Definition >200 mL/24 h and Bristol Types 1-7.
Link Type numbers to stool form and clinical label.
Severe constipation (1) through severe diarrhea (7) in strict order.

Luminal → Mucosal (small intestine, maximum) → Post mucosal.
Fat is most calorie-dense and most specific in malabsorption.
List carbs and proteins as the other macronutrients.

Acute <2w (nuisance), Persistent >2w, Chronic >4w.
Acute viral m/c overall: Norovirus adults, Rotavirus children, self-limiting.
Classify by duration first in the flowchart.

Chronic D/d: Osmotic→malabsorption, Secretory→tumor/toxin, Inflammatory→IBD.
Malassimilation = maldigestion + malabsorption.
Diminished digestion/absorption of one or more nutrients.

Osmotic = most consistent symptom of malabsorption.
Steatorrhea = hallmark: pale bulky fatty malodorous greasy stools.
Pathology: ↓ fat absorption → ↑ stool osmolality → draws water → osmotic diarrhea.

72-h fecal fat = gold standard with 100 g/day fat input.
Normal <7 g/day; steatorrhea >7 g/d for 3 d (D3-D5) or ≥7% excretion.
Qualitative: Sudan III, Sudan IV, Oil red O.

Secretory: ETEC/V. cholera heat-labile toxin + rotavirus; VIPoma→WDHA + hypoK + acidosis; no structural damage.
Gap table: Osmotic >100 + pH<5.5 vs Secretory <50 + ↑Na+K + pH>6.0 + no change on fasting.
Formula 290−2(Na⁺+K⁺), normal 50-100; factitious case adolescent female.

Factitious unsupervised ~16 vs supervised ~279.
Small vs Large etiology + full clinical table (volume, consistency, frequency, pus/blood/mucus, tenesmus, dyschezia, pain, fever, cramps, bloating, weight loss, vomiting, steatorrhoea) in order.
Weight loss/vomiting/steatorrhoea distinguish persistent small intestinal.

Duration first: <2w = infection, >4w = small vs large.
<2w Small (large volume, viral/ETEC/cholera, self-limiting) vs Large (fever/pain/blood, Shigella etc).
>4w Small osmotic (>100 gap, improves) vs secretory (VIPoma) vs Large inflammatory (UC).

Three stages in order: Luminal → Mucosal → Post mucosal.
Luminal is enzymes mediated; mucosal is the enterocyte brush border.
Post mucosal is movement from the mucosal epithelial cell into blood.

Proximal 2/3 = maximum absorption (jejunum > duodenum).
Distal 1/3 = bile acid, vitamin B12 and Mg2+ (ileum).
Fix the segment before learning each nutrient.

Villi are the specific feature and are surrounded by crypts of Lieberkühn.
Paneth cells sit at the crypt base and make alpha defensins, lysozymes, phospholipase A2.
Renewal every 48-72 hrs; interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemaker cells.

Layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, serosa.
Peyer's patches are macroscopic lymphoid aggregates of the ileal submucosa.
In typhoid they hypertrophy.

Bile acids + pancreatic lipase act on triglyceride → lipolysis → fatty acids + glycerol.
Micelles then pass into enterocytes by passive diffusion.
Chronic pancreatitis removes the lipase step.

Body pool 4 g, maintained by enterohepatic circulation.
Synthesis (7α-hydroxylase, rate limiting) → cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid → conjugation with glycine/taurine → bile salts.
Colonic bacterial deconjugation gives deoxycholic and lithocholic acid.

Luminal: chronic pancreatitis (lipase) and bile acid defect (secretion/synthesis/reabsorption).
Bile duct destruction in cirrhosis, PBC, PSC; ileal dysfunction in TB/Crohn's; early deconjugation in SIBO.
Mucosal: coeliac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue.
Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids

LCFA + glycerol → esterification → chylomicrons → intestinal lymphatics.
Disorders: abetalipoproteinaemia and intestinal lymphangiectasia.
Chain length >12 / 8-12 / <8; only long chain needs lipolysis and micelles; short chain is colonic and substantial in stool.

Disaccharidases on the brush border: lactase, maltase, sucrase, trehalase.
Gut: SGLT1 (active) for glucose/galactose, GLUT5 for fructose.
Liver: GLUT2 entry then galactokinase, fructokinase, glucokinase.

Congenital forms are autosomal recessive.
Selective = lactase deficiency; global = small intestinal mucosal defect (coeliac, Whipple's, tropical sprue).
Primary (m/c) lactase deficiency is allele persistence; secondary follows infections and IBS.

Trypsinogen → trypsin → activates chymotrypsin and elastase.
Selective defects: enterokinase deficiency, Hartnup's disease (pellagra), cystinuria (COLA).
COLA = cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine.

Lactose (milk, cheese) → lactase (brush border) → glucose + galactose.
Congenital autosomal recessive versus acquired ↓ activity (primary allele persistence, secondary infections/IBS).
Unabsorbed carbohydrate is fermented to acid and H2, methane, CO2.

90 min post prandial distension, bloating, cramps; acidic diaper dermatitis in children.
Stool pH acidic; lactose hydrogen breath test positive at H2 > 20 ppm.
Lactose-glucose blood test is obsolete; treat with diet and calcium.

AKA neuroacanthocytosis; autosomal recessive; apoB48 → defective esterification → no chylomicrons.
Triad: ataxia (vitamin E), retinitis pigmentosa, steatorrhea; smear shows acanthocytes.
Post prandial endoscopic biopsy is 100% diagnostic with enterocyte vacuolation.

Chylomicrons cross intestinal lymphatics into blood.
Primary = dilated channels; secondary = lymphoma or Crohn's with lymphatic obstruction.
Protein losing enteropathy with fecal α-1 antitrypsin elevated; treat with medium chain triglyceride diet.

Confirm the diagnosis (clinically and by investigations).
Then confirm global versus selective malabsorption.
Finally confirm the aetiology.

Small intestinal, >4 weeks, osmotic, improves on fasting — the most consistent symptom.
Fat → steatorrhea; carbohydrate → bloating and dyspepsia.
Protein → foul smelling stools, ascites, edema; plus unexplained weight loss.

Musculoskeletal: fat malabsorption with impaired vitamin D and Ca2+ → tetany, fracture, bone pain.
Niacin → hyperpigmentation; vitamin C → perifollicular hemorrhage and curly hair.
Vitamin K → bruisability; Zn/EFA → acrodermatitis; vitamin A → follicular hyperkeratosis.

Coeliac → growth retardation; proximal disease → folate/iron deficiency; distal → B12 deficiency.
B12/E → neuropathy and ataxia; B12 → glossitis, cheliosis, stomatitis; vitamin A → night blindness.
Free oxalate is absorbed in the colon → oxaluria → Ca2+ oxalate stones; pain, constipation and fever are NOT features.

Qualitative: Sudan III.
Quantitative (gold standard): fecal fat excretion >7 g/day.
The fecal fat excretion test is the gold standard investigation for malabsorption.

Best and most specific test; D-xylose is a pentose monosaccharide.
It assesses intact small intestinal mucosa.
25 g orally after fasting; urine collected over 4-6 hours; normal ≥4.5 g, <4.5 g positive.

False positives: renal failure (defective excretion), rapid transit (hyperthyroidism, vomiting), SIBO (organisms utilise D-xylose), ascites.
Lactose H2 breath test: for lactase deficiency, positive >20 ppm.
Lactulose H2 breath test: H2 within 90 minutes = SIBO; after 90 minutes = normal.

Obsolete: acid steatocrit and C-14 triolein breath test (fat); C-13 egg white breath test (protein).
Stool elastase/chymotrypsin → pancreatic insufficiency; fecal α-1 antitrypsin → lymphangiectasia; NIRA is newer.
Biopsy diagnoses: Whipple's disease, agammaglobulinaemia, abetalipoproteinaemia.

Phase I: 1000 μg unlabelled B12 IM to saturate stores, then 1 μg oral radiolabelled B12, then urine B12.
<7% positive, 7-10% normal.
Phase II: intrinsic factor → pernicious anaemia; pancreatic enzymes → chronic pancreatitis; antibiotics → SIBO; still <7% = ileal disease.

Defective absorption of carbohydrate, fat and protein from small intestinal mucosal dysfunction.
Fat is the most sensitive, most specific and most energy dense nutrient.
Three causes: celiac disease, Whipple's disease, tropical sprue.

AKA celiac sprue / gluten sensitive enteropathy / non-tropical sprue.
Iceberg phenomenon: only 50% present classically, missed through physician unawareness.
HLA DQ2/DQ8 is the most important predisposition; the disease is proximal small intestinal.

Classical: 50% present with symptoms of malabsorption.
Atypical: symptoms other than malabsorption; silent: asymptomatic, serology positive.
Latent: asymptomatic, antibodies negative, HLA susceptibility present.

HLA DQ2/DQ8 → gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats) → prolamine (most toxic) → gliadin (chief antigen).
Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin-bound glutamine → activates T cells.
Gluten-free diet: 90% revert (clinically 3 weeks, histologically 6 months); 10% refractory → steroids.

Classical: osmotic diarrhea, distension, foul smelling stool, weight loss; IBS symptoms in 30%.
Atypical: short stature, fracture/osteopenia, ataxia/neuropathy, iron deficiency anemia not due to blood loss.
Other: secondary hyperparathyroidism, cerebral calcification, hyposplenism with Howell-Jolly bodies, follicular hyperkeratosis, edema/ascites, cryptogenic cirrhosis.

Definite: dermatitis herpetiformis (most important), Down syndrome, type I DM, IgA nephropathy, IgA deficiency, bird-fancier lung, lymphocytic colitis, cerebral calcification with epilepsy.
Dermatitis herpetiformis: papulovesicular extensor lesions with linear IgA at the dermoepidermal junction.
Probable: cryptogenic transaminitis, idiopathic short stature, refractory iron deficiency anemia, cerebellar ataxia.

Anti-TTG IgA: most important for diagnosis and monitoring; specificity 98%.
Anti-endomysial IgA: indirect immunofluorescence, sensitivity 99%, specificity 73%, subjective and cumbersome.
Anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgG for IgA deficiency; anti-gliadin obsolete. Biopsy: mucosal total villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, normal thickness, lamina propria lymphocytes, Marsh score.

Both positive = celiac; both negative = not celiac (test HLA DQ2/DQ8 if suggestive).
Serology positive/biopsy negative: repeat biopsy; serology negative/biopsy positive: non-specific (tropical sprue, cow's milk intolerance).
Refractory disease is premalignant: EATL, small intestinal adenocarcinoma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma; diet is rice/corn/maize/potato/soybean with gluten restriction.

Chronic multisystem disease of joints, GIT, CNS and CVS; M > F, 50-60 years.
Pan-intestinal, proximal more than distal; Tropheryma whipplei is a gram positive actinobacterium that cannot be cultured because of slow doubling time.
Diagnosis is by biopsy.

Joints first in >80%: large joints, migratory arthralgia > arthritis.
GIT 2-3 years later: diarrhea (most consistent), weight loss, abdominal pain with mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
Neuro 40%: rapidly progressive dementia (m/c) and oculomasticatory myorhythmia (m/c specific); CVS: culture negative endocarditis, mitral valve > myocarditis > pericarditis, HACEK group.

Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is 100% diagnostic; PCR identifies Tropheryma whipplei.
PAS positive foamy macrophages in epithelium, lamina propria and submucosa with enlarged villi.
Induction IV ceftriaxone 2 g for 14 days (best); maintenance co-trimoxazole prevents relapse and penetrates the CNS.

Most common cause of malabsorption in India, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Infective diarrhea → toxigenic coliforms (E. coli, Klebsiella) → fermentation products, mainly ethanol.
Structural damage impairs folic acid absorption → 2-3 weeks → pan-intestinal involvement with defective B12, bile acid and Mg2+ absorption.

Chronic watery voluminous small bowel diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, prominent folic acid deficiency, hyperpigmentation from B12 deficiency.
Biopsy resembles celiac disease but serology is negative; stool examined for ova, cyst and trophozoite to rule out giardiasis.
Folic acid 5 mg daily plus tetracycline 250 mg QID for 3-6 months; relapse in 20%.
Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea

Bile acid diarrhea (cholorrhea) is seen in tropical sprue from defective FGF-19; limited ileal disease leaves compensatory excess hepatic bile acid removing Na+, Cl− and K+.
Fatty acid diarrhea needs severe ileal disease: no compensatory release → malabsorption → fatty acid in colon → steatorrhea >20 g.
Cholestyramine helps bile acid diarrhea; a low-fat diet helps fatty acid diarrhea.

Short bowel syndrome: < 200 cm; very severe: < 100 cm.
Adult: mesenteric vascular disease (ischemia with resection) more than Crohn's disease.
Child: necrotising enterocolitis.

Hyperoxaluria: unabsorbed LCFA bind calcium, free oxalate is absorbed and forms oxalate stones.
Absent ileum → cholesterol gallstones from supersaturation.
D-lactic acidosis from gram positive anaerobes (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) causing CNS features; hypergastrinemia; hypomagnesemia; defective ileal break with rapid gastric emptying.

Iron: absent duodenum > jejunum; Ca2+, folate, vitamins A, D, E: absent jejunum; vitamin K rarely because bacteria migrate when the ileocecal valve is lost.
SIBO from loss of the ileocecal valve.
Diet: medium chain fatty acids and complex carbohydrates; total parenteral nutrition when the colon is absent; teduglutide is an oral GLP-2 analogue.

AKA blind loop syndrome / stagnant bowel syndrome.
Proximal small intestine normally has no bacteria; ileum has Enterobacteriaceae; colon has anaerobes.
Overgrowth of non-toxigenic anaerobes proximally; causes are anatomical defects, motility disorders (IBS, scleroderma, diabetes, amyloidosis), immunodeficiency and HIV.

Bacteria compete for nutrients and consume B12: bloating and belching are most common; B12 deficiency, macrocytic anemia, steatorrhea, unexplained diarrhea.
Jejunal aspirate >10^3 CFU/mL is gold standard; lactulose H2 breath test is preferred; indican is obsolete; B12 low, folate and vitamin K high.
Rifaximin 550 mg BD for 7-10 days; avoid macrolides.

Four entities are listed, but IBD currently means UC and CD only.
Microscopic colitis follows long-term PPI and NSAID use: chronic non-bloody voluminous watery diarrhea with a normal examination and normal endoscopy.
Biopsy: collagenous colitis (collagen band, Sjogren's) versus lymphocytic colitis (intra-epithelial lymphocytes, celiac disease).
Diversion Colitis & Normal Histology of Colon

Diversion colitis occurs in patients using colostomy bags after surgery for bowel malignancies.
Normal colonic layers, innermost to outermost: mucosal epithelial cells, lamina propria, muscularis mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, serosa.
Learn the order — it anchors every depth-of-invasion comparison that follows.

Colonic mucosa has no villi.
Crypts contain microvilli for water absorption; goblet cells secrete mucus.
Diarrhea is defined as a stool volume above 200 mL.
Epidemiology of UC and Crohn's Disease

Overall CD > UC and males > females; peaks at 15-30 and 70-90 years.
Ethnicity: Jews > non-Jewish white > African American > Hispanic > Asian.
Smoking protects against UC but causes CD; appendicectomy protects against UC; OCP raises CD risk; concordance is significant and greater in CD; antibiotics in the first year triple the risk.

Childhood IBD is grouped as UC-like non-granulomatous versus CD-like granulomatous; Turner's syndrome is listed as most common.
Wiskott-Aldrich: WASP mutation, X-linked recessive, eczema plus sino-pulmonary infection plus microplatelet thrombocytopenia.
Hermansky-Pudlak: autosomal recessive with platelet dysfunction, pulmonary fibrosis and oculocutaneous albinism; von Gierke type I with glucose-1-phosphatase deficiency.
IPEX Syndrome & Early Onset Childhood IBD

Loss of Foxp3 function reduces regulatory T-cell tolerance and causes IPEX.
Triad: dermatitis, endocrinopathy (type I DM / thyroiditis) and UC-like enteropathy.
Supportive care, gene therapy and genetic testing; T-reg marker is CD25; early onset IBD reflects IL-10 pathway defects.

Exogenous and endogenous factors drive a dysregulated mucosal immune response in a genetically susceptible host.
UC: unclear pathogenesis with Th2 overactivity.
Crohn's: NOD2/CARD15 on chromosome 16, defective innate immunity (intracellular organisms, Paneth cell defensins), defective autophagy, Th1 overactivity and loss of protective Faecalibacterium.

Rectum alone is involved in 50%.
Hemorrhagic, edematous, ulcerated granular mucosa with pseudopolyps from epithelial regeneration.
Chronic disease rarely gives a lead pipe atrophic featureless colon; fulminant colitis rarely gives toxic megacolon with a diameter above 6 cm.

Cryptitis with loss of crypt architecture.
Paneth cell metaplasia distal to the hepatic flexure.
Basal plasma cells and lymphoid aggregates are the earliest finding and flag relapse; transmural disease, skip lesions, fistulas, strictures and fissures all argue against UC.

Anywhere from mouth to anus; ileocolitis 40-50%, ileitis 30-40%, colitis 15-20%.
Deep transmural asymmetric skip lesions; aphthous ulcers are earliest, linear serpiginous ulcers most visible.
Cobblestoning, perianal fissures and fistulas, terminal ileal fibrosis and stenosis, and creeping fat.

Involvement up to the muscularis propria with non-caseating granulomas at any level, even extraintestinal.
Mesenteric lymphadenopathy; cryptitis and crypt abscesses with normal crypt architecture.
Pyloric metaplasia, lymphoid aggregates and fibrosis; granuloma differential includes sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, cat scratch disease, berylliosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Features are described by the level of involvement: proctitis, proctosigmoiditis and proctocolitis.
Proctitis gives painless bleeding per rectum (differential: hemorrhoids and malignancies); proctosigmoiditis gives streaks of blood onto formed stool; proctocolitis gives large bowel diarrhea with small frequent stools containing blood, pus and mucus, plus tenesmus.
Physical examination is normal, slow proximal transit causes constipation, systemic symptoms are very rare because the lineage is Th2, and 90% have a relapsing course.

Fecal calprotectin is the most sensitive biomarker and is used to assess severity, treatment response and relapse.
Endoscopy shows symmetrical, superficial, continuous involvement.
Erythematous red velvety mucosa is earliest; vascularity is decreased; the mucosa shows ulcerations with fine granulations and friability; inflammatory pseudopolyps and, very rarely, a lead pipe colon.

Barium enema is the radiological heading for ulcerative colitis.
Fine mucosal granularities are the earliest change, followed by serrations giving a hazy margin, mild luminal narrowing and loss of rectal valves.
Deep ulcers reaching the submucosa give collar stud ulcers; backwash ileitis inflames the terminal ileum; chronic disease gives a lead pipe and fulminant disease toxic megacolon.

Ileocolitis is the commonest pattern: episodic right lower quadrant pain relieved by diarrhea.
Fever, weight loss and systemic symptoms reflect the Th1 profile with IL-2 and interferon gamma.
Jejunoileitis causes malabsorption; a palpable inflammatory mass comes from bowel wall thickening; obstruction, enterovesical more than perianal fistulas, and fissures progressing to fibrosed strictures complete the list.
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's

The target sign, mucosal ulcers with a translucent mound of edema, is the earliest radiological and endoscopic finding.
Rose thorn ulcers, fissures and the string sign reflect transmural disease; the string sign itself is fibrosed bowel.
CT has a limited role because MR enterography is preferred: target appearance from wall thickening, comb sign from a hypervascular mesentery, and fat halo sign with soft tissue inner and outer layers around a fatty middle layer.

Crohn's: ileocaecal valve commonly involved, four or more segments especially terminal ileum and ileocaecal valve, longitudinal ulcers, and frequent cobblestoning, aphthous and perianal lesions.
Tuberculosis: ileocaecal valve usually strictured and patulous, fewer than four segments especially ileocaecal valve and ascending colon, transverse ulcers, and rare cobblestoning, aphthous and perianal lesions.
Transverse ulcers plus a patulous strictured valve with fewer than four segments is the tuberculosis pattern.

Most extraintestinal manifestations are most common in Crohn's disease; uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis and pyoderma gangrenosum are most common in ulcerative colitis.
Eye: episcleritis extends from conjunctivitis and parallels bowel activity; uveitis is more dangerous, can cause vision loss and is unrelated to bowel activity.
Skin: painful pretibial papules of erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, pyoderma vegetans, aphthous ulcers and Sweet syndrome. Joints: type I pauciarticular arthritis parallels the bowel; type II axial arthritis does not.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is most common in ulcerative colitis and fibroses intra and extrahepatic ducts; two thirds of PSC patients have UC and 5% of UC patients have PSC.
Others: gallstones and oxalate renal stones, osteopenia and osteoporosis in over 40% from long term drug use, hepatic steatosis and raised thromboembolic risk.
Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin separate relapse from infectious diarrhea and rise during relapse. Serology: p-ANCA and anti-goblet cell antibody for UC; ASCA, Omp-C, anti-pancreatic antibody, anti-Ia and anti-flagellin for Crohn's.

Mild: fewer than four stools per day, no fever, no tachycardia, mild anemia, ESR below 30 mm per hour.
Moderate sits between mild and severe.
Severe: more than ten stools per day with blood, fever above 37.5 °C, heart rate above 90, hemoglobin below 75% of normal and ESR above 30 mm per hour.

5-ASA is the mainstay, but plain 5-ASA is absorbed in the small intestine and never reaches the rectum; delayed release mesalamine is the drug of choice for mild disease.
Induction: topical 5-ASA or oral mesalamine for mild, add oral steroids for moderate, intravenous steroid for severe.
Steroid refractory moderate disease moves to azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine; severe disease adds intravenous anti-TNF or cyclosporine, and maintenance uses azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine with low dose anti-TNF or oral cyclosporine.

Sulfasalazine is 5-ASA carried by sulfapyridine, absorbed at the rectum, and abandoned in G6PD deficiency.
Azathioprine side effects are hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression and pancreatitis.
Surgery is proctocolectomy with ileoanal anastomosis for toxic megacolon, perforation, uncontrollable hemorrhage, dysplasia or carcinoma, and medically refractory disease.

Grading: mild-moderate has no dehydration, obstruction, weight loss or systemic features; moderate-severe lies between; severe-fulminant means fever, cachexia, obstruction and peritoneal signs despite steroids.
Objectives are endoscopic mucosal healing and prevention of strictures and fistulae.
Drugs: antibiotics, corticosteroids with their dependency risk, 5-ASA, immunomodulators and biologics such as infliximab, adalimumab and certolizumab pegol.

Induction: oral budesonide 9 mg per day for mild-moderate, oral steroids for moderate-severe, intravenous steroids for severe-fulminant.
Maintenance: none for mild-moderate, azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine for moderate-severe, periodic anti-TNF for severe-fulminant.
Fistulizing disease needs anti-TNF with or without immunomodulators then surgery; avoid smoking and NSAIDs; never maintain with oral 5-ASA, corticosteroids or budesonide. Newer agents: natalizumab, ustekinumab and vedolizumab.

Risk exists in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease: lymphoma, leukemia, myelodysplasia and cholangiocarcinoma from primary sclerosing cholangitis.
IBD related carcinoma arises ten to fifteen years younger, in any segment of diseased colon, as a signet ring cell carcinoma.
Genetics invert the sporadic pattern: sporadic is APC early and p53 late, IBD related is p53 early and APC late. Five year survival is 50% for both.

Acute diarrhoea ≤2 weeks is infectious unless proved otherwise.
Duration branches: <1 week benign/viral or complicated/bacterial; >1 week protozoal.
Separate small-bowel large-volume watery stool from large-bowel small-volume bloody stool.

Small bowel: ETEC/V. cholerae toxins, preformed-toxin bacteria, Cryptosporidium, microsporidium, Giardia.
Large bowel: Shigella, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella, EIEC, V. parahaemolyticus, Entamoeba.
Typhoid is a small-bowel invasion with fever/pain and no diarrhoea in the note.

S. aureus: preformed heat-stable toxin, 1–6 h, custard/pork/canned meat, vomiting via 5-HT3.
B. cereus heat-stable: fried rice/vomiting; heat-labile: formed toxin, 6–12 h, diarrhoea/cAMP.
The source also lists Yersinia and E. coli among heat-stable-toxin producers.

V. cholerae is non-invasive; toxin activates adenyl cyclase; TCP attaches to mucosa.
Large-volume watery stool, dehydration and hypokalaemic normal-gap acidosis; the page names Ringer lactate.
V. parahaemolyticus: raw fish/Kanagawa; ETEC LT raises cAMP and is linked to travellers' diarrhoea.

Childhood HUS: 90% EHEC O157:H7/Shigella dysenteriae toxins; 10% pneumococcal neuraminidase.
Shigella invasion affects all four bowel-wall layers; enterotoxin causes diarrhoea and Shiga-like toxin is cytotoxic.
The note contrasts diarrhoea with arthritis against IBD markers and extraintestinal signs.

Typhoid: diarrhoea in week two, perforation, marrow suppression and intestinal bleeding.
C. jejuni is faeco-oral, incubates 2–4 days, and is linked to IBD, GBS and IPSID/lymphoma.
The page's culture and azithromycin notes are explicitly not routine for small-bowel diarrhoea.

GDH + toxin A/B EIA → confirm if both positive; discordant results go to PCR/NAAT.
The p51 flowchart separates non-severe, severe and fulminant disease by WBC/creatinine and ileus/shock/megacolon.
Treatment entries reproduce the book for study; they are not current clinical guidance.

Fundus above GES; body between GES and incisura; antrum below incisura.
Fundic, oxyntic and pyloric glands contain region-specific ECL, parietal, chief, mucous and G cells.
Review secretions and the diagram labels: rugae, curvatures, papillae and duodenum.

Defence layers: pre-epithelial, epithelial/restitution and subepithelial.
Separate damaging exposures from mucus, bicarbonate, blood-flow, barrier and repair protection.
Auerbach = motility; Meissner = secretion; ICC generate BER.

Histamine/cAMP, gastrin/CCK-B and acetylcholine/M3-Ca²⁺ cooperate to increase acid.
The BAO/MAO threshold is >0.6; the page gives MAO at 6 pm and least output at 6 am.
Gastritis is histologic; acute phlegmonous gastritis is severe and linked to neutrophils.

Type A: less common autoimmune, patchy corpus, parietal-cell antibodies; Type B: commoner, multifocal, H. pylori.
Follow each type's complications and malignancy arrow; retain the four gastritis associations.
Ménétrier disease: TGF-α/foveolar hyperplasia → mucus/protein loss; surgery is main treatment in the text.

Gram-negative, urease/oxidase/catalase positive; antral, flagellated, non-invasive and deep in mucosal gel.
Transmission is faeco-oral; the source lists ulcer/cancer associations and enzyme actions.
Know the roles of VacA, LPS, outer proteins, type IV secretion and CagA effectors.

Antral-predominant → duodenal ulcer; corpus atrophy → metaplasia/dysplasia/carcinoma; pan-gastritis → MALToma.
Dyspepsia symptom cluster, one-week PPI note and alarm indications precede H. pylori investigations.
Rapid urease uses antral biopsy; stool antigen and urea-breath testing confirm eradication after a one-month gap.

The p58 first-line and OBTM second-line regimens are transcribed as printed.
The p59 algorithm tests, treats, waits at least one month and branches by stool antigen/urea breath result.
Persistent positivity proceeds to later-line sensitivity-guided specialist review; this is book study, not current guidance.

Sporadic (80%) versus MEN1-associated (20%) differ in number/size, age, sex, location and risk.
Sporadic tumours are listed as more aggressive; MEN1 disease is usually smaller and less aggressive.
Keep the note separating insulinoma as the commonest functional pancreatic NET overall.

Triangle points: cystic duct/CBD, D2–D3 and pancreatic body–neck junctions.
Gastrin → parietal cells → HCl; mucosal injury yields GU/DU.
Acid can inactivate pancreatic enzymes, linking to diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and malabsorption.

Abdominal pain is the most important symptom; PUD is the commonest manifestation.
Unusual D2+ ulcers, refractory GU/DU, recurrence and diarrhoea raise suspicion in the page.
Diarrhoea has secretory and enzyme-inactivation/steatorrhoea components.

Fasting gastrin: <200 normal, 200–1000 needs confirmation; preserve the source's >1000 wording.
Secretin gives a paradoxical gastrin rise ≥200 pg/mL in the printed test.
SRS/¹¹¹In, octreotide rationale, EUS caveat, BAO/MAO and DOTATATE note are inventoried.

MEN1: high-dose PPI 60–80 mg; surgery when >2.5 cm.
Sporadic: PPI + octreotide then surgery; procedure follows head/body-tail/duodenal location.
The page says gastrectomy is not required and names liver as the commonest metastasis site.

IBS is presented as a functional bowel disorder/reaction to stress.
Associations: lactose intolerance, celiac disease, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue and generalized anxiety.
The clinical list is more common in women and under age 45.
Clinical Pattern, Rome IV & Red Flags

Pain: crampy lower abdomen, at least weekly, aggravated by stress/eating and relieved by defecation.
Rome IV line as printed: ≥3 months and ≥2 of stool-frequency change, stool-form change or defecation relation; the source omits onset ≥6 months before diagnosis (see audit/known-source-caveats.md).
Nocturnal diarrhoea, blood, fever, weight loss, anaemia, malabsorption and raised ESR argue against IBS.

Visceral hypersensitivity, increased colonic motor potentials and cingulate activation are listed.
The page also notes serotonin-containing enterochromaffin cells and TRP-V1 channels.
The graph shows pain/sensation at lower rectal distending volumes in IBS.

Diet/lifestyle changes improve about 70%; walking target is 6,000–8,000 steps.
Reduce fermentable oligo-, di-, monosaccharides and polyols; examples include apple, mango, wheat, honey, legumes and cauliflower.
Water draw in small bowel and fermentation/gas in colon explain the diagrammed symptoms.

D+: loperamide, pre-meal antispasmodic, antidepressant; the table labels several drugs obsolete.
C+: psyllium/PEG, lubiprostone, linaclotide and tenapanor.

IDA and ACD are normocytic normochromic initially; RA and miliary TB cause microcytic hypochromic ACD.
Sideroblastic anemia is dimorphic (microcytic + macrocytic); thalassemia trait is microcytic hypochromic.
Hepcidin (liver peptide) inhibits ferroportin; IL-6/activin, HFE (chr 6), hemojuvelin and Tfr2 stimulate it, while hypoxia inhibits it.

HFE mutation causes hemochromatosis; in ACD, ferritin and hepcidin are normal/high while Sr. iron, TIBC, TSAT and sTfR are low.
Sideroblastic anemia is inherited (X-linked ALA synthase deficiency) or acquired (MDS, Cu deficiency, alcohol, chloramphenicol/INH/PZA, lead).
Normal heme synthesis proceeds from Succinyl Co-A + Glycine + B6 (via ALA synthase) → ALA → Protoporphyrin + Fe → Heme → Hb.

ALA synthase deficiency leaves unbound iron around the erythroblast nucleus as ring sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain.
Sideroblastic investigations show dimorphic cellularity, EM Pappenheimer bodies, high Sr. iron/TSAT, normal/high ferritin and low TIBC.
Thalassemia trait (ββ⁰, ββ⁺) has one normal and one defective β gene, absent ineffective erythropoiesis, and normal iron indices.

Thalassemia trait shows normal RDW, Mentzer index <13, rare target/stippled cells, and HbA₂ 4–8% (normal 1.5–3%).
The master table contrasts Sr. iron, ferritin, TIBC and TSAT across IDA, ACD, sideroblastic anemia and thalassemia trait.
Inherited IDA includes IRIDA (defective matriptase-2 → ↑ hepcidin), DMT-1 mutation (no endosome-to-cytoplasm transport) and atransferrinemia.

The diagnostic protocol begins with Lineage (Single vs Multiple) followed by Reticulocyte Production Index (Low vs High).

Types, Causes & B12 vs Folate Stores

Macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL) divides into megaloblastic (lagging nuclear maturation) and normoblastic causes.
Megaloblastic causes include B12/folate/thiamine deficiency, DNA-synthesis inhibitors (cytarabine, hydroxyurea, 6-MP) and orotic aciduria.
B12 stores (2–5 mg; RDA 3–7 µg/d) last 2–5 years (>3 yr in vegetarians); folate stores (5–10 mg; RDA 50 µg/d) deplete in a few weeks.

Dietary B12 (animal origin: adenosyl- and methylcobalamin) binds salivary R-factor/haptocorrin in the stomach.
Pancreatic enzymes split the complex in duodenum (parts 2 & 3) so B12 binds parietal-cell Intrinsic Factor (IF).
Ileal CUBAM receptors absorb IF-B12; plasma TC-2 forms holotranscobalamin for marrow RBC maturation.

Causes: Pernicious anemia (most important), ileal disease (Crohn's, tropical sprue, TB), SIBO, TC-2/CUBAM defects (Imerslund–Gräsbeck), and D. latum.
Only B12, bile acids and Mg are absorbed solely in the ileum; TC-1 (from granulocytes) rises in MPN, while TC-2 mediates transport.
B12 is a cofactor for Homocysteine → Methionine and Methylmalonyl CoA → Succinyl CoA.

Folate is absorbed in proximal small bowel (jejunum/duodenum); dietary monoglutamate becomes circulating/storage 5-methyl THFA → THFA.
B12 deficiency causes the 'folate trap' (5-methyl THFA accumulation) and raises both homocysteine and methylmalonyl CoA (MMA is normal in pure folate deficiency).
Folate deficiency stems from ↓ intake (nutritional, major cause), celiac disease, ↑ demand (pregnancy, growth, hemolysis) and drugs (MTX, sulfasalazine, PPIs, pyrimethamine, triamterene, phenytoin).

Serum B12 >300 pg is normal, <200 pg is deficient, and 200–300 pg prompts MMA, folate and homocysteine testing.
Smear shows megaloblasts, hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes, earliest change; <2 lobes = pseudo-Pelger–Huët in MDS), Cabot rings, basophilic stippling and Howell–Jolly bodies.
Pancytopenia occurs in 15–20% and warrants bone marrow smear (dyserythropoiesis, erythroid hyperplasia, ↓ M:E ratio, giant metamyelocytes).

Anti-parietal cell antibody is sensitive; anti-intrinsic factor antibody is specific; body involvement with antral sparing is classic.
Associated with Addison's disease, Type 1 DM and vitiligo; affects middle-aged to elderly females who are often asymptomatic.
Clinical features include lemon-yellow pallor (hemolytic jaundice), angular cheilitis, beefy-red atrophic glossitis and hyperpigmentation.

SCD involves dorsal and lateral columns plus peripheral neuropathy and late cortical/optic changes (folate deficiency spares the spinal cord).
Increases risk of gastric carcinoid type 1 (m/c) and gastric adenocarcinoma (rare); workup shows oval macrocytosis, anti-IF Ab, ↑ gastrin and ↓↓ B12.
Hydroxycobalamin (1000 µg OD × 1 wk → weekly × 1 mo → monthly lifelong) raises reticulocytes by day 2–3 (peak day 6–8) and normalizes MCV in 10 weeks.

Hyperproliferative anemia (RPI >2.5, reticulocytosis) is classified as inherited vs acquired, intracorpuscular vs extracorpuscular, and intravascular vs extravascular.
Inherited intracorpuscular causes include hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemia), membrane defects (HS, elliptocytosis) and enzymopathies (G6PD, PK, 5'-nucleotidase); inherited extracorpuscular is atypical (familial) HUS.
Acquired causes split into immune (AIHA: warm, cold, PCH; alloimmune: HDN, transfusion reaction; drug-induced) and non-immune (HUS/TTP fragmentation, intracorpuscular PNH, sepsis, toxins/drugs).

PNH results from a PIGA gene mutation; intravascular hemolysis occurs inside blood vessels with ↑ LDH, hemoglobinemia, reticulocytosis and ↑ MCV.
Free Hb binds haptoglobin, making ↓ serum haptoglobin the most sensitive and specific test for hemolysis; urine shows hemoglobinuria (acute, dark urine) or hemosiderinuria (chronic).
Acute onset (m/c) causes are mismatched transfusion, sepsis, toxins and G6PD deficiency; chronic/acute-on-chronic causes are PNH, MAHA/HUS and PCH.

Extravascular hemolysis occurs in the spleen with moderate splenomegaly; globin returns to the amino acid pool, iron raises stores/ferritin, and protoporphyrin becomes unconjugated bilirubin (↑ urine urobilinogen, ↑ fecal stercobilinogen).
The summary table contrasts intravascular (plasma/urine Hb ++, urine hemosiderin ++, LDH ↑↑↑, haptoglobin ↓↓↓) with extravascular (tissue iron/ferritin ++, bilirubin ↑↑, splenomegaly ↑↑).
Inherited causes are intracorpuscular (except atypical HUS) and extravascular (except acute G6PD); acquired causes are extracorpuscular (except PNH) and intravascular (except warm/cold AIHA; PCH is intravascular).

Immune hemolytic anemia divides into autoimmune (warm IgG, cold IgM, PCH IgG/Donath–Landsteiner), alloimmune (HDN IgG, transfusion reaction) and drug-induced.
AIHA presents as rapidly progressive extravascular hemolytic anemia; the Coombs test differentiates immune from non-immune anemia.
Direct Coombs (DAT) uses polyvalent anti-human Ig to detect RBC surface antibodies (3+/4+ agglutination), followed by monovalent anti-IgG and anti-C3d.
DAT Subtyping & Warm vs Cold Etiology

Anti-IgG+ / C3d± indicates warm AIHA (or drug-induced if negative); Anti-IgG– / C3d+ indicates cold AIHA, PCH (DL test+) or drug-induced (Ab+, DL–); multiple transfusions cause false-positive Coombs.
Warm AIHA (m/c, IgG, 37°C, subacute 1–2 mo) is 50% idiopathic or secondary to SLE/CLL/HIV, autoimmune diseases (RA, PAN, IBD, scleroderma) and drugs (cephalosporins, drug-independent α-methyldopa).
Cold AIHA (IgM, 0–4°C, chronic indolent) is idiopathic cold agglutinin disease or secondary to Waldenström's (MYD88), lymphoma, infections (IM, EBV, CMV, Mycoplasma) and lenalidomide.

Warm AIHA: splenic macrophage Fc receptors mediate pan-agglutination and extravascular destruction in the spleen, causing anemia, spherocytosis, moderate splenomegaly, jaundice and urobilinogen (+).
Cold AIHA: IgM agglutinates RBCs in peripheral extremities (causing acrocyanosis) and Kupffer cells mediate predominantly extravascular destruction in the liver (minimal intravascular).
Warm AIHA smear shows variable spherocytes, fragmented/nucleated/polychromatic RBCs; cold AIHA smear shows agglutinated RBCs.

Schistocytes are fragmented/helmeted RBCs; warm AIHA is treated with steroids (1 mg/kg/d × 4 wk) + rituximab (100 mg/m² weekly × 4) with slow taper, and rituximab/cyclophosphamide/MMF/splenectomy on relapse.
Cold AIHA is treated with rituximab (best prognosis); C3b activation occurs in cold agglutinin disease.
Evans syndrome (warm AIHA + thrombocytopenia) associates with CVID; spherocytes also occur in hereditary spherocytosis (uniform), G6PD deficiency, transfusion reaction and CuSO₄ poisoning.

Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH) causes Coombs-positive acute intravascular hemolysis: polyclonal IgG binds RBC P-antigen at 4°C and lyses cells at 37°C (Donath–Landsteiner test, tertiary syphilis, conservative Rx).
Drug-induced autoantibody hemolysis includes drug-independent methyldopa (m/c) and procainamide, penicillin, cephalosporins and cold-reacting lenalidomide.
Immune-complex hemolysis is caused by quinidine, rifampicin and isoniazid; adsorption hemolysis is caused by high-dose penicillin (extravascular).

Non-immune hemolysis comprises infections (malaria, Babesia, Oroya fever, C. perfringens), drugs/toxins (dapsone, primaquine), PNH and fragmentation hemolysis.
PNH causes chronic intravascular hemolysis with acute exacerbations and affects all 3 blood lineages due to an acquired X-linked PIGA gene mutation.
PIGA codes for GPI anchor protein (anchoring CD55/DAF and CD59/MIRL to prevent complement attack), neutrophil alkaline phosphatase, and UPAR; PNH is the sole acquired intracorpuscular hemolytic anemia.

PIGA mutation leads to CD55/CD59-deficient PNH III RBC lysis, ↓ neutrophil alkaline phosphatase (seen in CML and PNH), and thrombosis from defective UPAR and NO scavenging.
Sleep-induced acidotic pH triggers nocturnal hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria with high-colored morning urine.
Hepatic vein thrombosis (m/c) causes Budd–Chiari syndrome (also caused by PCRV); pancytopenia (hypercellular marrow m/c) and the 25/10 aplastic anemia rule (plus rare AML progression) are classic.

Flow cytometry is the investigation of choice (detects PNH III RBC percentage; >50% is significant); Coombs test is negative and Ham's test is not used.
Centrifuged urine supernatant is clear in hematuria (RBCs) and high-colored in Hb/myoglobinuria; after resting 3–6 hours, myoglobin clears (T₁/₂ 3–6 h) while Hb stays dark.
Bone marrow involvement is treated with allogeneic HSCT; hemoglobinuria/thrombosis is treated with anti-C5 antibodies (ravulizumab > eculizumab) plus meningococcal vaccination.
Fragmentation: MAHA, TMA & HUS vs TTP

Fragmentation hemolysis combines MAHA (small-vessel endothelial injury → large vWF multimers → Gp Ib-IX & Gp VI platelet plug → thrombocytopenia + RBC fragmentation) and TMA.
TMA is small-vessel renal disease caused by HUS (most important), catastrophic APS, diffuse scleroderma, HELLP and malignant hypertension.
HUS targets renal capillaries causing a triad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal failure); TTP targets brain/GIT vessels causing lacunar stroke and a pentad (adding fever and neurological signs; renal failure is rare).

Childhood HUS (<5 yr, D⁺, benign, good prognosis) follows bloody diarrhea: 90% from EHEC O157:H7 (m/c, non-fermenter on Sorbitol MacConkey) or Shigella dysenteriae, and 10% from S. pneumoniae neuraminidase.
Childhood HUS blood work shows schistocytes, ↑↑ LDH, –ve Coombs, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin and normal PT/APTT; Rx is supportive (saline, bowel rest; avoid antibiotics).
Adult HUS (D⁻/atypical, leads to ESRD) stems from alternate complement mutations (CFH m/c, CFB worst prognosis, MCP good prognosis) or sporadic causes; Rx is plasmapheresis within 24 h and rituximab/eculizumab.

TTP is 95% acquired (IgG autoantibodies against ADAMTS-13, or ticlopidine/clopidogrel) and 5% congenital.
Failure to cleave vWF causes vWF accumulation, MAHA and microvascular thrombosis/ischemia (predominantly CNS, plus GIT/CVS); Rx is plasmapheresis + steroid + rituximab while monitoring ADAMTS-13.
Fragmentation hemolysis types: MAHA/march hemolysis (HUS, low platelets), Cardiac (prosthetic valve macroangiopathic, normal platelets) and Consumption (Kasabach–Merritt cavernous hemangioma + 2° DIC, low platelets).
Inherited Hemolytic Anemias & Hereditary Spherocytosis: Genetics and RBC Membrane Structure

Inherited hemolytic anemias classify into hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemia), membrane cytoskeleton disorders (HS), and enzymopathies (G6PD most common, pyruvate kinase, 5'-nucleotidase).
5'-nucleotidase deficiency shows basophilic stippling; cholestasis markers include 5'-nucleotidase, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT.
Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic compensated extravascular hemolysis from vertical/tangential membrane-cytoskeleton defects — AD (ankyrin ANK-1 > Band 3) more common than AR (β-spectrin).
Band 3 (abundant in membrane; ovalocytosis/stomatocytosis; protects against P. falciparum), spectrin dimer (biconcavity, abundant in cytoskeleton; severe AR HS & hereditary elliptocytosis), and glycophorin (P. falciparum receptor).
Hereditary Spherocytosis: Pathogenesis, Clinical Features & Investigations

Lipid bilayer defect → membrane microvesicle formation and detachment → spherical RBCs with the least surface-area-to-volume ratio.
7–8 μm spherocytes fail to elongate through 3–4 μm splenic capillaries and undergo extravascular destruction by splenic macrophages.
Presents with anemia, moderate splenomegaly, parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis, gallstones, and intermittent jaundice; indices show decreased MCV and markedly elevated MCHC with microspherocytes lacking central pallor.
Ektacytometry is most preferred, SDS-PAGE electrophoresis is the gold standard, EMA flow cytometry is less specific for ankyrin, osmotic fragility is not used, and glycerol lysis/pink test is obsolete.
Hereditary Spherocytosis Treatment & G6PD Deficiency: Genetics, HMP Shunt and Triggers

HS treatment by severity: mild (adults) gets supportive care; moderate (anemia, gallstones) gets splenectomy at puberty; severe (children with jaundice/complications) gets splenectomy at 3–4 years.
Cholecystectomy is performed only if gallstones are positive; splenectomy requires pre-op vaccination and carries post-op risk of sepsis and thrombosis.
G6PD deficiency is X-linked intermediate (Class 2 Mediterranean has decreased G6PD) and causes combined hemolysis with acute intravascular > chronic extravascular hemolysis.
HMP shunt generates NADPH and reduced glutathione to protect RBCs from oxidative injury triggered by oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone, cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, high-dose aspirin/vitamin C, methylene blue, chloroquine), infections, and fava beans.
G6PD Deficiency: Peripheral Smear, Diagnosis, Treatment & Anemia of Blood Loss

Peripheral smear morphology includes Heinz bodies (denatured globin precipitates), blister cells (hemighosts), bite cells, triangle cells, Howell-Jolly bodies, helmet cells, echinocytes (CKD, PK deficiency), and basophilic stippling (5'-pyrimidine nucleotidase).
G6PD diagnosis uses the fluorescent spot test for screening and quantitative enzyme assay for confirmation; management is stopping the precipitating agent and symptomatic care.
Anemia of blood loss progresses through Stage I (hypovolemia), Stage II (extravascular-to-intravascular volume shift), and Stage III (increased EPO and reticulocytes).
The lethal triad in severe hemorrhage/blood loss comprises hypothermia, acidosis, and DIC.
Overview: CMP Physiology, MPN Pathology and the Printed MPN List with Mutations

Physiology diagram: CMP → terminal myeloid cells (RBC, platelets, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils); pathology = proliferation of mature cells of multiple lineages with no dysplastic/immature cells.
MPN list: 1 PCRV (m/c), 2 PMF, 3 ET — bracketed under JAK-2 (PMF additionally deletion on chr 9p); 4 CML = BCR-ABL t(9;22); 5 CNL = CSF3R; 6 CEL = PDGFRA; 7 JMML and 8 MPN-NOS are BCR-ABL negative.
Notes: 1° myelofibrosis (myelophthisis) = bone marrow failure; systemic mastocytosis (c-kit) is excluded from MPN.
Clinical Features of MPN, Polycythemia Thresholds and Relative Polycythemia (Gaisböck's)

EMH at spleen (m/c), skin, liver; splenomegaly massive in CML/PMF, moderate in PCRV, mild in ET; classical B symptoms in 20%; MPN can transform into each other or AML; MDS = ineffective proliferation → pancytopenia; MDS/MPN overlap in WHO 5th edition.
Polycythemia table: male Hb ≥16.5 gm%/PCV 49, female ≥16/48; types relative and absolute.
Relative polycythemia (Gaisböck's): ↓ plasma volume (dehydration) → ↑ Hb%, post-viral; investigations show normal RBC mass/TC/PLC with ↑ Hb.
Absolute Polycythemia: Types, EPO/TC/PLC Table and Secondary Etiologies

Absolute = increased RBC mass; primary (PCRV) vs secondary; table: EPO normal-to-low in PCRV vs increased in secondary; TC/PLC increased in PCRV vs normal in secondary.
EPO = erythropoietin (cortex and outer medulla of kidney); hypoxic causes: COPD, OSAS, high altitude, CO intoxication, hepatopulmonary syndrome; renal artery stenosis separate.
Paraneoplastic: renal carcinoma (hypernephroma), cerebellar hemangioblastoma (von Hippel-Lindau), meningioma, pheochromocytoma (pallor ⇒ malignancy), hepatoma, uterine fibroids; features headache, dizziness, hypertension in paraneoplastic patients.
Polycythemia Rubra Vera: JAK2 Mutations and Clinical Features

PCRV = m/c MPN, age 50–60, female > male; JAK-2 in 100% (exon 14 V617F 95%, exon 12 5%).
Erythrocytosis: hyperviscosity, thrombosis arterial > venous (arterial stroke in young; venous Budd-Chiari/DVT; microvascular erythromelalgia), hypertension.
Granulocytosis: neutrophilia, basophilia → histamine → aquagenic pruritus, ↑ transcobalamin-I → ↑ B12 binding capacity; thrombocytosis → dysfunctional platelets → bleeding (epistaxis, acquired vWD); moderate splenomegaly; hyperuricemia (↑ turnover).
Investigations: ↑ RBC with ↓ MCV/normal MCH, low ESR (↓ rouleaux), PS microcytosis with erythrocytosis, LAP high, ↑ B12 binding capacity.
PCRV Investigations, Diagnostic Criteria and Management; Primary Myelofibrosis Etiology

Note: ↓ MCV (to conserve MCH) → no rouleaux; microcytosis list hypoxia, thalassemia, PCRV; transcobalamin from neutrophils for transport (liver, etc.).
Criteria: major Hb >16.5 men/>16 women, marrow hypercellularity, JAK-2; minor subnormal serum EPO.
Management: low risk <60 yrs — phlebotomy weekly (Hb 13–14) + aspirin; high risk >60 yrs/h/o thrombosis — phlebotomy + aspirin 75 mg + ruxolitinib 10 mg BD (or) hydroxyurea 0.5–2 g/day.
PMF etiology: JAK-2 50%, CALR 30–40%, MPL (codes for thrombopoietin) 10–20%, triple negative = poor prognosis, deletion 13q.
Primary Myelofibrosis: Pathogenesis and Clinical Features

Dysplastic megakaryocytes (lack CXCR4) in hypercellular marrow release TGF-β (most potent fibrogenic cytokine) and PDGF → marrow fibrosis (↑ type-III collagen); premature-cell release → leukoerythroblastosis and pancytopenia.
Most present in fibrotic stage; age >60; male = female; thrombosis risk PCRV > ET > PMF; B symptoms 20%; fatigue (m/c) from anemia; gout in proliferation stage.
EMH: massive splenomegaly (75%), osteosclerosis, hepatomegaly (portal hypertension), skin febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (Sweet syndrome — note: characteristic of AML); cutaneous photos show annular lesions (A,B,D), erythematous lower-limb lesions, erythematous papules and plaques.

PS: anisopoikilocytosis with teardrop cells/dacryocytes; cloud-like megakaryocytes; serum type-III procollagen peptide increased; aspirate dry tap; biopsy silver impregnation reticulin ± collagen fibrosis with hypercellular marrow; note megakaryocytes in peripheral smear.
Megakaryocyte glossary: staghorn ET, giant ITP, cloud-like PMF, dwarf CML.
Median survival 5 years; medical oral ruxolitinib (JAK-2) and lenalidomide; definitive AHSCT limited by complete-match requirement and ↑ infection risk.
Essential Thrombocytosis: Etiology, Clinical Features, Investigations and Complications

Benign disease, good prognosis; JAK-2 50–60%, CALR 30–40%, MPL 10–20%; mild splenomegaly; thrombosis (hyperplasia) > bleeding (dysplastic cells); female > male.
RBC/WBC normal, PLC >4.5 lakhs; biopsy megakaryocyte hyperplasia (few dysplastic) with staghorn cells (giant, mature cytoplasm, hyperlobulated nuclei); photos: ↑ megakaryocytes, hyperlobulated nuclei, megakaryocyte in aspirate.
Least conversion to myelofibrosis; AML order PCRV > PMF > ET.
Essential Thrombocytosis: Evaluation and Risk-Stratified Management

Diagnosis by exclusion: rule out reactive thrombocytosis (normal RBC/WBC, response to inflammation) and other MPN/MDS (JAK-2, calreticulin, MPL).
Low risk <60 yrs: aspirin 75 mg/day; high risk (>60 yrs, h/o thrombosis, platelets >1.5 × 10⁶): aspirin + hydroxyurea > interferon > anagrelide.
CML Pathophysiology: Myelopoiesis, BCR-ABL Molecular Genetics & the Philadelphia Chromosome

Myeloid origin cells: eosinophil, basophil, RBC, platelets, monocyte; myelopoiesis myeloblast → promyelocyte, segmented forms → mature neutrophils.
BCR on long arm of ch 22; ABL on long arm of ch 9; MBS autoinhibits ABL kinase.
Pathology: balanced reciprocal (pair) BCR-ABL translocation in 100% (myeloid > B > T), ABL exon onto BCR exon 13/14; Ph chromosome = shortened long arm of ch 22 in 95%; absent MBS → constitutively active ABL kinase → ATP docking → tyrosine phosphorylation.
CML Versus AML, TKI Note, Risk Factors & Clinical Features

CML vs AML: differentiation fairly normal vs complete arrest; proliferation high (multiple lineage) vs very high (single lineage); EMH massive splenomegaly; asciminib acts on MBS.
Risk factors: age 50–70, male > female, high-dose ionizing radiation (6–8 years), germ line susceptibility very low; 5-year survival 85–90%.
Chronic phase: asymptomatic leukocytosis (WBC ~1 lakh, m/c), fatigue D/t anemia, massive splenomegaly symptoms, gouty arthritis (↑ turnover), basophil histamine skin signs; blast crisis ≥20% within 4 years untreated; WBC >2 lakh → hyperviscosity (headache, blurred vision, priapism, vertigo); B symptoms 10–15% (classically Hodgkin's).
CML Investigations: Peripheral Smear, LAP, Tryptase, Cytogenetics & Bone Marrow Study

Smear: anemia, ↑ WBC (lakh), blasts <5%, all stages with myelocyte bulge (left shift), eosinophilia, basophilia, thrombocytosis without hemorrhage/thrombosis.
LAP low (low LAP in PNH, CML); tryptase increased (hematological neoplasm); cytology = smear, immunophenotyping = flow cytometry, G-banding = metaphase, FISH = interphase; cytogenetics for t(9;22), molecular for quantitative BCR-ABL.
BM study: mandatory conventional karyotyping to rule out additional abnormality (double Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17, del 20q), quantify blasts, grade fibrosis; FISH images normal vs BCR-ABL+; dwarf megakaryocytes.
CML Bone Marrow Picture, Accelerated Phase (Obsolete) & Prognostic Scales

Aspirate: marked hypercellularity, granulopoiesis (30:1), ↓ erythropoiesis, ↑ dwarf megakaryocytes, sea-blue histiocytes (Gaucher cells), fibrosis; images: blast >20%, trilineage hypercellular marrow, sea-blue histiocytosis, G-banding.
Accelerated phase (obsolete): basophilia ≥20%, blasts 10–19%, therapy-unresponsive thrombocytosis, uncontrolled thrombocytopenia, persistent/increased WBC.
Obsolete prognosis: Hasford scale and Sokal index (irrelevant post-TKIs) with parameters a–e (circulating blasts, spleen size, platelet count, age, eosinophils/basophils).
CML Management: Hydroxyurea, the TKI Table, Response Milestones & Monitoring

Hydroxyurea ↓ cell turnover; TKI table: imatinib 400 mg chronic / 600–800 mg blast crisis (hypopigmentation, periorbital edema, muscle cramps); IInd gen for TK domain mutation — bosutinib 500 mg/day (colitis), nilotinib 300 mg BD (peripheral vascular disease, pancreatitis), dasatinib 100 mg/day (pleural/pericardial effusion, periorbital edema, pulmonary hypertension); T315I — ponatinib 45 mg/day, asciminib (—).
Outcome: CCR in 6 months (no Ph on cytogenetics) = most important long-term survival predictor; molecular response by DNA PCR: 3 months <10%, 6 months <1%, 1 year <0.1% (MMR); monitor platelet count, smear, no symptoms.
Approach to Pancytopenia: Marrow Cellularity Flowchart & Aplastic Anemia Overview

Diseases: aplastic anemia, MDS, pure red cell aplasia, myelophthisis (secondary myelofibrosis); workup: bone marrow aspiration + biopsy → cellularity.
Hypercellular arm: acute leukemia (unless proven otherwise; adults AML 80%/ALL 20%), MDS, PMF, hairy cell leukemia (good prognosis), megaloblastic anemia (good prognosis), PNH, systemic (SLE, HIV, TB, brucellosis, leishmaniasis, sarcoidosis).
Hypocellular arm: + pancytopenia (aplastic anemia, 20% of MDS, aleukemic leukemia, copper deficiency, lymphoma); ± pancytopenia (Q fever, Legionella, anorexia, TB); PMF = pancytopenia + fibrosis; hairy cell = pancytopenia + massive splenomegaly.
Aplastic anemia intro: p121 prints 'hypercellular' as a slip (flowchart and p123 show hypocellular); bimodal (inherited <20 yrs, acquired >60 yrs); m/c cause drug dependent (good prognosis); m/c infection non-A, non-B hepatitis; 'bad prognosis' as printed.
Inherited vs Acquired Aplastic Anemia: Fanconi, Dyskeratosis Congenita, Shwachman-Diamond

Inherited: Fanconi (AR, FANCA > FANCB/FANCC, complex DNA-repair defect; short stature, café au lait macules, gonadal dysgenesis, ↑ AML & head-neck SCC, esophageal atresia; panels A facies, B hand/thumb anomaly, C chromosome breakage), dyskeratosis congenita (DKC mutation, telomere repair; captioned photos reticular skin pigmentation and dystrophic nails), Shwachman-Diamond (ribosomopathy; pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, metaphyseal dysplasia).
Acquired: idiopathic (m/c), drugs, toxins (benzene), virus (non-A, B, C hepatitis), others (PNH), autoimmune eosinophilic fasciitis (scleroderma mimic).
Drugs Causing Aplastic Anemia, Presentation, Severity Criteria & Treatment

Dose dependent (anticancer → temporary myelosuppression): fluorouracil, mercaptopurine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, busulfan; dose independent: chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, gold, acetazolamide, PTU, D-penicillamine.
Presentation bleeding (m/c) > anemia > infection; features against diagnosis: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, fever.
Severe thresholds (as printed): Hb <9 g/dl, reticulocyte <30.0 × 10⁹/L, ANC <0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelet <30.0 × 10⁹/L → Rx AHSCT; marrow hypocellular with fat cells; treatment equine ATG + cyclosporine (6 months to act, 50% success), AHSCT, eltrombopag (TPO analogue).
Pure Red Cell Aplasia & MDS Overview: Global Versus India Presentation

PRCA: acquired thymoma/CLL; transient aplastic crisis = sudden reticulocytopenia, giant pronormoblasts on smear, Rx IVIG.
MDS AKA myeloid neoplasm: dysplasia + ineffective erythropoiesis; MDS/MPN overlap = CMML; myeloblast proliferation = AML.
Global 70 yrs, M > F, single/multilineage vs India 40–60 yrs (5q deletion), female predominance, RBC-lineage disease, lenalidomide good response; hypercellular 80%/hypocellular 20%; AML progression 25%; no EMH; fatigue m/c.
RBC parameters: anemia (m/c), ringed sideroblasts (SF3B1), oval macrocytes (m/c), megaloblasts/nucleated RBCs, HJ bodies/basophilic stippling/Cabot rings; Perls staining image.
MDS Blood Parameters, Prognostic Scoring & Treatment Flowchart

WBC: blasts 5–19%, pseudo-Pelger-Huët (2 lobes), hypersegmented, toxic granules, Döhle bodies; platelet images: pawn-ball multinucleated, binucleate and dysplastic megakaryocytes.
Diagnostic features: pancytopenia with >10% dysplastic cells, hypocellular, cytogenetic abnormality, no AML, no other cause; R-IPSS named; prognosis poor = 7q deletion/monosomy 7 (paediatric), good = 5q/20q deletion, best = 11q deletion.
Treatment: single lineage → 5q deletion present lenalidomide / absent erythropoietin; trilineage → bone marrow transplantation or hypomethylating agent (azacytidine, decitabine).
Epidemiology of Acute Leukemia, Myeloid Precursor Lineages & AML Pathogenesis

Leukemia distribution: Adults → 80% AML, 20% ALL; Children/adolescents → 90% ALL, 10% AML; Myeloid precursor stem cell → Myeloblast (granulocyte), Monoblast (monocyte), RBC, Platelets.
AML pathogenesis: (1) Clonal proliferation of myeloid precursors — Myeloblast (m/c) → myeloblastic leukemia (70–80%), Monoblast → monoblastic/myelomonocytic leukemia, RBC precursor → erythro-leukemia, Platelet precursor → megakaryocytic leukemia.
(2) Complete arrest of differentiation (myeloblast takes over marrow): high turnover → short history (2–3 months), acute presentation without CNS/testes/organ (spleen/liver/lymph nodes) involvement, pancytopenia manifesting as bleeding; marrow replacement → blood blasts → ↑↑ counts (poor prognosis) → late CNS involvement.
Hyperviscosity Note, 5-Point Hematological Diagnosis, AML Definition, Survival & Hereditary Risk Factors

Hyperviscosity: absent in AML, present in CML. 5-point diagnosis: 1. Morphology (bone marrow/blood cells), 2. Cytology/Cytochemistry (MPO/Sudan black), 3. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry (CD markers), 4. Cytogenetics (recurrent genetic abnormalities), 5. Molecular genetics (inversion/deletion).
Definition: generalised neoplastic (clonal) proliferation of immature leucocytes ± blood/non-hematopoietic tissues; Leukemia = clonal WBC-lineage proliferation in marrow/blood; m/c cell = myeloblast; median age 65 yrs (seen in all ages); M > F.
5-year survival: >75 yrs almost NIL, >50 yrs ~20% with transplant. Notes: chronic disorders = mature cells; lymphoma = lymph node proliferation. Hereditary risk factors: defective DNA repair (Bloom, ataxia-telangiectasia), Diamond-Blackfan (inherited PRCA), inherited aplastic anemia (Fanconi, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond).
AML Risk Factors: Germline/Syndromic Predisposition, Down Syndrome, Environmental & Hematological Diseases

Hereditary continued: germline susceptibility (very minimal familial inheritance: germline CEBPA, germline GATA2), Kostmann syndrome (congenital agranulocytosis), Noonan syndrome.
Down syndrome: (a) Transient abnormal myelopoiesis — m/c hematological abnormality, seen at birth, resolves spontaneously in 2–3 months, d/t GATA-1 mutation; (b) AML — in 20%, within 4 years of age, megakaryocytic (M7) subtype, better prognosis than in a normal child.
Environmental: radiation, benzene, smoking, drug-induced (alkylating agents after 5–6 yrs; topoisomerase II inhibitors after 1–3 yrs: etoposide). Hematological: MPNs (PCV, PMF, ET, CML), PNH, aplastic anemia (eosinophilic fasciitis), myeloma, 25% of MDS (10–19% blasts) → AML (20% blasts).
Classification of AML: FAB Subtypes, WHO (2016) & WHO-5 (2023) Categories, and Recurrent Genetic Abnormalities

FAB classification (does not give prognosis): M2 myeloblast, M3 promyelocyte, M4 myelomonocyte, M5 monocyte, M6 erythroid, M7 megakaryocyte.
WHO (2016): AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities (blasts ≥20%), AML–MDS related & AML–therapy related (M6) [both poor prognosis], AML–NOS (M2, M3, M4), myeloid sarcoma. Recurrent genetic abnormalities (blasts ≥20% not required): good prognosis = t(15;17)/t(PML;RARα) [APML], t(8;21)/t(RUNX1;RUNX1 as printed), t(16;16)/inv(16) [CBFβ], NPM-1, CEBPA; bad = t(BCR;ABL)/t(9;22); very bad = FLT3-ITD.
WHO-5 (2023): 1. AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities (blasts ≥20% not required except CEBPA and t(BCR,ABL)), 2. AML–MDS, 3. AML–therapy related, 4. AML defined by differentiation (FAB). ICC classification: not used now.
Clinical Features of AML: Presenting Pancytopenia, Infections Note & Myeloid Sarcoma (Chloroma)

Presenting features: acute presentation (3-month history); pancytopenia → m/c complication is abnormal bleeding d/t prominent thrombocytopenia (bruising, petechiae, epistaxis, gingival bleeds, excess menstrual bleeding) and anemia (pallor, fatigue, weakness, palpitation).
ANC is normal → only minor infection/pustules; no fever (no cytokine production)/lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly; bone pains rare (m/c in ALL); life-threatening hemorrhage in APML; meningeal/cardiac/urogenital rare. Note: complex infections in aplastic anemia (profound neutropenia) and hairy cell leukemia (neutropenia, monocytopenia).
Myeloid sarcoma/Chloroma: d/t extramedullary blast proliferation, uncommon, m/c site orbit, can occur independent of marrow involvement, associated with t(8;21), also in children; m/c cells myeloblast/monoblast (M4/M5) infiltrate gingiva (gum hypertrophy/gingivitis), liver, spleen, dental abscess, proctitis.
Skin Involvement (Leukemia Cutis vs Sweet Syndrome), Blood Picture & Myeloblast vs Promyelocyte Morphology

Skin involvement: Leukemia cutis (non-tender violaceous nodular lesions on extensor forearms; M4/M5 AML; Rx chemotherapy) vs Sweet syndrome (tender erythematous/violaceous papules/plaques with dermal neutrophilic infiltration + fever on face, neck; AML, post G-CSF, PMF; Rx steroids).
Blood picture: normocytic normochromic anemia, platelets ↓↓ (<1 lac cells), total WBC count <4000 cells.
Morphology: Myeloblast (large uniform blast, high N:C ratio, pale blue scanty cytoplasm + granules, 1–4 prominent nucleoli, Auer rods ⊕ M3 > M2, fine dispersed chromatin) vs Promyelocyte (larger cell, more visible granules, nucleoli absent, clustering of Auer rods = faggot cells, M3/promyelocytic leukemia).
AML Cytology Stains, Immunophenotyping CD Markers, Cytogenetics, Molecular Mutations & European Risk Stratification

Cytology: MPO (+), Sudan black (+), NSE (M4, M5, M7), PAS (M6, M7). Immunophenotyping: Myeloblast (CD11b, CD13, CD33, CD117, HLA-DR), Promyelocyte (CD13, CD33), Myelomonoblast (+CD14), Monoblast (+CD11c), Erythroid (glycophorin, spectrin), Megakaryocytic M7 (CD41, CD61).
Cytogenetics & mutations: t(8;21) RUNX1–RUNX1T1 (m/c, children, chloroma, M2, CD19+, good prognosis); t(16;16)/inv(16) (abnormal eosinophils = AML M4 Eo, organ infiltration, good prognosis); t(9;22) bad prognosis (except CML); c-Kit (in t(8;21)/t(16;16), bad prognosis); NPM1 (cup-shape blasts, good prognosis, m/c gene mutated); CEBPA (good prognosis, requires >20% blasts); FLT3-ITD (bad prognosis).
European risk stratification: Favourable = t(8;21), t(16;16), NPM1 without FLT3-ITD, CEBPA; Intermediate = no cytogenetic abnormalities; Unfavourable = all other mutations.
Bad Prognostic Factors, Treatment Risk Groups, 7+3 Induction Regimen, Post-Induction Care & Targeted Agents

Bad prognostic factors: elderly age, high presenting WBC count, cytopenias (anemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia) >1 month before diagnosis, therapy-associated AML, MDS-associated AML, chromosomal translocations.
Treatment risk groups: Standard = t(8;21), t(16;16), age <60 yrs, NPM1, CEBPA; High = all other cases. Induction (7+3 regimen, 2 cycles): Cytarabine 7 days continuous low-dose infusion + Daunorubicin I.V 3 days low dose (ECHO prior d/t cardiotoxicity).
Post-treatment: marrow takes 10–14 days to regenerate → high infection risk (catheters, gut flora) → mortality; start antibiotics at first sign (tachycardia/tremors/fasciculations). Targeted: Midostaurin (oral FLT3-ITD inhibitor if FLT3-ITD+), Oral venetoclax (BCL-2 inhibitor, promotes apoptosis).
Post-Induction Bone Marrow & MRD Evaluation, Consolidation Phase, Regimens in Unfit/Elderly, New Drugs & APML Intro

Evaluation after 2 induction cycles: Blast % (<5% → hematological remission, risk of relapse +; >5% → refractory AML, inevitable death) and MRD (<0.01% blasts in marrow → MRD– → consolidation; >0.01% → MRD+ → bad prognosis).
Consolidation: 1. Allogenic HSCT (indication: MRD–); 2. High-dose cytarabine (indication: standard risk with MRD–; transplant not mandatory). Unfit/elderly for 7+3: hypomethylating agents (azacitidine, decitabine) + venetoclax (BCL-2 inhibitor).
New drugs: Gemtuzumab–Ozogamicin (anti-CD33), Ivosidenib (IDH inhibitor). APML (AML M3) intro: young patient with bleeding & pancytopenia, t(15;17)/t(PML;RARα), good prognosis with treatment, smear shows hypergranular myeloblasts (as printed).
APML (AML M3): DIC Pathogenesis, Hypergranular vs Hypogranular Types, Sanz Criteria & Differentiation Syndrome

Pathogenesis: promyelocyte granules contain thromboplastin → activates extrinsic cascade → DIC → early mortality from severe hemorrhage (medical emergency). Note: cells abundant in marrow but few in blood; start ATRA early if suspected; ↑ TF expression.
Types: Hypergranular (2/3, low WBC, faggot cells +, dark large granules, dumbbell-shaped bilobed nucleus) vs Hypogranular (1/3, high WBC, faggot cells –, few granules, butterfly-shaped bilobed nucleus).
Sans (Sanz) risk criteria: Low risk (WBC <10,000, platelets >40,000 → ATRA + arsenic trioxide, good prognosis) vs High risk (WBC >10,000, platelets <40,000 → ATRA + arsenic trioxide + idarubicin). APML differentiation syndrome (10 days post therapy): rapid count rise, fever, edema, pleural effusion, weight gain, lung infiltrates/dyspnea d/t cell adhesion to vascular epithelium & cytokine release; Rx I.V dexamethasone.
ALL Pathophysiology, Survival by Age, B-Cell vs T-Cell Lineage & Lymphoblast vs Myeloblast Morphology

Epidemiology & survival: ALL = 20% of adult leukemias (40–45% survival) and 90% of child/adolescent leukemias (10–19 yrs: 70–75% survival; <10 yrs: 90–95% survival); median age 13 years.
Lineages: Precursor B-cell ALL (80%) only involves marrow (only leukemias); Precursor T-cell ALL (20%) has poor prognosis, involves bone marrow ± mass (leukemias/lymphomas) in thymus → mediastinal widening, dyspnea, common in adolescent boys.
Lymphoblast vs Myeloblast: Lymphoblast is smaller, nucleoli absent, granules absent, MPO negative, Sudan black negative, PAS positive, acid phosphatase positive (myeloblast is larger, nucleoli & granules present, MPO & Sudan black positive, Auer rod).
ALL Risk Factors, Presenting Features (B-ALL, T-ALL, High-Count Sanctuary Sites) & Laboratory Features

Risk factors: Down syndrome (m/c malignancy: transient abnormal myelopoiesis > ALL > AML), defective DNA repair (ataxia-telangiectasia, Bloom's syndrome — in AML, ALL), radiation (printed note: in AML, ALL, CLL).
Presenting features: B-cell ALL in adults = pancytopenia, in children = limping, bone tenderness, inability to walk; T-cell ALL in adolescents = dyspnea d/t mediastinal widening (anterior mediastinal mass); High-count ALL = very poor prognosis, involves sanctuary sites (CNS, testes → cause for relapse, requires intrathecal chemotherapy); organomegaly rare in B-ALL, ± in T-ALL.
Lab features: (1) Blood — anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, circulating blasts, highly variable counts, hypereosinophilia precedes blasts by several months; (2) CSF — leukemic blasts +ve.
B-Cell Subtypes (Pro-B, Pre-B, Early Pre-B CALLA, Immature B), B-ALL vs T-ALL Clinical Features & Smear Notes

B-cell subtypes: Pro B cell, Pre B cell (m/c; includes Early pre B-cell → best prognosis, CD10⁺ = CALLA antigen), Immature B cell.
B-cell ALL: m/c childhood cancer, bone marrow failure features, fever in 50% d/t cytokine production by lymphoblasts, marrow cavity expansion, bleeding, CNS involvement; misdiagnosed as ITP or aplastic anemia.
T-cell ALL: classical presentation = mediastinal mass + pleural effusion, CNS involvement, pancytopenia (+) = T-cell leukemia vs (–) = T-cell lymphoma. Smears show large lymphoblasts; Note: AML has no fever; HTLV-1 produces adult T-cell lymphoma.
ALL Prognostic Factors Table, BFM-19 Treatment Protocol (Induction, MRD, Consolidation, Maintenance) & Other Drugs

Prognostic factors (Good vs Bad): White vs Black; 2–9 yrs vs <1 or >10 yrs; Female vs Male; CNS/testes/HSM/LAP/mediastinal mass – vs +; L1 vs L2, L3; Hyperdiploidy vs Hypodiploidy; t(12;21) vs t(9;22), t(4;11), t(1;19); NOTCH-1, HOX 11 vs –; Early pre B cell vs T cell.
Treatment: 1. Induction (2 cycles, BFM-19 protocol: Steroids + Vincristine + Daunorubicin + Cyclophosphamide; L-asparaginase not used now d/t widespread thrombosis) → 2. Bone marrow MRD status: Negative → 3. Consolidation (another 2 cycles) → 4. Maintenance (Methotrexate + 6-MP for 2–3 yrs); Positive → 3. 2 cycles chemo → 4. Transplant.
Other drugs: Rituximab (add if CD20 +ve), Intrathecal methotrexate (↓ CNS relapses), Blinatumomab (bispecific T-cell engager: Anti-CD19 + Anti-CD3), TKIs (if BCR-ABL +ve → better prognosis).
Initial Investigations, Common Lymphoid Progenitor Markers, Precursor B-Cell Maturation & CLL Origin

Investigations: FNAC, trucut/excision biopsy shows loss of lymph node architecture; immunophenotyping is diagnostic. Common lymphoid progenitor → B cell (CD 19), T cell (CD 3), NK cell (CD 56).
Precursor B-cell stages (Precursor B-cell ALL; m/c = Pre-B ALL): Pro-B = incomplete heavy chain, CD 19 + CD 34/HLA-DR/PAX-5 (bad prognosis); Pre-B = complete heavy chain, CD 10 (CALLA), TdT, CD 20/21/22/79a/79b + CD 19, loses CD 34/HLA-DR (good prognosis); Immature-B = complete heavy & light chain, S.IgM, loses CD 10/TdT (bad prognosis).
Naive B cell (no antigen encounter; CD 19/20/21/22/79a/79b, S.IgM): failure of apoptosis → clonal proliferation → CLL (acquires CD 5, CD 23).
Lymph Node Zones (Pre-Germinal, Germinal Centre, Post-Germinal/Marginal Zone), Myeloma Markers & CD Summary

LN zones: 1. Pre-germinal centre/mantle layer (after Naive B cell gains S.IgD in interfollicular area) → Mantle cell lymphoma (CD 5, Cyclin D); 2. Germinal centre (CD 10, CD 23, BCL-6): Centroblast (dark zone) → DLBCL, Burkitt's; somatic hypermutation & affinity maturation → Centrocyte (light zone) → Follicular lymphoma, Plasma blast, or Marginal zone.
Plasma blast proliferation → ABC-DLBCL; Plasma cell → Multiple myeloma (CD 38, CD 138, C19 [printed]; loses all other markers). Post-germinal/marginal zone → Marginal zone lymphoma; Memory B cell → Hairy cell leukemia, SLL, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia.
Summary panel: CD5+ CD10– CD23+ = CLL; CD5+ CD10– CD23– = MCL; CD5– CD10+ CD23+ = GC; CD5– CD10– CD23– = MZL.
CLL Overview, Epidemiology, Defective Apoptosis Pathophysiology, Small Lymphocytic Leukemia (SLL) & Etiology

Overview: CLL is the most common lymphoid leukemia (AML = m/c myeloid leukemia), Males > Females, low-grade; 80–85% asymptomatic/indolent, median age 72 yrs, median survival 10 yrs, 1–2% spontaneous regression.
Pathophysiology: Defective apoptosis of naive B-cells (CD19, CD20, CD21, CD22, CD79a, CD79b, S.IgM) → clonal expansion + acquire CD5, CD23 → monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis → CLL if lymphocytes >5000 cells/µL.
SLL & Etiology: SLL arises from memory B cell with identical immunophenotype/features and painless lymphadenopathy ± splenomegaly; CLL has strong familial inheritance and no risk with radiation.
CLL Investigations, Smudge Cells, Richter Transformation, Warm AIHA, Staging Table & Indications for Treatment

Investigations: Unexplained lymphocytosis (~60,000–70,000; rarely normocytic normochromic anemia, thrombocytopenia); smear shows small blue round CLL lymphocytes (pale cytoplasm, no granules, moderate chromatin condensation) + Smudge cells; LN biopsy shows diffuse effacement (SLL).
High-risk indicators: (1) Richter transformation — low-grade (classically SLL) → high-grade (classically DLBCL) with ↑ lymphadenopathy & B symptoms (>10% weight loss in 6 mo, fever >100.4°F, ↑↑ LDH, ↑ PET nodal uptake); (2) Warm antibody AIHA (DAT/Coomb's test).
Staging & Rx indications: Stages 0 (lymphocytosis) & 1 (+ lymphadenopathy) = no treatment; Stages 2 (HSM), 3 (anemia), 4 (pancytopenia, as printed) = treatment required. Rx indications: Richter features, steroid-refractory AIHA, Stages 2–4 (massive splenomegaly, marrow failure).
CLL Prognostic Factors Table, FCR & BR Treatment Regimens, and Hairy Cell Leukemia Overview & Pathogenesis

CLL prognosis & Rx: Good = hypermutated Ig heavy chain, chr 13q del; Bad = unmutated Ig heavy chain, other deletions (11q del, 17p del, trisomy 12), β2-microglobulin, ↑ LDH, Zap-70. Regimens: FCR (Fludarabine + Cyclophosphamide + Rituximab, TOC if fit); BR (Bendamustine + Rituximab, more commonly used).
Hairy Cell Leukemia: Rare low-grade B-cell neoplasm arising from memory B cell, >60 yrs (M > F). Pathogenesis: Memory B cell + BRAF mutation → Hairy cell → Spleen (massive splenomegaly) & Bone marrow (pancytopenia with neutropenia + monocytopenia, fibrosis → Aspergillosis, MAC, M. kansasii).
Hairy Cell Leukemia Investigations (Smear, Fried-Egg Marrow, Immunophenotype), Treatment & PAN Association

Investigations: Smear shows mononuclear hairy cells (bilobed eccentric nuclei, hairy projections, low N:C ratio, abundant cytoplasm); marrow biopsy shows hairy cells, fibrosis & fried-egg / honeycomb appearance.
Immunophenotyping: Positive = CD19, CD20, CD22, CD11c, CD25, CD103, CD123, Annexin, TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase); Negative = CD10, CD21.
Treatment & association: Purine nucleoside analogue (TOC) = Cladribine (DOC) > Pentostatin; BRAF inhibitor Vemurafenib (relapse); Rituximab (maintenance). Note: Polyarteritis nodosa is associated with hairy cell leukemia & hepatitis B.
Classification by Cell of Origin, Mature T-Cell Lymphomas (ALCL to Hepatosplenic) & Grade-Based Classification

Cell of origin: Precursor T → T-ALL/LBL; Mature T → mature T-cell lymphoma; Precursor B → ALL; Pre-GC → MCL; Centroblasts → DLBCL, Burkitt's; Centrocytes → Follicular; Post-GC → MZL; Plasmablast → ABC-DLBCL.
Mature T-cell lymphomas: (1) ALCL — ALK (CD30)+, t(2;5), breast implants, hallmark cells; (2) Angioimmunoblastic; (3) Enteropathy/Celiac T-cell; (4) Mycosis fungoides/Sezary; (5) Extranodal NK/T (EBV+); (6) HTLV-1 adult T-cell; (7) Hepatosplenic.
Prognosis & grade: B-cell > T-cell; m/c NHL = DLBCL. Grade: Low (SLL, MZL, Follicular); Intermediate–high (MCL); High (DLBCL, Burkitt's).
Causative Organisms Table (EBV 100/70/40/20 Rule, HIV, HCV, H. pylori, HHV-8, HTLV-1) & Ann-Arbor Staging

Organisms: EBV → Hodgkin 100/70/40/20 rule (LD 100%, MC 70%, NS 40%, LR 20%) & NHL (B-cell: Burkitt's, Post-transplant & Primary CNS [DLBCL morphology]; T-cell: Extranodal NK/T); HIV → DLBCL, Burkitt's; HCV → Waldenstrom's, Splenic MZL; H. pylori → MALToma; HHV-8 → Primary effusion lymphoma, Castleman's; HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
Ann-Arbor staging: I (single LN region), II (≥2 LN regions same side of diaphragm), III (both sides of diaphragm), IV (diffuse extralymphatic: lung, liver, bone).
Risk grouping: Stages I–II = Early (Unfavourable if Age ≥60, ↑ LDH, >1 extranodal site, poor PS); Stages III–IV = Late/advanced (Unfavourable by default).
NHL General Features, Mantle Cell Lymphoma (t(11;14), SOX-11, R-CHOP Resistance) & Follicular Lymphoma Genetics

General NHL features: Age 60 yrs, M > F, m/c asymptomatic painless lymphadenopathy, m/c nodal site = supraclavicular; extranodal = GIT (m/c), Waldeyer's ring, BM (30–40%); B-symptoms & CNS very rare.
Mantle cell lymphoma: Pre-GC origin; CD5+, Cyclin D1+, SOX-11+, t(11;14), CD10–, CD23–; aggressive (GIT lymphomatoid polyposis, BM, blood, spleen; unresponsive to R-CHOP); Classical = SOX-11+, Leukemic non-nodal = SOX-11– (printed good prognostic factor: SOX-11 upregulation).
Follicular lymphoma genetics: CD10+, CD23+ & BCL-6 dysregulation (all GC malignancies) + aberrant BCL-2 from t(14;18) (chr 14 IgG heavy chain [printed] + chr 18 BCL-2).
Follicular Lymphoma Histology/Course/Rx, Germinal Centre Malignancies Table & MALToma (t(11;18), H. pylori, Sjögren)

Follicular lymphoma: Paratrabecular lymphoid aggregates with small cleaved + large non-cleaved cells; B-symptoms rare, spontaneous remission & relapse common; treat symptomatic only (low burden: Rituximab); Richter transformation 3%/yr. GC table: Centrocyte = Follicular (low grade); Centroblast = Burkitt's & DLBCL (aggressive).
MALToma: m/c MZL (purely extranodal), post-GC origin, F > M (autoimmune), H. pylori non-atrophic pan-gastritis in 95%; CD5–, CD10–, CD23–, t(11;18); upper GI symptoms.
MALToma Rx & notes: H. pylori eradication (80% respond) → R-CHOP trial if no response; printed good prognosis = H. pylori +ve, t(11;18); Richter conversion to DLBCL; Sjögren MZL involves salivary gland.
High-Grade Lymphomas Overview, Clinical Features & Prognostic Factors, and Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)

High-grade lymphomas: (1) DLBCL, (2) Burkitt's, (3) Anaplastic large lymphoma [printed 'B-cell' on p150] — t(2;5), CD30+, hallmark & flower cells.
High-grade features: Rapidly progressive painless lymphadenopathy causing compression, extensive B-symptoms, extranodal (e.g., GIT), 'no involvement of BM or CNS' (general note), bad prognosis = LDH & hypoalbuminemia.
DLBCL overview: Age >60 yrs, M > F, aggressive, m/c NHL; primary nodal site = Neck; extranodal = mainly GIT.
DLBCL Subtypes (GCB vs ABC-DLBCL), Double/Triple-Hit vs Double-Expressor Venn Diagram & R-CHOP Regimen

DLBCL subtypes: Germinal centre (CD10+, CD23+, BCL-6+; good prognosis) vs Activated B-cell / ABC-DLBCL (plasmablast origin; CD10–/BCL-6+/MUM-1+ or CD10–/BCL-6–; CNS, mediastinal, organ transplant & body cavity lymphomas = ABC-DLBCL unless proven otherwise; HIV-defining; bad prognosis).
Genetics & Venn diagram: Dysregulated BCL-6 > aberrant BCL-2 t(14;18) (opposite in follicular). Double hit (c-myc + BCL-2/BCL-6 rearrangements, GCB) & Triple hit (c-myc + BCL-2 + BCL-6) = bad prognosis; Double expressor (high MYC + BCL-2 protein, ABC).
Treatment: R-CHOP = Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Hydroxy-daunorubicin + Oncovirin (Vincristine) + Prednisolone.
DLBCL Interim-PET Flowchart & Burkitt's Lymphoma (c-myc Translocations, Endemic vs Sporadic, CODOX-M/IVAC, Starry Sky)

DLBCL response-adapted Rx: 2 cycles R-CHOP → Interim PET: Good score → +2 cycles R-CHOP (early favourable) or +4 cycles R-CHOP (early unfavourable); Advanced disease → Autologous stem cell transplant.
Burkitt's lymphoma: 30% of childhood NHL, CNS involvement, chemosensitive, CD10+ & BCL-6+; chr 8 c-myc translocations t(8;14) [m/c], t(8;2), t(8;22) → highest Ki67 among NHL.
