The Acute-Pulmonary-Edema Treatment Bundle and Cardiogenic-Shock Features, Investigations and Phenotype-Specific Support

Acute pulmonary edema management uses IV furosemide 360 mg split 100 + 100 + 100 + 60 mg, semi-recumbent 45°, high-flow O₂ by NRBM/NIV, morphine 4 mg IV for extravascular fluid shift and BP control with NTG 5 µg/min (p329).
Cardiogenic shock has narrow pulse pressure with SBP <90 mmHg, fatigue, altered mentation, cyanosis and cold extremities, with a poor-prognosis note. Lactic acid rules out occult shock; early ECHO excludes ACS-related acute AR/MR.
HFrEF support uses dobutamine (common inotrope), milrinone (common inodilator) and IABP/ECMO; HFpEF uses vasopressors vasopressin/desmopressin.
Non-Recovering Pulmonary Edema, SCUF, BNP/NT-proBNP and Early Vasodilator Therapy in Acute AR or MR

If pulmonary edema with maintained BP is not recovering, the page offers dialysis or SCUF via central/femoral catheter; SCUF is expanded as slow continuous ultrafiltration (p330).
BNP/NT-proBNP >900 pg/mL is printed for patients with probability of HF; values are lower in obesity because of adipocyte metabolism, and the note flags diagnostic value in renal failure.
Early vasodilator therapy for acute AR/MR prefers nitroprusside > NTG (nitroglycerine); the printed chain is reduced aortic pressure → reduced transvalvular gradient.
The Cardiomyopathy Definition and Seven Types, the DCMP Presentation Table, MRI Uses and Pathophysiology

Cardiomyopathy is myocardial disease with a structurally/functionally abnormal heart after excluding CAD, hypertension, valvular disease and congenital disease (p331). Seven types are DCMP, HCM, RCMP, Takotsubo, arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia, LV non-compaction and tachycardia-induced disease.
DCMP systolic presentation has fatigue/palpitations, tachycardia from low CO/sympathetic overactivity, a down-and-out apex and prominent S3; diastolic presentation has dyspnea, edema/raised JVP and crepitations. Males > females.
MRI is gold standard for EF, RV function, amyloidosis/sarcoidosis and ischemia versus infarction. DCMP runs LV dilatation/thinning/systolic dysfunction → diastolic failure → LV failure → RV failure, with global hypokinesia and 25% of all heart-failure cases.
Other Heart-Failure Causes, the Genetic Table and Variable Penetrance, Etiology Branches, Complications and the Thrombus Figure

Other heart-failure causes are valvular, congenital and ischemia-related (p332). Genetics accounts for 30% with a positive family history: DCMP is autosomal dominant (TV titin > myosin heavy chain 7 > troponin I), ARVD autosomal recessive (desmosome) and LV non-compaction X-linked recessive (tafazzin), with variable penetrance/expression.
Peripartum and alcohol-induced CMP have good prognoses; drug-induced CMP is bad. Toxin/nutrition deficiencies are thiamine, selenium (sub-Himalayan Keshan disease) and carnitine; autoimmune sarcoidosis/hemochromatosis have a dilated > restrictive component; endocrine causes are pheochromocytoma, thyroid disease and obesity; inflammatory CMP is myocarditis.
Complications are thromboembolism, arrhythmias from a dilated LV, sudden cardiac death and decompensation with increased mortality; the figure shows a DCMP intraventricular thrombus on POCUS ECHO.
DCMP Investigations, Transplant, Angina with Normal Coronaries, and Peripartum Cardiomyopathy

DCMP ECG shows small-voltage limb-lead complexes (high voltage chest leads), sinus tachycardia and poor R-wave progression; ECHO shows cardiomegaly, a large roomy thin-walled LV with raised end-diastolic dimensions/reduced EF and global hypokinesia (p333). MRI/angiogram rule out CAD in all, especially first presentation after age 30.
Angina with normal coronaries is boxed as myocarditis, HCM or Takotsubo CMP; treatment is transplant. Peripartum CMP has the best DCMP prognosis but high recurrence, is associated with pregnancy age >30 and hypertension, and presents postpartum or in the third trimester.
Its pathology is SFLT1 (soluble fibrin-like tyrosine kinase I, anti-angiogenic); LV systolic failure, dyspnea with minimal exertion/breastfeeding and diaphoresis appear, with advice to avoid pregnancy again and expected resolution in 3–4 months.
Drug-Induced Cardiomyopathy and Anthracycline Regimens, Alcohol-Induced Disease, and Myocarditis Onset and Etiology

Drug-induced CMP includes anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin, mitoxantrone), trastuzumab, cyclophosphamide, VEGF inhibitors, proteasome inhibitors, anabolic steroids, lead, mercury, hydrocarbons and cocaine (p334). Anthracycline regimens noted are hydroxydaunorubicin in R-CHOP for NHL, Adriamycin/doxorubicin in ABVD for Hodgkin lymphoma and 7 + 3 for AML.
Alcohol-induced disease follows ACE polymorphism → acetaldehyde; added risks are holiday-heart AF, stroke and ACS, aggravated by thiamine/magnesium/selenium deficiency. Avoiding alcohol can improve EF after 3–6 months.
Myocarditis is focal or diffuse inflammatory dilated CMP, acute more than chronic (3 months), from post-viral HHV-6 (m/c) or Trypanosoma cruzi (Chaga's disease as printed), acting through systemic infection → severe cytokine release → reduced LV function.
The Clinical Spectrum of Myocarditis, ECG, Blood, HPE and MRI Findings, and Supportive Treatment

Most myocarditis is subclinical (p335). Unexplained tachycardia/hypotension after febrile infection can present with chest pain/angina despite normal coronaries or exertional dyspnea; refractory hypotension in infection and new-onset HF are poor-prognosis markers, while giant-cell myocarditis with rapidly progressive HF is linked to sarcoidosis.
ECHO shows global/LV dysfunction, ECG non-specific ST/T changes with low-voltage QRS and sinus tachycardia, blood shows troponin I elevation, HPE uses Dallas criteria and the MRI caption marks peripheral enhancement.
Treatment is no specific therapy, supportive care and steroids only for autoimmune disease.
HCM Epidemiology, Mutations, Pediatric Mimics, Complications, the 15-mm Definition and the Athlete-versus-HCM Table

HCM is the most common genetic cardiovascular disease worldwide and the most common cause of SCD; it is autosomal dominant, with myosin binding protein C ranked above myosin heavy chain (p336). Incidence is M = F, females progress more to HF with poor prognosis and 95–99% are asymptomatic.
Paediatric mimics are Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type 2, short PR), Fabry disease, Noonan syndrome and Friedreich ataxia; complications are HF progression, arrhythmias/AF and SCD.
HCM is LV thickness ≥15 mm without dilatation after excluding other capable cardiac/systemic disease; systemic HTN and AS are the other ≥15 mm causes. Athlete's heart has LV thickness <15 mm (10–12 mm), a large cavity, normal diastolic filling and improvement with rest; HCM has ≥15 mm, a small cavity, abnormal filling and no improvement.
Asymmetric and Inappropriate Hypertrophy, the Three LVOT States, Yamaguchi Disease and Diastolic Pathophysiology

Asymmetric HCM involves only the left side, septal and anterior wall, sparing apex and posterior wall; hypertrophy is inappropriate because afterload is not raised (p337). LVOT obstruction is present in one third, absent/normal in one third and dynamic in one third.
Yamaguchi disease is a Japanese-population HCM variant with apical hypertrophy and deep/giant T inversions. Diastolic dysfunction runs concentric LVH → smaller cavity → raised LVEDP → raised LAP.
Atrial stretch/dilatation raises the atrial CO contribution from 25 to 40% and AF risk; raised PCWP produces pulmonary edema and dyspnea, with tachycardia-related exertional dyspnea.
Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy, SAM, the Two Murmurs, the 30-mmHg Gradient and Aortic-Stenosis Types

Asymmetrical septal hypertrophy projects into the LVOT, narrows it and creates a high-velocity jet with low-pressure zones that draw the anterior mitral leaflet into the septum/LVOT; SAM is printed after two thirds of systole (p338).
Mild secondary MR causes a PSM at the apex, while increased LVOT obstruction causes an ESM at the lower left sternal border. A 30 mmHg gradient reflects subaortic/subvalvular obstruction and determines progression to HF (most important) and symptom severity.
The AS-location note labels valvular most common, subvalvular as the HCM form and supravalvular/Williams least common; angina with normal coronaries is due to microvascular dysfunction.
HCM Symptoms, Pulse and Apex Signs, Heart Sounds, Murmurs and the Principle of Dynamic Auscultation

Again 95–99% are asymptomatic (p339). Raised LAP/LVEDP gives exertional dyspnea/fatigue, orthopnea and PND in advanced disease; LVOT obstruction gives angina/syncope/dyspnea; palpitations come from arrhythmias with AF the commonest sustained arrhythmia, and syncope is repeated separately.
BP and JVP are normal, the pulse is jerky and bisferiens has two systolic peaks with percussion > tidal and the second peak related to SAM obstruction. The double apical impulse is due to SAM and the triple impulse to presystolic accentuation.
S1 is normal, S2 reverse split from prolonged ejection, S3 is + from reduced filling of a non-compliant ventricle and S4 ++ from a vigorously contracting sinus-rhythm atrium. Murmurs are ESM at LLSB and PSM at apex; ESM intensity follows the LV–aorta gradient and preload, afterload and inotropy.
Preferred Loading States, Relieving and Aggravating Factors, Manoeuvres, the Valsalva Exceptions and ECG

HCM prefers high preload, high afterload and low inotropy (p340). Reduced preload and afterload shrink the cavity/LVOT and raise obstruction; increased inotropy draws septum and mitral valve into the LVOT.
Hydration relieves. Venodilators/diuretics, aggressive BP reduction, moderate–severe activity and inotropes such as digoxin aggravate; inotropes are contraindicated for elevating BP in HCM.
Standing Valsalva, amyl nitrite and isoproterenol increase murmur intensity by lowering preload/afterload or raising contractility; hand grip and phenylephrine reduce it by raising afterload. All murmurs decrease with standing Valsalva except MVP (duration ↑) and HCM (intensity ↑). ECG shows LVH and precordial ST–T changes/deep giant T inversions in Yamaguchi.
ECHO and the Dagger Sign, Medical Treatment and Beta-Blocker Advantages, CCBs and ICD Indications

ECHO is the gold standard for HCM and requires ≥15 mm LV thickening without dilatation or another valvular/systemic/cardiac cause; Doppler shows the dagger sign (p341). Medical management is beta blocker or CCB plus disopyramide.
Beta blocker is DOC; propranolol is printed at 2 mg/kg (max 480 mg), reducing exercise HR response and rest/exercise LVOT gradient, relieving angina by lowering myocardial O₂ demand and increasing diastolic filling. CCBs are used for beta-blocker contraindication/intolerance; named drugs are verapamil and diltiazem.
ICD indications are previous cardiac arrest, family history of SCD, sustained VT, abnormal Holter, unexplained syncope and LVH >30 mm.
Disopyramide, Surgical Management, Restrictive Cardiomyopathy Physiology and Its Clinical Features

Disopyramide is class Ia, added to beta blocker/CCB if no relief, with QT prolongation, anticholinergic effects and reduced EF (p342). Surgery is for refractory HCM with gradient >50 mmHg despite medical therapy, by septal myomectomy or alcohol septal ablation.
RCM is introduced as non-genetic, more common than HCM and nested inside diastolic dysfunction. Constrictive pericarditis is the constrictive branch; restrictive physiology and restrictive CMP are the more severe restrictive branch.
RCM ventricles are stiff/non-compliant (R > L), non-dilated and of normal thickness, raising filling pressure and RAP. Systemic congestion gives JVP, ascites, edema and hepatomegaly; atrial stretch raises AF risk. Systolic function is almost normal, dimensions normal/rarely reduced, atria massively enlarged and RVEDP > LVEDP. Subtle exercise intolerance is first, restrictive physiology is the severest diastolic dysfunction and biventricular diastolic failure is R > L.
RCM Causes and Storage Patterns, the Most Common Mutations, Amyloidosis Classification and Features

RCM causes are non-infiltrative DM/scleroderma; intracellular iron (hemochromatosis, dilated > RCM), glycosphingolipid (Fabry) and glycogen (Pompe) accumulation (the latter two HCM > RCM); and intercellular amyloidosis, sarcoidosis (DCM > RCM), Loeffler syndrome and tropical endomyocardial fibrosis (p343). The figure labels lamellar bodies and zebra/onion-skin appearance in Fabry disease, with Ascaris lumbricoides printed as the most common associated infection.
The mutation recap gives DCMP truncated-variant titin, HCM myosin-binding-protein and RCM amyloidosis.
Amyloidosis is classified as primary AL, secondary AA (no heart, only kidney) and familial ATTR, with heart involved in all except secondary AA. ATTR is split into wild senile systemic amyloidosis and mutant familial amyloid polyneuropathy; localized amyloidosis produces atrial natriuretic factor and involves the heart. Features are bilateral thickened ventricles, biatrial dilatation, interatrial septal thickening and diastolic > systolic HF.
Amyloidosis Investigations, Arrhythmogenic RV Dysplasia, Tachycardia-Induced CMP and Takotsubo Presentation

Amyloidosis ECG shows low-voltage complexes and a pseudo-infarct pattern; ECHO shows hypertrophy (L > R); cardiac MRI shows a glittering hyperrefractile/sparkling myocardium due to interatrial septal thickening, and prognosis is poor (p344).
ARVD is autosomal recessive with mutated desmosomes, fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium and arrhythmias/SCD. Tachycardia-induced CMP follows recurrent tachycardia → myocardial-fibre disruption → CMP → AF.
Takotsubo is also called broken-heart syndrome, transient apical ballooning, neurogenic myocardial stunning, stress-induced CMP and catecholamine-induced CMP. It affects middle-aged females (F >>> M), follows chronic stress/sympathetic overactivity and causes transient LV dysfunction with a hypokinetic ballooned apex (catecholamine-induced transient myocardial stunning).
Takotsubo Investigations, Angiographic and ECHO Findings, Prognosis, Short-Term Complications and Treatment

Takotsubo ECG can mimic ACS or acute HF; troponin I rises but with a reduced rate of rise, and NT-proBNP rises markedly (p345).
Angiography shows normal coronaries, a hypokinetic apex and a hypercontractile base; ECHO shows regional wall-motion abnormality not confined to one coronary territory.
Long-term prognosis is excellent. Short-term complications are shock, LV rupture and thromboembolism, bracketed as the same as MI. Treatment is no specific therapy and carvedilol.
Mitral Valve Components, MR Features and the Acute-versus-Chronic Classification Tree

The mitral valve prints 2 leaflets, 2 commissures, 1 annulus plus chordae tendineae, papillary muscles and adjacent LV myocardium (p346). MR is systolic retrograde LV→LA flow, a pure volume overload lesion with normal diastolic function.
Acute MR arises from papillary muscle rupture (inferior wall MI; posteromedial wall supplied only by RCA, m/c; infection) or chordae rupture (infective endocarditis); chronic MR splits into primary/organic (RHD m/c in developing, MVP m/c in developed, SLE/RA) and secondary/functional (annular abnormality, LV dysfunction m/c, annular dilatation with MR begets MR, HCM via SAM).
RHD Timeline and Combinations, Autoimmune Notes, and the Physiology-versus-Pathology Chains

Acute valvulitis at around 10 yrs leads after 15–20 yrs to RHD with MS+MR (m/c), MS+AR and AR+AS; m/c heart disease d/t RHD is MS while m/c rheumatic heart disease is MR (p347). Other autoimmune diseases are listed under the printed heading 'causing AR': Takayasu arteritis, Behcet's, ankylosing spondylitis.
Physiology runs S1 → isovolumetric contraction → AV valve open → rapid + reduced ejection → LV to aorta (high afterload). Pathology runs coaptation-zone failure (soft S1) → incompetence → LV→LA leak (LA gives ↓↓ afterload) → ↑ LA blood → ↑ LA→LV blood → eccentric hypertrophy with dilatation (↑ radius, thickness not increased) → eventual contractility impairment (severe MR) → LVF.
Laplace's Law, Afterload Reduction, the Severity Table, Normal EF and the Pulse/BP/Apex/JVP Findings

Laplace: wall stress = pressure × radius/(2 × thickness); stress ∝ radius which keeps ↑ in MR till LVF; thin-walled LV needs less filling pressure (p348). NTG/sodium nitroprusside ↓ aortic afterload → more aortic flow, used in acute MR; strict BP control follows the same logic.
Severe/decompensated MR shows dyspnea +++ (LV failure), EF normal/↓↓ and ↑↑ LVEDP/LVESP against asymptomatic/palpitations, normal/↑↑ EF and normal pressures; normal EF in MR is 70% and <60% is bad prognosis needing treatment. Pseudocollapsing pulse keeps a well sustained peak and normal volume against collapsing's ill sustained peak and high volume (rapid up/downstroke shared); BP normal, severe MR → LV failure → narrow pulse pressure; apex down-out hyperkinetic; JVP v wave prominent in acute MR.
Soft S1 to S4, the Pansystolic Murmur Columns, Loudness Order, 60/40 Rule and MVP Features with the Venn Diagram

Soft S1 follows loss of coaptation zone and ↓ dp/dt; severe MR gives early A2 (wide split S2); S3 is universal even without failure and S4 never occurs (p349). The pansystolic murmur reflects a whole-systole gradient, except acute MR's short decrescendo murmur; heard at apex, left lateral, breath held in expiration, diaphragm; high-frequency soft blowing without thrill, no respiratory variation; radiation axilla/back (jet backwards) or base (jet to interatrial septa); loudness ∝ gradient, MVP < RHD < LVD.
Treatment indications: symptomatic, or asymptomatic with EF ≤60%/LVESD ≥40 mm (60/40 rule); repair > replacement, and post-repair sudden ↑ afterload can cause LVF. MVP: redundant leaflet buckling into LA (floppy), posterior leaflet m/c, F > M 15–30 yrs, m/c asymptomatic; Venn A = myxomatous disease (pathology), B = MVP on ECHO, C–E in the hatched overlap.
MVP Complications Flowchart, NEC and Murmur Auscultation and Dynamic Auscultation with Cavity Size

Excess leaflet tissue buckling into LA may carry GAG deposition: in annulus → weakening/dilatation/calcification → MR; in chordae → rupture → acute MR; pulling of chordae (papillary→LV myocardium) causes ischemic symptoms (palpitation, angina)/ectopics (p350). Auscultation: NEC and murmur, both or any one independently; murmur is high-pitched whooping (cooing dove), mid-systolic crescendo-decrescendo at apex, radiating to axilla (anterior leaflet) or aortic area (posterior leaflet).
Dynamic auscultation: Valsalva/sudden standing (↓ preload/↓ afterload) → ↓ ventricular blood → ↓ cavity → ↓ chordal stretch → more prolapse → click closer to S1 + longer murmur (figure ↓ impedance, ↑ contractility, ↓ volume); squatting/leg raising/standing-to-supine/isometric (↑ preload/↑ afterload) → ↑ cavity → more stretch → less prolapse → click away from S1 + shorter murmur (figure ↑ impedance, ↓ contractility, ↑ volume).
Brockenbrough Phenomenon, the MVP-versus-HCM Table and Acute MR Pathogenesis, Murmur and Treatment

Brockenbrough: post-VPC → compensatory pause → prolonged filling (↑ preload); in HCM ↑ force of contraction > ↑ preload → ↑ murmur intensity → ↑ gradient; in MVP cavity size stays normal so murmur is unchanged/↓ (p351). Table: standing/Valsalva ↑ duration (MVP) vs ↑ intensity (HCM); after VPC unchanged/↓ (MVP) vs ↑ intensity & duration (HCM).
Acute MR: rupture → non-compliant LA → ↑ LAP → ↑ PCWP → dyspnea (pulmonary edema); LV systolic function low/normal yet soon LVF → cardiogenic shock; short systolic decrescendo murmur; NTG/sodium nitroprusside till intervention, emergency CTVS surgery, bad prognosis.
Mitral Valve Components Diagram, Normal Valve Area, Etiology and the Rheumatic Pathology Chain

The p352 diagram numbers 1a/1b annulus (assymmetrical ellipsoidal fibrous ring), 2a/2b leaflets attached to annulus (posterior 3 lobes), 3a/3b commissures present b/w leaflets, 4 chordae attached to papillary muscle, 5a/5b papillary muscles (medial single vessel supply → involved) and 6 adjacent LV myocardium; normal valve surface area is 4–6 cm².
Etiology is RHD with a 2-decade latent period and death in 2–5 years once symptomatic without intervention. Acute rheumatic fever + valvulitis with MR leads after 15–20 years to RHD (40% of patients) with MS+MR (m/c), MS+AR and AR+AS; chronic inflammation → commisural fusion → fish mouth deformity → calcification → immobilized leaflet → ↑ stenosis, predisposing to thrombosis (m/c left atrial appendage).
AHA Classification, the ARF Carditis Note, Diastolic Cycle Gradient and Mild-to-Moderate MS Chain

AHA stages: progressive >1.5 cm², severe (asymptomatic/symptomatic) <1.5 cm², very severe <1.0 cm²; largest valve is tricuspid and ARF carditis gives 65% MR / 35% MR+AR (p353). Diastole runs S2 → IVR (MV opens incompletely) → gradient → ↑↑ LAP → ↑↑ PCWP → rapid filling → reduced filling → atrial systole; normally LAP = LVEDP – PCWP = PAEDP = 8–10 mmHg.
Mild-moderate MS: stress/exercise/pregnancy/fever/AFib → tachycardia → shortened diastole → ↓ filling time → ↑↑↑ LAP → ↑↑↑ PCWP → dyspnea with orthopnea, PND and pulmonary edema; presentation is dyspnea on tachycardia and β-blocker keeps HR down.
Severe and Very Severe MS: Pulmonary Hypertension Arms, Second-Stenosis Theory and Forward-Flow Signs

Severe MS: ↑↑↑↑ PCWP → ↑↑ PAEDP → PHTN via back pressure and reflex pulmonary vasoconstriction; presentation branches RVH→failure, TR, loud palpable P2, prominent pulsations, parasternal heave and prominent v wave (p354). The 2nd-stenosis theory: PHTN → pulmonary vasoconstriction → ↓ blood entering LA → patient feels better but is going to severe MS; very severe MS adds LV failure → ↓ cardiac output.
Forward flow: A2 ↔ OS over IVR; LA ↑↑ opens MV earlier so A2–OS shortens ∝ severity; murmur begins at end of IVR and its longer duration ∝ severity; pre-systolic accentuation is atrial contraction at the end of MDM and is absent in AF; loud S1 follows leaflets open at the bottom (↑ velocity of contraction) with delayed closure.
Backward Pressure Table, LAP Compression Syndromes, Hemoptysis Causes and the Clinical Findings Table

Backward pressure: PVH dyspnea, PAH with PHTN→RVH/TR, RAP ↑ JVP, IVC RHF features (ascites, edema) (p355). ↑↑ LAP stretches/dilates atria → AF → hypotensive shock and compresses esophagus (dysphagia) and RLN (hoarseness, Ortner's); LA clots embolise.
Hemoptysis causes: pulmonary apoplexy (↑ LAP rupturing thin-walled pulmonary/bronchial veins), winter (chronic) bronchitis → blood-streaked sputum, pulmonary edema → capillary rupture, anticoagulants, pulmonary infarction/hemosiderosis. Findings table: S1 loud, S2 palpable/wide split (failure), S3/S4 absent, rumbling MDM (left lateral, bell, end-expiration, no radiation); pulse normal/AFib, BP normal, JVP prominent 'a' wave, tapping apex displaced laterally.
Associated Murmurs, the MDM Note, MS-versus-Austin-Flint Table, ECG P Waves and CXR Findings

Caravallos sign (pansystolic TR) rises with inspiration at the lower left sternal border; Graham Steele murmur (diastolic decrescendo PR) sits at the same border (p356). MDM murmurs: Carey Coombs (acute MR), TS, Austin Flint (AR), MS. MS vs Austin Flint: AF frequent vs sinus rhythm, tapping vs hyperdynamic apex, loud vs soft S1, OS +++ vs absent, S3 absent vs + in AR with failure, PHTN present vs absent.
ECG: P pulmonale = increased P amplitude (II, V1); P mitrale = enhanced second hump (II) and enhanced negative deflection (V1). CXR straightening of left heart border is due to hypoplastic aorta, dilated pulmonary artery, LVH and ↓ cavity site (as printed).
Echocardiography, Warfarin and NOAC, PMBV with Contraindications and Balloon Valvotomy Figure

TTE stages MS and shows MR and calcification; TEE rules out LA clots; left atrial myxoma mimics MS (p357). Warfarin is indefinite for AF/clots and NOAC has no role in MS/prosthetic valve issue.
PMBV(C) = percutaneous mitral balloon valvotomy (commisurotomy); contraindications are calcific MS (requires valve replacement), thrombus formation and predominant regurgitation, all bracketed to mitral valve replacement; ↓ heart rate with β-blockers is life saving. The A–D figure carries stiffening cannula and guide wire labels, captioned mitral balloon valvotomy.
Pericardial Anatomy Table, Fluid Volume, Pressure Transmission and Interventricular Dependence

Pericardium: outer parietal fibrous (somatopleuric mesoderm, pain sensitive, pericarditis) vs inner visceral collagen + elastic fibres (splanchnopleuric mesoderm, pain insensitive, acute rheumatic fever only); fluid 50 mL (p358). Function 1: inspiration ↓ intrathoracic pressure → transmitted to chambers → augments filling; SVC extrathoracic vs heart intrathoracic gives the SVC–RA gradient so the rt heart fills more in inspiration.
Function 2: ↑ rt filling → septum to the left → ↓ CO; SBP fall upto 10 mm Hg in inspiration is normal, >10 mm is pulsus paradoxus (Normalis aggregans) in tamponade and 1/3 CCP. Function 3: TFP = intracavitatory − intrapericardial pressure; IPP ↑ → TFP ↓ → diastolic dysfunction. Function 4: systolic concordance with diastolic discordance (LV & RV) in inspiration.
CCP Etiology, Rock-Like Pericardium, Hemodynamics, Pulse, JVP and the Square-Root Sign

CCP etiology: repeated acute viral pericarditis (m/c), TB (and m/c), IgG4 related disease, histoplasmosis, malignancy (Ca breast), radiation (p359). Pathophysiology: symmetric fibrosis + thickening + adhesion + calcification → rock-like pericardium → impaired ventricular filling.
Hemodynamics: systole and initial 1/3 diastole normal, later 2/3 dysfunction → ↑ RAP → ↑ SVC/↑ JVP and ↑ IVC/edema-ascites-hepatomegaly → RHF; late diastole elevation & equalization of diastolic preanse in all 4 chambers → no filling (as printed). Pulse: pulsus paradoxus 1/3rd; JVP sharp prominent x and y descents with Kussmaul's sign; ventricular pressures show the square-root sign with pericardial knock, early dip → rapid filling → plateau.
CCP ECG and Broadbent's Sign, Differentials, the Tamponade-CCP-RCM Table and Tamponade Opening

CCP ECG: low voltage complexes; systolic retraction of apex = Broadbent's sign; D/D chronic liver disease and RCM; Kussmaul's sign also in RCM and TS; definitive Rx pericardial resection (p360). Comparison table: pulsus paradoxus +++/+/+; prominent y descent –/++/–; prominent x descent +++/++/absent; Kussmaul's –/+++/+; third heart sound –/–/+; pericardial knock –/++/–; low ECG voltage ++ in all; electrical alternans ++/–/–; thickened pericardium and calcification only in CCP (+++/++); effusion +++/+++/–; RV size usually small/normal/normal; equalization +++/+++ (post 1/3rd)/–.
Tamponade opens as a core emergency: abrupt rise in pericardial pressure alt fluid accumulation, cause trauma (m/c).
Tamponade Pathophysiology, Holodiastolic Equalization, JVP, Beck's Triad, Alternans and Pericardiocentesis

Tamponade: rapid fluid → ↑ pericardial pressure → exaggerated interventricular dependence with pulsus paradoxus in all patients, and LV compression with ↓ BP, obstructive shock, dyspnoea, tachycardia (p361). Holodiastolic elevation & equalization of diastolic pressure in all 4 chambers → no filling.
JVP: sharp rapid prominent x descent with absent y descent; Beck's triad = hypotension, prominent JVP, muffled heart sounds; ECG electrical alternans (alternating high & low volume complexes). Treatment: immediate pericardiocentesis, subxiphoid between xiphoid and left costal margin at 30–45°, aim left mid-clavicle toward the RV anterior wall, 16–18 gauge needle.
Acute Pericarditis Causes, the Paradoxical Friction Rub, ECG Stages, Investigations and Management

Acute pericarditis causes: infections (post viral m/c Coxsackie, TB, HIV), drugs (procainamide, hydralazines, anthracyclines, minoxidil), tumors (breast cancer), autoimmune (IgG4, SLE), post traumatic, post MI, uremia (daily intensive heparin free dialysis) (p362). Pain is sharp, pleuritic, relieved by sitting up & leaning forward; the paradoxical rub (more prominent with effusion, as printed) is high-pitched, leathery/scratchy, heard very close, triphasic, best sitting, at the lower left sternal border.
ECG: global ST elevation followed by Spodick's sign (TP depression) with stage I–IV panels; CXR +/- effusion; echo rules out tamponade. Management: aspirin 325 mg TDS/NSAIDs, colchicine, bed rest, steroids C/I.
CCP Complication, the MI-versus-Pericarditis Table and Dressler's Syndrome

Repeated pericarditis attacks lead to CCP (p363). MI vs pericarditis: sharp stabbing occasionally dull vs pressure-like heavy squeezing; worsened with inspiration vs no; worse supine/improved sitting-forward vs no; hours to days vs minutes (ischemia)/hours (infarction); nitroglycerin no change vs improved; rub present in most vs absent unless pericarditis; widespread concave vs localized convex ST elevation; PR depression frequent vs rare.
Dressler's syndrome: >2–6 wks post MI, autoimmune, fever + pleuritic pain + polyserositis, rub (+), ECG (N)/acute-pericarditis features, Rx NSAIDs.
Pulse-versus-JVP Indicators, Arterial Pulse Introduction, Waveform Letters and Pulse Apex Deficit

Pulse indicates left-sided ejection while JVP indicates right-sided filling (p364). The arterial pulse is a pressure wave originating in the aorta d/t LV systolic ejection, travelling at 5 m/s (faster than the 50 cm/s blood column); it indicates LV performance and the vascular reaction, with character/contour best felt at carotids.
Waveform: P percussion (SV/LV contraction), T tidal (aortic recoil), D dicrotic (reflected wave from PVR), DN dicrotic notch (S2). LV markers: ↑ SV gives sharper upstroke + higher peak; ↑ ejection velocity sharper upstroke + earlier peak. Pulse apex deficit: supine, neck turned to palpation side, carotid palpated while auscultating; > 10 means atrial fibrillation.
Brachiofemoral Delay, Coarctation Captions, Central-to-Periphery Changes and Assessment Features

Normal delays: carotid 30 ms, brachial 60 ms, radial 80 ms, femoral 75 ms; exaggerated delay = coarctation of aorta, whose captions are LVH on ECG, 3 sign on CXR, coarctation in cardiac MRI and serrated flow on continuous wave doppler (p365). Central→periphery: upstrokes steeper; ↓ peripheral resistance smooths the dicrotic notch and makes the dicrotic wave less prominent.
Assessment features: rate, rhythm, volume, character, vessel wall, peripheral pulses, radiofemoral delay.
Rate: Tachycardia and Bradycardia Causes, Myxedema and Cushing Notes, Relative Bradycardia

Sinus tachycardia: fever (infection), anxiety, exercise, high output states, hypovolemia, myocarditis, anterior wall MI, cardiac tamponade, cardiogenic shock. Sinus bradycardia: athletes, β blockers/CCB, ↑ ICT, hypothermia, inferior wall MI, myxedema (p366). Myxedema coma = unconscious, altered sensorium, bradycardia, hypothermia; Cushing's reflex = ↑ ICT + bradycardia + hypertension.
Relative bradycardia: HR rise not corresponding to temperature (10 beats/min per 1°; 101°F→100, 102°F→110, 103°F→120); infectious typhoid/Q fever/Legionella, non-infectious drug fever/lymphoma/CNS lesions/factitious fever; rule out heart block and β blockers/CCB; dengue, malaria, leptospirosis usually do not cause it.
Rhythm Tree, Hyperkinetic Pulse Notes and the Collapsing-versus-Pseudocollapsing Table

Rhythm: regular rapid = SVT/VT; irregularly irregular = AF, atrial flutter, SVT with varying conduction; regularly irregular = VPCs (p367). Hyperkinetic = high amplitude/volume with ↑ SV → ↑ CO; elderly rigid vessel means SV does not increase yet volume is high d/t non-distensibility; ↓ PVR makes the dicrotic wave less prominent; complete heart block has ↓ CO but ↑ amplitude (CO = SV ↑ × HR ↓).
Collapsing (Corrigan's/water hammer): rapid up/downstroke, ill sustained peak, high volume, from two-outlet conditions (AR, aortic sinus rupture, aorto-pulmonary window, PDA); pseudocollapsing: well sustained apex (as printed), normal volume, seen in MR.
Hypokinetic Pulse, Pulsus Tardus versus Parvus et Tardus and the Bisferiens-versus-Dicroticus Table

Hypokinetic = ↓ amplitude → ↓ SV (LV dysfunction); pulsus tardus reaches desired amplitude in time (severe AS) while parvus et tardus does not (very severe AS) (p368). Bisferiens = 2 systolic peaks (severe AR with P = T and T > P, AR with mild AS, HCM with P > T); mechanism: AR ↑ SV → large amplitude wave with P & T prominent; AS+AR ↑ turbulent velocity → ↓ lateral aortic pressure (venturi); HCM → SAM; palpation radial preferred.
Dicroticus = 1 systolic + 1 diastolic peak in LV failure (LVF → ↓ CO → ↑ PR); tracing panel prints QS2 = 280, LVET = 190, PEP = 90.
Alternans versus Bigeminus, Post-Extrasystole Pulse Volume, Pulsus Paradoxus and Its Reverse

Alternans = alternating high & low volume (alternating SV) with fluctuating Ca2+ uptake/release, rhythm regular; bigeminus = normal beat alternating with premature contractions (PMB SV diminished → pause → ↑ filling → ↑ next volume), rhythm regularly irregular (p369). Post-extra-systole pulse volume separates MVP (↑: ↑ filling → ↑ SV → ↑ SBP/volume) from HCM (↓, Brockenbrough sign: ↑ gradient/worsen SAM → ↓ CO/volume, ↑ murmur duration & intensity).
Pulsus paradoxus = systolic BP fall >10 mmHg in inspiration: tamponade, 1/3rd CCP, COPD, PE, SVC obstruction; femoral pulse for palpation. Reverse paradoxus (SBP ↑ with inspiration): IPPV in LV failure, isorhythmic AV dissociation, HCM.
Right-Heart Window, Its Three Indicators, Why the Right IJV Is Preferred and the Neck-Vessel Figures

JVP is the window to the right heart / natural non-invasive RH catheter measuring RA pressure, indicating RH hemodynamics, venous blood volume and venous tone (p370). The right IJV is preferred: carotid triangle between sternal & clavicular heads of SCM, lateral to carotid and deep to SCM, straight line with RA, less extrinsic compression.
Figure labels: carotid sinus, common carotid artery, internal/external jugular veins, subclavian vein & artery, anterior jugular vein, innominate vein, SVC; path of IJv with SCM heads and clavicle. The EJV is not preferred: valves interfere with measurement, invisible in hypotension (vasoconstriction), multiple fascial planes.
IJV-versus-Carotid Table, Abdominojugular Reflex and the Two-Scale Measurement of JVP

IJV vs carotid: superficial & lateral, better seen than felt, 2 peaks & 2 troughs with descents more obvious than crests, digital compression abolishes it, falls with inspiration, elevates with abdominal compression — against deeper & medial, better felt, single brisker visible upstroke, no compression or respiratory effect (p371).
AJR (old hepatojugular reflex): compress periumbilical region 10 sec; ↑ JVP <1 cm for <10 sec transient = normal, ↑ JVP >3 cm for >10 sec = impending right heart failure; principle = compression ↑ venous return which a faulty/dilated RV cannot receive without raised mean pressure. Measurement: scale 1 at JVP top, scale 2 perpendicular at sternal angle, measure x, patient 45° with neck & trunk in line; sternal angle is 5 cm above RA centre.
Measurement Inferences, Elevated-JVP Cause Groups, Kussmaul's Sign and Waveform Components

Inferences: JVP >3 cm above sternal angle elevated; RA pressure = (5 + JVP height cm) cm H2O with >8 elevated; RV end-diastolic pressure = RA pressure (p372). Pulseless rise = SVC obstruction; overload = renal failure, cirrhosis, excess fluid; ↑ RV pressure & ↓ compliance = PS, pulmonary HTN, RVF/RVH, RV infarction; inflow impedance = TS/atresia, RA myxoma, CCP. Kussmaul's sign = JVP rise with inspiration in CCP, TS, RCM.
Waveform: positive a, c, v with descents x, x', y across diastole–S1–systole–S2–diastole; panel aligns a with P, c with S1, x in systole and v after S2.
a Wave Mechanism and Position, Large a Waves, Cannon and Absent a Waves and the c Wave

a wave = RA contraction in diastole just before S1, preceding the carotid upstroke and following the P wave (p373). Large a wave = atria contracting against resistance (RV hypertrophy, RCM, TS, RA myxoma, pulmonary hypertension); giant/cannon a wave = atria against closed TV (regular AVNRT/AVRT; irregular VT with AV dissociation, CHB); absent a wave = AF and hyperkalemia.
c wave = upward bulge of TV during isovolumetric contraction, coinciding with S1; figure captions are large a wave and cannon waves.
x and x' Descents with Their Variations and the v Wave with Prominent and Reduced Causes

x descent = atrial relaxation (position line diastole) while x' = pulmonary valve opening pulling TV down → ↑ RA volume → ↓ RA pressure in systole; prominent x in CCP/CT, reduced/absent in RVF/TR/AF; figure stacks normal, tamponade and constrictive pericarditis (p374).
v wave = atrial filling, mostly systolic with S2 just before its peak; prominent v from ↑ RA volume in ventricular systole (TR, cor pulmonale, RCM, ASD + MR → high venacava pressure d/t RVF); reduced v in hypovolemia/hypotension; photo JVP in TR.
Lanscisis Sign, y Descent Variations, h Wave and the Closing Valve-Disease Note

Lanscisis sign (as printed) = giant v wave in TR with severe/mild/normal traces (p375). y descent = RA emptying → ↓ RA pressure in diastole after AV-valve opening; rapid y in CCP (Friedreich sign) and causes of prominent v wave; slow y with impaired RA emptying/RV filling in TS and RA myxoma; trace captioned rapid y descent with I, II, K marks.
h wave sits just prior to the a wave in long diastole d/t ↓ HR. Closing note: AS, AR, MR usually no change in JVP; MS prominent a wave d/t pulmonary HTN.

Ulcerative colitis endoscopy: symmetrical, superficial, continuous involvement with decreased vascularity, fine granulations, friability and inflammatory pseudopolyps. (Book p37)
The earliest change on barium enema in ulcerative colitis is:
Barium enema: earliest change is fine mucosal granularities. (Book p38)
Serrations on barium enema in ulcerative colitis produce:
Barium enema: serrations producing a hazy margin. (Book p38)
Deep ulcers extending to the submucosa correspond to the named lesion:
Deep ulcers extending to the submucosa produce collar stud ulcers. (Book p38)
Backwash ileitis is inflammation of the:
Backwash ileitis is inflammation of the terminal ileum. (Book p38)
Which structure is lost on barium enema in ulcerative colitis?
Barium enema findings include loss of rectal valves. (Book p38)

Match the barium enema appearance to its printed stage — 1) Earliest change 2) Deep ulcers 3) Chronic long-standing disease 4) Fulminant disease … A) Lead pipe appearance B) Toxic megacolon C) Collar stud ulcers D) Fine mucosal granularities

Fine mucosal granularities are the earliest change; collar stud ulcers reflect deep ulcers; lead pipe appearance reflects chronic long-standing disease; toxic megacolon complicates fulminant disease. (Book p38)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a listed barium enema finding in ulcerative colitis:

Barium enema findings in ulcerative colitis: fine mucosal granularities, serrations, collar stud ulcers, mild narrowing of lumen, loss of rectal valves, backwash ileitis. The string sign belongs to Crohn's disease. (Book p38)
The commonest site pattern of Crohn's disease is:
Crohn's disease clinical features: ileocolitis is the most common pattern. (Book p38)
Episodic right lower quadrant pain in ileocolitis is:
Ileocolitis: episodic right lower quadrant pain relieved with diarrhea (large bowel diarrhea due to colitis). (Book p38)
Fever, weight loss and systemic symptoms in Crohn's disease reflect a ____ profile acting through IL-2 and interferon gamma.
Fever, weight loss and systemic symptoms are due to the Th1 profile (IL-2, interferon gamma). (Book p38)
A palpable inflammatory mass in Crohn's disease is due to:
Palpable inflammatory mass: due to thickening of the bowel wall. (Book p38)
The fistula frequency listed for Crohn's disease is:
Fistulas: enterovesical more than perianal. (Book p38)
Fissures in Crohn's disease progress to ____ strictures.
Fissures progress to fibrosed strictures. (Book p38)

Match the Crohn's disease feature to its printed mechanism — 1) Palpable inflammatory mass 2) Malabsorption 3) Fistulas 4) Strictures … A) Enterovesical more than perianal B) Thickening of the bowel wall C) Fissures leading to fibrosis D) Jejunoileitis
The palpable inflammatory mass comes from bowel wall thickening; malabsorption from jejunoileitis; fistulas are enterovesical more than perianal; strictures follow fibrosis of fissures. (Book p38)
A young man has episodic right lower quadrant pain relieved by diarrhea, low grade fever, weight loss, bowel obstruction and a palpable right lower quadrant mass. The book's picture is:
Crohn's ileocolitis: episodic right lower quadrant pain relieved with diarrhea, fever, weight loss, systemic symptoms, obstruction, palpable inflammatory mass. (Book p38)
The target sign on barium enema is:
Mucosal ulcers with a surrounding translucent mound of edema
A fatty middle layer in the bowel wall
Barium enema: target sign — mucosal ulcers with a surrounding translucent mound of edema. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
The target sign is described as the:
The target sign is the earliest radiological and endoscopic finding. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
Rose thorn ulcers, fissures and the string sign are grouped as reflecting:
Rose thorn ulcers, fissures and the string sign reflect transmural ulcers. (Book p39)

Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
The role of CT scan in inflammatory bowel disease is:
Limited, with MR enterography preferred instead
CT scan has a limited role in the diagnosis of IBD; MR enterography is preferred instead. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's

Match the CT sign to its printed meaning — 1) Target appearance 2) Comb sign 3) Fat halo sign … A) Hypervascular mesentery B) Inner and outer soft tissue attenuation with a fatty middle layer C) Colonic wall thickening

Target appearance reflects colonic wall thickening; the comb sign reflects a hypervascular mesentery; the fat halo sign shows inner and outer soft tissue attenuation with a fatty middle layer. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
The comb sign in Crohn's disease indicates:
Comb sign in Crohn's disease: hypervascular mesentery. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
In the fat halo sign the middle layer shows:
Fat halo sign: inner and outer layers show soft tissue attenuation, the middle layer fatty attenuation. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a listed CT scan finding in inflammatory bowel disease:
CT scan findings listed: target appearance from colonic wall thickening, comb sign and fat halo sign. Sinus tract appears among the barium enema images. (Book p39)
Endoscopy & Cross Sectional Imaging in Crohn's

Match the feature to the Crohn's disease finding — 1) Ileocaecal valve 2) Colon 3) Ulcers … A) Four or more segments, especially terminal ileum and ileocaecal valve B) Longitudinal C) Commonly involved
Crohn's disease: ileocaecal valve commonly involved; four or more segments especially terminal ileum and ileocaecal valve; longitudinal ulcers. (Book p40)

Match the feature to the intestinal tuberculosis finding — 1) Ileocaecal valve 2) Colon 3) Ulcers … A) Fewer than four segments, especially ileocaecal valve and ascending colon B) Transverse C) Usually strictured and patulous
Intestinal tuberculosis: ileocaecal valve usually strictured and patulous; fewer than four segments especially ileocaecal valve and ascending colon; transverse ulcers. (Book p40)
Cobblestone appearance, aphthous lesions and perianal lesions are:
Frequent in Crohn's disease and rare in intestinal tuberculosis
Frequent in intestinal tuberculosis and rare in Crohn's disease
Cobblestone appearance, aphthous lesions and perianal lesions are frequent in Crohn's disease and rare in intestinal tuberculosis. (Book p40)
TRUE or FALSE — in the book's comparison, transverse ulcers with a usually strictured and patulous ileocaecal valve favour intestinal tuberculosis over Crohn's disease.
True — transverse ulcers and a strictured patulous valve favour tuberculosis
False — those findings favour Crohn's disease
False — the valve is never involved in tuberculosis
True — but only when more than four segments are involved
Intestinal tuberculosis: transverse ulcers, usually strictured and patulous ileocaecal valve, fewer than four segments, perianal lesions rare. (Book p40)
A patient with ileocaecal disease has transverse ulcers, a patulous but usually strictured ileocaecal valve and involvement of fewer than four segments. The book favours:

Intestinal tuberculosis: transverse ulcers, usually strictured and patulous ileocaecal valve, fewer than four segments especially ileocaecal valve and ascending colon, perianal lesions rare. (Book p40)
Most extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease are most common in:
Most extraintestinal manifestations are most common in Crohn's disease. (Book p40)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not listed as most common in ulcerative colitis:
Listed as most common in ulcerative colitis: uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis and pyoderma gangrenosum. Erythema nodosum is not in that list. (Book p40)

Match the eye manifestation to its printed descriptor — 1) Episcleritis 2) Uveitis … A) More dangerous, can lead to loss of vision, unrelated to bowel activity B) Extension of conjunctivitis, parallels bowel activity
Episcleritis is an extension of conjunctivitis and parallels bowel activity; uveitis is more dangerous, can lead to loss of vision and is unrelated to bowel activity. (Book p40)
Erythema nodosum is described by the book as:
Pruritic vesicles on the extensor surface
Erythema nodosum: painful, pretibial papules. (Book p40)

Match the arthritis pattern to its printed descriptor — 1) Peripheral arthritis type I 2) Peripheral arthritis type II … A) Ankylosing spondylitis like axial arthritis, unrelated to bowel activity B) Large joint migratory asymmetrical pauciarticular arthritis, parallels bowel activity

Peripheral arthritis type I is large joint migratory asymmetrical pauciarticular arthritis that parallels bowel activity; type II is ankylosing spondylitis like axial arthritis unrelated to bowel activity. (Book p40)
Peripheral arthritis type I in inflammatory bowel disease:
Peripheral arthritis type I parallels bowel activity. (Book p40)
Which of the following skin lesions is listed among the manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease?
Skin lesions listed: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, pyoderma vegetans, aphthous ulcers and Sweet syndrome. (Book p40)
A patient with quiescent colitis develops large joint migratory asymmetrical pauciarticular arthritis that flares whenever the bowel symptoms flare. The book's type is:
Peripheral arthritis type I: large joint migratory asymmetrical pauciarticular arthritis that parallels bowel activity. (Book p40)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis in inflammatory bowel disease is:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is most common in ulcerative colitis. (Book p41)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is described as fibrosing destruction of:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis: fibrosing destruction of intra and extrahepatic bile ducts. (Book p41)
What proportion of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis are ulcerative colitis positive?
Two thirds of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis are ulcerative colitis positive. (Book p41)
What proportion of patients with ulcerative colitis are primary sclerosing cholangitis positive?
5% of patients with ulcerative colitis are primary sclerosing cholangitis positive. (Book p41)
The stones listed under OTHERS in inflammatory bowel disease are:
Stones: cholelithiasis and nephrolithiasis of the oxalate type. (Book p41)
Match the OTHERS item to its printed content — 1) Musculoskeletal 2) Liver 3) Vascular … A) Steatosis B) Increased risk of thromboembolism C) Osteopenia and osteoporosis
Musculoskeletal: osteopenia and osteoporosis; liver: steatosis; vascular: increased risk of thromboembolism. (Book p41)
Osteopenia and osteoporosis are reported in what proportion of patients as most common?
Musculoskeletal: osteopenia and osteoporosis, most common in more than 40% of patients. (Book p41)
Osteopenia and osteoporosis in inflammatory bowel disease are attributed to:
Osteopenia and osteoporosis occur due to long term drug use. (Book p41)
Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin help to differentiate:
IBD relapse from infectious large bowel diarrhea
Irritable bowel syndrome from microscopic colitis
Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin help differentiate IBD relapse from infectious large bowel diarrhea. (Book p41)
Levels of fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin are:
Levels of fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin are increased in IBD relapse. (Book p41)
Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin, and correlation with extraintestinal manifestations
Relapse is identified by fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin, and by correlation with extraintestinal manifestations. (Book p41)

Match the serological marker to its printed meaning — 1) ASCA 2) Omp-C 3) APB 4) Anti-Ia … A) Anti-pancreatic antibody B) Elevated levels mean bad prognosis and need for surgery C) Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody D) Outer membrane porin C antibody
ASCA is anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody; Omp-C is outer membrane porin C antibody; APB is anti-pancreatic antibody; anti-Ia elevated means bad prognosis and need for surgery. (Book p41)
Elevated anti-Ia in Crohn's disease indicates:
Bad prognosis and need for surgery
Anti-Ia elevated means bad prognosis and need for surgery. (Book p41)
Ulcerative colitis serology: atypical p-ANCA correlates with disease activity. (Book p41)
ASCA is common to Crohn's disease and:
Note: ASCA is common to Crohn's disease and Behcet's disease. (Book p41)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not listed under Crohn's disease serology:
Crohn's disease serology: ASCA, Omp-C, APB, anti-Ia and anti-flagellin. Anti-goblet cell antibody is listed under ulcerative colitis. (Book p41)

Match the Truelove and Witt's grade to its printed stool criterion — 1) Mild 2) Moderate 3) Severe … A) Fewer than four stools per day B) More than ten stools per day with blood C) Between mild and severe
Mild: fewer than four stools per day; moderate: between mild and severe; severe: more than ten stools per day with blood. (Book p42)
The stool frequency that defines mild ulcerative colitis is:
Fewer than four stools per day
Fewer than ten stools per day
More than ten stools per day
Mild ulcerative colitis: fewer than four stools per day. (Book p42)
The stool frequency that defines severe ulcerative colitis is:
More than ten stools per day with blood
More than four stools per day
Fewer than four stools per day
More than twenty stools per day
Severe ulcerative colitis: more than ten stools per day with blood. (Book p42)
The fever threshold for severe ulcerative colitis is:
Severe ulcerative colitis: fever above 37.5 °C. (Book p42)
The heart rate threshold listed for severe ulcerative colitis is:
Severe ulcerative colitis: heart rate above 90 per minute. (Book p42)
The anemia threshold for severe ulcerative colitis is a hemoglobin below:
Severe ulcerative colitis: anemia with hemoglobin below 75% of normal. (Book p42)
The ESR threshold that separates severe from mild ulcerative colitis is:
Mild ulcerative colitis has ESR below 30 mm per hour; severe disease has ESR above 30 mm per hour. (Book p42)
Mild ulcerative colitis is characterised by:
No fever, no tachycardia and mild anemia
More than ten bloody stools per day
Mild ulcerative colitis: fewer than four stools per day, no fever, no tachycardia, mild anemia, ESR below 30 mm per hour. (Book p42)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a Truelove and Witt's severe criterion:
More than ten stools per day with blood
Severe criteria: more than ten stools per day with blood, fever above 37.5 °C, heart rate above 90 per minute, hemoglobin below 75% of normal, ESR above 30 mm per hour. (Book p42)
The mainstay of treatment in ulcerative colitis is:
5-ASA (aminosalicylic acid) is the mainstay of treatment. (Book p42)
Plain 5-ASA is absorbed at the small intestine and therefore does not reach the ____.
Disadvantage of plain 5-ASA: absorbed at the small intestine, so it does not reach the rectum, the site of active disease. (Book p42)
Delayed or controlled release 5-ASA, that is mesalamine, is the drug of choice for:
Mesalamine is a delayed or controlled release 5-ASA and is the drug of choice for mild ulcerative colitis. (Book p42)

Match the ulcerative colitis severity to its printed induction therapy — 1) Mild 2) Moderate 3) Severe … A) Oral mesalamine and oral steroids B) Intravenous steroid C) Topical 5-ASA or oral mesalamine
Induction: mild disease gets topical 5-ASA or oral mesalamine; moderate disease gets oral mesalamine and oral steroids; severe disease gets intravenous steroid. (Book p42)
Maintenance therapy in mild ulcerative colitis is:
Maintenance: mild ulcerative colitis is maintained on topical 5-ASA. (Book p42)
Steroid resistant or refractory moderate ulcerative colitis is treated with:
Steroid resistant or refractory moderate ulcerative colitis: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine. (Book p42)
Severe ulcerative colitis is induced with:
Intravenous steroid, intravenous anti-TNF-alpha or intravenous cyclosporine
Severe ulcerative colitis induction: intravenous steroid, intravenous anti-TNF-alpha or intravenous cyclosporine. (Book p42)
Maintenance in severe ulcerative colitis is with:
Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, low dose anti-TNF-alpha or oral cyclosporine
Severe ulcerative colitis maintenance: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, low dose anti-TNF-alpha or oral cyclosporine. (Book p42)
A patient with severe ulcerative colitis settles after intravenous steroid and now needs maintenance. According to the book you would choose:
Severe ulcerative colitis maintenance: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, low dose anti-TNF-alpha or oral cyclosporine. (Book p42)
Sulfasalazine is 5-ASA linked to a carrier molecule called ____.
Sulfasalazine: 5-ASA plus sulfapyridine as the carrier. (Book p43)
Sulfasalazine: 5-ASA plus sulfapyridine carrier, absorbed at the rectum. (Book p43)
The note 'G6PD deficiency, no longer used' appears against:
Sulfasalazine note: G6PD deficiency means it is no longer used. (Book p43)
The side effects listed for azathioprine are:
Hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression and pancreatitis
Side effects of azathioprine: hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression and pancreatitis. (Book p43)
The surgical procedure listed for ulcerative colitis is:
Surgical management of ulcerative colitis: proctocolectomy with ileoanal anastomosis. (Book p43)
Which of the following is a listed indication for surgery in ulcerative colitis?
Indications for surgery in ulcerative colitis: colonic dysplasia or carcinoma, uncontrollable colonic hemorrhage, colonic perforation, toxic megacolon and medically refractory disease. (Book p43)
Match the surgical indication to its printed wording — 1) Bleeding 2) Perforation 3) Neoplasia … A) Colonic perforation B) Uncontrollable colonic hemorrhage C) Colonic dysplasia or carcinoma
Surgical indications: uncontrollable colonic hemorrhage, colonic perforation and colonic dysplasia or carcinoma, plus toxic megacolon and medically refractory disease. (Book p43)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a listed indication for surgery in ulcerative colitis:

Indications for surgery in ulcerative colitis: toxic megacolon, colonic perforation, uncontrollable colonic hemorrhage, colonic dysplasia or carcinoma and medically refractory disease. Perianal fistula is not listed. (Book p43)

Match the Crohn's disease severity grade to its printed descriptor — 1) Mild-moderate 2) Moderate-severe 3) Severe-fulminant … A) Between mild and severe B) No dehydration, no obstruction, no weight loss and no systemic features C) Despite steroid intake the patient has fever, cachexia, obstruction and peritoneal signs

Mild-moderate: no dehydration, no obstruction, no weight loss, no systemic features. Moderate-severe: between mild and severe. Severe-fulminant: despite steroid intake the patient has fever, cachexia, obstruction and peritoneal signs. (Book p43)
Severe-fulminant Crohn's disease is defined by the book as:
Persistence of fever, cachexia, obstruction and peritoneal signs despite steroid intake
Severe-fulminant: despite steroid intake the patient has fever, cachexia, obstruction and peritoneal signs. (Book p43)
The objectives of medical management in Crohn's disease are:
Endoscopic mucosal healing and prevention of complications such as strictures and fistulae
Objectives: endoscopic mucosal healing and prevention of complications such as strictures and fistulae. (Book p43)
Corticosteroids in Crohn's disease carry a high risk of:
Corticosteroids carry a high risk of dependency and resistance. (Book p43)
The anti-TNF agents listed for Crohn's disease are:
Biologics: anti-TNF agents are infliximab, adalimumab and certolizumab pegol. (Book p43)
Biologics play an important role in:
Continuously active disease and prolonged symptomatic remission
Biologics play an important role in the treatment of continuously active disease and prolonged symptomatic remission. (Book p43)
Which drug class is listed among the drugs used in Crohn's disease?
Drugs listed for Crohn's disease: antibiotics, corticosteroids, 5-ASA, immunomodulators and biologics. (Book p43)
Mild-moderate Crohn's disease is induced with oral ____ at 9 mg per day.
Mild-moderate Crohn's disease induction: oral budesonide 9 mg per day. (Book p44)
The dose of oral budesonide used for induction in mild-moderate Crohn's disease is:
Oral budesonide 9 mg per day for mild-moderate Crohn's disease. (Book p44)
Maintenance therapy in mild-moderate Crohn's disease is:
Mild-moderate Crohn's disease: maintenance is not required. (Book p44)
Match the Crohn's severity to the printed induction steroid — 1) Mild-moderate 2) Moderate-severe 3) Severe-fulminant … A) Intravenous steroids B) Oral budesonide C) Oral steroids
Induction: mild-moderate gets oral budesonide, moderate-severe gets oral steroids, severe-fulminant gets intravenous steroids. (Book p44)
Maintenance in severe-fulminant Crohn's disease is:
Severe-fulminant Crohn's disease maintenance: periodic anti-TNF-alpha. (Book p44)
Maintenance in moderate-severe Crohn's disease is with:
Moderate-severe Crohn's disease maintenance: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine. (Book p44)
Fistulizing Crohn's disease is managed with:
Anti-TNF-alpha with or without immunomodulators, followed by surgery
Fistulizing disease: anti-TNF-alpha with or without immunomodulators followed by surgery. (Book p44)
The drug listed in moderate-severe Crohn's disease alongside azathioprine and anti-TNF-alpha is:
Moderate-severe Crohn's disease drugs: oral steroids, azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate, anti-TNF-alpha and periodic anti-TNF-alpha. (Book p44)
The note on maintenance therapy in Crohn's disease advises avoiding:
Note: avoid smoking and NSAIDs. (Book p44)
The drugs to be avoided in maintenance therapy of Crohn's disease are:
Drugs to be avoided in maintenance therapy: oral 5-ASA, corticosteroids and budesonide. (Book p44)
Match the newer drug to its printed target — 1) Natalizumab 2) Ustekinumab 3) Vedolizumab … A) Anti-IL-12 and IL-23 B) Anti-alpha-4 integrin C) Anti-integrin
Newer drugs: natalizumab is anti-alpha-4 integrin, ustekinumab is anti-IL-12 and IL-23, vedolizumab is anti-integrin. (Book p44)
Newer drugs: natalizumab is anti-alpha-4 integrin. (Book p44)
A patient with moderate-severe ileocolonic Crohn's disease is in remission after oral steroids. The book's maintenance choice is:
Moderate-severe Crohn's disease maintenance: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine. (Book p44)
The risk of malignancy in inflammatory bowel disease is:
Present in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease
Risk of malignancy is present in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. (Book p45)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not listed as an increased malignancy risk in inflammatory bowel disease:
Increased risk: non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and cholangiocarcinoma. Gastric carcinoma is not listed. (Book p45)
Cholangiocarcinoma in inflammatory bowel disease is attributed to the association with:
Cholangiocarcinoma occurs due to the association with primary sclerosing cholangitis. (Book p45)

Match the sporadic colorectal carcinoma feature to the IBD related carcinoma feature — 1) Age of onset 2) Genetic sequence 3) Site of lesion … A) Adenoma to carcinoma sequence B) Any segment of diseased colon C) Ten to fifteen years younger

Sporadic carcinoma presents after 50 years; IBD related carcinoma presents ten to fifteen years younger, follows an inflammation-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence in sporadic terms, and arises in any segment of diseased colon. (Book p45)
The age of onset quoted for sporadic colorectal carcinoma is:
Sporadic colorectal carcinoma: age of onset above 50 years. (Book p45)
IBD related colorectal carcinoma presents how much earlier than sporadic carcinoma?
IBD related carcinoma: ten to fifteen years younger. (Book p45)
The five year survival rate quoted in the comparison table is:
90% for sporadic and 50% for IBD related
50% for sporadic and 90% for IBD related
Five year survival rate: 50% for both sporadic and IBD related carcinoma. (Book p45)
The pathological feature of IBD related carcinoma is:
IBD related carcinoma is a signet ring cell carcinoma; sporadic carcinoma is an adenocarcinoma. (Book p45)
Sporadic colorectal carcinoma is common on the left side. (Book p45)
Mutation timing in sporadic colorectal carcinoma is:
APC mutation early and p53 mutation late
p53 mutation early and APC mutation late
Sporadic colorectal carcinoma: APC mutation early, p53 mutation late. (Book p45)
Mutation timing in IBD related carcinoma is:
p53 mutation early and APC mutation late
APC mutation early and p53 mutation late
IBD related carcinoma: p53 mutation early, APC mutation late. (Book p45)
A patient with long-standing colitis develops a signet ring cell carcinoma in a segment of diseased colon at 38 years of age. Compared with sporadic carcinoma the book would describe this as:
Ten to fifteen years younger, arising in any segment of diseased colon
Due to APC mutation occurring early
IBD related carcinoma: ten to fifteen years younger, signet ring cell type, any segment of diseased colon, inflammation-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence with p53 early and APC late. (Book p45)
In the book's opening definition, acute diarrhoea lasting no more than two weeks is considered:
Protozoal until an organism is identified
Non-infectious unless a stool culture is positive
Inflammatory only when blood is visible
Acute diarrhoea (≤2 weeks) is considered infectious unless proved otherwise. (Book p46)
Which duration boundary is used in the opening definition of acute diarrhoea?
The introductory definition uses acute diarrhoea of ≤2 weeks. (Book p46)
The first classification diagram organizes infectious diarrhoea by:
The first diagram is headed 'Based on duration and severity'. (Book p46)
A brief episode is placed in the diagram's benign, short-lasting, self-limiting branch. Which class is written at its end?
The <1-week benign, short-lasting, self-limiting branch ends in viral diarrhoea. (Book p46)
In the same duration diagram, the <1-week episode marked 'complicated' leads to which broad cause?
The complicated <1-week branch is labelled bacterial. (Book p46)
The diagram associates diarrhoea lasting more than one week with which broad group?
The >1-week branch in the duration diagram is labelled protozoal. (Book p46)
The site-based classification distinguishes small bowel, large bowel, and:
Enterocolitis involving small and large bowel
The third site category is enterocolitis (small bowel + large bowel). (Book p46)
In the site classification, Yersinia is singled out for causing:
Yersinia is listed under enterocolitis and causes severe ileocolitis. (Book p46)
Right-lower-quadrant tenderness during Yersinia ileocolitis is emphasized because it can mimic:
The note states that severe Yersinia ileocolitis produces right-lower-quadrant tenderness and mimics appendicitis. (Book p46)
Which stool pattern best fits the small-bowel column on the clinical-features table?
Large-volume watery stool without blood, pus or mucus
Painless formed stool streaked with blood
Frequent stools with fecal leukocytes and mucus
Small-volume bloody stool with urgency and tenesmus
Small-bowel diarrhoea is described as large-volume and watery, without blood, pus, mucus, increased frequency, urgency or tenesmus. (Book p46)
A patient has small-volume bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fecal leukocytes. The table localizes this pattern to the:
Fever, small-volume bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fecal leukocytes are in the large-bowel column. (Book p46)
Match each stool pattern to its site — 1) Large-volume watery stool without blood, pus or mucus 2) Small-volume bloody stool with fecal leukocytes … A) Large bowel B) Small bowel
The table places large-volume watery non-bloody stool in small-bowel disease and small-volume bloody stool with fecal leukocytes in large-bowel disease. (Book p46)
Among adults, which virus is marked as the most common cause in the small-bowel column?
Norovirus is marked most common in adults. (Book p46)
The virus marked most common in children is:
Rotavirus is marked most common in children. (Book p46)
A post-transplant patient develops sore throat, diarrhoea and leucopenia. Which virus is named beside this presentation?
The page associates post-transplant CMV with sore throat, diarrhoea and leucopenia. (Book p46)
The table places cytomegalovirus more prominently in which site?
Small bowel rather than large bowel
Equal involvement of small and large bowel
Large bowel rather than small bowel
The printed comparison is cytomegalovirus (large bowel > small bowel). (Book p46)
TRUE or FALSE — the site table places fecal leukocytes with the large-bowel pattern, not the large-volume watery small-bowel pattern.
True — fecal leukocytes are in the large-bowel column
False — the table does not mention fecal leukocytes
False — fecal leukocytes are listed only for small bowel
True — but the small-bowel stool is also described as bloody
Fecal leukocytes are listed in the large-bowel column; small-bowel stool is large-volume and watery without blood, pus or mucus. (Book p46)
The small-bowel bacterial mechanism described as in-vivo toxin production raises which second messenger before secretory diarrhoea?
The table links in-vivo toxin production to increased cAMP and secretory diarrhoea. (Book p47)
Which organism is labelled the most common small-bowel in-vivo secretory-toxin cause?
ETEC is marked most common under small-bowel in-vivo toxin production. (Book p47)
Which second organism is listed alongside ETEC under small-bowel in-vivo toxin production?
The listed small-bowel in-vivo toxin producers are ETEC and Vibrio cholerae. (Book p47)
Which set is grouped as preformed-toxin food poisoning in the small-bowel bacteria column?
Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens
Shigella flexneri, Campylobacter and non-typhoid Salmonella
The preformed-toxin group contains Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens. (Book p47)
Which organism is listed as an invasive large-bowel bacterium and is linked to shigellosis?
Shigella flexneri is listed among invasive organisms in the large-bowel column and causes shigellosis. (Book p47)
Which complete group lists the invasive bacteria named in the large-bowel column?
Shigella flexneri, V. parahaemolyticus, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella and EIEC
ETEC, V. cholerae and Staphylococcus aureus
The complete large-bowel invasive list includes Shigella, V. parahaemolyticus, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella and EIEC. (Book p47)
Which Vibrio species appears in the large-bowel invasive-organism list rather than the small-bowel secretory list?
V. parahaemolyticus is listed among large-bowel invasive organisms; V. cholerae is in the small-bowel secretory group. (Book p47)
Which protozoal distribution matches the table?
Small bowel: Entamoeba; large bowel: Giardia and Cryptosporidium
Small bowel: Entamoeba and microsporidium; large bowel: Cryptosporidium
Small bowel: Cryptosporidium, microsporidium, Giardia; large bowel: Entamoeba histolytica
Small bowel: Giardia only; large bowel: all other protozoa
The table lists Cryptosporidium, microsporidium and Giardia in small bowel; Entamoeba histolytica in large bowel. (Book p47)
The note distinguishes Salmonella typhi from diarrhoeal small-bowel pathogens because small-bowel invasion is associated with:

Classification of Vasculitis and Large Vessel Vasculitis
Adult-Onset Still's Disease and Septic Arthritis
u:
Read the ECG in the book's fixed chronology: QRS → P wave → regularity (start on lead II / rhythm strip) → rate → axis → QT.
Calibrate first: 1 small box = 40 ms. The QRS is the maximum deflection because ventricular depolarisation is synchronous; narrow = 2–2.5 small boxes (100 ms / 0.1 s), wide > 0.12 s, very wide > 0.16 s.

Sinus node → atria → AV node → Bundle of His → bundle branches → fascicles → Purkinje fibres → ventricles; depolarisation runs endocardium → epicardium.
Septal, free-wall and posterobasal events sum as QRS = Vector (1+2+3). Current TOWARDS the +ve electrode = upward deflection; AWAY = downward.

Vector 1 (IV septum; LBB shorter than RBB) heads right-anterior-inferior — positive right, negative left, most predominant right lead.
Vector 2 (free wall) runs Rt→Lt, endo→epi: deep S in V1, big R in V5–V6. Vector 3 (posterobasal, last) is superior-posterior with no deflection. V4 = 5th ICS midclavicular, V5 = anterior axillary, V6 = mid axillary line. Alternate-pathway wide QRS > 0.16 s: idioventricular 15–40, accelerated 40–100, VT >100 bpm.

Wide QRS on a normal-but-blocked pathway = 0.12–0.16 s (RBBB / LBBB).
Rate = 1500 ÷ small boxes between two QRS complexes; sinus 60–100, atrial/junctional 40–60, ventricular 15–40 bpm. Regularity = QRS complexes at regular, fixed intervals.
P Wave, PR Segment & PR Interval

P wave = 1st wave, atrial depolarisation by the SA node; ascending limb = RA, descending limb = LA; 2.5/2.5 rule; smooth, rounded, upright in II (biphasic/inverted in V1); normal only with SA-nodal activation and a P before every QRS.
PR segment (atria → His) ends electrically inert, hence flat. PR interval = P + PR segment = 0.12–0.2 s (3–5 boxes); prolonged = block on the regular pathway; shortened = Bundle of Kent.
Approach to the QRS & the Limb Leads

Narrow QRS: normal PR & P → SAN; short PR → WPW; prolonged PR → 1° AV block; abnormal P → atrial rhythm; absent P → junctional rhythm.
Wide ≥ 0.16 s → ventricular arrhythmia; 0.12–0.16 s → BBB. Bipolar: I = RA–LA, II = RA–LL, III = LA–LL. Augmented: aVR ⊥ III, aVL ⊥ II, aVF ⊥ I. Angles: I 0°, II +60°, III +120°, aVF +90°, aVL −30°, aVR −150°.

Axis: count QRS heights in I, II, III, aVL, aVF — it lies between the two tallest; an equiphasic lead (R = S) puts the axis ⊥ to it.

2. Site of Lesion, Pathology and Radiculopathy

Pure motor effects arise from AHC, NMJ and muscle (myopathy); sensorimotor from root, plexus and nerve; pure sensory from ganglion.

4. Polyneuropathy Types, Sensory Columns and Fibre Types

Polyneuropathy types: sensorimotor (m/c, sensory >> motor) splits into large fibre (posterior column) and small fibre (spinothalamic + autonomic); pure sensory is ganglionopathy.
Pure motor causes are lead poisoning, dapsone and MMN-CB. Sensory columns map proprioception to A-alpha and position/fine touch/vibration/joint sense to A-beta.
Spinothalamic lateral pain is sharp-localised A-delta and dull-chronic C; temperature is C; ventral crude touch/pressure is A-beta; A-gamma is thick myelinated motor.

Large fibre causes: Friedreich ataxia, B12 deficiency (posterolateral cord syndrome with neuropathy), pyridoxine toxicity, taxanes. Small fibre (m/c, LADU): leprosy, amyloidosis, diabetes (m/c), uremic, vasculitis (SLE/RA/EGPA/GPA), HIV, Fabry and Tangier.
Positive symptoms: large fibre tingling/pin-and-needle/cotton wool; small fibre burning pain with stocking-glove evolution. Negative symptoms (>50% axons lost): large fibre numbness and sensory ataxia with Romberg +ve as surest sign; small fibre burns and non-healing ulcers from lost temperature sense.
Reflexes: large fibre loses DTR; small fibre DTR normal +/- ankle jerk. ANS features occur only in small fibre neuropathy.

Ganglionopathy is a pure sensory neuropathy/neuronopathy with large fibre and truncal involvement, arms >> legs and severe asymmetrical truncal ataxia; DTR is variable.
Causes: Sjogren's syndrome (DTR lost), anti-Hu paraneoplastic syndrome (DTR +), cisplatin, Vit B6 toxicity, HIV and thalidomide.

1. Radiculopathies: Axonal vs Demyelinating Features and Causes

Axonal neuropathy (prototype DM) is gradual and insidious except porphyria; demyelinating radiculoneuropathy (prototype GBS) is acute or subacute except CIDP.
Axonal disease hits large long axons early with stocking-glove distal signs, ankle jerk lost early, wasting, normal CSF proteins, slow recovery and residual deformity; demyelinating disease is diffuse with generalized weakness, areflexia, raised CSF proteins, rapid recovery and slowed conduction.
Demyelinating causes split into acute (AIDP <4 weeks, diphtheria, drugs amiodarone/chloroquine/gold), chronic (CIDP >8 weeks, POEMS, myeloma, HIV, CTS) and inherited (CMTD, Refsum's).
2. Notes, ANS Predominant Neuropathies and Patterns of LMN Lesions

Pure sensory neuropathy is ganglionopathy; pure motor neuropathies are lead, dapsone and MMNCB; severe pain ranks small fibre > large with Fabry's > Tangier's > HIV > vasculitis.
Relapsing neuropathies are CIDP, Refsum's and porphyria; diabetic amyotrophy is asymmetric lumbosacral plexopathy; ANS predominant neuropathies use mnemonic PAD.
The eight patterns of LMN lesions map symmetric and asymmetric, proximal and distal, sensory and motor combinations to AIDP, diabetes, radiculopathy, plexopathy, pure motor neuropathy, spinal cord, muscle/NMS and ganglion.

1. Types of Inherited Neuropathy and CMT-1 vs CMT-2

Demyelinating inherited neuropathies are CMTD and Refsum's; axonal are FAP (transthyretin: wild type senile systemic amyloidosis, mutant FAP), porphyria and Tangier's.
Acute neuropathies are predominantly demyelinating (AIDP, GBS) with acute intermittent porphyria the axonal exception.
CMT combines motor and sensory involvement (HMSN); HSAN is its autonomic variant. CMT-1 and CMT-2 are both autosomal dominant; CMT-1 is more common, demyelinating with onion bulbs, nerve thickening and early onset, CMT-2 axonal, mild and later.
2. CMT-4, Features of CMT-1 and Thickened Nerves

CMT-4 (Dejerine sottas) is AD/AR congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. CMT-1 has a long slow 10-30 year course with pes cavus as the m/c presentation, hammer toes, palpable hypertrophic nerves, positive family history and mild kyphosis in 1/10th.
Sensory symptoms are absent although large-fibre signs are positive; motor disease is distal > proximal, lower limb predominant, non-debilitating with slow conduction, normal amplitude, prolonged distal latency and temporal dispersion, ending in inverted champagne leg.
Reflexes show generalised hypo/areflexia with ankle jerk universally absent; thickened nerves occur in leprosy, CIDP and CMT.
3. Familial Amyloid Polyneuropathy and Porphyric Neuropathy

FAP is mutant transthyretin axonal sensory-motor polyneuropathy with ANS involvement, painful neuropathy and large + small fibre symptoms.
Porphyric neuropathy manifests as neurovisceral (AIP) or less common cutaneous (variegate, hereditary coproporphyria with blisters, hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, skin fragility).
It is autosomal dominant with predominant ANS plus PNS and CNS involvement, acute onset, females > males, 3rd-4th decade and menstruation as precipitant; GIT acute abdominal pain is the most frequent symptom and neuropathy is acute axonal, proximal predominant with rare sensory glove-and-stocking or bathing suite pattern.
4. Porphyric ANS and CNS Features, Tangier's and Refsum Disease

ANS features are the hallmark of porphyric neuropathy: orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, urinary incontinence, persistent tachycardia > bradycardia and labile hypertension leading to hypertensive encephalopathy (PRES).
CNS features include mild neuropsychiatric symptoms, seizures, motor > sensory neuropathy, facial and bulbar weakness progressing to GBS-like flaccid quadriparesis with respiratory involvement, and rapidly progressive wasting from anterior horn cell involvement; SIADH causes hyponatremia.
Tangier's is autosomal recessive with an ATP binding cascade protein defect, low HDL, orange tonsil, axonal asymmetric mononeuropathy. Refsum's is demyelinating from a phytanic oxidase (alpha-oxidation) defect with the triad retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy.
5. Romberg's Sign, Wash Basin Sign, Fabry's and Autonomic Neuropathies

Romberg's sign components are semicircular canal, vestibulo-cerebellar fibres, visual stimulus and proprioception; standing with mild flexed posture and hands close to body eliminates the first two and eye closure eliminates vision, isolating proprioception.
The wash basin sign shows improper posture plus no visual component with posterior column tract disorder giving no compensation and a fall.
Fabry's disease shows angiokeratoma with painful acroparesthesia (painful small fibre neuropathy), digital paresthesia, severe ANS symptoms, axonal pathology and renal manifestation; autonomic neuropathies are seen in diabetes, amyloidosis, porphyria, Fabry and vincristine.
1. Definition, Classification Subtypes and AIDP Pathophysiology

GBS is acute (<=4 weeks) bilaterally symmetrical inflammatory autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy; CIDP is its chronic (>8 weeks) counterpart.
Subtypes: AIDP (anti-GM1, demyelinating, best prognosis), AMAN (children and young adults, anti-GD1a, axonal), AMSAN (mostly adults, axonal) and MFS (rarest; ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; anti-GQ1b); AMAN, AMSAN and MFS share poor prognosis and all antibodies are IgGs.
AIDP is m/c with mean age 40 years and male > female; antibodies bind myelin, activate complement, invite macrophage invasion and cause vesicular degeneration.
2. Clinical Presentation, Examination, Progression and Prognosis

Presentation flows from sensory symptoms (B/L tingling and numbness of lower limbs, rubbery legs) through mild transient bowel and bladder dysfunction to motor symptoms (bilateral lower limb weakness).
Examination early shows normal higher mental function, cranial nerves and upper limb motor with bilateral atonic areflexic paraparesis (proximal + distal) of lower limbs and large fibre (A-alpha) sensory loss.
Progression is rapid: >=24 hours since incident, areflexic ascending paralysis from lower to upper limb, cranial nerve involvement in 30% (4-15% mortality), brainstem involvement, respiratory centre affection and ventilation. 80% recover (5-10% with persistent weakness); survival is 85-90% with early intervention; bad prognostic factors are ANS manifestations.

Inciting factors: gastroenteritis/URTI in the past 4 weeks in 60-70% of GBS cases; associated infections C. jejuni, CMV, EBV, mycoplasma, Hep A/B and HIV; vaccination association; molecular mimicry. C. jejuni also links to IPSID.
