Essential features are progressive weakness in both arms and legs (legs -> arms) and areflexia; strong support includes progression over days up to 4 weeks, relative symmetry, mild sensory signs, cranial nerve involvement (m/c VII > III, B/L LMN VII palsy with sarcoidosis as D/d), recovery beginning 2-4 weeks after progression ceases, autonomic dysfunction and absence of fever at onset.
Lumbar puncture shows albuminocytological dissociation in 90% (not detected <7 days and in GBS variants), pleocytosis of 10-30 cells in 5%, findings lasting only 1 month; NCS shows latency prolongation, conduction block, reduced velocity, absent or prolonged F-wave and H reflex and temporal dispersion. Exclusions: botulism, myasthenia gravis, diphtheria, abnormal porphyrin metabolism and pure sensory syndrome.
4. Treatment, MFS/Bickerstaff Encephalitis and CIDP vs AIDP

Treatment: IVIg 0.4 gm/kg x 5 days; PLEX (one filter : 5 cycles) preferred for ANS manifestations, each cycle removing 1.5 times plasma volume replaced with 50% NS and 50% FFP; no role for steroids.
MFS (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia, anti-GQ1b +) plus brain stem encephalitis and hyperreflexia defines Bickerstaff encephalitis; treatment is PLEX.
CIDP runs >8 weeks with subacute/chronic non-emergency presentation, 30% preceding infection, secondary causes (myeloma/POEMS/HIV/SLE/Hodgkins/DM/IBD), absent ANS symptoms, 10% cranial nerve involvement, no precise onset point, no ventilator need and nil mortality; treatment is steroid (DOC), PLEX for resistant cases and IVIg for pure motor CIDP, whereas AIDP uses IVIg/PLEX and not steroids.
5. CIDP Affected Systems, POEMS Syndrome and MMN-CB

CIDP shows prominent sensory involvement with large fibre symptoms and distal-to-proximal spread plus gradually progressive distal-to-proximal lower-limb-predominant motor symptoms, while AIDP is predominantly motor with minimal sensory involvement.
CIDP is associated with relapsing neuropathy and nerve thickening; large fibre sensory symptoms are tingling, numbness, dysesthesia, paraesthesia, cotton wool sensation and sensory ataxia; nerve thickening also occurs in leprosy and CMT.
POEMS shows increased VEGF, lambda light chain myeloma, polyneuropathy referring to CIDP and osteosclerotic lesions, with Castleman syndrome refractory to therapy. MMN-CB is a pure motor neuropathy with atrophy lasting years, asymmetric, upper limb predominant, demyelinating on NCS with anti-GM1 antibody (D/d GBS); other pure motor causes are lead poisoning and dapsone toxicity.
1. Pure Motor LMN Comparison, NMJ Disorders and Power Grades

LMN disorders split into sensory-motor (radiculopathy, plexopathy, neuropathy) and pure motor disorders of anterior horn cells (motor neuron disease), muscle and neuromuscular junction (myasthenia gravis).
AHC weakness shows wasting >>> weakness, asymmetry, distal > proximal upper limb painless distribution, absent reflexes and fasciculations; muscle weakness shows weakness > wasting in late stages, symmetry, proximal B/L limb painless-predominant distribution, late hyporeflexia and no fasciculations.
NMJ disorders give fluctuating weakness with diurnal variation, weakness on repetitive movements, ophthalmoplegia + ptosis and masseter involvement causing chewing difficulties. The power table grades 5 to 0.
2. Muscle Etiology A and the Inherited Myopathy Classes

Etiology A splits inherited (chronic) muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies, metabolic myopathies and channelopathies of Na+/K+/Cl- from acquired (subacute > acute) inflammatory muscle disease, drugs, toxins, infections and endocrine (hypothyroidism).
Muscular dystrophies lose structural proteins, are progressive and replace necrotic muscle with adipose tissue (Duchenne and Becker). Congenital myopathies lose contractile proteins with slow non-progressive weakness (central core, centronuclear, nemaline).
Metabolic/mitochondrial myopathies alter carbohydrate or lipid metabolism with exercise-induced symptoms.
3. Episodic vs Persistent Matrix, Symptoms and Weakness Tasks

Inherited episodic muscle disease comprises rhabdomyolysis in glycogen storage disease type V (McArdle's), channelopathies, metabolic myopathy and NMJ disorders; inherited persistent is dystrophies (chronic); acquired episodic is rhabdomyolysis and acquired persistent is inflammatory muscle disease (acute/subacute).
Negative symptoms are weakness, fatigue and exercise intolerance; positive symptoms are myalgia, cramps, contractures and myotonia. Myoglobinuria is a positive sign of rhabdomyolysis with high colored urine; muscle atrophy is a negative sign of late muscle disease.
Bilaterally symmetrical painless weakness is proximal (lower limbs: climbing stairs, rising from low chair/squatting; upper limbs: washing clothes, taking things off a rack above, putting hooks on a blouse) or distal (upper limbs: tear paper, screw something on, put a key in; lower limbs: wearing sandals).
4. Exception Patterns, Fatigue/Exercise Intolerance and Myalgia

Exceptions to symmetrical myopathy: asymmetrical muscle weakness in inclusion body myositis (elderly fall d/t asymmetrical quadriceps involvement) and FSHD; pure distal myopathies Welander, Miyoshi, Nonaka; proximal UL + distal LL in FSHD; proximal LL + distal UL in myotonic dystrophy and inclusion body myositis.
Ptosis with ophthalmoplegia plus dysarthria is oculo-pharyngeal muscle dystrophy and without dysarthria is CPEO; B/L symmetrical ptosis with facial muscle involvement occurs in FSHD and myotonic dystrophy.
Fatigue/exercise intolerance: mitochondrial myopathy gives abnormal fatigability without significant weakness on trivial exercise; rhabdomyolysis gives severe pain, cramps and high colored urine after unaccustomed activity. Myalgia is non-specific with orthopedic and rheumatological causes exceeding muscular; muscular causes with pain are mitochondrial myopathy, inflammatory muscle disease (30%) and rhabdomyolysis; polymyalgia rheumatica associates with giant cell arteritis, has late onset RA and myositis as D/d, early morning stiffness around shoulder, hip and pelvic girdle with raised ESR and responds to low dose steroids.
5. Fibromyalgia, Cramps vs Contractures and Myotonia vs Paramyotonia

Fibromyalgia affects females (F:m 9:1) with stress as risk factor, easy fatigability, muscle pain, positive trigger points and normal muscle enzymes and ESR; treatment is psychiatric therapy.
Cramps are short and electrically active on needle EMG (dehydration, hyponatremia, ALS, Duchenne muscular dystrophy) whereas contractures are long and electrically silent (Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, mitochondrial myopathy).
ALS adds cramps, atrophy, fasciculations and wasting; mitochondrial myopathies add contractures, pain, cramps and weakness associated with exercise. Myotonia is impaired relaxation after forceful voluntary contraction; it improves with exercise and worsens with cold (myotonic dystrophy, hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, Na+ channelopathy) while paramyotonia worsens with both (paramyotonia congenita, Na+ channelopathy).
1. Structural Myopathies, Dystrophin Defect, DMD Timeline and Becker

Dystrophin defect is structural protein involvement with necrosis of muscle replaced by adipose and fibrous tissue, X linked deletion and steroid treatment; the photograph is captioned lordosis.
Duchenne's muscular dystrophy is progressive muscle degeneration with a 0-18 year timeline: gross motor delay (walking late), frequent falls presenting to clinic, toe walking with Gower's sign, cramps unrelated to exercise and lordosis, supported walking, wheelchair bound, upper limb involvement and finally respiratory involvement with aspiration pneumonia as the m/c cause of death.
Additional involvement covers scoliosis leading to ILD, pseudohypertrophy (calf > other muscles), mental retardation, cardiomyopathies and nocturnal hypoventilation leading to pooling of secretions and aspiration. Becker's is milder: cardiac death (dilated cardiomyopathy), CK/EMG/biopsy similar to DMD, presentation 5-60 years, survival >40 years, contracture absent, less weakness and mental retardation absent.
2. Limb Girdle, Emery Dreifuss, Facioscapulohumeral, Oculopharyngeal and Myotonic Dystrophy

LGMD is autosomal dominant/recessive, the m/c adult onset muscle dystrophy, associated with cardiomyopathy, involves lamin and caveolin and shows the diamond on thigh sign (vastus medialis hypertrophy with atrophy of other muscles); photographs show winging of scapula in LGMD.
Emery Dreifuss is X-linked recessive/autosomal dominant with prominent contractures and cardiomyopathy. FSHD is autosomal dominant with muscle asymmetry, proximal upper limb plus distal lower limb involvement and B/L ptosis with facial muscle involvement.
Oculopharyngeal is autosomal dominant with ptosis, ophthalmoplegia and dysphagia. Myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disease of chromosome 19 with DM1 > DM2 and proximal lower limb plus distal upper limb involvement with myotonia; photograph shows hatchet facies.
3. Myotonic Dystrophy Presentation and Metabolic/Mitochondrial Myopathies

Hatchet facies combines ptosis, temporal hollowing (temporalis), elongated face and facial muscle involvement; investigation shows percussion myotonia with contraction on repeated percussion and failure to release.
Associated findings are cardiac conduction abnormalities, mental retardation, gonadal atrophy, insulin resistance, SNHL and posterior subcapsular cataract; photographs show percussion myotonia, B/L winging of scapula and humeral atrophy with winging.
Mitochondrial myopathies are maternally inherited with ragged red fibers on trichrome stain and exercise induced weakness/fatiguability/cramps. CPEO gives ptosis + ophthalmoplegia without dysarthria or diplopia and is a D/D for NMJ disorders (myasthenia gravis). Kearns Sayre syndrome is CPEO before 20 years with retinitis pigmentosa, complete heart block and cerebellar ataxia; MERRF and MELAS complete the list.

Channelopathies show an LMN pattern of acute onset, B/L symmetrical, episodic motor weakness with electrolyte imbalance as D/d.
Calcium channel diseases (mnemonic E2 S6 HOm) are episodic ataxia type 2, spinocerebellar ataxia type 6, hypokalemic periodic paralysis and familial hemiplegic migraine; sodium gives hyperkalemic and normokalemic periodic paralysis and paramyotonia congenita; chloride gives myotonia congenita; potassium gives Anderson-Tawil syndrome, episodic ataxia type 1 and benign neonatal familial convulsions on day 5 of birth.
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is autosomal dominant, adolescent, m > F, precipitated by a high carbohydrate meal, with pure proximal limb weakness, propensity for arrhythmias and hypokalemia during episodes; treatment is oral potassium and acetazolamide. Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis and Anderson-Tawil syndrome share AD inheritance, childhood (1st decade) onset and episodic weakness; hyperkalemic PP has myotonia (+), K+ may be normal, worsening by cold and precipitation by rest, whereas Anderson-Tawil has no myotonia, variable K+ and dysmorphic facies with arrhythmias.

Myasthenia gravis is an NMJ disorder: autoantibody (B-cell) plus T-cell attack on postsynaptic AChR.
The NMJ figure labels ChAT, V/Q Ca++ channel, AChE, agrin, the active zone and voltage-gated Na+/K+/Ca+ channels; ACh vesicle release binds AChR, Na influx and muscle contraction.
Ocular symptoms are m/c; 15-20% stay ocular (good prognosis) while progressors (maximum first 2-3 years) go pharyngeal then proximal then respiratory; the most crucial period is the first 1 year after ocular symptoms.
2. Demographics, Antibodies, Thymus and Classical MG

Bimodal peaking: first peak 20-40 yr with females >>> males; second peak >60 years with males > females.
AChR antibody is specific (85% generalised, 50% ocular); MuSK 10-20% of generalised and 40-50% of AChR-negative MG; LRP4 sits in the double-negative population.
MuSK MG is absent in ocular disease, female-predominant, neck-drop with tongue fasciculations, no thymus involvement and pyridostigmine-refractory. In 80% of seropositive cases 70% have thymic hyperplasia and 10% thymoma; thymectomy in adult-onset generalised MG has very good prognosis. Clinical MG is a pure motor syndrome with diurnal variation, fatiguability and fluctuating UL proximal weakness on repetitive movement. Early-onset classical MG is 65% of cases, females >>> males, 20-40 years, antibodies (++++), HLA-DR3, B8, DR9 and thymic hyperplasia; FSHD has symmetrical ptosis and CPEO (mitochondrial) has ptosis + ophthalmoplegia.

Ocular symptoms are m/c: asymmetrical ptosis + diplopia + ophthalmoplegia, binocular diplopia, pupils spared, medial rectus maximal. Limb weakness is 10%; bulbopharyngeal involvement includes fatigue while chewing (masseter — specific for MG), dysarthria and dysphagia, plus expressionless facies and drooped posture.
Examination: peek sign, curtain sign, Cogan's lid twitch, sustained upgaze producing ptosis, unable to count digits 1-10 quickly.
Ice pack (cold improves conduction), edrophonium 2 mg IV and neostigmine 1 mg IM all improve symptoms. AChR antibody is most specific; single-fibre EMG (increased jitter) is most sensitive. NCS: MG has normal baseline CMAP, 3 Hz decremental and high-frequency incremental responses; LEMS has reduced CMAP, variable 3 Hz and >100% high-frequency increment.
4. LEMS, Drugs, Treatment and Cholinergic Crisis

LEMS: antibodies against V/Q Ca2+ channel on the pre-synaptic membrane; paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer; proximal lower limbs (+), ANS (+++), ocular mild; improves with 3,4 di-aminopyramidine. Notes: Anti-Hu is ganglionopathy; Anti-MA2 and anti-CRPM5 are viral encephalitis.
Drugs that exacerbate MG: aminoglycosides, quinolones, macrolides, magnesium (antacids), d-penicillamine, azathioprine, propranolol.
First attack: pyridostigmine 30-60 mg every 6th hourly. From second attack: initial pyridostigmine, maintenance steroids ± azathioprine. IVIg + plasma exchange for myasthenic crisis, life-threatening MG, severe bulbar dysfunction, refractory MG and planned surgery. Cholinergic crisis is overdose of cholinesterase inhibitors with DUMBELLS.
1. MND Classification and Features of ALS

MND is anterior horn cell disease of α/γ motor neurons at the ventral horn. Classification: pure UMN = primary lateral sclerosis; UMN+LMN = ALS (90% sporadic, 10% genetic copper-zinc superoxide dismutase defect); pure LMN = SMA, X-linked Kennedy disease and multifocal motor neuropathy with paraproteinemia.
ALS: age >50, M>F, survival maximum 3 years. LMN degeneration of AHC and medullary nuclei 9-12; UMN degeneration of CST and the printed corticospinal tract (CBT). Cognition, HMF, ANS and sensory system are spared. AHC is the 1st structure to degenerate; CST gives brisk reflexes and loss of dexterity/tone. Presentation is distal asymmetric UL (classically forearm/hand) atrophy with fasciculations and cramps.
2. Bulbar versus Pseudobulbar Palsy, Diagnosis and Treatment

Bulbar palsy (40% pts) is LMN of cranial nerves 9-12: nasal twang regurgitation, flaccid fasciculating tongue, bulbar dysarthria progressing to dysphagia, absent gag. Pseudobulbar palsy (25%) is UMN fibres to 9-12: dysphonic (laryngeal > nasal) with aspiration risk, brisk jaw jerk and emotional incontinence, small spastic tongue, pseudobulbar dysarthria, exaggerated gag.
Photographs: ALS patient with distal UL & LL atrophy; tongue atrophy in ALS; thenar atrophy; thenar > hypothenar atrophy. Needle EMG: polyphasic fasciculations and fibrillations. MRI: B/L symmetrical high intensities. Treatment: no effective drugs; riluzole and edaravone maybe tried.
3. ALS Variants — Kennedy, Hirayama and Madras MND

X-linked SMA (Kennedy's disease) is pure LMN trinucleotide-repeat disease with androgen insensitivity and spinobulbar involvement: tremor + fasciculations, proximal wasting = pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles, tongue wasting + perioral fasciculation.
Benign monomelic amyotrophy (Hirayama's disease): young male (<20 yrs), asymmetrical UL weakness + wasting, non-progressive; MRI impingement of dura from tight dural canal tearing in flexion/growth discrepancy, with atrophy/thinning of C8-T1.
Madras MND: bilfacial weakness + ocular involvement + SNHL + asymmetrical atrophy of limbs; a variant of MND. MRI of BMA and clinical photos A-D are labelled Finding of Madras MND.
1. Spinal Cord, Vertebrae and Segment Levels

Cord function is printed as motor output to and sensory output from trunk and limbs; length 45 cm; continuation of medulla from the upper border of atlas (C1) to adult L1-L2 or childhood L3-L4. Pia reaches the tip of coccyx; dura and arachnoid end at S2.
Neural tube forms in the 4th embryonic week; caudal tubular part becomes spinal cord. Spinal canal 70 cm; 33 vertebrae (C7, T12, L5, S5, C4); 31 segments (C8, T12, L5, S5, C1); roots are dorsal + ventral. Vertebra-to-segment offsets run same / +1 / +2 / +3 then T10 = L1,L2, T11 = L3,L4, T12 = epiconus, L1 = conus. The figure labels conus medullaris, internal and external terminal filum, cauda equina, dural sac termination and coccygeal nerve.
2. Conus Medullaris, Cauda Equina and Root Values

Conus medullaris is the terminal portion of spinal cord. Cervical enlargement is C3-T2. Lumbar enlargement roots L2,L3; epiconus L4,L5,S1,S2; conus S3,S4,S5,C0. Filum terminale is pia to the tip of coccyx, length 20 cm.
Conus medullaris syndrome is B/L symmetric, roots S3-S5 & C1, motor weakness absent, B/L saddle anaesthesia, dribbling/incontinence (micturition centre S3,S4), absent bulbocavernosus and anal reflexes (patulous anal canal), tumour, insidious/acute (malignancy). Cauda equina is asymmetric radiculopathy of L2-L5, S1-S5, C1, motor weakness present, variable sensory loss, urinary symptoms only in extensive disease, absent and variable reflexes, disc abnormality, insidious.
Root actions: L1>L2 hip flexion; L2>L3 hip adduction; L4>L3 knee extension plus TA dorsiflexion/inversion and knee jerk; L5 EHL, eversion, hip abduction; S1 hip extension, knee flexion, plantar flexion, ankle jerk.
3. Cross-Section, Myelopathy Types and Grey Matter

Cross-section labels posterior column (cuneatus/gracilis), dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts, lateral spinothalamic (pain, temperature), ventral spinothalamic (pressure, touch, minor role), ventral uncrossed corticospinal (distal limb, minor role), anterior horn, lateral corticospinal (pyramidal) with rubrospinal for distal limb movements, and vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal and tectospinal for axial and proximal limb movements.
Myelopathies are sensory/autonomic/motor symptoms d/t spinal cord disease. Compressive splits into intramedullary tumour (ependymoma, syringomyelia cavity expansion) and extramedullary disc compression; non-compressive is transverse myelitis. Above the lesion is normal (complete sparing); at the lesion based on anterior horn cells; below is motor (UMN) and sensory loss. Grey ventral column is AHC (α and γ). At the level: motor LMN, absent reflexes (maximum localizing value), sensory symptoms; L4 example = absent knee jerk plus knee-extension weakness, quadriceps atrophy and fasciculation.
4. Dorsal Column and Lateral Spinothalamic Pathology

White matter is tracts/funiculi (funicular pain). Dorsal column is ascending: first-order DRG, fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus, decussation in medulla (internal arcuate fibers) via medial leminiscus to VPL thalamus, third-order to postcentral gyrus (3,1,2). Sensations: proprioception, fine touch, vibration, position and joint sense.
Brown-Sequard: I/L loss of posterior column sensations. Posterior compression (glove and stocking / cervical compression myelopathy) starts cervical (UL) and progresses to sacral (LL). Diabetic neuropathy is stocking and glove.
Lateral spinothalamic: pain and temperature; decussates in the cord 1 to 2 segments above; hemisection gives C/L sensory loss. Intradural/extramedullary lesion list: dissociative sensory loss, sacral sparing (cervical > sacral), suspended sensory loss, prominent early LMN features.
5. Remaining Ascending Tracts, Corticospinal and Rubrospinal

Remaining ascending tracks: 2 spinocerebellar, 3 spinotectal, 4 spinoreticular, 5 spino-olivary. Lateral CST: pre-central gyrus → cerebral peduncle/midbrain → pyramidal decussation in medulla → lateral CST (and anterior CST) to LMN and skeletal muscle. Extramedullary lesion: early involvement; hemisection: I/L motor weakness.
Rubrospinal tract is the only extra pyramidal pathway in the lateral column; action flexion of upper limb. Decorticate (lesion above red nucleus, tract spared, UL flexed, LL extended) vs decerebrate (below red nucleus, tract affected, UL and LL extended).
6. Ventral Tracts, Brown-Sequard and Blood Supply

Ventral/anterior ascending: ventral/anterior spinothalamic tract = pressure, crude touch (minor role). Ventral (uncrossed) CST = distal limb movements (minor role). Descending extrapyramidal: vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal, tectospinal; action extension.
Early descending-tract pathology: paraplegia in extension (CST); late: paraplegia in flexion (extrapyramidal). Brown Sequard: ipsilateral posterior-column loss and motor weakness; contralateral lateral spinothalamic (pain and temperature) loss.
Blood-supply figure labels gracilis, cuneatus, CST, rubrospinal, anterior lateral system, vestibulospinal, ventral spinal artery, dorsal spinal and radicular arteries, plus vertebral, basilar, anterior spinal, PICA, superior cerebellar, posterior spinal, ascending cervical, intercostal and lumbar feeders.
7. Arterial Supply, Infarction and Denticulate Ligament

Origin is the vertebral artery. Two posterior spinal arteries supply posterior 1/3; one anterior spinal artery supplies anterior 2/3. Radicular (feeder) arteries reinforce from the lower cervical segment down. Artery of Adamkiewicz / arteria radicularis magna (largest) originates near T8-T12 and supplies the entire lower half. T4-T5 has fewer radicular arteries and higher ischaemic risk. Arteria vasocorona is the circumferential anastomosis; CST in the watershed → myelopathy.
ASA thrombosis: acute, generalized atherosclerosis, posterior-column sparing. PSA injury: traumatic accidents. Ligamentum denticulatum: pia attaching cord to dura; in compressive myelopathy it compresses the corticospinal tract.
1. Myelopathy Definition and the Compressive Compartments

Myelopathy is printed as sensory, motor or ANS symptoms d/t disease of spinal cord, divided into compressive and non-compressive; compressive myelopathy runs a chronic course.
The type table splits compressive myelopathy into intramedullary versus extramedullary, and extramedullary into intradural versus extradural, with extradural marked m/c.
Intramedullary = tumours (ependymoma, oligodendroglioma, medulloblastoma) plus expansion of cavity (syringomyelia); intradural = neurofibroma, meningioma, arachnoid cyst, pachymeningitis; extradural = vertebral lesions (fracture, TB/syphilis, pyogenic abscess, prostate & ovary metastasis), IVDP (m/c) and aneurysm of aorta.
2. Clinical Features, Claudication Table and Examination

Chronic back pain is moderate to severe, worse on erect posture (canal diameter ↓ in standing) and relieved on bending or cycling; with band-like hyperesthesia at the involved level (umbilicus if T10), these are printed as definitive symptoms of compression.
The note table separates neurogenic claudication (variable distance, relieved by sitting/bending, painless uphill, bicycle test negative, pulses present, back pain common, numbness proximal→distal) from vascular claudication (fixed distance, relieved by standing, painful uphill, bicycle test positive, pulses absent, cramping distal→proximal).
Examination shows normal HMF and cranial nerves, intact upper-limb power and sensation with compression below T1, reduced lower-limb power with B/L UMN features, spinothalamic plus posterior-column loss, exaggerated knee and ankle jerks, extensor plantars, and bowel-bladder involvement in intramedullary compression.
3. Level Localization and the Beevor Procedure

LMN findings, wasting, band-like sensation, hyperesthesia, hypesthesia and hypoalgesia localise at the level of lesion, while UMN findings with lost superficial and exaggerated deep reflexes sit below it; upper limbs normal means the lesion is below T1, with everything above spared.
Sensory symptoms plus weakness in both legs place the lesion above L1; a positive Beevor's sign indicates a lesion below T9; once the spinal segment is found, the compression is localized to the corresponding vertebral segment, and the reflex level carries the best localizing value.
Beevor's sign: ask the patient to rise from supine; normally upper (T7-T9) and lower (T9-T12) abdomen contract together with no umbilical deviation, whereas lower-abdominal weakness lets the upper muscles pull the umbilicus upward, which is a positive sign.

Intramedullary damage runs centrifugal from centre to periphery; extramedullary damage runs centripetal from periphery to centre, so pain is funicular inside the cord and root pain outside it.
The table marks dissociative sensory loss, suspended sensory loss, sacral sparing and trophic changes as intramedullary positives; pyramidal signs are late intramedullary but early extramedullary, LMN signs and bowel-bladder involvement early intramedullary but late extramedullary, while spinal deformity, spinal tenderness and raised CSF protein favour the extramedullary side.
5. Tract Layout, Root Pain versus Lhermitte Sign and the Intramedullary Logic

The mid-thoracic cross-section labels fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis (CTLS from lateral to medial), dorsal and ventral roots, dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts, lateral spinothalamic (pain, temperature) and ventral spinothalamic (pressure, touch), ventral uncrossed corticospinal (distal limb, minor role), anterior horn motor neurons, and the lateral corticospinal plus rubrospinal tracts for distal limb movements with reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts for axial and proximal limb movements.
Root or girdle pain is brief, shock-like, initially unilateral then bilateral, provoked by coughing or Valsalva, caused by posterolateral compression and useful for localization; Lhermitte sign is shooting pain down the cord to the sacrum on neck flexion from posterior extramedullary compression but is not useful for localization.
Funicular pain is constant and dull from within; suspended sensory loss reflects loss of crossing spinothalamic fibres at the level with normal sensation above and below; CTLS lamination explains sacral sparing, central bladder fibres explain early sphincter involvement, peripheral corticospinal tracts explain late UMN signs, raised CSF protein reflects root involvement, and cervical intramedullary extension can interrupt sympathetics to give Horner's syndrome.
6. Conus versus Cauda Equina, Epiconus and the VITAMIN Causes

Conus medullaris involvement is printed as B/L S3-C1 inside the spinal cord with sudden onset, uncommon root pain, saddle sensory loss, dissociated sensory loss, no weakness, normal knee and ankle jerks with lost anal and bulbocavernous reflexes, and early bladder, bowel and sexual involvement; cauda equina is asymmetrical L2-C1 roots with insidious onset, unilateral root pain in leg, thigh and bladder, saddle or any-leg sensory loss, weakness and wasting of leg muscles, lost knee and ankle jerks, and later sphincter involvement.
Epiconus involves L4, L5, S1 and S2 with hip flexion and adduction spared, thigh sensation spared, both knee and ankle jerks lost and an UMN-type bladder.
Non-compressive myelopathy causes run on the VITAMIN mnemonic: vascular (ASA thrombosis) and demyelinating (MS, NMO), inherited Friedreich's ataxia, arsenic toxin, sarcoid autoimmunity, metabolic subacute combined degeneration, infection and neoplasia.
7. Dermatomes, Causes and Clinical Features of ATM

Infection and neoplasia close the VITAMIN list: acute transverse myelitis as a post-infectious complication and syphilis or TB among the infections.
Acute transverse myelitis is printed as rapid-onset full-thickness or segmented monophasic inflammation of the spinal cord, a demyelinating disease that can affect a variable number of segments; the dermatome table runs from C5 (clavicles) and C6 (thumb) through C8 (ring and little fingers), T4 (nipples), T10 (umbilicus), T12 (groin), L1-L4 anterior and inner leg, L4 great toe, L4-L5-S1 foot, S1 outer foot and little toe and S2-S4 perineum.
Causes are post-infectious (m/c), vaccination, MS, sarcoidosis, paraneoplastic, neuromyelitis optica and Behcet's disease, the last four bracketed as longitudinally extending transverse myelitis; features are ascending paresthesia from the feet, back pain evolving into spastic weakness, peak within 4 hours to 21 days, a plateau of about a week, a definite sensory level with band-like constriction, complete loss below it, half-cord patterns, symmetrical or asymmetrical paraparesis, prominent sphincter involvement with urinary retention and brisk reflexes below the level.
8. Differentiating ATM from GBS, Investigations, Treatment and Combined Degeneration

GBS is separated from ATM by progressive lower-limb weakness that is proximal greater than distal, ascending paralysis, areflexia, a normal sensory examination, absence of a band-like definite sensory level and absence of bladder symptoms.
Work-up is MRI T2 of the spine showing hyperintensities at the level, with CSF pleocytosis above 10 cells and a raised IgG index; treatment is high-dose methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg IV in 100 ml NS over 1 hour, escalating to plasma exchange when there is no response, the exchange indications being inability to walk, markedly impaired autonomic function, sensory loss in the lower extremities and no or little improvement after 5-7 days of IV steroids.
Subacute combined degeneration is printed as posterolateral cord syndrome from B12 deficiency, progressing from posterior-column first symptom of distal tingling and first sign of lost vibration, to lateral-tract spinothalamic and corticospinal involvement with extensor plantars, then large-fibre neuropathy with lost reflexes and glove-and-stocking changes, and, if untreated, dementia and optic atrophy.

Friedreich's ataxia is printed as the commonest spinocerebellar degeneration with a normal cerebellum, FRATAXIN gene defect on chromosome 9 with GAA repetition, autosomal-recessive early onset between 8 and 20 years and a later-onset autosomal-dominant form, cerebrum and cranial nerves spared, males greater than females, and sagittal MRI showing a normal cerebellum while ataxia-telangiectasia shows an atrophic one.
Involvement runs dorsally from root ganglion to spinocerebellar tract, cord and finally nerve: severe sensory ataxia, cerebellar ataxia with horizontal nystagmus and dysarthria, extensor plantars from posterior and lateral columns, then reflexes lost from demyelinating neuropathy, with scoliosis, myocardial fibrosis in 90%, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, optic atrophy, deafness, pes cavus and hammer toe.
Tabes dorsalis, a neurosyphilis manifestation, gives DRG sensory ataxia with bowel and bladder involvement plus root pain, lost reflexes and absent plantar responses.
1. Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Disorders of the CNS

The chapter opens by listing the chronic inflammatory demyelinating disorders of the CNS: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, anti-MOG antibody disease, sarcoidosis and chronic graft-vs-host disease, with a note that non-inflammatory demyelination means osmotic demyelination from rapid sodium correction.
MS is defined as chronic inflammatory demyelination of the subcortical area, brainstem, spinal cord and cortical area while sparing the peripheral nerve system and organ systems.
Features are autoimmune disease, females greater than males, significant family history and HLA DR2/15; risk factors are EBV, smoking, vitamin D deficiency and high socio-economic status.
2. Pathogenesis, Target Antigens, Imaging Correlates and the BBB Figure

Pathogenesis is inflammation, demyelination, gliosis and secondary neuronal injury; astrocytes disrupt the blood-brain barrier and raised VEGF causes exudation from capillaries, giving hyperintense lesions on T2 and contrast enhancement on T1.
T cells and B cells act on the target antigens myelin basic protein and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, producing demyelination with loss of saltatory conduction and cumulative axonal destruction that branches into cortical atrophy and progressive neuronal damage.
The blood-brain-barrier figure labels tight junction, pericyte, astrocyte, endothelial cell, microglia, basement membrane, peg-socket junction, leukocyte and neuron.
3. Disease Patterns, Sensory and Motor Features and Optic Neuritis

Disability curves divide MS into relapsing-remitting in 90%, secondary progressive in 5-6% following the relapsing-remitting form, and primary progressive, for which the printed Rx is anti-CD20 with ocrelizumab.
Major features are long-tract sensory manifestations, the m/c complaint, with tingling, numbness, paraesthesia, hypaesthesia, unpleasant sensations and allodynia; UMN motor weakness with loss of strength and speed, loss of tone, loss of dexterity, spasticity and exercise-induced fatigue; and optic neuritis that is unilateral, asymmetric if bilateral, with retrobulbar pain, anterior-pathway involvement, drug responsiveness and diplopia.
4. Minor Features, Other Presentations and the McDonald Criteria

Minor features are ataxia, vertigo, bladder involvement, Lhermitte sign, dementia and myokymia, while other presentations include bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia, bilateral trigeminal neuralgia, pseudobulbar involvement and acquired pendular nystagmus.
McDonald criteria need dissemination in time plus dissemination in space: dissemination in time is satisfied clinically or radiologically by two lesions four weeks apart, a new T2 hyperintense lesion, or a T1 lesion enhancing with contrast; dissemination in space requires two lesions at different sites among juxtacortical, periventricular, spinal cord and infratentorial (cerebellar and middle cerebellar peduncle).
5. Ancillary Symptoms, MRI Patterns, CSF and VER

Ancillary symptoms are Uhthoff's phenomenon with unilateral blurring of vision during a hot shower, Lhermitte's symptom from neck flexion which is also seen in compressive myelopathy, and the Pulfrich phenomenon in which a two-dimensional image is perceived as three-dimensional.
T2 hyperintensities are common in periventricular white matter and typical in the corpus callosum as Dawson's fingers, illustrated by the MRI panels showing hyper-intense lesions and a periventricular lesion; CSF shows oligoclonal bands with IgG increased in 90%, and the visually evoked response has a sensitivity of 80-85%.
6. Acute Attack Therapy and Disease-Modifying Options

Acute attacks and relapse-remission episodes are treated with IV steroids, and the prevention list is grouped by route.
Infusables are natalizumab (anti-α4 integrin, side effect progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy), ocrelizumab for the primary-progressive type and alemtuzumab (anti-CD52); injectables are glatiramer acetate and IFN β.
Orals are fingolimod as a sphingosine receptor modulator, teriflunomide as a dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibitor and dimethyl fumarate.
7. NMO (Devic's Disease) and Its Distinction from MS

Neuromyelitis optica, also called Devic's disease, is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of females more than males, around 40 years of age, associated with autoimmune disease such as SLE in 40% of cases, and driven by antibody against aquaporin 4.
Clinically optic neuritis is present and myelitis is variable, with hearing loss also listed: optic neuritis is bilateral and symmetrical with chiasmal involvement, poor response to treatment and severe visual loss, while myelitis shows long-segment involvement with longitudinal extension of transverse myelitis, poor prognosis and a monophasic course; recurrent intractable hiccup is attributed to area postrema involvement.
Investigations show oligoclonal bands in only 30% and a normal MRI brain, and treatment is steroids with plasma exchange.
8. Anti-MOG Antibody Disease and Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis

Anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein disease is printed as covering optic neuritis, myelitis, aquaporin-4-negative NMO spectrum disorders and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
ADEM is a disease of children under 12 years with males more than females, usually post-infectious after measles more often than chicken pox with an incubation of 4-21 days, or post-vaccination, and pathologically driven by molecular mimicry of myelin basic protein and myelin oligodendrocyte protein.
Clinically it combines acute inflammatory demyelination of white matter predominantly with grey matter, basal ganglia and thalamus in a monophasic course with large foci of hyperintensity and fluffy lesions, together with encephalitis producing seizure, raised intracranial tension, loss of consciousness, bilateral hypertonia with hyper-extensive response, meningismus and a wide motor and sensory repertoire.
9. ADEM Imaging and the Printed ADEM versus MS Comparison

Investigation of ADEM is MRI showing large foci of hyperintense lesions, illustrated by sagittal brain and cervical cord and axial FLAIR images captioned hyper-intensity in MRI.
The comparison table separates ADEM (under 12 years, males more than females in children, triggers and constitutional symptoms present, bilateral optic neuritis, complete myelopathy rare, encephalopathy common, monophasic, large usually symmetrical lesions, centripetal location, mass effect and grey matter involvement) from MS (over 12 years, females more than males at 3:1, no triggers or constitutional symptoms, unilateral optic neuritis, complete myelopathy common, encephalopathy less common, relapsing-remitting, variable-size asymmetric lesions, periventricular location and none of the other features).
1. Blood Supply of the Brain and the Circle of Willis

The anterior circulation figure traces the brachiocephalic trunk to the right common carotid and the right internal carotid artery, with the basilar, vertebral, subclavian and posterior communicating arteries and the C1-C6 levels all labelled, and gives the terminal branches of the internal carotid artery under the mnemonic OPAAm.
Those branches are the ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, anterior choroidal artery, anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery.
The circle-of-Willis diagram then names the A1 and A2 segments of the ACA around the anterior communicating artery, the MCA, anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries at the ICA, and the P1 and P2 segments of the posterior cerebral artery on the basilar artery with its superior cerebellar, pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar and posterior inferior cerebellar branches, the vertebral arteries and the anterior spinal artery.
2. Blood Supply of the Surface of the Brain

The three colour-coded brain diagrams shade the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral artery territories over the superolateral, medial and inferior surfaces.
In the ACA-MCA-PCA table the ACA supplies most of the medial surface with the paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus and a narrow strip of cortex along the superomedial border; the MCA supplies most of the superolateral surface including most of the primary motor and sensory areas, the frontal eye field, Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere and the temporal pole; the PCA supplies most of the inferior surface except the temporal pole.
3. ACA, MCA and PCA Injury Features

ACA injury gives weakness that is LL greater than UL, urinary incontinence from paracentral lobule involvement, and the cingulate gyrus picture of apathy as the mild form, abulia, amotivation and akinetic mutism as the severe form.
MCA injury gives UL greater than LL weakness, temporal-pole involvement with macular involvement, and a cortical aphasia pairing Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus with Wernicke's area in the superior temporal gyrus, in contrast to internal capsule lesions where there is no aphasia.
PCA injury produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing from visual-area damage.
4. Parts of the Internal Capsule and Their Fibre Content

The internal capsule is drawn between the caudate head, lentiform nucleus and thalamus, with the genu carrying the corticobulbar tract, the anterior limb the anterior thalamic radiation and frontopontine and other corticofugal fibres, and the posterior limb the corticospinal tract with superior thalamic, auditory and optic radiations around the medial and lateral geniculate nuclei; the corona radiata, caudate, putamen, globus pallidus and thalamus are labelled on the coronal section.
The parts list assigns frontopontine fibres with lacunar strokes and cerebellar involvement to the anterior limb, corticospinal fibres for head and neck with predominant corticobulbar fibres to the genu, the corticospinal tract in the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb with UL equal to LL weakness and corticorubral fibres, the posterior thalamic optic radiation to the retrolentiform part and the inferior thalamic auditory radiation to the sublentiform part.
5. Corticobulbar Injury Patterns, Capsular Notes and the HHH Triad

Unilateral corticobulbar injury produces no cranial nerve palsy because of bilateral cortical innervation, except a contralateral upper-motor-neuron seventh palsy due to its contralateral supply, while bilateral corticobulbar injury gives pseudobulbar palsy as seen in ALS or motor neuron disease; a dense capsular lesion causes contralateral facial palsy with hemiplegia.
An internal capsule lesion is printed as the HHH triad of hemiplegia that is dense with UL equal to LL and a contralateral UMN seventh palsy, hemisensory loss, and homonymous hemianopia, and the closing note separates MCA involvement with UL greater than LL, ACA involvement with LL greater than UL, and posterior-limb weakness with UL equal to LL.
6. Arterial Supply of the Internal Capsule

The upper diagram lists four supply lines: striate branches of the middle cerebral artery, the recurrent branch of the anterior cerebral artery, branches from the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries, and the anterior choroidal artery, with the annotation that retrolentiform injury gives a mild HHH triad in which hemisensory loss predominates.
The boxed anterior limb is supplied by anterior cerebral striate branches, including the longest branch, the recurrent artery of Heubner, together with middle cerebral branches; the genu receives anterior and middle cerebral striate branches plus direct internal carotid branches.
The posterior limb is supplied by middle cerebral striate branches including the large Charcot artery of cerebral haemorrhage and by the anterior choroidal artery, while the sublentiform part takes posterior cerebral and anterior choroidal branches and the retrolentiform part takes posterior cerebral branches only.
7. MCA Segments, Sylvian Divisions and Lenticulostriate Occlusion

The MCA figure labels the horizontal M1, sylvian M2 and cortical M3 segments with the medial and lateral lenticulo-striate arteries against the putamen, globus pallidus, internal capsule and caudate head.
The M2 annotation supplies the sylvian fissure and splits into a superior division whose stroke causes contralateral hemiplegia with Broca's aphasia and an inferior division whose stroke causes Wernicke's aphasia without weakness, while both divisions together give contralateral hemiplegia with global aphasia.
The M1 segment supplies the internal capsule, caudate nucleus, putamen and globus pallidus through lenticulostriate arteries and 30-300 micrometre perforators; occlusion gives internal capsule stroke with the HHH triad plus a UMN seventh palsy and parkinsonian features when bilateral, and lipohyalinosis of the perforators gives lacunar stroke with pure motor hemiparesis.
8. Complete MCA Syndrome versus Capsular Lesions, and the ACA Segments

Complete MCA syndrome follows involvement of the M1, M2 and M3 segments, giving aphasia with a seventh nerve palsy only if corticobulbar involvement is bilateral, plus the HHH triad; the comparison table keeps the HHH triad as the common feature but separates the cortical syndrome by aphasia, agnosia, apraxia, loss of consciousness and seizures, with non-dominant unstructured dressing apraxia and hemispatial neglect, against the dense hemiplegia with UL equal to LL of a capsular lesion.
The ACA splits at the anterior communicating artery: the A1 segment proximal to it supplies the anterior hypothalamus, caudate lobe and anterior limb of the internal capsule and, because of significant collaterals, its occlusion produces no clinical symptoms, while the A2 segment distal to it supplies the medial cerebral surface with contralateral hemiplegia worse in the leg, the paracentral lobule with urinary incontinence and the cingulate gyrus with apathy and abulia.
9. PCA Segments, Unilateral and Bilateral Involvement

The PCA is divided at the posterior communicating artery into a P1 segment supplying the midbrain, subthalamus and thalamus, and a P2 segment whose unilateral involvement produces the medial-temporal picture of visual agnosia, peduncular hallucinosis, alexia without agraphia from splenium involvement and memory disturbance from the hippocampus, and occipital involvement giving congruent contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
Bilateral P2 involvement produces Anton syndrome of cortical blindness with pupillary sparing and Balint syndrome of optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, simultanagnosia and palinopsia, and a note separates ataxia with agraphia as Gerstmann syndrome.
10. Types of Posterior Circulation, Artery of Percheron and Dejerine-Roussy Syndrome

Four schematic types of posterior circulation are drawn, each labelling the midbrain, both thalami, the posterior cerebral artery and the basilar artery, with type IIB showing the artery of Percheron.
Infarction of that single thalamic perforator is printed as a triad of drowsiness or confusion, vertical gaze palsy and memory disturbance.
Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, the burning hand syndrome from thalamogeniculate artery occlusion, produces contralateral hemisensory loss with burning pain in the upper and lower limb, illustrated by the axial MRI captioned for that syndrome.
11. Watershed Territories and Their Predisposing Conditions

The watershed panel of axial FLAIR and diffusion images is set against a schematic that labels the cortical border zone between the ACA and MCA, the internal border zone between the lenticulostriate circulation, printed as LCA, and the MCA, and the cortical border zone between the MCA and PCA.
Watershed areas are stated to be prone to infarct, with predisposing conditions of hypoalbuminaemia, sudden hypotension and dehydration, alongside the printed reminder to maintain adequate hydration of the patient.

The opening comparison table separates embolic from thrombotic stroke by the tempo of deficit and by recovery, site and vessel size.
Embolic stroke presents with full weakness at onset, rapid recovery of consciousness and cortical findings, multiple lesions at different areas, grey-white matter interphase involvement, hemorrhagic transformation and small-vessel involvement, and the table marks thrombectomy as not useful with a worse prognosis; thrombotic stroke evolves its weakness over 48-72 hours, lacks those rapid recoveries and multifocal features, involves large vessels, and is the one for which thrombectomy is useful with better prognosis.
The note adds that weakness evolving beyond 72 hours suggests bleeding or tumour.
2. MCA Stroke Patterns in the UMN Approach

The MCA flowchart splits the approach into three arms, beginning with the lenticulostriate branches from M1, which produce internal capsule findings.
The M2 arm gives variable contralateral weakness with aphasia, separating into a superior division with Broca's aphasia and an inferior division with Wernicke's aphasia without weakness.
The third arm is complete MCA involvement, printed as weakness, hemianopia, hemisensory loss, cortical findings and global aphasia.

The differentials open with internal capsule lesions: dense hemiplegia, hemisensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, a more prominent seventh nerve palsy and an absence of cortical findings.
Brainstem lesions are printed as crossed hemiplegia, with an ipsilateral LMN cranial nerve nuclear palsy plus contralateral weakness.
Spinal cord lesions are the third entry, marked by bilateral involvement with a specific level of lesion.
4. Upper Motor Neurons: Definition, Functions and Tracts

Upper motor neurons are descending fibres that merge on the anterior horn cell in the spinal cord and on the cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem.
The corticospinal tract integrates highly skilled fine discrete movements of the distal extremities and supplies lower centres with inhibitory impulses, so a lesion inside the spinal cord gives LMN features at the level and UMN features below it; the extrapyramidal system maintains tone and posture and inhibits proximal and antagonistic muscles.
The fibres included are the pyramidal corticospinal tract, which merges on the AHC, and the extrapyramidal fibres, with the rubrospinal tract in the lateral white matter and the vestibulospinal, tectospinal and reticulospinal tracts in the ventral white matter.
5. Corticobulbar Fibres, Facial Palsy and the Motor Homunculus

Corticobulbar fibres merge on the cranial nerve nuclei, and the note divides them into bilateral involvement, which produces pseudobulbar palsy as seen in ALS, and unilateral involvement, which is usually symptomless because of bilateral representation.
The single printed exception is the seventh cranial nerve, whose lower half receives contralateral innervation only, so an internal capsule or cortical lesion gives an UMN seventh nerve palsy; the paired diagrams contrast a supranuclear UMN lesion, with drooping of the angle of the mouth and preserved forehead movement, against a facial nerve nucleus or nerve lesion, with deviation of the angle of the mouth and a Bell's palsy picture.
The motor homunculus places the lower limb with ACA lesions and the upper limb and face with MCA lesions, running from hip, leg, trunk, neck, head, shoulder and arm through the wrist, hand and individual digits to the eye, nose, face, lips, teeth and jaw, tongue and pharynx.
6. Pyramidal Tract: Cortical Origin and Capsular Course

The pathway begins in the cortex, with the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus providing pyramidal cells of Betz with the lowest threshold at 30%, premotor and supplementary motor cortex at 30% and the primary sensory cortex at 40%.
Fibres converge on the corona radiata and pass through the internal capsule at the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb, accompanied by corticonuclear and corticorubral fibres, and then run in the cerebral peduncle and brainstem towards the medullary pyramids, the decussation of pyramids and the lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts to the upper and lower motor neurons and skeletal muscles.
7. Midbrain to Cord: Brainstem Levels, Decussation and Segmental Distribution

The midbrain panel labels the superior colliculus, oculomotor nucleus, tectum, tegmentum, crus cerebri as the cerebral peduncle, red nucleus, decussation of the rubrospinal tract, oculomotor nerve, cerebral aqueduct, medial longitudinal fasciculus, lemnisci as sensory, substantia nigra, the middle three-fifths carrying corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres and the frontopontine fibres, with a note that the trochlear nerve is not seen at the superior collicular level.
The fibres then run through the basilar part of the pons and decussate at the pyramidal level in the caudal medulla before entering the spinal cord, where the printed distribution is cervical 50%, thoracic 30% and lumbosacral 30%.
8. Clinical Features: The Pyramidal Pattern of Weakness

The clinical features begin with an UMN facial palsy involving the lower half with sparing of the upper half, voluntary fibres for skilled learned actions failing before emotional fibres, and preserved deglutition and articulation.
The upper limb loses shoulder abduction and external rotation, leaving it adducted and internally rotated, loses elbow extension and supination, leaving it flexed and prone, and loses wrist dorsiflexion, leaving the hand palmar flexed.
The lower limb loses hip adduction and flexion, leaving it abducted and externally rotated, loses knee flexion, leaving it extended, and loses ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, leaving the foot plantarflexed and inverted, which produces a circumduction gait.
9. Tone: Spasticity versus Rigidity, and the Reflex Root Values

Tone change in a pyramidal lesion is printed as clasp-knife spasticity, and the comparison table separates spasticity as velocity and length dependent, resisting movement in one direction during the initial part, and typed as clasp-knife, from rigidity, which is neither velocity nor length dependent, resists in both directions and is typed as lead-pipe or cog-wheel.
The closing root-value note gives biceps jerk C5-C6, triceps jerk C7, finger flexion C8-T1, knee jerk L3-L4 and ankle jerk S1.

The chapter opens with the time-based definitions: stroke is abrupt focal/global neurological deficit lasting 24 hours or more with evidence of infarction or hemorrhage, while TIA is focal brain/retinal ischaemia lasting under 1 hour without infarction.
Diffusion-weighted MRI then separates the two: a normal DWI study means only TIA, whereas a hyperintense lesion means minor stroke even when the patient has clinically recovered.
The chapter's printed stroke line reads 'lasting ≥24 hrs' (OCR 'a4' = 24).

The ABCD² score predicts the risk of stroke following TIA, summing points across five components: age above 60 years and BP ≥140/90 mmHg at initial evaluation give 1 point each; clinical features give 1 for speech disturbance without weakness and 2 for unilateral weakness; duration gives 1 for 10-59 minutes and 2 for 60 minutes or more; diabetes gives 1 point.
The points column digits were re-read glyph by glyph from the scan (each cell is a single digit).
Total score therefore runs from 0 to 7.

The risk table stratifies stroke risk after TIA by total score at 2, 7 and 90 days: Low 0-3 = 1.0/1.2/3.1%, Moderate 4-5 = 4.1/5.9/9.8% and High 6-7 = 8.1/11.7/17.8%.
The High-row values were resolved glyph by glyph at high zoom (OCR had merged the digits) and match the Johnston Lancet 2007 validation table the book reproduces.
Risk rises monotonically with the score band.

The printed Notes state the key indications for dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) in neurology: TIA, mini stroke and intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD) with more than 50% occlusion.
Every other condition gets a single antiplatelet.
For the DAPT combination the book ranks aspirin/ticagrelor above clopidogrel.
5. Atherosclerotic Causes and Cerebral Venous Thrombosis

The causes section opens with '1. Atherosclerotic', which branches into arterial and venous disease; the venous branch is cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT).
CVT causes are split into inherited (Factor V Leiden mutation) and acquired (antiphospholipid syndrome, pregnancy/postpartum), with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting and seizures.
Arterial disease splits into ischaemic (85%) and haemorrhagic (15%).

Arterial stroke divides into ischaemic (85%) and haemorrhagic (15%); the haemorrhagic examples are SAH, EDH and IVH, all managed by a neurosurgeon.
The ischaemic arm divides into thrombotic (large vessel, evolving, weakness rising over 48-72 hours), embolic (hyperacute, cortical features, rapid recovery, distal vessel) and lacunar (30-300 μm vessels, lipohyalinosis).
Emolic disease splits into cardioembolic (mitral stenosis, AF, prosthetic valve, dilated cardiomyopathy, recent MI within 4-10 weeks, sick sinus syndrome) and artery-artery (the m/c stroke, from neck vessels).
7. Thrombotic versus Embolic Table and CT Imaging

The comparison table separates the two by tempo: onset (stroke in evolution versus hyperacute), features (↑headache versus LOC/seizures), weakness (rising over 48-72 hours versus full at onset), clot (fibrin clot versus red clot) and transformation (haemorrhagic transformation belongs to the embolic column).
CT imaging then shows the ischaemic stroke as a hypodense lesion and acute blood as a hyperdense lesion, with the three printed images being ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
8. Non-Atherosclerotic Causes and the Ischaemic Cascade

Non-atherosclerotic causes comprise moya-moya disease (multiple collaterals with 'puff of smoke' appearance from internal carotid artery vasculopathy), vasculitis, Fabry's disease, fibromuscular dysplasia, carotid artery dissection, dissection and Takayasu arteritis.
The pathology flowchart runs ATP depletion → failure of the Na+-K+ ATPase pump → glutamate release → calcium entry → liquefactive necrosis, on a Day 1 to Day 24 timeline captioned 'Hemorrhagic transformation of stroke'.
9. Treatment Goals and Early CT Signs

Goals of stroke treatment are revascularization (reperfusion), avoiding secondary injury and establishing collateral blood flow; the secondary-injury column lists 4-5 days of raised ICT (cerebral edema), SIADH/metabolic issues and haemorrhagic transformation.
Investigations rank MRI above CT, and the early CT findings in stroke are the hyperdense MCA sign (6 hrs) with the MCA dot sign as the earliest, the insular ribbon sign (6-48 hrs) and obscuration of the lentiform nucleus (8-24 hrs).
10. Lacunar Stroke and Small Vessel Disease Markers

Lacunar stroke occurs in the elderly with F > M and hypertension as the risk factor; the handwritten definition note reads '…cm size infarct in a 30-300 μm vessel d/t lipohyalinosis'.
The types table maps pure motor stroke to the lenticulostriate artery and internal capsule, pure sensory stroke to the thalamogeniculate artery and VPL nucleus, and ataxic hemiparesis/dysarthria-clumsy-hand to the basilar artery and basi pons.
The MRI small-vessel-disease markers with their modalities are recent small subcortical infarct (DWI), white matter hyperintensity (FLAIR), lacune (FLAIR), perivascular space and cerebral microbleeds (T2'/SWI); microbleeds point to cerebral amyloid angiopathy and CADASIL is expanded in full.

Ataxic hemiparesis is the same as dysarthria with clumsy hands.
The pathway diagram shows corticopontocerebellar (CPC) fibres running cortex → basi pons → contralateral cerebellum and the corticospinal (CS) tract running cortex → pyramid → contralateral body; CPC damage gives contralateral cerebellar findings and CS damage contralateral weakness.
A lesion at the basis pontis therefore produces ataxic hemiparesis / dysarthria with clumsy hands, and the DRTC (Dentato Rubro Thalamo Cortical) fibres pass via the red nucleus while spinocerebellar fibres degenerate in Friedreich's ataxia.

The brainstem runs rostral (midbrain), central (pons) and caudal (medulla) between brain and spinal cord.
Its hallmark presentation is crossed hemiplegia: ipsilateral LMN cranial nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia, because the corticospinal tract decussates while the cranial nerve nucleus is lesioned ipsilaterally.
The note contrasts hallmark presentations at other sites: cortical lesions give aphasia and internal capsule lesions give contralateral UMN 7th nerve palsy.

Brainstem structures divide by position: the midline 4M are the motor nuclei of CN 3, 4, 6 and 12, the medial longitudinal fasciculus (lesion → internuclear ophthalmoplegia), the medial lemniscus (posterior column fibres after decussation at the medulla) and the motor tract (corticospinal).
The lateral 4S are the spinothalamic tract, spinocerebellar fibres, sympathetic fibres (lesion → Horner's syndrome) and the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve carrying sensory fibres.
This medial-lateral map predicts which tracts each brainstem syndrome spares or involves.

The anterior view shows the crus cerebri of the midbrain bounded by the interpeduncular fossa with the oculomotor nerve exiting between the crura, above the pons; posteriorly the tectum carries the superior and inferior colliculi.
At the level of the superior colliculus the cross-section shows the cerebral aqueduct, oculomotor nucleus, MLF, red nucleus, substantia nigra, decussation of the rubrospinal tract and lemnisci, with the crus cerebri's middle 3/5th carrying corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres flanked by frontopontine fibres.
At the level of the inferior colliculus the trochlear nerve exits — the only cranial nerve to leave the brainstem posteriorly — with the mesencephalic nucleus of V, the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles and the temporoparietopontine fibre groups labelled.

Ventral midbrain syndromes share a vascular origin from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery.
Weber's syndrome lesions the base of the midbrain (cerebral peduncle): CN-3 fibres plus corticospinal tract, giving ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
Claude's syndrome lesions the tegmentum: CN-3 fibres plus the red nucleus/superior cerebellar peduncle (dentato-rubro-thalamic fibres), giving ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral ataxia and tremor; Benedikt's syndrome combines both — extensive tegmentum plus base — adding the substantia nigra (nigrostriatal pathway) for contralateral hemichorea and hemiathetosis, printed as Weber + Claude.

Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud's) syndrome is most commonly caused by pinealomas, lesioning the dorsum of midbrain — pretectal nucleus, periaqueductal grey matter and CN-3 fibres.
Its features are vertical gaze palsy (upgaze), sunsetting sign (looking down), Argyll Robertson pupil (accommodation present, light reflex absent), Collier's sign (levator palpebrae superioris overshoot → lid retraction), pseudo abducent pupil (printed as such), convergence-retraction nystagmus (overactive convergence centre) and skew deviation.
Nothnagel's syndrome is the anterior version of Parinaud's (CN-3 fibres plus superior cerebellar peduncle close to the red nucleus), the cerebellar peduncles connect superior→midbrain, middle→pons, inferior→medulla, and a note separates Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome of tularemia (Francisella tularensis).

Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg's/PICA syndrome) arises from the V4 segment of the vertebral artery and PICA, usually by large vessel thrombosis or artery-to-artery infarction, with cardiac embolism printed as rare.
Higher mental functions and the motor system are normal; cranial nerves 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 are spared while the spinal nucleus of V gives hemifacial sensory loss, the vestibular nuclei give vertigo/ataxia/nystagmus, the NTS of VII impairs anterior 2/3rd taste, the nucleus ambiguus (IX, X) gives dysphagia with nasal regurgitation, the dorsal vagal nucleus gives autonomic symptoms and the cervical sympathetic chain gives ipsilateral Horner's.
Sensory findings are contralateral pain and temperature loss with posterior column sparing, and spinocerebellar fibres give ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia.

The Horner's diagram on this page localises the lesion along the three-neuron ophthalmosympathetic pathway.
A central (first-order) lesion gives central Horner syndrome, the printed example being Wallenberg syndrome; a preganglionic (second-order, C8-T1 to superior cervical ganglion) lesion's example is a Pancoast tumour; a postganglionic lesion travelling with the carotid artery gives carotid artery dissection, in which anhidrosis is absent because the sudomotor fibres leave with the external carotid.
8. Medial Medullary Syndrome and Horizontal Gaze

Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome involves the XII nerve nucleus (ipsilateral 12th palsy with paralysis and atrophy of one half of the tongue), the corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiplegia), the MLF (ipsilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia) and the medial lemniscus (contralateral posterior column loss — touch and proprioception).
The horizontal gaze pathway runs from the frontal eye field to the contralateral PPRF and the VI nerve nucleus, whose internuclear fibres cross via the MLF to the opposite medial rectus subnucleus.
MLF lesion alone gives INO (ipsilateral adduction weakness with contralateral abduction nystagmus); MLF plus PPRF gives one-and-a-half syndrome; adding a VII palsy gives eight-and-a-half; bilateral VII palsy with one-and-a-half gives fifteen-and-a-half.
9. Cruciate Paralysis and the Avellis-Jackson Table

Cruciate paralysis results from early decussation of upper limb fibres at the pyramidal decussation, presenting either as brachial diplegia (both arms weak with legs spared) or weakness of one arm and the opposite leg.
The note restates crossed hemiplegia as I/L LMN CN palsy plus C/L hemiplegia.
The Avellis versus Jackson table compares two medullary syndromes: both sit in the tegmentum of medulla; Avellis involves the X nerve and spinothalamic tract giving ipsilateral LMN X palsy with contralateral body pain-temperature loss and no weakness, while Jackson adds the hypoglossal nucleus for ipsilateral LMN XII palsy.

The dorsal pons cross-section labels 23 structures from the floor of the fourth ventricle down: cochlear and vestibular nuclei, abducens nucleus, nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and MLF on the median sulcus; raphe and pontine reticular formation in the tegmentum; spinal nucleus of V with its root, facial nucleus, lateral and superior olivary nuclei, lemnisci and central tegmental tract laterally; then the middle cerebellar peduncle, pontocerebellar fibres, corticospinal tract, pontine nuclei and basilar sulcus at the basis.
The printed note is that the pons has no tectum.
Blood supply is basilar artery for the majority, with lateral pons supplied by AICA plus basilar.

The pontine syndrome table lists site, vascular origin and clinical features.
Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral, basal pons, basilar artery) is ipsilateral LMN facial and sixth nerve palsies with contralateral hemiplegia — the FSH syndrome; Raymond syndrome is ipsilateral sixth nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia, printed as the SH syndrome.
Foville syndrome (dorsal tegmentum, basilar artery) adds ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy (PPRF) to the Millard-Gubler picture — the FGH syndrome; Marie-Foix syndrome (lateral pons, AICA plus basilar) is ipsilateral ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle), contralateral pain-temperature loss and contralateral hemiplegia — the ASH syndrome.
Locked-in syndrome follows bilateral extensive pontine infarction with an alert patient (reticular activating system normal), quadriplegia from corticospinal and corticobulbar lesions, and preserved vertical eye movements; top-of-basilar occlusion gives absent visual/oculomotor findings with bilateral medial temporal lobe features — behavioural change, fluctuating alertness, amnesia and visual hallucinations. Posterior stroke presents with the 5 D's: diplopia, dizziness, dystaxia, dysarthria and dysphagia.

The goals of treatment are recanalisation/reperfusion, preventing secondary brain damage and optimising collateral blood flow.
The printed causes of secondary brain damage are the raised intracranial pressure cascade — ↑ICT from cerebral oedema leading to herniation/coning — plus haemorrhagic transformation and SIADH with hyponatraemia.
Each goal maps to a threat: reperfusion to the infarct core, secondary-damage prevention to oedema and metabolic injury, and collateral flow to the penumbra.
2. Immediate Management and the CT Protocol

Immediate management is used when the onset of stroke is known: the CT protocol table maps scenarios to investigations — presentation within 6 hours needs no additional imaging, suspected TIA needs diffusion-weighted MRI to rule out stroke, and presentation within 4.5 hours of symptom onset with CT excluding bleed proceeds to thrombolysis with alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10% bolus, 90% infusion over 1 hour) or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, which can be given without CT angiogram if thrombolysis is indicated.
The steps are supportive care with oxygen and vitals, checking random blood sugar, ECG plus troponin I, and BP correction — labetalol 20 mg IV up to two times when BP is ≥220/110 mmHg, or above 185/110 mmHg when thrombolysis or thrombectomy is planned.
Step 5 is CT: plain CT to rule out bleed, then CT angiography.

The printed contraindications to thrombolysis are age under 18 years, BP above 185/110 despite treatment, CT hypodensity over one third, intra-axial neoplasm, aortic dissection or infective endocarditis, recent heparin within 48 hours or LMWH within 24 hours, platelet count under 1,00,000 cells/μl, bleeding within the last 3 weeks (especially GI bleed) and surgery, trauma or stroke within the last 3 months.
Each item is an absolute block to the 4.5-hour alteplase/tenecteplase pathway.
4. CT and the MRI Protocol for Wake-up Stroke

The printed order continues on p701 with step 5 — CT: plain CT to rule out bleed, then CT angiography.
The MRI protocol is used for wake-up stroke, when the time of onset is unknown: diffusion-weighted MRI first establishes the diagnosis (hyperintense white lesions = stroke); the T2 FLAIR sequence then times the event, the lesion appearing white or black depending on how long ago the patient presented; a DWI-white versus FLAIR-black mismatch is indicative of very new onset, and such a patient can be considered for thrombolysis — ADC (apparent diffusion coefficient) is then performed to confirm restricted diffusion.

Step 4 is perfusion imaging, which compares DWI and PWI: the infarct core shows on DWI, part of the penumbra appears on PWI, and the complete penumbra is the region identified on MR perfusion imaging — the PWI-DWI mismatch (PDM).
The printed CBF thresholds are below 10 ml/100 g/min for infarcted tissue, above 20 ml/100 g/min for normal perfusion, and 10-20 ml/100 g/min for the penumbra region.

After 24 hours the printed sequence is: repeat imaging; anticoagulation for cardioembolic stroke — for valvular AF only warfarin is used, the causes printed being mitral stenosis and prosthetic valve; antiplatelet therapy — single (aspirin in most cases) or dual temporarily as aspirin plus ticagrelor for corresponding cardiac disease, minor stroke/TIA and ICAD over 50%; carotid endarterectomy over carotid stenting — endarterectomy for all cases except high-risk cardiac cases, stenting used in high-risk cardiac cases; and cholesterol management with target LDL below 100 on atorvastatin/rosuvastatin.
Indications for both revascularisation procedures are over 50% block in a symptomatic patient and over 70% block in an asymptomatic patient.
q: Match each step of the book's 'Chronology of reading ECG' to its correct position — 1) QRS complex 2) P wave 3) Rate 4) Axis 5) QT interval … A) Sixth B) First C) Fourth D) Fifth E) Second
The fixed chronology is: 1. QRS complex, 2. P wave, 3. Regularity of QRS (start from lead II / rhythm strip), 4. Rate, 5. Axis, 6. QT interval. (Book p377)
Match the tracing call-outs — 1) V1 call-out 1a 2) V1 call-out 1b 3) V5–V6 call-out 1a 4) V5–V6 call-out 1b … A) Big R B) Small Q C) Small R D) Deep S
The figure labels V1 with small R (1a) and deep S (1b), and V5–V6 with small Q (1a) and big R (1b). (Book p377)
The regularity call-out instructs you to start from ____.
Start from lead II / rhythm strip to assess QRS regularity. (Book p377)
Calibration note beside the 12-lead tracing: 1 small box = ____.
The book marks '1 small box = 40 ms' beside the tracing — i.e. 0.04 s, so 2.5 small boxes = 100 ms. (Book p377)
The QRS complex produces the MAXIMUM deflection in the ECG because it represents:
Features of the QRS: maximum deflection in ECG, due to synchronous ventricular depolarisation. (Book p377)
Normal / narrow QRS occupies 2–2.5 small boxes on the book's paper. In milliseconds and seconds that equals:
Normal/narrow QRS = 2–2.5 small boxes = 100 ms / 0.1 s (1 small box = 40 ms). (Book p377)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — the pairing that contradicts the book's QRS duration definitions:
Normal/narrow QRS is 2–2.5 small boxes (100 ms); wide QRS is > 0.12 s and very wide QRS is > 0.16 s. Calling a narrow QRS '> 0.12 s' is the odd one. (Book p377)

Match each station of the route of depolarisation to the station it hands the impulse to NEXT — 1) Sinus node 2) AV node 3) Bundle of His 4) Left anterior fascicle … A) Bundle of His B) Purkinje fibres C) Atria D) Right & left bundle branches
Route: Sinus node → Atria → AV node → Bundle of His → Right BB / Left BB → (Left anterior & posterior fascicles) → Purkinje fibres → ventricles. (Book p378)
TRUE or FALSE — per the book's note, ventricular depolarisation spreads from the epicardium towards the endocardium.
True — the epicardium is reached first by Purkinje fibres
False — the note runs endocardium → epicardium
False — depolarisation has no transmural direction, only base-to-apex
True — the note actually describes repolarisation
The book's note is explicit: Depolarisation: Endocardium → Epicardium. (Book p378)
Match each ventricular depolarisation event to its vector — 1) Septal depolarisation 2) Free wall depolarisation 3) Posterobasal LV depolarisation … A) Vector 3 B) Vector 1 C) Vector 2
Ventricular depolarisation: 1. Septal = Vector 1; 2. Free wall = Vector 2; 3. Posterobasal LV = Vector 3. (Book p378)
The book's margin equation: QRS complex = Vector (____).
QRS complex = Vector (1 + 2 + 3) — septal, free-wall and posterobasal vectors summed. (Book p378)
TRUE or FALSE — a DOWNWARD deflection is recorded when the flow of current is TOWARDS the positive electrode.
True — the +ve electrode always draws the trace down
True — but only in the chest leads
False — downward deflection occurs when current flows AWAY from the +ve electrode; towards it the deflection is upward
False — deflection direction depends only on the −ve electrode
Flow of current: downward deflection if flow is away from the +ve electrode; upward deflection if flow is towards the +ve electrode. (Book p378)

You wire a lead exactly like the book's diagram: right arm = −ve electrode (R), left arm = +ve electrode (L), galvanometer in between. A depolarisation wavefront now sweeps from the right arm towards the left arm. The galvanometer records:
No deflection — the current is perpendicular to the lead
Current flowing towards the +ve electrode (left arm) records an upward deflection — case A in the book's flow-of-current figure. (Book p378)
Vector 1 activates the LEFT side of the interventricular septum first because:
The LBB is shorter than the RBB
The left septum has a lower stimulation threshold
The right septum is supplied by the left posterior fascicle
Vector 1 = IV septum; LBB shorter than RBB, hence the left side of the IV septum is activated first. (Book p379)

Match each vector to its direction of spread — 1) Vector 1 2) Vector 2 3) Vector 3 … A) Superiorly & posteriorly B) Right side, anteriorly & inferiorly C) Rt → Lt, endocardium → epicardium (leftward, posteriorly & superiorly)
Vector 1: right side, anteriorly & inferiorly. Vector 2: Rt → Lt + endocardium → epicardium (left posteriorly & superiorly). Vector 3: superiorly & posteriorly. (Book p379)
TRUE or FALSE — Vector 1 gives a positive deflection in right-sided leads, a negative deflection on the left side, and is the most predominant vector in the right lead.
True — towards the right side it is positive, on the left negative, most predominant right lead
False — Vector 1 is positive on the left and negative on the right
False — Vector 1 is negative in all leads
True — but it is most predominant in the left lead
Vector 1: right-sided leads positive deflection, left-sided negative, and it is the most predominant, right lead. (Book p379)
Vector 2 writes a ____ in V1 and a ____ in V5–V6.
small q wave; tall T wave
Vector 2: right side −ve deflection in V1 → deep S wave; left side +ve in V5, V6 → big R. (Book p379)
Three of these belong to Vector 3 as written in the book. Pick the ODD ONE OUT:
Last part (posterobasal portion) to be depolarised
Most predominant vector, best seen in the right lead
Vector 3 = last (posterobasal) part, direction superiorly & posteriorly, no deflection. 'Most predominant, right lead' describes Vector 1. (Book p379)
Match each chest lead to its surface position in the book's lead-position diagram — 1) V4 2) V5 3) V6 … A) Anterior axillary line B) Mid axillary line C) 5th ICS, midclavicular line
Position of leads: V4 at the 5th ICS on the midclavicular line, V5 on the anterior axillary line, V6 on the mid axillary line. (Book p379)
In the lead-position figure, the sternal-angle landmark is labelled ____ ICS.
The sternal angle identifies the second intercostal space in the diagram. (Book p379)
Ventricular activation via an ALTERNATE pathway (myocardial cell-to-cell conduction) produces a wide QRS measuring:
Wide QRS cause 1: ventricular activation via alternate pathway — > 0.16 s, myocardial cell-to-cell conduction. (Book p379)
Match each ventricular-generated rhythm to its rate — 1) Idioventricular 2) Accelerated idioventricular 3) Ventricular tachycardia … A) 40–100 bpm B) >100 bpm C) 15–40 bpm
Ventricular generated rhythm: idioventricular 15–40 bpm; accelerated idioventricular 40–100 bpm; ventricular tachycardia >100 bpm. (Book p379)
Wide QRS via the NORMAL pathway with block measures ____ and corresponds to ____.
Cause 2: normal pathway with block — 0.12–0.16 s — Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) / Left BBB (LBBB). (Book p380)
On the lead II rhythm strip you count 20 small boxes between two consecutive QRS complexes. Applying the book's formula (1500 / no. of small boxes b/w 2 QRS), the rate is:
Rate = 1500 / 20 = 75 bpm — inside the sinus range of 60–100 bpm. (Book p380)
Match the pacemaker site to its rate range — 1) Sinus 2) Atrial / junctional 3) Ventricular … A) 15–40 bpm B) 60–100 bpm C) 40–60 bpm
Sinus rate 60–100 bpm; atrial/junctional rate 40–60 bpm; ventricular rate 15–40 bpm. (Book p380)
TRUE or FALSE — 'Regularity of QRS' means the QRS complexes occur at regular, FIXED intervals.
False — regularity permits gradually shortening intervals
False — regularity is judged on V1 only
True — but only when the rate exceeds 100 bpm
Regularity of QRS: QRS complexes occur at regular, fixed intervals. (Book p380)
The P wave is the 1st wave of the ECG. It is produced by:
Atrial depolarisation by the SA node
Atrial repolarisation by the AV node
P wave: 1st wave of ECG, due to atrial depolarisation by the SA node. (Book p380)
Match each P-wave component to its meaning — 1) Ascending limb 2) Descending limb 3) Tall P >2.5 mm in leads II, III, aVF … A) Lt atrial depolarisation B) Rt atrial depolarisation C) P-pulmonale
Rt atrial depolarisation = ascending limb; Lt atrial depolarisation = descending limb; a P wave taller than 2.5 mm in II, III or aVF is labelled P-pulmonale. (Book p380)
The 2.5/2.5 rule: normal height & width of the P wave = ____ mm.
2.5/2.5 rule — height & width of P wave = 2.5 mm. (Book p380)
TRUE or FALSE — the P wave is normal ONLY when the SA node depolarises the atria, and in normal sequence every QRS is preceded by a P wave.
True — SA-nodal atrial activation plus a P before every QRS
False — a junctional P wave counts as normal too
False — only every second QRS needs a preceding P wave
True — but the AV node may replace the SA node without changing P morphology
