Morphology: smooth, rounded; normal only when SA node depolarises atria; normal = every QRS is preceded by P wave. (Book p380)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — the descriptor that does NOT belong to the normal P wave in lead II per the book:
Normal P is smooth, rounded and upright in lead II; biphasic / inverted morphology belongs to lead V1, not lead II. (Book p380)
Match the P-wave morphology panels — 1) Normal lead II panel 2) Lead V1 normal panel 3) Tall inferior-lead panel … A) Biphasic B) Upright C) P-pulmonale, greater than 2.5 mm
The panels show upright P in II, biphasic P in V1 and P-pulmonale above 2.5 mm in II, III or aVF; an inverted morphology is also illustrated. (Book p380)
The PR segment shows NO deflection on the tracing because the last leg of its journey (AV node → upper part of Bundle of His) is:
Too fast for the galvanometer to record
PR segment parts: Atria → AV node; intra AV nodal (normal AV nodal delay); AV node → upper part of Bundle of His — electrically inert: no deflection. (Book p380)
Match each stage of the PR segment journey to what happens there — 1) Atria 2) Intra AV nodal 3) AV node → … A) Normal AV nodal delay B) Upper part of Bundle of His C) AV node
Parts of the PR segment: Atria → AV node; intra AV nodal = normal AV nodal delay; AV node → upper part of Bundle of His. (Book p380)
PR interval = P wave + PR segment = 0.12–0.2 s. On the book's paper that width equals how many small boxes?
PR interval 0.12–0.2 sec = 3–5 small boxes; > 0.2 s = prolonged PR interval. (Book p380)
Match the abnormal PR interval to its mechanism — 1) Prolonged PR 2) Shortened PR … A) Aberrant pathway b/w atria & ventricle (Bundle of Kent) B) Defect / block on the regular pathway
Abnormal PR: prolonged = defect/block on regular pathway; shortened = aberrant pathway b/w atria & ventricle (Bundle of Kent). (Book p380)

Narrow / normal QRS arm of the book's approach flowchart: match the PR / P-wave finding to the rhythm — 1) Normal PR & P wave 2) Short PR 3) Prolonged PR 4) Abnormal P wave 5) Absent P wave … A) 1° AV block B) Junctional rhythm C) SAN D) WPW E) Atrial rhythm
Look into PR interval: normal PR & P wave → SAN; short PR → WPW; prolonged PR → 1° AV block; abnormal P wave → atrial rhythm; absent P wave → junctional rhythm. (Book p381)

Wide QRS arm of the flowchart: match the finding to its branch — 1) Wide QRS ≥ 0.16 s 2) Wide QRS 0.12–0.16 s 3) VT, idioventricular & accelerated idioventricular rhythms … A) Bundle Branch Block branch (RBBB / LBBB) B) Ventricular arrhythmia branch C) A rhythm sitting under the ≥ 0.16 s branch
Wide ≥ 0.16 s → ventricular arrhythmia (idioventricular rhythm, accelerated idioventricular rhythm, VT); wide 0.12–0.16 s → Bundle Branch Block (RBBB/LBBB). (Book p381)
Match each bipolar lead to the two limbs it spans — 1) Lead I 2) Lead II 3) Lead III … A) Lt arm & Lt leg B) Rt arm & Lt arm C) Rt arm & Lt leg
Bipolar leads: Lead I b/w Rt arm & Lt arm; Lead II b/w Rt arm & Lt leg; Lead III b/w Lt arm & Lt leg. (Book p381)
Match each augmented unipolar lead to the bipolar lead it is PERPENDICULAR to — 1) aVR 2) aVL 3) aVF … A) ⊥ to lead II B) ⊥ to lead I C) ⊥ to lead III
Augmented unipolar leads: aVR perpendicular to lead III; aVL ⊥ to lead II; aVF ⊥ to lead I. (Book p381)
Match each lead to its angle on the book's hexaxial diagrams — 1) aVF 2) aVL 3) aVR 4) Lead III … A) −30° B) +90° C) −150° D) +120°
Hexaxial angles in the diagrams: I = 0°, II = +60°, III = +120°, aVF = +90°, aVL = −30°, aVR = −150°. (Book p381)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — the axis-zone pairing that CONTRADICTS the book's axis wheel:
Northwest axis — a fixed, determinable value at +60°
On the wheel: normal axis ~0 to +90°, leftward/LAD −30 to −90°, RAD +90 to ±180°, and the northwest axis (aVR zone) CANNOT be determined — it is not a fixed +60°. (Book p382)
The axis wheel labels the +90° aVF direction ____.
At +90°, aVF is labelled Rightward axis; this call-out is distinct from the RAD sector. (Book p382)
Counting QRS heights in I, II, III, aVL & aVF, you find the two TALLEST complexes in lead II (+60°) and aVF (+90°). Per the book's rule, the axis lies:
Determining the axis: count QRS height in I, II, III, aVL & aVF; the axis lies b/w the 2 leads with max height — here between +60° and +90°. (Book p382)
Axis shortcut: if a lead is EQUIPHASIC (R wave = S wave), the axis lies ____ to that lead.
Identify the equiphasic lead (R wave = S wave) → the axis lies ⊥ to it. (Book p382)
The QT interval (ventricular repolarisation) is measured from:
Beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave
End of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave
Beginning of the P wave to the end of the T wave
Beginning of the QRS complex to the peak of the T wave
QT interval = beginning of QRS complex to end of T wave; equivalently QRS complex + ST segment + T wave. (Book p382)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT — the QT value that does NOT match the book:
Book values: females 0.44 s, males 0.42 s, prolonged > 0.48 s. 'Males — 0.44 s' repeats the female value and is the odd one. (Book p382)
TRUE or FALSE — the QT interval equals QRS complex + ST segment + T wave.
True — QRS + ST segment + T wave
False — it excludes the ST segment
False — it equals QRS + T wave only
True — but only when the PR interval is normal
Features of QT: beginning of QRS to end of T; QRS complex + ST segment + T wave. (Book p382)
Per the book, the upper normal QT duration quoted for FEMALES is:
QT: females 0.44 s; males 0.42 s; prolonged > 0.48 s. (Book p382)
In the atrial-enlargement approach, an abnormal P wave localises the primary waveform abnormality to which origin?
The atrial-enlargement section identifies abnormal P waves with pathology of atrial origin. (Book p383)
A patient with COPD has tall, peaked, pointed P waves. Which pairing matches this section?
Pointed P is P-pulmonale and indicates right atrial enlargement; tall, peaked P waves are associated with COPD. (Book p383)
With an atrial-origin rhythm, which rate crosses the printed threshold for atrial tachycardia?
The rate threshold printed here is greater than 100 bpm, not merely equal to 100. (Book p383)
The right-atrial-enlargement figure groups pointed P-wave panels in ____ alongside a V1 panel.
The labelled small panels are II, III, aVF and V1; the inferior panels and the marked full tracing illustrate P-pulmonale/right atrial enlargement. (Book p383)
A bifid rather than pointed P wave is identified. What is the book’s atrial-enlargement interpretation?
Left atrial enlargement produces a bifid P wave, called P-mitrale. (Book p383)
Which panel set belongs to the left-atrial-enlargement illustration, showing bifid P waves and a prominent terminal negative component in V1?
The left-atrial-enlargement panels are labelled I, II, aVF and V1; arrows/circles in the accompanying ECG draw attention to the abnormal P waves. (Book p383)
Complete the note’s corrected-QT equation: QTc = ____.
The note gives QTc = QT divided by the square root of RR. (Book p383)
The LVH axis line places the leftward axis between ____ (the aVL angle is printed without a minus sign on this page).
The line gives aVL (printed 30°) to lead I (0°), called leftward axis. The conventional aVL angle is −30°, as on p382; the missing sign is a source discrepancy. (Book p383)
True or false: LVH pushes the net vector leftward because left-sided muscle mass increases.
True — right-sided muscle mass increases and reverses the septal vector
False — increased left mass pushes the vector rightward
False — hypertrophy changes PR duration but not the net vector
True — the increased left mass pulls the net vector leftward
The LVH flowchart links increased left muscle mass to a vector pushed to the left. (Book p383)
The LVH tracing highlights large leftward forces. Which polarity pair follows the printed explanation?
Larger positive left-sided and larger negative right-sided deflections
Larger positive deflections on both sides
Larger negative left-sided and larger positive right-sided deflections
Larger negative deflections on both sides
LVH increases positive deflections on the left and negative deflections on the right; the ECG is captioned left ventricular hypertrophy. (Book p383)
The precordial Sokolow–Lyon expression printed here is ____.
S in V5 or V6 + S in V1 or V2
R in V5 or V6 + R in V1 or V2
R in V5 or V6 + S in V1 or V2
R in V1 or V2 + S in V5 or V6
The expression adds the lateral R wave (V5 or V6) to the anterior S wave (V1 or V2), rather than swapping the wave types or lead groups. (Book p384)
Under the book’s Sokolow–Lyon rule, R in V5 is 23 mm and S in V1 is 13 mm. Which interpretation fits?
Sum 36 mm — proves RVH using an R/S cutoff
Sum 36 mm — exceeds the >35 mm LVH cutoff
Sum 36 mm — below a >40 mm LVH cutoff
Difference 10 mm — fails a >11 mm precordial cutoff
The book adds R in V5 or V6 to S in V1 or V2 and uses >35 mm for LVH. Here 23 + 13 = 36 mm. (Book p384)
The alternative aVL voltage criterion for LVH is ____.
The second printed Sokolow–Lyon line is aVL >11 mm → LVH. (Book p384)
Which combination explains the secondary ST/T changes listed with LVH?
Primary PR shortening from aortic stenosis or chronic hypertension
Atrial repolarisation from mitral stenosis or SA exit block
Pressure-overload strain from aortic stenosis or chronic hypertension
Volume-overload strain from isolated COPD or sinus arrest
Secondary ST/T changes accompany strain/pressure overload, with aortic stenosis and chronic hypertension as the listed examples. (Book p384)
Which proposed leftward-axis cause does NOT belong with the book’s LVH/LBBB list?
LVH with increased left-sided positive deflection
Isolated RVH with axis between III and aVF
LVH with increased left muscle mass
The two leftward-axis causes listed are LVH and LBBB; the next section places RVH between III and aVF. (Book p384)
The RVH axis is described between ____ and is termed rightward.
RVH is placed between lead III at 120° and aVF at 90°, a rightward axis. (Book p384)
A tracing with rightward axis has R taller than S in V1 and secondary ST changes in a patient with mitral stenosis. Which printed combination fits?
LBBB — V1 R/S >1, isolated P-wave changes with MS
LVH — V1 R/S <1, secondary ST changes with MS + LVH
RVH — V1 R/S <1, primary PR changes with MS
RVH — V1 R/S >1, secondary ST changes with MS + RVH
The RVH section specifies V1 R/S >1 and secondary ST changes due to mitral stenosis plus RVH; its tracing is captioned RVH. (Book p384)
For the P-pulmonale highlighted in the COPD tracing, which lead set and most-common association are listed?
P-pulmonale is listed in II, III and aVF, most commonly with COPD; those inferior P waves are circled in the figure. (Book p384)
Which sequence reproduces the COPD axis flowchart?
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed upward → axis shifts to 120°
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed downward → axis shifts to −30°
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed upward → axis shifts to 0°
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed downward → axis shifts to 90°
The flowchart runs COPD → hyperinflated lung → downward push of diaphragm → axis shifts to 90°. (Book p384)
At the end of that flowchart, prominent complexes occur in ____, while absent complexes in ____ define the lead I sign.
The two arms are prominent complexes in aVF and II, and absent complexes in I, called the lead I sign. (Book p384)
Which finding contradicts the four ECG signs of COPD listed here?
Poor R-wave progression from V1 to V6
Wide QRS as the listed baseline QRS feature
The listed signs are narrow QRS, poor R progression V1–V6, P-pulmonale and a positive lead I sign. (Book p384)
In the book’s RVH-with-RBBB example, R/S >1 accompanies an axis between I and aVL. What combined enlargement is inferred?
No hypertrophy — RR′ alone explains the axis
Biventricular hypertrophy — RVH plus leftward axis
Isolated RVH — leftward axis excludes LVH
The example labels R/S and RR′, assigns R/S >1 to RVH and I–aVL to leftward axis, then calls RVH plus leftward axis biventricular hypertrophy. (Book p385)
Match the RBBB morphology call-outs — 1) V1 terminal force 2) V6 terminal force 3) Blocked branch in the cartoon … A) Right bundle branch B) Wide S wave C) R′ wave
The RBBB cartoon marks the right bundle. V1 variants rr′, RR′ and rsR′ share terminal R′; V6 qRS/RS variants share a wide terminal S. (Book p385)
The morphology figure places ____ in V1 and ____ in V6.
rS / QS; broad isolated R only
Broad isolated R only; rS / QS
The labelled RBBB panels give rr′, RR′, rsR′ in V1 and qRS, RS in V6. (Book p385)

Match the first three fascicular-classification lines — 1) RBBB alone 2) RBBB plus LAFB or LPFB 3) LBBB alone … A) Bifascicular combination with a left fascicular block B) Bifascicular block by itself C) Unifascicular block
The book calls RBBB alone unifascicular, RBBB with either left fascicular block bifascicular, and LBBB bifascicular by itself. (Book p385)
True or false: the next line calls bifascicular block plus increased PR interval or Mobitz block trifascicular.
True — but only a shortened PR satisfies that line
False — only isolated RBBB is labelled trifascicular
False — the line instead calls this unifascicular
True — that is the printed classification
The line says bifascicular block + increased PR interval/Mobitz block = trifascicular. This is source terminology; prolonged PR alone does not prove disease of the remaining fascicle. (Book p385)
For LBBB, the text gives an I–aVL leftward axis and asks you to inspect ____ for LBBB morphology.
The LBBB bullets give I–aVL leftward axis and V5, V6, aVL morphology; the adjacent tracing marks LVH and lateral LBBB features. (Book p385)

Match the LBBB figure’s morphology and conduction panels — 1) V1 rS / QS variants 2) V6 broad R / RR′ variants 3) Cartoon with left-sided conduction interruption … A) Left bundle branch block B) W pattern C) M pattern
The left-bundle cartoons accompany a V1 W-pattern row and a V6 M-pattern row; the latter includes both notched RR′ and broad R forms. (Book p385)
Which timing pair agrees with the LBBB figure’s small-print call-outs?
R-peak time >0.16 s in both V1 and V6
R-peak time normal in V1; prolonged >0.05 s in V6
R-peak time >0.05 s in V1; normal in V6
R-peak time normal in V1; prolonged >0.12 s in V6
The figure labels onset of intrinsicoid deflection (R-peak time) normal in V1 and prolonged in V6, measuring >0.05 seconds. (Book p385)
The Sgarbossa section addresses diagnosis of which combination?
Its stated purpose is to diagnose MI along with LBBB. (Book p385)

Match the three ST-change descriptions in the text — 1) V1 or V2, concordant change 2) V1 or V2, discordant change 3) V5 or V6, concordant change … A) ST depression B) ST elevation with the QRS C) ST elevation opposite the QRS
The text lists concordant ST depression and discordant ST elevation in V1/V2, and concordant ST elevation in V5/V6. (Book p385)
Which pair reproduces numbered panels 1 and 2?
Concordant elevation >5 mm with positive QRS; concordant depression >5 mm in V1–V3
Concordant elevation >1 mm with positive QRS; concordant depression >1 mm in V1–V3
Discordant elevation >1 mm with positive QRS; concordant depression >5 mm in V5–V6
Concordant depression >1 mm with positive QRS; discordant elevation >1 mm in V1–V3
Panel 1 labels concordant ST elevation >1 mm with positive QRS; panel 2 labels concordant ST depression >1 mm in V1–V3. (Book p385)
At the labelled J point, discordant ST elevation is 5 mm and preceding S depth is 15 mm. Which calculation matches panel 3?

The figure divides J-point discordant STE height (5 mm) by preceding S-wave height (15 mm): 0.33, above 0.25 or 25%. This proportional panel is distinct from the absolute >5 mm criterion on the next page. (Book p385)
Match each textual criterion to its lead group and threshold — 1) Concordant ST elevation 2) Discordant ST elevation 3) Concordant ST depression … A) V1/V2, >5 mm B) V1/V2, >1 mm C) V5/V6, >1 mm
The three textual criteria use strict > thresholds: lateral concordant elevation >1 mm, V1/V2 discordant elevation >5 mm and V1/V2 concordant depression >1 mm. (Book p386)
In the V1–V3 morphology panels, which pair is labelled LBBB + acute MI rather than LBBB without MI?
Concordant ST elevation only in aVL or isolated P-mitrale
Concordant ST depression ≥1 mm or abnormally discordant elevation ≥5 mm
Ordinary discordant elevation or concordant depression <1 mm
Ordinary discordant depression or an isolated tall R in V1

The left panel group contrasts ordinary discordant ST in LBBB without MI against concordant ST ≥1 mm and abnormally discordant ST ≥5 mm in LBBB + acute MI. These diagram labels use ≥, whereas the prose above uses >. (Book p386)
True or false: the V5, V6, II, III and aVF panels label concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm as LBBB + acute MI, in contrast to the no-MI discordant pattern.
False — those panels are labelled V1, V2 and V3
True — the no-MI panel also requires concordant elevation ≥1 mm
True — concordance and ≥1 mm identify the acute-MI panel
False — only discordant depression ≥5 mm is labelled acute MI
The right-hand group is labelled V5, V6, II, III, aVF and contrasts discordant ST in LBBB without MI with concordant ST ≥1 mm in LBBB + acute MI. (Book p386)
The two bottom annotated ECGs are captioned, from left to right, ____ and ____.
LBBB without MI, concordant elevation >1 mm; ordinary discordant elevation <5 mm
Acute MI with LBBB, concordant elevation >1 mm; discordant elevation >5 mm
Acute MI with LBBB, discordant elevation >5 mm; concordant depression >1 mm
LVH, concordant elevation >5 mm; RVH, discordant elevation >1 mm
The arrows and circles on the left mark concordant elevation >1 mm in acute MI with LBBB; the right caption is discordant elevation >5 mm. (Book p386)
The first table row defines chronotropy as ____ and assigns its regulation to ____.
Heart rate; SA node / pacemaker potential
Conduction velocity; SA node / ventricular potential
Chronotropy means heart rate; its regulator is the SA node through pacemaker potential. (Book p387)
Which meaning and regulator belong to the inotropy row?
Myocardial contractility; ventricle (left > right), ventricular potential
Myocardial relaxation; ventricle (right > left), ventricular potential
Myocardial contractility; atria (left > right), pacemaker potential
Heart rate; SA node, pacemaker potential
Inotropy is myocardial contractility, regulated by the ventricle (Lt > Rt) and ventricular potential. (Book p387)
Match the remaining rows; all three regulator cells are printed as dashes — 1) Dromotropy 2) Bathmotropy 3) Lusitropy … A) Cardiac conduction velocity B) Cardiac excitability C) Cardiac relaxation
Dromotropy is conduction velocity, bathmotropy excitability and lusitropy relaxation. Their regulator cells are all dashes; no regulator is supplied. (Book p387)
Using only this page’s printed heart-failure split, which pair is correct?
The printed flowchart uses <50% and >50%, leaving exactly 50% unspecified. These are book-specific cutoffs, not the full contemporary EF classification. (Book p387)
In the older-classification table, impaired contractility and impaired relaxation map respectively to which dysfunctions?
The older table pairs systolic dysfunction with impaired contractility and diastolic dysfunction with impaired relaxation. (Book p387)
True or false: the older table says diastolic dysfunction always requires accompanying systolic dysfunction.
True — impaired relaxation is another name for impaired contractility
False — diastolic may occur with or without systolic dysfunction; systolic is listed as always accompanied by diastolic
True — the table gives an obligatory systolic component for diastolic dysfunction
False — neither type can ever coexist with the other
The systolic column says always associated with diastolic dysfunction; the diastolic column says ± systolic dysfunction. (Book p387)
Which treatment-row wording belongs to the book’s explicitly older classification (not current prescribing advice)?
Systolic: treatment options present; diastolic: “No drugs to Rx”
Systolic: no drugs; diastolic: treatment options present
Both columns: no drugs to treat

The older table prints Rx options + under systolic and No drugs to Rx under diastolic. The latter is a historical/source statement and must not be used as contemporary HFpEF treatment advice. (Book p387)
Automaticity means the heart can beat ____.
Only when AV conduction is intact
The book defines automaticity as the ability of the heart to beat in the absence of stimuli. (Book p387)
Which listed site is singled out as the pacemaker with maximum potential?
The SA node is specifically marked pacemaker (maximum potential). (Book p387)
Which replacement would make the printed automaticity-site list incorrect?
Dense fibrous tissue instead of atrial cells
Distal AV node alongside the SA node
Ventricular myocardium alongside the His–Purkinje system
The listed sites are SA node, distal AV node, atrial cells, His–Purkinje system and ventricular myocardium—not dense fibrous tissue. (Book p387)
For the pacemaker-potential phase, the book pairs transient outward K channels with ____ and inward rectifying K channels with ____.
The printed sequence is TOK: transient outward K, closure; IRK: inward rectifying K, opening. This item tests the source’s channel wording rather than silently rewriting it. (Book p387)
The funny-current channel is expanded as ____ and is listed as opening during pacemaker potential.
The line names hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide (HCN) channel and labels funny currents (opening). (Book p387)
Which combination matches all three continuation bullets for HCN/funny-current channels?
Na channels; rods, cones and olfactory epithelium; digoxin
Ca channels; rods, cones and atrial septum; ivabradine
Na channels; rods, cones and olfactory epithelium; ivabradine
K channels; rods, cones and olfactory epithelium; a beta-blocker

The book lists Na channels, sites in rods/cones/olfactory epithelium, and blockade by ivabradine. HCN current is physiologically a mixed-cation current; “Na channels” is the source’s shorthand. (Book p388)

Match each phase to the printed channel event — 1) Late pacemaker-potential sequence 2) Depolarisation 3) Repolarisation … A) L-type calcium channel activity B) L-type calcium closure plus delayed rectifier K opening C) T-type calcium channel opening
T-type calcium opening completes the pacemaker-potential list. Depolarisation uses L-type calcium; repolarisation closes L-type calcium and opens DRK, delayed rectifier K channels. (Book p388)
On the pacemaker-potential graph, which reading correctly follows the labelled slope, upstroke and downstroke?
The pacemaker slope is flat; Na efflux drives the upstroke; K influx drives the downstroke
Membrane potential falls toward threshold; K influx drives the upstroke; Ca efflux drives the downstroke
Membrane potential rises toward threshold; Ca influx drives the upstroke; K efflux with reduced Ca permeability accompanies the downstroke
The slope starts only after the upstroke; Ca permeability falls on the upstroke and rises on the downstroke

The axes are membrane potential (mV) against time (s). The labelled pacemaker slope approaches threshold; the upstroke is marked increased Ca permeability/influx, and repolarisation increased K with decreased Ca permeability and K efflux. (Book p388)

Match the four numbered markers on the pacemaker-potential curve — 1) Marker 1 2) Marker 2 3) Marker 3 4) Marker 4 … A) Falling repolarisation limb B) Rapid rising limb C) Transition from slow slope to threshold/upstroke D) Near the most negative potential

Markers 1–4 sit near the negative trough, the threshold transition, the rising limb and the falling limb respectively. They are diagram call-out numbers, not ventricular action-potential phase numbers. (Book p388)
Which pair reproduces the scale/time call-outs on the pacemaker-potential illustration?
Voltage scale −90 to +40 mV; time annotation 800 msec
Voltage scale −90 to +40 mV; time annotation 80 msec
Voltage scale −60 to +20 mV; time annotation 80 msec
Voltage scale −60 to +20 mV; time annotation 800 msec
The figure’s membrane-potential scale runs from −60 to +20 mV and its time annotation reads 800 msec; these are figure labels, not universal cycle durations. (Book p388)
In the bradyarrhythmia impulse-pathway figure, the sequence after sinus node and atria is ____.
Bundle of His → AV node → bundle branches → ventricles
AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → ventricles
AV node → bundle branches → bundle of His → ventricles
Bundle branches → bundle of His → AV node → ventricles
The figure shows sinus node in the atria, then AV node, His bundle, bundle branches and ventricles. (Book p388)
Which description correctly identifies the diagram’s bracket and separating tissue?
His and sinus node form the bracketed AV system; Purkinje fibres form the separating sheet
AV node, His and bundle branches form the bracketed AV system; dense fibrous tissue separates atria and ventricles
Only the ventricles form the bracketed AV system; atrial muscle is labelled dense fibrous tissue
Sinus node and atria form the bracketed AV system; ventricular muscle separates the chambers
The bracket encloses AV node, bundle of His and bundle branches; dense fibrous tissue is labelled at the atrioventricular boundary. (Book p388)
Which is NOT one of the four level categories listed under heart blocks?
AV block of first, second or third degree
The listed levels/categories are SA node, sinoatrial block, AV block (1°, 2°, 3°), and fascicular block. (Book p388)

Match each arm of the fascicular-block flowchart — 1) Unifascicular 2) Bifascicular 3) Trifascicular … A) LAFB, LPFB or RBBB alone B) Bifascicular block plus increased PR interval C) RBBB plus LAFB/LPFB, or LBBB
These are the three arms exactly as classified on this page. Prolonged PR alone does not establish the anatomical site of additional conduction delay. (Book p388)
The sinus-node-dysfunction strip A illustrates loss of ____ after the last displayed beat.
Only S waves with preserved sinus P waves
Only T waves with preserved sinus P waves
Only the PR segment with continuing normal beats
The heading states absent P waves; strip A shows a preceding beat followed by a flat continuation, captioned sinus node dysfunction. (Book p388)
After sinus failure, a regular escape rhythm is 50 bpm with no P waves. Which comparison matches the compensation line?
Atrial escape has no P; junctional escape has abnormal P; both are 40–60 bpm
Junctional escape has no P; atrial escape has abnormal P; both are listed at 40–60 bpm
Both escape types require normal P waves and rates of 15–40 bpm
Junctional escape has normal P; atrial escape has absent P; both are 60–100 bpm
The line gives junctional rhythm (no P wave) or atrial rhythm (abnormal P wave), 40–60 bpm; the illustrated strip is junctional escape rhythm. (Book p388)
The first extrinsic cause in the sinus-dysfunction flowchart is ____.
The causes branch into extrinsic and intrinsic; hyperkalemia heads the extrinsic list. (Book p389)
Which drug is NOT in this page’s three-item extrinsic drug list?

The printed drug list is digoxin, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers. Ivabradine appears in the earlier HCN discussion, not this particular list; this is not a claim that it cannot cause bradycardia. (Book p389)
The increased-PaCO2 (hypercapnia) bullet names ____ as its associated syndrome.
The extrinsic-cause list links increased PaCO2/hypercapnia to obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome. (Book p389)
Match the remaining extrinsic-cause lines — 1) Low body temperature 2) Myxedema coma 3) Increased intracranial tension … A) Bradycardia–hypertension reflex B) Hypothyroidism C) Hypothermia
The remaining bullets are hypothermia, hypothyroidism (myxedema coma), and increased intracranial tension with the bradycardia–hypertension reflex. (Book p389)
After the extrinsic list, which diagnosis occupies the intrinsic arm?
The intrinsic arm contains sick sinus syndrome, in contrast to the preceding extrinsic metabolic, drug and systemic causes. (Book p389)
Which combination is explicitly marked on the upper-right SA-nodal-dysfunction tracing?
The figure annotations identify hyperkalemia in the tall-wave area and junctional rhythm in the circled rhythm-strip complexes. (Book p389)
A regular 48-bpm tracing has normal P waves before its complexes. Which source-based interpretation and cause weighting fit?
Atrial escape; equal weighting of extrinsic and intrinsic causes
Sinus bradycardia; extrinsic causes far outweigh intrinsic causes
Junctional escape; intrinsic causes far outweigh extrinsic causes
Sinus bradycardia; intrinsic causes far outweigh extrinsic causes
The sinus-bradycardia bullets specify regular rhythm, 40–60 bpm, normal P waves and extrinsic >> intrinsic causes; the adjacent strip illustrates this pattern. (Book p389)
In the two labelled pause diagrams, sinus pause/arrest has ____ and sinoatrial exit block has ____.
Distance A = B; distance A > B
Distance A < B; distance A = B
Distance A = B; distance A < B
Distance A > B; distance A = B
The captions under the diagrams explicitly read distance A > B for sinus pause/arrest and distance A = B for sinoatrial exit block. These refer to the labelled diagram spans. (Book p389)
The third manifestation’s strip alternates rapid activity with a slow phase. Which caption belongs to it?
The third ECG manifestation is captioned tachy-brady syndrome. (Book p389)
The idioventricular-rhythm heading explicitly associates IVR with a ____ QRS complex.
IVR is followed by an arrow to wide QRS complex. (Book p389)
Which pair matches the first two printed ventricular-rate categories?
IVR up to 40 bpm; AIVR 40–100 bpm
IVR up to 60 bpm; AIVR 60–100 bpm
IVR 40–100 bpm; AIVR up to 40 bpm
IVR up to 40 bpm; AIVR >100 bpm
The bullets give IVR up to 40 and accelerated IVR 40–100 bpm. Exactly 40 overlaps in the printed wording and is not a reliable discriminator here. (Book p389)
Following reperfusion, a wide-complex ventricular rhythm runs at 70 bpm. What does the AIVR sub-bullet suggest?
Ordinary IVR — a marker of failed reperfusion
Junctional escape — because all escape rhythms are 40–100 bpm
Ventricular tachycardia — because any rate above 40 is VT
Accelerated IVR — a marker of successful reperfusion
The AIVR sub-bullet calls the rhythm a marker of successful reperfusion. (Book p389)
The final rate bullet labels a ventricular rhythm at 110 bpm ____.
The book labels a ventricular rhythm with HR >100 bpm ventricular tachycardia. (Book p389)
The adjacent wide-complex ECG with circled rhythm-strip complexes is captioned AIVR. Which expansion belongs to that caption?
AIVR expands to accelerated idioventricular rhythm, the caption beneath the marked ECG. (Book p389)
True or false: the bottom AV-block strip B contrasts with sinus dysfunction by showing absent QRS complexes while atrial P waves continue.
True — the AV-block bullet identifies absent QRS complexes
False — the missing components are only T waves
True — AV block is defined here by loss of all P waves as well
False — the AV-block caption refers to an isolated prolonged QT
The AV-block heading says absent QRS complexes; its strip continues P waves without the corresponding ventricular complexes. (Book p389)
Which pair is listed under causes of first-degree AV block?
The two listed causes are beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers. (Book p390)
Which finding contradicts the clinical-feature list for first-degree block on this page?
Loud S1 as the listed first-heart-sound finding
The source lists asymptomatic, soft S1 and cannon waves on JVP. Cannon waves are contextualised below by unusually prolonged PR; they are not a universal first-degree-block finding. (Book p390)
For the uncomplicated first-degree presentation described here, which management/prognosis pair is printed?
No treatment needed; very good prognosis
Permanent pacing for all; very good prognosis
No treatment needed; uniformly poor prognosis
The management column states no Rx needed and very good prognosis; this is the book’s uncomplicated presentation, not a blanket rule for symptomatic patients. (Book p390)
The source prints delayed atria-to-ventricle conduction with prolonged PR and a threshold of ____; this question asks what is printed, not the usual diagnostic cutoff.

The scanned line reads PR interval >100 ms and the figure marks prolonged PR. This appears inconsistent with the usual first-degree AV-block definition of PR >200 ms; retain the distinction rather than using >100 ms clinically. (Book p390)
True or false: first-degree AV block here retains regular sinus rhythm, normal P/QRS morphology and a QRS after every P.
False — normal P waves must be replaced by absent P waves
True — conduction is delayed but every P is followed by QRS
True — the prolonged PR requires intermittent dropped QRS complexes
False — the defining feature is complete P–QRS independence
The bullets specify regular sinus rhythm, normal P and QRS complexes and every P followed by QRS. (Book p390)
In the unusually prolonged-PR example, arrows mark P waves on T waves. Which consequence chain is printed?
Synchronous contraction → increased cardiac output and isolated giant v waves
Loss of all atrial activity → reduced output without any P waves
Synchronous atrial/ventricular contraction → reduced cardiac output and cannon JVP waves
Asynchronous atrial/ventricular contraction → increased cardiac output and absent JVP waves
The source links P superimposed on T to synchronous contraction of atria and ventricles, then branches to decreased cardiac output and cannon waves on JVP. (Book p390)
The second-degree flowchart divides into ____ and ____; the latter is described as not meeting the former’s criteria.
Mobitz (types I and II); advanced second-degree AV block
Mobitz type I; isolated sinus arrest
Second-degree block branches to Mobitz (types I and II) and advanced second-degree block, with the note that Mobitz criteria are not met in the latter. (Book p390)
What conducted/missed-beat pattern does the Mobitz branch specify at a time?
Only one beat missed with no conducted beats
Every third P missed regardless of the number conducted
Only one beat missed with at least two conducted
At least two beats missed with only one conducted
The flowchart specifies only one beat missed and ≥2 beats conducted at a time. (Book p390)
The top-left Mobitz-I example brackets three conducted beats and one missed beat. What is the resulting atrial-to-conducted-beat ratio for that group?
Three conducted plus one missed gives four atrial opportunities for three conducted ventricular beats; the figure labels three conducted and one missed. (Book p391)
Which pair of call-outs identifies the two advanced second-degree examples?
Exactly one missed; at least two conducted
More than one beat missed; fewer than two beats conducted
Exactly one missed; at least three conducted
No beats missed; all beats conducted
The advanced examples are annotated >1 beat missed and <2 beats conducted, in contrast to the preceding Mobitz criteria. (Book p391)

Match the first three Mobitz comparison rows; each right item gives type I followed by type II — 1) Pathology 2) QRS complex 3) Etiology label … A) Benign / malignant B) Narrow / wide C) AV nodal / infranodal

In row order the table contrasts AV nodal with infranodal pathology, narrow with wide QRS and benign with malignant. These are source-characteristic patterns, not universal QRS-width requirements. (Book p391)
A strip shows progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat. Which table entry and name fit?
Type I shows progressive PR prolongation, named Wenckebach; type II has a constant PR in conducted beats. (Book p391)
The table describes RR intervals as ____ in type I and ____ in type II.
The RR row says progressively shortens for type I and constant for type II. This describes the pattern among conducted beats, not the pause itself. (Book p391)
Which presentation pairing agrees with the Mobitz table?
Type I hemodynamic compromise; type II always asymptomatic
Type I Stokes–Adams syndrome; type II isolated soft S1 only
Type I asymptomatic; type II symptomatic with hemodynamic compromise or Stokes–Adams syndrome
Both types asymptomatic; syncope belongs only to sinus bradycardia
The table contrasts asymptomatic type I with symptomatic type II, listing hemodynamic compromise and Stokes–Adams syndrome. (Book p391)
The associated-infarct row pairs type I with ____ and type II with ____.
The table associates type I with inferior-wall MI and type II with anterior-wall MI. (Book p391)
Which is the printed type-II cause list, while the type-I cell contains a dash?
Sx, SLE, decreased K, aortic stenosis
The type-II cell reads Sx/SLE/↑K/Amyloid. “Sx” is retained as printed shorthand rather than silently expanded; type I has a dash. (Book p391)
What do the site-of-block cartoons contrast?
Type I at sinus node; type II only at AV node
Type I at the AV node; type II at infranodal His/bundle levels
Both types confined to the sinus node
Type I at the ventricular apex; type II only in atria
The type-I cartoon marks the AV nodal region; type-II cartoons show blocks below it along the His/bundle pathways. (Book p391)
In the ECG row, what distinguishes the left dropped-beat arrow from the right dropped-beat/star example?
Both: complete independence of all P and QRS complexes
Left: absent P throughout; right: absent T throughout
Left: constant PR before the drop; right: progressive PR before the drop
Left: progressive PR before the drop; right: constant conducted PR before a drop
The type-I strip illustrates Wenckebach prolongation then a dropped QRS; the type-II strip marks P waves and a dropped complex with constant PR in conducted beats. (Book p391)
True or false: the notes associate AWMI with infranodal block, described as rare and due to structural heart disease, and IWMI with AV nodal block.
True — both infarct types are described as exclusively SA nodal
False — the notes state that structural disease is never involved
False — AWMI is linked to AV nodal and IWMI to infranodal block
True — those are the two printed infarct-site associations
The AWMI notes say infranodal, rare and due to structural heart disease; the IWMI note says AV nodal block. (Book p391)
Which pair reproduces the page’s management branches, rather than imposing a new protocol?
Asymptomatic (type I > II): observe; symptomatic: permanent pacemaker

The printed branches are asymptomatic (type I > II) → observe, symptomatic → permanent pacemaker. This simplified source algorithm must not be read as permission to observe all asymptomatic Mobitz II/high-grade blocks; clinical pacing decisions require guideline-based assessment. (Book p391)
The upper ECG circles ST elevation in II, III and aVF and marks dropped ventricular beats in the rhythm strip. Which caption matches it?
AWMI with isolated first-degree AV block
The inferior-lead ST elevations and rhythm-strip marks accompany the caption IWMI with Mobitz AV block; the bracket identifies second-degree AV block. (Book p392)
The second IWMI tracing marks alternate nonconducted P waves. What degree and ratio are printed in its caption?
The caption reads IWMI with advanced second-degree AV (2:1) block; stars identify nonconducted atrial activity. (Book p392)
Third-degree block can occur anywhere along the conduction system; no atrial impulse reaches the ventricle, producing ____.
Sinus arrest with absent atrial activity
The features specify block anywhere along the conduction system and no impulse transmitted from atria to ventricle, leading to AV dissociation. (Book p392)
True or false: complete AV dissociation can show regular P waves and regular QRS complexes even though the two are unrelated.
False — dissociation requires an irregular ventricular rhythm
True — regularity means every P must still conduct to a QRS
True — atrial and junctional/ventricular rhythms can each be regular independently
False — dissociation requires an irregular atrial rhythm
The ECG bullets specify regular atrial P waves, regular junctional/ventricular QRS complexes and no relationship between P and QRS. (Book p392)
The escape-pathway diagram links junctional rhythm to ____ and ventricular rhythm to ____.
Short QT; prolonged PR with 1:1 conduction
Along the atria → AV node → bundle branch → ventricle diagram, junctional escape is linked to narrow QRS and ventricular escape to wide QRS. (Book p392)
Arrows on the complete-dissociation strip identify P waves appearing at differing positions relative to broad QRS complexes. What should be inferred?
Independent atrial activity and a ventricular escape rhythm
Progressive PR prolongation followed by a single dropped QRS
Sinus arrest with no continuing atrial depolarisation
A fixed prolonged PR with every P conducted
The strip is captioned complete AV dissociation; arrows mark continuing P waves unrelated to the broad ventricular complexes. (Book p392)
Which set reproduces the first three arms of the AV-dissociation cause flowchart?
Complete AV block; atrial flutter with fixed conduction; sinus arrest
Complete AV block; VT with complete AV dissociation; AIVR with complete AV dissociation
First-degree block; VT with 1:1 conduction; ordinary sinus bradycardia
Mobitz I; atrial tachycardia; AIVR with 1:1 atrial conduction
The first three arms are complete AV block, ventricular tachycardia with complete AV dissociation, and accelerated idioventricular rhythm with complete AV dissociation. (Book p393)
The final two arms are ____ with complete AV dissociation.
Sinus bradycardia and first-degree AV block
Both junctional tachycardia and junctional rhythm with complete AV dissociation are separately listed. (Book p393)
The full ECG’s inferior-infarct pattern is accompanied by arrows marking independent P waves. Which printed diagnosis combines these findings?
The tracing is captioned IWMI with third-degree AV block; arrows on the rhythm strip emphasise the independent atrial activity. (Book p393)
In the first summary row, a P precedes every QRS with a consistently prolonged PR. The row is labelled ____.
The first summary row is first-degree AV block, with delayed but retained 1:1 AV conduction. (Book p393)
In the next summary strip, PR lengthens before a missing ventricular complex. Which row is this?
The second summary row is type I second-degree AV block, showing the Wenckebach pattern. (Book p393)
The third summary row shows broad/notched conducted QRS complexes and an intermittent dropped QRS without progressive PR lengthening. Which label belongs to it?
The third row is type II second-degree AV block; the drawing uses broad/notched QRS complexes with intermittent nonconduction. (Book p393)
In the advanced 2:1 summary strip, how many atrial depolarisations correspond to each conducted QRS?
The fourth row is advanced 2:1 second-degree AV block: two atrial depolarisations for one conducted ventricular complex. (Book p393)
In the following advanced 3:1 summary strip, how many P waves fail to conduct between successive conducted beats?
The fifth row is advanced 3:1 second-degree AV block: one conducted beat for three P waves, so two are nonconducted. (Book p393)
The final two summary rows show complete block with ____ QRS for the AV-nodal row and ____ QRS for the infranodal row.
The final rows contrast complete AV block at AV-nodal level with narrow escape complexes and infranodal complete block with broad/notched escape complexes; P and QRS remain dissociated. (Book p393)
By definition, tachyarrhythmias require a heart rate exceeding which threshold, and are morphologically classified into which two QRS complex durations?
Tachyarrhythmias are defined by HR > 100 bpm and are divided morphologically into narrow and wide QRS complexes. (Book p394)
Which triad of fundamental electrophysiological mechanisms accounts for all tachyarrhythmias listed on this page?
Enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, and re-entry
Decreased threshold, delayed repolarisation, and conduction block
Early repolarisation, ion channel arrest, and sodium overload
Parasystole, accelerated conduction, and wandering pacemaker
The three fundamental causes listed are enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, and re-entry. (Book p394)
Ventricular impulses originating above the bifurcation of the Bundle of His traverse Purkinje fibers to produce bilateral synchronous activation and a normal/narrow QRS complex lasting ____.
Impulses originating above the His bifurcation conduct via Purkinje fibers yielding bilateral synchronous activation and a narrow QRS (< 0.12 s). (Book p394)
When impulses arise below the bifurcation of the Bundle of His, how are the ventricles activated and what is the resulting QRS complex duration?
Ventricular myocardium activates ventricles; Wide QRS (≥ 0.16 s)
Purkinje fibers activate ventricles; Narrow QRS (< 0.12 s)
Accessory bypass tract conducts impulse; Intermediate QRS (0.10 - 0.12 s)
Bundle branches conduct synchronously; Slightly wide QRS (0.12 - 0.14 s)
Below the His bifurcation, ventricular myocardium activates the ventricles directly, creating a wide QRS complex (≥ 0.16 s). (Book p394)
An ECG reveals an SVT conducted with an underlying bundle branch block. According to the origin-of-impulses section, what is the expected QRS complex duration?
Supraventricular tachycardias associated with bundle branch block manifest with an intermediate QRS duration of 0.12 - 0.16 s. (Book p394)

Match each tachyarrhythmia category to its characteristic QRS complex morphology — 1) Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) 2) SVT with conduction block (RBBB/LBBB) 3) Ventricular tachycardia (VT) … A) Narrow QRS complex B) Slightly wide QRS C) Wide QRS
Under Classification: SVT yields narrow QRS; SVT with conduction block yields slightly wide QRS; VT yields wide QRS. (Book p394)
Which statement regarding normal enhanced automaticity is accurate according to the mechanism diagram?
True — Sinus tachycardia represents normal enhanced automaticity originating from normal sinus impulses at the SA node
True — Sinus tachycardia originates from ectopic atrial foci outside the SA node
False — Normal enhanced automaticity produces wide QRS complexes exceeding 0.16 s
False — Sinus tachycardia is driven exclusively by micro re-entry within the sinoatrial junction
Normal enhanced automaticity corresponds to sinus tachycardia, where normal sinus impulses originate from the SA node. (Book p394)
Which finding is NOT correctly listed under abnormal enhanced automaticity on this page?
Atrial tachycardia is driven solely by enhanced automaticity and cannot exhibit re-entry
Atrial tachycardia can be focal or multifocal and has all 3 mechanisms of tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is listed under abnormal enhanced automaticity
Ventricular tachycardia (specifically ischemic VT) is listed under abnormal enhanced automaticity
The source specifically notes that atrial tachycardia (focal/multifocal) possesses all 3 mechanisms of tachycardia, not merely automaticity. (Book p395)
A heart failure patient receiving digoxin presents with paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with AV block. Which metabolic disturbance precipitates this condition and what is the underlying mechanism?
Hypokalemia; Tachycardia due to enhanced automaticity
Hyperkalemia; Tachycardia due to macro re-entry
Hypercalcemia; Tachycardia due to early afterdepolarisations
Hyponatremia; Tachycardia due to conduction block alone
PAT with AV block is associated with digoxin toxicity, precipitated by hypokalemia, and occurs due to enhanced automaticity. (Book p395)
Under triggered activity, early afterdepolarisation (EAD) is linked to which clinical entity?
Long QT syndrome leading to Torsades de pointes
Early afterdepolarisation is specifically paired with Long QT Syndrome and Torsades de pointes. (Book p395)

A young athlete develops non-sustained VT during strenuous exertion. Electrophysiological testing demonstrates late afterdepolarisations driven by sympathetic tone and elevated intracellular calcium. Which rhythm fits this late afterdepolarisation category?
Right ventricular outflow tract VT (RVOT VT)
Torsades de pointes in Long QT type 1
Late afterdepolarisations cause catecholamine-sensitive arrhythmias (d/t sympathetic activity & elevated intracellular Ca2+), including RVOT VT, LVOT VT, and sympathetic VT. (Book p395)
Re-entry tachycardias are classically precipitated by premature complexes (PAC/PVC) and are characteristically highly responsive to ____.
Re-entry is precipitated by premature complexes (PAC/PVC) and is highly responsive to DC cardioversion. (Book p395)

Match each arrhythmia to its re-entry circuit classification — 1) AVNRT 2) AVRT 3) Atrial fibrillation … A) Micro re-entry circuit in the AV node B) Macro re-entry circuit involving bypass tract C) Micro re-entry circuits in atrial tissue
Micro re-entry: AVNRT, Brugada syndrome, Atrial Fibrillation. Macro re-entry: AVRT, Atrial Flutter, Scar VT. (Book p395)
Which statement accurately reflects the structural heart requirements for wide QRS ventricular tachycardia on this page?
True — VT occurs only in a structurally abnormal heart (due to previous infarction or scar)
True — VT occurs primarily in completely normal hearts without pre-existing structural disease
False — Wide QRS tachycardias never arise from previous myocardial scars
False — Re-entrant narrow QRS tachycardias require prior extensive myocardial infarction
Under causes based on QRS, wide QRS VT (Scar VT/Long QT) is annotated: 'VT: Occurs only in a structurally abnormal heart (D/t previous infarction)'. (Book p395)
When interpreting a narrow QRS tachycardia with 10 small boxes between consecutive R waves, what heart rate is calculated using the 1500 small-box rule?
HR calculation shown: HR = 1500 / 10 = 150 bpm, confirming tachycardia. (Book p396)
Which sequence correctly reflects the frequency hierarchy of supraventricular tachycardias (m/c SVT) stated on this page?
Sinus tachycardia > AF > AVNRT > AVRT > SART
AF > Sinus tachycardia > AVRT > AVNRT > SART
AVNRT > AVRT > AF > Sinus tachycardia > SART
Sinus tachycardia > AVNRT > AF > SART > AVRT
The printed hierarchy is: m/c SVT: Sinus tachycardia > AF > AVNRT > AVRT > SART. (Book p396)
What are the baseline clinical features of AVNRT regarding cardiac structure, sex predilection, and clinical prognosis?
Can occur in structurally normal heart; F > M; Good prognosis
Requires severe structural heart disease; M > F; Guarded prognosis
Occurs only after extensive MI; Equal sex ratio; Poor prognosis
Always associated with congenital ASD; F > M; High mortality
Features listed: Can occur in structurally normal heart; F > M; Good prognosis. (Book p396)
In the dual AV nodal pathway model, the slow pathway conducts slowly and has a ____ refractory period, whereas the fast pathway conducts rapidly and has a longer refractory period.
Slow pathway: conducts slowly, shorter refractory period. Fast pathway: conducts rapidly, longer refractory period. (Book p396)
A premature supraventricular beat arrives when the fast AV nodal pathway is refractory but the slow pathway has recovered. How does the impulse circulate to sustain AVNRT?
Impulse enters slow pathway, activates ventricles, and joins fast pathway retrogradely to activate atria
Impulse enters fast pathway, activates atria antegradely, and exits via the accessory bypass tract
Impulse blocks antegradely in both pathways and travels down the His bundle via ventricular myocardium
Impulse circulates entirely within the left atrium without engaging the AV junction
The premature impulse enters the recovered slow pathway, splits to reach ventricles (narrow QRS), and joins the fast pathway retrogradely to activate atria. (Book p396)
Due to retrograde activation of the atria via the fast pathway during AVNRT, what P-wave morphology is characteristically seen in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF)?
P waves are inverted in leads II, III and aVF
P waves are peaked and upright > 2.5 mm in II, III and aVF
P waves are bifid with a terminal negative deflection in lead II
P waves are completely flat and isoelectric across all leads
Retrograde activation of atria results in P waves that are inverted in leads II, III and aVF. (Book p396)
In what proportion of AVNRT patients are the P and QRS complexes formed simultaneously, causing the P wave to be completely buried within the QRS complex?
The text states: '2/3rd patients: P & QRS formed simultaneously -> P wave buried in QRS complex.' (Book p397)
A regular narrow-complex tachycardia runs at a rate of 210 bpm. What physiological boundary excludes sinus tachycardia and which diagnosis is strongly favored?
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 180 bpm; Rate 200–250 bpm favors AVNRT >> AVRT
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 150 bpm; Rate > 200 bpm favors atrial flutter exclusively
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 220 bpm; Rate 200–250 bpm favors ventricular tachycardia
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 100 bpm; Rate > 200 bpm favors junctional tachycardia
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 180 bpm; at a rate of 200 - 250 bpm, AVNRT >> AVRT. (Book p397)

Match each feature of atypical AVNRT to its clinical detail — 1) Incidence of atypical AVNRT 2) Triggering premature beat 3) Differential diagnosis on ECG … A) 5% of cases B) Premature ventricular complex (PVC) C) Atrial tachycardia
Table shows: Typical (95%, PAC, Slow-Fast) vs Atypical (5%, PVC trigger, Fast-Slow pathway, D/d Atrial tachycardia). (Book p397)
While typical AVNRT enters via the slow pathway and exits via the fast pathway, atypical AVNRT conducts antegradely by entering the ____ pathway and exiting via the slow pathway.
Under Pathway in the table: Typical enters Slow; exit Fast. Atypical enters Fast; exit Slow. (Book p397)
In the 1/3rd of typical AVNRT patients where P waves fall outside the QRS complex, which pseudo-wave description is NOT listed?
Pseudo delta wave: P wave distorting the initial PR segment
Pseudo S wave: P wave just outside QRS
Pseudo r' wave: P wave on r wave
Pseudo Q wave: P wave just before Q wave
The three listed pseudo waves on p398 are Pseudo S wave, Pseudo r' wave, and Pseudo Q wave. Pseudo delta wave is not part of this list. (Book p398)
A 28-year-old woman in regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 205 bpm receives a rapid IV push of adenosine. Which electrocardiographic response is demonstrated on the rhythm strip?
Conversion of AVNRT back to normal sinus rhythm
Persistent tachycardia with progressive PR prolongation
Development of complete third-degree heart block requiring pacing
The strip caption states: 'Can be converted to normal rhythm by adenosine', showing abrupt termination into normal sinus rhythm. (Book p398)
Which statement correctly describes the clinical associations and relative frequency of AVRT compared to AVNRT?
True — AVRT is rarer than AVNRT and is fundamentally associated with WPW syndrome
True — AVRT is far more common than AVNRT and occurs exclusively in elderly patients
False — AVRT has no association with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome or bypass tracts
False — AVNRT is an extranodal macro re-entry tachycardia whereas AVRT is strictly intranodal
Under AVRT: Features: Rarer than AVNRT; Associated with WPW syndrome. (Book p398)

Match each AVRT subtype to its impulse entry limb and resulting QRS complex width — 1) Orthodromic AVRT entry 2) Orthodromic AVRT QRS 3) Antidromic AVRT entry 4) Antidromic AVRT QRS … A) AV node B) Narrow QRS C) Bundle of Kent D) Wide QRS
Orthodromic AVRT: Entry AV node, Exit Bundle of Kent, Narrow QRS. Antidromic AVRT: Entry Bundle of Kent, Exit AV node, Wide QRS. (Book p398)
In orthodromic AVRT initiated by a well-timed PAC, which anatomical sequence describes the path of impulse propagation?
Enters AV node slowly, activates ventricles synchronously, conducts retrogradely via bypass tract, and re-enters AV node
Enters bypass tract rapidly, activates ventricles eccentrically, conducts retrogradely via AV node, and re-enters bypass tract
Blocks in AV node, travels down His bundle via slow pathway, and exits through ventricular myocardium
Enters pulmonary veins, activates left atrium, conducts retrogradely via sinus venosus, and terminates

Orthodromic AVRT: PAC enters AV node (conducted slowly), both ventricles activated synchronously, impulse enters bypass tract from ventricles to atrium retrogradely, and re-enters AV node. (Book p399)
On the ECG of orthodromic AVRT, the retrograde P wave falls just outside the QRS complex with an RP interval measured as:
ECG findings for orthodromic AVRT state: RP interval: 2 boxes ~ 80 - 100 ms, where P falls just outside QRS. (Book p399)
Comparing AVNRT versus AVRT in the summary table, which parameter is NOT correctly paired?
Underlying structural disease: AVNRT is linked to WPW syndrome, whereas AVRT has no structural link
Synchronous A-V activation: Present (+) in AVNRT, absent (-) in AVRT
RP interval: < 80 ms in AVNRT, 80 – 100 ms in AVRT
Re-entry circuit: Micro re-entry in AVNRT, macro re-entry in AVRT
Structural heart disease is absent (-) in AVNRT and associated with WPW syndrome in AVRT. The option reverses this association. (Book p399)
Both AVNRT and AVRT are categorized overall as short RP, long PR tachycardias; however, AVNRT displays an ultra-short RP interval of ____, while AVRT exhibits an RP interval of 80–100 ms.
In the comparison table, the RP interval is < 80 ms in AVNRT and 80 - 100 ms in AVRT. (Book p399)
Which statement regarding the hemodynamic status of patients with AVNRT compared to AVRT is stated in the comparison table?
True — AVNRT patients are characteristically stable, whereas AVRT patients may be stable or unstable
True — AVNRT patients are uniformly hemodynamically unstable requiring immediate DC shocks
False — AVRT patients are never hemodynamically unstable regardless of heart rate
False — Both AVNRT and AVRT uniformly cause immediate cardiogenic shock
In the table under Hemodynamic status: AVNRT is 'Stable', whereas AVRT is 'Stable/unstable'. (Book p399)
According to the concluding note on page 399, what distinct interval pattern differentiates atrial tachycardia from AVNRT and AVRT?
The note explicitly highlights: 'Atrial tachycardia: Long RP, short PR.' (Book p399)
Why is producing an AV nodal block the shared primary therapeutic goal in AVNRT, AVRT, and atrial tachycardia?
Because all three tachyarrhythmias operate through the AV node
Because the AV node is the primary source of ectopic ventricular automaticity
Because AV nodal blockade eliminates sympathetic outflow to peripheral vessels
Because the AV node directly dissolves micro re-entry within the coronary sinus
Under Goal: AVNRT, AVRT, Atrial tachycardia operate through AV Node -> mx: AV nodal block. (Book p400)
A patient in rapid narrow-complex tachycardia presents with severe hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg) and acute pulmonary edema. What is the immediate treatment of choice?
Intravenous verapamil 5 mg infusion over 2 minutes
For hemodynamically unstable patients, the indicated management is immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. (Book p400)
In a hemodynamically stable patient with SVT, which agent is the drug of choice (DOC) for AV nodal block, and what is its dual mechanism of action?
Adenosine; Blocks PAC in AVNRT/AVRT and decreases HR in atrial tachycardia
Verapamil; Prolongs ventricular refractoriness and terminates sinus node firing
Digoxin; Directly cardioverts macro re-entry and stimulates vagal tone
Amiodarone; Blocks fast sodium channels and inhibits thyroid release
DOC for AV nodal block in stable patients is Adenosine. MOA: AVNRT/AVRT: Blocks PAC; Atrial tachycardia: decreases HR. (Book p400)
What are the elimination half-life, arm-to-arm transit time, and arm-to-heart circulation time of intravenous adenosine?
T1/2: 6 s; Arm to arm: 15 s; Arm to heart: 7.5 s
T1/2: 30 s; Arm to arm: 60 s; Arm to heart: 20 s
T1/2: 2 min; Arm to arm: 10 s; Arm to heart: 5 s
T1/2: 6 s; Arm to arm: 30 s; Arm to heart: 15 s
Pharmacokinetics of adenosine: T1/2: 6 s; Arm to arm circulation: 15 s; Arm to heart circulation: 7.5 s. (Book p400)
What is the initial recommended bolus dose of adenosine via the brachial vein, and what is the cumulative maximum dose when repeated?
6 mg initial bolus; repeat 12 mg + 12 mg up to max 30 mg
3 mg initial bolus; repeat 6 mg + 6 mg up to max 15 mg
12 mg initial bolus; repeat 12 mg up to max 24 mg
6 mg initial bolus; repeat 6 mg up to max 18 mg
Administration: 6 mg through brachial vein (Repeat: 12 mg + 12 mg, max: 30 mg), followed by immediate saline flush/push/chase. (Book p400)
During the administration of adenosine via a peripheral line, what procedural posture and arm position are instructed on page 400 to optimize drug delivery?
Put patient in 45° supine position, administer adenosine, then shift patient to prone position and raise arm overhead
Keep patient strictly upright at 90°, administer adenosine, and lower both arms below heart level
Position patient in steep Trendelenburg at -30° throughout administration with bilateral leg elevation
Place patient in left lateral decubitus with arm held flush against the chest wall
Procedure: Put patient in 45° supine position -> Administer adenosine -> Shift patient to prone position + Raise arm overhead. (Book p400)
Why is it mandatory to have a defibrillator immediately ready when administering adenosine to a patient with suspected AVRT?
Adenosine can trigger atrial fibrillation which degenerates via the bypass tract: AF -> VT -> VF -> Death
Adenosine routinely precipitates rupture of the interventricular septum during SVT
Adenosine induces prolonged electrical systole and permanent electromechanical dissociation
Adenosine causes severe hypocalcemia triggering immediate asystole
Safety protocol: Have defibrillator ready: If AVRT treated with adenosine -> AF -> VT -> VF -> Death. (Book p400)
A known patient with COPD and bronchial asthma develops stable AVNRT. Why is adenosine contraindicated, and which alternative drug dosages are listed?
Causes bronchospasm; alternatives are verapamil 2.5–5 mg IV (max 15 mg), metoprolol 5 mg IV (max 15 mg), or esmolol
Causes laryngospasm; alternatives are amiodarone 300 mg bolus or flecainide 100 mg orally
Causes metabolic acidosis; alternatives are atropine 1 mg IV or dopamine infusion
Causes coronary vasodilation; alternatives are digoxin 0.5 mg IV or sotalol 80 mg IV
Adenosine is contraindicated in COPD/BA as it can cause bronchospasm. Alternatives: verapamil 2.5-5 mg IV (max 15 mg), metoprolol 5 mg IV (max 15 mg), or esmolol. (Book p400)
Which pharmacological agent is specifically indicated for managing AVNRT occurring in a patient with concurrent congestive heart failure?
Under alternatives/protocols on p400: 'Heart failure with AVNRT: Digoxin.' (Book p400)
What are the clinical features and underlying heart status in atrial tachycardia?
Structurally abnormal heart; chronic runs cause tachyarrhythmia-related cardiomyopathy; follows all 3 mechanisms (m/c enhanced automaticity)
Structurally normal heart; never causes cardiomyopathy; follows re-entry exclusively
Congenital accessory pathway; young athletic males; triggered early afterdepolarisations
Severe coronary calcification; elderly smokers; isolated macro re-entry circuits
Features: Structurally abnormal heart; Chronic: Tachyarrhythmia related cardiomyopathy; Follows all 3 mechanisms of tachycardia (m/c: enhanced automaticity). (Book p401)
What is the primary management strategy for atrial tachycardia to restore sinus rhythm, and what is reserved for rare failures?
Rate reduction using beta-blockers (metoprolol) or CCBs (verapamil); antiarrhythmics on failure
Immediate high-energy unsynchronized defibrillation followed by magnesium
Primary catheter ablation within 2 hours of symptom onset
Observation alone without pharmacological rate slowing
Management: decrease Rate -> Sinus rhythm with beta-blockers (metoprolol) or CCB (verapamil); failure (rare) -> Antiarrhythmics. (Book p401)

An ECG demonstrates a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm with uniform abnormal P waves, long RP, and short PR intervals. Over several minutes, the rate slowly accelerates before gradually slowing down. What rhythm and phenomenon does this represent?
Unifocal atrial tachycardia exhibiting warm-up and cool-down phenomenon
Typical AVNRT with sudden paroxysmal onset and termination
Orthodromic AVRT with variable accessory pathway conduction
Atrial flutter with fluctuating 3:1 and 4:1 AV block
Unifocal AT: Narrow QRS, Rate ~150 bpm, regular rhythm, uniform abnormal P waves, RP Long, PR Short. Note: Warm up & cool down phenomenon (slow increase & decrease of rate). (Book p401)

A COPD patient receiving theophylline develops an irregular rhythm. ECG shows irregular RR intervals with 3 distinct P-wave morphologies. What is the most common cause and the first step in management?
COPD / theophylline toxicity; Stop theophylline, then give beta-blocker/CCB to decrease heart rate
Digoxin toxicity; Administer digoxin-specific Fab fragments immediately
Severe hyperkalemia; Administer calcium gluconate followed by insulin-dextrose
Acute pulmonary embolism; Initiate systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
Multifocal AT: RR interval irregular + ≥ 3 P wave morphologies. m/c cause: COPD/theophylline. mx: Stop theophylline -> Beta-blocker/CCB: decrease HR. (Book p401)
Under the types of atrial tachycardia listed on page 401, atrial tachycardia with AV block is classically associated with ____.
Under Types: Unifocal AT, Multifocal AT, and AT with AV block: A/w digoxin. (Book p401)
An ECG rhythm strip shows atrial tachycardia with 2:1 AV block. How do the P waves and RR intervals appear on this tracing?
Normal conducted P waves alternating with buried/missed P waves, producing an irregular RR interval
Uniformly absent P waves with a strictly regular ventricular rate > 200 bpm
Chaotic fibrillatory waves with no discernible discrete atrial deflections
Biphasic flutter waves at 300 bpm conducted in a constant 1:1 ratio
AT with AV block: Normal P wave + Buried P wave; Irregular RR. Tracing annotates conducted P (circles) and missed P (squares) in 2:1 AV block. (Book p402)
In a narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves, what ventricular heart rate favors junctional tachycardia over AVNRT or AVRT?
Junctional tachyarrhythmia: No P wave (seen in AVNRT, AVRT, Junctional tachycardia); HR ~ 100 - 110 bpm favors Junctional >> AVNRT/AVRT. (Book p402)
According to the summary flowchart for narrow-complex tachycardia, which rhythm is classified under REGULAR R-R intervals rather than irregular R-R intervals?
Irregular R-R: MAT, Atrial flutter with variable block, Atrial fibrillation, and Focal AT with varying block. Sinus tachycardia has regular R-R intervals. (Book p402)

In regular narrow-complex tachycardias with present P waves, match each interval configuration to its diagnosis — 1) Short RP (< 80 ms), long PR 2) Short RP (> 80 ms), long PR 3) Long RP, short PR … A) AVNRT B) AVRT C) Atrial tachycardia
Summary tree: RP short, PR long -> AVRT (> 80 ms) and AVNRT; RP long, PR short -> Atrial tachycardia. (Book p402)
Where does atrial fibrillation rank among all sustained cardiac arrhythmias, and which rhythm is the most common overall?
2nd most common sustained arrhythmia (1st is sinus tachycardia)
1st most common sustained arrhythmia (2nd is sinus tachycardia)
3rd most common sustained arrhythmia (behind sinus tachycardia and AVNRT)
4th most common sustained arrhythmia (behind ventricular fibrillation, VT, and sinus tachycardia)
Under Features: 2nd m/c sustained cardiac arrhythmia (1st is sinus tachycardia). (Book p403)
Atrial fibrillation is characterized by chaotic, disorganised, ineffective atrial contractions that cause stasis of blood, leading to ____ and ultimately stroke.
Features: Chaotic, disorganised, ineffective contractions. Complication: Stasis of blood -> Embolism -> Stroke. (Book p403)
Which two primary clinical risk factors (R/F) are explicitly listed on page 403 for atrial fibrillation?
Under Features: R/F: Age, Hypertension. (Book p403)
What is the most common anatomical site (m/c site) of thrombus formation resulting from blood stasis in atrial fibrillation?
Features: m/c site: Appendages (specifically the left atrial appendage). (Book p403)
On the ECG in atrial fibrillation, while the ventricular rate is variable with irregular R-R intervals, what is the characteristic underlying atrial rate?
ECG features: Narrow QRS tachycardia, Rate: Variable (Atrial rate: 300-600 bpm), R-R interval: Irregular, Fibrillatory waves present. (Book p403)

Match each temporal classification of atrial fibrillation to its defining duration — 1) Paroxysmal AF 2) Persistent AF 3) Long standing persistent AF … A) Self-terminating < 48 hrs or cardioverted < 7 days B) Lasts > 7 days C) Lasts > 1 year
Classification table: Paroxysmal: Self terminating (Usually < 48 hrs) or cardioverted AF < 7 days; Persistent: Lasts > 7 days (> 1 year: Long standing persistent). (Book p403)

An echocardiogram in a patient with chronic AF reveals a left atrium dilated to > 4 cm in the context of structural heart disease. Cardioversion is abandoned. What category does this represent and what is the management strategy?
Persistent AF; Urgent electrical rhythm control
Valvular AF; Immediate high-dose IV amiodarone
Permanent AF: LA dilated > 4 cm: Structural heart disease; mx: Rate control (Accepting A. fib). (Book p403)
Which statement correctly defines Valvular versus Non-valvular atrial fibrillation according to the classification table?
True — Valvular AF is strictly defined by mitral stenosis (MS) or the presence of a prosthetic valve; all other AF is non-valvular
True — Any patient with mitral regurgitation or aortic stenosis is classified under Valvular AF
False — Prosthetic valve replacement converts a patient to Non-valvular AF
False — Mitral stenosis with AF is managed as Non-valvular AF in all clinical guidelines
Valvular AF: ms (mitral stenosis) + A.fib OR Prosthetic valve + A.fib. Non-valvular: All other A.fib. (Book p403)
Which systemic condition is NOT listed under the etiology of atrial fibrillation on page 403?
Etiology lists: OSAS, CKD, Psoriasis, Thyroid disease, Alcohol, Any cardiac/lung disease, and Electrolyte abnormalities. SLE is not listed on this page. (Book p403)
Under electrolyte abnormalities causing atrial fibrillation, the two specific disturbances identified are ____ and hypomagnesemia.
Electrolyte abnormalities listed are: Hypokalemia and Hypomagnesemia. (Book p403)

Match each clinical symptom of atrial fibrillation to its underlying pathophysiological mechanism — 1) Angina 2) Syncope 3) Dyspnoea 4) Palpitation … A) Increased myocardial oxygen demand B) Decreased cerebral circulation C) Decreased cardiac output D) Increased heart rate
C/F: Angina: increased demand; Syncope: decreased circulation; Dyspnoea: decreased cardiac output; Palpitation: increased HR. (Book p403)
How is the average ventricular heart rate calculated in an irregular rhythm like AF using the 6-second marker rule?
HR = Number of QRS complexes in 30 large boxes × 10
HR = Number of QRS complexes in 15 large boxes × 10
HR = 300 divided by the number of large boxes in the longest RR interval
HR = Number of QRS complexes in 6 large boxes × 30
Investigations: 6 second marker rule: HR = No. of QRS complexes in 30 large boxes x 10 (30 large boxes = 6 seconds). (Book p404)
A patient with irregular narrow tachycardia is evaluated on ECG. Which feature distinguishes the two primary differential diagnoses (MAT vs AT with AV block) from AF?
MAT has ≥ 3 morphologically different P waves; AT + AV block shows conducted + missed P waves
MAT has identical tall peaked P waves; AT + AV block exhibits chaotic fibrillatory baseline
MAT displays wide monomorphic QRS; AT + AV block displays complete lack of atrial activity
MAT shows short PR with delta waves; AT + AV block shows retrograde P waves in inferior leads
D/d: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT): ≥ 3 morphologically different P waves; Atrial tachycardia + AV block: Conducted + missed P waves. (Book p404)
What is the immediate treatment of choice for atrial fibrillation occurring in a hemodynamically unstable patient or in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?
Synchronised DC cardioversion (Start: 100 J -> max: 200 J)
Intravenous verapamil 10 mg push over 1 minute
Intravenous digoxin 0.5 mg bolus followed by beta-blockers
Oral flecainide 200 mg single loading dose
Hemodynamically unstable / WPW: Synchronised DC cardioversion; Start: 100 J -> max: 200 J. (Book p404)
A hemodynamically stable patient presents with newly detected AF. Initial 2D echocardiography reveals a left atrium dilated to 4.6 cm (> 4 cm). What strategy does the algorithm dictate?
Transesophageal echo followed by immediate pharmacological cardioversion
Stable pathway: 2D Echo of LA -> Dilated > 4 cm -> Rate control. (Book p404)
A hemodynamically stable patient with a normal LA size on 2D echo presents within 24 hours (< 48 hrs) of acute palpitation onset. What is the indicated management?
Mandatory 3 weeks of oral anticoagulation prior to any rhythm attempt
Transesophageal echocardiography to rule out left ventricular thrombus
Long-term rate control alone accepting permanent AF
Normal LA dimension with onset < 48 hrs -> No risk of embolism -> Rhythm control. (Book p404)
In a stable AF patient with normal LA size but symptom duration > 48 hours or unknown, what investigation is required to assess embolic risk before attempting cardioversion?
Onset > 48 hrs / unknown -> Risk of embolism (+) -> Trans Esophageal Echo (TEE) / Cardiac CT to check for clot. (Book p404)
If TEE or cardiac CT reveals an intracardiac clot in stable AF > 48 hours, the patient must receive ____ weeks of anticoagulants before pharmacological rhythm control is attempted.
Clot (+) pathway: 3 wks of anticoagulants -> Pharmacological rhythm control -> 4 wks of anticoagulants -> Assess CHA2DS2-VASc. (Book p404)
Following pharmacological rhythm control in a previously clot-positive patient, how many weeks of anticoagulation are mandatory before assessing the CHA2DS2-VASc score for long-term therapy?
Flowchart: Pharmacological rhythm control -> 4 wks of anticoagulants -> Assess CHA2DS2-VASc Score -> +/- Long term anticoagulants. (Book p404)
Which two drugs are listed as Class Ic antiarrhythmics for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation?
Rhythm control: Flecainide, Propafenone -> Class Ic antiarrhythmics. (Book p405)
Which drug is the overall DOC for rhythm control (not available in India), and which is the 2nd DOC (most commonly used in India)?
Vernakalant (DOC, not in India); Ibutilide (2nd DOC, m/c used: 1 mg IV over 10 mins)
Ibutilide (DOC, not in India); Flecainide (2nd DOC, m/c used: 100 mg orally)
Amiodarone (DOC, not in India); Vernakalant (2nd DOC, m/c used: 3 mg/kg IV)
Propafenone (DOC, not in India); Dofetilide (2nd DOC, m/c used: 500 mcg IV)
Vernakalant: DOC (Not available in India); Ibutilide: 2nd DOC (m/c used), 1 mg IV over 10 mins. (Book p405)
What is the drug of choice (DOC) for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation occurring in a structurally abnormal heart, and what is its dosing schedule?
Amiodarone: 150 mg IV bolus OR 5 mg/kg over 1 hr -> 1 mg/kg over 8 hrs -> 0.5 mg/kg over 16 hrs
Ibutilide: 1 mg IV bolus over 1 min repeated every 5 minutes up to 4 mg
Flecainide: 200 mg IV bolus over 10 minutes followed by oral propafenone
Dabigatran: 150 mg orally twice daily with immediate electric cardioversion
Amiodarone: DOC for structurally abnormal heart: 150 mg IV bolus OR 5 mg/kg over 1 hour -> 1 mg/kg over 8 hrs -> 0.5 mg/kg over 16 hours. (Book p405)

Match each rate control drug to its specific clinical indication or dosing protocol — 1) Verapamil rate control 2) Esmolol rate control 3) Propranolol rate control 4) Digoxin rate control … A) 5–10 mg over 2 mins (max: 20 mg) B) 500 mcg/kg over 1 min C) 1 mg IV over 2 mins (max: 5 mg) D) Indicated in failed LV
Rate control: Verapamil: 5-10 mg over 2 mins (max: 20 mg); Esmolol: 500 mcg/kg over 1 min; Propranolol: 1 mg IV over 2 mins (max: 5 mg); Digoxin: Failed LV. (Book p405)
Calculate the CHA2DS2-VASc score for a 77-year-old female patient with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and a history of ischemic stroke.
Score points: C=0, H=1, A (≥75)=2, D=1, S (stroke)=2, V=0, A (65-74)=0, S (female)=1. Total = 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7. (Book p405)
According to the CHA2DS2-VASc score recommendations, what score threshold requires anticoagulants, and what is indicated for a score of 1?
Score ≥ 3: Requires anticoagulants; Score = 2: Aspirin alone
Score ≥ 4: Requires anticoagulants; Score = 1–3: No therapy
Which clinical score is specifically noted on page 405 for assessing bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation patients?
Note: HAS-BLED score: Bleeding risk assessment in A.fib. (Book p405)
What is the general drug of choice (DOC) for anticoagulation in AF, and in which two exceptions is Warfarin the mandatory DOC?
DOC is Dabigatran; Warfarin for Valvular A.fib and A.fib + ESRD
DOC is Warfarin; Dabigatran for Valvular A.fib and A.fib + ESRD
DOC is Apixaban; Rivaroxaban for severe mitral regurgitation and CKD stage 3
DOC is Heparin; Aspirin for prosthetic heart valves and liver failure
Anticoagulants: DOC: Dabigatran. Exception: Valvular A.fib, A.fib + ESRD -> DOC: Warfarin. (Book p405)
In the 'pills in the pocket' technique for paroxysmal AF, patients are advised to consume oral flecainide combined with ____ at the acute onset of symptoms.
Pills in the pocket technique: Oral flecainide + β-blockers, in patients with paroxysmal A.fib, advised to consume at symptom onset. (Book p405)
In typical atrial flutter, what is the anatomical direction of right atrial re-entry, and how do flutter waves appear in lead II?
Counterclockwise re-entry; Flutter waves inverted in lead II
Clockwise re-entry; Flutter waves upright in lead II
Figure-of-eight re-entry; Flutter waves biphasic in lead II
Radial re-entry from pulmonary veins; Flutter waves absent in lead II
Typical atrial flutter: counterclockwise circuit in Right atrium (upward Left atrium activation), flutter waves inverted in lead II. (Book p406)
Which statement regarding reverse typical atrial flutter is accurate according to the diagram on page 406?
True — Re-entry in the right atrium is clockwise, left atrial activation is directed downwards, and flutter waves are upright in lead II
True — Reverse typical flutter produces deeply inverted sawtooth flutter waves across leads II, III, and aVF
False — Reverse typical flutter originates strictly from the left atrial appendage
False — In reverse typical flutter, the re-entry circuit moves counterclockwise around the tricuspid valve
Reverse typical atrial flutter: clockwise circuit in right atrium, downward left atrium activation, flutter waves upright in lead II. (Book p406)

A patient develops palpitations 4 days after undergoing open-heart bypass surgery. ECG demonstrates classic sawtooth waves. What anatomical site accounts for 90% of these cases and what is the typical post-op timing?
Lateral wall of Rt. Atrium (90%); Onset < 1 wk of open heart surgery
Left atrial posterior wall; Onset > 1 month of open heart surgery
Interventricular septum; Onset within 24 hours of thoracic trauma
Coronary sinus ostium; Onset 2 to 3 weeks following valve replacement
Features: Site: Lateral wall of Rt. Atrium (90%); Onset: < 1 wk of open heart surgery; ECG: Sawtooth appearance. (Book p406)
What is the treatment of choice (TOC) for acute atrial flutter, and what energy level is delivered?
Management: DC Cardioversion (TOC): 25-50 J; Ibutilide. (Book p406)
For definitive curative management of typical atrial flutter, catheter ablation is performed targeting the ____ isthmus.
Under management: 'Catheter ablation: Site -> Cavotricuspid isthmus.' (Book p406)
