In broad QRS tachyarrhythmias arising from the ventricle, impulses bypass specialized conduction fibers and propagate slowly via ____ transmission to widen the QRS complex.
Pathophysiology: Source: Ventricle generates impulse -> Cell-to-cell transmission -> Broad QRS. (Book p407)

Match each ventricular rhythm to its characteristic rate range — 1) Idioventricular tachycardia (IVT) 2) Accelerated idioventricular tachycardia (AIVT) 3) Ventricular tachycardia (VT) … A) 15 – 40 bpm B) 40 – 100 bpm C) > 100 bpm
Rate: IVT: 15-40 bpm; AIVT: 40-100 bpm; Ventricular Tachycardia (VT): > 100 bpm. (Book p407)
Following thrombolytic therapy for acute inferior STEMI, a patient develops a wide-complex rhythm at 75 bpm. What rhythm is this and what is its clinical significance?
Accelerated idioventricular tachycardia (AIVT); Sign of successful thrombolysis
Monomorphic VT; Sign of extensive reperfusion injury requiring immediate DC shock
Idioventricular escape rhythm; Sign of complete AV node necrosis
Antidromic AVRT; Sign of accessory pathway unmasking
Accelerated Idioventricular Tachycardia (AIVT): rate 40-100 bpm, indicates successful thrombolysis. (Book p407)
Which QRS duration definitively indicates true ventricular tachycardia, as opposed to the intermediate 0.12–0.16 s range seen in SVT with BBB or antidromic AVRT?
Causes: QRS > 0.16 s: VT; QRS 0.12 - 0.16 s: SupraVT with bundle branch block (BBB) or Antidromic AVRT (WPW syndrome). (Book p407)
What is the defining electrophysiological mechanism of a ventricular premature complex (VPC / extrasystole)?
Premature discharge from ventricle occurring earlier than next anticipated sinus beat
Delayed conduction through AV node resulting in an escape ventricular contraction
Continuous macro re-entry circulating around the tricuspid valve ring
Triggered early afterdepolarisation arising from prolonged atrial repolarisation
Mechanism of VPC: Extrasystole; Premature discharge from ventricle; Occurs earlier than next anticipated sinus beat. (Book p407)
Which finding is NOT among the six diagnostic criteria for VPC listed on page 407?
Preceded by a normal peaked P wave with short PR interval
Very wide QRS complex with ST/T changes in opposite direction
Always constant coupling interval between VPC and preceding QRS

Criteria for VPC: 1. Not preceded by P wave; 2. Very wide QRS complex; 3. ST/T changes in opposite direction; 4. Coupling interval always constant; 5. Compensatory pause; 6. R on T phenomena. (Book p407)
In classic unifocal VPCs, the coupling interval (distance between the VPC and the preceding QRS complex) is characteristically ____.
Criteria: 4. Coupling interval: Distance b/w VPC & preceding QRS complex: Always constant. (Book p407)
On the ECG measuring a fully compensatory pause following a VPC, how does the distance between two sinus impulses across the VPC compare to normal sinus cycles?
Distance across VPC equals distance across two normal beats (2 × RR interval)
Distance across VPC is shorter than a single normal RR interval
Distance across VPC is exactly equal to one normal sinus RR interval
Distance across VPC equals three times the baseline QT interval
Compensatory pause: Distance b/w 2 sinus impulses across VPC = Distance b/w 2 sinus impulses across normal beat (2 x RR; e.g. A = 1340 ms = B = 1340 ms). (Book p407)
A monitoring strip captures a premature ventricular contraction falling directly upon the preceding T wave. What is this phenomenon called and what risk does it carry?
R-on-T phenomenon; Can precipitate ventricular fibrillation or polymorphic VT
Ashman phenomenon; Signifies physiological rate-dependent bundle aberrancy
Wenckebach phenomenon; Leads to progressive PR prolongation and sinus arrest
Concealed conduction; Guarantees immediate termination of all ventricular ectopy
Criterion 6: R on T phenomena: VPC lies on previous wave (T wave), risking lethal ventricular arrhythmias. (Book p407)
An ECG rhythm strip reveals frequent VPCs with variable coupling intervals measured at 760 ms, 640 ms, 580 ms, and 460 ms. What diagnosis does this variation establish?
Note: Parasystole: VPCs with different coupling intervals (tracing demonstrates varying intervals: 760 ms, 640 ms, 580 ms, 460 ms). (Book p408)
How are multifocal ventricular premature complexes defined on the electrocardiogram?
VPCs occurring at different times of the diurnal cycle
VPCs that conduct retrogradely into both atria simultaneously
VPCs originating alternately from the left and right bundle branches

An ____ VPC is defined as a premature ventricular complex sandwiched between two normal sinus impulses without disturbing the sinus rhythm or creating a compensatory pause.

Match each ventricular ectopy frequency pattern to its exact definition — 1) Ventricular bigeminy 2) Ventricular trigeminy 3) Couplet … A) Isolated VPB after every sinus beat B) Isolated VPB after every 2 sinus beats C) 2 VPBs in a row
Frequency: Ventricular bigeminy: Isolated VPBs after every sinus beat; Ventricular trigeminy: Isolated VPBs after every 2 sinus beats; Couplet: 2 VPBs in a row. (Book p408)
According to the frequency criteria on page 408, what consecutive run of VPBs and what heart rate threshold officially define Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)?
≥ 3 VPBs in a row + HR > 100 bpm
≥ 2 VPBs in a row + HR > 120 bpm
≥ 5 VPBs in a row + HR > 90 bpm
≥ 6 VPBs in a row + HR > 150 bpm
Under Frequency: 'VT : ≥ 3 VPBs in a row + HR > 100 bpm.' (Book p408)
A patient with no structural heart disease is found to have asymptomatic isolated VPCs causing occasional palpitations. What is the indicated treatment and what is contraindicated?

Immediate oral amiodarone loading; Beta-blockers are contraindicated
Elective catheter ablation within 2 weeks; Observation is contraindicated
Intravenous lidocaine infusion; Defibrillator implantation is contraindicated

Increased frequency of episodes, multifocal VPCs, and bigeminy/couplets
First episode presenting at age > 40 years
Ectopy not affected by exercise, parasystole, and underlying LV dysfunction

Wide QRS tachycardia (> 0.16 s), Rate > 200 bpm, and all complexes look alike
Narrow QRS tachycardia (< 0.12 s), Rate 150 bpm, and changing polarities
Intermediate QRS (0.12–0.16 s), Rate 100 bpm, with sawtooth flutter waves
Irregular wide QRS complexes with continually twisting electrical axes

Which statement regarding the transition shown on the 12-lead ECG panel at the bottom of page 409 is accurate?

True — The 12-lead ECG strip shows typical AVNRT transitioning into normal sinus rhythm after adenosine

On a monitor strip of wide-complex tachycardia, one beat displays hybrid features of both a normal sinus impulse and a ventricular ectopic focus, while another beat is completely narrow where the sinus beat briefly captured the ventricles. What are these beats called?

Distance from J-point to peak of T wave > 440 ms
PR interval duration exceeding 200 ms during tachycardia
Peak-to-peak amplitude of QRS complex > 25 mm in precordial leads
Brugada sign: Distance from onset of QRS complex to nadir of S wave: > 100 ms. (Book p410)

The presence of distinct notching at the nadir of the S wave in a wide QRS tachycardia is designated as ____ sign.

What is meant by positive or negative precordial concordance, and what is its clinical significance in wide-complex tachycardia?
All precordial leads (V1–V6) show completely positive or completely negative QRS complexes; strongly indicates VT
Precordial leads alternate strictly between upright and inverted deflections; confirms SVT with aberrancy
Limb leads match chest leads in frontal axis direction; rules out structural heart disease
Lead V1 and V6 share identical RS ratios; diagnostic of uncomplicated bundle branch block
Cardinal features list +ve or -ve concordance (all precordial leads positive or all negative), which points to ventricular tachycardia. (Book p410)

Which statement regarding Brugada criteria for diagnosing VT on this page is accurate?
True — Brugada criteria include RS complex absent or > 100 ms, alongside no P waves / AV dissociation
True — Brugada criteria mandate normal PR interval and absence of S waves across all 12 leads
False — AV dissociation on ECG rules out ventricular tachycardia and confirms sinus mechanism
False — Brugada criteria apply exclusively to narrow QRS tachycardias lasting < 30 seconds

Lignocaine: 500 mg IV infusion over 1 hour followed by oral mexiletine

How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia defined, and what condition is it typically associated with when accompanied by a prolonged QT interval?
Multiple different complexes with changing polarities; Torsades de pointes (TdP)
Identical uniform complexes at 150 bpm; Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
Narrow QRS complexes with absent P waves; Inappropriate sinus tachycardia
Sawtooth oscillations around baseline; Reverse typical atrial flutter
Polymorphic VT: multiple different complexes with changing polarities; usually a/w prolonged QT: Torsades de pointes (TdP). (Book p411)

Decreased K+, decreased Ca2+, decreased Mg2+, and hypothermia

What is the characteristic sex predilection stated for Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?

Which electrocardiographic finding is NOT part of the classic ECG pattern of WPW syndrome listed on page 413?
Short PR interval and delta waves
Near normal QRS with secondary ST and T wave changes
ECG features: Normal P wave, Short PR interval, Delta waves, Near normal QRS, Secondary ST & T wave changes. PR is short, not prolonged. (Book p413)
The electrophysiological mechanism of WPW syndrome involves an aberrant accessory pathway known as the Bundle of ____ that causes pre-excitation of the ventricle.
Mechanism: Bundle of Kent: Aberrant pathway -> Pre-excitation of ventricle. (Book p413)

Match each WPW type to its 12-lead ECG appearance and antegrade conduction pathway — 1) Concealed WPW 12-lead ECG 2) Concealed WPW antegrade limb 3) Manifest WPW 12-lead ECG 4) Manifest WPW antegrade limb … A) Normal B) Via AV node C) Abnormal D) Via Bundle of Kent (BOK)
Types table: Concealed: 12-lead ECG Normal, Antegrade via AV node; Manifest: 12-lead ECG Abnormal, Antegrade via Bundle of Kent (BOK). (Book p413)
Which two arrhythmias can be triggered by a premature atrial complex (PAC) in both concealed and manifest WPW syndrome?
Sinus arrest and Mobitz type II block
Under Arrhythmias triggered by PAC: Both Concealed and Manifest forms can develop Orthodromic AVRT and A.fib. (Book p413)
Which statement accurately reflects the clinical prognosis of Atrial Fibrillation occurring in concealed versus manifest WPW on page 413?
True — In concealed WPW, A.fib carries a bad prognosis and responds only to DC cardioversion, whereas manifest WPW has a better prognosis due to early diagnosis
True — In concealed WPW, A.fib responds promptly to intravenous verapamil and carries an excellent prognosis
False — Manifest WPW carries a uniformly fatal prognosis because early diagnosis cannot be achieved

Prognosis: Concealed: A.fib: Bad prognosis, responds only to DC Cardioversion. Manifest: Better prognosis (d/t early diagnosis). (Book p413)
In the classification of WPW by accessory pathway location, which is the most common anatomical subtype?
Left sided WPW is designated as Type A (m/c). (Book p414)

A 22-year-old male undergoes a routine sports physical. ECG shows a short PR interval, small delta wave, and a tall positive R wave in lead V1. What type of WPW is present and what is the direction of ventricular activation?
Left-sided WPW (Type A); Conduction proceeds from Left to Right
Right-sided WPW (Type B); Conduction proceeds from Right to Left
Concealed WPW; Conduction proceeds solely through the AV node
Mahaim fiber pre-excitation; Conduction proceeds from Apex to Base

An ECG reveals a large delta wave with a predominantly negative R wave / deep QS complex in lead V1. Which accessory pathway variant does this morphology indicate?
Right-sided WPW (Type B) with Right-to-Left conduction
Left-sided WPW (Type A) with Left-to-Right conduction
Anterior fascicular block with isolated septal pre-excitation
Typical AVNRT with slow-fast dual AV nodal physiology
Right sided WPW (Type B): Delta wave large, Conduction Rt -> Lt, V1 lead: -ve R wave + delta wave. (Book p414)

Match each WPW variant to its delta wave size and lead V1 morphology — 1) Type A left-sided delta wave 2) Type A lead V1 appearance 3) Type B right-sided delta wave 4) Type B lead V1 appearance … A) Small (less myocardial activation) B) Positive tall R wave C) Large D) Negative R wave
Type A: Small delta, +ve tall R wave in V1. Type B: Large delta, -ve R wave in V1. (Book p414)

In manifest WPW, the lack of delay across the Bundle of Kent initiates early ventricular pre-excitation (producing the short PR and delta wave), after which the AV nodal impulse ____ to complete a near-normal QRS duration.
Manifest WPW diagram: Bundle of Kent (no delay) -> Pre-excitation (Short PR, delta wave); AV node -> Catch up -> Near normal QRS complex. (Book p414)
In a patient known to have concealed WPW who develops acute Atrial Fibrillation, what is the indicated management on page 414?
Under Management of Concealed WPW: If AVRT -> Adenosine -> Refer to Electrophysiologist; If A.fib -> Synchronised DC cardioversion. (Book p414)
What is the definitive curative treatment (Definitive Rx) for manifest WPW syndrome identified on early diagnosis?
Surgical division of the AV node

In manifest WPW, what electrocardiographic pattern is observed after acute tachycardia (AVRT or A.fib) is successfully terminated?
True — Conversion reveals sinus rhythm accompanied by the baseline delta wave, after which the patient is referred to an electrophysiologist
True — Conversion produces permanent complete AV block with an idioventricular escape pacemaker
False — Following cardioversion, the delta wave disappears permanently from all subsequent ECGs
False — Manifest WPW cannot be converted with adenosine or DC cardioversion

In the flowchart for manifest WPW: AVRT treated with Adenosine and A.fib treated with Synchronised DC cardioversion both yield 'Sinus rhythm + delta wave', followed by 'Refer to Electrophysiologist'. (Book p414)
A ruptured coronary plaque causes a critical, fibrin-rich occlusive thrombus. Which acute coronary syndrome is the source most directly linking to this lesion?

Which set contains only determinants of myocardial oxygen demand in the source?
Coronary diameter, heart rate and perfusion pressure

A patient with central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia is described as having the page's ‘Syndrome Z’. What associated condition is specifically listed?

Which is listed as a non-plaque cause of large-vessel coronary artery disease?

An hs-CRP result is 3.4 mg/dL in the source's risk-factor scheme. How is this tier marked?

Which lipoprotein pattern is specifically identified as a plaque risk factor on this page?

Which three consequences are listed under hypertension as a risk factor for plaque formation?

Which cluster of factors follows hyperlipidaemia in the plaque-risk list and includes diabetes with centripetal obesity, age 40–50 and a gender pattern?

Which lipid result meets the source's first listed statin indication and its stated target?

The HOPE trial note on this page associates ramipril with reduction in fatal and non-vascular events. Which drug class is highlighted as superior to ARBs in that note?

What does the Agatston score use to determine the degree of coronary calcification?

Which note under lifestyle modifications links protein malnutrition to a laboratory marker of atherosclerosis?

A person with a plaque burden above 70% is asymptomatic. According to the patient-presentation flowchart, which outcome is linked to that branch?

A middle-aged patient reports squeezing retrosternal tightness with exertion, lasting 12 minutes, relieved promptly by sublingual nitroglycerin. Which presentation does this most support?

Under the printed Bruce-protocol criterion, which treadmill finding is positive and warrants angiography?

Which investigation is called the investigation of choice for both myocardial fibrosis and ejection fraction, and the gold standard for ejection fraction?

A stable-angina patient has persistent symptoms after three sublingual NTG tablets over 20 minutes. What does the source flowchart direct the clinician to consider?
Acute coronary syndrome and first-line NTG plus beta-blocker strategy
Long-term ivabradine as the only option
No further action because the symptoms are stable

In the alternatives table for stable angina, which first- and second-line drug effects are correctly stated?

Nitrates increase pump function and have no tolerance

CCBs only increase HR without BP effect

Which antianginal is listed as a funny-current inhibitor that can cause visual disturbance?

Which new antianginal drug is identified as a Rho-kinase inhibitor?

Which three agents are identified as GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors used around stenting to reduce periprocedural events?

A patient has recurrent midnight-to-early-morning rest pain lasting 10 minutes, transient ST elevation, normal angiography, and rapid nitrate relief. Which treatment precaution follows the source?

Prinzmetal angina is rest angina, lasts 5–15 min, has transient ST elevation and normal angiography; beta-blockers are to be avoided. (Book p420)
What anatomical interval is also called the Kingmaker segment?
PR segment, from end of P to QRS onset
QT interval, from QRS onset to T-wave end
TP segment, from T-wave end to P-wave onset
ST segment, from the end of J point to onset of T wave
Kingmaker segment is stated to be the ST segment: end of J point to onset of T wave. (Book p420)
Subepicardial/transmural injury creates a current directed toward injured myocardium. Which ST change does the page associate with this direction?

Systolic current from subepicardial/transmural injury flows toward injured myocardium and produces ST elevation (MI or pericarditis); subendocardial diastolic current flows away and produces non-localising ST depression. (Book p420)
Which ST-elevation contour is attributed to pericarditis in the current-of-injury diagrams?
The diagrams contrast non-concave/convex ST elevation in MI with concave/saddle-shaped elevation in pericarditis. (Book p420)
What calibration and intervals are shown in the ECG intervals diagram on page 420?
Calibration 1 mV = 10 mm with only QT interval
Only QRS width is shown without intervals
Small box 0.04 s (40 ms) and 0.20 s (200 ms); PR interval, ST interval, TP interval and QT interval are labelled
Small box 0.12 s only with QRS width alone
The diagram labels PR interval, ST interval, TP interval, QT interval and RR interval with calibration 0.04 s =40 ms and 0.20 s =200 ms. (Book p420)
Which condition is NOT listed among the page's other causes of ST elevation?
Listed alternatives are Prinzmetal angina, hyperkalaemia > hypokalaemia, LBBB, benign early repolarisation and LV aneurysm. (Book p421)
Which ST-elevation morphology is treated as ACS on the figure rather than a low-likelihood pattern?
Convex and coved morphologies are labelled ACS; horizontal/plateau is ‘ACS unless proven otherwise’; oblique is <30% ACS and concave <15% ACS. (Book p421)
For a male older than 40 years, what precordial ST elevation in V2–V3 is the significant threshold printed on the page?
Significant V2–V3 elevation is ≥2.5 mm if <40 years, ≥2 mm if >40 years, and ≥1.5 mm in females; reciprocal changes must be present in the source's MI diagnosis note. (Book p421)
Which ECG change appears earliest in the displayed STEMI evolution sequence?
The sequence progresses from hyperacute T wave to hyperacute T waves with ST elevation, then pathological Q/decreasing R and further ST/T changes over hours to days. (Book p421)
ST elevation is present in I and aVL with reciprocal ST depression in inferior leads. How is this ECG example labelled on the page?
The illustrated tracing is captioned ST elevation with reciprocal changes and marks a high lateral MI pattern. (Book p421)
An ECG shows ST elevation in V2–V3 at the transient zone without reciprocal changes. How is this labelled on page 421?
Normal ST elevation at the transient zone
Benign early repolarisation with PR depression
The page marks normal ST elevation at the transient zone in V2–V3 without pathological reciprocal changes. (Book p421)
An ECG shows ST elevation with J-point notching (‘hook effect’) but no PR-segment depression. Which diagnosis is most consistent with the source?
Benign early repolarisation has ST elevation and J-point hook effect; PR depression supports pericarditis instead. (Book p422)
A patient with acute illness has diffuse concave-upward ST elevation, PR depression, and no reciprocal changes. What diagnosis fits best?
The pericarditis block gives clinical features/acute illness, global concave upward ST elevation, PR depression and no reciprocal changes. (Book p422)
Which ECG deflection is the classic marker of hypothermia on the page?
Hypothermia is labelled with an Osborne wave. The page also illustrates post-DC-cardioversion tracing and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. (Book p422)
A middle-aged woman develops catecholamine-induced cardiac failure after emotional stress and mimics ST elevation. Which source term applies?
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is labelled catecholamine-induced cardiac failure/broken-heart syndrome and most common in middle-aged females. (Book p422)
Which description best distinguishes the page's pericarditis tracing from benign early repolarisation?
A J-point hook is obligatory in pericarditis
Reciprocal change is universal in pericarditis
The printed differential says BER has no PR depression; pericarditis has PR depression, global concave elevation and no reciprocal changes. (Book p422)
In the page's V1–V3 summary, which diagnosis is paired with a pseudo-infarction pattern due to hyperkalaemia?
The summary panel lists LVH, LBBB, acute pericarditis, pseudo-infarction pattern (hyperkalaemia), acute anteroseptal MI, acute anterolateral MI and Brugada syndrome. (Book p423)
A depressed ST segment has a horizontal contour. What interpretation is written below that morphology?
The summary labels horizontal ST depression ‘probable ischemia’; sloping ST is strain-related and scoop-shaped ST is digoxin-related. (Book p423)
A patient on digoxin has a characteristically scooped ST depression. This contour should be attributed to:
The ‘scoop’ example is explicitly labelled digoxin related; morphology must be interpreted in clinical context. (Book p423)
What ECG pattern is noted to evolve to MI on the page?
The final tracing is captioned ‘de Winter T waves: evolves to MI.’ (Book p423)
Tall, peaked T waves are illustrated as the repolarisation pattern of which ischaemic location?
The page contrasts normal myocardium, tall/peaked T waves in subendocardial ischaemia, and deep symmetrical inversion in transmural ischaemia. (Book p424)
Deep, symmetrically inverted T waves most strongly indicate the source's:
Deep symmetrical T inversion is labelled transmural ischaemia; tall/peaked T waves are subendocardial ischaemia. (Book p424)
In the illustrated progression, hyperacute T waves develop into which major acute ECG pattern?
The lower paired ECGs show hyperacute T waves progressing to STEMI. (Book p424)
A prominent U wave on the source strip points to which electrolyte disorder?
The note beneath the strip states ‘U waves: Hypokalemia.’ (Book p424)
The serial ST-depression tracings on the page are time-stamped at 60, 90 and:
The page presents serial ST-depression changes at 60, 90 and 120 minutes before its T-wave panels. (Book p424)
Which infarct territories are assigned to right coronary circulation on the source overview?
Apical, high-lateral and anterior MI only
Right coronary circulation is linked to IWMI, PWMI and RVMI; left circulation is linked to AWMI, septal MI and LWMI. (Book p425)

Which chamber forms the anterior sternocostal surface of the heart in the source anatomy list?
Surface list: anterior sternocostal = RV; inferior diaphragmatic = RV+LV; posterior = LA. (Book p425)

A patient has a posterior descending artery arising from the RCA. Which dominance pattern and approximate frequency does the page give?

Which leads are listed for inferior-wall involvement in right coronary circulation?
Inferior leads are II, III, aVF; RV free-wall V3R/V4R/V5R and posterior V7/V8/V9 are not represented on a standard 12-lead ECG; lateral V5/V6 show reciprocal changes. (Book p425)

Which named lead group assesses right-ventricular free wall in this chapter?
Right free-wall leads are V3R–V5R. The source separately lists V7–V9 for posterior wall assessment. (Book p425)

What is the stated origin of the right coronary artery?
The RCA is shown arising in the right AV sulcus. (Book p426)

An inferior MI is accompanied by sinus bradycardia after proximal RCA occlusion. Which RCA branch mechanism is most directly implicated?
The SA nodal branch section states proximal RCA occlusion can cause sinus bradycardia; bradycardia can also reflect vagal stimulation or nodal ischaemia. (Book p426)

Atrial arrhythmias after proximal RCA occlusion are linked to compromise of which branch group?
Atrial branches in the right AV sulcus
Atrial branches run in the right atrioventricular sulcus; proximal RCA occlusion is linked to atrial arrhythmias. (Book p426)
Coronary Territories, Dominance & Right Coronary Artery
An RCA occlusion proximal to the acute marginal artery is most likely to have which implication?
RVMI is present and prognosis is poorer
Occlusion relation to acute marginal artery: proximal means RVMI always positive and poorer prognosis; distal means RVMI always negative. (Book p426)
Coronary Territories, Dominance & Right Coronary Artery
Which structure does the acute marginal artery supply?
The acute marginal artery supplies the RV free wall. (Book p426)
Coronary Territories, Dominance & Right Coronary Artery
An IWMI patient is hypotensive, has clear lung fields and elevated JVP. What is the source's immediate management direction?
The page's RVMI triangle is hypotension, clear lung fields and raised JVP, with management IV fluids. (Book p426)
Coronary Territories, Dominance & Right Coronary Artery
In a right-dominant circulation, distal RCA occlusion produces which infarct pattern?
RCA occlusion flowchart: right dominant proximal → RVMI+IWMI±PWMI; right dominant distal → IWMI±PWMI. Left-dominant distal RCA causes no MI. (Book p426)
Coronary Territories, Dominance & Right Coronary Artery
Which complication group is listed under IWMI?
LBBB with high-grade infra-His block only
SA/AV nodal dysfunction, complete heart block, atrial tachycardia, RVMI and posteromedial papillary-muscle rupture
VT/VF, external rupture and septal rupture only
IWMI list includes SA node/AV node/complete heart block, atrial tachycardia, RVMI, and posteromedial papillary muscle rupture causing secondary MR. (Book p426)
Coronary Territories, Dominance & Right Coronary Artery
Inferior ST elevation is greater in lead III than lead II, with ST depression in aVL greater than aVR. Which culprit artery does the source favour?
For RCA: ST↑ in II/III/aVF, reciprocal V1/V5/V6; III > II and ST↓ aVL > aVR. LCx instead has II > III. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
An IWMI ECG has ST depression in V1 discordant to V2–V3. What associated extension does the page indicate?
Proximal RCA: ST depression in V1 discordant to V2/V3 is marked RVMI positive. ‘Wrap around’ indicates RCA supplies all regions. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
Which lead relationship favours LCx occlusion in an inferior/posterior MI pattern?
ST elevation in II greater than III
ST elevation in III greater than II
ST depression in aVL greater than aVR
The LCx note lists IWMI+PWMI and ST elevation in II > III; in left dominance, LCx lateral-wall supply may add LWMI. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
After an inferior MI and PCI, a patient has pulmonary congestion, an LV S3, no murmur, good EF, and a normal/near-normal ECG. Which mechanical diagnosis should still be suspected?
The page identifies papillary muscle rupture → secondary MR in post-IWMI PCI with CCF; it notes LV S3, absent murmur, good EF and normal/near-normal ECG. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
Where does the LAD run according to the left-coronary-circulation diagram?
LCA branches into LCx and LAD; the LAD site is the left anterior interventricular sulcus. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
Which branch–territory association is correctly stated?
D1 supplies high lateral wall and septal branches supply septal wall
D1 supplies posterior wall and S1 supplies lateral wall
LCx/LAD branch map: D1 high lateral wall, S1 septal wall, D2 anterior wall, D3 lateral wall; D=diagonal and S=septal. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
Which lead grouping is designated as high lateral MI territory?
LAD/LCx lead map: anterior V2–V4, lateral V5–V6, high lateral I/aVL, septal V1>>V2, apical V1. (Book p427)
Inferior MI Localisation & Left Coronary Anatomy
Which LAD-occlusion location is listed before the first diagonal (D1) branch?
The localisation list proceeds: before D1; between D1 and S1; and below S1 (with branches S1–D2 or D2–D3). (Book p428)
An anteroseptal high-lateral MI has ST elevation in V2–V4, V1, and I/aVL. Which localisation bundle does the page assign?
LAD above S1 and before D1
For anteroseptal high-lateral MI: V2–V4 elevation indicates LAD, V1 elevation indicates above S1, and I/aVL elevation indicates before D1. (Book p428)
ST elevation in V2–V4 is present but V1 lacks elevation. What LAD localisation does this support?
The wrap-around section says V2–V4 elevation is above D2; V1 no elevation is below S1; II/V5/V6 elevation identifies wrap-around. (Book p428)
An anterior infarct has ST elevation in II, V5 and V6 in addition to anterior leads. Which anatomical pattern is represented?
The page explicitly labels II, V5 and V6 elevation as wrap-around phenomenon; course enters posterior interventricular sulcus and anastomoses with PDA. (Book p428)
An anterolateral MI is anatomically described as which relationship?
S1 before D1 with occlusion between S1 and D1
D1 before S1 with occlusion below S1
The source states anterolateral MI has anatomical S1 before D1 and occlusion between S1 and D1. (Book p428)
V1 ST elevation with ST depression in I and aVL is shown under which infarct localisation?
The anteroseptal section labels V1 ST elevation as above S1 and I/aVL ST depression as between D1 and S1. (Book p428)
An ECG shows ST elevation in aVR with ST depression in all other leads. What urgent intervention does the source prescribe?
Immediate PCI for proximal left-coronary/left-main occlusion
Proximal LCA occlusion: aVR ST elevation, all other leads ST depression, 100% mortality if untreated; immediate PCI is specified. (Book p429)
Which electrical complications are listed for LV involvement in AWMI?
Ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death
Atrial flutter and sinus bradycardia only
AWMI LV involvement includes VT, VF and sudden cardiac death; mechanical complications include external cardiac rupture and septal rupture, plus infra-Hisian blocks. (Book p429)
Which conduction abnormality is named among AWMI complications?
The AWMI complication list includes infra-Hisian blocks, in contrast to the nodal problems emphasised in IWMI. (Book p429)
After fixed plaque rupture, which thrombus–clinical-syndrome pairing is correct in the source's older ACS flowchart?
Platelet-rich incomplete occlusion → chronic stable angina
Critical fibrin-rich occlusion → unstable angina with normal enzymes
The obsolete scheme maps critical fibrin-rich thrombus to STEMI/STE-ACS and incomplete platelet-rich thrombus to NSTE-ACS; normal enzymes mean unstable angina and raised enzymes NSTEMI. (Book p430)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
What is the current universal definition of acute MI stated on the page?
ST elevation in a single ECG lead
A fixed plaque found on angiography
Myocardial injury plus or minus clinical evidence of myocardial ischaemia
Any chest pain with a positive stress test
The page replaces the older model with myocardial injury ± clinical evidence of myocardial ischaemia. (Book p430)

Which troponin pattern fulfils the page's definition of myocardial injury?
A stable value below the 50th percentile
One high troponin with no serial measurement
At least one value above the 99th percentile with an acute rise and fall
Myocardial injury is cardiac troponin T/I with at least one value above the 99th percentile and an acute rise and fall. (Book p430)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
A septic ICU patient has elevated troponin without evidence of acute coronary ischaemia. Which category of cause is the page illustrating?

Non-cardiac causes listed include sepsis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, CKD, critical illness and pulmonary embolism. Cardiac causes include myocarditis, Takotsubo, defibrillator shocks, tachyarrhythmia and spasm/embolism/dissection. (Book p430)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
A patient with sustained tachyarrhythmia develops myocardial oxygen demand excess and troponin elevation. Which mechanism category is explicitly shown?
The causes tree lists increased O2 demand from tachyarrhythmia and decreased supply from spasm, embolism or dissection. (Book p430)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
Which clinical finding is one of the page's five forms of evidence for myocardial ischaemia?
Clinical evidence listed: symptoms, new ECG changes, pathological Q waves, imaging evidence of new RWMA, and angiographic evidence of coronary thrombus. (Book p431)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
Which MI subtype is defined by demand–supply mismatch, with ICU patients and severe anaemia given as examples?
Type 1 is atherothrombotic occlusion; Type 2 is supply/demand mismatch (ICU patients, severe anaemia); Type 3 sudden cardiac death; Type 4 post-PCI; Type 5 post-CABG. (Book p431)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
Which universal MI subtype is related to percutaneous coronary intervention?
The list gives Type 4 as post-percutaneous coronary intervention and Type 5 as post-coronary artery bypass graft. (Book p431)

Ultra-sensitive troponin assays can detect enzyme elevation down to approximately which concentration in the source?
The graph note says ultrasensitive troponin assays can detect as low as 0.01 ng/mL of enzyme elevation. (Book p431)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
A rising/falling troponin above the 99th-percentile URL occurs with acute ischaemia and plaque rupture/erosion. What diagnosis does the source flowchart assign?

Rise/fall with acute ischaemia is acute MI; the atherosclerosis/thrombosis arm is Type 1 (plaque rupture/erosion). Without acute ischaemia it is acute injury; stable troponin is chronic injury. (Book p431)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
A stable troponin elevation in a patient with structural heart disease or chronic kidney disease is classified as:
The stable-troponin branch is chronic myocardial injury and gives structural heart disease and CKD as examples. (Book p431)
Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
How does the page distinguish reinfarction from recurrence by timing?
Reinfarction within 28 days; recurrence after 28 days
Reinfarction after 90 days; recurrence within 90 days
Reinfarction within 24 hours; recurrence after one week
The table defines reinfarction within 28 days and recurrence after 28 days. (Book p432)
For suspected reinfarction/recurrence, what serial troponin change is requested by the source?
More than 20% increase between immediate and 3–6-hour values
A fall of more than 50% over 7 days
Two troponin values are obtained immediately and 3–6 h later; a >20% increase is specified. The table says no role for CPK-MB. (Book p432)
Which culprit-lesion process is most common and more associated with men and elevated cholesterol?
Plaque rupture is 60–70% (most common), associated with men and elevated cholesterol; erosion 30–40% is associated with younger females and smoking. (Book p432)
Which feature is part of the page's vulnerable-plaque profile?
Thick fibrous cap with abundant smooth muscle
Vulnerable plaque features: thin cap, necrotic lipid core >40%, increased macrophages, reduced smooth-muscle cell content and spotty calcification. (Book p432)
A chronically underperfused myocardium has reduced function but viable tissue on evaluation. Which term is correct?
Hibernating myocardium is chronic, viable and has reduced function due to low perfusion; MRI should be used for evaluation. (Book p432)
After relief of acute ischaemia, perfusion is restored but function remains reduced for several hours in viable tissue. Which term applies?
Stunned myocardium is acute/post-ischaemic: restoring perfusion for a few hours precedes low function in viable tissue. (Book p432)
A patient has rest angina lasting more than 20 minutes, new severe crescendo symptoms, ST depression/T inversion and elevated troponin. What diagnosis is most consistent?
NSTEMI features listed are rest angina >20 min, new-onset severe/crescendo angina, ST depression/T inversion and elevated troponin. (Book p433)
Which score determines mortality risk in NSTEMI according to this page?
The NSTEMI feature list states TIMI score determines mortality risk. (Book p433)
An Indian patient in the source's typical NSTEMI age range presents with atypical symptoms; what sex pattern is stated for India?
Clinical presentation states age 40–50 in India (50–60 outside), females > males in India (reverse outside), vague symptoms in females and absent classic pain in diabetic patients. (Book p433)
Significant ST depression in the page's examples is associated with which acute coronary syndrome?
The lower ECG caption identifies significant ST depression as NSTEMI; the comparison example is non-significant ST depression. (Book p433)
Which chest-pain descriptor has the highest positive likelihood ratio for AMI in the source table?
Radiation to the right arm or shoulder
The table gives right arm/shoulder radiation 4.7 (0.9–12.0), both arms 4.1, exertion 2.4, left arm 2.3, diaphoresis 2.0, nausea/vomiting 1.9 and pressure 1.3. (Book p434)

A middle-aged patient is woken by new chest pain and cannot return to sleep. How does the source frame this presentation?

Which symptom is included as an angina equivalent?

Management continuum: pre-CCU morphine/sedation 30% one-month mortality; CCU beta-blocker/defibrillator 15%; reperfusion with thrombolysis/PCI 5%. (Book p434)

Which two measures are listed under the source's reperfusion arm?
The source places thrombolysis and percutaneous intervention under reperfusion (since 1975). (Book p434)

Which artery is listed as most commonly involved in STEMI?
The artery list ranks LAD most common, then RCA, then LCx. (Book p435)

What time window is called the ‘golden hours’ for progression of myocardial damage?

Reperfusion is performed after 6 hours of chest pain. Which source-stated benefit remains the emphasis?
Reduce pain and prevent electrical/mechanical complications

The central primary goal of PCI/lysis is expressed how on the mortality-salvage graph?
The graph says opening the artery is the primary goal (PCI/lysis) and time to treatment is critical for mortality/salvage. (Book p435)

Which is listed as a determinant of salvageable myocardium?

What principle is emphasised above the STEMI target-time flowchart?

Reopening the artery matters more than the mode of reperfusion
Thrombolysis is always superior to PCI
The source specifically notes reopening the artery is more important than the mode of reperfusion. (Book p436)

From chest pain to first medical contact, what target is printed?
The flowchart sets first medical contact <10 min and defines it as medical/paramedical staff able to take/interpret ECG and use a defibrillator. (Book p436)

A 24-hour PCI centre is available and diagnosis-to-wire-crossing time can be below 60 minutes. What route does the source direct?
Wire crossing within 90 minutes (with 30 minutes allowed for transfer)
If a 24-hour PCI centre is available and diagnosis-to-wire crossing <60 min, wire crossing is to be done within 90 min (+30 min transfer). (Book p436)

A patient cannot be shifted to a PCI centre within 120 minutes. What reperfusion option and time are specified?
Thrombolysis within 10 minutes with tenecteplase or reteplase
If timely transfer is not possible, thrombolysis within 10 min with tenecteplase or reteplase is shown, then transfer to a PCI centre. (Book p436)

After lysis, ST resolution at 60–90 minutes is below 70%. Which next step is listed?
No further intervention because lysis is successful
ST resolution >70% is successful and leads to pharmaco-invasive PCI; <70% is unsuccessful and calls for rescue/emergency PCI. (Book p436)

Following successful thrombolysis, the pharmaco-invasive approach schedules PCI within:
Successful lysis is followed by PCI within 2–24 hours to prevent recurrence of thrombus formation. (Book p436)

Which thrombolytic is non-fibrin-specific, antigenic, and has the lowest source-listed risk of intracranial haemorrhage?
Streptokinase is non-specific, 50% potent, antigenic, has lowest ICH risk and is 1.5 million U in 100 mL NS over 1 hour. (Book p437)
Which thrombolytic is described as having maximal fibrin specificity and highest fibrin selectivity?
Tenecteplase is specific (max), 75% potent, half-life 10–12 min, dose 0.5 mg/kg, and highest fibrin selectivity. (Book p437)
What reteplase regimen is printed in the agent table?
10 U in two doses 30 minutes apart
Reteplase is specific, 80% potent and dosed 10 U ×2, 30 min apart. (Book p437)
What characteristic distinguishes alteplase in the table?
Alteplase is specific, 75% potent and has a very short 4–8 minute half-life. (Book p437)
Within the first hour of ACS, how does the source compare thrombolysis with PCI for effect?
The source states effect within 1 h of ACS: thrombolysis = PCI, while PCI is otherwise more superior and mandatory after thrombolysis. (Book p437)
What is the source’s timing comparison for thrombolysis?
Benefits exceed risk within 6–12 h; risk exceeds benefits after 12 h
Only the first 15 minutes are useful
Thrombolysis benefits > risk within 6–12 h, risk > benefit after 12 h; pre-hospital lysis is noted to have a great outcome. (Book p437)
Which initial aspirin dose and formulation are listed for thrombolysis?
Loading-dose section gives aspirin 325 mg, non-enteric chewable; statins: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg. (Book p437)
An IWMI patient is bradycardic after a proximal RCA lesion and shows V1–V2 discordance. Which associated diagnosis is noted?
Note: RVMI has hypotension, clear lung and raised JVP; IWMI has bradycardia due to proximal occlusion and V1–V2 discordance. (Book p437)
What clopidogrel loading dose is stated for an adult undergoing thrombolysis?
For thrombolysis: clopidogrel 300 mg adult dose; age >75 receives 75 mg, with blood-cholesterol monitoring at 3–6 months. (Book p438)
For PCI, which P2Y12 loading strategy is marked ‘best’ on the page?
PCI section: aspirin/statin same dose; ticagrelor 180 mg best, clopidogrel 600 mg, prasugrel 60 mg. (Book p438)
What two flow goals define the stated aim of PCI?
No ST change and zero troponin
TIMI 3 epicardial flow and MPG 3 microvascular flow
TIMI 1 and MPG 1 to prevent bleeding
Normal venous flow and lymphatic drainage
PCI aim is restore normal epicardial coronary flow (TIMI 3) and attain normal microvascular flow (MPG 3). (Book p438)
After thrombolysis a patient develops hypotension and bradycardia. What does the source interpret this combination as?
Post-lysis hypotension + bradycardia indicates vessels reopening; hypertension + tachycardia suggests noncompliance/allergic reaction. (Book p438)
Post-lysis blood pressure is low and prognosis is poor. Which cause–action pairing is correct?
Cardiogenic shock → assess IVC diameter only
Low BP causes listed: hypovolaemia → assess IVC; RVMI (IWMI) → IV fluids; cardiogenic shock → intra-aortic balloon pump. (Book p438)
Why are anticoagulants continued after thrombolysis according to the flowchart?
Raw plaque areas are exposed and recurrence must be prevented

Within what timeframe does the note say young thrombus responds better to lysis?
Young thrombus responds better if lysed within 1–2 h; if primary PCI cannot be performed after STEMI diagnosis, fibrinolytic therapy is recommended within 12 h. (Book p438)
Which agents are the GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors listed for downstream bailout therapy?
GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors are abciximab, tirofiban, eptifibatide; use is downstream bailout in cath lab if no TIMI 3/MPG 3 flow or high thrombus burden. (Book p439)
When initiated within the first 24 hours, which two drug classes are stated to confer survival advantage?
ACE inhibitors/beta-blockers have survival advantage if started within first 24 h, but are avoided with heart-failure signs/low-output state. (Book p439)
A PCI centre is available for a STEMI patient. Which initial regimen matches the source algorithm?
Aspirin 325 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg or clopidogrel 600 mg, and rosuvastatin 40 mg
Clopidogrel 75 mg alone and delayed statin
Tenecteplase 0.5 mg/kg before angiography in all cases
Available PCI centre branch lists aspirin 325 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg or clopidogrel 600 mg, rosuvastatin 40 mg, then cath lab. (Book p439)
No PCI centre is available. Which thrombolysis branch is printed?
Clopidogrel 300 mg plus tenecteplase 0.5 mg/kg, then repeat ECG in 60–90 min
No-centre branch: thrombolysis with clopidogrel 300 mg + tenecteplase 0.5 mg/kg, repeat ECG after 60–90 min, then enoxaparin 30 mg IV and pharmaco-invasive/rescue PCI. (Book p439)
After normal TIMI 3 and MPG 3 flow, which long-term schedule is shown?
Rosuvastatin 20 mg and aspirin 75 mg lifelong; clopidogrel 75 mg for one year
CCU/discharge box: rosuvastatin 20 mg lifelong, aspirin 75 mg lifelong, clopidogrel 75 mg ×1 year. (Book p439)
Which item is NOT listed as a contraindication to thrombolysis on the page?
Intracranial haemorrhage or structural cerebrovascular mass
Stroke within three months (except acute stroke within 4.5 h)
Uncomplicated remote appendicectomy ten years ago

Contraindications include intracranial haemorrhage/structural mass, recent stroke, bleeding disorder/aortic dissection, recent severe head/facial trauma, intracranial/intraspinal surgery, uncontrolled HTN, and recent streptokinase use. (Book p439)
An RVMI patient is hypotensive with elevated JVP and clear lungs. Which hemodynamic treatment appears on the STEMI-complication page?
Hemodynamic complication: RVMI hypotension presents with raised JVP and clear lungs; management is IV fluids. (Book p440)
How much myocardial damage is associated with acute LV failure in the source complication chart?
Acute LVF is linked to 25% myocardial damage and proximal LAD lesion; cardiogenic shock to 40% damage/proximal LAD. (Book p440)
Proximal LAD lesion → isolated atrial flutter
Electrical complications: RCA lesion → atrial arrhythmias; proximal LAD lesion → VT/VF. (Book p440)
Three to five days after MI, a patient develops pain and a new murmur at the left lower sternal border with a thrill. Which mechanical complication is described?
Septal rupture is described as rare, after 3–5 days, with pain, new LLSB murmur and thrill. (Book p440)
Sudden pulseless electrical activity with no BP/pulse and tamponade after infarction is most suggestive of:
Free-wall rupture causes electromechanical dissociation/PEA, no BP/no pulse and tamponade, with poor prognosis. (Book p440)
Acute pulmonary oedema after an RCA infarct is attributed to involvement of which structure?
Posteromedial papillary muscle causing acute MR
Acute MR: RCA involvement affects posteromedial papillary muscle and presents as acute pulmonary oedema. (Book p440)
Why does the page state thrombolytics have no role in NSTEMI?
All NSTEMI cases have normal ECGs
The thrombus is platelet-rich with reduced fibrin content
NSTEMI pathogenesis is plaque rupture in elderly/comorbid people with critical/subtotal occlusion, ST/T changes, platelet-rich thrombus and decreased fibrin, so no thrombolytic role. (Book p440)
Chest pain has increased in nature, duration beyond 20 minutes and frequency and is not relieved by nitrates or rest. Which presentation is being described?
Clinical presentation on p441 describes increasing nature/duration (>20 min)/frequency and pain not relieved by nitrates/rest. (Book p441)
Which initial treatment bundle is listed for NSTE-ACS on this page?
Oxygen if SpO2 <90%, aspirin 325 mg, rosuvastatin 40 mg, SL nitrate and morphine
Treatment: O2 if SpO2<90%, aspirin 325 mg chewable non-enteric, rosuvastatin 40 mg, SL nitrate 5 mg repeated three times, morphine, PCI within 24 h (high risk within 2 h). (Book p441)
What is the source’s treatment of choice in its NSTE-ACS ‘landmark changes’ note?
Landmark changes list intervention-based guideline: PCI TOC; angiography within 24 h (high risk 2 h), with P2Y12 inhibitor in cath lab. (Book p441)
Which peri-interventional enoxaparin dose is written for NSTE-ACS before reaching the cath lab?
Peri-interventional anticoagulation: enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg bolus until cath lab. (Book p441)
Which P2Y12 loading dose is given for prasugrel in the NSTE-ACS cath-lab list?
Cath-lab loading options: prasugrel 60 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg, or clopidogrel 600 mg. (Book p441)
After discharge, which source schedule is stated for dual antiplatelet therapy?
Ticagrelor 90 mg BD for one year, or clopidogrel 75 mg OD for one year, or prasugrel 10 mg for one year
After discharge: aspirin 75 mg lifelong, rosuvastatin 20 mg lifelong, and ticagrelor 90 mg BD ×1 y or clopidogrel 75 mg OD ×1 y or prasugrel 10 mg ×1 y (best). (Book p441)
Within the connective-tissue-disorder map, which disorder is marked most common and which is second most common?
Rheumatoid arthritis first; Sjogren syndrome second
Inflammatory muscle disease first; SLE second
The CTD map marks rheumatoid arthritis as most common and Sjogren syndrome as second most common. (Book p442)
Which demographic profile is given for Sjogren syndrome?
Women aged 40–60 years with F:M about 9:1
Sjogren syndrome is described as a multisystem autoimmune inflammatory CTD in middle-aged females (40–60) with F:M = 9:1. (Book p442)
Secondary Sjogren syndrome is most strongly associated with which sequence of CTDs on the page?
Inflammatory muscle disease more than RA
RA more than SLE more than inflammatory muscle disease
SLE more than RA more than systemic sclerosis
Secondary Sjogren has CTD association, ranked RA > SLE > IMD; primary has no such association. (Book p442)
What proportion split is used for glandular and extraglandular Sjogren pathology?
Classification by pathology divides glandular (50%) and extraglandular (50%); extraglandular disease is multisystem and 15% is severe/life-threatening. (Book p442)
What clinical hallmark is highlighted before the pathology section?
The clinical hallmark is dry eye and dry mouth; thyroid is noted as the simple endocrine organ involved and Sjogren can be an extrahepatic manifestation of HCV. (Book p442)
Which is NOT listed among the page's extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis C virus?
HCV extrahepatic manifestations listed are cutaneous lichen planus, porphyria cutanea tarda, cryoglobulinaemia, Sjogren syndrome and MPGN. (Book p443)

A patient develops dry eye, xerostomia, dry skin, dry throat and vaginal dryness after autoimmune lymphocytic exocrinopathy. Which process directly precedes these clinical symptoms in the page’s pathogenesis flow?
Genetic/environmental factors → autoantibodies → autoimmune lymphocytic exocrinopathy (periductal/perivascular) → ductal epithelial activation → the listed sicca symptoms. (Book p443)
Which HLA association is stated for Sjogren syndrome?
Genetic factors list HLA-DR3; the note identifies SLE as another disease associated with HLA-DR3. (Book p443)
Which helper-T-cell direction is drawn in Sjogren inflammation?
Th1 greater than Th2, leading to B-cell involvement
Th2 greater than Th1 with absent B cells
Th17 only with no B-cell role
The inflammation line states T cell (Th1 > Th2) > B cell. (Book p443)
Painless parotid enlargement in Sjogren is attributed to which cellular finding on the page?
IL-18-positive macrophages are linked to salivary-gland enlargement/painless parotid enlargement. (Book p443)
A patient with anti-M3 muscarinic antibodies has troublesome dryness. Which pharmacologic class is linked to treatment in the source?
Antibodies list anti-M3 (muscarinic) → cholinergic agonist cevimeline for treatment, and anti-α-fodrin. (Book p443)
Which salivary-gland biopsy is the gold standard in Sjogren syndrome?
Histopathology states minor salivary gland is gold standard and shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with T cells; major gland has benign lymphoepithelial lesions with B cells. (Book p444)
Which immunohistochemical marker is shown with B-cell infiltration in the major salivary-gland panel?
The major-gland B-cell infiltration panel is labelled CD20; the T-cell infiltration panel is CD3. (Book p444)
Which cellular pattern defines the minor-gland lesion of Sjogren in the source?
Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with T cells
Minor salivary gland biopsy is gold standard and demonstrates focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with T-cell infiltration. (Book p444)
A patient describes a gritty, sandy eye sensation and glare. Which mechanism is named in the dry-eye section?
Dry eyes are non-specific and may result from aqueous plus lipid/meibomian-gland dysfunction, producing irritation, gritty/sandy sensation and glare. (Book p444)
What Schirmer-test result is used for dry eye on the page?
Dry-eye diagnosis: Schirmer <5 mm after 5 min; tear-film breakup time <10 s; ocular staining may use lissamine green or fluorescein. (Book p444)
Which tear-film breakup time is marked abnormal for dry eye?
The source marks tear-film breakup time <10 seconds as dry eye. (Book p444)
Which statement correctly contrasts dry mouth with dry eyes in the clinical-features block?
The source calls dry eyes non-specific and dry mouth more specific. (Book p444)
A patient must drink water to swallow, has chewing difficulty and dental caries. Which Sjogren manifestation is most directly illustrated?
Dry mouth manifestations: unable to swallow without water, chewing difficulty and dental caries. (Book p444)
Which oral feature is listed alongside altered taste in Sjogren dry-mouth manifestations?
Continuation lists oral thrush, altered taste, and 25% salivary-gland swelling. (Book p445)
About what proportion of Sjogren patients have salivary-gland swelling according to the page?
The source gives 25% salivary-gland swelling, usually bilateral painless symmetric. (Book p445)
A child has recurrent episodes of acute parotitis due to duct blockade. Which source diagnosis context does this support?
Childhood Sjogren is described as recurrent acute parotitis due to duct blockage. (Book p445)
A Sjogren patient develops asymmetric painful nodular parotid swelling with palpable nodes. What complication must be suspected?
B-cell lymphoma of extranodal marginal-zone type
Asymmetric painful swelling with palpable nodules signals B-cell lymphoma (extranodal marginal-zone B-cell lymphoma), associated with cryoglobulinaemia and low C3/C4. (Book p445)
Which laboratory pattern predicts extraglandular Sjogren on the page?
Low C3/C4, anti-Ro/La, positive rheumatoid factor and cryoglobulins
Predictors listed: low complement (C3/C4), anti-Ro/La (SS-A/SS-B), positive RF and cryoglobulins. (Book p445)
A diagnosed Sjogren patient has high anti-Ro/La titres and early onset/long duration. What prognostic association is stated?
Extraglandular disease, poorer prognosis, B-cell lymphoma risk and salivary enlargement

Positive anti-Ro/La in diagnosed Sjogren indicates extraglandular disease, poorer prognosis, B-cell lymphoma risk and salivary-gland enlargement; ~5% may develop disease after 10–15 years. (Book p445)
Jaccoud arthropathy in Sjogren is characterised as:
Manifestations include fatigue and arthralgia/arthritis with non-erosive Jaccoud arthropathy. (Book p445)
A Sjogren patient develops dorsal-root-ganglion involvement with truncal ataxia. Which severe-system category is implicated?
Severe manifestations (15%) include CNS ganglionopathy from dorsal-root-ganglion involvement, causing truncal ataxia. (Book p446)
What is the most common interstitial lung pattern listed in Sjogren?
Lung: risk ILD; most common NSIP. Most characteristic is lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP) with GGO, cysts and nodules. (Book p446)
HRCT in Sjogren shows ground-glass opacity, cysts and nodules. Which lung disorder is described as most characteristic?
LIP is marked most characteristic and has GGO, cyst and nodules. (Book p446)
Which renal manifestation is specifically attributed to tubulointerstitial kidney disease in Sjogren?
Renal: tubulointerstitial kidney disease causes distal RTA and has minor CKD risk. (Book p446)
A patient reports Raynaud phenomenon that preceded sicca symptoms. Which additional warning is provided on the page?
It is restricted to the first week of disease
It may produce critical limb ischaemia
It proves an absence of vasculitis
Raynaud may precede sicca in one-third and may produce critical limb ischaemia. (Book p446)
What is the hallmark lesion of the most common vascular complication in Sjogren?
Small-vessel vasculitis is most common and hallmark lesion is palpable purpura. Medium-vessel disease is severe, with ulcers/gangrene, MPGN and neuropathy. (Book p446)
A Sjogren patient develops ulceration, gangrene, MPGN and neuropathy. Which vascular category is indicated?
The source describes severe medium-vessel vasculitis with ulcer/gangrene and association with MPGN and neuropathy. (Book p446)
Which combination supports concern for B-cell lymphoma in Sjogren?
Persistent asymmetric painful nodular parotid enlargement with lymphadenopathy
High saliva flow with normal nodes

Lymphadenopathy prompts exclusion of lymphoma; indicators include persistent asymmetric painful nodular parotid enlargement with nodes, cryoglobulinaemia, low C3/C4, high Ro/La, purpura and leukopenia. (Book p446)
Which disorders are associated with lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis according to the note?
Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis is associated with Sjogren and HIV. (Book p447)
Which trio of disorders is listed as causing lung cysts?
Cysts in lung: LIP, Langerhans-cell histiocytosis and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. (Book p447)
How often is ANA positive in Sjogren according to the investigation section?
ANA is a CTD screening test and is positive in 85% with Sjogren; if positive, ANA profile can detect anti-Ro/La. (Book p447)
Which antibody has no independent diagnostic value in the source despite being positive in roughly one-third?
Anti-Ro is positive in 50%; anti-La has no independent value despite 33% positivity. (Book p447)
ANA IIF shows fine-speckled pattern with negative metaphase cells. What does the source say this pattern suggests?
Fine speckled is most common, metaphase cells negative, and suggests anti-Ro/La/Sjogren. Dense fine speckled has DFS-positive metaphase cells and rules out CTD. (Book p447)
Which test is called the investigation of choice/gold standard for Sjogren in this section?
Minor salivary gland biopsy is IOC/gold standard and shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (T cell). (Book p447)
What unstimulated salivary flow is given as abnormal in the (now less-used) sialography note?
Sialography note: unstimulated salivary flow rate <1.5 mL/15 min; it is marked ‘not done now.’ Ultrasound shows loss of gland homogeneity. (Book p447)
In 2016 ACR/EULAR classification, which two findings each carry three points?
Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis focus score ≥1/mm² and anti-Ro/SS-A positivity
Schirmer ≤5 mm and low salivary flow
Ocular staining and Rose Bengal score
Score 3: histopathology focus score ≥1/mm² and anti-Ro/SS-A. Score 1: ocular staining/Rose Bengal, Schirmer ≤5 mm/5 min, and salivary flow <0.1 mL/min. (Book p448)
What total is required for primary-Sjogren classification after at least one oral/ocular dryness symptom?
Rules: at least one symptom of ocular/oral dryness plus total score ≥4. (Book p448)
Which condition is NOT in the printed exclusion list for Sjogren classification?
Exclusions include prior head/neck radiation, active HCV, AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, GVHD and IgG4-related disease. (Book p448)
A pregnant woman with high anti-Ro/La titres is counselled about which fetal risk stated in the note?
Tetralogy of Fallot in all pregnancies
High anti-Ro/La in pregnancy increases congenital heart block risk (2–5%). The source contrasts offspring risk for CTD in Sjogren male versus SLE female contexts. (Book p448)
Which salivary-gland-enlargement differential pairs IgG4-related disease with the correct pathology/association?
Storiform fibrosis, plasmacytic infiltrate and pancreatitis
Focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with dry eyes
Differential: sarcoidosis = ILD + uveitis + hilar adenopathy; IgG4-RD = storiform fibrosis + plasmacytic infiltrate + pancreatitis. (Book p448)
Which treatment is assigned to severe life-threatening extraglandular Sjogren manifestations?
High-dose steroid plus immunosuppressant such as mycophenolate mofetil

Treatment: glandular saliva substitute/cevimeline/artificial tears. Fatigue/arthralgia uses low-dose steroid <7.5 mg/day + NSAIDs + HCQ; severe life-threatening disease uses high-dose steroid + immunosuppressant/MMF. (Book p448)
Which condition heads the IgG4-related-disease spectrum as the most common manifestation on the next page?

The spectrum lists type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis, Mikulicz disease, Riedel thyroiditis, mediastinal fibrosis, primary sclerosing cholangitis and periaortitis; p450 calls type 1 AIP the most common manifestation. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
How is IgG4 characterised among IgG subclasses in the source?
IgG4 is listed as least common (<5%). (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
Which functional property of IgG4 is specifically stated?
It is the principal opsonin for bacteria
IgG4 is anti-inflammatory, blocks IgG–C1q binding, does not fix complement, and is a bispecific antibody with two antigen-binding sites that binds/sequesters antigen. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
A biopsy shows tumefactive plasma-cell-rich inflammation, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. What disease is most strongly suggested?
Histology lists IgG4-predominant lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, tumour-like lesions, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis and mild eosinophilia. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
Which cytokine is called the most potent fibrogenic cytokine in the pathogenesis flowchart?
Antigenic stimuli → IgG4 plasma-lymphocytic infiltrate → myofibroblast activation → TGF-β/PDGF → fibrosis; TGF-β is called most potent fibrogenic cytokine. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
Obliterative phlebitis is noted as occurring in IgG4-related disease and which other disease?
The page's note pairs obliterative phlebitis with IgG4-related disease and Behcet disease. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
Which demographic pattern is given for IgG4-related disease?
Men more than women, age 40–70, subacute onset
Women more than men, childhood onset
Clinical features: M>F, age 40–70 years, subacute onset; symptoms weight loss and myalgia. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
Which finding is listed as arguing against IgG4-related disease?
Features against IgG4-RD: fever, arthritis, neutrophil involvement and granuloma. Mild eosinophilia appears among histology/atopy-allergy history. (Book p449)
IgG4 Biology, Pathology & Core Clinical Profile
A patient has obstructive jaundice, diffuse irregular pancreatic-duct narrowing on ERCP, and a ‘sausage pancreas’ with homogeneous enhancement on CT. What manifestation is most likely?
Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is most common in IgG4-RD and presents with obstructive jaundice; ERCP is IOC and CT shows sausage pancreas/homogeneous enhancement. (Book p450)
Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis can be associated with which endocrine and exocrine consequences?
AIP is associated with endocrine insufficiency → type 3c DM and exocrine insufficiency → malabsorption. (Book p450)
A patient has bilateral painless submandibular enlargement but minimal sicca symptoms. Which IgG4 manifestation is represented?
Salivary involvement is bilateral painless submandibular enlargement with minimal sicca symptoms. (Book p450)
What is the most common orbital manifestation of IgG4-related disease on the page?
Orbital/periorbital lesions include orbital inflammatory pseudotumours; lacrimal enlargement/dacryoadenitis is marked most common orbital manifestation. (Book p450)
Which CNS manifestation is specified in postpartum women with raised intracranial tension?
Minor CNS manifestations are lymphocytic hypophysitis (postpartum women with ↑ICT) and pachymeningitis without parenchymal involvement. (Book p450)
What is the most common renal manifestation of IgG4-related disease?
Tubulointerstitial disease is most common renal manifestation, with minimal CKD risk and no renal tubular acidosis; membranous nephropathy is glomerular involvement. (Book p450)
Which bile-duct manifestation is listed under IgG4-related disease?
The organ list continues with bile duct: primary sclerosing cholangitis. (Book p451)
Which lung finding is described for IgG4-related disease?
NSIP with thickening of the bronchovascular bundle
LIP with cysts as the defining pattern
Lung: non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and thickening of bronchovascular bundle. (Book p451)
Which vascular manifestation may be associated with a paravertebral mass?
Aorta manifestation is periaortitis, associated with paravertebral mass. (Book p451)
A patient has membranous nephropathy as an IgG4 manifestation. What complement pattern is noted?
The page notes membranonephropathy manifestation of IgG4 disease → low complements. (Book p451)
What three domains compose the RCD 2020 criteria as shown?
Pathologic findings, serology and clinical features
RCD 2020 criteria show pathologic/histologic features + serology + clinical features; serum IgG4 correlates with activity and is elevated in 40% cases. (Book p451)
Which ratio is stated to be a better marker than serum IgG4 alone?
Other findings: IgG4/IgG ratio is a better marker. (Book p451)
Mikulicz disease involves enlargement of which glands?
Mikulicz disease is enlargement of parotid, submandibular and lacrimal gland; history includes chronic sinusitis/nasal obstruction with eosinophilia. (Book p451)
What first-line treatment and relapse-prevention steroid-sparing agent are listed for IgG4-related disease?
Steroids first line; rituximab to prevent relapse
NSAIDs first line; IVIG for relapse
Steroids are first line with good response within two weeks but relapse risk; rituximab is the steroid-sparing agent to prevent relapse. (Book p451)
A patient has pronounced salivary enlargement, little sicca, and good steroid response but relapse risk. Which diagnosis is favoured over Sjogren in the comparison table?

Comparison: IgG4 has increased salivary enlargement, decreased sicca, good steroid response and relapse risk; Sjogren has decreased enlargement, increased sicca and sicca symptoms not steroid responsive. (Book p451)
Which population profile is given for SLE on the opening page?
SLE is described as a disease of women of reproductive age (20–40) with 9:1 female predominance. (Book p452)
What concordance is cited for identical twins in SLE?
The source lists positive concordance in >40% of identical twins and strong family history. (Book p452)
What lupus-nephritis frequency contrast is shown?
Lupus nephritis is shown in adults 50–60% and childhood SLE 100%. (Book p452)
An elderly person develops new postmenopausal SLE. Which clinical profile is favoured in the source?
Good prognosis with no CNS/renal symptoms and sicca/serositis/musculoskeletal symptoms
Severe nephritis with low complement in every case
Postmenopausal SLE has good prognosis, no CNS/renal symptoms, sicca/serositis/musculoskeletal symptoms, anti-Ro positive, anti-dsDNA negative and normal complements. (Book p452)
Which statement is made about prognosis and active-serology in SLE?
Active SLE has anti-Ro only with normal complement
Male SLE has poor prognosis; active SLE has anti-dsDNA positivity and low complement
Male SLE has better prognosis and high C3
The bottom notes state male SLE has poor prognosis; active SLE markers are anti-dsDNA positive and low complements. (Book p452)
What defective-clearance substrates initiate the printed SLE pathogenesis pathway?
Genetic/environmental causes lead to defective clearance of apoptotic and NETotic debris, triggering immune dysregulation. (Book p453)
Which innate receptors are explicitly shown in the SLE pathogenesis diagram?
TLR-7 and TLR-9 are labelled pattern-recognition receptors; hydroxychloroquine is drawn inhibiting this step. (Book p453)
What is called the central key pathogenic cytokine in SLE?
Activated plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I interferon/IFNα, identified as the central key pathogenic cytokine; anifrolumab is shown blocking it. (Book p453)
Which helper-T-cell balance is drawn in SLE?
Treg greater than all helper cells
Th2 greater than Th17 with Th1 also shown
The diagram depicts Th1, Th2 > Th17; Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 aid B-cell activation. (Book p453)
Which ligand/cytokine is marked upregulated in SLE and promotes B-cell stimulation?
BAFF/B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) is shown upregulated in SLE; belimumab inhibits it. (Book p453)
Immune-complex deposition in which three sites is depicted as type-III hypersensitivity?
B cells form immune complexes/type-III hypersensitivity that deposit in glomerulus (GN), synovial cavity (synovitis) and vessels (vasculitis). (Book p453)
Which HLA alleles are listed as genetic factors for SLE?
HLA factors listed: HLA-DR3 (seen in subacute cutaneous lupus) and HLA-DR2. (Book p454)
What is the strongest complement-deficiency risk factor ranking printed for SLE?
C1q deficiency greater than C2 deficiency greater than C4 deficiency
C4 deficiency greater than C2 greater than C1q
Early complement deficiency affects debris clearance; ranking is C1q > C2 > C4 deficiency. (Book p454)
Which chromosome/gene association is explicitly given?
Non-HLA factors include increased X-chromosome number → increased risk/IRAK gene, and chromosome 3 → TREX gene. (Book p454)
Which environmental exposure is listed as an autoimmune trigger through stimulation of pulmonary alveolar macrophages?
Environmental factors include OCP, HRT, UV-B, EBV, silicosis (stimulates pulmonary alveolar macrophage → autoimmune trigger), vitamin-D deficiency and smoking. (Book p454)
Which factor is labelled as having only minimal association in the source?
A bracket labels vitamin-D deficiency and smoking as minimal association; the source separately lists OCP, HRT, UV-B, EBV and silicosis. (Book p454)
Which hormonal exposures are listed among SLE environmental factors?
Oral contraceptive pills and hormone replacement therapy
OCP and HRT head the environmental-factor list. (Book p454)
Which drug is shown blocking TLR-7/TLR-9 in the SLE pathogenesis illustration?
HCQ is drawn over TLR-7/TLR-9; belimumab targets BLyS and anifrolumab blocks type-I interferon signalling in the diagram. (Book p454)
How long before clinical features can antibodies appear in SLE according to the opening comparison?
Antibodies can appear before clinical features: SLE 3 years; Sjogren syndrome 10–15 years. (Book p455)
When ANA is positive, which technique is identified as useful for assessing pattern?
ANA methodology: ELISA is only for quantitative assessment; IIF/indirect IF on HEp-2 cells, with titre >1:80, is used to look for pattern. (Book p455)
What ANA titre threshold is shown in the positive-ANA flowchart before proceeding to pattern review?
The flowchart shows IIF (HEp-2) and titre >1:80, then look for pattern. (Book p455)
ANA shows dense fine speckling in mitotic-phase cells. What is the disease implication given in the table?
Dense fine speckled pattern in mitotic-phase cells has no probable antibody listed and rules out CTD. (Book p455)
A fine-speckled ANA pattern is accompanied by anti-Ro/La. Which disease association should be selected?
Fine speckled pattern is linked to anti-Ro/La and Sjogren syndrome. (Book p455)
A coarse-speckled ANA pattern with anti-Smith antibody is associated with which disease?
Coarse speckled patterns include anti-Smith → SLE, anti-U1 RNP → MCTD, and anti-RNA polymerase 3 → systemic sclerosis. (Book p455)
Which antibody–disease association is correct for coarse-speckled ANA?
The coarse-speckled table maps anti-U1 RNP to MCTD. (Book p455)
A nucleolar ANA pattern with PM/Scl-70 points to which overlap?
Nucleolar pattern with PM/Scl-70 is linked to polymyositis–scleroderma overlap. (Book p455)
Which antibody is linked to cytoplasmic ANA pattern and antisynthetase syndrome?
Cytoplasmic pattern with anti-Jo-1 is linked to polymyositis/dermatomyositis (antisynthetase syndrome). (Book p455)
Which homogeneous ANA pairing is correctly stated?
Homogeneous pattern: anti-dsDNA associates with SLE and antihistone with drug-induced SLE. (Book p455)
A centromere ANA pattern is associated with which disease?
The final row maps centromere pattern to CREST syndrome (scleroderma). (Book p455)
After a positive ANA and IIF pattern, what is the source’s next diagnostic step?
Further evaluation to confirm antibodies with ANA or ENA profile
Immediate renal biopsy in every patient
Clinical suspicion → ANA positive → IIF pattern → further evaluation to confirm antibodies, using ANA profile or ENA profile. (Book p456)
Which statement describes the ANA profile on the page?
Immunoblot-based, costly multiple-antibody analysis, done once without repeat values
A cheap bedside test repeated daily
ANA profile: by immunoblot, costly/multiple antibody analysis, done once (no repeat values). ENA profile tests six antibodies. (Book p456)
Which disease is stated to have ANA positivity in 100% of cases in the flowchart?
Mixed connective-tissue disease, drug-induced lupus and type 1 autoimmune hepatitis
ANA positivity chart: 100% MCTD, DILE and type 1 autoimmune hepatitis; 85% Sjogren; 50% IgG4-related disease. In SLE it is positive in 97%. (Book p456)
What caution is given about ANA in rheumatoid arthritis?
ANA is not diagnostic despite RA being the most common multisystem CTD
The source says RA is the most common multisystem CTD but ANA is not diagnostic. (Book p456)
A patient has DILE. Which antibody and IIF pattern combination fits the source?
Antihistone antibody with homogeneous IIF pattern
DILE features: 100% ANA positive, homogeneous IIF pattern, antihistone antibody positive, and procainamide cause. (Book p456)
Which drug is named as a cause of drug-induced lupus erythematosus?
The DILE block lists procainamide as a cause. (Book p456)
What atypical antibody pattern is noted in elderly SLE?
Anti-dsDNA positive with low complement always
Note: elderly SLE → anti-Ro positive and ANA negative. (Book p456)
Which technique is listed for anti-dsDNA titre measurement?
Anti-dsDNA: ELISA for titre; Crithidia luciliae (flagella) is a qualitative IIF method marked obsolete. (Book p457)
Which test organism/method is used qualitatively for anti-dsDNA in the source, though marked obsolete?
Crithidia luciliae (flagella) is specified as qualitative IIF, obsolete. (Book p457)
Which comparison of anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith is correct on the page?
Anti-dsDNA sensitivity 75% (preferred); anti-Smith 25% but more specific
Anti-Smith is 75% sensitive and anti-dsDNA 25% specific
Table: anti-dsDNA sensitivity 75% preferred; anti-Smith 25% more specific. (Book p457)
Serial anti-dsDNA titres are rising. Which risks are specifically noted to rise?
The source states increased anti-dsDNA titres increase nephritis and vasculitis risk; no prognostic effect is listed for anti-Smith. (Book p457)
What is the source’s general interpretation of anti-Ro/La in an asymptomatic person?
Anti-Ro/La is non-specific in CTD and has no significance in asymptomatic patients. (Book p457)
In a patient with SLE, anti-Ro/La positivity indicates which associated condition?
Within SLE, anti-Ro/La indicates secondary Sjogren; it is also linked to pregnancy CHB, SCLE/HLA-DR3/photosensitive lesions, good prognosis and lupus myocarditis. (Book p457)
What congenital-heart-block risk is given for pregnancy with anti-Ro/La positivity?
In pregnancy, anti-Ro/La is linked to 2–5% congenital heart block, increased in female child. (Book p457)
A patient with SCLE, photosensitive lesions and HLA-DR3 positivity has anti-Ro/La. What is the source’s renal/vascular prognosis association of higher titres?
Lower risk of nephritis and vasculitis
Higher risk of nephritis and vasculitis

Anti-Ro/La is associated with SCLE/HLA-DR3/photosensitivity and good prognosis: higher titres → reduced risk of nephritis/vasculitis; it is protective in skin/myocardium and linked to shrinking-lung syndrome. (Book p457)
About what fraction of SLE patients have antiphospholipid-syndrome antibodies according to the page?
APS antibodies are positive in one-third of SLE patients. (Book p457)
Warm-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia in SLE is associated with which antibody?
The antibody list identifies anti-RBC antibody in warm-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. (Book p457)
Anti-platelet antibody is listed in secondary ITP associated with which group?
SLE, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori and RA
Secondary ITP list: SLE, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori and RA, with bleeding/anaemia. (Book p457)
Which antibody is specific for psychosis/depression in CNS lupus on the source page?
Anti-ribosomal P is specific for psychosis/depression in CNS lupus; anti-glutamate/anti-neuronal antibody is most common in CNS lupus. (Book p457)
What is the most common CNS manifestation of lupus according to the note?
The note names cognitive decline as the most common CNS manifestation in lupus. (Book p457)
Which combination is listed as biomarkers of SLE disease activity?
Anti-dsDNA titre, low C3/C4, and raised ESR with low CRP
Anti-Ro titre, high C3/C4, and high CRP
Biomarkers: anti-dsDNA titre, ↓C3/↓C4, and ↑ESR with ↓CRP. (Book p457)
The clinical-features list for SLE opens with which constitutional triad?
Fatigue with weight loss, pyrexia of unknown origin and leucopenia
Fever with night sweats and generalised lymphadenopathy
Weight gain, bradycardia and cold intolerance
Migratory arthralgia, morning stiffness and rash
Constitutional symptoms are listed as fatigue and weight loss, pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) and leucopenia. (Book p458)
Which classification is named for dividing the cutaneous lesions of lupus?
Gilliam-Sontheimer classification: lupus specific versus lupus non-specific
The cutaneous section opens with the Gilliam-Sontheimer classification into lupus specific and lupus non-specific lesions. (Book p458)
Which cutaneous lupus category is marked as the most common (m/c) in the source?
ACLE is listed first among lupus-specific lesions and marked (m/c); its localised form (malar rash) is also marked m/c. (Book p458)
Which description is least compatible with the page's localised ACLE (malar/butterfly rash)?
Symmetrical, erythematous rash over the malar eminences
