Highly photosensitive and associated with onset at a younger age
A scaly, scarring rash that permanently destroys follicles
Localised ACLE is symmetrical, erythematous, scaly and NON-scarring (with or without oedema); scarring belongs to discoid/CCLE disease. (Book p458)
Besides the malar rash, which mucocutaneous findings are linked to the ACLE block?
Painless oral/nasopharyngeal ulcers and non-scarring alopecia
Painful oral ulcers and scarring alopecia
Nasal septal perforation and nasal bridge collapse
The ACLE block associates painless oral/nasopharyngeal ulcers and non-scarring alopecia with the malar rash. (Book p458)
How does the source describe the generalised form of ACLE?
It is confined to sun-protected skin
It spares the knuckles and may present as a TEN-like lupus eruption
It preferentially involves the knuckles with Gottron-like papules
It is a scarring alopecia of the scalp
Generalised ACLE is annotated as sparing the knuckles; the TEN-like lupus image is attached to the same ACLE arm. (Book p458)
Which triad is attached to SCLE on the classification page?
Anti-centromere positivity, pulmonary hypertension and CREST
Anti-Jo-1 positivity, mechanic's hands and ILD
Anti-Ro/La positivity, HLA-DR3 association and photosensitivity
Anti-dsDNA positivity, low complement and nephritis
SCLE is listed with anti-Ro/La (+), association with HLA DR3 and photosensitivity. (Book p458)
A patient being worked up for SLE has a facial rash that involves the nasolabial fold. Which diagnosis does the source's note raise?
Acne rosacea (the note also lists dermatomyositis)
The note lists rash involving the nasolabial fold under acne rosacea (a) and dermatomyositis (b); SLE malar rash spares the nasolabial fold. (Book p459)
The discoid-lupus note is printed as a '5/20 rule'. Which pairing matches it?
5% of patients with discoid rash have SLE; 20% of patients with SLE have discoid rash
50% of patients with discoid rash have SLE; 2% of patients with SLE have discoid rash
5% of patients with SLE have discoid rash; 20% of patients with discoid rash have SLE
15% of patients with discoid rash have SLE; 25% of patients with SLE have discoid rash
The 5/20 rule: 5% of patients with discoid rash have SLE and 20% of patients with SLE have a discoid rash. (Book p459)
A scarring, circular, raised erythematous plaque on the scalp shows follicular plugging, keratotic scaling and dermal atrophy on biopsy. Which long-term risk does the source attach?
Transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

CCLE/discoid rash: circular raised erythematous patching with scarring; biopsy shows follicular plugging, keratotic scaling and dermal atrophy; there is a risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma. (Book p459)
Which alopecia type is paired with discoid lupus on this page?
CCLE is associated with cicatricial (scarring) alopecia, shown with the carpet-track sign of DLE. (Book p459)
A patient with SCLE has a psoriasiform rash pattern. According to the source, which implication follows?
Lower rate of conversion to SLE
Higher rate of conversion to SLE
SCLE patterns listed are annular and psoriasiform, the latter marked with increased conversion to SLE. (Book p459)
Which statement about SCLE epidemiology and serology matches the source?
About 20% of patients with SCLE have SLE, more often in the white population, with anti-Ro and less renal involvement
About 20% of patients with SLE have SCLE, with anti-dsDNA and severe nephritis
SCLE never occurs without systemic SLE
SCLE is associated with anti-centromere and pulmonary hypertension
SCLE: 20% of patients with SCLE have SLE, white population, association with HLA DR3, anti-Ro with reduced renal involvement. (Book p459)
Which lesion is listed under lupus NON-specific skin disease on this page?
Lupus panniculitis (profundus) with subcutaneous tender erythematous nodules
Lupus non-specific lesions listed are chilblain lupus and lupus panniculitis/profundus (subcutaneous, tender erythematous nodules). (Book p459)
A referral letter describes a patient as having 'lupus pernio' and the team clarifies the terminology. Which note does the source print?
Both terms describe discoid lupus variants
Lupus pernio is sarcoidosis; lupus vulgaris is tuberculosis
Lupus pernio is tuberculosis; lupus vulgaris is sarcoidosis
The note states lupus pernio is sarcoidosis and lupus vulgaris is TB. (Book p460)
Which system is flagged as the most commonly involved in SLE, and what is the typical joint pattern?
Renal: glomerular disease dominates the presentation
Pulmonary: interstitial disease dominates the presentation
Musculoskeletal: small joints of the upper limb much more than the lower limb, wrist involved
Musculoskeletal manifestations are marked (m/c system involved); the site is upper limb >> lower limb with small-joint and wrist involvement progressing to arthritis. (Book p460)
A patient with SLE has reducible, deforming hand deformities with non-erosive arthritis on imaging. Which term and mechanism does the source use?
Jaccoud arthropathy due to ligament laxity (also seen in Sjogren's)
Rhupus due to anti-CCP positive erosive disease
Avascular necrosis due to corticosteroid therapy
SLE arthritis is non-erosive and deforming from ligament laxity, producing Jaccoud arthropathy, which is also seen in Sjogren syndrome. (Book p460)
Erosive arthritis with a positive anti-CCP antibody in a patient with SLE is labelled:
SLE with erosive arthritis is labelled Rhupus (RA/SLE overlap) and anti-CCP is positive. (Book p460)
A patient on treatment for SLE develops a single hot joint that is involved out of proportion to the rest. Which complication is most feared here?

Under complications, septic arthritis is the concern in a patient on SLE treatment with a single joint involved out of proportion; the monoarthritis note lists crystal arthropathy and septic arthritis in the differential. (Book p460)
Three months into SLE treatment a patient develops acute joint pain. Which investigation does the source mark as the investigation of choice?
Avascular necrosis presents as acute joint pain after about three months of disease; MRI is marked as the investigation of choice. (Book p460)
A patient with SLE has fatigue, a malar rash and wrist synovitis but no kidney, lung or CNS involvement. How does the source classify this pattern?
SLE with constitutional, skin and joint involvement is labelled non-organ/life-threatening SLE, in contrast to organ-system involvement which carries a bad prognosis. (Book p460)
Which figures are printed for renal involvement and its renal outcome in SLE?
Kidney involved in 25%; about 25% progress to CKD
Kidney involved in 50-60%; about 10% progress to CKD
Kidney involved in 10%; about 50-60% progress to CKD
Kidney involved in 90%; about 50% progress to CKD
Organ-system involvement: kidney involved in 50-60%, and 10% progress to CKD. (Book p460)
Which cause-of-death pairing is printed for SLE across the disease course?
Renal failure in the first 10 years; malignancy after 10 years
CNS vasculitis in the first 10 years; renal failure after 10 years
Infection from immunosuppression in the first 10 years; acute coronary syndrome after 10 years
Acute coronary syndrome in the first 10 years; infection after 10 years

Immunosuppressive therapy leading to infection is the most common cause of death in the first 10 years; acute coronary syndrome is the most common cause of death after 10 years, in keeping with accelerated atherosclerosis being an MI equivalent. (Book p460)
A patient with SLE develops acute abdominal pain from mesenteric ischaemia and a week later an ischaemic stroke. Which vascular territory does the source flag as dangerous?
Vascular disease is noted in one-third of patients (thrombosis and accelerated atherosclerosis); dangerous vasculitis is medium-vessel, involving mesenteric and CNS vessels. (Book p460)
Which anaemia pairing is printed for the RBC line in SLE?
Anaemia of chronic disease is most common; a rapidly progressive anaemia indicates autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Iron-deficiency anaemia is most common; a rapidly progressive anaemia indicates marrow aplasia
Megaloblastic anaemia is most common; a rapidly progressive anaemia indicates haemorrhage
Sideroblastic anaemia is most common; a rapidly progressive anaemia indicates thalassaemia
RBC: anaemia of chronic disease is the most common; rapidly progressive anaemia is autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. (Book p461)
Which lymphoma association is attached to the leucopenia note in SLE, and how is it contrasted?
SLE carries a raised risk of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; Sjogren carries a raised risk of marginal zone B-cell lymphoma
SLE carries a raised risk of marginal zone lymphoma; Sjogren carries a raised risk of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Both carry a raised risk of Hodgkin lymphoma
WBC: leucopenia/lymphopenia with a raised risk of DLBCL; the note contrasts Sjogren syndrome, which raises the risk of marginal zone B-cell lymphoma. (Book p461)
The platelet line of the haematological block is labelled:
Platelet: secondary ITP is listed in the haematological manifestations. (Book p461)
A patient with SLE is assessed for interstitial lung disease. Which source statement governs the expectation?
ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation of SLE
Usual interstitial pneumonia is the characteristic SLE pattern
Pulmonary fibrosis is the leading cause of death in SLE
The lung parenchyma is spared in SLE, so ILD is not expected
The lung block states the lung parenchyma is spared in SLE, therefore there is no ILD; pleuritis and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage dominate instead. (Book p461)
A patient with SLE has pleuritic chest pain and a small bilateral pleural effusion. Which description of SLE pleuritis does the source print?
Most common lung manifestation: small, bilateral, exudative effusion
Only seen with associated pulmonary embolism
Pleuritis is the most common lung manifestation, with or without a small, bilateral, exudative effusion. (Book p461)
A patient with SLE develops cough, haemoptysis and bilateral air-space opacification on the chest radiograph. What does the source require?
Active immunosuppression for diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Stopping immunosuppression because the likely cause is viral or tuberculous infection

Cough, haemoptysis and bilateral air-space opacification indicate diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, which requires active immunosuppression; the contrasting branch (viral/TB) is managed by stopping immunosuppression. (Book p461)
Why is diffuse alveolar haemorrhage emphasised in the lung block?
It is the commonest cause of pulmonary hypertension in SLE
It has a poor prognosis and is the most important marker of SLE disease activity in the lung
It is benign and needs no treatment
DAH is flagged as carrying a poor prognosis and as the most important marker of SLE disease activity in the lung. (Book p461)
Which biomarker pattern is printed for assessing SLE disease activity?
Falling anti-dsDNA, rising C3/C4, raised ESR with raised CRP
Rising anti-Ro, normal C3/C4, normal ESR
Rising anti-Smith with a raised CRP and normal ESR
Rising anti-dsDNA, falling C3/C4, raised ESR with CRP below 10 mg/dL
Activity assessment: clinically active disease with new-onset rashes, rising anti-dsDNA titres, falling C3 and C4, and a raised ESR with a low CRP (below 10 mg/dL). (Book p461)
A patient with SLE has central chest pain relieved by leaning forward and a rub on examination, without hypotension. Which cardiac manifestation does the source list as most common?
Cardiac: pericarditis without tamponade is the most common manifestation; myocarditis is associated with anti-Ro antibody. (Book p461)
Where are the vegetations of Libman-Sacks endocarditis located according to the source?
On the chordae of the mitral valve only
On the undersurface of the valve leaflet
Libman-Sacks endocarditis is described with vegetations on the undersurface of the valve leaflet; mitral regurgitation is the most common valvular lesion. (Book p461)
A patient with SLE is found to have a raised transaminase with a positive autoantibody panel but no abdominal symptoms. Which gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary statements does the source print?
Both the gut and liver are commonly involved with granulomas
The gut is spared but the pancreas is the target organ
The gut is generally spared; the hepatobiliary link is type 1 autoimmune (lupoid) hepatitis
The gut is commonly involved with vasculitis; the liver is never involved
GIT: generally spared. Hepatobiliary: type 1 autoimmune hepatitis (lupoid hepatitis). (Book p461)
Which thresholds are printed as indications for renal biopsy in SLE?
Proteinuria above 150 mg/day on a single sample
Proteinuria above 1 g/day, or proteinuria of at least 500 mg/day with at least 3 RBCs in urine
Indications for renal biopsy: proteinuria >1 g/day, or proteinuria ≥500 mg/day plus ≥3 RBCs in urine (microhaematuria). (Book p461)
Two biopsies are compared: one shows only mesangial immune-complex deposits with no clinical renal disease, and one shows mesangial proliferation. How does the source pair class with prognosis?
Class I minimal mesangial is asymptomatic with an excellent prognosis; class II mesangial proliferative has a poor prognosis
Both are class I disease with an excellent prognosis
Both require active immunosuppression as class III disease
Both are class V membranous disease with a better prognosis

Class I minimal mesangial lupus nephritis shows mesangial immune-complex deposits, is asymptomatic and has an excellent prognosis, whereas class II mesangial proliferative disease is marked as having a poor prognosis. (Book p462)
How does the printed table separate class III from class IV lupus nephritis?
Class III is focal with under 50% glomerular involvement; class IV is diffuse with over 50%
Class III is diffuse with over 90% involvement; class IV is focal with under 50%
Class III is membranous; class IV is sclerotic
Class III focal lupus nephritis has <50% glomerular involvement; class IV diffuse has >50% glomerular involvement. (Book p462)
A biopsy report describes focal lupus nephritis with RPGN. What does the source say about this group?
They respond to ACE inhibition alone
Class III focal lupus nephritis is linked with RPGN and the table states these patients require active immunosuppression. (Book p462)
Which pairing is printed for class V (membranous) lupus nephritis?
Mesangial immune-complex deposits, asymptomatic, excellent prognosis
Membranous nephropathy, adult-onset nephrotic syndrome, steroid-resistant, better prognosis
Class V shows membranous nephropathy with adult-onset nephrotic syndrome, is resistant to steroid, and carries a better prognosis. (Book p462)
Which class carries the worst prognosis with over 90% glomerular sclerosis and CKD?
Class VI advanced sclerotic lupus nephritis
Class I minimal mesangial lupus nephritis
Class II mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis
Class VI advanced sclerotic lupus has >90% glomerular sclerosis and CKD, and is marked as the worst prognosis. (Book p462)
Which light-microscopy description is printed for class III/IV lupus nephritis?
Purely mesangial proliferation without capillary involvement
Class III and IV lupus nephritis: HP shows endocapillary plus mesangial proliferation. (Book p462)
Which immunofluorescence pattern is described in class III/IV lupus nephritis, and what caution is added?
Isolated IgA deposition, as in IgA nephropathy
Linear IgG along the basement membrane, as in Goodpasture syndrome
Full-house pattern: IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q and C3 deposits, a pattern also seen in HIV
IF shows IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q and C3 deposits, the full-house pattern; the note adds that it is also seen in HIV. (Book p462)
Which electron-microscopy and specific histological findings are printed for class III/IV disease?
Subepithelial spikes only; no specific inclusions
Mesangial IgA dominance; tubuloreticular inclusions are the most specific
Subendothelial wire-loop deposits with mesangial deposits; hematoxylin bodies of Gross are the most specific
EM shows subendothelial (wire loop lesion) and mesangial deposits; hematoxylin bodies of Gross are described as most specific, and tubuloreticular inclusions are also shown. (Book p462)
Which CNS manifestation is listed as the most common in SLE, and which vascular risk is added?
Cognitive decline is most common, with a raised stroke risk from antiphospholipid antibodies
Seizures are most common, with a raised haemorrhage risk from thrombocytopenia
Psychosis is most common, with a raised risk of CNS lymphoma
Aseptic meningitis is most common, with a raised risk of venous sinus thrombosis
CNS: cognitive decline is the most common manifestation, with a raised risk of stroke due to antiphospholipid antibodies; small-fibre neuropathy and CNS vasculitis are also listed. (Book p463)
Which weights are printed for the constitutional and arthritis domains?
Fever scores 2; synovitis or tenderness in at least 2 joints scores 6
Fever scores 6; synovitis or tenderness in at least 2 joints scores 2
Constitutional domain: fever 2. Arthritis domain: synovitis or tenderness in at least 2 joints, 6. (Book p463)
How is the cutaneous domain weighted in the classification table?
Only acute cutaneous lupus is scored, at 10
Acute cutaneous lupus 6, SCLE or discoid lupus 4, oral ulcers 2 and non-scarring alopecia 2
Acute cutaneous lupus 2, SCLE or discoid lupus 4, oral ulcers 6 and non-scarring alopecia 6
Cutaneous domain: non-scarring alopecia 2, oral ulcers 2, subacute cutaneous or discoid lupus 4 and acute cutaneous lupus 6. (Book p463)
Which neurological weights are printed in the clinical domains column?
Neurologic domain: delirium 2, psychosis 3, seizure 5. (Book p463)
How is the serositis domain weighted in the classification table?
Pleural or pericardial effusion 5; acute pericarditis 6
Pleural or pericardial effusion 6; acute pericarditis 5
Serositis domain: pleural or pericardial effusion 5 and acute pericarditis 6. (Book p463)
How are the haematologic domain items weighted?
Only autoimmune haemolysis is scored, at 6
Haematologic domain: leukopenia 3, thrombocytopenia 4, autoimmune haemolysis 4. (Book p463)
Which renal-domain weights are printed in the classification table?
Proteinuria above 0.5 g/24 h scores 4; class II or V lupus nephritis 8; class III or IV lupus nephritis 10
Proteinuria above 0.5 g/24 h scores 10; class II or V scores 4; class III or IV scores 2
Renal domain: proteinuria >0.5 g/24 hr = 4 points; class II or V lupus nephritis = 8; class III or IV lupus nephritis = 10. (Book p463)
How is the antiphospholipid-antibody domain scored in the immunologic column?
4 points only when lupus anticoagulant is present
It is not scored in this table
2 points for anticardiolipin IgG above 40 GPL, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG above 40 units, or lupus anticoagulant
Antiphospholipid antibody domain: anticardiolipin IgG >40 GPL, or anti-β2 glycoprotein I IgG >40 units, or lupus anticoagulant scores 2. (Book p463)
Which immunologic-domain weights are printed for complement and highly specific antibodies?
Low C3 or low C4 scores 3, low C3 and low C4 scores 4, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm each score 6
Low C3 or low C4 scores 6, both low scores 8, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm each score 3
Complement proteins domain: low C3 or low C4 = 3; low C3 and low C4 = 4. Highly specific antibodies domain: anti-dsDNA = 6 and anti-Sm = 6. (Book p463)
What are the entry criterion and the classification threshold printed with the criteria table?
Low complement and at least 12 points
ANA at least 1:80 as the entry criterion and at least 10 points to be classified as SLE
ANA at least 1:160 and at least 6 points
Anti-dsDNA positivity and at least 4 points
The table notes that all patients classified as having SLE must have ANA ≥1:80 (entry criterion) and patients must have ≥10 points to be classified as SLE. (Book p463)
Which caution is printed beside the classification table?
A negative ANA still allows classification
Fewer than 10 points still allows classification
Classification criteria are not diagnostic criteria
Classification criteria replace the need for ANA testing
The note states that classification criteria are not diagnostic criteria. (Book p463)
What defines the target in the treat-to-target loop printed at the top of the management page?
Discontinuation of all therapy within 3 months
SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) driven to 0 as the indicator of remission
Treat to target: SLE diagnosis to active disease to initial treatment to remission; the target is the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) to 0, which is the indicator of remission. (Book p464)
A patient with SLE has only constitutional symptoms. What initial therapy is printed?
Initial Rx: constitutional symptoms are managed with HCQ (hydroxychloroquine) and observation. (Book p464)
Which regimen is printed for non-life-threatening SLE?
Low-dose steroid below 7.5 mg/day plus hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/day
Non-life-threatening SLE: low-dose steroid (<7.5 mg/day) plus HCQ 5 mg/kg/day. (Book p464)
A patient with SLE on hydroxychloroquine is reviewed for long-term toxicity. Which monitoring investigation does the source attach to this drug?
Optical coherence tomography to look for retinal toxicity
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is listed to look for retinal toxicity during HCQ therapy. (Book p464)
What pulse steroid regimen is printed for life-threatening or organ-threatening SLE?
Hydrocortisone 100 mg three times daily for 10 days
Methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g in 100 ml normal saline over 1-2 hours, pulsed for 3 days
IV steroid: methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g IV infusion in 100 ml normal saline over 1-2 hours, given as a pulse for 3 days. (Book p464)
After the intravenous pulse for organ-threatening SLE, what oral regimen follows?
Oral steroid 1 mg/kg/day tapered over 3 months down to 5 mg/day
Oral steroid 1 mg/kg/day continued for 12 months without taper
Oral steroid 0.1 mg/kg/day for one week
The pulse is followed by oral steroid 1 mg/kg/day, tapered over 3 months to 5 mg/day. (Book p464)
Which steroid-sparing induction options are listed alongside the intravenous steroid?
Oral mycophenolate mofetil 2-3 g/day or intravenous cyclophosphamide 500 mg in two doses two weeks apart
Alongside IV steroid: oral MMF (mycophenolate mofetil) 2-3 g/day or IV cyclophosphamide 500 mg, two doses two weeks apart. (Book p464)
A patient who received cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis is counselled about long-term risks. Which adverse effects does the source list?
Adverse effects with long-term cyclophosphamide use: secondary malignancy (AML) and gonadal toxicity. (Book p464)
How is remission judged in the printed management algorithm?
By anti-dsDNA alone after one week
By complement levels alone after one month
By SLEDAI assessment after more than 3 months
The algorithm states: assess remission after more than 3 months using the SLEDAI index. (Book p464)
What maintenance regimen is printed once remission is achieved?
Steroid below 7.5 mg/day plus mycophenolate mofetil 1 g/day or azathioprine for 2-3 years
Maintenance Rx: steroid (<7.5 mg/day) plus MMF (1 g/day) or azathioprine for 2-3 years. (Book p465)
Which steroid-sparing agent is named for maintenance therapy in SLE?
Belimumab is listed as the steroid-sparing agent in the maintenance block. (Book p465)
Maintenance therapy fails to produce remission after more than three monthly assessments. Which escalation is printed next?
The flowchart takes the no-remission (>3 months) branch to switching to cyclophosphamide, and if there is still no response the case is labelled refractory lupus. (Book p465)
Which agents are listed for refractory lupus?
Rituximab, voclosporin with MMF, belimumab (anti-BLyS) and anifrolumab (anti type I interferon)
Refractory lupus: rituximab, voclosporin (a calcineurin inhibitor) with MMF, belimumab (anti-BLyS) and anifrolumab (anti type I interferon). (Book p465)
A patient with refractory lupus has diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with CNS vasculitis. Which additional therapy does the source list?
The refractory-lupus block adds that plasma exchange is done if DAH or CNS vasculitis is present. (Book p465)
Which goals of therapy are printed at the end of the lupus treatment sequence?
Normalisation of ESR and CRP only
Asymptomatic, normal urine, normal complement and no fever or cytopenias
Goals of Rx: asymptomatic, urine normal, complement normal, and no fever and no cytopenias. (Book p465)
Which mnemonic is printed for drugs causing drug-induced lupus?
CHImP: carbamazepine, chlorpromazine, hydralazine, isoniazid, interferon, infliximab, methyldopa, procainamide, phenytoin
ABCDE: amiodarone, bleomycin, cyclophosphamide, dapsone, ethambutol
The CHImP mnemonic lists carbamazepine, chlorpromazine, hydralazine, isoniazid, interferon, infliximab, methyldopa, procainamide and phenytoin. (Book p465)
Which serological profile is printed for drug-induced lupus?
Anti-dsDNA positive, antihistone negative and ANA negative
Anti-dsDNA negative, antihistone positive and ANA positive in 100% of cases
Clinical features: M = F, CNS and renal not involved, anti-dsDNA negative, antihistone antibody positive, ANA positive in 100% and skin plus joint involvement. (Book p465)
Which feature is least compatible with the source's drug-induced lupus profile?
Immune-complex glomerulonephritis with a rising anti-dsDNA titre
Good prognosis after withdrawing the offending drug
Drug-induced lupus spares the CNS and kidneys and is anti-dsDNA negative; nephritis with a rising anti-dsDNA belongs to SLE. (Book p465)
Which apparent paradox about these drugs is printed as a note?
These drugs make antihistone antibodies disappear
Drugs that cause drug-induced lupus are safe to use in patients who already have SLE
These drugs must never be used in any patient with a positive ANA
The note states that drugs causing SLE (drug-induced lupus) are safe in lupus patients. (Book p465)
Which earlier name for antiphospholipid syndrome is printed at the head of the chapter?
The heading notes the syndrome was earlier called antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLA). (Book p466)
What proportion of SLE cases is printed as antiphospholipid-syndrome positive?
The chapter notes that one-third of SLE cases are APS positive. (Book p466)
A patient with SLE is found to have antiphospholipid antibodies and asks about the thrombotic tendency. Which pattern does the source describe?
Increased arterial dissection risk without thrombosis
Increased susceptibility to thrombus formation, venous more than arterial
Increased susceptibility to haemorrhage, venous more than arterial
Increased capillary fragility with purpura only
In the complications-of-SLE note, APS is described as increasing susceptibility to thrombus formation, with venous more than arterial events. (Book p466)
Which complication listed under SLE involves medium vessels of the gut and CNS?

The SLE complications note lists accelerated atherosclerosis, glomerular disease (class III/IV lupus nephritis), complications of immunosuppression, vasculitis of medium vessels (GIT/CNS) and APS. (Book p466)
How does the source divide primary and secondary APS?
About 90% primary; secondary disease does not exist
About 10% primary; the rest are secondary to malignancy
All cases are secondary to SLE
About 50% primary, associated with HLA DR4 and DRw53; at least 50% secondary, most commonly from SLE
APS: 50% of cases are primary, associated with HLA DR4 and HLA DRw53; 50% or more are secondary, most commonly due to SLE (one-third of APS). (Book p466)
Which HLA-disease pairing is printed in the side note beside the APS epidemiology block?
HLA DR3 positivity is linked to Sjogren syndrome and SLE; the most common cause of secondary Sjogren is rheumatoid arthritis
HLA DR4 positivity is linked to Sjogren syndrome and SLE
HLA DR5 positivity is linked to Sjogren syndrome
No HLA association is noted for Sjogren syndrome
The side note states the most common cause of secondary Sjogren is RA and that HLA DR3 positivity is associated with Sjogren syndrome and SLE. (Book p466)
Against which targets are the antiphospholipid antibodies directed according to the pathophysiology diagram?
Phospholipid-binding proteins: beta-2 glycoprotein I, the prothrombin-phosphatidylserine complex and annexin

Antibodies are directed against phospholipid-binding proteins: beta-2 glycoprotein I, the prothrombin-phosphatidylserine complex and annexin, with platelet surface proteins shown alongside. (Book p466)
Which platelet count range is printed alongside the raised propensity to thrombosis?
A normal platelet count is mandatory
Thrombocytopenia of about 50,000 to one lakh
The pathway ends in thrombocytopenia (50,000 to one lakh) with an increased propensity to thrombosis. (Book p466)
Which downstream mechanisms are printed after antigen-antibody complex formation?
Platelet inhibition and fibrinolysis leading to bleeding
Complement inhibition with no thrombotic tendency
Increased affinity for platelets and complement activation, plus reduced inhibition of coagulation factors, leading to thrombosis

The diagram shows the Ag-Ab complex with increased affinity for platelets, activation of the complement cascade, thrombocytopenia with a raised thrombotic tendency, and reduced inhibition of coagulation factors progressing to thrombosis. (Book p466)
What are the two hits printed in the APS model?
First hit: antibody causing endothelial injury; second hit: oestrogen, smoking, obesity or other prothrombotic states
First hit: infection; second hit: malignancy
First hit: platelet antibodies; second hit: complement deficiency
First hit: trauma; second hit: immobilisation only
The two hits are the antibody causing endothelial injury and a second hit such as oestrogen, smoking, obesity or other prothrombotic states. (Book p467)
A young woman presents with an unprovoked venous thrombosis and thrombophilia testing is planned. Which ranking of causes does the source print?
Acquired and inherited causes are equally common
Acquired: antiphospholipid syndrome is the most common; inherited: factor V Leiden mutation
Acquired: malignancy is the most common; inherited: protein C deficiency
Inherited: factor V Leiden is more common than any acquired cause
The most common cause of thrombophilia is acquired (APS), greater than inherited factor V Leiden mutation. (Book p467)
How is the thrombosis spectrum ranked in the clinical-features list?
Stroke more than DVT more than Budd-Chiari syndrome
DVT more than arterial thrombosis (stroke) more than Budd-Chiari syndrome
Budd-Chiari syndrome more than DVT more than stroke
Thrombosis: DVT is more common than arterial thrombosis (stroke), which is more common than Budd-Chiari syndrome. (Book p467)
A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome presents with painful hepatomegaly and ascites, and later with a cerebral venous thrombosis. Which venous territories does the source name?
Portal vein causing portal hypertension only
Renal vein causing nephrotic syndrome only
Hepatic vein causing Budd-Chiari syndrome and cerebral veins causing cortical vein thrombosis
Veins involved: hepatic vein gives Budd-Chiari syndrome and cerebral veins give cerebral venous thrombosis. (Book p467)
Which organs are listed under microvascular APS involvement?
Microvascular involvement affects the kidneys more than the adrenals. (Book p467)
A young patient has livedo reticularis and an ischaemic stroke. Which syndrome does the source name?
Sneddon's syndrome is listed with livedo reticularis and stroke in the APS clinical-features block. (Book p467)
A young woman presents with hepatic vein thrombosis and antiphospholipid antibodies are considered. Which differential diagnosis does the source list?
APS, polycythemia rubra vera and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
The note gives the differential for hepatic vein thrombosis as APS, polycythemia rubra vera and PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria). (Book p467)
A young patient with antiphospholipid syndrome has an acute neurological deficit with a cranial nerve palsy and pyramidal weakness. Which stroke profile does the source highlight?
Insidious onset with a purely sensory deficit
Acute onset, cranial nerve palsy and a pyramidal pattern of weakness
The note describes the stroke as acute in onset with cranial nerve palsy and a pyramidal pattern of weakness. (Book p467)
What persistence requirement is printed for the Sapporo laboratory criteria?
Any antibody positive twice, at least 12 weeks apart
A single positive antibody at any time
Three positive results within one week
Antibody positivity for five consecutive years
Laboratory criteria: any antibody positive twice over 12 weeks. (Book p467)
Which assay is attached to anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies in the Sapporo criteria?
ELISA for IgG or IgM anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I
Anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I (IgG/IgM) is detected by ELISA. (Book p467)
Which anticardiolipin threshold and performance are printed?
IgA above 40 units; described as specific
Any titre; described as neither sensitive nor specific
IgG or IgM above 40 units; described as sensitive
IgG or IgM above 4 units; described as specific
Anti-cardiolipin antibody (IgG/IgM >40 units) is described as sensitive. (Book p467)
A patient has an unexplained prolonged aPTT and a positive lupus anticoagulant. How does the source characterise this test, and which assays are named?
Sensitive but not specific: normal aPTT with a raised bleeding time
Both highly sensitive and specific: prolonged prothrombin time only
Of no diagnostic value in APS
Specific but not sensitive: raised aPTT and a raised dilute Russell's viper venom test (dRVVT)
Lupus anticoagulant is specific but not sensitive, with a raised aPTT and a raised dRVVT (diluted Russell's viper venom test). (Book p467)
Which vascular event satisfies the clinical criterion for APS?
A vascular event due to venous or arterial thrombosis
Clinical criteria: a vascular event due to venous or arterial thrombosis. (Book p468)
Which obstetric criteria are printed for APS?

Any one miscarriage at or beyond 10 weeks, or three or more miscarriages before 10 weeks, or premature delivery before 34 weeks of a morphologically normal neonate due to pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or HELLP syndrome
Any two first-trimester losses with a chromosomal abnormality
Delivery before 37 weeks for any reason

Pregnancy criteria: one miscarriage ≥10 weeks, or ≥3 miscarriages before 10 weeks, or premature delivery <34 weeks of a morphologically normal neonate due to pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or HELLP syndrome. (Book p468)
A woman with recurrent pregnancy loss after 10 weeks of gestation is evaluated for antiphospholipid syndrome. Which obstetric role does the source highlight?
APS causes loss only in the third trimester
APS is the most common cause of second-trimester abortion, that is loss after 10 weeks
The note states APS is the most common cause of second-trimester abortion (after 10 weeks). (Book p468)
A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome has chorea and a pansystolic murmur from mitral regurgitation. Which non-criteria manifestations does the source list?
CNS: stroke only; cardiac: myocardial infarction only
CNS: chorea, epilepsy and migraine; cardiac: Libman-Sacks endocarditis and mitral regurgitation
Non-criteria APS: CNS shows chorea, epilepsy and migraine; cardiac shows Libman-Sacks endocarditis and MR. (Book p468)
Which haematological manifestations are listed under non-criteria APS?
Warm-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and Evan's syndrome
Cold agglutinin disease and sickle cell crisis
Hematological: warm-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and Evan's syndrome, with thrombocytopenia not significant enough to cause bleeding. (Book p468)
A renal biopsy in a patient with antiphospholipid antibodies shows thrombotic microangiopathy. How does the source describe the renal lesion?
APS nephropathy: thrombotic microangiopathy from microvascular involvement of the kidney
Renal: APS nephropathy is a thrombotic microangiopathy due to microvascular involvement of the kidney. (Book p468)
A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome collapses in shock and livedo reticularis is noted over the legs. Which non-criteria entries explain these findings?
Endocrine: adrenal-vessel infarction with adrenal insufficiency; dermatological: venous obstruction and venular dilatation producing livedo reticularis
Endocrine: infarction of adrenal vessels leads to adrenal insufficiency (shock); dermatological: venous obstruction with venular dilatation gives livedo reticularis. (Book p468)
Which domains are listed under the clinical and laboratory columns of the APS domain table?
Clinical: fever and rash; laboratory: ESR and CRP
Clinical: renal and hepatic; laboratory: complement and immunoglobulins
Clinical: neurologic and pulmonary; laboratory: imaging and biopsy
Clinical: macrovascular venous, macrovascular arterial, microvascular, obstetric, cardiac valve and haematology; laboratory: lupus anticoagulant test and other antibody tests

Domains: clinical domains 1-6 (macrovascular venous, macrovascular arterial, microvascular, obstetric, cardiac valve, haematology) and laboratory domains 7-8 (lupus anticoagulant test, other antibody tests). (Book p469)
How is catastrophic APS defined in the note?
Three or more organ systems involved within one week, with small-vessel involvement
One organ system involved over one year
Two organ systems over one month with large-vessel disease
Any thrombotic event with a positive antibody

Catastrophic APS: three or more organ systems involved within one week, with small vessels involved; presentations include thrombotic microangiopathy of the kidney and adrenal insufficiency. (Book p469)
An asymptomatic adult with antiphospholipid antibodies but no events is reviewed. What does the source advise?
Management: an asymptomatic adult requires no treatment. (Book p469)
Which anticoagulation targets and regimens are printed for an adult with a thrombotic episode?
Target INR 3.5-4.5 with warfarin alone for six weeks
Target INR 2.5-3 with a direct oral anticoagulant
Target INR 2.5-3 using heparin 5000 units three times daily subcutaneously or LMWH 60 mg twice daily, overlapped with warfarin continued lifelong
To attain an INR of 2.5-3: heparin 5000 units TDS SC or LMWH 60 mg BD SC, with warfarin overlapped with heparin/LMWH and continued lifelong; the note adds there is no role for NOACs. (Book p469)
A pregnant patient with known APS and a history of previous thrombosis asks about prophylaxis. What is printed?
Aspirin alone for the first trimester only
Prophylactic low-dose aspirin plus heparin throughout pregnancy and for 6-12 weeks post-partum
Pregnancy management: prophylactic low-dose aspirin with heparin throughout pregnancy and for 6-12 weeks post-partum; warfarin is continued lifelong if APS is diagnosed. (Book p469)
Which regimen is printed for catastrophic APS?
Steroids plus intravenous immunoglobulin plus plasmapheresis
Catastrophic APS is managed with steroids, IV Ig and plasmapheresis. (Book p469)
A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome on warfarin asks whether a direct oral anticoagulant can replace it. Which caution does the source print?
NOACs replace warfarin after one year
There is no role for new oral anticoagulants (NOACs) in APS
NOACs are the first-line choice in all APS patients
The note states there is no role for new oral anticoagulants (NOACs) in APS. (Book p469)
A tutorial compares a biopsy from active lupus nephritis with one from early systemic sclerosis. Which inflammation contrast does the source draw?
SSc shows more inflammation than SLE
SLE shows marked inflammation while SSc shows only mild inflammation with a low or normal ESR
Both show equally intense inflammation with a raised ESR
The general-features diagram contrasts inflammation: SLE +++ versus SSc + with a low or normal ESR. (Book p470)
Which pathogenetic triad is drawn for systemic sclerosis?
Neutrophilic infiltration, pustule formation and scarring
Amyloid deposition, light-chain production and cast nephropathy
Fibrosis, vasculopathy and immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis with capillary hypoxia

SSc pathogenesis: fibrosis (with interstitial lung disease), vasculopathy from small-vessel endothelial injury with anti-endothelial antibody causing thrombosis, and immune-complex-mediated small-vessel vasculitis producing capillary hypoxia. (Book p470)
Which sequence is drawn for the severe vascular form of systemic sclerosis?
Medium-vessel involvement (mesenteric and CNS) with TGF-beta release driving mesenchymal cells to myofibroblasts
Severe form: involvement of medium vessels (mesenteric and CNS vessels) with TGF-beta release acting on mesenchymal cells to produce myofibroblasts. (Book p470)
A patient with systemic sclerosis develops exertional breathlessness and is found to have pulmonary arteriolar hypertension. How does the source frame this complication?
Pulmonary arteriolar hypertension (group 1) with a bad prognosis
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease with an excellent prognosis
Chronic thromboembolic disease cured by thrombolysis
Pulmonary arteriolar hypertension (class 1) is attached to the vasculopathy arm and marked as carrying a bad prognosis. (Book p470)
What does the source give as the definition of scleroderma itself?
Thickening and induration of the skin
Ulceration of the skin with necrosis
Scleroderma is defined as thickening and induration. (Book p470)
How does the classification page divide the scleroderma spectrum?
Only by antibody status, with no skin-based division
By the presence or absence of Raynaud phenomenon only
Local manifestation (localised scleroderma: morphoea and linear scleroderma) versus systemic manifestation (systemic sclerosis, subdivided by extent of skin involvement)

Local manifestations are localised scleroderma (morphoea, linear scleroderma); systemic manifestation is systemic sclerosis, subdivided by extent of skin involvement into diffuse and limited SSc. (Book p470)

Two patients with systemic sclerosis are compared: one has skin thickening over the trunk with ILD, the other has skin changes only distal to the elbows with pulmonary hypertension. Which subset pairing does the source print?
Diffuse: skin changes over all parts of the body, ILD, fibrosis with vasculopathy and minimal inflammation; limited: skin distal to elbow and face, pulmonary hypertension, vasculopathy predominant
Diffuse: skin distal to elbow, pulmonary hypertension; limited: skin over all parts of the body, ILD
Both have identical skin distribution and complications

Diffuse SSc: skin lesion over all parts of the body, complications of ILD, pathogenesis of fibrosis plus vasculopathy with minimal inflammation. Limited SSc: skin distal to elbow and face, pulmonary hypertension, vasculopathy predominant. (Book p470)
A patient with indurated skin plaques who received gadolinium contrast is referred as possible scleroderma. Which mimics does the source list?
Eosinophilic fasciitis with groove sign and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis after gadolinium contrast
Dermatomyositis with Gottron papules and SLE with malar rash
Scleroderma mimics: eosinophilic fasciitis with groove sign, and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, which is drug induced after gadolinium contrast. (Book p470)
How is the epidemiology of systemic sclerosis summarised?
A disease of the elderly with equal sex distribution
A tropical infection with vector transmission
An orphan disease of unknown cause, aged 35-50 years, with a female-to-male ratio of 5:1
A common disease of childhood with male predominance
Etiology: orphan disease with unknown cause; age 35-50 years; F:M = 5:1. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
Which susceptibility genes and infections are listed under etiology?
No genetic or infective associations are listed
HLA DRB1/DQB1 (DR5) with EBV, CMV and parvovirus B19
Immune susceptibility is listed as HLA DRB1/II (DR5) and viral associations are EBV, CMV and parvovirus B19. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
Which agent is printed as having the strongest association with systemic sclerosis?
Agents inducing scleroderma: vinyl chloride, bleomycin, pentazocine, contaminated L-tryptophan and silica, with silica carrying the maximum association with SSc. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
Which HLA-disease pairings are printed in the side note?
DR3 with SLE and Sjogren syndrome, DR4 with APS and RA, DR5 with SSc, and silica also associated with SLE
DR3 with SSc, DR4 with SLE, DR5 with Sjogren syndrome
DR2 with multiple sclerosis, DR3 with myasthenia
The note pairs HLA DR-3 with SLE and Sjogren syndrome, DR-4 with APS and RA, DR-5 with SSc, and adds that silica is also associated with SLE. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
How is very early systemic sclerosis (VESS) characterised?
VESS never progresses to systemic sclerosis
About two-thirds of cases progress to SSc over 3-5 years
All cases progress to SSc within 6 months
Very early systemic sclerosis: 3-5 years, with two-thirds of cases progressing to SSc. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
A patient with Raynaud phenomenon and a positive ANA is assessed for very early systemic sclerosis. Which investigation completes the source's triad?
The triad pairs Raynaud's phenomenon and ANA positivity with the investigation nail-fold capillaroscopy. (Book p471)

A worker reports finger colour change and pain while using a vibrating tool in a cold store and during stressful periods. Which triggers does the source list?
Raynaud's phenomenon is episodic vasoconstriction in response to stimuli; triggers listed are cold, stress and vibration. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
A patient describes digital colour change with pain and a tight, swollen hand. Which sequence and associated sign does the page list?
Pallor only, with no reactive phase
Pallor, cyanosis and redness on rewarming, with pain and tightness of digits and a puffy hand
Persistent erythema with no colour change
Clinical manifestations listed: pallor, cyanosis, redness on rewarming, pain and tightness of digits and a puffy hand. (Book p471)
Etiology, Very Early SSc & Raynaud's Phenomenon
A young woman with triphasic cold-induced colour change has a negative ANA, symmetric self-limiting symptoms and a mother with the same complaint. Which column does this fit?
ANA positive with a positive family history
ANA negative with a negative family history
ANA negative with a positive family history and a good prognosis
ANA positive with a negative family history
Primary (Raynaud's disease): ANA negative, family history positive, symptoms self-limiting and symmetric, and other features listed as a good prognosis. (Book p472)

Which features are printed in the secondary Raynaud column?
Mild self-limiting disease with a good prognosis
Purely arterial disease without tissue loss
Severe disease with critical limb ischaemia, ulcer and gangrene, associated with SSc, Sjogren syndrome, MCTD and inflammatory muscle disease

Secondary Raynaud phenomenon: severe with critical limb ischaemia, ulcer and gangrene of the extremities, and associated diseases (SSc, Sjogren syndrome, MCTD and inflammatory muscle disease). (Book p472)

Nail-fold capillaroscopy in a patient with suspected secondary Raynaud phenomenon shows capillary dropout with dilated tortuous loops and microhaemorrhages. Which column does this match?
Dropout of capillaries, dilated tortuous capillaries and microhaemorrhages
Giant capillaries only in the primary form
Nail-fold capillaroscopy in secondary disease: dropout of capillaries, dilated tortuous capillaries and microhaemorrhages; the primary column is normal. (Book p472)

A patient with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis has a centromere pattern on ANA testing. Which antibody does the source pair with this pattern?
Anti-U1 RNP with a coarse-speckled pattern
Anti-centromere antibody with a centromere ANA pattern
Anti-RNA polymerase III with a nucleolar pattern
Limited SSc: ANA pattern centromere with anti-centromere antibody; diffuse SSc: fine speckled with anti-topoisomerase and anti-RNA polymerase III. (Book p472)

How does the printed table contrast Raynaud phenomenon between limited and diffuse SSc?
Limited: long-standing and severe with critical limb ischaemia, from predominant vasculopathy; diffuse: short-lasting and less severe, from predominant fibrosis
Limited: short-lasting and mild; diffuse: long-standing and severe

Raynaud phenomenon: limited SSc is long standing and severe (due to predominant vasculopathy) with critical limb ischaemia present; diffuse SSc is short lasting and less severe (due to predominant fibrosis) with critical limb ischaemia not extensive. (Book p472)
Primary vs Secondary Raynaud's & Diffuse vs Limited SSc
Which antibody pair is printed for diffuse systemic sclerosis?
Diffuse SSc: anti-topoisomerase and anti-RNA polymerase III, with a fine-speckled ANA pattern. (Book p472)

What does the C and the E of the CREST association stand for on this page?
C: calcinosis in the tissues; E: oesophagitis, which is far more common in limited than diffuse disease
C: calcinosis; E: equally common in both subsets
CREST: C is calcinosis of the tissues; E is oesophagitis, marked limited much greater than diffuse. (Book p473)

Which two components complete the CREST association?
R: restrictive lung disease; S: stenosis; T: thrombosis
R: Raynaud phenomenon; S: sclerodactyly, that is scleroderma of the fingers; T: telangiectasia
R: renal crisis; S: synovitis; T: tenosynovitis
R: rash; S: sicca; T: thyroiditis
CREST: R is Raynaud's phenomenon, S is sclerodactyly (scleroderma of fingers) and T is telangiectasia, with minimal fibrosis noted for limited disease. (Book p473)
Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
A patient with limited systemic sclerosis is breathless, yet spirometry is normal and only the DLCO is reduced. Which functional pattern does the source describe?
Obstructive pattern with a low FEV1/FVC
Normal spirometry and a normal DLCO
Asymptomatic with normal FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC but a reduced DLCO
Marked restriction with a low FVC and a normal DLCO
Pulmonary artery hypertension is asymptomatic with normal FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC but a reduced DLCO. (Book p473)

Why is pulmonary artery hypertension emphasised prognostically?
It is benign and never progresses
It responds dramatically to calcium-channel blockers alone
It only occurs in diffuse disease
It carries a poor prognosis because of increased mortality
Pulmonary artery hypertension: poor prognosis due to increased mortality. (Book p473)
Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
Which features are listed as arguments AGAINST limited systemic sclerosis?
Extensive fibrosis, ILD, cardiac involvement and renal involvement
Features against limited SSc: extensive fibrosis, ILD, cardiac involvement and renal involvement. (Book p473)

A patient with diffuse disease reports tight facial skin, a small mouth with pursed lips and patchy pigment change on the face. Which description does the source give?
Salt-and-pepper hypo- and hyperpigmentation with hair loss, progressing to face tightening, microstomia, pursed lips, a puckered mouth and mask facies

Skin manifestations: dry tight skin, facial hypo- and hyperpigmentation (salt-and-pepper appearance), hair loss, intense itching, and progression to face tightening with microstomia, pursed lip, puckered mouth and mask facies. (Book p473)

Which general skin description is printed for diffuse SSc?
Diffuse SSc skin manifestations include bilateral symmetrical skin thickening. (Book p473)
Limited SSc, PAH & Diffuse Cutaneous Features
How are the joint manifestations divided between diffuse and limited SSc?
Diffuse: acral osteolysis; limited: arthritis and myositis
Both subsets show identical erosive arthritis
Joint disease never occurs in SSc
Diffuse: arthritis and myositis from inflammation; limited: acral osteolysis with severe Raynaud phenomenon
Joint manifestations: diffuse SSc shows arthritis/myositis due to inflammation; limited SSc shows acral osteolysis (falling off of fingers) with diffuse severe Raynaud's phenomenon. (Book p474)
Which mechanism is given for acral osteolysis?
Other manifestations include acral osteolysis, attributed to fibrosis or vasculopathy. (Book p474)
A patient with systemic sclerosis has dysphagia and bloating, and imaging shows dilated bowel loops with gas in the bowel wall. Which gastrointestinal sequence does the source describe?
Oesophageal hypomotility leading to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and pneumatosis intestinalis
Peptic ulcer disease leading to perforation
Oesophageal hypomotility progresses to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and pneumatosis intestinalis. (Book p474)
How is the watermelon stomach lesion identified according to the source?
The watermelon-stomach image is labelled as seen on upper GI endoscopy. (Book p474)
Which manifestation is listed as the most common cause of death in systemic sclerosis?
Disease progression: pulmonary manifestations leading to interstitial lung disease, which is the most common cause of death; cardiac and renal manifestations are also listed. (Book p474)
A patient with limited systemic sclerosis and anti-centromere antibodies is monitored for complications. Which complication does the source link to this antibody?
Anti-centromere is limited-type SSc with CREST syndrome and pulmonary hypertension as the complication. (Book p474)
A patient with diffuse systemic sclerosis is found to have anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Which complication is most strongly linked to this antibody?
Anti-RNA polymerase III (diffuse) is linked to scleroderma renal crisis, more than anti-topoisomerase, and to malignancy of lung and breast. (Book p474)
Which findings are attached to anti-topoisomerase-1 (anti Scl-70)?
Malignancy of lung and breast only
Isolated Raynaud phenomenon without organ disease
Renal thrombotic microangiopathy, lung ILD, tendon friction rubs (diffuse more than limited), GAVE and rapidly progressive skin involvement with joint contractures

Anti-topoisomerase-1 (anti-Scl-70), diffuse: renal TMA progressing to scleroderma renal crisis, lung ILD, tendon friction rubs on passive movement (diffuse more than limited), GAVE (watermelon stomach) and rapidly progressive skin involvement with joint contractures and tendon friction rubs. (Book p474)
Which overlap antibodies are printed, and how do they differ by lung involvement?
Both are associated with severe ILD
Anti-PM/Scl-70 overlap has ILD; anti-Ku overlap has no ILD
The antibody table lists anti-PM/Scl-70 in overlap disease with ILD positive and anti-Ku in overlap disease with no ILD. (Book p474)
Three years after diagnosis of diffuse systemic sclerosis, a patient develops accelerated hypertension with acute kidney injury. How does the source characterise this presentation?
It presents within the first 4 years, affects small vessels of the kidney and shows thrombotic microangiopathy
It presents after 20 years and affects large renal arteries
It is a glomerulonephritis with immune-complex deposits
It is caused by analgesic nephropathy
Renal disease in diffuse SSc presents within the first 4 years, affects small vessels of the kidney and is a thrombotic microangiopathy. (Book p475)
Which triad of findings is printed for the thrombotic microangiopathy of scleroderma renal crisis?
Accelerated hypertension, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia
Thrombotic microangiopathy: accelerated hypertension plus microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia plus thrombocytopenia. (Book p475)
Which drug class is printed as the treatment of choice for scleroderma renal crisis?
Angiotensin-receptor blockers combined with renin inhibitors
Rx for scleroderma renal crisis: ACE inhibitors, described as the drug of choice. (Book p475)
Which phases of diffuse systemic sclerosis are described?
An early fibrotic phase followed by an oedematous phase
A single static phase with no progression
A granulomatous phase followed by a caseating phase
An early oedematous phase with non-pitting oedema, progressing to a fibrotic phase
Phases of diffuse SSc: the oedematous phase, more common in diffuse disease and associated with non-pitting oedema, progresses to the fibrotic phase. (Book p475)
A patient with systemic sclerosis has progressive dyspnoea with a markedly reduced DLCO and basal subpleural reticular change on the chest radiograph. Which pattern does the source print?
DLCO markedly reduced with reduced FRC, and bilateral basal subpleural reticular infiltrates on the chest radiograph
Obstructive pattern with a raised FRC and hyperinflation
Isolated reduced FEV1 with normal volumes
Normal PFTs with a normal radiograph
Investigations: PFT for ILD shows DLCO markedly reduced and FRC reduced; the chest radiograph shows bilateral basal subpleural reticular infiltrates. (Book p475)
A patient with systemic sclerosis needs imaging for suspected interstitial lung disease. Which investigation of choice and pattern ranking does the source give?
Bronchoscopy is the investigation of choice; LIP predominates
HRCT is the investigation of choice; NSIP is more common than UIP in scleroderma
Chest radiography is the investigation of choice; UIP is more common than NSIP
PET-CT is the investigation of choice; COP predominates
HRCT: IOC. Scleroderma: NSIP more than UIP. (Book p476)
How does the table contrast NSIP with UIP in scleroderma?
Both patterns are identical in findings and treatment
UIP has the better prognosis of the two

NSIP: no parenchymal destruction, ground-glass opacities, treated with steroid and mycophenolate with a better prognosis; UIP: destruction with cystic change, honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, no effective treatment
NSIP: honeycombing and no treatment; UIP: ground-glass opacities responding to steroids

NSIP shows no destruction with ground-glass opacities and is treated with steroids and mycophenolate mofetil (better prognosis); UIP shows destruction with cystic changes, honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis with no treatment listed. (Book p476)
Which disease associations are printed in the interstitial-pattern note?
UIP with SLE and LIP with sarcoidosis
NSIP with rheumatoid arthritis and UIP with Sjogren disease
LIP with systemic sclerosis and NSIP with sarcoidosis
UIP with rheumatoid arthritis and LIP with Sjogren disease, while NSIP is the pattern in others
The note attributes UIP to RA, LIP as characteristic of Sjogren's disease, and NSIP to others. (Book p476)
What is the printed first-line treatment for Raynaud phenomenon in systemic sclerosis?
A calcium-channel blocker, with or without a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil
A beta-blocker with or without a nitrate
Rx of RP: first line is a calcium-channel blocker, with or without a PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil). (Book p476)
A patient with systemic sclerosis has Raynaud phenomenon that has not responded to a calcium-channel blocker. Which second-line agent and class does the source print?
Second line for Raynaud phenomenon is bosentan, an endothelin antagonist. (Book p476)
Which regimen is printed for SSc-associated interstitial lung disease?
Nintedanib plus mycophenolate mofetil, as the disease does not respond to steroid
ILD: nintedanib plus MMF, and the source notes the disease is non-responsive to steroid. (Book p476)
Which treatments are listed for skin, joint and muscle disease in systemic sclerosis?
Cyclophosphamide for skin; rituximab for joints
Hydroxychloroquine for skin; sulfasalazine for joints
D-penicillamine for skin; colchicine for joints
Mycophenolate mofetil for skin; steroid plus methotrexate for joints and muscle
Treatment: skin is treated with mycophenolate mofetil, and joint plus muscle involvement with steroids and methotrexate; scleroderma renal crisis is treated with ACE inhibitors. (Book p476)
Which definition is printed for the inflammatory muscle diseases?
A motor-neuron disease with fasciculations and wasting
A multisystem autoimmune connective-tissue disease with mononuclear inflammation within skeletal muscle and subacute weakness, lasting 6-8 weeks
A monophasic post-viral myalgia of the calves lasting days
A dystrophic muscle disease with dystrophin loss
Definition: a multisystem autoimmune CTD characterised by mononuclear inflammation within skeletal muscle, with subacute muscle weakness and fatigue, lasting 6-8 weeks. (Book p477)
Which entities are listed in the OLD classification of the inflammatory muscle diseases?
Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
Dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome and juvenile dermatomyositis
Old classification: polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy. (Book p477)
Which term does the CURRENT classification declare obsolete?

Current classification opens with polymyositis, now an obsolete term, and then lists dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome, necrotizing myopathies, juvenile DM, paraneoplastic myositis, inclusion body myositis and amyopathic DM. (Book p477)
A patient reports progressive difficulty rising from a chair and lifting the head off the pillow over two months, with new dysphagia. Which Bohan-Peter criterion does this satisfy?
Proximal and symmetrical weakness of the pelvic and scapular girdle and anterior neck flexors progressing over weeks to months, with or without dysphagia or respiratory-muscle involvement
Muscle biopsy showing necrosis and inflammatory exudate

Criterion A: proximal and symmetrical muscle weakness of the pelvic and scapular girdle and anterior flexors of the neck, progressing for weeks to months, with or without dysphagia or involvement of respiratory muscles. (Book p477)
Blood tests in a patient with suspected myositis show a raised creatine kinase with raised AST, LDH and aldolase. Which Bohan-Peter criterion does this satisfy?
Creatine kinase, aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase and aldolase
Alanine aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase only
Criterion B: elevation of serum levels of skeletal-muscle enzymes, namely creatine kinase, aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase and aldolase. (Book p477)
Electromyography in a weak patient shows short small motor units with fibrillation, positive sharp waves and insertional irritability. Which criterion does this satisfy?
Myasthenic decremental response on repetitive stimulation
A purely neuropathic pattern with fibrillation only

What is printed under Bohan-Peter criterion D?
A normal muscle biopsy with no inflammation

Criterion D: muscle biopsy showing necrosis, phagocytosis and inflammatory exudate. (Book p477)
A weak patient has a violaceous periorbital rash with periorbital oedema and vasculitic lesions over the MCP joints. Which Bohan-Peter item does this fulfil?

Which HLA-disease pairings are printed in the note on HLA risk factors?
DR3 with scleroderma; DR4 with SLE; DR5 with Sjogren syndrome
DR2 with myasthenia; DR3 with vasculitis
HLA associations are not printed for myositis
DR3 with SLE, Sjogren syndrome and dermatomyositis; DR4 with APS and RA; DR5 with scleroderma

Ascending areflexic paralysis with sensory involvement

Which examination findings are printed for the muscular presentation?
Normal power with fasciculations and absent reflexes
Reduced power with a sensory level
Normal bulk with reduced power and tone, normal reflexes and an intact sensory system
Reduced bulk with brisk reflexes and sensory loss
Examination findings: bulk normal, power reduced, tone reduced, reflexes normal and sensory system intact. (Book p478)

30% have acute-subacute proximal pain and weakness; 10% have chronic proximal plus distal weakness
10% have acute-subacute proximal pain and weakness; 30% have chronic proximal plus distal weakness

Which clinical syndrome in the frequency table runs over years rather than months?
Insidious proximal and distal weakness over 1-10 years
Acute or subacute proximal pain and weakness over weeks to months

A patient with proximal weakness has violaceous flat-topped papules over the knuckles and a periorbital violaceous rash. Which lesions does the source call pathognomonic?
Gottron's papules and the heliotrope rash

Pathognomonic skin lesions: Gottron's papule (scaly erythematous flat-topped violaceous papule/plaque over the dorsal MCP, PIP and DIP) and heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema). (Book p479)
A tender subcutaneous nodule over the shins
A purpuric macule on the buttocks
A keratotic plug on the palms only
A scaly, erythematous, flat-topped violaceous papule or plaque over the dorsal surface of MCP, PIP and DIP joints
Gottron's papule: scaly erythematous flat-topped violaceous papule/plaque on the dorsal surface of MCP, PIP and DIP joints. (Book p479)
A patient with myositis has violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema. What is this rash called?
A violaceous plaque over the knuckles
A photosensitive rash over the upper back
Heliotrope rash: violaceous periorbital oedema and erythema. (Book p479)
How does the source distinguish Gottron's sign from Gottron's papule?
There is no difference between the two
Gottron's sign is the macular erythema over the papule, typically on extensor surfaces and photosensitive, with linear erythema over the dorsum of the hand
Gottron's sign is the same lesion on the elbow only
Gottron's sign is a scarring variant
Other skin lesions: Gottron rash/sign is macular erythema over Gottron's papule, typically on extensor surfaces, photosensitive, with linear erythema over the dorsum of the hand. (Book p479)
A patient has a photosensitive erythematous rash over the chest and upper back, with a further patch on the lateral thigh. Which signs does the source name?
All three are on the face
All three are on the lower legs
V sign over the chest; shawl sign posteriorly over the back; holster sign on the lateral aspect of the thigh
V sign over the back; shawl sign over the chest; holster sign on the arm
V sign is located over the chest, shawl sign posteriorly over the back and holster sign is erythema on the lateral aspect of the thigh; scalp involvement is generally pruritic. (Book p479)
Which nail-fold findings are listed under telangiectasia?
Periungual erythema or oedema with cuticular hyperplasia
Telangiectasia: nail-fold capillary involvement with periungual erythema or oedema, and cuticular hyperplasia also seen. (Book p479)
A child with dermatomyositis develops firm subcutaneous deposits over the extremities. Which statements does the source make about calcinosis cutis?
It is due to deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite, is seen in juvenile dermatomyositis and also occurs in CREST syndrome
It is due to urate deposition and occurs only in gout
It is due to amorphous calcium phosphate and occurs only in SLE
It is a feature of adult dermatomyositis alone
Calcinosis cutis: also seen in CREST syndrome and in juvenile dermatomyositis, and due to deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite. (Book p479)
How does the dermatomyositis rash differ from the SLE rash on this page?
The DM rash is always associated with oral ulcers
The DM rash involves the knuckles, spares the nasolabial fold, is pruritic and is not associated with oral ulcers
The DM rash spares the knuckles and involves the nasolabial fold

SLE rash: never involves the knuckles, may involve the nasolabial fold, associated with painless oral cavity ulcers and non-pruritic. Dermatomyositis rash: involves the knuckles (MCP joint), does not involve the nasolabial fold, not associated with oral cavity ulcers and pruritic. (Book p480)
Which statement about mechanic's hand is printed?
It is diagnostic of systemic sclerosis
It is not specific for dermatomyositis and forms part of the antisynthetase syndrome
Mechanic's hand: not specific for dermatomyositis and part of the antisynthetase syndrome. (Book p480)
A definitive test is needed in a patient with suspected inflammatory muscle disease. Which investigation does the source call the gold standard?
Muscle biopsy is described as the gold standard test. (Book p480)
Which muscle-biopsy features are printed for dermatomyositis?
Mononuclear (CD4-positive T-cell) infiltrate with perifascicular atrophy
CD8-positive T-cell endomysial invasion without atrophy
Muscle biopsy shows a mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate of CD4+ T cells and perifascicular atrophy. (Book p480)
Which MRI sequence and finding are printed?
T1 sequence showing hypointense fibrosis only
MRI: the STIR sequence shows hyperintense areas within muscle. (Book p480)
Which electromyographic findings are listed in the investigations block?
A decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation
Prolonged insertion with myotonic discharges only
Polyphasic short-duration small-amplitude potentials with high-frequency discharges and spontaneous fibrillation
Large polyphasic units with a reduced interference pattern
EMG: polyphasic short-duration small-amplitude potentials, high-frequency discharges, and spontaneous fibrillation or denervation. (Book p480)
Enzymes in a patient with myositis show a creatine kinase above the AST. Which enzyme relationship does the source print?
LDH is the only useful enzyme
Enzymes: CPK is greater than AST. (Book p480)
Which antibody and prognostic profile is printed on this page?
Anti-Mi-2 alpha: good prognosis, low risk for ILD and responsive to conventional therapy with steroid and MMF
Anti-Jo-1: good prognosis with no ILD risk
Anti-MDA-5: low risk of rapidly progressive ILD
Antibody associated: anti-Mi-2 alpha with good prognosis, low risk for ILD and responsiveness to conventional therapy (steroid plus MMF). (Book p480)
How do the age groups differ between polymyositis and dermatomyositis in the comparison table?
Polymyositis occurs only in adults; dermatomyositis is also seen in the elderly and in juveniles
Dermatomyositis occurs only in adults; polymyositis also occurs in children
Both are confined to middle-aged adults
Age group: polymyositis only in adults; dermatomyositis seen in the elderly or juvenile. (Book p481)
A patient with biopsy-proven myositis has no skin rash and no calcinosis. Which rows of the source's comparison table best separate the two entities?
Serum enzymes: raised in polymyositis, normal in dermatomyositis
EMG: abnormal in polymyositis, normal in dermatomyositis
Skin changes and calcinosis: absent or rare in polymyositis, present in dermatomyositis
Weakness distribution: distal in polymyositis, proximal in dermatomyositis

Skin changes are absent in polymyositis and present in dermatomyositis; calcinosis is rare in polymyositis and seen in dermatomyositis. Both share subacute onset, proximal symmetric weakness, systemic features and normal-to-high enzymes. (Book p481)
Which overlap statement is printed for the two entities?
Dermatomyositis never exists on its own
Neither is associated with overlap syndromes
Both always occur as isolated diseases
Polymyositis never exists on its own, whereas dermatomyositis can exist on its own
Associated systemic conditions or overlap syndrome: yes for polymyositis, which never exists on its own, and yes for dermatomyositis, which can exist on its own. (Book p481)
Which biopsy immunology distinguishes the two conditions?
Polymyositis shows CD8-positive T-cell involvement; dermatomyositis shows CD4-positive and B-cell involvement with perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation
Both show identical CD8-positive endomysial infiltrates
Biopsy findings: polymyositis shows CD8+ T-cell involvement while dermatomyositis shows CD4+ and B cells with perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation. (Book p481)
Which prognostic statement opens the antisynthetase syndrome block?
It is treatable if diagnosed early
It is uniformly fatal within a year
The antisynthetase syndrome block opens with the statement that it is treatable if diagnosed early. (Book p481)
A patient with myositis has roughened skin on the radial side of the index finger, Raynaud phenomenon, cardiomyopathy and an SLE-like arthritis. Which syndrome and features does the source list?
Proximal myalgia with a normal CK
Isolated ILD with no systemic features
Mechanic's hand, Raynaud phenomenon, cardiomyopathy and an SLE-like arthritis (Jaccoud arthropathy)
Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules and calcinosis
Antisynthetase syndrome clinical features: mechanic's hand, Raynaud's phenomenon, cardiomyopathy and an SLE-like arthritis (Jaccoud's arthropathy). (Book p481)
How does the source describe mechanic's hand in the antisynthetase syndrome?
Violaceous papules over the dorsal MCP joints
Painless nodules over the Achilles tendon
Crusted hyperkeratotic lesions on the radial aspect of the index and middle fingers
Mechanic's hand is seen on the radial aspect of the index and middle finger and is characterised by crusted hyperkeratotic lesions. (Book p481)
Which additional disease association is printed for Jaccoud's arthropathy?
It is also seen in Sjogren syndrome
It is also seen in sarcoidosis
It is pathognomonic of rheumatoid arthritis
It occurs only in the antisynthetase syndrome
The note adds that Jaccoud's arthropathy is also seen in Sjogren's syndrome. (Book p481)
A patient with the antisynthetase syndrome has fever and pulmonary infiltrates on the chest radiograph. What does the source warn about?
It is a benign self-limiting finding
It can be mistaken for viral pneumonia and can progress to ILD, which is the most common cause of death
It is always a bacterial pneumonia needing antibiotics
It indicates an acute coronary syndrome

Investigations: CXR shows fever with infiltrates, which can be mistaken for viral pneumonia and can progress into ILD; ILD can be the first presentation of the syndrome and is the most common cause of death. (Book p481)
HRCT in a patient with myositis shows ground-glass opacities with areas of consolidation. Which interstitial patterns does the source print?
NSIP and COP, with NSIP most common and identified by ground-glass opacities
UIP and LIP, with UIP most common
ILD pattern: NSIP plus COP. NSIP is most common and identified by ground-glass opacities; COP is identified by consolidations. (Book p482)

Which imaging signature is attached to a UIP pattern in these patients?

Anti-MDA-5 with a poor prognosis that is not treatable

An 8-year-old girl with dermatomyositis has no cardiac involvement, no malignancy and no interstitial lung disease. Which pattern does the source print for juvenile disease?
Boys are affected twice as often as girls

Juvenile DM commonly affects girls aged 5-15 years and malignancy, cardiac involvement and ILD are absent. (Book p482)

Which antibodies are printed for juvenile dermatomyositis, and what does their presence in an adult imply?

Anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1-gamma; in adults they indicate cancer-associated myositis

Which antibody and treatment-response pairings are printed for immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy?
Both antibodies respond fully to steroids alone
Anti-SRP responds rapidly and anti-HMG-CoA reductase does not
Neither antibody is associated with treatment response
Anti-SRP in severe disease with ILD and cardiac involvement does not respond; anti-HMG-CoA reductase after statin therapy responds to steroid, IVIG and rituximab

An elderly man presents with recurrent falls and slowly progressive weakness. Which demographic and presenting pattern does the source print?
Most common in the elderly with male predominance, presenting with recurrent falls and a chronic course
Most common in young women with an acute febrile onset
Most common in children with a rash

IBM: most common in the elderly (males more than females), presenting with recurrent falls and a chronic presentation. (Book p483)
How is the weakness of inclusion body myositis described?
Asymmetrical proximal and distal involvement, including quadriceps, vastus and finger flexors
IBM weakness is asymmetrical, proximal plus distal, and involves the quadriceps, vastus and finger flexors. (Book p483)
A muscle biopsy shows red-rimmed vacuoles and the patient has not improved on steroids. Which histology and treatment response does the source print?

Perifascicular atrophy with an excellent steroid response
IBM histology shows red-rimmed vacuoles and the disease is steroid unresponsive. (Book p483)
Which malignancies are paired with dermatomyositis on this page?
Breast cancer is characteristic and colon cancer the most common
Gastric cancer is characteristic and lymphoma the most common

Which antibody is printed for the antisynthetase syndrome in the antibody table?

Which antibodies are listed as OTHER associated antibodies, and what is noted for two of them?
Anti-RNA polymerase III and anti-U1 RNP
Anti-Ro, anti-Ku (which may develop ILD) and anti-PM/Scl (polymyositis with scleroderma with or without ILD and a nucleolar ANA pattern)

Which antibodies are shared by juvenile dermatomyositis and cancer-associated myositis?

What is the printed first-line treatment for the inflammatory muscle diseases?
Steroid alone in pulsed doses only
Steroid plus methotrexate, or steroid plus mycophenolate mofetil
