Which agents are listed as second-line treatment?
Rituximab and JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib
Second-line treatment: rituximab and JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib). (Book p483)
What is stated as the goal of treatment for the inflammatory muscle diseases?
Clinical elimination of all disease activity
The treatment goal is clinical elimination of all disease activity. (Book p483)
A 35-year-old woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and a lymph-node biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas. Which definition does the source give?
A chronic, multisystem, granulomatous immunological disorder with non-caseating granulomas on biopsy
An acute suppurative infection with neutrophilic abscesses
A vasculitic disorder of medium vessels
An eosinophilic infiltration of the lung and skin
Sarcoidosis is defined as a chronic, multisystem, granulomatous, immunological disorder; biopsy usually shows non-caseating granulomas. (Book p484)
What exception to the non-caseating rule is printed?
Caseation occurs only in the skin
Caseating granulomas can be seen in one-third of cases
Caseating granulomas never occur in sarcoidosis
Caseation is seen in every case
Biopsy usually shows non-caseating granulomas, but caseating granulomas can occur in one-third of cases. (Book p484)
Which outcome spread is printed for sarcoidosis?
All patients develop chronic fibrotic disease
About 50% resolve spontaneously, about 25% become chronic (mostly lung) and about 5% mortality attributed to ILD and infections
About 90% resolve and mortality is unknown
Outcome: 50% spontaneous resolution, 25% become chronic (mostly the lung is affected) and 5% mortality, attributed to interstitial lung disease and infections. (Book p484)
A biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas and tuberculosis is being considered. Which other conditions does the source list as producing non-caseating granulomas?
30% of TB cases, lymphoma, berylliosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Crohn disease and cat-scratch disease
Diseases that can have non-caseating granulomas: 30% of TB cases, lymphoma, berylliosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), Crohn's disease and cat-scratch disease. (Book p484)
Which three items make up the ACR criteria for the diagnosis of sarcoidosis?
A compatible clinical picture, histological non-caseating granulomas and exclusion of other causes
Raised ACE, a positive Mantoux test and hypercalcaemia
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever and weight loss
A positive gallium scan, BAL lymphocytosis and skin anergy
ACR criteria: compatible clinical picture, histological non-caseating granulomas and exclusion of other causes. (Book p484)
Which named syndromes head the acute and chronic branches of the classification?
Acute: Sweet syndrome; chronic: Sjogren syndrome
Acute: Lofgren syndrome; chronic: Heerfordt syndrome
Acute: Heerfordt syndrome; chronic: Lofgren syndrome
Acute: Garland syndrome; chronic: Mikulicz syndrome
Classification: acute sarcoidosis is represented by Lofgren syndrome and chronic sarcoidosis by Heerfordt syndrome; hilar adenopathy is the important finding. (Book p484)
A patient with sarcoidosis has lung, skin, eye and joint involvement and asks which organ is usually spared. Which ranking and spared organ does the source print?
Eyes more than lung, with the liver spared
Joints most often, with the kidney spared
Lung (ILD) more than skin more than eyes more than joints, with only the testes spared
Skin more than lung more than eyes, with the spleen spared
Major manifestations: lung (ILD) more than skin more than eyes more than joints; multisystem manifestations include cardiac and renal disease, and the only organ spared is the testes. (Book p484)
Which risk factors are listed for sarcoidosis?
Propionibacterium acnes infection and excessive firewood burning
Risk factors: Propionibacterium acnes infection and excessive firewood burning. (Book p484)
A patient with Lofgren syndrome is HLA typed. Which association and prognosis does the source print?
HLA-DRB1*03, associated with Lofgren syndrome and a good prognosis
HLA-DRB1*11, which marks CNS and cardiac disease
HLA DRB1*03 is associated with Lofgren syndrome and a good prognosis. (Book p485)

Which HLA types are printed as protective and as markers of poor prognosis respectively?
HLA-DRB1*04 is protective; HLA-DRB1*11 marks CNS and cardiac sarcoidosis with a bad prognosis
HLA-DRB1*11 is protective; HLA-DRB1*04 marks severe disease
HLA DRB1*04 has a protective role, while HLA DRB1*11 is associated with CNS and cardiac sarcoidosis, which carries a bad prognosis. (Book p485)

Which HLA-disease pairs are repeated in the note on other diseases?
DRB1*05 with SLE and Sjogren syndrome
DRB1*03 with SLE, Sjogren syndrome and dermatomyositis; DRB1*04 with APS and RA; DRB1*05 with scleroderma
DRB1*03 with scleroderma; DRB1*04 with SLE
The note repeats: HLA DRB1*03 with SLE, Sjogren syndrome and dermatomyositis; DRB1*04 with APS and RA; DRB1*05 with scleroderma. (Book p485)

A patient with sarcoidosis has a negative Mantoux test despite previous BCG vaccination and has recurrent chest infections with lymphopenia. What does the source call this?
Lymphocytosis with a strongly positive Mantoux test
Neutropenia with a false-positive Mantoux test
Eosinophilia with a normal immune response
Lymphopenia in the blood with a raised risk of infection, and a false-negative Mantoux test
Immune paradox/anergy: lymphopenia in blood leading to increased risk of infection, and a Mantoux test that is false negative because of low lymphocytes. (Book p485)
HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
Which observation is printed about HIV infection and sarcoidosis?
HIV positivity lowers the lymphocyte count and lowers the risk of sarcoidosis
HIV positivity raises the risk of sarcoidosis
HIV has no relationship to sarcoidosis
The note states HIV positivity leads to lymphopenia and a reduced risk of sarcoidosis. (Book p485)
HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
A young patient presents with tender pretibial nodules, ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar adenopathy. Which syndrome does the source name?
Fever, night sweats and weight loss
Erythema nodosum, arthritis and hilar adenopathy
Uveitis, parotitis and facial nerve palsy
Lupus pernio, bone cysts and uveitis
Lofgren syndrome is drawn with erythema nodosum, arthritis and hilar adenopathy. (Book p485)
HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
How is the rash of sarcoidosis-associated erythema nodosum described?
A vesicular rash on sun-exposed skin
A scarring panniculitis of the thighs
Erythema nodosum in Lofgren syndrome is described with the 3 P's: painful, pretibial, papule. (Book p485)

Which features are listed for the arthritis or tenosynovitis of acute sarcoidosis?
Chronic, unilateral large-joint disease in the elderly
Acute onset, ankle involvement, bilateral and symmetrical, occurring in young patients
Arthritis/tenosynovitis is acute, involves the ankle joint, is bilateral and symmetrical and is seen in the young. (Book p485)
HLA Associations, Immune Paradox & Lofgren Syndrome
How does the source distinguish the erythema nodosum of Behcet disease?
It has a fourth P: pigmentation, in addition to painful, pretibial papules
It is confined to the arms
It is identical to the sarcoid lesion
In Behcet's disease, erythema nodosum has 4 P's: painful, pretibial, papules with pigmentation. (Book p486)

Which statement is printed about hilar adenopathy in sarcoidosis?
It is a feature of tuberculosis, not sarcoidosis
It is the most consistent feature and is generally bilateral
It is rare and always unilateral
It occurs only in chronic disease
Hilar adenopathy is described as the most consistent feature and is generally bilateral, with right paratracheal and left hilar nodes shown. (Book p486)
Hilar Adenopathy, Heerfordt Syndrome & Chronic Sarcoidosis
A patient with sarcoidosis has uveitis, bilateral facial nerve weakness and parotitis. Which syndrome and features does the source list?
Lupus pernio, bone cysts and panuveitis
Uveitis, bilateral lower-motor-neuron seventh-nerve palsy and parotitis
Erythema nodosum, ankle arthritis and hilar adenopathy
Heerfordt-Waldenstrom syndrome: uveitis, bilateral LMN seventh-nerve palsy and parotitis. (Book p486)

Which uveitis statements are printed for sarcoidosis?
The eye is never involved in sarcoidosis
Any type or compartment can be involved, acute anterior uveitis is more common and uveitis is the most common ocular manifestation
Uveitis: any type or compartment, acute anterior uveitis more common, and the most common ocular manifestation of sarcoid. (Book p486)

A patient with sarcoidosis develops bilateral lower-motor-neuron facial weakness. What does the source call this manifestation?
Bilateral LMN seventh-nerve palsy is the most common neurological manifestation in sarcoid; the note pairs it with Guillain-Barre syndrome as its main differential. (Book p486)

What is the clinical paradox of chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis?
Nodes and parenchyma are unrelated to the disease stage
As the lung disease worsens, the nodal enlargement regresses, which helps identify chronicity
Nodes enlarge in proportion to the parenchymal disease
Nodes calcify while the parenchyma remains normal
Clinical paradox: it helps identify chronicity, because as the lung disease worsens the nodal enlargement regresses. (Book p486)

Serial imaging shows hilar nodes regressing as parenchymal infiltrates appear, and later fibrosis. How does the source stage chronic sarcoidosis?
Staging is based on symptoms, not imaging
Stage 1 bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; stage 2 nodal enlargement with parenchymal disease; stage 3 parenchymal disease only; stage 4 fibrosis
Stage 1 fibrosis; stage 2 nodes; stage 3 infiltrates; stage 4 calcification

Stages: 1 bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with nodal enlargement only, 2 nodal enlargement plus parenchymal disease (node size starts to fall as infiltrate rises), 3 parenchymal disease only, 4 fibrosis. (Book p486)

Which features are printed for the fibrosis pattern of sarcoidosis?
Thickening of the bronchovascular bundles with upper-lobe traction bronchiectasis
Fibrosis pattern: thickening of bronchovascular bundles and traction bronchiectasis of the upper lobe; upper-lobe fibrosis is also listed for ankylosing spondylitis and sarcoidosis. (Book p487)
A patient has violaceous indurated plaques over the central face that respond poorly to treatment. How does the source describe this lesion?
Violaceous or erythematous, indurated infiltrative plaques on the central face that respond poorly to treatment
A painless pretibial nodule that resolves spontaneously

The current classification splits memory by mode of retrieval into which two branches?

Mode of retrieval (current classifications): explicit (declarative) - episodic and semantic - and implicit (non-declaratives): procedural, priming, associative (conditional), non associative. (Book p569)
Episodic memory per the flowchart is based on time and context (autobiographical), is hippocampal, and is affected early in which disease?

Episodic: based on time and context (autobiographical), area hippocampus, affected early in Alzheimer's disease; semantic: based on facts, association areas, rarely affected in late Alzheimer's disease. (Book p569)

Procedural: basal ganglia, supplementary motor area, cerebellum (e.g. driving); priming: neo cortex (remembering facts d/t exposure, duration or intensity); associative (conditional): amygdala (not seen in humans - animals associating fear to lion and environment); non-associative: reflex pathway (habitual response). (Book p570)
An animal's fear-association response to a predator in its environment is mapped in the table to which area?

Per the cortex anatomy table, which lobe's area stores semantic memory?

Which subcortical area is labelled the 'gateway of memory' storing long-term memory?

The Papez circuit is also known as what, and which station is annotated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndromes?

Papez circuit aka mammillo-thalamic circuit: hippocampus/subiculum -> fornix -> mammillary body (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndromes) -> mammillo-thalamic tract -> thalamus -> internal capsule -> cingulate gyrus -> parahippocampal gyrus -> entorhinal cortex (gateway of memory) -> back to hippocampus. (Book p571)

ADL: basic = self-care related; instrumental = handling own phone, money, etc. Cognitive impairment: minor = ADL unaffected; major = ADL affected. (Book p572)

Definition as printed: major cognitive impairment + >=1 out of 6 cognitive domains affected. (Book p572)
The language domain in the 6-domain table maps to which areas?
Inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's) and superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's)

Domain table: episodic memory -> hippocampus (median temporal lobe); language -> inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's) + superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's); complex attention, executive function and social cognition -> prefrontal cortex; perceptual motor (praxicons) -> superior parietal lobule. (Book p572)
The four causes of dementia listed on this page are:
Alzheimer's disease (m/c), diffuse Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia, normal pressure hydrocephalus

Causes: 1. Alzheimer's disease (m/c); 2. diffuse Lewy body (DLB) dementia; 3. vascular dementia (branches: post-stroke, multi-infarct dementia, white matter dementia/Binswanger disease); 4. normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). (Book p572)
Based on the parts of brain affected, the subcortical-dementia list includes:
DLB dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy, Binswanger disease, NPH
Dementia -> cortical; subcortical -> diffuse Lewy body (DLB) dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy, Binswanger disease, NPH. (Book p572)
The PFC-functions note assigns which function to the orbital PFC?
Note - functions of PFC: dorsolateral PFC executive function; medial PFC energisation and motivation; orbital PFC behaviour. (Book p572)
A reversible-cause workup lists benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants and lithium under which mnemonic letter?

Reversible causes: D drugs (benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, lithium); E endocrine (hypothyroidism: metabolic slowing); M metabolic (vit B12 deficiency); E chronic infections of ear; N normal pressure hydrocephalus; T trauma, tumors; I infections (chronic meningitis); A anemia, autoimmune encephalitis. (Book p573)
Peripheral neuropathy plus dementia plus subacute combined cord degeneration points to which reversible cause?
Note: vit B12 deficiency -> peripheral neuropathy, dementia and subacute combined cord degeneration; Rx of NPH: surgery. (Book p573)
The treatment of NPH stated in the reversible-causes note is:
Note under reversible causes: Rx of NPH - surgery. (Book p573)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the condition NOT listed under young-onset dementia:
Young onset dementia: frontotemporal dementia (Pick's disease) m/c, prion disease, Huntington's disease, DLB dementia. (Book p573)
Among rapidly progressive dementias, which two are bracketed as non-degenerative?
Rapidly progressive: FTD (Pick's) m/c, prion, DLB, HIV and Whipple's (bracketed non-degenerative), tumors (based on location). (Book p573)
The pathology note says entorhinal cortex atrophy is specific for which disease?
Atrophy of: entorhinal cortex - specific for Alzheimer's; dentate nucleus - occurs with ageing. Alzheimer's disease: m/c cause of dementia; most important risk factor age; sporadic. (Book p573)
The book prints what chance of Alzheimer's for age >85 years?
Most important risk factor: age (>85 years: 40% chance of Alzheimer's). (Book p573)
In the APP pathway, abnormal kinetics with metabolism by which enzyme produces A-beta amyloid (beta-pleated sheets)?

APP (amyloid precursor protein, gene on chr 21) with abnormal kinetics is metabolised by beta-secretase producing A-beta amyloid (beta-pleated sheets); note: normal metabolism uses alpha-secretase. (Book p574)
A-beta 40 and A-beta 42 diverge in the pathway: which outcome pairs with A-beta 40?
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy with microhemorrhages in brain
A-beta 40 -> cerebral amyloid angiopathy (microhemorrhages in brain); A-beta 42 -> Alzheimer's disease -> depositions of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins (tauopathy). (Book p574)
Deposited inside the neuron, hyperphosphorylated tau forms what, and which sequence follows?
Neurofibrillary tangles -> mitochondrial injury -> progressive neuronal destruction
Amyloid/neuritic plaques -> toxic response from glia

Inside neuron: neurofibrillary tangles -> mitochondrial injury to neurons -> progressive neuronal destruction; outside neuron: amyloid/neuritic plaques elicit toxic response from oligodendrocytes, microglia, astrocytes. (Book p574)
In 'type 3 DM / brain diabetes', why does A-beta 42 accumulate?
Hyperinsulinemia uses up the insulin degrading enzyme, leaving A-beta 42 undegraded
Normal physiology: insulin degrading enzyme (IDE) degrades insulin and A-beta 42; in diabetes hyperinsulinemia -> IDE used up in degrading insulin -> A-beta 42 accumulates. (Book p574)
The AD pathology list on MRI includes atrophy of which regions?
Median temporal lobe, lateral temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus and entorhinal cortex

Pathology: atrophy of median temporal lobe, lateral temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus and entorhinal cortex (gateway of memory) - seen on MRI; plus Hirano bodies and granulovacuolar degeneration. (Book p574)
Depleted cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert justify which DOC class?
Depleted cholinergic neurons of nucleus basalis of meynert -> DOC: cholinesterase inhibitors. (Book p574)
The genetic-basis list places Presenilin-1, Presenilin-2 and ApoE4 on which chromosomes respectively?

Genetic basis: Presenilin-1 (chr 14) and Presenilin-2 (chr 1) - m/c defect in familial AD -> early onset -> characteristic features (<45 years, seizures, sleep disturbances); ApoE4 (chr 19) in late-onset dementia, ineffective degradation of A-beta amyloid, most important risk factor (biomarker) for sporadic AD in elderly. (Book p575)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the item that IS a risk factor, against the printed 'Not risk factors' list:

Risk factors: age, positive family history (Presenilin 1 > 2), F > m, h/o head trauma/concussions, h/o stroke, metabolic syndrome, hypertension, diabetes. Printed NOT risk factors: low IQ, smoking, NSAIDs. Note: theory of cognitive reserve - individuals with daily use of cognitive domains are protected from AD. (Book p575)
A patient who uses cognitive domains daily is described as protected from AD by which printed theory?
Note - theory of cognitive reserve: individuals with daily use of cognitive domains -> protected from AD. (Book p575)
In the clinical-stages loop, naming and comprehension abnormalities (stage II) follow hippocampal stage I and arise at which structure?
Angular gyrus feeding the association areas

Loop: hippocampus -> stage I (Korsakoff amnestic stage: episodic memory loss, difficulty in consolidating memory) -> angular gyrus -> association areas (stage II: stage of anomia, naming and comprehension abnormalities) -> superior parietal lobe praxicons (stage III: visuo-spatial disorientation; apraxia) -> PFC (stage IV: behavioural abnormalities and personality changes). Note: memory = time dependant, contextual, autobiographic. (Book p575)
The CSF analysis findings printed for Alzheimer's are:
Down A-beta 42 levels with up hyperphosphorylated tau levels

Investigations: EEG normal/non-specific slowing; CSF analysis down A-beta 42 levels, up hyperphosphorylated tau levels; PET scan IOC detecting hypometabolism and amyloid fibrils (PiB PET scans shown for AD vs control). (Book p576)
The PET scan is marked as what for AD, and what does it detect?
PET scan: IOC; detects hypometabolism and amyloid fibrils. (Book p576)
The cholinesterase-inhibitor (DOC) list contains which three drugs?
Treatment: 1. cholinesterase inhibitors (DOC): donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine; 2. NMDA antagonist: memantine; 3. monoclonal antibody against A-beta 42: aducanumab. (Book p576)
The obsolete drug retired for hepatotoxicity in the note is:
The page prints what percentage of FTD (Pick's disease) as sporadic?
FTD (Pick's disease): 70% sporadic, young onset dementia (50-60 years), rapidly progressive dementia; note contrasts Alzheimer's -> 90-95% sporadic (cerebral atrophy MRI pair). (Book p577)
FTD pathology involves the MAPT gene on which chromosome, with which m/c protein?

Pathology involves MAPT gene chromosome 17; proteins involved: TDP-43 (m/c), tau (hyperphosphorylated: loss of function of tau molecule) -> Pick's bodies, FUS; b/l prefrontal cortex atrophy. (Book p577)
Loss of social embarrassment, apathy, impaired planning and judgement with relatively preserved memory - which FTD type is the m/c one?

Clinical features: m/c type behavioural variant; loss of social embarrassment; social and emotional systems dysfunction (apathy, overeating - temporal); impaired planning and judgement; memory relatively preserved; hyperorality - temporal lobe involvement. (Book p577)
The side notes pair hyperphosphorylated tau with which diseases, and split the PFC into which three parts?
CJD and Binswanger; ego, id, memory
PSP and MSA; attention, memory, motor
Alzheimer's and Pick's; Id, superego, ego

Notes: tauopathy -> hypophosphorylated tau / hyperphosphorylated tau (Alzheimer's, Pick's); PFC -> Id, superego, ego. Diffuse Lewy Body Dementia: 2nd m/c cause of dementia; part of Parkinson-plus/atypical Parkinson's syndrome. (Book p577)
Which pairing lists only the 'alpha synuclein'-opathies in the Parkinson-plus components tree?
Multiple system atrophy and diffuse Lewy body dementia
Progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration

Components of Parkinson plus syndrome: 'Tau'opathies - progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration; 'alpha synuclein'-opathies - multiple system atrophy, diffuse Lewy Body dementia. (Book p577)
Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions whose content is:

Lewy bodies: intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions; content alpha-synuclein. Note: Parkinson's = alpha synucleinopathy; Alzheimer's = 'Tau'pathy (degenerated cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of meynert); anticholinergics are the Rx of drug-induced parkinsonism. (Book p578)
Characteristic changes of 'alpha synuclein'-opathies precede disease onset by how long?

Characteristic changes 5-10 years before onset of disease: 1. REM sleep disorders; 2. autonomic nervous system symptoms - postural hypotension, erectile > ejaculatory dysfunction, urinary abnormalities. (Book p578)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the autonomic symptom NOT listed for 'alpha synuclein'-opathies:
Listed ANS symptoms: postural hypotension, erectile > ejaculatory dysfunction and urinary abnormalities. (Book p578)

Cognitive impairment within 1 year of motor manifestations, visual hallucinations before motor symptoms, b/l axial rigidity with rocket sign, tremor uncommon, antipsychotics worsening, L-dopa unresponsive - which diagnosis?

DLB v/s PD table: DLB - cognitive impairment precedes/within 1 year (predominant rapidly progressive dementia), visual hallucinations and fluctuating alertness precede motor symptoms, tremors uncommon, b/l axial rigidity (rocket sign +), gait abnormalities common, antipsychotics worsen (d/t D2 receptor inhibition), L-dopa no improvement, treatment none available; PD - after 4-5 years of motor manifestations, tremor common, asymmetrical rigidity, gait uncommon, L-dopa improves, Rx L-dopa and deep brain stimulation. (Book p578)
The rocket sign is defined in the note as:
Falling backwards immediately after trying to get up from a chair
Forward lean on the pull test
Note: rocket sign - falling backwards immediately after trying to get up from a chair. (Book p578)
Severe memory impairment, early dysphasia, apraxia/agnosia/acalculia present, visuo-spatial defects more severe, indifferent personality - which column of the comparison table?
Subcortical dementia (examples DLB, PSP, NPH, Binswanger)

Cortical column: examples Alzheimer's, FTD; affected hippocampus, medial temporal lobe; memory severe; apraxia (superior parietal lobe lesion) / agnosia (association areas) / acalculia (angular gyrus) (+); early dysphasia; visuo-spatial more severe; personality indifferent; mood depressed (subcortical > cortical); coordination normal; cognitive and motor speed normal; abnormal movements rare; extrapyramidal symptoms -. (Book p579)
The subcortical dementia column's affected regions are:
Subcortical grey matter (basal ganglia, thalamus) and white matter (corticospinal, corticobulbar fibres)

Subcortical column: examples DLB dementia, PSP, NPH, Binswanger's disease; regions subcortical grey matter (basal ganglia, thalamus) plus subcortical white matter (corticospinal, corticobulbar fibres); memory less severe; language normal; personality apathetic; coordination impaired; speed slow; abnormal movements common; extrapyramidal symptoms +. (Book p579)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the row value NOT from the subcortical dementia column:
Subcortical column values: language normal (cortical: early dysphasia), personality apathetic, speed slow, abnormal movements common. (Book p579)
Prion is defined on the page as:
An infectious protein with no nucleic acid
A misfolded peptide carrying nucleic acid
Prion: infectious protein with no nucleic acid; genetic/sporadic. Pathology: beta-pleated PrPsc protein -> spongiform degeneration of cortex -> neuronal loss. (Book p579)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the prion disease NOT in the types list:

Types of prion diseases: 1. CJD, 2. familial fatal insomnia, 3. kuru, 4. Gerstmann Straussler Scheinker disease. Common features: young onset dementia, rapidly progressive dementia, no immune response. (Whipple's appears only in the p573 rapidly-progressive list.) (Book p580)
CJD: spongiform cortical changes with cortical ribboning, basal ganglia hyperintensities, dementia with myoclonus, long incubation and no immune response - which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
CJD investigations: EEG - low voltage background, high voltage sharp waves; CSF normal; brain biopsy to confirm diagnosis; Rx flupirtine maleate (centrally acting non-opioid analgesic). (Book p580)
The dementia-protein table pairs DLB with which protein?
Dementia-protein table: Alzheimer's A-beta; FTD tau; DLB alpha synuclein; CJD PrPsc. Vascular dementia: types large vessel disease (post-CVA dementia) and small vessel disease. (Book p580)
Large-vessel vascular dementia: the m/c site of infarct per the page is:

Large vessel disease: m/c site of infarct b/l PCA lesion; criteria: 1. dementia; a. cerebrovascular disease - multi-infarct state with 'strategic territory' infarct (infarct in these areas leads to dementia). (Book p580)
The 'relationship between the two disorders' requires dementia onset when after a stroke?
3. Relationship between the two disorders: onset of dementia within 3 months of stroke; stepwise decline in cognitive function (stepwise graph). (Book p581)
Binswanger disease pathology involves penetrating vessels of what size range?

Small vessel disease - Binswanger disease: most important risk factor HTN; lacunar infarct; pathology lipohyalinotic infarct involving penetrating vessels (size 30-300 um); MRI finding white matter hyperintensities in elderly (gradual cognitive-decline graph); features similar to vascular Parkinson's. (Book p581)
A small-vessel patient with gait apraxia, magnetic foot and falls - which tract's lower-limb fibres (close to the ventricle) are affected per the table?

Fibres affected -> manifestation: corticobulbar tract -> pseudobulbar palsy; corticospinal tract (affects lower limb fibres close to the ventricle) -> gait disturbances and falls, gait apraxia, magnetic/ignition foot phenomenon (feet 'stuck' to floor); fibres from paracentral lobule -> urinary abnormalities; corticostriate fibres (PFC to striatum) -> personality changes. (Book p581)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the item NOT a feature of cerebral amyloid angiopathy:
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy: A-beta 40 protein deposition, elderly, microhemorrhages. (NOTCH3 is the CADASIL mutation.) (Book p581)
CADASIL is the m/c inherited vascular dementia with which mutation and presentation?

CADASIL: cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with small vessel ischemic change/leukoencephalopathy, or CADA with stroke and ischemic leukoencephalopathy; m/c inherited vascular dementia; NOTCH3 mutation; presentation aura + migraine + dementia + stroke. (Book p582)
The NPH hydrocephalus tree places aqueductal stenosis under which branch?

Hydrocephalus: occlusive (non-communicating) -> aqueductal stenosis; non-occlusive (communicating) -> up CSF production or down CSF adsorption -> idiopathic (NPH) / familial (congenital: arachnoid granulations; acquired: trauma, SAH). Note: atrophy - obtuse interventricular angle. (Book p582)
NPH per the page: the GUD abnormalities, CSF profile and Rx are:
Gait apraxia (magnetic foot), urinary incontinence, subcortical dementia; normal CSF pressure (20 ml/day produced); shunting
Spastic paraparesis, urgency, cortical dementia; raised CSF pressure; acetazolamide
Tremor, ataxia, aphasia; low CSF pressure; fenestration
Apraxia, incontinence, amnesia; xanthochromic CSF; shunt revision

NPH pathology: adsorption defect > outflow resistance of CSF -> ventriculomegaly, no atrophy. Clinical: symptoms progress over weeks to months; GUD - gait (gait apraxia/magnetic foot), urinary (incontinence), dementia (subcortical type); arrest in initiation of ambulation; gait instability with multiple falls; generalized slow movements; CSF pressure normal (20 ml/day produced); Rx shunting (good prognosis if effective); MRI - interventricular angle acute. (Book p582)
The subcortex tree: grey matter and white matter give rise to which structures?
Basal ganglia; corticospinal tract and corticobulbar fibres passing through the internal capsule
Subcortex -> grey matter -> basal ganglion; white matter -> corticospinal tract, corticobulbar fibres (pass through internal capsule). (Book p583)
Per the nuclei diagram, the corpus striatum and lenticular nucleus are formed by which pairings?
Nuclei: caudate nucleus (CN), putamen, globus pallidus (GP: GPi, GPe), subthalamic nucleus (STN), substantia nigra (SN); corpus striatum = CN + putamen; lenticular nucleus = putamen + GP. (Book p583)
A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus produces which movement disorder per the diagram?
Lesion -> hypokinetic movements: caudate -> chorea; putamen/striatum -> dystonia/athetosis; STN -> hemiballismus. (Book p583)
The basal-ganglia physiology functions listed are:
Respiratory drive, heart rate, blood pressure
Complex motor activity; initiation and scaling of movement; cognitive part; activity set for movement (planning, programming, initiation)
Sensory discrimination, memory consolidation, language naming

Functions: complex motor activity; initiation and scaling of movement; cognitive part of motor activity; activity set for movement (planning, programming and initiation). Note: premotor cortex and supplementary motor area also involved in planning and programming. (Book p583)
The three general features of the direct and indirect pathways are:
All input from thalamus; output via STN; only inhibitory nucleus is GPi
Input from brainstem; output via SN; only excitatory is caudate
All input from cerebellum; output via thalamus; subthalamus inhibitory
All input from cortex to striatum; all output leaves through GPi; the only excitatory BG nucleus is the subthalamus
General features: 1. all input from cortex -> striatum; 2. all output leave through GPi; 3. the only excitatory nucleus in BG: subthalamus. (Book p584)
The nigrostriatal pathway (SN -> corpus striatum) acts via D1 and D2 receptors to do what?
D1 activates the direct pathway and D2 inhibits the indirect pathway, together stimulating the cortex
D1 inhibits the direct pathway and D2 activates the indirect pathway
D1 excites STN and D2 excites GPe
Nigrostriatal pathway: via D1 activate direct pathway; via D2 inhibits indirect pathway - together stimulating of cortex. (Book p584)
Degeneration of the nigrostriatal pathway in PD produces which applied-aspect outcome?
Inhibition of the cortex -> akinesia and bradyphrenia (slowness of thoughts)

Applied aspect: degeneration of NS pathway (Parkinson's disease) -> inhibition of cortex -> akinesia, bradyphrenia (slowness of thoughts). Disorders of BG: hyperkinetic vs hypokinetic (paucity of movement - down amplitude, slowness - unrelated to weakness/spasticity). Idiopathic PD: and m/c neurodegenerative disease; majority cases sporadic, elderly > 60 years. (Book p584)
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: the majority cases are which distribution and age?
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: and m/c neurodegenerative disease; majority cases: distribution sporadic, age elderly > 60 years. (Book p584)
The 'typical symptomatic appearance' figure labels which constellation?
Hyperextended posture, lively facies, flaccidity, wide-based ataxic gait
Forward lean with brisk arm swing and long strides

Stooped posture, masked facial expression, rigidity, forward tilt of trunk, flexed elbows and wrists, reduced arm swinging, slightly flexed hips and knees, trembling of extremities, shuffling short-stepped gait

Figure labels: stooped posture, masked facial expression, rigidity, forward tilt of trunk, flexed elbows and wrists, reduced arm swinging, slightly flexed hips and knees, trembling of extremities, shuffling short-stepped gait. (Book p585)
The tremor-comparison table gives Parkinson disease tremor frequency as:
Frequency row: PD tremor 4-6 Hz; essential tremor 5-12 Hz. (Book p585)

A rest tremor with re-emergent component, asymmetric, hands and legs, micrographia, progressive course, 1% family history, extrapyramidal signs present, levodopa-responsive, DBS at STN or GPi - which tremor?

PD column: at rest +/- re-emergent tremor, asymmetric, hands +/- legs, small writing (micrographia), progressive, family history uncommon (1%), extrapyramidal signs (bradykinesia, rigidity, loss of postural reflex) present, relieved by levodopa/dopamine agonists/anticholinergics, DBS site subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna. Essential column: postural tremor, mostly symmetric, hands/head/voice, large and tremulous writing, stable or slowly progressive, family history common (>30%), EPS absent, relieved by alcohol/propranolol/primidone/topiramate/gabapentin/clonazepam, DBS ventral intermediate thalamus. (Book p585)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the relieving factor NOT for Parkinson disease tremor per the table:
PD relieving factors: levodopa, dopamine agonists, anticholinergics; essential tremor relieving factors include alcohol, propranolol, primidone, topiramate, gabapentin, clonazepam. (Book p585)
The sheet for printed p586 is absent from the supplied scan. Which statement correctly places it in the Parkinson's sequence?
It lies between the p583 title page and the p584 pathway diagram
It lies between the p589 L-dopa list and the p592 agonist examples
No sheet is missing - p587 follows p585 directly in the scan
It lies between the p585 tremor-comparison table and the p587 rigidity list

Printed p586 is absent from the supplied scan (it proceeds p585 -> p587); its bracketing content is the p585 PD-versus-essential tremor table and the p587 rigidity/akinesia list. Content verification of p586 remains unresolved, as with the missing p527 in Chapter 26. (Book p586)
Cogwheel and lead-pipe rigidity are distinguished at which sites per the page, and what is Froment's sign?
Cogwheel (rigidity + tremor) at the wrist; lead pipe at the elbow; Froment's sign = activity-induced increase in c/l rigidity
Cogwheel at the elbow; lead pipe at the wrist; Froment's sign = thumb pinch sign
Both at the ankle; Froment's sign = falling backwards
Both at the neck; Froment's sign = tremor vanishing in action
Hypertonia - 2 types: cogwheel rigidity (rigidity + tremor) at wrist; lead pipe rigidity at elbow. Froment's sign: activity-induced increase in c/l rigidity (as printed on the page). (Book p587)

Bradyphrenia, reduced arm swing, stooped posture from flexion hypertonia, short quick steps with freezing, narrow-based festinant gait, micrographia, hypomimia, hypophonia and reduced blinking - this printed cluster is:

Akinesia/bradykinesia: bradyphrenia; reduced arm swing (difficulty with limb movements); flexion hypertonia (stooped posture); short quick steps and freeze in between; festinant gait (narrow-based); micrographia; hypomimia (minimal expression); hypophonia (down voice); reduced blinking - glabellar tap sign positive. (Book p587)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the item NOT on the atypical-PD/hypokinesia note on this page:

Note: atypical PD - b/l axial rigidity: difficulty turning in bed, rising from a chair (wheelchair sign); non-parkinsonian lesion having hypokinesia: hypothyroidism. (Visual hallucinations with fluctuating alertness are DLB features on p588.) (Book p587)
The pull test shows the patient falls backward (normal: takes 2-3 steps backwards to correct posture) - which feature is demonstrated?
Postural instability: unsteadiness and falls; pull test - patient falls backward (normal: takes 2-3 steps backwards to correct posture). (Book p587)
The investigation line for Parkinson's disease states the diagnosis is:
MRI at midbrain level shows b/l grey-matter hyperintensities surrounded by hypointense red nuclei and crural fibres, with absent swallow-tail sign - the sign's origin per the note is:
The substantia nigra (swallow tail sign d/t SN)
MRI midbrain level: hyperintensities b/l in grey matter surrounded by hypointense red nuclei and crural fibres; absence of swallow tail sign (swallow tail sign d/t SN). (Book p587)
The 'PD patient can also have' note lists which symptom groups?
PD patients can also have sensory symptoms (pain, anosmia), neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression > dementia) and gastrointestinal symptoms (dysphagia). (Book p587)
Atypical Parkinson's disease is also called what, with which listed hallmarks?
Parkinson minus syndromes - slow progression, late dementia
Parkinson plus syndromes - rapid progression, early onset dementia, symmetrical bradykinesia, facial dyskinesia

Atypical PD aka Parkinson plus syndromes: rapid progression, early onset dementia, symmetrical bradykinesia, facial dyskinesia. Classifications: tauopathy (PSP, CBD) and alpha synucleinopathy (MSA, DLB). (Book p588)
The features common to atypical PD itself per the list are:
Absence of tremor, unresponsiveness to L-dopa, rapidly progressive
Prominent rest tremor, good L-dopa response, slowly progressive

Atypical PD: absence of tremor, unresponsiveness to L-dopa, rapidly progressive; DLB: dementia at presentation, visual hallucination, fluctuating alertness; CBD: myoclonus, cortical signs; PSP: falls d/t postural instability, dementia component, b/l axial rigidity, supranuclear gaze palsy; MSA: ANS symptoms, disproportionate cerebellar signs. (Book p588)
Supranuclear gaze palsy with b/l axial rigidity and falls from postural instability - which atypical PD?
PSP: falls d/t postural instability, dementia component, b/l axial rigidity, supranuclear gaze palsy. (Book p588)
CBD: myoclonus, cortical signs; DLB: dementia at presentation, visual hallucination, fluctuating alertness; MSA: ANS symptoms, disproportionate cerebellar signs. (Book p588)
MSA per the page: age range and defining inclusions are:
45-55 years; glial cytoplasmic inclusions staining for alpha synuclein
MSA: 45-55 yrs; glial cytoplasmic inclusions (stain for alpha synuclein) - alpha synucleinopathy; REM sleep disorders (years before diagnosis); ANS predominant. (Book p588)
The MSA classification prints what proportion as MSA-P (parkinson predominant)?
MSA classification: MSA-P (80%) parkinson predominant; MSA-C cerebellar predominant; MSA-A/Shy-Drager syndrome (15%) ANS predominant. (Book p588)
L-dopa is combined with a decarboxylase inhibitor because:
Peripheral metabolism of L-dopa is high
L-dopa cannot cross the blood-brain barrier without it

Drugs: L-Dopa - peripheral metabolism is high; combined with: dopa decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa, benserazide); COMT inhibitors - not used now: tolcapone (hepatotoxic), entacapone (hepatotoxic, orange coloured urine); L-Dopa + dopa decarboxylase inhibitor is the combination started. (Book p589)
The L-dopa administration details printed on the page are:
Only when symptoms are severe, fasting
Small doses, multiple times, crushed and mixed with carbonated water
Single large dose at night with plain water

All patients are started on L-dopa: small doses, multiple times, crushed and mixed with carbonated water. Symptoms non-responsive to L-dopa: freezing, falls, dysphagia, dysarthria, ANS symptoms. (Book p589)
Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the symptom NOT printed as non-responsive to L-dopa:
Symptoms non-responsive to L-dopa: freezing, falls, dysphagia, dysarthria, ANS symptoms. (Book p589)
Peak-dose choreiform dyskinesia and off-period dystonia differ by what per the page?
High dose versus low drug concentration respectively

Side effects: nausea/vomiting, postural hypotension; motor fluctuations - wearing off (space drug without much gap), on/off, delayed onset of action, drug failure; dyskinesias - peak dose dyskinesia: choreiform movements (d/t high dose), off period dyskinesia: dystonia (d/t low drug concentration). (Book p589)
The drug the page assigns to tackle motor fluctuations is:
Motor fluctuations (wearing off, on/off, delayed onset of action, drug failure) - to tackle: amantadine. (Book p589)
Central anticholinergics and the dopaminergic-agonist disadvantage note state:
Propranolol is used in drug-induced PD; DDS brings pain and anosmia
Carbidopa is a central anticholinergic; DDS brings seizures and aphasia
Trihexyphenidyl is used in drug-induced PD; DDS brings visual hallucinations, impulse control issues, addiction
Trihexyphenidyl is the DOC for idiopathic PD; DDS brings depression and amnesia

Central anticholinergics: trihexyphenidyl; used in drug-induced PD. Dopaminergic agonists: found as replacement for L-dopa; disadvantages - dopamine dysregulation syndrome (neuropsychiatric manifestations: visual hallucinations, impulse control issues, addiction). (Book p589)
The supplied scan proceeds directly from p589 to p592. What is absent between them?
Nothing is missing - p592 follows p589 in the book
Printed p590 and p591, both missing from the supplied scan

Printed p590 and p591 are absent from the supplied scan, so the dopaminergic-agonist material between the p589 disadvantages list and the p592 examples list cannot be visually verified; this follows the unresolved-missing-page precedent set by p527 in Chapter 26. (Book p590)
The p591 sheet is absent from the supplied scan. Which visible page carries the 'Example: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine' list that follows it?
Printed p592, which opens with that examples list
Printed p589, which ends with the DDS note

With p591 (and p590) absent from the supplied scan, the next visible sheet - p592 - opens with the dopaminergic-agonist examples list: pramipexole (antidepressant action also), ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine (used in rescue therapy, IV route). (Book p591)
The dopaminergic-agonist examples list on this page includes which drug used in rescue therapy by the IV route?
Example: pramipexole (antidepressant action also), ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine - i. used in rescue therapy, ii. IV route. (Book p592)
Amantadine's printed mechanisms of action number how many, and which are they?

Amantadine: 3 mechanisms of action - dopaminergic agonist, anticholinergic, NMDA antagonist. Newer drugs: istradefylline (A2a antagonist - minimizes motor fluctuations), pimavanserin (5HTa antagonist). (Book p592)
The treatment protocol prints which first-line choice for a patient <60 years with mild symptoms?
Treatment protocol: <60 yrs old + mild symptoms -> dopaminergic agonist; >60 yrs / significant disease present -> L-dopa + carbidopa. (Book p592)
Which of these structures is pain-INSENSITIVE per the relevant-anatomy list?

Pain sensitive: dural venous sinuses, dura around vessels, large veins, circle of Willis, dural arteries (meningeal arteries), first few centimeters of medium sized vessels, pia mater, small cerebral vessels; pain insensitive: choroid plexus, ependyma. (Book p593)
The primary headache causes listed in the classification are:
Giant cell arteritis, SAH, brain tumour

Mesoderm splits into paraxial, intermediate and lateral plate derivatives. The lateral plate divides into somatopleure (outer serosal layers) and splanchnopleure (inner serosal layers). The cloaca — the hindgut distal to the allantois — divides into the primitive urogenital sinus and the primitive rectum. The sinus's epithelial buds, vesicourethral canal and definitive urogenital sinus form the prostate, bladder and urethral segments, while the rectum carries the anal canal only up to the pectinate line, below which the canal is proctodermal.

The metanephros is the permanent kidney.

Light microscopy: parietal epithelial proliferation with fibrin crescents (number matters). Step 1 checks: ECG (hyperkalaemia → calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 2–3 min), ABG (metabolic acidosis → NaHCO₃ or dialysis) and volume status (IVC diameter → diuretics). Pulmonary renal syndrome = RPGN + diffuse alveolar haemorrhage; list Goodpasture, microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and active SLE. Goodpasture disease targets the noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of type-IV collagen with triggers smoking, hydrocarbons, fluid overload and lung infection; DR2/15 and DR4 are high risk, DR1 and DR7 low risk. Dialysis disequilibrium: first session <1 hour, subsequent 4 hours, else ↓osmolality drives water into cells → cerebral oedema, seizure, death.

Lung involvement in 75% with cough, haemoptysis, smoking history and no fever; renal involvement means poor prognosis. DLCO is increased, X-ray shows B/L diffuse infiltrate and CT shows diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Active management for ongoing pulmonary haemorrhage, creatinine <5.5 mg/dL with normal urine output, new cellular crescent and type IV RPGN; mainstay PLEX + steroid/cyclophosphamide for 3–6 months; transplant after 6 months of antibody negativity. Ciliopathy overview: cilia function and the four types

Ciliopathies are hereditary cystic disorders of the kidney in which a ciliary defect strips the tubular epithelium of its differentiated phenotype; polycystin regulates this function. The TYPES flowchart gives four entities: ADPKD, ARPKD, juvenile nephronophthisis and MCDK.

ADPKD is autosomal dominant with variable expression, 10% spontaneous mutations, multiple bilateral cysts as the hallmark and only 5% of nephrons involved. ARPKD is autosomal recessive, diagnosable in utero with small medullary cysts. PKHD1 on chromosome 6 makes the fibrocystin-polyductin complex; its defect affects the cilia/centrosome complex in the collecting duct (medullary cyst) and biliary duct (congenital hepatic fibrosis/Caroli/biliary ectasia). Pulmonary hypoplasia kills 70% within a year, portal hypertension the remaining 30% at adolescence, ESRD rarely. USG: hyperechoic medulla with loss of corticomedullary differentiation.

CKD definition and the causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disease

CKD = >5% interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy/glomerular sclerosis with fewer functional nephrons. The causes table maps vascular (RAS/TMA), glomerular (IgAN/MPGN/FSGS/membranous and diabetes) causes to secondary tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and primary tubulointerstitial fibrosis to CTID. Pathology is scarring with fibrosis and atrophy >5%.
Etiology of CTID: from ciliopathies to metabolic and autoimmune causes

Etiology runs from ciliopathies, reflux nephropathy (VUR) and obstructive nephropathy, through drugs (lithium microcysts; calcineurin-inhibitor striped pattern with afferent arteriolar hyalinosis; PPIs) and toxins (lead saturnine gout; cadmium ouch ouch nephropathy) to metabolic causes (hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia/urate nephropathy, hyperoxaluria, hypokalemic vacuolization of PCT > DCT), then autoimmune causes (sarcoidosis, Sjogren's, IgG4) and finally CKDu.
CTID features, investigations and the CKDu concept

CTID is asymptomatic with an insidious onset. The clinical-features table links each sign to its cause: polyuria/nocturia (concentration defect), anaemia (peritubular interstitial fibroblast EPO), nephrogenic DI (cortical collecting duct fibrosis), RTA IV (beta cell fibrosis) and RTA I (alpha intercalated cell fibrosis), with rickets in children from phosphate loss. Anaemia is maximal in CTID and minimal in ADPKD. Investigations: proteinuria <2 g/day with beta-2 microglobulin, inactive sediment, deranged RFT, small kidneys. CKDu: unknown pathophysiology, theories of heat stress, agrochemicals, fluoride, cadmium and communicable disease; eastern coast of India, middle-aged men, asymptomatic until ESRF.
AKI definition, KDIGO staging and pre-renal causes

AKI = abrupt fall in renal function over hours to days causing ECF volume expansion, uremia, hyperkalemia and acidosis. KDIGO stages by urine output and creatinine; newer markers NGAL, KIM-1, LFABP, IL-18. The CAUSES flowchart splits pre-renal (commonest hospital AKI) from renal (ATN, AIN) and post-renal; pre-renal causes run from volume depletion through reduced effective volume, low cardiac output, sepsis, renal vasoconstriction and compartment syndrome.
Pre-renal pathophysiology, ATN and AIN mechanisms

Pre-renal failure is usually non-oliguric; oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction. Long-standing profound pre-renal failure causes ischemic ATN with tubuloglomerular feedback. ATN arises from ischemia and endogenous (hemoglobin, myoglobin, uric acid, light chains) or exogenous (drugs, contrast) toxins; AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction from drugs, infections (leptospirosis, scrub typhus) and infiltration (lymphoma, sarcoidosis).

Acute interstitial nephritis and drug-induced nephropathy

AIN is a T4-mediated hypersensitivity with reversible AKI: rash and eosinophilia, asymptomatic renal failure, no oedema or HTN, impaired RFT and mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts, interstitial infiltrates with normal glomeruli on biopsy; treatment is stop the insult then steroids after a week. NSAID nephropathy (PG inhibition to RAAS) gives oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion; aminoglycosides bind megalin in the PCT brush border, accumulate in lysosomes and cause non-oliguric AKI 5-10 days later, prevented by single daily dosing.
