ATN has three phases (tubular injury, tubuloglomerular feedback with adenosine-mediated afferent vasoconstriction, recovery) with raised phosphorus/magnesium and low calcium; hypercalcemia and hypernatremia are not seen in AKI. Sepsis: pre-renal predominant over ATN, vasodilation with microthrombi and endothelial leak, PAMPs/DAMPs to inflammatory cascade to oxidative stress; causes and perfusion signs; investigations - IVC diameter 2-2.5 cm, lactate >1 and >4 mmol/L and the (obsolete) passive leg raising test.
Sepsis treatment ladder and uric acid nephropathy

Sepsis-AKI treatment: crystalloid first, vasopressor second (norepinephrine > dopamine), dobutamine, cortisol; SAFE trial note; diuretics not used in prevention or treatment of AKI. Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) follows chemotherapy of hematological malignancy with oliguric AKI, markedly raised uric acid, raised K/PO4/mg and low calcium, treated with IV rasburicase and dialysis, prevented by 5-6 L/day hydration, alkalinization and allopurinol.

Causes from electric shock and seizures to statins, hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia, McArdle disease, hypothyroidism and myositis; pathophysiology combines PCT injury, vasoconstriction and uric acid casts with myoglobin toxicity, cast obstruction and hypovolemia. Clinical features (cramps, swelling, non-oliguric AKI, pigmented granular casts), CPK kinetics with the compartment-syndrome caveat, HAGMA with FeNa <1, and treatment with vigorous hydration, alkalinization and hemodialysis.
Contrast-induced AKI and athero-embolic renal disease

Contrast-induced AKI: reduced by low volume iso-osmolar contrast (iohexol/iopamidol), medullary hypoxia with tubular injury, creatinine rise at 24-48 hrs peaking at 3-5 days and normal in 7-10 days, no treatment required and prevention by hydration. Athero-embolic renal disease (cholesterol embolism) after endovascular intervention in extensive aortic atherosclerosis, with subacute renal failure over weeks, blue toe, livedo reticularis, Hollenhorst plaque, poor prognosis, hypocomplementemia, eosinophiluria with Hansel's stain, raised amylase, skin (never kidney) biopsy showing birefringent biconvex cholesterol crystals and ACE inhibitor avoidance.
Cardiorenal syndrome types and acute cortical necrosis

CRS 1-5 table: acute cardiorenal, chronic cardiorenal, acute renocardiac, chronic renocardiac and secondary, each with its definition. The closing note: snake bite, placental abruption and pancreatitis cause acute cortical necrosis (urine output failing to recover) that can progress to CKD.
Definition, pathogenesis flowchart and the causes line

CKD is the net consequence of ↓ viable nephrons (fixed at birth weight, never replaced) → intraglomerular hypertension → proteinuria. GFR = viable nephrons × sn GFR: ↓ nephron number → ↑↑ sn GFR → hyperfiltration → intraglomerular hypertension → mechanical stretching — capillary (↑ pore diameter, tubulotoxic proteinuria), podocyte (local RAAS via AT-II, ↓ nephrin), mesangial cell (proliferation → GS). Mnemonic IF TA GS; TGF-β from interstitial inflammation drives IF+TA; tubulointerstitium is 85-90% of the kidney and the determinant of decline; progression becomes etiology-independent after 50% nephron loss. Causes line: DKD (m/c, worst prognosis) > CGN (and m/c) > IN > CTID > ADPKD.
CKD causes table: DKD, CGN, IN, CTID
Rate of fall of GFR (ml/min/year): DKD 8-10, CGN 6-8, IN 4-6, CTID 2-4. Complications row: DKD ↑↑ vascular, IN ↑↑ macrovascular; CGN and CTID are '-'.

G table: G1 ≥90 (needs radiological/biochemical/histological evidence), G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15 = ESRD (uremic phase), mx dialysis. A table (ACR): A1 ≤30 normal, A2 30-300 moderately ↑, A3 >300 severely ↑↑.
Complications of CKD: the ABCDE mnemonic

A — anemia (unfit for transplant, ↓ GFR independently), metabolic acidosis (↓ cardiac function), access for dialysis; B — BP, bone mineral disease (renal osteodystrophy); C — cardiac (m/c cause of death): LVH → HFpEF, calcification → unfit for transplant; D — dry weight; E — electrolyte (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁺, K⁺); U — uremic symptoms.
Diagnosis and the five reversible causes

Diagnosis: B/L contracted kidney; diabetic nephropathy = proteinuria, edema, hypertension, retinopathy (all of); biopsy looks for IF/TA/GS. Address reversible causes: 1 obstruction, 2 drugs/toxins/alternate medicines, 3 uncontrolled hypertension, 4 ECF volume ↓ (diuretic excess, ↓ albumin), 5 hypercalcemia (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, afferent arteriole vasoconstriction).
Protocol: transplant hurdles, mortality graph, dialysis indications and access

Protocol starts with confirming CKD diagnosis. Transplant fit: hurdles = vascular complications (medial calcifications) → ↓ success; success ranking CGN, CTID > DKD, IN. Dialysis-mortality co-relation: mortality rate highest in the first 30 days (≈34% at day 15-50 in age >65, ≈22% all patients, ≈6-7% age <65) and falls over 360 days. Dialysis indications: uremic symptoms (definitive); volume, K⁺, acidosis (relative). Access: AV fistula, 6 weeks to mature.
Variation of GFR with plasma concentration (curves A, B, C)

Two zones: overt renal failure (<25% GFR) and zone of compensation. Curve A — creatinine, urea, uric acid: depend largely on GFR, inverse relation. Curve B — PO₄, uric acid, K, H: rise only in late CKD via tubular secretion/decreased reabsorption. Curve C — sodium: normal throughout CRF because Na excretion per surviving nephron increases.
KDIGO 23 holistic approach: lifestyle, BP, proteinuria, LDL

Holistic approach is first line. Lifestyle: salt 2-3 g/day, activity, stop tobacco, weight management, risk-factor reassessment every 3-6 months. First-line drugs: proteinuria — ACE(-)/ARBs + SGLT2i (curb ↓GFR), 2nd line finerenone (nonsteroidal aldosterone antagonist); BP <120/80 mmHg with 24-hr ambulatory monitoring, ACE(-)/ARB or aliskiren (never combined with ACE(-)/ARB), non-DHP CCB; LDL <100 mg/dl — rosuvastatin 20 mg/kg. LDL targets: CKD 100, diabetic CKD 70, diabetic CKD with prior CVD 55. ACE(-) C/I: pregnancy, B/L or unilateral RAS, Cr ↑>30% or K+ >5.5 after starting, hereditary angioedema.
Consequences of CKD: the acidosis branch

CKD consequences: access dialysis, acidosis, anemia. Acidosis: NAGMA → HAGMA, myocardial depressant; monitor venous HCO₃⁻ (normal 20-22 mEq/L); Rx oral/IV sodium bicarbonate. Anemia appears below GFR 75 ml/min (male) / 40 ml/min (female).
Anemia thresholds: ISN, KDIGO and the ESA target
Start evaluation: ISN <11 gm/dl; KDIGO male <13 g/dl, female <12 g/dl. Target Hb on exogenous erythropoietin (ESA): 11.5-12.5 g/dl; >13 gm/dl → stroke, thrombosis.

Hematopoietic stem cell → BFU-E → CFU → erythroblast → reticulocyte → RBC. EPO-independent (stem cell → BFU-E); erythropoietin-dependent (BFU-E → CFU → erythroblast, 10-14 days); iron + erythropoietin dependent (erythroblast → reticulocyte 4 days → RBC 1-2 days).
Causes: EPO, iron, inflammation, PTH and deficiencies

Normocytic normochromic anemia: ↓ RBC production (more common) >> ↑ RBC destruction (↓ survival span). ↓EPO inappropriately low for anemia/hypoxia via the HIF-α/HIF-PH axis (normal O₂ degrades HIF-α; hypoxia → HIF-α+HIF-β → EPO from peritubular interstitial fibroblasts, cortex > outer medulla). Low iron: anorexia, ↓ absorption, blood loss (1 ml = 0.5 mg Fe). Inflammation → activin/CRP/interleukin → ↑ hepcidin → ↓ EPO response. Raised PTH → marrow fibrosis. Deficiency: vitamin B₆, folic acid. Note: uremic toxins inhibit erythropoiesis; RBC glutathione depletion shortens survival — EPO effect ↑↑ after dialysis.
Effects of anemia and STEP 1 iron replenishment

Anemia independently raises the risk of fall in GFR; LVH; cardiovascular mortality (m/c cause of death) via LVH, calcification, endothelial dysfunction. STEP 1: replenish iron store = 2.2 × BW × (Hb deficit) + 1000 mg (as printed; the common Ganzoni 2.4 is not the page's value).
Iron therapy: oral and IV, ferritin and TSAT

Oral: ferrous sulfate 60 mg elemental iron — non-dialysable patients, less effective. IV: ferric carboxymaltose 1 gm in 100 ml NS over 10-15 min; iron sucrose 200 mg; iron isomaltose 1 gm. Note: low s. ferritin → anemia; normal → check TSAT = s. iron/TIBC × 100; s. iron ↓ = TSAT ↓ (TSAT: transferrin saturation; TIBC: total iron binding capacity).
ESA: prerequisites, contraindications, generations and dosing

STEP 2 ESA. Prerequisites (enough iron store): TSAT ≥30%, s. ferritin ≥500 ng/ml. C/I: absolute — stroke; relative — malignancy. SC preferred (30% less dose); IV. 1st gen EPO-α: T½ 8.5 hrs, 50-100 U/kg/week or 4000-10000 U/week, up to 300 U/kg/week. No response = ESA hyporesponsiveness (m/c: iron deficiency; chronic disease). Daprodustat: prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, oral, high cost. 2nd gen (2 extra N-linked glycosylation chains): darbepoetin α T½ 25.3 hrs, 60-200 µg/2 weekly; EPO-β (CERA) T½ 130 hrs, 0.6 µg/kg/2 weekly.
High bone turnover pathophysiology and the FGF23 axis

CKD-MBD (previously renal osteodystrophy). High turnover (30%): osteitis fibrosa cystica; GFR ↓↓ → ↑ P; endothelial cells convert to osteoblasts → trap Ca → irreversible medial vascular calcification. Osteocytes secrete FGF23 (phosphaturic) via klotho receptor → blocks Na-P cotransporter PCT2a → phosphate excretion; actions: LVH, 1,2-hydroxylase inhibition → calcitriol deficient → hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia); grade 5 CKD: klothoreceptor resistance. ↑ bone formation << ↑ bone resorption; amorphous Ca₃(PO₄)₂ → trivial trauma fracture (↓ mineralization); bone + fibrous tissue + cyst → osteitis fibrosa cystica.
Low bone turnover and the CKD-MBD Venn triad

Low turnover (10%): adynamic bone disease — middle to elderly aged female, DM, obese; prone for calcification. Venn diagram: biochemical changes + bone abnormality + calcification (vascular + soft tissue).
Target values, phosphate binders and tertiary hyperparathyroidism

High turnover → medial calcification: ↑ P, ↑ Ca₃(PO₄)₂, ↑ PTH. Targets: PTH 2-7× ULN (50-100 pg/ml), Ca <9.5, P <5.5. 1st line pure binders: sevelamer carbonate 400 mg TDS (↓ LDL), ferric citrate, sucroferric oxyhydroxide; calcium binders only in significant hypocalcemia (may worsen calcification); calcitriol 0.25 µg alternate days (vit D <20). Tertiary HPT: autonomous nodule after long-standing 2° HPT → PTH ↑↑↑, ↑ Ca⁺ ↑ P (Ca always low in CKD except tertiary); Rx cinacalcet (CaSR agonist) → parathyroidectomy if unresponsive.
Adynamic bone disease and extraskeletal calcification

Adynamic: worst prognosis, bone pain. Causes: excess Ca supplementation (PTH <400 pg → high Ca & P → vascular/soft tissue calcification → death) and aluminum (dialysis dementia). Extraskeletal calcification in CRF: arterial, pulmonary, periarticular. Treatment: stop all supplements; dialysis in low calcium dialysate.
DEXA, calciphylaxis, NSF and atheroembolic disease

DEXA assesses bone mass; low bone mass → bisphosphonates; Ca/vit D with caution. Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy): medial calcification of subcutaneous/dermal arterioles; precipitated by vit-K antagonist (vit-K regenerates matrix Gla protein); pulse preserved; female obese; ischemic necrosis of dermis/subcut fat; violaceous painful plaque → nodule → ulcer on buttock/trunk; livedo reticularis-like rare; clinical diagnosis; poor prognosis (secondary infection); Rx vit-K + sodium thiosulfate. NSF (scleroderma-like): gadolinium-based contrast, GFR <30 — finger contracture, swelling/fibrosis, peau d'orange. Atheroembolic renal disease: blue toes.
CVD in CKD: non-traditional causes, features, MI and transplant

>>Leading cause of mortality: ESRD 50% cardiac deaths; young CKD 500× risk vs controls. Non-traditional: uremic toxins (uremic cardiomyopathy), medial calcification, LVH (HFpEF), endothelial dysfunction (ADMA ↑ → NO ↓, loss of fetuin), malnutrition-inflammation-nephrosclerosis (insulin resistance, protein-energy malnutrition). Arteries: endothelial dysfunction, medial calcification, ↑ wall thickness → ↑ carotid systolic BP, ↓ augmented pulse velocity. Heart: LVH, myocardial fibrosis, uremic cardiomyopathy. Flower: CKD-MBD, endothelial dysfunction, protein carbamylation, oxidative stress, uremic toxins, gut dysbiosis. Treat early: early dialysis, phosphate binders early, transplant before calcification. Uremia → pericarditis, hyperkalemia → arrhythmias. MI marker: Trop-I rate of rise, ↑20% in 9 hours (most specific). Transplant pre-requisites: iliac vessel doppler, peripheral artery doppler, CT for calcification → normal → coronary angiogram. Oxidative stress: malnutrition, bacterial products in dialysate, CKD, blood-membrane interactions, loss of antioxidants during dialysis.

RISK: 50-60% of diabetic patients, ↑ with age; T1 DM screen 5 yearly, T2 DM at diagnosis. Screening: check for albuminuria every 3-6 months — 24-hr urine protein (superior, but cumbersome) or early morning albumin:creatinine (ACR). Levels: <30 normal; 30-300 microalbuminuria (endothelial injury, ↑ thrombosis risk); >300 albuminuria.
Hyperfiltration pathogenesis and the SGLT2i mechanism

Afferent vasodilation + efferent vasoconstriction → glomerular hyperfiltration → intraglomerular hypertension. Net ↓ afferent resistance: NO bioavailability, prostaglandins, kallikrein-kinins, ANF, angiotensin (↓); net ↑ efferent resistance: angiotensin II, thromboxane A2, endothelin-1 (ETA). Panels: A normal (appropriate tone, normal TGF/GFR); B early DN (afferent vasodilation + ↑ Na/glucose reabsorption → ↓ Na delivery to macula densa → impaired TGF); C SGLT2i (proximal Na reabsorption ↓ → ↑ Na to macula densa → afferent constriction → GFR normalized; glucosuria). SGLT2i: 1st line for hyperfiltration injury.

Mogensen: on the model of T1 DM; not very accurate for T2 DM; stage V = ESRD. Table: I hyperfiltration (GFR ↑, BP =/↑); II silent + microalbuminuria (GFR ↓/↑, BP ↑ — 24-hr ambulatory monitoring: absence of nocturnal dipping, wide pulse pressure); III macroalbuminuria (GFR =/↓, BP ↑↑); IV renal impairment (GFR ↓, BP ↑↑↑).
Traver histology, nodular diseases and DN criteria

Traver et al: histological; characteristic pattern nodular glomerulosclerosis. I GBM thickening (earliest); II mesangial expansion (m/c 90%; afferent & efferent hyalinosis); III nodular sclerosis — KW lesions (Kimmelstiel wilson), only 50% pts, most specific; IV advanced diabetic glomerulosclerosis. Nodular kidney diseases: diabetes (KW nodules), MPGN, lichen deposition diseases, amyloidosis, smokers. Diabetic nephropathy = albuminuric DKD; criteria (all of): proteinuria (albuminuria) nephrotic range without syndrome; no micro/macro hematuria.
DN criteria continued, non-albuminuric DKD and NDRD red flags

Criteria continue: hypertension; edema extra > intravascular d/t Na⁺, glucose transporters; retinopathy concordance T1 100%, T2 65%; if any absent → biopsy. Non-albuminuric DKD: tubulointerstitial & vascular damage. Non-diabetic RPD: nephrotic syndrome; renal dysfunction onset <10y of DM (T1 > T2); absent nephropathy (T1 > T2); mx biopsy; hematuria/RBC casts; extra-renal vasculitis, myeloma; RPRF. Hypertension in DKD diagram: exogenous + genetic → obesity ↔ T2DM → insulin resistance/hyperleptinemia, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia → sympathetic activation, micro/macrovasculopathy → angiotensin II → hypertension.
Management: glucose target, DM drug table, proteinuria control

Target glucose >7 mg/dl as printed (to avoid hypoglycemia). DM control & weight loss: lifestyle; DOC metformin if GFR >30 ml/min. Macrovascular (CKD/ASCVD): DOC SGLT2i — canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin; initiated GFR >30. Table: metformin neutral/neutral-potential benefit/high/low/neutral; SGLT2i benefit/benefit/benefit/intermediate/low/loss; GLP-1 benefit/benefit/potential benefit/high/low/loss; DPP-4 neutral/neutral/potential risk (saxagliptin)/intermediate/low/neutral; insulin neutral/neutral/neutral/highest/high/gain; sulfonylureas neutral/high/high/gain; TZD neutral/potential benefit (pioglitazone)/increased risk/high/low/gain; α-glucosidase inhibitors neutral/neutral/neutral/intermediate/low/neutral. Proteinuria: 1st line SGLT2i + ACEi; 2nd line finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) — monitor s. K⁺ (hyperkalemia risk).
Other DM drugs in CKD: preferred agents and eGFRD-safe list

GLP-1 RA: most preferred liraglutide; oral semaglutide; no dose adjustment. DPP-4: most preferred linagliptin (no dose adjustment); others require adjustment. Sulfonylureas: not preferred; renal safe glipizide, gliclazide. Drugs safe in eGFRD: insulin; glipizide, gliclazide; imeglimin (CKD) = oxidative phosphorylation blocker.
Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering

Functions work only across a narrow pH range; daily H⁺ production is 7 crore nmol against a blood H⁺ of 40 nmol/L at pH 7.4. Excess H⁺ is cellulotoxic, altering cellular morphology before the buffering system renders it safe. Buffering types: chemical (immediate), respiratory (fast), renal (slow). Chemical buffering = [H⁺] + [A⁻] → HA, with H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ the most potent extracellular buffer; pKa is the pH at which 50% A⁻ = 50% HA, and weak acids (mostly A⁻) are the best buffers.
The Siggaard–Andersen nomogram and the three buffer types

Nomogram: x-axis arterial pH 7.0–7.8, y-axis arterial plasma HCO₃⁻ 0–60 mmol/L, right-hand [H⁺] scale 100→20 nmol/L, isobars labelled pCO₂ 120→10 mmHg, and printed zones for normal, acute/chronic respiratory acidosis and alkalosis, and metabolic acidosis/alkalosis. Buffer types: bicarbonate system (1st compensation in metabolic acidosis, CO₂ exhaled so PaCO₂ falls = 2nd compensation), phosphate (pKa 6.8, 2nd most effective, better intracellularly) and haemoglobin (pKa 7.3, best intracellular buffer).
Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA

Causes of metabolic acidosis = acid generation (exogenous: methanol; endogenous: ketoacids) and alkali loss (GI and renal). Anion gap derivation from measured/unmeasured cations and anions, giving AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). NAGMA = hyperchloremic acidosis with GI loss (VIPoma, ureterosigmoidostomy) and renal loss (RTA); HAGMA = rise in unmeasured anions with the KUSMAL list — ketoacidosis (DKA, starvation, alcoholic), uremia, salicylates/paraldehyde, methanol, ethylene glycol (alcohol) and lactic acidosis.
Terminology, H⁺ estimation and the buffering systems

Acidemia < 7.36, alkalemia > 7.44, with acidosis/alkalosis defined as those states left unopposed. H⁺ estimation: 40 nmol/L at pH 7.4, ×1.25 per 0.1 pH fall, ×0.8 per 0.1 pH rise (7.2 = 63, 7.3 = 50, 7.5 = 32, 7.6 = 25). Respiratory buffering drives CO₂ out with ↑ respiratory rate → respiratory alkalosis → ↓PaCO₂. Renal buffering: non-volatile acids (sulphuric, phosphoric) excreted 1 mEq/kg/day (80 mEq/day) as titratable acid and ammonia; volatile H₂CO₃ is exhaled. 4330 mEq/day of HCO₃⁻ (24 × 180 L) is filtered and 100% reabsorbed — PCT ≈ 4000 mEq > thick AL > DCT — so urine HCO₃⁻ is nil.
PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram

Luminal Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger; luminal CA IV converts HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ to H₂CO₃ (step ①), which splits into H₂O + CO₂ (step ②). CO₂ enters the cell where CA II rebuilds H₂CO₃ (step ③), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (step ④); HCO₃⁻ leaves on the basolateral Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger. H₂O, Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ are reabsorbed along with CO₂.
Proximal (type 2) RTA: the 4400 mEq H⁺ problem and the PCT defect

For 1 mEq HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed, 1 mEq H⁺ is used; 4330 mEq of HCO₃⁻ plus 80 mEq of non-volatile acid demands 4400 mEq H⁺ daily — not practically possible, hence the requirement of the buffering system. Type 2 RTA = generalised PCT dysfunction from a Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger or carbonic anhydrase defect: Fanconi's syndrome in childhood (cystinosis m/c, Lowe's disease, Wilson disease in adolescence) and myeloma or drugs (tenofovir, cyclophosphamide, outdated tetracycline, gentamicin) in adults. The PCT defect cascades to NAGMA, salt water wasting, RAS activation and hypokalemia; the phosphate arm gives rickets-like changes and the glucose arm glycosuria.
The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion

Cortical collecting system diagram of the α-intercalated cell: luminal H⁺-ATPase and H⁺,K⁺-ATPase (both ATP-dependent), cytoplasmic CA II making H₂CO₃ from CO₂ and H₂O, and H⁺ secreted into the lumen. HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻ is titratable acid and NH₃ → NH₄⁺ is non-titratable acid. Net acid secretion = urine NH₄⁺ + urine titratable acid − urine HCO₃⁻.
Distal (type 1) RTA and the distal vs proximal RTA table

Distal RTA = H⁺-ATPase / H⁺,K⁺-ATPase defect, giving severe NAGMA, severe hypokalemia, salt water wasting with RANS activation, ↑Ca²⁺ resorption in bone with rickets-like change and kidney stones, an alkaline urine and no glycosuria. The distal vs proximal table: severity of NAGMA + hypokalemia (severe vs mild), mechanism of rickets (Ca²⁺ resorption vs loss of phosphorus), stones (present vs absent), urine pH (alkaline vs normal), glycosuria (absent vs present), inherited causes (AR H⁺ ATPase/H⁺ K⁺ ATPase defect vs Fanconi's syndrome) and acquired causes (Sjögren's syndrome vs myeloma).
Urine anion gap and the ammonia-forming pathway

Urine anion gap = urinary Na⁺ + urinary K⁺ − urinary Cl⁻ = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation, normally slightly negative. A positive UAG indicates RTA; a negative UAG indicates GI loss. Ammonia formation is predominantly in the proximal tubules from glutamine → glutamate → α-keto glutarate, releasing NH₃ at each step.
Henderson–Hasselbalch and renal handling of excess HCO₃⁻

pH = pKa + log [HCO₃⁻]/PaCO₂ and [H⁺] = 24 × PaCO₂/HCO₃⁻. A rise in HCO₃⁻ (metabolic alkalosis) leads to a rise in PaCO₂ to keep H⁺ constant. Whether the alkalosis persists depends on the kidney: excess HCO₃⁻ excreted with Cl⁻ conserved means no metabolic alkalosis, whereas failure to excrete it produces metabolic alkalosis.
Saline-unresponsive alkalosis: ECF volume expansion and its causes

ECF volume expansion = saline unresponsive metabolic alkalosis with normal urine Cl⁻ (> 40 mEq/L). Major causes by renin–aldosterone pattern: ↓renin/↑aldosterone = primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome); ↑renin/↑aldosterone = RAS and renin-secreting tumours; ↓renin/↓aldosterone = Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutation). Other causes: Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess → mineralocorticoid excess), apparent mineralocorticoid excess (blocked cortisol → cortisone step) and glucocorticosteroid remediable aldosteronism (ACTH → aldosterone).
The alkalosis triad, urine chloride and the acidosis note

Features triangle: alkalosis with hypokalemia and HTN. ECF volume contraction = secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism (hypokalemia, alkalosis), ↓GFR (↓urine Cl⁻, ↓urine K⁺) and saline responsive alkalosis, caused by GI (vomiting, NG aspiration) or renal factors (diuretics, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, Mg²⁺/K⁺ depletion, Bartter, Gitelman). The urine chloride ladder reads low (< 25 mEq/L: GI loss, post hypercapnia, cystic fibrosis, late-phase diuretics), normal (> 40 mEq/L: ECF volume expansion) and high (renal loss: early-phase diuretics, Bartter, Gitelman). The closing note splits metabolic acidosis into acid generation (high anion gap) and alkali loss — GI causes NAGMA with a negative UAG (VIPoma) versus renal causes NAGMA with a positive UAG (RTA).
ABG methodology: equipment, prerequisites and procedure

Equipment (ABG analyzer, 1 ml heparinized syringe with 0.5 ml heparin and no excess, 70% alcohol wipe and gauze, gloves and cover roll) and prerequisites (> 50% blood, syringe 3 ml or less, no air bubbles because they cause ↑PO₂/↓PCO₂, cold chain maintained). Allen's test determines radial artery patency; the wrist of the non-dominant hand is extended 20–30°, the radial artery palpated, the area sterilised and the needle inserted at 45°, then capped and transported.
Precautions, the delay table, contraindications and sites

Precautions: flush with 0.5 ml 1 : 1000 heparin and empty the syringe (excess heparin → dilutional ↓HCO₃⁻ and ↓PCO₂), transport earliest via cold chain; delay changes pH 0.01, pCO₂ 1 mmHg and pO₂ 0.1% per 10 minutes at 37°C, versus 0.001, 0.1 mmHg and 0.01% iced at 4°C. Contraindications: abnormal Allen's test, local infection or distorted anatomy, severe peripheral vascular disease, active Raynaud's syndrome. Sites: radial, femoral, brachial, axillary, dorsalis pedis. Measured parameters (pH, pCO₂, pO₂, cCa²⁺, cCl⁻, cK⁺, cNa⁺, cGlucose, hematocrit) yield the derived ones (HCO₃⁻, anion gap, base excess).
The primary problems, reading methods and the Boston method

Four primary problems: metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, respiratory acidosis (↑PaCO₂) and respiratory alkalosis (↓PaCO₂), the respiratory arms being further labelled acute or chronic. Three reading methods: Boston, Copenhagen, Stewarts. Boston normal values: pH 7.4, pCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L, with [H⁺] = 24 × PaCO₂/HCO₃⁻ and [HCO₃⁻] = 24 × PaCO₂/H⁺; a valid ABG requires the calculated [HCO₃⁻] to lie within ±2 mEq of the venous sample. Step 1: pH < 7.4 acidosis, > 7.4 alkalosis.
Steps 2 and 3: primary abnormality and compensation

Step 2: HCO₃⁻ and PaCO₂ following the line of pH identifies the primary problem — decreased pH with ↓HCO₃⁻ = metabolic acidosis or with ↑PaCO₂ = respiratory acidosis; increased pH with ↑HCO₃⁻ = metabolic alkalosis or with ↓PaCO₂ = respiratory alkalosis. Step 3 compensation: metabolic acidosis ↓HCO₃⁻/↓PaCO₂ (respiratory alkalosis) and metabolic alkalosis ↑HCO₃⁻/↑PaCO₂ (respiratory acidosis), with ↓1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ → ↓1.2 mmHg pCO₂ and ↑1 mEq/L → ↑0.7 mmHg pCO₂; respiratory acidosis ↑PaCO₂/↑HCO₃⁻ (metabolic alkalosis) and respiratory alkalosis ↓PaCO₂/↓HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis), with ↑10 mmHg pCO₂ → ↑1 mEq/L (acute) or ↑4 mEq/L (chronic) HCO₃⁻ and ↓10 mmHg pCO₂ → ↓2 mEq/L (acute) or ↓4 mEq/L (chronic).
Adequacy of compensation and the compensatory limits

Adequacy flowchart: for metabolic acidosis/respiratory alkalosis a compensatory metabolite ≤ expected value means adequate compensation and between expected and normal means partial compensation; for metabolic alkalosis/respiratory acidosis the rule is mirrored (≥ expected value = adequate). Compensatory limits: respiratory acidosis ↑up to 30 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ (acute) and ↑up to 45 mEq/L (chronic); respiratory alkalosis ↓up to 20 mEq/L (acute) and ↓up to 12–14 mEq/L (chronic).
Anion gap, osmolal gap and delta ratio

Anion gap: measured cation + unmeasured cation = measured anion + unmeasured anion, so mc − ma = ua − uc and AG = uc − ua = Na⁺ − (HCO₃⁻ + Cl⁻) = 12 ± 2 mEq/L, with corrected AGc = AG + 2.5 (4.5 − S.albumin). Osmolal gap = measured osmolality (osmomoter) − calculated osmolality, where calculated osmolality = 2(Na) + BUN/2.8 + Glucose/18 + 1.25 × EtOH; normal < 10 mOsm/kg and ≥ 10 mOsm/kg suggests unmeasured osmotically active molecules such as methanol or ethylene glycol. Delta ratio = ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻, where ΔAG = measured AG − normal AG: < 1 = HAGMA + NAGMA, 1–2 = HAGMA, > 2 = HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis.

Amino-acid derivatives: tyrosine → T3/T4 and catecholamines (adrenaline 80%, noradrenaline, dopamine); tryptophan → serotonin, melatonin. Vitamin derivatives: A and D. Peptides: small (<50 AA) = ACTH, ADH, oxytocin, all hypothalamic; large (>50 AA) = GH 191, prolactin 199, insulin 51, PTH, renin; glycoproteins (protein > carbohydrate) = FSH/LH/TSH, >200 AA with common α subunit. Steroids: glomerulosa aldosterone, fasciculata cortisol, reticularis DHEAS/androstenedione; sex hormones estrogen/progesterone/testosterone. DHEAS = most abundant adreno-cortical hormone in fetal life.
Tryptophan derivatives, sleep–wake cycle and the 80/20 rules

Serotonin (enterochromaffin cells of GIT) keeps us alert; melatonin (pineal) aids sleep. Morning light → retinal ganglion cells → raphe nuclei → serotonin; night (9:30–10 pm) serotonin falls and melatonin rises to a 2–2:30 am peak. Night gadget overuse → serotonin stays up → melatonin cannot rise → disrupted sleep–wake → depression. Happiness hormones DOSE. Adrenal 80/20: cortex/medulla; medulla 80% adrenaline/20% noradrenaline.
Mechanism-based classification and Group I (nuclear) hormones

Group I: intracellular receptor, lipophilic, carrier protein (+), long t½; act via gene transcription >> transport channels. Type I/homodimer = cytoplasm, steroids; Type 2/heterodimer = nucleus, T3/T4/vitamin A&D. Steroid receptor held inactive by Hsp-90; hormone binding releases Hsp-90 and the R–H complex binds GREs.
Type II nuclear receptors, orphan receptors and PPAR agonists

VDR (calcitriol = 1,25(OH)2D3) heterodimerizes with RXR and binds VDREs; TR on TRE sheds co-repressor and recruits co-activator on T3 binding. Homodimers = steroid receptors; heterodimers = TR, VDR, RAR, PPAR; orphans (no ligand) = SF1, DAX1 (gonadotrophs + adrenal cortex) and HNF4α (defect → MODY type 1). PPARα clofibrate (TG >440 mg/dL); PPARγ pioglitazone (insulin resistance; risks salt-water retention, fractures, bladder cancer); dual saroglitazar (DOC diabetic dyslipidaemia, NAFLD, NASH). Metformin also combats insulin resistance.
Group II hormones: second messengers and the GPCR cycle

Group II act through second messengers on transport channels, translation, modification and transcription. Receptor types: GPCR, TKR, JAK/cytokine, STKR. GPCR: hormone → GDP→GTP on α, α dissociates to the effector. Gs/Gi → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation; Gq → PLC on PIP2 → DAG (PKC) + IP3 (Ca2+/calmodulin); Gt = transducin (cAMP).
The GPCR hormone map, cGMP vasodilators and TKR

cAMP users: CRH; ACTH/FSH/LH/TSH; V2; β and α2 (Gi); secretin/glucagon/somatostatin (Gi); PTH/calcitonin. IP3/DAG users: TRH/GnRH; V1/V3/oxytocin; AT II/substance P; α1/ACh; CCK/gastrin. Gi lowers cAMP. cGMP vasodilators: NO and ANF; urotensin = most potent vasoconstrictor. TKR: ligand → dimerisation → autophosphorylation; insulin → PI3K/Akt → GLUT4 (adipose, skeletal muscle, heart); growth factors all use TKR except TGF β.

JAK–STAT: ligand → dimerisation → STAT phosphorylation → transcription; users GH, prolactin (twin hormones), EPO; JAK2 mutations in PRV, primary myelofibrosis, essential thrombocytosis. STKR phosphorylates SMAD; users activin, inhibin, BMP, TGF-β (most potent pathogenic fibrogenic cytokine, 'stroke master').
Adrenal anatomy, embryology and blood supply

Gland = 80% cortex/20% medulla on the kidney. Embryology: 6 wks urogenital ridge (mesoderm) → adrenal primordium (coelomic epithelium); 8 wks hormone synthesis; 9–10 wks urine formation; 12 wks development complete; kidney complete 32–36 wks; fetal:adult ratio 4:1; TFs SF-1, DAX1 (orphans), WNT4. Arteries: superior (inferior phrenic), middle (aorta), inferior (renal). Veins: right → IVC; left → left renal vein → IVC.
Relations, fetal zone and the definitive zones

Right anterior IVC + right liver lobe, posterior right crus; left anterior stomach/pancreas/spleen, posterior left crus. Fetal zone: DHEAS principal, regresses after birth. Definitive: ZG (at birth, RAAS, 15%, aldosterone), ZF (at birth, pituitary, 75%, cortisol, lipid-rich clear cells), ZR (by 2–3 y, pituitary, 10%, DHEAS >20 mg/day; adrenarche 6–8 y, regresses post-reproductive).
Steroidogenesis: the enzyme ladder and zone specificity

Cholesterol (LDL) → pregnenolone via StAR (steroid acute regulatory protein; rate-limiting; defect → congenital lipid hyperplasia). 17α-hydroxylase on both Δ pairs; 17,20 lyase → DHEA; 3β-HSD → progesterone; 21α-hydroxylase → DOC/11-deoxycortisol; 11β-hydroxylase → corticosterone/cortisol; 18-hydroxylase then aldosterone synthase (only in ZG) → aldosterone. Gonadal: 17β-HSD3 → testosterone/estradiol; 5α-reductase II → DHT (testis); aromatase (POR = P450 oxidoreductase) → estrone (ovary).

11β-HSD2 normally converts cortisol → cortisone. Inherited defect = AME; acquired inhibition by Cushing's disease and licorice excess. Excess cortisol acts as mineralocorticoid → salt + water retention → HTN with alkalosis and hypokalaemia.
Primary hyperaldosteronism: causes and the P-cell mechanism

PHA = 90% acquired (B/L micronodular hyperplasia 60%; U/L adenoma 30% = Conn's) + 10% familial (Type I GRA, AD; Type II ClCN2). Aldosterone→MR→AIP (aldosterone-induced protein)→ENaC in P-cells: Na+ in, K+/H+ out; ANP activation explains no edema. Triad HTN (diastolic > systolic) + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis. AME (AR, 11β-HSD2 defect) vs GRA (AD, chimeric ACTH-driven aldosterone; Rx steroids).
Presentation, who to screen and the drug-aware work-up

HTN + proximal/distal weakness; confirm renal K+ loss (urine K+/creatinine, spot K+ ↑). ABG: acidosis → RTA; alkalosis → acquired (Cushing, PHA) vs inherited (AME AR, GRA AD, Liddle AD = ENaC gain-of-function). Normal BP + hypokalaemic alkalosis = Gitelman/Bartter. Screen every new HTN; HTN + TOD (LVH, fundus, microalbuminuria, ↑ central systolic BP) → secondary work-up. ARR obsolete; false + β-blocker/NSAIDs/clonidine, false − ACEi/ARB/spironolactone/dihydropyridine; bridge with α-blocker, hydralazine, non-DHP. Screen: PAC ≥10 ng/dl + PRA ≤1 ng/ml/hr.
Saline infusion confirmation and CT lateralisation
Saline infusion test: 2 L NS over 4 h; normal suppression vs PHA unsuppressed (>10 ng/dL). Repeat PAC ≥10 ng/dl → CT abdomen (IOC) → B/L hyperplasia vs U/L adenoma.
Hypercortisolism: definitions, causes and metabolic effects

Cushing's = hypercortisolism from zona fasciculata (75% of cortex). Causes: exogenous steroid (m/c), inherited AME, acquired ↑cortisol; pseudocushing = chronic stress of obesity/alcohol/depression. Cortisol (GC+MC)→cortisone (GC) via 11β-HSD2. Effects: protein catabolism → proximal myopathy; carbohydrate (adrenal diabetes) with gluconeogenesis alanine >> FFA; fat redistribution (centripetal, buffalo hump); MC triad HTN+mA+hypokalaemia; sex-steroid acne/hirsutism/amenorrhoea; CNS steroid psychosis.
Systemic effects, the eosinophil clue and the cause tree

Eye ↑IOP/cataract/glaucoma; GI ulceration; ↓ linear growth; IL-6 inhibition (anti-inflammatory); ↑WBC yet infection-prone with eosinopenia and hypercoagulable thrombosis. Eosinopenia +infection → typhoid, −infection → Cushing's; eosinophilia → Addison's. Causes: ACTH-dependent 90% (pituitary adenoma 75% = Cushing's disease = m/c endogenous; paraneoplastic 15% m/c squamous cell carcinoma); ACTH-independent 10% (adenoma; carcinoma m/c in toddlers); others: McCune-Albright (GSα defect; triad precocious puberty/fibrous dysplasia/café-au-lait; m/c infancy) and PPNAD (micronodular, Carney's). Adult F>M.
Important symptoms, childhood Cushing's and first cut-offs

Protein catabolism: B/L proximal symmetric myopathy (LL>UL), facial plethora (thin skin, lost SC fat), bruising, young-onset osteoporosis/fractures with short stature and delayed bone age, violaceous striae (loss of collagen). Plus DM/HTN metabolic syndrome and incidental adrenal mass + central obesity → screen. Childhood: m>>F, adrenal > pituitary, less catabolism, obesity, androgen → precocious puberty; Rx radiotherapy. Rule-out: midnight serum cortisol ≤1.8 µg/dL and salivary ≤5.5 mmol/L.
The diagnostic algorithm: diurnal rhythm, DSTs and ACTH

8 AM cortisol >1.8 µg/dl (loss of diurnal variation = earliest) → endogenous; too low → exogenous. ONDST 1 mg 11 pm → <1.8 rules out. LDDST 0.5 mg Q6H ×2d for pseudocushing/obesity/PCOS/OCP. ACTH <10 = adrenal (CT adrenal; U/L adenoma → unilateral adrenalectomy; B/L hyperplasia → B/L adrenalectomy with Nelson risk). ACTH >10: 10–50 pituitary, 50–100 both, >100 PNS (PET). MRI: ≥6 mm → hypophysectomy; <6 mm → IPSS; none → PET.
IPSS, high-dose DST, PNS and medical therapy

IPSS petrosal/peripheral ACTH ratio >2:1 → pituitary adenoma → trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy; <2 → PET → PNS. High-dose DST 2 mg Q6H ×2d, >50% suppression = pituitary. PNS: hyperpigmentation, less catabolism, MC action. TOC trans-sphenoidal surgery (75% remission); radiotherapy 3rd line; relapse-prevention drugs ketoconazole, pasireotide, cabergoline, metyrapone, mifepristone (GR inhibitor), mitotane (adrenolytic).
Addison's disease: causes and hormone-deficiency features

1° = Addison's; 2° (m/c) = abrupt steroid withdrawal, pituitary/hypothalamic dysfunction. Causes: autoimmune m/c (PGA/APS 1&2, anti-21-OH antibody; isolated adrenalitis); inherited — Aladin (3A/4A: alacrimia, achalasia cardia, Addison's, ANS), X-ALD (↑VLCFA), T-pit (corticotrophs only); infective — TB m/c in India, meningococcaemia → Waterhouse-Friderichsen. Glands enlarged/normal/atrophic/asymmetrical. GC↓: asthenia, anorexia, weight loss, hypoglycaemia, euvolemic hyponatremia, eosinophilia; MC↓: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypovolemic hyponatremia, salt craving, ↑BUN/Cr; SS↓: dry skin, lost axillary/pubic hair, lost libido; ACTH↑: hyperpigmentation 90% (sun-exposed, oral mucosa); plus normocytic anemia and hypercalcaemia → auricular calcification (adrenal calcification absent).
Crisis, 1° vs 2° differences and the cortisol/Synacthen work-up

Crisis precipitants: infection/any stress, abrupt steroid withdrawal; features acute abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, hypoglycaemia, hypotension/circulatory failure; Rx fluids + steroids. 1° vs 2°: MC ↓ vs normal; ACTH ↑ vs ↓; pigmentation, salt craving/postural hypotension, vitiligo + vs −; K+ ↑ vs normal; Na+ ↓↓ both. Fasting cortisol <3 = Addison's, >20 rules out, 3–20 → Synacthen 250 µg IM/IV, peak <18 confirms, >18 rules out.
Replacement therapy: maintenance, equivalence and crisis protocol

Maintenance oral hydrocortisone DOC 20 mg/day (10+5+5); prednisolone/dexamethasone alternatives; fludrocortisone 50–100 µg if MC deficiency. Fever/infection double dose; hospitalisation 50–75 mg/day; surgery day 50–100 mg IV. Equivalence 0.75 dexa = 4 methylpred = 5 prednisolone = 20 hydrocortisone = 25 cortisol. Crisis: 100 mg IV stat + 50 mg Q6H (day 1 = 300 mg), 200/100/50 mg days 2–4, oral 25 mg (10,10,5) ×1 week → 20 mg (10,5,5) ± fludrocortisone; fluids NS/DNS 1 L over 1 h then 2–3 L over 12 h.
Medullary development, catecholamines and the PNMT rule

Medulla = neuroectoderm (20%), cortex = mesoderm (80%); complete by day 45 IUL. Catecholamines pulsatile, 80/20 adrenaline/NA; smaller granules adrenaline, larger dense NA. Metabolites (easier to measure): metanephrine/VMA, HVA, normetanephrine. Synthesis: tyrosine →(tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) DOPA → dopamine → NE →(PNMT) epinephrine. PNMT adrenal-only → extra-adrenal pheo makes only NE; cortisol stimulates PNMT.
Adrenomedullin and the pheochromocytoma types tree

Adrenomedullin (endothelium): vasodilation, inhibits endothelial apoptosis (prevents septic shock); granules also contain opioids, chromogranin A. Pheo: 4th–5th decade, M=F; neural-crest tumour making catecholamines + metabolites. Adrenal 75% vs extra-adrenal paraganglioma 25% (high malignant potential; sympathetic 20% organ of Zuckerkandl; parasympathetic 5% non-functional carotid body > jugular bulb). Rule of 10 obsolete; current bilateral 40/extra-adrenal 25/familial 40/malignant 50. Familial: MEN strongest, VHL, NF-1; B/L except NF-1. Malignancy: metastasis surest; SDH-B ↑ metastatic potential. Book conflict: p853 tree labels vs p852 PNMT mechanism.
Pathophysiology, the triad and BP patterns

Sustained sympathetic activity → ↑ intravascular volume (↓GFR → hypercalcaemia → acute abdominal pain; postural hypotension), DM, weight loss; EPO → 2° paraneoplastic polycythaemia. Triad: episodic headache 95% (m/c symptom), palpitation/tachycardia, profuse sweating. Others: abdominal pain, perspiration, panic attack 75%, pallor (suspect malignancy), weight loss, hyperadrenergic spells. Signs: episodic HTN 75–85% (m/c sign; sustained only 20% = resistant young HTN), normal BP 15%, postural hypotension 75% (↑HR >30/min, ↓SBP >20, ↓DBP >10).
Incidentaloma alarms, cardiac effects, histology and pre-test drugs

Benign m/c; functional cortisol-producing > pheo. Non-functioning alarms (any 1 → adrenalectomy): >4 cm, CT >20 HU, washout <40%. Heart ↑ rate/excitability/O2/force; dilated cardiomyopathy (other: sarcoidosis). Hypercalcaemia associates: Addison's, pheo, thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly. m/c cause of panic attack is NOT pheo. Zellballen pattern; markers chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100. Stop TCAs, L-Dopa, NSAIDs before testing.

Screening: 24 hr fractionated metanephrine/NM (98%/98%); plasma 100% sensitivity (with urine if strong family history). MRI abdomen IOC (T2 hyperintense, hemorrhagic/cystic); MIBG/FDG-PET obsolete; Ga-DOTATATE PET IOC if MRI −ve but biochemically +ve (SSTR2 binding). TOC laparoscopic retroperitoneal adrenalectomy. 10 days before: admit + liberal fluids + α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine DOC, non-selective irreversible non-competitive; prazosin/terazosin; CCB if needed; metyrosine rarely); 3 days before: β-blocker atenolol; intraop crisis: sodium nitroprusside/nicardipine.
MEN1: gene, 3P majors and minor tumours

MEN types 1, 2A, 2B/3, 4. MEN1 AD, M=F, MENIN (tumour suppressor, 11q), intron inversion > base-pair deletion. Major <20 yrs 3P: parathyroid 100%, pancreas 50–70%, pituitary 30–50%. Minor skin angiofibroma > collagenoma > lipoma; benign adreno-cortical adenoma (m/c), meningioma (m/c neuro), pheo <1%; malignant PNET, thymic & foregut carcinoid.
MEN1 organ-by-organ and the MEN2A gene

1° HPT: MEN1 asymmetric hyperplasia <20 yrs M=F vs sporadic adenoma F>40 (peak 60); IOC 99mTc sestamibi; Rx 3½ near-total parathyroidectomy. m/c hypercalcaemia symptom = fatigue. Pancreas: enteropancreatic NET = m/c cause of death; gastrinoma > insulinoma > glucagonoma (migratory necrolytic erythematous rash) > VIPoma (WDHA, NAGMA). Gastrinoma MEN1: duodenum, small multifocal, <5%, endoscopic US, lymph; sporadic: Passaro's, large, >50–60%, SRS, blood; >2 cm surgery; streptozocin+octreotide vs high-dose PPI. Pituitary prolactinoma aggressive macro. MEN2A = RET (10q, point mutation).

Classical MEN2A: MTC 100% + pheo 50% + parathyroid hyperplasia 25%; variants + cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, + Hirschsprung's, FMTC. MEN2B/3: MTC 100% + pheo 50% + marfanoid habitus, mucosal & intestinal ganglioneuromatosis (tongue photo), myelinated corneal nerves. MEN4 = CDKN1B: parathyroid + pituitary + renal/adrenal + testicular/ovarian tumours.
Syndrome gene table and Carney's triad

HPT-jaw tumour (parafibromin/CDC73; ossifying jaw fibroma; parathyroid Ca), Carney's complex (PRKAR1A; atrial myxoma lepidic; PPNAD thin Cushing's, GH adenoma; lentigenes), VHL (Chr3; RCC, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, islet tumours, papillary cystadenoma broad ligament, epididymal cyst, endolymphatic sac; pheo; pancreatic cysts), NF1 (Chr17; optic sheath > meningioma; pheo U/L), Cowden (PTEN; breast Ca, hamartomatous polyps; nodular goitre/Hashimoto's), McCune-Albright (not inherited, post-zygotic GNAS; PFD, precocious puberty, café-au-lait). Carney's triad = pulmonary chondroma + GIST + paraganglioma.
RCC comparisons, Cushing's by age and the APS 1/2 table

VHL RCC B/L young lymphatic vs sporadic U/L elderly blood-stream. TS: kidney cysts + angiomyolipoma vs VHL pancreatic cysts (m/c) + RCC. Cushing's m/c cause: adults pituitary adenoma; infants McCune-Albright; toddlers adrenocortical carcinoma. PGA = APS: type 1 childhood M=F AR, APECED/AIRE, anti-21-hydroxylase + anti-interferon, skin/nail +, Graves > Hashimoto's + hypoparathyroidism + Addison's, candidiasis; type 2 adult F>M polygenic HLA DR3/DR4, Hashimoto's > Graves + Addison's, coeliac association; minor both type 1 DM + hypogonadism.
Bone types, constituents and the collagen table

Skeleton 10% cardiac output. Cortical 80% (diaphysis, osteon, Haversian +, PTH/thyroid, low turnover) vs trabecular 20% (epiphysis/vertebrae, trabeculae, steroids, high turnover d/t surface:mass); osteoporosis judged on trabecular bone via BMD + TBS (normal 1.432 good; low 1.124 degraded). Constituents: cells 2%, matrix 98% (organic 30–40% type I collagen + osteopontin/osteocalcin/thrombospondin/matrix GLA (warfarin-inhibited → calcification)/fibronectin/proteoglycans; inorganic 60–70% Ca/P/Mg). Collagen disorders: I OI/EDS VII; V EDS classical; II chondrodysplasia; III EDS IV; IV Alport/Goodpasture; VII epidermolysis bullosa; VIII none.
Bone formation hypotheses, ALP and the bone cells

Amorphous Ca phosphate → hydroxyapatite. Old: osteoblast lays type I matrix, mineralised by ALP/annexin/5'-nucleotidase; new: osteoblast → osteocyte lays matrix. ALP hydrolyses mineralisation inhibitors; not ↑ in myeloma; sources bone/kidney/placenta; GGT liver-only confirms hepatic ALP. Osteoblast mesenchymal (RUNX2 → intramembranous skull/clavicle; defect cleidocranial dysplasia). Osteocyte master regulator, mechanoreceptor, estrogen kills osteoclasts; sclerostin (unloading/estrogen deficiency) inhibits WNT1 + activates osteoclasts; FGF23 most potent phosphaturic. Osteoclast macrophage origin, CA type 2 protons, Howship lacunae.
RANKL/OPG, calcitonin, bone cycle and turnover markers

PTH/vit D ↑ RANKL on osteoblasts → RANK + M-CSF activates osteoclast; OPG inhibits RANK–RANKL. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast + renal Ca clearance → hypocalcaemia (Rx hypercalcaemia). Cycle: activation → resorption (3 wks) → reversal → formation → mineralisation (3 months). Resorption markers TRAP/CTP/NTX; formation total & bone ALP, osteocalcin, PICP, PINP. Vit D = Group I nuclear heterodimer (type 2), VDR+RXR on VDRE.
Vitamin D metabolism, jejunal action and PTH basics

D3 (animal/skin) vs ergocalciferol (plant); liver 25-hydroxylase → calcidiol (long t½, storage, assay form); 24-α-hydroxylase → inactive 24,25; renal PCT 1α-hydroxylase (PTH-stimulated) → calcitriol → intestinal Ca-binding protein/Ca-ATPase/ALP → ↑Ca → inhibits PTH. Drugs: phenytoin resistance, INH inhibits 25-hydroxylase, steroids/ketoconazole inhibit 1α. Nephrotic: DBP lost, vit D normal. Jejunum TRPV5/6-calbindin-NCX1-PMCA1b; VDR anti-proliferative (skin/breast/prostate). PTH 84 aa (PTHrP 139), bioactive 1-34, t½ 2-4 min (cold chain), 2nd-gen assay 50-100 pg/mL, ↑Ca ↓P.
Parathyroid anatomy and the PTH–vitD–FGF23 axis

Endodermal, 5-7 wks: 3rd pouch → inferior (ectopic intrathyroid m/c), 4th → superior. TFs: Tbx1 → DiGeorge (22q); GATA3 → hypoPT+SNHL+renal; GCMB/SOX3 → hypoPT. Oxyntic cells (mitochondria, sestamibi). Loop: FGF23 (−)vitD (−)PTH; PTH (+)vitD (+)FGF23; vitD (−)PTH (+)FGF23; PTH via 1α-hydroxylase. FGF23: (−)Na-P 2a phosphaturic, (−)1α, (−)PTH via Klotho (CKD resistance). PTH kidney ↑Ca ↑P-excretion; vit D ↓excretion; bone PTH resorption (intermittent low dose formation); vitD 1,25 resorption / 24,25 formation. Assay: <12 deficient 50k IU/wk ×6-8 + 600-2000/day; 12-19 ≥400/day; >20 sufficient; RDA 600/800; hydroxylation impaired calcitriol 0.25-0.5 µg.
PTH receptors, sigmoid rule, CaSR mutations and senile osteoporosis

CVS: medial calcification, atherosclerosis, HTN. GPCR cAMP/PKA; type 1 receptor also binds PTHrP (SCC head-neck/lung paraneoplastic). Sigmoid: ↑Ca activates CaSR → ↓PTH; ↓Ca (more sensitive) → ↑PTH; ionised Ca most important; P deficiency impairs release. CaSR loss → FHH; gain → Bartter type 5. Senile osteoporosis MSC → adipocyte; claudin 16 renal Ca reabsorption.
Calcium stores, corrected calcium and intestinal absorption

Total 1000–1300 g: 99.3% bone, 0.6% soft tissue (48% ionized, 40% albumin, 12% other), 0.1% ECF. Corrected Ca 8.6–10.3; formula +0.8(4−albumin); <8.4 hypo, >10.5 hyper. Ionized Ca: CaSR sensitisation, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity, bone mineralization; acidosis ↑ free Ca (0.1 pH → 0.1 meq/L). Absorption jejunum > duodenum, 20% net (~200 mg), acid enhances; 95% transcellular calcitriol-controlled (nuclear receptor → calbindin → TRPV5/6 → Ca-ATPase), 5% paracellular independent.
Urinary thresholds, milk-alkali syndrome and renal calcium handling

~200 mg/day urinary loss; 4 mg/kg/24 h; stones '4/7/11': hypercalciuria >4 (m/c), hyperuricosuria >7 (2nd), hypocitraturia <11. Milk-alkali: >4 g/day intake → paracellular entry → hypercalciuria/stones + hypercalcaemia → CaSR → ↓absorption & ↓ADH → volume depletion → RAAS → metabolic alkalosis. Renal: PCT 65% paracellular independent; TAL 25% dependent; DCT 10% active most dependent. ↑Ionized Ca: seconds → parathyroid CaSR ↓PTH (immediate); days → TAL CaSR ↓reabsorption → hypercalciuria (delayed). TAL CLDN16/19 + claudin-14.

Half-lives PTH 2–4 min, calcitriol 6–8 h, 25(OH)D3 2–3 wks (assay form). Gain-of-function CaSR = Bartter type V (AD; others AR): ↑↑↑ excretion → hypocalcaemia (others hypercalcaemia). Loss-of-function = FHH (children, AD): no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia.
Hypercalcemia thresholds and the three cause groups

>10.5 mg/dl starts evaluation (adjusted 8.6–10.3; 0.25 mmol = 0.5 meq/l = 1 mg/dl). Parathyroid dependent 80%: primary HPT (m/c overall, F>M, 6th decade; adenoma 85% inferior gland; hyperplasia MEN1>2A, MEON CDC73 carcinoma, sporadic), FHH (AD CaSR loss, low urine Ca), lithium inhibits CaSR, tertiary in CKD, PTHrP (SCC lung/head-neck). Vit-D 20%: hypervitaminosis; 1α-hydroxylase tumors lymphoma/sarcoidosis/acromegaly. Misc: endocrine (Addison's, pheo, thyrotoxicosis), milk-alkali, thiazide, osteolytic (breast m/c, lung, myeloma).

M/c asymptomatic. Acute: abdominal pain/vomiting/constipation (mimics pancreatitis), neuropsychiatric drowsiness/lethargy/confusion/disorientation, short QT. Chronic: fatigue (2nd m/c), painful bones, recurrent stones/UTI, myopathy, band keratopathy, pseudoclubbing. Mnemonic Bone/Stone/Groan/Moans/Overtone. Renal: neurogenic DI → polyuria → dehydration → pre-renal AKI; CTD. No diarrhea/seizures; hypocalcemia = long QT.

iPTH 2nd gen immunoradiometric, normal 50–100 pg/ml. High Ca with 'normal' PTH → suspect parathyroid dependent. >50 + ↓PO4 + ↑↑urine Ca → adenoma (inferior m/c), Tc99 sestamibi IOC (binds oxyphil). <50 → independent: 25↑&1,25↑ = hypervitaminosis D; 25 N & 1,25↑ = ↑1α-hydroxylase tumors (lymphoma, acromegaly, sarcoidosis); <20 = PTHrP paraneoplastic (SCC lung m/c) → CT/PET. CTD adds hypokalemia, hyperoxaluria, hyperuricosuria.

1°: adenoma m/c/hyperplasia MEN1-2A, PTH >50, Ca↑ PO4↓. 2°: CKD, PTH 500–1000, Ca↓ PO4↑. 3°: long-standing CKD, PTH >1000, Ca↑↑ PO4↑↑. Bones: 1 diffuse resorption (m/c) — subperiosteal radial side proximal/middle phalanx index+middle finger (most characteristic); 2 rugger jersey (intercortical); 3 brown tumor; 4 salt-pepper skull; 5 endosteal scalloping; 6 acral osteolysis; 7 osteitis fibrosa cystica (resorption > formation → fracture → fibrous/cystic).
Adenoma surgery indications and hypercalcemic crisis

Adenoma: surgery absolute, single-gland excision curative, no medical role. Asymptomatic indications: <50 yr, renal failure, urine Ca >400 mg/day, osteoporosis, S.Ca >1 mg/dl above baseline. Crisis 1st line: fluids 300–400 ml/hr + IV Lasix (not recommended) + calcitonin 4 U/kg S/C BD + IV bisphosphonate (zoledronate 4 mg in 50 ml saline + 50 ml dextrose 5% preferred; pamidronate). 2nd line: oral prednisolone (only osteolysis/Vit-D dependent) + denosumab.

Malignancy: PTHrP m/c (humoral, a/w SCC lung); lymphoma 1α-hydroxylase; osteolysis → crisis (breast m/c, myeloma, lung). Paediatric: Jansen (X-linked, activation mutation PTH type 1 receptor; short stature, dementia, disorientation, abnormal facies, severe bone) vs FHH (AD, CaSR loss; mild, fatigue, weakness).

Distinguish acute excitability, long QT and seizures from chronic calcification, cataract and dry skin. Elicit latent tetany with facial tapping or cuff inflation; the two tests are not interchangeable. ECG intervals require rate correction in clinical use.

Use phosphate and PTH together: low PTH suggests deficient secretion; normal/high PTH directs attention to renal failure, cell injury and other causes. DiGeorge: TBX1/22q11.2 and CATCH22; adult autoimmune disease: APECED.
Drug causes, hungry bone and PTH resistance

Confirm corrected/ionized calcium, assess magnesium, then evaluate PTH. Compare hungry bone with gland failure. Read PHP types across biochemical resistance, cAMP response and AHO, while recognizing the printed PPHP response wording is misleading.
AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment

AHO combines brachydactyly, short stature, round facies and cognitive impairment. Separate 3rd-, 4th-, and 4th/5th-knuckle patterns. Source calcium regimens are learning references, not unmonitored prescribing instructions.
Compare Ca and phosphate stores, albumin binding and intestinal fractions. Serum phosphate assays measure inorganic extracellular phosphate; do not apply the calcium correction formula to phosphate.
Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis

Follow PCT transport through Fanconi syndrome, compensatory phosphaturia in early CKD and impaired signaling in advanced CKD. Distinguish medial vascular calcification from atherosclerotic intimal calcification.

Clinical significance and pathogenesis of portal HTN

Portal HTN can manifest with or without cirrhosis and leads to hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites (1st sign of decompensation) → hepatorenal syndrome; jaundice + liver failure = decompensation with average survival without transplant printed as ‘a years’ (≈1 year) versus mean survival of 12 years without decompensation/transplant. Pathogenesis: portal venous pressure ≥ 12 mm Hg, sinusoidal pressure ≥ 6 mm Hg (clinically significant ≥ 10 mm Hg); cirrhosis (loss of fenestration, compression by nodules, ↑ septae) raises splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). The cirrhotic sinusoid diagram: collagen deposition in space of Disse, activation of hepatic stellate cells, constriction and defenestration of sinusoids; nodules and fibrous septae compress sinusoids → ↑ portal → ↑ splenic vein pressure (caput medusae = back flow of blood from portal veins).

Portal vein: development — inferior segment of left and right vitelline veins joins to form it; formation — splenic vein + superior mesenteric vein join behind the neck of pancreas, 7.5 cm long, hilum posterior to hepatic (artery) and bile duct. High compliance, low resistance. Branching diagram: umbilical vein drains into left portal vein, cystic vein into right portal vein, 1st order = main trunk, 3rd order (Bifurcation), ‘…rd order (Entry)’ label garbled in print. Hepatic buffer response: hepatic ischaemia is rare d/t dual blood supply (portal vein, hepatic artery).
