Extreme fatigue, tachypnoea/tachycardia/splenomegaly and mild myalgia in uncomplicated disease; complications from cyto-adherence, rosetting and agglutination of RBCs with organ ischaemia and the spleen as the major trapping organ; species table — falciparum (younger cells, 48 h, black pigment, no relapses), vivax (reticulocytes and cells up to 2 weeks old, 48 h, yellow-brown, relapses), ovale (reticulocytes, 48 h, dark-brown, relapses), malariae (older cells, 72 h, brown-black, no relapses); complicated falciparum disease with anaemia, cerebral malaria, hypoglycaemia, shock, black water fever and jaundice; diagnosis by thick smear with Giemsa and light microscopy as gold standard, thin smear not sensitive, QBC with acridine orange and three tests 12 hours apart to exclude malaria, HRP2 rapid test not validated; oral artemether 80 mg plus lumefantrine 480 mg four tablets BD for 3 days first line with atovaquone-proguanil, clindamycin-mefloquine, doxycycline-quinine, artesunate-amodiaquine and artesunate-mefloquine as alternatives; complicated disease IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours then daily on days 2 and 3.

First reported case in 1981 from an African patient, formerly lymphadenopathy-associated virus; CDC stages: 0 early HIV infection, 1 ≥500 cells/mm³, 2 200-499 cells/mm³ with CD4 14-28%, 3 <200 cells/mm³ or CD4 <14% with AIDS-defining conditions; AIDS-defining groups: malignancies (Burkitt's, EBV-mediated immunoblastic and primary CNS lymphoma, invasive cervical cancer, Kaposi's sarcoma), viral (CMV outside liver/spleen/nodes, HSV except zoster, JC virus PML), fungal (candidiasis of bronchi/trachea/lungs/oesophagus, extrapulmonary cryptococcosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii), parasitic (cerebral toxoplasmosis) and bacterial (MAC, MTB, Salmonella septicemia); category B non-defining conditions include vulvovaginal and oropharyngeal candidiasis, pelvic inflammatory disease, cervical dysplasia/carcinoma in situ, fever above 38.5 °C or diarrhoea beyond a month, ITP, herpes zoster, peripheral neuropathy and hairy leukoplakia; first Indian case in Chennai in 1986; Retroviridae with HTLV-1 (delta) causing adult T-cell lymphoma/leukemia and tropical spastic paraparesis, and lentiviruses HIV-1 and HIV-2 (less virulent, simian family, West African), envelope gp120/gp41, enzymes, capsid p17/p24, subtype C commonest and subtype B spread through blood and homosexuals.

Two copies of ssRNA; env codes gp120 spike and gp41 transmembrane pedicle protein, pol codes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease, gag codes p17 matrix and p24 core (nucleocapsid) protein; non-structural genes Nef (negative effector downregulating host CD4), Vif, Rev, Tat, Vpr and Vpu/Vpx; sources with high concentration are blood, semen and vaginal fluid (as high as blood), pus from sores and CSF, while tears, saliva (with salivary lymphocyte inhibitory protein), urine and breast milk are low; transmission frequency sexual > parent to child > IV drug abuse > transfusion > needlestick, with the highest per-exposure risk being transfusion at 9,250 per 10,000; replication step 1 entry with gp120 change, CXCR4 (lymphocytes) or CCR5 (macrophages) co-receptor binding, gp41 change then fusion and uncoating (co-receptor blocker oral, fusion inhibitor subcutaneous), step 2 RNA to DNA, step 3 integration (oral integrase inhibitors), step 4 proliferation and release with protease cleavage (protease inhibitors); acute HIV infection after a 3-6 week incubation mimicking infectious mononucleosis with fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, diarrhoea and rash, no opportunistic infections, over 90% resolving and about 10% fulminant with meningoencephalitis, then establishment in GALT with long subclinical replication (clinical latency).

Pathogenesis: HIV-specific immune response, massive viraemia with wide dissemination to lymphoid organs, GALT seeding, chronic persistent infection with trapping of virus, partial immunologic control, then destruction of the immune system with accelerated replication, immune activation driven by cytokines and HIV envelope-mediated aberrant cell signalling and rapid CD4 T-cell turnover; untreated course runs primary infection with or without acute HIV syndrome, dissemination and lymphoid seeding, clinical latency, constitutional symptoms with skin and mucous-membrane defects and systemic deficiency, opportunistic disease and death; graph shows CD4 count, HIV RNA copies and anti-HIV antibody over weeks then years; HIV RNA detectable around day 10 (1-2 weeks), p24 by day 16 (2-3 weeks) and antibody last; testing uses the 4th-generation HIV-1/HIV-2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay, negative means no HIV, positive goes to the HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay, and if no antibodies are detected HIV-1 NAT decides between acute HIV-1 infection and a negative result; opportunistic infections by CD4: lymphadenopathy/thrombocytopenia near 600, Kaposi's sarcoma at any count, oral hairy leukoplakia/TB, mucocutaneous herpes, cryptosporidiosis and microsporidiosis near 300, Pneumocystis, miliary TB and oesophageal candidiasis near 200, cerebral toxoplasmosis and cryptococcal meningitis near 100, primary CNS lymphoma at 50-100, and HIV-associated dementia, PML, CMV retinitis and MAC at the lowest counts.

CMV retinitis has the pizza-pie fundus; MAC presents with disseminated disease — fever, night sweats, weight loss and lymphadenopathy with rare pulmonary involvement — at an average CD4 below 10, treated with clarithromycin plus ethambutol and prevented with azithromycin when CD4 falls below 50; all HIV must be treated; drug classes are CD4 receptor inhibitors (ibalizumab IV), co-receptor inhibitors (maraviroc oral), fusion inhibitors (enfuvirtide subcutaneous), integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir, raltegravir), protease inhibitors (ritonavir, nelfinavir, atazanavir) and reverse-transcriptase inhibitors — NRTIs abacavir, lamivudine and emtricitabine, NNRTIs nevirapine, efavirenz and delavirdine, and the nucleotide RTI tenofovir disoproxil; preferred three-drug combination is TED (tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, dolutegravir 50 mg, all once daily) with the NACO/TLD regimen substituting lamivudine 300 mg for emtricitabine; post-needlestick prophylaxis uses the TED regimen for 4 weeks and is optimally effective within 72 hours; tenofovir carries bone toxicity.
q: Which set gives the three primary mesoderm branches in the embryology diagram?
Lateral plate, foregut and neural tube
The tree branches from mesoderm into intermediate mesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and lateral plate mesoderm. (Book p705)
Which set is linked to paraxial mesoderm?
The paraxial branch lists somites, muscles and myotomes. (Book p705)
Fill up: Lateral plate mesoderm divides into somatopleuric and ______ layers.
The two daughter branches of lateral plate mesoderm are somatopleuric and splanchnopleuric. (Book p705)
Which pleural layer is assigned to the somatopleuric branch?
The first somatopleuric bullet is outer parietal pleura. (Book p705)
Fill up: The somatopleuric contribution to the peritoneum is its ______ layer.
Mesothelial layer only in the pelvis
Visceral layer only in the foregut
The second somatopleuric bullet is outer peritoneum. (Book p705)
Which pericardial layer is listed under somatopleuric mesoderm?
The third somatopleuric bullet is outer pericardium. (Book p705)
Which pleural layer is assigned to the splanchnopleuric branch?
The first splanchnopleuric bullet is inner visceral pleura. (Book p705)
Fill up: The splanchnopleuric contribution to the peritoneum is its ______ layer.
Parietal layer only in the pelvis
Parietal layer only in the foregut
The second splanchnopleuric bullet is inner peritoneum. (Book p705)
Which pericardial layer is listed under splanchnopleuric mesoderm?
The third splanchnopleuric bullet is inner pericardium. (Book p705)
Which combination is linked to the cloaca in the urogenital-development line?
Lateral plate mesoderm plus neural crest
The line reads intermediate mesoderm + endoderm: cloaca. (Book p705)
A trainee asks the embryological origin of the anal canal below the pectinate line. Which answer fits?
The adjacent note assigns the anal canal below the pectinate line to proctoderm, also called the anal pit. (Book p705)
Fill up: The cloaca is the segment of hindgut ______ the allantois.
The definition beneath CLOACA is hindgut distal to allantois. (Book p705)
Which two structures are the immediate branches of the cloaca diagram?
Primitive urogenital sinus and primitive rectum
The diagram divides the cloaca into primitive urogenital sinus on the left and primitive rectum on the right. (Book p705)
Fill up: Epithelial buds of the primitive urogenital sinus form the ______.
The leftmost sinus branch is epithelial buds → prostate. (Book p705)
Which urinary reservoir is a derivative of the vesicourethral canal?
The first derivative under the vesicourethral canal is the bladder. (Book p705)
In males, the vesicourethral canal forms the prostatic urethra up to the opening of which duct?
The male sub-bullet specifies prostatic urethra up to the opening of the ejaculatory duct. (Book p705)
Fill up: In females, the vesicourethral canal forms ______.
The female sub-bullet is part of the urethra. This is tested before moving to the definitive urogenital sinus. (Book p705)
The definitive urogenital sinus divides into which two parts?
The definitive urogenital sinus branches into pelvic and phallic parts. (Book p705)
Which male urethral segments are assigned to the pelvic part?
The pelvic-part male sub-bullet lists the remaining prostatic urethra and membranous urethra. (Book p705)
Which statement about the female pelvic-part derivative is TRUE?
It forms part of the urethra
The female derivative under the pelvic part is part of the urethra. (Book p705)
Fill up: The male urethral derivative of the phallic part is the ______ urethra.
The first derivative listed under the phallic part is spongy urethra. (Book p705)
Which female structure is listed under the phallic part?
The second phallic-part derivative is the vestibule in females. (Book p705)
The right-hand cloacal branch directly gives rise to which bowel structure?
The primitive rectum gives rise to the rectum. (Book p705)
The anal-canal contribution of the primitive rectum extends up to which landmark?
The primitive-rectum branch labels the anal canal up to the pectinate line. (Book p705)
Which set contains the three branches of the intermediate-mesoderm diagram?
Mesonephric duct, paramesonephric duct, urogenital ridge
Primitive rectum, anal pit, phallic urethra
The diagram branches into the mesonephric duct, paramesonephric duct and urogenital ridge. (Book p706)
Fill up: The mesonephric duct is also called the ______ duct.
Wolffian duct is the synonym printed beneath mesonephric duct. (Book p706)
Which bud arises from the mesonephric duct in the diagram?
The arrow from mesonephric duct leads to the ureteric bud. (Book p706)
Fill up: The ureteric bud develops into the kidney’s ______ system.
The next arrow links the ureteric bud to the collecting system of the kidneys. (Book p706)
The paramesonephric duct is also known as which duct?
The middle branch labels the paramesonephric duct as the Müllerian duct. (Book p706)
Over which embryonic regions does the urogenital ridge extend?
The first ridge bullet gives extension from the cervical to the sacral region of the embryo. (Book p706)
The urogenital ridge lies adjacent to which duct?
The second ridge bullet states that it is adjacent to the Wolffian duct. (Book p706)
How does the text describe the swellings of the urogenital ridge?
One unpaired swelling ventral to the heart
Three pairs beside the neural crest
Four pairs within the primitive gut
Two pairs, on either side of the dorsal aorta
The third bullet describes two pairs of swellings on either side of the dorsal aorta. (Book p706)
Fill up: The medial swelling is the ______ ridge.
The medial swelling is named the genital ridge. (Book p706)
Which pair of organs is linked to the genital ridge?
The arrow from the genital ridge leads to ovary and testis. (Book p706)
The lateral swelling of the urogenital ridge is the:
The lateral swelling is named the nephrogenic cord. (Book p706)
Which part of the kidney is linked to the nephrogenic cord?
The lateral-swelling arrow links the nephrogenic cord to the excretory part of the kidney. (Book p706)
The appendix of the epididymis is a remnant of which duct?
The first note identifies the appendix of the epididymis as a mesonephric-duct remnant. (Book p706)
Fill up: The appendix of the testis is a remnant of the ______ duct.
The bracketed note assigns the appendix of the testis to the paramesonephric duct. (Book p706)
Which ductal origin is assigned to the hydatid of Morgagni?
The same note assigns the hydatid of Morgagni to the paramesonephric duct. (Book p706)
Which embryonic structure is identified as the kidney in the final note?
The final note reads metanephros: kidney. (Book p706)
On which day does the timeline place pronephros formation?
The first timeline row gives day 22 (fourth week) for formation of the pronephros. (Book p706)
What happens to the pronephros after its formation?
It regresses in a few days
It persists as the adult kidney
The second event in the first row is regression in a few days. (Book p706)
When does the timeline place formation of the mesonephros?
The second timeline row begins with mesonephros formation at the end of the fourth week. (Book p706)
Fill up: The mesonephros regresses by ______ in the timeline.
The next mesonephros bullet gives regression by four months. (Book p706)
Which qualification is essential when reading this timeline’s statement that the mesonephros has “no role in humans”?
It is the book’s shorthand, not a denial of all transient embryonic roles
It proves the mesonephric duct has no human derivatives
It means human embryos never form a mesonephros
It establishes mesonephros as the permanent human kidney

The scan says “No role in humans.” Treat that as source wording, not a literal claim that the embryonic mesonephros or its duct has no developmental roles. The same page describes human mesonephric-duct derivatives. (Book p706)
Which animals are named in the book’s parenthesis beside the mesonephros?

The printed parenthesis says “Kidney of amphibians, reptiles.” This records the source wording; it should not be generalized as a comparative-anatomy rule that adult reptiles lack a metanephros. (Book p706)
In the fifth week, mesenchyme of the metanephric blastema forms from which structure?
The first fifth-week event is formation of mesenchyme of the metanephric blastema from the nephrogenic cord. (Book p706)
In the fifth week, epithelium of the ureteric bud forms from which duct?
The second fifth-week event is formation of ureteric-bud epithelium from the mesonephric duct. (Book p706)
During which weeks is epithelial–mesenchymal interaction/transition placed in the timeline?
The continuation table places epithelial–mesenchymal interaction/transition in weeks 6–8. (Book p707)
Which two tissues participate in the interaction described for weeks 6–8?
The parenthesis names epithelium of the ureteric bud and mesenchyme of the metanephric bud. (Book p707)
Fill up: WT1 is described as a ______.
The first WT1 sub-bullet identifies it as a transcription factor. (Book p707)
On which chromosome is WT1 located?
The second WT1 sub-bullet specifies chromosome 11. (Book p707)
When does the first fully formed nephron appear in the timeline?
The next row gives end of the eighth week for the first fully formed nephron. (Book p707)
At which stage does urine formation by filtration begin in the table?
The first event at 9–10 weeks is formation of urine (filtration). (Book p707)
Which movement of the kidney accompanies the 9–10-week stage?
The second event in the 9–10-week row is ascent of the kidney with rotation. (Book p707)
Fill up: Nephrogenesis is completed at ______ gestational weeks.
The next row places completion of nephrogenesis at 32–36 weeks. (Book p707)
What proportion of nephrons is formed in the third trimester?
The next bullet states that 60–70% of nephrons form in the third trimester. (Book p707)
At birth, how is the number of nephrons described?
The at-birth row states fixed number of nephrons. (Book p707)
Which statement about nephron formation after birth matches the table?
No new nephron is formed or replaced
The first after-birth bullet states that no new nephron is formed or replaced. (Book p707)
How does urine-concentrating capacity change after birth?
The final row shows an increase in urine concentration capacity after birth. (Book p707)
By what age does urine-concentrating capacity reach the adult level?
The final arrow gives adult-level urine concentration capacity by 1.5 years. (Book p707)
Fill up: The nephron-number defining parameter highlighted here is ______.
The line immediately under Pathogenesis of CKD identifies birth weight as the nephron-number defining parameter. (Book p707)
In this flowchart, lower birth weight is linked first to which change?
The opening arrow connects reduced birth weight to a reduced number of functional nephrons. (Book p707)
A patient born at low birth weight has fewer functional nephrons. Which compensatory change follows in the diagram?
The next arrow links fewer functional nephrons to increased single-nephron GFR. (Book p707)
Total GFR equals single-nephron GFR multiplied by which quantity?
The parenthetical equation is GFR = single-nephron GFR × number of functional nephrons. It is tested at its printed position, before the downward cascade. (Book p707)
What is the next labelled state beneath the GFR equation?
The downward arrow from increased single-nephron GFR leads to glomerular hyperfiltration. (Book p707)
Glomerular hyperfiltration is followed by which pressure change?
The next arrow leads from glomerular hyperfiltration to intraglomerular hypertension. (Book p707)
Fill up: Intraglomerular hypertension leads to ______ injury in the cascade.
The next labelled step is hyperfiltration injury. (Book p707)
Which capillary-pore change immediately follows hyperfiltration injury?
The next arrow leads to stretching of the capillary pore. (Book p707)
What happens to capillary-pore diameter after stretching?
The next step is increased diameter of the capillary pore. (Book p707)
After increased capillary-pore diameter, which urinary abnormality is labelled in the flowchart?

The flowchart labels proteinuria. Its parenthesis reads “Albuminemia,” which refers to blood rather than urine and appears to be a wording error here; albumin in urine is albuminuria. The printed wording is flagged, not silently treated as correct terminology. (Book p707)
Which injury directly follows proteinuria in the cascade?
The arrow from proteinuria leads to tubular injury. (Book p707)
Which process follows tubular injury along the leftward arrow?
The lower flowchart turns left from tubular injury to interstitial inflammation. (Book p707)
Fill up: Interstitial inflammation is followed by release of ______.
The next leftward arrow leads to TGF-β release. (Book p707)
Which two compartments undergo fibrosis after TGF-β release?
The upward arrow from TGF-β release leads to fibrosis of tubules and interstitium. (Book p707)
What is the final disease endpoint of this fibrosis cascade?
The final upward arrow ends at CKD. (Book p707)
The first CKD feature on this page is a reduction in what?
The opening CKD-features bullet describes a decrease in the number of functional nephrons. (Book p708)
Which interstitial change is included in the listed CKD features?
The second CKD-features bullet first names interstitial fibrosis. (Book p708)
Fill up: The tubular change paired with interstitial fibrosis is tubular ______.
The next component in the CKD-features line is tubular atrophy. (Book p708)
Which glomerular change completes the CKD-features line?
The line ends with glomerulosclerosis. No numerical percentage is supplied in the scan. (Book p708)
Which maternal condition follows “age of conception” in the diagram?
The diagram begins age of conception → pre-eclampsia/hypertension. It gives no age threshold and should not be read as an inevitable outcome at any particular age. (Book p708)
Which placental problem follows maternal pre-eclampsia/hypertension?
The next arrow leads to placental insufficiency. (Book p708)
Placental insufficiency is followed by which fetal growth problem?
The printed term is intra-uterine growth retardation (IUGR), commonly termed intrauterine growth restriction. (Book p708)
Fill up: The next outcome after IUGR in the diagram is a ______ baby.
The next box is small for gestational age (SGA) baby. (Book p708)
Which renal risk is listed for the small-for-gestational-age offspring?
The first listed increased risk is CKD. (Book p708)
Which blood-pressure disorder is listed as an increased risk for these offspring?
The second listed increased risk is hypertension. (Book p708)
Which urate-related abnormality is included in the risk list?
The next listed increased risk is hyperuricaemia. (Book p708)
Which glucose-metabolism disorder is included in the offspring risk list?
The next listed increased risk is diabetes. (Book p708)
Which syndrome completes the list of increased risks after SGA birth?
The last listed risk is metabolic syndrome. (Book p708)
Fill up: ______ is important for formation of the epithelium of the ureteric bud.
The first note identifies PAX-2 as important for formation of ureteric-bud epithelium. (Book p708)
What vertebral range is listed for the adult kidney?
The adult-kidney location is T12–L3. (Book p708)
What vertebral range is listed for the fetal kidney?
The fetal-kidney location is S1–S2. (Book p708)
WAGR is introduced under mutation of which gene?
The heading WT1 Gene Mutation is followed by WAGR mutation. (Book p708)
Which renal tumour forms the W component of WAGR?
The first numbered WAGR photograph is captioned Wilms tumour. (Book p708)
A child with WAGR has the eye abnormality illustrated in the second panel. Which abnormality is named?
The second photograph is captioned aniridia. (Book p708)
Which category of abnormalities corresponds to G in WAGR?
The third figure caption is genitourinary abnormalities. (Book p708)
Which developmental feature completes the four-part WAGR description?
The fourth caption uses the older term “mental retardation.” Intellectual disability is the preferred term; the caption’s intended feature is preserved. (Book p708)
Which tumour is the first feature illustrated for Denys–Drash syndrome?
The first Denys–Drash figure is captioned Wilms tumour. (Book p709)
The second Denys–Drash illustration is labelled as which developmental problem?

The caption states disorders of sexual development (DSD), followed by the historical term “male pseudohermaphroditism.” The older wording is recorded without adopting it as preferred clinical terminology. (Book p709)
Which glomerular lesion is illustrated for Denys–Drash syndrome?
The third figure is captioned diffuse mesangial sclerosis. (Book p709)
By which age does the Denys–Drash caption place early-onset CKD?
The caption links diffuse mesangial sclerosis to early-onset CKD by 3–5 years. (Book p709)
Which gonadal tumour is listed under Frasier syndrome?
The first gonadal bullet under Frasier syndrome is gonadoblastoma. (Book p709)
Fill up: The gonadal developmental abnormality listed in Frasier syndrome is gonadal ______.
The second gonadal bullet is gonadal dysgenesis. (Book p709)
How does this book’s Frasier diagram describe external genitalia?
The third gonadal bullet says external genitalia normal. This is the source’s description, not a universal exclusion of sex-development differences in every patient with Frasier syndrome. (Book p709)
Which biopsy lesion is listed for Frasier syndrome?
The middle branch, Biopsy, lists focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. (Book p709)
By which age does the Frasier diagram place renal failure?
The right-hand branch states renal failure by 15–20 years. (Book p709)
Which statement matches the WT2 section’s opening line?
It is the ureteric-bud epithelial marker PAX-2
It is identified as a renal sodium channel
No role in epithelial–mesenchymal interaction is assigned here
It is the named driver of that interaction

The WT2 section opens with no role in epithelial mesenchymal interaction. “WT2” is the book’s historical locus/section label and should not be mistaken for a fully specified modern single-gene diagnosis. (Book p709)
Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is described as what type of anomaly?
The line beneath Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome reads genomic imprinting anomaly. (Book p709)
Which tongue finding is illustrated in Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome?
The left photograph is captioned macroglossia. (Book p709)
Which abdominal-wall finding is named in the middle Beckwith–Wiedemann photograph?
The middle photograph is captioned umbilical hernia. This is kept distinct from the later omphalocele bullet. (Book p709)
Which renal size change is included in the organomegaly caption?
The organomegaly caption first lists nephromegaly; the ultrasound montage also labels bilateral nephromegaly. (Book p709)
Which pair of enlarged abdominal organs is named next in the organomegaly caption?
The next listed finding is hepatosplenomegaly, meaning enlargement of the liver and spleen. (Book p709)
Fill up: Enlargement of the adrenal glands in the organomegaly caption is termed ______.
The organomegaly caption ends with adrenomegaly. (Book p709)
Which limb-growth finding is listed among the other Beckwith–Wiedemann features?
The first Others bullet is hemihypertrophy of limbs. (Book p709)
Which abdominal-wall defect is separately listed under “Others”?
The second Others bullet is omphalocele; it is separate from the earlier umbilical-hernia photograph. (Book p709)
Which childhood renal tumour is listed in Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome?
The next Others bullet is Wilms tumour. (Book p709)
Which head-size term is actually printed in this book’s Beckwith–Wiedemann list?

The scan prints microcephaly. This is an atypical/questionable feature for Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome and is retained only as a flagged source claim, not promoted as a defining clinical diagnostic feature. (Book p709)
Which ear finding follows the head-size term in the Beckwith–Wiedemann list?
The same bullet lists an ear-lobe crease after the slash. (Book p709)
A newborn with Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is screened for the glucose abnormality listed here. Which is it?
The next Others bullet is hypoglycaemia. (Book p709)
Which adult renal association is listed for Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome?
The final Others bullet is medullary sponge kidney, with the qualifier in adults. (Book p709)
Which facial shape is named for Russell Silver syndrome?
The first Russell Silver bullet is triangular facies. (Book p709)
Which developmental feature does this book list beside triangular facies in Russell Silver syndrome?

The scan uses the historical wording “mental retardation.” This is recorded as a source claim, not as a universal feature or diagnostic requirement of Russell Silver syndrome; normal intellectual development can occur. (Book p709)
Which sex predominance is printed for unilateral renal agenesis in this book?
The first bullet prints F > M. This question records the book’s epidemiological claim rather than asserting a universal sex distribution. (Book p710)
What incidence does the book give for unilateral renal agenesis?
The second bullet prints 1 in 10,000 live births. This is a source-specific figure, not a claim that all epidemiological references agree. (Book p710)
Which mutation is associated with unilateral renal agenesis in this section?
The next bullet lists PAX-2 mutation as an association; this does not mean every case has that mutation. (Book p710)
Which ocular association is listed for unilateral renal agenesis?
The first association is optic nerve coloboma. (Book p710)
Which cardiac-position abnormality is associated with unilateral renal agenesis here?
The next association is dextrocardia. (Book p710)
Which blood-pressure abnormality is listed among these associations?
The next association is hypertension. (Book p710)
What explanation is supplied for hypertension in unilateral renal agenesis?
The parenthetical explanation is decreased nephron number. (Book p710)
Which foot abnormality completes the association list?
The final association is flat foot. (Book p710)
Congenital absence of one kidney, the condition named by the upper imaging montage’s caption, is called:

The montage is captioned u/l renal agenesis. Its chest, abdominal, ultrasound and foot images accompany the unilateral association list; no additional unlabelled radiographic diagnosis is assumed. (Book p710)
Which named syndrome is used for bilateral renal agenesis in this section?
Under Bilateral Renal Agenesis, the book uses Potter’s syndrome. Clinically, Potter sequence describes the effects of severe oligohydramnios and is not limited to one cause. (Book p710)
The book calls Potter syndrome the “most common cause of death immediately after birth.” How should this be handled?
Flag it as an unsupported broad source claim, not a universal mortality statistic
Accept it as the leading cause of every neonatal death worldwide
Infer that unilateral agenesis is invariably lethal
Infer that all affected infants have normal lung development

The sentence is present in the scan, but its unqualified “most common” claim should not be taught as an established universal neonatal mortality statistic. Bilateral renal agenesis can be lethal, notably through severe oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia. (Book p710)
Which gene is named in the RET/GDNF line under bilateral renal agenesis?
The line names RET gene / GDNF protein mutation. This records an association, not a claim that all bilateral agenesis is explained by RET. (Book p710)
Which protein is paired with RET in the bilateral-agenesis line?
The protein named alongside RET is GDNF. (Book p710)
The scan abbreviates the expansion to “Glial derived neurotrophic factor.” The standard expansion is glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor. (Book p710)
The Potter figure caption prints “pulmonary hyperplasia.” Which clinical interpretation is appropriate?
Pulmonary hypoplasia; the printed caption appears erroneous
Pulmonary hyperplasia is the typical consequence
The caption proves that both lungs are absent
The caption means only transient neonatal tachypnoea

The actual caption says pulmonary hyperplasia. In Potter sequence the characteristic problem is pulmonary hypoplasia from severe oligohydramnios, not hyperplasia. The source error is made explicit rather than silently corrected or taught as clinical fact. (Book p710)
What renal finding is named in the second Potter image caption?
The second caption begins absent kidney, within the bilateral renal agenesis section. (Book p710)
Which vascular structures are also named as absent in that caption?
The same caption lists absent renal arteries after absent kidney. (Book p710)
Which adrenal-gland shape is described in the final Potter image?
The last image is captioned disc shaped adrenal gland. (Book p710)
Which fetal kidney level is printed in the gross-anatomy level line?
The scan reads S1–S2, not S1–S3. This corrects the previous bank transcription. (Book p711)
Fill up: Fetal kidneys ascend with ______.
The arrow is labelled ascend with rotation. (Book p711)
What vertebral range is given for the adult kidneys?
Fill up: The renal hilum corresponds to vertebral level ______.
Why is the left kidney higher than the right in this description?
The liver occupies the right side
The spleen pushes the left kidney down
The bladder pulls the right kidney down
The pancreas pushes the left kidney up
The line says left kidney higher due to liver on the right side. (Book p711)
The renal artery is discussed among which aortic branches?
Terminal branches of the pulmonary trunk
Lateral branches of the abdominal aorta
Anterior branches of the thoracic aorta
Posterior branches of the aortic arch
Arterial supply: lateral branches of abdominal aorta (Book p711)
Which artery is first in the book’s lateral-branch sequence?
The printed sequence starts with inferior phrenic artery; this is the book’s ordering, not a claim of invariant branching anatomy. (Book p711)
Which artery is second in this lateral-branch sequence?
Aortic lateral branch 2: middle suprarenal artery (Book p711)
Which artery is third in this lateral-branch sequence?

All of the following are components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus EXCEPT:
JGA components: JG cells, macula densa and mesangial/lacis/supporting (Polkissen) cells; podocytes are glomerular, not JGA. (Book p726)

Macula densa composition: modified tall columnar cells. (Book p726)
Fill up: The macula densa sits in the cortical portion of the thick ascending limb (TAL), also called the distal ______ tubule.
Site: cortical portion of thick ascending limb of loop of Henle (TAL)/distal straight tubule. (Book p726)
Tubulo-glomerular (TG) feedback by the macula densa is mediated by:
Function of macula densa: TG feedback mediated by adenosine. (Book p726)
Match each macula densa fact with its detail — 1) Composition 2) Site 3) Function … A) TG feedback mediated by adenosine B) Modified tall columnar cells C) Cortical TAL / distal straight tubule
Macula densa: modified tall columnar cells (composition) in the cortical TAL/distal straight tubule (site), doing TG feedback via adenosine (function). (Book p726)
Which of the following statements about the macula densa is TRUE?
It lies in the cortical portion of the thick ascending limb / distal straight tubule
It lies in the medullary portion of the thin descending limb
It lies in the proximal convoluted tubule
It lies within the glomerular capillary tuft
Site of macula densa: cortical portion of TAL/distal straight tubule, where it senses tubular load. (Book p726)
In the JG-apparatus figure, the arteriole labelled leaving the glomerulus beside the smooth-muscle layer is the:

The JG apparatus figure labels the efferent arteriole with its smooth muscle layer, plus internal elastic lamina, glomerular epithelium, JG cells, basement membrane, distal tubule (straight) and macula densa. (Book p726)

Match each label in the JG apparatus figure with where its leader points — 1) Internal elastic lamina 2) Glomerular epithelium 3) Basement membrane … A) Wall of the distal tubule in cross-section B) Top wall of the arteriole C) Covering of the glomerular tuft
Internal elastic lamina → top arteriole wall; glomerular epithelium → tuft covering; basement membrane → distal tubule wall. (Book p726)
All of the following are labelled in the JG apparatus figure EXCEPT:

The figure labels distal tubule (straight), macula densa and JG cells (with efferent arteriole, smooth muscle layer, internal elastic lamina, glomerular epithelium and basement membrane); no thin ascending limb. (Book p726)
In the sequence-of-tubular-injury table, the phase of tubular injury lasts:

Renal tubular injury from tubulotoxic drugs (eg. gentamicin) → PCT injury within < 24 hrs. (Book p726)
Fill up: In phase 1, PCT injury lowers reabsorption of solute + H2O and increases their loss in ______.
↓ reabsorption of solute + H2O → ↑ loss of solute + H2O in urine. (Book p726)
All of the following are findings of the TG-feedback phase EXCEPT:
TG-feedback phase findings: ↓GFR, ↑S.creatinine, ↑K+ → cardiac arrhythmias, ↑H+ → metabolic acidosis; GFR falls, not rises. (Book p726)
In the TG-feedback phase, the raised H+ load leads to:
Phase-2 findings: ↑H+ → metabolic acidosis (with ↓GFR, ↑S.creatinine and ↑K+ → cardiac arrhythmias). (Book p726)
Match each sensing priority of the macula densa with the ion — 1) First sensed 2) Second sensed 3) Third sensed … A) Na+ B) Cl- C) K+
Macula densa senses Cl- > K+ > Na+ load delivered to the TAL. (Book p726)
Fill up: Sensing the increased tubular load, the macula densa triggers release of ______, which constricts the afferent arteriole.
Impaired reabsorption → macula densa senses load → release of adenosine → constricts afferent arteriole. (Book p726)
The management listed for the TG-feedback phase of tubular injury is:
Supportive care with monitored fluid intake
Mx: supportive care; monitor fluid intake (↑ chance of edema due to renal failure). (Book p727)
Which of the following statements about the TG-feedback MOA is TRUE?
Afferent arteriolar constriction lowers GFR (glomerular filtration rate) and prevents further salt + H2O loss
Afferent constriction raises GFR to flush the tubule
Efferent dilatation is the protective step

Constricts afferent arteriole → ↓GFR (glomerular filtration rate) → ↑S.creatinine and prevents further salt + H2O loss due to impaired reabsorption. (Book p727)
In the sequence-of-tubular-injury table, the MOA column for the recovery phase (3) shows:
Row 3 'Recovery phase' carries only a dash in the MOA column. (Book p727)
A patient with prolonged vomiting becomes dehydrated and develops pre-renal failure. The first event in the book's chain is:
Dehydration (eg. ↑ vomiting → pre-renal failure) begins with loss of intravascular volume. (Book p727)
Fill up: Loss of intravascular volume lowers glomerular ______ pressure and therefore GFR.
Loss of intravascular volume → ↓ glomerular hydrostatic pressure → ↓ GFR. (Book p727)
Which of the following statements about the dehydration chain is TRUE?
Proximal tubular absorption increases and feeds the macula densa signal
Proximal tubular absorption falls to zero
The macula densa senses an increased Na+/Cl-/K+ load

↑ proximal tubular absorption (+) → macula densa senses ↓Na+/Cl-/K+ → dilatation of afferent arteriole. (Book p727)
Fill up: In dehydration, afferent arteriolar dilatation that restores GFR is mediated by ______.
Dilatation of afferent arteriole is mediated by prostaglandins → ↑ GFR. (Book p727)
The final outcome of the dehydration/TG-feedback chain is:
Prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation ends with ↑ GFR. (Book p727)
Which of the following statements about the book's AKI cause groups is TRUE?
Inside-kidney causes are ATI/ATN and acute interstitial nephritis
Pre-renal causes arise inside the kidney
Post-renal causes arise inside the kidney
Outside kidney = pre-renal + post-renal; inside kidney = ATI/ATN + AIN. (Book p727)
Match each AKI cause group with its members — 1) Outside kidney 2) Inside kidney … A) ATI/ATN and acute interstitial nephritis B) Pre-renal and post-renal causes
Both groups contain only pre-renal causes
Outside kidney = pre-renal + post-renal; inside kidney = ATI/ATN + AIN. (Book p727)
Fill up: JG cells are composed of ______ cells.
JG cells composition: granular cells. (Book p727)
Fill up: JG cells sit in the tunica ______ of the afferent arteriole (more than the efferent).
Site: tunica media of afferent arteriole > efferent arteriole. (Book p727)

JG cell function: produce renin. (Book p727)

β1-receptors (with prostaglandins and ↓ perfusion pressure) positively stimulate JG cells to secrete renin. (Book p728)

β1-receptors (with prostaglandins and ↓ renal perfusion pressure) act positively on JG cells → renin, so β-blockade blunts the response. (Book p728)
The renal artery is described in the circulation chain as a:
Renal circulation starts: renal artery (end artery). (Book p728)

Renal artery → 5 segmental arteries (4 anterior + 1 posterior). (Book p728)

Segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular/cortical radial → afferent arteriole. (Book p728)

Afferent arteriole supplies glomerular capillary plexus (in cortex). (Book p728)

Glomerular plexus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillary plexus. (Book p728)

Peritubular capillary plexus → blood supply to medulla (mediated by vasa recta). (Book p728)

Ascending limb of vasa recta → renal vein → IVC (inferior vena cava). (Book p728)

Forward order is interlobar → arcuate (not arcuate → interlobar); the other pairs follow the chain as written. (Book p728)

Cortex: supplied by renal artery, good supply; medulla: supplied by vasa recta, poor supply. (Book p728)

Medulla: poor supply; pars recta/proximal straight tubule is m/c vulnerable to hypoxia. (Book p728)

The medulla has a richer supply than the cortex
The cortex is supplied by vasa recta
Both zones are equally vulnerable to hypoxia
Cortex = renal artery, good supply; medulla = vasa recta, poor supply with the pars recta m/c vulnerable to hypoxia. (Book p728)

CKD: chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis/disease → RTA type 4. (Book p729)

Small vessel disorders → TMA → hypertensive crisis → progress to CKD (ischemic nephropathy). (Book p729)

Function: prevent proteinuria (albuminuria) → prevent nephrotoxicity. (Book p730)

Hyperfiltration → ↓ functional nephrons → proteinuria → intraglomerular HTN → capillary stretching
Proteinuria → ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration → capillary stretching → intraglomerular HTN
Intraglomerular HTN → ↓ functional nephrons → hyperfiltration → proteinuria → capillary stretching
↓ number of functional nephrons → hyperfiltration by remaining nephrons → intraglomerular hypertension → stretching of capillaries with ↑ pore diameter → proteinuria. (Book p730)

Stretching of capillaries → ↑ capillary pore diameter → proteinuria (albuminuria). (Book p730)

Proteinuria splits into tubulotoxicity and interstitial inflammation; the inflammation branch gives TGF-β formation → tubulo interstitial fibrosis. (Book p730)

TGF-β formation → tubulo-interstitial fibrosis closes the chain. (Book p730)

Which of the following statements about the charge rule of the filtration barrier is TRUE?
Molecules of effective diameter 4–8 mm are repelled if they carry a negative charge
Molecules of effective diameter 4–8 mm are repelled if positively charged
Charge plays no role between 4 and 8 mm
Only molecules above 10 mm are charge-repelled

α1α1α2 at birth; α3α4α5 in GBM, cochlear BM and ocular BM; α5α5α6 in epidermal BM. (Book p731)
A defect in type 4 collagen produces:
Type 4 collagen defect → Alport syndrome. (Book p731)
Match each Alport syndrome form with its profile — 1) The 85% form 2) The 10–15% form … A) AD/AR inheritance, α3+/α4 defect, normal skin stain B) X-linked inheritance, α5 defect, absent skin stain
Both are X-linked with absent stain
Both are AD/AR with normal stain

85% X-linked with alpha5 defect and absent skin/epidermal stain; 10-15% AD/AR with the printed 'alpha3+/ alpha4' defect cell and normal stain. The column header prints 'Immunoflorescence' (one u) — taught as printed. (Book p731)
Fill up: The negative charge of the GBM comes from heparin sulfate proteoglycans such as perlecan and ______.
Negative charge: heparin sulfate proteoglycans (eg: perlecan, agrin) — 'Heparin sulfate' is the printed spelling; standard nomenclature is heparan sulfate. (Book p731)
In the GBM visualisation tree, the method listed first (printed as '1.') is:

Normal GBM thickness on electron microscopy is:

Thin GBM disease: < 200 nm against a normal 350–400 nm. (Book p731)

The supporting cells of the filtration barrier named in the book's note are the:

The m/c prototype disease of mesangial cell/matrix expansion listed is:

Match each label in the light-microscope image with what its arrows mark — 1) Mesangial cells 2) Bowman's space 3) PT … A) Proximal tubule profiles  B) The urinary space around the tuft  C) Cells in the mesangial regions

The left-hand figure on this page (the histology photograph) is captioned:
Caption as printed: 'Light microscope image'. (Book p731)

Match each label in the juxtaglomerular-apparatus figure with the structure it names — 1) PCT 2) GC 3) AA … A) Proximal convoluted tubule  B) Afferent arteriole  C) The four capillary circles inside the tuft

HCV extrahepatic: porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus, Sjogrens syndrome, cryoglobulinemia. (Book p771)
A hepatitis C patient with arthralgia develops palpable purpuric spots on both legs with a normal platelet count. The note on this page attributes the picture to:
Cryoglobulinemia, one of the listed extrahepatic features
Porphyria cutanea tarda, the other cutaneous manifestation named
Hepatitis C-associated membranous nephropathy with subepithelial deposits
Thrombocytopenic purpura from the underlying liver disease
Cryoglobulinemia → non thrombocytopenic palpable purpura. (Book p771)
Fill up: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease, Henoch-Schonlein nephritis) carries the tag of being the ______ glomerular disease.
AKA Henoch-Schonlein nephritis/Berger's disease; m/c glomerular disease. (Book p771)

Match each IgA fact with its type — 1) mIgA (monomeric) production site 2) pIgA (polymeric) production site 3) pIgA normal clearance organ … A) Liver B) Bone marrow C) MALT (mucosa associated lymphoid tissue)
mIgA produced in bone marrow; pIgA produced in MALT; normally cleared by liver. (Book p771)
Which IgA-type statement is TRUE as per the etiopathogenesis tree?
Monomeric IgA is produced in the mucosa
Polymeric IgA is produced in bone marrow
Monomeric IgA is normally cleared by the kidney
Polymeric IgA is made in MALT and cleared by the liver
mIgA (monomeric): bone marrow; pIgA (polymeric): MALT, normally cleared by liver. (Book p771)
The mucosal-injury causes of secondary IgA nephropathy include all of these EXCEPT:
Mucosal injury: coeliac, Whipple, tropical sprue, Crohns, ulcerative colitis, HIV. (Book p772)
HIV sits in the mucosal-injury list, but its m/c associated glomerular lesion is:
HIV (m/c collapsing FSGS) in the mucosal injury list; the liver-disease table pairs HIV with collapsing FSGS. (Book p772)
Cirrhosis appears as a secondary cause of IgA nephropathy because the damaged liver cannot clear immune complexes.
True — and the identical reason is printed against hepatitis B
True — the bracket reads 'liver cannot clear immune complex'

Cirrhosis: (liver cannot clear immune complex). (Book p772)
The spondyloarthritis examples in adults are ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis and IBD-associated arthritis, where the book ranks:
In the innocent bystander mechanism, mucosal injury drives ↑↑ production of galactose-deficient pIgA, which is not cleared by liver; the antibodies formed against pIgA are:
Anti glycan antibodies formed against pIgA → large immune complex. (Book p772)
In the innocent bystander mechanism, the large IgA complex cannot cross the sinusoids into the liver parenchyma and is finally deposited in the mesangium.

Match each condition with its m/c associated glomerular disease — 1) HIV 2) Cirrhosis (alcoholic & non alcoholic) 3) Hepatitis C … A) Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis B) Collapsing FSGS C) IgA nephropathy
HIV → collapsing FSGS; cirrhosis → IgA nephropathy; hepatitis C → MPGN. (Book p772)

Match each condition with the glomerular lesion printed against it in the liver-disease block — 1) Hepatitis B 2) Hepatitis C 3) Cirrhosis … A) Membranous nephropathy B) MPGN pattern C) IgA nephropathy D) Minimal change disease
Which pairing statement is TRUE per the m/c-associated-disease table?
HIV is paired with membranous nephropathy in the same table
Hepatitis C is the infection paired with collapsing FSGS
Hepatitis B is the virus listed beside an MPGN pattern
Cirrhosis, alcoholic and non-alcoholic, pairs with IgA nephropathy
Cirrhosis → IgA nephropathy; HIV → collapsing FSGS; HBV → MN; HCV → MPGN. (Book p772)
The sex preponderance written for IgA nephropathy presentation is:

Isolated oliguria with a normal urine sediment
Adolescents, synpharyngitic, episodic macrohematuria, intervening microhematuria + proteinuria. (Book p773)
The asymptomatic arm with microhematuria and proteinuria covers what share of IgA patients?
30-40% patients: asymptomatic + microhematuria and proteinuria. (Book p773)
The 1% RPGN arm of IgA nephropathy is annotated as:
1% patients: RPGN (adult HSP); 5% nephrotic; 5% directly as CKD. (Book p773)
A 30-year-old has BP 160/100, proteinuria, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL and bilaterally contracted kidneys; biopsy shows mesangial IgA. Which printed arm of IgA nephropathy is this?
The >50% adolescent cluster with intervening microhematuria and proteinuria
The 1% RPGN arm annotated as adult Henoch-Schonlein purpura
The 5% straight-to-CKD arm with a contracted kidney

The IgA prognosis rule of 1/3 splits into spontaneous resolution, develop CKD and:
Near normal RFT with stable course
1/3 spontaneous resolution; 1/3 near normal RFT, stable course; 1/3 develop CKD. (Book p773)

In the MEST-C discussion, mesangial IgA alone carries normal features; the bad-prognosis indicators are IgA deposits outside mesangium (eg. capillary loops), any proliferation other than mesangial and:
Tamm-Horsford protein casts within the tubules
Isolated C3 staining along the capillary loops
Bad prognosis: IgA outside mesangium; any non-mesangial proliferation; non IgA deposits (IgG, IgM). (Book p773)
In the prognostic list on this page, crescents (the RPGN lesion) sit with the bad-prognosis findings.
True — and gross hematuria is listed alongside them as a bad sign
True — crescents are grouped with the bad-prognosis entries
False — crescents are given no prognostic value at all
False — endocapillary hypercellularity is called chronic and inactive
Endocapillary hypercellularity → bad prognosis (active disease); segmental sclerosis + tubular atrophy → CKD → bad prognosis; crescents (RPGN) → bad prognosis. (Book p773)
Among the 'others' prognostic notes, macrohematuria earns a good prognosis because it permits:
Macrohematuria: early diagnosis → good prognosis. (Book p773)
Both serum complement levels and serum IgA are marked on this page as having no value in IgA nephropathy.
True — but the note applies only to children
True — serum C3/C4 and serum IgA are each followed by 'no value'
False — serum IgA is the recommended screening test
False — a low C3 must be shown before biopsy is considered
Serum C3/C4 → no value; serum IgA → no value. (Book p773)
IgA nephropathy investigations: light microscopy shows pure mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis, while immunofluorescence shows:
Subepithelial IgG spikes with a doubled membrane
Full house staining of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q
Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
IF: pIgA1 in mesangium ± C3 deposits. (Book p774)
Conservative management targets: salt restriction <2 g Na+/day, protein 1 g/kg/day, BP control below:
Salt <2 g Na+/day; protein 1 g/kg/day; manage HTN (BP <140/90); ACE inhibitor/ARBs for proteinuria control. (Book p774)
Steroid (short course oral) indications include proteinuria >1 g/day after 6 months of conservative management, nephrotic or RPGN (crescents) presentation, high E score and:

Steroids are withheld in IgA nephropathy when GFR falls at or below:
Transplant in IgA nephropathy is indicated if CKD occurs, and the book notes what about recurrence post transplant?
Transplant: indication if CKD occurs; ↓ rate of recurrence post transplant. (Book p774)

Match each complement pattern with its interpretation — 1) C3↓ and C4↓ 2) Transiently low C3 3) ↓C3 with normal C4 … A) eg. PSGN B) Classical complement pathway affected, eg. MPGN Type I C) Alternate complement pathway affected, eg. C3GN, adult HUS
C3↓+C4↓ classical (MPGN Type I); transiently low C3 eg. PSGN; ↓C3 normal C4 alternate (C3GN, adult HUS). (Book p774)
IgA deposits are seen in IgA nephropathy, IgA-predominant PSGN (adult PSGN), full house effect (SLE) and light chain deposition disease, the last showing IgA & κ light chain deposit as part of:
Light chain deposition disease: IgA & κ light chain deposit (part of myeloma). (Book p774)
All of the following carry IgA deposits per the note EXCEPT:
IgA deposits: IgA nephropathy, IgA-predominant PSGN, full house (SLE), light chain deposition disease; MN is not listed. (Book p774)

Which steroid-indication statement is TRUE as per this page?

A GFR of 30 or below is itself a steroid indication
A high E score is an indication; GFR ≤30 or sclerosis/atrophy is not
Proteinuria >1 g/day at the first visit mandates steroids immediately
High E score (endocapillary cellularity) indicates steroid; GFR ≤30/sclerosis/atrophy → no steroids; proteinuria >1 g/day only after 6 months conservative. (Book p774)
Fill up: In the conservative management of IgA nephropathy, proteinuria is controlled with ______ inhibitor/ARBs.
ACE inhibitor/ARBs for proteinuria control. (Book p774)
Which demographic profile belongs to PIGN/IRGN (infection-related GN) rather than to PSGN?
Immunocompetent school child presenting after a streptococcal sore throat
Healthy adolescent presenting after a GABHS skin infection
Immunodeficient child, male > female, predisposed by diabetes mellitus
Immunocompetent child, male > female, aged 2–7 years

The TYPES table contrasts the two entities: PIGN/IRGN arises in the immunodeficient child (male > female) with diabetes mellitus as the predisposing factor, whereas PSGN arises in the immunocompetent child. (Book p775)
A 5-year-old immunocompetent boy, previously healthy, develops cola-coloured urine and hypertension 10 days after a sore throat, with a low C3. Which table entry does he fit?
Thin basement membrane disease with persistent microhaematuria
PSGN — the commonest presentation is acute proliferative GN
PIGN/IRGN — the commonest presentation is RPGN
PSGN = immunocompetent child, age 2–7 years, streptococcal sore throat preceding by 7–10 days, presenting as acute proliferative glomerulonephritis with low C3. (Book p775)
PSGN follows infection with group A beta-haemolytic streptococci; as printed in the table, sore throat < skin infection as the predisposing infection.
True — skin infection is the commoner predisposing infection
False — sore throat is the commoner predisposing infection

The table's inequality 'sore throat < skin infection' means skin infection is the commoner predisposing streptococcal infection in PSGN — consistent with anti-DNAase B (a skin-infection antibody) being the marker used. (Book p775)
In the TYPES table, the PSGN age band is:
PSGN demographic row: immunocompetent child, male > female, age 2–7 years. (Book p775)

Match each PSGN table entry with its meaning — 1) Strains 1, 3, 4, 12  2) Strains 47, 49, 55, 57  3) Anti-DNAase B … A) Skin infection  B) Antibody that appears after a preceding skin infection  C) Sore throat

The TYPES table splits nephritogenic GABHS strains by the infection they follow: strains 1, 3, 4 and 12 cause sore throat, strains 47, 49, 55 and 57 cause skin infection, and anti-DNAase B is the antibody highlighted after a preceding skin infection. (Book p775)
All but one of these GABHS strains are listed against skin infection in PSGN. Which strain is the odd one out?
Strain 12 belongs to the pharyngitis group (1, 3, 4, 12); strains 47, 49, 55 and 57 are the skin-infection strains. (Book p775)
The organism responsible for PIGN/IRGN in the TYPES table is:
PIGN/IRGN is caused by MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), typically in an immunodeficient diabetic child. (Book p775)
Fill up: In PIGN/IRGN the commonest predisposing infection in a diabetic child is diabetic ______.
Predisposing factors for PIGN/IRGN: diabetes mellitus, with diabetic foot/cellulitis as the commonest infection. (Book p775)
Match the incubation period with the triggering event — 1) Sore throat  2) Skin infection  3) PIGN/IRGN … A) 7–10 days  B) 2–4 weeks  C) Alongside the infection (no incubation period)
PSGN incubation is 7–10 days after sore throat and 2–4 weeks after skin infection; PIGN/IRGN arises alongside the infection, with no incubation period. (Book p775)
PIGN/IRGN characteristically appears 2–4 weeks after the predisposing staphylococcal infection.
True, but only when the skin is the portal of entry
False — it appears 7–10 days after the infection
False — it appears alongside the infection, with no incubation period
True — the incubation period is 2–4 weeks
The incubation-period row reads 'alongside infection (no IP)' for PIGN/IRGN; the 2–4 week interval applies to PSGN after skin infection. (Book p775)
In the TYPES table, PSGN presents with a low C3 in what percentage of patients?
PSGN presentation row: acute proliferative GN (commonest) with ↓C3 in 90% of patients. (Book p775)
An immunodeficient diabetic man with an infected foot develops rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with a raised C3. The table's prognostic entry for this entity is:
Good prognosis with no risk of CKD
PIGN/IRGN presents as RPGN with ↑C3 in 60% and carries a poor prognosis, whereas PSGN has a good prognosis with no risk of CKD. (Book p775)
Match each row of the TYPES table with its entry — 1) PSGN prognosis  2) PIGN/IRGN prognosis  3) C3 in PIGN/IRGN … A) Poor  B) Good, with no risk of CKD  C) Raised in 60% (as printed in this table)

The HLA associations listed specifically for glomerular diseases with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis are:
HLA associations in glomerular diseases: HLA DR4 and HLA DR1. (Book p775)
Fill up: NAPlr stands for nephritis-associated ______ receptor.
NAPlr = nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor, one of the two PSGN antigens. (Book p775)
SPEB, the second PSGN antigen listed, is:
Antigens in PSGN: NAPlr (nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor) and SPEB (streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B). (Book p775)

Match each PSGN marker with its description — 1) NAPlr  2) SPEB  3) Anti-DNAase B … A) Nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor  B) Antibody appearing after a preceding skin infection  C) Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin
NAPlr = nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor; SPEB = streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B; anti-DNAase B is the antibody raised after a preceding skin infection. (Book p775)
A 7-year-old girl develops PSGN after an infected insect bite that became impetiginised. Which antibody titre is expected to rise in this setting?
Anti-DNAase B is the antibody highlighted after a preceding skin (pyoderma) infection; NAPlr and SPEB are antigens, not antibodies. (Book p775)
The clinical features of PSGN become acute within:

Diastolic BP fluctuation in PSGN raises the risk of PRES, which then may cause:
Diastolic BP fluctuation → increased risk of PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome)/hypertensive encephalopathy → seizures. (Book p775)

PRES = posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, the consequence of diastolic BP fluctuation/hypertensive encephalopathy in PSGN. (Book p775)
Pulmonary oedema and hyperkalaemia are listed among the 'other features' of acute PSGN, separate from the classical triad.
False — both belong to the triad itself
True, but only in immunodeficient children
False — hyperkalaemia is never seen in PSGN
Other features of acute PSGN: pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia and diastolic BP fluctuation with PRES/hypertensive encephalopathy and seizures. (Book p775)

Complete the pathogenesis flowchart of hypertension and pulmonary oedema in PSGN — 1) NAPlr + plasmin  2) ENaC  3) Na⁺ and H₂O retention … A) Activates the channel  B) End result: hypertension and pulmonary oedema  C) Epithelial sodium channel that is activated

Renal function tests in PSGN typically show:

A 6-year-old with PSGN has the following urinalysis: RBCs 3+, albumin 1+, and white cell casts on microscopy. This picture is:

Typical of PSGN — ↑↑ RBC with 1+/2+ albumin and WBC casts

Typical of acute interstitial nephritis — sterile pyuria with WBC casts only
Urine examination in PSGN: ↑↑ RBC, albumin 1+/2+, and WBC casts. (Book p776)
A child with PSGN has a persistently low C3 beyond 8 weeks. The book's stated action is:

Start empirical steroids for nephrotic syndrome

A second episode of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is common and simply needs a repeat course of penicillin.
False — PSGN does not recur, so a recurrence needs evaluation for an alternative diagnosis

The histopathology of PSGN is best described as:
Membranous nephropathy with spike-and-dome subepithelial deposits

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with podocyte effacement
Histopathology in PSGN: DPGN (diffuse proliferative GN) with exudative neutrophilic capillary infiltration > mesangial proliferation. (Book p776)
Fill up: The histopathology of PSGN is abbreviated DPGN, i.e. diffuse ______ glomerulonephritis.
DPGN = diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, with neutrophils in capillary loops exceeding mesangial proliferation. (Book p776)

Match the immunopathology with its PSGN phase — 1) Clinical phase on immunofluorescence  2) Recovery phase on immunofluorescence  3) Electron microscopy … A) Subepithelial camel-hump deposits  B) Only C3 in the mesangium  C) Granular IgG ± C3 in capillary walls > mesangium

A 7-year-old with PSGN has a BP of 150/100 mmHg. According to the treatment table, the drug of choice and its dose are:

A child with PSGN has a serum potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. Per the treatment table, the monitoring that must accompany this is:

Match each sign in the PSGN treatment table with its prescription — 1) Hypertension  2) Pulmonary oedema  3) Hyperkalaemia … A) Torsemide 5–10 mg  B) ECG monitoring and serial serum K⁺  C) Amlodipine 2.5–5 mg with hourly BP charting

Treatment table: hypertension → CCB amlodipine 2.5–5 mg + hourly BP charting; pulmonary oedema → diuretic torsemide 5–10 mg; hyperkalaemia → ECG monitoring (tall T waves) + regular serum K⁺. (Book p776)
The ECG change specifically named for hyperkalaemia in the PSGN treatment table is the tall T wave.

Hyperkalaemia row: ECG monitoring (check for tall T waves) and serum K⁺ levels checked regularly. (Book p776)
The histopathology figure labelled 'DPGN histopathology' on this page illustrates:

A glomerulus with spikes along the subepithelial space
A normal glomerulus with thin basement membranes

An immunofluorescence image in a child with acute PSGN is reported as a 'starry sky pattern'. This corresponds to:
Granular IgG ± C3 in capillary walls, more than in the mesangium
Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Mesangial IgA with C3 in a garland pattern
Extensive crescent formation with fibrinogen staining
Clinical-phase IF in PSGN: granular IgG ± C3 in capillary walls > mesangium, described as the starry sky pattern (figure 'IF: starry sky pattern'). (Book p776)

What is the indication for antibiotics in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
A low serum C3 at presentation
Antibiotics in PSGN are indicated for an active sore throat; they do not alter the course of the established glomerulonephritis. (Book p777)

Match the antibiotic regimen for an active sore throat — 1) Benzathine penicillin  2) Oral penicillin V  3) Penicillin allergy … A) 500 mg BD for 5–10 days  B) Erythromycin  C) Single dose of 1.2 million units
Regimens: single-dose benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units; oral penicillin V 500 mg BD × 5–10 days; erythromycin when penicillin-allergic. (Book p777)

Single-dose benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units is one of the listed options for an active sore throat. (Book p777)
Oral penicillin V for an active sore throat in PSGN is given as 500 mg twice daily for:
Oral penicillin V: 500 mg BD × 5–10 days, as an alternative to single-dose benzathine penicillin. (Book p777)

The note on this page states that nephrotic syndrome shows no pulmonary oedema.

False — pulmonary oedema is the rule in nephrotic syndrome
True, but only in children under 5 years
False — the note is about PIGN, not nephrotic syndrome
Note: 'Nephrotic syndrome: no pulmonary oedema' — contrasting the intravascular-volume depletion of nephrotic syndrome with the volume overload of the nephritic syndrome. (Book p777)
With prompt treatment, what percentage of PSGN patients recover in 3–5 days?
Recovery: 99% recover in 3–5 days with prompt treatment. (Book p777)
Six months after an episode of PSGN, a boy still has 5–10 RBCs/hpf on urine microscopy but normal BP, creatinine and serum C3. What is the correct advice?
Long-term steroid therapy to clear the haematuria

Immediate repeat renal biopsy for recurrent disease

A 6-year-old treated for PSGN is reviewed at 8 weeks: haematuria persists but serum C3 has normalised. The correct interpretation is:
Both findings indicate a recurrence of PSGN, which requires a second course of penicillin
The persistent haematuria indicates progression to CKD, and C3 must be rechecked monthly for one year
A normal C3 at 8 weeks excludes PSGN, so the original diagnosis must be revised
Persistent microhaematuria after PSGN has no significance, whereas a C3 still low beyond 8 weeks would suggest C3 GN and warrant biopsy

Recovery point: 99% recover in 3-5 days with prompt treatment, and microhaematuria may persist after treatment with no significance; follow-up is by serum C3, normally normal by 8 weeks, and persistence beyond that points to C3 GN and biopsy. PSGN also does not recur. (Book p777)
Follow-up after an episode of PSGN is done with:
Follow-up: serum C3, expected to be normal after 8 weeks; persistence beyond 8 weeks suggests C3 GN and needs biopsy. (Book p777)
In the management of PIGN/IRGN, serum C3 is low in what proportion of patients?
Investigations in PIGN/IRGN: serum C3 is low in 60% of patients (in contrast to 90% in PSGN). (Book p777)
The biopsy findings described for PIGN/IRGN are:
C3-dominant deposits with camel-hump subepithelial humps

IgA-predominant ± C3 deposits, or C3-predominant deposits with a garland/rope pattern
Linear IgG along the GBM with crescents
PIGN/IRGN biopsy: IgA-predominant ± C3, or C3-predominant deposits showing a garland/rope pattern. (Book p777)
A 5-year-old with post-streptococcal GN has C3 measured at presentation, and his cousin with MRSA-related infection-associated GN is also tested. The expected results are:

↓C3 in 60% of PSGN versus ↓C3 in 90% of PIGN/IRGN

↑C3 in 90% of PSGN versus ↓C3 in 60% of PIGN/IRGN

The prognosis and management described for PIGN/IRGN are:

Match the following source iodine entries — 1) Adult requirement 2) Pregnancy requirement 3) Daily urinary repletion entry … A) >100 µg B) 220 µg/day C) 150 µg/day

After several days of fasting during critical illness, a patient has low T3, high reverse T3, and initially normal T4 and TSH. Which pattern matches the source?

Assess thyroid testing in critical illness: I ICU admission excludes coexisting intrinsic thyroid disease. II Thyroid testing remains appropriate when there is a specific clinical suspicion.

Activating mutation in the TSH receptor causing autonomous thyroid follicle hyperplasia

I is true; II is false
