Toxic adenoma of the left lobe
The scintigraphy image on page 903 shows a Tc-99m scan of ectopic thyroid, with 'No uptake in normal location' and 'Uptake in ectopic location'. (Book p903)
Match the thyroid disorder to its effect on the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) — 1) Hypothyroidism 2) Hyperthyroidism … A) Decreased (↓) BMR B) Increased (↑) BMR
Thyroid hormone maintains BMR: hypothyroidism leads to decreased BMR, whereas hyperthyroidism causes increased BMR. (Book p903)
Which receptor family is explicitly listed under 'Cardiac actions' of thyroid hormone on page 903?
Page 903 explicitly notes: 'Cardiac actions (α-receptors): ↑ Cardiac output (CO), ↑ O2 utilization, ↑ heart rate'. (Book p903)
Thyroid hormone stimulates tissue oxygen (O2) utilization throughout the body, with the explicit exception of the ___ and ___.
Thyroid hormone causes increased O2 utilization '(Except brain & gonads)'. (Book p903)

Regarding the vascular and hemodynamic effects on page 903: I Toxicosis leads directly to increased cardiac output (CO). II Hyperthyroidism increases peripheral resistance, leading to increased blood pressure (BP).
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Page 903 notes: 'Toxicosis -> ↑ CO' and 'Hyperthyroidism -> ↑ peripheral resistance -> ↑ BP'. (Book p903)
Thyroid hormone drives thermogenesis by acting as an uncoupler of ___; a severe deficiency in myxedema coma causes ___.
The citric acid cycle; heat stroke
Thyroid hormone acts as an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation producing thermogenesis; its lack in myxedema coma results in hypothermia. (Book p903)
What two key effects of thyroid hormone on carbohydrate metabolism are outlined on page 903?
Direct inhibition of hepatic glucokinase and activation of intestinal SGLT-1
Suppression of pancreatic glucagon release and acceleration of glycolysis
Gluconeogenesis stimulation and glucose uptake into cells (with insulin resistance in hypothyroidism)
Glycogen synthesis stimulation and peripheral insulin sensitization
In carbohydrate metabolism, thyroid hormone drives: 1. Gluconeogenesis, and 2. Glucose uptake into cells (with hypothyroidism predisposing to insulin resistance). (Book p903)
Regarding fat metabolism: I Thyroid hormone causes minimal lipolysis. II Thyroid hormone stimulates cholesterol clearance; therefore, hypothyroidism results in hypercholesterolemia.
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
Under fat metabolism: 1. Lipolysis (minimal), 2. Cholesterol clearance (Hypothyroidism : Hypercholesterolemia). (Book p903)

A patient with severe long-standing thyrotoxicosis develops proximal muscle wasting, osteopenia with pathological fractures, and hypercalcemia with nephrolithiasis. What catabolic mechanism explains these findings?
Enhanced gluconeogenesis depleting muscle glycogen and causing secondary hyperparathyroidism
Impaired cholesterol clearance inducing osteoclast atheromatous emboli
Potent catabolic proteolysis causing myopathy, osteopenia/osteoporosis, and hypercalcemia leading to hypercalciuria and stones
Severe uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation causing muscular lactic acidosis and stone deposition
In significant toxicosis, thyroid hormone acts as a potent catabolic hormone driving proteolysis -> myopathy, osteopenia -> osteoporosis, and hypercalcemia -> hypercalciuria -> stones. (Book p903)
Match the physiological action of thyroid hormone to its target organ — 1) CNS 2) Vitamin metabolism 3) Bone marrow … A) Myelination B) β-Carotene conversion to Vitamin A C) Stimulates erythropoiesis
Thyroid hormone promotes myelination of the CNS, converts beta-carotene to vitamin A, and stimulates erythropoiesis in bone marrow. (Book p903)
Why can hypothyroid patients exhibit yellowish-orange skin discoloration while sparing the sclerae?
Extensive accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the sclerae
Accelerated breakdown of red blood cells from erythropoietic arrest
Impaired conversion of β-carotene to Vitamin A leads to carotenemia
Thyroid hormone is responsible for converting beta-carotene to vitamin A; in hypothyroidism this conversion is impaired, leading to hypercarotenemia and yellowing of skin. (Book p903)
Thyroid hormone maintains reproductive fertility; the sequential menstrual derangement noted in untreated hypothyroidism is: menorrhagia → ___ → infertility.
Under fertility maintenance: 'Hypothyroidism -> menorrhagia -> Oligo/amenorrhea -> Infertility'. (Book p903)
Which of the following is NOT listed on page 903 as a physiologic function or target of thyroid hormone?
Inhibition of erythropoiesis in bone marrow
Myelination of the central nervous system
Conversion of β-carotene to vitamin A
Thyroid hormone stimulates erythropoiesis, not inhibits it. It also maintains BMR, promotes CNS myelination, and converts beta-carotene to vitamin A. (Book p903)

Match the drug categories affecting thyroid function tests — 1) Deiodinase inhibitors 2) Enzyme inducers (↑ hormone metabolism) … A) Steroids, Propranolol, Iodine, Amiodarone, Propylthiouracil B) Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Rifampicin, Sertraline, Ritonavir
Deiodinase inhibitors listed are steroids, propranolol, iodine, amiodarone, PTU; enzyme inducers increasing metabolism are phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin, sertraline, ritonavir. (Book p904)
Which of the following drugs is NOT listed on page 904 as a deiodinase inhibitor?
Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer that increases hormone metabolism; steroids, propranolol, iodine, amiodarone, and PTU are deiodinase inhibitors. (Book p904)

Match the drug to its specific effect on thyroid hormone economy — 1) Lithium 2) Al(OH)3, Cholestyramine, Calcium carbonate, Ferrous sulfate … A) Directly causes hypothyroidism B) Decreases thyroid hormone absorption
Lithium causes hypothyroidism, while aluminum hydroxide, cholestyramine, calcium carbonate, and ferrous sulfate decrease thyroid hormone absorption. (Book p904)
What is the normal reference range for TSH tested by 4th-generation CLIA as specified on page 904?
Page 904 states: 'TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) : 0.5 - 5 mIU/L (by CLIA 4th generation)'. (Book p904)
Regarding thyroid testing rules on page 904: I Clinicians should always look for all three: fT3, fT4, and TSH. II Thyroid function tests should not be checked in critically ill patients.
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Under TESTS: 'Always look for all of: fT3, fT4, TSH' and 'Do not check in critically ill patients'. (Book p904)
A patient's laboratory report reveals: TSH elevated (↑), while total T4, free T4, total T3, and free T3 are all normal (N). What is the condition?
TSH ↑ with normal T4, FT4, T3, and FT3 represents Subclinical 1° hypothyroidism. (Book p904)
In overt primary hypothyroidism (TSH ↑, T4 ↓, FT4 ↓, T3 ↓, FT3 ↓), what is the most common etiology and clinical association noted on page 904?
Dietary iodine deficiency, associated with endemic goiter
Consumptive hemangioma, associated with deiodinase-3 excess
Pituitary mass lesion, associated with Sheehan syndrome
Autoimmune etiology, associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis
For primary hypothyroidism, page 904 notes: 'm/c : Autoimmune' and 'A/w : Hashimoto's thyroiditis'. (Book p904)
A patient's thyroid panel shows elevation of all parameters: TSH ↑, T4 ↑, FT4 ↑, T3 ↑, and FT3 ↑. Clinically, the patient is euthyroid. What is the diagnosis?
When TSH, T4, FT4, T3, and FT3 are all elevated, the condition is RTH if the patient is euthyroid, or TSH-secreting adenoma if toxic features are present. (Book p904)

When TSH, T4, FT4, T3, and FT3 are all simultaneously elevated, match the clinical presentation to the diagnosis — 1) Euthyroid state 2) Toxic features present … A) RTH (Resistance to Thyroid Hormone) B) TSH secreting adenoma
For elevated TSH + elevated T4/FT4/T3/FT3: RTH presents as euthyroid; TSH secreting adenoma presents with toxic features. (Book p904)
In hypothalamo-pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism: I TSH is normal or decreased (N/↓). II T4, FT4, T3, and FT3 are all decreased (↓).
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
In hypothalamo-pituitary hypothyroidism, TSH is normal or low (N/↓) while peripheral hormones T4, FT4, T3, and FT3 are all low (↓). (Book p904)
A patient has TSH ↓, total T4 normal, free T4 ↑, total T3 normal, and free T3 ↑. Which causes does the page 904 interpretation table list for this pattern?
Subclinical hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid syndrome
Overworking gland (Autoimmune Graves) or stored hormone release (Thyroiditis, Hydatidiform mole/pregnancy)
Under thyrotoxicosis (TSH ↓, T4 N, FT4 ↑, T3 N, FT3 ↑), causes include overworking gland (Autoimmune Graves) and stored hormone release (Thyroiditis, Hydatidiform mole/pregnancy). (Book p904)
Serum thyroglobulin is elevated in all forms of thyrotoxicosis EXCEPT ___, where exogenous hormone suppresses endogenous thyroglobulin release.
Serum thyroglobulin is increased in all thyrotoxicosis except thyrotoxicosis factitia (hormone supplementation). (Book p904)
What is the most common (m/c) cause of primary hypothyroidism on page 905?
Under Primary Hypothyroidism: '1. Autoimmune hypothyroidism (m/c) AKA Hashimoto thyroiditis'. (Book p905)
Autoimmune hypothyroidism is associated with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes (APS); clinicians should specifically check for ___ before initiating treatment.
Autoimmune hypothyroidism is associated with APS-1/2; clinicians 'Should check for APS2 before treatment'. (Book p905)
A patient with undetected coexisting adrenal insufficiency (APS-2) is prescribed L-thyroxine without prior cortisol supplementation. What acute consequence is cautioned on page 905?
Adrenal insufficiency: shock in children, profound adrenal insufficiency in adults
Sudden thyrotoxic crisis with hyperpyrexia and delirium
Acute hypocalcemic tetany from suppressed parathyroid reserve
If L-thyroxine is given without cortisol supplementation in APS-2, it precipitates adrenal insufficiency: shock in children, and profound adrenal insufficiency in adults. (Book p905)

Match the pharmacologic agent causing hypothyroidism to its specific clinical characteristic — 1) Lithium 2) Interferon-alpha (IFN-α) 3) Amiodarone … A) Associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI) B) Drug-associated thyroid destruction (irreversible side effect) C) Can produce both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism
Lithium causes hypothyroidism and nephrogenic DI; IFN-α causes irreversible thyroid destruction; amiodarone can produce both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism. (Book p905)
Regarding side effects of interferon-alpha (IFN-α): I Thyroid destruction is an irreversible side effect. II Flu-like syndrome is a reversible side effect.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Page 905 notes for IFN-α: 'Irreversible S/E: thyroid destruction' and 'Reversible S/E : Flu like syndrome'. (Book p905)
Which of the following is NOT listed under causes of primary hypothyroidism on page 905?
Pituitary mass effect from lymphocytic hypophysitis
Pituitary mass effect is a cause of secondary hypothyroidism, not primary hypothyroidism. (Book p905)
In secondary hypothyroidism due to a pituitary mass effect, what is the most common (m/c) underlying etiology listed?
Under Secondary Hypothyroidism: 'Pituitary cause : No significant hypothyroidism; Primary Cause - MASS effect - (m/c) Lymphocytic hypophysitis'. (Book p905)

Assess secondary hypothyroidism from pituitary disease: I It characteristically causes severe, profound isolated hypothyroidism. II Its primary mechanism is mass effect, most commonly from lymphocytic hypophysitis.
I is true; II is false
Both I and II are false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are true
Page 905 states: 'No significant hypothyroidism' for pituitary cause, and its primary cause is mass effect, most commonly lymphocytic hypophysitis. (Book p905)
A 2-month-old infant with a large hepatic hemangioma develops profound hypothyroidism requiring massive doses of levothyroxine. What is the mechanism of this consumptive hypothyroidism?
Suppression of hypothalamic TRH secretion by circulating angiogenin
Increased deiodinase-III expression in the hemangioma converting active hormone to reverse T3
Direct destruction of the infant thyroid follicles by hemangioma-derived antibodies
Failure of intestinal absorption of thyroid hormone due to splanchnic steal
Consumptive hypothyroidism in hemangioma is driven by increased deiodinase-III expression leading to decreased active hormones and increased reverse T3. (Book p905)
Consumptive hypothyroidism associated with hemangioma is mediated by increased expression of ___, which accelerates the formation of ___.
Hemangioma -> ↑ Deiodinase-III expression -> ↓ Hormones (↑ formation of Reverse T3). (Book p905)
What is the primary underlying cause of congenital hypothyroidism on page 905?
Under Congenital Hypothyroidism: 'mostly due to thyroid dysgenesis'. (Book p905)

Match the newborn physical sign of congenital hypothyroidism to its system — 1) Cranial sign 2) Gastrointestinal sign 3) Hepatic sign … A) Open posterior fontanelle B) Delay in passing meconium C) Prolonged physiological jaundice
Features of congenital hypothyroidism listed on page 905 are: open posterior fontanelle, delay in passing meconium, and prolonged physiological jaundice. (Book p905)
Which of the following is NOT listed on page 905 as a feature of congenital hypothyroidism?
Delay in passing meconium and prolonged physiological jaundice
Very little crying and excessive sleep
Features of congenital hypothyroidism are open posterior fontanelle, delay in passing meconium, prolonged physiological jaundice, very little crying, and excessive sleep. (Book p905)
In which demographic group is Hashimoto's thyroiditis most common?
Under Hashimoto's Thyroiditis FEATURES: 'most common in middle-aged female'. (Book p906)
Match the immunogenetic associations of Hashimoto's thyroiditis — 1) HLA alleles 2) Immune checkpoint polymorphisms … A) HLA-DR3, DR4, DR5 (can be ANA positive) B) CTLA-4 and PTPN-22 polymorphisms
HLA associations are DR-3 / DR-4 / DR5 (can be ANA +ve); non-HLA gene polymorphisms are CTLA-4 / PTPN-22. (Book p906)

Assess gland changes in Hashimoto's thyroiditis: I The thyroid gland is commonly not enlarged. II When goitre is present, it is characteristically an irregular, firm, heterogeneous, non-tender enlargement.
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Gland changes: 'Commonly not enlarged' and 'If goitre present : Irregular/ firm/ heterogeneous non tender enlargement of gland'. (Book p906)
On gross examination of a resected thyroid from a middle-aged woman with autoimmune hypothyroidism, the gland appears fibrosed, pale, and firm. What accounts for the pale appearance?
Diffuse fatty infiltration of stromal tissue
Under Gross appearance: 'Fibrosed gland' and 'Pale gland d/t lymphoid infiltration'. (Book p906)
On microscopic examination of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the prominent lymphocytic infiltration characteristically organizes into ___ formation.
Microscopic appearance: 'Lymphocytic infiltration -> Germinal center formation'. (Book p906)
What are the transformed, hypereosinophilic epithelial cells with abundant granular cytoplasm seen in Hashimoto's thyroiditis called?
Page 906 notes: 'Hypereosinophilic cells : Hürthle cells' and 'Oxyphilic metaplasia'. (Book p906)
Regarding the microscopic findings in Hashimoto's thyroiditis: I The follicular lumen characteristically shows an absence of colloid. II Oxyphilic metaplasia with Hürthle cells is a key hallmark.
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Microscopic hallmarks on page 906 include: 'Absence of colloid' and 'Oxyphilic metaplasia' with Hürthle cells. (Book p906)
Which malignancy has the highest associated relative risk in patients with longstanding Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid
Under Associated malignancy: 'Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid'. (Book p906)

Match the malignancy associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis to its relative frequency order — 1) Most strongly associated malignancy 2) Secondary associated thyroid carcinoma … A) Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma B) Papillary carcinoma thyroid
Associated malignancy hierarchy: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma is more strongly associated than papillary carcinoma of thyroid. (Book p906)
The cellular and cytokine mediators driving thyroid destruction in Hashimoto's include T-cells (both CD-8 and ___), plasma cells, and the cytokine ___.
Pathological mediators: 'T-cell (CD-8, CD-4)', 'IFN-gamma', and 'Plasma cell'. (Book p906)
Which of the following is NOT listed on page 906 as a histological feature or mediator of Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
Lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation
Abundant colloid retention in dilated follicles
In Hashimoto's, there is characteristically an 'Absence of colloid', not abundant colloid retention. (Book p906)

A 50-year-old woman with a 15-year history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis presents with a rapidly enlarging thyroid goiter. Biopsy demonstrates extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma. What is the classic risk hierarchy noted on page 906?
Follicular thyroid carcinoma > marginal zone lymphoma
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid
Papillary carcinoma thyroid > follicular carcinoma thyroid
Medullary thyroid carcinoma > anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
Page 906 explicitly highlights: 'Associated malignancy : Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid'. (Book p906)
What is the most common (m/c) presenting symptom of generalized slowing (decreased BMR) in primary and secondary hypothyroidism?
Under Classical Symptoms: '1. Generalized slowing (↓ BMR) : Fatigue/tiredness (m/c)'. (Book p907)

Match the manifestations of generalized slowing in hypothyroidism — 1) Speech & Gait 2) Bowel movements 3) Neurologic reflexes 4) Body weight … A) Slow speech and slow gait B) Constipation C) Delayed deep tendon reflexes (DTR) D) Poor appetite with weight gain
Generalized slowing affects: speech/gait (slow), bowel (constipation), reflexes (delayed DTR), and weight (poor appetite with weight gain). (Book p907)
In primary hypothyroidism, elevated TSH stimulates fibroblasts to produce matrix ___, which trap water and cause non-pitting myxedema.
In 1° Hypothyroidism: ↑ TSH elevation -> Stimulates Fibroblast -> Stimulates Accumulation of matrix GAG's -> Traps water -> Nonpitting edema. (Book p907)

Assess the clinical consequences of matrix GAG accumulation trapping water in 1° hypothyroidism: I Facial puffiness, periorbital edema, and hoarse voice. II Macroglossia leading to obstructive sleep apnea syndrome.
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Trapped water from matrix GAGs causes puffiness (face), periorbital edema, macroglossia -> obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, hoarse voice, and nonpitting edema. (Book p907)
Which of the following is NOT listed on page 907 as a symptom predominant in young females with hypothyroidism?
Symptoms predominant in young females are hair loss, irregular menstrual cycle, dry skin, and mood swings. (Book p907)
Which endocrine disorder is noted on page 907 as causing 'False positive Hypothyroidism' (transiently elevated TSH)?
Page 907 explicitly contains the note: 'Note : False positive Hypothyroidism -> Addison's disease'. (Book p907)

An adult with severe longstanding primary hypothyroidism presents with prominent pseudohypertrophy of both calf muscles accompanied by slowness and muscle stiffness. What eponymous disorder is depicted in the photo on page 907?
The clinical photo on page 907 demonstrates: 'Hoffman syndrome Pseudohypertrophy in calf muscle'. (Book p907)
Match the serous cavity effusions seen in hypothyroid polyserositis — 1) Pleural cavity 2) Pericardial space 3) Peritoneal cavity … A) Pleural effusion B) Pericardial effusion C) Ascites
Complications of hypothyroidism include serous effusions in three spaces: pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and ascites. (Book p907)
What is the most common cause of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) in females versus males on page 907?
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS): 'm/c cause in females : Hypothyroidism' and 'm/c cause in males : Amyloidosis'. (Book p907)
Regarding Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) epidemiology on page 907: I Hypothyroidism is the most common cause in females. II Amyloidosis is the most common cause in males.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Page 907 notes for CTS: - m/c cause in females : Hypothyroidism, - m/c cause in males : Amyloidosis. (Book p907)

A 48-year-old obese woman with untreated hypothyroidism presents with severe loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, and witnessed nocturnal apneas. What anatomical mechanism links this to her thyroid disease?
Macroglossia secondary to TSH-induced matrix GAG accumulation causing obstructive sleep apnea syndrome
Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve compression from thyroid fibrosis
Direct neuromuscular weakness of the diaphragm from hypothyroid myopathy
Tracheal deviation from subacute granulomatous expansion
GAG accumulation traps water, producing macroglossia that leads directly to obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. (Book p907)
Although page 907 prints 'Hypocholesterolaemia' among complications (an editorial misprint in the scan), the classical metabolic consequence of reduced LDL clearance in hypothyroidism is ___.
Page 907 lists 'Hypocholesterolemia' in its complications column, but clinically and on page 903, impaired cholesterol clearance classically causes hypercholesterolemia. (Book p907)
Which of the following is NOT listed on page 907 as a complication of hypothyroidism?
Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome and Carpal tunnel syndrome

Hypercalcemia and nephrolithiasis are complications of severe thyrotoxicosis (p903), not hypothyroidism. Complications on p907 are myxedema coma, encephalopathy, bradycardia, effusions, OSA, and CTS. (Book p907)
In a patient presenting with newly identified hypothyroidism, autoantibody screening returns completely negative. What diagnostic entity is considered on page 908?
Transient hypothyroidism due to thyroiditis (postviral or post-vaccine)
In the workup for Hashimoto's, negative autoantibodies indicate: 'Transient Hypothyroidism : Thyroiditis (Postviral / Post vaccine) -> may/may not require treatment'. (Book p908)

Match the autoantibody in Hashimoto's disease to its percentage association on page 908 — 1) Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody 2) Thyroglobulin antibody 3) TSH Receptor Antibody … A) 90 - 100% B) 80 - 90% C) 10 - 20%
Autoantibody associations in Hashimoto's: TPO Ab 90 - 100%, Thyroglobulin Ab 80 - 90%, and TSH Receptor Ab 10 - 20%. (Book p908)
The single most sensitive and prevalent autoantibody in Hashimoto's disease is ___, present in ___ of cases.
Thyroid peroxidase antibody is the most strongly associated antibody, present in 90 - 100% of Hashimoto's patients. (Book p908)

Match the combination of elevated TSH (↑ TSH) and free T4 level to the diagnosis — 1) ↓ Free T4 2) ↑ Free T4 3) Normal Free T4 … A) 1° Hypothyroidism B) TSH Secreting Adenoma C) Subclinical 1° Hypothyroidism
↑ TSH + ↓ Free T4 = 1° Hypothyroidism; ↑ TSH + ↑ Free T4 = TSH Secreting Adenoma; ↑ TSH + Normal Free T4 = Subclinical 1° Hypothyroidism. (Book p908)
What is the definitive TSH cut-off value that provides an absolute indication for L-thyroxine treatment in confirmed Hashimoto's disease regardless of symptoms?
Under Treatment Indications: 'Confirmed Hashimoto's (TSH value > 10 mcu/ltr)'. (Book p908)

For patients with a TSH value between 5 and 10 mcu/ltr: I Treatment is indicated if vague symptoms are present with TPO positivity, positive family history, or pregnancy. II Treatment is indicated if severe symptoms are present.
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
When TSH is 5 - 10 mcu/ltr, treatment is indicated for vague symptoms + (TPO +ve, Family history, Pregnancy) or severe symptoms. (Book p908)
A 27-year-old woman in early pregnancy is found to have a TSH of 6.8 mcu/ltr with normal free T4. Her anti-TPO antibody titre is elevated. What is the correct management per page 908?
Defer treatment and recheck TSH postpartum
Wait until TSH exceeds 10 mcu/ltr before treating
In pregnancy with TSH 5 - 10 mcu/ltr and TPO positivity, L-thyroxine treatment is explicitly indicated. (Book p908)
What is the recommended starting dose of L-thyroxine for a symptomatic hypothyroid patient under 60 years of age?
In patients under 60 years of age on L-thyroxine, subsequent dosage adjustments should be titrated by ___ µg/day.
Under drugs: 'Dose change can be by 25-50 µg/day' for patients under 60 years. (Book p908)
In elderly patients (> 60 years of age), what is the recommended starting dose and dose adjustment step for L-thyroxine?
Starting dose 50 µg/day; dose change by 50 µg/day
Starting dose 100 µg/day; dose change by 25 µg/day
Starting dose 10 µg/day; dose change by 5 µg/day
Starting dose 25 µg/day; dose change by 25 µg/day
In elderly (>60 yr): starting dose is '25 µg/day' and 'Dose change by 25 µg/day'. (Book p908)
Why must elderly patients (> 60 years) be started on a low dose of L-thyroxine (25 µg/day)?
Because older patients do not convert T4 to T3
Due to the risk of cardiotoxicity (e.g., precipitating angina or arrhythmias)
Because of rapid hepatic clearance of levothyroxine in older adults
Due to the high risk of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Elderly patients start at 25 µg/day explicitly '(Due to cardiotoxicity)'. (Book p908)
Which of the following is NOT an indication to treat subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH 5 - 10 mcu/ltr on page 908?
Vague symptoms with a positive family history
Pregnancy or presence of severe symptoms
Indications for TSH 5-10 mcu/ltr are: vague symptoms + TPO +ve, family history, pregnancy, or severe symptoms. (Book p908)
What specific administration instructions must be given to patients taking oral L-thyroxine on page 909?
Take dissolved in hot milk twice daily after meals
Take on an empty stomach in the morning (7 - 7:30 am) with a glass of water, and wait 30 minutes before meals
Take with a full meal at dinner time to maximize lipid-phase absorption
Take at bedtime co-administered with calcium and iron supplements
Instructions: 'Empty stomach (morning 7-7:30 am) with glass of water. Take meal after 30 minutes'. (Book p909)

Match the drug that inhibits L-thyroxine absorption to its formulation — 1) FeSO4 2) CaCO3 3) Al(OH)3 / Sucralfate … A) Ferrous sulfate iron salt B) Calcium carbonate C) Aluminum hydroxide antacid / mucosal protectant

What is the mortality rate of myxedema coma reported on page 909?

What are the primary trigger factors listed for precipitating myxedema coma?

Albumin colloid indicated; normal saline strictly avoided
Hypertonic saline indicated; hypotonic saline strictly avoided

What is the complete medical treatment regimen for myxedema coma on page 909?
IV Levothyroxine 25 µg daily, Furosemide infusion, Potassium chloride

External active warming with heated blankets, Hydrocortisone, Hypotonic saline

Which autoantibody and HLA allele are characteristically elevated and associated with SREAT on page 909?

Prolactin induces and maintains lactation in a breast already primed by estrogen and progesterone. (Book p941)

Match the regulatory factor to its effect on prolactin secretion — 1) Estrogen 2) Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) 3) Dopamine (PRIF) 4) REM sleep … A) Stimulates prolactin release B) Stimulates prolactin release C) Inhibits prolactin release D) Stimulates prolactin release
Estrogen, TRH, VIP, oxytocin, and REM sleep stimulate prolactin release; dopamine (PRIF) inhibits prolactin release. (Book p941)
Prolactin physiology, molecular forms and regulation
A 26-year-old woman undergoes polysomnography. Prolactin secretion exhibits physiological episodic nocturnal surges correlated with:
Awake state immediately prior to sleep
Prolactin release is physiologically stimulated during REM sleep. (Book p941)

Identify the factor that does NOT stimulate prolactin release:
Dopamine is the primary prolactin inhibitory factor (PRIF); TRH, VIP, and oxytocin stimulate release. (Book p941)

Assess the classification of pituitary adenomas by size: I Microadenomas measure less than or equal to 1 cm. II Macroadenomas measure greater than or equal to 1 cm.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
Pituitary microadenomas are defined as <= 1 cm and macroadenomas as >= 1 cm. (Book p941)
Prolactin physiology, molecular forms and regulation

Match the fasting serum prolactin range to its clinical interpretation — 1) Less than 25 ug/L 2) 25 to 40 ug/L 3) 40 to 100 ug/L 4) Greater than 200 ug/L … A) Normal reference level B) Physiological elevation (sleep, stress, chest wall stimulation) C) Drug-induced or systemic conditions D) Definite prolactinoma (rule out macroprolactin)
Fasting prolactin < 25 is normal, 25-40 is physiological, 40-100 is drug-induced/systemic, > 100 suggests adenoma, and > 200 confirms adenoma. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
What peak physiological prolactin level can be attained during pregnancy?
During pregnancy, prolactin levels rise physiologically and can reach up to 180 ug/L. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
Which clinical entity is characterized by markedly elevated serum prolactin in a completely asymptomatic individual?
Macroprolactin presents with high measured prolactin levels while the patient remains completely asymptomatic. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
A 40-year-old male with a 4 cm giant pituitary macroadenoma has an initial serum prolactin reported as only 45 ug/L. Suspecting the Hook effect, what is the best laboratory corrective step?
Assay the sample using gel filtration chromatography
Switch from chemiluminescence to high-performance liquid chromatography
Perform serial dilution of the serum sample
Precipitate the sample with polyethylene glycol

The hook effect occurs in giant prolactinomas where antigen excess saturates assay antibodies yielding artifactually low prolactin; 1:100 serum dilution reveals the true massive elevation. (Book p942)

A prolactinoma exceeding ___ cm in maximal diameter is categorized as a giant prolactinoma.
A prolactinoma measuring > 4 cm is designated as a giant prolactinoma. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
Which medication is NOT listed as a pharmacological cause of hyperprolactinemia?
Risperidone, metoclopramide, verapamil, opiates, H2 blockers, and alpha-methyldopa cause hyperprolactinemia; levothyroxine suppresses TRH and lowers prolactin. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
A 32-year-old psychiatric patient on haloperidol develops bilateral galactorrhea. D2 receptor blockade in which central nervous system pathway produces her worsening negative symptoms?
Conventional antipsychotics block D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway, worsening negative symptoms, while tuberoinfundibular blockade causes galactorrhea. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
Following discontinuation of an offending pharmacological agent, drug-induced hyperprolactinemia typically demonstrates a good response and normalizes within:
Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia shows a good response and normalizes if the offending drug is stopped for < 72 hours. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
How does primary hypothyroidism induce hyperprolactinemia?
Direct thyroid hormone toxicity impairs hypothalamic dopamine release
Thyroid peroxidase autoantibodies cross-react with D2 receptors
Thyroxine clearance of renal prolactin is drastically diminished
Elevated TRH acts as a prolactin-releasing hormone on lactotrophs
In primary hypothyroidism, compensatory high TRH levels stimulate lactotrophs to release prolactin. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
Which systemic condition is NOT a recognized cause of hyperprolactinemia?
Systemic causes of hyperprolactinemia include primary hypothyroidism, PCOS, CKD, and CLD; primary hyperparathyroidism does not elevate prolactin. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
Assess the characteristics of prolactinomas: I Prolactinomas are the most common pituitary adenoma. II Microprolactinomas occur more frequently than macroprolactinomas.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
Prolactinomas are the most common pituitary adenoma, with microprolactinomas outnumbering macroprolactinomas. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
Metoclopramide induces prominent hyperprolactinemia because, unlike domperidone, it readily crosses the ___ barrier.
Metoclopramide crosses the blood-brain barrier to block hypothalamic/pituitary dopamine receptors. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies

Match the condition to its prolactin diagnostic hallmark — 1) Macroprolactin 2) Hook effect … A) Elevated prolactin levels with completely asymptomatic patient B) Falsely low or mismatched prolactin in presence of a massive tumor
Macroprolactin is high but asymptomatic; the hook effect features a large tumor with discordant prolactin. (Book p942)
Fasting prolactin levels, macroprolactin and hyperprolactinemia etiologies
What is the female-to-male ratio in patients diagnosed with microprolactinoma?
Microprolactinomas show a marked female preponderance with an F:M ratio of 20:1. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
Assess gender patterns in prolactinomas: I Macroprolactinomas have an equal female-to-male ratio of 1:1. II Men with prolactinoma typically present late with compressive mass effects.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
Macroprolactinomas show F:M = 1:1 because men lack menstrual cues and present late with mass effects. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features

Match the patient age group to its prolactinoma clinical pattern — 1) 25 to 45 years 2) Less than 20 years … A) Most common peak age of presentation B) Genetic/syndromic causes (MEN 1, McCune-Albright, Carney complex)
Peak incidence occurs at 25-45 years; presentations under 20 suggest MEON syndromes (MEN 1, McCune-Albright, Carney). (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
In the galactorrhea-amenorrhea complex, hyperprolactinemia suppresses the hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis leading to hypogonadism and ___.
Elevated prolactin inhibits the HPG axis, producing hypogonadism and luteolysis. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
A 29-year-old female presents with secondary amenorrhea, milky breast discharge, and hot flushes. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) demonstrates osteopenia localized predominantly to the:
Hypogonadism in hyperprolactinemia leads to osteopenia and osteoporosis involving predominantly the spine. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
Why does hypogonadism in males with prolactinoma often go unnoticed until late stages?
Testosterone levels are paradoxically maintained by direct adrenal stimulation
Gynaecomastia occurs in 100% of cases providing an immediate visible cue
Men do not experience bone density loss from hypogonadism
Symptoms such as loss of libido and erectile dysfunction are subtle and insidious
In males, hypogonadal symptoms like loss of libido and erectile dysfunction go unnoticed until mass effects emerge. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
What percentage of patients harboring a macroprolactinoma present with visual field defects?
In macroprolactinomas, 35% of patients have visual field defects and 45% have hypopituitarism of other axes. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
In patients with macroprolactinoma, what proportion demonstrate deficiency of other anterior pituitary hormones?
Deficiency of other pituitary hormones is found in 45% of macroprolactinoma patients. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
What is the confirmatory investigation of choice (IOC) for suspected prolactinoma?
Basal serum prolactin measurement at 8 AM
TRH dynamic stimulation testing with serum prolactin curve
The confirmatory investigation of choice is Gadolinium-enhanced MRI (T1 sagittal post-contrast). (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features

Assess the MRI appearance of a pituitary microadenoma: I Pre-contrast features include gland asymmetry, depression of the sellar floor, and infundibular stalk deviation. II Post-contrast imaging shows the whole normal gland enhancing except the hypointense adenoma.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
Pre-contrast microadenoma signs are asymmetry, floor depression, and stalk deviation; with contrast, the normal gland enhances while the adenoma remains hypoenhancing. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features

A 35-year-old male undergoes sellar MRI for bitemporal visual deficits. The coronal post-contrast sequence demonstrates a 2.5 cm heterogeneous mass composed of cystic (non-enhancing) and solid (enhancing) areas. This lesion is a:
Macroprolactinomas characteristically show heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement with non-enhancing cystic areas and enhancing solid components. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features

Match the pituitary imaging finding on MRI to its structural entity — 1) Pre-contrast sellar floor depression and stalk deviation 2) Non-enhancing fluid compartment within macroadenoma 3) Diffuse uniform avid post-contrast enhancement … A) Microadenoma B) Cystic component C) Normal pituitary parenchyma
Microadenomas produce floor depression and stalk deviation; cystic components do not enhance; normal pituitary parenchyma enhances uniformly. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
Which syndrome is NOT part of the MEON genetic complex associated with young-onset prolactinomas (< 20 years)?
Genetic syndromes associated with early prolactinomas include MEN 1, McCune-Albright, and Carney complex; MEN 2 is not linked to pituitary adenomas. (Book p943)
Prolactinoma prevalence, clinical syndrome and MRI features
What is the recommended initial management for a patient diagnosed with an asymptomatic pituitary microadenoma?
Wait and watch with repeat MRI in 3 to 6 months
For asymptomatic microadenoma, management is wait and watch with repeat MRI after 3-6 months; treat only if size increases. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
What is the first-line medical drug of choice (DOC) for symptomatic prolactinomas and macroadenomas?
Cabergoline is the first-line medical drug of choice for prolactinomas. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
Due to its prolonged elimination half-life, cabergoline is typically initiated at a weekly dose of ___ mg twice weekly.
Cabergoline has an increased half-life allowing weekly dosing at 0.25 mg twice weekly. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
Which is NOT a recognized acute adverse effect of dopamine agonists such as cabergoline?
Dopamine agonists cause nausea, vomiting, postural hypotension, and dizziness, rather than severe hypertension. (Book p944)

At cumulative cabergoline doses exceeding 2 g/week, what major cardiopulmonary toxicities can occur?
Cumulative cabergoline > 2 g/week (or high doses) can cause tricuspid regurgitation (valvulopathy) and lung fibrosis. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
What proportion of prolactinoma patients exhibit dopamine agonist resistance to cabergoline?
Dopamine agonist resistance to cabergoline occurs in 20% of patients. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
A 28-year-old woman with a microprolactinoma desires pregnancy. Which dopamine agonist is preferred because of its extensive safety record in gestation?
Bromocriptine is used in pregnancy due to extensive historical safety data. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
If a woman taking bromocriptine during pregnancy intends to breastfeed after delivery, when should the drug be discontinued?
Stop at onset of active labor
Bromocriptine must be stopped 7 days before lactation to allow prolactin-mediated milk production. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma

Match the therapeutic milestone in prolactinoma management to its expected timeframe — 1) Normalization of serum prolactin levels 2) Significant shrinkage of tumor volume … A) Within 4 weeks B) Within 3 to 6 months
Prolactin levels normalize within 4 weeks; tumor shrinkage is achieved by 3-6 months. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
Which condition is NOT an established indication for surgical resection of a prolactinoma?
Persistent visual field defects after 1 month of medical therapy
Asymptomatic microadenoma with serum prolactin of 60 ug/L
Surgical indications include dopamine agonist resistance, persistent visual defects after 1 month of medical Rx, unstable apoplexy, and pregnancy unresponsive to therapy. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
What immunohistochemical proliferation marker is utilized to evaluate extremely rare malignant prolactinomas?
Malignant prolactinoma is very rare and identified by the Ki67 proliferation marker. (Book p944)
Medical, surgical and radiation management of prolactinoma
What modality serves as the last resort for patients with refractory prolactinoma who are unfit for surgical resection?
Gamma Knife stereotactic radiotherapy is the last resort if the patient is unfit for surgery. (Book p944)

Assess the primary goals of prolactinoma therapy: I Normalize serum prolactin and restore gonadal axis function. II Induce tumor shrinkage and normalize anterior pituitary function.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
Goals of therapy are tumor shrinkage by 3-6 months, prolactin normalization by 4 weeks, pituitary function normalization, and restoration of gonadal function. (Book p944)

What proportion of anterior pituitary cells are constituted by growth hormone-secreting somatotrophs?
Somatotrophs account for 50% of the anterior pituitary cell population. (Book p945)

Growth hormone is a single polypeptide chain comprising ___ amino acids.
Growth hormone contains 191 amino acids. (Book p945)

During which physiological sleep stage does the primary nocturnal surge of growth hormone occur?
GH secretion occurs predominantly during deep slow-wave Stage 3 and 4 NREM sleep. (Book p945)

Assess the kinetics of growth hormone measurement: I A single random basal GH level is unreliable due to its pulsatile secretion and short half-life of 5 to 20 minutes. II IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 provide a stable integrated estimation with a half-life of 12 to 15 hours.
Both I and II are false

GH has a short half-life of 5-20 minutes, while IGF-1 bound to IGFBP-3 has a half-life of 12-15 hours, making it the preferred indirect measure. (Book p945)

Which circulating hormone does NOT stimulate hepatic IGF-1 synthesis independently of growth hormone?
Thyroid hormones, insulin, and gonadal hormones independently stimulate IGF-1; cortisol does not. (Book p945)

An 8-year-old obese boy demonstrates accelerated height velocity despite paradoxically suppressed circulating basal GH levels. What biochemical mechanism drives his rapid linear growth?
Hyperinsulinemia downregulates IGFBP-1 and IGFBP-2, increasing free IGF-1 bioavailability
Adipocytes secrete authentic pituitary growth hormone into the systemic circulation
Elevated leptin binds directly to hepatic somatotroph receptors stimulating gigantism
Aromatization of androgens completely suppresses epiphyseal plate maturation
In obesity, increased insulin levels suppress IGFBP-1 and IGFBP-2, increasing free IGF-1 bioavailability and accelerating growth despite low GH. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics

Match the physiological regulator to its effect on growth hormone secretion — 1) Hypoglycemia 2) Ghrelin 3) Somatostatin 4) Obesity … A) Stimulates GH release B) Stimulates GH release C) Inhibits GH release D) Inhibits GH release
Hypoglycemia, GHRH, and ghrelin stimulate GH; somatostatin, ageing, and obesity inhibit GH secretion. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics
What paradoxical hormonal response occurs following TRH administration in patients with acromegaly?
Massive surge of ACTH with acute adrenal crisis
In acromegaly, TRH administration produces a paradoxical rise in growth hormone. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics
A hypocaloric state or severe malnutrition induces peripheral ___ to growth hormone, resulting in high GH but low IGF-1.
Malnutrition and hypocaloric states cause GH resistance with elevated GH and depressed IGF-1. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics
Growth hormone exerts its intracellular actions by binding to cell-surface cytokine receptors that signal via:
Growth hormone signals through the JAK-STAT cytokine receptor pathway. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics
Match the molecule to its circulating half-life — 1) Growth hormone (GH) 2) IGF-1 complexed with IGFBP-3 … A) 5 to 20 minutes B) 12 to 15 hours
GH has a short half-life of 5-20 minutes, while IGF-1 bound to IGFBP-3 circulates with a half-life of 12-15 hours. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics
Assess regulatory dynamics of growth hormone: I Ghrelin acts as a potent physiological stimulus for GH release. II Ageing is associated with progressive decline and inhibition of GH secretion.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
Ghrelin stimulates GH release, while ageing is a recognized inhibitor of GH secretion. (Book p945)
Growth hormone physiology, secretion and obesity dynamics
Match the hormone to its specific action on carbohydrate metabolism — 1) Growth hormone 2) IGF-1 … A) Diabetogenic (induces insulin resistance) B) Anti-diabetogenic (insulin-like action)
On carbohydrates, GH is diabetogenic while IGF-1 is anti-diabetogenic. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
Match the hormone to its action on lipid metabolism — 1) Growth hormone 2) IGF-1 … A) Lipolytic (increases circulating free fatty acids) B) Anti-lipolytic
On lipids, GH is lipolytic increasing free fatty acids, whereas IGF-1 is anti-lipolytic. (Book p946)

What shared metabolic effects are exerted concordantly by both GH and IGF-1?
Bone growth, epiphyseal growth, muscle anabolism, and protein anabolism
Adipose tissue lipolysis and ketone body formation
Hepatic glycogenolysis and systemic insulin resistance
Both GH and IGF-1 stimulate bone growth, epiphyseal growth, muscle anabolism, and protein anabolism. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
Under the BEAMS mnemonic for GH actions independent of IGF-1, which action is NOT included?
Bile acid synthesis and cholesterol excretion
BEAMS represents Bone growth, Epiphyseal growth, Adipose tissue lipolysis, Muscle anabolism, and Salt and water retention; bile acid synthesis is not included. (Book p946)

Why is IGF-1 referred to as a 'wonder molecule' in cellular physiology?
Promotes genetic stability, stress resistance, and regulates telomere shortening
Completely suppresses oncogenic transformation across all cell types
Permits indefinite cellular replication without requirement of ATP
Serves as an irreversible suicide inhibitor of somatostatin receptors
IGF-1 promotes genetic stability, stress resistance, and modulates telomere shortening. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
Assess the feedback loop of IGF-1: I Circulating IGF-1 exerts negative feedback by inhibiting pituitary GH secretion. II IGF-1 stimulates hypothalamic somatostatin release.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
IGF-1 inhibits pituitary GH secretion and stimulates hypothalamic somatostatin release in a classic negative feedback loop. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
A full-term infant with congenital isolated GH deficiency is delivered with normal birth length and weight. What explains normal intrauterine somatic growth in the absence of GH?
Placental lactogen independently activates adult somatotroph receptors
Thyroid hormone completely substitutes for GH in epiphyseal chondrocytes
Intrauterine growth and development is primarily dependent on IGF-2
Maternal GH crosses the placental syncytiotrophoblast in high concentrations
In GH deficiency, height at birth is normal because intrauterine growth depends on IGF-2 (Multiplication Stimulation Activity), which is not GH-dependent. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
IGF-2 was historically designated in experimental physiology as Multiplication Stimulation Activity (___).
IGF-2 is also called Multiplication Stimulation Activity (MSA). (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2

Match the somatomedin to its primary tissue source and physiological regulator — 1) IGF-1 2) IGF-2 … A) Liver tissue; regulated by growth hormone B) Diverse tissues; regulation is not known / GH-independent
IGF-1 is produced by liver tissue under GH regulation; IGF-2 is synthesized in diverse tissues and is independent of GH. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
What cardiovascular action is exerted by IGF-1 on the systemic circulation?
IGF-1 promotes cardiovascular development, cardioprotection, and vasodilation. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
Which central nervous system effect is NOT attributed to IGF-1?
IGF-1 promotes neural development, myelination, amyloid-beta clearance, and anti-inflammatory protection; it does not cause tau accumulation. (Book p946)
Actions of GH versus IGF-1, BEAMS mnemonic and IGF-2
In the BEAMS mnemonic for GH actions, the letter 'S' stands for ___ and water retention.
The 'S' in BEAMS denotes salt and water retention. (Book p946)

A 7-year-old child presents with severe dwarfism and craniofacial disproportion. Biochemical evaluation demonstrates elevated circulating growth hormone with profoundly low levels of IGF-1 and IGFBP-3. This condition is caused by:
Laron dwarfism is caused by an inactivating GHR mutation; GH is elevated but downstream IGF-1 and IGFBP are markedly decreased. (Book p947)

In Laron dwarfism, mutated GHR leads to low IGF-1 and low insulin, which causes an increase in nuclear ___ transcription factors.
Mutated GHR in Laron dwarf leads to decreased IGF-1/insulin and elevated nuclear FoxOs. (Book p947)

Which dynamic provocative investigation serves as the gold standard test to evaluate suspected growth hormone deficiency?
The insulin tolerance test (inducing hypoglycemia) is the gold standard provocative test for GH deficiency. (Book p947)

Match the dynamic provocative GH test to its current clinical status — 1) Insulin tolerance test 2) Glucagon-mediated stimulation 3) Arginine, Clonidine, L-Dopa, GHRH … A) Standard provocative test B) Recognized provocative test C) Other stimulation tests no longer in active use
ITT and glucagon stimulation are active provocative tests; arginine, clonidine, L-dopa, and GHRH are obsolete tests not in routine use. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology
What percentage of acromegaly cases are caused by a primary GH-secreting pituitary adenoma?
Pituitary gland adenomas account for 98% of all cases of acromegaly. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology
What proportion of somatomammotropin adenomas causing acromegaly contain co-expressed lactotrophic cells?
Somatomammotropin adenomas causing acromegaly contain lactotroph cells in 20% of cases. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology

A 48-year-old female presents with signs of acromegaly. Pituitary MRI is completely normal, but abdominal CT reveals a functional neuroendocrine tumor. Ectopic authentic GH secretion is classically caused by:
Ectopic growth hormone secretion is a classical finding in pancreatic islet cell tumors. (Book p947)

Match the ectopic source to the hormone it hypersecretes in acromegaly — 1) Pancreatic islet cell tumor 2) Bronchial carcinoid / small cell lung cancer … A) Direct ectopic GH secretion B) Ectopic GHRH secretion
Pancreatic islet cell tumors classically secrete ectopic GH; bronchial carcinoid and small cell lung cancer secrete ectopic GHRH. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology
Which neoplasm is NOT recognized as a source of ectopic GHRH hypersecretion causing acromegaly?
Ectopic GHRH is secreted by bronchial carcinoid, small cell lung cancer, and medullary carcinoma of the thyroid; adrenal carcinoma does not secrete GHRH. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology
In the hypothalamus, autonomous secretion of GHRH causing acromegaly can arise from a ___.
Hypothalamic hamartomas can secrete excess GHRH causing secondary acromegaly. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology

Assess GH provocative testing in suspected deficiency: I Insulin tolerance test acts by inducing hypoglycemia to provoke counter-regulatory GH release. II Baseline random serum GH alone is sufficient to exclude GH deficiency.
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
ITT triggers counter-regulatory GH secretion via hypoglycemia; random baseline GH is uninformative due to pulsatility. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology
What initial laboratory biomarker provides the most accurate indirect evaluation of integrated 24-hour GH activity?
Serum IGF-1 provides an indirect integrated evaluation of growth hormone activity. (Book p947)
Laron dwarfism, provocative testing and acromegaly etiology

Match the pituitary tumor to its epidemiological characteristics — 1) GH adenoma 2) Prolactinoma … A) Macroadenoma; peak age 35 to 50 years; Males > Females B) Microadenoma; peak age 25 to 40 years; Females > Males
GH adenomas are typically macroadenomas presenting at 35-50 yrs (M>F); prolactinomas are microadenomas presenting at 25-40 yrs (F>M). (Book p948)

If acromegaly or prolactinoma is diagnosed under 20 years of age, which genetic syndrome is NOT part of the MEON differential?
Diagnosis under 20 warrants evaluation for MEN 1, McCune-Albright, and Carney complex; VHL does not cause pituitary adenomas. (Book p948)

Match the GH adenoma histopathological pattern to its clinical prognosis — 1) Sparsely granulated adenoma 2) Densely granulated adenoma … A) Bad prognosis (more aggressive, poorer response to somatostatin analogs) B) Good prognosis
Sparsely granulated GH adenomas have a bad prognosis; densely granulated adenomas have a good prognosis. (Book p948)

What triad of pathological actions is produced by a GH-secreting macroadenoma?
Immune suppression, Cytokine storm, and Carcinoid syndrome
Primary aldosteronism, Salt wasting, and Nephrocalcinosis
Hormonal excess, Stalk effect, and Mass effect
GH macroadenomas cause hormonal excess (high GH), stalk effect (hypopituitarism/hyperprolactinemia), and mass effect (headache/visual deficits/cavernous sinus thrombosis). (Book p948)

Because epiphyseal plate fusion is complete in adults, growth hormone excess produces ___ enlargement affecting the hands and feet.
Epiphyseal fusion is complete in adults, so growth is restricted to acral enlargement of the hands and feet. (Book p948)
Adenoma histopathology, acral features and coarse facies

A 44-year-old male notes that his shoe size and wedding ring diameter have progressively enlarged over the past five years. Internal organomegaly is present. Which visceral organ is spared from acromegalic enlargement?
Acromegaly causes generalized visceromegaly of internal organs, but the brain is spared. (Book p948)

Which feature is NOT part of the classical coarse facies of acromegaly?
Prominent supraorbital ridge and frontal bossing
Coarse facies involves macroglossia, thickened lips/nose, prominent supraorbital ridges, frontal bossing, and prognathism; microglossia is incorrect. (Book p948)

Protrusion of the mandible resulting from excessive mandibular periosteal bone growth in acromegaly is termed:
Protrusion of the mandible in acromegaly is called prognathism. (Book p948)

Assess the mass effects of pituitary macroadenomas: I Suprasellar extension causes chiasmatic compression with visual impairment. II Lateral expansion can compress the cavernous sinus causing thrombosis.

Mass effect causes headaches, visual deficits from chiasm compression, and cavernous sinus thrombosis from lateral extension. (Book p948)

Match the facial manifestation of acromegaly to its anatomical basis — 1) Widely spaced teeth and underbite 2) Prominent forehead bulge 3) Airway obstruction and speech change … A) Prognathism with jaw malocclusion B) Frontal bossing C) Macroglossia
Prognathism causes malocclusion; frontal bossing creates the forehead bulge; macroglossia causes airway compromise and speech changes. (Book p948)
Adenoma histopathology, acral features and coarse facies
Histologically, GH adenomas with dense secretory granules on electron microscopy carry a ___ prognosis.
Densely granulated GH adenomas carry a good prognosis. (Book p948)
Adenoma histopathology, acral features and coarse facies

A 40-year-old male presents with visual field loss and headaches. MRI confirms a 2.5 cm pituitary mass. His serum prolactin is mildly elevated at 45 ug/L despite lack of prolactin staining in the tumor. This finding represents:

Match the subject response on the metyrapone test to its biochemical outcome — 1) Normal individual with intact ACTH axis 2) Patient with pituitary ACTH deficiency … A) Absence of cortisol stimulates ACTH release, causing marked accumulation of 11-deoxycortisol B) Inability to produce ACTH prevents precursor stimulation, resulting in low 11-deoxycortisol

What is the standard daily replacement dose of levothyroxine in secondary hypothyroidism?

For central diabetes insipidus in hypopituitarism, what is the standard desmopressin dosing?

What is the pediatric growth hormone replacement dosing range aimed at achieving > 12 cm height velocity per year?
Children receive 0.18-0.35 mg/kg/week SC targeting > 12 cm height increase/year (adults receive 0.3 mg/day SC). (Book p957)

Which adverse effect is NOT typically associated with growth hormone replacement therapy in children?

A 42-year-old female who underwent bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory Cushing disease two years ago presents with profound generalized hyperpigmentation of her abdominal surgical scar and bitemporal hemianopsia. Sellar MRI reveals an aggressive macroadenoma. What condition is this?
Nelson syndrome occurs post bilateral adrenalectomy due to loss of negative feedback, resulting in massive ACTH elevation, pituitary tumor expansion, and intense hyperpigmentation. (Book p957)

Assess hormone replacement priorities in hypopituitarism: I Corticosteroid replacement must ALWAYS be initiated prior to starting levothyroxine to prevent precipitating adrenal crisis. II If fertility is desired in gonadotroph deficiency, therapy utilizes hCG or GnRH.

Which molecule is an ineffective osmole that freely permeates cell membranes?

Translocational pseudohyponatremia due to systemic absorption of effective solute glycine
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion triggered by surgical pain
Excessive primary renal sodium wasting from acute tubular necrosis
Psychogenic water intoxication during perioperative recovery
Glycine is an effective solute that stays in blood without crossing cell membranes, drawing water from cells and causing translocational hyponatremia. (Book p958)

In translocational hyponatremia from hyperglycemia, for every 100 mg/dL elevation in blood glucose, serum sodium falls by approximately:
For every 100 mg/dL rise in blood glucose, serum sodium falls by 1.6 mEq/L. (Book p958)

Match the hyponatremic state to its serum osmolality profile — 1) True hyponatremia 2) Pseudohyponatremia … A) Low serum sodium with low serum osmolality B) Low serum sodium with normal or increased serum osmolality
True hyponatremia is low sodium with low osmolality; pseudohyponatremia features low sodium with normal or elevated osmolality. (Book p958)

Which solute is NOT listed among the effective solutes causing translocational hyponatremia?
Glucose, mannitol, glycine, and maltose are effective solutes; ethanol is an ineffective osmole that crosses membranes freely. (Book p958)

Assess the osmotic characteristics of solutes: I Effective osmoles draw intracellular water into the vascular compartment, diluting serum sodium. II Ineffective osmoles alter effective tonicity and drive transcellular fluid shifts.

Both I and II are false
Effective osmoles cause water shifts and hyponatremia; ineffective osmoles cross membranes freely without changing effective osmolality. (Book p958)

Match the serum sodium concentration to its severity classification tier — 1) 130 to 135 mEq/L 2) 120 to 129 mEq/L 3) 100 to 119 mEq/L 4) Less than 100 mEq/L … A) Mild hyponatremia B) Moderate hyponatremia C) Severe hyponatremia D) Very severe hyponatremia
130-135 is mild, 120-129 is moderate, 100-119 is severe, and < 100 is very severe hyponatremia. (Book p959)

Which obsolete laboratory methodology artifacts produce artifactual pseudohyponatremia due to volume displacement?

At what serum osmolality threshold is endogenous ADH (vasopressin) release triggered?
ADH secretion is activated when serum osmolality exceeds 280 mmol/kg. (Book p959)

Increased osmolality triggers ADH (> 280) and thirst (> 290), so elevated sodium is not normally seen. (Book p959)

Vasopressin is synthesized in the hypothalamus within the supra-optic and ___ nuclei.

What specialized hypothalamic neuronal cell population synthesizes pro-vasopressin?
Magnocellular neurons produce the pro-vasopressin precursor. (Book p959)

Match the pro-vasopressin cleavage fragment to its role — 1) ADH (Vasopressin) 2) Neurophysin 3) Copeptin … A) Active antidiuretic hormone stored in posterior pituitary B) Carrier protein during axonal transport C) Equimolar C-terminal cleavage marker
Pro-vasopressin is cleaved into ADH, neurophysin, and copeptin at the pituitary stalk. (Book p959)

Which stimulus is the MOST important physiological driver for ADH release?
Osmotic stimulus (at 280 mOsm/kg) is the most important physiological trigger for ADH release. (Book p959)

Match the vasopressin receptor subtype to its intracellular secondary messenger pathway — 1) V1 and V3 receptors 2) V2 receptor … A) IP3 / DAG pathway B) cAMP pathway

Which vasopressin receptor located on anterior pituitary corticotrophs stimulates ACTH release?

A 19-year-old male with mild von Willebrand disease is administered desmopressin (DDAVP) prior to dental extraction. Desmopressin acts on which endothelial receptor to stimulate vWF release?

Assess the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (THAL): I THAL actively reabsorbs solutes (Na+ and Cl-) while remaining impermeable to water. II THAL delivers hypertonic fluid with osmolality exceeding 800 mOsm/kg into the distal tubule.

Counter-current exchange is maintained by medullary interstitium, urea gradient, and the vasa recta; ADH acts only when interstitial osmolality is maintained. (Book p960)

Match the nephron segment to its role in urine concentration — 1) Descending loop of Henle 2) Thick ascending loop of Henle (THAL) 3) Cortical collecting duct (under ADH) … A) Counter-current multiplier reabsorbing water and raising osmolality 4-fold B) Active solute (Na+/Cl-) reabsorption creating a diluting segment C) ADH-mediated water reabsorption producing concentrated urine (800–900 mOsm/kg)
Descending limb multiplies osmolality 4-fold; THAL reabsorbs solutes; collecting duct concentrates urine under ADH to 800-900 mOsm/kg. (Book p960)

Medullary interstitial hypertonicity is preserved by urea recycling, which is maintained by the hairpin capillary loops of the ___.
The vasa recta maintain the medullary urea gradient and interstitial osmolality. (Book p960)

Under maximal ADH stimulation, the collecting duct concentrates tubular urine to an osmolality of:
ADH action in the collecting duct concentrates urine to 800-900 mOsm/kg. (Book p960)

Under what condition does ADH effectively produce antidiuresis in the collecting ducts?
When glomerular filtration rate is reduced by 50%

When the hypertonic medullary interstitial osmolality is maintained
ADH acts to concentrate urine only when the medullary interstitial osmolality is maintained. (Book p960)

On which membrane surface of the cortical collecting duct principal cell does ADH bind to the V2 receptor?

Match the signaling cascade step of ADH in the collecting duct to its mediator — 1) Receptor binding on basolateral membrane 2) Secondary messenger activation 3) Luminal water channel expression … A) V2 receptor B) Adenylyl cyclase - cAMP - Protein Kinase A pathway C) Exocytosis of stored aquaporin-2 into apical membrane
ADH binds basolateral V2, stimulates cAMP and Protein Kinase A, and promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. (Book p961)

Match the aquaporin subtype to its nephron localization and physiological regulation — 1) Aquaporin 1 2) Aquaporin 2 3) Aquaporin 3 and 4 … A) Proximal convoluted tubule (ADH-independent obligatory water reabsorption) B) Luminal membrane of cortical collecting duct (ADH-dependent facultative water reabsorption) C) Basolateral membrane of cortical collecting duct (constitutive water exit)
AQP1 mediates obligatory PCT water reabsorption; AQP2 mediates facultative ADH-dependent apical reabsorption; AQP3/4 mediate basolateral exit. (Book p961)

Water reabsorption mediated by aquaporin-1 in the proximal convoluted tubule is termed ___ water reabsorption.
AQP1 in the PCT mediates obligatory water reabsorption independent of ADH. (Book p961)
Collecting duct aquaporins, cellular mechanism and water homeostasis
Water reabsorption governed by aquaporin-2 insertion into the luminal membrane of collecting ducts is termed ___ water reabsorption.
AQP2 in the CCD mediates facultative water reabsorption dependent on ADH. (Book p961)
Collecting duct aquaporins, cellular mechanism and water homeostasis

A 24-year-old male with X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus has an inactivating mutation in the AVPR2 gene. Despite high circulating ADH, he excretes 10 liters of dilute urine daily. What step in water reabsorption is defective?
Failure of cAMP-dependent exocytosis of aquaporin-2 into the apical luminal membrane
Loss of constitutive basolateral aquaporin-3 and aquaporin-4 water channels
Complete downregulation of proximal tubular aquaporin-1 channels
Direct inhibition of thick ascending limb solute reabsorption
Without functional V2 receptors, cAMP is not generated, preventing the apical expression of aquaporin-2 and free water reabsorption. (Book p961)

Which is NOT one of the three physiological reasons why a healthy person does not normally develop hyponatremia?
Circulating ADH is negligible in the baseline resting state
Aldosterone stimulates rapid continuous water excretion in the distal tubule
Only solute is reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb of Henle (THAL)
A healthy person resists hyponatremia because PCT reabsorption is iso-osmotic, THAL reabsorbs only solute, and resting ADH is negligible; aldosterone does not excrete water. (Book p961)

Through which aquaporin channels does reabsorbed free water exit the principal cell across the basolateral membrane into the renal interstitium?
Water exits across the basolateral membrane into the interstitium via aquaporin 3 and 4. (Book p961)
Collecting duct aquaporins, cellular mechanism and water homeostasis
Following maximal ADH-driven free water reabsorption across luminal aquaporin-2 channels, urine osmolality reaches:
Free water reabsorption concentrates urine up to 800-900 mOsm/kg. (Book p961)

Assess aquaporin physiology: I Aquaporin-1 is ADH-independent and drives obligatory water reabsorption. II Aquaporin-2 expression on the apical membrane is strictly ADH-dependent.

Both I and II are true
AQP1 is ADH-independent (obligatory); AQP2 is ADH-dependent (facultative). (Book p961)

Match the nephron water handling characteristic to its anatomical segment — 1) Iso-osmotic reabsorption of fluid 2) Pure solute reabsorption without water 3) ADH-regulated water permeability … A) Proximal convoluted tubule B) Thick ascending limb of Henle (THAL) C) Cortical collecting duct
PCT is iso-osmotic; THAL reabsorbs only solute; collecting duct has ADH-regulated water permeability. (Book p961)

What is the baseline activity of antidiuretic hormone in a healthy, well-hydrated resting individual?
In the resting baseline state, circulating ADH is negligible, preventing water retention and hyponatremia. (Book p961)

Stop the test and move on to the urine osmolality step
