What are the minimal free peritoneal fluid volumes required sequentially for ultrasonographic detection, clinical shifting dullness, and eliciting a fluid thrill?
Peritoneal fluid detection thresholds are: <100 mL on ultrasonography (USG), 500 mL on clinical examination for shifting dullness, and 1.5 L for elicitation of a fluid thrill. (Book p1007)
By definition in decompensated chronic liver disease, refractory ascites refers to peritoneal fluid accumulation that exhibits:
Secondary bacterial infection following diagnostic paracentesis
Development of acute intrinsic tubular necrosis during diuretics
No therapeutic response to maximum doses of diuretic medications
Persistent recurrence despite weekly large-volume paracenteses
Refractory ascites is defined as peritoneal fluid accumulation that shows no response to maximum doses of diuretics (spironolactone up to 400 mg/day plus furosemide up to 160 mg/day). (Book p1007)
Following large-volume paracentesis (LVP) for tense ascites, which adjunctive intervention should routinely be administered to preserve effective circulating volume?
Large volume paracentesis (LVP) should be followed by intravenous albumin replacement to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, noted in text as expensive. (Book p1007)
Match each diagnostic modality for ascitic fluid detection with its corresponding minimum fluid threshold: 1. Ultrasonography (USG) 2. Shifting dullness 3. Fluid thrill
Ultrasonography detects free fluid at volumes <100 mL; clinical shifting dullness requires 500 mL; elicitation of a fluid thrill requires 1.5 L of peritoneal fluid. (Book p1007)

A 52-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presents with massive abdominal distension. On examination, a prominent fluid thrill is elicited. Based on physical diagnostic thresholds, what is the minimum volume of free ascitic fluid present?
Around 500 to 750 mL of peritoneal fluid
Strictly less than 100 mL of fluid
At least 1.5 L of free peritoneal fluid
A fluid thrill requires at least 1.5 L of free peritoneal fluid to be elicited clinically. Shifting dullness requires 500 mL, whereas USG can detect volumes <100 mL. (Book p1007)
What is the most common causative organism and bacterial class responsible for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
The primary cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is Gram-negative bacteria, most commonly Escherichia coli. (Book p1007)

In the diagnostic criteria for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), the ascitic fluid analysis must demonstrate a total WBC count of at least ________ or a polymorphonuclear (PMN) neutrophil count of at least ________.
Diagnostic criteria for SBP require: (1) Ascitic fluid WBC ≥500 cells/mL OR PMNs ≥250 cells/mL, (2) positive ascitic fluid culture, and (3) no surgically treatable source of infection. (Book p1007)
Which of the following is NOT one of the three established diagnostic criteria for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
Positive monobacterial culture from ascitic fluid inoculation
Absence of any surgically treatable intra-abdominal infection source
Ascitic fluid serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) less than 1.1 g/dL
Ascitic fluid WBC count ≥500 cells/mL or PMN count ≥250 cells/mL

The 3 criteria for SBP are: (1) ascitic fluid WBC ≥500 cells/mL OR PMNs ≥250 cells/mL, (2) positive culture, and (3) absence of a surgically treatable source of infection. SAAG <1.1 g/dL is not a criterion (cirrhotic ascites has high SAAG ≥1.1). (Book p1007)

A 58-year-old cirrhotic patient presents with fever and diffuse abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis reveals an ascitic fluid PMN count of 380 cells/mL (elevated). Ascitic fluid cultures show no bacterial growth at 48 hours, and surgical abdominal sources are ruled out. This entity represents:
Culture-negative neutrocytic ascites (CNNA): criteria 1 and 3 present, 2 absent
Monobacterial non-neutrocytic ascites (MNNA): criteria 2 and 3 present, 1 absent
Secondary bacterial peritonitis requiring emergent exploratory laparotomy
Pseudochylous ascites secondary to thoracic duct obstruction

Culture Negative Neutrocytic Ascites (CNNA) is defined by presence of criteria 1 (PMN ≥250) and 3 (no surgical source), with absence of criterion 2 (culture negative). It represents a milder degree of SBP seen in patients with minimal immunity and good opsonization. (Book p1007)
Match each variant of SBP with its criteria profile and characteristic microbiology: 1. Culture Negative Neutrocytic Ascites (CNNA) 2. Monobacterial Non-Neutrocytic Ascites (MNNA)
1: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent); 2: Criteria 1+2 present (3 absent), Polymicrobial > Monomicrobial
1: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent); 2: Criteria 2+3 present (1 absent), Gram-positive > Gram-negative
1: Criteria 2+3 present (1 absent); 2: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent), Gram-negative > Gram-positive
1: Criteria 1+2 present (3 absent); 2: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent), Anaerobic > Aerobic

CNNA has criteria 1+3 present (PMN elevated, no surgical source) and criterion 2 absent (culture negative). MNNA has criteria 2+3 present (culture positive, no surgical source) and criterion 1 absent (PMN <250/mL), with Gram-positive organisms predominating over Gram-negative. (Book p1007)
True or False: Differentials of SBP criteria such as CNNA and MNNA represent milder degrees of SBP observed in patients possessing minimal host immunity combined with good opsonization capacity.
False: Severe fulminant peritonitis observed only in patients lacking opsonization
False: Iatrogenic contamination artifacts occurring strictly after repeated taps
False: Secondary surgical catastrophes requiring emergency surgical peritoneal toilet
True: Milder SBP spectrum seen with minimal immunity and good opsonization
As documented under differentials of criteria, CNNA and MNNA represent a milder degree of SBP seen in patients with minimal immunity plus good opsonization (+). (Book p1007)
In monobacterial non-neutrocytic ascites (MNNA), how does the microbiological profile characteristically contrast with classic SBP?
Fungal hyphae such as Candida albicans predominate over bacterial pathogens
Gram-positive organisms are isolated more frequently than Gram-negative organisms
Polymicrobial anaerobic enteric flora predominate over single aerobes
Strict anaerobes such as Clostridium species account for nearly all isolates
In MNNA, isolated pathogens characteristically show Gram-positive organisms > Gram-negative organisms, contrasting with classic SBP where Gram-negative E. coli predominates. (Book p1007)
In a patient with ascites presenting with acute peritonitis, which triad of ascitic fluid findings strongly points to secondary surgical peritonitis rather than spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
Protein >3 g/dL, glucose >120 mg/dL, and absence of peritoneal neutrophils
Protein <0.5 g/dL, glucose <10 mg/dL, and elevated amylase without LDH
Protein >1 g/dL, glucose <50 mg/dL, and markedly elevated LDH (LDH ↑↑)
Protein <1 g/dL, glucose >100 mg/dL, and normal peritoneal LDH level
As noted in the book, surgical peritonitis features ascitic protein >1 g/dL, sugar (glucose) <50 mg/dL, and markedly elevated LDH (LDH ↑↑). (Book p1007)
What is the first-line empirical antibiotic regimen recommended for treating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), CNNA, and MNNA?
Inj Vancomycin 1 g IV BD plus Metronidazole for 7 days
Inj Cefotaxime 2 g IV TDS for 5 days
Inj Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OD for 14 days
Inj Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV BD for 10 days
The drug and regimen of choice for SBP, CNNA, and MNNA is Inj Cefotaxime 2 g IV TDS for 5 days (printed in text with degraded numeral 'ag IV TDS x 5days'). (Book p1007)
A 56-year-old cirrhotic patient recovers successfully from an acute episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. What secondary antibiotic prophylaxis should be instituted upon discharge?
Tab Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 6 months
Tab Rifaximin 550 mg BD lifelong only
Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life
Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg BD for 7 days
Prophylaxis with Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life is indicated for: prior SBP, Child-Pugh score ≥9, or ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL in cirrhosis. (Book p1007)
In a patient with cirrhosis and ascites presenting with acute upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding, the recommended prophylactic antibiotic regimen to prevent SBP is Tab Norfloxacin ________.
For upper GI bleed in cirrhosis, the specific prophylaxis is Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg BD for 7 days. (Book p1007)

Match each clinical scenario with its recommended Norfloxacin prophylactic regimen: 1. Patient with history of prior SBP 2. Cirrhotic patient with Child's score ≥9 or ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL 3. Cirrhotic patient presenting with acute UGI bleed
1: 400 mg OD for life; 2: 400 mg OD for life; 3: 400 mg BD for 7 days
1: 400 mg BD for 7 days; 2: 400 mg BD for 7 days; 3: 400 mg OD for life
1: 400 mg OD for life; 2: 400 mg BD for 7 days; 3: 400 mg OD for life
1: 400 mg BD for 14 days; 2: 400 mg OD for life; 3: 400 mg BD for life

Lifelong prophylaxis (Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life) is indicated for prior SBP, Child's score ≥9, and ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL. Acute UGI bleed warrants short-term prophylaxis: Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg BD for 7 days. (Book p1007)
What specific clinical staging and laboratory cutoffs mandate secondary norfloxacin prophylaxis (400 mg OD lifelong) in cirrhotic ascites?
Child's score ≥9 and ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL
Child's score ≥10 and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL
Child's score ≥7 and ascitic fluid protein <1.0 g/dL
Child's score ≥12 and ascitic fluid protein <0.5 g/dL
Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life is indicated when the Child-Pugh score is ≥9 or the ascitic fluid protein is <1.5 g/dL in a cirrhotic patient. (Book p1007)
What distinguishes diuretic-resistant ascites from diuretic-intractable ascites in patients with chronic liver disease?
Resistant has high SAAG with low protein; intractable has low SAAG with high protein
Resistant fails to respond to full doses; intractable cannot tolerate full doses due to complications
Resistant is caused by portal vein thrombosis; intractable is caused by hepatic vein thrombosis
Resistant responds only to loop diuretics; intractable responds only to aldosterone antagonists

Diuretic-resistant ascites shows no response to full-dose diuretics, whereas diuretic-intractable ascites cannot receive full-dose diuretics due to development of diuretic-induced complications. (Book p1008)

Diuretic-resistant ascites is characterized by lack of response to full-dose diuretics, defined in the notes as spironolactone (printed as 40 mg / intended full dose 400 mg) combined with furosemide (Lasix) ________.
In diuretic-resistant ascites, there is no response to full-dose diuretics: spironolactone (printed as 40 mg, full dose 400 mg) plus 160 mg lasix. (Book p1008)
Untreated or worsening diuretic-resistant ascites typically progresses directly to which life-threatening complication?
Diuretic resistant ascites is noted as: 'Progresses to HRS'. (Book p1008)
Match each subtype of refractory ascites with its clinical definition and features: 1. Diuretic Resistant Ascites 2. Diuretic Intractable Ascites
1: Inability to tolerate full doses due to complications like hypo/hyperkalemia or renal failure; 2: Lack of response to full doses (Lasix 160 mg + spironolactone), progresses to HRS
1: Responsive only to salt restriction alone without medications; 2: Complete resolution following a single diagnostic paracentesis
1: Caused by bacterial translocation into the ascitic space; 2: Caused by lymphatic rupture into the peritoneal space
1: Lack of response to full doses (Lasix 160 mg + spironolactone), progresses to HRS; 2: Inability to tolerate full doses due to complications like hypo/hyperkalemia or renal failure

Diuretic-intractable ascites occurs when full diuretic doses cannot be administered due to medical complications. Which of the following is NOT an example of such a diuretic complication?
Examples given for diuretic-intractable ascites complications are hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, and renal failure. (Book p1008)
What definitive interventional radiological procedure is indicated for the management of refractory ascites?
Under refractory ascites, the designated management is TIPSS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt). (Book p1008)
In the pathogenesis of hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), what is the initial vascular event that subsequently triggers severe compensatory neurohumoral activation?
Splanchnic vasodilation is the primary event, which stimulates ADH, SNS, and RAAS pathways, resulting in renal vasoconstriction. (Book p1008)
In hepatorenal syndrome, splanchnic vasodilation stimulates three primary neurohormonal systems that mediate renal vasoconstriction: ________, ________, and ________.
Splanchnic vasodilation stimulates ADH (antidiuretic hormone), SNS (sympathetic nervous system), and RAAS (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system). (Book p1008)
Match each hepatorenal syndrome subtype with its progression pathway and clinical outcome: 1. HRS-AKI (Acute Kidney Injury) 2. HRS-NAKI (Non-AKI)
1: Develops over time in the setting of chronic refractory ascites; 2: Mediated by acute renal vasoconstriction and pre-renal failure, has terrible prognosis with 100% mortality without transplant
1: Resolves spontaneously without medical therapy; 2: Characterized by massive glomerular basement membrane immune deposits
1: Exclusively caused by direct nephrotoxicity of paracetamol; 2: Caused by bacterial invasion of the renal parenchyma
1: Mediated by acute renal vasoconstriction and pre-renal failure, has terrible prognosis with 100% mortality without transplant; 2: Develops over time in the setting of chronic refractory ascites

HRS-AKI arises from severe renal vasoconstriction and pre-renal failure, carrying a terrible prognosis and 100% mortality without liver transplant. HRS-NAKI develops over time in association with refractory ascites. (Book p1008)
True or False: In patients who develop HRS-AKI, the prognosis is universally dismal, with 100% mortality expected in the absence of liver transplantation.
False: Fully cured in over 90% of cases by oral loop diuretics alone
False: Fatal only when accompanied by overt hepatic encephalopathy grade 4
True: Terrible prognosis with 100% mortality without liver transplantation
False: Benign self-limiting condition with less than 5% mortality on saline hydration
As emphasized in the text, HRS-AKI has a 'terrible prognosis' and '100% mortality without transplant'. (Book p1008)
Hepatorenal syndrome is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion established in a patient who must have which foundational underlying clinical triad?
Hepatomegaly, normal portal pressures, and pleural effusion
Acute viral hepatitis, splenomegaly, and macroscopic hematuria
Biliary atresia, normal spleen size, and lower limb edema
HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with the triad of Cirrhosis, PHTN, and Ascites. (Book p1008)
To confirm hepatorenal syndrome, pre-renal and intra-renal etiologies must be systematically excluded. Which of the following is NOT an intra-renal condition listed in the diagnostic workup?
Structural renal parenchymal abnormalities on USG
Severe hypoalbuminemia (marked reduction in serum albumin)

Marked hypoalbuminemia (↓↓ S. albumin) is classified under pre-renal causes to rule out, along with diuretic excess and UGI bleed. Proteinuria and hematuria are intra-renal markers, and USG rules out structural abnormality. (Book p1008)

A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis, ascites, and portal hypertension develops a serum creatinine rise to 2.8 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no proteinuria or hematuria, renal ultrasonography shows normal kidney morphology, there is no history of shock or nephrotoxic drug ingestion, and diuretic withdrawal with volume expansion does not reverse the renal dysfunction. This confirms:
Primary bilateral polycystic kidney disease complicated by infected renal cysts
Hepatorenal syndrome diagnosed after ruling out pre-renal, intra-renal, and structural etiologies
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis with persistent nephrotic proteinuria
Contrast-induced acute tubular necrosis responding rapidly to furosemide diuresis

HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with cirrhosis, PHTN, and ascites after ruling out pre-renal failure (diuretic excess, UGI bleed, hypoalbuminemia), intra-renal disease (proteinuria, hematuria), structural abnormalities on USG, shock, and nephrotoxic drugs (diuretics, NSAIDs). (Book p1008)
Match the diagnostic exclusion category with the specific factors that must be ruled out when evaluating for HRS: 1. Pre-renal etiologies 2. Intra-renal etiologies 3. Nephrotoxic exposures
1: Structural abnormalities on USG; 2: NSAIDs; 3: Marked hypoalbuminemia and hematuria
1: Diuretics and NSAIDs; 2: Diuretic excess; 3: Proteinuria and hematuria
1: Diuretic excess, marked hypoalbuminemia, and UGI bleed; 2: Proteinuria and hematuria; 3: Diuretics and NSAIDs
1: Proteinuria and hematuria; 2: Diuretic excess and UGI bleed; 3: Hypoalbuminemia and shock

Pre-renal factors to rule out are diuretic excess, severe hypoalbuminemia (↓↓ S. albumin), and UGI bleed; intra-renal factors are proteinuria and hematuria; nephrotoxic drugs include diuretics and NSAIDs. (Book p1008)
What is the definitive and curative management for hepatorenal syndrome (HRS)?
Liver transplantation is the definitive management for hepatorenal syndrome. (Book p1009)
What is the recommended dosing and titration schedule for intravenous terlipressin used to reverse splanchnic vasodilation prior to liver transplantation in HRS?
0.5 mg IV continuous infusion doubling every 24 hours (max 6 mg/day)
4 mg IV every 8 hours with rapid taper after 48 hours (max 16 mg/day)
1 mg IV every 4–6 hours, titrating up to 2 mg IV every 4–6 hours (max 12 mg/day)
2 mg IV stat followed by 1 mg IV every 12 hours (maximum 4 mg/day)
Terlipressin is administered as 1 mg IV every 4-6 hours, titrated up to 2 mg IV every 4-6 hours, with a maximum dose of 12 mg/day. (Book p1009)
Which medical regimens are used to counter splanchnic vasodilation and serve as a pharmacological bridge to liver transplantation in HRS?
Dopamine infusion, oral furosemide, and intravenous loop diuretics
Nitroprusside, oral hydralazine, and intravenous labetalol
Terlipressin, subcutaneous Octreotide plus oral Midodrine, or Norepinephrine
Medical therapy to prevent splanchnic vasodilation until transplant includes: Terlipressin, subcutaneous Octreotide + oral Midodrine (oral alpha agonist), or Norepinephrine. (Book p1009)
In the medical management of hepatorenal syndrome, midodrine is administered as an ________ and functions pharmacologically as an ________.
Midodrine is an oral alpha-agonist (oral α agonist) used in combination with subcutaneous octreotide. (Book p1009)

A 49-year-old patient with decompensated cirrhosis and type 1 hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) is listed for urgent orthotopic liver transplantation. While awaiting donor organ availability, what medical regimen should be instituted immediately to reverse splanchnic vasodilation?
Aggressive volume resuscitation with 5% dextrose and forced furosemide diuresis
Empirical high-dose oral spironolactone 400 mg daily with potassium chloride
Bilateral renal denervation via catheter-based radiofrequency ablation
Terlipressin 1 mg IV Q4-6H titrated up to 2 mg Q4-6H (or octreotide plus midodrine)

Medical management to counter splanchnic vasodilation until liver transplant includes terlipressin (1 mg IV Q4-6h up to 2 mg Q4-6h, max 12 mg/d), octreotide plus midodrine, or norepinephrine. (Book p1009)
Match each pharmacological agent used in hepatorenal syndrome with its specific administration detail: 1. Terlipressin 2. Midodrine 3. Octreotide
1: 1 mg IV Q4-6h titrating to 2 mg IV Q4-6h (max 12 mg/d); 2: Oral alpha agonist; 3: Subcutaneous (S/C) administration
1: Subcutaneous administration; 2: 1 mg IV Q4-6h (max 12 mg/d); 3: Oral alpha agonist
1: Oral alpha agonist; 2: Subcutaneous administration; 3: 1 mg IV Q4-6h titrating to 2 mg
1: 1 mg IV Q4-6h; 2: Subcutaneous administration; 3: Oral alpha agonist
Terlipressin is given IV 1 mg Q4-6h up to 2 mg Q4-6h (max 12 mg/d); midodrine is an oral alpha agonist; octreotide is given subcutaneously (S/C) in combination with midodrine. (Book p1009)
In hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS), chronic liver disease leads to excessive pulmonary production of which potent gaseous vasodilator?
Chronic liver disease stimulates excess nitric oxide (NO) production, resulting in intrapulmonary capillary dilatation. (Book p1009)
In hepatopulmonary syndrome, what is the extent of intrapulmonary capillary dilatation compared to normal pulmonary capillary diameter?
Pulmonary capillary diameter expands dramatically from normal 8-15 µm up to 50-500 µm in HPS. (Book p1009)
The marked intrapulmonary capillary dilatation in HPS leads to decreased oxygenation and arteriovenous shunts, causing hypoxia/hypoxemia via ________.
The combination of decreased oxygenation and AV shunts causes hypoxia/hypoxemia through ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch. (Book p1009)
Platypnea is defined as dyspnea provoked by standing upright. What are the two physiological factors identified in the text that produce platypnea in HPS?
Pulmonary capillary constriction and diaphragm descent
Increased AV shunt activation and diaphragm moving up
Decreased bronchial caliber and left ventricular failure
Carotid sinus denervation and alveolar collapse
Platypnea is dyspnea on standing due to: (1) ↑ AV shunt activation and (2) diaphragm moves up. (Book p1009)
Orthodeoxia is a hallmark clinical sign of hepatopulmonary syndrome defined by which specific arterial oxygen saturation change on standing?
Orthodeoxia is explicitly defined as a drop of SpO2 > 3% on standing. (Book p1009)
What is the investigation of choice (IOC) to demonstrate intrapulmonary vascular dilatations in hepatopulmonary syndrome?
Invasive right heart catheterization with pulmonary angiography
The investigation of choice (IOC) for HPS is Bubble Echocardiography / Contrast Transthoracic Echocardiography. (Book p1009)
What is the definitive curative treatment for hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS)?
The definitive treatment for HPS is liver transplantation. (Book p1009)

A 50-year-old woman with cirrhosis complains of progressive shortness of breath when sitting up, improving when lying flat. Pulse oximetry reveals SpO2 of 96% supine, dropping to 91% on standing. Bubble echocardiography is positive for intrapulmonary shunting. What is the diagnosis and definitive management?
Large hepatic hydrothorax; Tube thoracostomy and chemical pleurodesis
Portopulmonary hypertension; Sildenafil and bosentan therapy

The triad of chronic liver disease, platypnea-orthodeoxia (drop in SpO2 > 3% on standing), and positive bubble echocardiography confirms hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS), for which the definitive treatment is liver transplantation. (Book p1009)

Statement I is true ('Glutamate: ↓ in blood, ↑ in CSF'). Statement II is false because HE features Alzheimer type-2 astrocytes; Alzheimer type-1 cells occur in PMLE. (Book p1010)

A 50-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites develops severe confusion. Serum ammonia is markedly elevated. In the cerebral cortex, excessive glutamine accumulation within astrocytes leads to osmotic swelling and triggers secondary neuronal injury via which receptor?
Ammonia and glutamine toxicity leads to 'NMDA -> Secondary Neuronal damage'. (Book p1010)

u: Newborn period = first 4 weeks: 1st week is early, next 3 weeks are late. Birth weight categories: LBW < 2.5 kg, VLBW < 1.5 kg, ELBW < 1 kg. (Book p2)
SGA can be constitutional (normal) or pathological (IUGR). Identification points of IUGR: loose skin folds, skin peeling, thin umbilical cord. (Book p2)

Symmetrical: maternal etiology (uteroplacental insufficiency), onset 2nd-3rd trimester, brain-sparing present (normal head, small body), good outcome. Asymmetrical: fetal etiology (trisomy, organ anomalies), onset 1st trimester, no brain-sparing (uniformly small), poor outcome. (Book p2)

New AIMS intrauterine growth curves: LGA = upper percentile curve, SGA = lower percentile curve; male and female charts are different. Ponderal index (PI) = weight (g) / [length (cm)] cubed x 100: >2 = symmetrical IUGR, <2 = asymmetrical IUGR. (Book p2)
Preterm < 37 wks, term 37-41 wks, post-term 42 wks onwards. Antenatal assessment of gestation is based on mother's LMP and 1st trimester ultrasound scan. (Book p3)

Expanded New Ballard Score (ENBS) is postnatal, based on neuromuscular maturity + physical maturity. Total range -10 to +50 (-10 = 20 wks, +50 = 44 wks), accuracy +/-1 week. Physical maturity: each sign scored -1 to +5, and scores map to gestation (0 = 24 wks, 10 = 28 wks, 30 = 36 wks, 45 = 42 wks). (Book p3)

Preterm: extended posture, square window negative, no arm recoil, scarf sign positive (elbow crosses midline), obtuse popliteal angle, heel reaches ear, breast buds <5 mm, labia minora visible, empty scrotum, abundant lanugo, slow pinna recoil. Term: the opposite of all; testes fully descended by 36 wks. (Book p4)

Organ immaturity causes RDS (surfactant deficiency), NEC, IVH (germinal matrix bleeding into ventricles) and kernicterus (bilirubin crosses immature BBB -> brain damage). Decreased nutrient reserve causes hypoglycemia, anemia (low iron stores) and hypothermia. (Book p4)

APGAR = Activity, Pulse, Grimace, Appearance, Respiratory effort; each 0-2, total 0-10. Timing: 1 min after birth, followed by repeats. Normal 7-10/10, low <7/10. Grimace is elicited by irritating nasal mucosa with a nasogastric tube. Normal newborn heart rate: 120-160/min. (Book p4-5)

Heart rate >100/min (term 100-160/min, preterm 120-180/min); respiratory rate 40-60/min; CRT <= 3 sec (checked by pressing ball of finger over sternum: blanching of skin, then skin becomes pink); temperature 36.5-37.5 C. (Book p5)

Erythema toxicum: papulosaquamous lesions, eosinophils, onset >24 hr. Pustular melanosis: pustules + hyperpigmented patches, neutrophils, onset <24 hr. Epithelial inclusion cyst: keratin deposits (milia); palate = Epstein pearls, gum = Bohn's nodules. Mongolian spots: melanocytes in dermis, arrest in neural-crest migration. Salmon patch/stork bite/birthmark: forehead or nape of neck, vascular ectasia. (Book p5)

Breast engorgement and witch's milk (milk-like nipple discharge); bleeding per vagina in females (uterine shedding after sudden withdrawal of maternal hormones); small subconjunctival/retinal hemorrhage (stress of normal delivery); hymenal skin tags (female); physiological phimosis (male). None require treatment - only reassurance. (Book p6)

Caput succedaneum: more common; diffuse swelling; superficial; scalp. D/t prolonged labour -> venous congestion -> fluid leakage. Content: fluid. Onset: at birth/soon after. Recovery: 2-3 days. No associations. (Book p6)

Cephalohematoma: localised, deep, sub-periosteal; d/t trauma to skull in instrumental delivery; blood; slowly increases after 12-24 hr; recovery 3-8 wks; associated with linear skull fractures and jaundice (heme breakdown). Subgaleal hemorrhage: below galea aponeurotica; vacuum extraction -> separation of scalp layers -> blood accumulation; fluctuant; appears soon after birth; most severe - shock, pallor, jaundice. (Book p6)
Priority of management in newborn: 1st Respiration (crying after birth), 2nd Temperature, 3rd Circulation. (Book p7)

Golden minute (1 min): initial action = temperature, airway, circulation (if no cry). Assess HR + respiratory effort. HR<100 -> PPV (30 sec). HR<60 -> chest compressions with ventilation (30 sec). No response -> adrenaline. Still no response -> consider volume expansion (NS 10 ml/kg; only if documented significant maternal ante-partum blood loss). Total duration 20 min; if no response -> declare death. (Book p7)

4 pre-birth questions to predict and plan for outcome of delivery: 1. Term gestation? 2. Clear amniotic fluid? 3. Risk factors present (maternal or fetal)? 4. Umbilical cord management plan: delay cord clamping 30-60 sec (only if baby cried after birth); cord blood for newborn screening token. (Book p7)

1. Temperature: keep baby under warmer. 2. Breathing: gentle tactile stimulation (rubbing back with cotton towel, flicking soles). 3. Airway: slight neck extension (sniffing position) with towel under shoulder; suctioning only if visible secretions, order mouth -> nose (nose first -> blocked nose -> mouth breathing -> secretions aspirated). (Book p8)

No cry (no breathing) -> significant hypoxia -> HR <100/min (normal newborn HR >100/min). HR>100 + poor/labored breathing -> O2 via hood (commonly used) or nasal prongs; if preterm (<32 wks) CPAP -> opens alveoli in collapsed premature lung. HR<100 or apnoea -> PPV: initially non-invasive BMV; upon failure invasive ET tube. (Book p8)

BMV: volume 40-750 ml, rate 40-60/min, response = HR>100/min. Pressure: 1st 30-40 cm H2O (open stiff airway), subsequent 15-30 cm H2O (prevent hyperinflation/alveolar rupture). FiO2: >=35 wks room air (21%); <35 wks start 21-30% and titrate to target SpO2 (right hand): 1 min 60-65, 2 min 65-70, 3 min 70-75, 4 min 75-80, 5 min 80-85, 10 min 85-95%. Excess O2 (preterm) -> hyperoxia damage: ROP -> blindness. (Book p8-9)

Inadequate response -> correction in order, mnemonic MRSOPA: Mask repositioning (incorrect position = m/c cause), Readjust head position, Suction (remove all secretions), Open mouth, Pressure increase over bag, Alternate airway (ET tube) if all fail. Absolute C/I: congenital diaphragmatic hernia (air via esophagus -> inflates intrathoracic viscera -> lung compression). Ambu-bag: goal RR 40-60/min; mask should adequately cover nose and mouth (no leak). (Book p9)

Airway visualization via straight blade laryngoscope (size 0: preterm, size 1: term; on back of blade). ET type: uncuffed (prevent pressure tracheal necrosis). Inner diameter by weight: <1 kg 2.5 mm, 1-2 kg 3 mm, >2.5 kg 3.5 mm. Best confirmation: EtCO2 (capnography). Insertion depth: naso-tragal length (cm) + 1 cm. (Book p10)

Chest compression done alongside ventilation (2 person), ratio 3:1 (90 compressions : 30 ventilations in 1 min), response monitored on cardiac monitor (HR>60); 2-thumb technique from head end, lower 1/3 sternum, depth 1/3 AP diameter. Adrenaline: preferred IV (umbilical vein), if inaccessible intraosseous; dose 0.1 ml/kg, strength 1:10,000. (Book p10)

NEC: m/c and devastating surgical emergency in neonates. Causes: prematurity (<32 wks, GI immaturity), top feeds without breastmilk (formula, cow milk -> pathogenic bacterial colonisation), other factors (asphyxia, maternal cocaine use) -> vasoconstriction of splanchnic circulation -> necrosis; inflammatory necrosis d/t infection. (Book p11)

Stage I (Suspect NEC): bacterial colonisation + inflammation -> non-specific features (vomiting, abdominal distension); IA occult blood in stools, IB gross blood in stools; imaging normal. Stage II (Definite NEC): breaks in intestinal epithelium -> air in intestinal walls (pneumatosis intestinalis); IIa absent bowel sounds. Stage III (Complicated NEC): air + bacteria enter peritoneal cavity -> pneumoperitoneum + peritonitis; IIIa induration/redness/tenderness of abdominal wall; IIIb intestinal perforation. Air in wall -> venous drainage -> SMV -> portal vein: pneumatosis portalis. (Book p11-12)

Triad of lab findings (thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia): seen only after stage IIb; do not have great relevance in diagnosis. Until stage IIIa: medical management - NPO, TPN, IV antibiotics (penicillin gram+ve, aminoglycoside gram-ve, metronidazole anaerobes). Antibiotic duration: stage Ia 3 days, Ib 7-10 days, II and IIIa 14 days. Stage IIIb: unstable -> 1st peritoneal drainage (emergency), after stabilization -> laparotomy -> resection + anastomosis; stable -> laparotomy directly. Untreated: m/c cause of neonatal mortality. (Book p12)

Types: generalised (septicemia); localised (specific organ systems: respiratory - pneumonia, CNS - meningitis, bones & joints - osteomyelitis, arthritis). Early onset: first 72 hrs of life, source maternal, risk factors chorioamnionitis/foul smelling liquor/ROM >72 hrs, type: pneumonia >> sepsis. Late onset: >72 hrs, hospital acquired infection, risk factors unclean hands of health professionals & caregivers, LBW (down immunity), lack of breastfeeding; equal incidence of sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis. (Book p13)

India: 1. Klebsiella (m/c), 2. Acinetobacter, 3. S. aureus. Worldwide: 1. Group B Streptococcus (GBS), 2. E. coli, 3. Listeria. Weak immune response -> non-specific symptoms -> suspect sepsis in any sick baby. Early symptoms: change in feeding pattern, lethargy, hypothermia >> fever. Pneumonia: respiratory distress. Meningitis: fever and irritability (non specific), seizures. (Book p13)

Blood culture: gold standard; disadvantage time-consuming. Sepsis screen: presence of >2 findings: TLC down (<5000/mm3), ANC down (<1800/mm3), I/T neutrophil ratio up (>0.2), micro-ESR up (>15 mm/hr), CRP up (>1 mg/dl). Newest marker: up procalcitonin. LP: indication = suspicion of meningitis in all symptomatic babies; C/I = asymptomatic babies (even with risk factors). (Book p14)

Empirical antibiotics (while awaiting culture): low resistance: penicillin (gram+ve cover) + aminoglycoside (amikacin/gentamicin); suspected meningitis: ampicillin + 3rd gen cephalosporin (cefotaxime); high resistance: ciprofloxacin (+amikacin) or piperacillin-tazobactam + amikacin (m/c). Duration: culture negative 5-7 days (1 week); culture positive: meningitis 3 weeks, others 2 weeks. (Book p14)

Suspected sepsis: early onset (<72 hrs) with risk factors -> start antibiotics + blood culture; then symptoms (LP indications): present -> perform LP, absent -> no LP; no risk factors -> close monitoring. Late onset (>72 hrs): no symptoms -> close monitoring; symptoms: sick baby -> antibiotics, blood culture, LP; not sick -> sepsis screen (+ -> same triad). (Book p15)

Clinical features: 1. Respiratory rate increased (>60 breaths/min; normal newborn RR 40-60/min). 2. Chest retraction: d/t involvement of accessory respiratory muscles. 3. Severe hypoxia (severe cases): central cyanosis (involves mucosa as well), grunting (expiration against partially closed glottis -> prevents airway/alveolar collapse). (Book p16)

Used for preterm babies. 5 criteria scored 0/1/2: upper chest retraction (0 synchronized chest-abdomen, 1 lag, 2 see-saw), lower chest retraction, nasal flaring, xiphoid retractions (not seen/mild/severe), grunting (not present/audible with stethoscope/audible without). Interpretation: <5 mild, 5-7 moderate, >7 severe. (Book p16)

Used for term and preterm babies. Mnemonic for criteria: CRAG (Cyanosis, Respiratory rate, Air entry, Grunting). Scored 0/1/2. Interpretation: <3 mild, 4-6 moderate, >6 severe (impending respiratory failure). (Book p16)
Onset within 6 hours of birth: TTNB (m/c overall), RDS, meconium aspiration syndrome. Onset any time after birth: pneumonia, pneumothorax. Also: anomalies of lung development. (Book p17)

AKA wet lung syndrome. m/c in term neonates and neonates delivered by LSCS. Pathogenesis: term neonate -> adequate stimulation and compression at birth (birth canal) -> clearance of lung fluids; without it -> delayed clearance of lung fluids. CXR: perihilar radio-opaque streaks (fluid in hilium -> bronchovascular structures -> white streaks, AKA sunburst appearance); fluid in interlobar fissure. Management: supportive (O2 inhalation) sufficient (transient); improvement in 48-72 hours. (Book p17)

AKA hyaline membrane disease (HMD). m/c in preterm (<34 wks) born to mothers who haven't received antenatal steroids (m/c: dexamethasone) and infants of diabetic mothers (up insulin -> down surfactant). Down surfactant -> up surface tension -> alveolar collapse and respiratory distress. Surfactant keeps alveoli open by decreasing surface tension. Histology: eosinophilic substances in lung tissue (resembles hyaline). CXR: white out/ground glass (collapsed alveoli, no air entry); air bronchogram sign (open airway tract). (Book p17-18)

Severity by Silverman score: mild (<5) and moderate (5-7) -> CPAP (PEEP of 5-7 mm H2O maintained -> keeps alveoli open); severe (>7) -> mechanical ventilation; surfactant replacement therapy. SRT types: natural (beractant bovine, poractant pigs), recombinant synthetic (with SP-B). Administration: endotracheal; technique: ET tube (mnemonic INSURE: intubation, surfactant, extubation) or surfactant tracheal catheter (STC) - less invasive. Earlier synthetic surfactants leaked SP-B -> down efficacy. (Book p18)

Pathogenesis: post-term baby (>42 wks) / IUGR baby stress -> meconium expulsion before birth -> aspiration of meconium stained liquor (MSL). Consequences: 1. Atelectasis (d/t complete airway obstruction); 2. Air trapping (partial obstruction) -> hyperinflation/obstructive emphysema; 3. Chemical pneumonitis -> inactivation of surfactant -> impaired gas exchange -> hypoxia, hypercapnia -> chronic pulmonary vasoconstriction -> PPHN. CXR: infiltrates in lung field. Diagnosis: by exclusion + with h/o MSL. Management: supportive (O2, CPAP, MV in severe); inhaled nitric oxide (iNO): pulmonary vasodilator for PPHN. (Book p19)

Pathogenesis: anatomical defect in diaphragm. Types: Bochdalek (m/c, postero-lateral), Morgagni (antero-medial). Features: respiratory distress (compression of lung in utero d/t movement of intestines into mediastinum -> pulmonary hypoplasia), mediastinal shift -> heart sound heard on right side, sunken/scaphoid abdomen. Investigations: USG antenatal; CXR postnatal (intestinal air shadows, absent diaphragm shadow on affected side). Management: no cry at birth -> resuscitation; cries: medical (first 48 hrs: NG tube -> down lung compression, MV via ET tube -> up lung expansion) then surgical (>48 hrs: hernia repair). CDH is absolute C/I for bag and mask ventilation (air into esophagus -> bowel loop inflation -> lung compression). Prognosis: antenatal USG LHR <1 and liver in thorax bad; postnatal PPHN (most important) and onset of distress <24 hrs bad. (Book p19-20)

Incidence: seen in upto 60% newborns -> pathological 5-10% (require treatment), physiological majority (no treatment required). Bilirubin metabolism: breakdown of RBCs -> haem -> biliverdin -> unconjugated bilirubin (water insoluble) --UDPGT (uridine diphosphate glucuronyl transferase, in liver)--> conjugated bilirubin (water soluble) -> through bile duct -> intestines: stercobilinogen (in colon) 90% excreted in stools, urobilinogen 10% excreted in urine; enterohepatic circulation loops back. (Book p21)

1. Serum bilirubin levels: best investigation; value = total serum bilirubin (TSB) -> Direct = conjugated, Indirect = unconjugated. 2. Screening of baby: initial clinical assessment; Kramer method (visual, cephalo-caudal progression): face & neck 5-7 mg/dL (seen first in eyes), chest & upper abdomen 7-9, lower abdomen & thighs 9-11, legs/arms/forearms 11-13, palms & soles = danger sign >13-15 mg/dL (risk of kernicterus). Transcutaneous bilirubinometry (TcB): tip on skin (m/c sternum), visualizes appropriate TSB; better than visual assessment; unreliable in high bilirubin (>15 mg/dL) and preterm babies. (Book p21-22)

Table: incidence common vs less common; TSB mildly elevated vs largely elevated >15 mg/dL; rate of increase >5 mg/dL (pathological); onset usually 24-72 hrs vs <24 hrs; duration 1-2 weeks vs beyond 3-4 weeks; peak 3rd-5th day; palms & soles not affected vs affected; treatment not required (wait & watch) vs required. Any 1 positive = pathological. Note: clay/pale stools = obstruction (bile duct or intestine); conjugated bilirubin pathological if >1 mg/dL or >20% of TSB -> absorbed into blood -> urobilinogen -> dark yellow urine; cannot pass into colon -> absence of stercobilinogen -> pale/yellow stools. (Book p22)

Pathological jaundice: up unconjugated bilirubin (hemolytic disorders = up breakdown of RBC e.g. hereditary spherocytosis, G6-PD deficiency; blood group incompatibility = maternal antibodies e.g. ABO/Rh; down UDPGT enzyme activity = sepsis, hypothyroidism; inherited defect of UDPGT = Crigler Najjar syndrome [Type I complete absence-severe, Type II partial absence]; extravasation of blood = cephalhemotoma) and up conjugated bilirubin (biliary atresia = obstruction of bile flow to intestine). (Book p22)

Breast feeding jaundice: AKA suboptimal intake hyperbilirubinemia; down breast milk intake -> up enterohepatic circulation -> bilirubin re-enters liver -> up bilirubin levels; onset 5-7 days (upto 1 week); feature: excessive weight loss (>10% body weight); management: increase breastfeeding frequency and duration. Breastmilk jaundice: jaundice >3 weeks, diagnosis of exclusion; beta-glucuronidase in milk -> down conjugation -> up unconjugated bilirubin; management: continue breastfeeding, transient & self resolving. (Book p23)

Normogram: used to decide course of treatment (serum bilirubin vs age in hours; plotted curve abnormal vs highest/normal curve). Phototherapy: blue-green LED (400-490 nm), protection of eye & gonads (testis); mechanism: a. structural isomerism (bilirubin -> lumirubin -> excreted), b. photoisomerisation (light -> bilirubin isomers), c. photooxidation; minimum irradiance 30 microwatt/cm2/nm; minimum distance 30-45 cm; terminate when at least 2 consequent values within normal curves on normogram; C/I: conjugated bilirubin (brown pigment formation -> Bronze baby syndrome). (Book p23-24)

DVET indications: very high bilirubin level (abnormal in normogram); Rh isoimmunization with cord blood bilirubin >5 mg/dL or cord blood hemoglobin <10 mg/dL. Mechanism: simultaneous removal of blood with up bilirubin and replacement with equal volume of fresh blood. Amount: normal blood volume in body 80-90 mL/kg; volume exchanged 160-180 mL/kg. (Book p24)

Newborn jaundice screening every 12 hours for 3-5 days post-birth. Serious jaundice present? d. onset <24 hours; e. yellow palms/soles; f. signs of bilirubin encephalopathy (hypertonia: opisthotonus; high pitched cry). Yes -> start phototherapy immediately + serum bilirubin testing -> plot on normogram, decide further management. No -> assess if jaundice is pathological: Yes -> serum bilirubin testing; No -> observation + followup. (Book p24)

Neonatal Hypoglycemia: Definition, Screening & Risk Factors

Hypoglycemia = blood glucose <45 mg/dL. Can be asymptomatic yet dangerous → screen (heel prick, routine newborn care). Risk factors: inadequate substrate (SGA <3rd percentile, preterm <35 wks), relative hyperinsulinemia (LGA, IDM), sick neonates (sepsis, birth asphyxia, severe hypothermia). High-risk period first 72 hrs. (Book p27)

1. Asymptomatic; 2. Symptomatic: jitteriness/tremors m/c & earliest (stops with stimulus), seizure not stimulus-sensitive, lethargy, refusal of feeds, autonomic symptoms uncommon. Management: symptomatic IV 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose → continuous infusion GIR 6 mg/kg/min ↑ by 2 mg/kg/min → 12 mg/kg/min; asymptomatic <40 mg/dL start infusion, 40–45 mg/dL trial of oral breastfeeds → reassess after 20–30 min. (Book p27)

Resistant = GIR >12 mg/kg/min or persists >7 days. Causes: hypopituitarism (↓ ACTH), metabolic (glycogen storage, galactosemia), nesidioblastosis (β-islet hyperplasia → congenital hypoglycemia). Treatment: stimulate gluconeogenesis (hydrocortisone, glucagon) & ↓ insulin (diazoxide, octreotide); avoid diazoxide/glucagon in SGA babies. (Book p28)

Pedersen's hypothesis: maternal hyperglycemia ↑ glucose → placenta → fetus ↑ insulin → anabolism & growth → LGA. Effects of ↑ insulin: asymmetric septal hypertrophy (resolves when insulin ↓), inactivation of surfactant → alveoli collapse → RDS, lazy left colon (↓ gut motility → delayed meconium). LGA side effect: ↑ O2 → ↑ RBC/polycythemia → hyperviscosity → thromboembolism. Congenital anomalies if hyperglycemia in 1st trimester (embryogenesis): cardiac m/c VSD, most specific TGA; CNS m/c NTD, most specific caudal regression (lumbosacral agenesis). Metabolic: ↑ insulin → ↓ PTH → functional hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcemia <8 mg/dL & hypomagnesemia <1.5 mg/dL; hypoglycemia m/c cause of seizure (> hypocalcemia). (Book p28-29)

Infections ↓immunity usual signs absent Empirical treatment all SAM m/c Ampicillin+Amikacin Penicillin+Aminoglycoside If no improvement 48hrs 3rd gen cephalosporin Ceftriaxone m/c bacteria Gram-negative Electrolytes Na ↑ total body Excess Na avoided Serum Na Low/normal intracellular & dilution edema Hypokalemia Hypomagnesemia Supplementation Dehydration Thirst urine output Dryness Treated irrespective No shock ReSoMal Shock Ringers lactate 5% dextrose K+ First 2 hrs 15 ml/kg Oral fluids Micronutrient multivitamin Twice RDA Iron absorption first week ↓ Free radical bacterial proliferation.

Obesity Excess adipose tissue deposition Seen >20% children urban India Energy intake >> expenditure ↑↑ deposition primarily abdomen (Central obesity ↑↑ risk complications) Note body unlimited capacity for fats, not carbs/proteins. DEFINITIONS BMI >5 yrs Wt kg/Ht m2 x100 plotted BMI charts Overweight >23 adult eq Obesity >27 adult eq. Wt for Ht <5 yrs WHO charts +2 to +3 SD Overweight >+3 SD Obesity. Skinfold ↑subcutaneous fat Harpenden caliper >85th %ile Obesity. Waist circumference indicator abdominal obesity >75th %ile >80 cm girls >90 cm boys. Waist-hip ratio age independent >1 males >0.85 females. Waist-height ratio age independent >0.5 obesity. BMI interpretation per IAP BMI chart.

Obesity 2 branches Constitutional (Exogenous) m/c vs Pathological. Constitutional Cause Excess food intake + Inadequate exercise. Characteristics Child has Tall stature d/t ↑insulin and ↑Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF) + Generalized obesity. Pathological Usually child is of short stature.
Pathological Obesity — Monogenic and Endocrine Causes

1. Monogenic Hereditary single gene defects (Positive family history) a. mineralocorticoid-4-receptor defect (MC4R) m/c b. Leptin deficiency ↓leptin/resistance to leptin → uncontrolled appetite. Note Leptin deficiency first reported monogenic cause. 2. Endocrine Cushing's (Truncal obesity + buffalo hump + striae + moon-face) Hypothyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism Growth hormone deficiency.

3. Hypothalamic obesity Lesion in Ventro-medial nucleus (VMN) Satiety centre → uncontrolled appetite. Causes Head injury, Radiation, Tumor, Infection. ROHHAD mnemonic R Rapid Onset, O Obesity with, H Hypothalamic dysfunction, H Hypoventilation, A Autonomic, D Dysregulation.

4. Syndromic a. Prader-Willi Syndrome Genetic imprinting disorder Features Hypogonadism, small hands & feet, almond-shaped eyes. b. Beckwith-Wiedemann Obesity, Macroglossia, Organomegaly, Hemi hypertrophy. c. Laurence-Moon (LM) + Biedl-Bardet (BB) shared Obesity, Hypogonadism, Intellectual disability, Retinitis pigmentosa; LM Syndactyly; BB Polydactyly. 5. Drugs Anti-epileptic (Valproate, Lamotrigine) Steroids → Cushingoid appearance.

Metabolic complications Obesity (↑adipose) → Insulin resistance → Metabolic syndrome/Syndrome X + PCOS in women. Insulin resistance marker Acanthosis nigricans (Hyperpigmented velvety patches on neck and axilla). Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) Leads to Steatohepatitis (Inflammatory changes in liver) → Chronic → Fibrosis.
Management of Obesity — Lifestyle, Medical, Surgical

Steps Lifestyle changes → (No response) Medical management → (No response) Surgical management. Lifestyle Sugars avoid processed (sweetened beverages, packaged foods) Fats avoid trans + saturated ↑ unsaturated ↑ vegetables fruits nuts grains Salt <5 g/day Physical activity moderate-strenuous >60 min/day (>30 min school hours). Medical Treatment of endocrine disorders Orlistat (inhibits gastric & pancreaticlipase ↓ fat breakdown & absorption) GLP-1 analogue Liraglutide (slows gastric emptying ↓ fat absorption) Metformin (Known diabetes, Women with PCOS). Surgical Last resort LAGB ↓ capacity stomach ↓ Food intake.

Rickets Occurs due to Vitamin D deficiency (Sunshine vitamin). Etiology Dietary deficiency (Fish, fish liver oil, egg yolk) Drugs Anti-epileptics (Phenytoin, phenobarbitone, carbamazepine) + Antitubercular (Isoniazid + Rifampicin) ↓ sunlight exposure Malabsorption Chronic liver disease. Pathophysiology Vit D deficiency → ↓ absorption Ca²⁺ & PO₄³⁻ → ↓ mineralization of bone → Weak bones (Disproportionate short stature: Short limbs, Pathological fractures, Deformity) + Cartilage hypertrophy at growth plate → Osteoid expansion → Swelling.

Head 1. Craniotabes Softening of skull bone, Sponge ball/ping pong ball like consistency. Note Craniotabes also seen in Congenital syphilis, Hydrocephalus, Osteogenesis imperfecta. 2. ↑ size of fontanelles (Wide open) 3. Frontal bone bossing. Chest 1. Costochondral junction widening Rachitic rosary (Painless & round) AKA string of beads appearance. 2. Harrison's sulcus groove d/t pull of diaphragm on weakened ribs.
Rickets — Limbs, Other Findings and Investigations

Limbs 1. Widening of wrist 2. Genu varum/bow leg 3. Genu valgum/knock knees 4. Double malleolus sign (Cartilage hypertrophy Swelling above lateral malleolus). Other findings Delayed dentition Seizures/tetany in infants d/t acute hypocalcemia. Blood ↓ Vit D (↓ as HCC) ↓S.Ca²⁺→↑PTH→Normal S.Ca²⁺ ↓S.PO₄³⁻ D/t ↑ bone resorption by PTH ↑ALP. Vit D table Sufficiency >20, Insufficiency 12-20, Deficiency <12 ng/ml. X-Ray primary tool Loss of zone of provisional calcification (ZPC) white line Fraying (First sign) Cupping.

1. Daily dose of Vitamin D → Recommended Duration 12 weeks. Dose <1 year 2000 IU/day; >1 year 3000 IU/day. 2. Ca²⁺ supplement 50-75 mg/kg/day. Monitoring 1. X-Ray Preferred method, shows changes by 4 weeks, Healing with line of rickets (1st visible sign) 2. Biochemical investigation shows changes in 12 weeks.
Refractory Rickets — Definition and Familial Hypophosphatemic Rickets

Refractory Rickets No response to Vitamin D supplementation. Disorders seen 1. Familial hypophosphatemic rickets 2. Vitamin D dependent rickets (VDDR) 3. RTA associated rickets 4. CKD associated rickets. Familial hypophosphatemic X-linked dominant, m/c inherited form, PHEX gene mutation (phosphate regulation endopeptidase). Normal PHEX → Endopeptidase → Inactivated phosphatonin (FGF-23); mutation → No endopeptidase → Phosphatonin always active → ↑ PO₄³⁻ excretion urine → Hypophosphatemia. Features Lower limb deformities, No features of hypocalcemia (e.g. Tetany), Dental abnormalities Pulp exposure ↑ risk dental abscess.
Refractory Rickets — Treatment, VDDR and Approach Algorithm

Familial hypophosphatemic Treatment 1. Phosphate supplementation Joule solution (elemental phosphates) 2. Burosumab newer drug monoclonal antibody against FGF-23. VDDR Autosomal recessive, Defects in Vit D metabolism → Hypocalcemia. Features Classic rickets + Type II additional Ectodermal defects (Milia, epidermal cysts), Oligodontia (↓ teeth), Alopecia. Treatment Type I α calcidiol (active form of Vit D) + Ca²⁺ supplements; Type II High doses Vit D → partially overcome resistance → improves symptoms. Approach (biochemical values) High PO₄³⁻ → CKD associated (↓ excretion PO₄³⁻); Low PO₄³⁻ → ABG Acidosis(+) → RTA; Acidosis(−) → PTH High (response to ↓Ca²⁺) → VDDR; Normal → Familial hypophosphatemic.
Scurvy — Role of Vitamin C, Etiology, Features, X-Ray, Treatment

Scurvy D/t Vitamin C deficiency. Role of Vit C 1. Collagen formation (Proline + Lysine → Hydroxylation requires Vit C → mature collagen) 2. Wound healing 3. Osteoid/bony trabeculae formation. Etiology Vit C deficient diet (Citrus fruits Lemon orange, Green vegetables) Intake of boiled/evaporated cow milk without fruit/vegetables. Early features Abnormal irritability ↓ appetite Anemia (Vit C needed for iron absorption). Bleeding Characteristic Gum bleeds, Perifollicular bleeding + corkscrew hair, Bone subperiosteal bleeding → Pain(+) → Pseudo paralysis → frog leg posture. Rosary Painful, Sharp or angulated. Diagnosis Mainly clinical; X-Ray Subperiosteal hemorrhage, Area of rarefaction (Trümmerfeld's zone central), Ring epiphysis, White line of Frankel, Pelken's spur (lateral). Treatment Oral Vit C 100-200 mg/day until lesion subsides.
Aneuploidies — Down Syndrome Pathogenesis, Face and Limbs

Aneuploidies Abnormal number of chromosomes. TRISOMIES Presence of three chromosomes in place of a pair. Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21) m/c trisomy. Pathogenesis 1. Maternal meiotic non-disjunction (95%) m/c genetic cause 2. Translocation (4%) t(4;21) t(14;21) 3. Mosaic (1%) abnormal pair of ch.21 with 3 others. Face Brachycephaly, Flat face, Flat occiput, Redundant skin, Low set ears, Flat nose, Brushfield spots, Upslanting palpebral fissures/mongoloid slant, Epicanthal fold, Open mouth with protruding tongue (D/t hypoplastic mandible). Limbs Simian crease (Single transverse palmar crease), 5th/little finger Clinodactyly (Curved finger d/t hypoplasia of phalanx), Foot Sandal gap (↑ed gap between 1st and 2nd toe).
Down Syndrome — Internal Manifestations, Associations, Recurrence Risk

Heart Congenital Heart Defect m/c 40%, Endocardial cushion/AVSD, m/c cause of morbidity/mortality. Brain Low IQ, Hypotonia. GI Intestinal atresia (m/c Duodenum) → obstruction, Hirschsprung/aganglionosis, annular pancreas. Associations 1. Hypothyroidism (congenital/acquired, autoantibodies e.g. Antithyroid peroxidase Ab) 2. Leukemia ALL m/c overall; AML-M7 megakaryoblastic m/c in <3 yrs 3. Presenile Alzheimer's 35-40yrs (Trisomy 21 → Overexpression APP gene → Amyloid ↑ → brain deposition) 4. Atlanto-axial subluxation/instability 10-30% (Upon hyperflexion e.g. sports → sudden spinal cord compression; Dx Lateral X-ray neck; Avoid contact sports). Recurrence risk General 1%; Maternal age >35 yrs up to 4%; Robertsonian translocation parents t(4;21) mother 10% father 5%; t(14;21) 100% 100%.

Edwards Syndrome Trisomy 18 — 2nd m/c trisomy. External Microphthalmos (Short palpebral fissures), Short neck, Limited hip abduction, Clenched hands with overlapping fingers, Prominent heels, Rocker bottom feet, Occiput/back of skull prominent, Dysplastic/malformed ears. Internal CHD >90% VSD > PDA > ASD; Renal horseshoe kidney. Patau Syndrome Trisomy 13 Scalp defects (Aplasia cutis), Microphthalmos, Cleft lip and/or palate, Dysplastic ears, Absent/missing ribs, Undescended testes/cryptorchidism, Clenched hands and polydactyly (Postaxial polydactyly). Heart defects 80-90% VSD > PDA > ASD; CNS Holoprosencephaly.
Turner Syndrome — Karyotype and External Features

Karyotype 45,X0/monosomy X (57%) > Mosaicism (39%) > Partial monosomy X (14%) (monosomy X in some cells) (Ring/iso chromosome X). Gender Female. External Short stature (Adults <145 cm), Lymphedema (May involve foot/hand/neck, Cystic hygroma, Seen during infancy), Neck Web neck + Loose skin folds, Normal IQ, Low hairline, Shield-shaped thorax, Widely spaced nipples, Fold of skin, Shortened metacarpal IV, Small finger nails, Streak ovaries, Cubitus valgus carrying angle >135° (Increased, lateral deviation of limbs at elbow).
Turner Internal Features, Noonan and Klinefelter Syndromes

Turner internal Heart Bicuspid aortic valve/Coarctation of aorta; Kidney 50% Horseshoe kidney; Delayed puberty & Infertility in adulthood. Pseudo Turner/Noonan Inheritance Autosomal dominant (Males and Females affected); Gene PTPN (Protein tyrosine phosphatase non-Receptor) ch.12q24. Table Turner vs Noonan — Gender Females vs Both; IQ Normal vs Low; Gonadal Streak ovaries vs Cryptorchidism (male); m/c heart Bicuspid aortic valve/Coarctation vs Pulmonary stenosis. Klinefelter Eunuchoid body habitus Taller stature (long limbs), Low (hairline), Reduced facial/axillary hair, Breast development (Gynaecomastia), Cryptorchidism → ↓Testosterone → Delayed progression of puberty; ↑Aromatase Testosterone→Estrogen → breast tissue → persistent → ↑risk breast carcinoma; Long term ↑ Risk extragonadal germ cell tumors anterior mediastinum.

Deletion of a tiny part of chromosome → Undetectable on karyotyping. DiGeorge Affected ch.22q11.2; Defective development of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches → Defect in thymus, parathyroid. Features Hypertelorism (Widely separated eyes), Low lying notched ears, Thin upper lip, Small jaw. Associations CATCH-22 C Cardiac conotruncal defects (Tetralogy of Fallot m/c), A Abnormal face, T T cell deficiency (absence of thymus), C Cleft lip/palate, H Hypocalcemia (PTH deficiency), 22 Chromosome 22. Williams 7q11.23 Elfin face (Prominent forehead, Puffiness of eyes and cheeks, Wide mouth); Hypercalcemia; Heart defect Supravalvular aortic stenosis m/c; Low IQ, learning disabilities.

Imprinting Silencing. Pathophysiology 1 Gene → 2 Alleles (Active/Inactive) → Genomic imprinting disorders Deletion (active allele) or Disomy (inactive allele). Prader-Willi Genetic defect Chromosome 15q11-13 → Deletion of paternal allele / Disomy of maternal allele. Clinical 1. Massive Obesity ↑Ghrelin → ↑appetite → ↑food intake; 2. Short stature (compared to children of similar age); 3. Small hands and feet; 4. Small eyes Almond shaped; 5. Hypogonadism → Delayed puberty → Low IQ.
Angelman Syndrome and Fragile X (Trinucleotide Repeat)

Angelman AKA happy puppet syndrome. Gene defect 15q11-13 Deletion of maternal allele / Disomy of paternal allele. Neurological ↑incidence of seizures, Hypotonia, Low IQ, Speech defects (Communicate in sign language), Abnormal movements of hands & feet Ataxia. Fragile X (TRD) CGG repeats <55 Normal, >200 TRD; Gene defect FMR1 (Fragile messenger ribonucleoprotein) protein gene. Clinical Large ears, Long face, Prominent chin, Macroorchidism (Large testes) post puberty, ↑Behavioural (ADHD, Autism). Other associations Connective tissue defects (Hyperextensive joints, High arched palate, Mitral valve prolapse MVP), Low IQ.

Childhood exanthems: Infectious diseases characterized by rash. Classification Arranged in order of historical importance. 1st disease Measles; 2nd disease Scarlet Fever; 3rd disease Rubella; 5th disease Erythema Infectiosum; 6th disease Roseola infantum/exanthema subitum.

Measles (ss RNA virus, _oviridae). Incubation 8-12 days; Respiratory droplets; Secondary attack rate >90%; Infectivity/isolation 4 days before to 5 days after onset of rash. 1. Prodromal Day 1-3 Fever (intensity ↑ after rash), 3C's Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis. 2. Enanthem Day 2-3 Koplik spot (white spot surrounded by reddish hue, usually opposite 2nd lower molar; Rice grain/grain of sand). 3. Exanthematous Day 4-8 Maculopapular, behind ear/face → downward trunk & extremities, leaves brownish pigmentation, ↑ fever after rash. Complications Acute m/c Otitis media, most severe Pneumonia (viral giant cell/HECHT; bacterial Staph aureus/Strep pneumoniae); Chronic SSPE (1 in 1,000,000, latent 7-13 yrs, myoclonic seizures, cognitive impairment, personality changes, Dx IgG anti-measles Ab in CSF, fatal). Management Supportive (nutrition, antipyretic, IV fluids); Vitamin A ↓ morbidity/mortality by 50%, 2 doses 24 hrs apart: >1 yr 1 lakh IU, <1 yr 1/2 lakh IU.
Scarlet Fever — Etiology, Features, Complications, Management

Etiology Group A β hemolytic streptococci → Toxin: Pyrogenic exotoxin (Erythrogenic toxin); Age 5-15 yrs. Clinical Fever, Sore throat, Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, Strawberry tongue (D/t hypertrophy of papillae), Rash starts on 2nd day of fever (spares palms and soles), Fine maculopapular sandpaper rash (face, trunk, extremities), Pastia's lines (rash accentuation at skin creases). Post streptococcal complications Acute rheumatic fever, PSGN, Post streptococcal reactive arthritis. Management Investigations Throat swab culture; Treatment Oral Penicillin V for 10 days > Amoxicillin for 10 days.

Rubella AKA German measles/3 day measles (Similarity in C/P's). Etiology Togaviridae (ss RNA virus). Incubation 14-21 days; Respiratory droplets; Infectivity 5 days before - 6 days after onset of rash. Clinical 1. Rash First sign/starts Day 1 (without prodromal stage), Maculopapular, behind ear/face → downwards, No desquamation/discoloration after disappearance. 2. Enanthem Forchheimer spots (tiny rose lesions in oropharynx); Lymphadenopathy suboccipital, posterior auricular, anterior cervical. Complications 1. Post infectious thrombocytopenia (2-3 wks after infection, self-limiting) 2. Arthritis (older children) 3. Progressive Rubella Panencephalitis (PRP) most severe, features similar to SSPE.

Etiology Parvovirus B19 (ss DNA virus). Incubation 4-28 days; Age >5 years. Clinical 1. Prodromal Fever 1-2 days. Exanthematous Stage 1 Slapped-cheek appearance, Facial flushing; Stage 2 Diffuse macular erythema (trunk & extremities); Stage 3 Central clearing of rash, lacy/reticulated appearance. Associations Arthralgia (older children); Transient aplastic crisis (Pre-existing hemolytic anemia + B19, presents pancytopenia); Infection in mother (during pregnancy). Management Supportive (good prognosis).

Etiology Human herpes virus (HHV) 6, 7, echovirus 16; Age 6 months - 3 years. Clinical 1. Prodromal stage (1-4 days) Fever, Cough, Running nose. 2. Exanthematous phase (Day 4) Maculopapular rash, starts in trunk, ↓ fever after rash appears, No residual pigmentation. 3. Enanthem Nagayama spots: erythematous macules in soft palate and uvula. Treatment Supportive; Prognosis Good.

HFMD Age Preschool (<5 years). Causative Coxsackie A16, Enterovirus 71. Spread Direct contact/infected fomites (Eg used towel). Clinical Fever; Vesicles resolve over 4-5 days; Papulovesicular lesions in soles and palms; Blisters around oral cavity (First manifestation). Treatment Supportive. m/c complication Temporary loss of nails 4 weeks after initial infection.
Varicella / Chickenpox — Features, Complications, Treatment, Prevention

Varicella Causative varicella-zoster virus (ds DNA virus); Incubation 10-21 days; Droplet spread; Infectivity 24-48 hrs before rash → crusting of all lesions; Secondary attack rate 80%. Clinical Fever; Rash Day 2 of fever, lasts 3-5 days, Macule → Papule → Vesicle (pruritic), trunk → other areas, leaves hypo/hyperpigmented macules, Pleomorphic, Dew drop on a rose petal, Fluid filled vesicles. Complications Secondary bacterial (Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes), Neurological (Cerebellar ataxia, meningo-encephalitis), Reye's syndrome (Aspirin usage, hepatic encephalopathy). Diagnosis Clinical; Tzanck smear multinucleated giant cells (poor sensitivity); Serology Anti-IgM. Treatment Antipyretics Paracetamol; Acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose x 4/day start within 48 hrs; Avoid Ibuprofen (↑ risk necrotizing fasciitis). Prevention Varicella vaccine (Live attenuated Oka strain, 2 doses SC: 15-18 months, 4-6 years); Post exposure (if not administered) Varicella vaccine + VZIG (immunocompromised, pregnant, neonate born to affected mother 5 days before to 2 days after delivery).

TORCH Intrauterine infection transmitted from mother to baby: Toxoplasmosis; Others: Syphilis, Zika virus, Parvo B19 virus; Rubella; Cytomegalovirus (CMV); Herpes simplex. Type of maternal infection 1. Primary (mother infected during pregnancy; m/c transmitted) 2. Secondary/reactivation (Latent infection reactivation; Transmission of syphilis, CMV). Time of gestation 1st trimester m/c (Organ anomalies, ↑ risk congenital anomalies, Highest transmission risk). Common manifestations Antenatal IUGR m/c, IUD, Preterm delivery, Abortions; Postnatal Bone marrow suppression (Anemia, thrombocytopenia), Hepatosplenomegaly, Lymphadenopathy, Jaundice/abnormal LFT (Subclinical).
Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) — Triad, Features, Diagnosis, Management

CRS Severe maturation infection. Clinical Triad Heart defects (PDA, Pulmonary artery stenosis PS, VSD), Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) m/c, Cataract. Other features 1. Salt and pepper retinopathy (Black and white spots on retina; m/c ocular finding) 2. Blueberry muffin lesion (Purpuric spots non-blanching dome-shaped papules; severe CRS; dermal erythropoiesis; non-specific). Chronic manifestations 1. Progressive rubella panencephalitis (PRP) school going age, similar to SSPE (measles) poor scholastic performance, seizures, intellectual impairment 2. Adult-onset Diabetes 3. Hypothyroidism. Diagnosis Fetal IgM antibodies against rubella (maternal IgM cannot cross placenta); IgG not used (maternal IgG crosses placenta). Management No treatment (damage permanent); Prevention immunization of parent (during their childhood).
Congenital CMV — Transmission, Triad, Diagnosis, Treatment

Congenital CMV m/c TORCH infection. Transmission rate 3rd trimester (90%) → Organogenesis complete → Asymptomatic; 1st trimester → Organogenesis incomplete → Congenital cytomegalic inclusion disease. Triad Microcephaly, Chorioretinitis, Intracranial calcification (periventricular). Other SNHL (m/c long term sequelae; m/c cause of non-syndromic hearing loss in children), Rash (Petechiae d/t ↓ platelets; Blueberry muffin lesion), Hepatosplenomegaly. Diagnosis PCR (Urine > blood > saliva; Screening; as early as possible); Serology (Low sensitivity) IgM antibodies against CMV. Treatment Ganciclovir IV 6 weeks → Oral 6 months; Goal prevent progression neurological disorders, decrease risk of SNHL in future.

Transmission risk highest in 3rd trimester. Triad Hydrocephalus (unique), Chorioretinitis, Intracranial calcification (Diffuse calcification). Other Low IQ, Deafness (SNHL), Some cases A/W microcephaly. Diagnosis Serology IgM/IgA ELISA (more sensitive), Immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) test; PCR in CSF/tissue sample (if neurological involvement +). Treatment Infected child All cases symptomatic and asymptomatic should be treated: [Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine x 1 year] + [Folic acid (To prevent bone marrow suppression cause by Rx)]; Infected mothers Spiramycin ↓ transmission risk.

Congenital Varicella Syndrome Intrauterine transmission of herpes zoster; Period of risk 2nd trimester (13-20 weeks of gestation). Clinical 1. Cerebral atrophy 2. Microcephaly 3. Limb hypoplasia 4. Cicatrix (Irregular scarring, resembles burn scar). Perinatal Varicella more common than congenital varicella; Period of highest risk 5 days before to 2 days after delivery; Management immediately after birth Varicella zoster > IV Ig (Prevention); If lesions (+) Acyclovir.
Congenital Syphilis — Early and Late Features, Management

Unique feature Recurrent Abortion; Period of risk >4 months of gestation (≥ 2nd trimester). Early onset <2 years 1st Rhinitis (Snuffles) 2nd Vesiculobullous rash palms and soles (Pemphigus syphiliticus) 3rd Bone (metaphysis, Osteochondritis, Periostitis) → Bone pain, If severe Pseudo paralysis + Edema of affected limb (Soft tissue shadow on xray). Late onset >2 years 1. Hutchinson's triad (SNHL, Interstitial keratitis, Hutchinson's teeth notching/peg shaped incisors) 2. Mulberry molars (Irregular surface d/t rudimentary cups; usually 1st molar) 3. Deformed nose (Preceded by Saddle Nose deformity; Perforations; bony deformities) 4. Rhagodes (Fissures around mouth/nose) 5. Saber shin (Bowing of tibia) 6. Clutton's joint (B/L knee effusion). Management Diagnosis VDRL (baby and mother) 4 fold ↑ titres diagnostic; Treatment Aqueous crystalline penicillin/Penicillin G > 3rd generation cephalosporin: Ceftriaxone.

Vector Aedes aegypti mosquito → Infected mother → Baby; Period of risk 1st trimester. 1. Skull manifestations Partial collapse of skull, Internal abnormalities (Overlapping of sutures), Brain damage (Microcephaly, Hypertonia/spasticity, Extrapyramidal chorea/athetosis, D/t basal ganglionic damage, Occipital prominence). 2. Limb manifestations Abnormally curved limbs (d/t multiple contractures); Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita. 3. Eye manifestations Coloboma, Pigmentary retinal mottling, Scar + in macula. 4. Others SNHL.

Transmitted across all trimesters; most sensitive period of transmission 2nd trimester. Tropism for erythroid lineage (Primarily at the pronormoblast stage). Clinical 1. Severe anemia → High output cardiac failure 2. Direct cytopathic effects on myocardium → Myocarditis; Fetal cardiac arrest → IUD (Intrauterine death) 3. Non immune hydrops fetalis.

Guidelines for COVID-19 are given by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW). COVID appropriate behaviour = 3Ws & AVS: Watch your distance (> 2 metres), Wear mask, Wash your hands frequently, Ventilation (open space ventilation ↓ transmission) and Vaccination (for 15–18 years of age).

Symptoms: Mild/asymptomatic (m/c; incidental detection or h/o contact), fever, cough, rhinorrhoea, sore throat/throat irritation (Omicron variant m/c), myalgia/headache/malaise, diarrhoea, loss of sense of smell > taste (Delta variant m/c).
Severity Classification, Danger Signs & Tachypnoea Criteria

Severity: Asymptomatic / Mild (URT) / Moderate / Severe. RR normal in asymptomatic & mild, ↑ in moderate & severe. SpO2 in room air: normal (asymptomatic), > 94% (mild), 90–93% (moderate), < 90% (severe). Danger signs: grunting, lethargy, seizures, somnolence, severe chest retractions — present only in severe. Tachypnoea: < 2 mo > 60/min; 2–12 mo > 50/min; 1–5 yr > 40/min; > 5 yr > 30/min.

Investigations: Asymptomatic/mild — not required. Moderate — CBC, ESR, chest X-ray, blood glucose. Severe — above + CRP/ferritin (markers of inflammation), D-dimer assays (for thrombosis), LFT/RFT (for multi-organ dysfunction). CT chest: not indicated in paediatric COVID, except if terminally ill.
Treatment — Site of Care & Rx by Severity

Site of care: Asymptomatic — home isolation. Mild — home isolation ± teleconsultation (sos), COVID care centre. Moderate — ward of a COVID-19 hospital / DCHC (Dedicated COVID Health Centre). Severe — ICU / High Dependency Unit (HDU). Rx: Asymptomatic — no specific Rx. Mild — paracetamol for fever, warm saline gargles for sore throat. Moderate — O2 inhalation (target SpO2 94–96%), fluid & electrolyte balance, steroids in progressive disease, antimicrobials if needed. Severe — O2 support (94–96%), fluid & electrolytes, corticosteroids (most useful drug; indicated in all severe cases).

Steroids — Right time: avoided in first 3–5 days after onset of symptoms (prolongs viral shedding). Right dose: Dexamethasone 0.15–6 mg/kg once daily; Methylprednisolone 0.75–30 mg/kg once daily. Right duration: 5–7 days → tapered over 10–14 days. Anticoagulants: thrombosis confirmed by imaging/↑ D-dimer — LMWH (Enoxaparin) 1 mg/kg BD. Antimicrobials: clinical evidence/suspicion of bacterial infection, septic shock. Antivirals (Remdesivir, Favipiravir)/monoclonal antibodies: not recommended (efficacy unknown in children).

MIS-C (Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) presents 2–4 weeks after acute COVID. Risk factors: age < 1 year, co-morbidities (asthma, chronic lung disease), obesity, children with immunodeficiency.

WHO criteria: fever > 38°C for ≥ 3 days AND any 2 of — mucocutaneous inflammation (rash/bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis), hypotension or shock, myocardial dysfunction/myocarditis/valvulitis/coronary aneurysms/↑ troponin, coagulopathy (elevated D-dimers), severe GI involvement (uncontrolled abdominal pain/diarrhoea). Additional: ↑ inflammatory markers (CRP > 5 mg/dl, ESR > 40 mm/hr, procalcitonin), recent COVID (RTPCR +ve)/contact with confirmed case, no evidence of serious bacterial infection/alternative diagnosis. Management: hospitalization in ICU; methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day tapered over 2–3 weeks; IVIG 2 g/kg slow IV infusion (maximum 100 g).

Esophageal atresia = discontinuity in the esophagus. Associated anomalies: 1. Tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF) — m/c defect in mesenchymal separation b/w trachea & esophagus; Gross classification A–F. 2. VACTERL association.

Type A — isolated EA. Type B — proximal TEF with distal EA. Type C — proximal EA with distal TEF (m/c, 85% cases). Type D — proximal and distal TEF (with EA). Type E (or H) — TEF without EA. Type F — esophageal stenosis.
VACTERL: Vertebral anomalies, Imperforate anus, Cardiac defects, Tracheo-esophageal fistula, Renal anomalies, Limb anomalies.

Clinical: vomiting (multiple episodes) → aspiration pneumonitis; excessive frothy salivation; antenatal polyhydramnios (inability to swallow amniotic fluid). Investigations — chest X-ray: resistance during NG tube insertion; coiled NG tube in proximal esophagus. Treatment: surgery — anastomosis of esophageal ends + division & ligation of TEF.

GERD: onset < 6 months (infancy); recurrent vomiting (d/t short esophagus) → aspiration, malnutrition, failure to thrive. Sandifer syndrome: characteristic — spasmodic dystonia (posturing of back muscles): opisthotonus. Opisthotonus also seen in neonatal tetanus & bilirubin-induced neurological damage (BIND).

Investigations: 24-hr pH monitoring (pH ≤ 4 indicates GERD); pH-MII (multichannel intraluminal impedance) — best test, measures level up to which reflux occurs; upper GI endoscopy — erosions & breaks. Treatment: diet & lifestyle (small frequent feeds, thickened feeds, avoid caffeine/spicy/chocolates) → pharmacological (PPIs omeprazole/lansoprazole × 3 months to prevent recurrence) → surgery for refractory GERD: Nissen fundoplication (fundus wrapped around lower esophagus → ↑ LES tone/pressure → ↓ reflux).
Foreign Bodies in Esophagus — Features & Natural Course

Age ≤ 3 years; common FBs — coins, nuts, small toys. Dangerous: button batteries → coagulative necrosis; multiple magnets → stick across bowel loops → obstruction → perforation; sharp objects. Natural course: > 95% pass & excreted. Impaction sites: cricopharynx, mid-esophagus (tracheal bifurcation), right above LES.
Foreign Bodies — Clinical Features, Diagnosis & Management

H/o ingestion may be absent; may be asymptomatic; if symptomatic — drooling of saliva, refusal of feeds, chest discomfort/pointing; respiratory complaints — recurrent cough/wheeze (pressure on trachea). X-ray: only radio-opaque FBs; esophagogram: filling defect. Management: conservative (blunt & asymptomatic — observe 24 hrs); esophagoscopy removal — symptomatic, impacted > 24 hrs, batteries/magnets/sharp.

Diarrheal disorders are major contributors of under-5 mortality. Types: Acute — < 7 days, infections. Persistent — > 14 days, prolonged infection. Chronic — > 14 days (upto months), non-infectious causes (especially malabsorption).

Acute diarrhea: m/c cause — Rotavirus; other viral — Norwalk, adeno, astro & calicivirus; m/c bacteria — ETEC (enterotoxigenic E. coli). Dysentery = diarrhea + blood in stool; m/c cause — Shigella flexneri.

Dehydration is the primary concern in diarrhea — look, feel, decide & treat. No dehydration — active & alert, normal eyes/tears/mouth/thirst, pinch fast (< 1 sec). Some — irritable, sunken eyes, absent tears, dry mouth, severe thirst, pinch slow (< 2 sec). Severe — lethargy (cannot be aroused), very sunken eyes, very dry mouth, unable to drink, pinch very slow (> 2 sec). Skin pinch tests turgor/elasticity which depends on interstitial fluid.
Plan A — No Dehydration (Low Osmolarity ORS)

Plan A: low osmolarity ORS — glucose 75, Na 75, K 20, Cl 65, citrate 10; total 245 mosm/L; glucose:Na 1:1 for maximum absorption via SGLT-1. Home alternatives: salted rice water, salted yogurt, soup with salt, fresh fruit juice (no sugar), tender coconut water — avoid packed juices (added sugar). Amount of ORS (replace ongoing losses): < 2 yr 50–100 mL/stool; 2–10 yr 100–200 mL; > 10 yr ad lib.
Plan B — Some Dehydration (75 mL/kg over 4 hrs)

Plan B: ORS corrects dehydration — 1. Rehydration: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hrs. 2. Replacement of ongoing loss: same as Plan A. 3. Maintenance (Holliday–Segar): first 10 kg — 100 mL/kg; 10–20 kg — 1000 mL + 50 mL/kg after 10 kg; > 20 kg — 1500 mL + 20 mL/kg after 20 kg.
Plan C — Severe Dehydration (IV RL + 5% Dextrose) & Zinc

Plan C: IV fluids RL + 5% dextrose; rehydration 100 mL/kg. < 1 yr: 30 mL/kg over 1 hr + 70 mL/kg over 5 hrs = 6 hrs. > 1 yr: 30 mL/kg over 30 min + 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hrs = 3 hrs. Zinc for 14 days — GI re-epithelialisation, ↓ risk of persistent diarrhea; dose: < 6 months 10 mg/day, > 6 months 20 mg/day.

Additional drugs: dysentery — 3rd generation cephalosporin; vomiting — ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg/dose orally; probiotics (cost-benefit) — Lactobacillus rhamnosus & Saccharomyces boulardii. Convulsions with diarrhea: electrolyte/metabolic (hypo/hypernatremia, hypoglycemia), infections (febrile seizures, meningitis/encephalitis), dehydration → cerebral venous & sagittal sinus thrombosis.
Persistent Diarrhea — Risk Factors & Management (Vitamin A, Lactose, Diet Ladder)

Risk factors: malnutrition (↓ immunity), immunodeficiency. Management: ORS/IV fluids per dehydration; zinc; vitamin A single dose (< 8 kg 1 lakh IU, > 8 kg 2 lakh IU); lactose restriction — milk < 50 mL/kg/day. Persistent diarrhea → villi damage → ↓ lactase → lactose intolerance → unabsorbed lactose + colonic bacteria → H2 (gaseous stool) & lactic acid (↓ pH, perianal excoriation). Diet ladder: no-lactose diet (↓ sugars & starch; plain glucose, cereals, egg white, chicken) → no response → no lactose, no starch — only egg yolk/chicken (protein).
Celiac Disease — Gluten, Pathogenesis, Diagnosis & Treatment

Celiac disease: gluten hypersensitivity causing chronic diarrhea. Gluten foods (BROW): barley, rye, oats (relatively well tolerated), wheat (m/c implicated). HLA DQ2 & DQ8; T cell mediated autoimmune disorder: genetic predisposition + gluten → gliadin (intestinal absorption) → T cell → B cell → autoantibodies → intestinal injury. Associations: Down, Turner, Hashimoto, selective IgA deficiency, T1DM. Onset ≥ 6 months (after stoppage of exclusive breastfeeding). Anemia: iron (duodenum) + folate (terminal ileum) → dimorphic, iron-refractory. Diagnosis: anti-tTG (screening), anti-endomysial (best); duodenal biopsy — IOC in India (villous atrophy, ↑ crypt length, ↑ IEL > 30/100 enterocytes). Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet (substitute rice & maize).

Hereditary hyperbilirubinemias (AKA syndromic jaundice) — AR inheritance. ↑ Unconjugated BR: ↓ UDP-GT defect (Crigler Najjar, Gilbert). ↑ Conjugated BR: defect in secretion/excretion of conjugated BR from liver into bile (Dubin Johnson, Rotor).
Crigler-Najjar Syndrome — Type I vs Type II

Suspect type I if high bilirubin without hemolysis beyond 1st week after birth. Type I — UDP-GT absent; most severe (can be fatal); kernicterus risk high; serum BR > 20 mg/dl; supportive (phototherapy, exchange transfusion) + curative liver transplant; no response to phenobarbitone. Type II — partial deficiency; less severe; low kernicterus risk; BR < 20 mg/dl; only supportive; phenobarbitone (enzyme inducer) → ↓ jaundice.

Gilbert syndrome: m/c cause of hereditary hyperbilirubinemia; mild UDP-GT deficiency → m/c benign type. Onset: adolescence/puberty; mild unconjugated BR (1–6 mg/dl). Symptoms: intermittent fluctuant jaundice; any stressor (illness/fasting) precipitates. Treatment: reassurance — no intervention needed.

Transporter proteins carry conjugated bilirubin from hepatocyte to bile duct: MRP-2 (multidrug resistant protein) coded by ATP binding cassette subfamily C (ABCC) — defective in Dubin Johnson; OATP (organic anion transport protein) — defective in Rotor. Onset: adult/late adolescence; mild asymptomatic jaundice; treatment — reassurance.

Neonatal cholestasis: impairment of bile flow in hepatobiliary system → ↑ conjugated BR. Biochemical: TSB < 5 mg/dl → conjugated BR ≥ 1 mg/dl; TSB > 5 mg/dl → conjugated ≥ 20% of TSB. Clinically: persistent jaundice > 3 weeks (excluding other dx), pale/clay (especially core) stools, dark yellow urine.
Neonatal Cholestasis — Intrahepatic Causes (Hepatitis, Metabolic, Lysosomal)

Intrahepatic: 1. Idiopathic neonatal hepatitis (2nd m/c cause) 2. Infections — TORCH, sepsis 3.
