Metabolic — galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency (oil drop cataract, jaundice); tyrosinemia type I (fumaryl acetoacetate hydrolase deficiency; boiled cabbage odour of urine; hepatorenal syndrome — proximal tubular damage → Fanconi like); lysosomal storage disorders — Gaucher (glucocerebrosidase; hepatosplenomegaly, lytic bone lesions → Erlen meyer flask, pancytopenia; crumpled tissue paper HPE) & Niemann-Pick (sphingomyelinase; HSM + cherry red spots; foamy cells).

Alagille: JAGGED 1 & NOTCH 2 gene defects; ↓ intrahepatic bile ducts + pulmonary artery stenosis = arteriohepatic dysplasia; triangular facies; vertebral defects (hemivertebra & butterfly vertebra); posterior embryotoxon (white-gray ridge at cornea near limbus on slit lamp). Zellweger: peroxisomal (PEX gene → peroxins); VLCFA accumulation; misdiagnosed as Down (similar facies + profound hypotonia). Extrahepatic: EHBA (d/t severe fibrosis) — m/c cause of neonatal cholestasis; choledochal cyst — cystic dilatation of bile duct.
Neonatal Cholestasis — Evaluation, Biopsy & Management (Medical + Kasai)

Evaluation: history & exam; serum bilirubin (total & conjugated); imaging primarily useful in EHBA — USG (microgallbladder/ghost; hyperechogenic atretic duct; triangular cord sign), HIDA (↓ tracer excretion; high negative predictive value). Biopsy — best investigation; differentiates intrahepatic (damaged architecture, giant cells +++, portal inflammation) vs EHBA (normal architecture, giant cells +, portal fibrosis, neoductular proliferation +). Medical: MCT oil, vitamins A/D/E/K, Cu/Mg/Zn/PO4, twice-RDA multivitamins, UDCA & cholestyramine. Surgical: Kasai (hepatoportoenterostomy) — good if < 60 days; definitive — transplant. Choledochal cyst — excision + hepaticojejunostomy.

Wilson disease: AR; ATP7B gene (chromosome 13q) → P-type ATPase defect → ↑ free copper (toxic) + ↓ ceruloplasmin. Onset > 3 yrs. Liver (children): chronic liver disease → cirrhosis → ESLD. CNS (adults): tremor, seizures, extrapyramidal, psychosis/depression (basal ganglia). Eye: Cu in descemet membrane → KF ring; sunflower cataract. Coombs –ve hemolysis; arthralgia. Screening: urine Cu ↑, ceruloplasmin ↓. Gold standard: liver biopsy — Cu > 250 µg/g dry weight; macrovesicular steatosis. Rx: copper restriction; chelators (D-penicillamine, trientene); zinc (long-term maintenance); liver transplant (definitive).

GSD: fasting glycogen not broken down → defect. Presentation: recurrent fasting hypoglycemia; hepatomegaly (glycogen accumulation); muscle involvement in certain subtypes (exertional fatigue, ↓ ATP). Types: 0 — glycogen synthase (no glycogen deposit); I von Gierke — G6Pase (m/c); II (Cori, as per book) — debranching (muscle involvement); III (Anderson, as per book) — branching (2nd m/c; early cirrhosis, worst outcome); VI Hers — liver phosphorylase; IX — phosphorylase kinase. Von Gierke: doll facies, renomegaly, ↑ uric acid (PPP→purines), hyperlipidemia (pyruvate→acetyl CoA→FA), lactic acidosis; lactate & uric acid ↑↑↑ vs type III (–). Rx: frequent feeds 2–3 hrly; uncooked corn starch; night feeds (NG young, waxy maize starch older).

IHPS: hypertrophy of the circular muscles in pylorus → obstruction (stenosis). Associations: m/c in 1st born male child; erythromycin usage. Clinical: onset > 3 weeks after birth; vomiting — non-bilious, projectile; epigastric swelling — olive-shaped, usually after vomiting; visible gastric peristalsis — left → right, seen after feeding.

Chronic vomiting → loss of milk/feeds, H⁺, Cl⁻, K⁺ ions → hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. If no treatment: Na⁺ lost through vomitus → kidney reabsorbs Na⁺ & secretes K⁺ → depletion of K⁺ → secretion of H⁺ into urine instead → paradoxical aciduria.

Investigations: USG — IOC (pyloric muscle wall thickness ≥ 4 mm; pyloric channel length ≥ 16 mm). Barium contrast X-ray — not commonly used; narrowing of pyloric channel = string sign. Management: step 1 — correction of dehydration (IV ½ normal saline + K⁺ + 5% dextrose; corrects hypokalemia, hypoglycaemia, fluid loss); step 2 — Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy.

Duodenal atresia: m/c type of intestinal atresia. Pathology: failure of recanalization of duodenal lumen. Associations: Down’s syndrome (~30% babies with Down’s). Clinical: antenatal polyhydramnios; bilious vomiting soon after birth. Types: 1 (m/c) — mucosal web, windsock deformity, no complete obstruction; 2 — atretic ends connected by fibrous band; 3 — disconnected atretic ends, complete atresia.

X-ray: double bubble sign (also seen in annular pancreas — obstruction d/t part of pancreas surrounding duodenum). USG/CT — IOC: atresia distinctly seen. Treatment: duodeno-duodenostomy (preferred, ↓ risk of anastomotic leakage); duodeno-jejunostomy (atretic ends connected to jejunum).

Intussusception: m/c cause of intestinal obstruction in 5 months–3 years; m/c abdominal emergency < 2 years. Telescoping of one part of intestine into another → obstruction; m/c site — ileocolic junction; intussusceptum usually proximal, intussuscipiens distal. Pathogenesis: complimentary feeding/viral infection/vaccination → lead point (< 2 yr: swollen Peyer’s patches; > 2 yr: polyp/lipoma) → telescoping with mesentery → venous return obstruction → edema + mucosal bleeding → necrosis/perforation if untreated.

Triad: paroxysmal colicky pain (knees drawn to chest); vomiting (most common, PPV = 90%); currant jelly stools (mucus + blood; classic triad < 30% of patients) + RUQ mass (d/t telescoping) — triad together PPV = 100%. USG — IOC: longitudinal telescoping; transverse doughnut sign. Colour doppler — vascularity; barium enema (rare) — claw sign. Treatment: NPO/NG decompression + IV fluids → USG-guided reduction (hydrostatic saline / contrast — not preferred / aerostat — safest) → overnight observation (10–20% immediate recurrence) → surgical reduction.
Hirschsprung Disease — Pathology, Consequences & Clinical Features

Hirschsprung: failure of migration of neurons from neural crest → aganglionosis in submucosal & myenteric plexus; m/c site — rectum > sigmoid. Association: Down’s syndrome (m/c gastric association). Aganglionosis → sustained contraction with no relaxation → narrowing (m/c rectum); m/c congenital motility disorder; m/c cause of lower intestinal obstruction in infancy. Clinical: delayed meconium > 48 hrs; abdominal distension; PR exam — sphincter normal, lumen narrow; on removal of finger — sudden expulsion of meconium (transient dilatation).

Investigations: plain X-ray — ↓/absent air in pelvis; barium contrast enema — diagnostic (segments may not always be visualized; transitional zone); rectal manometry — absence of recto-anal inhibitory reflex (RAIR): no ↓ anal tone on rectal dilatation; rectal biopsy — IOC: ganglions absent, nerve fibres hypertrophied (stained with acetylcholinesterase). Treatment: early — pull-through (affected segment removed; unaffected proximal segment pulled through & attached to anus); delayed (older child constipation) — colostomy → pull-through.
Laryngomalacia: m/c congenital malformation of larynx. "Malacia" = softness/floppiness/laxity. Structures affected: supraglottic structures — epiglottis, arytenoids, aryepiglottic folds.

Stridor = sign of upper airway obstruction. Pathology: floppy structures → fall over glottic opening. Onset: soon after birth/within 2 weeks after birth. Characteristics: intermittent (when baby is crying/agitated/after feeding); postural variation — supine +, prone −.

Table — positional variation of stridor: laryngomalacia +, congenital subglottic stenosis −. Cry: muffled in laryngomalacia, normal in subglottic stenosis. Stridor: inspiratory in laryngomalacia, biphasic (inspiration and expiration) in subglottic stenosis.
Diagnosis: laryngoscopy (shows omega (Ω) shaped epiglottis). Treatment: reassurance; resolves by 6–12 months of age.

Pathogenesis: cartilaginous bronchial dysplasia → abnormal compliance of bronchi → near complete collapse of bronchi during expiration (ball valve effect) → air trapping → hyperinflation/emphysema. m/c sites: left upper lobe > right middle lobe. Distended lobe compresses other lobes → atelectasis → impaired oxygenation → respiratory distress in newborn; mediastinal shift to unaffected side. X-ray → CT chest: IOC. Treatment: lobectomy of emphysematous lobe.

CPAM: hamartomatous/dysplastic lung tissue → multiple cysts; m/c cause of cystic lung disease in newborn. Presentation: cysts are non-functional → no gaseous exchange → respiratory distress; ↑ risk of infection → recurrent pneumonia. Chest X-ray → CT chest: IOC (multiple cysts). Treatment: ↑ risk of lung tumours (sarcoma/carcinoma) → surgical resection within one year of age.

Pathology: segregation/isolation of a non-functioning part of lung (no communication with bronchus); blood supply systemic (lower thoracic aorta/abdominal aorta); ↑ risk of recurrent infections; site — lower lobe of lung fields. Types: intrapulmonary (common pleural covering), extrapulmonary (separate pleural covering). Chest X-ray → CT chest: IOC. Treatment: surgical resection.
Foreign Bodies in the Airway — Introduction & Presentation

Paediatric emergency; age group usually < 3 years; location: lower airway > upper airway → m/c bronchus (right > left); common foreign bodies: nuts, coins, small rounded plastic toys. Immediate presentation: choking; small child — acute recurrent coughing episodes; older child — choking sign (clutching of neck) or gag response (natural response to prevent choking). Note: caregiver may present child with h/o choking.
Foreign Bodies — Delayed Presentation, Consequences, Investigation & Management

Delayed presentation (d/t retained foreign body): recurrent unexplained wheeze/breathing difficulty mimicking asthma unresponsive to bronchodilators; suppurative complications — recurrent pneumonia localising to the same site → bronchiectasis, lung abscess. Consequences: complete obstruction → collapse/atelectasis; partial obstruction → ball valve effect → hyperinflation. Chest X-ray unreliable (only 10–20% of foreign bodies are radiopaque). Management initiated upon suspicion: suggestive history (acute presentation), focal abnormal lung findings, abnormal X-rays. Lower airway (bronchus) FB → rigid bronchoscope removal. Upper airway FB: > 1 year — Heimlich’s maneuver; < 1 year — 5 back blows + 5 chest compressions.

Characteristics: bronchoconstriction d/t hyper-responsiveness of airway + chronic airway inflammation (reversible airway obstruction); variable intensity & frequency of episodes over time → management according to subjective symptoms. Clinical phenotypes: allergic/atopic (m/c in children; associated family/personal history of allergic conditions e.g. atopic dermatitis; good treatment response), non-allergic (m/c in adults; no family history; difficult to treat), exercise-induced.
Phases of Allergic Asthma — Early & Late Phase

Early phase: allergen → IgE → IgE-bound mast cell → triggers → release of mediators (degranulation; starts within 10 min) — histamine (most important), prostaglandins, leukotrienes (C, D & E), bradykinin → bronchoconstriction, mucosal edema, ↑ secretions; treatment: β2-agonist (bronchodilator). Late phase: starts 3 to 4 h later; peak by 10 to 12 h; inflammatory cell recruitment (eosinophils, basophils & lymphocytes); repeated exposure → chronic airway inflammation; steroids (−) inhibit (inflammatory cell recruitment).
Clinical features: recurrent episodes of wheezing/cough/chest tightness. Varying intensity and frequency (↑ frequency late night/early mornings).

Table: Airflow limitation — FEV1 ↓, FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.8. Bronchodilator response — FEV1 ↑ by > 12%. Exercise challenge — airflow obstruction worsened: FEV1 ↓ by > 15%. Diurnal variation/AM to PM variation — FEV1 or PEF (Peak Expiratory Flow) ↑ by > 20%.
Management of Asthma — Overview & Stepwise Therapy (Age 6–11 yr)

Based on Global Initiative Network for Asthma (GINA) guidelines. Management → identification & elimination of exacerbating factors + pharmacotherapy (long-term management, acute exacerbations). Age > 12 yr: managed as in adults. Age 6 to 11 yr: stepwise management. Step 1 reliever therapy → short-acting β-agonist (SABA) (SOS for sudden exacerbation of symptoms). Steps — I: < 2/month → whenever SABA taken → ICS low dose; II: > 2/month, not daily → daily low dose ICS; III: daily symptoms + night symptoms ≥ 1/week → daily low dose ICS + LABA OR daily medium dose ICS; IV: daily + night symptoms ≥ 1/week + low lung function → daily medium dose ICS + LABA OR high dose ICS; V: uncontrolled on step IV → daily high dose ICS + LABA (+/−), biological agents (last resort).
Asthma Drugs — SABA, LABA, ICS Doses & Biological Agents

SABA: short-acting β-agonist. LABA: long-acting β-agonist (formoterol) — synergistic effect with steroid; steroid sparing effect (long-term). ICS: inhaled corticosteroid — budesonide used. Low dose: 200 to 400 mcg; medium dose: 400 to 800 mcg; high dose: > 800 mcg. Biological agents: immunomodulatory monoclonal antibodies — omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab (anti-IL5), dupilumab (anti-IL4 receptor), anti-TSLP (thymic stromal lymphopoietin): new drug.

Age < 5 yr (preschool): asthma may resolve > 5 yr in some patients. Classification of patient: episodic wheeze (during viral infection), multitrigger wheeze (during respiratory infection + other triggers: cold, exertion, food). Asthma probability: ↑ probability for future asthma (requires treatment) if symptoms last > 10 d after URI AND > 3 episodes. Treatment: controller — daily low-dose ICS therapy + reliever therapy — SABA → review after 2 months → improvement → stop treatment; no improvement → treat as per age 6 to 11 guidelines.

Classification of exacerbation episodes — Sensorium: mild normal, moderate anxious, severe agitated. Dyspneal retractions: mild absent, moderate moderately present, severe severe. SpO2: mild > 95%, moderate 90–95%, severe < 90%. PEFR (% of predicted): mild > 80%, moderate 60–80%, severe < 60%. PEFR: peak expiratory flow rate.

Mild: salbutamol in metered dose inhalers (MDI) — 4–10 puff every 20 minutes. Moderate: salbutamol + ipratropium (centrally acting anti-cholinergics) + O2 to keep SpO2 > 95% + oral prednisolone. Severe: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + oral prednisolone or iv hydrocortisone + inj magnesium sulphate.

Based on age of child: ≥ 12 yr — MDI; 4 to 12 yr — MDI + spacer (allows drug to be suspended in air → inhaled over few breaths); < 4 yr — MDI + spacer + face mask. Rotahaler (not commonly used) — mouth piece for inhalation of powdered rotacap; hole for inserting rotacap; tin; rota chamber: rota cap powdered on twisting.
Respiratory Tract Infections — URT vs LRT Overview
Infections of respiratory tract split into: Upper respiratory tract (URT) — croup, epiglottitis; Lower respiratory tract — acute bronchiolitis, pneumonia.
Croup AKA acute laryngo-tracheo bronchitis. Age 6 months to 5 yrs, peak 2 yrs. Etiology: viral — Parainfluenza virus (m/c): Type 1 m/c (intermediate severity), Type 2 mildest, Type 3 most severe.

URI symptoms (running nose, cough) for 2–3 d → severe barking/seal-like/brassy cough; inflammatory narrowing: larynx→stridor, trachea & bronchi→wheeze; child appears well despite symptoms unless severe. Severity: stridor mild only-on-exertion / moderate & severe at-rest; distress absent/present/severe; SpO2 normal/normal/decreased (<92%).

X-ray: subglottic narrowed air column = steeple/inverted-V sign. Management primarily supportive (self-limiting). Mild: oral dexamethasone (↓ inflammation). Moderate–severe: dexamethasone + O2 inhalation + neb racemic epinephrine (↓ edema in pre-capillary arterioles; 1:1 D and L isomers).

Age 3–6 yrs; bacterial: Hemophilus influenzae type b (m/c in India), Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae. Severe airway inflammation = medical emergency (↑ obstruction risk); sick-looking child, high-grade fever, supraglottic stridor; 3 D's: dysphagia, drooling, dyspnea; tripod posture opens airway. Note: low-grade fever in viral infections.

Investigations: X-ray thumb sign (soft-tissue shadow of swollen epiglottis); laryngoscopy shows inflamed cherry-red epiglottis but NOT done routinely (stimulation → laryngospasm → respiratory arrest). Management: 1. secure airway (priority) — intubation, if not possible tracheostomy; 2. IV antibiotics — 3rd-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime).

Incidence ↑ in winter; age < 2 yrs (peaks 3–6 months). Etiology: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) — Type A more severe, Type B; RSV can cause URIs and LRIs. Pathogenesis: inflammation of bronchioles → edema + ↑ mucus → airway obstruction → ↑↑ narrowing during expiration → air-trapping in lung fields.
Acute Bronchiolitis — Clinical Findings, Investigations, Management & Prevention

Clinical: air-trapping → ↑ AP diameter, hyper-resonance on percussion; narrowed bronchioles → wheeze. Investigations: X-ray peribronchial cuffing (inflammatory exudates) + bilateral hyperinflation; nasopharyngeal swab PCR for RSV. Management: self-limiting (3–7 d); supportive — moist O2 (goal SpO2 > 92%), fluids; antivirals not routine; inhaled ribavirin (nebulized) in at-risk (chronic lung disease, CHD). Prevention: palivizumab (monoclonal antibody against RSV proteins).
Pneumonia in Children — Definition, Etiology & Clinical Features

Infection of lung tissue/parenchyma; leading cause of under-5 mortality. Etiology bacterial > viral: Strep pneumoniae (overall m/c); E. coli & group-B streptococci (m/c in neonates); viral RSV (m/c). Etiological diagnosis not always feasible → X-ray more reliable. Features: fever, productive wet cough (may not be expectorated d/t swallowing), tachypnea, crepitations.
Pneumonia — IMNCI Community Management & Fast-Breathing Criteria

IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal & Childhood Illness) colour-coded 3 categories. No pneumonia (fever, cough/cold) → home paracetamol. Pneumonia (fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, normal SpO2) → home PCT + oral amoxicillin ×5 d; if wheeze + salbutamol ×5 d; cough > 2 wk → evaluate for TB. Severe pneumonia (SpO2 < 90% or ≥1 danger sign: lethargy, not feeding, convulsions, cyanosis) → urgent referral + 1st dose IV ampicillin + gentamicin. Fast breathing: <2 m >60/min; 2–12 m >50/min; >12 m >40/min.

Mode of transmission: droplet; season ↑ incidence: winter. Features: lobar consolidation on chest X-ray; ↓ air entry, crepitations, rusty sputum (if expectorated), bronchial sounds, dull/impaired note on percussion. Treatment: Penicillin G 50,000 IU/kg/day IV 5–7 d; if not available → 3rd-generation cephalosporins (IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime).

Bacteria: Staph aureus. Seen in: spread from another focus (pyoderma/skin), secondary to viral infection (measles, influenza), cystic fibrosis (recurrent pneumonia). X-ray: pneumatocele (air-filled cystic spaces, pathognomonic) → rupture → pneumothorax; B/L patchy consolidation (with pus) → empyema (if < 2 yr → m/c staph) and purulent pericarditis. Treatment: co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) OR ceftriaxone + cloxacillin ×7–10 d; suspected MRSA → + vancomycin.

Organisms: m/c Mycoplasma; age > 5 yr (rarely < 5 yr). Features: low-grade fever, cough, scattered crepitations, hemolysis may be seen. Investigations: X-ray more significant than clinical findings (interstitial pneumonia); cold agglutination test positive (IgM against RBC → hemolysis). Treatment: macrolide antibiotics oral (azithromycin OR erythromycin) ×7–10 d.

Multi-system AR disorder affecting GIT, respiratory, genitourinary & sweat glands; m/c life-limiting genetic disorder. Pathogenesis: CFTR gene (CF transmembrane regulator) on chr 7q codes for CFTR protein (Cl⁻ channel); m/c mutation ΔF508 = deletion of phenylalanine at the 508th position. Mucoviscidosis = thick mucus secretions; defective CFTR → Cl⁻ not transported into lumen → thick mucus, mucus secretion & inflammation.

GIT features are the EARLIEST. Meconium ileus: 10–15% of patients, virtually diagnostic of CF; inspissation of thick meconium in ileum → ileal obstruction → delayed meconium passage + abdominal distension. Investigations: contrast enema — microcolon + filling defects, distended small intestine proximal to terminal ileum, air-fluid levels, ground-glass appearance. Older children: fecal impaction in distal ileum → DIOS; rectal prolapse (rare, d/t early pancreatic enzyme supplementation).

Pancreatic insufficiency (85% cases): initially exocrine (steatorrhea, Vit A/D/E/K deficiency) → later endocrine (diabetes, 4th decade). Respiratory: recurrent infections — early childhood: Staph aureus (m/c), H. influenzae b; late childhood/adults: Pseudomonas (mucoid → biofilm → antibiotic resistance); Burkholderia cepacia = ↑ risk of death; bilateral nasal polyps. Other: biliary cirrhosis/neonatal cholestasis; males azoospermia (Wolffian duct failure), females ↓ fertility; sweat glands — ↑ Na⁺/Cl⁻ loss (↓ reabsorption): salty skin on kissing, frosting, hyponatremic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, ↑ sweat Cl⁻.
Diagnosis — Criteria, Lab Evidence & Sweat Test

Clinical criteria: positive for ANY ONE → confirmatory lab test: typical respiratory/GIT/genitourinary features, history of CF in a sibling (AR), positive newborn screen (immunoreactive trypsin, IRT). Lab evidence: ANY 1 positive lab test confirms CF — sweat chloride >60 mEq/L on separate days; identification of 2 CF mutations; 1 abnormal value of trans-epithelial nasal potential difference. Sweat chloride test = pilocarpine iontophoresis: pilocarpine into skin via electrodes, sweat collected and processed for Cl⁻ levels.
Respiratory Care — Physiotherapy, Mucolytics, Antibiotics & Prophylaxis

Three pillars: airway clearance (physiotherapy; mucolytics — inhaled hypertonic saline 3%, human recombinant DNase/dornase alfa), antibiotics (co-amoxiclav DOC, fluoroquinolone, azithromycin) and prophylaxis for Pseudomonas (3×/week decreases colonization — inhaled tobramycin/aztreonam, oral azithromycin).

Dietary measures: high fat, protein, calories; salt supplementation (more during dehydration); pancreatic enzyme supplements (enterically coated microspheres); fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K. CFTR modulators (↑ CFTR channel activity): ivacaftor (>2 yrs); ivacaftor + lumacaftor (>6 yrs, useful in ΔF508); ivacaftor + tezacaftor (>12 yrs); triple combination (ivacaftor + tezacaftor + elexacaftor) covers most mutations.

Salient features: pulmonary vascular resistance is HIGH (d/t non-functional lungs) → ↑ BP in the right side of the heart. Communications in a fetus: ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus, foramen ovale, umbilical vessels (2 umbilical arteries + 1 umbilical vein).
Circulation Before Birth — Pathway & SaO₂ Values

Placenta (O₂ + nutrients) → umbilical vein (SaO₂ 80%) → fetal portal veins → IVC (SaO₂ 70%). Deoxygenated blood selectively shunted → RV (SaO₂ 55%) → PA → ductus arteriosus (d/t ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance) → aorta. FO: RA → LA → LV (SaO₂ 65%) → aorta → systemic (SaO₂ 50–60%); umbilical arteries (SaO₂ 50–60%); ductus venosus = low resistance by-pass.
Circulatory Changes at Birth & Outcome of Fetal Structures

At birth: placenta cut off → closure of umbilical vessels → closure of ductus venosus; breathing → O₂ enters lungs → ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance → ↓ RV & RA pressures → closure of ductus arteriosus; cord clamping removes low-resistance placental circulation → ↑ systemic (aortic) → LV → LA pressures → closure of foramen ovale. Outcomes: ductus venosus (soon/7 d → ligamentum venosum); foramen ovale (soon/3 months up to 1 yr → fossa ovalis); ductus arteriosus (10–15 h/10–21 d → ligamentum arteriosum).
CHD — Prevalence, Inheritance & p134 Associations (Genetic + Maternal)

Prevalence 6–8/1000 live births; inheritance multifactorial. Most common CHD = VSD; most common cyanotic CHD = TOF. p134 rows: Down — endocardial cushion (AVSD); Turner — bicuspid aortic valve + coarctation of aorta; Noonan — PS + ASD; Overt's diabetes — VSD (m/c) + TGA (most specific); Rubella — PDA, PS, VSD; SLE — heart block d/t Anti-Ro (SS-A) & Anti-La (SS-B).

p135 rows: DiGeorge (CATCHaa, microdeletion) — TOF + conotruncal defects; Williams (microdeletion) — supravalvular aortic stenosis + elfin facies; Holt-Oram (autosomal dominant) — ASD + skeletal anomalies (absent radius/thumb); Alagille — PS, triangular face, cholestasis. Teratogens: Lithium → Ebstein's anomaly; Phenytoin → VSD; Alcohol → VSD.

Diagnosis: presence of 1 major OR 2 minor criteria. Major: 1. systolic murmur ≥ grade 3; 2. any diastolic murmur; 3. central cyanosis with NO improvement on O₂ inhalation (improvement → respiratory etiology); 4. features of CCF. Minor: systolic murmur < grade 3, abnormal BP, abnormal ECG, abnormal X-ray, abnormal S3.

Acyanotic congestive heart defects: Left-to-right (L→R) shunts (oxygenated mixes with deoxygenated → no cyanosis): 1. ASD (5–10%); 2. VSD (m/c, 45%); 3. PDA. Obstructive lesions: coarctation of aorta.

Outlet/subarterial VSD (AKA doubly committed): defect in surrounding structures (aorta, PA) → ↑ risk of aortic defect (m/c AR). Perimembranous VSD (m/c): upper membranous part of IVS. Muscular VSD: lower muscular part of IVS, ↑ spontaneous closure, swiss-cheese pattern (multiple defects). Inlet VSD: never closes spontaneously, ↑ valve defect (m/c mitral).

Turbulent flow → pansystolic (shunt) murmur at left parasternal area of 4th ICS. Mitral valve ↑ flow → delayed diastolic murmur at mitral area (flow murmur); ↑ PA flow → ejection systolic murmur (flow murmur). Shunt murmurs: diagnostic; flow murmurs: not diagnostic.

CT ratio = (a+b)/c (a+b = widest cardiac length each side, c = widest thorax); normal children <0.55, infant <0.6; higher = cardiomegaly, ↑ in VSD; LV enlargement, apex pushed outwards. Early: CCF, forceful flow → RV wall injures → infective endocarditis (m/c Streptococcus viridans), lung congestion → recurrent pneumonia. Late: Eisenmenger (RV hypertrophy → RV > LV → R→L reversal → cyanosis). Medical (non-curative): digoxin + furosemide, antibiotics. Surgery: CCF after supportive Rx, Qp:Qs > 2:1, valve defect (esp AR); Dacron patch or percutaneous device.

Ostium secundum ASD: upper part of septum (m/c). Ostium primum ASD: lower part of septum — associated with valve defects (esp mitral insufficiency) and conduction defects d/t location. Sinus venosus ASD (SVC type at SVC opening; IVC type at IVC opening): rare. Coronary sinus ASD: between atrium and coronary sinus — rare.

Minimal pressure difference → smooth flow → no shunt murmurs; flow murmurs (delayed diastolic, ejection systolic); delayed closure of pulmonary valves → delayed P2 → wide fixed splitting of S2 (diagnostic). ECG determines location: secundum = right-axis deviation; primum = left-axis deviation (left fascicular block; mitral insufficiency → left chamber overload). Elective closure: >3–5 y (upto school-going age, no spontaneous closure), size >8 mm; early closure: uncontrolled CCF or Qp:Qs > 2:1.

Incidence: preterm (kept patent by prostaglandin) > term babies; association: congenital rubella. Aorta → via PDA → pulmonary artery; turbulent flow (large pressure difference) → loud continuous machinery murmur at parasternal area & left ICS. Complications: congestion d/t ↑ flow — lungs (first) → recurrent pneumonia, heart → CCF; Eisenmenger (reversal of shunt, late): upper limbs spared, only lower limbs cyanotic = differential cyanosis.

Medical: supportive (CCF: digoxin + furosemide; pneumonia: antibiotics); curative only in preterm — NSAIDs ↓ prostaglandin → PDA closure, ibuprofen > indomethacin (↓ nephrotoxicity, NEC). Surgical: preterm not responding or C/I to medical (platelets <80,000, creatinine >1.8 mg/dl, active bleeding) + all term babies; techniques: ligation, percutaneous catheterization with occluders/coils.

m/c location: juxta-ductal (near ductus arteriosus). Near complete (uncommon): severely restricted flow → shock in neonates. Partial narrowing (m/c): ↓ flow to lower limbs — claudication pain, feeble femoral pulses, radio-femoral delay; ↓ renal flow (ischemia) → renin → RAAS (↑ aldosterone) → hypertension++; systemic hypertension d/t ↑ resistance. Note: hypertension → hypertensive encephalopathy → presents with seizures.

Older children (>10 y): formation of collaterals → blood diverted to intercostal arteries → dilated & tortuous IC arteries → pressure on lower border of rib → inferior rib notching. X-ray: pre-stenotic dilatation + stenosis + post-stenotic dilatation = 3-sign. Treatment: balloon dilatation of coarctation ± stenting.

Cyanotic CHD are rarely seen compared to acyanotic CHD. ↑ pulmonary blood flow: HLHS, truncus arteriosus, TGA, TAPVC. ↓ pulmonary blood flow (m/c group): TOF (m/c), tricuspid atresia, Ebstein's anomaly.

4 components: 1. overriding of aorta (shift of aorta towards right); 2. PA output inversely proportional to severity of sub-pulmonary stenosis (determinant of cyanosis); 3. VSD; 4. subpulmonary stenosis (aka infundibular hypertrophy / RVOT obstruction) with RVH.

Cyanosis: onset within 4 months after birth (varies with severity of sub-pulmonary stenosis). Single S2: A2 heard, P2 not heard d/t stenosis. Murmur: ejection systolic in pulmonary area — disappears during cyanotic spell (surest sign of TOF); VSD non-restrictive → no turbulent flow → no pansystolic murmur (free flow across VSD). X-ray: boot-shaped heart (RVH, uplifting of apex).

Cyanotic spell: ↑ severity of cyanosis; disappearance of shunt murmur = surest sign of TOF. Cycle: infundibular spasm (narrowing) → worsening hypoxia → lactic acidosis → stimulation of respiratory centre → hyperventilation → ↑ venous return → more spasm. Management: O2, sodium bicarbonate, morphine (depress respiratory centre), β-blockers, squatting (older children)/knee-to-chest (infants) → femoral artery compression; α-agonist (phenylephrine) → ↑ SVR (aorta) → ↑ afterload for LV → ↓↓ RV→LV flow → ↓ cyanosis.

Definitive: VSD repair + correction of stenosis (performed < 3 months). Palliative shunt surgery → improve pulmonary blood flow → improve cyanosis: in delayed presentations or C/I to definitive surgery; method — shunting systemic artery to pulmonary artery: classic Blalock-Taussig (B-T) with subclavian artery; modified B-T (artificial conduit, m/c); Waterston with ascending aorta; Potts with descending aorta.

Atresia of tricuspid valve → ↓ blood flow to RV → ↓ blood flow to PA → cyanosis. PFO or ASD mandatory → overload of blood to LA and LV → hypertrophy of left heart. ECG: left-axis deviation. Note: all CHD are diagnosed by ECHO cardiography. Treatment: staged shunt surgery — 1. modified B-T shunt (immediately) → 2. Glenn shunt (SVC to PA) → 3. Fontan shunt (IVC to PA).

Inferior/apical displacement of septal leaflet of tricuspid valve (normal position shown) → atrialization of RV; ↑ RA size; ↓ RV size → ↓ RV blood volume → ↓ blood flow to PA → cyanosis. X-ray: box-shaped heart (increased PA size). Associations: lithium exposure; accessory pathways on right side — WPW (Bundle of Kent: RA→RV) → early pre-excitation of RV → slurred QRS (delta wave, short PR, wide QRS). Treatment: cone repair of tricuspid valve, return valve to original position.

1. atresia of mitral valve → no communication between LA and LV; 2. hypoplastic LV; 3. hypoplastic aorta → severely ↓ systemic flow → shock in neonates. ASD seen in majority of cases → ↑ blood flow to RA & RV → early onset CCF (< 1 week). Treatment: fatal if untreated/delayed; Norwood procedure — surgical creation of Neo (new) aorta to ↑ blood flow.

Common outflow tract (TA) — mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from RV and LV → cyanosis. A type of conotruncal defect (includes TOF, interrupted aortic arch etc.); associated with DiGeorge syndrome. Treatment: Rastelli's procedure — truncus arteriosus partitioned → normal blood outflow.

TGA with intact ventricular septum: parallel circulation (separate tracts for oxygenated and deoxygenated blood) → early onset cyanosis (within few minutes) → fatal. TGA with VSD: blood flows LV→RV, mixing → less intense cyanosis + pansystolic murmur + CCF. X-ray: egg (heart) + string (narrow positioning of great arteries) = egg-on-string appearance. Treatment (intact septum): emergency — 1. PGE-1 infusion immediately at birth (keeps DA open: O2 blood PA→aorta); 2. atrial septostomy (RA↔LA connection → ↑ O2 status); definitive: Jatene's arterial switch repair. TGA with VSD: electively (few weeks after birth) → Jatene's.

Abnormal connections between PV and RA. Types by route: 1. supracardiac (m/c) — PV → superior vena cava → RA; 2. cardiac — PV → RA directly; 3. infracardiac — PV → portal veins → RA. Obstructive type: pulmonary venous obstruction → congestion of lungs → severe cyanosis. Non-obstructive (m/c): equal O2 saturation in all heart chambers; ASD with wide fixed splitting of S2; mixed blood in aorta → cyanosis. X-ray: supracardiac TAPVC — snowman/figure-of-8 appearance (d/t ↑ SVC size).

Post-streptococcal disorder → Group A β-hemolytic streptococci; school-going children (5–15 yrs); m = F; pharyngitis → rheumatic fever in 10 days to few weeks via molecular mimicry; antibodies cross-react with heart, joints and skin; probability 0.3% (epidemic 1–3%). Risk stratification (India = moderate–high risk): ARF incidence per lakh school-going children: low risk < a vs moderate–high > a; RHD prevalence per 1000 population: low < 1 vs moderate–high > 1.

Major (moderate–high risk): 1. pancarditis (clinical or subclinical ECHO+); 2. arthritis (mono/polyarthritis/polyarthralgia); 3. subcutaneous nodules; 4. erythema marginatum; 5. Sydenham's chorea. Low risk: only polyarthritis counts as major. Minor (moderate–high / low risk): arthralgia mono/poly; fever ≥38 / ≥38.5; ESR ≥30 / ≥60 mm/hr and/or CRP ≥3 mg/dl; PR interval listed only for moderate–high risk.

Essential (preceding streptococcal infection): elevated ASO titer (preferred); throat swab culture (false +/− → not preferred); history of preceding sore throat (< 50%). Diagnosis + essential criteria: first episode — 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor; recurrence — 2 major OR 1 major + 1 minor OR 3 minor.

m/c feature of ARF (90%); early finding (within 2 weeks); all 3 layers → pancarditis; most serious (permanent valve damage). Pericarditis: chest pain + friction rub. Valvular m/c → mitral (F > m) > aortic (m > F): mitral valvulitis → Carey Coombs murmur (delayed diastolic); mitral regurgitation → soft S1, pansystolic murmur, hemodynamic overload → LVF (morbidity/mortality in ARF).
Large joints (knee, ankle, elbow) migratory arthritis; early finding, 30–50% of affected children; excellent response to aspirin; complete recovery (no residual joint damage).

EM: rare, early stages; erythematous with pale center → coalesce → serpiginous rash; non-pruritic; starts in trunk then limbs; face not involved; induced by warmth/heat. Nodules: late finding (≥ 6 weeks); painless; around bony prominences (elbow, shin, occiput, ankle); high risk of carditis.

Last manifestation (3 months after onset); semi purposeful jerky movements of limbs → abnormal coordination & posturing; associated: hypotonia, emotional lability, jerky speech; milkmaid grip sign (alternate tightening/loosening of grip); darting tongue sign (uncontrollable sliding in & out of tongue on protrusion); self resolving (2–6 weeks); if not resolving — diazepam, haloperidol.

Treatment: bed rest for 2 weeks; penicillin — Inj. Penicillin G (Benzathine) single dose OR oral Penicillin V 250 mg QID × 10 days OR if allergic erythromycin 450 mg QID × 10 days; anti-inflammatories (steroids/aspirin). 2° prophylaxis: Benzathine/Penicillin G >30 kg: 12 lakh IU every 3 weeks; <30 kg: 6 lakh IU every 2 weeks; oral Pen V 250 mg BD; if allergic erythromycin 250 mg BD.

Anti-inflammatory (for 12 weeks): steroids preferred (esp. cardiac problems) — oral prednisolone (2–40 mg/kg/day) × 3 weeks → taper over 9 weeks; aspirin 90–120 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses × 10 weeks → taper over next 2 weeks. Prophylaxis duration: no carditis — next 5 years or till age 18 (whichever longer); carditis (without RHD) — next 10 years or till age 25 (whichever longer); established RHD/undergone surgery — till age 40 (ideal: life long).

Normal contralateral kidney → hypertrophy → normal overall renal function → asymptomatic; incidental finding on USG; treatment: reassurance, avoid contact sports (trauma to unaffected kidney); female: associated MRKH (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser) syndrome — pelvis USG rules out uterine maldevelopment, vaginal aplasia, normal ovaries.

Both kidneys not developed: severe presentation. ↓ urine output → ↓ amniotic fluid (severe oligohydramnios antenatal) → fetal compression → Potter's syndrome. Facial: prominent epicanthal folds, low/depressed nasal bridge, low set ears, redundant skin, receding chin. Body: pulmonary hypoplasia (d/t chest compression; if severe → death), limb deformities (CTEV: congenital talipes equino varus).

Dysplasia = abnormal differentiation. M/c: cystic dysplasia → M/c: multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) d/t abnormal metanephric differentiation; M/c cystic renal malformation. Pathogenesis: 20–40% VUR → kidney damage; hypertrophy → renal function normal; usually unilateral (L > R); cysts compress normal kidney structures → dysfunctional kidney; spontaneous involution by 5–7 years of age.

Bilateral condition → ↓ kidney function → progression to CKD, uncontrolled HTN; characterized by multiple cysts; gene defect: PKHD1 gene (chromosome 6p) → hepatic manifestations: liver cirrhosis (periportal fibrosis); O/E: bilateral abdominal mass (loin area). Diagnosis: gene testing (PKHD1); USG: hyperechoic bright kidneys + loss of cortico medullary differentiation. Treatment: dual transplantation (renal + hepatic).
Defect: fusion of lower poles of kidney (isthmus). Genetic association: Turner's syndrome (30%). Complications: ureteral obstruction → hydronephrosis, UTI, stone, ↑ risk of Wilms' tumor (4 fold).

Anomalies causing obstructive uropathy: PUJ obstruction > PUV. PUJ: congenital; usually unilateral L > R; antenatal: ↑ size of kidney (hydronephrosis); postnatal: abdominal mass, stone, UTI; older child: Dietl's crisis (intermittent severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting). Investigations: DTPA scan (kidney, bladder, PU obstruction, kidney retaining tracer; helps assess renal function → management); IVU: contrast retained in kidneys. Management: normal renal function → follow-up (spontaneous resolution); abnormal → Anderson Hynes pyeloplasty (relieving obstruction).

Only seen in male child; m/c severe cause of obstructive uropathy. Pathophysiology: membrane valve causing obstruction; location: prostatic urethra (lower part), just distal to verumontanum. Features: dilated ureter, bladder with dilated trabeculations, dilated posterior urethra. Clinical: poor urine stream, abdominal mass, UTI, hydronephrosis. Investigation: MCU (dilated bladder, dilated posterior urethra, PUV). Management: primary — catheter (relieve obstruction); definitive — endoscopic (cystoscopic) fulguration of valve.
Defects shown: omphalocele; bladder exstrophy (fleshy mass); ileal exstrophy (terminal part of ileum).

1. massive proteinuria (hall mark): excretion > 40 mg/m2/hr or > 1 g/m2/day; spot dipstick 3+/4+; P:C ratio > 2. 2. hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin < 3 g/dl) → ↓ oncotic pressure. 3. anasarca. 4. hyperlipidemia (d/t ↑ production of lipoprotein and lipid by liver).

MCD: m/c. Significant glomerular lesions: FSGS, mesangial proliferative glomerulonephropathy, C3 glomerulopathy. MCD pathogenesis: effacement of negatively charged foot process of podocyte → negatively-charged protein not repelled → ↑ protein excretion. Management: diet (high protein, no added salt); prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day daily (upto 60 mg) × 6 weeks then 1.5 mg/kg/day alternate days (upto 40 mg) × 6 weeks; response (confirms MCD without biopsy): urine protein < 4 mg/m2/hr or dipstick nil/trace; P:C ratio < 0.2; diuretic for significant edema: furosemide → if no response add spironolactone.

Course: presentation → remission / relapse (recurrence of proteinuria; daily steroids 2 mg/kg/day → alternate day 1.5 mg/kg/day; continue 4 weeks; relapse during alternate-day therapy or relapse within 14 d of stoppage = steroid dependence). Frequent relapses: ≥ 2 relapses in 6 months OR ≥ 3 relapses in 1 year. Management: avoid steroids (toxicity); immunomodulatory: levamisole, mycophenolate. Steroid resistant NS: usually d/t significant glomerular lesions / congenital NS (onset > 3 months). Investigations: renal biopsy, GFR estimation, genetic testing — NPHS1 (Finnish type; nephrin; AR), NPHS2 (podocin; AR), WT1 (Denys-Drash; AD; ↑ Wilms risk, ambiguous genitalia in male). Management: calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporin, tacrolimus).

Proteinuria of → ↓ immunoglobulins/complement proteins → impaired opsonization → ↑ risk of encapsulated bacterial infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type B) → spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), cellulitis, pneumonia. Also: ↓ anticoagulant proteins (Protein C / Protein S) + ↑ fibrinogen production in liver → hypercoagulability → infarctions (eg: stroke).

Clinical features: hematuria (hall mark; cola-colored urine; urine microscopy: > 5 RBC/hpf, dysmorphic RBC, RBC casts); oliguria; localized edema (eg: periorbital puffiness of eyes); hypertension (HTN); mild proteinuria. Diseases seen: post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, hereditary nephritis.

Post-infectious phenomenon; course 7–10 days; pathogenesis: Group A β hemolytic streptococci. Initial infection (pharyngitis/pyoderma) → formation of immune complexes → deposited in kidney → nephritis. Lag period: 1–2 wks: pharyngitis (M4, M12 strains); 3–6 wks: pyoderma (M49 strain).

Incidence: m/c age 5–15 years (school-going); male > female. Presentation: abrupt onset hematuria, oliguria, edema, HTN; preceding h/o infection not requisite for diagnosis; degree of oliguria decides severity. Complications: hypertensive encephalopathy (seizures), left ventricular failure. Investigations: antibody titre (ASO; anti-DNAase B additionally in skin infection); serum C3 ↓ in immune complex-mediated disorders, normalises within 8–12 weeks; renal biopsy not routinely — indications: persistent low C3 > 12 weeks, systemic illness (high fever, rash, joint pain), no resolution > 10 days. Findings: EM sub-epithelial immune complex deposits → humps; IF IgG + C3 in capillary walls and mesangium → starry sky appearance. Management: self-limiting; supportive for HTN (amlodipine, nifedipine); no prophylactic role of antibiotics (unlike rheumatic fever).

Berger's disease: m/c cause of chronic and recurrent nephritis (associated with CKD). Pathogenesis: any viral/bacterial URTI → IgA in mesangium and capillary walls. Investigations: C3 normal; ASO titre no increase; renal biopsy mesangial proliferation + IgA deposits. Management: chronic nephropathy (constant follow-up) → 10–20% cases → CKD; ACE inhibitors/ARB → ↓ renal progression → ↓ CKD risk; fish oil (omega-3 PUFA) → ↓ macrophage entry into mesangium → no initiating factors for IgA deposition.

AKA Alport syndrome. m/c inheritance: X-linked dominant. Genetic defect: COL4A5 gene (α5 chain of type IV collagen). Clinical: triad — hematuria, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, ocular findings (anterior lenticonus = diagnostic, macular flecks, corneal erosions). Investigations: COL4A5 gene testing; renal biopsy: lamellations (basket weave), thinning + thickening of GBM. Management: regular follow-up (many develop ESRD by 2nd–3rd decade); supportive; ACE inhibitors → ↓ renal progression.

Tubular defects reduce reabsorption: water loss causes polyuria with compensatory polydipsia, electrolyte loss causes imbalance, and nutrient loss causes failure to thrive. Fanconi is a generalized proximal-tubule/type II RTA defect.
Fanconi retains distal urinary acidification (urine pH <5.5). Its associations include cystinosis, Lowe syndrome, Wilson disease and galactosemia; cystinosin failure traps cystine in lysosomes.

Bartter is an autosomal-recessive ascending-loop defect beginning in infancy. Na-K-2Cl transport failure causes salt and calcium loss, RAAS activation, hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis; ROMK or Barttin-related chloride defects have key distinctions.
Gitelman is an autosomal-recessive DCT disorder presenting in older children. Na-Cl and magnesium loss activates RAAS and causes hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia.

Liddle is an autosomal-dominant gain-of-function ENaC disorder: sodium retention gives hypertension and suppressed aldosterone, while potassium loss produces hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Use acid-base status, BP, urinary calcium and magnesium to separate the inherited tubulopathies.
Acute Kidney Injury — Definition, Staging & Biomarkers

AKI is acute impairment of kidney function, diagnosed by a creatinine rise or oliguria. Learn the KDIGO-style stage thresholds, Schwartz eGFR and the limitations of serum creatinine alongside newer biomarkers.

Classify AKI into pre-renal hypoperfusion, renal parenchymal causes and post-renal obstruction. Restore perfusion in pre-renal AKI; restrict fluid in renal AKI and treat important electrolyte/acid-base complications safely.

Typical diarrhea-positive HUS follows Shiga toxin from Shigella dysenteriae or EHEC O157:H7. Endothelial injury drives microangiopathic hemolysis and renal injury; distinguish complement-mediated diarrhea-negative HUS and treat appropriately.
CKD is persistent functional decline or renal abnormality for at least three months. Know the GFR bands, including initial hyperfiltration, and link advanced disease to its complications.

Congenital anomalies are the most common CKD cause. Correct reversible structural disease surgically; otherwise support growth and prevent/treat anemia, mineral bone disease, short stature and hypertension.

Progressive CKD refractory to medical therapy needs KRT at GFR <12. Dialysis is accessible while awaiting a donor; renal transplantation is definitive. Compare home peritoneal dialysis with hospital hemodialysis.

VUR is usually congenital backward flow from bladder to ureter due to a short/absent submucosal tunnel. It is autosomal dominant, promotes recurrent UTI and renal scarring, and is confirmed/graded by MCU (VCUG).

VUR often resolves spontaneously. Grade it by the extent of reflux/dilatation. Support fluids and bowel-bladder function; give prophylaxis in grade 3–5, and consider reimplantation after breakthrough UTI.

In infants UTI may be fever without a focus; E. coli is most common. Distinguish simple from complicated and recurrent infections. Urine culture is definitive and CFU thresholds depend on collection method.

Hospitalize complicated UTI and young infants. Treat complicated and simple UTI with their respective duration/regimens. After the first episode, sequence USG KUB, delayed MCU when indicated and DMSA for scars.

NTDs are the commonest congenital CNS malformations. Learn maternal risks, anterior/posterior neuropore timing and the spectrum from occult spina bifida through meningocele to severe myelomeningocele.
Cranial NTDs include lethal anencephaly, occipital encephalocele, iniencephaly and craniorachischisis. Diagnose antenatally by ultrasound and markers; folate before conception markedly lowers risk.

Migration defects include smooth agyric lissencephaly, cleft-like schizencephaly, white-matter-lined porencephalic cysts, agenesis of corpus callosum/Aicardi syndrome and SHH-related holoprosencephaly.

Hydrocephalus is increased intracranial CSF volume. Separate obstructive causes (especially aqueductal stenosis) from non-obstructive overproduction or impaired absorption, and know Dandy-Walker, Chiari and vein-of-Galen patterns.

Raised CSF volume in infants causes macrocephaly and features of raised ICP, including sunset eyes. Screen with neurosonography, confirm with MRI, reduce CSF medically with acetazolamide or divert it with VP shunt; remember shunt infection.
Seizures & Febrile Seizures — Definition and Types

Seizures are paroxysmal abnormal brain electrical activity. Fever-provoked febrile seizures occur in neurologically normal 6-month to 5-year-olds without CNS infection or prior unprovoked seizures; classify simple versus complex accurately.
Febrile Seizures — Recurrence, Epilepsy Risk & Management

Recurrence risk rises with early age, early-in-fever onset and high fever, plus family/complex and other minor risks. Use LP selectively to exclude meningitis, control fever, and reserve intermittent prophylaxis for substantial recurrence risk.
Absence Seizures & Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy — Core Features
Absence seizures cause brief vacant staring in schoolchildren and have characteristic 3-Hz EEG; JME affects adolescents with morning myoclonus, preserved consciousness and 4–6-Hz polyspike-wave EEG.

JME causes awakening myoclonus, often with GTCS/absence, and is treated lifelong with valproate. West syndrome begins before one year with infantile spasms, regression and hypsarrhythmia; urgent ACTH is key.

Dravet is severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy due to SCN1A and may need stiripentol. Lennox-Gastaut combines delay, refractory seizures and slow spikes. Treat status after 5 minutes; neuronal injury risk rises beyond 30.

For seizures beyond five minutes, stabilize ABCD and obtain IV access, correct glucose first, then give IV benzodiazepine, second-line antiseizure therapy and continuous anesthetic infusions for refractory status with EEG monitoring.
Cerebral Palsy — Introduction, Etiology & Spastic Topography

CP is static encephalopathy—the commonest chronic motor disability of childhood—with non-progressive injury to the developing brain. Learn causes across time periods and the spastic diplegia/hemiplegia/quadriplegia map.
Cerebral Palsy — Other Types, Clinical Features & Management

Dyskinetic CP follows basal-ganglia injury (asphyxia/kernicterus); ataxic CP reflects cerebellar vermis injury. Recognize delayed development, persistent primitive reflexes and spasticity, then manage symptoms in a multidisciplinary plan.
Pyogenic meningitis organisms vary by age, with pneumococcus overall most common. Identify increased-ICP and meningeal signs, avoid LP in severe raised ICP, and recognize the bacterial CSF profile.

Treat pyogenic meningitis with third-generation cephalosporin, add vancomycin after nonresponse, and give dexamethasone with initial therapy to reduce SNHL. TB meningitis follows rupture of a hematogenously seeded Rich focus.

TB meningitis has a nonspecific 1–4-week prodrome before meningeal disease. Diagnose basal-cistern exudates and the CSF pattern, then treat 9–12 months with HRZE intensive phase followed by HR, plus corticosteroids.

Encephalitis produces cortical-lobe signs. Japanese encephalitis is mosquito-borne rural disease targeting basal ganglia/thalamus; HSV is the commonest sporadic cause and targets temporal lobe with PLEDs—each has distinctive tests and treatment.

NCC is Taenia solium disease in children over three, acquired through undercooked pork or fecal-oral eggs. Recognize scolex-containing cysts and their imaging patterns, reduce edema first, then select cysticidal and antiseizure therapy.
Spinal Muscular Atrophy — Genetics & Clinical Features

Neuromuscular disorders combine spinal-cord/peripheral-nerve involvement with muscle weakness. SMA is autosomal recessive 5q SMN disease causing lower-motor-neuron hypotonia, atrophy and fasciculations while sparing extraocular muscles and mentation.
SMA — Severity Types, Complications & Modern Therapy

SMA severity spans fatal prenatal type 0 through ambulant types 3–4. Swallowing-muscle hypotonia causes aspiration pneumonitis, a key mortality cause. Disease-modifying treatments restore SMN/exon-7 function but SMA is not classically curable.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy — Basis & Early Features

DMD is the commonest neuromuscular-dystrophy variant: X-linked recessive dystrophin loss destabilizes muscle, producing fiber death and fibrofatty replacement. Learn the early milestones, proximal weakness, Gower maneuver and calf pseudohypertrophy.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy — Progression, Tests & Treatment

DMD progression brings axial deformity, bulbar dysfunction and eventually cardiorespiratory death. Confirm with marked CK elevation/gene testing or biopsy; steroids slow apoptosis and targeted drugs address exon skipping or nonsense mutations.

Becker is a milder dystrophin allelic variant with later onset but early cardiomyopathy. FSHD is autosomal dominant with facial, scapular and humeral weakness. Limb-girdle disease affects shoulder/hip girdles with preserved neck/bulbar muscle and normal IQ.
Type 1 myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant DMPK disease from expanded CTG repeats. Recognize the hatchet face, delayed relaxation, distal weakness, cataract and endocrine associations.
Growth Hormone Deficiency — Types & Laron Dwarfism

GHD is mostly idiopathic; isolated congenital forms follow developmental pituitary anomalies or GH1/GHRHR mutations, while acquired forms follow craniopharyngioma, germinoma, infiltration or irradiation. Laron dwarfism = defective hepatic GH receptor so IGF-1 is low despite GH action failing.

Isolated GHD: normal at birth (GH has no fetal role), then proportionate short stature with growth velocity < 4 cm/yr, more than 2 SD below mid-parental height, apparent adiposity, prominent cheeks, overweight and delayed bone age. With hypopituitarism add micropenis, hypoglycemia and prolonged jaundice.

Screen with IGF-1 (or IGFBP-3 when malnourished); confirm with provocative GH testing (insulin, clonidine, arginine) — a stimulated GH < 10 ng/ml is diagnostic. Treat with nightly subcutaneous rGH until epiphyseal closure; other rGH uses spell GTCS-IN-P.

Early detection matters because thyroid hormone drives brain development — undetected CH is the m/c preventable intellectual disability. Thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia/hypoplasia/ectopic lingual thyroid) is the m/c cause; features emerge after the 1st week once maternal hormones wane.

Screen every newborn: heel-prick dried blood spot TSH at 3–4 days; > 40 mU/L → send TFT → start treatment stat. Confirm anatomy with USG/radionuclide (I-131 preferred over Tc-99m). Treat early with oral thyroxine 10–15 μg/kg/day, targeting normal free T4, lifelong.

Endemic cretinism (severe iodine deficiency) is neurological (most severe, goitre, deaf-mutism, spasticity) or myxedematous (madarosis, periorbital puffiness, no goitre). Acquired hypothyroidism = Hashimoto thyroiditis in adolescent females: short stature, weight gain, firm nodular goitre.

All adrenal steroids derive from cholesterol. Glucocorticoid synthesis is ACTH-regulated; aldosterone is regulated by intravascular volume, plasma K+ and RAAS. StAR (steroidogenic acute regulatory protein) shuttles cholesterol into mitochondria.

Cushing syndrome = excess glucocorticoids; the m/c cause overall is exogenous steroid therapy. Endogenous disease is ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma, young children) or ACTH-dependent (pituitary microadenoma = Cushing disease; ectopic ACTH from neuroblastoma, Wilms tumour, carcinoid).

Glucocorticoid excess blocks lipolysis → fat deposition: moon facies, abdominal obesity, striae and buffalo hump. Hypertension (intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity), hirsutism (ACTH-driven androgens), delayed puberty (cortisol inhibits gonadotropins), proximal muscle weakness and short stature.

Screen with 24-hour urine free cortisol and the overnight dexamethasone suppression test; confirm with low-dose DST (5 μg/kg q6H × 2 days). ACTH level separates ACTH-independent (<15 pg/mL) from pituitary (>15) and ectopic (>100); high-dose DST confirms pituitary suppressibility. Treat by tumour resection, trans-sphenoidal surgery, or medical adrenalectomy.

CAH is the m/c adrenal disorder of childhood, autosomal recessive. Enzyme blockade lowers glucocorticoids → loss of feedback → ↑ACTH → tropic stimulation → adrenal hyperplasia with shunting of precursors. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the m/c form; 11-β-OH and 17-α-OH are the other classics.

21-OH deficiency blocks aldosterone and cortisol → salt wasting (hyponatremia, shock, hyperkalemia) with androgen excess (precocious puberty in males, ambiguous genitalia in females) and ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation. Screen with 17-OHP; replace hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone lifelong with stress dosing.

11-β-OH deficiency piles up 11-deoxycorticosterone — a mineralocorticoid — so the child is hypertensive despite low aldosterone, with androgen excess (virilisation/precocious puberty) and ACTH-mediated hyperpigmentation.

17-α-OH deficiency: hypertension with undervirilised males and delayed puberty (low androgens). 3-β-HSD deficiency: salt wasting with undervirilised males and mildly virilised females (DHEA). Pointers: salt wasting + high androgen → 21-OH; salt wasting + low androgen → 3-β-HSD; HTN + high androgen → 11-β-OH; HTN + low androgen → 17-α-OH.
Puberty Basics & Delayed Puberty — Definition, Central Causes

Puberty is defined by appearance of secondary sexual characters — thelarche first in girls, testicular enlargement first in boys. Delayed puberty: no pubertal change by 14 y (boys), no thelarche by 13 y or menarche by 16 y / 5 y after thelarche (girls); constitutional delay is the m/c cause.
Delayed Puberty — Peripheral Causes & Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome

Peripheral (hypergonadotropic) causes: Turner streak ovaries, Klinefelter cryptorchidism, 17-α-OH CAH and androgen-action defects. Classical AIS: AR gene mutation, X-linked recessive, 46 XY — phenotypic female, uterus absent, sparse pubic hair, inguinal testes.

At puberty AIS testes make very high testosterone, aromatised to estrogen for breast development; partial forms may virilise ("apparent change of gender"). Replace sex steroids: ethinylestradiol (girls) with progesterone 2 years later, testosterone (boys) — early use fuses epiphyses → short stature.

Precocious puberty: pubertal changes before 8 y (girls) or 9.5 y (boys). Central (gonadotropin-dependent): idiopathic m/c in girls, CNS pathology (hypothalamic hamartoma) m/c in boys — think gelastic seizures. Peripheral: testicular Leydig/Sertoli tumours, autonomous ovarian cyst (McCune-Albright), CAH.

McCune-Albright = GNAS1 gain-of-function (Gs α-subunit) → autonomous endocrine hyperfunction (thyroid, pituitary, adrenal, ovaries). Triad: polyendocrinopathy (precocious puberty), café-au-lait spots with irregular Coast-of-Maine margins not crossing midline, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (skull base, proximal femur — Shepherd crook).

Treat the underlying condition. Central precocious puberty: long-acting GnRH analogue (leuprolide) — sustained stimulation desensitises the pituitary, lowering LH/FSH and sex steroids. McCune-Albright: aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) cut the final step of estrogen synthesis.

DKA is based on ISPAD guidelines. Severe insulin deficiency (insulinopenia) together with a rise in counter-regulatory hormones (growth hormone, glucagon, cortisol) — precipitated by infection or trauma — produces hyperglycemia with increased lipolysis: the osmotic effect of glucose causes intracellular dehydration and pseudohyponatremia, while hepatic oxidation of fatty acids forms ketone bodies (acetone, aceto-acetate, β-hydroxybutyrate) → Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, fruity breath.

Three components: hyperglycemia > 200 mg/dl + acidosis (venous pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate < 18 mmol/l) + raised ketones (ketonemia β-hydroxybutyrate ≥ 5.3 mmol/l — not used because of low accuracy — or ketonuria ≥ 2+ on dipstick).

Severity is graded by venous pH, serum bicarbonate and estimated dehydration: mild 7.2–7.3 / < 18 mmol/L / 5% of body weight; moderate 7.1–7.2 / < 10 mmol/L / 7% BW; severe < 7.1 / < 5 mmol/L / 10% BW.

Three pillars: correct the pathology (insulin for hyperglycemia), correct dehydration (fluid restoration), identify & treat the precipitating event (e.g. focus of infection). Minimal dehydration → oral fluids + s/c insulin. Moderate or greater dehydration → 10–20 ml/kg IV 0.9% NS over 20–30 min, insulin started after fluids as 0.05–0.1 U/kg/hr infusion → s/c on improvement. Shock → secure ABC then 20 ml/kg 0.9% NS bolus. C/I: insulin bolus (↑↑ insulin during resuscitation → cerebral edema).

Cerebral edema → slow deficit correction over 24–48 hr. Insulin-induced hypokalemia → NS + 40 mEq/L KCl; bicarbonate therapy is contraindicated (worsens CNS acidosis & hypokalemia). Blood glucose < 300 mg/dl → add 5% dextrose to IV fluids to prevent hypoglycemia. Hypernatremia restores on treating the hyperglycemia.

Leukemia is the m/c hematological malignancy. Its hallmarks are clonal proliferation plus arrest of maturation (the tumour cells are of immature cell series). Acute leukemia (ALL, AML) is far more common than chronic leukemia in children.

ALL is the m/c malignancy in children, peak age 2–5 years, males > females. Increased-risk conditions: ataxia telangiectasia, Bloom's syndrome, SCID, Down syndrome, Fanconi's anemia, Le Fraumeni syndrome and environmental factors such as ionizing radiation.

Based on cell type (CD markers by flow cytometry): pre-B cell — m/c: 85% — CD10 (marker of good prognosis), CD19, CD20, CD45 → good prognosis with treatment; mature B cell (and most common) — CD19, CD20, CD21 with surface Ig positivity → intensified treatment required; T cell — CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8 → mediastinal involvement plus CNS manifestations. The cytogenetic classification uses chromosome number and translocations.

Bone marrow failure → pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia — seen as petechiae — and leukopenia; a few patients may still show leukocytes) with night bone pains from infiltration. Extramedullary involvement in > 60%: hepatosplenomegaly/splenomegaly, superficial lymphadenopathy (non-tender, firm, fixed, confluent), mediastinal involvement (tracheal compression, SVC syndrome with facial flushing/edema and jugular vein distension), CNS leukemia (cranial neuropathies, seizures, ↑ICT features) and painless testicular swelling.

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy; aspiration may be normal. ≥ 25% lymphoblasts confirms ALL. Standard-risk/good prognosis: age 2–10 y, female, no CNS involvement, initial WBC < 50,000/mm³, pre-B cell subtype, hyperdiploidy (> 50 chromosomes) or trisomy 4, 10. High-risk/poor prognosis: age ≤ 1 y or > 10 y, male, CNS involvement, WBC > 50,000/mm³, B or T cell subtype, hypodiploidy (< 44 chromosomes), t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome or t(4;11) infantile leukemia (< 1 y old).

Phase I induction (prednisolone, L-asparaginase, anthracycline, vincristine) — induce remission and look for response: ↓ WBC count, no blasts in marrow and circulation = good response/good prognosis; minimal residual disease (MRD) is beyond conventional detection and is tested by flow cytometry/PCR. Phase II prophylactic CNS therapy — intrathecal methotrexate for subclinical CNS involvement. Phase III consolidation/intensification — methotrexate, epipodophyllotoxin, cyclophosphamide, cytosine-arabinoside — to tackle drug resistance and sustain remission. Phase IV maintenance (once a week for a year) — 6-mercaptopurine and methotrexate — to prevent relapse.

AML is the 2nd m/c type of leukemia. FAB: M0 minimal differentiation, M1 without maturation, M2 with maturation, M3 APML, M4 myelomonocytic leukemia, M5 monocytic leukemia, M6 erythroleukemia, M7 megakaryoblast leukemia. WHO/favourable: inversion 16, t(8;21), CEBPA gene mutation (transcription factor for myeloid maturation), NPM1 gene mutation; high risk: monosomy 5/7 and 5q deletion. Favourable genetics are treated with chemotherapy; high-risk disease needs hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

Features resemble ALL, except that hepatosplenomegaly is rarely seen (present in M4, M5) and there is no lymphadenopathy. Very high WBC count → leukostasis → lung infiltrates and stroke manifestations; DIC in M3; gum hypertrophy (M4); chloroma/myeloid sarcoma = deposition of leukemia cells in skin due to extramedullary hematopoiesis. Diagnosis: marrow aspiration > 20% myeloblasts. Induction — cytosine arabinoside + daunorubicin; consolidation — cytosine arabinoside + etoposide; M3 (APML) — ATRA/tretinoin drives differentiation of the malignant cell into a mature cell.

Reed-Sternberg (RS) cell present (40%) = Hodgkin lymphoma/disease; RS cell absent (60%) = non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Hodgkin lymphoma affects 15–19-year-olds with male predominance; risk factors are infections (HHV6, CMV, EBV — EBV raises risk 4×) and autoimmune disorders such as SLE.

Lymphadenopathy (m/c cervical) that is painless, matted, with firm rubbery consistency. Constitutional symptoms — high-grade fever (> 38°C), drenching night sweats, weight loss > 10% in 6 months — if absent = grade A (good prognosis), if present = grade B (poor prognosis). Classical HD: CD15/CD30 positive, RS cell (malignant transformation of a germinal B cell) with owl-eye inclusion body; nodular lymphocyte-predominant: CD20/CD45 with popcorn cells. Classical subtypes: nodular sclerosis (m/c worldwide, F > M, lacunar variant, EBV −, excellent), mixed cellularity (m/c in India, M > F, EBV +, good), lymphocyte rich (mononuclear, EBV +, excellent) and lymphocyte depleted (reticular, EBV +, poor).
Hodgkin Lymphoma — Ann Arbor Staging & Treatment

Modified Ann Arbor staging: I single lymph node; II ≥ 2 lymph nodes on one side of the diaphragm; III multiple lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm; IV multiple nodes plus organs affected. Stage annotations: X = bulky > 10 cm, E = extension into an extralymphatic site. Stages I–IIIB are favourable — ABVD chemotherapy (adriamycin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine); unfavourable disease (stage IV, or any stage with X or E) — chemotherapy plus radiotherapy, including involved field radiation therapy (IFRT).

NHL occurs at 5–15 years and is typed by lymphocyte of origin: B cell (Burkitt's lymphoma — m/c worldwide; diffuse large B cell lymphoma), T cell (lymphoblastic lymphoma — m/c in India; anaplastic large cell lymphoma) and intermediate cell. Endemic Burkitt (endemic to Africa, m/c worldwide) presents with jaw lesions (lytic bone lesions, draining sinuses, diffuse swelling) and generalized abdominal distension; sporadic Burkitt (m/c in India) presents with intra-abdominal tumours — mass per abdomen, unexplained abdominal pain, intussusception with tumour as lead point. EBV association is positive in endemic and ↓↓ in sporadic. T cell type resembles ALL and presents as a mediastinal mass.

St. Jude staging: low risk — stage 1 (single lymph node, no other lesion) and stage 2 (multiple lymph nodes with a single resectable GI lesion); high risk — stage 3 (multiple nodes with non-resectable GI lesions) and stage 4 (non-resectable GI lesions with bone marrow/CNS involvement). Chemotherapy: cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisolone and doxorubicin for low risk; methotrexate is added for high risk.

LCH (histiocytosis X) is a clonal proliferation of Langerhans-like cells with a wide, potentially multisystemic spectrum. Sites: bone (m/c; skull > jaw, missing/loose teeth), skin (scales with discharge, mimics seborrheic dermatitis and does not respond to its treatment — cradle cap), pituitary infiltration destroying the stalk → block in release of vasopressin/ADH from posterior pituitary granules → diabetes insipidus (MRI: loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot), lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Spectrum with increasing severity: eosinophilic granuloma (older children, lytic bone in skull) → Hand-Schüller-Christian disease (2–6 years; skull defect, DI, exophthalmos) → Letterer-Siwe disease (severe form, < 2 years; seborrheic dermatitis, ear discharge, hepatosplenomegaly with abnormal LFT, lymphadenopathy).

Diagnosis on biopsy: immunohistochemistry for CD1a and CD207 (langerin); electron microscopy shows Birbeck granules with a tennis racket appearance. Treatment: simple lesion — curettage and intralesional steroids; multiple lesions — vinblastine (m/c), 6-mercaptopurine and prednisolone; refractory disease — cladribine.

Neuroblastoma is the m/c intra-abdominal tumour, the m/c extra-cranial solid tumour and the 2nd m/c solid tumour (after intracranial/brain tumours) of children — and the m/c malignancy of infancy. It arises from neuroblasts (neural crest cells), most often in the adrenal gland (suprarenal tumour), then the paravertebral sympathetic chain/ganglia, posterior mediastinum and pelvis. Microscopy: small round uniform blue cells with scanty cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei forming Homer-Wright rosettes with central eosinophilic neuropil (cytoplasmic processes). Features: firm fixed irregular midline abdominal mass, constitutional symptoms, Horner syndrome and heterochromia iridis; metastases to bone (m/c → bony pain), retro-orbital region (raccoon eyes) and skin (blueberry muffin lesions).
Neuroblastoma — Paraneoplastic Effects, Investigations, Staging & Treatment

Paraneoplastic: opsoclonus-myoclonus ataxia (dancing eye/dancing feet syndrome, anti-neuronal antibodies) and VIP hypersecretion → intractable watery diarrhea with hypokalemia. Investigations: urine catecholamine metabolites VMA and HVA (initial, non-specific), NSE (most specific); CT abdomen (m/c) shows stippled calcifications and a mass displacing the kidney inferolaterally (unlike Wilms); I¹²³ MIBG and PET-CT rule out metastases. INSS stages I, 2 (2a/2b), 3 (crosses midline or contralateral nodes), 4 (disseminated), 4S (infant, good prognosis). Low risk: stages I, II, 4s, onset < 18 months, hyperdiploidy, TRK A expression; high risk: stages 3/4, onset > 18 months, hypodiploidy, N-myc amplification, loss of heterozygosity (1p, 11q). Treatment: localised → resection; disseminated → surgery + cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, etoposide; no response → radiotherapy; refractory → autologous HSCT.
Wilms Tumour — Features, Associations & Clinical Picture

Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is the m/c solid tumour of the kidney in childhood and the 2nd m/c intra-abdominal tumour; usually unilateral. Cell of origin: nephrogenic rest (undifferentiated mesenchyme of the kidney); age 2–5 years. Risk factors: horseshoe kidney (4× risk), cryptorchidism and hypospadias. WT-1 (11p13) mutation → WAGR (Wilms tumour, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, mental Retardation) and Denys-Drash syndrome (diffuse mesangial sclerosis → congenital nephrotic syndrome; ambiguous genitalia in males). WT-2 (11p15) mutation → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (LGA with hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele, organomegaly, ear lobe creases). Clinical: asymptomatic loin mass, hypertension from ↑ renin, hematuria. Metastasis: lung (m/c) > lymph node > liver.

Children's Oncology Group (COG) staging is POST-SURGICAL: stage 1 confined to kidney and completely resectable; stage 2 extends outside the kidney but completely resectable with uninvolved nodes; stage 3 residual tumour confined to abdomen, regional node metastasis or tumour extension into IVC; stage 4 nodal metastasis outside the abdomen or hematogenous metastasis to organs like lung and liver; stage 5 bilateral kidney involvement. Treatment: radical nephrectomy for stages 1–4 — stages 1/2 get vincristine + actinomycin D for 18 weeks; stages 3/4 get vincristine + actinomycin D + doxorubicin for 24 weeks AND radiotherapy. Partial nephrectomy for stage 5, with surgery + chemotherapy + radiotherapy.

JDM is a multisystem disorder and the m/c cause of inflammatory myopathy in children (5–14 years, F > M). Non-suppurative inflammation involves skin and muscles, and the vessels show systemic vasculopathy. Features: proximal symmetrical muscle weakness (shoulder and hip muscles early → difficulty rising from a chair/climbing stairs, Gower's sign positive), skin findings (Gottron's papules over the extensor aspects of MCP and IP joints, heliotrope rash with periorbital edema, shawl sign) and nail findings (periungual erythema, dilated nail-fold capillaries on capillaroscopy).

Essential criterion: rash — heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules. Other criteria (any 3): proximal symmetrical muscle weakness; elevated muscle enzymes (CPK, aldolase, LDH); EMG showing fasciculations with high-frequency discharges (replaced by MRI in practice); muscle biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltrates. Myositis-specific antibodies monitor prognosis: anti-TNF IV antibodies indicate severe skin involvement refractory to treatment; anti-Mi-2 antibodies predict good response. Treatment: steroids (IV methylprednisolone initially, tapered with oral prednisolone) and methotrexate (DMARD) as weekly maintenance for 2 years.

JIA is the m/c chronic rheumatic arthritis of children — an autoimmune disorder. Definition: age of onset < 16 years, duration ≥ 6 weeks, involvement of at least 1 joint and exclusion of other conditions. Oligoarticular JIA is the m/c type (F > M), with ≤ 4 joints involved, large joints affected in the order knee > ankle > wrist, and extra-articular findings of uveitis strongly associated with a positive ANA.
JIA — Polyarticular, Systemic, Psoriatic & Enthesitis Types

Polyarticular JIA (RF-negative): any age up to 16 years, > 4 joints (knee, hip, wrist), asymmetrical, with uveitis (ANA+). Polyarticular RF-positive: 9–11 years, small joints — MCP, PIP, cervical spine, TMJ — symmetrical, with rheumatoid nodules (elbow, occiput, Achilles tendon). Systemic JIA: m > F, quotidian fever with 1–2 spikes/day, arthritis, plus salmon-coloured evanescent maculopapular rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or serositis; Koebner phenomenon is a hypersensitivity reaction. Psoriatic arthritis: F > m; arthritis with psoriasis OR nail pitting, dactylitis (sausage digits) or a first-degree relative with psoriasis. Enthesitis-related arthritis: m > F, inflammation of tendons/ligaments, asymmetrical lower-limb arthritis and HLA-B27 association (sacro-iliitis, precursor to ankylosing spondylitis).
JIA — Macrophage Activation Syndrome, Work-up & Treatment

Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS): hyperinflammation with ↑↑ interleukins/cytokines, continuous fever, drop in cell counts (especially thrombocytopenia), hypofibrinogenemia from consumptive coagulopathy (→ low ESR), ↑ ferritin and ↑ triglycerides, and hemophagocytosis on marrow biopsy. JIA is a clinical diagnosis — lab tests are not required; ↑ ESR and ↑ CRP have prognostic use. Treatment: oligoarticular — NSAIDs (analgesia), then intra-articular triamcinolone if unresponsive; polyarticular — NSAIDs + DMARDs (methotrexate > hydroxychloroquine); systemic — biologicals: anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), adalimumab/etanercept (anti-TNF α antibody) and tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 antibody).

HSP is a multisystem small-vessel vasculitis and the m/c childhood vasculitis worldwide (4–8 years). Pathogenesis: leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophil debris in inflamed vessel walls, fibrinoid necrosis and IgA deposits. Palpable purpura is the m/c and characteristic feature — non-blanching, non-thrombocytopenic, in dependent areas (lower limbs, genital area in males). Others: post-prandial intermittent peri-umbilical colicky abdominal pain, ankle/knee arthritis or arthralgia, and renal involvement — hematuria/nephritis in 30% and nephrotic-range proteinuria in 10%.

Biopsy (skin/kidney) is usually not required — it is a clinical diagnosis — and shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition on immunofluorescence. Essential criterion: raised palpable hemorrhagic skin lesions without thrombocytopenia (platelet count normal or ↑). Additional (at least one): abdominal pain, arthritis/arthralgia, positive biopsy findings, renal involvement. Acute complication: intussusception and GI bleed; chronic: renal involvement — age > 6 years predisposes to long-term renal problems, monitor renal function for at least 1 year, 1–5% develop progressive kidney disease (CKD). Prognosis is good with long-term follow-up if renal involvement; treatment is supportive (self-limiting), steroids for severe GI involvement, and 10–20% recur.

Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis primarily of the coronary arteries, the m/c childhood vasculitis in India (< 5 years, idiopathic). Acute stage (1–2 weeks; ↓ morbidity if diagnosed here): fever > 5 days without discernible cause plus the CREAM findings — Conjunctivitis (b/l non-purulent, sparing the limbus), Rash (non-specific maculopapular), Extremities (non-pitting edema and erythema of limbs), Lymphadenopathy (u/l cervical), and mucocutaneous involvement (oral cavity erythema with cheilitis, strawberry tongue, cracked lips). Subacute/complication stage (2–4 weeks, most dangerous): coronary aneurysm in 25% (myocardial ischemia/thrombosis/rupture), periungual desquamation and thrombocytosis. Convalescent (6–8 weeks): recovery with Beau's lines. Other features: BCG scar reactivation, perianal desquamation, aseptic meningitis with high irritability, hydrops of the gallbladder (right hypochondrial pain), sterile pyuria from urethritis, and joint involvement.

Clinical diagnosis: fever ≥ 5 days + 4 of 5 CREAM findings. Investigations: platelet count normal in the acute phase and increased in the subacute phase; ↑ CRP and ↑ ESR; echocardiography at diagnosis, 2nd week, 6–8 weeks, then after 1 year — abnormal at any point means frequent evaluation. Atypical/incomplete KD: fever ≥ 5 days with 2–3 CREAM features, or an infant with fever ≥ 7 days and no other manifestations, with ESR ≥ 40 mm/hr or CRP ≥ 3 mg/dl — echocardiography showing cardiac involvement means treat as Kawasaki disease. Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg is the treatment of choice (↓ coronary abnormalities to 2–3%); aspirin at anti-inflammatory dose 75 mg/kg till afebrile for 48 hours, then anti-platelet dose 3–5 mg/kg for 6–8 weeks, then stop if echocardiography is normal or continue long term if abnormal.

WHO Hb cut-offs: 6 months–5 years < 11 g/dl; 5–11 years < 11.5 g/dl; 12–13 years < 12 g/dl; non-pregnant women < 12 g/dl; men < 13 g/dl. Hb is higher in males than females due to the effect of androgens. Nomograms (based on Hb and hematocrit, with different graphs for males and females) are the best method to define anaemia in a child: anaemia = < 2 SD from the mean for age and gender (< -2SD).

Age of onset of history suggestive of anaemia: since birth → congenital haemolytic disorders (enzyme deficiency such as G6PD deficiency; RBC membrane defects such as hereditary spherocytosis); > 6 months → β-globin chain defects such as thalassaemia (HbF present up to 6 months does not contain the β-globin chain); 9–24 months → iron deficiency anaemia, the m/c cause. Diet history: strict vegetarian/vegan → vitamin B12 deficiency and goat's milk diet → folic acid deficiency (both → megaloblastic anaemia); exclusive cow milk diet → iron and vitamin C deficiency (vitamin C aids iron absorption); pica → iron deficiency anaemia. Other history: chronic disease → anaemia of chronic inflammation; family history → haemolytic anaemia (anaemia with jaundice, gallstones, splenectomy).

Universal feature: pallor. Associated congenital defects: skeletal defects such as absent radius/thumb — seen in Fanconi anaemia (bone marrow failure). Petechiae/purpura (thrombocytopenia): leukaemia, aplastic anaemia, haemolytic uraemic syndrome (acute onset). Splenomegaly: haemolytic anaemia; splenomegaly with hepatomegaly or generalised lymphadenopathy: leukaemia.
Investigations — MCV, Iron Trial & Reticulocyte Algorithms

MCV classifies anaemia: low MCV (microcytic) — iron deficiency anaemia (m/c), anaemia of chronic disease/inflammation (ACD/ACI), thalassaemia; normal MCV (normocytic); high MCV (macrocytic).
