Low MCV algorithm: history/findings suggestive of IDA → trial of therapeutic iron → assess response — (+) treat as IDA, (−) do serum ferritin — low IDA, normal thalassaemia, high ACD/ACI. Normal/high MCV anaemia: evaluate the reticulocyte count (normal 1–2%), which indicates the marrow response. Corrected reticulocyte count = reticulocyte count × patient's Hb ÷ normal Hb for age/gender (taken as 15); > 2% indicates adequate marrow response. Normocytic/macrocytic anaemia: corrected reticulocyte count low (< 2%) or high (> 2%) → look for evidence of haemolysis (peripheral smear positive, ↑ LDH, ↑ bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin). Low count with no haemolysis: normal WBC and platelets → pure red cell aplasia (Diamond-Blackfan syndrome); pancytopenia → bone marrow failure (aplastic anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia). High count with haemolysis → haemolytic anaemia (aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia); without haemolysis → acute blood loss.
Iron Deficiency Anaemia — Pathogenesis & Predisposing Factors

IDA is the m/c cause of anaemia in children worldwide. Pathogenesis: ↓ total body iron stores (↓ serum ferritin) → ↓ erythropoiesis → anaemia; iron stores fall only after a few months of markedly reduced dietary intake. Predisposing factors: decreased intake (↓ dietary iron); increased demand (growth spurts at 0–2 years and puberty); decreased absorption (malabsorption, e.g. celiac disease); increased blood loss (worm infestation — hookworm). Onset is at 9–24 months — late because of the good iron stores acquired from the mother in utero. Rare causes: atransferrinemia (defective iron transfer to red cell precursors in marrow) and transferrin receptor antibodies.
Iron Deficiency Anaemia — Features, Work-up & Response to Iron

Features: tiredness, easy fatigability; the most reliable sign is pallor (oral mucosa, nail beds, palpebral conjunctiva); koilonychia (spooning of nails), platynychia (flat nails) and atrophic glossitis (shiny, smooth tongue). Associations: pica, temper tantrums, breath-holding spells and restless leg syndrome. Investigations: peripheral smear — hypochromia (pallor > 1/3 of the cell), microcytes and anisopoikilocytosis (varying size and shape); blood parameters — low MCV and low serum ferritin (screening). Treatment: ferrous sulphate, the most effective and economical iron (20% elemental iron), 3–6 mg/kg/day (maximum 300 mg/day) for 4–6 months to replenish stores. Response: 12–24 h replenishment of intracellular iron enzymes (subjective improvement); 36–48 h bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia; 48–72 h reticulocytosis peaking by 5–7 days; 4–30 days ↑ Hb; 1–3 months replenishment of iron stores. Supplementary: dietary modification with iron-rich food and deworming with albendazole.

Macrocytes (large RBCs) are seen on the peripheral smear. Predisposing causes — ↓ vitamin B12: pure vegetarian/vegan diet, pernicious anaemia (autoantibodies against intrinsic factor), malabsorption (vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum) and inborn errors of metabolism (homocystinuria, orotic aciduria, methyl malonic acidemia). ↓ folic acid: diet with excess goat milk, infection (giardiasis) and drugs interfering with folate utilisation (6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate). Features: pallor, tiredness, easy fatigability; characteristic — beefy red tongue, hepatosplenomegaly in 30–40% and knuckle hyperpigmentation. Neurological manifestations occur in vitamin B12 deficiency (↓ methylation reactions in the nervous system) and may precede the anaemia: earliest loss of position/vibration sense, ataxia, paresthesia, peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord. Investigations: macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (at least 1 neutrophil with ≥ 6 lobes among 5% of neutrophils with 5 lobes) due to nuclear maturation delay; pancytopenia may be present on CBC; ↑ MCV (100–120 fl).

Vitamin B12 deficiency: 1000 mcg IM daily for the first 2 weeks, then 1000 mcg weekly until the hematocrit normalises; for pernicious anaemia, monthly vitamin B12 lifelong. Folic acid deficiency: oral folic acid 1–5 mg daily for 3–4 weeks plus dietary supplementation. Note: folic acid given without vitamin B12 → persistence or worsening of neurological manifestations; in megaloblastic anaemia treat with both vitamin B12 and folic acid.

Congenital haemolytic anaemia is classified into three groups. Defects of red cell membrane → hereditary spherocytosis. Disorders of red cell metabolism → glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Haemoglobinopathies (defect in the globin chain of Hb) → sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia.
Hereditary Spherocytosis — Inheritance, Pathogenesis & Membrane Proteins

Hereditary spherocytosis has autosomal dominant inheritance. Pathogenesis: a normal discoid RBC with an RBC cytoskeletal protein defect becomes a spherical RBC → decreased deformability → entrapment in the splenic microcirculation → haemolysis → splenomegaly (characteristic). The membrane diagram labels ConA, Band 3 and Glycophorin A crossing the lipid bilayer, with the underlying skeleton of spectrin, ankyrin, actin and Band 4.1; Band 4.1 is annotated as the m/c defect and spectrin as the 2nd m/c and the most severe.

Clinical features: variable onset of anaemia and jaundice due to increased lysis of RBCs, with 50% presenting as neonatal jaundice; splenomegaly; positive family history; pigment gallstones from increased bilirubin production; and aplastic crisis as an acute presentation. Parvovirus B19 infection in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis → bone marrow dysfunction → pancytopenia.

1. Peripheral smear: lack of central pallor in spherocytes; a small surface area of the RBC is lost during the shape change → cellular dehydration → increased concentration of Hb inside the RBC → hyperchromia. 2. Red cell indices: increased MCHC (characteristic). 3. Screening tests: osmotic fragility is increased — increased permeability to Na+ in spherocytes → increased Na+/H2O transport into the RBC → increased swelling and lysis at a lower concentration of hypotonic saline; incubated osmotic fragility incubates the patient's blood at 37°C for 24 hours and improves the sensitivity of testing; osmotic fragility is also seen in other haemolytic disorders. 4. Confirmatory tests: flow cytometry showing decreased binding of eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) to proteins, and molecular testing for deletion of mutations in RBCs.
Hereditary Spherocytosis — Management & Consequences of Splenectomy

Management: 1. Lifelong folic acid supplementation — because of megaloblastic erythropoiesis from chronic haemolysis; given to all children with chronic haemolytic anaemias. 2. Splenectomy — the best treatment modality; decreased lysis → increased lifespan of RBCs → decreased severity of anaemia; laparoscopic partial splenectomy is preferred; concomitant cholecystectomy if gallstones are present. Consequences of splenectomy: absence of splenic macrophages → risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria (especially if age < 6 years) — Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcus. Precautions: surgery after 6 years of age, immunization, and penicillin for 2 years post surgery.

G6PD deficiency is the m/c RBC enzyme deficiency, X-linked recessive, and is commonly seen in Africans, Mediterraneans and Asians. Pathophysiology — the HMP shunt: glucose-6-phosphate is acted on by G6PD; NADP is converted to NADPH, which converts glutathione to reduced glutathione (via 6-phosphoglycerate), and reduced glutathione protects RBCs from oxidative stress. When G6PD is deficient the shunt is blocked → decreased levels of reduced glutathione → oxidative stress → haemolysis.

Clinical features: variable onset — early presentation is neonatal jaundice, late presentation is episodic haemolysis. Risk factors for episodic haemolysis are fever, fava beans and drugs. Drug-induced haemolysis starts 2–3 days after exposure and is self-limiting; the drugs listed are primaquine, nitrofurantoin, sulfonamides, nalidixic acid and phenazopyridine.

Investigations: 1. Peripheral smear — Heinz bodies: oxidative stress converts Hb to methaemoglobin → condensation → Heinz bodies; the Heinz bodies are engulfed by splenic macrophages, producing bite cells. 2. Enzyme assay in RBCs is the confirmatory test, showing decreased enzyme levels in RBCs. Management is supportive: most episodes are self-limiting, and implicated drugs must be avoided.

Sickle cell anaemia is autosomal recessive with a high incidence in the tribal populations of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Pathogenesis: a mutation in the gene for the β-globin chain of haemoglobin → glutamate is replaced by valine at the 6th position → production of defective Hb, HbS (normal Hb is HbA). The RBC with HbS sickles under hypoxia, dehydration, fever and metabolic acidosis; repeated sickling makes RBCs fragile → haemolysis, while sickle cells blocking blood flow cause ischaemia → infarction.
Sickle Cell Anaemia — Clinical Features & Crises

Sickle cell anaemia manifests after 6 months of age because HbF predominates for the first 6 months and is protective. Features: icterus, pallor, vaso-occlusive crisis with painful episodes (characteristic), dactylitis/hand-and-foot syndrome (swelling of fingers and toes, manifesting in infancy), acute chest syndrome (fever and breathing difficulty resembling pneumonia with new-onset infiltrates on chest X-ray) and stroke episodes. Sickling of cells in the spleen: repeated infarcts → autosplenectomy by 6 years of age (functional hyposplenism) → recurrent infection by encapsulated bacteria; venous blockade → acute pooling of blood → ≥ 2% Hb reduction → pallor and shock. Aplastic crisis is pancytopenia precipitated by parvovirus B19 infection.
Sickle Cell Anaemia — Investigations & Sickle Cell Trait

Investigations: 1. Peripheral smear — sickled RBCs. 2. Screening test — the sickling test, inducing sickling by adding 2% sodium metabisulphite. 3. Hb electrophoresis — the initial, best diagnostic test. 4. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) — the gold standard test, which detects and quantifies HbS. Note: in sickle cell trait, HbA + HbS are present, giving less severe manifestations.
Sickle Cell Anaemia — Management & Preventive Care

Management: good hydration; analgesics for pain episodes; PRBC transfusion for aplastic and sequestration crises (to increase the oxygen carrying capacity of blood); exchange transfusion for acute chest syndrome and stroke — sequential removal of HbS from the circulation with the goal of HbS concentration < 30% of Hb; haematopoietic stem cell transplant is curative; newer agents reduce vaso-occlusive episodes — crizanlizumab, a monoclonal antibody against P-selectin that decreases attachment of sickled RBCs to the vessel wall, and voxelotor, which decreases HbS polymerization and hence sickling. Preventive care: penicillin prophylaxis from infancy to 5 years of age; immunization against encapsulated organisms; hydroxyurea to increase HbF production and thereby decrease sickling episodes, started after 9 months of age.

β-thalassaemia is autosomal recessive. Types arise from reduction or absence of β-globin chain synthesis; normally 2 alleles code for the β-globin chain. Key: β = normal, β+ = decreased production, β0 = no production. Genotype table — β/β normal; β/β+ β-thalassaemia trait (mild), asymptomatic; β+/β+ or β+/β0 β-thalassaemia intermedia, mild to moderate severity (β+/β0 more severe than β+/β+); β0/β0 β-thalassaemia major or Cooley's anaemia, the most severe form, needing transfusion every 3–4 weeks.

Absent β-globin chain synthesis → accumulation of α-chains in RBCs → instability of cells → early destruction → ineffective erythropoiesis. This produces severe anaemia (transfusion dependent) and extramedullary haematopoiesis — hepatosplenomegaly and expansion in the skull. Thalassemic facies comprises frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge, maxillary prominence and dental malocclusion; the skull X-ray shows prominent vertical trabeculae — the hair-on-end appearance. Note: α and β chains are normally produced in a 1:1 ratio.

Investigations: 1. Peripheral smear — nucleated RBCs and microcytic hypochromic RBCs with central pallor > 1/3. 2. Haemoglobin electrophoresis — the initial diagnostic test. 3. HPLC — the gold standard test. Management: supportive — blood transfusion every 3–4 weeks using leukocyte-depleted/irradiated blood products (to reduce the risk of allergic reactions), with a pre-transfusion target Hb of 9–10 g/dL to reduce deformities and promote growth. Curative treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplant.

Iron overload complicates repeated transfusions (monitor after over 1 year of transfusion) and is the major cause of morbidity and mortality through cardiotoxicity. Organs damaged: liver, spleen and heart. High transferrin saturation decreases the bacteriostatic properties of lactoferrin → increased risk of infection, most commonly Yersinia enterocolitica. Investigations: serum ferritin > 1000 pg/L, and MRI — R2 or R2* weighted liver MRI (best) and T2-weighted cardiac MRI. Management: iron chelators — deferasirox (oral) is preferred and causes only mild GI disturbances; deferoxamine (s.c.) causes ototoxicity and retinal toxicity; deferiprone (oral) causes neutropenia and cartilage damage.

Normal hemostasis depends on three components — blood vessel, platelets and clotting factors. The hemostasis diagram shows circulating vWF with Factor VIII, X→Xa, the clotting cascade, activated aggregated platelets, fibrinogen, GpIIb/IIIa and GpIb gathering at an endothelial defect over subendothelial vWF and collagen. Causes of bleeding split into vascular (HSP vasculitis, scurvy from Vit C deficiency, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia/Osler-Weber-Rendu) and non-vascular (thrombocytopenia, clotting factor defects).

Platelet disorders bleed mucocutaneously with petechiae present, multiple small ecchymoses, bleeding after minor trauma but no delayed post-surgical bleeding. Coagulation disorders bleed deep into muscles and joints (hemarthrosis) with absent petechiae, single large ecchymoses, no bleeding after minor trauma but delayed bleeding after surgery.

ITP arises by molecular mimicry after viral infection in a 1–7 year old: autoantibodies against GP IIb/IIIa receptors coat platelets, the coated platelets enter the spleen, are recognised by Fc receptors on splenic macrophages and undergo lysis, producing autoimmune thrombocytopenia. The bone marrow compensates with increased megakaryocyte production.

Acute ITP (< 3 months) is the m/c type (60–75%) with spontaneous recovery; persistent lasts 3–12 months and chronic > 12 months. Acute ITP affects 1–7 year olds, starting 1–4 weeks after a viral infection with sudden mucocutaneous bleeds (petechiae >> epistaxis, oral oozing) in a well-appearing child; GI bleeds, hematuria and fatal CNS bleeds are rare, and lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly — if present — demand evaluation for another etiology such as leukemia.

Blood count shows thrombocytopenia with marrow compensation — peripheral smear with normal-sized and large young platelets and bone marrow aspiration with increased megakaryocytes. Most cases are self-limiting (supportive care); treatment is decided by clinical symptoms (organ bleeds, rising bleed count), not platelet counts. IV immunoglobulins are best (↓ macrophage activity → ↓ destruction), steroids raise production, and platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeds. Other listed causes of thrombocytopenia include aplastic anemia, marrow infiltration, SLE, parvovirus/EBV/varicella/rubella/mumps and drugs (heparin, valproate, phenytoin, NSAIDs, penicillins and cephalosporins).

Hemophilia is a clotting factor defect → delayed clot formation → bleeding manifestations. Type A (m/c, Factor VIII) and B (Factor IX) are X-linked recessive affecting males more; type C (Factor XI) is autosomal recessive. Hemarthrosis (bleeding into a joint) is the hallmark; the knee is affected most (knee > elbow, ankle), and a target joint — repeated bleeding into the same joint — fibroses and restricts movement, the m/c cause of morbidity.

Mild hemophilia (5–40% activity, no spontaneous bleeds) goes unnoticed until adolescence; moderate (1–4%, bleeds mostly absent) bleeds after trauma or surgery; severe (< 1%, spontaneous bleeds present) shows hemarthrosis, muscle hematoma, rare CNS and iliopsoas bleeds (→ shock) and neonatal clues (IM-injection hematoma, circumcision bleed, large cephalhematoma). Coagulation profile shows ↑ APTT from intrinsic pathway compromise, and factor assay — the best test — estimates clotting factor levels in blood.

Factor replacement is dosed by desired % increase — 40% for hemarthrosis, 100% for CNS bleeds — using Dose = % increase × body weight × K (0.5 for A, 1.4 for B). Other options are FFP and cryoprecipitate (Factor VIII + fibrinogen, useful only in hemophilia A). Antibodies to clotting factor are the most serious complication (patients stop responding); treatment is bypass agents — factor type (recombinant VIIa, APCs/FEIBA) or non-factor type (emicizumab, anti–Factor VIII monoclonal antibody, hemophilia A only).

Von Willebrand disease is the m/c inherited bleeding disorder worldwide, most commonly autosomal dominant. VWF binds Factor VIII (↑ VIII half-life) and bridges platelets to subendothelial collagen. Type 1 (m/c, 80%) is a quantitative partial deficiency; type 2 is qualitative dysproteinemia (abnormal function, normal levels); type 3 — most severe — is complete absence of VWF, resembling Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A).

VWD presents with mucocutaneous bleeds (epistaxis, gum bleeds) and menorrhagia in females; severe disease resembles hemophilia A. Coagulation profile shows ↑ APTT (Factor VIII activity affected); vWF antigen levels are used in type 1 and 3, while multimer testing (protein structure and functioning) and the ristocetin cofactor assay (ristocetin induces VWF–platelet binding, decreased in VWD) are used in type 2. Desmopressin releases stored endothelial VWF (useful in type 1); plasma-derived or recombinant VWF concentrates are used in type 2 and 3.

Respiratory causes exceed cardiac causes of cardiopulmonary arrest in children — respiratory failure and terminal stages of shock. Initial assessment splits into pulse+breathing absent (start CPR with compression + ventilation, reassess every 2 cycles, attach AED) and pulse present with breathing absent (positive pressure ventilation at 20–30 breaths/min, assess every 2 min, start CPR if pulse is lost or HR < 60 bpm with poor perfusion), while reversible causes are sought on both sides. Outside hospital the compression–ventilation ratio is 15:2 with two rescuers and 30:2 with one; intubated children (two people) receive 100–120 compressions and 20–30 breaths per minute in hospital.

Shockable rhythm: deliver 2 J/kg, continue CPR and reassess, repeat shocks up to 10 J/kg; no response means refractory disease treated with Inj. lidocaine and amiodarone. Non-shockable rhythm: immediate IV push of epinephrine 0.1 ml/kg of 1:10,000, repeated every 3–5 min, with CPR continued for 2 min before reassessment.

Verify scene safety; position supine on a flat hard surface and immobilise if fracture is suspected (RTA). Check responsiveness by looking for body movements; if unresponsive, shout for help, activate the emergency response system in public, and check breathing chest movements plus pulse — brachial in infants, carotid or femoral beyond 1 year — simultaneously for under 10 seconds. Circulation: compress the lower third of the sternum at 100–120/min to one-third of the AP chest diameter, allowing full recoil for cardiac filling — push hard, push fast.

Airway: head tilt–chin lift first, then jaw thrust. Breathing is non-invasive (bag-and-mask ventilation) or invasive (endotracheal intubation, preferred in hospital CPR and prolonged CPR). The tube is cuffed with size (Age + 4)/4, cuff pressure below 20–25 cm H2O to prevent pressure necrosis, and depth of insertion 3 × Age in years. Routine cricoid pressure is avoided (cartilage damage); breathing rate is 20–30/min, i.e. one breath every 2–3 seconds.

Vascular access aims at drug administration — IV preferred (femoral is the large accessible vein), intraosseous alternate (proximal tibia > distal femur, below the tibial tuberosity). The AED displays rhythm to decide management and delivers shock by asynchronous depolarisation of the myocardium. Shockable (wide QRS): irregular V-fib and regular pulseless VT; non-shockable: asystole and pulseless electrical activity.

Reversible causes are recalled as 6H and 4T. The H bullets are hypovolemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis) and hypo/hyperkalemia; the T bullets are thromboembolism (pulmonary, coronary), toxin, tamponade (pericardial) and tension pneumothorax.

Shock is circulatory dysfunction with decreased oxygen delivery and cellular perfusion insufficient for metabolic demands. Hypovolemic shock (m/c — hemorrhage, dehydration) joins cardiogenic (congenital heart disease, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy), distributive (anaphylactic, neurogenic) and septic shock (features of all three). Compensated shock maintains vital brain–heart–kidney function via sympathetic activation (↑ SVR, ↑ contractility, blood diverted from skin); prolonged shock decompensates into multiorgan dysfunction. Circulatory adequacy is judged by capillary refill time — blanching the thumb — normal ≤ 2 sec, > 3 sec in shock.

Compensated shock shows agitation or confusion, increased heart rate, CRT > 3 sec, normal urine output, normal BP and increased respiratory rate. Decompensated shock shows drowsiness, markedly increased heart rate, CRT > 5 sec, oliguria/anuria, decreased BP and increased respiratory rate.

Hypovolemic shock is suspected with fluid loss or ↓ oral intake: dry mouth, ↓/absent tears, sunken eyes, oliguria with ↑ creatinine and ↑ urea, and ↓ CVP as lost volume lowers preload. Cardiogenic shock is impaired contractility with venous pooling: ↑ CVP, ↑ JVP, S3 gallop, congestive hepatomegaly, plus primary cardiac clues (murmurs, pericarditis friction rub) and a ventricular-failure diagram.

Distributive shock is warm shock — warm extremities, bounding pulses, flash CRT (< 1 sec) — from vasodilatation due to ↓ SVR with ↓ afterload and ↓ cardiac output. Septic shock splits into cold type (cold extremities, CRT > 3 sec, feeble/decreased pulses) and warm type (warm extremities, flash CRT, bounding pulses).

Recognise shock quickly; stabilise A, B, C with high-flow O2 and IV access (intraosseous if IV is inaccessible for 60 seconds); check and treat hypoglycemia and sepsis. Give an initial 10–20 ml/kg bolus over 15–20 min, then 20 ml/kg over 15–20 min repeated up to 60 ml/kg in the first hour; no response for 60 min is fluid-refractory shock. Cold shock needs vasodilation (epinephrine or dopamine 5–9 µg/kg/min); warm shock needs vasoconstriction (norepinephrine or dopamine ≥ 10 µg/kg/min); epi/norepi start at 0.05 and titrate to 3 µg/kg/min. Catecholamine-resistant shock gets corticosteroids (if adrenal insufficiency is suspected), cardiac monitoring and transfusion to Hb > 10 g/dl.

Cold shock with normal BP gets vasodilators (nitroprusside/milrinone, nitroglycerin/levosimendan); cold shock with ↓ BP gets titrated epinephrine to the highest dose plus norepinephrine to normalise diastolic BP, then milrinone/levosimendan if there is no response; warm shock with ↓ BP gets volume titration to normal, added vasopressin for vasoconstriction, and milrinone/levosimendan if cardiac output falls. Persistent failure prompts a search for reversible causes (pericardial effusion, pneumothorax) and then ECMO — oxygenation of blood through a machine outside the body.
IO Sites, Rules of 60, Fluids, Vasoactives & Endpoints

IO sites are proximal tibia and distal femur. Rules of 60: IO if IV is unavailable in 60 sec, boluses up to 60 ml/kg in the first 60 min, vasoactives 60 min after starting fluids. Crystalloids (↓ price, easy availability) beat colloids (long-term paediatric risk unknown); normal saline 0.9% and Ringer lactate — isotonic solutions only. Sepsis is managed with a 3rd-generation cephalosporin + vancomycin. Vasopressors alter resistance (epinephrine, norepinephrine, vasopressin); inotropes raise contractility (epinephrine, dobutamine, milrinone/PDE-III inhibitor, levosimendan/Ca sensitizer); vasodilators dilate vessels (nitroglycerine, nitroprusside). Endpoints: normal HR/BP, urine > 1 ml/kg/hr, CRT < 2 sec, normal mentation.
q: The newborn period extends up to ___
Newborn period = first 4 weeks after birth. (Book p2)
In the newborn period, the 'late' phase comprises next 3 weeks.
True — 1st week: Early; next 3 weeks: Late. (Book p2)
Low birth weight (LBW) is defined as a birth weight less than ___
Very low birth weight (VLBW) is defined as ___
Very Low Birth Weight (VLBW): < 1.5 kg. (Book p2)
Extremely low birth weight (ELBW) is a birth weight of ___
Extremely Low Birth Weight (ELBW): < 1 kg. (Book p2)
A baby weighing 1.8 kg at birth is best classified as ___
1.8 kg is < 2.5 kg so LBW, but > 1.5 kg so not VLBW. (Book p2)

A term male is delivered by vacuum extraction. Within 2 hours he has a diffuse, fluctuant swelling of the scalp that crosses suture lines. He is pale, tachycardic (182/min) and his capillary refill is 4 seconds.

The most likely diagnosis is —
Vacuum extraction → separation of scalp layers below galea aponeurotica → blood accumulation; diffuse, fluctuant, crosses sutures, appears soon after birth, most severe (shock, pallor). (Book p6)

A baby boy is born at 34 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 1.4 kg. He is active and feeding well. His mother wants to know how his weight will be categorised.

This baby's birth weight is best classified as —
VLBW = birth weight < 1.5 kg; this baby (1.4 kg) is VLBW (and also LBW since < 2.5 kg, but not ELBW which is < 1 kg). (Book p2)

At 1 minute of life a term baby has: heart rate 110/min, slow irregular breathing, some flexion of extremities, a grimace with weak cry when the nasal mucosa is irritated with a nasogastric tube, and a pink trunk with blue extremities.

The 1-minute APGAR score of this baby is —
Pulse >100 = 2; irregular breathing = 1; some flexion = 1; grimace with weak cry = 1; acrocyanosis = 1 → total 6/10 (low; moderate asphyxia range 4-6). (Book p4)

A well, full-term breastfed baby develops scattered papules and pustules on the trunk and face on day 3 of life. He is afebrile and feeds normally. Lesion smear shows abundant eosinophils.

The most likely diagnosis is —
Erythema toxicum: papulopustular lesions, eosinophils on smear, onset > 24 hr, baby otherwise well. (Pustular melanosis: neutrophils, onset < 24 hr.) (Book p5)
In the book's classification, small-for-gestational-age (SGA) is divided into symmetrical and Asymmetrical only.
False — correct: Constitutional (Normal) and Pathological. SGA -> Constitutional (Normal) / Pathological (IUGR). (Book p2)

Identification points: loose skin folds, skin peeling, thin umbilical cord. (Book p2)
Skin peeling in a newborn is an identification point of ___
Identification points of IUGR include skin peeling. (Book p2)
A thin umbilical cord is characteristic of ___
Identification points: a. Loose skin folds, b. Skin peeling, c. Thin umbilical cord. (Book p2)
Symmetrical IUGR: etiology maternal, cause uteroplacental insufficiency. (Book p2)
Uteroplacental insufficiency is the cause of ___
Symmetrical IUGR cause: uteroplacental insufficiency. (Book p2)
Asymmetrical IUGR: etiology fetal (genetic defects, organ anomalies). (Book p2)
Genetic defects (eg: Trisomy) and organ anomalies cause asymmetrical IUGR.
True — Asymmetrical IUGR cause: genetic defects (eg: Trisomy), organ anomalies. (Book p2)
Asymmetrical IUGR begins in which trimester?
Symmetrical IUGR develops in the 2nd and 3rd trimester, i.e. during ___
Symmetrical IUGR onset: 2nd and 3rd trimester (during placenta-dependent growth of body). (Book p2)
A brain-sparing effect with normal-sized head and body small for gestational age is seen in ___
Symmetrical IUGR: brain-sparing effect present -> normal size head, body size small for gestational age. (Book p2)
In asymmetrical IUGR, there is no brain-sparing effect, so the baby is ___
Asymmetrical IUGR: no brain-sparing effect -> uniformly small baby. (Book p2)
Which type of IUGR has a poor outcome?
Outcome: symmetrical = good, asymmetrical = poor. (Book p2)
On the new AIMS intrauterine growth curves, LGA lies on the ___
New AIMS curves: LGA -> upper percentile curve. (Book p2)
On the new AIMS intrauterine growth curves, SGA lies on the ___
New AIMS curves: SGA -> lower percentile curve. (Book p2)

Male and female charts are different

Weight of baby (g) / [Length of baby (cm)] cubed x 100
PI = weight of baby (g) / [length of baby (cm)]^3 x 100. (Book p2)
A ponderal index greater than 2 indicates asymmetrical IUGR.
False — correct: Symmetrical IUGR. PI interpretation: > 2 : Symmetrical IUGR. (Book p2)

Mother's LMP and 1st trimester ultrasound scan

Based on: LMP + 1st trimester ultrasound scan. (Book p3)
The Expanded New Ballard Score (ENBS) is based on ___
ENBS based on: neuro muscular maturity + physical maturity. (Book p3)

In ENBS physical maturity, leathery, cracked and wrinkled skin is scored 4.

In ENBS, skin that is smooth, pink with visible veins is scored ___
Skin scores: -1 sticky/friable/transparent; 0 gelatinous, red, translucent; 1 smooth, pink, visible veins. (Book p3)
In ENBS, parchment-like skin with deep cracking and no vessels is scored ___
Skin: 4 = parchment, deep cracking; no vessels. (Book p3)
Abundant lanugo in ENBS physical maturity corresponds to a score of ___
Lanugo: none = -1, sparse = 0, abundant = 1, thinning = 2, bald areas = 3, mostly bald = 4. (Book p3)

A raised areola with a 3-4 mm bud in ENBS is scored ___

The popliteal angle (angle between thigh and leg when flexed) is obtuse in ___
Popliteal angle: preterm obtuse, term acute. (Book p4)

Surgical correction of ambiguous genitalia in CAH (clitoroplasty) should be done within —
Surgical correction of ambiguous genitalia: should be done within 2–6 months (clitoroplasty). (Book p207)
The surgical procedure named for correction of clitoromegaly in CAH is ___.
Surgical correction of ambiguous genitalia (clitoroplasty) within 2–6 months. (Book p207)

A 12-day-old 46,XX neonate with clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds presents with poor feeding, shock, Na 122 mEq/L, K 6.4 mEq/L. Newborn screen reports markedly elevated 17-OHP.

A 46,XX newborn has clitoromegaly and labial fusion; at day 12 she develops shock with Na 122, K 6.4 mEq/L and hypoglycemia. Newborn screen shows high 17-OHP. Diagnosis —
Ambiguous genitalia in a female + salt wasting (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, shock) + high 17-OHP = 21-OH deficiency. (Book p207)

2. ACTH acting on MSH receptor

4. Low aldosterone (salt wasting)
Correct pairs: Shock→Low aldosterone (salt wasting); Clitoromegaly→High androgens; Hyperpigmentation→ACTH acting on MSH receptor; Precocious puberty in males→Virilisation from androgens. (Book p207)

A child with known CAH on hydrocortisone develops chickenpox. The dose should be —
In 11-β-hydroxylase deficiency, the compound that accumulates and acts as a mineralocorticoid is —
High 11-deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid action) d/t enzyme deficiency. (Book p207)
11-deoxycorticosterone accumulates in 11-β-OH deficiency because the block prevents its conversion to —
11-deoxycorticosterone → (11-β-OH) → corticosterone; the block piles up DOC. (Book p206–207)
The striking electrolyte/BP finding in 11-β-OH deficiency is —
High 11-deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid action): HTN in spite of decreased aldosterone. (Book p207)
Hypertension with which feature points to 11-β-OH deficiency rather than renal disease?
11-β-OH deficiency: HTN (DOC) + androgen excess → ambiguous genitalia in females / precocious puberty in males. (Book p207)
Androgen effects of 11-β-OH deficiency include precocious puberty in males and ambiguous genitalia in —
High androgens: precocious puberty (males), ambiguous genitalia (females). (Book p207)
Hyperpigmentation in 11-β-OH deficiency is mediated by —
High androgens, high ACTH, high DOC, low aldosterone/cortisol
Low androgens, low ACTH, high aldosterone
High aldosterone, low ACTH, high cortisol
Clinical triad: high androgens + high ACTH + high 11-deoxycorticosterone, with decreased aldosterone and cortisol. (Book p207)

A 3-week-old 46,XX infant has clitoromegaly, hyperpigmented scrotal-like labia and BP above the 95th centile. Electrolytes are normal; cortisol is low, ACTH high.

A hypertensive 46,XX newborn has clitoromegaly, hyperpigmentation, Na 138, K 4.0 mEq/L, low cortisol and high ACTH. Diagnosis —
Ambiguous genitalia + HTN despite low aldosterone (DOC mineralocorticoid action) + hyperpigmentation = 11-β-OH deficiency. (Book p207)
In 11-β-OH deficiency, blood pressure is high "in spite of" decreased ___.
HTN in spite of decreased aldosterone — because accumulated 11-DOC has mineralocorticoid action. (Book p207)
Both shunt to increased androgens (virilisation) with high ACTH (hyperpigmentation); they differ in BP/DOC. (Book p207)
The feature that best distinguishes 11-β-OH from 21-OH deficiency is —
11-β-OH: HTN (DOC excess); 21-OH: salt-wasting hypotension — both share virilisation and hyperpigmentation. (Book p207)
11-β-hydroxylase deficiency causes hypertension through increased aldosterone.
False — Aldosterone is low; HTN is d/t mineralocorticoid action of accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone. (Book p207)
In 11-β-OH deficiency the accumulated steroid just proximal to the block in the cortisol pathway is 11-deoxy___.
A male with 11-β-OH deficiency may present with precocious puberty.
True — High androgens cause precocious puberty in males. (Book p207)
In 17-α-hydroxylase deficiency, cortisol is decreased and ACTH rises; the pathway that benefits is —
Decreased enzyme → decreased cortisol → increased ACTH → increased increased aldosterone (aldosterone pathway favoured) + decreased testosterone. (Book p208)
The BP abnormality of 17-α-hydroxylase deficiency is —
17-α-OH deficiency → decreased testosterone (androgen pathway blocked). (Book p208)
A 46,XY newborn with 17-α-hydroxylase deficiency may show —
Low androgens in males: undervirilization — hypospadias, bifid scrotum, delayed puberty; severe cases: ambiguous genitalia. (Book p208)
Male genital findings in 17-α-OH deficiency include hypospadias, bifid scrotum and delayed ___.
In males: undervirilization — hypospadias, bifid scrotum, delayed puberty; severe: ambiguous genitalia. (Book p208)
Delayed/slow progression of puberty in 17-α-OH deficiency females is due to decreased —
Slow/delayed progression of puberty d/t decreased aromatization of testosterone (decreased estradiol). (Book p208)
Hyperpigmentation in 17-α-OH deficiency is due to —

A 15-year-old phenotypic female with 46,XY karyotype has hypertension, absent uterus, no thelarche, and very low testosterone and cortisol with high ACTH.

A 15-year-old 46,XY patient raised as female has no breast development, primary amenorrhoea, absent uterus, hypertension and low testosterone. Diagnosis —
HTN (high aldosterone) + undervirilised 46,XY + delayed puberty (low estradiol from low androgen substrate) = 17-α-OH deficiency. (Book p208)
In 3-β-HSD deficiency, the hormones that DECREASE include cortisol, aldosterone, androgens and —
Decreased enzyme → decreased cortisol, decreased aldosterone, decreased androgens, decreased estradiol (with high ACTH). (Book p208)
Low BP with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia
Low aldosterone: decreased BP + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia. (Book p208)
Low androgens in males: undervirilization. (Book p208)
Females with 3-β-HSD deficiency may show mild virilisation due to increased —
In females: mild virilization d/t increased DHEA (mild androgen) in the older child. (Book p208)
Mild virilisation of an older female child with 3-β-HSD deficiency includes acne, menstrual irregularities and —
Features: acne, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities (d/t increased DHEA). (Book p208)
DHEA, the mild androgen increased in 3-β-HSD deficiency, stands for ___.
Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) — a mild androgen upstream of the 3-β-HSD block. (Book p208)

A 46,XY newborn with hypospadias and bifid scrotum develops salt-wasting crisis; his 8-year-old sister has acne, hirsutism and menstrual irregularities with normal BP.

A salt-wasting 46,XY newborn has hypospadias and bifid scrotum; an older sister has acne and hirsutism. The enzyme deficiency —
3-β-HSD: salt wasting + undervirilised males + mildly virilised older females (DHEA). (Book p208)
The diagnostic pointer table combines salt-wasting features with ___ status to differentiate enzyme deficiencies.
Pointers for diagnosis use salt-wasting features and serum androgen to separate the enzyme deficiencies. (Book p208)
Salt-wasting features with HIGH serum androgens point to —
Salt wasting + increased androgen = 21-OH deficiency. (Book p208)
Salt-wasting features with LOW serum androgens point to —
Salt wasting + decreased androgen = 3-β-HSD deficiency. (Book p208)
Hypertension with HIGH serum androgens points to —
Hypertension with LOW serum androgens points to —

Salt-wasting belongs to 21-OH and 3-β-HSD deficiencies; 17-α-OH causes HTN with undervirilisation. (Book p207–208)
Hyperpigmentation is a shared feature of 21-OH, 11-β-OH, 17-α-OH and 3-β-HSD deficiencies because ACTH is high in all.
True — All CAH blocks lower cortisol → high ACTH → MSH-receptor cross-stimulation → hyperpigmentation. (Book p207–208)
Puberty is defined by the appearance of —
Puberty is defined by the appearance of secondary sexual characters. (Book p209)

First change in puberty in females: thelarche (occurs earlier than in males). (Book p209)

First change in puberty in males: increase in size of testis. (Book p209)
Puberty basics and delayed puberty definition
Thelarche occurs ___ than the first pubertal change in males.
Thelarche (females) occurs earlier than males. (Book p209)
Puberty basics and delayed puberty definition
Delayed puberty in MALES is defined as pubertal changes not occurring beyond —
In male: pubertal changes do not occur > 14 years of age. (Book p209)

Delayed puberty in FEMALES includes absence of thelarche beyond —
In female: absence of thelarche > 13 years of age. (Book p209)

> 14 years of age OR > 3 years after thelarche

Absence of menarche by > 16 years of age OR > 5 years after thelarche. (Book p209)

Menarche delayed beyond 16 years OR beyond ___ years after thelarche defines delayed puberty in girls.
Absence of menarche by > 16 years of age OR > 5 years after thelarche. (Book p209)

The overall most common cause of delayed puberty is —
Constitutional delay in growth and puberty
Overall m/c cause: constitutional delay in growth and puberty. (Book p209)

Constitutional delay in growth and puberty is also the most common cause of —
Constitutional delay (also m/c cause of short stature). (Book p209)

A 14.5-year-old boy has prepubertal testes (3 ml), height just below the 3rd centile with delayed bone age, healthy appetite and normal exam. His father finished school at a "late bloomer" pace.

A 14.5-year-old boy has no testicular enlargement but normal growth velocity, delayed bone age and a family history of "late bloomers". Diagnosis —
Constitutional delay in growth and puberty
Overall m/c cause of delayed puberty is constitutional delay in growth and puberty — typical late bloomer pattern. (Book p209)

Central (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism results from a disorder of the —
Central/hypogonadotropic: d/t pituitary gland and/or hypothalamus disorder. (Book p209)

Central: decreased LH, FSH → decreased sex steroids. (Book p209)

The syndrome associated with anosmia among central causes of delayed puberty is —

Kallmann syndrome combines hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with ___.
Kallmann syndrome: associated with anosmia. (Book p209)

Lawrence-Moon-Biedl-Bardet syndrome features include obesity, retinitis pigmentosa and —
Lawrence-Moon-Biedl-Bardet: obesity, polydactyly, retinitis pigmentosa. (Book p209)

CNS injury causes of central delayed puberty include trauma and —
CNS injury (e.g., trauma); infiltrative disorders of pituitary: histiocytosis, sarcoidosis, etc. (Book p209)

Infiltrative disorders of the pituitary causing delayed puberty include histiocytosis and —
Infiltrative disorders of pituitary: histiocytosis, sarcoidosis, etc. (Book p209)

In central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, LH and FSH are elevated.
False — Central disease lowers LH and FSH (→ low sex steroids); high LH/FSH marks peripheral disease. (Book p209)

The overall most common cause of delayed puberty is chronic systemic illness.
False — Constitutional delay in growth and puberty is the overall m/c cause. (Book p209)

Low LH, low FSH with low sex steroids

The gonadal lesion of Turner syndrome causing delayed puberty is —
In Klinefelter syndrome, delayed puberty/hypogonadism follows —
Klinefelter: cryptorchidism → decreased testosterone production. (Book p209)
The CAH enzyme causing delayed puberty in males (peripheral cause) is —
CAH: 17-α-hydroxylase → delayed puberty in males. (Book p209)
Insufficient androgen action as a cause of delayed puberty includes AIS and —
Insufficient androgen action: androgen insensitivity syndrome, 5-α-reductase deficiency. (Book p209)
Odd one out (peripheral causes of delayed puberty):
Kallmann is a CENTRAL (hypogonadotropic) cause; the other three are peripheral/hypergonadotropic or androgen-action causes. (Book p209)
AIS pathology: resistance to androgen action. (Book p209)
The genetic defect in androgen insensitivity syndrome is a mutation of the —
Genetic defect: AR (androgen receptor) gene mutation. (Book p209)
Inheritance of androgen insensitivity syndrome is —
Mode of inheritance: X-linked recessive. (Book p210)
Karyotype of a patient with classical androgen insensitivity syndrome is —
Phenotypic appearance of the CLASSICAL form of AIS is —
Phenotypic appearance of classical form: female (features vary with severity of resistance). (Book p210)
Features of classical AIS vary with —
Phenotypic appearance of classical form (features vary with severity of resistance). (Book p210)
Breast development in AIS occurs because high testosterone is converted by ___ and the product acts on breast tissue.
AIS → increased testosterone —(aromatase)→ estrogen acts on breast tissue. (Book p210)
In classical AIS, the uterus is —
Uterus: absent (Sertoli AMH acts normally). (Book p210)
Body hair pattern in classical AIS is —
Pubic and axillary hair: absent/sparse (androgen action blocked at hair follicles). (Book p210)
The undescended testes in classical AIS typically present as —
Undescended testis: palpable inguinal mass. (Book p210)

A 15-year-old "girl" is evaluated for primary amenorrhoea. Breasts are Tanner 4, pubic and axillary hair nearly absent, a right inguinal mass is palpable, and ultrasound shows no uterus.

A 15-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea has normal breasts, absent pubic/axillary hair, a palpable inguinal mass and no uterus on USG. Karyotype —
Breast development + absent uterus + sparse pubic hair + inguinal testis = classical AIS (46,XY). (Book p210)
The pathophysiology of AIS involves decreased development of male external genitalia, specifically fusion of scrotum and ___.
Decreased development of male external genitalia (fusion of scrotum, lengthening of penis). (Book p210)

B. Breast development
C. Absent uterus
D. Inguinal mass

List II
1. Sertoli AMH acts normally
2. Undescended testis
3. Aromatase converts testosterone to estrogen
4. Resistance to androgen action

Correct pairs: Phenotypic female→Resistance to androgen action; Breast development→Aromatase converts testosterone to estrogen; Absent uterus→Sertoli AMH acts normally; Inguinal mass→Undescended testis. (Book p210)
In AIS the testes produce AMH normally, which is why the uterus is absent.
True — Sertoli cell AMH action is intact in AIS (only androgen action is blocked), so Müllerian structures regress. (Book p210)
Pubic and axillary hair are normal in classical androgen insensitivity syndrome.
False — Pubic and axillary hair are absent/sparse (their growth needs androgen action). (Book p210)
Peripheral hypergonadotropic hypogonadism is caused by decreased sex steroids feeding back to raise LH and FSH.
True — Decreased sex steroids → feedback → increased LH, FSH. (Book p209)
At puberty in AIS, testosterone levels become —
Puberty: markedly increased testosterone levels (testes functional, receptors resistant). (Book p210)
In PARTIAL androgen insensitivity at puberty, high testosterone can cause —
Puberty with increased testosterone → spontaneous virilization; apparent change of gender (partial forms, features vary with severity). (Book p210)
"Apparent change of gender" at puberty is described in —
Spontaneous virilization with apparent change of gender occurs when resistance is partial (features vary with severity of resistance). (Book p210)

A 12-year-old raised as a girl presents with deepening voice, clitoromegaly and increasing muscle mass. Karyotype is 46,XY and testosterone is very high.

A child raised as a girl begins virilising at puberty (voice deepening, clitoral growth). The likely mechanism —
Partial androgen insensitivity with rising testosterone
Puberty: increased testosterone → spontaneous virilization → apparent change of gender (partial resistance). (Book p210)
Clinical hallmark of AIS in childhood is female-like features with the child —
Female-like features: child raised as a girl. (Book p210)
Testosterone injections in classical AIS girls
Management: replacement of sex steroids. (Book p210)
In AIS raised female, the estrogen used for replacement is —
Ethinylestradiol replacement in AIS (raised female) is started beyond ___ years of age.

Oral progesterone is added to AIS (female) hormone replacement —
Oral progesterone 2 years later (to achieve break-through bleeding). (Book p210)
The purpose of adding oral progesterone in AIS (raised female) is to achieve —
Oral progesterone (to achieve break-through bleeding). (Book p210)
In AIS raised male (partial forms), replacement therapy uses —
Early (premature) administration of sex steroids in AIS causes —
Early fusion of epiphysis → short stature
Early administration → early fusion of epiphysis → short stature. (Book p210)
Sex steroid replacement in AIS must be timed carefully because early administration fuses the ___.
Early administration → early fusion of epiphysis → short stature. (Book p210)

In classical AIS, breast development at puberty is driven by testosterone converted to estrogen.
True — Increased testosterone is aromatized; the estrogen acts on breast tissue. (Book p210)
Precocious puberty in FEMALES is defined as pubertal changes before —
Pubertal changes occurring in females < 8 years. (Book p211)
Precocious puberty in MALES is defined as pubertal changes before —
Pubertal changes occurring in males < 9.5 years. (Book p211)
Central (gonadotropin-dependent) precocious puberty arises from disorders of the —
The most common cause of central precocious puberty in FEMALES is —
The most common cause of central precocious puberty in MALES is —
CNS pathology: m/c in males. (Book p211)
The most common CNS lesion causing central precocious puberty is —
A hypothalamic hamartoma may also cause gelactic seizures characterised by —
Other features: gelastic seizures (uncontrollable laughter). (Book p211)
Gelastic seizures, defined by uncontrollable ___, point to hypothalamic hamartoma with precocious puberty.
Gelastic seizures = uncontrollable laughter, associated with hypothalamic hamartomas. (Book p211)

A 7-year-old boy develops pubic hair, penile growth and accelerated height velocity over 6 months. Mother describes daily 30-second bouts of uncontrollable laughing. MRI shows a non-enhancing suprasellar mass.

A 7-year-old boy has rapid growth, pubic hair and 8 ml testes; he also has brief daily fits of uncontrollable laughter. MRI shows a suprasellar mass. Diagnosis —
Hypothalamic hamartoma with central precocious puberty
CNS pathology (m/c in males): hypothalamic hamartoma with gelastic seizures → central precocious puberty. (Book p211)
Functioning tumours in peripheral precocious puberty are more commonly found in the —
Functioning tumours: more common in testis → increased testosterone production. (Book p211)
Testicular tumours causing peripheral precocious puberty include —
Leydig/Sertoli cell tumours → increased testosterone production. (Book p211)
The most common cause of an autonomously functioning ovarian cyst with precocious puberty is —
Autonomously functioning ovarian cyst: m/c McCune-Albright syndrome (increased estrogen production). (Book p211)
CAH causing peripheral precocious puberty in males is due to deficiency of —
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: deficiency of 21-hydroxylase, 11-β-hydroxylase → precocious puberty in males. (Book p211)
The sex in which CAH classically produces precocious puberty is —
21-OH/11-β-OH deficiency → precocious puberty in males. (Book p211)
In peripheral precocious puberty, gonadotropin levels are —
Peripheral/gonadotropin-independent: sex steroids rise independent of gonadotropin stimulation. (Book p211)

A 3-year-old girl has thelarche and vaginal bleeding with a large ovarian cyst on ultrasound. LH and FSH are prepubertal; estradiol is very high. She also has bony deformity of the femur.

A 3-year-old girl has breast development, pubic hair and recurrent ovarian cysts with low LH/FSH but high estrogen. Likely diagnosis —
Autonomously functioning ovarian cyst (m/c with McCune-Albright) → increased estrogen, gonadotropin-independent puberty. (Book p211)

In males, pubertal changes before 8 years define precocious puberty.
False — In males the cut-off is < 9.5 years; < 8 years is the female cut-off. (Book p211)
McCune-Albright syndrome results from autonomous endocrine hyperfunction of one or more glands — thyroid, adrenal, ovaries and —
Autonomous endocrine hyperfunction of: thyroid, pituitary, adrenal gland, ovaries. (Book p211)
The genetic defect in McCune-Albright syndrome is —
Genetic defect: GNAS1 gene mutation (gain of function). (Book p211)
The GNAS1 mutation in McCune-Albright is a ___ of function mutation.
GNAS1 gene mutation (gain of function) → autonomous uncontrolled receptor activation. (Book p211)
GNAS1 codes for the α-subunit of ___ receptors.
Codes for α-subunit of Gs receptors (→ constitutive cAMP signalling). (Book p211)
The functional consequence of the GNAS1 mutation is —
Gain-of-function Gs α-subunit → autonomous uncontrolled receptor activation. (Book p211)
The clinical TRIAD of McCune-Albright syndrome includes polyendocrinopathy (precocious puberty), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and —
Triad: café-au-lait spots (skin finding), polyendocrinopathy (precocious puberty), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. (Book p211)
Irregular margins — "Coast of Maine" appearance; spots do not cross midline. (Book p211)

Irregular margins, "Coast of Maine" appearance. (Book p211)

Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright appears as —
Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia: multiple lytic lesions in bones. (Book p211)

M/c sites affected: base of skull; proximal femur → bowing (Shepherd crook deformity). (Book p211)

Proximal femur → bowing → Shepherd crook deformity. (Book p211)

Shepherd's crook deformity (proximal femur bowing). (Book p211)
Lytic lesions of the skull in McCune-Albright can be seen on —
Lytic lesions in skull (with base of skull as a m/c site). (Book p211)

Triad of precocious puberty (polyendocrinopathy), café-au-lait spots (Coast of Maine, not crossing midline) and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (femoral bowing) = McCune-Albright. (Book p211)

Langerhans cell histiocytosis is also known as ___.

Bone involvement: skull > jaw (missing/loose teeth). (Book p220)

Stalk destruction blocks vasopressin/ADH release from posterior pituitary granules → diabetes insipidus. (Book p220)

False — LCH skin lesions mimic seborrheic dermatitis but do NOT respond to treatment of the same. (Book p220)
