c: Medical Disorders: Anemia, Drugs and Heart Disease
MTP, Ectopic Pregnancy & Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
u: Gametogenesis starts with primordial germ cells arising from the epiblast and ectoderm. These bipotent cells differentiate into spermatogonia when the SRY gene on chromosome Y is present, or into oogonia when it is absent. The SRY locus sits on the distal end of the short arm of chromosome Y.

Spermatogenesis initiates at puberty in the seminiferous tubules. Type A spermatogonia maintain the stem pool while Type B spermatogonia enter meiosis, yielding 16 primary spermatocytes, which divide into secondary spermatocytes and then 64 spermatids. Spermiogenesis remodels round spermatids into spermatozoa without any cell division.

A mature spermatozoon measures 50–60 µm with an acrosome from the Golgi apparatus, a middle piece powerhouse packed with mitochondria, and a 9+2 axoneme from the centriole. Motility is acquired in the distal epididymis over 12–14 days, bringing total development time to 90 days. Once ejaculated, sperm reach the ampulla in 30 minutes and remain fertilisable for 48–72 hours.

Oogenesis begins in intrauterine life. Primary oocytes enter Meiosis I and arrest in the diplotene stage of prophase I (dictyate state) until the preovulatory LH surge triggers resumption. Meiosis II arrests at metaphase II and completes only upon fertilization. Follicles peak at 6–7 million at 5 months of fetal life, falling to 1–2 million at birth and 4–5 lakh at puberty.

Early zygotic blastomeres are totipotent, capable of building embryonic and extraembryonic structures, whereas germ cells are pluripotent. Primordial germ cells migrate from the epiblast across the yolk sac to the genital ridge; failure of migration with aberrant germ cell arrest along the midline produces teratomas.

Capacitation occurs in the female tract over 6–8 hours (2 hours in vitro), conferring hypermotility. Sperm bind the ZP3 receptor on the zona pellucida and release hyaluronidase during the acrosome reaction. Fusion of the sperm head with the oolemma triggers the cortical and zona reactions to prevent polyspermy.

Fertilization occurs in the ampulla on day 14 of a 28-day cycle. Cleavage yields a 2-cell embryo at 30 hours and a 16-cell morula that enters the uterine cavity on day 4 (cycle day 18), propelled by ciliated columnar cells and tubal peristalsis. On day 5, zona hatching frees the blastocyst; tubal immobility from Kartagener syndrome or progestin-only pills risks ectopic pregnancy.

Implantation occurs on day 6 post-fertilization (cycle day 20) during the receptive window from day 20 to 24. Apposition is mediated by selectins, adhesion by integrins, and penetration by matrix metalloproteinases. Progesterone drives decidualisation with marked stromal edema, creating the decidua basalis, capsularis, and parietalis, and giving the double decidual sign on ultrasound.

On day 8 post-fertilization, the blastocyst divides into the embryoblast and trophoblast. The inner cell mass generates all three definitive germ layers, while the trophoblast splits into syncytiotrophoblast—the placental hormone factory producing hCG and hPL—and cytotrophoblast. Extravillous trophoblasts remodel maternal spiral arteries, while chorion frondosum builds the fetal placenta.

Chorion arises from chorion laeve on day 8 as the outermost fetal membrane. Amnion forms on day 10 from embryonic ectoderm as an avascular, aneural inner membrane that supplies tensile strength. The yolk sac produces alpha-fetoprotein and serves as the initial site of hematopoiesis, while membrane rupture releases PGF2α to accelerate labor.

Preimplantation Genetic Testing screens embryos in assisted reproduction prior to transfer. It detects monogenic conditions such as sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, and thalassemia, as well as aneuploidies and translocations. Polar body biopsy detects only maternal disorders and blastomere removal risks embryo injury, making trophectoderm biopsy at the blastocyst stage the gold standard.

Fetal growth periods from fertilization comprise the preimplantation period (0–2 weeks, governed by the all-or-none law), the embryonic period (3–8 weeks, the peak teratogenic phase of organogenesis), and the fetal period (≥9 weeks). Maximum permissible radiation is 5 Rads (0.05 Gy); doses >5 Rads cause microcephaly and IUGR, while ≥10 Rads trigger abortion. Ultrasound and non-contrast MRI are safe.
Teratogenic Drugs: Category X & Specific Malformations

Category X medications carry proven fetal harm that far outweighs benefit, including androgens, DES, warfarin, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, thalidomide, lithium, and valproate. Alcohol causes smooth philtrum and cognitive impairment; phenytoin triggers fetal hydantoin syndrome; lithium induces Ebstein anomaly; thalidomide causes phocomelia; and warfarin causes chondrodysplasia punctata with stippled epiphyses.

CMV is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss, classically presenting with periventricular calcifications. Toxoplasmosis shows chorioretinitis and diffuse intracranial calcifications, treated with spiramycin for mother and pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine for the fetus. Rubella causes cataracts, PDA, and SNHL; Parvovirus B19 attacks erythroid precursors causing hydrops; and maternal SLE causes complete congenital heart block.

The human placenta is discoid, deciduate, and hemochorial, weighing ~500 g at term with a 1:6 placenta-to-fetal weight ratio and equal weight at 17 weeks. Central thickness measures 2.5–4 cm; thickness >4 cm defines placentomegaly from diabetes, hydrops, or syphilis. The shiny fetal surface forms 4/5th of the placenta, while the dull red maternal surface forms 1/5th and is divided into 15–20 cotyledons.

The placental barrier separates maternal and fetal blood via syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, extraembryonic mesoderm, and fetal capillary endothelium. Primary villi form on day 13, secondary villi acquire a mesodermal core on day 16, and tertiary villi develop fetal vessels on day 17. Cytotrophoblast invades maternal spiral arteries, replacing their elastic coats to lower resistance and expand flow.

Uteroplacental circulation in the intervillous space is established by day 12–13, carrying 500–700 ml/min at term out of a total uterine flow of 750 ml/min. Fetoplacental circulation in villi is established by day 17, flowing at 400 ml/min via the oxygenated umbilical vein and two deoxygenated umbilical arteries. Nitabuch's fibrinoid layer limits trophoblast penetration; its absence triggers placenta accreta.

The placenta carries out respiratory, endocrine, nutritive, and excretory duties. Intervillous space blood matches umbilical vein oxygen saturation at 65–75% with a PO2 of 30–35 mm Hg. The corpus luteum peaks on day 22 and is rescued by syncytiotrophoblastic hCG from day 8 post-fertilization, sustaining progesterone until the luteal-placental shift at 8–10 weeks.

The placenta converts maternal cholesterol into progesterone to sustain pregnancy and quiet the myometrium. Lacking 17α-hydroxylase, the placenta depends on fetal adrenal DHEA-S for estrogen synthesis via placental sulfatase and aromatase. Labor onset follows functional progesterone withdrawal and an estrogen surge; absent fetal DHEA-S in anencephaly precipitates post-term pregnancy.

Human placental lactogen shares 96% homology with growth hormone, peaking at 36 weeks as an anti-insulin agent that spares glucose for the fetus. Human chorionic gonadotropin has a common alpha subunit and a unique beta subunit, peaking at 10 weeks (~100,000 IU/L) with a 36-hour half-life. The discriminatory zone is 2000 IU/L on TVS and 6500 IU/L on TAS.

Placenta accreta spectrum grades depth of villous attachment from accreta (superficial myometrium) to increta (deep invasion) and percreta (serosal penetration). Placenta bilobata features two equal parts with one cord, while placenta succenturiata has an accessory lobe connected by bridging vessels that risk retained lobe PPH. Extrachorial placentas form a ring, with circumvallate showing a raised rolled fold predisposing to abruption and IUGR.
Cord Insertion Anomalies, Vasa Previa & Apt Test

Battledore placenta inserts marginally, while velamentous insertion attaches to membranes where vessels lack Wharton's jelly. When these membranous vessels cross the internal os, vasa previa results; rupture causes catastrophic fetal bleeding. Transvaginal color Doppler is the IOC, and an elective Cesarean is done at 34–37 weeks. The Apt alkali test stays pink with fetal HbF, confirming vasa previa over placenta previa.

Hematopoiesis shifts from the yolk sac (<6 weeks) to the liver (6–30 weeks, producing HbF) and then the bone marrow (≥20 weeks, producing HbA). Newborn Hb is 16–18 g/dL with 75–90% HbF, falling to 1% by 6 months. In the third stage, placental separation cleaves along the decidual zona spongiosa via the Schultze mechanism (80%, central, shiny side first) or Duncan mechanism (20%, peripheral, dull side first).

Amniotic fluid has a specific gravity of 1.008–1.010, pH of 7.2, and osmolarity of 260 mOsm/L, peaking at 1000 ml at 32–34 weeks before declining to 800 ml at term and 200 ml at 42 weeks. Fetal urination provides 1000 ml/day after 20 weeks, balanced by fetal swallowing. Amniotic fluid color signals pathology: green indicates meconium, golden indicates Rh incompatibility, dark red reflects abruptio, and tobacco juice marks IUFD.

Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for amniotic fluid assessment. The Amniotic Fluid Index sums the vertical diameter of the largest pocket across all four quadrants (normal 5–24 cm; <5 cm defines oligohydramnios and ≥25 cm defines polyhydramnios), though it cannot be used in twins. The Single Deepest Pocket measures 2–8 cm normally (<2 cm is oligohydramnios and >8 cm is polyhydramnios) and is valid in twin gestations.

Mild polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios are most often idiopathic. Severe polyhydramnios stems from gross congenital anomalies—gastrointestinal obstructions like duodenal and esophageal atresia surpassing neural tube defects—as well as maternal diabetes causing fetal osmotic diuresis. Severe oligohydramnios is driven by fetal renal anomalies in the second trimester and uteroplacental insufficiency or PPROM in the third trimester, requiring a sterile speculum exam.

Antepartum surveillance for fluid disorders starts at 28 weeks with weekly NST and BPP, and delivery at 39 weeks uncomplicated or 37 weeks complicated. Early oligohydramnios causes lethal pulmonary hypoplasia, while in labor it causes variable decelerations managed by left lateral rest and amnio-infusion. Amniotic band syndrome from early rupture creates constriction rings and digital amputations, distinct from thalidomide's proximal phocomelia.

In severe symptomatic polyhydramnios, serial therapeutic amniocentesis slowly drains up to 1.5–2.0 L, with tocolytics used before 34 weeks (indomethacin before 32 weeks), while ARM is contraindicated. High-yield imaging features include the keyhole sign in posterior urethral valves (causing oligohydramnios), the double bubble sign in duodenal atresia (causing polyhydramnios and linked to Down syndrome), and CTEV clubfoot from oligohydramnios compression.

Gestational age is calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), while fetal age is reckoned from fertilization, creating a 2-week difference. Naegele's rule calculates the EDD by adding 9 months and 7 days to the LMP, adjusting for variations in cycle length. Pregnancy spans three trimesters: T1 (up to 13w6d), T2 (14w to 27w6d), and T3 (28w to delivery).
ART Dating, Preterm Categories & Fetal Death / IUD

In assisted reproduction, EDD is calculated from the embryo transfer date (+263 days for Day 3, +261 days for Day 5 blastocyst). Preterm delivery is classified by ACOG into early (<34w) and late (34w-36w6d), and by WHO into extreme (<28w), very (<32w), and moderate-to-late. Intrauterine fetal death (demise at >=20 weeks or >=500g) presents with lost movements and characteristic imaging signs like Spalding's and Robert's.

Obstetrical history uses the GTPAL system: Gravida, Term (>=37w), Preterm (20-36w6d), Abortions (<20w), and Living children. Multiple gestations (twins/triplets) count as a single gravidity and parity event, but count individually as living children. Viability in India is defined at 28 weeks, and an elderly primigravida is defined as a woman conceiving for the first time at 35 years or older.
Symptoms, Pelvic Signs & Diagnostic Signs of Pregnancy

Pregnancy manifestations are categorized into presumptive symptoms (amenorrhea, morning sickness, quickening), probable pelvic signs, and positive/definitive signs. Classical probable signs include Goodell's (cervical softening), Hegar's (isthmic softening), Chadwick's (bluish mucosal vascularity), Palmer's (rhythmic uterine contractions), and Osiander's sign (lateral fornix pulsations). Definitive proof requires sonographic cardiac activity, auscultated FHS, or palpated fetal parts.

The gravid uterus ascends from a pelvic organ at 12 weeks (pubic symphysis) to midway at 16 weeks, umbilicus at 24 weeks, and xiphisternum at 36 weeks before descending at 40 weeks due to fetal head engagement (lightening). Fundal height in centimeters matches gestational age in weeks between 20 and 36 weeks. A discrepancy of >=3 weeks/cm warrants urgent sonographic evaluation for polyhydramnios, twins, IUGR, or erroneous dates.

The normal umbilical cord measures 40-70 cm, wrapped in Wharton's jelly, and contains 2 umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta and 1 left umbilical vein delivering oxygenated blood to the fetus. Umbilical artery Doppler shows forward flow in both systole and diastole with progressively decreasing vascular resistance and an S/D ratio normally <3 as pregnancy advances.
Abnormal Doppler: UPI, AEDF, REDF & MCA Doppler

In uteroplacental insufficiency, increased placental resistance elevates the S/D ratio (>=3), progressing to absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) and reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF). Delivery is indicated at 33-34 weeks for AEDF and 30-32 weeks for REDF after corticosteroids. Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler peak systolic velocity (PSV >=1.5 MoM) is the gold standard for non-invasive diagnosis of fetal anemia.

Single umbilical artery (SUA) is the most common vascular abnormality of the umbilical cord, strongly associated with renal and cardiovascular malformations; finding an associated anomaly necessitates fetal karyotyping. High-risk pregnancies require surveillance from 32 weeks with NST and biophysical scoring. Characteristic CTG signatures include late decelerations in UPI, variable decelerations in cord compression, and sinusoidal patterns in fetal anemia.
Antenatal Care Schedules, Mandatory & Optional Labs

Antenatal care guidelines mandate a minimum of 8 contacts by WHO and 4 visits by the Government of India (<12w, 14-26w, 28-34w, and 36w to term). Essential initial investigations include ABO/Rh typing, complete blood count, urine microscopy/culture, opt-out HIV screening, HBsAg, and VDRL/syphilis serology. Optional tests comprise maternal TSH, aneuploidy screening, rubella IgG/IgM susceptibility, and Group B Streptococcus swabs at 35-37 weeks.
Td/Tdap Vaccines, Risk Coding & Alert Signs

Pregnant women receive two doses of Td vaccine 4 weeks apart (or a single booster if fully vaccinated within 3 years), alongside Tdap between 27-37 weeks for neonatal pertussis protection. The Mother and Child Protection card and PMSMA utilize color stickers (Green for low risk, Red for high risk requiring 3 additional visits). Critical alert signs demanding emergency evaluation include fever >=38°C for >=24 hours, persistent vomiting, severe headache, bleeding, and decreased fetal movements.
Folic Acid Prophylaxis & IFA / Anemia Mukt Bharat

Periconceptional folic acid (400 mcg/day for low-risk, 4-5 mg/day for women with previous NTD) is initiated at least 1-3 months before conception through the first trimester. From the 4th month onwards, the Anemia Mukt Bharat programme provides daily red IFA tablets (60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid) for 180 days during pregnancy and continued for 180 days postpartum.

Recommended gestational weight gain is scaled to pre-pregnancy BMI: 11.5-16 kg for normal BMI, 12.5-18 kg for underweight, and 5-9 kg for obese mothers. Daily maternal energy demands increase by an average of +350 kcal/day (National guidelines: +85 in T1, +280 in T2, +470 in T3), accompanied by 1000 mg/day elemental calcium, 250 mcg/day iodine, and additional protein (+9.5g in T2, +22g in T3).
Vaccines, Air Travel & Exercise in Pregnancy

Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, chickenpox, BCG) are contraindicated during pregnancy, with conception advised at least 1 month post-immunization; killed and mRNA vaccines are safe. Commercial air travel is generally safe up to 36 weeks of gestation in uncomplicated pregnancies. Moderate exercise (30-45 minutes walking daily) is recommended, while vigorous exertion is contraindicated in placenta previa, pre-eclampsia, and heart disease.

Morning sickness typically resolves by 12-16 weeks; first-line therapy is doxylamine (10 mg) combined with pyridoxine (10 mg). Hyperemesis gravidarum is characterized by intractable vomiting, >5% pre-pregnancy weight loss, ketonuria, and electrolyte disturbances. The Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis (PUQE) score stratifies severity; management centers on fluid resuscitation, antiemetics, and mandatory thiamine (vitamin B1) supplementation to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Minor Ailments: Supine Hypotension, Varices & Neuropathies

Supine hypotensive syndrome results from IVC compression by the gravid uterus causing reduced venous return, maternal hypotension, and tachycardia, promptly corrected by left lateral positioning. Progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation and increased venous pressure produce lower limb varices, vulval varicosities, and hemorrhoids. Gestational fluid retention predisposes to compression neuropathies like carpal tunnel syndrome and Bell's palsy.

Transvaginal sonography (TVS, 5-10 MHz) identifies gestational landmarks approximately one week earlier than transabdominal scans. The gestational sac appears as an eccentric, fluid-filled rim at 4.5-5 weeks, followed by the yolk sac at 5-5.5 weeks (mean sac diameter 10 mm), which definitively confirms intrauterine pregnancy and excludes an ectopic pseudogestational sac.
Fetal Pole, Cardiac Activity & Missed Abortion Criteria

The embryonic fetal pole is visible by TVS at 5.5-6 weeks with cardiac flicker evident on M-mode (normal baseline 110-130 bpm at 6 weeks, peaking at 160-170 bpm at 8 weeks; <85 bpm signifies poor prognosis). Definitive criteria for missed abortion include a CRL >=7 mm without cardiac activity or a mean sac diameter (MSD) >=25 mm without an visible embryo.
Discriminatory hCG Titer & True vs Pseudogestational Sac

The discriminatory zone of beta-hCG is 1500-2000 mIU/mL for TVS and 6000-6500 mIU/mL for TAS; absence of an intrauterine sac above these titers strongly indicates an ectopic pregnancy. A true gestational sac is eccentrically located, exhibits a double decidual sign, and grows 1 mm/day, whereas a pseudogestational sac is centrally located, devoid of a yolk sac or double bleb sign, and lacks a double decidual contour.

Early transvaginal sonography identifies sequential gestational hallmarks: the intradecidual sign representing interstitial blastocyst burrowing, the double decidual sign confirming intrauterine pregnancy, and the double bleb sign pairing yolk and amniotic sacs. Crown-rump length (CRL) serves as the gold standard parameter for dating up to 13 weeks + 6 days.
Second Trimester Biometry, Cervical Length & Fetal Echo

Beyond 14 weeks, fetal biometry relies on biparietal diameter (BPD, measured outer-to-inner in the transthalamic plane), head circumference, abdominal circumference (AC, single best growth marker), and femur length. Transvaginal cervical length screening identifies preterm birth risk (<25 mm), while specialized fetal echocardiography at 22-24 weeks evaluates cardiac anomalies.
Anomaly Scan (TIFFA) & Cranial NTDs: Anencephaly & Acrania

Targeted Imaging for Fetal Anomalies (TIFFA / Level 2 scan) is universally performed between 18 and 22 weeks. Failure of anterior neuropore closure yields acrania and anencephaly, marked by absent calvarium, deep shallow orbits ('frog-eye' or 'Mickey Mouse' appearance), absent fetal adrenals causing post-term gestation, and polyhydramnios.
Spina Bifida, Arnold-Chiari II Signs & Craniorachischisis

Spina bifida results from failure of caudal vertebral arches to close, ranging from spina bifida occulta to open meningomyelocele. Classic sonographic hallmarks of Chiari II malformation include the 'lemon sign' (scalloped frontal bones), 'banana sign' (downward displaced cerebellum obliterating the cisterna magna), and hydrocephalus.
Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele vs Gastroschisis

Omphalocele is a midline umbilical defect enclosed within an amnioperitoneal sac with the umbilical cord inserting onto its apex, carrying high aneuploidy risks. Gastroschisis is a right paraumbilical defect with bowel loops floating freely in amniotic fluid without a membrane, exhibiting normal cord insertion and marked AFP elevation.

Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP), synthesized by the fetal yolk sac, liver, and gut, is evaluated between 15 and 20 weeks. Elevated MSAFP signifies open NTDs, abdominal wall defects, or multiple gestations, whereas decreased MSAFP is seen in fetal aneuploidies, maternal diabetes, and gestational trophoblastic disease ('Diabetic GOAT').

Aneuploidies stem from chromosomal non-disjunction, Robertsonian translocations, or mosaicism, with Trisomy 16 being the most common cause of early miscarriage. Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most viable autosomal trisomy, carrying a 100% recurrence risk if a parent harbors a balanced t(21;21) Robertsonian translocation.
First Trimester Screening: Dual Test & Combined Test

First trimester screening at 11w0d to 13w6d (CRL 45-84 mm) combines biochemical analytes and sonography. The Dual test measures PAPP-A (decreased) and free beta-hCG (increased in Down syndrome). Combining the Dual test with nuchal translucency (Combined test) achieves an 85-87% detection rate.

Nuchal translucency (NT) is measured in the mid-sagittal plane with a neutral fetal head, considered abnormal when >=3 mm. Increased NT associates with Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and congenital heart defects. Cystic hygroma is a larger, multiseptated posterior neck lymphangioma with a very high predictive value for aneuploidy.
Second Trimester Markers: Triple, Quad & Soft Sonographic Signs

Second trimester biochemical screening between 15 and 20 weeks comprises the Triple test and Quad test (adding Inhibin-A). Down syndrome exhibits high hCG and Inhibin-A with low AFP and uE3 ('HI' is high). Key sonographic soft markers include thickened nuchal fold (>=6 mm), absent nasal bone, echogenic intracardiac focus, and choroid plexus cysts.
Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT / cffDNA) & Integrated Screening

NIPT analyzes cell-free fetal DNA derived from apoptotic syncytiotrophoblasts in maternal plasma from 10 weeks onward, offering >99% sensitivity for Trisomy 21. Integrated screening fuses first-trimester Combined testing with second-trimester Quad screening to achieve 85-95% detection rates while minimizing invasive procedures.

Screening results are expressed as personalized risk ratios, using established cutoffs of 1:250 for Down syndrome and 1:100 for Trisomies 18 and 13. Screen-positive findings prompt counseling for secondary screening via NIPT or definitive invasive diagnostic confirmation via CVS (T1) or amniocentesis (T2).
Invasive Prenatal Diagnostic Procedures: CVS vs Amniocentesis

Invasive prenatal diagnosis provides definitive karyotyping when screening indicates aneuploidy. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) biopsies rapidly dividing cytotrophoblasts at 10-14 weeks, yielding swift results within 48 hours but carrying a 1% procedure-related loss rate and risk of confined placental mosaicism. Amniocentesis samples amniocytes between 15 and 20 weeks with a lower loss rate (<0.5%) and definitive cytogenetic accuracy.

Amniocentesis is performed under continuous real-time ultrasound guidance using a 20-22G spinal needle, aspirating approximately 20 mL of amniotic fluid for cytogenetics, viral PCR, or fetal lung maturity testing. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS / cordocentesis) accesses the umbilical vein beyond 18 weeks to measure fetal hemoglobin in severe Rh alloimmunization or non-immune hydrops.
Antepartum Fetal Surveillance Principles & Movement Counts

Antepartum fetal surveillance is universally initiated at 32 weeks in high-risk pregnancies (or 2-4 weeks prior to a prior gestational demise). Maternal kick charts, such as the Cardiff 'count-to-10' (10 movements in 2 hours at rest or 12 hours during daily activity), provide a cost-free screening tool; diminished movement reflects early compensatory fetal motor quiescence to preserve central oxygenation.

The Non-Stress Test (NST) evaluates fetal autonomic integrity by recording fetal heart rate (FHR) responses to fetal movement with the mother in a left lateral tilt. A normal baseline FHR spans 110-160 bpm with moderate baseline variability (6-25 bpm). At >=32 weeks, a reactive acceleration requires a heart rate increase of >=15 bpm lasting >=15 seconds (15x15 rule).

A sinusoidal heart rate pattern (smooth regular oscillations, 2-5 cycles/min, amplitude 5-15 bpm) is an ominous sign pathognomonic of severe fetal anemia or acute profound acidemia, demanding immediate delivery. Tracings lacking accelerations over 20 minutes are extended to 40 minutes to account for fetal sleep cycle, followed by acoustic stimulation or biophysical scoring if non-reactivity persists.
Biophysical Profile (BPP / Manning Score) & Modified BPS

Manning's Biophysical Profile combines four ultrasound dynamic variables (tone, gross movement, breathing movements, and single deepest pocket >=2 cm) with the NST, scoring each parameter as 0 or 2. Under progressive hypoxic acidemia, early-developing acute neurological centers (NST, breathing) fail first, while the primitive fetal tone center fails last. A score <=4/10 signals significant acidemia and mandates prompt delivery.

Uterine contractions physiologically compress intramyometrial blood vessels, transiently reducing intervillous perfusion. While well-oxygenated fetuses tolerate this stress, compromised fetuses develop decelerations and progressive metabolic acidemia. Routine surveillance in low-risk labor utilizes intermittent auscultation (every 30 mins in first stage, every 15 mins in second stage), switching to continuous electronic monitoring for high-risk conditions.

CTG interpretation assesses baseline rate (110-160 bpm), baseline variability (moderate 6-25 bpm), and decelerations. Absent variability is the most reliable single herald of fetal hypoxia. Prolonged decelerations (drop >=15 bpm lasting 2-10 minutes) commonly arise from uterine tachysystole induced by oxytocin, managed immediately by stopping uterotonics, lateral repositioning, and acute tocolysis.
Deceleration Morphologies: Early, Late & Variable Decelerations

Early decelerations mirror contractions with a nadir coinciding with the peak of the contraction, caused by vagal stimulation from fetal head compression (benign). Late decelerations lag behind contractions with a delayed nadir, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal myocardial hypoxia. Variable decelerations exhibit an abrupt drop caused by umbilical cord compression.

Cardiotocography tracings are stratified into Category 1 (Normal/reassuring), Category 2 (Suspicious/indeterminate), and Category 3 (Pathological/non-reassuring). Category 3 tracings (absent variability with late decelerations, severe variable decelerations, bradycardia, or sinusoidal wave) dictate urgent intrauterine resuscitation—discontinuing oxytocin, maternal left lateral positioning, high-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus, and rapid delivery.
Fetal Scalp Blood Sampling, Scalp Stimulation & Pulse Oximetry

Fetal scalp blood sampling directly measures capillary pH when CTG is abnormal (>=7.25 normal, 7.20-7.24 pre-acidotic, <7.20 severe acidosis dictating immediate operative delivery). Prior to incision, fetal scalp stimulation that elicits an acceleration confirms a normal pH in virtually 100% of cases, avoiding unnecessary invasive blood sampling.
Maternal Adaptations: Cutaneous, Uterine & Cervical Shifts

Elevated estrogen and progesterone stimulate melanogenesis, producing linea nigra, melasma ('mask of pregnancy'), and palmar erythema. The uterus enlarges dramatically from 50 g to 1100 g, driven predominantly by myometrial hypertrophy. The cervix exhibits vascular engorgement (Chadwick/Goodell signs), glandular hyperplasia forming a protective mucus operculum, and benign columnar ectropion.
Vaginal Ecosystem, Endocrine Shifts & Fluid Retention

Lactobacilli ferment vaginal glycogen into lactic acid, dropping vaginal pH to 3.5-4.0; this acidic shield inhibits bacterial pathogens but predisposes to Candida vulvovaginitis. High placental steroids suppress gonadotropins and maintain decidual quiescence. Maternal fluid retention expands extracellular volume by 6.5-8.5 liters, producing benign dependent edema that readily resolves upon recumbency.

Maternal plasma volume expands by 40-50% while erythrocyte mass increases by only 20-30%, creating physiological hemodilution where hemoglobin normally remains >=11.0 g/dL. Pregnancy induces a marked prothrombotic state: fibrinogen doubles (to 400-600 mg/dL), Factors VII, VIII, IX, and X increase, and fibrinolysis is suppressed, while bleeding and clotting times remain unchanged.

Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, inducing physiological hydroureter (right > left due to dextrorotated uterine compression) and predisposing to ascending pyelonephritis from asymptomatic bacteriuria. Renal blood flow jumps by 70-80% and GFR by 50%, reducing normal serum creatinine to 0.4-0.6 mg/dL. Progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation delays gallbladder emptying and relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, exacerbating GERD.

The maternal respiratory system adapts through progesterone-mediated stimulation of the medullary respiratory center, increasing tidal volume by 30-50% while respiratory rate remains constant. Diaphragmatic elevation of 4 cm and subcostal widening decrease functional residual capacity by 20%, while chronic hyperventilation creates a compensated respiratory alkalosis facilitating fetal CO2 transfer.
Maternal Oxygen Dynamics, Endocrine & Visceral Changes

Total maternal oxygen consumption and binding capacity increase alongside a narrower arteriovenous oxygen gradient. The anterior pituitary gland enlarges by 135% with heightened vascularity, rendering it susceptible to ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome) during postpartum hemorrhage. Fetal skeletal demands absorb 30 g of maternal calcium via enhanced active intestinal absorption.
Iron Requirements, Metabolism & Anemia Mukt Bharat / I-NIPI

Total pregnancy iron requirement is 1000 mg (fetal/placental demands 300 mg, RBC expansion 500 mg, basal losses 200 mg), rising to 7.5 mg/day in the third trimester. Because anemia affects 50% of Indian mothers, the Anemia Mukt Bharat (I-NIPI 6x6x6) initiative distributes daily red IFA tablets (60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid) paired with mid-trimester albendazole deworming.

IFA tablets should be consumed 2 hours post-prandially with water or citrus juices, maintaining a 2-hour separation from calcium or tea to maximize absorption. WHO classifies anemia as <11 g/dL (Mild: 10-10.9, Moderate: 7-9.9, Severe: <7 g/dL), while ICMR designates <4.0 g/dL as very severe anemia. Nutritional iron deficiency accounts for 80% of pathological anemia.
Maternal & Fetal Complications of Anemia in Pregnancy

Severe maternal anemia impairs myometrial oxygenation leading to uterine inertia, postpartum hemorrhage, subinvolution, and heart failure (peaking immediately postpartum due to autotransfusion). While active placental transport shields the fetus from developing microcytic anemia, maternal hypoxemia triggers compensatory placentomegaly, preterm labor, and fetal growth restriction.
Clinical Evaluation & Physical Workup of Gestational Anemia

Clinical history evaluates pica, menorrhagia, and worm infestation; physical examination inspects the conjunctiva, tongue, and palmar creases (pallor evident when Hb <7 g/dL). Severe deficiency produces platonychia, koilonychia (spoon nails), or angular cheilosis. Government guidelines mandate checking hemoglobin at all four routine antenatal visits.
Diagnostic RBC Indices & Iron Profile Interpretation

Peripheral blood smear demonstrates microcytic hypochromic red cells in iron deficiency anemia (MCV <75-80 fL, MCHC <30%). The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC count) cleanly differentiates IDA (>13) from beta-thalassemia trait (<13). Serum ferritin (<20-30 mcg/L) serves as the gold-standard biochemical marker of depleted iron stores, accompanied by elevated TIBC (>400 mcg/dL) and transferrin saturation <16%.
Oral Iron Therapy & Assessing Treatment Response

Treatment of mild-to-moderate anemia initiates with 2 IFA tablets daily (120 mg elemental iron). Therapeutic response is verified earliest by a reticulocyte surge within 5-7 days (peaking at 10 days), followed by a hemoglobin rise of 0.7-1.0 g/dL per month. Dark stools confirm medication compliance, and treatment continues until target hemoglobin is reached.
Parenteral Iron Therapy, Ganzoni Formula & Blood Transfusion

Parenteral iron (IV iron sucrose, max 200 mg/day; ferric carboxymaltose) is indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption, or moderate anemia diagnosed beyond 30-34 weeks. Total deficit is calculated via the Ganzoni equation: Weight x (11 - Hb) x 2.4 + 500 mg. Packed red blood cell transfusion is reserved for acute hemorrhage, heart failure, Hb <5 g/dL at any gestation, or severe anemia near term.
Trimester-Wise Gestational Management Protocol for Anemia

Anemia algorithms integrate gestational age and severity: before 34 weeks, mild-to-moderate anemia receives oral iron; beyond 34 weeks, moderate cases switch to parenteral iron to secure rapid replenishment. Severe anemia (<7 g/dL) near term warrants blood transfusion with furosemide diuresis, while extreme anemia (<5 g/dL) mandates immediate transfusion regardless of gestational age.
Antimicrobial Safety & Teratogenic Hazards in Pregnancy

Penicillins and cephalosporins remain safe throughout gestation, while nitrofurantoin serves as first-line therapy for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Tetracyclines (bone hypoplasia, permanent enamel discoloration), aminoglycosides (eighth cranial nerve ototoxicity), chloramphenicol (Gray baby syndrome), and fluoroquinolones (fetal arthropathy) are strictly avoided.

Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) does not cross the placental barrier and serves as the anticoagulant of choice throughout gestation, monitored by anti-Factor Xa levels. Warfarin crosses the placenta, causing embryopathy and fetal intracranial hemorrhage. In women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves, warfarin <5 mg/day may be continued in early pregnancy or switched sequentially to LMWH/UFH prior to labor.

Warfarin exposure at 6-9 weeks produces DiSaia syndrome, featuring nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata), microcephaly, and optic atrophy. Among antiepileptics, valproate is the most potent teratogen (neural tube and cardiac defects); levetiracetam and lamotrigine display the safest clinical profiles, always co-prescribed with high-dose folic acid.
Maternal Cardiovascular Hemodynamics & Peak Stress Periods

Maternal cardiac output surges by 40-50% while systemic vascular resistance declines, producing a mid-trimester blood pressure nadir. Peak cardiovascular decompensation risks concentrate at 28-32 weeks, during the second stage of labor, and immediately postpartum due to autotransfusion of 300-500 mL of blood from the contracted uterus.
Heart Failure vs Pregnancy Signs, RHD & Congenital Lesions

Physiological systolic flow murmurs (grade <=2/6) and an S3 gallop are benign in pregnancy, whereas any diastolic murmur, systolic murmur >=grade 3/6, or elevated JVP signifies structural heart disease. Rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis (MS) is the leading cause of maternal cardiac mortality in developing nations; atrial septal defect represents the most common acyanotic congenital lesion.
Lesion Prognosis & WHO Class IV Contraindications

Stenotic valvular lesions (MS, AS) poorly tolerate gestational tachycardia due to shortened diastolic filling times, precipitating pulmonary edema. Regurgitant lesions (MR, AR) improve due to reduced peripheral vascular resistance. Modified WHO Class IV conditions (Eisenmenger syndrome, severe pulmonary hypertension, severe MS, LVEF <30%, Marfan with aortic root >=45 mm) carry extreme maternal mortality (30-50%), contraindicating pregnancy.
Intrapartum & Postpartum Management of Heart Disease

Vaginal delivery in a semi-recumbent left-lateral position with early epidural analgesia is preferred for cardiac patients, using vacuum or forceps to shorten second-stage pushing. Fluid infusion is restricted to 75 mL/hr. In the third stage, slow IV oxytocin is the agent of choice; methylergometrine is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED because severe vasoconstriction triggers fatal pulmonary edema.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) presents with heart failure (LVEF <45%) between 36 weeks and 5 months postpartum without prior cardiac disease, managed with diuretics, beta-blockers, and bromocriptine. Severe mitral stenosis (mitral valve area <1.5 cm^2) requires heart rate control with beta-blockers and diuretics, with percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy performed in the second trimester if medical therapy fails.

Detect mid-pelvic and outlet contraction by their diameters, then add the posterior sagittal diameters, inclination angle and sub-pubic angle. Focus for this checkpoint: Mid-pelvis & pelvic outlet, Sagittal diameters & pelvic angles.
Significance of the ischial spine & stations

Use the ischial spine for stations, engagement, internal rotation, deep transverse arrest, levator ani attachment and the pudendal block landmark. Focus for this checkpoint: Significance of the ischial spine & stations.

Apply contraction cut-offs at inlet, mid-pelvis and outlet, then diagnose and manage CPD by level and severity with trial of labour as the best test. Focus for this checkpoint: Contracted pelvis & cephalopelvic disproportion.

Remember that CPD is fetus-relative and bars VBAC, then classify gynaecoid, android, anthropoid and platypelloid pelves by inlet shape, walls and angles. Focus for this checkpoint: CPD notes & Caldwell-Moloy pelvic types.
Presenting parts of the fetal skull & head attitude

Map the vertex, brow and face onto their fontanelle and facial landmarks, then link each degree of flexion to the part that presents. Focus for this checkpoint: Presenting parts of the fetal skull & head attitude.

Label the diagram of the fetal skull – bones, sutures, bregma and lambda – and lock in the exact meaning of each terminology word used in later chapters. Focus for this checkpoint: Sutures, fontanelles & skull terminology.
Diameters of the fetal skull & engaging diameters

Rank the six AP and four transverse diameters by length, then tie each presentation and attitude to the diameter that must pass the pelvis. Focus for this checkpoint: Diameters of the fetal skull & engaging diameters.
Engagement timing, moulding & swellings on the head

Time the descent of the head in primi versus multi, grade moulding, and separate caput succedaneum from cephalhematoma feature by feature. Focus for this checkpoint: Engagement timing, moulding & swellings on the head.

Define lie, presentation and presenting part with their m/c examples, manage transverse lie in each period, and sort hand versus head-plus-hand prolapse. Focus for this checkpoint: Lie, presentation, prolapse & presenting part.

Assign the correct denominator to each presentation, then walk the eight occipital positions to know which are delivered vaginally and which are most common at each stage. Focus for this checkpoint: Denominator, attitude & position.
Practise the three-step P/V method for locating the occiput and translating the examiner's right into the mother's left. Focus for this checkpoint: Identification of fetal position.
Leopold's manoeuvres: preparation & the four grips

Run through the seven preparatory steps, then interpret what each of the four grips palpates and infers about lie, presentation, position and engagement. Focus for this checkpoint: Leopold's manoeuvres: preparation & the four grips.
Fixation & engagement of the fetal head (Crichton method)
Count the fifths of head palpable above the brim to distinguish a free, fixed and engaged head. Focus for this checkpoint: Fixation & engagement of the fetal head (Crichton method).
The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase

Fix the boundaries of the four stages, then compare the latent and active phases by guideline cut-off, event and duration in primi and multi. Focus for this checkpoint: The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase.

Define prolonged latent phase numerically and match each of its three causes with the correct management, remembering it is never a C-section indication. Focus for this checkpoint: Prolonged latent phase.
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase

Learn the cm/hr benchmarks for dilatation and descent, the old vs new WHO 1 cm/hr rule, and the P/V-based protocol for slow active-phase progress. Focus for this checkpoint: Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase.
Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest

State the arrest criteria in hours and Montevideo units, the prerequisites for arrest of descent, and read the classic arrest partogram. Focus for this checkpoint: Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest.
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management

Hold the average and maximum second-stage durations with and without epidural, then decide between C-section, forceps and vacuum by station and cause. Focus for this checkpoint: Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management.
Recognise obstructed labour clinically, from the exhausted mother to the Bandl's ring, and know what to do – and what to avoid. Focus for this checkpoint: Obstructed labour & Bandl's ring.

Contrast the retraction ring of obstructed labour with the oxytocin-induced constriction ring across cause, site, stage, palpability and relief. Focus for this checkpoint: Bandl's ring vs Schroeder's ring.
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care

Sort the recommended from the not-recommended at admission, then apply the rules for ambulation, oral intake, bladder care, pain relief and monitoring frequency. Focus for this checkpoint: WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care.
Management of second stage & prevention of perineal tear

List the four perineal protection measures, the two things not recommended, and the two-hand technique of the modified Ritgen manoeuvre. Focus for this checkpoint: Management of second stage & prevention of perineal tear.
Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide

Trace the evolution from Friedman's sigmoid curve through Philpott's alert line to the 2020 Labour Care Guide and what each one plots. Focus for this checkpoint: Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide.

Record FHR, amniotic fluid codes and moulding grades exactly as they appear in the fetal section of the modified WHO partograph. Focus for this checkpoint: Modified WHO partograph: upper (fetal) parameters.
Cervicograph: alert & action lines and colour zones

Interpret the green–yellow–pink zones of the cervicograph and apply the rule that the first plot always goes on the alert line. Focus for this checkpoint: Cervicograph: alert & action lines and colour zones.
Lower part: maternal parameters & uterine contractions

Know what the lower part records, what it omits, and how adequate contractions are counted, timed, shaded and rescued when hypertonic. Focus for this checkpoint: Lower part: maternal parameters & uterine contractions.
Labour Care Guide: sections, supportive care & alert column

Memorise the seven LCG sections with the mnemonic, the alert-box concept, and how companion, pain relief, fluids and posture are coded. Focus for this checkpoint: Labour Care Guide: sections, supportive care & alert column.
Code every fetal parameter of Section 3 and identify which values trigger the red alert box. Focus for this checkpoint: LCG Section 3: care of baby.
LCG Sections 4–7: woman, progress, medication & plan

Fix the maternal alert thresholds, the contraction and time-bound dilatation alerts, the WHO second-stage limits and the final sections. Focus for this checkpoint: LCG Sections 4–7: woman, progress, medication & plan.
Definition, criteria & the four phases of labour

Define normal labour by its five criteria and walk through the four uterine phases from quiescence to postpartum with their hormonal drivers. Focus for this checkpoint: Definition, criteria & the four phases of labour.
Pre-labour state & true vs false labour pain

Recognise lightening, false pains and the biochemistry of cervical ripening, then separate true from false labour pain across six features. Focus for this checkpoint: Pre-labour state & true vs false labour pain.
The 3 Ps & physiology of uterine contractions

Quantify the origin, speed, pressure thresholds and stage-wise strengths of contractions, and understand Montevideo units and segment formation. Focus for this checkpoint: The 3 Ps & physiology of uterine contractions.

Define tachysystole and precipitate labour with their causes and consequences, and manage hypertonic and hypotonic uterine activity. Focus for this checkpoint: Tachysystole, precipitate labour & hypotonic contractions.

Identify Kocher's forceps, the prostaglandin logic of ARM, its absolute and relative contraindications, and the engaged/unengaged sequencing rule. Focus for this checkpoint: Augmentation of labour: ARM & sequence.
Cardinal movements & the process of labour

Order the seven cardinal movements and know the degree of rotation, the definition of crowning, restitution and WHO perineal protection steps. Focus for this checkpoint: Cardinal movements & the process of labour.
Engagement: definition, signs, causes of non-engagement & engaging diameters

Define engagement by the biparietal diameter, its clinical signs, why a primigravida's head may float at term and which AP diameter engages in each attitude. Focus for this checkpoint: Engagement: definition, signs, causes of non-engagement & engaging diameters.

Distinguish synclitic from anterior and posterior asynclitic engagement by where the sagittal suture points, and recall how the head is delivered in vertex vs breech/face. Focus for this checkpoint: Synclitic & asynclitic engagement.
Pain pathways of labour & epidural analgesia

Trace the spinal segments carrying 1st and 2nd stage pain, and set the level, drugs, effects, monitoring and contraindication of epidural analgesia. Focus for this checkpoint: Pain pathways of labour & epidural analgesia.

Locate the pudendal and paracervical block sites, their uses and hazards, then cover prostaglandin receptors, synthesis sites and obstetric uses. Focus for this checkpoint: Pudendal & paracervical blocks and prostaglandins.

Score every Bishop parameter with the DELHI POLICE mnemonic, know the most and least important items, the simplified and modified versions, and interpret the totals. Focus for this checkpoint: Induction of labour: Bishop score.
Methods of induction: sweeping & mechanical methods

Group the ripening, induction and augmentation methods, then detail membrane sweeping, Foley, EASI and laminaria – the options preferred in a scarred uterus. Focus for this checkpoint: Methods of induction: sweeping & mechanical methods.
Dose misoprostol, cerviprime gel and Cervidil correctly, rank their tachysystole risk, and prepare and titrate oxytocin safely. Focus for this checkpoint: Prostaglandins & oxytocin for induction.
Contraindications to IOL & IOL in special cases

Recall the ten conditions where vaginal delivery – and hence induction – is contraindicated, and the protocols for scarred uterus and intrauterine death. Focus for this checkpoint: Contraindications to IOL & IOL in special cases.
Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview
Master placental separation physiology, the signs, passive vs active management and the four steps of AMTSL. Focus for this checkpoint: Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview.

Dose and store oxytocin, methylergometrine, syntometrine, carboprost and misoprostol, and contrast oxytocin with methylergometrine. Focus for this checkpoint: Step 1: uterotonics – oxytocin & alternatives.

Time delayed clamping, its iron benefit and programme link, and list every absolute and relative indication for early clamping including the HIV nuance. Focus for this checkpoint: Step 2: delayed cord clamping.
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage

Perform controlled cord traction correctly, handle the special cases (cord snap, inversion, PAS, succenturiate lobe), then run fourth-stage monitoring. Focus for this checkpoint: Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage.

Pin down every PPH definition (volume, ACOG, clinical, WHO severe), the primary/secondary split, and the 4 T causes with their m/c examples. Focus for this checkpoint: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts.
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
Sort the maternal, placental, uterine and intrapartum risk factors, and recall the five specific risks for traumatic PPH. Focus for this checkpoint: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH.
Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH

Run the six-point resuscitation, then use per-abdominal massage to split atonic from traumatic PPH and decide the next examination. Focus for this checkpoint: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH.
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid

Perform bimanual massage, give tranexamic acid at the right dose and timing, and start the WHO first-choice uterotonic. Focus for this checkpoint: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid.
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost

Dose each second-line drug, identify its unique contraindications and side effects, and know which is the gold standard. Focus for this checkpoint: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost.
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery

Follow the escalation ladder from first-line uterotonics through balloon tamponade, compression sutures, devascularisation and hysterectomy. Focus for this checkpoint: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery.
Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing

Place the O'Leary suture correctly, quote its success rate, compute the shock index and remember which old method is obsolete. Focus for this checkpoint: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing.
Define retained placenta and manage each of its three causes – trapped, adherent-non-invasive and morbidly adherent. Focus for this checkpoint: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm.
Grade accreta, increta and percreta by depth, know the risk factors, etiology, Doppler signs and definitive treatment. Focus for this checkpoint: Placenta accreta spectrum.
Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features

Distinguish inversion from prolapse, classify by time and degree, and recognise the neurogenic-then-hemorrhagic shock picture. Focus for this checkpoint: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features.
Apply Johnson's manual replacement principles, know the surgical fall-backs and outdated methods, and the four post-replacement steps. Focus for this checkpoint: Uterine inversion: management.

Explain AFE pathophysiology and its two clinical phases, the clinical diagnostic criteria, and differentiate the three causes of postpartum collapse. Focus for this checkpoint: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse.

Identify the artery, cause and presentation of vulval hematoma, decide between conservative and surgical care, and recognise the hidden broad-ligament bleed. Focus for this checkpoint: Vulval hematoma & broad ligament hematoma.
Grade perineal tears including the 3A/3B/3C subdivisions, and sequence the repair by degree, setting, suture and timing. Focus for this checkpoint: Perineal tear: classification & repair.

List the indications, compare median with mediolateral episiotomy feature by feature, know the correct moment to cut and which muscles are divided. Focus for this checkpoint: Episiotomy: indications, types, timing & anatomy.

Define malposition, rank the OP positions and causes, and contrast OP with OA on abdominal findings and engaging diameters. Focus for this checkpoint: Occipito-posterior malposition: features, causes & findings.
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest

Work through complete forward rotation, incomplete rotation with deep transverse arrest, and posterior rotation with face-to-pubes delivery. Focus for this checkpoint: Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest.

Characterise transverse lie by denominator, position, causes and examination, know its cord-prolapse risk and the C-section-only rules including neglected shoulder. Focus for this checkpoint: Transverse lie & shoulder presentation.
Prepare for ECV with the right prerequisites and USG checks, know its procedure, contraindications and what to do after success or failure. Focus for this checkpoint: External cephalic version (ECV).
Describe face presentation's attitude and denominator, its risk factors, positions with the m/c one, and management by mento-anterior vs mento-posterior. Focus for this checkpoint: Face presentation.
Recognise brow presentation by its landmarks and 14 cm diameter, and know why it can only deliver by C-section unless it converts. Focus for this checkpoint: Brow presentation.

Track breech incidence by gestation, its m/c causes, and distinguish complete, frank, knee and footling breech by posture, P/V findings and cord-prolapse risk. Focus for this checkpoint: Breech: features, incidence, causes & types.
Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery

Use USG to screen for ECV, follow the ECV flowchart, and apply the absolute and relative indications for caesarean section. Focus for this checkpoint: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery.
Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites

Know the denominator, engaging diameter and m/c position of breech, the deadly complication of the after-coming head, and the safety prerequisites. Focus for this checkpoint: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites.
Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks

Follow the RSA mechanism from oblique engagement to spontaneous buttock delivery, and apply groin traction, Pinard's manoeuvre and the Savage technique. Focus for this checkpoint: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks.
Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre

Trace the bisacromial diameter through the pelvis and rescue extended arms with Lovset's manoeuvre or cubital fossa delivery. Focus for this checkpoint: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre.

Deliver the after-coming head with Burns-Marshall, Bracht, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit, Piper's forceps and Prague manoeuvre – and know when each applies. Focus for this checkpoint: After-coming head of breech: manoeuvres.
Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction

Manage the entrapped head differently in preterm and term breech, recall the m/c cause of death, and define breech extraction for the second twin. Focus for this checkpoint: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction.

Learn the indications, the FORCEPS mnemonic of prerequisites, the favourable positions, and when vacuum can replace forceps. Focus for this checkpoint: Instrumental delivery: indications, prerequisites & choice.

Recall the vacuum-specific and absolute contraindications, then set up the silastic cup pressures and the flexion-point application. Focus for this checkpoint: Contraindications & vacuum delivery technique.

Name the parts of the obstetric forceps, the two lock types, how to identify left from right, and the four classic forceps with their unique features. Focus for this checkpoint: Forceps: parts, locks, handedness & types.
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications

Classify low vs outlet forceps, pull in the correct sequence of directions, quote traction forces, and compare complications of forceps and vacuum. Focus for this checkpoint: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications.
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section

Place the Pfannenstiel and Joel-Cohen incisions, weigh transverse-incision pros and cons, and compare Sanger's, Kerr's and Krönig's uterine incisions by rupture risk and VBAC eligibility. Focus for this checkpoint: Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section.
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section

Choose between TOLAC and repeat section, list the risks of each path, and master the inter-delivery interval numbers and anaesthesia levels. Focus for this checkpoint: Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section.

Separate absolute from relative contraindications to VBAC, remember what is NOT a contraindication, identify prognostic markers and monitor the scar. Focus for this checkpoint: VBAC: contraindications, prognosis & monitoring.
Classical caesarean indications & anaesthesia for caesarean

Know when the lower segment cannot be used, the 4-minute perimortem rule, and match spinal, epidural and general anaesthesia to their indications. Focus for this checkpoint: Classical caesarean indications & anaesthesia for caesarean.

Separate puerperium from the fourth trimester, schedule ACOG and GOI postnatal visits, and chart the uterus shrinking week by week. Focus for this checkpoint: Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution.
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function

Track the lower segment, cervix and os, sequence the lochia, time placental-site healing and return of ovulation in breast- and non-breastfeeding women. Focus for this checkpoint: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function.
Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains

Recall the blood-count and fluid shifts after delivery, when each parameter normalises, and the nature of after-pains. Focus for this checkpoint: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains.
Identify the m/c cause of subinvolution, its clinical features, USG findings and the uterotonic-then-curettage management. Focus for this checkpoint: Subinvolution of the uterus.

Distinguish prolactin from oxytocin roles, what colostrum lacks, and which maternal conditions truly contraindicate breastfeeding. Focus for this checkpoint: Breastfeeding: hormones, colostrum & contraindications.
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis

Diagnose postpartum endometritis by site and risk factors, recognise septic pelvic thrombophlebitis clinically and manage with heparin for the correct duration. Focus for this checkpoint: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.
Match burning thigh, quadriceps weakness and foot drop to the injured nerve and its mechanism, and know the nerves most often injured after caesarean. Focus for this checkpoint: Obstetric neuropathy.
q: Fill up: Gametogenesis begins with the primordial germ cell (PGC), which is embryologically derived from ______.
Primordial germ cells are derived from the epiblast and ectoderm. (Book p265)
Fill up: Primordial germ cells are described as bipotent because they possess the developmental capability to form ______.
All three embryonic germ layers only
PGCs are bipotent cells that can differentiate into either spermatogonia or oogonia. (Book p265)
Fill up: Sexual differentiation of the primordial germ cells into male or female gametogonia is fundamentally determined by the ______.
Differentiation is determined by the SRY gene (sex-related gene on chromosome Y). (Book p265)
Fill up: The SRY gene is located on the ______.
Distal end of the short arm of chromosome Y
The SRY gene is located on the distal end of the short arm of chromosome Y. (Book p265)
Fill up: When the SRY gene on chromosome Y is absent, primordial germ cells normally differentiate into ______.
When the SRY gene is absent, PGCs differentiate into oogonia. (Book p265)

Match the following germ-cell milestones with the time they occur — 1) Spermatogenesis first begins 2) Oogenesis first begins 3) Primordial germ cells reach the genital ridge … A) Puberty B) Intrauterine life C) 5th-6th week of gestation
Spermatogenesis starts only at puberty, oogenesis starts in intrauterine life, and PGCs migrate to the genital ridge by the 5th-6th week. (Book p265)
Fill up: Spermatogenesis begins ______, unlike oogenesis which starts in intrauterine life.
Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, unlike oogenesis which starts in intrauterine life. (Book p265)
Fill up: ______ divide and replenish the stem stores of spermatogonia.
Type A spermatogonia divide and replenish the stem stores of spermatogonia. (Book p265)
Fill up: The male germ cells that undergo maturation and enter spermatogenesis are designated as ______.
Type B (pale) spermatogonia undergo spermatogenesis to form primary spermatocytes. (Book p265)
One spermatogonium produces 16 primary spermatocytes. (Book p265)
Fill up: During Meiosis I of spermatogenesis, chromosome reduction occurs when one primary spermatocyte (46, XY) divides to form ______.
Two secondary spermatocytes (23, X and 23, Y)
One secondary spermatocyte and one polar body
In Meiosis I, chromosome number is halved, yielding two secondary spermatocytes (23, X and 23, Y) from each primary spermatocyte. (Book p265)
Fill up: Each primary spermatocyte produces ______, and one spermatogonium yields 64 spermatids.
Each primary spermatocyte produces 4 spermatids, and one spermatogonium yields 64 spermatids. (Book p265)
Fill up: The developmental process termed spermiogenesis is best defined as the ______.
Morphological transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa without cell division
First meiotic division reducing chromosome number to haploid
Second meiotic division producing round spermatids
Release of mature spermatozoa into the tubule lumen
Spermiogenesis is the morphological transformation of round spermatids into spermatozoa without meiosis or mitosis. (Book p265)
Fill up: The process by which mature spermatozoa detach from Sertoli cells and are released into the seminiferous tubule lumen is termed ______.
Spermiation is the process of release of sperm into the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. (Book p265)
Fill up: The time taken for spermatogenesis is ______.
The time taken for spermatogenesis is 70–74 days (~72 days). (Book p265)
Fill up: The time required specifically for the morphogenetic phase of spermiogenesis is ______.
The time taken for spermiogenesis is 10–14 days. (Book p265)
Fill up: A full cycle of spermatogenesis takes ______ days, of which the morphogenetic phase of spermiogenesis alone occupies ______ days.
Spermatogenesis takes 70-74 days (~72 days) and spermiogenesis alone takes 10-14 days. (Book p265)
Fill up: The basal compartment contains ______; adluminal holds secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and sperms.
The basal compartment contains spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes; adluminal holds secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and sperms. (Book p266)
Fill up: The adluminal compartment contains ______ sperms, while the basal compartment contains spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes.
Primordial germ cells and Leydig interstitial cells
Only Type A and Type B spermatogonia
The adluminal compartment contains secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and sperms, while the basal compartment contains spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes. (Book p266)
Fill up: The blood-testis barrier that physically partitions the seminiferous tubule into basal and adluminal compartments is formed by specialized tight junctions between ______.
Specialized tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli sustentacular cells establish the blood-testis barrier, dividing the seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments. (Book p266)
Fill up: The acrosomal cap is formed by the ______ of the spermatid.
The acrosomal cap is formed by the Golgi apparatus of the spermatid. (Book p266)
Fill up: The middle piece of the mature spermatozoon is termed the powerhouse of the cell because it is composed of condensed ______.
Mitochondria aggregate in the middle piece, serving as the powerhouse of the sperm. (Book p266)
Fill up: The axial filament forming the flagellar tail of the mature spermatozoon originates from the spermatid's ______.
The axial filament/tail is formed by the centriole. (Book p266)
Fill up: The axoneme within the flagellar tail of the spermatozoon exhibits which characteristic microtubular arrangement is ______.
The tail of the sperm has a characteristic 9+2 arrangement of microtubules. (Book p266)
Fill up: The total size of a mature spermatozoon is ______ (compared to 120 µm for an ovum).
The total size of a mature spermatozoon is 50–60 µm (compared to 120 µm for an ovum). (Book p266)
Fill up: The fertilisable lifespan of sperm is ______, whereas the ovum's lifespan is 12–24 hours.
The fertilisable lifespan of sperm is 48–72 hours, whereas the ovum's lifespan is 12–24 hours. (Book p266)
Fill up: In the male reproductive tract, spermatozoa attain structural maturity in the proximal epididymis, while progressive forward motility is acquired in the ______.
Sperm maturity is attained in the proximal epididymis, while motility is attained in the distal epididymis. (Book p266)
Fill up: The total duration required to produce fully mature, motile spermatozoa (testicular spermatogenesis plus epididymal maturation) is ______.
Total time taken to form mature sperm (spermatogenesis + epididymal maturation) is ~90 days. (Book p266)
Fill up: Time taken by sperm to reach the fertilization site after ejaculation is ______.
Time taken by sperm to reach the fertilization site after ejaculation is 30 minutes. (Book p266)
Which of the following statements about human spermatozoa is TRUE?
Sperm acquire progressive motility only during epididymal transit, not in the testis
Sperm gain the ability to fertilise an oocyte while still inside the seminiferous tubules
Ejaculated sperm are immediately capable of fertilising an oocyte without further change
Spermatozoa normally remain motile in the female genital tract for barely two to three hours
Motility is acquired during epididymal transit; fertilising capacity requires capacitation in the female tract, and sperm survive there for days. (Book p266)
Fill up: Unlike spermatogenesis which begins at puberty, oogenesis in the female commences during ______.
Oogenesis begins in intrauterine life, with oogonia entering meiosis before birth. (Book p266)
Fill up: Primary oocytes arrest in the ______, also known as the dictyate state.
Primary oocytes arrest in the diplotene stage of prophase I, also known as the dictyate state. (Book p266)
Which statement about Meiotic arrest — arrested primary oocyte is TRUE?
The arrested primary oocyte resting phase is called the Dictyate state (absent in spermatogenesis)
The arrested primary oocyte resting phase is called the Syncytial state (absent in spermatogenesis)
The arrested primary oocyte resting phase is called the Diakinesis state (absent in spermatogenesis)
The arrested primary oocyte resting phase is called the Zygotene state (absent in spermatogenesis)
The arrested primary oocyte resting phase is called the dictyate state (absent in spermatogenesis). (Book p266)

A 24-year-old G2P1L1 at 9 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding primordial follicles and ovarian reserve. According to the notes, the ovary functions as a biological reservoir of follicles; ovarian reserve tests check for the presence of an adequate number of resting primordial follicles. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that the presence of an adequate pool/reservoir of resting follicles within the ovary is the correct primordial follicles and ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that the mitotic division rate of granulosa cells within preantral follicles is the correct primordial follicles and ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that the functional competence of the meiotic spindle in metaphase ii is the correct primordial follicles and ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that the rate of follicular fluid accumulation within the graafian antrum is the correct primordial follicles and ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
The ovary functions as a biological reservoir of follicles; ovarian reserve tests check for the presence of an adequate number of resting primordial follicles. (Book p266)
Which statement about Meiosis resumption — Meiosis I resumes is TRUE?
Meiosis I resumes due to the preovulatory LH surge (hormone dependent)
Meiosis I resumes due to the preovulatory Progesterone peak (hormone dependent)
Meiosis I resumes due to the preovulatory Inhibin B surge (hormone dependent)
Meiosis I resumes due to the preovulatory Human placental lactogen surge (hormone dependent)
Meiosis I resumes due to the preovulatory LH surge (hormone dependent). (Book p266)
Fill up: Ovulation marks the transition from primary oocyte to ______ along with the extrusion of the 1st polar body.
Secondary oocyte and first polar body
Mature ovum and second polar body
Ovulation marks the transition from primary oocyte to secondary oocyte along with the extrusion of the 1st polar body. (Book p266)
Which statement about Meiosis II arrest — secondary oocyte arrested is TRUE?
The secondary oocyte is arrested in Metaphase II of meiosis II until fertilisation occurs
The secondary oocyte is arrested in Anaphase II of meiosis II until fertilisation occurs
The secondary oocyte is arrested in Prophase II of meiosis II until fertilisation occurs
The secondary oocyte is arrested in Diplotene I of meiosis II until fertilisation occurs
The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II of meiosis II until fertilisation occurs. (Book p266)
Fill up: Meiosis II resumes and finishes at ______, giving the female pronucleus and 2nd polar body.
Meiosis II resumes and finishes at fertilization, giving the female pronucleus and 2nd polar body. (Book p266)
Match the germ-cell population with its number — 1) Oogonia at 20 weeks' gestation 2) Oocytes at birth 3) Oocytes at puberty … A) ~7 million B) 1-2 million C) 300,000-400,000
Peak oogonial number is ~7 million at 20 weeks, falling to 1-2 million at birth and 300,000-400,000 by puberty. (Book p266)
Which statement about Gamete yield — Unlike spermatogenesis where is TRUE?
One mature ovum and three non-functional polar bodies is the listed gamete yield as per the notes
Four mature ova, all of them fertilisable is the listed gamete yield as per the notes
Sixteen mature ova, all of them fertilisable is the listed gamete yield as per the notes
Sixty-four mature ova, all of them fertilisable is the listed gamete yield as per the notes
Unlike spermatogenesis, where one spermatogonium yields 64 spermatids, each oogonium ultimately gives rise to a single mature ovum (female pronucleus) plus non-functional polar bodies. (Book p267)
Which statement about Gamete dimensions — size of mature is TRUE?
The size of a mature human ovum is 120 µm
The size of a mature human ovum is 50–60 µm
The size of a mature human ovum is 18–20 mm
The size of a mature human ovum is 1–2 mm
The size of a mature human ovum is 120 µm. (Book p267)
Fill up: The fertilisable lifespan of an ovum is ______.
The fertilisable lifespan of an ovum is 12–24 hours. (Book p267)
Which statement about Follicle size — size of mature is TRUE?
The size of the mature preovulatory follicle just before ovulation is 18–20 mm
The size of the mature preovulatory follicle just before ovulation is 50–60 mm
The size of the mature preovulatory follicle just before ovulation is 120 µm
The size of the mature preovulatory follicle just before ovulation is 2–4 mm
The size of the mature preovulatory follicle just before ovulation is 18–20 mm. (Book p267)
Fill up: Follicle formation begins at 14 weeks and is completed by ______ of intrauterine life.
Follicle formation begins at 14 weeks and is completed by 22–24 weeks of intrauterine life. (Book p267)
Which statement about Ovarian reserve — maximum peak of is TRUE?
The maximum peak of 6–7 million follicles occurs at the 5th month of intrauterine life
The maximum peak of 6–7 million follicles occurs at the Birth
The maximum peak of 6–7 million follicles occurs at the Puberty
The maximum peak of 6–7 million follicles occurs at the 14 weeks of gestation
The maximum peak of 6–7 million follicles occurs at the 5th month of intrauterine life. (Book p267)

A 32-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding ovarian reserve. According to the notes, at birth, the number of follicles in the ovary drops to 1–2 million. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that 1–2 million is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 6–7 million is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 4–5 lakh is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 1000 follicles is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
At birth, the number of follicles in the ovary drops to 1–2 million. (Book p267)

A 32-year-old G3P1L1 at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding ovarian reserve. According to the notes, by puberty the ovarian follicular pool is further reduced to 4-5 lakh (400,000-500,000) follicles. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that 4-5 lakh, that is 400,000-500,000 follicles is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 1-2 million, that is 1,000,000-2,000,000 follicles is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 6-7 million, that is 6,000,000-7,000,000 follicles is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 10,000, that is ten thousand follicles only is the correct ovarian reserve for this patient at this gestation
By puberty the ovarian follicular pool is further reduced to 4-5 lakh (400,000-500,000) follicles. (Book p267)
Fill up: During the active reproductive years, approximately how many ovarian follicles undergo atresia every month is ______.
Every month, roughly 1000 follicles undergo atresia while normally only one reaches ovulation. (Book p267)

Match the menopause reserve with the correct detail — 1) At the onset of menopause, the number of 2) Primordial germ cells are classified as pluripotent because 3) The human zygote up to the 8-cell stage … A) Zero (depleted) B) Form all three embryonic germ layers C) Form both embryonic and extraembryonic tissues
At menopause, there are virtually no follicles remaining in the ovary. (Book p267)

Match the cell potency with the correct detail — 1) Primordial germ cells are classified as pluripotent because 2) The human zygote up to the 8-cell stage 3) is the correct sequential migratory route taken by … A) Form all three embryonic germ layers B) Form both embryonic and extraembryonic tissues C) Epiblast → Yolk sac wall → Genital ridge → Gonads
Germ cells are pluripotent, meaning they have the ability to form all 3 germ layers. (Book p267)

A 28-year-old G3P1L1 at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding cell potency. According to the notes, a zygote up to the 8-cell stage is totipotent, capable of forming both embryonic and extraembryonic tissue. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that form both embryonic and extraembryonic tissues is the correct cell potency for this patient at this gestation
Advise that form only the three definitive embryonic germ layers is the correct cell potency for this patient at this gestation
Advise that differentiate solely into the central nervous system is the correct cell potency for this patient at this gestation
Advise that form the placenta without an embryo is the correct cell potency for this patient at this gestation
A zygote up to the 8-cell stage is totipotent, capable of forming both embryonic and extraembryonic tissue. (Book p267)

A 30-year-old second gravida at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding germ cell migration. According to the notes, pGCs migrate from the epiblast to the yolk sac wall, then to the genital ridge where gonads develop. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that epiblast → yolk sac wall → genital ridge → gonads is the correct germ cell migration for this patient at this gestation
Advise that neural crest → hypoblast → genital ridge → gonads is the correct germ cell migration for this patient at this gestation
Advise that splanchnic mesoderm → allantois → amnion → gonads is the correct germ cell migration for this patient at this gestation
Advise that dorsal aorta → mesonephros → yolk sac → gonads is the correct germ cell migration for this patient at this gestation
PGCs migrate from the epiblast to the yolk sac wall, then to the genital ridge where gonads develop. (Book p267)
Which statement about Teratoma pathogenesis — Failure of PGC is TRUE?
Failure of PGC migration (aberrant location) results in the formation of Teratomas
Failure of PGC migration (aberrant location) results in the formation of Choriocarcinomas
Failure of PGC migration (aberrant location) results in the formation of Pheochromocytomas
Failure of PGC migration (aberrant location) results in the formation of Hydatidiform moles
Failure of PGC migration (aberrant location) results in the formation of teratomas. (Book p267)
Fill up: A teratoma shows tissue from all three embryonic layers, so its cell of origin behaves as a ______ cell, whereas a normal primordial germ cell is only ______.
Teratomas reveal the totipotent potential of germ cells, while normal PGCs are bipotent — able to form spermatogonia or oogonia only. (Book p267)
Which statement about Capacitation definition — Capacitation process by is TRUE?
Sperms become capable of fertilizing the ovum is the listed capacitation definition as per the notes
Spermatids shed excess cytoplasm to form flagella is the listed capacitation definition as per the notes
Spermatozoa acquire progressive motility in the epididymis is the listed capacitation definition as per the notes
