Sperm heads fuse with the second polar body is the listed capacitation definition as per the notes
Capacitation is the process by which sperms become capable of fertilizing the ova. (Book p268)
Fill up: In vivo capacitation takes ______ (compared to 2 hours for in vitro capacitation).
In vivo capacitation takes 6–8 hours (compared to 2 hours for in vitro capacitation). (Book p268)
Which statement about Capacitation site — Capacitation begins at is TRUE?
Begins in the cervix; main site is the fallopian tube is the listed capacitation site as per the notes
Begins in the vagina; main site is the uterine cavity is the listed capacitation site as per the notes
Begins in the epididymis; main site is the ampulla is the listed capacitation site as per the notes
Begins in the vas deferens; main site is the cervix is the listed capacitation site as per the notes
Capacitation begins at the cervix, but its main site of completion is the fallopian tube. (Book p268)

A 32-year-old G3P1L1 at 11 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding in vitro capacitation. According to the notes, in vitro capacitation takes approximately 2 hours. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that 2 hours is the correct in vitro capacitation for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 6–8 hours is the correct in vitro capacitation for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 30 minutes is the correct in vitro capacitation for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 24 hours is the correct in vitro capacitation for this patient at this gestation
In vitro capacitation takes approximately 2 hours. (Book p268)
Fill up: Motility is acquired in the distal epididymis, whereas hypermotility is attained in the ______ tract.
Motility is acquired in the distal epididymis, whereas hypermotility is attained in the female reproductive tract. (Book p268)
Fill up: The zona pellucida contains specific receptors for the sperm head known as ______s.
The zona pellucida contains specific receptors for the sperm head known as ZP3 receptors. (Book p268)

Match the acrosome reaction with the correct detail — 1) The acrosomal reaction releases which key hydrolytic enzyme 2) Following sperm-oolemma fusion, the secondary oocyte completes Meiosis 3) Hardening and biochemical alteration of the zona pellucida … A) Hyaluronidase B) Calcium ions (Ca2+) and lysosomal enzymes C) Cortical reaction and zona reaction
The acrosome reaction releases enzymes including hyaluronidase to digest the zona pellucida. (Book p268)
Which statement about Cortical reaction — Cortical granules in is TRUE?
Calcium ions (Ca2+) and lysosomal enzymes is the listed cortical reaction as per the notes
Progesterone and estrogen is the listed cortical reaction as per the notes
Glycogen and mucin is the listed cortical reaction as per the notes
Nitabuch fibrinoid material is the listed cortical reaction as per the notes
Cortical granules in the secondary oocyte cytoplasm release Ca2+ and enzymes to trigger the zona reaction. (Book p268)
Fill up: Polyspermy is prevented by the ______ and subsequent zona reaction (hardening of zona pellucida).
Polyspermy is prevented by the cortical reaction and subsequent zona reaction (hardening of zona pellucida). (Book p268)

A 32-year-old woman's oocytes fail to fertilise in vitro until albumin is added to the culture medium; albumin acts as a sterol acceptor and strips cholesterol from the sperm membrane. Which step was being reproduced?
Capacitation — removal of cholesterol and seminal glycoproteins from the sperm membrane
Acrosome reaction — release of acrosin and hyaluronidase from the acrosomal cap
Cortical reaction — enzyme release that hardens the zona pellucida around the oocyte
Spermiation — detachment of mature spermatozoa from recesses in the Sertoli cell
Capacitation is cholesterol and glycoprotein removal from the sperm membrane (reproduced in vitro by albumin), and it must precede the acrosome reaction. (Book p268)
Which statement about Fertilization site — Fertilization normally occurs is TRUE?
Fertilization normally occurs in the Ampulla of the fallopian tube
Fertilization normally occurs in the Isthmus of the fallopian tube
Fertilization normally occurs in the Infundibulum near the fimbriae
Fertilization normally occurs in the Endometrial cavity
Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. (Book p269)
In a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, the day of fertilization corresponds to which cycle day?
Day of fertilization equals the day of ovulation, which is Day 14 in a standard 28-day cycle. (Book p269)
The first mitotic cleavage division of the unicellular diploid zygote to form a 2-cell embryo occurs at approximately:
The 2-cell zygote stage is reached 30 hours after fertilization. (Book p269)
The developing conceptus typically enters the uterine cavity at which developmental stage?
The 16-cell morula enters the uterine cavity from the fallopian tube. (Book p269)
Transport of the dividing morula through the fallopian tube towards the uterine cavity is driven by:
Tubal peristalsis and beating of ciliated columnar epithelial cells
Active flagellar motility of the blastomeres
The morula is propelled by tubal peristalsis and ciliary movement of the ciliated columnar lining. (Book p269)
The dividing embryo resides in the fallopian tube for 3 days nourished by secretory peg cells, entering the uterus on:
The 16-cell morula enters the uterine cavity on the 4th day after fertilization (Day 18 of the cycle). (Book p269)
Zona hatching, the shedding of the acellular zona pellucida to allow fluid influx and blastocyst expansion, occurs on:
On the 5th day after fertilization, the zona pellucida is lost (zona hatching) and fluid enters to form a blastocyst. (Book p269)
Which of the following conditions increases the risk of tubal ectopic pregnancy by impairing normal tubal ciliary motility or peristalsis?
Kartagener syndrome and progestin-only contraceptive pills
Combined oral contraceptives with high estrogen
Kartagener syndrome (immotile cilia) and progestin-only pills (smooth muscle relaxation) impair tubal transport, predisposing to ectopic pregnancy. (Book p269)
Fill up: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ______ of the fallopian tube and the zygote reaches the uterine cavity about ______ days later.
Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla and the conceptus takes roughly 3-4 days of tubal transport to reach the uterine cavity. (Book p269)
On which day after fertilization does normal blastocyst implantation into the endometrium initiate?
Implantation occurs on Day 6 after fertilization, which corresponds to Day 20 of the menstrual cycle. (Book p270)
The receptive endometrial window during which the uterine lining is optimal for blastocyst attachment spans:
Day 20 to Day 24 of the menstrual cycle
Day 10 to Day 14 of the menstrual cycle
Day 25 to Day 28 of the menstrual cycle
Day 14 to Day 18 of the menstrual cycle
The implantation window is Day 20 to Day 24 of the cycle, when the endometrium is maximally receptive. (Book p270)
Slight, painless vaginal spotting occurring around cycle day 20–22 due to blastocyst burrowing into the endometrium is termed the:
Hartmann sign, also called the placental sign
Palmer sign of regular uterine pulsation
Slight painless spotting around cycle day 20-22 from blastocyst burrowing into the endometrium is the Hartmann sign (placental sign). (Book p270)
On early obstetric ultrasound, the very first sonographic sign confirming an intrauterine pregnancy is the:
The intradecidual sign (gestational sac deep inside the thickened endometrium) is the first sign seen on ultrasound. (Book p270)
Match the correct molecular mediator with the respective stage of blastocyst implantation:
Apposition: Selectin; Adhesion: Integrin; Penetration: Matrix metalloproteinases
Apposition: Integrin; Adhesion: Selectin; Penetration: Hyaluronidase
Apposition: Collagenase; Adhesion: Cadherin; Penetration: Selectin
Apposition: MMPs; Adhesion: Fibrinogen; Penetration: Integrin
Apposition is mediated by selectins, adhesion by integrins (most important), and penetration by matrix metalloproteinases. (Book p270)
Following implantation, the endometrium beneath the blastocyst that will directly form the maternal component of the placenta is the:
Decidua basalis lies directly beneath the conceptus and forms the maternal side of the placenta. (Book p270)
The layer of decidua that arches over and encapsulates the expanding blastocyst, separating it from the uterine cavity, is the:
Decidua capsularis overlies the blastocyst and separates it from the remaining uterine cavity. (Book p270)

Match the implantation landmark with its post-ovulation timing — 1) Blastocyst enters the uterine cavity 2) Blastocyst attaches to the endometrium 3) Implantation is completed … A) Day 3-4 B) Day 6-7 C) Day 11-12
The blastocyst enters the cavity on day 3-4, attaches on day 6-7 and implantation is complete by day 11-12. (Book p270)
On ultrasound examination, the double decidual sac sign is formed by the concentric echogenic rings of which two layers?
The double decidual sac sign is formed by the decidua capsularis and decidua parietalis. (Book p271)
Obliteration of the uterine cavity occurs when the decidua capsularis fuses completely with the decidua parietalis at:
Decidua capsularis fuses with decidua parietalis, obliterating the uterine cavity at 14–16 weeks of pregnancy. (Book p271)
Fertilization of two ova released in two different menstrual cycles by two separate acts of coitus is termed superfetation, which in humans is:
Not seen, but theoretically possible only until 14–16 weeks
A common mechanism for dizygotic twins
Superfetation is not seen in humans; theoretically it could only occur before cavity obliteration at 14–16 weeks. (Book p271)
Under the influence of progesterone, endometrial thickness increases to 10–12 mm primarily as a consequence of:
Exudation of fibrinoid material into the glands
Progesterone causes marked stromal edema (most important histological finding), increasing endometrial thickness to 10–12 mm. (Book p271)
On day 8 after fertilization, the blastocyst differentiates into which two primary structural components?
Inner cell mass (embryoblast) and outer trophoblast
On Day 8 after fertilization, the blastocyst segregates into inner cell mass (embryoblast) and trophoblast. (Book p272)
All three definitive embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) and the embryo proper are derived from the:
The embryo proper and all 3 germ layers are formed entirely from the inner cell mass. (Book p272)
The syncytiotrophoblast is clinically characterized as the 'hormone factory' of the placenta because it synthesizes:
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and human placental lactogen (hPL)
The syncytiotrophoblast functions as the hormone factory of the placenta, synthesizing peptide hormones like hCG and hPL. (Book p272)
Which population of trophoblastic cells invades maternal spiral arterioles to establish low resistance and prevent pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH)?
Extravillous trophoblasts invade maternal spiral arteries, transforming them into dilated low-resistance conduits and preventing PIH. (Book p272)
The villous trophoblast adjacent to the decidua basalis proliferates into bushy, villous projections termed the:
Villous trophoblast near the decidua basalis forms the chorion frondosum, which becomes the fetal side of the placenta. (Book p272)
The smooth, non-villous portion of the trophoblast that surrounds the remaining conceptus is termed:
Chorion laeve, which becomes the chorionic part of the fetal membranes
Chorion frondosum, where the villi persist and form the definitive placenta
The Nitabuch layer, where maternal and fetal tissues meet and mix
Decidua vera, the maternal lining away from the implantation site
Villi regress over the abembryonic pole giving chorion laeve; opposite the implantation site they persist as chorion frondosum. (Book p272)
Which of the following statements about trophoblast differentiation is TRUE?
Syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer that secretes hCG and invades the endometrium
Cytotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer and is the main source of hCG secretion
Syncytiotrophoblast forms by fusion of decidual stromal cells around the implanting blastocyst
Cytotrophoblast alone erodes maternal sinusoids, since it is the invasive layer in the first trimester
Cytotrophoblast is the inner mononuclear stem layer; syncytiotrophoblast is outer, multinucleated, hCG-secreting and invasive. (Book p272)
Which statement accurately describes the developmental origin and characteristics of the fetal chorion?
Formed by chorion laeve on day 8; forms the outermost fetal membrane
Formed by ectoderm on day 10; forms the innermost membrane
An avascular membrane that contains no collagen
Formed from the secondary yolk sac on day 14
Chorion is formed by chorion laeve (cytotrophoblast) on Day 8 and is the outermost fetal membrane. (Book p272)
The fetal amnion is derived embryologically from ectoderm on day 10 and is histologically notable for being:
Avascular, without nerves or lymphatics, providing tensile strength
Highly vascularized with maternal capillary loops
Derived from endoderm and producing hCG
Richly innervated by fetal autonomic nerve fibers
Amnion is the innermost membrane formed from ectoderm on Day 10; it is avascular, aneural, lacks lymphatics, and gives tensile strength. (Book p272)
In early embryonic development, the primary physiological functions of the yolk sac include:
First site of fetal hematopoiesis and primary source of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
Synthesis of human placental lactogen and progesterone
Differentiation into the permanent umbilical arteries
Storage of maternal glycogen for the fetus
The yolk sac is the first site for fetal hematopoiesis and the primary early source of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). (Book p272)
All of the following are derived from the inner cell mass EXCEPT:
The trophoblast (and hence syncytiotrophoblast) comes from the outer cell mass; the embryo, amnion and yolk sac come from the inner cell mass. (Book p272)
Embryologically, the allantois is an endodermal diverticulum that connects the fetal hindgut to the:
The allantois is a diverticulum connecting the embryonic hindgut to the connecting stalk. (Book p273)
During a lower-segment Cesarean section, what is the correct anatomical sequence of layers traversed from outside to inside to reach amniotic fluid?
Skin → Abdominal wall muscles → Uterine serosa → Myometrium → Endometrium (Decidua) → Chorion → Amnion
Skin → Peritoneum → Amnion → Chorion → Myometrium → Decidua
Skin → Myometrium → Uterine serosa → Chorion → Decidua → Amnion
Skin → Abdominal wall → Decidua → Chorion → Uterine serosa → Myometrium → Amnion
Layers traversed: Skin, abdominal muscles, uterine serosa, myometrium, endometrium (decidua vera), chorion, and amnion. (Book p273)
Rupture of the fetal membranes during active labor accelerates uterine contractions primarily through the local release of:
Membrane rupture releases PGF2α, which stimulates myometrial contractility and accelerates labor. (Book p273)
Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT) is exclusively performed in assisted reproductive technology (ART) with the primary goal of:
Selecting and transferring only genetically healthy embryos into the uterus
Inducing artificial zona hatching before cleavage
Preventing ectopic implantation in the fallopian tube
PGT involves genetic testing before implantation so that only healthy unaffected embryos are transferred into the uterus. (Book p273)
Which of the following conditions represents a classic monogenic disorder frequently evaluated using PGT-M?
Sickle cell anemia, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, and thalassemia
Down syndrome and Edwards syndrome exclusively
Congenital rubella syndrome and CMV infection
Monogenic disorders tested by PGT-M include sickle cell anemia, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, and thalassemia. (Book p273)
In addition to single-gene monogenic mutations, PGT is indicated for detecting aneuploidies, HLA typing, and:
Fetal hemoglobin variants in maternal blood
Neural tube defects via alpha-fetoprotein assay
PGT can detect aneuploidies, structural chromosomal rearrangements like balanced translocations, and enable HLA typing. (Book p273)
A major developmental limitation of polar body biopsy during preimplantation genetic testing is that:
Only maternally inherited genetic disorders can be tested
It causes inevitable destruction of the embryoblast
It cannot be performed in assisted reproduction
It transmits mitochondrial mutations to the fetus
The key drawback of polar body testing is that only maternally inherited genetic disorders can be evaluated. (Book p273)
What is considered the safest and most reliable biopsy specimen for comprehensive PGT in modern ART?
Trophectoderm biopsy at the blastocyst stage
Trophectoderm biopsy (sampling extraembryonic cells from the blastocyst) is the best material and avoids harming the inner cell mass. (Book p273)
Fill up: Preimplantation genetic testing is performed on a biopsy of the ______ taken on day ______ of development.
Blastocyst-stage trophectoderm biopsy on day 5-6 is standard, because sampling the inner cell mass would risk the embryo itself. (Book p273)
When calculating developmental milestones from the day of fertilization, the embryonic period spans:
3 to 8 weeks after fertilization (5th to 10th menstrual week)
The embryonic period spans 3–8 weeks after fertilization (5th to 10th week of pregnancy calculated from LMP). (Book p274)
Teratogenic insult occurring during the first 2 weeks after fertilization (period of fertilized ovum) obeys the 'All-or-none law', meaning the conceptus:
Either escapes injury completely or undergoes spontaneous abortion
Always develops major neural tube defects
During the first 2 weeks, exposure follows the all-or-none law: the embryo either completely recovers or aborts. (Book p274)
The developmental window of maximum susceptibility to gross structural teratogenic malformations is the:
The embryonic period (3–8 weeks post-fertilization) is the period of active organogenesis and the most teratogenic period. (Book p274)
What is the recognized maximum permissible cumulative radiation exposure dose throughout pregnancy?
The maximum permissible radiation exposure in pregnancy is 5 Rads (0.05 Gy). (Book p274)
In utero radiation exposure exceeding 5 Rads increases the risk of intellectual disability, IUGR, and microcephaly, whereas a dose ≥10 Rads (≥0.1 Gy) causes:
Radiation exposure ≥10 Rads (≥0.1 Gy) causes severe fetal death, abortion, and gross structural devastation. (Book p274)
A pregnant woman who underwent two accidental diagnostic abdominal X-rays before realizing she was pregnant (<0.5 Rads total) should be counseled to:
Continue the pregnancy, as diagnostic X-rays fall well below 5 Rads
Undergo immediate medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)
Up to 2 diagnostic X-rays impart <0.5 Rads (far below the 5 Rad threshold); the pregnancy should be safely continued. (Book p274)
Which of the following diagnostic imaging or contrast agents is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy?
Dental X-rays with lead abdominal shielding
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI, radioactive iodine, and paramagnetic contrast agents are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. (Book p274)
A woman at 8 weeks of gestation has an abdominal CT scan; the calculated fetal dose is 4 rad (40 mGy). She asks whether the pregnancy must be terminated. What is the most appropriate counselling?
Termination is not indicated — doses below 5 rad show no measurable rise in malformation or loss
Termination is advised — any exposure above 1 rad after 6 weeks causes microcephaly
Termination is advised — 4 rad lies above the 2 rad threshold for organogenic damage
Termination is not indicated — before 10 weeks radiation can only cause growth restriction
Below 5 rad there is no detectable increase in malformation, growth restriction or loss, so termination is not medically indicated. (Book p274)
Which of the following medications is classified as an FDA Category X teratogen that is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?
Category X drugs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and include warfarin, thalidomide, isotretinoin, and DES. (Book p275)
First-trimester gestational exposure to sodium valproate is classically associated with an increased incidence of:
Neural tube defects (spina bifida) and cleft lip/palate
Epstein anomaly and floppy infant syndrome
Valproate exposure produces neural tube defects (NTDs), CNS defects, cardiac anomalies, and cleft lip/palate. (Book p275)
The classic facial dysmorphology of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS) characteristically includes:
Smooth/flat philtrum, thin vermilion border, and short palpebral fissures
Broad prominent philtrum, thick lips, and hypertelorism
Microtia, low-set ears, and cleft palate exclusively
Cloverleaf skull deformity and severe proptosis
FAS features growth restriction, microcephaly, smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, and short palpebral fissures. (Book p275)
Fetal hydantoin syndrome resulting from antenatal phenytoin exposure is characterized by midfacial hypoplasia, upturned nose, and:
Distal digital and nail hypoplasia ± cardiac defects
Cranial nerve VI and VII palsies
Phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome: midfacial hypoplasia, upturned nose, and distal digital/nail hypoplasia. (Book p275)
Administration of ACE inhibitors or ARBs during the second and third trimesters produces fetal renal dysgenesis leading to:
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
ACE inhibitors impair fetal renal perfusion, causing anuria, severe oligohydramnios, and hypoplastic lung development. (Book p275)
In utero lithium exposure during cardiac organogenesis is classically associated with which congenital cardiac defect?
Ebstein anomaly, with downward displacement of the tricuspid leaflets
Tetralogy of Fallot, with an overriding aorta and pulmonary stenosis
Coarctation of the aorta, with hypertension confined to the upper limbs
Patent ductus arteriosus, with a continuous machinery murmur
Lithium in cardiac organogenesis is classically linked to Ebstein anomaly, where the tricuspid leaflets are displaced into the right ventricle. (Book p275)

Match the drug with its classic fetal effect — 1) Warfarin 2) Sodium valproate 3) Lithium … A) Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve B) Nasal hypoplasia with stippled epiphyses C) Lumbosacral neural tube defect
Warfarin causes nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata, valproate causes neural tube defects, and lithium causes Ebstein anomaly. (Book p275)
Teratogenic drugs: category X & specific malformations
First-trimester exposure to the retinoid isotretinoin (used for cystic acne) characteristically causes:
Microtia/anotia, CNS malformations, and cleft palate
Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the cervix
Isotretinoin causes craniofacial defects (microtia/anotia), CNS anomalies, thymic defects, and cleft palate. (Book p276)
Thalidomide is notorious for causing which severe proximal limb reduction defect where hands or feet attach directly to the torso?
Thalidomide causes phocomelia (seal-like limbs due to severe proximal long-bone reduction) and stillbirth. (Book p276)
Fetal Warfarin Syndrome (DiSaia syndrome) resulting from first-trimester exposure manifests as depressed nasal bridge, cataracts, and:
Chondrodysplasia punctata with stippled epiphyses on radiography
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Warfarin embryopathy causes defective cartilage formation (chondrodysplasia), stippled epiphyses, and nasal hypoplasia. (Book p276)
Antenatal exposure to methotrexate during cranial bone ossification can cause severe craniosynostosis giving rise to a:
Methotrexate produces severe craniosynostosis leading to the classic cloverleaf skull deformity. (Book p276)
Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) with DES-like teratogenicity, requires what minimum washout period before conception?
The minimum time gap between stopping tamoxifen and attempting pregnancy is 3 months. (Book p276)
Failed first-trimester termination with misoprostol causes vascular disruption leading to limb defects and Moebius syndrome, which involves:
Congenital 6th and 7th cranial nerve palsies with facial diplegia
Bilateral renal agenesis with flat facies
Misoprostol vascular disruption causes Moebius syndrome (6th and 7th cranial nerve palsy) and transverse limb reduction defects. (Book p276)
Indomethacin is an effective tocolytic before 32 weeks, but administration beyond 32 weeks gestation is contraindicated because it causes:
Premature in utero closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios
Beyond 32 weeks, indomethacin causes premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios. (Book p276)
The most common congenital viral infection in humans and the leading non-genetic cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is:
CMV is both the most common congenital infection and the leading congenital cause of sensorineural hearing loss. (Book p277)
What is the hallmark cranial sonographic or CT neuroimaging finding characteristic of Congenital Cytomegalovirus Syndrome?
Congenital CMV syndrome classically manifests with periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and SNHL. (Book p277)
The classic congenital triad of Toxoplasmosis consists of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and:
Congenital toxoplasmosis presents with hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis. (Book p277)
What is the drug of choice for a pregnant woman diagnosed with acute toxoplasmosis, and what is given if fetal infection is confirmed?
Spiramycin for mother; Pyrimethamine + Sulphadoxine for confirmed fetal infection
Pyrimethamine alone for mother; Acyclovir for fetus
Penicillin G for mother; Erythromycin for fetus
Ganciclovir for mother; Valganciclovir for fetus
Maternal toxoplasmosis is treated with spiramycin; if fetal infection is confirmed on amniocentesis, give pyrimethamine + sulphadoxine. (Book p277)
The classical Gregg's triad of Congenital Rubella Syndrome following first-trimester maternal viremia comprises:
Cataracts/glaucoma, cardiac defects (PDA/pulmonary stenosis), and SNHL
Spina bifida, clubfoot, and renal dysgenesis
Congenital rubella syndrome causes heart disease (PDA/pulmonary stenosis), eye anomalies (cataract/glaucoma), and sensorineural hearing loss. (Book p277)
A pregnant woman in the first trimester is found to be rubella-IgG negative on antenatal screening. The recommended management is to:
Administer the MMR vaccine after delivery and advise avoiding pregnancy for 1 month post-vaccine
Administer MMR vaccine immediately in the first trimester
Give high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) within 24 hours
Rubella vaccine is a live vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy; vaccinate postpartum and advise avoiding pregnancy for 1 month. (Book p277)
All of the following are recognised features of congenital cytomegalovirus infection EXCEPT:
PDA and pulmonary stenosis belong to congenital rubella; CMV gives periventricular calcification, chorioretinitis and sensorineural deafness. (Book p277)
Congenital varicella syndrome resulting from early maternal chickenpox exposure classically presents with:
Cicatricial zigzag skin scars in a dermatomal pattern and limb hypoplasia
Severe neonatal jaundice and bilateral cataracts
Patent ductus arteriosus and congenital glaucoma
Congenital varicella syndrome is characterized by cicatricial skin scarring along dermatomes and hypoplastic limb deformities. (Book p278)
The highest risk of severe, life-threatening neonatal varicella occurs when maternal chickenpox rash erupts within:
5 days before to 2 days after delivery
Maternal chickenpox from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery exposes the neonate to severe varicella without maternal antibodies. (Book p278)
Maternal Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy targets fetal erythroid progenitor cells, leading to profound fetal anemia, high-output failure, and:
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Parvovirus B19 lyses erythroid progenitors, causing fetal anemia, high-output heart failure, hydrops fetalis, and polyhydramnios. (Book p278)
Which non-invasive Doppler ultrasound parameter is the investigation of choice to assess the severity of fetal anemia in Parvovirus B19 infection?
Middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity
Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler peak systolic velocity is the investigation of choice to detect and monitor fetal anemia. (Book p278)
Zika virus exhibits strong placental tropism via TIM-1 and TAM-AXL receptors on Hofbauer cells, causing fetal brain devastation characterized by:
Severe cortical brain atrophy, microcephaly, and arthrogryposis/limb contractures
Zika virus attacks placental Hofbauer cells and fetal neural tissue, causing severe cortical atrophy, microcephaly, and arthrogryposis. (Book p278)
In a pregnant woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), transplacental transfer of which maternal autoantibodies causes congenital complete heart block in the fetus?
Anti-Ro and Anti-La antibodies cross the placenta to cause inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node, producing complete heart block. (Book p278)
The human placenta is morphologically and histologically classified as:
Human placenta is discoid in shape, deciduate (sheds after birth), and hemochorial (villi bathe directly in maternal blood). (Book p279)
At term, what is the average weight of the human placenta and the typical placenta-to-fetal weight ratio?
The term placenta weighs ~500 grams, with a placenta-to-fetal weight ratio of 1:6. (Book p279)
At what gestational age is the weight of the developing human placenta equal to the weight of the fetus?
At 17 weeks of gestation, the weight of the placenta equals the weight of the fetus. (Book p279)
Under normal term physiological conditions, the diameter and central thickness of the placenta measure approximately:
Diameter: 15–20 cm; Thickness at center: 2.5–4 cm
Diameter: 25–30 cm; Thickness at center: 5–6 cm
Diameter: 8–10 cm; Thickness at center: 1–2 cm
Diameter: 10–12 cm; Thickness at center: 0.5–1 cm
The normal placenta measures 15–20 cm in diameter and 2.5–4 cm in central thickness. (Book p279)
Placentomegaly is defined as a placental thickness exceeding 4 cm, which can be caused by:
Maternal diabetes, hydrops fetalis, and congenital syphilis
Preeclampsia and severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
Post-term dysmaturity syndrome and severe oligohydramnios
Placentomegaly (>4 cm thick) is caused by diabetes, multifetal gestation, hydrops fetalis, severe fetal anemia, and syphilis. (Book p279)
Which of the following clinical conditions characteristically results in an abnormally small, thin, hypoplastic placenta?
Uteroplacental insufficiency, pre-eclampsia (PIH), and IUGR characteristically result in a small, underperfused placenta. (Book p279)
Fill up: At term the placenta weighs about ______ g, which is roughly ______ of the fetal weight.
The term placenta weighs about 500 g and its ratio to the fetus is about 1:6. (Book p279)
Which set of features accurately describes the fetal surface compared to the maternal surface of the human placenta?
Fetal: shiny, grey-blue, forms 4/5th; Maternal: dull, fleshy-red, forms 1/5th with 15–20 cotyledons
Fetal: dull red with cotyledons, forms 1/5th; Maternal: covered by amnion, forms 4/5th
Fetal: derived from decidua basalis; Maternal: derived from chorion frondosum
Fetal: divided by decidual septa into 30 lobes; Maternal: smooth and completely avascular
The fetal surface forms 4/5th (shiny, covered by amnion/chorion frondosum); the maternal surface forms 1/5th (dull red decidua basalis, 15–20 cotyledons). (Book p280)
What is the correct anatomical sequence of histological layers composing the placental membrane/barrier from maternal blood to fetal blood?
Syncytiotrophoblast → Cytotrophoblast → Extraembryonic mesoderm → Fetal capillary endothelium
Cytotrophoblast → Syncytiotrophoblast → Amniotic epithelium → Capillary wall
Syncytiotrophoblast → Decidua basalis → Mesoderm → Fetal blood
Placental barrier from outside to inside: Syncytiotrophoblast, Cytotrophoblast, Extraembryonic mesoderm, and Fetal capillary endothelium. (Book p281)
Primary chorionic villi appear on day 13 after fertilization and are histologically composed of:
A cytotrophoblastic core surrounded by syncytiotrophoblast (trophoblastic shell)
Cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, and a mesodermal core
Trophoblastic shell, mesenchyme, and functional fetal capillaries
Amniotic ectoderm and maternal vascular lacunae
Primary villi (Day 13) consist of a central cytotrophoblast core covered by syncytiotrophoblast (trophoblastic shell). (Book p281)
Secondary chorionic villi form on day 16 after fertilization when which structure invades the core of the primary villus?
Secondary villi form on Day 16 when extraembryonic mesoderm grows into the center of the trophoblastic shell. (Book p281)
Tertiary chorionic villi are definitively established on day 17 after fertilization by the appearance of:
Fetal blood vessels / capillaries within the mesodermal core
Tertiary villi are established on Day 17 when fetal blood vessels and capillaries differentiate within the villous core. (Book p281)
The total blood volume contained within the human term placenta is 500 ml, which is partitioned into:
350 ml of fetal blood (in villi) and 150 ml of maternal blood (in intervillous space)
250 ml of fetal blood and 250 ml of maternal blood
150 ml of fetal blood and 350 ml of maternal blood
450 ml of fetal blood and 50 ml of maternal blood
Placental blood totals 500 ml: 350 ml fetal blood within villous capillaries and 150 ml maternal blood in the intervillous space. (Book p281)
During physiological trophoblastic invasion, cytotrophoblast cells remodel maternal spiral arteries by replacing their muscular coats, which converts them into:
Dilated, flaccid, low-resistance vessels that deliver high blood flow to the intervillous space
Narrow, highly coiled, high-resistance muscular sphincters
Venous sinusoids that drain retroplacental clots
Cytotrophoblasts replace the muscular media of spiral arteries, transforming them into dilated low-resistance conduits that maximize IVS flow. (Book p281)
Which of the following statements about trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries is TRUE?
Extravillous trophoblast replaces the musculoelastic media of spiral arteries by 20-24 weeks
Endovascular trophoblast invasion stops at the decidua and never reaches the myometrial segment
Spiral arteries keep their smooth muscle throughout pregnancy, so intervillous flow stays pulsatile
Cytotrophoblast plugs persist until the third trimester and only dissolve after 28 weeks
The second wave of trophoblast invasion converts spiral arteries into low-resistance flaccid tubes by 20-24 weeks; plugs disappear by 10-12 weeks. (Book p281)
In the developing human placenta, uteroplacental and fetoplacental circulations are established on which post-fertilization days?
Uteroplacental by Day 12–13; Fetoplacental by Day 17
Uteroplacental by Day 6; Fetoplacental by Day 14
Uteroplacental by Day 28; Fetoplacental by Day 32
Uteroplacental by Day 20; Fetoplacental by Day 24
Uteroplacental circulation in the IVS is established by Day 12–13; fetoplacental circulation in the villi is established by Day 17. (Book p282)
In fetoplacental circulation, physiological gas and nutrient transport between placenta and fetus is conducted by:
Umbilical vein carrying oxygenated blood to fetus; two umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to placenta
Two umbilical veins carrying oxygenated blood; one umbilical artery carrying deoxygenated blood
Umbilical artery carrying oxygenated blood; umbilical vein carrying waste to placenta
Spiral arteries carrying fetal blood; uterine veins carrying maternal blood
The single umbilical vein transports oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus; two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood. (Book p282)
At term gestation, what are the normal volumetric blood flow rates through the uteroplacental space and the total uterine circulation?
At term, uteroplacental blood flow is 500–700 ml/min, total uterine blood flow is 750 ml/min, and fetoplacental flow is 400 ml/min. (Book p282)
A placental cotyledon, the basic functional unit of the human placenta, is anatomically defined as the territory supplied by:
One main stem villus and its branching hierarchy
The entire chorion laeve combined with amnion
Two adjacent decidual septa without villous tissue
A placental cotyledon is the functional unit of the placenta supplied by one main stem villus and all its branches. (Book p282)
Nitabuch's layer is a zone of fibrinoid degeneration situated between the invading trophoblast and decidua basalis whose primary role is to:
Limit the invasive penetration of the blastocyst into the myometrium
Prevent maternal immunological rejection of syncytiotrophoblast
Stimulate continuous production of human placental lactogen
Facilitate immediate postpartum separation of the amnion
Nitabuch's layer is a zone of fibrinoid degeneration between blastocyst and decidua basalis that limits deep invasion into the myometrium. (Book p282)
Congenital or iatrogenic absence of Nitabuch's layer permits blastocyst invasion directly into the myometrium, producing:
Absence of Nitabuch's layer allows chorionic villi to attach directly to myometrium, causing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). (Book p282)
Fill up: The term placenta contains about ______ cotyledons, and each is supplied by a single ______ artery.
There are roughly 15-20 cotyledons, each supplied by one truncal (stem villous) artery arising from the chorionic plate vessels. (Book p282)
In addition to acting as an endocrine organ, the placenta carries out crucial fetal life-support functions, the most vital of which is:
Immunological suppression of all maternal IgG
Thermal regulation through brown fat synthesis
Direct erythropoiesis for the fetal marrow
The two primary placental functions are respiratory gas exchange and hormone production. (Book p283)
The oxygen saturation and partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) in maternal intervillous space blood normally equal those in the umbilical vein, measuring:
Oxygen saturation in the IVS and umbilical vein is 65–75%, with a partial pressure of O2 around 30–35 mm Hg. (Book p283)
In a non-conception menstrual cycle, the corpus luteum reaches its maximum morphological size and peak progesterone secretion on:
Day 22 of the cycle (8 days after ovulation)
Day 14 of the cycle (day of ovulation)
Day 1 of the cycle (onset of menses)
The corpus luteum attains maximum size and peak progesterone production on Day 22 of the cycle (8 days post-ovulation). (Book p283)
When fertilization occurs, luteolysis of the corpus luteum is prevented by which hormone secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast from day 8 post-fertilization?
Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG from Day 8 after fertilization (Day 22 of cycle), which rescues the corpus luteum from degeneration. (Book p283)
A 29-year-old at 6 weeks of gestation has a corpus luteum removed at laparotomy for a large haemorrhagic cyst. If no hormonal support is given, what is the most likely outcome?
Pregnancy loss, because the luteo-placental shift is not complete until 8-10 weeks
Normal continuation, because hCG alone maintains the decidua from the fourth week onward
Normal continuation, because the fetal adrenal axis takes over progesterone synthesis immediately
Preterm labour at 32 weeks, since progesterone is what suppresses myometrial contractility
Before the luteo-placental shift at 8-10 weeks the corpus luteum is the sole source of progesterone, so its removal without support causes loss. (Book p283)
The functional lifespan of the corpus luteum of pregnancy, maintaining early gestational hormone support, is approximately:
The lifespan of the corpus luteum of pregnancy is 10–12 weeks. (Book p284)
The critical transition known as the luteal-placental shift, during which the placenta takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum, occurs at:
Progesterone originates from the CL until 7 weeks, shifts between 8–10 weeks, and is solely produced by the placenta after 10 weeks. (Book p284)
An asymptomatic simple ovarian cyst detected on first-trimester ultrasound should be managed conservatively without surgery because surgical excision before 7 weeks will cause:
Immediate miscarriage due to loss of luteal progesterone support
The cyst is almost certainly the corpus luteum; removal before 7 weeks removes essential progesterone and precipitates abortion. (Book p284)
The human placenta is incapable of de novo cholesterol synthesis from acetate; it synthesizes progesterone using which circulating maternal precursor?
Placental progesterone is synthesized directly from circulating maternal cholesterol. (Book p284)
The essential physiological action of progesterone in sustaining pregnancy throughout gestation is to:
Maintain profound myometrial smooth muscle relaxation and prevent preterm labor
Stimulate active myometrial oxytocin receptor expression
Promote rapid cervical ripening and effacement
Increase peripheral vascular resistance to maintain blood pressure
Progesterone acts as a uterine smooth muscle relaxant that maintains quiescence and prevents preterm labor. (Book p284)
Because the human placenta lacks 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-desmolase, it relies on which fetal adrenal precursor for estrogen biosynthesis?
The placenta requires fetal adrenal DHEA-S because it lacks the 17α-hydroxylase and desmolase needed to convert C21 steroids to C19 androgens. (Book p284)
Which two placental enzymes convert fetal adrenal DHEA-sulfate into active estrogens (estrone and estradiol)?
Placental sulfatase removes the sulfate from DHEA-S, and aromatase converts the androgens into estrogens. (Book p284)

Match the following about placental steroidogenesis — 1) Substrate the placenta takes from the mother 2) Enzyme pair the placenta lacks 3) Principal estrogen of pregnancy … A) 17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase B) Maternal LDL cholesterol C) Estriol
The placenta uses maternal LDL cholesterol, lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase, and makes estriol from fetal DHEA-S and 16-alpha-OH-DHEA-S. (Book p284)
The physiological endocrine trigger initiating the onset of spontaneous labor contractions at term involves:
Functional withdrawal of progesterone accompanied by an increase in estrogen
Sudden surge in maternal progesterone and decrease in estrogen
Complete cessation of placental relaxin and hPL
Acute drop in fetal cortisol and oxytocin
Onset of labor is triggered by functional progesterone withdrawal combined with elevated estrogen, initiating uterine contractions. (Book p285)
Fetal anencephaly is classically complicated by post-term pregnancy because the absence of the hypothalamus and pituitary results in:
Adrenal hypoplasia with absence of DHEA-S, leading to deficient placental estrogen production
Excessive secretion of human placental lactogen
In anencephaly, adrenal hypoplasia means no DHEA-S is produced; lack of placental estrogen fails to trigger labor, causing post-term pregnancy. (Book p285)
In addition to fetal anencephaly and wrong menstrual dates (most common), endocrine causes of post-term pregnancy include:
Placental sulfatase and placental aromatase deficiencies
Elevated hCG levels and hyperemesis gravidarum
Placental sulfatase deficiency, aromatase deficiency, and intrauterine fetal death cause deficient estrogen and post-term gestation. (Book p285)
Placental and luteal relaxin mediates which physiological cardiovascular and musculoskeletal adaptations during pregnancy?
Joint laxity (pelvic ligaments), smooth muscle relaxation, decreased PVR, and increased GFR
Closure of the ductus arteriosus and decreased renal blood flow
Elevation of systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure
Relaxin causes pelvic joint laxity, uterine quiescence, systemic vasodilation (decreased PVR), and increased renal blood flow/GFR. (Book p285)
Human placental lactogen (hPL), synthesized by the syncytiotrophoblast, exhibits 96% structural homology with which pituitary hormone?
hPL is a polypeptide hormone synthesized by syncytiotrophoblasts that has 96% structural homology with growth hormone. (Book p285)
What is the biological half-life (T1/2) of human placental lactogen in maternal plasma?
The biological half-life of hPL is 15 minutes (in contrast to hCG which is 36 hours). (Book p285)
Production of hPL begins at the 3rd week, peaks at 36 weeks, and serves as an indicator of placental mass whose primary metabolic action is to:
Exert an anti-insulin diabetogenic effect, sparing maternal glucose and amino acids for the fetus
Inhibit maternal lipolysis and increase maternal glycogen storage
hPL produces maternal insulin resistance (diabetogenic effect) and lipolysis, ensuring continuous glucose availability for the fetus. (Book p286)
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a heterodimeric glycoprotein whose α-subunit is structurally identical to that of LH, FSH, and TSH, while biological specificity is determined by its:
The alpha subunit is shared with LH, FSH, and TSH; the beta subunit is unique and imparts hormone-specific biological identity. (Book p286)
In early embryonic development, the initial stimulus prompting fetal testicular Leydig cells to produce testosterone for male differentiation is:
Placental hCG provides the initial stimulus for fetal Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone. (Book p286)
In normal gestation, beta-hCG can be detected earliest in maternal serum and maternal urine at:
Serum: 8 days post-fertilization (Day 22); Urine: Day of missed period (Day 28)
Serum: Day of missed period; Urine: 8 weeks of gestation
Serum: 14 days post-fertilization; Urine: 3 weeks after missed period
Serum: 30 hours post-fertilization; Urine: Day 20 of cycle
hCG is detectable in blood as early as 8 days after fertilization (Day 22 of cycle) and in urine by the day of the missed period. (Book p286)
Which of the following statements about human chorionic gonadotropin is TRUE?
The beta subunit is hCG-specific and is what assays measure; the alpha subunit is shared with TSH, LH and FSH
Serum hCG keeps rising through the second trimester and peaks only at around 28 weeks
A doubling time slower than seven days is entirely normal between 4 and 8 weeks of gestation
hCG first appears in maternal blood only after implantation is complete at about day 14
hCG peaks at 8-10 weeks and then falls; the beta subunit is assay-specific, and hCG is detectable from about day 8-9, well before day 14. (Book p286)
Serum levels of hCG peak at approximately 10 weeks of gestation (60–80 days) reaching what typical concentration?
hCG peaks at 10 weeks (60–80 days) at ~100,000 IU/L (10^5), declining to a plateau of ~10,000 IU/L by 16 weeks. (Book p287)
What is the biological plasma half-life of hCG, and how soon after delivery does it become undetectable in maternal serum?
Half-life: 36 hours; undetectable by 2 weeks postpartum
Half-life: 15 minutes; undetectable by 24 hours postpartum
Half-life: 7 days; undetectable by 6 months postpartum
Half-life: 12 hours; undetectable by 6 weeks postpartum
The plasma half-life of hCG is 36 hours; levels clear to zero by 2 weeks after normal delivery (2–4 weeks post-abortion). (Book p287)
In a patient presenting at ≤4 weeks gestation with an empty uterus on ultrasound, a 48-hour repeat beta-hCG that rises by only 15% most strongly suggests:
A completely normal viable intrauterine pregnancy
A viable intrauterine pregnancy rises by 33%–66% in 48 hours; a suboptimal rise <30–33% strongly suggests an ectopic pregnancy. (Book p287)
The discriminatory zone—the serum beta-hCG titer at which an intrauterine gestational sac must be visualized—is defined as:
An intrauterine sac must be seen at beta-hCG ≥2000 IU/L on TVS and ≥6500 IU/L on TAS; absence indicates an ectopic pregnancy. (Book p288)
Which of the following clinical conditions is characteristically associated with pathologically elevated serum beta-hCG levels?
Molar pregnancy, multifetal gestation, and Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
Intrauterine growth restriction and placental sulfatase deficiency
hCG is elevated in twin pregnancies, molar pregnancy/GTN, Rh-negative hydrops, and Down syndrome (Trisomy 21). (Book p288)
Anatomically, placenta previa is defined as abnormal implantation of the placenta within the:
Placenta previa is located in the lower uterine segment, rather than the normal upper uterine segment. (Book p289)
In the Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS), when chorionic villi invade deeply into the myometrial muscular wall without reaching serosa, it is designated as:
Accreta attaches to superficial myometrium; increta invades deeply into myometrium; percreta penetrates through to serosa or bladder. (Book p289)
Placenta percreta represents the most aggressive form of morbidly adherent placenta, wherein chorionic villi:
Penetrate through the entire myometrium to the uterine serosa or adjacent pelvic organs
Attach superficially to the basal layer of the endometrium
Are confined strictly to the decidua basalis without muscular contact
Are attached to an accessory placental lobe across membranes
In placenta percreta, chorionic villi penetrate through the entire myometrium and uterine serosa, potentially invading the urinary bladder. (Book p289)
Placenta bilobata (bipartita) is morphologically characterized by:
Placenta divided into two roughly equal lobes connected by blood vessels with a single umbilical cord
Two separate placentas with two separate umbilical cords
One major placenta with a tiny rudimentary accessory lobe
A central depression encircled by a double fold of membranes
Placenta bilobata consists of two roughly equal lobes connected by vessels, with a single umbilical cord (unlike twin placentas). (Book p289)
Placenta succenturiata features a separate accessory lobe connected by intramembranous vessels, presenting clinical risks of:
Retention of the succenturiate lobe causing PPH and placenta previa
Immediate fetal phocomelia with amputation of the digits
Complete congenital heart block appearing in the newborn
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus in the fetus

Placenta succenturiata has a separate accessory lobe joined by intramembranous vessels, risking a retained succenturiate lobe with postpartum hemorrhage and an increased risk of placenta previa. (Book p289)
All of the following predispose to placenta accreta spectrum EXCEPT:
Grand multiparity without any uterine surgery
Previous caesarean section with an anterior low-lying placenta
Previous endometrial curettage or Asherman syndrome
Accreta spectrum needs a deficient decidua from endometrial damage — scar, curettage, previa or myomectomy; parity alone does not scar the myometrium. (Book p289)
In an extrachorial placenta, the maternal surface is larger than the fetal surface, resulting in:
Fetal membranes failing to extend to the placental margin, forming a ring on the fetal surface
The umbilical cord inserting directly into the cervical canal
The chorionic villi attaching directly to the ovarian surface
In extrachorial placenta, maternal surface exceeds the fetal surface, so membranes insert inward and form a ring around the fetal surface. (Book p290)
A circumvallate placenta is distinguished on gross examination by a thick, raised, rolled white ring at the margin with a central depression, predisposing to:
Intrauterine growth restriction and antepartum hemorrhage from abruption
Fetal macrosomia together with polyhydramnios in the third trimester
Down syndrome and maternal hyperthyroidism in the index pregnancy
Post-term pregnancy with a persistently high serum hCG level
A circumvallate placenta shows a thick raised rolled white ring at the margin with central depression, and predisposes to IUGR and antepartum hemorrhage (abruptio placentae). (Book p290)
Unlike circumvallate placenta, a circummarginate placenta exhibits a flat, smooth transition between membranes and placenta at the same level and is:
Clinically benign and of no significant clinical consequence
An absolute indication for immediate Cesarean section
Associated with a 50% incidence of fetal mortality
Circummarginate placenta shows a flat, smooth transition without a raised fold and carries no clinical significance. (Book p290)
A placenta in which the umbilical cord is inserted directly into the lateral placental margin rather than near the center is termed a:
In battledore placenta, the umbilical cord is attached to the lateral margin of the placenta like a table tennis bat. (Book p291)
In velamentous cord insertion, the umbilical cord inserts into the fetal membranes away from the placenta, leaving fetal vessels vulnerable because:
Protective Wharton's jelly is absent as vessels traverse the bare membranes
The umbilical vein is completely obliterated
The vessels are surrounded by a thick calcified sheath
The vessels carry only maternal blood
In velamentous insertion, cord vessels run through membranes devoid of protective Wharton's jelly, predisposing them to tearing. (Book p291)
The catastrophic consequence of vasa previa occurs when membrane rupture tears unsupported fetal vessels crossing the internal os, producing:
Rapid fetal exsanguination and high perinatal mortality
Severe maternal hemorrhagic shock with normal fetal heart
Vasa previa involves fetal vessels traversing the internal os; rupture causes direct fetal hemorrhage and catastrophic perinatal mortality. (Book p291)
Type 1 vasa previa is caused by velamentous cord insertion, while Type 2 vasa previa results from:
Vessels traversing between the lobes in placenta bilobata or succenturiata
Dehiscence of a previous caesarean section scar in the lower segment
Complete congenital absence of the single umbilical vein
A circumvallate ring forming around the margin of the placenta
Type 1 vasa previa comes from velamentous cord insertion, while type 2 results from vessels traversing between the lobes in placenta bilobata or placenta succenturiata. (Book p292)
What is the investigation of choice (IOC) for vasa previa, and what is the definitive delivery recommendation upon antenatal diagnosis?
Color Doppler ultrasound; Elective Cesarean section at 34–37 weeks
Digital vaginal examination; Induction of labor at 39 weeks
Non-stress test alone; Expectant management until spontaneous rupture
Color Doppler ultrasound is the IOC; antenatal detection mandates elective Cesarean delivery at 34–37 weeks (ARM is contraindicated). (Book p292)
In a laboring patient presenting with painless vaginal bleeding immediately following amniotomy, which finding specifically points to vasa previa over placenta previa?
Profound fetal distress (bradycardia/sinusoidal CTG) entirely out of proportion to slight maternal vaginal bleeding
Profuse maternal bleeding with completely normal fetal heart tones
The presence of a visible retroplacental clot on ultrasound
A high maternal pulse pressure with maternal hypovolemia
In vasa previa, the blood lost is fetal, causing severe, rapid fetal distress out of proportion to the minimal external blood seen. (Book p292)

At 38 weeks, membranes rupture spontaneously and are immediately followed by fresh vaginal bleeding and fetal bradycardia. Vaginal blood is mixed with water; after adding alkali the supernatant stays pink. What is the diagnosis and the immediate step?
Vasa previa with fetal haemorrhage — immediate caesarean section
Placental abruption with maternal bleeding — stabilise and aim for vaginal delivery
Bloody show from cervical dilatation — reassure and await spontaneous labour
Uterine rupture — laparotomy and repair of the uterine scar
A positive Apt test (alkali-resistant fetal haemoglobin turning the supernatant pink) means the blood is fetal — vasa previa demands immediate caesarean. (Book p292)
Cord insertion anomalies, vasa previa & Apt test
The Apt test (Singer's alkali denaturation test) differentiates fetal from maternal vaginal bleeding by adding 1% NaOH or KOH to vaginal blood because:
Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is alkali-resistant (remains pink), while adult hemoglobin (HbA) denatures (turns yellow-brown)
Adult hemoglobin is alkali-resistant, while fetal hemoglobin rapidly precipitates
Maternal platelets clump immediately in the presence of alkali
Fetal leukocytes lyse and release peroxidase enzymes
HbF is alkali-resistant, so vaginal blood containing HbF remains pink (+ve Apt test = vasa previa); HbA denatures to brown (placenta previa). (Book p293)
Which comparison correctly contrasts the Apt test with the Kleihauer-Betke test?
Apt test: qualitative test for vasa previa using NaOH; Kleihauer-Betke: quantitative acid elution test to dose anti-D in Rh -ve mothers
Apt test: quantitative test for fetal anemia; Kleihauer-Betke: qualitative test for placenta accreta
Both tests utilize identical alkaline reagents on maternal urine
Kleihauer-Betke test is used exclusively to diagnose ectopic pregnancy
Apt test is a qualitative alkali test for vasa previa; Kleihauer-Betke is a quantitative acid elution test on maternal blood to calculate anti-D dose. (Book p293)
What is the chronological sequence of anatomical sites of hematopoiesis and primary hemoglobin types during embryonic and fetal development?
<6 weeks: Yolk sac (Gower/Portland); 6–30 weeks: Liver (HbF); ≥20 weeks: Bone marrow (HbA)
<6 weeks: Liver; 6–30 weeks: Spleen; ≥20 weeks: Yolk sac
<6 weeks: Bone marrow; 6–30 weeks: Yolk sac; ≥20 weeks: Liver
<6 weeks: Thymus; 6–30 weeks: Bone marrow; ≥20 weeks: Spleen
Hematopoiesis originates in yolk sac (<6 wks, embryonic Hb), shifts to liver (6–30 wks, HbF), and establishes in bone marrow (≥20 wks, HbA). (Book p293)
Fill up: Fetal erythropoiesis begins in the ______, and the predominant haemoglobin at term is ______.
The mesoblastic (yolk-sac) phase starts first, and HbF still predominates at term, with HbA rising only after birth. (Book p293)
At birth, fetal hemoglobin (HbF) comprises approximately 75%–90% of total hemoglobin, but by 6 months of age it normally declines to:
At birth, HbF accounts for 75%–90% of total hemoglobin, falling to approximately 1% by 6 months of postnatal life. (Book p294)
What is the normal physiological hemoglobin concentration in a healthy term newborn infant?
The normal hemoglobin concentration in a healthy term neonate is 16–18 g/dL. (Book p294)
During the third stage of labor, normal physiological placental detachment occurs along which histological cleavage plane?
Zona spongiosa of the decidua basalis
Zona compacta of the decidua basalis
Normal placental separation occurs cleanly through the spongy layer (zona spongiosa) of the decidua basalis. (Book p294)
Which features correctly distinguish the Schultze method from the Duncan method of placental separation?
Schultze: central separation, shiny fetal surface first; Duncan: peripheral separation, dull maternal surface first
Schultze: peripheral separation, dull maternal surface first; Duncan: central separation, shiny fetal surface first
Schultze: continuous bleeding from the start; Duncan: bleeding appears only after expulsion
Schultze: peripheral detachment with no retroplacental clot; Duncan: central detachment with a large clot

Schultze (80%) separates centrally, the shiny fetal surface is expelled first and bleeding is seen only after expulsion; Duncan (20%) separates peripherally, the dull maternal surface is expelled first and bleeding is continuous. (Book p294)
The four classic clinical signs confirming complete placental separation in the third stage of labor are:
Gush of blood, umbilical/suprapubic bulge, fundus rising and becoming firm/globular, and permanent lengthening of the cord
Sudden maternal hypotension, severe fetal bradycardia, uterine relaxation, and cord shortening
Absence of vaginal bleeding, flattening of the fundus, disappearance of the cord, and pelvic pain
Immediate cervical dilatation to 10 cm, descent of presenting part, caput formation, and crowning
The 4 signs of separation are: a sudden gush of blood, suprapubic bulge, uterine fundus rising and becoming globular, and permanent cord lengthening. (Book p294)
What are the normal physical and biochemical properties of term amniotic fluid?
Normal amniotic fluid has a specific gravity of 1.008–1.010, slightly alkaline pH (7.2), and osmolarity of ~260 mOsm/L. (Book p295)
The volume of amniotic fluid reaches its physiological maximum of approximately 1000 ml at 32–34 weeks, thereafter declining to:
800 ml at 40 weeks (term) and ~200 ml at 42 weeks (post-term)
500 ml at 36 weeks and 100 ml at term
1500 ml at 38 weeks and 1200 ml at term
800 ml at 36 weeks and remaining at 800 ml until 43 weeks
Amniotic volume peaks at 1 L at 32–34 weeks, drops to ~800 ml at term (40 weeks), and declines sharply to ~200 ml at 42 weeks. (Book p295)
What is the primary physiological source of amniotic fluid production after 20 weeks of gestation?
Maternal transudate across the vaginal mucosa
Direct amniotic epithelial active water secretion
After 20 weeks, fetal urine is the main contributor to amniotic fluid, producing ~1000 ml/day at term. (Book p295)
Transudation of fluid across fetal skin ceases to contribute to amniotic fluid when cutaneous keratinization completes at:
Keratinization of fetal skin is complete by 22–25 weeks of pregnancy, after which transudation across the skin stops. (Book p295)
The primary mechanism responsible for clearing and maintaining normal amniotic fluid turnover is:
Fetal swallowing (500–1000 ml/day absorbed by the fetal gut)
Intramembranous transport into maternal pelvic veins
Direct filtration across the umbilical cord Wharton's jelly
Passive diffusion across maternal abdominal wall muscles
Fetal swallowing (500–1000 ml/day) is the primary clearance pathway; impaired swallowing results in polyhydramnios. (Book p295)

Match the amniotic fluid colour with its usual meaning — 1) Golden yellow 2) Green 3) Port-wine or red-brown … A) Meconium staining B) Rh isoimmunisation with bilirubin C) Old blood, as in abruptio placentae
Golden fluid means bilirubin from haemolysis, green means meconium, and port-wine or red-brown means old intrauterine bleeding. (Book p295)
On amniocentesis or artificial rupture of membranes, normal amniotic fluid appears:
Straw-colored at term and completely colorless in preterm gestation
Golden-yellow at term and deep green preterm
Port-wine colored at term and cloudy white preterm
Dark brown at term and straw-colored preterm
Normal amniotic fluid is colorless and watery in early/preterm pregnancy, becoming pale straw-colored at term. (Book p296)
Green amniotic fluid indicates meconium staining, which is classically seen in fetal distress, breech or transverse lie presentations, and:
Green staining is caused by meconium passage due to fetal distress, breech/transverse lie, or intrauterine Listeria infection. (Book p296)
A golden-yellow coloration of amniotic fluid on amniocentesis is pathognomonic of excessive bilirubin accumulation due to:
Rh isoimmunization / hemolytic disease of the fetus
Fetal duodenal atresia with bile reflux
Premature placental separation with lysed blood
Golden-yellow amniotic fluid is due to bilirubin pigments released during severe fetal hemolysis in Rh incompatibility. (Book p296)
Match the abnormal amniotic fluid appearance with its correct underlying clinical condition:
Dark red (port-wine): Concealed abruption; Tobacco-juice (dark brown): Intrauterine fetal death; Saffron: Post-term pregnancy
Dark red: Rh incompatibility; Tobacco-juice: Normal term; Saffron: Listeria infection
Dark red: Ectopic pregnancy; Tobacco-juice: Duodenal atresia; Saffron: Hydatidiform mole
Dark red: Meconium staining; Tobacco-juice: Abruptio; Saffron: Normal preterm
Dark red (port-wine) indicates concealed abruption, tobacco-juice (dark brown) indicates IUFD, and saffron indicates post-term dysmaturity. (Book p296)
The clinical investigation of choice (IOC) for the quantitative assessment of amniotic fluid volume is:
Ultrasound is the non-invasive investigation of choice for measuring amniotic fluid parameters. (Book p296)
The Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) is calculated by ultrasound as the sum total of the largest vertical pocket of fluid in:
All four quadrants of the maternal abdomen (RUQ + LUQ + RLQ + LLQ)
The right and left upper quadrants only
A single deepest vertical pocket across the entire uterus
The retroplacental space and lower uterine segment
AFI is calculated by summing the deepest vertical pocket in each of the 4 abdominal quadrants (AFI = a + b + c + d). (Book p296)
What is the normal physiological reference range for the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) in a singleton pregnancy?
The normal range for AFI is 5–24 cm; values <5 cm define oligohydramnios, and ≥25 cm define polyhydramnios. (Book p296)
By definition, oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios are diagnosed when the AFI values are respectively:
Oligohydramnios below 5 cm, and polyhydramnios at 25 cm or more
Oligohydramnios below 2 cm, and polyhydramnios above 8 cm
Oligohydramnios below 10 cm, and polyhydramnios at 35 cm or more
Oligohydramnios below 1 cm, and polyhydramnios at 15 cm or more
By amniotic fluid index, oligohydramnios is below 5 cm and polyhydramnios is 25 cm or more; the 2 cm and 8 cm values belong to the deepest pocket method. (Book p296)
A major technical clinical limitation of using the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) is that it:
Cannot be accurately utilized in twin or multiple gestations
Exposes the fetus to excessive ionizing radiation
Requires invasive needle puncture of the amniotic sac
Can only be measured after 37 completed weeks of pregnancy
AFI cannot be used in multifetal pregnancies because the quadrants overlap both sacs; SDP must be used instead. (Book p296)
A 34-year-old at 37 weeks has an amniotic fluid index of 4.2 cm with a single deepest vertical pocket of 3.1 cm. How should this scan be reported, and what follows?
Oligohydramnios by AFI, though the deepest pocket is still adequate — look for rupture and monitor
Normal study, because both the AFI and the deepest vertical pocket are within normal limits
Polyhydramnios, because the AFI is above the 95th centile for gestational age
Severe oligohydramnios by both criteria, so immediate caesarean delivery is indicated
AFI at or below 5 cm is oligohydramnios, while a deepest pocket of 3.1 cm is still above the 2 cm threshold — the two methods disagree and must both be reported. (Book p296)
What is the normal reference range for the Single Deepest Pocket (SDP) / Maximum Vertical Pocket (MVP) on ultrasound?
Normal SDP is 2–8 cm; an SDP <2 cm defines oligohydramnios, and >8 cm defines polyhydramnios. (Book p297)
What are the key clinical advantages of measuring the Single Deepest Pocket (SDP) over the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI)?
It is more sensitive than AFI and can be reliably used in twin pregnancies
It provides a direct biochemical analysis of fetal hemoglobin
It measures maternal renal blood flow simultaneously
It can diagnose fetal neural tube defects without imaging
SDP is more sensitive than AFI, avoids overdiagnosis of oligohydramnios, and is valid in twin gestations. (Book p297)
What is the most common etiology for mild polyhydramnios and mild oligohydramnios, respectively?
Mild cases of both polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios are most commonly idiopathic in origin. (Book p297)
In severe polyhydramnios, what represents the single most common category of underlying etiologies?
Gross congenital anomalies (Gastrointestinal tract obstructions > Neural tube defects)
Severe polyhydramnios is most commonly caused by gross congenital anomalies, with GIT defects (atresias) outnumbering NTDs. (Book p297)
What is the leading cause of severe oligohydramnios diagnosed in the second trimester?
Fetal renal anomalies (e.g., bilateral renal agenesis, PUV)
Severe oligohydramnios is most commonly due to fetal renal malformations impairing fetal urine production. (Book p297)
The pathophysiological mechanism causing marked polyhydramnios in poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus is:
Maternal hyperglycemia causing fetal hyperglycemia, which induces fetal osmotic polyuria
Impaired fetal swallowing due to cleft palate
Excessive transudation across fetal skin after 25 weeks
Placental hypoplasia with decreased fluid clearance
Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, driving fetal osmotic diuresis and massive polyuria into the amniotic sac. (Book p297)
All of the following are causes of polyhydramnios EXCEPT:
Renal agenesis removes fetal urine output and causes oligohydramnios; obstruction, impaired swallowing and fetal polyuria cause polyhydramnios. (Book p297)
Which of the following fetal malformations causes polyhydramnios specifically by impairing the fetal swallowing mechanism?
Esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula, and duodenal atresia
Posterior urethral valves and prune belly syndrome
Bilateral renal agenesis and multicystic kidney
Fetal coarctation of the aorta and tetralogy of Fallot
Swallowing defects preventing amniotic clearance include esophageal atresia, TEF, duodenal atresia, and cleft lip/palate. (Book p298)
Chronologically, the most common cause of oligohydramnios in the second trimester vs the third trimester is:
T2: Fetal renal anomalies; T3: Uteroplacental insufficiency (UPI) or PROM
T2: Gestational diabetes; T3: Fetal anemia
T2: Fetal swallowing defects; T3: Rh isoimmunization
In the 2nd trimester, fetal renal anomalies are the leading cause; in the 3rd trimester, UPI/IUGR and PROM predominate. (Book p298)
In every patient diagnosed with oligohydramnios, what essential initial clinical step must be performed to exclude membrane rupture?
Sterile speculum (P/S) examination to inspect for amniotic pooling and rule out PROM
Immediate digital vaginal examination with Bishop scoring
A sterile speculum examination must be performed in all oligohydramnios cases to rule out premature rupture of membranes (PROM). (Book p298)
Which clinical entity can present with both oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios in the same pregnancy?
Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS: oligohydramnios in donor, polyhydramnios in recipient)
Fetal anencephaly in a singleton gestation
Bilateral renal agenesis in a singleton gestation
TTTS classically produces polyhydramnios in the recipient twin and severe oligohydramnios in the donor twin. (Book p298)
In high-risk pregnancies complicated by significant amniotic fluid disorders, antepartum surveillance initiates at 28 weeks and includes:
Weekly NST, weekly Biophysical Profile (BPP), and fetal growth USG every 3 weeks
Daily oxytocin challenge tests and daily amniocentesis
Monthly urine pregnancy testing and pelvic X-ray
Surveillance starts at 28 weeks with weekly NST, weekly biophysical score, and ultrasound for fetal growth every 3 weeks. (Book p299)
What is the recommended gestational age for delivery by induction of labor in uncomplicated vs complicated amniotic fluid disorders?
Labor induction is scheduled at 39 completed weeks for uncomplicated cases and at 37 weeks for complicated disorders. (Book p299)
Severe, prolonged oligohydramnios present early in pregnancy (first or early second trimester) is clinically most devastating because it causes:
Pulmonary hypoplasia, the most lethal complication, and limb contractures
Duodenal atresia together with macroglossia in the newborn
A complete hydatidiform mole developing in the uterus
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus before delivery
Severe early oligohydramnios is devastating because it causes pulmonary hypoplasia, the most lethal complication, and severe limb reduction contractures. (Book p299)
In late pregnancy and active labor, oligohydramnios predisposes the fetus to which cardiotocographic (CTG) abnormality due to loss of fluid cushioning?
Repetitive variable decelerations due to umbilical cord compression
Late decelerations occurring only after complete delivery
Loss of amniotic cushioning leads to umbilical cord compression, presenting on CTG as repetitive variable decelerations. (Book p299)
Which of the following statements about oligohydramnios is TRUE?
Potter sequence follows prolonged severe oligohydramnios beginning before about 22-24 weeks
Amniotic band syndrome is caused by oligohydramnios and is prevented by amnioinfusion
An amniotic fluid index of 8 cm is diagnostic of oligohydramnios in the third trimester
Isolated oligohydramnios at term is by itself an indication for immediate caesarean delivery
Only early, severe, prolonged oligohydramnios causes pulmonary hypoplasia with Potter facies and limb deformities; bands are a separate amnion-rupture problem. (Book p299)
What constitutes the conservative mainstay of management for antenatal oligohydramnios?
Strict bed rest in maternal left lateral position and aggressive maternal hydration
Mainstay conservative management includes bed rest in the left lateral position to optimize uterine perfusion and oral/IV hydration. (Book p300)
Amnio-infusion of warm normal saline is specifically indicated and performed during active labor for:
Persistent, severe variable decelerations due to cord compression
Antenatal treatment of pulmonary hypoplasia at 20 weeks
Preventing postpartum hemorrhage in twin pregnancy
Amnio-infusion with normal saline is indicated during active labor to alleviate persistent variable decelerations caused by cord compression. (Book p300)
In uteroplacental insufficiency (UPI), the fetal 'brain-sparing effect' leads to oligohydramnios through which sequence?
Cardiac output is preferentially shunted to the brain → Renal blood flow falls → GFR drops → Oliguria → Oligohydramnios
Blood is shunted to kidneys → Excessive urination → Bladder rupture
Renal vessels dilate → Glomerular filtration surges → Polyhydramnios
Systemic vasoconstriction causes pulmonary edema and amniotic fluid reabsorption
In UPI, blood is shunted to vital brain tissue, reducing renal perfusion; diminished GFR produces fetal oliguria and oligohydramnios. (Book p300)
Potter's syndrome is primary bilateral renal agenesis with pulmonary hypoplasia and flat facies, whereas Potter's sequence refers to:
The identical constellation of deformities resulting secondarily from any chronic severe oligohydramnios
The association of duodenal atresia with Down syndrome
Placental chorangioma combined with fetal hydrops
Potter's sequence describes the classic phenotypic triad arising secondary to any cause of severe oligohydramnios (such as PROM or PUV). (Book p300)
Amniotic Band Syndrome (Streeter's syndrome) occurs when early rupture of the amnion produces loose fibrous strands that:
Wrap tightly around fetal digits or extremities, forming constriction rings and causing amputations
Infiltrate the maternal myometrium to cause placenta percreta
Cross the internal os to cause vasa previa
Stimulate excessive fetal swallowing and severe polyhydramnios
Amniotic bands wrap tightly around fetal digits or limbs, producing deep constriction rings, distal digital hypoplasia, or amputation. (Book p300)

In distinguishing limb reduction deformities, distal digital hypoplasia/amputation is characteristic of amniotic band syndrome and phenytoin, whereas proximal long-bone phocomelia is pathognomonic of:
Proximal limb reduction (phocomelia/seal limbs) is caused by thalidomide, whereas distal digital amputations occur in amniotic band syndrome. (Book p301)
In severe symptomatic polyhydramnios (SDP ≥10 cm or AFI ≥35 cm) with maternal respiratory distress, therapeutic amnioreduction should remove:
A maximum of 1.5 to 2.0 Liters slowly
Up to 5 Liters rapidly within 10 minutes
All fluid until the SDP measures <1 cm
Amnioreduction should slowly remove a maximum of 1.5–2.0 L to avoid abruptio placentae from rapid uterine decompression. (Book p301)
When uterine irritability complicates symptomatic polyhydramnios, the recommended tocolytic regimens according to gestational age are:
<32 weeks: Indomethacin; 32–34 weeks: Nifedipine; ≥34 weeks: Tocolytics not given
At all gestational ages: Indomethacin exclusively
Only intravenous magnesium sulfate throughout the third trimester
Indomethacin is used before 32 weeks, nifedipine is given from 32–34 weeks, and tocolytics are avoided at ≥34 weeks. (Book p301)
In a patient in labor with marked polyhydramnios, artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is strictly contraindicated because sudden gush of fluid precipitates:
Umbilical cord prolapse and abruptio placentae
ARM is contraindicated in polyhydramnios because rapid decompression risks catastrophic umbilical cord prolapse and placental abruption. (Book p301)
Overdistension of the uterus in severe polyhydramnios increases maternal and obstetric risks of:
Preterm labor, unstable lie, placental abruption, and uterine atony PPH
Complete congenital heart block and Ebstein anomaly
Polyhydramnios predisposes to preterm labor, cord prolapse, abruptio placentae, malpresentation, and postpartum uterine atony. (Book p301)
On fetal pelvic ultrasound, the classic 'keyhole sign' consisting of a distended bladder and dilated proximal posterior urethra is diagnostic of:
Posterior urethral valves (PUV) causing severe oligohydramnios
Bilateral renal agenesis with empty bladder
The keyhole sign represents a distended bladder and dilated posterior urethra in male fetuses with PUV, producing severe oligohydramnios. (Book p301)
The classic sonographic 'double bubble sign' on fetal abdominal imaging represents a fluid-filled stomach and dilated duodenum pathognomonic of:
Duodenal atresia, which is associated with polyhydramnios and Down syndrome
The double bubble sign represents duodenal atresia, which prevents fluid absorption causing polyhydramnios and is strongly tied to Down syndrome. (Book p301)
Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV / clubfoot) occurring as a secondary deformation in late gestation is classically associated with:
Prolonged severe oligohydramnios with uterine crowding and compression
Maternal exposure to thalidomide in the third trimester
Excessive production of human placental lactogen
Prolonged severe oligohydramnios late in pregnancy restricts fetal movements and compresses extremities, leading to CTEV (clubfoot). (Book p301)
Fill up: In severe polyhydramnios, amnioreduction removes fluid at about ______ mL per hour, and the drug used to reduce fetal urine output is ______.
Slow decompression at about 500 mL/hour limits abruption and preterm labour, and indomethacin reduces fetal urine output (with ductal constriction as the caveat). (Book p301)
Fill up: In an obstetric patient with regular 28-day menstrual cycles, the clinical gestational age (menstrual age) of the pregnancy is calculated from ______.
The first day of the last menstrual period (LMP)
Gestational age is calculated from the first day of the last normal menstrual period (LMP). (Book p302)
Which of the following statements about Basics of pregnancy is TRUE?
Gestational age is 2 weeks greater than fetal age
Gestational age is 2 weeks less than fetal age
Gestational age is 1 week greater than fetal age
Gestational age is identical to fetal age
Because fertilization typically occurs 2 weeks after the LMP in a 28-day cycle, gestational age = fetal age + 2 weeks. (Book p302)
All of the following are Basics of pregnancy EXCEPT:
5th week of gestational age — Cardiac activity starts 3 weeks after fertilization, corresp
3rd week of gestational age — Cardiac activity starts 3 weeks after fertilization, corresp
4th week of gestational age — Cardiac activity starts 3 weeks after fertilization, corresp
6th week of gestational age — Cardiac activity starts 3 weeks after fertilization, corresp
