Cardiac activity starts 3 weeks after fertilization, corresponding to the 5th week of gestational age (fetal age + 2 weeks). (Book p302)

A 28-year-old woman at 13 weeks with basics of pregnancy presents with trimester 1 spans lmp to 13 weeks + 6 days, trimester 2 spans 14 weeks to 27 weeks + 6 days, and tri. According to standard obstetric definitions, the second trimester of pregnancy spans from:?
14 weeks to 27 weeks + 6 days with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
12 weeks to 24 weeks with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
13 weeks to 26 weeks with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
16 weeks to 28 weeks + 6 days with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
Trimester 1 spans LMP to 13 weeks + 6 days, Trimester 2 spans 14 weeks to 27 weeks + 6 days, and Trimester 3 spans 28 weeks to delivery. (Book p302)
A 24-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles is sure her last menstrual period started on 12 March 2026. Using Naegele's rule, what is her expected date of delivery?
Naegele's rule adds 9 months and 7 days to the first day of the LMP: 12 March 2026 + 9 months + 7 days = 19 December 2026. (Book p302)
Fill up: ______ are the only pregnancy events calculated from the day of fertilization rather than the first day of the LMP.
Fetal growth periods (period of fertilized ovum, embryo, and fetus)
Estimated date of delivery (EDD) by Naegele's rule
Fetal growth periods are the only pregnancy events calculated from the day of fertilization rather than the first day of the LMP. (Book p303)
Which of the following statements about Basics of pregnancy regarding 3rd week to the end of is TRUE?
3rd week to the end of the 8th/9th week after fertilization
Day of fertilization up to 2 weeks
9th week after fertilization up to birth
12th week to 24th week of gestational age
The embryonic period extends from the 3rd week to the end of the 8th/9th week after fertilization, preceded by the period of the fertilized ovum (up to 2 weeks). (Book p303)
All of the following are Basics of pregnancy regarding 7 days to the first day EXCEPT:
7 days to the first day of the LMP and add 9 calendar months
7 days to the last day of the LMP and add 9 calendar months
14 days to the first day of the LMP and add 9 calendar months
280 days from the day of missed period — Naegele's formula adds 7 days to the 1st day of the LMP and
Naegele's formula adds 7 days to the 1st day of the LMP and then adds 9 months (or subtracts 3 months and adds 1 year and 7 days). (Book p303)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with basics of pregnancy presents with for a 28-day cycle, edd = jan 10 + 7 days + 9 months = oct 17. A pregnant woman reports an LMP of January 10th and has a regular menstrual cycle length of 35 days. What is her corrected EDD?
October 24th with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
October 17th with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
October 10th with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
November 7th with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
For a 28-day cycle, EDD = Jan 10 + 7 days + 9 months = Oct 17. The cycle difference is 35 - 28 = +7 days. Adding 7 days gives October 24th. (Book p303)
Fill up: For Day 5 transfer, EDD = ______ transfer + 261 days (for Day 3 transfer, EDD = Date of transfer + 263 days; conception + 266 days).
For Day 5 transfer, EDD = Date of transfer + 261 days (for Day 3 transfer, EDD = Date of transfer + 263 days; conception + 266 days). (Book p304)
Which of the following statements about Dating and fetal demise is TRUE?
Dating and fetal demise — Early term
Dating and fetal demise — Full term
Dating and fetal demise — Late term
Early term is 37w0d to 38w6d; Full term is 39w0d to 40w6d; Late term is 41w0d to 41w6d; Post-term is >=42 weeks. (Book p304)
All of the following are Dating and fetal demise EXCEPT:
Extreme preterm birth (<28 weeks) — Extreme preterm is <28 weeks, very preterm is <32 weeks (or
Very preterm birth (28 to <32 weeks) — Extreme preterm is <28 weeks, very preterm is <32 weeks (or
Late preterm birth (34 to 36+6 weeks) — Extreme preterm is <28 weeks, very preterm is <32 weeks (or
Extreme preterm is <28 weeks, very preterm is <32 weeks (or 28-31+6 wks), moderate PTB is 32-33+6 wks, and late PTB is 34-36+6 weeks. (Book p304)
Match the gestational band with its label — 1) Below 28 weeks 2) 34+0 to 36+6 weeks 3) 32+0 to 33+6 weeks … A) Late preterm (ACOG) B) Extreme preterm (WHO) C) Moderate preterm (WHO)
WHO calls <28 weeks extreme and 32-33 weeks moderate, while ACOG splits preterm into early (<34 weeks) and late (34+0 to 36+6 weeks). (Book p304)
ART dating, preterm categories & fetal death / IUD

A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks with dating and fetal demise presents with iud/stillbirth is pregnancy loss at >=20 weeks (or birth weight >=500 g by who criteria; stillbirth . Intrauterine fetal death (IUD) / stillbirth is defined under standard obstetric criteria as fetal demise occurring at or beyond:?
>= 20 weeks of gestation (or birth weight >= 500 g)
>= 12 weeks of gestation with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
>= 16 weeks of gestation with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
>= 24 weeks of gestation without weight criteria
IUD/stillbirth is pregnancy loss at >=20 weeks (or birth weight >=500 g by WHO criteria; stillbirth >=28 weeks in India/WHO international comparisons). (Book p305)
Fill up: While idiopathic is common overall, ______ IUGR is the most common single identifiable cause of IUD.
While idiopathic is common overall, unrecognized IUGR is the most common single identifiable cause of IUD. (Book p305)
Which of the following statements about Dating and fetal demise regarding Gas/bubbles within the fetal great vessels is TRUE?
Gas/bubbles within the fetal great vessels and heart
Overlapping of skull bones due to cerebral liquefaction
Hyperflexion or hyperextension of the fetal spine
Dating and fetal demise — Crowding of the fetal ribs
Robert's sign is the earliest sign of IUD, characterized by radiolucent gas bubbles in the fetal cardiac chambers and great vessels. (Book p305)
All of the following are Dating and fetal demise regarding Overlapping of the cranial vault bones EXCEPT:
Overlapping of the cranial vault bones due to liquefaction of brain tissue
Gas within the fetal abdominal wall — Spalding's sign is the collapse and overlapping of fetal sku
Abnormal angulation of the fetal extremities
Spine hyperextension in a circular configuration
Spalding's sign is the collapse and overlapping of fetal skull bones occurring after intrauterine death due to loss of intracranial pressure. (Book p305)

Match the dating and fetal demise with the correct detail — 1) A patient with a confirmed IUD retained for 2) A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks with dating 3) Fill up: While idiopathic is common overall, ______ … A) Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) B) >= 20 weeks of gestation (or birth weight >= 500 g) C) Unrecognized intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
Retention of a dead fetus for >=4 weeks releases thromboplastin from degenerating fetal-placental tissues into maternal circulation, precipitating DIC. (Book p305)
Fill up: Gravida ______ the total number of times a woman has been pregnant, including the current pregnancy regardless of gestational age.
Is always included in the gravidity count
Is excluded from gravidity until viability is reached
Is only included if it has progressed past the first trimester
Is counted as parity, not gravidity
Gravida is the total number of times a woman has been pregnant, including the current pregnancy regardless of gestational age. (Book p306)
Which statement about Obstetrical terminology — In India period is TRUE?
28 completed weeks of gestation is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
20 completed weeks of gestation is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
24 completed weeks of gestation is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
22 completed weeks of gestation is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
In India, the period of viability (beyond which a fetus is capable of independent extrauterine life) is designated as 28 weeks. (Book p306)
Which statement about Obstetrical terminology — In GTPAL term is TRUE?
Number of preterm deliveries (20-36w6d) and number of abortions (<20w) is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
Number of living children and number of abortions is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
Number of term deliveries and number of preterm deliveries is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
Number of stillbirths and number of ectopic gestations is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
In GTPAL: a = term deliveries (>=37w), b = preterm deliveries (20-36w6d), c = abortions (<20w), and d = living children. (Book p306)
Fill up: She conceived 3 times (G3). Deliveries: 1 term (a=1), 1 twin delivery at 34w (counts as 1 preterm birth, b=1), 1 abortion (c=1), and 3 living children (d=3): ______.
She conceived 3 times (G3). Deliveries: 1 term (a=1), 1 twin delivery at 34w (counts as 1 preterm birth, b=1), 1 abortion (c=1), and 3 living children (d=3): G3 P 1+1+1+3. (Book p306)

A woman's obstetric history is: one delivery at 39 weeks, one delivery at 33 weeks, two first-trimester miscarriages, and three living children because the term delivery was a twin pregnancy. How is she recorded?
Gravidity counts every pregnancy (4); T counts term births (1, the twins count once), P counts the 33-week birth, A counts the two losses, and L counts three living children. (Book p306)
Which statement about Obstetrical terminology — multipara has given is TRUE?
Given birth 5 or more times is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
Given birth 2 or more times is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
Conceived 5 or more times regardless of outcome is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
Conceived 3 or more times is the listed obstetrical terminology as per the notes
A multipara has given birth >=2 times; a grand multipara has given birth >=5 times beyond the age of viability. (Book p307)

A 26-year-old second gravida at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding obstetrical terminology. According to the notes, an elderly primigravida is a woman who is pregnant for the very first time at >=35 years of age. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that conceives for the first time at or above 35 years of age is the correct obstetrical terminology for this patient at this gestation
Advise that conceives for the first time at or above 30 years of age is the correct obstetrical terminology for this patient at this gestation
Advise that delivers for the second time above 40 years of age is the correct obstetrical terminology for this patient at this gestation
Advise that conceives via art above 32 years of age is the correct obstetrical terminology for this patient at this gestation
An elderly primigravida is a woman who is pregnant for the very first time at >=35 years of age. (Book p307)

A 24-year-old G3P1L1 at 6 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding clinical signs of pregnancy. According to the notes, goodell's sign is the earliest probable sign on bimanual examination; Hegar's and Piskacek's follow a little later. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that goodell's sign, softening of the cervix felt from about six weeks is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that hegar's sign, softening of the lower uterine segment is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that piskacek's sign, asymmetrical softening of the uterine cornu is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that palmer's sign, rhythmic contraction of the uterus felt on examination is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Goodell's sign is the earliest probable sign on bimanual examination; Hegar's and Piskacek's follow a little later. (Book p307)
Which statement about Clinical signs of pregnancy — Piskacek s sign is TRUE?
Asymmetrical enlargement of the uterus due to eccentric implantation is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
Softening of the lower uterine segment/isthmus is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
Pulsations felt in the lateral vaginal fornix is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
Violet discoloration of the vulva is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
Piskacek's sign is an asymmetrical enlargement and prominence of one uterine cornu due to eccentric blastocyst implantation. (Book p307)

A 32-year-old G3P1L1 at 8 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding clinical signs of pregnancy. According to the notes, osiander's sign refers to marked pulsations felt in the lateral vaginal fornices due to increased blood flow in the descending vaginal branches of the uterine arteries. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that osiander's sign is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that chadwick's sign is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that goodell's sign is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that palmer's sign is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Osiander's sign refers to marked pulsations felt in the lateral vaginal fornices due to increased blood flow in the descending vaginal branches of the uterine arteries. (Book p307)
Fill up: Hegar's sign is present when bimanual examination detects a soft, compressible, and empty lower uterine isthmus between ______ cervix and the uterine corpus.
The abdominal and vaginal examining fingers easily approximate each other through the softened, empty lower uterine isthmus
The cervix exhibits a velvety softening and purplish coloration
Rhythmic, painless uterine contractions are palpated
The uterine body can be separated from the adnexa on deep palpation
Hegar's sign is present when bimanual examination detects a soft, compressible, and empty lower uterine isthmus between the cervix and the uterine corpus. (Book p307)

Match the clinical signs of pregnancy with the correct detail — 1) of the following signs or symptoms provides definitive 2) Quickening—the maternal perception of initial fetal movements—is typically 3) At approximately 12 weeks of gestation, the uterine … A) Demonstration of fetal cardiac activity on ultrasound B) 18-20 weeks and 16-18 weeks, respectively C) At the upper border of the pubic symphysis
Definitive/positive signs diagnostic of pregnancy include sonographic fetal cardiac activity, fetal heart sounds on auscultation, and palpable fetal parts by the examiner. (Book p308)
Which statement about Clinical signs of pregnancy — Quickening perceived around is TRUE?
18-20 weeks and 16-18 weeks, respectively is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
14-16 weeks and 12-14 weeks, respectively is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
20-22 weeks and 18-20 weeks, respectively is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
16-18 weeks and 18-20 weeks, respectively is the listed clinical signs of pregnancy as per the notes
Quickening is perceived around 18-20 weeks in primigravidae and 16-18 weeks in multigravidae. (Book p308)

Match the probable sign of pregnancy with what is felt or seen — 1) Goodell's sign 2) Hegar's sign 3) Palmer's sign … A) Softening of the uterus at the isthmus, so the cervix and body feel separate B) Rhythmic uterine contraction felt on bimanual examination C) Softening of the cervix, like touching the lips rather than the nose
Goodell is cervical softening, Hegar is isthmic softening, and Palmer is the rhythmic contraction felt during bimanual examination. (Book p308)
Symptoms, pelvic signs & diagnostic signs of pregnancy
Fill up: Hand-held Doppler detects FHS at ______, whereas a Pinard fetoscope/stethoscope detects FHS by 18-20 weeks.
10-12 weeks by Doppler and 18-20 weeks by stethoscope
6 weeks by Doppler and 12 weeks by stethoscope
14 weeks by Doppler and 24 weeks by stethoscope
16 weeks by Doppler and 20 weeks by stethoscope
Hand-held Doppler detects FHS at 10-12 weeks, whereas a Pinard fetoscope/stethoscope detects FHS by 18-20 weeks. (Book p309)

A 32-year-old G2P1L1 at 16 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding clinical signs of pregnancy. According to the notes, internal ballottement is elicited per vaginam from 16 weeks, while external abdominal ballottement is evident by 20 weeks. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that 20 weeks of gestation is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 12 weeks of gestation is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 28 weeks of gestation is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Advise that 32 weeks of gestation is the correct clinical signs of pregnancy for this patient at this gestation
Internal ballottement is elicited per vaginam from 16 weeks, while external abdominal ballottement is evident by 20 weeks. (Book p309)
Which statement about Fundal height landmarks — At 12 weeks is TRUE?
At the upper border of the pubic symphysis is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
Midway between pubic symphysis and umbilicus is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
At the lower border of the umbilicus is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
It remains entirely an intrapelvic organ and cannot be felt is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
At 12 weeks, the uterus ascends out of the pelvis and its fundus is palpable at the pubic symphysis. (Book p308)
Fill up: The fundus reaches the lower border of the umbilicus at 20 weeks and the upper border of the umbilicus at ______.
The fundus reaches the lower border of the umbilicus at 20 weeks and the upper border of the umbilicus at 24 weeks. (Book p310)
Which statement about Fundal height landmarks — fundal height reaches is TRUE?
The fundal height reaches the Xiphisternum at 36 weeks, causing maximal maternal breathlessness
The fundal height reaches the Costal margin at 36 weeks, causing maximal maternal breathlessness
The fundal height reaches the Umbilicus at 36 weeks, causing maximal maternal breathlessness
The fundal height reaches the Two-thirds distance between umbilicus and xiphisternum at 36 weeks, causing maximal maternal breathlessness
The fundal height reaches the xiphisternum at 36 weeks, causing maximal maternal breathlessness. (Book p310)
Which statement about Fundal height landmarks — When fundal height is TRUE?
Lightening, or the welcome sign, from engagement of the head is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
Uteroplacental insufficiency with a falling fundal height is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
Pathological oligohydramnios with reduced fetal growth is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
Arrest of engagement with a persistently floating head is the listed fundal height landmarks as per the notes
When the fundal height at 40 weeks matches that at 32 weeks, the phenomenon is lightening ('welcome sign'), due to engagement of the fetal head. (Book p310)
Fill up: ______ weeks, the fetal head is engaged/felt on deep pelvic palpation and flanks are full; at 32 weeks the head is not engaged and flanks are empty.
At 40 weeks the fetal head is engaged in the pelvis and the flanks are full
At 32 weeks the fetal head is deeply engaged in the pelvis
At 40 weeks the flanks are entirely empty and narrow
At 32 weeks there is marked pelvic lightening
At 40 weeks, the fetal head is engaged/felt on deep pelvic palpation and flanks are full; at 32 weeks the head is not engaged and flanks are empty. (Book p310)
A discrepancy between fundal height and gestational age is considered clinically significant and warrants ultrasound evaluation when it equals or exceeds:
A discrepancy of >=3 cm (or >=3 weeks) between fundal height and period of gestation indicates a pathological cause and mandates ultrasound. (Book p310)
Which of the following clinical conditions causes fundal height to be significantly LESS than the calculated gestational age?
Fundal height < gestational age is seen in IUGR, oligohydramnios, transverse lie, wrong dates, and IUD. (Book p310)
Fill up: The uterine fundus reaches the umbilicus at about ______ weeks and the xiphisternum at about ______ weeks.
The fundus is at the umbilicus around 24 weeks and at the xiphisternum around 36 weeks, then drops as the head engages. (Book p310)
What is the normal average length and physiological range of the human umbilical cord at term?
Normal cord length is 40-70 cm (average ~55 cm); <30-32 cm is short cord, and >70-100 cm is long cord. (Book p311)
At term, the umbilical cord normally contains which vascular arrangement enclosed within Wharton's jelly?
Two umbilical arteries and one left umbilical vein
One umbilical artery and two umbilical veins
Two umbilical arteries and two umbilical veins
One umbilical artery and one left umbilical vein
The term cord contains 3 vessels: two umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta, and one left umbilical vein. (Book p311)
The anatomical anastomosis that connects the two umbilical arteries just prior to their placental insertion is named the:
The Hyrtl anastomosis connects the two umbilical arteries approximately 1-2 cm from the placental insertion, equalizing pressures. (Book p311)
Which vessel in the feto-placental circulation carries fully oxygenated blood from the placenta to the developing fetus?
The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus under low resistance and low pressure. (Book p311)
Which of the following statements about the umbilical cord and its Doppler waveform is TRUE?
Two arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood away, and the single vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus
Two veins carry oxygenated blood to the fetus, and the single artery returns deoxygenated blood
End-diastolic flow is normally absent in the umbilical artery until about 28 weeks of gestation
The umbilical artery Doppler systolic-diastolic ratio falls steadily because placental resistance rises with gestation
The cord has two umbilical arteries and one vein; end-diastolic flow appears well before 28 weeks and placental resistance falls with gestation. (Book p311)
As normal gestation advances towards term, how do the resistance and diastolic flow within the umbilical artery Doppler waveform evolve?
Placental vascular resistance decreases and end-diastolic flow increases
Placental vascular resistance increases and end-diastolic flow decreases
With advancing gestation, tertiary villous branching lowers placental vascular resistance, causing diastolic flow to increase and S/D ratio to decrease. (Book p312)
In normal third-trimester pregnancies, the umbilical artery systolic-to-diastolic (S/D) ratio should normally measure:
A normal umbilical artery S/D ratio at and beyond 30 weeks is <3.0; an S/D ratio >=3.0 indicates increased placental vascular resistance. (Book p312)
In uteroplacental insufficiency (UPI) associated with pre-eclampsia, what primary hemodynamic change occurs in the umbilical artery Doppler?
Vasoconstriction raises resistance, resulting in decreased end-diastolic flow and S/D ratio >= 3
Vasodilation increases end-diastolic flow and lowers resistance
Complete absence of systolic forward flow
Sudden reversal of flow within the umbilical vein
Placental vasoconstriction and obliterative vasculopathy increase resistance, reducing diastolic flow and elevating S/D ratio >=3. (Book p312)
When absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) is identified on umbilical artery Doppler in a growth-restricted fetus, delivery is recommended at:
33 to 34 weeks of gestation (after steroid coverage)
Immediate termination irrespective of gestational age
AEDF warrants admission, steroid coverage, close monitoring, and planned delivery at 33-34 weeks of gestation. (Book p313)
When reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) is detected on umbilical artery Doppler, pregnancy termination/delivery is recommended at:
REDF indicates extreme placental resistance with impending fetal death; delivery is indicated at 30-32 weeks following corticosteroid administration. (Book p313)
Why is Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) Doppler NOT utilized to diagnose intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?
Due to the 'brain-sparing effect' which causes compensatory cerebral vasodilation
Because MCA blood flow is absent in early pregnancy
Because MCA resistance always equals umbilical artery resistance
Because fetal movements prevent MCA insonation
In hypoxia, the brain-sparing effect vasodilates the MCA to protect vital cerebral circulation; thus MCA Doppler is normal or hyperdynamic in early UPI. (Book p313)
What is the primary clinical indication for measuring the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) Peak Systolic Velocity (PSV)?
Non-invasive detection of moderate-to-severe fetal anemia (PSV >= 1.5 MoM)
Diagnosis of macrosomia in diabetic mothers
In fetal anemia (Rh alloimmunization, Parvovirus B19), hyperdynamic circulation increases MCA-PSV >=1.5 MoM, making it the non-invasive test of choice. (Book p313)

At 34 weeks a growth-restricted fetus has absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, a middle cerebral artery Doppler showing brain sparing and a normal CTG. What is the appropriate next step?
Give antenatal corticosteroids and plan delivery, as absent end-diastolic flow at 34 weeks is an indication
Repeat the Doppler in two weeks and continue the pregnancy to 38 weeks
Perform immediate caesarean section within thirty minutes for suspected fetal acidosis
Admit for bed rest and discharge once the middle cerebral artery Doppler normalises
Absent end-diastolic flow at or beyond 34 weeks is an indication for delivery after steroids; reversal of end-diastolic flow is even more urgent. (Book p313)
Abnormal Doppler: UPI, AEDF, REDF & MCA Doppler
In severe fetal anemia due to Rh isoimmunization or Parvovirus B19, which heart rate pattern is characteristically observed on cardiotocography (CTG)?
Persistent marked tachycardia without loss of variability
A sinusoidal heart rate pattern (smooth sine wave with 2-5 cycles/min, amplitude 5-15 bpm) is pathognomonic of severe fetal anemia. (Book p314)
Single umbilical artery (SUA) is the most common vascular anomaly of the cord. The most commonly associated fetal organ systems affected are:
SUA is most frequently associated with renal malformations, followed by major cardiovascular anomalies. (Book p314)
When a single umbilical artery (SUA) is diagnosed on prenatal ultrasound, what is the protocol regarding fetal karyotyping?
Karyotyping is indicated only if associated gross congenital anomalies are present
Karyotyping is mandatory in every isolated SUA
Immediate chorionic villus sampling is required in all cases
Karyotyping is never indicated for cord vascular defects
If gross congenital anomalies (GCA) are detected alongside SUA, karyotyping is indicated; isolated SUA does not require karyotyping. (Book p314)
Which of the following maternal factors significantly predisposes to the development of a single umbilical artery (SUA)?
Twin pregnancy and maternal diabetes mellitus
Twin pregnancy and pre-existing maternal diabetes mellitus are established predisposing factors for single umbilical artery. (Book p314)
In all high-risk pregnancies, routine antepartum fetal surveillance (NST, BPP, growth scans) should routinely be initiated at:
In high-risk pregnancies, antepartum fetal monitoring with NST and BPP is recommended starting from 32 weeks of gestation. (Book p314)
On CTG interpretation, late decelerations reflect uteroplacental insufficiency, whereas variable decelerations characteristically indicate:
Fetal head compression by the cervix
Variable decelerations are triggered by umbilical cord compression, whereas early decelerations reflect head compression and late decelerations reflect UPI. (Book p314)
All of the following are classically associated with a single umbilical artery EXCEPT:
A single umbilical artery is linked to trisomy 18, renal and cardiac anomalies and growth restriction; the association with trisomy 21 is weak. (Book p314)
What is the minimum number of antenatal contacts recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO 2016 model) for a positive pregnancy experience?
The WHO recommends a minimum of 8 antenatal contacts (1 in T1, 2 in T2, and 5 in T3). (Book p315)
According to the Government of India (RCH) guidelines, what is the minimum mandatory number and schedule of antenatal visits?
6 visits: every 6 weeks starting at 12 weeks
The GOI mandates at least 4 visits: 1st within 12w, 2nd at 14-26w, 3rd at 28-34w, and 4th at 36w to term. (Book p315)
At the first antenatal visit, HIV screening is conducted under an 'opt-out' approach. What are the screening and confirmatory tests, respectively?
Screening by ELISA, confirmatory by Western blot
Screening by Western blot, confirmatory by PCR
Screening by rapid card test, confirmatory by CD4 count
Screening by PCR, confirmatory by ELISA
HIV screening is done with ELISA/rapid immunoassay; confirmatory testing is performed with Western blot or second dual ELISA. (Book p315)
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) testing is performed at the initial antenatal booking visit:
In all pregnant women, regardless of prior vaccination status
Only in women with a history of jaundice or tattooing
Only if the partner is known to be HBsAg positive
Universal screening for HBsAg is mandatory in every pregnant woman regardless of her previous Hepatitis B vaccination status. (Book p315)
Which of the following statements about antenatal laboratory testing is TRUE?
Blood grouping with Rh typing and an indirect Coombs test at booking identify who needs anti-D prophylaxis
A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is mandatory at the first visit in every pregnancy
Serum alpha-fetoprotein at 16 weeks is a mandatory investigation in every antenatal clinic
Urine culture is recommended at every antenatal visit for all pregnant women
Grouping, Rh typing and the indirect Coombs test are mandatory at booking; the GTT is done at 24-28 weeks and AFP screening is optional. (Book p315)
Antenatal care schedules, mandatory & optional labs
Rubella susceptibility screening in pregnancy checks for IgG and IgM antibodies. If a woman is found to be IgG-negative and IgM-negative, the correct management is:
Vaccinate with MMR immediately after delivery, as the live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy
Administer MMR vaccine immediately in the first trimester
Administer rubella vaccine at 28 weeks of gestation
Reassure that she is immune and no action is required
Negative IgG and IgM indicate susceptibility. MMR is a live attenuated vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy; immunization is given postpartum. (Book p316)
According to ACOG guidelines, universal screening for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization is performed using a rectovaginal swab at:
Universal GBS screening is performed at 35-37 weeks using a lower vaginal and rectal swab to direct intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. (Book p316)
Under the National Immunization Schedule in India, the recommended tetanus and adult diphtheria (Td) toxoid schedule in pregnancy is:
Td-1 at first contact, followed by Td-2 after 4 weeks
Single dose of Td at 36 weeks
Three doses of Td spaced 1 month apart
Td-1 at 20 weeks and Td-2 at 36 weeks
Two doses of Td are given 4 weeks apart (Td-1 as early as possible, Td-2 four weeks later). (Book p316)
If a pregnant woman received full, documented Td immunization during a previous pregnancy 2 years ago, what is indicated in her current pregnancy?
Only a single Td booster dose during the current pregnancy
Two complete doses of Td spaced 4 weeks apart
No tetanus immunization is needed for 5 years
If a woman received complete Td vaccination within the preceding 3 years, only a single Td booster dose is required. (Book p316)
According to ACOG guidelines, a single dose of Tdap (tetanus, reduced diphtheria, and acellular pertussis) vaccine should be administered during:
27 to 36 weeks of gestation in every pregnancy
Only if the mother has an open dirty wound
Tdap is recommended between 27 and 36 weeks of gestation in each pregnancy to optimize transplacental maternal pertussis antibody transfer. (Book p316)
On the antenatal Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card, what color sticker represents high risk factors present?
Under MCP card color-coding: Green = no risk factors, Red = high risk factors present (Blue = PIH, Yellow = GDM/comorbidity). (Book p316)

Match the vaccine with its recommendation in pregnancy — 1) MMR 2) Tdap 3) Yellow fever … A) Contraindicated, being live attenuated B) Given once in every pregnancy, preferably 27-36 weeks C) Avoided in pregnancy unless travel to an endemic area is unavoidable
Live vaccines such as MMR are contraindicated, Tdap is given once each pregnancy, and yellow fever is only used when travel risk outweighs fetal risk. (Book p316)
Td/Tdap vaccines, risk coding & alert signs
Under the Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA, held on the 9th of every month), pregnant women flagged with a RED sticker are advised:
At least 3 additional specialist antenatal visits
PMSMA flags high-risk pregnancies with a red sticker and advises 3 additional antenatal visits by obstetricians. (Book p317)
Which of the following maternal complaints is recognized as an obstetric alert symptom requiring emergency hospital evaluation?
Fever >= 38°C for >= 24 hours or sudden blurring of vision
Mild morning nausea subsiding by noon
Increased urinary frequency in the first trimester
Alert danger signs include fever >=38°C for >=24h, persistent vomiting, severe headache/blurring of vision, vaginal bleeding/fluid leak, and reduced fetal movement. (Book p317)
To prevent primary neural tube defects (NTD), the recommended periconceptional prophylactic dose of folic acid for a low-risk woman is:
400 mcg/day starting at least 1 month before conception through the first trimester
4 mg/day starting at 12 weeks of gestation
100 mcg/day starting after positive urine pregnancy test
Low-risk women require 400 mcg/day of folic acid starting at least 1 month prior to conception and continued through the first 3 months. (Book p317)
A woman with a history of a previous infant affected by spina bifida desires another pregnancy. What dose of folic acid should she receive?
4 mg/day (therapeutic dose) starting >=3 months before conception through the first trimester
400 mcg/day starting from the day of missed period
To prevent recurrence of NTD, high-risk women should take 4-5 mg/day of folic acid starting at least 3 months pre-conceptually through 12 weeks. (Book p317)
Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat programme (I-NIPI), what are the constituents of the daily red IFA tablet provided to pregnant women from the 4th month?
60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid
100 mg elemental iron + 1 mg folic acid
30 mg elemental iron + 400 mcg folic acid
200 mg elemental iron + 5 mg folic acid
The red IFA tablet contains 60 mg elemental iron (as ferrous sulfate) and 500 mcg folic acid. (Book p317)
For how long should prophylactic IFA supplementation be continued during pregnancy and after childbirth?
For at least 180 days during pregnancy plus 180 days postpartum
IFA is taken for 180 days during pregnancy (from the 2nd trimester) and continued for 180 days postpartum to replenish iron stores. (Book p317)
What is the recommended therapeutic dosage of IFA tablets for a pregnant female diagnosed with nutritional iron deficiency anemia?
2 IFA tablets per day (120 mg elemental iron)
4 IFA tablets per day with meals
For treating established anemia in pregnancy, the dose is doubled to 2 IFA tablets daily (total 120 mg elemental iron). (Book p317)
Fill up: Periconceptional folic acid ______ mg daily reduces neural tube defects and should be started ______.
0.4; at least three months before conception
Standard prophylaxis is 0.4 mg (400 microgram) started at least three months before conception; 4-5 mg is reserved for women with a previously affected child. (Book p317)
Folic acid prophylaxis & IFA / Anemia Mukt Bharat
Between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation, which laboratory investigations are specifically recommended for repeat screening?
Hemoglobin/hematocrit, GDM screening (DIPSI), and Indirect Coombs test if Rh-negative
Thyroid profile, rubella IgG, and toxoplasma serology
Nuchal translucency and ductus venosus Doppler
Between 24-28 weeks: repeat Hb/Hct, oral glucose tolerance test (DIPSI) for GDM, and Indirect Coombs test in Rh-negative mothers at 28w. (Book p318)
According to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) guidelines, what is the recommended total gestational weight gain for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5-24.9)?
Recommended weight gain: Underweight (<18.5) = 12.5-18 kg; Normal (18.5-24.9) = 11.5-16 kg; Overweight (25-29.9) = 7-11.5 kg; Obese (>=30) = 5-9 kg. (Book p318)
What is the average recommended additional caloric requirement per day for a pregnant woman in India?
+350 kcal/day on average (National: +85 in T1, +280 in T2, +470 in T3)
+500 kcal/day exclusively in the first trimester
ICMR recommends an average additional +350 kcal/day (trimester-wise: T1 +85, T2 +280, T3 +470 kcal/day). (Book p318)
Which of the following statements about gestational weight gain is TRUE?
Recommended total gain is higher for underweight women and lower for women with obesity
Every woman should gain exactly 11 to 12 kg irrespective of her pre-pregnancy body mass index
Weight loss is recommended in pregnancy for women whose body mass index exceeds 30
Most of the maternal weight gain of pregnancy occurs during the first trimester
Institute of Medicine targets vary with pre-pregnancy BMI; weight loss is never advised and most gain occurs in the second and third trimesters. (Book p318)
What is the recommended daily dietary allowance (RDA) for elemental calcium in pregnancy, and what is the rule regarding its co-administration with iron?
1000 mg/day, taken with a minimum 2-hour interval from iron tablets
500 mg/day, taken simultaneously with iron tablets to enhance absorption
2000 mg/day, administered only in the first trimester
1200 mg/day, taken exclusively with tea or milk
RDA for calcium is 1000 mg/day (started from 14 weeks); calcium and iron compete for absorption and must be spaced at least 2 hours apart. (Book p319)
What is the daily recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for iodine during pregnancy to prevent fetal cretinism and neurodevelopmental delay?
The RDA for iodine increases to 250 mcg/day in pregnancy (compared to 150 mcg/day in non-pregnant adults). (Book p319)
Which of the following vaccines is absolutely CONTRAINDICATED during pregnancy due to the risk of live viral transmission to the fetus?
Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, BCG, yellow fever, oral polio) are contraindicated during pregnancy. (Book p319)
If a woman accidentally receives a live attenuated rubella vaccine, she should be advised to avoid conception for at least:
After accidental live attenuated rubella vaccine, conception should be avoided for at least 1 month (4 weeks). (Book p319)
Up to what gestational age is commercial air travel considered generally safe for an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy?
Commercial flying is safe up to 36 weeks in uncomplicated singleton pregnancies (32 weeks for multiples) before airline restrictions apply. (Book p319)
Moderate aerobic exercise such as 30-45 minutes of brisk walking daily is encouraged in pregnancy, but vigorous physical exertion is contraindicated in:
Placenta previa, pre-eclampsia, and maternal heart disease
Strenuous physical exercise is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia/PIH, placenta previa, patients at risk of preterm labor, and heart disease. (Book p319)
All of the following are reasons to stop exercise in pregnancy EXCEPT:
Mild fatigue during the first trimester
Calf pain and swelling suggesting thrombosis
Bleeding, thromboembolic symptoms, presyncope and chest pain are red flags; first-trimester tiredness alone merely calls for a gentler routine. (Book p319)
Vaccines, air travel & exercise in pregnancy
What is the first-line pharmacotherapy recommended by ACOG for mild-to-moderate nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness)?
Doxylamine (10 mg) + Pyridoxine / Vitamin B6 (10 mg)
The combination of doxylamine (antihistamine, 10 mg) and pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 10 mg) is the first-line drug of choice for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. (Book p320)
Hyperemesis gravidarum is characterized by severe vomiting leading to ketonuria and >5% weight loss. What is its primary hormonal driver?
Rapidly rising peak levels of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Hyperemesis gravidarum correlates with peak serum hCG levels (hence increased incidence in twin and molar pregnancies). (Book p320)
A pregnant patient with severe hyperemesis gravidarum develops intractable vomiting and confusion. What critical nutrient must be given BEFORE administering IV dextrose fluids?
Thiamine 100 mg intravenously, to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy
Folic acid 5 mg intravenously, to prevent a megaloblastic crisis
Vitamin K 10 mg intravenously, to correct the coagulopathy
Vitamin C 500 mg intravenously, to hasten tissue healing
Prolonged vomiting with confusion means thiamine must be given before any glucose, or Wernicke's encephalopathy follows. (Book p320)
Why is the use of ondansetron generally avoided during early organogenesis (<10 weeks of gestation) unless other therapies fail?
A possible small increased risk of oral clefts, lip or palate
A high incidence of neural tube defects in the fetus
Induction of fetal renal agenesis in the first trimester
A definite risk of phocomelia after first-trimester use
Ondansetron is generally avoided during early organogenesis (under 10 weeks) because of a possible association with a small increased risk of oral clefts (cleft lip or palate). (Book p321)
The PUQE (Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis) scoring system classifies the severity of nausea and vomiting into mild, moderate, and severe using cutoffs of:
<=6 is mild, 7 to 12 is moderate, and >=13 is severe
<=3 is mild, 4 to 8 is moderate, and >=9 is severe
<=10 is mild, 11 to 20 is moderate, and >=21 is severe
<=5 is mild, 6 to 15 is moderate, and >=16 is severe
PUQE score: 4 to 6 indicates mild emesis, 7 to 12 indicates moderate emesis, and >=13 indicates severe hyperemesis gravidarum. (Book p321)

A 26-year-old at 9 weeks vomits five times a day, retches through most of the day and has kept nothing down for twelve hours. Pulse 108/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, urine ketones 3+. What is the most appropriate initial management?
Admit, give intravenous saline with thiamine and potassium, and start parenteral antiemetics
Reassure her and advise small frequent dry meals at home with oral antacids
Start total parenteral nutrition immediately because oral intake has failed
Recommend termination of pregnancy because the condition is intractable
Ketosis with tachycardia and orthostasis means hyperemesis needing admission, thiamine-supplemented rehydration and antiemetics before any enteral feeding. (Book p321)
A pregnant woman in the late third trimester experiences dizziness, nausea, and pallor when lying flat on her back. What is the initial compensatory sign?
Maternal tachycardia, followed by a fall in blood pressure
Sudden maternal bradycardia without blood pressure change
Rapid increase in systemic vascular resistance
In supine hypotension syndrome, compression of the IVC reduces venous return; maternal tachycardia is the first compensatory response before BP crashes. (Book p321)
What is the immediate, life-saving corrective maneuver for supine hypotensive syndrome in pregnancy?
Turning the patient into the left lateral tilt position
Placing the patient in reverse Trendelenburg position
Rapid infusion of ephedrine in the supine position
Turning the patient onto her left side displaces the gravid uterus off the inferior vena cava, instantly restoring venous return and cardiac output. (Book p321)
Why is elective medical or surgical excision of varicose veins and hemorrhoids strictly avoided during pregnancy?
Most pregnancy-induced varicosities regress spontaneously within 6-12 weeks postpartum
They carry a 100% recurrence rate during labor
Varices protect against deep vein thrombosis
Varicose veins and hemorrhoids in pregnancy are managed conservatively (elevation, stockings, fiber) as they typically regress postpartum. (Book p322)
When a pregnant patient develops acute, painful nocturnal calf muscle cramps, the immediate relieving physical maneuver is to:
Extend the knee and strongly dorsiflex the foot/toes
Flex the knee and plantarflex the toes
Apply an ice pack to the popliteal fossa
During an acute calf cramp, extending the knee and forcibly dorsiflexing the toes stretches the gastrocnemius, immediately relieving the spasm. (Book p322)
Carpal tunnel syndrome during pregnancy presents with tingling and numbness in the lateral three and a half digits due to compression of which nerve?
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Gestational fluid retention and perineural edema compress the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum, treated conservatively with wrist splints. (Book p322)

Match the complaint with its mechanism or remedy — 1) Supine hypotension 2) Meralgia paraesthetica 3) Carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy … A) Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh B) Aortocaval compression relieved by the left lateral position C) Median nerve compression giving nocturnal paraesthesia of the thumb and index finger
Supine hypotension is aortocaval compression, meralgia paraesthetica is entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, and carpal tunnel is median nerve compression. (Book p322)
Minor ailments: supine hypotension, varices & neuropathies
Bell's palsy (idiopathic facial nerve paralysis) occurring during the third trimester is primarily attributed to:
Perineural edema, hypercoagulability and physiological immunosuppression
Direct herpes zoster encephalitis involving the facial nucleus
Compression by an intracranial aneurysm of the posterior circulation
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis occurring late in the third trimester
Bell's palsy in the third trimester is attributed mainly to perineural edema, hypercoagulability and physiological immunosuppression. (Book p323)
In early pregnancy ultrasound, what are the characteristic transducer probe frequencies utilized for transabdominal scan (TAS) and transvaginal scan (TVS)?
3-5 MHz for TAS and 5-10 MHz for TVS
7-12 MHz for TAS and 2-3 MHz for TVS
1-2 MHz for TAS and 3-5 MHz for TVS
TAS utilizes 3-5 MHz probes for deeper penetration, whereas TVS uses higher frequency 5-10 MHz probes for superior near-field resolution. (Book p324)
What is the earliest anatomical structure identifiable within the uterus on transvaginal sonography (TVS) at 4.5 to 5 weeks?
The gestational sac, a symmetrical fluid collection with an echogenic rim
The secondary yolk sac, which appears before the gestational sac
The embryonic fetal pole, seen as soon as the sac becomes visible
The amniotic membrane, which separates first and outlines the sac
At 4.5-5 weeks the gestational sac is the first structure seen; the yolk sac follows at about 5 weeks and the embryo later. (Book p324)
The visualization of an isolated fluid-filled sac in the uterine cavity on ultrasound does NOT definitively confirm intrauterine pregnancy because:
An ectopic pregnancy can produce a central decidual pseudogestational sac
The yolk sac may be outside the uterus
Molar pregnancy always mimics a gestational sac
Blighted ovum never forms a gestational sac
A pseudogestational sac (blood/fluid within decidual reaction) occurs in 10-20% of ectopic pregnancies; true IUP requires yolk sac or embryo. (Book p324)
The secondary yolk sac appears as a distinct circular echogenic bleb within the gestational sac on TVS when the Mean Sac Diameter (MSD) reaches:
The yolk sac is visualized on TVS when the mean sac diameter reaches 10 mm (at approximately 5-5.5 weeks of gestation). (Book p324)
Fill up: On transvaginal sonography the gestational sac is first seen when the mean sac diameter is about ______ mm, and the yolk sac becomes visible at about ______ weeks.
The sac is visible on TVS at a mean sac diameter of 2-3 mm (about 4-4.5 weeks) and the yolk sac appears around 5 weeks. (Book p324)
The presence of a definite yolk sac within an intrauterine gestational sac provides definitive sonographic confirmation of:
An authentic intrauterine pregnancy, ruling out a pseudogestational sac
Immediate fetal viability and normal karyotype
Exclusion of any possibility of miscarriage
Seeing a yolk sac definitively confirms a true intrauterine gestational sac and excludes an ectopic pseudogestational sac. (Book p325)
On transvaginal sonography, the fetal pole and embryonic cardiac flicker (M-mode) are normally detectable by:
5.5 to 6.5 weeks of gestation (CRL 1-5 mm, MSD 13-18 mm)
The fetal pole with cardiac flicker is detected on TVS at 5.5-6.5 weeks (CRL 1-5 mm, MSD 13-18 mm). (Book p325)
What is the normal baseline fetal heart rate at 6 weeks versus 8 weeks of gestation, and what cutoff indicates a poor prognosis?
110-130 bpm at 6w, 160-170 bpm at 8w; <85 bpm indicates poor prognosis
70-90 bpm at 6w, 120 bpm at 8w; <100 bpm is normal
160-180 bpm at 6w, 110 bpm at 8w; >200 bpm is normal
140 bpm throughout; any variation indicates demise
Embryonic FHR rises from 110-130 bpm at 6 weeks to 160-170 bpm at 8 weeks; an embryonic FHR <85 bpm signifies high risk of demise. (Book p325)
According to established sonographic guidelines, an anembryonic pregnancy (blighted ovum / missed abortion) is definitively diagnosed when:
The Mean Sac Diameter (MSD) is >= 25 mm with no visible embryo/fetal pole
The MSD is >= 15 mm without a yolk sac
The CRL is >= 3 mm without cardiac motion
The gestational sac is irregularly contoured at 4 weeks
An MSD >=25 mm with no embryo on TVS is a definitive criterion for non-viable/missed abortion (blighted ovum). (Book p325)
Fill up: Absent cardiac activity reliably confirms pregnancy loss once the crown-rump length is ______ mm or more, but a sac without a pole must measure over ______ mm mean diameter.
Modern criteria: CRL of 7 mm or more with no heartbeat, or a mean sac diameter over 25 mm with no embryo, before declaring a missed abortion. (Book p325)
Fetal pole, cardiac activity & missed abortion criteria
Which of the following is a definitive sonographic criterion for diagnosing a missed abortion on transvaginal ultrasound?
A Crown-Rump Length (CRL) of >= 7 mm with absence of cardiac activity
A CRL of >= 4 mm with absence of cardiac activity
An MSD of >= 16 mm without a fetal pole
Absence of yolk sac when MSD is 8 mm
A CRL >=7 mm without cardiac motion is a major definitive criterion for missed abortion. (Book p326)
If an initial ultrasound demonstrates a gestational sac without a yolk sac, after how many days must a repeat scan without cardiac activity be observed to confirm non-viability?
Absence of an embryo with cardiac activity >=14 days after a scan that showed a gestational sac without a yolk sac definitively confirms missed abortion. (Book p326)
If an initial scan shows a gestational sac WITH a yolk sac, missed abortion is confirmed if cardiac activity is absent on a repeat scan performed after at least:
Absence of cardiac activity >=11 days after a scan that demonstrated a gestational sac with a yolk sac is diagnostic of pregnancy failure. (Book p326)
What is the discriminatory zone (critical titer) of serum beta-hCG above which an intrauterine gestational sac must be visualized on TVS and TAS, respectively?
1500-2000 IU/L for TVS and 6000-6500 IU/L for TAS
500-1000 IU/L for TVS and 2000-3000 IU/L for TAS
3000-4000 IU/L for TVS and 8000-10000 IU/L for TAS
1000 IU/L for both TVS and TAS
The discriminatory zone of beta-hCG is 1500-2000 IU/L for TVS and 6000-6500 IU/L for TAS; empty uterus above this strongly indicates ectopic. (Book p326)
A hemodynamically stable patient has a serum beta-hCG of 2500 IU/L, but no intrauterine gestational sac is seen on TVS. What is the presumptive diagnosis?
Blighted ovum within the endometrial cavity
When serum beta-hCG exceeds the TVS discriminatory threshold (1500-2000 IU/L) and the endometrial cavity is empty, ectopic pregnancy must be presumed. (Book p326)
In a healthy, viable early intrauterine pregnancy, repeat serum beta-hCG titers measured 48 hours apart should normally demonstrate:
A doubling of titer (or an increase of at least 66%)
In a viable early intrauterine pregnancy, serum beta-hCG approximately doubles every 48 hours (minimum 66% rise). (Book p326)
A 48-hour serial beta-hCG that rises suboptimally (increases but does not double) is highly suspicious of:
An increase that fails to double (suboptimal rise) is characteristic of an ectopic pregnancy or failing intrauterine gestation. (Book p326)
Which of the following sonographic features definitively distinguishes a true intrauterine gestational sac from an ectopic pseudogestational sac?
Eccentric location within decidua with double decidual sac sign
Central location within the endometrial cavity
Absence of yolk sac or double bleb sign
Lack of progressive growth on serial scans
A true gestational sac implants eccentrically within the decidua, displays a double decidual sign, contains a yolk sac, and grows ~1 mm/day. (Book p326)
A woman at about 6 weeks with pain and spotting has a serum beta-hCG of 3200 mIU/mL and a transvaginal scan showing an empty uterus with no adnexal mass. What is the safest next step?
Treat as pregnancy of unknown location: repeat beta-hCG in 48 hours and rescan
Perform an immediate dilatation and curettage to obtain chorionic villi
Give methotrexate now, because an empty uterus proves ectopic pregnancy
Discharge her, since a beta-hCG below 3500 rules out ectopic pregnancy
Below the discriminatory zone the diagnosis is pregnancy of unknown location; blind methotrexate or curettage could destroy a viable intrauterine pregnancy. (Book p326)
Discriminatory hCG titer & true vs pseudogestational sac
Fill up: The intradecidual sign is the first sonographic sign of pregnancy, reflecting ______ within the decidua.
Interstitial implantation of the blastocyst within the thickened endometrium
Complete separation of the amnion and chorion
Decidual capsularis stretching over the developing embryo
Appearance of the secondary yolk sac
The intradecidual sign is the first sonographic sign of pregnancy, reflecting interstitial implantation of the blastocyst within the decidua. (Book p327)
Which of the following statements about First trimester ultrasound is TRUE?
Inner ring: Decidua capsularis; Outer ring: Decidua parietalis
Inner ring: Decidua basalis; Outer ring: Decidua capsularis
Inner ring: Amnion; Outer ring: Chorion laeve
Inner ring: Decidua parietalis; Outer ring: Myometrium
The double decidual ring consists of an inner ring (decidua capsularis) and an outer ring (decidua parietalis), confirming intrauterine pregnancy. (Book p327)
All of the following are First trimester ultrasound EXCEPT:
The yolk sac and the developing amniotic sac
The gestational sac and the pseudogestational sac
The right and left lateral cerebral ventricles
The vitelline duct and the allantois — The double bleb sign represents the transient side-by-side a
The double bleb sign represents the transient side-by-side appearance of the secondary yolk sac and the expanding amniotic sac with the embryonic disc between them. (Book p327)

A 28-year-old woman at 9 weeks with first trimester ultrasound presents with crown-rump length (crl) measured between 7 and 9 weeks (usable up to 13w6d) is the single most accur. What is the single most accurate ultrasound parameter for determining gestational age across the entire pregnancy?
Crown-Rump Length (CRL) measured in the first trimester
Femur length (FL) measured in the second trimester
Abdominal circumference (AC) measured in the third trimester
Crown-rump length (CRL) measured between 7 and 9 weeks (usable up to 13w6d) is the single most accurate parameter for pregnancy dating (+/- 3-5 days). (Book p327)
Fill up: First-trimester dating uses the ______, which is accurate to within ______ days.
The crown-rump length dates pregnancy to within 5-7 days, far better than second-trimester biparietal diameter. (Book p327)
Fill up: ______ in days can be estimated from early sac dimensions using: MSD (in mm) + 30 = gestational age in days.
Gestational age (in days) = MSD (in mm) x 7
Gestational age in days can be estimated from early sac dimensions using: MSD (in mm) + 30 = gestational age in days. (Book p328)
Which of the following statements about First trimester ultrasound regarding First trimester ultrasound — 84 mm is TRUE?
CRL is used up to 13 weeks + 6 days and CRL < 84 mm; once CRL >= 84 mm, biparietal diameter (BPD) and head circumference are utilized. (Book p328)
All of the following are First trimester ultrasound regarding The CRL measurement of the larger EXCEPT:
The CRL measurement of the larger twin — In twin pregnancies with growth discrepancy, gestational age
The CRL measurement of the smaller twin — In twin pregnancies with growth discrepancy, gestational age
The mathematical average of both CRL measurements
Discarding the ultrasound and relying strictly on LMP
In twin pregnancies with growth discrepancy, gestational age dating and EDD calculation are based on the larger fetus to avoid missing early growth restriction. (Book p328)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with biometry and specialized imaging presents with bpd is measured in the transthalamic plane from the outer table of the skull on the near field to th. When measuring the Biparietal Diameter (BPD) in the second trimester, the ultrasound calipers should be placed on which anatomical skull margins?
From the outer table of the proximal parietal bone to the inner table of the distal parietal bone
From the outer table to the outer table of both parietal bones
From the inner table to the inner table of both parietal bones
Across the fronto-occipital axis with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
BPD is measured in the transthalamic plane from the outer table of the skull on the near field to the inner table of the skull on the far field. (Book p328)
Fill up: ______ reflects fetal liver size and subcutaneous abdominal fat stores, making it the most sensitive biometry parameter for fetal growth.
Abdominal circumference reflects fetal liver size and subcutaneous abdominal fat stores, making it the most sensitive biometry parameter for fetal growth. (Book p328)
Which of the following statements about Biometry and specialized imaging is TRUE?
Biometry and specialized imaging — 18 to 22 weeks of gestation
Biometry and specialized imaging — 11 to 13 weeks + 6 days
Biometry and specialized imaging — 24 to 28 weeks of gestation
Biometry and specialized imaging — 32 to 34 weeks of gestation
The Level II anomaly scan (TIFFA) is universally recommended for all pregnant women between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation. (Book p328)
In women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth, transvaginal cervical length screening is indicated; a cervical length is considered abnormal when it measures:
A TVS cervical length < 25 mm prior to 24 weeks identifies high risk for recurrent preterm labor and is an indication for vaginal progesterone or cerclage. (Book p329)
What is the optimal gestational age to assess definitive placental localization to diagnose or exclude placenta previa, and when should borderline cases be repeated?
Best evaluated at 32 weeks, and repeated at 36 weeks
Evaluated at 12 weeks, repeated at 18 weeks
Evaluated at 20 weeks, repeated at 24 weeks
Placental localization is best assessed at 32 weeks (accounting for trophotropism/apparent placental migration) and confirmed at 36 weeks if low-lying. (Book p329)
A specialized fetal echocardiogram is ideally performed between 22 and 24 weeks of gestation. Which of the following is a recognized maternal indication?
First-trimester lithium exposure (risk of Ebstein anomaly)
Indications for fetal echo include lithium exposure (Ebstein anomaly), maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (congenital heart block), maternal pregestational DM, and aneuploidy. (Book p329)
A 29-year-old primigravida with no prior preterm birth has a transvaginal cervical length of 20 mm at 22 weeks and no contractions. What is the most appropriate management?
Start vaginal micronised progesterone 200 mg nightly and repeat the cervical length
Perform an immediate McDonald cerclage, because 20 mm is an absolute operative indication
Advise strict bed rest alone, since no intervention has proven benefit
An incidental short cervix of 25 mm or less in a woman without a prior preterm birth is treated with vaginal progesterone, not immediate cerclage. (Book p329)
Second trimester biometry, cervical length & fetal echo
What is the fundamental embryological defect underlying anencephaly?
Failure of closure of the cranial (anterior) neuropore around day 24-26
Failure of closure of the caudal (posterior) neuropore around day 26-28
Premature fusion of the sagittal cranial suture
Anencephaly results from failure of closure of the cranial neuropore, leaving neuroectoderm exposed to amniotic fluid where it degenerates. (Book p330)
What is the most frequent anatomical site for the development of a fetal encephalocele?
Encephaloceles most commonly arise in the occipital region through a calvarial defect in the occipital bone. (Book p330)

Match the cranial defect with its sonographic appearance — 1) Acrania 2) Exencephaly 3) Anencephaly … A) Skull vault absent but formed brain tissue still present B) Disorganised brain tissue floating in amniotic fluid with no skull C) No brain tissue above the orbits, giving the frog-face appearance
Acrania and exencephaly are successive stages of the same process that ends as anencephaly with absent cerebrum. (Book p330)
Anomaly scan (TIFFA) & cranial NTDs: anencephaly & acrania
Anencephaly is characteristically associated with post-term pregnancy (>42 weeks). What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism?
Absence or hypoplasia of fetal pituitary and adrenal glands leading to deficient DHEAS and reduced estrogen
Excessive production of fetal progesterone by the placenta
Anencephalic fetuses lack hypothalamus/pituitary-adrenal stimulation, leading to deficient DHEAS, low maternal estrogen, and failure of labor initiation. (Book p331)
Why is polyhydramnios frequently seen in fetuses affected by anencephaly during the late second and third trimesters?
Impaired fetal swallowing reflex combined with transudation of fluid from exposed neural tissue
Excessive fetal urination secondary to renal hypertrophy
Severe fetal cardiac failure causing polyuria
Overproduction of lung surfactant into amniotic fluid
Polyhydramnios develops because the anencephalic fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid due to lack of cerebral swallowing centers. (Book p331)
What is the earliest gestational age at which anencephaly can be recognized on transvaginal sonography, and what is the classic facial sign?
From 10-12 weeks, with the frog-eye or Mickey Mouse sign from the bulging orbits
From 18 weeks onwards, once the lemon sign has appeared
From 24 weeks onwards, once the banana sign has appeared
From 6 weeks onwards, with the double bleb sign
Anencephaly is recognisable from 10-12 weeks: absent calvarium with prominent orbits gives the frog-eye appearance. (Book p331)
What is the empiric recurrence risk of a neural tube defect in a subsequent pregnancy after ONE previously affected child?
The recurrence risk of an NTD is approximately 3-5% after one affected pregnancy, rising to 10% after two affected pregnancies. (Book p331)
Maternal hyperthermia or fever (body temperature elevated by >= 1.5°C) during the first trimester is recognized as a teratogenic risk factor for:
Neural tube defects, microcephaly, and neurodevelopmental delay
First-trimester hyperthermia/fever (elevated >=1.5°C) disrupts mitotic neurogenesis and neuropore closure, causing NTDs and microcephaly. (Book p332)
What is considered the gold-standard, most sensitive biochemical marker measured in amniotic fluid to confirm an open neural tube defect?
Amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the best, highly specific biochemical marker for open neural tube defects. (Book p332)
In spina bifida aperta, what is the anatomical difference between a meningocele and a meningomyelocele?
Meningocele involves herniation of meninges only; meningomyelocele involves herniation of both meninges and spinal cord elements
Meningocele is covered by intact skin; meningomyelocele is completely open
Meningocele contains brain tissue; meningomyelocele contains spinal cord
Meningocele occurs only in the occiput; meningomyelocele occurs only in the sacrum
A meningocele contains only meninges and cerebrospinal fluid in the herniated sac; a meningomyelocele contains neural tissue/spinal cord as well. (Book p332)
On cranial ultrasound of a fetus with open spina bifida, the 'Banana sign' refers to:
Anterior curvature and caudal displacement of the cerebellum around the brainstem, obliterating the cisterna magna
Scalloping and inward indentation of the frontal cranial bones
Severe asymmetrical dilation of the lateral ventricles
Absence of the cavum septum pellucidum
The 'banana sign' describes the cerebellar vermis herniating into the foramen magnum and curving anteriorly around the brainstem in Arnold-Chiari II malformation. (Book p332)
The 'Lemon sign' seen on second-trimester fetal cranial sonography is characterized by:
Inward scalloping and concavity of the frontal calvarial bones
A narrow, elongated anterior fontanelle seen on the scan
Widening of the cisterna magna in the posterior fossa
Bulging parietal bones with premature coronal synostosis
The lemon sign is inward scalloping and concavity of the frontal calvarial bones, due to reduced intracranial pressure. (Book p332)
Fill up: On the axial head view, scalloping of the frontal bones gives the ______ sign and the displaced cerebellum gives the ______ sign of Arnold-Chiari II malformation.
The lemon sign is frontal bone scalloping and the banana sign is the herniated, flattened cerebellum of the Chiari II malformation. (Book p332)
Spina bifida, Arnold-Chiari II signs & craniorachischisis
The severe lethal malformation termed 'Craniorachischisis' is characterized by:
Combined continuous failure of neural tube closure encompassing both anencephaly and total open spina bifida
Occipital encephalocele accompanied by polycystic kidneys
Herniation of the posterior fossa contents into an occipital sac (Chiari III)
Isolated sacrococcygeal teratoma with open spine
Craniorachischisis is the most extreme form of NTD, with complete non-closure of the neural tube extending from the brainstem throughout the entire spine. (Book p333)
What is the critical anatomical covering that distinguishes an omphalocele from gastroschisis?
An omphalocele is enclosed within a protective peritoneal-amniotic sac; gastroschisis is completely uncovered
Gastroschisis is enclosed within a thick amnion sac; omphalocele is uncovered
Both defects are always enclosed within Wharton's jelly
Both defects lack any peritoneal covering
An omphalocele is enclosed by a two-layered sac (peritoneum internally, amnion externally); gastroschisis is an open defect without any covering sac. (Book p333)
Where is the abdominal wall defect located in gastroschisis relative to the umbilical cord insertion?
Full-thickness defect located to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord
Directly through the midline umbilical ring
Full-thickness defect to the left of the umbilical cord
Supraumbilical midline defect involving the lower sternum
Gastroschisis is located almost always immediately to the right of an intact, normally attached umbilical cord. (Book p334)
In which anterior abdominal wall defect is the insertion of the umbilical cord situated directly onto the apex of the herniated sac?
In omphalocele, the umbilical cord inserts directly onto the apex of the membranous sac, with umbilical vessels radiating across its surface. (Book p334)
Which abdominal wall defect carries a very high rate of associated chromosomal aneuploidies (particularly Trisomy 18 and 13) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
Gastroschisis (aneuploidy is extremely rare; karyotyping not routinely indicated)
Omphalocele is associated with major chromosomal trisomies (Trisomy 18 > 13 > 21) and syndromes in >50% of cases, warranting karyotyping. (Book p334)
Why must a definitive sonographic diagnosis of omphalocele NEVER be made before 11 completed weeks of gestation?
Because physiological midgut herniation into the umbilical cord normally persists until 9-11 weeks
Because the liver does not develop until 12 weeks
Because amniotic fluid volume is insufficient for visualization
Because fetal abdominal muscles do not form until the second trimester
Physiological midgut rotation and herniation into the umbilical coelom is normal between 6 and 10 weeks; diagnosis of omphalocele is made after 11 weeks. (Book p334)
All of the following describe omphalocele EXCEPT:
Bowel loops float freely with no covering membrane over them
The umbilical cord inserts into the covering sac
It is a midline defect and often contains the liver
It is strongly associated with chromosomal anomalies and cardiac defects
An uncovered sac is gastroschisis; omphalocele is a midline, membrane-covered defect with the cord on the sac and a high anomaly rate. (Book p334)
Abdominal wall defects: omphalocele vs gastroschisis
During human fetal development, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is predominantly synthesized by which tissues?
Fetal yolk sac, fetal liver, and gastrointestinal tract
AFP is a fetal-specific glycoprotein synthesized primarily by the secondary yolk sac in early gestation, and later by the fetal liver and GI tract. (Book p334)
At what gestational age does fetal serum concentration of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) reach its maximal peak?
Fetal serum AFP levels peak at approximately 13 weeks of gestation, following which concentrations decline in fetal serum while rising in maternal serum. (Book p334)
What is the optimal gestational age window for screening maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP)?
16 to 18 weeks of gestation, acceptable 15 to 20 weeks
11 to 13 weeks and 6 days of gestation, acceptable 10 to 14
24 to 28 weeks of gestation, acceptable 22 to 30 weeks
6 to 8 weeks of gestation, acceptable 5 to 9 weeks
The optimal window for maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein screening is 16 to 18 weeks, with 15 to 20 weeks acceptable. (Book p334)
Which of the following conditions is characteristically associated with a pathologically ELEVATED maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) level?
An open neural tube defect such as anencephaly or spina bifida aperta
Down syndrome, that is trisomy 21 of the fetus
A complete hydatidiform mole within the uterine cavity
Overestimation of the gestational age at the time of testing
A pathologically elevated MSAFP is characteristically associated with an open neural tube defect (anencephaly, spina bifida aperta). (Book p334)
Using the clinical mnemonic 'Diabetic GOAT', which of the following causes a DECREASE in maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP)?
Maternal pregestational diabetes, Gestational trophoblastic disease, Overestimated dates, and Aneuploidy/Trisomies
Gastroschisis, Omphalocele, Anencephaly, and Twin gestation
Gestational diabetes, Oligohydramnios, Abruptio, and Teratoma
Glomerulonephritis, Open spina bifida, Atresia, and Turner syndrome
Decreased MSAFP ('Diabetic GOAT'): Diabetes, Gestational trophoblastic disease, Overestimated gestational age, Aneuploidy (Trisomy 21, 18, 13), Trisomies. (Book p334)
Which of the following statements about alpha-fetoprotein is TRUE?
Open spina bifida raises amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase, while gastroschisis raises AFP alone
A low maternal serum AFP is diagnostic of trisomy 21 and needs no further assessment
Maternal serum AFP interpretation is unaffected by incorrect gestational dating
Amniotic fluid AFP is normally far higher than fetal serum AFP in a closed neural tube defect
Amniotic fluid AFP plus acetylcholinesterase is specific for open defects; wrong dating is the commonest cause of a spurious AFP result. (Book p334)
What is the single most common chromosomal trisomy identified in first-trimester spontaneous miscarriages?
Trisomy 16, which is always lethal in early embryogenesis
Trisomy 21, which is the commonest trisomy seen among liveborn infants
Trisomy 18, which is the commonest trisomy causing loss in the second trimester
Trisomy 13, which is the commonest trisomy associated with holoprosencephaly
Trisomy 16 accounts for about a third of first-trimester losses and is incompatible with life; trisomy 21 is commonest at birth. (Book p335)
What is the primary genetic mechanism responsible for approximately 95% of cases of Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
Maternal meiotic non-disjunction (strongly linked to advanced maternal age)
Paternal meiotic deletion of the long arm of chromosome 21
95% of Down syndrome cases arise from meiotic non-disjunction (overwhelmingly maternal Meiosis I), which correlates with maternal age. (Book p335)

If a father or mother is an asymptomatic balanced carrier of a Robertsonian translocation between homologous chromosomes 21;21 [t(21q21q)], what is the chance of having a child with Down syndrome in every pregnancy?
A balanced homologous 21;21 translocation carrier can only produce gametes with either two 21s (Down) or zero 21s (monosomy 21, lethal), giving a 100% risk. (Book p335)

In a family where a parent carries a balanced non-homologous Robertsonian translocation t(14;21), what is the empirical risk of Down syndrome in offspring when the MOTHER is the carrier versus when the FATHER is the carrier?
10-15% when mother is carrier; 2-5% when father is carrier
For balanced t(14;21) carriers, recurrence risk is 10-15% if the mother is the carrier, but only 2-5% if the father is the carrier. (Book p335)
Fill up: About ______% of Down syndrome is caused by meiotic non-disjunction, and the extra chromosome is of ______ origin in the great majority.
Roughly 95% is non-disjunction, mostly maternal and rising with maternal age; the rest is translocation or mosaic. (Book p335)
What is the gold standard diagnostic test to confirm fetal chromosomal aneuploidy when screening is positive?
Karyotyping (G-banding) of fetal cells via CVS or amniocentesis
Fetal karyotyping (or chromosomal microarray/FISH) obtained via invasive testing provides the definitive diagnostic confirmation of chromosomal abnormalities. (Book p336)
What are the two maternal serum biochemical analytes measured in the first-trimester 'Dual test' between 11 and 13+6 weeks?
Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and free beta-hCG
The Dual test measures serum PAPP-A and free beta-hCG between 11w0d and 13w6d (CRL 45-84 mm). (Book p336)
In a fetus affected by Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), what typical pattern of PAPP-A and free beta-hCG is found on first-trimester biochemical screening?
Decreased PAPP-A and increased free beta-hCG
Increased PAPP-A and decreased free beta-hCG
Both PAPP-A and free beta-hCG are markedly decreased
Both PAPP-A and free beta-hCG are markedly increased
Down syndrome displays reduced PAPP-A (<0.5 MoM) and elevated free beta-hCG (>2.0 MoM); in Trisomy 18 and 13, both analytes are significantly decreased. (Book p336)
Beyond screening for chromosomal aneuploidies, an isolated finding of very low first-trimester maternal serum PAPP-A (<0.4 MoM) is an established predictor for:
Placental insufficiency, with fetal growth restriction and pre-eclampsia
Fetal macrosomia with polyhydramnios in the third trimester
Gestational diabetes mellitus needing early screening
A prolonged pregnancy that runs well past the expected date
A very low PAPP-A reflects poor placentation and is associated with growth restriction, pre-eclampsia and stillbirth. (Book p336)
What components constitute the 'Combined test' for first-trimester Down syndrome screening, and what is its approximate detection rate?
Dual test (PAPP-A + free beta-hCG) plus sonographic Nuchal Translucency (NT); detection rate 82-87%
Triple test plus Level II targeted ultrasound; detection rate 65%
Nuchal translucency plus ductus venosus Doppler; detection rate 50%
Quad test plus NIPT; detection rate 70%
The first-trimester Combined test incorporates maternal age, Dual test analytes, and ultrasound NT, yielding an 82-87% detection rate for Down syndrome. (Book p336)

Match the test with what it measures — 1) Dual test 2) First-trimester combined test 3) Quadruple test … A) Nuchal translucency plus beta-hCG and PAPP-A with maternal age B) Beta-hCG and PAPP-A alone C) AFP, beta-hCG, unconjugated estriol and inhibin A
The dual test is biochemical only; adding nuchal translucency makes it the combined test, and the quad test belongs to the second trimester. (Book p336)
First trimester screening: dual test & combined test
Between what gestational age and CRL range must fetal Nuchal Translucency (NT) be measured?
11 weeks + 0 days to 13 weeks + 6 days (CRL 45 mm to 84 mm)
9 weeks + 0 days to 11 weeks + 0 days (CRL 25 mm to 44 mm)
14 weeks + 0 days to 16 weeks + 0 days (CRL 85 mm to 110 mm)
16 weeks + 0 days to 20 weeks + 0 days (CRL > 120 mm)
NT measurement is strictly validated between 11w0d and 13w6d when the embryonic CRL is 45 to 84 mm. (Book p337)
What is the normal upper physiological cutoff for Nuchal Translucency (NT), above which it is classified as abnormally increased?
Above 3.0 mm, or above the 95th percentile for the crown-rump length
Above 1.5 mm, or above the 50th percentile for the crown-rump length
Above 6.0 mm, or above the 99th percentile for the crown-rump length
Above 10.0 mm, or above the 99.9th percentile for the crown-rump length
Nuchal translucency up to 3.0 mm (or below the 95th percentile for the CRL) is regarded as normal at 11 to 13+6 weeks. (Book p337)
A thickened fetal Nuchal Translucency (>= 3.0 mm) with a normal fetal karyotype is an established indication to evaluate for which structural defect?
Congenital heart disease, with a fetal echocardiogram at 22-24 weeks
Duodenal atresia, with serial scans looking for the double bubble
Polycystic kidney disease, with detailed imaging of the renal tract
Unilateral clubfoot, with careful limb views at every subsequent visit
A thickened nuchal translucency with a normal karyotype is an established indication for specialist fetal cardiac assessment. (Book p337)
What technical criteria must be fulfilled to obtain an accurate, standardized Nuchal Translucency (NT) measurement?
Mid-sagittal plane, neutral fetal head (not flexed/extended), separate visualization of amnion, and calipers placed inner-to-inner
Transverse axial plane across the orbits with head fully extended
Coronal plane through the cervical spine with amnion touching the skin
Any plane showing the neck with calipers placed outer-to-outer
