Standard NT criteria: mid-sagittal view, neutral head, magnification of head/thorax, separate amnion, and calipers placed inner-to-inner across widest lucency. (Book p337)
Which of the following statements about nuchal translucency is TRUE?
With a nuchal translucency above 3.5 mm and a normal karyotype, a fetal echocardiogram and detailed anatomy scan are indicated
Cystic hygroma is a thin, septation-free collection that always resolves by the middle of the second trimester
Nuchal translucency may be measured at any gestational age between 14 and 20 weeks
A nuchal translucency of 2.5 mm is above the 99th centile at every crown-rump length
NT is measured at 11 to 13+6 weeks; a very thick NT with normal chromosomes warrants cardiac and anatomical follow-up, and septated cystic hygroma has a worse prognosis. (Book p337)
How does a Cystic Hygroma differ sonographically and clinically from simple increased Nuchal Translucency?
Cystic hygroma is a larger, widespread, multiseptated lymphatic sac extending beyond the neck, carrying higher aneuploidy risk
Cystic hygroma never contains internal septations and is limited to the subocciput
Cystic hygroma has no association with chromosomal abnormalities
Nuchal translucency always exhibits internal vascular flow on color Doppler
Cystic hygroma is a bilateral, multiseptated cystic lymphangioma extending along the posterolateral neck/body, carrying a >60% aneuploidy risk. (Book p338)
Which biochemical analyte is added to the classic Triple test (AFP, hCG, uE3) to construct the Quadruple test for Down syndrome screening?
The Quadruple test adds dimeric Inhibin-A to the Triple test, improving Down syndrome detection rate from ~70% to 80-83%. (Book p338)
In a second-trimester quadruple test for Down syndrome, which two markers are elevated ('HI' is high)?
hCG and Inhibin-A are elevated; AFP and uE3 are decreased
AFP and Inhibin-A are elevated; hCG and uE3 are decreased
uE3 and hCG are elevated; AFP and Inhibin-A are decreased
In Down syndrome, hCG and Inhibin-A ('HI') are abnormally high, while AFP and unconjugated estriol (uE3) are low. (Book p338)
On second-trimester ultrasound (15-20 weeks), what cutoff for Nuchal Skinfold Thickness (NSFT) is considered an abnormal soft marker for Down syndrome?
In the second trimester (15-20 weeks), a nuchal fold thickness >=6 mm measured in the transcerebellar plane is a major soft marker for Down syndrome. (Book p338)
Which of the following second-trimester sonographic soft tissue markers has the LOWEST individual risk of aneuploidy and is found in 11-17% of completely normal fetuses?
Choroid plexus cysts carry the lowest isolated risk for aneuploidy (found in 1-2% of normal fetuses, weak association with Trisomy 18); when isolated, normal outcome is expected. (Book p338)
All of the following are soft sonographic markers of trisomy 21 EXCEPT:
Choroid plexus cysts are the classic trisomy 18 marker; nuchal fold thickening, short long bones and echogenic bowel are trisomy 21 markers. (Book p338)
Second trimester markers: triple, quad & soft sonographic signs
Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) analyzes cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) extracted from maternal blood. What is the tissue source of this cffDNA?
Intact fetal red blood cells that crossed the placenta
Fetal leukocytes in maternal bone marrow
Amniotic fluid leaking into maternal capillaries
cffDNA in maternal plasma consists of short fragments (~150 bp) originating predominantly from apoptotic placental syncytiotrophoblast cells. (Book p339)
From what gestational age onwards can Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) be reliably performed?
>= 10 weeks of gestation (when fetal fraction is >= 4%)
NIPT can be performed from 10 weeks onward, when the placental cffDNA fraction consistently exceeds the minimum testing threshold of 4%. (Book p339)
What is the primary clinical limitation of Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT)?
It is a screening and not a diagnostic test, so positives need confirmation
Its sensitivity for Down syndrome is under 70% in practice
It carries about a 1% risk of procedure-related miscarriage
It cannot be performed at all in Rh-negative mothers
The primary limitation of NIPT is that it is an advanced screening test and not definitive; positive results must be confirmed invasively. (Book p339)
What is 'Integrated Screening' for Down syndrome, and what is its major ethical/clinical drawback?
First-trimester (Dual + NT) and second-trimester (Quad) tests combined; results are withheld until second-trimester testing is completed
Sequential testing with immediate termination offered in the first trimester
Simultaneous NIPT and amniocentesis for all patients
Integrated screening combines 1st trimester Dual+NT with 2nd trimester Quad (detection rate 85-95%), but results are withheld until T2, delaying diagnosis. (Book p339)

Match the test with what it is — 1) cffDNA or NIPT 2) Chorionic villus sampling 3) Amniocentesis … A) Screening test using placental DNA fragments in maternal blood B) Diagnostic test on placental tissue from 10-13 weeks C) Diagnostic test on amniotic fluid, usually after 15 weeks
NIPT remains a screening test because the DNA is placental; CVS and amniocentesis give a definitive fetal karyotype. (Book p339)
Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT / cffDNA) & integrated screening
What is the standard clinical cutoff ratio used to define a 'screen-positive' result for Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
1 in 250 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
1 in 1000 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
1 in 50 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
1 in 10 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
The standard second-trimester cut-off is 1 in 250: a risk of 1 in 150 is screen-positive and 1 in 500 is screen-negative. (Book p339)
What is the standard screening cutoff ratio used to classify a pregnancy as high risk for Trisomy 18 (Edwards) and Trisomy 13 (Patau)?
For Trisomy 18 and Trisomy 13, the standard screen-positive cutoff ratio is typically set at 1:100. (Book p339)
A 32-year-old woman receives a combined first-trimester screening report indicating a Down syndrome risk of 1:80. What is the most appropriate next step in clinical management?
Offer CVS or amniocentesis for diagnosis, or secondary screening with NIPT
Reassure the patient that the fetus is entirely normal on this result
Perform an immediate emergency caesarean delivery of the fetus
Repeat exactly the same biochemical test again next week
A combined first-trimester risk of 1:80 is screen positive, so offer diagnostic confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis, or secondary screening with NIPT. (Book p339)

If a pregnant woman presents with positive first-trimester aneuploidy screening and chooses definitive invasive diagnostic testing, what procedure is performed at 11 to 13+6 weeks versus after 15 weeks?
Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) in the first trimester; Amniocentesis after 15 weeks
Amniocentesis in the first trimester; CVS after 15 weeks
Targeted ultrasound only at both gestational ages
Invasive diagnosis is achieved via CVS in the first trimester (10-14 weeks, ideally 11-13+6w) and via amniocentesis in the second trimester (15-20 weeks). (Book p339)
A 38-year-old at 12 weeks has a combined-test risk of 1 in 80 for trisomy 21. She wants certainty but is frightened of procedure-related loss. What is the correct counselling?
Offer diagnostic testing by CVS or amniocentesis, because NIPT remains a screening test at this risk
Reassure her that 1 in 80 is screen-negative and no further testing is needed
Offer NIPT and terminate the pregnancy if it is high risk, without confirmatory testing
Repeat the combined test at 16 weeks to obtain a definitive result
A screen-positive result must be confirmed by a diagnostic test before any irreversible decision, and screening tests cannot be repeated as if they were diagnostic. (Book p339)
Fill up: CVS aspirates and cultures the ______ (and mesenchyme) of the chorion frondosum.
Rapidly dividing cytotrophoblast and mesenchyme of the chorion frondosum
Desquamated fibroblasts from the fetal dermis in the amniotic fluid
Epithelial cells shed from the amniotic membrane surface
Fetal nucleated red blood cells from the circulating blood
CVS aspirates and cultures the rapidly dividing cytotrophoblast (and mesenchyme) of the chorion frondosum. (Book p340)
Which of the following statements about Invasive diagnostic tests is TRUE?
10 to 14 weeks of gestation, ideally 11 to 13 weeks and 6 days
15 to 20 weeks of gestation, ideally 16 to 18 completed weeks
6 to 8 weeks of gestation, ideally at 7 completed weeks
18 to 22 weeks of gestation, ideally at 20 completed weeks
The optimal window for chorionic villus sampling is 10 to 14 weeks, ideally 11 to 13 weeks and 6 days. (Book p340)
All of the following are Invasive diagnostic tests EXCEPT:
It carries a substantial risk of severe fetal transverse limb reduction defects and oromandibular/omphalocele anomalies
It causes immediate maternal Rh sensitization in 100% of cases
It induces premature rupture of membranes in the first trimester
The placenta is not yet attached to the decidua
CVS performed <10 weeks causes fetal vascular disruption, leading to severe limb reduction defects and micrognathia. (Book p340)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with invasive diagnostic tests presents with the main cytogenetic disadvantage of cvs is that in 1-2% of cases results are confounded by confined. What is the primary cytogenetic diagnostic disadvantage of Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) compared to amniocentesis?
In 1-2% of cases confined placental mosaicism confounds the result
CVS cannot detect numerical aneuploidies such as trisomy 21
CVS takes at least 4 weeks to obtain the initial karyotype
Cytotrophoblast cells do not possess any nuclear chromosomes
The main cytogenetic disadvantage of CVS is that in 1-2% of cases results are confounded by confined placental mosaicism, requiring confirmatory amniocentesis. (Book p340)
Fill up: is the standard gestational window for performing mid-trimester diagnostic amniocentesis, and what is its associated procedure-related fetal loss rate is ______.
15 to 20 weeks of gestation (ideal 16-18 weeks); procedure loss rate < 0.5%
10 to 12 weeks of gestation; procedure loss rate 5%
24 to 28 weeks of gestation; procedure loss rate 2%
Any time in the first trimester; procedure loss rate 0%
Amniocentesis is routinely performed between 15 and 20 weeks; the procedure-related loss rate is low (<0.5%). (Book p340)
Which of the following statements about Invasive diagnostic tests regarding Higher fetal loss, talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) is TRUE?
Higher fetal loss, talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) and amniotic fluid leakage
Amniocytes cannot be karyotyped before 15 weeks of gestation
The fetal heart is arrested by the needle puncture in every case
Amniotic fluid is devoid of alpha-fetoprotein before 15 weeks
Early amniocentesis before 15 weeks is not recommended because of significantly higher fetal loss rates, talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) and fluid leakage. (Book p340)

Match the procedure with its timing and caveat — 1) Chorionic villus sampling 2) Early amniocentesis before 14 weeks 3) Standard amniocentesis … A) From 15 weeks, the safest window with the lowest loss and talipes risk B) 10-13 weeks, transabdominal or transcervical placental sampling C) Avoided, because it raises pregnancy loss and fetal talipes
CVS is the 10-13 week option, amniocentesis is best from 15 weeks, and amniocentesis before 14 weeks is linked to loss and talipes. (Book p340)
Invasive prenatal diagnostic procedures: CVS vs amniocentesis
All of the following are Specialized fetal procedures EXCEPT:
20 to 22-gauge spinal needle; approximately 20 mL of fluid
16-gauge Trocar needle; 50 mL of fluid — Amniocentesis uses a 20-22G spinal needle under continuous r
18-gauge bone marrow needle; 30 mL of fluid
Amniocentesis uses a 20-22G spinal needle under continuous real-time USG guidance, discarding the first 1-2 mL and collecting ~20 mL. (Book p341)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with specialized fetal procedures presents with in the third trimester, amniocentesis was historically performed to assess fetal pulmonary maturity . In the third trimester, what was the classic indication for performing diagnostic amniocentesis?
Assessing fetal lung maturity via the Lecithin-to-Sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio
Testing for sickle cell anemia carrier status
Measuring fetal head circumference with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
Assessing maternal alpha-fetoprotein with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
In the third trimester, amniocentesis was historically performed to assess fetal pulmonary maturity via the L/S ratio (>=2.0 indicates mature lungs). (Book p341)
Fill up: Cordocentesis samples fetal blood by puncturing ______ vein approximately 1 cm from the placental insertion site.
The umbilical vein, near its placental insertion site
The right umbilical artery near the fetal abdominal wall
Cordocentesis samples fetal blood by puncturing the umbilical vein approximately 1 cm from the placental insertion site. (Book p341)
Which of the following statements about Specialized fetal procedures is TRUE?
Fetal hemoglobin and hematocrit assessment, and direct intrauterine transfusion
Routine first-line screening for Down syndrome in all pregnancies
Evaluation of the fetal risk of an open neural tube defect
Measurement of maternal serum human placental lactogen levels
The primary contemporary indication for cordocentesis is direct assessment of fetal hemoglobin and hematocrit, with direct intrauterine transfusion in severe Rh isoimmunization. (Book p341)
What is the most common congenital cardiovascular malformation diagnosed in infants with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
Endocardial cushion defect / Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD)
Endocardial cushion defect (complete AV canal defect) is the most frequent cardiac lesion in Down syndrome, followed by VSD and ASD. (Book p341)
Fill up: Cordocentesis is generally performed after ______ weeks and samples blood from the ______.
Cordocentesis (percutaneous umbilical blood sampling) is done after 18 weeks, usually from the umbilical vein. (Book p341)
In all high-risk pregnancies (e.g., pre-eclampsia, diabetes, IUGR), formal antepartum fetal surveillance is recommended to commence at:
Formal antepartum fetal surveillance (NST, BPP) is routinely started at 32 weeks in high-risk pregnancies. (Book p342)
When a pregnant woman has a history of an unexplained stillbirth in a previous pregnancy, when should antepartum fetal surveillance begin in the index pregnancy?
2 to 4 weeks before the gestation of the previous adverse outcome
At 37 completed weeks of gestation, whatever the prior outcome
From the day the pregnancy test first becomes positive
Only once labour contractions have begun spontaneously
After an unexplained stillbirth, antepartum fetal surveillance should begin 2 to 4 weeks prior to the gestational age at which the previous adverse outcome occurred. (Book p342)
Under the Cardiff 'Count-to-10' protocol for daily fetal movement assessment, fetal activity is considered normal when the mother perceives:
At least ten discrete movements within two hours while resting in the left lateral position
At least three discrete movements recorded in any twenty-four hour period
At least twenty discrete movements recorded within a single hour
At least one discrete movement every ten minutes, by day and by night
The Cardiff count-to-ten asks the woman to note the time to ten movements; fewer than ten in 12 hours, or a clear slowing, warrants testing. (Book p342)
What is the primary physiological mechanism leading to decreased fetal movements in chronic placental insufficiency?
Fetal behavioural adaptation to hypoxemia, reducing energy and oxygen use
Complete motor paralysis of the fetal spinal cord from ischemia
Compression of the fetal brainstem by amniotic bands in utero
Maternal hypoglycaemia producing fetal lethargy and weakness
Reduced fetal movements in chronic placental insufficiency reflect fetal compensatory behavioural adaptation to reduce energy and oxygen consumption in the face of hypoxemia. (Book p342)
Fill up: With the Cardiff count-to-ten chart, the woman reports if she feels fewer than ______ distinct movements in ______ hours.
Fewer than ten fetal movements in 12 hours (or a marked fall from her own baseline) triggers further testing. (Book p342)
Antepartum fetal surveillance principles & movement counts
How does an external cardiotocography machine monitor and record fetal well-being during a Non-Stress Test (NST)?
An ultrasound Doppler transducer records the fetal heart rate and a tocodynamometer records contractions, with an event marker
A scalp electrode is attached directly to the fetal skull during the test
A pressure catheter is placed inside the amniotic cavity for the recording
Maternal pulse oximetry is recorded continuously alongside the fetal electrocardiogram
External cardiotocography uses an abdominal Doppler transducer for the heart rate and a tocodynamometer for uterine activity. (Book p343)

At 40 weeks a non-stress test shows a baseline of 140 bpm, moderate variability, two accelerations of 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds in a 20-minute window and no decelerations. How is this tracing reported?
Reactive and reassuring — continue routine antenatal care
Non-reactive — extend for 40 minutes and use vibroacoustic stimulation
Equivalent to a positive contraction stress test — deliver the fetus
A sinusoidal pattern — proceed to immediate caesarean delivery
Two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds in 20 minutes with moderate variability make the NST reactive, which is reassuring. (Book p343)
What is the normal physiological baseline fetal heart rate (FHR) range on cardiotocography, evaluated over a minimum 10-minute window?
The normal physiological baseline fetal heart rate on CTG is 110 to 160 bpm, evaluated over a minimum 10-minute window. (Book p344)
Normal baseline fetal heart rate variability represents healthy autonomic cardiac control and is quantified as:
Fluctuations of 6 to 25 bpm around the baseline
Fluctuations of < 5 bpm around the baseline
Fluctuations of > 30 bpm around the baseline
Moderate (normal) baseline variability is 6-25 bpm, reflecting balanced sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic inputs. (Book p344)
At >= 32 weeks of gestation, a reactive fetal heart rate acceleration is strictly defined as an increase in FHR above baseline of at least:
15 bpm lasting for at least 15 seconds (15x15 rule)
10 bpm lasting for at least 10 seconds (10x10 rule)
20 bpm lasting for at least 2 minutes
30 bpm lasting for at least 30 seconds
At >=32 weeks, acceleration is defined as >=15 bpm above baseline lasting >=15 seconds from onset to return (15x15 rule). (Book p344)
If an NST is conducted in a preterm fetus between 28 and 31+6 weeks of gestation, what criteria define an acceleration?
An increase in FHR of >= 10 bpm above baseline lasting for >= 10 seconds (10x10 rule)
An increase in FHR of >= 15 bpm lasting >= 15 seconds
An increase of >= 25 bpm lasting >= 30 seconds
Accelerations are not evaluated before 34 weeks
Before 32 weeks, immature autonomic innervation permits the 10x10 rule (>=10 bpm for >=10 seconds) to qualify as an acceleration. (Book p344)
A sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern on cardiotocography is an ominous finding that characteristically indicates:
Severe fetal anaemia from isoimmunisation, parvovirus or vasa previa, or acute severe hypoxia
A benign physiological quiet sleep cycle in a healthy fetus
The normal fetal response to a meal eaten by the mother
Simple head compression as the head enters the pelvic inlet
A sinusoidal pattern is ominous and points to severe anaemia or acute hypoxia, never to a benign sleep cycle. (Book p344)
All of the following can produce a sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern EXCEPT:
Severe fetal anaemia from Rh isoimmunisation
A sinusoidal pattern signals severe anaemia or hypoxia; the fetal sleep cycle reduces variability but never produces a smooth sine wave. (Book p344)
What criteria define a 'Reactive' (negative) Non-Stress Test over a 20-minute monitoring period at term?
At least 2 accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds in 20 minutes, with variability
No accelerations at all, with a flat baseline over the full 20 minutes
One continuous acceleration lasting longer than 10 minutes throughout
Early decelerations with every contraction, with normal variability
A reactive non-stress test over 20 minutes at term shows at least 2 qualifying accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds, with normal baseline and moderate variability. (Book p345)
If an initial 20-minute NST demonstrates fewer than 2 accelerations, what is the mandatory immediate next step?
Extend the monitoring for a further 20 minutes to allow for the fetal sleep cycle
Perform an immediate emergency caesarean delivery for fetal distress
Administer a high-dose oxytocin infusion to stress the fetus
Discharge her with reassurance and repeat the test next week
A non-reactive trace is extended to 40 minutes first, because the fetus may simply be asleep. (Book p345)
What is the diagnostic accuracy profile of a reactive NST versus a non-reactive NST?
A reactive NST has a very high negative predictive value; a non-reactive one has a false-positive rate near 50%
A non-reactive NST is completely specific for imminent fetal death
A reactive NST still carries a false-negative rate of about 50%
Both results carry an identical positive predictive value of 90%
A reactive NST is excellent for ruling out compromise; a non-reactive trace is poorly predictive and needs further testing. (Book p345)
In Manning's Biophysical Profile (BPP), how are each of the five biophysical parameters scored?
Either 0 (abnormal/absent) or 2 (normal/present), for a maximum composite score of 10
Scored from 0 to 4 based on gestational age
Scored 0 or 1, for a maximum score of 5
BPP evaluates 5 parameters (NST, fetal breathing, gross movement, tone, amniotic fluid), scoring each as either 0 or 2 (maximum 10). (Book p345)
To receive a normal score of 2 for 'Amniotic Fluid Volume' in the Biophysical Profile, what ultrasound criterion must be met?
At least one vertical pocket of amniotic fluid measuring 2.0 cm or more
An amniotic fluid index of 15 cm or more on the scan
A fluid pocket completely filled with fetal limbs throughout
A single fluid pocket measuring 8 cm or more in depth
A score of 2 for amniotic fluid volume in the biophysical profile requires at least one vertical pocket measuring 2.0 cm or more (single deepest pocket). (Book p345)
Fill up: The full biophysical profile scores ______ components, and a total score of ______ or less is considered abnormal at term.
Five components are scored out of two each; a score of 4 or less is abnormal, 6 is equivocal and 8-10 is reassuring. (Book p345)
Biophysical profile (BPP / Manning score) & modified BPS
In progressive fetal hypoxemia and acidemia, in what order are the biophysical parameters compromised and lost?
NST and fetal breathing are lost earliest; gross body movements and fetal tone are lost latest
Fetal tone is lost first, followed by breathing and NST
Amniotic fluid volume is lost immediately within minutes
All parameters cease simultaneously at pH 7.30
Under hypoxia, regulatory centers in the brainstem fail in reverse embryological order: NST and breathing disappear first; tone is lost last. (Book p346)

A patient at 38 weeks of gestation undergoes a Biophysical Profile that yields a score of 8/10, but the 2 points lost are for decreased amniotic fluid volume (oligohydramnios). What is the management?
Delivery of the fetus, because oligohydramnios indicates chronic placental insufficiency
Reassurance and repeat BPP in 1 week
Bed rest and maternal IV hydration with discharge
Emergency Caesarean section under general anesthesia within 15 minutes
An 8/10 score with oligohydramnios indicates chronic compromised placental perfusion; delivery is indicated if the pregnancy is >=36-37 weeks. (Book p346)
What two components constitute the 'Modified Biophysical Profile' used as an efficient antenatal screening tool?
Non-stress test for acute oxygenation, plus amniotic fluid assessment for chronic function
Fetal breathing movements for tone, plus umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry
Fetal tone and body movement, plus maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
Cardiotocography tracing, plus fetal scalp blood pH estimation
The modified biophysical profile combines the non-stress test, reflecting acute oxygenation, with amniotic fluid assessment / single deepest pocket, reflecting chronic placental function. (Book p346)
Why do normal uterine contractions during labor pose a physiological stress to fetal oxygenation?
Contractions raise intramural pressure and briefly compress the spiral vessels
Contractions raise the maternal blood pressure to pathological levels
Contractions trigger fetal hypothermia and shivering while in utero
Contractions cause permanent thrombosis of the umbilical vein and arteries
Normal contractions raise intramyocardial or intramural pressure, temporarily compressing the spiral vessels and reducing intervillous blood flow. (Book p347)
According to WHO recommendations for low-risk labor, what is the frequency of intermittent fetal heart sound auscultation during the first and second stages of labor?
Every 30 minutes in the first stage; every 15 minutes in the second stage
Every 15 minutes in the first stage; every 5 minutes in the second stage
Every 60 minutes in the first stage; every 30 minutes in the second stage
In low-risk labor: auscultate every 30 minutes in the first stage (active phase), and every 15 minutes in the second stage. (Book p347)
In high-risk intrapartum cases monitored by intermittent auscultation, what is the required frequency of auscultation in the first and second stages of labor?
Every 15 minutes in the first stage; every 5 minutes in the second stage
Every 30 minutes in the first stage; every 15 minutes in the second stage
Every 5 minutes in the first stage; continuously in the second stage
For high-risk labor: auscultate every 15 minutes during the first stage, and every 5 minutes during the second stage. (Book p347)
Which of the following statements about intrapartum fetal surveillance is TRUE?
In low-risk labour, intermittent auscultation every 15 minutes in the first stage is an accepted alternative to continuous CTG
Continuous electronic monitoring is mandatory for every labour, whatever the risk status
Auscultation should be performed for a full minute before a contraction rather than after it
A handheld Doppler device cannot be used for intermittent auscultation in labour
Low-risk labours may be monitored by intermittent auscultation, counting for at least a minute immediately after a contraction. (Book p347)
When performing intermittent auscultation during labor, for how long should the fetal heart rate be counted, and when in relation to a contraction?
Counted for at least 1 full minute, continuing immediately after the end of a uterine contraction
Counted for 15 seconds during the peak of a contraction
Counted for 30 seconds before contractions begin
Counted only during uterine relaxation between contractions
Auscultation is performed for 60 seconds immediately following a contraction to detect potential late decelerations. (Book p348)
What is the most common maternal cause of persistent baseline fetal tachycardia (>160 bpm) during active labor?
Maternal pyrexia and chorioamnionitis are the most frequent causes of intrapartum baseline fetal tachycardia. (Book p348)
Which parameter on cardiotocography is considered the single most reliable indicator of fetal normoxemia and absence of cerebral acidemia?
Moderate baseline variability (6-25 bpm) is the single most reliable sign of normal central fetal oxygenation and normal cord pH. (Book p348)

Match the CTG term with its definition — 1) Fetal tachycardia 2) Minimal variability 3) Prolonged deceleration … A) Amplitude range of 5 bpm or less persisting for 40 minutes or more B) Baseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more C) A fall of 15 bpm or more lasting over 2 minutes but under 10 minutes
Tachycardia exceeds 160 bpm for 10 minutes, minimal variability is an amplitude of 5 bpm or less, and a prolonged deceleration lasts 2 to 10 minutes. (Book p348)
A prolonged deceleration on CTG is defined as a decrease in fetal heart rate of >= 15 bpm below baseline lasting for:
At least 2 minutes but less than 10 minutes
At least 30 seconds but less than 1 minute
A prolonged deceleration is a drop in FHR >=15 bpm lasting >=2 minutes but <10 minutes; if >=10 minutes, it is a baseline change. (Book p349)
What is the most frequent iatrogenic cause of acute prolonged fetal heart rate decelerations during induced labor?
Uterine hyperstimulation or tachysystole from oxytocin or misoprostol
Administration of prophylactic ampicillin during the induction
Artificial rupture of membranes performed to augment labour
Maternal oral hydration with plain water throughout the labour
The most frequent iatrogenic cause of acute prolonged decelerations in induced labour is uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole) from oxytocin or misoprostol. (Book p349)
Early decelerations on intrapartum CTG are characterized by a gradual decrease in FHR that mirrors the uterine contraction. What is their physiological cause?
Fetal head compression, raising intracranial pressure and causing vagal stimulation
Umbilical vein compression, which reduces venous return to the fetal heart
Uteroplacental insufficiency, which reduces gas exchange at the villi
Placental abruption, which separates the placental bed from the uterus
Early decelerations mirror contractions and are benign; late decelerations come from uteroplacental insufficiency and variable ones from cord compression. (Book p350)
Why are late decelerations considered the most ominous deceleration pattern on cardiotocography?
Their nadir follows the contraction peak, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency
They indicate fetal head compression against the pelvic floor and skull
They reflect rapid cord prolapse through the cervix with cord compression
They are caused by maternal sleep and the resulting reduced placental flow
Late decelerations are the most ominous pattern because the nadir occurs after the peak of the contraction, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal myocardial hypoxia. (Book p350)

Match the deceleration with its cause and shape — 1) Early deceleration 2) Late deceleration 3) Variable deceleration … A) Uniform, mirrors the contraction, nadir at the peak, from head compression B) Uniform, nadir after the contraction peak, from uteroplacental insufficiency C) Abrupt V-shaped fall and recovery, from cord compression
Early decelerations mirror contractions from head compression, late decelerations lag behind from placental insufficiency, and variable decelerations are abrupt from cord compression. (Book p350)
Deceleration morphologies: early, late & variable decelerations
Variable decelerations exhibit an abrupt drop (<30 seconds to nadir) and vary in shape, depth, and duration. What is their primary cause?
Variable decelerations are triggered by umbilical cord occlusion/compression (transient umbilical vein and artery collapse). (Book p351)
On a cardiotocograph showing variable decelerations, what are 'shoulders' (transient accelerations before and after the deceleration)?
A reassuring compensatory response of a healthy fetus to transient cord occlusion
An ominous sign of impending fetal cardiac arrest and hypoxic decompensation
An artifact produced by maternal coughing or movement during the recording
Evidence of fetal seizure activity from cortical irritation by hypoxia
Shoulders are transient accelerations before and after a variable deceleration, a reassuring feature signalling intact fetal autonomic responsiveness and good prognosis. (Book p351)
Under the 3-tier ACOG/FIGO intrapartum CTG classification, what characterizes a Category 1 (Normal / Reassuring) tracing?
Baseline 110-160 bpm, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations
Absent baseline variability with a mild fetal tachycardia
Recurrent late decelerations with a normal baseline fetal rate
A sinusoidal pattern with superimposed fetal heart accelerations
A Category 1 intrapartum tracing has a baseline of 110-160 bpm, moderate variability (6-25 bpm), no late or variable decelerations, and early decelerations either present or absent. (Book p351)
Which of the following CTG abnormalities places a tracing into Category 3 (Abnormal / Non-reassuring)?
Absent baseline variability accompanied by recurrent late decelerations or a sinusoidal pattern
Early decelerations during the second stage of labor
Baseline FHR of 150 bpm without decelerations
Category 3 includes absent baseline variability with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, bradycardia, or sinusoidal pattern. (Book p351)
What is the initial pharmacological step in intrauterine resuscitation when acute fetal decelerations occur in the presence of uterine hyperstimulation?
Stop the oxytocin infusion and give terbutaline 0.25 mg SC for acute tocolysis
Increase the oxytocin infusion to accelerate the delivery urgently
Give an intravenous bolus of methylergometrine to contract the uterus
Give a high-dose magnesium sulfate bolus for fetal neuroprotection
For acute decelerations with uterine hyperstimulation, discontinue the oxytocin infusion immediately and give terbutaline 0.25 mg SC for acute tocolysis. (Book p351)
A labouring woman's CTG shows a baseline of 110 bpm, minimal variability and recurrent late decelerations with no accelerations. How should this tracing be categorised and managed?
Category III — start intrauterine resuscitation and expedite delivery
Category I — normal tracing needing no intervention
Category II — continue monitoring and review again in 30 minutes
Category III — but delivery can safely wait two hours for a trial of rest
Absent or minimal variability with recurrent late decelerations is a Category III tracing, requiring resuscitation and prompt delivery. (Book p351)
What cervical dilatation and fetal station are prerequisite before attempting fetal scalp blood sampling?
Cervix dilated >= 4 to 5 cm with vertex at or below -1.5 station
Cervix dilated 1 cm with floating head
Fully dilated cervix with head on perineum
Prerequisites for scalp sampling: ruptured membranes, cervix dilated >=4-5 cm, and vertex engaged at least at -1.5 station. (Book p352)
What fetal scalp capillary blood pH cutoffs represent normal, pre-acidotic, and acidotic states?
7.25 or more normal; 7.20 to 7.24 pre-acidotic; under 7.20 acidotic
7.40 or more normal; 7.30 pre-acidotic; under 7.25 acidotic
7.10 or more normal; under 7.00 acidotic; nothing in between
7.00 or more is normal in every labour, whatever the trace
Fetal scalp pH of 7.25 or more is normal, 7.20 to 7.24 is pre-acidotic and is repeated in 20-30 minutes, and under 7.20 is acidotic and requires immediate delivery. (Book p352)
During digital examination in labor, digital fetal scalp stimulation that elicits a fetal heart rate acceleration (>=15 bpm for >=15s) indicates:
Fetal scalp pH is >= 7.25 in 99-100% of cases, reliably ruling out significant acidemia and avoiding scalp sampling
Severe fetal hypoxia requiring immediate emergency C-section
An acceleration in response to scalp stimulation correlates with scalp pH >=7.25 in virtually 100% of cases, reliably excluding acidemia. (Book p352)
During intrapartum fetal pulse oximetry, a fetal arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) falling below which threshold is strongly associated with fetal acidosis?
A fetal SpO2 < 30% for at least 2 minutes on continuous intrapartum pulse oximetry correlates with fetal metabolic acidosis. (Book p352)
Fill up: Fetal scalp blood sampling is abnormal when the pH is below ______, while a value of 7.20 to 7.25 is ______.
A pH below 7.20 is abnormal and 7.20-7.25 is borderline, so the sample is repeated after resuscitation. (Book p352)
Fetal scalp blood sampling, scalp stimulation & pulse oximetry
Gestational hyperpigmentation (linea nigra, chloasma/melasma) is primarily driven by elevated estrogen and progesterone stimulating:
Estrogen and progesterone stimulate melanocytes and MSH release, producing hyperpigmentation along the midline (linea nigra) and face (chloasma). (Book p353)
The non-pregnant uterus weighs approximately 50-60 g and enlarges to approximately 1100 g at term. What is the primary cellular mechanism driving this enlargement?
Myometrial hypertrophy (hyperplasia occurs only in the first trimester)
Myometrial hyperplasia throughout all three trimesters
Deposition of adipose tissue within the perimetrium
Uterine enlargement is overwhelmingly due to hypertrophy of existing smooth muscle fibers (hyperplasia is limited to early first trimester). (Book p353)
All of the following are normal skin changes of pregnancy EXCEPT:
Generalised pruritus with jaundice and dark urine
Linea nigra over the lower abdomen
Chloasma or melasma over the cheeks
Striae gravidarum over the abdomen and thighs
Pruritus with jaundice suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; linea nigra, chloasma and striae are normal. (Book p353)
Maternal adaptations: cutaneous, uterine & cervical shifts
What are Montgomery's tubercles, which become prominent on the maternal breasts by 8-12 weeks of gestation?
Hypertrophied sebaceous glands located on the primary areola
Superficial thrombosed veins of the breast
Montgomery's tubercles are hypertrophic sebaceous glands on the areola that secrete a protective, lubricating lipoid fluid. (Book p354)

A pregnant woman presents with painless, minor post-coital vaginal spotting. Speculum examination reveals a red, velvety, glandular outgrowth of endocervical mucosa onto the exocervix. What is the diagnosis?
Cervical ectropion / eversion (benign physiological adaptation; no biopsy required)
Eversion of the endocervical columnar epithelium (ectropion) is a physiological response to estrogen; it is benign and requires reassurance. (Book p354)
During normal pregnancy, the vaginal pH becomes markedly acidic (pH 3.5 to 4.0) due to:
Döderlein's lactobacilli fermenting estrogen-induced mucosal glycogen into lactic acid
Direct transudation of amniotic fluid into the vaginal vault
Excess secretion of gastric hydrochloric acid
Secretion of acidic mucus from the Bartholin glands
Estrogen increases epithelial glycogen, which Döderlein's bacilli ferment to lactic acid, creating an acidic pH (3.5) protective against pathogens. (Book p354)
What is the most common form of infectious vaginitis encountered during pregnancy, thriving in the acidic vaginal microenvironment?
Candida albicans thrives in the acidic, glycogen-rich environment of the pregnant vagina, making candidiasis the most common vaginitis. (Book p354)
Which of the following statements about the vaginal environment in pregnancy is TRUE?
Physiological leucorrhoea is increased cervical mucus from oestrogen, and the vaginal pH stays acidic
Vaginal pH rises above 6 in normal pregnancy, which is why bacterial vaginosis is so common
Progesterone dries and thins cervical mucus, reducing the discharge of normal pregnancy
Total body water falls in pregnancy despite the rise in aldosterone and renin
Oestrogen increases cervical mucus and glycogen, keeping the vagina acidic; total body water rises by several litres in pregnancy. (Book p354)
Vaginal ecosystem, endocrine shifts & fluid retention
Why is lactation physiologically suppressed during pregnancy despite maternal prolactin levels rising up to 10-fold by term?
High placental oestrogen and progesterone block prolactin at the breast receptors
Low oxytocin from the posterior pituitary fails to trigger milk ejection
High maternal thyroid hormone inhibits milk synthesis within the alveoli
Prolactin secreted in pregnancy is biologically inactive at the receptor

Lactation is held in check during pregnancy by high circulating placental estrogen and progesterone, which competitively block prolactin action at the breast alveolar receptors; delivery lifts the block and unleashes lactation. (Book p355)
How can an examiner clinically differentiate physiological dependent edema of pregnancy from pathological pre-eclamptic edema?
Physiological is dependent and settles overnight; pathological involves the face and hands
Physiological edema is non-pitting on pressure, whereas pathological edema pits
Physiological edema is accompanied by marked proteinuria and hypertension
Pathological edema always disappears after walking about for a while
Physiological edema is restricted to the dependent lower extremities and subsides with overnight recumbency; pathological edema involves the face and hands and persists. (Book p355)
During normal singleton pregnancy, maternal plasma volume expands by 40-50%, whereas red blood cell volume increases by 20-30%. This physiological mismatch results in:
Physiological hemodilution ('physiological anemia of pregnancy') with decreased hematocrit and blood viscosity
Greater expansion of plasma volume over red cell mass causes physiological hemodilution, reducing blood viscosity and cardiac workload. (Book p356)
Under standard WHO and CDC definitions, maternal hemoglobin concentration during pregnancy is considered abnormal (anemic) when it falls below:
Below 11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, below 10.5 g/dL in the second
Below 12.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, below 11.0 g/dL in the second
Below 10.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, below 9.0 g/dL in the second
Below 11.0 g/dL in the second trimester, below 10.5 g/dL in the first and third

Under WHO and CDC definitions anemia in pregnancy is hemoglobin below 11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, or below 10.5 g/dL in the second (reflecting mid-trimester hemodilution). (Book p356)
What physiological changes occur in maternal leukocyte (WBC) and platelet counts during normal pregnancy and active labor?
Leukocytosis up to 15,000/mcL in pregnancy and 25,000/mcL in labour, with mild thrombocytopenia
Severe leukopenia with a marked reactive thrombocytosis in pregnancy
Pancytopenia affecting all cell lines across every trimester
Marked basophilia with severe thrombocytopenia below 50,000/mcL
Normal pregnancy shows leukocytosis (up to 15,000/mcL, or 25,000/mcL in labor) and mild gestational thrombocytopenia, with the count still at or above 100,000/mcL. (Book p356)
Pregnancy is a markedly prothrombotic state. Which coagulation factors exhibit significant physiological increases?
Fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, IX and X, and von Willebrand factor
Only factor XI and factor XIII, both of which also rise markedly
Antithrombin III and protein S, the natural anticoagulants
Tissue plasminogen activator, which keeps the maternal circulation fluid
Clotting factors and fibrinogen rise, while antithrombin and protein S fall — which is why pregnancy is prothrombotic. (Book p356)
Which of the following coagulation parameters remains physiologically UNCHANGED during normal pregnancy?
Bleeding time, clotting time, and aPTT remain unchanged in normal pregnancy despite elevation of specific procoagulant factors. (Book p356)
Fill up: In pregnancy the plasma volume expands by about ______%, but the red cell mass rises by only about ______%, producing physiological anaemia.
Greater plasma expansion than red cell expansion dilutes the haemoglobin, which is why the physiological nadir occurs around 30 weeks. (Book p356)
Why is physiological hydroureter and hydronephrosis in pregnancy significantly more pronounced on the RIGHT kidney than the left?
Dextrorotation of the gravid uterus compresses the right ureter at the pelvic brim
The right ureter has thinner smooth muscle walls than the left ureter does
The right kidney produces about three times more urine than the left
The left ureter is completely immune to the relaxant effect of progesterone

Physiological hydroureter and hydronephrosis are worse on the right because dextrorotation of the gravid uterus compresses the right ureter against the pelvic brim and it crosses the right ovarian vein. (Book p356)
In normal pregnancy, maternal Renal Blood Flow (RBF) increases by 70-80% and Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) increases by 50%. How does this alter normal serum creatinine levels?
Creatinine falls to about 0.4-0.6 mg/dL, so a value above 0.8 mg/dL is abnormal in pregnancy
Creatinine rises to between 1.5 and 2.0 mg/dL from the increased filtration load
Creatinine stays fixed at about 1.0 mg/dL whatever the filtration rate
Creatinine becomes undetectable because filtration is so greatly increased
With filtration up by half, creatinine falls; a value considered normal outside pregnancy is abnormal during it. (Book p357)

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy is defined as >= 10^5 CFU/mL of a single pathogen on midstream clean-catch urine. What is the most common causative organism and why is treatment mandatory?
Escherichia coli (80%); mandatory to prevent ascending acute pyelonephritis and preterm labor
Staphylococcus aureus; mandatory to prevent maternal sepsis
Group B Streptococcus; mandatory to prevent maternal liver failure
Proteus mirabilis; mandatory to prevent renal stone formation
E. coli is most common; untreated ASB leads to acute pyelonephritis in 25-30% of pregnant women and increases preterm labor risks. (Book p357)
Why is serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) physiologically elevated by two- to three-fold during the third trimester of pregnancy despite completely normal liver function?
Release of heat-stable alkaline phosphatase from the placental syncytiotrophoblast
Obstruction of the maternal biliary ducts by the gravid uterus
Severe maternal osteomalacia from calcium loss in pregnancy
Demineralisation of the fetal bones in the third trimester
Serum ALP rises two- to three-fold in the third trimester because of release of large quantities of heat-stable alkaline phosphatase from the placental syncytiotrophoblast. (Book p357)

Match the renal change with its direction in pregnancy — 1) Renal plasma flow and GFR 2) Serum creatinine 3) Ureteric and pelvic dilation … A) Falls to about 0.5-0.7 mg/dL, so a normal non-pregnant value may be abnormal B) Rises by 50-75% in the first half of pregnancy C) More marked on the right, from uterine compression of the ureter at the pelvic brim
Filtration rises, creatinine falls and the right ureter dilates more, which is why pyelonephritis is commoner on the right. (Book p357)
Fill up: Progesterone directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center to increase ______ by 30-50% (and minute ventilation by 40%).
Progesterone directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center to increase tidal volume by 30-50% (and minute ventilation by 40%). (Book p358)
Which of the following statements about Respiratory physiology is TRUE?
It remains essentially constant (or shows a negligible increase)
It doubles from 14 to 28 breaths per minute
The respiratory rate remains unchanged (or shows minimal increase); hyperventilation is achieved via increased tidal volume, not tachypnea. (Book p358)
All of the following are Respiratory physiology EXCEPT:
Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
Vital Capacity and Inspiratory Capacity — Elevated diaphragm position reduces Functional Residual Capa
Tidal Volume and Minute Ventilation — Elevated diaphragm position reduces Functional Residual Capa
Total Lung Capacity and Anatomical Dead Space
Elevated diaphragm position reduces Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) by ~20%. (Book p358)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with respiratory physiology presents with normal pregnancy shows a chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis, with pco2 28-32 mmhg, hco3 18-22. What physiological acid-base state is characteristically observed on maternal arterial blood gas analysis during normal pregnancy?
Compensated respiratory alkalosis: pCO2 28-32, HCO3 18-22, pH 7.40-7.45
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis: pCO2 45-50, HCO3 12-16, pH 7.20-7.28
Acute respiratory acidosis: pCO2 55-60, HCO3 26-30, pH 7.22-7.30
Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia: pCO2 45-50, HCO3 32-36, pH 7.50-7.55
Normal pregnancy shows a chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis, with pCO2 28-32 mmHg, HCO3 18-22 mEq/L and arterial pH held at 7.40-7.45. (Book p358)
Fill up: is the biological advantage of maternal physiological respiratory alkalosis (low maternal pCO2 of 28-32 mmHg) for the fetus is ______.
It creates a gradient that drives CO2 rapidly from fetal blood into maternal blood
It stimulates fetal renal surfactant synthesis and accelerates lung maturity
It prevents premature rupture of membranes by lowering amniotic fluid pressure
It inhibits fetal cardiac output so that placental flow is preferentially raised
Maternal physiological respiratory alkalosis (pCO2 28-32 mmHg) establishes a favourable partial pressure gradient promoting rapid transfer of CO2 from fetal circulation to maternal blood. (Book p358)
Fill up: In pregnancy, tidal volume increases by about ______%, which lowers maternal arterial PCO2 to roughly ______ mmHg.
Progesterone-driven hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 to about 30-32 mmHg, creating the gradient for fetal carbon dioxide transfer. (Book p358)
Which of the following statements about Systemic and visceral shifts is TRUE?
The 40-50% rise in cardiac output far exceeds tissue oxygen extraction
Fetal tissues consume no oxygen at all throughout the pregnancy
Maternal hemoglobin loses its ability to bind and carry oxygen
Maternal systemic vascular resistance rises during pregnancy
Oxygen consumption rises 20% but the A-V gradient falls because the disproportionate 40-50% surge in maternal cardiac output delivers oxygen far in excess of tissue extraction. (Book p358)
All of the following are Systemic and visceral shifts EXCEPT:
Sheehan syndrome — Enlargement of the anterior pituitary makes it vulnerable to
Simmonds disease — Enlargement of the anterior pituitary makes it vulnerable to
Nelson syndrome — Enlargement of the anterior pituitary makes it vulnerable to
Schmidt syndrome — Enlargement of the anterior pituitary makes it vulnerable to
Enlargement of the anterior pituitary makes it vulnerable to ischemic infarction during severe hypotension in PPH (Sheehan syndrome). (Book p358)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with systemic and visceral shifts presents with the fetus acquires ~30 g of calcium (mostly in t3), met by doubling maternal intestinal absorption s. Approximately how much total elemental calcium does the developing fetal skeleton accumulate across pregnancy, and how does maternal physiology supply this?
Approximately 30 g; supplied by doubled maternal intestinal calcium absorption under active 1,25-(OH)2 Vitamin D
Approximately 500 g; supplied by maternal bone resorption
Approximately 5 g; supplied by passive renal retention
Approximately 100 g; supplied by amniotic fluid ingestion
The fetus acquires ~30 g of calcium (mostly in T3), met by doubling maternal intestinal absorption stimulated by 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. (Book p358)
Which of the following statements about respiratory physiology in pregnancy is TRUE?
The fall in maternal PaCO2 is what allows fetal carbon dioxide to diffuse into maternal blood
Maternal arterial PO2 falls markedly because oxygen consumption outstrips the rise in ventilation
The gravid uterus pushes the diaphragm downwards, increasing the antero-posterior chest diameter
Functional residual capacity rises during pregnancy, giving the mother more oxygen reserve
PaO2 is normal or slightly higher, the diaphragm rises (transverse diameter widens) and FRC falls, so the pregnant woman desaturates faster. (Book p358)
Maternal oxygen dynamics, endocrine & visceral changes
Fill up: The total extra requirement is ______ mg of elemental iron, and the breakdown matters when explaining why supplementation is needed.
About 1000 mg: 300 mg for the fetus and placenta, 500 mg for red cell expansion and 200 mg excreted
About 300 mg: 100 mg for the fetus and placenta, 150 mg for red cell expansion and 50 mg excreted
About 2500 mg: 1000 mg for the fetus and placenta, 1200 mg for red cell expansion and 300 mg excreted
About 500 mg: 200 mg for the fetus and placenta, 250 mg for red cell expansion and 50 mg excreted
The total extra requirement is about 1000 mg of elemental iron, and the breakdown matters when explaining why supplementation is needed. (Book p359)
Which of the following statements about Iron physiology and national programs is TRUE?
Active transport via transferrin receptors against a concentration gradient
Simple passive diffusion through intercellular clefts
Placental syncytiotrophoblasts extract iron via transferrin receptors and actively pump it to the fetus against a concentration gradient. (Book p359)
What is the daily elemental iron requirement during the third trimester of pregnancy?
7.5 mg/day, compared with about 0.8 mg/day in the first trimester
1.0 mg/day, compared with about 0.8 mg/day in the first trimester
25 mg/day, compared with about 7.5 mg/day in the first trimester
0.5 mg/day, compared with about 7.5 mg/day in the first trimester
Elemental iron needs rise steeply to about 7.5 mg/day in the third trimester, largely for the expanding red cell mass. (Book p359)
Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat (I-NIPI) programme, what deworming regimen is routinely administered to pregnant women?
Albendazole 400 mg single oral dose in the second trimester (after 14 weeks)
Albendazole 400 mg daily for 7 days in the first trimester
Under Anemia Mukt Bharat, a single prophylactic dose of Albendazole 400 mg is administered during the 2nd trimester to treat hookworm infestation. (Book p359)
Fill up: The total extra iron requirement of a pregnancy is about ______ mg, of which roughly ______ mg goes to the fetus and placenta.
About 1000 mg extra iron is needed in total: the largest share expands the maternal red cell mass and about 300 mg goes to the fetus and placenta. (Book p359)
Iron requirements, metabolism & Anemia Mukt Bharat / I-NIPI
What are the two active pharmacological ingredients in the prophylactic RED IFA tablet distributed under the national programme?
60 mg elemental iron (as ferrous sulfate) and 500 mcg folic acid
100 mg elemental iron and 1 mg folic acid
30 mg elemental iron and 400 mcg folic acid
200 mg elemental iron and 5 mg folic acid
Each red IFA tablet contains 60 mg elemental iron (dried ferrous sulfate) and 500 mcg folic acid. (Book p360)
When is the optimal time for a pregnant woman to consume her daily oral iron tablet to maximize bioavailability and reduce GI discomfort?
2 hours after meals (or at bedtime), avoiding co-ingestion with tea, milk, or calcium tablets
Immediately before breakfast with a large cup of milk
With hot black tea to stimulate gastric acidity
Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach or 2 hours post-meal; tannins in tea and calcium in milk inhibit iron absorption. (Book p360)
Fill up: Anaemia in pregnancy is diagnosed when the haemoglobin is below ______ g/dL, and severe anaemia when it is below ______ g/dL.
WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as haemoglobin below 11 g/dL, with severe anaemia below 7 g/dL and moderate between 7 and 9.9 g/dL. (Book p360)
According to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria, what hemoglobin cutoffs define mild, moderate, and severe anemia in pregnancy?
Mild: 10.0 to 10.9 g/dL; Moderate: 7.0 to 9.9 g/dL; Severe: < 7.0 g/dL
Mild: 11.0 to 11.9 g/dL; Moderate: 9.0 to 10.9 g/dL; Severe: < 9.0 g/dL
Mild: 9.0 to 10.0 g/dL; Moderate: 6.0 to 8.9 g/dL; Severe: < 6.0 g/dL
Mild: 10.5 to 11.0 g/dL; Moderate: 8.0 to 10.4 g/dL; Severe: < 8.0 g/dL
WHO defines anemia in pregnancy as Hb <11.0 g/dL (Mild: 10-10.9; Moderate: 7-9.9; Severe: <7.0 g/dL; ICMR adds Very severe: <4.0 g/dL). (Book p361)
What is the single most common pathological cause of anemia in pregnant women worldwide?
Nutritional iron deficiency anemia (IDA, ~80% of cases)
Nutritional iron deficiency anemia accounts for approximately 80% of all pathological anemias encountered in pregnancy. (Book p361)
Why does maternal severe anemia stimulate compensatory placentomegaly (abnormally large placenta)?
To increase the villous surface area in an attempt to compensate for decreased maternal oxygen-carrying capacity
Due to excessive deposition of fetal fat in the cotyledons
Because iron accumulates within chorionic villi
In severe maternal anemia, chronic hypoxemia stimulates placental hypertrophy and capillary branching, causing placentomegaly. (Book p361)
All of the following are recognised consequences of severe maternal anaemia EXCEPT:
Preterm labour and low birth weight
Postpartum haemorrhage from poor myometrial contractility
Severe anaemia impairs oxygen transfer and myometrial function, so growth restriction and preterm birth occur; macrosomia does not. (Book p361)
Maternal & fetal complications of anemia in pregnancy
Why are severely anemic women at exceptionally high risk of developing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) immediately following placental delivery?
Myometrial tissue hypoxia impairs smooth muscle contractility, resulting in severe uterine atony
Anemia causes disseminated intravascular coagulation in all patients
Platelets cannot aggregate in anemic blood
Severe tissue hypoxia prevents the living ligatures (interlacing myometrial fibers) from contracting effectively, precipitating atonic PPH. (Book p362)
At what specific time point during childbirth is an anemic woman at the greatest risk of acute congestive heart failure and pulmonary edema?
Immediately postpartum, following placental delivery and uterine contraction
During the latent phase of the first stage of labor
Immediately postpartum, uterine contraction autotransfuses 300-500 mL of blood into the systemic circulation, acutely overloading the compromised heart. (Book p362)
Does moderate maternal iron deficiency anemia typically cause microcytic hypochromic anemia in the neonate at birth?
No, because the placenta actively extracts iron against a gradient, maintaining normal neonatal hemoglobin at the expense of maternal stores
Yes, the fetus always reflects the exact maternal hemoglobin concentration
Yes, fetal hemoglobin drops to zero
Only if the infant is male
The placenta actively transports iron, preserving normal fetal/neonatal hemoglobin; however, neonatal iron stores are depleted. (Book p362)
A pregnant woman presents with an intense craving to eat non-food substances such as dirt, clay, raw rice, or ice. This symptom is known as:
Pica, a classic clinical manifestation of severe iron deficiency
Bulimia nervosa, with repeated bingeing and purging behaviour
Hyperemesis gravidarum, with protracted vomiting and ketosis
Chorea gravidarum, with involuntary movements of the limbs
Craving and chewing non-food substances such as clay, raw rice or ice is pica, and it accompanies severe iron deficiency. (Book p362)
A 26-year-old at 30 weeks has a haemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL with pallor, koilonychia, a smooth sore tongue and pica. Which single investigation best confirms the underlying diagnosis?
Koilonychia, glossitis and pica point to iron deficiency, and serum ferritin is the most specific single test of iron stores. (Book p362)
Clinical evaluation & physical workup of gestational anemia
On physical examination of a pregnant female, clinical pallor becomes distinctly evident on inspection of the palmar creases when the hemoglobin level drops below:
Pallor of the palmar creases is a reliable clinical sign indicating severe anemia with hemoglobin < 7.0 g/dL. (Book p363)
Koilonychia—spoon-shaped concave nails with raised edges—is a specific physical sign indicative of:
Koilonychia (spooning of nails) and platonychia (flat nails) are pathognomonic physical signs of chronic tissue iron depletion. (Book p363)
According to Government of India (MOHFW) guidelines, how frequently should hemoglobin be screened during antenatal care?
At every routine antenatal visit (4 times during pregnancy)
Only once at the booking visit
Only in the third trimester at 36 weeks
Only if the patient appears visibly pale
In India, MOHFW mandates checking hemoglobin at each of the 4 routine antenatal visits to detect and manage progressive anemia. (Book p363)
What is the Mentzer Index formula, and what cutoffs differentiate Iron Deficiency Anemia from Beta-Thalassemia Trait?
Mentzer Index = MCV / RBC count; > 13 favors Iron Deficiency Anemia, < 13 favors Beta-Thalassemia Trait
Mentzer Index = Hb / MCV; > 20 favors IDA, < 20 favors Thalassemia
Mentzer Index = MCHC / Ferritin; > 5 favors IDA
Mentzer Index = Hematocrit / WBC; > 10 favors Thalassemia
Mentzer index = MCV (fL) / RBC count (millions/mcL). In IDA, RBC count is low, giving index >13; in thalassemia trait, RBC count is high, giving index <13. (Book p364)
What is considered the gold-standard, most sensitive non-invasive biochemical test to confirm depleted iron stores and diagnose Iron Deficiency Anemia?
Serum ferritin <20-30 mcg/L is the single best, earliest, and most sensitive biochemical marker of iron deficiency (normal 20-200 mcg/L). (Book p364)
In a patient with classical Iron Deficiency Anemia, what typical pattern of iron study parameters is expected?
Decreased serum iron (<40 mcg/dL), elevated TIBC (>400 mcg/dL), and decreased transferrin saturation (<16%)
Elevated serum iron, decreased TIBC, and elevated ferritin
Normal iron, normal TIBC, and elevated transferrin saturation
Decreased serum iron and decreased TIBC
IDA is characterized by low serum ferritin, low serum iron (<40 mcg/dL), elevated TIBC (>400 mcg/dL), and transferrin saturation <10-16%. (Book p364)
How does Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) differ between Iron Deficiency Anemia and Anemia of Chronic Disease?
TIBC is elevated in Iron Deficiency Anemia, but decreased/normal in Anemia of Chronic Disease
TIBC is decreased in IDA, but elevated in chronic disease
TIBC is identical and zero in both conditions
TIBC is elevated in both conditions
In IDA, transferrin synthesis rises, producing high TIBC (>400 mcg/dL); in chronic disease/inflammation, hepcidin and cytokines reduce TIBC. (Book p364)

Match the laboratory pattern with the diagnosis — 1) Microcytic hypochromic cells with a low ferritin 2) Macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils 3) Microcytosis with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 … A) Beta thalassaemia trait B) Iron deficiency anaemia C) Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency
Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils means megaloblastosis, and a raised HbA2 with normal iron means thalassaemia trait. (Book p364)
Diagnostic RBC indices & iron profile interpretation
When initiating oral therapeutic iron for anemia in pregnancy, what is the standard recommended daily dose of IFA tablets?
2 IFA tablets per day (delivering 120 mg of elemental iron)
4 IFA tablets per day with meals
Therapeutic oral iron therapy requires 2 IFA tablets daily (total 120 mg elemental iron) until target hemoglobin is achieved. (Book p365)
What is the EARLIEST objective hematological marker indicating an adequate therapeutic response to oral iron therapy?
An increase in reticulocyte count within 5 to 7 days (peaking at 10 days)
An increase in hemoglobin concentration within 24 hours
A drop in serum ferritin within 3 days
A sudden decrease in total iron binding capacity
A reticulocyte surge beginning at 5-7 days and peaking at 10 days is the earliest and preferred proof of therapeutic bone marrow response. (Book p365)
A pregnant woman taking oral iron therapy has a repeat hemoglobin checked after 1 month. What rise in hemoglobin defines an 'adequate' response?
A rise of >= 1.0 g/dL after 1 month of therapy
A rise of >= 4.0 g/dL after 1 month
A rise of 0.1 g/dL after 1 month
No change in hemoglobin is required
An adequate response is defined as an increase in hemoglobin of >=1.0 g/dL after 3-4 weeks of compliant oral iron therapy. (Book p365)
What is the most common reason for failure of oral iron therapy in a pregnant patient, and how can the clinician objectively verify adherence?
Non-compliance from gastrointestinal side effects, which blackening of the stool can confirm
Severe intestinal malabsorption, demonstrated by a negative stool test
Bone marrow aplasia, which should always be excluded by aspiration
Excessive urinary excretion of iron, measured in a 24-hour collection
The commonest reason is that she has stopped taking it because of nausea or constipation; asking about black stools is a simple objective check. (Book p365)
Fill up: An adequate response to oral iron is a haemoglobin rise of about ______ g/dL over ______ weeks.
A rise of roughly 1 g/dL in 3-4 weeks confirms adherence and absorption; failure prompts a search for malabsorption or non-iron causes. (Book p365)
Oral iron therapy & assessing treatment response
Which of the following is a recognized clinical indication for administering parenteral (intravenous) iron therapy in pregnancy?
Severe gastrointestinal intolerance or non-compliance to oral iron, or moderate anemia diagnosed late in gestation (>30-34 weeks)
Mild anemia diagnosed at 8 weeks of gestation
Patient preference for intravenous injections in the first trimester
Parenteral iron is indicated for oral intolerance, non-compliance, malabsorption, or moderate anemia presenting beyond 30-34 weeks. (Book p366)
What is the Ganzoni formula used to calculate total elemental iron deficit for parenteral iron therapy?
Total deficit (mg) = [Body weight (kg) x (Target Hb 11 - Actual Hb) x 2.4] + 500 mg (iron stores)
Total deficit (mg) = Body weight x Actual Hb x 10
Total deficit (mg) = Gestational age x (11 - Hb) x 100
Ganzoni formula: Iron deficit (mg) = [Weight in kg x (Target Hb 11 - Patient's Hb) x 2.4] + 500 mg for storage replenishment. (Book p366)
What is the maximum single daily dose and weekly ceiling for intravenous iron sucrose administration in pregnancy?
Up to 200 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 600 mg per week
Up to 1000 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, with no weekly ceiling
Up to 50 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 200 mg per week
Up to 200 mg per day diluted and infused over 15-30 minutes, and up to 2000 mg per week
Iron sucrose is given in divided doses: a maximum of 200 mg per day infused over 15-30 minutes and 600 mg per week. (Book p366)
One unit of packed red blood cells (PRBC) typically elevates the maternal hemoglobin concentration by approximately:
About 1.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about three percentage points
About 0.2 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about one percentage point
About 3.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about nine percentage points
About 5.0 g/dL, and the haematocrit by about fifteen percentage points
A rough rule is that one unit of packed cells raises the haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL and the haematocrit by about 3 per cent. (Book p366)
Which of the following statements about parenteral iron in pregnancy is TRUE?
Iron sucrose is the preferred parenteral preparation; iron dextran needs a test dose because of anaphylaxis risk
Intramuscular iron into the gluteal region is the preferred parenteral route in the third trimester
Total-dose iron infusion is the treatment of choice in the first trimester for severe anaemia
Parenteral iron must never be given once the haemoglobin has fallen below 7 g/dL
Iron sucrose and ferric carboxymaltose are safe after the first trimester; iron dextran risks anaphylaxis, and intramuscular iron is painful and stains the skin. (Book p366)
Parenteral iron therapy, Ganzoni formula & blood transfusion
A pregnant woman presents at 28 weeks of gestation with moderate anemia (Hb 8.5 g/dL). What is the appropriate initial management protocol?
Oral iron therapy (2 IFA tablets daily) with repeat hemoglobin assessment after 3-4 weeks
Immediate blood transfusion of 2 units of packed RBCs
At <34 weeks with mild-to-moderate anemia, oral iron (2 tablets/day) is first line; parenteral iron is reserved for failures or late presentation. (Book p367)
A pregnant woman is first diagnosed with moderate anemia (Hb 8.0 g/dL) at 35 weeks of gestation. Why is parenteral iron preferred over oral iron?
Parenteral iron replenishes stores rapidly, whereas oral iron takes 4-6 weeks
Oral iron is contraindicated in pregnancy after 34 weeks of gestation
Parenteral iron induces spontaneous cervical ripening before delivery
Parenteral iron crosses the placenta faster and corrects fetal anaemia
Parenteral iron replenishes iron stores rapidly and covers the calculated deficit before delivery, whereas oral iron takes 4-6 weeks to achieve an adequate hemoglobin rise. (Book p367)
A pregnant woman presents at 24 weeks of gestation with very severe, symptomatic anemia and a hemoglobin of 4.2 g/dL (< 5 g/dL). What is the immediate treatment of choice?
Packed red cell transfusion with IV furosemide, at any gestational age
Double-dose oral iron therapy continued for a full month
Intravenous iron sucrose 200 mg given daily for a week
Immediate termination of pregnancy after stabilisation
With very severe symptomatic anemia and Hb under 5 g/dL at 24 weeks, the immediate treatment is packed red blood cell transfusion with IV furosemide, irrespective of gestational age. (Book p367)
A primigravida at 14 weeks has a haemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL with breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs. What is the most appropriate plan?
Admit, start parenteral iron sucrose, continue oral iron to term and recheck the haemoglobin in four weeks
Transfuse packed cells immediately and deliver the pregnancy whatever the gestation
Continue oral iron alone and review the haemoglobin at 28 weeks
Recommend termination because severe anaemia before viability is unmanageable
In the second trimester a symptomatic woman with severe anaemia needs parenteral iron; transfusion is reserved for decompensation or an imminent need for delivery. (Book p367)
Trimester-wise gestational management protocol for anemia
Which of the following antibiotic classes is considered SAFE and serves as first-line therapy across all trimesters of pregnancy?
Beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) do not interfere with fetal development and are safe throughout gestation. (Book p368)
Why are tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) strictly contraindicated after the 15th week of gestation?
They chelate calcium in fetal bones and teeth, causing discoloration and enamel hypoplasia
They cause Gray baby syndrome from impaired hepatic conjugation in the fetus
They cause congenital deafness from direct damage to the eighth cranial nerve
They trigger fetal aplastic anaemia through direct bone-marrow suppression
After the 15th week tetracyclines chelate with calcium in fetal bones and teeth, causing permanent yellowish-brown discoloration, enamel hypoplasia and inhibition of bone growth. (Book p368)
What fetal adverse effect is specifically associated with maternal aminoglycoside (streptomycin, gentamicin) use during pregnancy?
Cranial nerve VIII damage causing permanent hearing loss and vestibular toxicity
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus in the third trimester
Phocomelia and amelia from inhibition of early limb-bud development
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve with neonatal cyanosis
Maternal aminoglycosides (streptomycin, gentamicin) damage the 8th cranial nerve, causing permanent sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular ototoxicity. (Book p368)
Why is the administration of sulfonamides (e.g., sulfamethoxazole) contraindicated during the late third trimester near delivery?
They displace bilirubin from albumin, precipitating neonatal kernicterus
They induce gestational diabetes in the mother towards term
They cause Gray baby syndrome in the exposed preterm neonate
They trigger fetal limb reduction defects in the third trimester
Sulfonamides near delivery displace bilirubin from albumin binding sites, precipitating neonatal kernicterus. (Book p368)
All of the following antimicrobials are regarded as safe in pregnancy EXCEPT:
Tetracyclines stain fetal teeth and bones and are avoided; penicillins, cephalosporins and macrolides are safe in pregnancy. (Book p368)
Antimicrobial safety & teratogenic hazards in pregnancy
Why is Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH, Enoxaparin) the anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy?
Because its large molecular weight and negative charge prevent it from crossing the placental syncytiotrophoblast barrier
Because it is an oral tablet with zero maternal bleeding risk
Because it permanently reverses prosthetic valve thrombosis
Because it accelerates fetal lung maturity
Heparins (both LMWH and UFH) do not cross the placenta and are neither teratogenic nor cause fetal hemorrhage. (Book p368)
What laboratory assay is standardly utilized to monitor the therapeutic efficacy and dosing of Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH)?
Anti-Factor Xa assay (therapeutic target 0.8 to 1.2 IU/mL for mechanical valves)
LMWH does not predictably prolong the aPTT; it is monitored using peak anti-Factor Xa levels (0.8-1.2 IU/mL for prosthetic valves). (Book p368)
At what gestational age is the teratogenic risk of maternal Warfarin exposure at its absolute peak?
First trimester between 6 and 9 weeks of gestation
Warfarin teratogenicity is maximal between 6 and 9 weeks (critical window for nasal cartilage and epiphyseal development). (Book p368)
A pregnant woman with a mechanical heart valve taking therapeutic Warfarin unexpectedly enters active labor at 37 weeks. What is the mandatory management?
Stop warfarin, deliver by caesarean, and give vitamin K to mother and neonate
Allow spontaneous vaginal delivery, shortened by vacuum extraction
Administer high-dose intravenous aspirin and continue warfarin
Discharge the patient until the warfarin has washed out completely
With a mechanical valve on warfarin in active labour, stop warfarin, perform caesarean delivery and give vitamin K to both mother and neonate to avoid fetal intracranial hemorrhage. (Book p369)

Match the exposure with its fetal consequence — 1) Warfarin between 6 and 12 weeks 2) Warfarin near term and in labour 3) Low molecular weight heparin … A) Does not cross the placenta and is the preferred agent B) Warfarin embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses C) Fetal and neonatal intracranial haemorrhage during delivery
Warfarin teratogenicity peaks in organogenesis, near-term use risks fetal bleeding, and heparin molecules do not cross the placenta. (Book p369)
DiSaia syndrome (Fetal Warfarin Syndrome), caused by early first-trimester coumarin exposure, is characterized by which classic triad?
Hypoplasia of the nasal bridge, stippled epiphyses and central nervous system abnormalities
Phocomelia, amelia and ano-rectal atresia in the affected infant
Ebstein anomaly, fetal goitre and bilateral renal agenesis
Cleft lip, cleft palate and postaxial polydactyly
DiSaia syndrome is warfarin embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia, chondrodysplasia punctata and central nervous system defects. (Book p369)
Which antiepileptic medication carries the HIGHEST risk of major congenital malformations (including neural tube defects, craniofacial, and cardiac anomalies)?
Valproic acid (sodium valproate) carries the highest risk of major congenital malformations, including neural tube defects, craniofacial and cardiac anomalies, and developmental delay. (Book p369)
If a woman with epilepsy conceives while on antiepileptic therapy, what is the recommended clinical management strategy?
Continue the same drug at the lowest effective dose as monotherapy, and prescribe high-dose folic acid (4 to 5 mg/day)
Immediately stop all antiepileptic drugs to prevent birth defects
Switch her to multiple high-dose antiepileptics
Abrupt drug withdrawal triggers status epilepticus (fatal to fetus); maintain seizure control with lowest effective monotherapy + high-dose folic acid. (Book p369)
Fill up: The critical window for warfarin embryopathy is between ______ and ______ weeks of gestation.
Exposure from 6 to 12 weeks produces nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata; later exposure mainly risks central nervous system and bleeding problems. (Book p369)
By how much does maternal cardiac output physiologically increase during normal singleton pregnancy, and when does this rise peak antenatally?
Rises by 40% to 50%, peaking antenatally at 28 to 32 weeks
Rises by about 10%, peaking antenatally at 12 weeks
Rises by about 100%, peaking antenatally at 40 weeks
Falls by about 20% during the course of the third trimester
Maternal cardiac output increases by 40% to 50% in a normal singleton pregnancy, reaching its antenatal peak at 28 to 32 weeks of gestation. (Book p370)
During normal pregnancy, maternal systemic blood pressure drops to its nadir during which period, and what physiological mechanism is responsible?
20-24 weeks, from progesterone- and nitric oxide-mediated vasodilatation
6 weeks in the first trimester, from maternal dehydration and hypovolaemia
38 weeks in the third trimester, from placental ischaemia and vasospasm
Blood pressure never falls, as cardiac output matches vascular resistance

Maternal systemic blood pressure reaches its nadir in the mid-second trimester (20-24 weeks), driven by progesterone- and nitric oxide-mediated systemic vasodilatation that lowers peripheral vascular resistance. (Book p370)
Which of the following cardiovascular physical findings is considered entirely PHYSIOLOGICAL during normal pregnancy and does not signify heart disease?
Grade 1-2/6 mid-systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left sternal border
Continuous machinery murmur over the left infraclavicular area
A functional ejection systolic murmur (grade <=2/6) over the pulmonary area and an S3 are normal in >90% of pregnant women due to hyperdynamic flow. (Book p370)
What normal anatomical displacement of the heart occurs on chest X-ray and ECG during the third trimester as the uterus elevates the diaphragm?
The heart is displaced upward and laterally to the left, producing mild apparent cardiomegaly and left-axis deviation on ECG
The heart is pushed downward into the abdomen
The cardiac apex rotates to the right hemithorax (dextrocardia)
The heart becomes completely obscured by pleural effusion
Diaphragmatic elevation pushes the apex beat to the 4th intercostal space lateral to the midclavicular line, simulating cardiomegaly and left axis shift. (Book p370)
Fill up: Maternal cardiac output rises by about ______% in pregnancy and peaks around ______ weeks.
Output rises early and peaks at 20-24 weeks; further surges occur during labour and immediately after delivery. (Book p370)
Maternal cardiovascular hemodynamics & peak stress periods
Which of the following physical signs or symptoms in a pregnant woman is unequivocally PATHOLOGICAL and diagnostic of organic cardiac disease?
Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, hemoptysis, diastolic murmur, and persistent Jugular Venous Pressure > 8 cm H2O
Mild dependent ankle edema subsiding after night rest
Mild breathlessness when climbing two flights of stairs
Resting heart rate increase of 10-15 bpm
Diastolic murmurs, hemoptysis, orthopnea, PND, clubbing, and elevated JVP (>8 cm H2O) are pathological signs of structural cardiac disease. (Book p371)
What is the most common cause of heart disease in pregnancy in developing countries like India, and which specific valvular lesion is most frequently encountered?
Congenital Heart Disease; Coarctation of the aorta
Ischemic coronary heart disease; Myocardial infarction
