Rheumatic heart disease accounts for the majority of maternal cardiac disease in developing nations, with mitral stenosis being the classic predominant lesion. (Book p371)
What is the most common acyanotic congenital heart disease encountered in pregnant women?
Atrial Septal Defect (ASD, ostium secundum type)
Secundum ASD is the most common congenital cardiac lesion seen in adult pregnancy, generally well tolerated unless pulmonary hypertension develops. (Book p371)
What is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease encountered in pregnant women?
Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic heart defect; uncorrected TOF carries high maternal mortality and fetal loss rates. (Book p371)
Which of the following best distinguishes pathological heart disease from the normal cardiovascular changes of pregnancy?
A loud P2, a third heart sound and persistent basal crepitations are pathological, while a soft systolic flow murmur is not
Exertional dyspnoea in a pregnant woman is always pathological and needs echocardiography
Any systolic murmur heard over the pulmonary area in pregnancy indicates organic valve disease
Pedal oedema in the third trimester always indicates incipient cardiac failure
Breathlessness, a soft ejection murmur and ankle oedema are common in normal pregnancy; a loud P2, gallop rhythm and persistent crepitations are not. (Book p371)
Heart failure vs pregnancy signs, RHD & congenital lesions
Why do stenotic cardiac lesions (e.g., Mitral Stenosis, Aortic Stenosis) decompensate severely during pregnancy, whereas regurgitant lesions (Mitral Regurgitation) often improve?
Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling in stenosis, while low resistance helps regurgitant lesions
Progesterone dilates stenotic valves and worsens the pressure gradient
Oestrogen closes regurgitant valves completely during pregnancy
Stenotic lesions are unaffected by the blood volume shifts of pregnancy
Stenotic lesions cannot increase output through a fixed orifice and tachycardia shortens filling; regurgitant lesions benefit from the fall in resistance. (Book p371)
Under the modified WHO classification of maternal cardiovascular risk, what is the defining feature of WHO Class IV conditions?
Pregnancy contraindicated; mortality up to 30-50%, so termination is advised
Pregnancy is safe with routine outpatient visits; mortality under 1%
Caesarean delivery must be performed at 28 weeks; mortality 5-10%
Only oral iron therapy is needed; no excess maternal mortality
In modified WHO class IV, pregnancy is strictly contraindicated, maternal mortality is extremely high (up to 30-50%), and termination is advised if conception occurs. (Book p371)
Which of the following maternal cardiac conditions is classified under WHO Class IV, carrying the HIGHEST risk of maternal mortality (30-50%)?
Eisenmenger syndrome and severe pulmonary arterial hypertension carry a catastrophic 30-50% maternal mortality, primarily peripartum. (Book p371)

A pregnant woman with Marfan syndrome undergoes echocardiographic evaluation of her ascending aorta. At what aortic root diameter is pregnancy strictly contraindicated or termination strongly advised?
Aortic root diameter >= 40 to 45 mm (due to high risk of fatal aortic dissection or rupture)
Aortic root diameter is irrelevant in Marfan syndrome
An aortic root diameter >=40-45 mm in Marfan syndrome carries an extreme risk of lethal aortic dissection or rupture during pregnancy and labor. (Book p371)
All of the following are WHO class IV lesions in which pregnancy is contraindicated EXCEPT:
Mild mitral stenosis in NYHA class I
Pulmonary arterial hypertension of any cause
Severe left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction below 30%
Severe mitral stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension
Mild mitral stenosis with good functional class is a class II lesion with a small risk; the others carry prohibitive maternal mortality. (Book p371)
Lesion prognosis & WHO class IV contraindications
In a pregnant woman with stable, compensated cardiac disease, what is the preferred mode of delivery?
Spontaneous or induced vaginal delivery, as Caesarean section entails greater blood loss, infection risk, and hemodynamic instability
Routine elective Caesarean section under general anesthesia at 34 weeks
Vaginal delivery is preferred for cardiac patients because Caesarean delivery produces twice the blood loss and dramatic hemodynamic shifts. (Book p372)
Why is an instrumental delivery (vacuum or low forceps) routinely planned to assist the second stage of labor in a patient with cardiac disease?
To cut short the maternal bearing-down efforts that cause cardiac workload swings
To prevent fetal macrosomia and the obstructed labour that it would cause
Because cardiac drugs cause complete paralysis of the uterine muscle
Because cardiac patients cannot feel uterine contractions at all

Instrumental delivery is planned to cut short and eliminate strenuous maternal bearing-down (Valsalva) efforts, which produce sharp cardiac workload swings and protect the heart from acute preload surges. (Book p372)
During the active management of the third stage of labor in a woman with heart disease, what is the drug of choice for uterotonic prophylaxis, and what drug is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED?
Slow IV oxytocin infusion is the drug of choice; Methylergometrine is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED
Methylergometrine is the drug of choice; Oxytocin is contraindicated
Carboprost is the drug of choice; Misoprostol is contraindicated
Ergometrine and oxytocin should be given simultaneously in high doses
Oxytocin infusion is the drug of choice. Methylergometrine is contraindicated because it induces sustained vasoconstriction, hypertension, and pulmonary edema. (Book p372)
What intravenous fluid rate restriction is recommended during intrapartum care of a woman with cardiac disease to avoid volume overload?
Restrict total IV fluids to <= 75 mL/hour
Rapid bolus of 500 mL/hour normal saline
IV fluids are restricted to <=75 mL/hr to prevent iatrogenic circulatory overload and flash pulmonary edema in cardiac mothers. (Book p372)
A primigravida with tight mitral stenosis reaches full cervical dilatation. Which intrapartum measure matters most for her safety?
Cut the second stage short with forceps or vacuum under epidural analgesia and avoid Valsalva pushing
Encourage a long second stage of spontaneous pushing to avoid any instrumentation
Give intramuscular ergometrine with the delivery of the anterior shoulder
Withhold analgesia so that warning symptoms of failure are not masked
Epidural analgesia and instrumental shortening of the second stage blunt the dangerous cardiac output surges, and ergometrine is avoided. (Book p372)
Intrapartum & postpartum management of heart disease
What clinical criteria define Peripartum Cardiomyopathy (PPCM)?
Heart failure from left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction below 45% in the last month or first five months postpartum
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection presenting at 20 weeks of gestation
Aortic valve vegetations appearing during the first year after delivery
A congenital ventricular septal defect first detected in the third trimester
Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined by its timing, by systolic dysfunction and by the absence of another identifiable cause. (Book p373)
In addition to standard heart failure pharmacotherapy, which novel drug targeting the 16-kDa prolactin cleavage fragment has shown therapeutic benefit in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy?
Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist that inhibits pituitary prolactin release)
Carbergoline in high doses for lactation induction
16-kDa prolactin promotes endothelial apoptosis in PPCM; bromocriptine blocks prolactin release and improves myocardial recovery. (Book p373)

Match the lesion with its description — 1) Peripartum cardiomyopathy 2) Mitral stenosis 3) Severe aortic stenosis … A) Systolic dysfunction appearing in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months after delivery B) Diastolic murmur with a loud first sound and opening snap; tachycardia is poorly tolerated C) Fixed cardiac output, so obstruction makes labour and delivery extremely dangerous
Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined by its timing, mitral stenosis is a diastolic lesion that cannot raise output through tachycardia, and aortic stenosis fixes output. (Book p373)
In a pregnant woman with moderate-to-severe Mitral Stenosis (valve area < 1.5 cm^2), what is the first-line medical therapy to prevent pulmonary edema?
Beta-blockers (e.g., Metoprolol) to control heart rate and prolong diastolic ventricular filling time
High-dose intravenous hydralazine to induce tachycardia
Digoxin monotherapy to increase heart rate
Atropine bolus to maintain pulse > 120 bpm
Beta-blockers slow the heart rate, prolonging diastolic filling across the narrowed mitral valve and lowering left atrial pressure to prevent pulmonary edema. (Book p374)
When medical therapy fails in a pregnant patient with severe, refractory symptomatic Mitral Stenosis, what surgical/interventional procedure is preferred, and in which trimester?
Percutaneous Transvenous Mitral Commissurotomy (PTMC / Balloon Valvotomy), ideally performed in the second trimester
Open cardiopulmonary bypass valve replacement in the first trimester
Emergency mechanical valve replacement during active labor
Transapical aortic valve implantation at 12 weeks
PTMC (balloon mitral valvotomy) is the intervention of choice for refractory severe MS, ideally performed in the 2nd trimester after organogenesis. (Book p374)
Fill up: does the size of the thyroid gland normally change during pregnancy according to the notes is ______.
It remains unchanged and goitre is expected
It doubles only in the third trimester
It increases; a goitre remains pathological
It decreases and goitre is physiological
The thyroid gland increases in size in pregnancy, but goitre is still pathological. (Book p375)
Which of the following statements about Thyroid physiology is TRUE?
Overt hyperthyroid state with high free T4
Hypothyroid state with low total T4
Absent TSH secretion with low free hormones
Euthyroid state with normal free T3 and free T4
Pregnancy is a euthyroid state; free T3 and free T4 remain normal. (Book p375)
All of the following are Thyroid physiology EXCEPT:
Progesterone destroys free thyroxine — Estrogen raises TBG, increasing the protein-bound and theref
Maternal TSH crosses the placenta — Estrogen raises TBG, increasing the protein-bound and theref
The fetal thyroid produces maternal T4 — Estrogen raises TBG, increasing the protein-bound and theref
Estrogen raises TBG, increasing the protein-bound and therefore total T3/T4 values. (Book p375)
Fill up: The stated RDA of iodine in pregnancy is ______ daily.
The stated RDA of iodine in pregnancy is 250 micrograms daily. (Book p375)
Which of the following statements about Fetal thyroid is TRUE?
Maternal thyroxine because the fetal thyroid is not producing thyroxine
Fetal TSH crossing to the mother
Before 12 weeks, fetal thyroid thyroxine production is absent, so development depends on maternal thyroxine. (Book p375)
All of the following are Fetal thyroid EXCEPT:
At fertilization — The fetal thyroid begins thyroxine production at or after 12
At 6 weeks of gestation — The fetal thyroid begins thyroxine production at or after 12
Only after birth — The fetal thyroid begins thyroxine production at or after 12
At or after 12 weeks of gestation — The fetal thyroid begins thyroxine production at or after 12
The fetal thyroid begins thyroxine production at or after 12 weeks. (Book p375)
Fill up: ______ is listed as the most common cause of hypothyroidism.
Hashimoto's thyroiditis is listed as the most common cause of hypothyroidism. (Book p375)
Which of the following statements about Hypothyroidism is TRUE?
Maternal T3/T4 can cross the placenta, whereas maternal TSH cannot. (Book p375)
All of the following are Hypothyroidism EXCEPT:
10–15% — The notes advise increasing thyroxine by 30–50% after concep
70–90% — The notes advise increasing thyroxine by 30–50% after concep
30–50% — The notes advise increasing thyroxine by 30–50% after concep
5–10% — The notes advise increasing thyroxine by 30–50% after concep
The notes advise increasing thyroxine by 30–50% after conception in hypothyroidism. (Book p375)
Fill up: In pregnancy total T4 rises because oestrogen increases ______, so the best screening test of thyroid function is ______.
Oestrogen raises TBG and hence total T4, which is why free T4 and TSH rather than total T4 are used to judge thyroid status in pregnancy. (Book p375)
Fill up: ______ is identified as the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
Graves' disease is identified as the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. (Book p375)
Which of the following statements about Hyperthyroidism is TRUE?
PTU is the drug of choice in the first trimester. (Book p375)
All of the following are Hyperthyroidism EXCEPT:
They prevent fetal thyroid formation after 20 weeks
They are associated with aplasia cutis and choanal atresia
They cause fetal renal agenesis — Methimazole/carbimazole are avoided in T1 because of aplasia
They cause neonatal hypoglycemia — Methimazole/carbimazole are avoided in T1 because of aplasia
Methimazole/carbimazole are avoided in T1 because of aplasia cutis and choanal atresia risk. (Book p375)
Fill up: ______ is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy. (Book p375)
Which of the following statements about Thyroid storm is TRUE?
The source lists PTU as the drug of choice for thyroid storm and propranolol for symptoms. (Book p375)
A 28-year-old at 12 weeks with known Graves disease presents with fever of 39 C, a pulse of 150/min, profuse vomiting and new atrial fibrillation. What is the diagnosis and the first drug?
Thyroid storm — start propylthiouracil, then iodine an hour later, with a beta blocker
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis — reassure and repeat the thyroid profile in 4 weeks
Graves disease in pregnancy — start methimazole and plan radioiodine ablation after delivery now
Thyroid storm — start carbimazole and proceed to immediate delivery of the fetus
Thyroid storm is a medical emergency: propylthiouracil blocks both synthesis and T4-to-T3 conversion, iodine is given after an hour, and beta blockade controls the rate. (Book p375)
All of the following are Diabetes physiology EXCEPT:
hCG alone — hPL is listed among the hormones associated with insulin res
Oxytocin — hPL is listed among the hormones associated with insulin res
Prolactin-inhibiting factor — hPL is listed among the hormones associated with insulin res
Human placental lactogen (hPL) — hPL is listed among the hormones associated with insulin res
hPL is listed among the hormones associated with insulin resistance in pregnancy. (Book p376)
Fill up: The source distinguishes ______ as not causing insulin resistance.
The source distinguishes hCG as not causing insulin resistance. (Book p376)
Which of the following statements about Diabetes physiology is TRUE?
Significant insulin resistance develops around 24–28 weeks. (Book p376)
All of the following are Diabetes physiology regarding Progressing gestation increases hPL secretion and EXCEPT:
Glycosuria never occurs in pregnancy — Increasing hPL with gestation increases insulin resistance,
Estrogen eliminates glucose production — Increasing hPL with gestation increases insulin resistance,
Progressing gestation increases hPL secretion and insulin resistance
Maternal insulin freely crosses to the fetus
Increasing hPL with gestation increases insulin resistance, making pregnancy diabetogenic. (Book p376)
Fill up: ______ crosses the placenta, whereas maternal insulin does not.
Maternal insulin crosses; maternal glucose does not
Neither maternal glucose nor insulin crosses
Both cross equally by active transport
Maternal glucose crosses; maternal insulin does not
Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, whereas maternal insulin does not. (Book p376)
Which of the following statements about Diabetes physiology regarding Diabetes physiology — Glucose is TRUE?
Diabetes physiology — Maternal ketone bodies only
The fetus depends on maternal glucose for its glucose requirement. (Book p376)
All of the following are Diabetes physiology regarding Glycosuria — Glycosuria is described as EXCEPT:
Proteinuria of any degree — Glycosuria is described as normal in pregnancy
Glycosuria — Glycosuria is described as normal in pregnancy
Persistent ketonuria — Glycosuria is described as normal in pregnancy
Gross hematuria — Glycosuria is described as normal in pregnancy
Glycosuria is described as normal in pregnancy. (Book p376)
Fill up: should a pregnant woman with diabetes avoid fasting, vomiting, or diarrhea is ______.
They prevent glucose transfer to the fetus
They make maternal insulin cross the placenta
They can cause hypoglycemia followed by ketone-body formation and ketosis
Fasting, vomiting, or diarrhea can produce hypoglycemia, acetone bodies, and ketosis. (Book p376)
Which of the following statements about Diabetes physiology regarding Free-radical formation that crosses the placenta is TRUE?
Maternal insulin transfer to the fetus
Free-radical formation that crosses the placenta
Hyperglycemia increases free radicals that cross the placenta and contribute to congenital malformations. (Book p376)
Which of the following statements about placental transfer in diabetic pregnancy is TRUE?
Glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion but insulin does not, so the fetal pancreas makes its own insulin
Maternal insulin crosses the placenta freely and is the main driver of fetal macrosomia
Neither glucose nor insulin crosses the placenta, so the fetus depends on amino acids and lactate alone
Anti-TSH receptor antibodies cross the placenta, but neither glucose nor insulin can cross it
Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia because glucose crosses freely while insulin, and most oral agents such as glyburide, cross poorly. (Book p376)
All of the following are Diabetes classification EXCEPT:
A normoglycemic woman develops diabetes only after 24 weeks
It resolves within 6 weeks after delivery
It has no free-radical formation before organogenesis
A diabetic woman conceives and hyperglycemia is present from day 1
In pregestational diabetes, the woman is diabetic at conception and blood sugar is high from day 1. (Book p377)
Fill up: are congenital malformations characteristic of pregestational diabetes but not typical gestational diabetes is ______.
In GDM, free radicals form after organogenesis
Pregestational diabetes never produces free radicals
GDM usually develops later, with free radicals forming after organogenesis, so congenital malformations are not typical. (Book p377)
Which of the following statements about Diabetes classification is TRUE?
It resolves only after insulin therapy
It resolves within 6 weeks after delivery
It progresses immediately to type 1 diabetes
The notes state that GDM resolves within 6 weeks postpartum. (Book p377)
All of the following are White classification EXCEPT:
Type 1 diabetes with nephropathy — Type A in the Priscilla White classification denotes gestati
Thyroid disease in pregnancy — Type A in the Priscilla White classification denotes gestati
Gestational diabetes — Type A in the Priscilla White classification denotes gestati
Pregestational diabetes — Type A in the Priscilla White classification denotes gestati
Type A in the Priscilla White classification denotes gestational diabetes. (Book p377)
Fill up: differentiates A1 from A2 gestational diabetes is ______.
A1 is pregestational; A2 is gestational
A1 needs cesarean delivery; A2 never does
A1 has fetal echo; A2 has no ultrasound
A1 is diet controlled; A2 is controlled with insulin or metformin
A1 GDM is diet controlled, while A2 is controlled with medication such as insulin or metformin. (Book p377)
Which of the following statements about GDM timing is TRUE?
GDM usually develops between 24 and 28 weeks. (Book p377)
All of the following are GDM timing EXCEPT:
Rh sensitization — Diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks is usually pregestational
Pregestational diabetes — Diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks is usually pregestational
Physiological glycosuria only — Diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks is usually pregestational
Inevitable abortion — Diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks is usually pregestational
Diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks is usually pregestational diabetes. (Book p377)
Fill up: Universal screening for gestational diabetes is performed at ______ weeks, and women with strong risk factors are additionally tested ______.
All women are screened at 24-28 weeks, and those with risk factors are screened early at booking and retested later if the first test is normal. (Book p377)
Which statement about GDM follow-up — source directs confirmation is TRUE?
Urine dipstick at 12 months is the listed gdm follow-up as per the notes
Fetal echocardiography at 6 weeks postpartum is the listed gdm follow-up as per the notes
A glucose test at 6 weeks postpartum is the listed gdm follow-up as per the notes
HbA1c on the day of delivery only is the listed gdm follow-up as per the notes
The source directs confirmation with a sugar-level test 6 weeks postpartum. (Book p377)
Which statement about Diabetes imaging — TIFFA done for is TRUE?
Only diet-controlled GDM at 10 weeks is the listed diabetes imaging as per the notes
Only pregestational diabetes after 34 weeks is the listed diabetes imaging as per the notes

Only at 20 and 22 completed weeks of gestation

The listed treatment is 3 teaspoons glucose in 100 mL water, or 6 teaspoons sugar in 100 mL water. (Book p386)
All of the following are maternal complications of diabetes in pregnancy EXCEPT:
Pre-eclampsia, candidiasis, polyhydramnios, infections and progression of retinopathy and nephropathy are all linked to diabetes; placenta previa is not. (Book p386)
In Pedersen hypothesis, maternal hyperglycemia first produces which fetal change?
Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia before stimulating the fetal pancreas. (Book p387)
What endocrine state results after fetal hyperglycemia stimulates the fetal pancreas?
Fetal hyperglycemia stimulates the fetal pancreas, producing hyperinsulinemia. (Book p387)
How does fetal hyperinsulinemia contribute to shoulder dystocia?
It increases growth and fat deposition around the fetal shoulder
Fetal hyperinsulinemia promotes macrosomia and shoulder fat deposition, leading to shoulder dystocia. (Book p387)
IUGR in a diabetic pregnancy is expected primarily when which condition coexists?
The notes restrict IUGR in diabetes to cases with vasculopathy or PIH. (Book p387)
Which hormones are identified as needed for fetal growth?
Insulin and IGFs are named as hormones needed for fetal growth. (Book p387)
Uncontrolled diabetes raises the risk of which early pregnancy outcome?
Uncontrolled diabetes increases the risk of abortion. (Book p387)
Why is stillbirth risk increased in diabetes according to the source?
All diabetic fetuses have structural renal anomalies
Macrosomia raises oxygen demand and hyperglycemia causes oxidative stress and chorionic-villus edema
Maternal insulin crosses and causes fetal bradycardia
Macrosomia increases oxygen demand, while hyperglycemia causes oxidative stress and villous edema that reduce oxygen transport. (Book p387)
When is diabetic stillbirth most common according to the notes?
In the last 2 weeks of pregnancy
The notes state that diabetic stillbirth is most common in the last 2 weeks of pregnancy. (Book p387)

Match the mechanism with its consequence — 1) Pedersen hypothesis 2) Diabetic embryopathy in the first trimester 3) Neonatal hypoglycaemia after cord clamping … A) Caudal regression and cardiac anomalies B) Fetal hyperinsulinaemia causing macrosomia and organomegaly C) Continued fetal insulin action once the maternal glucose supply stops
Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia (Pedersen), early hyperglycaemia malforms the embryo, and sustained fetal insulin causes postnatal hypoglycaemia. (Book p387)
Why does neonatal hypoglycemia occur after a diabetic pregnancy?
Maternal glucose supply stops at birth while fetal insulin remains high
Maternal insulin starts crossing after birth
Fetal insulin production stops abruptly before birth
The placenta continues supplying glucose after birth
At birth maternal glucose supply is lost but fetal insulin remains high, causing neonatal hypoglycemia. (Book p387)
Which neonatal electrolyte abnormalities are listed as triggered by hypoglycemia?
Hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia are listed with neonatal hypoglycemia. (Book p387)
Why is respiratory distress syndrome increased in the infant of a diabetic mother?
Maternal glucose cannot cross the placenta
It is caused only by fetal anemia
High fetal insulin suppresses surfactant production, increasing RDS risk. (Book p387)
Hypoxia in the infant of a diabetic mother leads to which sequence?
Increased erythropoietin, polycythemia, hyperviscosity, and hyperbilirubinemia
Hypoxia raises erythropoietin, causing polycythemia, hyperviscosity, and hyperbilirubinemia. (Book p387)
Which complication is specifically NOT seen in the neonatal complication list of diabetes?
The source explicitly notes that anemia is not seen as a neonatal complication. (Book p387)
Which late outcome is listed for a child born after a diabetic pregnancy?
Late child outcomes include obesity, metabolic syndrome, and a 1–3% risk of type 2 diabetes. (Book p388)
How is fetal lung maturity testing performed according to the notes?
By amniocentesis in the third trimester
By fetal echocardiography in the first trimester
Lung maturity tests are done on amniotic fluid obtained by third-trimester amniocentesis. (Book p388)
What is the most common fetal lung-maturity test listed?
The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio is listed as the most common lung-maturity test. (Book p388)
What L/S ratio indicates mature fetal lungs in the notes?
An L/S ratio of 2:1 or greater indicates lung maturity. (Book p388)
Which is identified as the best lung-maturity test when done at or after 35 weeks?
Phosphatidylglycerol is the best test, done at or after 35 weeks. (Book p388)
Which of the following statements about the infant of a diabetic mother is TRUE?
Fetal hyperinsulinaemia antagonises cortisol and delays surfactant maturation, raising the risk of respiratory distress at any gestation
Neonatal hypoglycaemia is rare, because the fetal pancreas involutes promptly after delivery
Neonatal polycythaemia and jaundice result from fetal hypo-insulinaemia and reduced oxygen consumption
Amniocentesis to document lung maturity is mandatory before every delivery in a diabetic pregnancy
Hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant, chronic intrauterine hyperglycaemia drives polycythaemia, and lung maturity testing is selective, not universal. (Book p388)
What does the presence of phosphatidylglycerol indicate?
Presence of phosphatidylglycerol indicates lung maturity. (Book p388)
Which lamellar-body count guarantees 100% lung maturity in the notes?
A lamellar-body count above 50,000/mL indicates 100% mature lungs. (Book p388)
What lamellar-body count is considered a positive test in amniotic fluid?
A lamellar-body count of 30,000–40,000/mL AF is termed positive. (Book p388)
In the obsolete Nile blue sulfate test, what result indicates mature lungs?
Orange cells are mature skin cells; more than 50% orange cells indicates mature lungs. (Book p388)
Fill up: Phosphatidylglycerol appears in amniotic fluid at about ______ weeks, and its presence is taken to indicate ______.
A lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio of 2:1 and the appearance of phosphatidylglycerol around 35 weeks both indicate that the fetal lungs are mature. (Book p388)
How is shoulder dystocia defined in the source notes?
Inability to deliver the fetal shoulder within 1 minute of head delivery
Failure to deliver the head within 10 minutes of crowning
Any prolonged second stage over 2 hours
Shoulder dystocia is inability to deliver the fetal shoulder within 1 minute after head delivery. (Book p388)
What is the turtle sign in shoulder dystocia?
Recession of the fetal head into the perineum
The turtle sign is recession of the delivered fetal head back into the perineum. (Book p388)
Fill up: The first manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia is ______, which works by ______.
McRoberts positioning; flattening the lumbar lordosis and rotating the symphysis pubis upwards
fundal pressure; driving the anterior shoulder below the symphysis pubis
the Zavanelli manoeuvre; replacing the head before caesarean delivery
the Woods corkscrew; widening the bisacromial diameter of the shoulders
Hyperflexing the maternal thighs on the abdomen flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis, freeing the impacted anterior shoulder. (Book p388)
What is the first action in the listed shoulder-dystocia management sequence?
Proceed directly to cesarean before assessment
The sequence begins by calling for help. (Book p389)
Which early surgical adjunct is listed in shoulder-dystocia management?
The management sequence includes liberal episiotomy. (Book p389)
What is the first and most effective maneuver for shoulder dystocia?
McRoberts maneuver is described as the first and most effective maneuver. (Book p389)
What does the McRoberts maneuver involve?
Delivery of the posterior arm first
Flexion and abduction of the legs against the abdomen
Extension of both legs below the table
Internal rotation of one shoulder only
McRoberts uses flexion and abduction of the maternal legs against the abdomen. (Book p389)
Why does the McRoberts maneuver help shoulder dystocia?
It rotates both fetal shoulders internally at the pelvic brim
It decreases the bisacromial diameter of the fetal shoulders
It straightens the sacrum and increases the space available
It increases the bony pelvic diameter by about 5 cm
The McRoberts manoeuvre straightens the sacrum relative to the lumbar spine and increases the available space, without increasing the pelvic diameter. (Book p389)
What is added if McRoberts maneuver alone fails?
If McRoberts fails, sustained suprapubic pressure in thrusts is added. (Book p389)
Which maneuver performs manual rotation of the shoulders in shoulder dystocia?
The Enter maneuver is manual rotation of the shoulders. (Book p389)
Which statement correctly compares Wood's corkscrew and Rubin maneuvers?
Wood's corkscrew rotates both shoulders; Rubin rotates one shoulder
Wood's rotates one shoulder; Rubin rotates both
Wood's corkscrew acts on both shoulders, whereas Rubin's maneuver acts on one. (Book p389)
What is the maneuver called when the posterior fetal arm is delivered?
Delivery of the posterior arm is the Jacquemier maneuver. (Book p389)
Which maneuver places the mother on all fours?
The all-fours maneuver is Gaskin maneuver. (Book p389)
What is the last-step Zavanelli maneuver?
Push the fetal head back into the uterus and perform cesarean section
Deliver the posterior arm with traction
Zavanelli replaces the fetal head into the uterus before cesarean delivery. (Book p389)
What can be done for shoulder dystocia in a dead baby according to the notes?
For a dead baby, clavicular fracture (cleidotomy) is listed. (Book p389)
Which intervention is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia management?
Fundal pressure is specifically contraindicated. (Book p389)
What is the maximum time allowed for each shoulder-dystocia maneuver before moving to the next step?
Each maneuver is performed for a maximum of 30 seconds before escalating. (Book p389)
McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure have failed and the anterior shoulder is still impacted behind the symphysis. Which manoeuvre should be attempted next?
Internal rotation with Woods corkscrew or Rubin II, or delivery of the posterior arm
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant while traction continues
Immediate Zavanelli manoeuvre and caesarean delivery
Symphysiotomy before any rotational manoeuvre is attempted
After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, internal rotation or posterior arm delivery reduces the bisacromial diameter; fundal pressure is contraindicated. (Book p389)
What is the most common fetal complication of shoulder dystocia?
Erb's palsy is listed as the most common fetal complication. (Book p389)
What arm position is characteristic of Erb palsy (policeman/porter tip hand)?
Both arms held above the head
Flexed at elbow with hyperextended wrist only
The source describes Erb palsy as an internally rotated, adducted, and pronated arm. (Book p389)
What is the most common maternal complication of shoulder dystocia?
Postpartum hemorrhage is the most common maternal complication. (Book p389)
Which nerve is most commonly injured during McRoberts maneuver?
The facial nerve, compressed against the maternal symphysis pubis
The ulnar nerve, compressed at the elbow during positioning
The phrenic nerve, stretched by the hyperflexed thighs
The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, compressed under the inguinal ligament
Hyperflexing the thighs compresses the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh under the inguinal ligament, causing meralgia paraesthetica. (Book p389)
All of the following are recognised fetal complications of shoulder dystocia EXCEPT:

Brachial plexus injury, long-bone fracture and asphyxia follow traumatic delivery and prolonged head-to-body interval; talipes is not caused by shoulder dystocia. (Book p389)
Fill up: Blood-pressure finding defines hypertension in pregnancy in the notes is ______.
At least 130/80 mmHg on one occasion
At least 160/110 mmHg on two occasions 24 hours apart
At least 150/100 mmHg after delivery only

Hypertension is BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two readings 4 hours apart. (Book p390)

Persistent severe BP after the 15-minute repeat requires antihypertensives. (Book p390)
Fill up: Chronic hypertension is present from day 1 in ______ who was hypertensive when she conceived.

BP is elevated only during labor
A woman with hypertension conceives and BP is high from day 1

Chronic hypertension is present from day 1 in a woman who was hypertensive when she conceived. (Book p390)

Hypertension occurs only during the first trimester

A previously normotensive woman develops hypertension after 20 weeks due to placental pathology
PIH begins after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive woman and is related to placental pathology. (Book p390)
Which statement about the postpartum course of pregnancy-induced hypertension is TRUE?
Blood pressure usually normalises within 12 weeks of delivery
Blood pressure usually normalises within 48 hours of delivery
Hypertension persisting beyond 12 weeks is still called gestational hypertension
Blood pressure never returns to normal after pregnancy-induced hypertension
PIH usually normalises within 12 weeks of delivery; a blood pressure still raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as chronic hypertension. (Book p390)

A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Transient hypertension only
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Chronic hypertension
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Gestational hypertension
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Mild pre-eclampsia
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as chronic hypertension. (Book p390)
Fill up: Gestational hypertension is a blood pressure of ______ mmHg or more recorded after 20 weeks in a woman without proteinuria.

Elevated blood pressure alone, above 140/90 mmHg
A history of a prior pregnancy affected by hypertension
Proteinuria and/or signs of maternal end-organ damage
Onset of the hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation
In the source comparison, proteinuria and/or signs of end-organ damage distinguish pre-eclampsia from gestational hypertension. (Book p390)

Match the proteinuria test with the threshold that makes it positive — 1) 24-hour urinary protein 2) Urine protein:creatinine ratio 3) Urine dipstick used for OPD screening … A) At least 300 mg per 24 hours B) At least 0.3 C) At least +1

Which statement about Proteinuria — urine protein creatinine is TRUE?
At least 0.03 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
At least 3.0 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
At least 30 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
At least 0.3 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes

A 32-year-old G3P1L1 at 9 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding proteinuria. Advise that at least +4 only is the correct proteinuria for this patient at this gestation

Serum uric acid only is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
24-hour urinary protein excretion is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
Urine dipstick is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
Fundus examination is the listed proteinuria as per the notes

Match the severe-feature test with its end-organ-damage threshold — 1) Platelet count 2) Serum creatinine 3) Hepatic transaminases … A) Below 1 lakh/mm³ B) At least 1.1 mg/dL C) At least twice the normal level

Which statement about End-organ damage — Serum creatinine 1 is TRUE?
At least 0.3 mg/dL is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
At least 0.8 mg/dL only is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
At least 5 mg/dL only is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
At least 1.1 mg/dL is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Serum creatinine ≥1.1 mg/dL is a listed severe feature. (Book p391)

A 32-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding end-organ damage. Advise that transaminases at least twice normal is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation

Advise that low bilirubin only is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation
Advise that low ldh only is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation
Transaminases at least two times normal are a severe feature; placental ALP normally rises in pregnancy. (Book p391)
Which statement about End-organ damage — Pulmonary edema and is TRUE?
Rh negativity and proteinuria alone is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Pulmonary edema and cerebral/visual symptoms is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Physiological pedal edema and glycosuria is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Anemia and hyperemesis is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Pulmonary edema and cerebral or visual symptoms are listed severe features. (Book p391)

A 36-year-old with known chronic hypertension, previously well controlled on methyldopa, is now 28 weeks pregnant. Her blood pressure has become uncontrollable and she has developed new 2+ proteinuria. What is the diagnosis?
Gestational hypertension alone, since she was hypertensive before
Transient hypertension of pregnancy, needing no treatment
Mild pre-eclampsia, which carries the best prognosis
Superimposed pre-eclampsia is chronic hypertension with uncontrollable blood pressure, new proteinuria or end-organ damage after 20 weeks, and it carries a bad prognosis. (Book p391)

Match the superimposed pre-eclampsia with the correct detail — 1) is aspirin considered in a woman with chronic 2) urine protein:creatinine ratio meets the listed proteinuria threshold 3) dipstick protein result is the OPD screening threshold … A) To prevent superimposed pre-eclampsia B) At least 0.3 C) At least +1
The source notes aspirin use to prevent superimposed PE in chronic hypertension. (Book p391)

Match the hypertensive disorder with its definition — 1) Pre-eclampsia 2) Superimposed pre-eclampsia 3) Gestational hypertension … A) New proteinuria, hypertension or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks B) Chronic hypertension with new proteinuria or a sudden worsening of control C) Hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria that settles by 12 weeks postpartum
Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ involvement; superimposed disease is a change in a woman who was already hypertensive. (Book p391)

A 32-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks has a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg with 2+ urine protein. Her platelets, creatinine and transaminases are normal and she has no headache or visual symptoms. How is this classified?
Mild pre-eclampsia, the pressure being 140/90 to under 160/110
Severe pre-eclampsia on the degree of proteinuria alone

Mild pre-eclampsia is a blood pressure of 140/90 to under 160/110 mmHg without severe features; the degree of proteinuria does not differentiate mild from severe. (Book p392)

Severe PE is defined by BP ≥160/110 or severe features/end-organ damage. (Book p392)
All of the following are listed as NON-differentiating between mild and severe pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
A blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or higher
The degree of proteinuria, oliguria and IUGR are all listed as non-differentiating; a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or higher does differentiate mild from severe pre-eclampsia. (Book p392)
Which statement about Severity assessment — Oliguria listed as is TRUE?
Visual symptoms is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
End-organ damage is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
Oliguria is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
Severe BP elevation is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
Oliguria is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both. (Book p392)

A 24-year-old G2P1L1 at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding severity assessment. According to the notes, iUGR is a non-differentiating feature in the source table. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that bp ≥160/110 mmhg is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
Advise that pulmonary edema is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
Advise that severe headache is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
Advise that iugr is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
IUGR is a non-differentiating feature in the source table. (Book p392)
Which statement about edema in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
Edema is pathological when it does not subside with rest and involves non-dependent parts
Edema is pathological only when it is confined to the ankles after standing
Any edema appearing in pregnancy is by definition a severe feature
Edema is always absent in pregnancy-induced hypertension
Pathological edema does not improve with rest and is present in dependent and non-dependent parts, unlike physiological dependent edema which settles overnight. (Book p392)
A woman with pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks reports a severe headache that has not responded to her usual analgesics, and her blood pressure is now 160/110 mmHg. Which feature is she showing?
Impending eclampsia, from a severe headache unrelieved by usual medication
Migraine with aura, occurring independently of her pre-eclampsia

The physiological headache of pregnancy, needing only reassurance

All of the following are listed visual warning symptoms of impending eclampsia EXCEPT:

Fill up: Fundus examination is part of evaluating visual symp______ms in PIH.
Fundus examination is part of evaluating visual symptoms in PIH. (Book p392)
All of the following suggest impending eclampsia EXCEPT:
Polyuria with a urine output above 200 mL per hour
Persistent frontal headache that does not respond to simple analgesia
Blurring of vision, scotomata or photophobia
Vomiting with severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
Oliguria, not polyuria, accompanies severe disease; headache, visual disturbance and epigastric pain are the classic warning symptoms. (Book p392)
Fill up: The notes state that all women with pre-eclampsia should be ______.
Observed at home without any tests
Managed on an OPD basis only
Discharged after a single blood-pressure reading
The notes state that all pre-eclampsia patients should be admitted. (Book p392)
Which statement about the investigations emphasised in all pre-eclampsia patients is TRUE?
Liver function tests, serum creatinine and platelet count are the three highlighted tests
Karyotyping, TORCH serology and VDRL are the three highlighted tests
Serum bile acids, indirect Coombs test and OGTT are the three highlighted tests
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, calcium and HbA1c are the three highlighted tests
LFT, serum creatinine and platelet count are the three investigations highlighted for every pre-eclampsia patient. (Book p392)
Fill up: Eclampsia is called atypical when convulsions occur before ______ weeks of gestation or more than ______ after delivery.

Which statement about Eclampsia — Eclampsia severe PE is TRUE?
Proteinuria without hypertension is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Chronic hypertension with edema only is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Severe pre-eclampsia with generalized tonic-clonic seizures is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Any seizure in a pregnant woman with normal BP is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Eclampsia is severe PE plus generalized tonic-clonic seizures. (Book p393)
A 26-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure before the onset of labour pain. Which type of eclampsia is this, and what is its prognosis?
Antepartum eclampsia, the commonest type and the worst prognosis
Intrapartum eclampsia, the commonest type and the worst prognosis
Postpartum eclampsia, which is uncommon and has the best prognosis
Atypical eclampsia, needing anticonvulsants for six months
Antepartum eclampsia is the most common type and has the worst prognosis; postpartum eclampsia is within 48 hours of delivery and onset beyond 48 hours is atypical. (Book p393)
Fill up: Postpartum eclampsia occurs after delivery ______.
Postpartum eclampsia occurs after delivery within 48 hours. (Book p393)

Match the atypical eclampsia with the correct detail — 1) seizure timing is atypical for eclampsia 2) antenatal seizure timing should be considered atypical eclampsia 3) is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia … A) More than 48 hours after delivery B) Before 20 weeks of pregnancy C) MRI
Onset beyond 48 hours postpartum is a feature of atypical eclampsia. (Book p393)
Which statement about Atypical eclampsia — seizure before 20 is TRUE?
During the second stage of labor is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
At 40 weeks only is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
Before 20 weeks of pregnancy is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
After 37 weeks is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
A seizure before 20 weeks is an atypical-eclampsia feature. (Book p393)
Which statement about Atypical eclampsia — MRI investigation of is TRUE?
Plain abdominal X-ray is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
DIPSI is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
Kleihauer–Betke test is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
MRI is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
MRI is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia. (Book p393)

A 30-year-old G3P1L1 at 11 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pres. According to the notes, pRES is described as edema localized to the posterior cerebral hemisphere. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that posterior cerebral hemisphere is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
Advise that pituitary gland is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
Advise that cerebellar vermis only is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
Advise that frontal sinus is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
PRES is described as edema localized to the posterior cerebral hemisphere. (Book p393)
Which statement about Gestational hypertension — source states that is TRUE?
The source states that about 0% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 50% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 5% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 100% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 50% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE. (Book p393)
How should gestational hypertension with BP at least 160/110 mmHg be managed?
Severe-range gestational hypertension is managed like severe PE. (Book p393)
A woman first found hypertensive after 20 weeks has no proteinuria or end-organ damage. What is the provisional diagnosis?

Which of the following statements about posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
PRES causes headache, visual loss and seizures with occipital vasogenic oedema on MRI, and is managed by blood pressure control and seizure control
PRES is a haemorrhagic stroke that needs immediate neurosurgical decompression
PRES occurs only in eclampsia and is never seen in non-obstetric patients

What is the role of extravillous trophoblast in normal pregnancy?
It constricts spiral arteries to reduce placental flow
It replaces spiral-artery lining and converts high-resistance vessels to low-resistance vessels
Extravillous trophoblast replaces spiral-artery lining, converting high-resistance arteries to low-resistance vessels. (Book p394)
Why is spiral-artery remodeling important in normal pregnancy?
Trophoblastic invasion and vascular remodeling maintain uteroplacental circulation. (Book p394)
When does the first phase of normal spiral-artery remodeling occur and what segment is replaced?
At 12 weeks; the decidual segment lining
The first phase occurs around 12 weeks and replaces the decidual segment lining. (Book p394)
When does the second phase of normal spiral-artery remodeling occur and what segment is replaced?
At 16–20 weeks; the myometrial segment lining
The second phase is 16–20 weeks and replaces the myometrial segment lining. (Book p394)
Which maternal immune cell type participates in spiral-artery remodeling?
Maternal NK cells play a role in vascular remodeling. (Book p394)
What is incomplete in trophoblastic invasion in PIH according to the notes?
In PIH, the second phase of trophoblastic invasion is incomplete. (Book p394)
What happens to spiral-artery resistance when trophoblastic remodeling is incomplete?
It becomes unrelated to placental blood flow
Incomplete invasion leaves resistance high. (Book p394)
What immediate placental consequence follows persistently high spiral-artery resistance?
Reduced blood volume in the intervillous space and placental ischemia
High resistance lowers intervillous blood volume, producing placental ischemia. (Book p394)
Fill up: Trophoblast normally converts spiral arteries into ______ vessels, and in pre-eclampsia this conversion fails to reach the ______ segment.
Failed remodelling of the myometrial segment leaves high-resistance vessels, so the placenta is under-perfused and releases anti-angiogenic factors. (Book p394)
How does placental ischemia affect placental size in the source pathway?
It has no effect on placenta
Placental ischemia decreases placental size and contributes to uteroplacental insufficiency. (Book p395)
What fetal growth consequence follows uteroplacental insufficiency in PIH?
Reduced fetal blood supply causes IUGR. (Book p395)
Why can oligohydramnios develop in PIH with placental insufficiency?
Fetal brain sparing reduces renal blood flow, causing oliguria
Maternal insulin crosses and stops urine formation
Placental ischemia increases fetal renal blood flow
Brain sparing directs blood to brain and away from kidneys, causing oliguria and oligohydramnios. (Book p395)
Which mediator is increased in PIH and is an antiangiogenic soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase?

Decreased thromboxane A2 with increased prostacyclin I2

Match the mediator with its role in pre-eclampsia — 1) Excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 2) Placental growth factor 3) Endothelin-1 … A) Falls in pre-eclampsia and forms the denominator of the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio B) Antagonises VEGF and PlGF, producing endothelial dysfunction and proteinuria C) A powerful vasoconstrictor released from damaged endothelium

Which three elements form the Virchow-triad pathway in PIH noted in the source?

Raised serum urea, uric acid, and creatinine
Low creatinine with low uric acid
Reduced filtration raises serum urea, uric acid, and creatinine. (Book p396)
Which process can lead from leaky cerebral capillary endothelium to eclamptic seizures?

Cerebral edema, hypoxia, and excitatory-neurotransmitter release

Why do visual disturbances occur in PIH according to the notes?
Cerebral hyperperfusion affects the occipital lobe
The retina is replaced by trophoblast
Maternal insulin crosses the optic nerve

Which of the following statements about death from severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia is TRUE?

Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the commonest cause of death in eclampsia

Which reproductive history represents first exposure to placenta and raises PIH risk?
