Antihistamines cure the condition, so pregnancy may safely continue to 42 weeks
Warfarin is the anticoagulant of choice when vitamin K deficiency causes a prolonged prothrombin time
A widespread urticarial rash always precedes the pruritus of intrahepatic cholestasis
Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line; vitamin K is given to the mother to prevent haemorrhage and warfarin is unsafe in pregnancy. (Book p409)
Where is the Rh antigen locus located according to the notes?
The Rh antigen locus is on the short arm of chromosome 1. (Book p410)
Which set lists the Rh antigens given in the source?
C, c, D, E, and e
The listed Rh antigens are C, c, D, E, and e. (Book p410)
Around what gestational age does Rh antigen formation occur according to the notes?
Rh antigen formation is stated to occur by 38 days of gestation. (Book p410)
What maternal-fetal pairing defines an Rh-negative pregnancy at risk?
An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is the high-risk pairing. (Book p410)
What paternal result makes the fetus definitively Rh-negative and removes the Rh-related high-risk concern in the source flowchart?
If the father is Rh-negative, the fetus will be Rh-negative and is not high risk in the source diagram. (Book p410)
What fetal Rh-positive probability is shown when the father is Rh-positive in the source flowchart?
The source diagram gives a 50% chance of an Rh-positive fetus when the father is Rh-positive. (Book p410)
Fill up: The clinically most important Rh antibody is ______, and without prophylaxis about ______ of Rh-negative women carrying an Rh-positive fetus become sensitised.
Anti-D is the antibody that matters; roughly 15% of at-risk women are immunised by a pregnancy or delivery unless anti-D immunoglobulin is given. (Book p410)
What testing should be done at the first antenatal visit before identifying an Rh-negative mother?
ABO and Rh typing are done at the first ANC visit. (Book p411)
What paternal assessment is required after identifying an Rh-negative pregnant woman?
No paternal assessment is ever relevant
The husband's Rh type must be assessed in an Rh-negative pregnancy. (Book p411)
Which events are listed as causes of fetomaternal hemorrhage in an Rh-negative mother?
Bleeding, invasive procedures, and versions are listed causes of fetomaternal hemorrhage. (Book p411)
What is the first antibody produced when an Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh antigen?
IgM is produced initially after Rh antigen exposure. (Book p411)
Why is the first Rh-positive pregnancy generally safe in an unsensitized Rh-negative mother?
All Rh-positive fetuses are Rh-negative in first pregnancy
Initially produced IgM cannot cross the placenta; IgG is produced after delivery
Maternal IgG cannot ever be made
Fetal red cells cannot enter maternal blood
The initial antibody is IgM, which cannot cross the placenta; significant IgG follows after delivery. (Book p411)
Why is a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy at risk after previous sensitization?
IgG is formed quickly and crosses the placenta to hemolyze fetal cells
Prior exposure prompts rapid IgG formation; IgG crosses the placenta and causes fetal hemolysis. (Book p411)

Match the manifestation with its mechanism — 1) Hydrops fetalis 2) Kernicterus 3) Early neonatal anaemia … A) Unconjugated bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei B) Severe anaemia with ascites, scalp oedema and an enlarged placenta C) Ongoing haemolysis in the first days of life needing phototherapy or exchange transfusion
Severe haemolysis causes hydrops in utero, bilirubin causes kernicterus after birth, and continuing antibody action causes early neonatal anaemia. (Book p411)
What is the initiating fetal complication of Rh isoimmunization?
Rh antibodies cause fetal hemolysis. (Book p412)
What severe sequence can follow fetal anemia in Rh isoimmunization?
Heart failure followed by hydrops fetalis
Severe fetal anemia causes heart failure and then hydrops fetalis. (Book p412)
What compensatory response produces erythroblastosis fetalis?
Hepatosplenomegaly and bone-marrow hyperplasia increasing erythrocytes
Reduced erythropoiesis within the fetal bone marrow and liver
Fetal insulin suppression from maternal antibody transfer
Maternal platelet activation with consumptive coagulopathy
Erythroblastosis fetalis reflects the compensatory response of hepatosplenomegaly and bone-marrow hyperplasia producing more erythrocytes. (Book p412)
Which maternal complications are linked to placentomegaly in Rh disease?
Placentomegaly can cause PIH and polyhydramnios. (Book p412)
What CTG/NST pattern can indicate fetal anemia?
A sinusoidal heart-wave pattern on CTG/NST is an indication of fetal anemia. (Book p412)
What MCA Doppler value indicates fetal anemia?
Peak systolic velocity less than 0.5 MoM
Peak systolic velocity at least 1.5 MoM
MCA peak systolic velocity ≥1.5 MoM signals fetal anemia. (Book p412)
Which is a listed cause of fetal anemia besides Rh isoimmunization?
Vasa previa or twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
The notes list Rh isoimmunization, vasa previa, and twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome as causes. (Book p412)
Fill up: Fetal anaemia is detected non-invasively by Doppler of the ______, where a peak systolic velocity above ______ multiples of the median suggests severe anaemia.
Anaemia lowers blood viscosity and raises middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity; above 1.5 multiples of the median it predicts severe anaemia. (Book p412)
An antigen that sensitizes the mother
Anti-D is an antibody against the Rh antigen. (Book p412)
How does externally administered anti-D prevent Rh sensitization?
It increases fetal haemolysis, clearing Rh-positive cells from the circulation
It converts the fetal Rh type from positive to negative while in utero
It neutralises Rh-positive fetal red cells before maternal antibodies form
It stimulates the mother to produce her own protective anti-D antibodies
Externally administered anti-D neutralises Rh-positive fetal red cells before the maternal immune system mounts stimulation and forms excess antibodies. (Book p412)
In which pregnancy is anti-D beneficial?
An Rh-positive mother with no antibody screen
Any pregnancy regardless of Rh type
Anti-D is beneficial only in Rh-negative unsensitized pregnancies. (Book p412)
Which of the following statements about anti-D immunoglobulin is TRUE?
Anti-D clears Rh-positive fetal red cells from the maternal circulation before the mother can mount her own immune response
Anti-D is a live vaccine that must be given before pregnancy to work
Anti-D given after delivery protects the infant by suppressing the fetal immune system
Anti-D is effective only in the first trimester and is never given after delivery
Passive anti-D causes rapid clearance of fetal cells so the mother never makes her own antibody; it is given after any sensitising event and at 28 weeks. (Book p412)
What low anti-D dose is listed for routine prophylaxis?
The routine low dose is 300 micrograms of anti-D. (Book p413)
A 300-microgram anti-D dose neutralizes up to what volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage?
Three hundred micrograms neutralizes up to 30 mL of fetomaternal hemorrhage. (Book p413)
A 300-microgram anti-D dose neutralizes up to what volume of fetal red cells?
The stated coverage is 15 mL of fetal RBCs. (Book p413)
What is the stated effect if prophylactic anti-D crosses the placenta?
It does not cause fetal hemolysis
The notes state that anti-D does not cause hemolysis even if it crosses the placenta. (Book p413)
What is the purpose of the indirect Coombs test in an Rh-negative pregnant woman?
To determine whether she is sensitized
ICT assesses whether an Rh-negative pregnant woman is sensitized. (Book p413)
What sample is used for indirect Coombs testing?
ICT is performed on maternal blood. (Book p413)
When is ICT performed in Rh-negative pregnancy?
At the first ANC visit and repeated at 28 weeks
ICT is done at booking and repeated at 28 weeks. (Book p413)
What does a negative ICT indicate in the Rh-negative management pathway?
Negative ICT indicates that the Rh-negative mother is unsensitized. (Book p413)
What does a positive ICT indicate in the Rh-negative management pathway?
Positive ICT indicates Rh sensitization. (Book p413)
What antepartum prophylaxis is given to an unsensitized Rh-negative woman whose ICT remains negative?
A negative ICT receives 300 micrograms or 1,500 IU anti-D antepartum. (Book p413)
What is the role of anti-D after ICT is positive?
Stop all fetal monitoring, since sensitisation is inevitable
No role; manage as a sensitized Rh-negative pregnancy
Give double the routine dose of anti-D immediately
Give anti-D every day until delivery is achieved
Once the indirect Coombs test is positive, anti-D has no role and the pregnancy is managed as a sensitized Rh-negative pregnancy. (Book p413)
Fill up: The indirect Coombs test detects ______ in the mother's serum, whereas the direct Coombs test detects ______.
free anti-D antibody; antibody already bound to fetal red cells
fetal red cells in maternal blood; free anti-D antibody
maternal red cell antigens; maternal anti-D antibody
Indirect Coombs screens maternal serum for free antibody; direct Coombs shows antibody already coating the infant's red cells and is positive in affected babies. (Book p413)
What delivery timing is listed for an unsensitized Rh-negative woman?
For unsensitized Rh-negative women, delivery is at 39–40 weeks. (Book p413)
What delivery mode is listed for an unsensitized Rh-negative woman?
Vaginal delivery is the listed mode. (Book p413)
What cord-clamping practice is stated to prevent sensitization during delivery of an unsensitized Rh-negative mother?
Early cord clamping is listed to prevent sensitization during delivery in an unsensitized mother. (Book p413)
After delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, which test is performed on the newborn blood?
Indirect Coombs test on maternal blood only
A Rh-positive newborn has direct Coombs test (DCT) on newborn blood. (Book p413)
When is 300 micrograms of postpartum anti-D given to the mother after an Rh-positive newborn?
If the newborn DCT is negative
A Rh-positive newborn with negative DCT leads to 300 micrograms anti-D to the mother. (Book p413)
Is postpartum anti-D prophylaxis required if the newborn is Rh-negative?
Only if maternal blood group is A
If the newborn is Rh-negative, postpartum prophylaxis is not required. (Book p413)
What is the aim of postpartum anti-D prophylaxis?
Postpartum anti-D is intended to protect a future pregnancy. (Book p413)
What is the ideal time for postpartum anti-D after vaginal delivery or cesarean?
Postpartum anti-D should ideally be given within 72 hours; the notes permit up to 28 days. (Book p413)
Should anti-D still be administered if postpartum sterilization is planned?
Only if the baby is Rh-negative
The notes state anti-D is given even if postpartum sterilization is to be done. (Book p413)
An Rh-negative woman with a negative antibody screen delivers an Rh-positive infant. The cord direct Coombs test is negative and the baby is well. What should she receive?
Anti-D immunoglobulin 300 microgram (1500 IU) intramuscularly within 72 hours of delivery
Anti-D only if the Kleihauer-Betke test shows a bleed larger than 30 mL
Nothing, because the baby is unaffected and her antibody screen is negative
Anti-D 50 microgram now and a further dose at her six-week postnatal visit
All non-sensitised Rh-negative women delivering an Rh-positive infant need anti-D within 72 hours; the Kleihauer-Betke test only decides whether extra doses are needed. (Book p413)
Why is maternal antibody titre measured in sensitized Rh-negative pregnancy?
To measure the maternal blood glucose concentration during treatment
To confirm the diagnosis of pregnancy-induced hypertension
To judge whether the antibody level is high enough to cross the placenta and cause haemolysis
To determine the sex of the fetus before planning delivery
A critical titre means there is enough antibody crossing the placenta to produce significant fetal haemolysis, and it triggers surveillance. (Book p414)
What is the critical maternal antibody titre in the source notes?
The critical titre is 1:16; serially diluted maternal antibody at or above this is significant. (Book p414)
Which titre is considered not significant in the management flowchart?
Titre below 1:16 is not significant. (Book p414)
How frequently is antibody titre repeated when it is below the critical level?
With titre below 1:16, repeat titres every 4 weeks. (Book p414)
When does fetal monitoring begin for antibody titre below the critical threshold?
Fetal monitoring begins from 32 weeks in this pathway. (Book p414)
When is delivery planned if the antibody titre remains below 1:16?
With non-significant titre, delivery is at 37–38 weeks. (Book p414)
What is the best noninvasive investigation for fetal anemia?
MCA Doppler is the best noninvasive investigation and screening test for fetal anemia. (Book p414)
At what MCA peak systolic velocity is fetal anemia considered positive?
MCA PSV ≥1.5 MoM indicates fetal anemia. (Book p414)
When MCA PSV is below 1.5 MoM in a sensitized pregnancy, how often should it be repeated?
If MCA PSV is <1.5 MoM, repeat it every 1–2 weeks. (Book p414)
What antenatal fetal surveillance is used from 32 weeks when MCA PSV remains below 1.5 MoM?
The pathway calls for weekly NST and BPP from 32 weeks. (Book p414)
Which of the following statements about Rh isoimmunisation is TRUE?
Sensitisation during one pregnancy usually spares that baby but endangers later Rh-positive pregnancies
A first Rh-positive pregnancy is always severely affected because antibodies form in the first trimester
Anti-D immunoglobulin given after sensitisation reverses the immune response
ABO incompatibility between mother and fetus makes Rh sensitisation more likely
Primary immunisation is slow, so the index pregnancy usually escapes; ABO incompatibility protects, because fetal cells are destroyed before they immunise. (Book p414)
What is the next diagnostic procedure if MCA PSV is 1.5 MoM or greater?
Cordocentesis to assess fetal Hb and hematocrit
MCA PSV ≥1.5 MoM indicates anemia and prompts cordocentesis for fetal Hb/hematocrit. (Book p414)
Cordocentesis obtains blood from the umbilical cord. (Book p415)
Which cordocentesis finding is classified as mild fetal anemia?
Fetal Hb less than 2 SD below mean or hematocrit below 30%
Fetal Hb more than 2 SD below mean only
Mild anemia is Hb <2 SD below mean or Hct <30% in the source flowchart. (Book p415)
Which cordocentesis finding is classified as severe fetal anemia?
Fetal Hb more than 2 SD below mean or hematocrit below 30%
Hb less than 2 SD below mean only
Severe anemia is Hb >2 SD below mean (i.e., deviation) or hematocrit <30% in the source diagram. (Book p415)
How are fetal Hb and hematocrit followed in mild fetal anemia?
For mild anemia, repeat fetal Hb and hematocrit weekly. (Book p415)
When is delivery planned for mild fetal anemia after surveillance?
Mild fetal anemia is delivered at 37–38 weeks. (Book p415)
What is the management for severe fetal anemia at 35 weeks or later?
Severe fetal anemia at ≥35 weeks is managed by delivery. (Book p415)
What is the management for severe fetal anemia before 35 weeks?
Severe anemia before 35 weeks is managed with intrauterine blood transfusion. (Book p415)
What cord-clamping practice is used when an Rh-negative mother is already sensitized (ICT positive)?
Because the mother is already sensitized, the source lists delayed cord clamping. (Book p415)
A sensitised woman with anti-D antibodies at 32 weeks has a middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity of 1.7 multiples of the median. What is the next step?
Cordocentesis with intrauterine transfusion if the fetal haemoglobin is low, after corticosteroids for lung maturity
Immediate delivery at 32 weeks without further testing
Repeat the middle cerebral artery Doppler in four weeks
Maternal intravenous immunoglobulin and expectant management to term
A peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median indicates severe anaemia, confirmed by cordocentesis and treated by intrauterine transfusion. (Book p415)
What volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage is considered normal in the source notes?
Normal FMH is less than 4 mL. (Book p415)
How much additional anti-D is given for every extra 1 mL of fetal blood above 30 mL FMH?
For each extra 1 mL fetal blood over 30 mL, add 10 micrograms anti-D. (Book p415)
Which event is a listed cause of increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
Abdominal trauma is among causes of increased FMH. (Book p415)
Which delivery/procedure event is a listed cause of increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
An early fetal echocardiogram performed before 20 weeks
A DIPSI glucose tolerance test in the second trimester
A routine fundal examination at the antenatal visit
Instrumental delivery or manual removal of the placenta
Delivery itself, especially instrumental delivery and manual removal of the placenta, is the commonest cause of a larger feto-maternal haemorrhage. (Book p415)
Which pregnancy events are listed as causes of increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
Twin pregnancy and intrauterine death are listed causes of increased FMH. (Book p415)

Match the test with what it does — 1) Kleihauer-Betke test 2) Rosette test 3) Flow cytometry … A) A screening test that detects a feto-maternal haemorrhage of more than about 10 mL B) A quantitative test that uses acid elution of adult haemoglobin to identify fetal cells C) The most accurate modern method of quantifying fetal red cells in maternal blood
The rosette test screens, Kleihauer-Betke quantifies by acid elution, and flow cytometry with anti-HbF is the most precise method. (Book p415)
What is the screening test for increased fetomaternal hemorrhage?
Rosette test is the screening test for increased FMH. (Book p416)
What does a positive rosette test indicate?
A positive rosette test indicates increased FMH. (Book p416)
Which test quantitatively estimates the exact volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage?
Kleihauer–Betke is the quantitative test for exact FMH volume. (Book p416)
Within what interval should the Kleihauer–Betke test be done according to the notes?
The source states the Kleihauer–Betke test should be done within 2 hours. (Book p416)
What type of test is the Singer alkali denaturation test?
Quantitative test of exact FMH volume
Singer alkali denaturation is a qualitative test. (Book p416)
What bleeding differential can Singer alkali denaturation test distinguish?
Singer alkali test differentiates vasa previa and placenta previa and also helps detect FMH. (Book p416)
Which first-trimester event is an indication for anti-D prophylaxis?
Routine fetal movement counting from 28 weeks of gestation onwards
Normal glycosuria detected on routine antenatal urine testing
Abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy or chorionic-villus sampling
Normal nausea and vomiting limited to the first trimester alone
First-trimester indications for anti-D prophylaxis include abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy and chorionic-villus sampling. (Book p416)
What anti-D dose is listed by ACOG/India for sensitizing events before 12 weeks?
No anti-D is used before 12 weeks
For <12 weeks, the source follows ACOG in India: 50 micrograms IM. (Book p416)
What anti-D dose is listed by RCOG for sensitizing events before 12 weeks?
The RCOG dose listed for <12 weeks is 300 micrograms IM. (Book p416)
Which second/third-trimester procedure is an indication for anti-D?
A detailed fetal echocardiogram performed before 20 weeks
Amniocentesis, or external cephalic or internal podalic version
A DIPSI glucose tolerance test in the second trimester
A routine non-stress test in the third trimester
Anti-D is given after any procedure that may cause feto-maternal haemorrhage, including amniocentesis and version. (Book p416)
Which second/third-trimester events are indications for anti-D prophylaxis?
Unexplained bleeding, APH, fetal death, or abdominal trauma
The source lists unexplained bleeding, APH, fetal death, and abdominal trauma. (Book p416)
What anti-D dose is given after sensitizing events beyond 12 weeks?
The stated dose after 12 weeks is 300 micrograms IM. (Book p416)
Fill up: A single 300 microgram dose of anti-D covers about ______ mL of fetal whole blood, so a 40 mL feto-maternal haemorrhage needs ______ doses.
300 microgram neutralises about 30 mL of fetal blood; the Kleihauer-Betke result is used to calculate any additional doses required. (Book p416)
Why is there no role for anti-D with cordocentesis?
The mother is already sensitized (ICT positive)
The procedure has no fetal blood exposure
The notes say no anti-D with cordocentesis because sensitization has already occurred. (Book p416)
Why is anti-D not required if delivery occurs within 28 days of a prior anti-D dose?
The half-life of anti-D is 28 days
Anti-D cannot cross placenta after 28 days
The source states anti-D half-life is 28 days, so no repeat is needed for delivery within that interval. (Book p416)
Which minor antigen carries the most common risk of sensitization?
Kell is listed as the most common minor antigen leading to sensitization, often after mismatched transfusion. (Book p416)
Which minor antigens are listed as carrying sensitization risk?
Kell, Kidd, and Duffy-A are in the risk-of-sensitization group. (Book p416)
Which minor antigens are listed as not carrying sensitization risk?
Lewis, I antigen, and Duffy-B are listed as no-risk minor antigens. (Book p416)
All of the following are indications for anti-D immunoglobulin EXCEPT:
A woman who is herself Rh-positive
Delivery of an Rh-positive infant by an Rh-negative mother
Antepartum haemorrhage in an Rh-negative woman
External cephalic version in an Rh-negative woman
Anti-D is only for Rh-negative non-sensitised women exposed to Rh-positive blood; Rh-positive women cannot form anti-D. (Book p416)
What is the most common non-D alloimmunization according to the notes?
Anti-E is listed as the most common non-D alloimmunization. (Book p417)
What is the most severe non-D alloimmunization according to the notes?
Anti-C is listed as the most severe non-D alloimmunization. (Book p417)
Only maternal edema without fetal findings
Mother and fetus mimic each other with edema
Only fetal edema with a normal mother
Mirror syndrome means the mother and fetus mirror each other; both are edematous. (Book p417)
Which pairing describes the mother and fetus in mirror syndrome?
Maternal oligohydramnios and fetal IUGR only
Maternal hyperglycemia and fetal hypoglycemia only
Maternal anemia and fetal polycythemia only
In mirror syndrome, maternal polyhydramnios accompanies fetal hydrops. (Book p417)
Which condition is associated with mirror syndrome?
Anti-D isoimmunisation, twin-to-twin transfusion, cystic hygroma or placental chorioangioma
An uncomplicated singleton pregnancy with a normal fetus and placenta
Diet-controlled gestational diabetes with a normal liquor volume
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy alone, with raised serum bile acids
Mirror syndrome is the maternal reflection of fetal hydrops, whatever its cause — immune, anastomotic, lymphatic or placental. (Book p417)
How is hydrops fetalis diagnosed by ultrasound?
Fetal anemia alone without ultrasound findings
At least two of pericardial effusion, ascites, pleural effusion, and subcutaneous edema
Hydrops is diagnosed if at least two of the four listed fluid/edema findings are present. (Book p417)
What is the first ultrasound sign of hydrops fetalis in the notes?
Buddha sign from scalp subcutaneous edema
The first USG sign is Buddha sign due to scalp subcutaneous edema. (Book p417)
Are placentomegaly and polyhydramnios diagnostic criteria for hydrops fetalis?
Yes; either one alone diagnoses hydrops
No; they are associated findings only
Placentomegaly and polyhydramnios are findings in hydrops, not diagnostic criteria. (Book p417)
What is the most common cause/type context of immune hydrops fetalis in the notes?
Immune hydrops is listed in Rh-negative pregnancy. (Book p417)
What fetal Hb and hematocrit thresholds are shown for immune hydrops?
The immune-hydrops box lists fetal Hb <40% and hematocrit <15%. (Book p417)
What is the most common cause of nonimmune hydrops fetalis?
Nonimmune hydrops is more common; CVS anomaly is its most common listed cause. (Book p417)
Which categories are listed as other causes of nonimmune hydrops?
Rh D isoimmunisation alone, which is the only listed cause
Maternal obesity alone, acting through an unexplained mechanism
Maternal hyperthyroidism alone, causing fetal tachycardia
Chromosomal anomalies, parvovirus B19 or TORCH infection, and fetal anaemia
Non-immune hydrops has chromosomal, infective, haematological and cardiac causes; Rh disease is the immune category. (Book p417)

Match the condition with its description — 1) Mirror syndrome 2) Immune hydrops 3) Non-immune hydrops … A) Maternal oedema, hypertension and proteinuria that parallel fetal hydrops and resolve after delivery B) Caused by red cell alloimmunisation, classically anti-D, anti-c or anti-Kell C) Caused by cardiac anomalies, arrhythmia, parvovirus B19 or twin-to-twin transfusion
Mirror syndrome is the maternal reflection of fetal hydrops; hydrops is now more often non-immune than immune in countries with anti-D prophylaxis. (Book p417)

Match each definition with the gestation or weight it uses — 1) Abortion 2) WHO definition of abortion 3) Intrauterine death … A) Fetal weight below 500 g, about 22 weeks B) Pregnancy loss at or after 20 weeks C) Pregnancy loss before 20 weeks
Abortion is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks; the WHO definition is fetal weight below 500 g, about 22 weeks; and intrauterine death is loss at or after 20 weeks. (Book p418)
Fill up: The WHO definition of abortion is a fetal weight below ______ g, approximately below ______ weeks.
The WHO definition uses a fetal weight below 500 g, approximately 22 weeks. (Book p418)
Fill up: Abortion is pregnancy loss before ______ weeks, whereas intrauterine death is loss at or after ______ weeks.
Abortion is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of gestation, and intrauterine death is pregnancy loss at or after 20 weeks. (Book p418)
Which statement about the period of viability is TRUE?
The notes state a period of viability of 28 weeks in India
The notes state a period of viability of 24 weeks in India
The source definition puts viability at 32 weeks
Viability is reached at 20 weeks in the source notes
The notes state a period of viability of 28 weeks in India. (Book p418)
Fill up: Spontaneous abortion is subdivided into an ______ single episode or ______ abortion.
Recurrent; isolated, meaning a single loss
In the source flowchart spontaneous abortion is subdivided into an isolated single episode and recurrent abortion with at least 3 abortions. (Book p418)
Fill up: An abortion that is induced medically is termed ______.
Induced abortion is medical termination of pregnancy. (Book p418)
A woman who had a surgical evacuation four days ago now has fever, lower abdominal pain and an offensive vaginal discharge, and her os is open. Which feature makes this a septic abortion?
The presence of septic foci in association with the abortion
Rh negativity of the mother on its own
An open internal os by itself, without any infection
Fetal cardiac activity still seen on the scan
Any abortion with septic foci is a septic abortion; neither Rh negativity, an open os alone nor fetal cardiac activity defines it. (Book p418)
Fill up: In India, abortion is defined as termination of pregnancy before ______ weeks of gestation or the birth of a fetus weighing less than ______ g.
Indian law uses the 28-week or 1000 g definition of viability, so expulsion before that limit and weight is called abortion. (Book p418)

A 30-year-old woman has a single isolated first-trimester pregnancy loss. She has no history of thrombosis, no cervical surgery and no systemic disease. What is the most common cause of this kind of loss?
Chromosomal anomaly is the most common cause of an isolated first- or second-trimester abortion, and aneuploidy is the most common category. (Book p418)
Which statement about chromosomal anomalies in isolated abortion is TRUE?
Aneuploidy is the most common category
Balanced translocation is the most common category
Triploidy accounts for most isolated abortions
Mitochondrial mutations are the leading category
Aneuploidy is listed as the most common chromosomal anomaly in isolated abortion. (Book p418)
All of the following are listed chromosomal abnormalities in isolated abortion EXCEPT:
The source order is aneuploidy, then trisomy, then monosomy (Turner syndrome), then trisomy 16; a mitochondrial mutation is not listed. (Book p418)
All of the following are listed causes or risk factors for isolated abortion EXCEPT:
Listed risk factors are a previous abortion and increasing maternal age, with chromosomal anomaly the commonest cause; daily walking is not a risk factor. (Book p418)
Which statement about maternal age and isolated abortion is TRUE?
The risk of isolated abortion increases with maternal age
Maternal age has no effect on the risk of isolated abortion
Only paternal age affects the risk of isolated abortion
The risk falls to zero after the age of 35 years
Increasing maternal age is a listed risk factor for isolated abortion. (Book p418)
Which statement about infection and recurrent abortion is TRUE?
Infections do not cause recurrent abortion
All infections are the commonest cause of recurrent abortion
TORCH serology always proves a diagnosis of recurrent abortion
VDRL testing is mandatory in every case of recurrent loss
The notes state that infections do not cause recurrent abortion. (Book p418)
Fill up: In congenital syphilis the pregnancy prognosis follows ______ law, improving as the number of pregnancies ______.
Kassowitz law states that the pregnancy prognosis is proportional to the number of pregnancies in syphilis; stillbirth is more common than abortion. (Book p418)
All of the following infections are associated with spontaneous abortion EXCEPT:
Human papillomavirus infection of the cervix
Cervical HPV causes warts and neoplasia, not pregnancy loss; listeria, syphilis, CMV, rubella, toxoplasma and parvovirus all cause loss. (Book p418)
Fill up: The most lethal trisomy is trisomy ______, while the most viable is trisomy ______.
Trisomy 16 is the most lethal in the note, and trisomy 21 is the most viable, with abortion its most common outcome. (Book p419)
A 38-year-old woman has a second-trimester loss and products of conception are sent for karyotyping, which returns trisomy 21. How is this trisomy described in the notes?
The most viable, with abortion as its commonest outcome
The most lethal of all the autosomal trisomies
Incompatible with implantation, so never seen in losses
Always inherited from a parental balanced translocation
Trisomy 21 is the most viable trisomy and abortion is its most common outcome; trisomy 16 is the most lethal. (Book p419)
Which statement about HIV and pregnancy loss is TRUE?
HIV is neither abortogenic nor teratogenic
HIV is abortogenic but not teratogenic
HIV is teratogenic but not abortogenic
HIV is always both abortogenic and teratogenic
The source explicitly states that HIV is neither abortogenic nor teratogenic. (Book p419)
Fill up: Recurrent abortion is defined as at least ______ consecutive pregnancy losses before ______ weeks.
Recurrent abortion is at least 3 consecutive pregnancy losses before 20 weeks. (Book p419)
Which statement about Recurrent abortion — ASRM defines recurrent is TRUE?
ASRM defines recurrent loss as At least 2 confirmed pregnancy losses
ASRM defines recurrent loss as At least 3 consecutive unconfirmed losses
ASRM defines recurrent loss as At least 4 losses after 20 weeks
ASRM defines recurrent loss as One biochemical pregnancy
ASRM defines recurrent loss as at least 2 confirmed pregnancy losses. (Book p419)
Fill up: Can pregnancy loss be confirmed for the ASRM recurrent-loss definition is ______.
Confirmation is by histopathological examination or USG. (Book p419)

Match the recurrent abortion causes with the correct detail — 1) is the most common group of causes of 2) is the most common individual cause of recurrent 3) Fill up: Recurrent abortion is defined as at … A) Endocrine causes B) APLA syndrome C) 3; 20
Endocrine causes are the most common group, ahead of uterine causes. (Book p419)
Fill up: ______ is the most common individual cause.
APLA syndrome is the most common individual cause. (Book p419)
Fill up: The commonest cause of a sporadic first-trimester abortion is a ______, and the single commonest chromosomal abnormality found is ______.

Both conditions always use exactly the same methotrexate regimen
Ectopic pregnancy is treated with folinic acid alone, never with methotrexate
Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia is never treated with methotrexate
The ectopic regimen is a single dose with day 4 and day 7 hCG checks, whereas GTN regimens use repeated doses alternated with folinic acid rescue. (Book p438)
What is done on day 1 of single-dose methotrexate therapy for ectopic pregnancy?
Measure beta-hCG and administer the entire methotrexate dose
Measure only beta-hCG with no drug
Day 1 includes beta-hCG measurement and the full methotrexate injection. (Book p438)
On which days is beta-hCG measured after single-dose methotrexate to estimate response?
Beta-hCG is measured on days 4 and 7. (Book p438)
Fill up: The single-dose methotrexate regimen for ectopic pregnancy is ______ mg per square metre intramuscularly, with beta-hCG measured on days ______.
The standard is 50 mg per square metre intramuscularly with beta-hCG on days 4 and 7 to judge the response. (Book p438)
What fall in beta-hCG between day 4 and day 7 indicates successful medical treatment?
A decline of at least 15% from D4 to D7 indicates successful medical therapy. (Book p439)
What is done if beta-hCG falls by less than 15% between day 4 and 7 after methotrexate?
Repeat the entire methotrexate dose as a new day 1, up to 3 doses
A <15% fall is inadequate; repeat full MTX as new D1, maximum three doses. (Book p439)
What defines failed medical therapy after up to three methotrexate injections?
A day-7 fall of less than 15% after three doses, or a rising hCG from day 4 to day 7
Any rise at all in the hCG measured on day 1 after the first injection
A fall of exactly 15% between the day 4 and the day 7 measurements
The absence of vaginal bleeding on the first day of treatment
Treatment is judged to have failed after three doses if the day-7 fall is under 15%, or if the hCG is still rising between days 4 and 7. (Book p439)
What does a rise in beta-hCG between day 1 and day 3 after methotrexate usually represent?
A normal release from the dying ectopic sac
A D1–D3 hCG rise can be normal due to release from the dying ectopic sac. (Book p439)
What is the preferred operative route for surgical management of unruptured ectopic pregnancy?
The surgical-management route listed is laparoscopy. (Book p439)
When is linear salpingostomy the surgery of choice for unruptured ectopic pregnancy?
Family complete and ectopic size at least 5 cm
Family not complete and ectopic size under 4 cm
Linear salpingostomy is chosen if family is incomplete and ectopic is <4 cm. (Book p439)
What is done in linear salpingostomy?
Incision with hydrodissection; tube left intact and incision left open
Linear salpingostomy uses incision/hydrodissection, preserves tube, and leaves incision open. (Book p439)
Which of the following statements about monitoring methotrexate treatment is TRUE?
A fall of 15 per cent or more in beta-hCG between days 4 and 7 predicts success; otherwise a second dose or surgery is considered
The beta-hCG must rise before it falls, so a rise on day 7 confirms that treatment is working
A single beta-hCG measurement at three weeks is sufficient follow-up
Surgery is mandatory whenever the beta-hCG has not halved by day 4
The day 4 to day 7 fall is the decision point: a fall of at least 15 per cent is reassuring, a lesser fall prompts a second dose or surgery. (Book p439)
When is unilateral salpingectomy the surgery of choice for unruptured ectopic pregnancy?
Family complete or ectopic size at least 5 cm
Family incomplete and ectopic below 4 cm
Unilateral salpingectomy is selected if family is complete or ectopic is ≥5 cm. (Book p439)
Which tubal procedures are labeled obsolete in the ectopic-surgery notes?
Milking of tubes and salpingotomy with closed incision
Milking tubes and salpingotomy with closed incision are obsolete. (Book p439)
What is the indication for expectant management of ectopic pregnancy?
Heterotopic pregnancy with a live IUP
Expectant management is wait and watch for spontaneously resolving ectopic pregnancy. (Book p439)
What beta-hCG value is a prerequisite for expectant ectopic management?
Expectant management requires beta-hCG <200 IU. (Book p439)
What beta-hCG trend is required for expectant ectopic management?
A spontaneous fall in beta-hCG is required. (Book p439)
What ultrasound prerequisite is listed for expectant ectopic management?
No gestational sac in the fallopian tube
Definite yolk sac in the tube
Expectant management requires no gestational sac in the tube. (Book p439)
A molar pregnancy with a fetus
Twin pregnancy with one intrauterine and one ectopic pregnancy
Heterotopic pregnancy has one IUP and one ectopic pregnancy. (Book p439)
Why is methotrexate contraindicated in heterotopic pregnancy?
It would harm the coexisting intrauterine pregnancy
Methotrexate is contraindicated because a desired intrauterine pregnancy coexists. (Book p439)
What is the management of heterotopic pregnancy in the source notes?
Heterotopic pregnancy is managed surgically. (Book p439)
All of the following favour salpingectomy over salpingostomy EXCEPT:
A first ectopic in a young woman with a healthy contralateral tube who wants children
A badly damaged or ruptured fallopian tube
Bleeding at the tubal site that cannot be controlled conservatively
A recurrent ectopic pregnancy in the same tube
Salpingostomy is preferred when future fertility matters and the tube is salvageable; damage, bleeding or recurrence favour salpingectomy. (Book p439)
What type of pregnancy is cornual pregnancy in the source comparison?
Cornual pregnancy is an ectopic pregnancy. (Book p440)
What type of pregnancy is angular pregnancy in the source comparison?
Where can a cornual pregnancy implant according to the notes?
Near the uterine angle only inside cavity
Interstitial fallopian tube or rudimentary uterine horn
Cornual ectopic is in the tubal interstitium or rudimentary horn. (Book p440)
Near the angle/cornua of the uterus
In the tubal interstitium lateral to round ligament
Angular pregnancy is intrauterine near the uterine angle/cornua. (Book p440)
How does cornual pregnancy relate to the round ligament?
Cornual pregnancy is lateral to the round ligament. (Book p440)
How does angular pregnancy relate to the round ligament?
Angular pregnancy is medial to the round ligament. (Book p440)
Which cervical finding is part of Paalman criteria?
Internal os open and external os closed
Internal os closed and external os partially open
Paalman criteria include a closed internal os and partially open external os. (Book p440)
Where is the gestational sac attached in Paalman criteria for cervical ectopic?
In cervical ectopic, the sac is attached to the endocervix. (Book p440)
What symptom is part of Paalman criteria for cervical ectopic?
Cervical ectopic presents with bleeding without uterine cramps. (Book p440)

Match the rare ectopic with its description — 1) Cornual or interstitial pregnancy 2) Angular pregnancy 3) Cervical ectopic pregnancy … A) Implantation in the lateral angle of the cavity medial to the round ligament, which may reach term B) Implantation in the interstitial tube surrounded by myometrium, with late catastrophic rupture C) Implantation in the endocervix giving a barrel-shaped cervix and painless brisk bleeding
Cornual pregnancy is surrounded by myometrium and ruptures late, angular pregnancy sits in the cavity angle, and cervical pregnancy bleeds painlessly. (Book p440)
Which finding is part of Spiegelberg criteria for ovarian ectopic?
Normal ovaries with sac in ampulla
Sac present in the ovary with normal tubes
Sac in endocervix with open internal os
Spiegelberg requires sac in ovary and normal tubes. (Book p440)
How is the gestational sac related to the uterus in Spiegelberg criteria?
Spiegelberg criteria include sac attached to uterus by ovarian ligament. (Book p440)
What histologic finding confirms ovarian ectopic under Spiegelberg criteria?
Ovarian tissue in the gestational sac
Decidua only with no ovarian tissue
Ovarian tissue must be identified in the gestational sac. (Book p440)
Which are Studdiford criteria for primary abdominal ectopic pregnancy?
Gestational sac in the ampulla with a visible yolk sac
No uteroperitoneal fistula, normal tubes and ovaries, peritoneal attachment
An open internal os with the gestational sac lying in the endocervix
A gestational sac in the ovary with ovarian tissue in its wall
Studdiford criteria for primary abdominal ectopic pregnancy are: no uteroperitoneal fistula, normal tubes and ovaries, and a pregnancy attached to the peritoneum. (Book p440)
Which abdominal ectopic is more common according to the note?
Secondary abdominal ectopic is more common. (Book p440)
Which two entities are grouped as molar pregnancy/hydatidiform mole?
Molar pregnancy/hydatidiform mole is partial or complete mole. (Book p441)
Which is a form of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia?
Invasive mole is a gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. (Book p441)
Which malignant trophoblastic condition is listed under GTN?
Choriocarcinoma is listed under gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. (Book p441)
Which tumors are listed under GTN besides invasive mole and choriocarcinoma?
Placental-site trophoblastic tumour and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour
Manual vacuum aspiration and manual removal of the placenta
Ventricular septal defect and transposition of the great arteries
Haemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Besides invasive mole and choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia includes placental-site and epithelioid trophoblastic tumours. (Book p441)
Fill up: Spiegelberg criteria for ovarian pregnancy require the gestational sac to lie within the ovary and the ______ on that side to be intact.
An intact ipsilateral tube separates a primary ovarian pregnancy from a tubal pregnancy that has secondarily involved the ovary. (Book p441)
What is the most important risk factor for molar pregnancy?
Previous molar pregnancy is the most important risk factor. (Book p441)
Which demographic factors are listed for molar pregnancy?
Only European origin and middle age
Southeast Asian origin and extremes of age
Southeast Asian countries and extremes of age are listed risk factors. (Book p441)
What pathologic processes are listed in molar pregnancy?
Undue trophoblastic proliferation and hydropic degeneration
Molar pregnancy involves undue trophoblast proliferation and hydropic degeneration. (Book p441)
What distinguishes partial from complete mole by fetal tissue?
Partial mole has some fetal tissue; complete mole has no fetal tissue
Complete mole has fetal tissue; partial has none
Both always have a normal fetus
Some fetal tissue is present in partial mole; no fetal tissue in complete mole. (Book p441)
How is molar pregnancy characterized biologically?
A benign disease with malignant potential
A strictly nonneoplastic condition with no follow-up relevance
Molar pregnancy is benign but has malignant potential. (Book p441)
What is the most common presentation of molar pregnancy?
Palmar itching in the third trimester
P/V bleeding in the first or early second trimester
P/V bleeding in first/early second trimester is the most common presentation. (Book p441)
What vaginal finding is classically associated with molar pregnancy?
Grape-like vesicles P/V are characteristic. (Book p441)
Why can PIH develop before 20 weeks in molar pregnancy?
Early-onset PIH before 20 weeks is due to increased placental tissue. (Book p441)
Which symptoms/findings are driven by elevated hCG in molar pregnancy?
Hyperemesis, thyrotoxicosis, and bilateral theca-lutein cysts
Hypoglycemia, low TSH, and renal failure only
Raised hCG is associated with hyperemesis, thyrotoxicosis, and bilateral theca-lutein cysts. (Book p441)
What can cause pulmonary embolism and breathlessness in molar pregnancy according to the notes?
Pulmonary embolism and breathlessness are attributed to vesicles in the source notes. (Book p441)

A 22-year-old at 14 weeks has vaginal bleeding and passage of grape-like vesicles. The uterus is larger than dates, no fetal parts are felt and the beta-hCG is 500,000 mIU/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Missed abortion with a blighted ovum
A very high beta-hCG, a uterus larger than dates, absent fetal parts and classic vesicles point to a complete mole rather than a partial mole. (Book p441)

A 24-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation presents with vaginal bleeding and passage of grape-like vesicles. On abdominal examination fundal height is larger than dates and fetal parts are not palpable. How does fundal height usually compare with POG in molar pregnancy?
Fundal height is larger than period of gestation, rarely smaller than dates
Fundal height is always smaller than period of gestation in molar pregnancy
Fundal height exactly equals period of gestation in all molar pregnancies
Fundal height cannot be assessed clinically in molar pregnancy due to obesity
The uterus is usually larger than dates (fundal height > POG), rarely ≤ POG. (Book p442)
Fill up: In molar pregnancy, fetal parts are ______ on palpation and fetal heart sounds are ______.
Fetal parts are not palpable and fetal heart sounds are absent in molar pregnancy. (Book p442)
Which of the following statements about uterine consistency in molar pregnancy is TRUE?
Uterine consistency is described as doughy in molar pregnancy on palpation
Uterine consistency is woody hard in molar pregnancy due to myometrial invasion
Uterine consistency is board-like rigid in molar pregnancy from acute abdomen
Uterine consistency is craggy and fixed in molar pregnancy from parametrial involvement
The notes describe a doughy uterine consistency in molar pregnancy. (Book p442)
Fill up: Investigation of choice for molar pregnancy is ______ and shows ______ appearance.
Ultrasound is the IOC and shows the snowstorm appearance. (Book p442)
All of the following are part of pre-treatment evaluation before evacuating a mole EXCEPT:
Liver function tests and kidney function tests with complete blood count and blood grouping
Chest X-ray to rule out pulmonary metastasis and baseline beta-hCG estimation
Blood group and Rh typing with complete blood count and thyroid function if indicated
Serum amylase estimation as routine part of molar pregnancy workup before evacuation
Pre-treatment evaluation lists LFT, KFT, β-hCG, chest X-ray, blood group/Rh and CBC – not amylase. (Book p442)
Which of the following statements about treatment of molar pregnancy is TRUE?
Suction evacuation followed by sharp curettage is the treatment of choice for molar pregnancy
Sharp curettage alone without suction is the treatment of choice for molar pregnancy
Hysterotomy followed by curettage is the treatment of choice for molar pregnancy today
Misoprostol priming alone followed by curettage is the treatment of choice for molar pregnancy
Suction evacuation followed by sharp curettage is the treatment of choice. (Book p442)

A 22-year-old woman undergoes suction evacuation for complete mole at 14 weeks. During the procedure she develops tachycardia, tremor and dyspnoea. Which two complications are flagged as increased risks during suction evacuation of a mole?
Thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm and pulmonary embolism of trophoblastic tissue
Uterine inversion and air embolism from excessive traction during evacuation
HELLP syndrome and eclampsia precipitated by molar tissue evacuation
Cervical tear and bladder injury from difficult dilatation during evacuation
The procedure carries ↑ risk of thyrotoxicosis/thyroid storm and pulmonary embolism. (Book p442)
Fill up: During suction evacuation of molar pregnancy, oxytocin is given ______.
Oxytocin is given after starting suction evacuation to limit embolisation risk. (Book p442)

A 42-year-old woman with 3 living children presents with complete mole at 10 weeks. She has completed her family and desires definitive management. In which patient is hysterectomy indicated for molar pregnancy?
Age 40 years or more with completed family desiring definitive treatment for mole
Any primigravida with molar pregnancy irrespective of age and parity status
Only if beta-hCG exceeds 10^5 IU/L with theca lutein cysts larger than 6 cm
Only in partial mole with fetal parts present and beta-hCG below 10^5 IU/L
Hysterectomy is indicated at age ≥ 40 years with a completed family. (Book p442)
Which of the following statements about follow-up after molar evacuation is TRUE?
Serial beta-hCG levels are the investigation of choice for follow-up after molar evacuation
Serial CA-125 levels are the investigation of choice for follow-up after molar evacuation
Serial placental lactogen levels are used for follow-up after molar evacuation routinely
Serial AFP levels are the investigation of choice for follow-up after molar evacuation
Serial β-hCG levels are the IOC for follow-up. (Book p442)

Match the beta-hCG follow-up step with its timing — 1) Baseline 2) 48 hours post-evacuation 3) Weekly till 3 consecutive normal 4) Monthly till 6 months … A) Before procedure B) After evacuation C) Until 3 normals D) Till 6 months
Baseline β-hCG, then 48 hrs after evacuation, weekly till 3 consecutive normal, then monthly till 6 months. (Book p442)
Fill up: After evacuation of molar pregnancy, pregnancy is contraindicated for ______ months.
Pregnancy is contraindicated for 6 months during β-hCG surveillance. (Book p442)
Which of the following statements about contraception during molar follow-up is TRUE?
OCP is the contraceptive of choice; IUCD is contraindicated during beta-hCG surveillance
IUCD is the contraceptive of choice; OCP is contraindicated due to thrombosis risk
Both OCP and IUCD are contraindicated during follow-up after molar evacuation
No contraception is needed if beta-hCG is falling after molar evacuation
OCPs are the contraceptive of choice while IUCD insertion is contraindicated. (Book p442)
Fill up: After evacuation of a hydatidiform mole, beta-hCG is measured ______ until it is normal for three consecutive readings, and then ______ for the rest of follow-up.
Weekly hCG until three consecutive normal values, then monthly for at least six months, reliably detects progression to neoplasia. (Book p442)
Fill up: Partial mole arises from ______ whereas complete mole arises from ______.
1 ovum with 2 sperms; an empty ovum with duplication of zygotic chromosomes
1 ovum with 1 sperm; 2 ova each fertilized by 1 sperm separately
2 ova with 2 sperms; 1 ovum fertilized by a single sperm only
1 ovum with 1 sperm in both partial and complete mole with different phenotype
Partial mole arises from 1 ovum fertilized by 2 sperms, whereas complete mole arises from an empty ovum with duplication of the zygotic chromosomes. (Book p443)
Fill up: Karyotype of partial mole is ______ with commonest being ______.
Partial mole is triploid: 69XXY (most common) or 69XXX. (Book p443)
Match partial vs complete mole — 1) Partial mole sperm number 2) Partial mole maternal genes 3) Complete mole maternal genes … A) Dispermic B) Present C) Absent
Partial mole is dispermic with maternal genes present; complete mole is monospermic with maternal genes absent. (Book p443)
Fill up: p57 KIP2 staining, a marker of maternal genes, is ______ in partial mole and ______ in complete mole.
Maternal genes are present in partial mole (p57 KIP2 +) and absent in complete mole (−). (Book p443)
Match mole type with clinical picture — 1) Partial mole symptoms 2) Partial mole uterine size 3) Complete mole uterine size … A) Less common B) Smaller than POG C) Larger than POG
Partial mole: symptoms less common and height < POG; complete mole: symptoms more common and height > POG. (Book p443)
Which ultrasound picture belongs to a partial mole?
Cystic spaces in placenta with fetal tissue and ↓ amniotic fluid; sac transverse > AP
Snowstorm appearance with bilateral theca lutein cysts
Absent amniotic fluid with no fetal tissue
Partial mole shows placental cystic spaces, fetal tissue (+), reduced fluid and a transverse > AP sac, resembling missed abortion. (Book p443)
A 'snowstorm' uterus with no fetal tissue, absent amniotic fluid and bilateral theca lutein cysts indicates:
Those features define the complete/vesicular mole on USG. (Book p443)
On HPE (gold standard), which feature separates partial from complete mole?
Vascular villi with less hydropic change in partial; avascular villi with extensive change in complete
Avascular villi in the partial mole; vascular villi in the complete mole
Villi are absent in both partial and complete molar pregnancies
Fetal tissue is absent in the partial mole but present in the complete mole
On HPE, the gold standard, partial mole shows vascular villi with less hydropic change, while complete mole shows avascular villi with extensive hydropic degeneration. (Book p443)
Fill up: Risk of GTN after partial mole is ______ and after complete mole is ______.
Subsequent GTN risk is 1% after partial mole and 15–20% after complete mole. (Book p443)
The risk of choriocarcinoma after a complete mole is quoted as:
Choriocarcinoma risk is <1% after partial mole and 4% after complete mole. (Book p443)
How long does hCG take to return to normal after partial vs complete mole, and what levels are typical before treatment?
6 weeks vs 7 weeks; <10^5 IU/L vs ≥10^5 IU/L
7 weeks vs 6 weeks; ≥10^5 IU/L vs <10^5 IU/L
12 weeks in both; levels not useful
hCG normalises by 6 weeks (partial) vs 7 weeks (complete); pre-treatment levels are <10^5 IU/L vs ≥10^5 IU/L. (Book p443)

Match the trophoblastic entity with its description — 1) Complete mole 2) Partial mole 3) Invasive mole … A) Triploid, usually 69 XXX or 69 XXY, with focal villous swelling and some fetal tissue B) Androgenetic 46 XX with diffuse villous swelling, trophoblastic hyperplasia and no fetus C) Molar villi that invade the myometrium after evacuation and may perforate the uterus
Complete moles are diploid and androgenetic with no fetus; partial moles are triploid with a fetus; invasive moles penetrate the myometrium. (Book p443)
All of the following antecedent pregnancies can be followed by choriocarcinoma EXCEPT:
Molar pregnancy, full term delivery, ectopic pregnancy and abortion can all precede choriocarcinoma
Molar pregnancy alone is the only antecedent that can be followed by choriocarcinoma
Full term and molar pregnancies alone are the only antecedents for choriocarcinoma
Ectopic and abortion alone are the only antecedents that can lead to choriocarcinoma
Choriocarcinoma (+) follows molar, full term, ectopic and abortion pregnancies. (Book p444)
Invasive mole arises only after which pregnancy?
Invasive mole is (+) only after molar pregnancy and (−) after the others. (Book p444)
PSTT is uniquely listed as possible after which antecedent pregnancy but NOT after ectopic or abortion?
A term delivery: it is not listed after an ectopic pregnancy or after an abortion
An ectopic pregnancy, which is the antecedent unique to placental site trophoblastic tumour
An abortion, which is the usual antecedent for placental site trophoblastic tumour
None of these, since placental site trophoblastic tumour has no antecedent pregnancy
Placental site trophoblastic tumour characteristically follows a term pregnancy, with a long latency and only modest hCG secretion. (Book p444)
Fill up: After a molar pregnancy the m/c GTN is ______, while after a full term pregnancy the m/c GTN is ______.
Molar pregnancy → m/c GTN invasive mole; full term pregnancy → m/c GTN choriocarcinoma. (Book p444)
What is the m/c cause of choriocarcinoma?
Molar pregnancy is the m/c cause of choriocarcinoma. (Book p444)
Which of the following is NOT among the listed signs/symptoms of GTN after hydatidiform mole?
Listed features are persistent bleeding, persistent theca lutein cyst, subinvolution, shock due to invasive mole and metastasis. (Book p444)
A plateau of β-hCG over 4 consecutive weekly values (D1, 7, 14, 21) within ±10% suggests:
A β-hCG plateau for 4 consecutive weeks (±10% of previous value) is suggestive of invasive mole. (Book p444)
A rise in β-hCG of ≥10% over previous values across 3 weeks (D1, 7, 14) suggests:
An increase ≥10% over 3 weekly values is suggestive of choriocarcinoma. (Book p444)
Under the OLD criteria, persisting β-hCG beyond how long after evacuation labelled the case as GTN?
β-hCG present after 6 months of evacuation was the old criterion. (Book p444)
What happens to the theca lutein cysts after suction evacuation of a mole?
Theca lutein cysts regress spontaneously in about 2 months after evacuation. (Book p444)
What is the m/c site of GTN metastasis and its FIGO stage?
Lung is the m/c metastatic site and corresponds to FIGO stage 3. (Book p444)
Which chest X-ray patterns are listed for lung metastases in GTN?
CXR shows cannon ball appearance (m/c) and snowstorm appearance. (Book p444)
The second m/c site of GTN metastasis and its typical presentation are:
The vagina just below the urethra, presenting as suburethral nodules
The liver, presenting months later with obstructive jaundice
The brain, presenting with seizures and focal neurological deficits
The pelvis, presenting with deep pelvic pain and a palpable mass
After the lungs, the vagina is the second commonest site: suburethral nodules that may bleed are the classic presentation. (Book p444)
Why is biopsy contraindicated in suspected vaginal metastatic nodules of GTN?
Risk of torrential bleeding from highly vascular deposits
Nodules are too small to sample
Biopsy is c/i on these vascular nodules; the notes simply mark it contraindicated. (Book p444)
All of the following are characteristic sites of metastasis in gestational trophoblastic neoplasia EXCEPT:
GTN spreads haematogenously to lung, vagina, pelvis, liver and brain; bony metastases are rare and suggest another diagnosis. (Book p444)
Match FIGO stage with site in GTN — 1) Stage 1 2) Stage 2 3) Stage 3 4) Stage 4 … A) Confined to uterus B) Pelvis and vagina C) Lung D) Brain or liver
Stage 1 is confined to the uterus, stage 2 spreads to pelvis and vagina, stage 3 to lung, and stage 4 to brain, liver or kidney. (Book p445)
In the WHO risk scoring table, which pair falls in the HIGH-risk column?
Age ≥ 40 years and antecedent full term pregnancy
High risk: age ≥40 yrs, full term antecedent, interval ≥12 months, hCG ≥10^5, size ≥5 cm, brain/liver sites, >8 mets, failed chemo. (Book p445)
Fill up: WHO scoring assigns low risk for an interval between pregnancies of ______ and high risk for ______.
Interval <4 months scores low risk while ≥12 months scores high risk. (Book p445)
Which hCG values mark the low- and high-risk ends of the WHO score?
Low risk hCG <10^3 IU; high risk ≥10^5 IU. (Book p445)
Tumour size and number of metastases in the WHO score: low vs high risk.
< 3 cm and < 4 mets vs ≥ 5 cm and > 8 mets
< 5 cm and < 8 mets vs ≥ 3 cm and > 4 mets
< 2 cm and < 2 mets vs ≥ 4 cm and > 6 mets
Size and mets are not scored
Low risk: <3 cm, <4 metastases; high risk: ≥5 cm, >8 metastases. (Book p445)
Which metastatic sites score as high risk in WHO scoring?
Lung/vagina are low-risk sites; brain/liver are high-risk sites. (Book p445)
Previous history of failed chemotherapy contributes to the WHO score as:
Always high risk irrespective of history
Previous failed chemotherapy is (−) in the low-risk column and (+) in the high-risk column. (Book p445)
Total WHO score interpretation: which cut-offs are used?
≤ 6 = low risk GTN; ≥ 7 = high risk GTN
Total score ≤6 is low risk GTN and ≥7 is high risk GTN. (Book p445)
GTN is chemosensitive, so chemotherapy is the backbone of management. (Book p445)
Choose the correct treatment for stage 1 and stage 2–3 GTN with a WHO score < 6.
Stage 1 low risk and stage 2–3 with score <6 are treated with methotrexate. (Book p445)
Stage 2–3 GTN with score ≥ 7, and all stage 4 disease, require:
Score ≥7 (stages 2–3) and stage 4 high-risk GTN receive multidrug chemotherapy. (Book p445)
Fill up: In the WHO prognostic scoring system, a total score of ______ or more defines high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is treated with ______ chemotherapy.
A score of 6 or less is low risk and treated with single-agent chemotherapy; 7 or more is high risk and needs multi-agent EMA-CO. (Book p445)
Which single drug is the DOC for low-risk GTN?
Methotrexate (MTX) is the DOC single-drug therapy. (Book p446)
In multidose MTX therapy, the equally divided dose is given on which days, alternated with what?
Equally divided MTX doses on days 1, 3, 5, 7 are alternated with folic acid. (Book p446)
After each MTX cycle, treatment is repeated until which endpoint, then followed up for how long?
3 consecutive normal β-hCG levels; follow-up 12 months
Cycles repeat till 3 consecutive normal β-hCG levels, with follow-up for 12 months. (Book p446)
EMA-CO (Bagshaw regime) is also known as which multidrug therapy, and what does each letter-day pairing say?
E etoposide D1, M MTX D2, A actinomycin D D3, C cyclophosphamide D4, O Oncovin D5
E etoposide D1, M MTX D1, A actinomycin D D1, C cisplatin D8, O Oncovin D8
E etoposide D4, M MTX D5, A actinomycin D D6, C cyclophosphamide D7, O Oncovin D8
E etoposide D2, M MTX D3, A actinomycin D D4, C cyclophosphamide D5, O Oncovin D6
As listed: etoposide D1, MTX D2, actinomycin D D3, cyclophosphamide D4, Oncovin D5. (Book p446)
If GTN becomes resistant to EMA-CO, the regime switches to EMA-EP. What changes?
Days 1–3 remain the same; etoposide on D4 and cisplatin on D5
All drugs stop and radiotherapy starts
In EMA-EP days 1, 2, 3 stay the same while etoposide is given on D4 and cisplatin on D5. (Book p446)
Radiotherapy has a role in GTN for which metastatic site?
Radiotherapy is reserved for brain metastasis. (Book p446)

Match the disease category with its treatment — 1) Low-risk GTN 2) High-risk GTN 3) Placental site trophoblastic tumour … A) Multi-agent EMA-CO chemotherapy B) Single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin D C) Hysterectomy, because it is relatively chemoresistant and secretes little hCG
Risk dictates intensity: single agent for low risk, EMA-CO for high risk, and surgery for the chemoresistant placental site tumour. (Book p446)
How long is follow-up, and how long is pregnancy contraindicated, after multidrug GTN therapy?
12 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 12 months
6 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 6 months
12 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 24 months
24 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 6 months
Follow-up is for 12 months and pregnancy is contraindicated for 12 months. (Book p446)
What is the management of PSTT/ETT?
PSTT/ETT is managed by hysterectomy followed by EMACO. (Book p446)
Which tumour markers are listed for PSTT?
Placental alkaline phosphatase and human placental lactogen
Beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein, both markedly elevated
CA-125 and inhibin, which closely track the tumour burden
Lactate dehydrogenase and calcitonin, which rise with metastases
Placental site trophoblastic tumour secretes placental alkaline phosphatase and human placental lactogen, with relatively little hCG. (Book p446)
Which is NOT a listed indication of hysterectomy in GTD?
Molar pregnancy with age ≥ 40 years + completed family
Indications are age ≥40 yrs with completed family, intractable hemorrhage during evacuation, PSTT/ETT, and stage I GTN with completed family. (Book p446)
Stage I GTN in a woman with a completed family is managed by:
Stage I GTN with completed family: hysterectomy followed by multidose MTX. (Book p446)
Match the histopathology: invasive mole vs choriocarcinoma vs PSTT.
Invasive mole – edematous chorionic villi of syncytio- and cytotrophoblast; choriocarcinoma – no villi with syncytio- and cytotrophoblast; PSTT – no villi, intermediate trophoblast
Invasive mole – no villi; choriocarcinoma – edematous villi; PSTT – syncytiotrophoblast only
PSTT shows edematous villi; invasive mole shows intermediate trophoblast only
Invasive mole keeps edematous villi; choriocarcinoma has no villi-like structure with both trophoblasts; PSTT has no villi and intermediate trophoblast. (Book p446)
Which of the following statements about the management of molar pregnancy is TRUE?
Hysterectomy may suit a woman who has completed her family, but hCG follow-up is still needed because metastases can still appear
Hysterectomy removes all risk of malignant change, so no hCG follow-up is required
Prophylactic chemotherapy is given routinely after every molar evacuation
Combined oral contraceptives are contraindicated during follow-up because they raise hCG
Hysterectomy reduces but does not abolish the risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia; contraception during follow-up is encouraged, not banned. (Book p446)
Fill up: Antepartum hemorrhage is any bleeding from or into the genital tract beyond the period of viability or ≥ ______ weeks of pregnancy.
APH is defined as bleeding from/into the genital tract beyond viability or ≥28 weeks. (Book p447)

Match each cause of antepartum haemorrhage with when or how often it occurs — 1) Commonest cause 2) Second commonest cause 3) Bleeding commonest at the time of labour … A) Abruptio placenta B) Placenta previa C) Uterine rupture
Abruptio placenta is the commonest cause of APH, placenta previa the second commonest, and uterine rupture is commonest at the time of labour. (Book p447)
Which statement about APH — Placenta previa 2nd is TRUE?
Placenta previa is the 2nd m/c cause of APH
Vasa previa is the 2nd m/c cause of APH
Preterm labour show is the 2nd m/c cause of APH
Uterine rupture is the 2nd m/c cause of APH
Placenta previa is the 2nd m/c cause of APH. (Book p447)
A woman at 38 weeks has painless vaginal bleeding with fetal bradycardia, and the blood lost is fetal blood coming out through the mother's vagina. What is the diagnosis?
Vasa previa, with fetal blood escaping through the mother's vagina
Abruptio placenta, with premature separation of the placenta
Placenta previa, with the placenta in the lower uterine segment
Uterine rupture, with bleeding from the previous scar site
Vasa previa means fetal blood loss coming out through the mother's vagina, which is why it presents with fetal bradycardia. (Book p447)
All of the following count as antepartum haemorrhage EXCEPT:
A blood-stained mucus show in preterm labour
Bleeding from placental abruption with a tender, contracting uterus
Painless recurrent bleeding from placenta previa in the third trimester
Bleeding from vasa previa accompanied by fetal bradycardia
A show is mucus with a little blood from the cervix; antepartum haemorrhage means bleeding from the placental site or vessels, so a preterm show is not APH. (Book p447)
Fill up: Uterine rupture is m/c ______.
Uterine rupture is m/c at the time of labour. (Book p447)

A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks presents with painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding and the placenta has not yet been located on scan. Which examination is contraindicated until placenta previa is ruled out?
Per vaginal examination, until placenta previa has been excluded
Per abdominal examination of the fundal height and lie
Recording of the maternal pulse and blood pressure
Speculum inspection performed after the ultrasound
Per vaginal examination is contraindicated in third-trimester APH until placenta previa is excluded. (Book p447)

Match the definition to the condition — 1) Placenta lying in the lower uterine segment 2) Premature separation of a normally located placenta 3) Fetal blood escaping through the mother's vagina … A) Abruptio placenta B) Placenta previa C) Vasa previa

Placenta previa is a placenta in the lower uterine segment; abruptio is premature separation of a normally located placenta; vasa previa means fetal blood loss coming out through the mother's vagina. (Book p447)

Match the pp vs abruptio with the correct detail — 1) abruptio placenta 2) Sequence of bleeding in placenta previa: uterine contraction/cervical 3) statement about bleeding in placenta previa is TRUE … A) Premature separation of a normally located (upper-segment) placenta B) Opening of venous sinuses of the intervillous space C) The placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released
Abruptio = premature separation of a normally located placenta in the upper uterine segment. (Book p447)
All of the following are PP vs abruptio — Sequence of bleeding in placenta EXCEPT:
The placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released
Premature separation of a normally located (upper-segment) placenta
Vasa previa, with fetal blood escaping through the mother's vagina
Opening of venous sinuses of the intervillous space
Shearing force opens the venous sinuses (intervillous space); the placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released. (Book p447)
Which statement about bleeding in placenta previa is TRUE?
The placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released
The placenta separates centrally, releasing thromboplastin
Fetal distress is the earliest and most constant feature
The bleeding is consistently painful and dark red
In placenta previa the shearing force opens venous sinuses of the intervillous space; the placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released. (Book p447)
Which statement about PP vs abruptio — Separation begets further is TRUE?
Separation begets Further bleeding, thromboplastin release and fetal distress
Separation begets Opening of intervillous sinuses only
Separation begets further bleeding, thromboplastin release and fetal distress. (Book p447)
Fill up: Antepartum haemorrhage is bleeding from or into the genital tract after ______ weeks of gestation, and its two commonest causes are placenta previa and ______.
After the period of viability (28 weeks in India), the classic causes are placenta previa and abruptio placentae, with local causes and vasa previa less common. (Book p447)
Fill up: For the diagnosis of placenta previa, the placenta must lie within ______ of the internal os.
Placenta previa is defined by a placenta-to-internal-os distance of 2 cm or less. (Book p448)
A low-lying placenta is noted on the 20-week anomaly scan of an asymptomatic woman. Why is placenta previa not diagnosed at this stage?
Placental migration occurs with differential growth of the lower segment in the third trimester
Ultrasound is unsafe before the third trimester of pregnancy
Bleeding from placenta previa never occurs before the third trimester
The internal os does not begin to dilate until the third trimester
Differential growth of the lower uterine segment in the third trimester migrates the placenta upwards, so the diagnosis is reserved for the third trimester. (Book p448)
Which statement about PP — best time for is TRUE?
The best time for ultrasound assessment of placenta previa is 32 weeks and 36 weeks, the third-trimester window in which the diagnosis is made
The best time for ultrasound assessment of placenta previa is 20 weeks and 24 weeks, the third-trimester window in which the diagnosis is made
The best time for ultrasound assessment of placenta previa is 28 weeks and 40 weeks, the third-trimester window in which the diagnosis is made
The best time for ultrasound assessment of placenta previa is 12 weeks and 16 weeks, the third-trimester window in which the diagnosis is made
The best time for ultrasound assessment of placenta previa is 32 weeks and 36 weeks, the third-trimester window in which the diagnosis is made. (Book p448)
Which statement about thromboplastin release in abruptio placenta is TRUE?
It produces a tense tender uterus, labour, tissue necrosis and DIC
It produces uterine relaxation with painless bleeding
It limits bleeding by promoting local clot formation at the site
It has no systemic effect and stays within the uterine cavity
Thromboplastin causes a tense, tender, rigid uterus, initiates labour, raises matrix metalloproteinase with tissue necrosis and blood loss, and can progress to DIC. (Book p448)
Fill up: Old classification: Type 1 placenta previa means the placental edge: is ______.
Lies within 2 cm of the internal os (lateral PP)
Reaches the margin of the internal os
Type 1 (lateral PP): edge within 2 cm of the internal os, with anterior and posterior subtypes. (Book p448)
Fill up: Type 2 = ______ PP (edge reaches the os margin); type 2 posterior PP is the dangerous variety.
Marginal PP; the dangerous variety of PP
Type 2 = marginal PP (edge reaches the os margin); type 2 posterior PP is the dangerous variety. (Book p448)

A 24-year-old second gravida at 11 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pp. According to the notes, type 3 = placenta covering the internal os partially (incomplete placenta previa). What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that partial covering of the internal os (incomplete pp) is the correct pp for this patient at this gestation
Advise that complete covering of the internal os is the correct pp for this patient at this gestation
Advise that edge within 2 cm of the os is the correct pp for this patient at this gestation
Advise that edge not reaching the lus is the correct pp for this patient at this gestation
Type 3 = placenta covering the internal os partially (incomplete placenta previa). (Book p448)
Which of the following statements about placenta previa is TRUE?
Classic placenta previa causes painless, recurrent, bright red bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus
Placenta previa typically causes severe abdominal pain with a rigid, tender uterus
Bleeding from placenta previa is always provoked by intercourse or trauma
The fetal head is usually deeply engaged in the pelvis in placenta previa
Painless bright bleeding with a soft relaxed uterus and a high or malpresenting head is previa; pain with a woody uterus is abruption. (Book p448)
Which statement about PP types & abruptio varieties — Type 4 placenta is TRUE?
Complete/central placenta previa is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Marginal placenta previa is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Lateral placenta previa is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Low-lying placenta is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Type 4 = placenta covering the internal os completely (complete/central PP). (Book p449)
Which statement about PP types & abruptio varieties — In new classification is TRUE?
Low-lying: type I — placenta previa: types I, II and III reaching or covering the os is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Low-lying: types I to IV — placenta previa: type I alone is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Low-lying: type II — placenta previa: types III and IV only is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Low-lying: type I — placenta previa: type IV alone is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
In the new classification low-lying placenta is type I, while placenta previa covers types I to III reaching or covering the os. (Book p449)

A 24-year-old G2P1L1 at 12 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pp types & abruptio varieties. According to the notes, revealed: clot −, bleeding +; concealed: clot +, bleeding −; mixed (m/c): clot + and bleeding +. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that revealed – clot (−), bleeding (+); concealed – clot (+), bleeding (−); mixed – clot (+), bleeding (+) is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that revealed – clot (+), bleeding (−); concealed – clot (−), bleeding (+); mixed – both (−) is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that revealed – both (+); concealed – both (−); mixed – clot (+) only is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that all three show bleeding with no clot is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Revealed: clot −, bleeding +; concealed: clot +, bleeding −; mixed (m/c): clot + and bleeding +. (Book p449)
Fill up: The ______ is the most common.
The mixed variety is the most common. (Book p449)
Which statement about PP types & abruptio varieties — Grade 0 retrospective is TRUE?
Retrospectively, based on the retroplacental clot is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
By maternal shock at presentation is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
By fetal distress on CTG is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
By DIC parameters is the listed pp types & abruptio varieties as per the notes
Grade 0 is a retrospective diagnosis based on the retroplacental clot. (Book p449)

A 26-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pp types & abruptio varieties. According to the notes, grade 1 has normal FHS; Grade 2 shows fetal distress, both with bleeding + pain. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that grade 1 – fhs normal; grade 2 – fetal distress is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that grade 1 – fetal death; grade 2 – fhs normal is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that both show fetal distress is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that grade 1 – distress; grade 2 – death is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Grade 1 has normal FHS; Grade 2 shows fetal distress, both with bleeding + pain. (Book p449)

A 24-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pp types & abruptio varieties. According to the notes, grade 3 = bleeding + pain, maternal shock, +/− DIC and fetal death. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that bleeding + pain, maternal shock, +/− dic and fetal death is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that painless bleeding with normal fhs is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that only a retroplacental clot found retrospectively is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that bleeding with fetal distress but stable mother is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Grade 3 = bleeding + pain, maternal shock, +/− DIC and fetal death. (Book p449)

A 32-year-old second gravida at 12 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pp types & abruptio varieties. According to the notes, risk factor is PIH; primigravida and smoking are predisposing. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
Advise that pih, primigravida and smoking is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that grand multiparity only is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Advise that diabetes only is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
