Advise that previous c-section only is the correct pp types & abruptio varieties for this patient at this gestation
Risk factor is PIH; primigravida and smoking are predisposing. (Book p449)

Match the grade of placenta previa with its description — 1) Type I 2) Type II 3) Type IV … A) The placenta reaches the lower segment but not the margin of the internal os B) The placenta reaches the margin of the internal os but does not cover it C) The placenta completely covers the internal os even when the os is fully dilated
Type I is low-lying, type II is marginal and reaching the os, type III partially covers it and type IV covers it completely. (Book p449)
All of the following are PP vs abruptio — m/c risk factor for placenta EXCEPT:
Diabetes, Rh-negative pregnancy, twins, a succenturiate lobe and placenta bilobata
Previous caesarean, uterine surgery or curettage, and smoking with endometritis
Previous placenta previa is m/c with a 5–8% recurrence rate. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Which statement about PP vs abruptio — bulky placenta covers is TRUE?
Diabetes, Rh-negative pregnancy, twins, a succenturiate lobe and placenta bilobata is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
Pregnancy-induced hypertension and maternal thrombophilia is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
Folic acid deficiency with severe maternal anaemia is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
Cocaine abuse with the placental infarction it produces is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
A bulky placenta covers more of the lower segment, so conditions that enlarge the placenta predispose to previa. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Fill up: Adhesion formation that prevents placental migration follows: is ______.
Previous caesarean, uterine surgery or curettage, and smoking with endometritis
Polyhydramnios, which stretches the uterus and thins the decidua
Folic acid deficiency, which impairs the development of the decidua
Primigravidity, since a first pregnancy leaves behind the most adhesions
Anything that scars or inflames the endometrium prevents the placenta from migrating away from the lower segment. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations

Match the pp vs abruptio with the correct detail — 1) The m/c risk factor for abruptio placenta and 2) is NOT a listed abruptio risk factor 3) Risk factors common to both placenta previa and … A) Previous abruptio; recurrence 15% B) Folic acid deficiency is listed; choose the odd one: young maternal age with first pregnancy C) Increased maternal age, increased parity and smoking
Previous abruptio placenta is m/c with a 15% recurrence rate. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Which statement about PP vs abruptio — Listed risks include is TRUE?
Folic acid deficiency is listed; choose the odd one: young maternal age with first pregnancy is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
Thrombophilia is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
Cigarette smoking and cocaine abuse is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes
Single umbilical artery with preterm rupture of membranes is the listed pp vs abruptio as per the notes

Listed risks include folic acid deficiency, ↑ age/parity, smoking/cocaine, thrombophilia, PIH/chronic HTN, fibroid, twins, polyhydramnios, SUA, PROM and trauma – not young first pregnancy. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Fill up: Risk factors common to both placenta previa and abruptio placentae are ______.
Increased maternal age, increased parity and smoking
Diabetes mellitus and Rh negativity of the mother
Thrombophilia and a fibroid uterus distorting the cavity
Cocaine use and blunt abdominal trauma in pregnancy
Risk factors common to both placenta previa and abruptio placentae are increased maternal age, increased parity and smoking. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Fill up: ______ is m/c with transverse lie more common than breech.
Malpresentation is m/c with transverse lie more common than breech. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Fill up: At term the m/c cause of transverse lie is ______ accreta, managed by C-section → hysterectomy.
At term the m/c cause of transverse lie is placenta accreta, managed by C-section → hysterectomy. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Overall (any gestation), the m/c cause of transverse lie is:
Overall m/c cause of transverse lie is preterm delivery; at term it is placenta previa/accreta. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
In posterior varieties of placenta previa, the fetal head pushed into the pelvis produces which sign?
Stallworthy's sign, where the head cannot be pushed into the pelvis, with fetal distress
Cullen's sign, with bluish discolouration around the umbilicus
Chadwick's sign, with bluish discolouration of the vaginal mucosa
Bandl's sign, with a rising retraction ring across the abdomen
In a posterior placenta previa the head is held up by the placental mass and cannot be pushed into the pelvis: Stallworthy's sign. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
A bluish, bruised uterus with blood clots in the myometrium in abruptio is called:
Retroplacental bleeding tracking into the myometrium gives the Couvelaire uterus. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
True or false per the notes: Couvelaire uterus is an indication for hysterectomy.
False – it is NOT an indication for hysterectomy
False – but it mandates internal iliac ligation
The notes state Couvelaire uterus is not an indication for hysterectomy. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Abruptio placenta is associated with increased chances of:
PPH, DIC from thromboplastin release, and preterm labour
Placenta previa in a subsequent pregnancy, but nothing else
Vasa previa with rupture of fetal vessels in labour
Uterine inversion from traction on the placental site
Abruptio placenta is associated with increased chances of PPH, DIC (from release of thromboplastin) and preterm labour. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
Name the rare associations of chronic abruption listed.
Chronic abruption oligohydramnios sequence and precipitate labour under 3 hours
Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome together with vasa previa
Uterine rupture together with acute inversion of the uterus
Cervical incompetence with a persistent bloody vaginal show
The rare associations listed for chronic abruption are chronic abruption oligohydramnios sequence (CAOS) and precipitate labour of under 3 hours. (Book p450)
PP vs abruptio: risk factors & associations
All of the following are risk factors for placenta previa EXCEPT:
A previous pregnancy complicated by placenta previa
Hypertensive disorders are linked to abruption rather than previa; scarring of the endometrium from surgery, parity and age are previa risks. (Book p450)
In a patient of preterm labour with a tense, tender, rigid uterus you should suspect:
A tense, tender, rigid uterus in PTL raises the chance of abruptio placenta. (Book p451)
In a PPH patient with sustained fetal distress, which diagnosis must be ruled out?
Sustained fetal distress with PPH mandates ruling out abruptio placenta. (Book p451)
Describe the bleeding of placenta previa.
Bright red, recurrent and painless, with no precipitating factor and often a small warning bleed
Dark red and non-recurrent, with severe abdominal pain and a tender uterus
A blood-stained mucus discharge mixed with the cervical show of labour
A continuous dark trickle of blood with a rigid, tender uterus
Previa bleeds bright and painlessly with no trigger; pain, darkness and tenderness point to abruption instead. (Book p451)
Describe the bleeding of abruptio placenta.
Dark red, non-recurrent, with abdominal pain and a precipitating factor such as trauma or hypertension
Bright red and painless, recurring at intervals through the third trimester
Recurrent with completely free intervals and a soft non-tender uterus
Only after sexual intercourse, with no pain or uterine tenderness at all
Abruption bleeds dark and often concealed, with pain and a trigger such as trauma or hypertension; previa is bright, painless and recurrent. (Book p451)
General examination in abruptio (mixed/concealed varieties) shows shock that:
Does not correspond to the amount of visible blood loss
In mixed and concealed varieties shock does not correspond to visible blood loss. (Book p451)
Per-abdominal findings in placenta previa include all EXCEPT:
Fetal parts easily palpable with FHS heard easily
Uterine height corresponding to POG with normal FHS
A tense tender rigid uterus belongs to abruptio; PP gives a soft relaxed non-tender uterus. (Book p451)
In abruptio placenta, the uterine height compared with POG and fetal status are:
Height of uterus > POG and fetal distress are features of abruptio. (Book p451)
Per vaginal examination in placenta previa is contraindicated because it leads to excessive bleeding. Which other activity is also contraindicated?
Intercourse is also contraindicated in PP. (Book p451)
In abruptio placenta, P/V examination is performed:
Only after ruling out placenta previa
P/V is done in abruptio only after excluding PP. (Book p451)
Investigation of choice in placenta previa and its purpose:
Transvaginal ultrasound, to measure the distance between external and internal os
Transabdominal ultrasound, to measure the distance between external and internal os
Transvaginal ultrasound, to grade the degree of placental calcification
MRI of the pelvis, to measure the distance between external and internal os
The investigation of choice in placenta previa is transvaginal ultrasound, which gives the exact distance between the external and internal os. (Book p451)
Abruptio is a clinical diagnosis aided by USG. (Book p451)
Screening USG pathway for suspected previa: first ______, and if the placenta is in the LUS then ______.
Suspected PP is screened by transabdominal USG; placenta in LUS prompts TVS. (Book p451)

A 32-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks has had a single painless episode of bright red bleeding that has now stopped. The uterus is soft and non-tender, the fetal heart is normal and the head is not engaged. What is the next step?
Ultrasound to locate the placenta, and no digital vaginal examination until placenta previa is excluded
Immediate digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix and confirm the source
Emergency caesarean section on clinical grounds before any imaging
Induction of labour with oxytocin because she is already 34 weeks
Every woman with antepartum haemorrhage is imaged before any digital examination, because examining a previa can cause torrential bleeding. (Book p451)
Initial resuscitation for third-trimester bleeding includes which cannulae and investigations?
2 large-bore IV cannulas No 14/16; ABO/Rh, PT, BT, CT
Resuscitation uses two 14/16 cannulas with ABO/Rh, PT, BT, CT, crystalloids, blood arrangement and catheterisation. (Book p452)
Which step is NOT part of the resuscitation checklist for third-trimester bleeding?
The checklist covers cannulas, investigations, crystalloids, blood, catheter, ABC and oxygen – not routine tocolysis. (Book p452)
The three assessment parameters after resuscitation are:
Maternal vitals, FHS and evaluation for DIC
Assess vitals, FHS and DIC. (Book p452)
If ANY ONE of the assessment parameters is abnormal, the action is:
Any abnormal parameter mandates immediate C-section irrespective of diagnosis. (Book p452)
With all three parameters normal, the next step is:
History and abdominal examination followed by a transabdominal screening ultrasound
Direct transvaginal scanning before any clinical assessment is made
Emergency caesarean section on the basis of the presenting complaint alone
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to map the placental site
Transabdominal screening comes first; transvaginal scanning is then used to measure the placental edge when needed. (Book p452)
Which triad confirms abruptio on imaging/examination?
Placenta in upper uterine segment, retroplacental clot, Jello sign positive
Placenta in LUS, snowstorm, theca lutein cysts
Abruptio (+): placenta in UUS, retroplacental clot and Jello sign (shimmering placenta on movement). (Book p452)
Shimmering of the placenta on movement
Jello sign = shimmering of the placenta on movement, seen in abruptio. (Book p452)
A placenta found in the LUS in T1/T2 without any history of P/V bleeding will migrate in what proportion of cases?
In 80–90% of such cases placental migration occurs. (Book p452)
Fill up: Until placenta previa has been excluded, a ______ examination must not be performed, since it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage.
A speculum examination and transvaginal ultrasound are safe, but a finger in the cervix can separate the placenta and cause massive bleeding. (Book p452)
Advice given to a patient with a low-lying placenta includes avoiding:
Intercourse, physical exercise, heavy lifting and standing 4 hours or more
All household work and walking about inside the house
Normal oral fluid intake and normal dietary salt intake
Transvaginal scans, which must be avoided after 28 weeks
With a low-lying placenta the patient is advised to avoid intercourse, physical exercise, heavy lifting and standing for 4 hours or more. (Book p453)
Follow-up scan schedule: no P/V bleeding → repeat USG at 32 weeks; if placenta still in LUS →
Placenta in LUS at 32 weeks → repeat TVS at 36 weeks. (Book p453)
If the placenta is STILL in the LUS at 36 weeks, delivery is planned as:
Persistent LUS placenta → plan C-section between 36–37 weeks + 6 days. (Book p453)
If at follow-up the placenta is in the upper uterine segment, the interpretation is:
Migration has occurred – not a case of placenta previa
Placenta in UUS means migration occurred; it is not placenta previa. (Book p453)
Mode of delivery: a low-lying placenta 1–2 cm from the internal os is best managed by:
Caesarean preferred, though vaginal delivery can be done
Mandatory caesarean section in absolutely every single case
Mandatory vaginal delivery, caesarean is never considered
Forceps delivery to shorten the second stage of the labour
A low-lying placenta 1-2 cm from the internal os is best managed by caesarean section, though vaginal delivery can be done. (Book p453)
A placenta within 1 cm of the internal os, and true placenta previa, require:
Within 1 cm → C-section; placenta previa → always C-section. (Book p453)
In placenta previa WITH active bleeding, expectant management aims to:
Continue pregnancy to attain fetal lung maturity without risking the mother
Terminate the pregnancy immediately by caesarean section in every case
Delay delivery until beyond 40 completed weeks regardless of bleeding
Avoid antenatal corticosteroids and transfuse only when symptomatic
In placenta previa with active bleeding, expectant management aims to continue pregnancy to attain fetal lung maturity without risking the mother's life. (Book p453)
Which of the following statements about delivery in placenta previa is TRUE?
Major or central previa needs caesarean section, while a minor previa whose edge lies more than 2 cm from the internal os may allow a trial of labour
Vaginal delivery is safe for every degree of placenta previa as long as the fetus is alive
A placental edge within 1 cm of the internal os is safe for a trial of labour
Caesarean section is needed only if bleeding recurs after 37 weeks
The measured distance from the placental edge to the internal os decides the mode: an edge beyond 2 cm permits a trial of labour. (Book p453)
Which combination favours EXPECTANT management of bleeding previa?
Stable vitals, no active bleeding, under 37 weeks, reactive CTG, no major anomaly
Unstable vitals with active bleeding, under 37 weeks, non-reactive CTG
Stable vitals, no active bleeding, under 37 weeks, fetal distress on CTG
A gross congenital anomaly in a non-viable fetus, with stable vitals
Expectant management of bleeding previa requires all of: stable vitals, absent active bleeding, under 37 weeks, reactive CTG, and no or only a minor anomaly. (Book p454)
Which single finding triggers ACTIVE management in bleeding previa?
ANY one of unstable vitals, active bleeding, ≥37 weeks (or ≥34 weeks with extreme loss), fetal distress or gross anomaly triggers active management. (Book p454)
At what gestation does active management become indicated even without extreme blood loss?
POG ≥37 weeks favours active management; ≥34 weeks only with extreme blood loss. (Book p454)
Expectant management of previa is also named the ______ regime and starts with:
MacAfee/Johnson's regime – admit the patient with bed rest
Expectant management = MacAfee/Johnson's regime beginning with admission and bed rest. (Book p454)
Maternal vitals, fetal heart sounds and bleeding, with blood arranged
Only a weekly serum beta-hCG measurement is required
Cervical length measured every single day by ultrasound
Serial magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis each week
Monitoring during expectant management covers maternal vitals, fetal heart sounds and bleeding, with blood arranged in advance. (Book p454)
An Rh-negative mother under expectant management should receive:
Anti-D is given if the patient is Rh-negative. (Book p454)
Steroid and tocolytic rules in expectant previa: POG <34 weeks gets ______ and POG <32 weeks adds ______.
Dexamethasone + tocolytics; MgSO4 for neural protection
<34 weeks: dexamethasone + tocolytics; <32 weeks: add MgSO4 for fetal neural protection; continue till 37 weeks then elective C-section (36–37 weeks). (Book p454)
In ALL cases of placenta previa the notes advise suspecting:
Every previa should raise suspicion of placenta accreta. (Book p454)
If Doppler USG in previa shows accreta features, the operative plan becomes:
With accreta present, C-section proceeds to hysterectomy (caesarean hysterectomy). (Book p454)
A 30-year-old at 30 weeks with major placenta previa has stopped bleeding, is haemodynamically stable and has a normal CTG. What is the best plan?
Expectant inpatient management with corticosteroids, cross-matched blood and planned delivery around 36-37 weeks
Immediate caesarean delivery at 30 weeks because the bleeding has been severe
Discharge home with instructions to return if the bleeding restarts
Induction of labour by amniotomy and oxytocin infusion at 30 weeks
When mother and fetus are stable, expectant management buys maturity; steroids are given and delivery planned electively around 36-37 weeks. (Book p454)
Expectant vs active management of previa
An abruptio patient presenting in labour pain with maternal vitals unstable, fetal distress, DIC or acute kidney injury needs:
These emergency conditions mandate immediate C-section. (Book p455)
In abruptio with FETAL DEATH, vaginal delivery is acceptable when:
Maternal vitals are stable and there is no DIC
Fetal death with stable mother and no DIC allows vaginal delivery; instability or DIC pushes to C-section. (Book p455)
A non-emergency abruptio (normal FHS) at ≥34 weeks is managed by:
Induction of labour for vaginal delivery
≥34 weeks → induction of labour/vaginal delivery; <34 weeks → expectant management. (Book p455)
DIC is also called ______ and includes which obstetric causes?
Consumptive coagulopathy, from abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, septic abortion, acute fatty liver and prolonged fetal death
Consumptive coagulopathy, caused by placenta previa and nothing else
Dilutional coagulopathy, caused by postpartum haemorrhage alone
A hypercoagulable state, caused by maternal sepsis alone
Obstetric DIC is consumptive: thromboplastin or tissue factor enters the circulation and consumes fibrinogen and platelets. (Book p455)
Cryoprecipitate, fresh frozen plasma and blood transfusion
A heparin infusion given on its own throughout
Platelet transfusion given on its own throughout
Vitamin K given alone by slow intravenous injection
Management of DIC includes cryoprecipitate, fresh frozen plasma and blood transfusion. (Book p455)
In abruptio WITH DIC, the first step is:
In abruptio + DIC, manage DIC first and then proceed to C-section. (Book p455)

Match the term with its meaning — 1) Couvelaire uterus 2) Consumptive coagulopathy in abruption 3) Concealed abruption … A) Blood tracking into the myometrium and beneath the serosa, seen at caesarean section B) Falling fibrinogen and platelets with prolonged clotting times from thromboplastin release C) Blood retained behind the placenta, so the uterus is larger than dates and woody hard
Concealed bleeding distends the uterus, thromboplastin triggers consumption coagulopathy, and extravasation produces the Couvelaire appearance. (Book p455)
Differential diagnosis of bleeding beyond 28 weeks includes all EXCEPT:
Cervical ectropion bleed as a listed APH cause
The D/D list is APH (abruptio, previa, vasa previa), preterm labour show and uterine rupture. (Book p456)
Labour vs abruptio: match P/V, cervix and fetus findings.
Labour – blood-mixed mucus discharge, progressive cervical dilatation, FHS normal; abruptio – bleeding, no progressive dilatation, fetal distress
Labour – frank bleeding, no dilatation, distress; abruptio – show, dilatation, normal FHS
Labour shows mucus-discharge, progressive dilatation and normal FHS; abruptio shows bleeding and fetal distress. (Book p456)
If the distinction between labour and abruptio is doubtful, the next step is:
When doubtful, ARM is performed to inspect the liquor. (Book p456)
ARM in abruptio yields which liquor and effects?
Dark red liquor; accelerates labour; increases bleeding
Meconium-stained liquor; no effect on labour
In abruptio ARM shows dark red liquor, accelerates labour and ↑ bleeding. (Book p456)
Abruptio vs ruptured uterus: which history and P/A pair belongs to ruptured uterus?
H/o previous LSCS; uterine contour not felt with fetal parts felt superficially in the peritoneal cavity
H/o trauma/PIH; tender rigid uterus with fundal height > POG
H/o trauma; fetal parts not palpable
H/o PIH; loss of fetal station on P/A
Ruptured uterus follows previous LSCS with loss of uterine contour and superficially felt parts; P/V shows loss of fetal station. (Book p456)
On P/V examination, loss of fetal station suggests:
Loss of fetal station on P/V is the ruptured-uterus counterpart to a palpable head in abruptio. (Book p456)
Placenta accreta spectrum was previously known as:
PAS was previously called morbidly adherent placenta. (Book p457)
Placenta accreta – villi superficially attached to myometrium (m/c)
Grade 1 = accreta with superficial myometrial attachment, the m/c grade. (Book p457)
Grade 2 increta: villi within the myometrium — grade 3 percreta: villi reach the serosa or beyond
Grade 2 percreta: villi through the serosa — grade 3 increta: villi within the myometrium
Grade 2 accreta: villi lying on the myometrium — grade 3 increta: villi within the myometrium
Grade 2 involves the bladder — grade 3 is limited to the serosa of the uterus
Grade 1 is accreta, grade 2 increta into the myometrium, and grade 3 percreta to the serosa, with 3b for bladder and 3c for other organs. (Book p457)
The three etiopathogenic mechanisms of PAS are:
Defective decidualisation, absence of Nitabuch's layer and excessive trophoblastic invasiveness
Hypertension, diabetes and cigarette smoking during pregnancy
Uterine overdistension, intrauterine infection and direct trauma
A thin myometrium, polyhydramnios and a twin pregnancy
Accreta spectrum is a decidua problem plus an invasive trophoblast: no decidua, no Nitabuch layer, and over-invasive cytotrophoblast. (Book p457)
Nitabuch's layer is a layer of fibrinoid degeneration between ______ and its function is to:
Trophoblast and decidua basalis; limit villous penetration into decidua
Nitabuch's layer lies between trophoblast and decidua basalis and limits penetration; its absence allows deeper invasion. (Book p457)
The foremost risk factor for PAS in the current pregnancy is:
Anterior placenta previa in the present pregnancy heads the risk list. (Book p458)
Previous surgeries predisposing to PAS include:
C-section, myomectomy, curettage and endometrial ablation
Prior C-section (risk ↑ with number), myomectomy, curettage and endometrial ablation predispose to PAS. (Book p458)
Maternal serum markers (not done routinely) that raise PAS risk are:
Maternal serum AFP ≥2.5 MoM and hCG ≥2.5 MoM indicate ↑ PAS risk. (Book p458)
Screening and definitive diagnosis of PAS are:
Anomaly scan (findings in T2); USG with colour Doppler (IOC) at 28 weeks
First-trimester NT scan; MRI at 12 weeks
Screening is the anomaly scan with characteristic T2 findings; definitive is colour Doppler USG (IOC) at 28 weeks. (Book p458)
Which USG sign of PAS describes sonolucent areas with a moth-eaten appearance and ↑ vascularity on Doppler?
Large placental lacunae, also called placental lakes
The twin peak sign of a dichorionic pregnancy
A snowstorm appearance filling the uterine cavity
The ring of fire seen around a corpus luteum
Large placental lacunae (placental lakes) are sonolucent areas with a moth-eaten appearance and increased vascularity on Doppler. (Book p458)
Thinning of the retroplacental myometrium in PAS is defined as a serosa–myometrium distance of:
A distance <1 mm between serosa and myometrium defines thinning. (Book p458)
Bridging vessels in PAS are seen between the placenta and:
The bladder-serosa interface, appearing hypervascular on Doppler
The umbilical cord insertion into the placental mass
The cervix and the adjacent lower uterine segment
The veins of the broad ligament and ovarian plexus
Bridging vessels in PAS are seen between the placenta and the bladder-serosa interface, appearing hypervascular on Doppler. (Book p458)
Two further USG signs of PAS listed are disruption of the continuous white line and:
Loss of the normal retroplacental hypoechoic area (decidua basalis)
Gain of a new retroplacental cystic lesion behind the placenta
Marked thickening of the amnion over the placental surface
Absent fetal breathing movements on a 30-minute scan
Besides disruption of the continuous white line, PAS shows loss of the normal retroplacental hypoechoic area (the decidua basalis). (Book p458)
MRI in PAS workup is reserved for:
Cases where USG + Doppler are inconclusive
MRI is used only when USG with Doppler is inconclusive. (Book p458)
Fill up: Accreta, increta and percreta differ by the depth of trophoblastic invasion into the ______, with percreta penetrating through to the ______.
Accreta adheres to myometrium, increta invades it and percreta penetrates the full thickness, sometimes into the bladder. (Book p458)
ACOG's management of choice for antenatally detected PAS is:
Elective caesarean at 34-35 weeks and 6/7 days, then hysterectomy with placenta in situ
Elective caesarean at 39 completed weeks, then removal of the placenta
Vaginal delivery followed by manual removal of the placenta at delivery
Methotrexate therapy, then curettage once the placenta separates
ACOG's management of choice for antenatally detected PAS is elective caesarean at 34-35 weeks and 6/7 days, followed by hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ. (Book p459)
During caesarean hysterectomy for PAS, which anaesthesia and incision are preferred?
General anaesthesia with classical C-section avoiding the placental site
Spinal anaesthesia with low transverse incision through the placenta
Local anaesthesia with vertical skin incision
General anaesthesia with incision through the placental site
GA is preferred and a classical C-section avoids the placental site. (Book p459)
Two intraoperative rules for PAS caesarean hysterectomy are:
Do not attempt to separate the placenta, and close the uterine incision first
Deliver the placenta manually before starting the hysterectomy
Leave the uterine incision open throughout the hysterectomy
Separate the placenta using controlled traction on the cord
Two intraoperative rules for PAS caesarean hysterectomy are: make no attempt to separate or deliver the placenta, and close the uterine incision before proceeding to hysterectomy. (Book p459)
Pre-operative ureteric catheterization in PAS offers which advantage and limitation?
Helps ureteric identification if bladder invasion exists; does NOT reduce urinary tract injury risk
Prevents all ureteric injury; no advantage in identification
Guides bladder repair; contraindicated in percreta
It aids identification but does not lower urinary tract injury risk. (Book p459)
Pre-operative internal iliac artery balloon catheters are inflated post-delivery to reduce pelvic blood flow. Why does ACOG NOT recommend them?
The ↑ embolization risk makes ACOG not recommend internal iliac balloon catheters. (Book p459)
Intractable PPH with no plane of cleavage, sometimes with haematuria from bladder invasion
Painless bright-red bleeding at 32 weeks with a soft non-tender uterus
A snowstorm ultrasound appearance with bilateral theca lutein cysts
Fetal distress with a rigid tender uterus and concealed bleeding
Postnatally detected accreta presents as a placenta that cannot be separated, with torrential bleeding and sometimes haematuria. (Book p459)
Management of postnatally detected PAS is:
Emergency hysterectomy is the management. (Book p459)
If fertility is desired in postnatal PAS, the conservative procedure includes:
Leave the placenta in situ with the cord ligated at its insertion and close the hysterotomy
Immediate hysterectomy, whatever the woman's wishes about future fertility
Manual piecemeal removal of the placenta until the cavity is empty
Vigorous curettage of the placental bed to remove all adherent tissue
Conservative management leaves the placenta in place; forced removal is what turns a controlled situation into a haemorrhage. (Book p459)
Follow-up investigations after conservative PAS management and the two interventions with NO role are:
Serial USG/MRI; no role for serial β-hCG or injection methotrexate
Serial β-hCG; no role for USG
Serial MTX levels; no role for MRI
Serial USG/MRI follow the patient; serial β-hCG and methotrexate have no role. (Book p459)
After conservative (fertility-sparing) management of PAS, what proportion ultimately require hysterectomy?
About 20% will ultimately need hysterectomy. (Book p459)
Antenatal imaging at 32 weeks in a woman with two previous caesareans and an anterior placenta previa suggests placenta percreta involving the bladder. What is the management plan?
Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-36 weeks with the placenta left in situ, by a multidisciplinary team with blood products ready
Attempt manual removal of the placenta at delivery and give oxytocin
Await spontaneous labour and plan a vaginal delivery
Give methotrexate to dissolve the placenta and deliver vaginally at term
Percreta means leaving the placenta in situ and performing a caesarean hysterectomy, planned early at a centre with surgical, urological and blood-bank support. (Book p459)
Fill up: Dizygotic twins form when ______, whereas monozygotic twins form when ______.
2 ova fertilized by 2 different sperms; 1 ovum fertilized by 1 sperm that then divides into 2
1 ovum fertilized by 1 sperm that then divides into 2; 2 ova fertilized by 2 different sperms
1 ovum fertilized by 2 different sperms; 2 separate ova fusing together after fertilisation
2 separate ova fusing together; 1 ovum fertilized by 2 different sperms after ovulation
Dizygotic twins form when 2 ova are fertilized by 2 different sperms, whereas monozygotic twins form when a single ovum fertilized by a single sperm divides into 2. (Book p460)
Fill up: The more common twin type is ______ twins, also called ______ twins.
Dizygotic twins are more common and are called fraternal; monozygotic are identical. (Book p460)
Which of the following statements about monozygotic twins is TRUE?
Monozygotic twins share sex, blood group, HLA and phenotype, but fingerprints differ due to environment
Monozygotic twins share sex alone, since blood groups and HLA types always differ between them
Monozygotic twins share blood group alone, because sex and HLA can differ even in identical twins
Monozygotic twins share nothing, since they differ genetically as much as any two siblings
Monozygotic twins share the whole genome, so sex, blood groups, HLA and phenotype match; fingerprints differ because they are formed by the environment. (Book p460)
Match the country with dizygotic twinning incidence — 1) Nigeria 2) Japan 3) India … A) 1 in 20 maximum B) 1 in 200 least C) 1 in 80
Incidence: Nigeria 1:20 max, Japan 1:200 least, India 1:80. (Book p460)
Which of the following statements about monozygotic twinning incidence is TRUE?
Monozygotic twinning incidence is uniform worldwide at about 1 in 250 births
Monozygotic twinning incidence is highest in Nigeria at 1 in 20 births overall
Monozygotic twinning incidence is lowest in Japan at 1 in 200 births worldwide
Monozygotic twinning incidence in India equals dizygotic twinning at 1 in 80 births
Monozygotic twinning is uniform worldwide (1 in 250). (Book p460)
Fill up: As per Hellin's rule, if twins occur 1 in 80, triplets occur 1 in ______ and quadruplets 1 in ______.
Hellin's rule: triplets 1 in 80² and quadruplets 1 in 80³. (Book p460)

Match the mechanism with its description — 1) Dizygotic twinning 2) Monozygotic twinning 3) Superfetation … A) One fertilised ovum splits, so the rate is constant across populations and the babies are genetically identical B) Two ova are fertilised, so the rate varies with maternal age, parity, race and ovulation induction C) A second conception occurs in a later cycle after a pregnancy is already established
Dizygotic rates vary with maternal factors and treatment; monozygotic splitting is a constant background event; superfetation is extremely rare. (Book p460)
Fill up: Two ova released in the same cycle but fertilized at different times by different acts of coitus is ______ and it is ______ in humans.
Superfecundation = same-cycle ova fertilized at different times; it is rare but possible in humans. (Book p461)
Which of the following statements about superfetation is TRUE?
Superfetation is not seen in humans; theoretically possible only until cavity obliterated at 14-16 weeks
Superfetation is common after IVF when several embryos are transferred in one cycle
Superfetation is seen only in multiparous women who have a larger uterine cavity volume
Superfetation is the same as superfecundation where two ova of one cycle are fertilised
Superfetation would need a second ovulation and fertilisation after a pregnancy is established, which the decidua prevents. (Book p461)
All of the following are recognised risk factors for dizygotic twinning EXCEPT:
IVF as the sole risk factor with no role for geography, age, parity or family history at all
Geographical distribution with Nigeria showing highest incidence at 1 in 20 and Japan lowest
Advanced maternal age and increased parity raising chance of multiple ovulation and twins
Maternal family history of twins and ovulation-induction drugs like clomiphene and hMG
Dizygotic risks: geography, ↑ age, ↑ parity, maternal family history, IVF and ovulation induction; IVF alone is the monozygotic risk. (Book p461)
The only listed risk factor for MONOZYGOTIC twins is:
Monozygotic twinning risk lists IVF only. (Book p461)
Fill up: Zygosity refers to ______ while chorionicity refers to ______.
type of conception; type of placentation
type of placentation; type of conception
number of sacs; number of embryos
Zygosity = type of conception; chorionicity = type of placentation. (Book p461)
Fill up: Chorion is ______ membrane formed on day ______ and amnion is ______ membrane formed on day ______.
Chorion is the outer membrane (day 8) and amnion the inner (day 10). (Book p461)
Dizygotic twins always have which membrane arrangement?
Dichorionic diamniotic, with a separate amnion and chorion for each twin
Monochorionic diamniotic, sharing a single placental mass
Monochorionic monoamniotic, with both fetuses in one sac
Dichorionic monoamniotic, a recognised though uncommon combination
Dizygotic twins are always dichorionic diamniotic, since each comes from a separate ovum with its own membranes. (Book p461)
Fill up: If the zygote splits before day 3 the result is ______ twins, whereas splitting between days 8 and 13 produces ______ twins.
Splitting before day 3 gives two placentas and two sacs; days 4-8 give monochorionic diamniotic; days 8-13 give monoamniotic; after day 13 the twins are conjoined. (Book p461)
Match division timing of monozygotic zygote with membrane pattern — 1) <4 days morula 2) 4-8 days blastocyst 3) 8-12 days 4) ≥12 days … A) DCDA B) MCDA C) MCMA D) Conjoined/Siamese
<4 days DCDA; 4–8 days MCDA (common chorion by day 8); 8–12 days MCMA; ≥12 days conjoined twins. (Book p462)
Which of the following statements about MCDA formation at 4-8 days is TRUE?
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because common chorion has formed by day 8 while amnions stay separate
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because amnion forms before chorion so both share one sac
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because both chorion and amnion are shared by the two fetuses
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because no fetal membranes have formed at blastocyst stage
Division at 4-8 days (blastocyst stage) yields MCDA twins because by day 8 a common chorion is already formed while the amnions remain separate. (Book p462)
Fill up: Division occurring after formation of single amnion, chorion and embryonic disc at ≥12 days results in ______.
Late division after the embryonic disc forms produces conjoined/Siamese twins. (Book p462)

A 28-year-old woman with monochorionic monoamniotic twins at 30 weeks is counselled. Ultrasound shows cord entanglement of both cords. What is the most appropriate counselling about complications and management?
Cord entanglement with sudden death of both twins; give steroids and plan caesarean at 32-34 weeks
Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome requiring laser ablation of anastomoses before 28 weeks
Preterm labour alone managed with cervical cerclage and bed rest until 38 weeks gestation
No specific risk in monoamniotic twins, so vaginal delivery at term is appropriate and safe
Monoamniotic twins risk cord entanglement and sudden loss, so steroids are given and delivery planned by caesarean at 32-34 weeks. (Book p462)
Fill up: The commonest variety of twins overall is ______ and among monozygotic twins is ______.
The commonest variety of twins overall is DCDA (dizygotic), and among monozygotic twins it is MCDA. (Book p462)
Which of the following statements about prognosis in twins is TRUE?
Prognosis depends on chorionicity: monochorionic twins fare worse than dichorionic in every outcome
Prognosis depends on zygosity alone, since monozygotic twins do badly whatever the placentation
Prognosis depends on fetal sex, since unlike-sex twins have worst perinatal outcome overall
Prognosis depends on maternal parity, since first twin pregnancy carries poorest outlook
Chorionicity determines prognosis because it decides whether the circulations are shared; zygosity and sex do not. (Book p462)
Fill up: Determination of chorionicity is best done by ______ at ______ weeks of gestation.
Chorionicity is best determined by transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) at 10-14 weeks in the first trimester. (Book p462)
Match twin type with number of membrane layers — 1) DCDA 2) MCDA 3) MCMA … A) 4 layers B) 2 layers C) 0 layers
DCDA 4 layers, MCDA 2 layers, MCMA none. (Book p463)
Fill up: Membrane thickness distinguishing DCDA from MCDA is ______ in DCDA vs ______ in MCDA.
DCDA membranes are ≥2 mm thick while MCDA are <2 mm. (Book p463)
Match chorionicity with vascular connections — 1) Dichorionic 2) Monochorionic diamniotic 3) Monoamniotic … A) None B) Deep arteriovenous C) Superficial
Dichorionic placentas have no connections; monochorionic diamniotic placentas have deep arteriovenous ones, and monoamniotic placentas superficial ones. (Book p463)
Which of the following statements about DCDA placental features is TRUE?
DCDA twins have two placentas or one fused single-looking with lambda or twin-peak sign
DCDA twins have single placenta with T sign at membrane insertion site
DCDA twins have single placenta with no distinguishing ultrasound sign at all
DCDA twins have two separate placentas but always show T sign between membranes
Dichorionic twins have two placentas, or a fused single-looking one, and always show the lambda or twin-peak sign. (Book p463)
Fill up: The T sign on USG, with single chorion and no intervening placenta, indicates ______.
T sign = single chorion without intervening placenta = MCDA. (Book p463)
Match twin type with its specific complications — 1) MCDA 2) MCMA … A) TTTS, TAPS, selective IUGR B) Cord entanglement and conjoined twins
MCDA twins specifically risk TTTS through deep vascular connections; MCMA twins specifically risk cord entanglement. (Book p463)
Fill up: Delivery timing is ______ for DCDA, ______ for MCDA and ______ for MCMA twins.
Delivery timing is 38 weeks for DCDA twins, 36 weeks for MCDA twins, and 32-34 weeks by caesarean after corticosteroids for MCMA twins. (Book p463)

Match the ultrasound sign with what it means — 1) Lambda or twin-peak sign 2) T sign 3) Conjoined twins … A) A wedge of placenta between the membranes, which indicates dichorionicity B) The intertwin membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle with no placental tissue between, indicating monochorionicity C) Splitting after day 13, so the fetuses share tissue and often share organs
The lambda sign proves dichorionicity in the first trimester, the T sign proves monochorionicity, and conjoined twins follow very late splitting. (Book p463)
DCDA vs MCDA vs MCMA & conjoined twins
USG in twin pregnancy is significant for assessing gestational age, chorionicity and ↑NT. Chorionicity can be determined earliest at ______ and best at ______.
Chorionicity: earliest 7 weeks, best 10 weeks. (Book p464)
USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
An increased nuchal translucency in a twin pregnancy raises suspicion of ______, and its ideal assessment time is the ______ trimester.
↑NT suggests TTTS; the ideal time is the 2nd trimester. (Book p464)
USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
Which is NOT a marker of dichorionicity on USG?
Dichorionicity markers: ≥4 membranes, ≥2 mm thickness, different sexes, 2 placentae and twin peak sign. (Book p464)
USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
Conjoined twins are a complication of which twin type, and how are the types named?
Monoamniotic twins; parapagus, thoracophagus, rachiphagus and craniophagus
Dichorionic twins, in whom only cephalopagus has ever been described
Monochorionic diamniotic twins, in whom only ischiopagus is described
Dizygotic twins, in whom only parapagus joining has been recorded
Conjoined twins follow splitting after day 13, so they are monoamniotic and monochorionic; the types are named for the shared part. (Book p464)
USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
Caesarean at 32-34 weeks after completing a steroid course
Vaginal delivery at 38 weeks after completing a steroid course
Fetal reduction at 12 weeks, then delivery at 38 weeks
Serial amnioreduction, then delivery at 34 completed weeks
Conjoined twins are managed by caesarean section between 32 and 34 weeks after completing the steroid course. (Book p464)
USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
Maternal complications of twin pregnancy include pronounced haemodynamic changes, ↑ placental size, polyhydramnios and which liver conditions?
Intrahepatic cholestasis and acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Cirrhosis and acute hepatitis E infection in pregnancy
Gilbert syndrome and Dubin-Johnson syndrome in pregnancy
Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal vein thrombosis in pregnancy

Maternal complications of twin pregnancy include pronounced haemodynamic changes, increased placental size, polyhydramnios, and the liver conditions intrahepatic cholestasis and acute fatty liver of pregnancy. (Book p465)
Twin pregnancy increases the risk of which obstetric complications?
Preterm labour, pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage, cord prolapse and malpresentation
Gestational diabetes alone, with no effect on the course of labour or delivery
Hyperemesis gravidarum alone, with no increase in risk later in the pregnancy
Iron deficiency anaemia alone, since only the maternal blood volume is affected
Overdistension of the uterus and a large placental mass explain the whole spectrum of increased obstetric risk in twins. (Book p465)
↑ hCG and ↑ human placental lactogen in twins explain which associations?
Pre-eclampsia in twin pregnancy is attributed to:
The notes attribute pre-eclampsia to increased paternal antigen exposure. (Book p465)
PIH prophylaxis in twin pregnancy uses:
Low-dose aspirin 80-150 mg/day started before 16 weeks, ideally 12
High-dose aspirin 300 mg/day started after 28 weeks
Calcium supplementation only, started after 20 weeks
Low-molecular-weight heparin from the time of conception
PIH prophylaxis in twin pregnancy uses low-dose aspirin 80-150 mg/day started before 16 weeks, ideally at 12 weeks. (Book p465)
Fetal complications are m/c in which order?
Monochorionic worse than dichorionic, and monozygotic worse than dizygotic, apart from cumulative chromosomal risk
Dichorionic twins do worse than monochorionic twins in every respect
Dizygotic twins always do worse than monozygotic twins
All types carry exactly the same risk of fetal complications
Shared circulation drives risk, so monochorionic and monozygotic twins do worse; dizygotic twins carry two independent chromosomal risks instead. (Book p465)
For aneuploidy testing, sampling differs by zygosity how?
Monozygotic – sample any one twin; dizygotic – sample both twins
Monozygotic – sample both; dizygotic – sample one
Monozygotic twins share genetics so one sample suffices; dizygotic need both sampled. (Book p465)
Prognosis depends on chorionicity and amnionicity EXCEPT for which two complications?
Preterm labour (related to number of twins) and IUGR
Preterm labour relates to twin number and IUGR is independent of chorionicity. (Book p465)
Fetal reduction in multifetal pregnancy: DOC, target and timing are:
Intracardiac KCl injection into the fetus with least chance of survival, at 10–13 weeks
Intracardiac KCl into the largest fetus at 20 weeks
Aspiration of amniotic fluid at 8 weeks
Intracardiac KCl to the least-viable fetus at 10–13 weeks; it does not affect the other fetus's survival. (Book p465)
All of the following are maternal complications that are commoner in twin pregnancy EXCEPT:
Twin pregnancies are delivered early; the others are all more frequent because of the larger placental mass and greater hormonal load. (Book p465)
The three complications common to ALL twin pregnancies are:
Preterm labour (m/c), IUGR and congenital anomalies
Cord prolapse, vasa previa and rupture
Preterm labour (m/c), IUGR and congenital anomalies affect all twins. (Book p466)
In a primigravida twin pregnancy without history of preterm labour or 2nd-trimester abortion, cervical cerclage is:
The notes state cerclage is not done in this scenario. (Book p466)
Congenital anomalies in twins are m/c compared with singletons and follow which pattern?
Twin above singleton; monochorionic above dichorionic; heart defects
Singleton above twin; dichorionic above monochorionic
Dichorionic above monochorionic; neural tube defects only
Twin above singleton; monochorionic above dichorionic; renal defects
Congenital anomalies are commoner in twins than singletons, commoner in monochorionic than dichorionic twins, and heart defects predominate. (Book p466)
For TTTS screening in monochorionic twins, echocardiography is done at ______ and a target/anomaly/level II scan is done in ______.
Echo at 18–22 weeks; the level II scan applies to all pregnant women. (Book p466)
Vanishing twin syndrome refers to ______ and is common in ______.
Early spontaneous reduction of a twin pregnancy to singleton; IVF pregnancies
Death of both twins at term; spontaneous conception
Late IUD of one twin; natural conception
Vanishing twin = early spontaneous reduction to singleton, common after IVF. (Book p466)
Effect of a vanishing twin on the surviving co-twin:
The second twin usually survives normally, ± LBW/SGA. (Book p466)
After death of one twin, complications in the survivor depend on chorionicity how?
Monochorionic survivors are at risk through the shared anastomoses; dichorionic survivors largely are not
Both monochorionic and dichorionic survivors are at equal risk of neurological injury
Dichorionic survivors are at greater risk, because the second placenta also fails
Neither twin is at any risk once one of them has died in utero
Acute transfusion through anastomoses at the moment of death is what injures the monochorionic survivor's brain. (Book p466)
In a dying monochorionic co-twin, the sequence in twin A (high-pressure system) flowing to twin B (low-pressure system) causes:
Twin A becomes hypotensive and anaemic, exsanguinating into the low-pressure twin
Twin A becomes polycythaemic as blood flows in from the dying co-twin
Twin B becomes hypertensive from the sudden increase in blood volume
No haemodynamic change occurs in either twin at the moment of death
When the monochorionic co-twin dies, the survivor's low-pressure circulation drains the dying twin, which is how the survivor is injured. (Book p466)
Which of the following statements about single intrauterine death in a twin pregnancy is TRUE?
In monochorionic twins the survivor risks neurological injury from acute inter-twin transfusion, while in dichorionic twins the main risk is preterm delivery
Death of a dichorionic co-twin is more dangerous to the survivor than death of a monochorionic co-twin
Immediate delivery is mandatory whenever one twin dies, whatever the gestation
Maternal disseminated intravascular coagulation appears within hours in a third of these pregnancies
Vascular anastomoses make monochorionic loss dangerous to the survivor's brain; maternal coagulopathy is rare and immediate delivery is not always best. (Book p466)
Management when USG shows impending death of the 1st twin:
Impending death of the 1st twin mandates immediate delivery of both. (Book p467)
The four complications specific to monochorionic twins are:
TTTS, TAPS, TRAP and selective IUGR
Cord entanglement, conjoining, vanishing twin, show
TTTS, TAPS, TRAP and selective IUGR are monochorionic-specific. (Book p467)
Differentiate IUGR from selective IUGR in twins.
Ordinary IUGR affects both twins; selective IUGR is monochorionic, one normal and one growth-restricted twin
The two terms mean exactly the same thing and are interchangeable
Selective IUGR is a complication confined to dichorionic twins
Ordinary IUGR affects only one twin of the pair
Selective growth restriction is a monochorionic problem of unequal placental sharing, with one twin normally grown. (Book p467)
Deep vascular anastomosis between artery and vein
Deep arterio-venous anastomoses cause TTTS. (Book p467)
Commonest in monochorionic diamniotic twins, least common in monoamniotic, and not seen in dichorionic twins
Commonest in dichorionic twins with two separate placentas, and never seen in monochorionic twins
Commonest in monoamniotic twins because of cord entanglement, and never in monochorionic diamniotic twins
Equally common in every type, since transfusion depends on cord insertion rather than chorionicity
Deep arteriovenous anastomoses in monochorionic diamniotic placentas drive TTTS; without shared circulation the syndrome cannot occur. (Book p467)
In TTTS, the DONOR twin shows which renal and fluid findings?
↓ renal blood flow (↑ renal failure risk), ↓ GFR and oligohydramnios
The donor has reduced renal perfusion and GFR with oligohydramnios; the recipient the opposite. (Book p467)
Donor: anaemia with heart failure — recipient: polycythaemia with thrombosis and failure
Donor: polycythaemia with thrombosis — recipient: anaemia and heart failure
Both twins become anaemic from the unbalanced transfusion
Both twins become polycythaemic from the shared circulation
The donor is volume depleted and anaemic; the recipient is volume loaded and polycythaemic, with thrombotic and cardiac complications. (Book p467)
Peak systolic velocity of the MCA in TTTS donor vs recipient:
MCA-PSV ≥1.5 MoM in the anemic donor and <0.8 MoM in the polycythemic recipient. (Book p467)
Serious complications listed for TTTS fetuses are:
Hydrops fetalis and death are the listed complications. (Book p467)
Fill up: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is driven by ______ anastomoses in a monochorionic placenta, and the donor twin becomes ______.
arteriovenous; oliguric with oligohydramnios and growth restriction
Unidirectional arteriovenous anastomoses make the donor hypovolaemic with oliguria and oligohydramnios, and the recipient hypervolaemic with polyhydramnios. (Book p467)
The best method for amniotic fluid assessment in twin pregnancy is:
Single largest vertical pocket on USG
Amniotic fluid index summing four quadrants
The single largest vertical pocket is the best method in twins. (Book p468)
Diagnostic criteria of TTTS in monochorionic diamniotic twins:
Polyhydramnios in one twin with oligohydramnios in the other
Poly-oligo sequence between MCDA twins defines TTTS. (Book p468)
The early marker of TTTS is:
Increased NT is the early marker of TTTS. (Book p468)
The 'stuck twin' appearance in TTTS results from:
Renin-angiotensin activation in the donor, causing oliguria, anuria and anhydramnios
Polyhydramnios in the recipient compressing the donor against the uterine wall
Cord entanglement between the two fetuses lying in a single sac
A uterine septum separating the two gestational sacs
The donor twin is volume depleted, activates the renin-angiotensin system and stops making urine, so it becomes the stuck twin in an anhydramniotic sac. (Book p468)
Quintero stage 1 vs stage 2 of TTTS differ by:
Stage 1: the donor bladder is still visible — stage 2: it is not visible, and Doppler is normal in both
Stage 1: the Doppler is already abnormal — stage 2: the Doppler becomes normal again
Stage 2: hydrops fetalis is already present in the recipient twin
Stage 2: one or both twins have already died in utero
Quintero stage 1 still shows a donor bladder; stage 2 loses it, while abnormal Doppler belongs to stage 3 and hydrops to stage 4. (Book p468)
Stage 3 abnormal Doppler; stage 4 hydrops fetalis in one/both; stage 5 death of one/both twins
Stage 3 hydrops; stage 4 abnormal Doppler; stage 5 anuria
Stage 3 anuria; stage 4 Doppler; stage 5 hydrops
Stage 3 death; stage 4 hydrops; stage 5 Doppler
Stages 3–5 add abnormal Doppler, hydrops and death respectively. (Book p468)

At 20 weeks a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy has a deepest vertical pocket of 8.5 cm in one sac and 1.5 cm in the other, and a bladder is visible in both fetuses. What is the most appropriate management?
Refer for fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
Reassure her and repeat the scan in four weeks, since both bladders are visible
Immediate delivery, since this is advanced disease
Serial amnioreduction alone, because laser offers no advantage
Oligo-polyhydramnios with both bladders visible is Quintero stage II, and laser ablation of anastomoses is the definitive treatment before 26 weeks. (Book p468)
Follow-up Doppler studies in monochorionic twins are done at 16–20 weeks and include:
Umbilical artery, vein, ductus venosus and PSV of MCA
Doppler at 16–20 weeks covers umbilical artery/vein, ductus venosus and MCA-PSV. (Book p469)
USG follow-up in TTTS-risk twins assesses:
Fetal biometry, liquor volume in each sac and Doppler for hydrops and abnormal waveforms
Cervical length alone, since transfusion does not affect growth or liquor volume
Placental grading alone, which predicts transfusion before any fetal change appears
Fetal sex determination alone, since chorionicity is already known from the first scan
Surveillance looks for the consequences of unbalanced transfusion: growth discordance, liquor discordance, abnormal Doppler and hydrops. (Book p469)
Echocardiography of the RECIPIENT twin in TTTS looks for:
Pulmonary stenosis or atresia, ventricular hypertrophy and predominantly right-sided dysfunction
Left ventricular hypoplasia with a small aortic root and coarctation
An isolated ventricular septal defect with no myocardial hypertrophy at all
A structurally and functionally normal heart in the great majority of recipient twins
The recipient twin is volume loaded, so the right side bears the brunt: pulmonary stenosis or atresia, hypertrophy and right-sided dysfunction. (Book p469)
Treatment of TTTS by gestational age: ≤28 weeks vs >28 weeks.
Fetoscopic laser ablation of vascular anastomoses; serial amnioreduction
≤28 weeks fetoscopic laser ablation; >28 weeks serial amnioreduction. (Book p469)
A chronic form of twin-to-twin transfusion through tiny anastomoses, with anaemia and polycythaemia but no fluid discordance
An acute severe form of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome with sudden polyhydramnios in both sacs
A complication confined to dichorionic twins in which one placenta has a velamentous cord insertion
A complication of cord entanglement in monoamniotic twins that causes sudden death of both twins
TAPS is chronic slow transfusion through anastomoses under 1 mm: the haemoglobin gap is large but the liquor volumes stay normal. (Book p469)
TAPS can occur spontaneously or after which procedure?
TAPS may follow laser ablation of TTTS. (Book p469)
Features of TAPS: haemoglobin, amniotic fluid and MCA-PSV.
Donor anaemia and recipient polycythaemia, with normal liquor volume in both sacs
An oligo-polyhydramnios sequence, with equal peak systolic velocities
Donor polycythaemia together with anaemia in the recipient
Abnormal liquor volume in both sacs from the very beginning
TAPS is defined by a large haemoglobin difference without the liquor discordance of classic twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. (Book p469)
TRAP sequence is a rare complication of monochorionic twins caused by:
An aberrant artery-to-artery anastomosis through which the pump twin perfuses the acardiac twin in reverse
Deep arteriovenous anastomoses of the kind that produce classic twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Superficial venous anastomoses that allow a slow transfusion between the two circulations
Complete absence of any anastomosis, so each twin keeps an entirely separate circulation
TRAP needs an artery-to-artery anastomosis: deoxygenated blood from the pump twin reaches the acardiac twin first and stunts its development. (Book p469)

Match the monochorionic complication with its description — 1) TRAP sequence 2) Twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence 3) Selective fetal growth restriction … A) An acardiac twin perfused in reverse through artery-to-artery anastomoses B) Chronic slow transfusion producing a large inter-twin haemoglobin difference without the oligo-polyhydramnios sequence C) One twin below the third centile with abnormal Doppler from unequal placental sharing
TRAP has a perfused acardiac twin, TAPS shows a haemoglobin gap without fluid discordance, and selective growth restriction reflects placental share. (Book p469)
Outcomes in the acardiac twin of TRAP are named:
Acardiac acephalus (lower body developed); acardiac amorphous (no formed parts)
Acardiac acephalus (lower body developed); acardiac anceps (head formed only)
Acardiac amorphous (no formed parts); acardiac acephalus (lower body developed)
Acardiac anceps (head formed only); acardiac amorphous (no formed parts)
Outcomes in the acardiac twin of TRAP are acardiac acephalus, in which only the lower part is developed, and acardiac amorphus, an amorphous mass with no formed parts. (Book p470)
Selective IUGR is defined by fetal weight < 10th percentile of the normal co-twin OR:
Discordance >25% in weight also defines selective IUGR. (Book p470)
Causes of selective IUGR listed are:
Unequal placental sharing and unequal splitting of the cell mass
Deep vascular anastomoses with artery-to-artery connections
Maternal diabetes causing symmetrical overgrowth of both twins
Cord entanglement restricting blood flow to one twin only
The listed causes of selective IUGR are unequal placental sharing and unequal splitting of the initial cell mass. (Book p470)
Complications specific to MONOAMNIOTIC twins and the cause of cord entanglement:
Cord entanglement and conjoined twins; true knots form the cause
TTTS and TAPS, caused by the deep vascular anastomoses
Selective IUGR, from unequal sharing of the placental mass
A vanishing twin, from thrombosis of the shared umbilical cord
Complications specific to monoamniotic twins are cord entanglement and conjoined twins, with true knots forming the cause of the entanglement. (Book p470)
Management of monoamniotic twins with cord entanglement risk:
C-section at 32–34 weeks is advised. (Book p470)
The 1st twin is defined as the one that:
Is closer to the internal os during pregnancy / comes out first during delivery
Is labelled by the sonologist arbitrarily
The twin closer to the internal os (delivered first) is the 1st twin. (Book p471)
The m/c and 2nd m/c presentation combinations in twins are:
Both-vertex is m/c; 1st vertex + 2nd breech is second m/c. (Book p471)
Interlocking of twins is seen with which combination and is managed by:
Interlocking occurs when the 1st is breech and 2nd cephalic; C-section is done. (Book p471)
Mode of delivery in twins depends on the presentation of the:
The first twin: a vertex first twin allows vaginal delivery whatever the second twin is doing
The second twin: any non-vertex second twin means both babies are delivered by caesarean section
The larger twin: whichever twin weighs more determines whether a caesarean is needed
The placental site: an anterior placenta makes a vaginal delivery of twins impossible
The presentation of the first twin governs the plan; a breech or transverse second twin can often still be delivered vaginally by an expert. (Book p471)
Match delivery plans when the 1st twin is vertex: 2nd vertex, 2nd breech, 2nd transverse.
Second vertex: vaginal delivery — second breech: assisted breech — second transverse: internal podalic version in theatre
Every combination is delivered by caesarean section once the first twin has been born vaginally
Every combination can be delivered vaginally by an experienced operator without preparation
Caesarean section for a breech second twin only, since version is never attempted for a transverse lie
When the first twin is vertex, a vertex or breech second twin can usually be delivered vaginally, and a transverse second twin by version and breech extraction. (Book p471)
After delivery of the 1st twin, which drug is contraindicated and why?
Methylergometrine, since it contracts the uterus and traps the second twin
Oxytocin, since it causes maternal hypotension at this stage
Misoprostol, since it causes pyrexia at this stage of labour
Magnesium sulfate, since it causes maternal sedation and drowsiness
After delivery of the first twin, methylergometrine is contraindicated because it causes uterine contractions that trap the second twin. (Book p471)
The maximum acceptable time gap between delivery of the twins is ______; beyond it the action is ______.
30 minutes; immediate C-section of the 2nd twin
A gap >30 minutes mandates immediate C-section of the second twin. (Book p471)
Internal podalic version has a single indication and one contraindication:
2nd twin in transverse lie; previous h/o C-section
IPV is indicated only for a transverse 2nd twin and c/i after previous C-section. (Book p471)
Under general anaesthesia a hand is passed into the uterus, the feet are grasped and the fetus is turned to a breech
Under spinal anaesthesia the head is rotated with forceps before delivery
External manipulation through the abdomen with the membranes left intact
Traction on the cord under continuous ultrasound guidance in the labour ward
Internal podalic version is an intrauterine manoeuvre under general anaesthesia, grasping a foot and converting the lie to a breech. (Book p471)
The note adds that EXTERNAL cephalic version is attempted only if:
The fetus is breech at 30 weeks
ECV requires intact membranes per the note. (Book p471)
Fill up: Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at about ______ weeks, whereas uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at about ______ weeks.
Monochorionic twins are delivered earlier because of the unpredictable risk from anastomoses and late single fetal death. (Book p471)
Fill up: Preterm labour is defined as labour beginning at ______ weeks.
PTL = labour process beginning before 37 weeks. (Book p472)
Fill up: The most common cause of preterm labour is ______ and an iatrogenic example is ______.
idiopathic; induction at 34 weeks in severe pre-eclampsia
induction at 34 weeks in severe pre-eclampsia; idiopathic
infection; induction at 40 weeks at term
Idiopathic is m/c; iatrogenic PTL occurs e.g. when labour is induced at 34 weeks in severe pre-eclampsia. (Book p472)
Which of the following statements about risk factors for preterm labour is TRUE?
Previous history of preterm labour is the most important risk factor for preterm birth
Short cervix alone is the most important risk factor, more than previous preterm birth
PROM is the most important risk factor for preterm labour in all populations
Twin pregnancy is the most important risk factor for preterm labour worldwide
Previous preterm labour is the most important risk factor. (Book p472)
All of the following cause uterine overdistension leading to preterm labour EXCEPT:
Twins and polyhydramnios causing uterine overdistension and preterm contractions
Fibroids and adenomyosis causing uterine overdistension and preterm labour
Oligohydramnios causing uterine overdistension and preterm contractions
Cervical polyps causing uterine overdistension and leading to preterm labour
Overdistension from twins or polyhydramnios predisposes to PTL. (Book p472)
Fill up: Bleeding in pregnancy causing preterm labour is most commonly due to ______.
Abruptio placenta is the m/c bleeding cause linked to PTL. (Book p472)
Match the stress contributor with its example — 1) Maternal stress 2) Fetal stress … A) PIH B) Uteroplacental insufficiency and IUGR
Maternal stress (PIH) and fetal stress (UPI, IUGR) are listed. (Book p472)
All of the following maternal infections are linked to preterm labour with no routine screening advised EXCEPT:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria and bacterial vaginosis, neither routinely screened for PTL prevention
Syphilis and HIV infection, neither routinely screened for PTL prevention in low-risk women
Tuberculosis and malaria, neither routinely screened for preterm labour prevention
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea, neither routinely screened for preterm labour prevention
Maternal infections linked to preterm labour for which no routine screening is advised are asymptomatic bacteriuria and bacterial vaginosis. (Book p472)

A 26-year-old woman with previous preterm birth at 32 weeks is now 18 weeks. She asks if her risk can be predicted. Which patients have preventable preterm labour and what is the IOC tool for prediction?
Previous preterm birth or short cervix; transvaginal sonography is the investigation of choice
All primigravid women screened by transabdominal sonography for cervical length routinely
Twin pregnancies alone screened by magnetic resonance imaging for cervical length
Preterm prelabour rupture alone monitored with cardiotocography for contractions
Prevention is aimed at women with a previous preterm birth or a short cervix, and transvaginal scan is how the cervix is measured. (Book p472)
Fill up: A short cervix on TVS risking preterm labour is defined as ______ cm or less.
Cervical length ≤2.5 cm denotes a short cervix at risk of PTL. (Book p472)
Fill up: As cervix dilates in preterm labour, its T shape changes in sequence ______.
The cervical shape changes T → Y → V → U as preterm labour progresses. (Book p472)
Fill up: ACOG recommends cervical length measurement by TVS between ______ weeks in women with history of PTL.
ACOG: TVS cervical length between 16–24 weeks in all with h/o PTL. (Book p472)
Which of the following statements about TVS cervical length measurement precautions is TRUE?
Measure with empty bladder from internal os to external os for cervical length assessment
Measure with full bladder and measure only the visible part of cervix on TVS
Measure with full bladder from external os to internal os with fundal pressure
Measure without bladder preparation and include lower uterine segment in length
The bladder must be empty and length measured internal-to-external os. (Book p472)
All of the following are risk factors for spontaneous preterm birth EXCEPT:
A short cervical length in the second trimester
Prior preterm birth, short cervix, multiples, infection and uterine anomalies raise risk; a previous uncomplicated term birth is reassuring. (Book p472)
Causes, risks & prediction of preterm birth
All of the following lifestyle measures help prevent preterm labour EXCEPT:
Quit smoking as a preventive measure for preterm labour in at-risk women
Strict bed rest as a proven preventive measure for preterm labour
Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria when detected in antenatal screening
Progesterone prophylaxis in women with previous preterm birth or short cervix
Quitting smoking is listed; bed rest, nutrient supplements and routine screening have no role. (Book p473)

A 29-year-old woman with previous preterm birth at 30 weeks, singleton pregnancy, TVS cervix 2.0 cm at 18 weeks. She asks about cerclage. Which three indications are required for cervical cerclage surgery?
Preterm birth history, cervical length 2.5 cm or less on TVS, singleton pregnancy
Preterm labour history, twin pregnancy and short cervix on transabdominal scan
Previous term delivery, cervical length 3.5 cm and singleton pregnancy at 20 weeks
No previous preterm birth but short cervix alone in twin pregnancy at 16 weeks
Cervical circlage requires all three of: a history of preterm birth, cervical length 2.5 cm or less on TVS, and a singleton pregnancy. (Book p473)
Fill up: Cervical cerclage timing is ______ weeks with ______ given alongside.
Circlage is done at 14–24 weeks and progesterone is given with it. (Book p473)
All of the following are indications for progesterone prophylaxis of preterm labour EXCEPT:
Previous preterm birth, cervical length ≤25 mm and adjunct to cervical cerclage as per notes
Twin pregnancy alone whatever the cervical length or obstetric history without other risk
Singleton pregnancy with short cervix on TVS between 16 and 24 weeks gestation
History-indicated cerclage with progesterone as adjunct therapy for prevention
Progesterone is given for a previous preterm birth, an incidental short cervix, or alongside cerclage in a classic history. (Book p473)
Match progesterone regimen with its details — 1) Hydroxyprogesterone caproate 2) Micronised progesterone … A) IM weekly 16-20 to 36 weeks B) PV daily
The listed progesterone regimens are hydroxyprogesterone caproate IM weekly starting at 16-20 weeks and stopping at 36 weeks, and micronised progesterone per vaginam daily. (Book p473)
Which of the following statements about progesterone mechanism in PTL prevention is TRUE?
Progesterone prevents preterm labour by acting as a smooth muscle relaxant maintaining quiescence
Progesterone acts as a tocolytic after contractions have started to stop established labour
Progesterone prevents preterm labour by increasing oxytocin receptor expression in myometrium
Progesterone prevents preterm labour by ripening the cervix and increasing gap junctions
Its function is smooth muscle relaxation. (Book p473)
Which of the following statements about progesterone as tocolytic is TRUE?
Progesterone is not a tocolytic and cannot stop labour once contractions have started
Progesterone is the first-line tocolytic agent in established preterm labour
Progesterone stops contractions within 30 minutes when given intravenously in labour
Progesterone is more effective than nifedipine for acute tocolysis in preterm labour
False: progesterone is not a tocolytic and cannot prevent preterm labour once contractions have started. (Book p473)
All of the following have NO role in preventing preterm labour EXCEPT:
Bed rest, nutrient supplementation and routine screening for infection have no role in PTL prevention
Progesterone and cerclage have no role in preventing preterm labour in at-risk women
Smoking cessation has no role in preventing preterm labour and can be ignored
Transvaginal cervical length screening has no role in predicting preterm labour
Bed rest, nutrient supplementation and routine infection screening have no role. (Book p473)

Match the preventive measure with its current place — 1) Vaginal progesterone 2) Cervical cerclage 3) Bed rest and hydration … A) Offered when a short cervix is found on ultrasound, even without a previous preterm birth B) Considered with a cervical length below 25 mm and a history of mid-trimester loss or preterm birth C) Widely used but never shown to prevent preterm birth, so not recommended
Progesterone treats the incidental short cervix, cerclage suits the classic history with a short cervix, and bed rest has no proven benefit. (Book p473)
Fill up: Established preterm labour is defined as regular contractions with cervical dilatation ≥______ cm and effacement ≥______%.
Dilatation ≥2 cm = established PTL requiring admission; <2 cm → admit and observe dilatation/effacement. (Book p473)
Which of the following statements about fetal fibronectin in PTL is TRUE?
Fetal fibronectin is a glycoprotein from choriodecidual interface predicting preterm labour
Fetal fibronectin is a hormone from corpus luteum maintaining pregnancy until term
Fetal fibronectin is a fetal lung maturity marker measured in amniotic fluid routinely
Fetal fibronectin is a maternal serum marker for Down syndrome screening in twins
Such patients are admitted for observation of dilatation and effacement. (Book p473)
The CONVENTIONAL definition of established PTL needs uterine contractions (4 in 20 min / 8 in 60 min) plus any one of:
Contractions plus a cervical length of 2 cm or less, dilatation of 3 cm or more, or a positive fetal fibronectin
Contractions plus cervical dilatation of 1 cm or more and nothing else
Contractions plus a fetal fibronectin of 10 ng per mL or more in cervicovaginal fluid
Contractions plus a Bishop score of 6 or more with a closed cervix
The conventional definition adds an objective marker: a short cervix, advanced dilatation or a positive fibronectin test. (Book p473)
Fill up: Preterm labour is regular uterine contractions with progressive cervical change occurring between ______ and ______ weeks of gestation.
The window runs from 20 weeks to 36 weeks and 6 days; before 20 weeks the loss is called an abortion rather than preterm labour. (Book p473)
A 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks with regular contractions, cervix 2 cm dilated, 80% effaced, membranes intact, no bleeding. Fetal fibronectin is positive. What is the diagnosis and best predictor?
Established preterm labour; fetal fibronectin positive predicts delivery within 7-14 days
False labour; fetal fibronectin positive rules out preterm labour completely
Term labour; fetal fibronectin is irrelevant after 37 weeks gestation
Braxton Hicks contractions; no need for steroids or tocolysis at 32 weeks
The current definition drops the add-on tests and requires progressive change, or dilatation of at least 2 cm at presentation. (Book p474)
Fetal fibronectin is a 'glue' present between the fetal membrane and decidua. In cervicovaginal secretions, a positive result between 22–35 weeks indicates:
Between 22–35 weeks fibronectin positivity suggests PTL or PPROM; after 35 weeks it is normal. (Book p474)
After how many weeks is fetal fibronectin in cervicovaginal secretions considered NORMAL?
Beyond 35 weeks its presence is normal. (Book p474)
Match intervention in established PTL with its purpose — 1) Corticosteroids 2) Tocolytics 3) MgSO4 4) Antibiotics … A) Fetal lung maturity B) Delay delivery 48h C) Neuroprotection D) GBS prophylaxis
Cerebral palsy risk is countered with neuroprotective MgSO4; RDS/NEC/IVH with corticosteroids. (Book p474)
Which neonatal complications of PTL are reduced by corticosteroids?
Steroids accelerate lung maturity and ↓ RDS, NEC and IVH. (Book p474)
Corticosteroids in PTL are indicated in:
All cases before 34 weeks, and from 34 weeks once chorioamnionitis and a previous course are excluded
Only below 28 weeks, since later gestation gains nothing
Only between 34 and 37 weeks, where the benefit is greatest
Every case regardless of infection, because the benefit outweighs the risk
Corticosteroids are given before 34 weeks, and in the late preterm window once infection and prior treatment are excluded. (Book p474)
Which condition CONTRAINDICATES corticosteroids in PTL?
The action of antenatal corticosteroids is seen ______ after the first dose, with maximum benefit ______.
Effect appears 48 hours after the first dose, maximal 2–7 days after. (Book p474)
Fill up: In established PTL, steroids are given as ______ IM 12 hours apart or ______ IM 24 hours apart.
Repeat courses are not given as they can cause cerebral palsy. (Book p474)
Match steroid regimens: dexamethasone (DOC in India) and betamethasone (DOC worldwide).
Dexamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg IM 12-hourly; betamethasone 2 doses of 12 mg 24-hourly
Dexamethasone 2 doses of 12 mg 24-hourly; betamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg 12-hourly
Dexamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg IM 12-hourly; betamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg 12-hourly
Both given as a single dose of 12 mg IM, repeated if delivery is delayed
Dexamethasone (DOC in India) is 4 doses of 6 mg IM 12 hours apart; betamethasone (DOC worldwide) is 2 doses of 12 mg 24 hours apart and carries a slightly higher fetal hypoglycaemia risk. (Book p474)
The role of tocolytics in PTL and their maximum duration of use:
To allow corticosteroid action; maximum use till 48 hours
Tocolytics buy 48 hours for steroid action. (Book p475)
Tocolytics + corticosteroids are recommended in which group, and have NO role in which three groups?
Preterm labour before 34 weeks; no role after 34 weeks, in twins, or with chorioamnionitis
Preterm labour after 34 weeks only, with no role before 34 weeks
Twin pregnancy alone, with no role in singleton pregnancies
Chorioamnionitis alone, since infection shortens the cervix
Tocolysis with steroids is for early preterm labour; it has no place in late preterm labour, twins or infection. (Book p475)
The m/c tocolytic used in India and its ACOG window:
Nifedipine is m/c in India with ACOG use at 32–34 weeks. (Book p475)
Atosiban, the oxytocin antagonist, is the tocolytic of choice in:
Atosiban is preferred in cardiac disease. (Book p475)
Indomethacin as a tocolytic leads to which fetal effects and is restricted by ACOG to:
Oligohydramnios and premature ductus arteriosus closure; <32 weeks
Indomethacin causes oligohydramnios and premature ductal closure; ACOG limits it to <32 weeks. (Book p475)
Nifedipine and atosiban, which are calcium and oxytocin antagonists
Indomethacin and sulindac, which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis
Magnesium sulfate and progesterone, which are used for other purposes
The beta-agonist group is terbutaline, salbutamol, ritodrine and isoxsuprine; the others belong to different drug classes. (Book p475)
Side effects of β-agonist tocolytics include tremors, hypotension, tachycardia, pulmonary oedema and:
Hyperglycaemia, which is why they are contraindicated in diabetes
Hypoglycaemia, which needs regular monitoring of blood glucose
Bradycardia, which limits the dose that can safely be given
Isolated hypokalaemia, with no other metabolic disturbance
