Beta-agonists cause tremor, tachycardia, hypotension, pulmonary oedema and hyperglycaemia, so they are avoided in diabetes. (Book p475)
Two 'not a tocolytic' notes: progesterone is not a tocolytic, and MgSO4 is not used as one because:
Its tocolytic effect appears only at 9-10 mg/dL, the same range as its toxicity
It causes persistent fetal tachycardia that masks the signs of fetal distress
It has no effect at all on the myometrium at any dose that can be given
It paradoxically induces labour by increasing local prostaglandin release
Magnesium relaxes myometrium only at levels that are already toxic, so it is used for neuroprotection rather than tocolysis. (Book p475)

A 30-year-old at 30 weeks is in established preterm labour with intact membranes. Corticosteroids and magnesium for neuroprotection have been started. Which tocolytic is most appropriate, and for how long?
Nifedipine or an oxytocin antagonist for up to 48 hours, to complete steroids and arrange transfer
No tocolytic at all, since delaying delivery never helps the baby
Indomethacin after 32 weeks, continued for seven days
Ritodrine for two weeks so that she can be managed at home
Tocolysis buys up to 48 hours for steroids and transfer; indomethacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of ductal constriction and oligohydramnios. (Book p475)
MgSO4 in PTL is used for its ______ action and is given in all cases of PTL < ______ weeks.
Neuroprotective action (prevents cerebral palsy); given when PTL is under 32 weeks
Tocolytic action (arrests uterine contractions); given when PTL is under 32 weeks
Neuroprotective action (prevents cerebral palsy); given when PTL is over 34 weeks
Tocolytic action (arrests uterine contractions); given when PTL is over 34 weeks
MgSO4 in preterm labour is given for its neuroprotective action (reducing cerebral palsy), and it is given in all cases of PTL before 32 weeks. (Book p476)
MgSO4 dosing for neuroprotection in PTL:
Loading 4 g followed by 1 g maintenance. (Book p476)
GBS screening in PTL/PPROM is done at presentation; routine screening in all pregnant women is by rectovaginal swab at:
Routine GBS screening is at 35–37 weeks by rectovaginal swab. (Book p476)
Antibiotics in PTL are indicated when:
GBS colonisation, intrapartum fever, or ruptured membranes for 18 hours or more
Routinely for every woman in preterm labour, whatever her colonisation status
Only after delivery, once the baby has been born and the cord has been clamped
Only when clinical chorioamnionitis is already established during labour
Intrapartum antibiotics are given for GBS colonisation, intrapartum fever or prolonged rupture, not routinely to everyone. (Book p476)
In the PTL summary table, corticosteroids and GBS screening are given in:
Both are listed for early preterm labour and both again for late preterm labour
Only in early preterm labour, since late preterm labour needs neither
Only in late preterm labour, since early delivery is already inevitable
In neither group, since both are given only after 37 completed weeks
In the summary table corticosteroids and GBS screening appear in both the early and the late preterm labour columns. (Book p476)
Tocolytics and MgSO4 in the summary table are reserved for:
Early preterm labour only, with magnesium given only below 32 weeks; none in late preterm labour
Late preterm labour only, since early preterm delivery is inevitable
Both groups equally, with the same agents and the same neuroprotection
Only when chorioamnionitis has been confirmed on amniocentesis
Tocolytics and magnesium belong to early preterm labour; neither has a place in late preterm labour. (Book p476)
Antibiotics in the PTL summary table are marked:
X in both late and early PTL
Routine antibiotics are not indicated in either group per the summary. (Book p476)
Induction of labour in PTL is generally avoided EXCEPT for:
Fetal distress, chorioamnionitis, abruptio placentae and intrauterine death
Maternal request for delivery at 34 weeks without any medical indication
A post-dates pregnancy that has reached 41 weeks with no sign of labour
An uncomplicated twin pregnancy at 36 weeks with intact membranes
Induction is avoided in preterm labour unless continuing the pregnancy is more dangerous than delivering, as with infection or distress. (Book p476)
Fill up: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given when delivery is anticipated before ______ weeks, using a loading dose of ______ g.

PROM and PPROM are defined as:
PROM – membrane rupture beyond 37 weeks before onset of labour; PPROM – rupture before 37 weeks
PROM – rupture before 37 weeks; PPROM – after 37 weeks
PROM is rupture beyond 37 weeks pre-labour; PPROM is rupture before 37 weeks. (Book p477)
Early PPROM and late PPROM span:
Early <34 weeks; late 34 weeks to 36 weeks + 6 days
Early PPROM <34 weeks; late PPROM 34 to 36+6 weeks. (Book p477)
Consequences of PROM include PTL within a week, ↑ chorioamnionitis, abruptio placenta, cord prolapse, oligohydramnios and:
RDS is among the listed consequences. (Book p477)
Her clothes are soaked and she reports a sudden gush followed by continued leaking
Painless bright-red bleeding with a soft and non-tender uterus
Fever with a rigid tender uterus and offensive-smelling lochia
Reduced fetal movements alone, without any loss of fluid or bleeding
Rupture of membranes presents as a sudden gush with continuing leak; bleeding suggests abruption or previa, and fever suggests infection. (Book p477)
On general examination in PROM, fever indicates:
Match P/A findings in PROM: ↓ fundal height, ↑ uterine tone with tense tender rigid uterus, uterine tenderness.

Digital P/V examination is avoided due to infection risk. (Book p477)
Sterile per speculum examination in PROM assesses:
Cervical dilatation, pooling of liquor, cord prolapse, and a high vaginal swab for culture
Cervical dilatation alone, since the rest is assessed later by ultrasound
Pooling of fluid alone, because a digital examination is still performed afterwards
Fetal presentation alone, since membrane status is decided from the history
A sterile speculum examination avoids introducing infection while assessing dilatation, liquor, cord and taking a swab. (Book p477)
Which of the following statements about prelabour rupture of membranes is TRUE?
The earlier the gestation at rupture, the higher the risk of chorioamnionitis, pulmonary hypoplasia and cord prolapse
Rupture of membranes before labour always demands immediate delivery, whatever the gestation
Rupture of membranes at term is labelled prelabour rupture of membranes
Prophylactic antibiotics have no effect on latency and are given only for established infection
At term, rupture before labour is called prelabour rupture (PROM); preterm rupture is PPROM, and antibiotics do prolong latency and reduce infection. (Book p477)
Differentiating amniotic fluid from urine relies on:
The ammoniacal smell of urine, and dribbling seen on coughing after the bladder is emptied
The colour of the fluid, which is reliably yellow for urine and clear for liquor
The volume passed, since urine is always lost in a single large gush
The characteristic sweet odour of amniotic fluid on the bed linen
Emptying the bladder with a catheter and then watching for further loss on coughing separates urine from amniotic fluid. (Book p478)
The Nitrazine test principle uses pH: amniotic fluid is ______ and vaginal discharge is ______.
Amniotic fluid pH 7.2 (alkaline) vs vaginal discharge pH 3.5 (acidic). (Book p478)
On litmus paper, amniotic fluid ______ while vaginal discharge ______.
Blue = alkaline amniotic fluid; yellow = acidic discharge. (Book p478)
False-positive Nitrazine tests can be due to:
Blood, semen, bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas infection and meconium
Contamination with urine, which is the only recognised cause
Contamination with the normal saline used for the examination
The cervical mucus plug alone, which is strongly alkaline
Nitrazine turns blue with any alkaline fluid, so blood, semen, infected discharge and meconium all give false positives. (Book p478)
The fern test is microscopy of vaginal discharge; a fern-like appearance indicates amniotic fluid because of:
Sodium chloride crystallisation produces the ferning pattern. (Book p478)
On USG in PROM you expect:
Reduced amniotic fluid because the membranes have ruptured
Polyhydramnios from accumulation of the leaking fluid
Normal amniotic fluid volume is always seen in these cases
A snowstorm appearance throughout the uterine cavity
On ultrasound in PROM one expects reduced amniotic fluid due to rupture of the membranes. (Book p478)
Match the bedside kit tests: the Actim test and the Amnisure test detect:

Actim: PAMG-1 — Amnisure: alpha-fetoprotein in the vaginal fluid
Both tests detect human chorionic gonadotrophin in vaginal fluid
Both tests detect fetal fibronectin in cervicovaginal secretions
Actim detects IGFBP-1 (placental protein 12) and Amnisure detects placental alpha microglobulin-1 in vaginal fluid. (Book p478)
All of the following help to diagnose rupture of membranes EXCEPT:
Sterile speculum examination showing pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix
Nitrazine or pH testing of vaginal fluid
Ferning of dried vaginal fluid seen under the microscope
Pooling on speculum, an alkaline pH and arborisation (ferning) diagnose rupture; amniotic fluid tests such as AFP belong to other diagnoses. (Book p478)
In the PROM/PPROM management table, the MAIN risk in term PROM vs early PPROM is:
Term PROM risks chorioamnionitis; early PPROM adds RDS. (Book p479)
Induction of labour is indicated (+) in which column of the PROM table?
Term prelabour rupture only; not in early or late preterm rupture
Early preterm rupture of membranes only, to avoid ascending infection
Late preterm rupture of membranes only, once the lungs are mature
All three groups, since rupture of membranes alone is an indication

Corticosteroids and tocolytics in the PROM table: steroids are given in ______ and tocolytics only in ______.
Early and late PPROM; early PPROM
Steroids (+) in both PPROM groups; tocolytics (+) only in early PPROM. (Book p479)
MgSO4 in the PROM table is given:
Only in early PPROM when the pregnancy is under 32 weeks
In all cases of PROM, whatever the gestation
Only in late PPROM, that is after 34 weeks
Never in PROM, since tocolysis is contraindicated
In the PROM table, MgSO4 is given only in early PPROM with period of gestation under 32 weeks. (Book p479)
GBS prophylaxis in term PROM is given only if:
Membranes ruptured ≥18 hours OR fever ≥100.4°F for 4 hours
Only with positive screening in early PPROM
Term PROM needs prophylaxis only with ROM ≥18 h or intrapartum fever ≥100.4°F for 4 h; both PPROM groups get it. (Book p479)
35–37 weeks in all pregnant women by rectovaginal swab
Universal rectovaginal swab at 35–37 weeks. (Book p479)
The role of GBS prophylaxis is to prevent:
Prophylaxis prevents early neonatal sepsis. (Book p479)
GBS prophylaxis WITHOUT needing screening is indicated for:
A previous infant with GBS sepsis, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, or a positive screening swab
Preterm labour alone, whatever the screening result or the previous obstetric history
Intrapartum fever alone, even with a negative screen and no other risk factor
Rupture of membranes for twelve hours alone, with no other risk factor present
A previous affected infant, bacteriuria in this pregnancy or a positive swab all justify prophylaxis without screening. (Book p479)
If GBS screening was NOT done, prophylaxis is still given for:
Preterm labour, preterm rupture, rupture for 18 hours or more, or intrapartum fever
Term labour alone with intact membranes and no other risk factor
An elective caesarean section before labour with the membranes intact
A post-term pregnancy that has gone beyond 41 completed weeks
When the GBS status is unknown, prophylaxis is given on the basis of these clinical risk factors. (Book p479)
Timing and DOC for GBS prophylaxis, with alternatives:
Intrapartum benzyl penicillin, with ampicillin or cefazolin and clindamycin if she is penicillin-allergic
Antepartum oral erythromycin given for a week before the expected date of delivery
Postpartum metronidazole started once the placenta has been delivered
Intrapartum gentamicin alone as a single intramuscular injection
Prophylaxis must be intrapartum to clear carriage at delivery: benzyl penicillin, with alternatives for allergy. (Book p479)
A woman at 34 weeks with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is afebrile, with a normal CTG and normal inflammatory markers. What is the management?
Expectant management with antibiotics, corticosteroids and close monitoring, planning delivery around 34-37 weeks
Immediate caesarean section to avoid infection
Induction of labour within twelve hours, whatever the gestation
Discharge home on oral antibiotics with weekly outpatient review
Expectant care with antibiotics and surveillance balances prematurity against infection; delivery is timed by gestation and any sign of infection or compromise. (Book p479)
Chorioamnionitis is best described as a:
It is a polymicrobial infection. (Book p480)
Presumptive clinical diagnosis of chorioamnionitis requires ruptured membranes + temperature ≥39°C plus any one of:
Fetal tachycardia, a maternal white cell count of 15,000 or more, or pus from the internal os
Maternal bradycardia with a falling blood pressure and cold peripheries
Oligohydramnios with a reduced amniotic fluid index on the ultrasound scan
Meconium-stained liquor with a normal maternal temperature and pulse rate
Presumptive chorioamnionitis is ruptured membranes with fever plus fetal tachycardia, maternal leucocytosis or purulent cervical discharge. (Book p480)
Maternal tachycardia and uterine tenderness in chorioamnionitis are:
They are features, not part of the diagnostic criteria. (Book p480)
Definitive diagnosis of chorioamnionitis is by:
Amniocentesis with Gram stain, culture and histology of the fetal membranes
Clinical criteria alone, which are sensitive and specific enough on their own
A raised maternal C-reactive protein measured on admission in labour
Ultrasound findings of debris and a thickened placenta
Clinical criteria make a presumptive diagnosis; definitive diagnosis needs amniotic fluid studies and membrane histology. (Book p480)
Ampicillin with gentamicin is the regimen. (Book p480)
Induction of labour with vaginal delivery preferred
Wait for spontaneous labour beyond 48 h
Induction and vaginal delivery are preferred. (Book p480)
Why is C-section not preferred in chorioamnionitis?
It increases chances of postpartum endometritis
C-section ↑ postpartum endometritis risk; it is reserved for obstetric reasons. (Book p480)
The ONLY indication for C-section in chorioamnionitis is an obstetric reason such as contracted pelvis or placenta previa; in that case which drug is added?
Metronidazole is added when C-section is performed. (Book p480)
Antibiotics in chorioamnionitis are stopped when:
The patient is afebrile for 24 hours
48 hours after delivery regardless of fever
Afebrile × 24 hours allows stopping antibiotics. (Book p480)

Match the feature with its significance in chorioamnionitis — 1) Maternal fever 2) Fetal tachycardia 3) Uterine tenderness with offensive liquor … A) A baseline above 160 bpm, often an early and easily missed fetal sign B) A core temperature of 38 C or more with maternal tachycardia C) Clinical evidence of intrauterine infection requiring delivery and intravenous antibiotics
Maternal fever plus fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor form the clinical triad that demands delivery and antibiotics. (Book p480)
The total normal duration of pregnancy is quoted as:
Normal duration: 9 months + 7 days = 40 weeks = 280 days. (Book p481)
42 weeks or more, that is 294 days or more
40 weeks or more, that is 280 days or more
41 weeks or more, that is 287 days or more
37 weeks or more, that is 259 days or more
Post-term pregnancy is defined as 42 weeks or more (294 days or more). (Book p481)
The FIRST step when a history of post-term pregnancy is given:
First review the menstrual history to confirm dates. (Book p481)
In post-term pregnancy the amniotic fluid colour and volume at ≥42 weeks are:
Fluid becomes saffron/yellowish-green and volume falls to about 300 ml. (Book p481)
Why can the placenta not synthesise estrogen independently?
The placenta lacks 17α-hydroxylase, making estrogen synthesis dependent on fetal adrenals. (Book p481)
Order the fetal-placental estrogen pathway for onset of labour.
Fetal adrenal C19 → 17α-hydroxylase → DHEA/DHEA-S → placental sulphatase and aromatase → estrogen → contractility
Placental estrogen → fetal adrenal C19 → 17α-hydroxylase → DHEA/DHEA-S → placental sulphatase → contractility
Fetal adrenal C19 → placental aromatase → DHEA/DHEA-S → 17α-hydroxylase → estrogen → myometrial contractility
Placental sulphatase → fetal adrenal C19 → DHEA/DHEA-S → placental aromatase → estrogen → myometrial relaxation
Fetal adrenal C19 steroids undergo 17α-hydroxylase action to DHEA/DHEA-S, then placental sulphatase and aromatase make estrogen (E1, E2, E3), which raises myometrial contractility. (Book p481)
The pathophysiology of post-term pregnancy is:
Falling estrogen reduces myometrial contractility, so labour is hard to start
Rising estrogen makes the labour precipitate and very short
Rising progesterone causes uterine rupture before labour
Falling prostaglandins alone, with normal estrogen levels
Post-term pregnancy is explained by reduced estrogen leading to reduced myometrial contractility, so initiating labour is difficult. (Book p481)
Causes of post-term pregnancy listed include:
Anencephaly, placental sulphatase deficiency, fetal demise and fetal Down syndrome
Maternal diabetes, polyhydramnios and an already macrosomic fetus
Cervical incompetence, placenta previa and multiple uterine fibroids
Hyperemesis gravidarum, severe maternal anaemia and Rh isoimmunisation
Post-term pregnancy is linked to an absent or hypoplastic fetal pituitary-adrenal axis and to sulphatase deficiency; maternal diabetes tends to shorten gestation. (Book p481)
Macrosomia in post-term pregnancy by Indian guidelines means fetal weight:
Indian guidelines define macrosomia as ≥4.0 kg. (Book p481)
Oligohydramnios in post-term pregnancy leads to:
Less space, so cord compression with variable decelerations, then fetal distress and meconium passage
Hydramnios with cord prolapse once the membranes rupture spontaneously in labour
Uterine overdistension leading to rupture of a previously scarred uterus
An entirely normal cardiotocograph, since liquor volume does not affect the trace
Falling liquor in a post-term pregnancy compresses the cord, giving variable decelerations, fetal distress and meconium-stained liquor. (Book p481)
Placental ageing in post-term pregnancy causes:
Uteroplacental insufficiency, giving late decelerations and fetal distress
Accelerated fetal growth from continued nutrient transfer
An increase in amniotic fluid volume from fetal polyuria
The early spontaneous onset of labour well before term
The ageing placenta fails, producing late decelerations on the CTG and fetal distress in labour; liquor falls rather than rises. (Book p481)
Fill up: Post-term pregnancy is defined as a gestation of ______ weeks or more, and the added fetal risk comes mainly from ______.
Beyond 42 weeks the ageing placenta may fail, liquor falls and the risk of meconium, macrosomia and stillbirth rises. (Book p481)
ACOG management of post-term pregnancy: termination of pregnancy at ______ by ______.
ACOG advises TOP at ≥41 weeks via induction of labour. (Book p482)
Post-term pregnancy is a ______ for VBAC.
It is a relative contraindication to vaginal birth after C-section. (Book p482)
Risk factors for macrosomia listed are:
Post-term pregnancy, maternal diabetes, maternal obesity and a male fetus
Maternal anaemia, cigarette smoking during pregnancy and first pregnancy
Pre-eclampsia, placental insufficiency and a female fetus
Maternal hypothyroidism, hyperemesis gravidarum and teenage pregnancy
Macrosomia follows excess substrate (diabetes, obesity, postmaturity) and male sex; smoking and vascular disease cause growth restriction. (Book p482)
Caesarean section, instrumental delivery, prolonged labour and shoulder dystocia
Postpartum haemorrhage alone, with no effect on the mode of delivery
Malpresentation alone, with no increase in operative delivery
Prelabour rupture of membranes alone, with no intrapartum complications
Macrosomia raises the whole spectrum of obstructed labour complications, including shoulder dystocia and operative delivery. (Book p482)
The organ LEAST affected by macrosomia is:
The brain is least affected per the note. (Book p482)
Best mode of delivery in macrosomia and C-section thresholds:
Vaginal delivery; C-section at 4.5 kg in diabetics or 5.0 kg in non-diabetics
Vaginal delivery; C-section at 4.0 kg in diabetics or 4.5 kg in non-diabetics
Elective C-section for all; no weight threshold is applied in either group
Vaginal delivery only; C-section at 4.5 kg in diabetics and non-diabetics alike
In macrosomia vaginal delivery is the usual mode; caesarean is advised at 4.5 kg in diabetics and at 5.0 kg in non-diabetics. (Book p482)
Macrosomia is a ______ contraindication for VBAC.
It is a relative contraindication for VBAC. (Book p482)
Best USG method and parameter for estimating fetal weight:
Formulae such as Hadlock or Shepherd, with abdominal circumference the most useful single parameter
Biparietal diameter and femur length measured in the second trimester
Head circumference combined with the placental grade
Three-dimensional volume measurement with the amniotic fluid index

Johnson's formula for clinical fetal weight estimation is:
(Fundal height in cm minus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
(Fundal height in cm plus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
Fundal height in cm times 155, minus n, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
(Abdominal circumference in cm minus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
Johnson's formula subtracts 12 when the head is above the ischial spines and 11 when it is engaged, and multiplies the result by 155. (Book p482)

Umbilical vein, portal sinus (hockey-stick sign) and fetal stomach

Reassure her and await spontaneous labour until 43 weeks without intervention
Immediate caesarean section, because post-term fetuses never tolerate labour
Admit for daily amniocentesis to test fetal lung maturity

Iliopectineal line forming the lateral boundary of the pelvic brim

true pelvis; the whole of labour from engagement to expulsion
mid pelvis; internal rotation of the fetal head during labour
pelvic outlet; extension of the head during delivery

Oblique diameters run from symphysis pubis directly backwards to sacral promontory

lower margin of the symphysis pubis; 13

junction of S4–S5; junction of S2–S3
Greatest plane posteriorly at S2–S3; least plane at S4–S5. (Book p484)

Both ischial spines can be touched at once with the fingers of one hand
Neither ischial spine can be reached at all on vaginal examination

The subpubic arch is unusually wide and the side walls are divergent

The pelvic outlet (anatomical) lies at the level of the:

The least-dimensions plane is superior and the outlet plane inferior. (Book p485)
The posterior sagittal diameter of the MID-PELVIS is measured from the sacrum to the:

The second Leopold (umbilical/lateral) grip identifies a smooth, continuous, rigid area as the ______ and multiple irregular knob-like structures as ______; back on the left means position ______.
Smooth rigid = back, knob-like = limbs; position of back = position of occiput, so back on left → LOA/LOP/LOT. (Book p496)
Leopold's manoeuvres: preparation & the four grips

Match the Leopold manoeuvre with what it determines — 1) Fundal grip 2) Lateral grip 3) Pawlik's grip … A) Which pole occupies the fundus, and whether it is the head or the breech B) The lie and the side on which the fetal back and limbs lie C) What lies above the pelvic inlet and whether the presenting part is engaged
The first grip identifies the fundal pole, the second the lie and back, the third engagement, and the fourth confirms the degree of flexion. (Book p496)
Third Leopold manoeuvre (Pawlik grip) – ballotable head means ______ and non-ballotable means ______; it infers presentation and ______.
Not fixed; fixed; it infers fixation and descent of the head
Fixed; not fixed; it infers the attitude of the head
Engaged; floating; it infers the lie of the fetus in utero
Deflexed; flexed; it infers the position of the fetal head
In the Pawlik grip, a ballotable head means it is not fixed and a non-ballotable head means it is fixed; the grip infers fixation, that is descent of the head into the pelvis. (Book p497)
Leopold's manoeuvres: preparation & the four grips
In the fourth Leopold manoeuvre (deep pelvic grip), fingers brought below the head that CONVERGE versus DIVERGE indicate:
Converge = head entered pelvis; diverge = head not entered pelvis
Converge = head not entered; diverge = head entered
Converging fingers → head entered pelvis; diverging → not entered. The 4th grip confirms Pawlik findings and gives attitude. (Book p497)
Leopold's manoeuvres: preparation & the four grips
Inference of the fourth Leopold manoeuvre – match occiput and sinciput findings: opposite directions, occiput higher : opposite directions, same level : same direction, occiput higher.
Opposite directions with occiput higher = flexion; same level = deflexed; same direction with occiput higher = completely extended. (Book p497)
Leopold's manoeuvres: preparation & the four grips
In the Crichton method the fetal head is taken to be about ______ fingers wide on abdominal palpation.
Head of fetus ≈ 5 fingers (Crichton method). (Book p498)
Fixation & engagement of the fetal head (Crichton method)
A ballotable head with 5/5 palpable (all 5 fingers accommodated) means:
Head has not entered the pelvis
5/5 palpable, ballotable = not entered the pelvis. (Book p498)
Fixation & engagement of the fetal head (Crichton method)
Match the non-ballotable head – 4/5 palpable : ≤2/5 palpable.
Non-ballotable head: 4/5 palpable = fixed; ≤2/5 palpable = engaged. (Book p498)
Fixation & engagement of the fetal head (Crichton method)
Fill up: By Crichton's method the head is said to be engaged when ______ of the head remains palpable above the pelvic brim.
Engagement means the widest part of the head has passed the brim, which corresponds to two-fifths or less of the head being felt abdominally. (Book p498)
Fixation & engagement of the fetal head (Crichton method)
Fill up: 1st: ______ → full dilatation; 2nd: → delivery of baby; 3rd: → delivery of placenta; 4th: 1–2 hrs observation after placenta.
True labour pain to full dilatation (10 cm) : full dilatation to delivery of baby : delivery of baby to delivery of placenta : 1–2 hrs observation after placenta
Onset of pain to engagement : engagement to crowning : crowning to birth : birth to placenta
True pain to 6 cm : 6 cm to full dilatation : full dilatation to birth : birth to placenta
Rupture of membranes to full dilatation : birth of baby : placenta : 24 hrs after placenta
1st: true labour pain → full dilatation; 2nd: → delivery of baby; 3rd: → delivery of placenta; 4th: 1–2 hrs observation after placenta. (Book p499)
The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase
Which of the following statements about The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase is TRUE?
ACOG: latent ends 5 cm, active begins 6 cm; New WHO: 4 cm / 5 cm; Old WHO: 3 cm / 4 cm. (Book p499)
The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase
All of the following are The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase EXCEPT:
Effacement with slow dilatation; then rapid dilatation with descent
Descent with slow dilatation; then effacement with no further change
Rapid dilatation with descent; then effacement with slow progress
Effacement only, no dilatation; then descent with slow cervical change
The latent phase is the event of effacement with slow dilatation; the active phase is rapid dilatation with partial descent of the fetal head. (Book p499)
The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with the four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase presents with primi: latent 12 h, active 4 h; multi: latent 8 h, active 3 h. Duration of latent and active phases – Primigravida : Multigravida?
Latent 12 hrs, active 4 hrs : latent 8 hrs, active 3 hrs
Latent 8 hrs, active 3 hrs : latent 12 hrs, active 4 hrs
Latent 20 hrs, active 6 hrs : latent 14 hrs, active 4 hrs
Latent 6 hrs, active 2 hrs : latent 4 hrs, active 1 hr
Primi: latent 12 h, active 4 h; multi: latent 8 h, active 3 h. (Book p499)
The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase
Fill up: Plotting of the active phase begins at ______ on the modified WHO partogram and at ______ on the WHO Labour Care Guide 2020; the latent phase is ______. is ______.
4 cm; 6 cm; plotted in the first column
Modified WHO partogram begins at 4 cm (old WHO); Labour Care Guide begins at 5 cm; latent phase is not plotted. (Book p499)
The four stages & the first stage: latent vs active phase
Fill up: The first stage of labour ends with ______, and the fourth stage is defined as the first ______ after delivery of the placenta.
delivery of the baby; two hours
delivery of the placenta; six hours
The stages are: first to full dilatation, second to delivery of the baby, third to delivery of the placenta, and fourth the first hour of observation. (Book p499)
Which of the following statements about Prolonged latent phase is TRUE?
≥20 hrs in primigravida or ≥14 hrs in multigravida
≥14 hrs in primigravida or ≥20 hrs in multigravida
≥12 hrs in primigravida or ≥8 hrs in multigravida
Prolonged latent phase — >24 hrs in either
≥20 h in primigravida or ≥14 h in multigravida. (Book p499)
All of the following are Prolonged latent phase EXCEPT:
Prostaglandins (PGE1 & PGE2) : wait for spontaneous delivery : therapeutic rest (best)
Oxytocin : C-section : prostaglandins — Unripe cervix → PGE1/PGE2; OP position → await spontaneous d
ARM : manual rotation : oxytocin — Unripe cervix → PGE1/PGE2; OP position → await spontaneous d
Unripe cervix → PGE1/PGE2; OP position → await spontaneous delivery; false labour pains → therapeutic rest (best management). (Book p499)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with prolonged latent phase presents with note: prolonged latent stage is not an indication for c-section. Prolonged latent stage as an indication for caesarean section – true or false?
False – prolonged latent stage is NOT an indication for C-section
True – always requires C-section with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
True – only in primigravida with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
True – only if membranes ruptured with appropriate counselling and management as per notes
Note: prolonged latent stage is not an indication for C-section. (Book p499)
Which of the following statements about a prolonged latent phase is TRUE?
It usually reflects an unfavourable cervix rather than obstruction, so rest and analgesia are the treatment
It is an immediate indication for caesarean section in every case
It is always caused by cephalopelvic disproportion or a contracted pelvis
It should be treated at once with high-dose oxytocin augmentation
Therapeutic rest with analgesia lets an unripe cervix resolve; most women then enter the active phase or are not in true labour. (Book p499)
Fill up: Dilatation: primi ______, multi 1.5 cm/hr.
Dilatation: primi 1.2 cm/hr, multi 1.5 cm/hr. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Which of the following statements about Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase is TRUE?
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase — 1 cm/hr : 2 cm/hr
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase — 1.2 cm/hr : 1.5 cm/hr
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase — 2 cm/hr : 1 cm/hr
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase — 0.5 cm/hr : 1 cm/hr
Descent: primi 1 cm/hr, multi 2 cm/hr. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Old vs new WHO recommendation on cervical dilatation:
Old: at least 1 cm/hr, the basis of the action line; New: under 1 cm/hr can be normal
Old: at least 2 cm/hr, the basis of the action line; New: under 1 cm/hr can be normal
Old: at least 1 cm/hr, the basis of the action line; New: alert and action lines retained
Old: under 1 cm/hr was normal; New: at least 1 cm/hr with the alert line retained

The old WHO recommendation was a minimum of 1 cm/hr, the basis of the action line; the new guidance accepts that under 1 cm/hr can be normal and removes the alert and action lines from the Labour Care Guide. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Protracted active phase is defined as cervical dilatation ______ OR descent of head ______.
Under 1 cm/hr dilatation; descent under 1 cm/hr in primigravida or 2 cm/hr in multipara
Under 2 cm/hr dilatation; descent under 1 cm/hr in both primigravida and multipara
Under 1 cm/hr dilatation; descent under 2 cm/hr in primigravida or 1 cm/hr in multipara
No progress in dilatation for 2 hours; no descent of the head for 1 hour
Protracted active phase is cervical dilatation under 1 cm/hr, or descent of the head under 1 cm/hr in a primigravida or under 2 cm/hr in a multigravida. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Management protocol for protracted active phase begins with vaginal examination — match the finding to the action: cephalopelvic disproportion : occipito-posterior position : inadequate contractions.
CPD: caesarean section — occipito-posterior: wait for spontaneous rotation — inadequate contractions: assess them abdominally
CPD: wait and observe — occipito-posterior: caesarean section — inadequate contractions: start oxytocin
CPD: start oxytocin — occipito-posterior: caesarean section — inadequate contractions: wait and observe
CPD: amniotomy — occipito-posterior: forceps delivery — inadequate contractions: caesarean section
The finding on examination decides the action: disproportion is delivered, a good pelvis with malposition is given time, and weak contractions are assessed then augmented. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
If contractions are hypotonic/inadequate, augmentation of labour consists of:
Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Sequence of augmentation – head engaged : head not engaged.
Head engaged: ARM, wait 30 minutes, then oxytocin; not engaged: oxytocin then ARM
Head engaged: oxytocin, wait 30 minutes, then ARM; not engaged: ARM then oxytocin
Head engaged: ARM alone, no oxytocin; not engaged: oxytocin alone, no ARM
Both engaged and not engaged: simultaneous ARM and oxytocin together
With the head engaged, augment by ARM, wait 30 minutes, then oxytocin; with the head not engaged, give oxytocin followed by ARM, since ARM first raises the risk of cord prolapse. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Fill up: In the active phase of the first stage, cervical dilatation normally proceeds at least at ______ cm per hour.
A rate below about 1 cm per hour in a primigravida is protraction, which prompts a search for poor contractions, malposition or disproportion. (Book p500)
Active phase: normal rates & protracted active phase
Arrest of active phase is diagnosed when there is no dilatation of cervix for:
≥4 hrs despite good contractions (≥200 Montevideo units) OR ≥6 hrs of inadequate contractions despite oxytocin
≥6 hrs with good contractions OR ≥4 hrs with inadequate contractions
No dilatation ≥4 h despite good contractions (≥200 MVU) or ≥6 h of inadequate contractions despite oxytocin. (Book p500)
Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest
Arrest of descent (a second criterion of arrest) = no descent of fetal head for:
≥2 hrs in primigravida, ≥1 hr in multigravida
≥1 hr in primigravida, ≥2 hrs in multigravida
≥4 hrs in primigravida, ≥2 hrs in multigravida
No descent for ≥2 h (primi) / ≥1 h (multi). (Book p501)
Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest
Prerequisites for diagnosing arrest of active phase are ______ and ______; management is ______.
Cervix ≥6 cm dilated; membranes ruptured; C-section
Cervix fully dilated; membranes ruptured; vacuum
Prerequisites: cervix ≥6 cm and membranes ruptured; management is C-section. (Book p501)
Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest
On the illustrated arrest partogram, arrest of cervical dilatation appears as ______ and falling FHR indicates ______.
A straight (flat) line for 3 hrs; fetal distress → immediate C-section
A line crossing the alert line only; wait
No dilatation for 3 h appears as a straight line; ↓FHR = fetal distress, an indication for immediate C-section. (Book p501)
Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest
Other features on the same arrest partogram were meconium in amniotic fluid, 3+ moulding and good uterine contractions. In the FIRST stage, fetal distress is managed by:
In the 1st stage of labour, management of fetal distress is C-section only. (Book p501)
Arrest of active phase, arrest of descent & partogram of arrest
A primigravida's partogram shows the cervix at 6 cm with no further change for four hours despite adequate contractions, and the head is at station zero. What is the diagnosis and next step?
Arrest of the active phase — reassess for disproportion and deliver by caesarean section
Normal progress — continue to observe for another four hours
Prolonged latent phase — give sedatives and allow her to rest
Precipitate labour — prepare for immediate delivery
No cervical change for four hours with adequate contractions, or two hours without, is arrest of dilatation and needs delivery after excluding disproportion. (Book p501)
Arrest of active phase & arrest of descent
The second stage of labour (from full dilatation of cervix, 10 cm) – main event, effect of epidural, and descent:
Delivery of baby; epidural prolongs it by 1 hr; maximum fetal head descent occurs here
Delivery of placenta; epidural shortens it; no descent
Delivery of baby; epidural has no effect; descent minimal
Effacement; epidural prolongs by 2 hrs; descent begins
Main event = delivery of baby; epidural prolongs 2nd stage by 1 hour; maximum head descent occurs in this stage. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Fill the second-stage duration table for PRIMIGRAVIDA – average : maximum without epidural : maximum with epidural.
Primi: average 50 min, max 3 h without epidural, 4 h with epidural. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Fill the second-stage duration table for MULTIGRAVIDA – average : maximum without epidural : maximum with epidural.
Multi: average 30 min, max 2 h without epidural, 3 h with epidural. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Prolonged second stage without epidural is defined as:
>3 hrs in primigravida; >2 hrs in multigravida
>2 hrs in primigravida; >1 hr in multigravida
>4 hrs in primigravida; >3 hrs in multigravida
Prolonged 2nd stage: >3 h primi, >2 h multi (without epidural). (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Arrest of descent in the second stage requires a pre-requisite of ______ and management depends on ______.
Normal FHR; maternal and fetal condition
Pre-requisite: normal FHR; management depends on maternal and fetal condition. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Fetal distress in 2nd stage with fully dilated cervix – management by station:
Station above +2: C-section; station at +2 or below: forceps
Station above +2: vacuum; at +2 or below: C-section
Above +2 → C-section; at or below +2 → forceps (forceps preferred in fetal distress). (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Which second-stage scenarios mandate C-section with NO instrumental delivery?
Bandl's ring + prolonged 2nd stage; CPD + prolonged 2nd stage with moulding/caput
Prolonged 2nd stage with normal FHR at station +2
Bandl's ring or CPD (with moulding/caput) in a prolonged 2nd stage → C-section; instrumental delivery is contraindicated. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Prolonged 2nd stage with normal FHR and no CPD/obstructed labour – management:
Station above +2: C-section; at +2 or below: forceps or vacuum
Above +2 → C-section; at/below +2 → forceps or vacuum. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Requisites for instrumental delivery and the instrument of choice in fetal distress:
Full cervical dilatation and station ≥ +2; forceps > vacuum
Cervix ≥8 cm and engaged head; vacuum > forceps
Requisites: full dilatation + station ≥ +2; in fetal distress forceps > vacuum. (Book p502)
Second stage of labour: durations & arrest of descent management
Fill up: In a primigravida the second stage normally lasts up to ______ hours without epidural analgesia, and up to ______ hours with an epidural.
Two hours (three with an epidural) is the accepted limit in a primigravida, and one hour (two with an epidural) in a multiparous woman. (Book p502)
The baby cannot be delivered despite good contractions and full dilatation, from obstruction in the passage
Failure of the cervix to dilate despite adequate oxytocin augmentation
A latent phase lasting more than 20 hours in a primigravida
Delayed delivery caused by contractions that are too weak
Obstruction means mechanical blockage with adequate powers; weak contractions are inertia, not obstruction. (Book p503)
Obstructed labour is seen in all EXCEPT:
Listed causes: transverse lie, conjoint twins, hydrocephalus, fibroid uterus. (Book p503)
On general examination in obstructed labour the mother appears:
Exhausted, dehydrated, tachypnoeic with acidotic breathing
Exhausted, dehydrated, tachypnoeic, acidotic breathing. (Book p503)
Bandl's ring on P/A examination is the ______ between the ______ upper segment and the ______ lower segment.
Groove; tonically contracted upper segment; passively distended lower segment
Groove; passively distended upper segment; tonically contracted lower segment
Bulge; relaxed and atonic upper segment; tonically contracted lower segment
Ridge; tonically contracted upper segment; hypertonic non-distended lower
Bandl's ring is the groove between the retracted (tonically contracted) upper segment and the distended (passively dilated) lower segment. (Book p503)
Complications of obstructed labour include rupture of uterus and vesicovaginal fistula (VVF). The VVF appears:
After 7-10 days, from ischaemic necrosis of the bladder with constant dribbling of urine
Immediately after delivery, from a direct laceration of the bladder wall
After six weeks, from a low-grade infection of the bladder
Within 24 hours, from trauma caused by the urethral catheter
Pressure necrosis declares itself a week or so later as continuous painless dribbling of urine per vaginam. (Book p503)
Management of obstructed labour and what must be AVOIDED:
Immediate caesarean with resuscitation; avoid waiting, oxytocin and instruments
Oxytocin augmentation to overcome the obstruction; avoid caesarean
Forceps delivery once fully dilated; avoid any further waiting
Wait for spontaneous delivery; avoid oxytocin in the meantime
Obstructed labour is managed by immediate caesarean section with maternal resuscitation; waiting, oxytocin and instrumental delivery must all be avoided. (Book p503)
All of the following are features of obstructed labour EXCEPT:
A well-flexed deeply engaged head with no caput or moulding
A retraction ring rising obliquely across the abdomen
A tonically contracted tender uterus in an exhausted, dehydrated woman
A distended bladder, ketosis and a hot dry vagina
Obstruction produces marked caput and moulding with non-engagement; a well-flexed engaged head with no caput is a favourable, unobstructed picture. (Book p503)
Match the alternate names – Bandl's ring : Schroeder's ring.
Bandl's = retraction ring; Schroeder's = constriction ring. (Book p504)
Match the cause – Bandl's ring : Schroeder's ring.
Bandl's: obstructed labour; Schroeder's: segment spasm from oxytocin
Bandl's: oxytocin overdose; Schroeder's: obstructed labour
Bandl's: prolonged latent phase; Schroeder's: cephalopelvic disproportion
Bandl's: uterine rupture; Schroeder's: placenta accreta spectrum
Bandl's ring is caused by obstructed labour; Schroeder's ring is a spasm of a uterine segment due to inadvertent oxytocin use. (Book p504)
Match the site and stage – Bandl's ring : Schroeder's ring.
Between upper and lower uterine segments, second stage : any site, first or second stage
Any site, first stage : between segments, second stage
Cervix, second stage : fundus, third stage
Lower segment, first stage : upper segment, second stage
Bandl's: junction of upper and lower segments in 2nd stage; Schroeder's: any site, 1st or 2nd stage. (Book p504)
Palpability, visibility and maternal/fetal condition – Bandl's ring : Schroeder's ring.
Palpable and visible P/A, maternal and fetal distress : palpable P/V, not visible, condition normal
Palpable P/V, visible, distress : palpable P/A, visible, normal
Not palpable, not visible, normal : palpable P/A, visible, distress
Both palpable P/A and visible with distress
Bandl's ring is palpable and visible per abdomen with maternal/fetal distress; Schroeder's ring is felt P/V, not visible and condition is normal. (Book p504)
Relief of Schroeder's ring is by ______, and if C-section is needed the incision is ______.
Stopping oxytocin and giving uterine relaxants; a vertical (Kronig) lower-segment incision
Continuing oxytocin to overcome the ring; a vertical (Kronig) lower-segment incision
Stopping oxytocin and giving uterine relaxants; a transverse lower-segment incision
Manual dilatation of the constriction ring; a classical upper-segment fundal incision
Schroeder's ring is relieved by stopping oxytocin and giving uterine relaxants such as terbutaline; if caesarean is needed the incision is a vertical (Kronig) lower vertical incision. (Book p504)

Match the ring with its description — 1) Physiological retraction ring 2) Bandl's ring 3) Constriction ring … A) A pathological ring that rises obliquely across the abdomen as obstructed labour advances B) The normal junction of active upper and passive lower segment that cannot be felt abdominally C) A localised spasm of uterine muscle around a fetal part, unrelated to the segmental junction
The physiological ring is normal and impalpable, Bandl's ring is the rising sign of obstruction, and a constriction ring is a focal spasm. (Book p504)
WHO recommended actions at admission in labour include all EXCEPT:
Auscultate fetal heart sounds / P/V exam (contraindicated in active bleeding)
Not recommended: routine enema, routine pelvic examination, routine CTG, routine pelvic shaving. (Book p504)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Which of the following are NOT recommended routinely at admission per WHO?
Routine CTG and routine pelvic shaving
Routine enema, pelvic examination, CTG and pelvic shaving are not recommended. (Book p504)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Ambulation in first stage – early labour : late labour/membranes ruptured.
Allowed : lie in left lateral position
Ambulation allowed in early labour; left lateral position in late labour or after membrane rupture. (Book p504)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Oral intake in first stage and pre-C-section fasting rules:
Solids not allowed, liquids allowed; for C-section stop solids 6 hrs and liquids 2 hrs before surgery
Solids and liquids allowed; stop both 8 hrs before surgery
Nil by mouth throughout labour; 12 hrs fasting before surgery
Solids allowed, liquids restricted; stop liquids 6 hrs before
Solids not allowed, liquids allowed; solids stopped 6 h and liquids 2 h before C-section. (Book p504)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Bladder function during first stage – the woman is encouraged to void every:
Encouraged to relieve bladder every 2 hours. (Book p504)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Which of the following is consistent with WHO recommendations for care in normal labour?
A companion of the woman's choice, oral fluids, freedom of movement and no routine enema or shaving
A routine admission enema, pubic shaving and nil by mouth for every woman
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring for every woman in labour
Routine episiotomy and routine early amniotomy to shorten labour
WHO supports respectful, low-intervention care; enemas, shaving, routine amniotomy and routine episiotomy are not recommended. (Book p504)
WHO recommendations for admission & first stage care
Which first-stage items (pain relief, companion of choice, ambulation, oral intake) are grouped under 'supportive care' in the Labour Care Guide?
Ambulation, oral intake, pain relief and a companion of the woman's choice
Pain relief alone, since the others are obstetric interventions
Bladder care and fetal monitoring, which together define supportive care
An enema and perineal shaving, as recommended routinely on admission
Supportive care bundles the low-technology measures: mobility, fluids, analgesia and continuous support. (Book p505)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Monitoring frequency in the first stage – maternal pulse/BP : temperature (membranes intact / ruptured) : contractions : P/V.
Hourly : hourly / 4th hourly : every 30 min : 4th hourly
Every 30 min : hourly / hourly : hourly : 2nd hourly
4th hourly : hourly / hourly : every 15 min : hourly
Hourly : 4th hourly / hourly : every 30 min : 2nd hourly
Pulse/BP hourly; temperature hourly (intact) or 4th hourly (ruptured); contractions every 30 min; P/V 4th hourly. (Book p505)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
FHR auscultation frequency – 1st stage low risk : 1st stage high risk : 2nd stage low risk : 2nd stage high risk.
1st stage: 30 min (low risk) / 15 min (high risk); 2nd stage: 15 min / 5 min. (Book p505)
WHO recommendations: admission & first stage care
Recommended measures to prevent perineal tear include all EXCEPT:
Controlled delivery of fetal head / modified Ritgen manoeuvre
Routine episiotomy and fundal pressure are NOT recommended. (Book p505)

One hand initially flexes then extends the head; the other supports the perineum. (Book p505)

Which statement about maternal position in the second stage is correct per the notes?
Delivery can be done in any position
Note: delivery can be done in any position. (Book p505)

warm compresses with hands-on support; avoiding routine episiotomy
a routine mediolateral episiotomy; fundal pressure
sustained Valsalva pushing; the lithotomy position
a routine episiotomy; early cord clamping
Warm compresses, hands-on support and spontaneous pushing reduce tears; episiotomy and fundal pressure increase trauma. (Book p505)
Management of second stage & prevention of perineal tear

Friedman curve = 1st partogram, sigmoid curve. (Book p506)

Which of the following statements about Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide is TRUE?
Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide — Philpott & Castle; 1 cm/hr
Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide — Friedman; 1.2 cm/hr
Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide — WHO 2020; 0.5 cm/hr
Types of partogram: Friedman curve, modified WHO & Labour Care Guide — Bishop; 2 cm/hr
Alert/action line introduced by Philpott & Castle; principle: minimum 1 cm/hr in the active phase. (Book p506)
