Third stage of labour – main factor affecting placental separation : plane of separation : m/c method of separation.
Uterine contractions : zona spongiosa : Schultz method
Cord traction : zona basalis : Duncan method
Separation depends on uterine contractions, occurs through zona spongiosa, m/c Schultz method. (Book p523)
Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview
The surest sign of placental separation is:
The placenta being felt in the vagina, with apparent permanent lengthening of the cord
A sudden gush of blood before the placenta appears at the introitus
The fundus becoming globular and firm on abdominal palpation
The uterus rising higher in the abdomen above the umbilicus
Feeling the placenta in the vagina, with the cord appearing to lengthen permanently, is the surest sign that separation has occurred. (Book p523)
Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview
Passive management of the third stage (not preferred) involves:
Waiting for spontaneous separation and expulsion, with more blood loss and a higher risk of PPH
A uterotonic within one minute of the birth, followed by controlled cord traction
Controlled cord traction with suprapubic counter-pressure and early clamping of the cord
Early cord clamping with immediate traction on the cord to hasten separation of the placenta
Passive management means waiting for signs of separation without a uterotonic; it increases blood loss, PPH and maternal mortality. (Book p523)
Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview
Shortens the third stage, reduces blood loss and prevents PPH, but slightly raises the chance of retained placenta
Lengthens the third stage but reduces PPH; the drawback is uterine inversion
Reduces blood loss only, with neonatal anaemia as its drawback
Prevents retained placenta entirely, but at the cost of more PPH
Active management shortens and de-bloods the third stage, at the price of a small increase in retained placenta from early uterotonics. (Book p523)
Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview
Arrange the four steps of AMTSL:
Uterotonic within one minute, delayed cord clamping, controlled cord traction, then intermittent assessment of uterine tone
Cord traction first, then the uterotonic, then clamping, then uterine massage
Early cord clamping, then the uterotonic, then traction, then assessment of tone
Uterine massage first, then the uterotonic, then traction, then late clamping
The four steps run: uterotonic, delayed clamping, controlled cord traction with counter-pressure, then regular assessment of the uterus. (Book p523)
Third stage of labour & AMTSL overview

Match the component of active management with its purpose — 1) Uterotonic within one minute of birth 2) Controlled cord traction 3) Delayed cord clamping … A) The single most effective step for preventing postpartum haemorrhage B) Shortens the third stage when combined with suprapubic counter-pressure, while guarding against cord avulsion C) Allows placental transfusion for 1-3 minutes and improves neonatal iron stores
Active management of the third stage is a package: uterotonic, traction with counter-pressure, and delayed clamping when the baby is well. (Book p523)
Third stage of labour & active management
WHO-recommended uterotonic for AMTSL – dose, route, storage:
Oxytocin 10 IU IM or IV infusion (in RL/NS); stored at 2–8 °C
Oxytocin 5 IU IV bolus; room temperature
Oxytocin 10 IU IM or IV infusion; stored 2–8 °C. (Book p524)
Oxytocin IV bolus is contraindicated because it causes ______; 5% dextrose preparation causes ______.
Hypotension, tachycardia and arrhythmias; and water intoxication from its antidiuretic effect
Severe hypertension with intracranial haemorrhage; and hyperglycaemia
Reflex bradycardia with heart block; and hypernatraemia from the salt load
High fever with rigors; and hypokalaemia from intracellular shift
An intravenous bolus of oxytocin causes hypotension and arrhythmias, and large volumes of 5% dextrose cause water intoxication. (Book p524)
If oxytocin is unavailable, methylergometrine is given as:
0.2 mg intramuscularly, since the intravenous route can cause severe hypertension
0.5 mg intravenously, with the ampoules kept refrigerated
0.2 mg intravenously, from ampoules that have been stored frozen
1 mg by mouth, stored at room temperature
Methylergometrine 0.2 mg is given intramuscularly; the intravenous route risks a dangerous rise in blood pressure. (Book p524)
Syntometrine is a fixed combination of ______ with the advantage of ______ but disadvantage of ______.
5 U oxytocin + 0.5 mg methylergometrine; ↑ efficacy; expensive and ↓ availability
10 U oxytocin + 0.2 mg ME; cheap; hypertension
5 U oxytocin + 250 mcg carboprost; long action; bronchospasm
0.5 mg ME + 600 mcg misoprostol; oral; fever
Syntometrine = 5 U oxytocin + 0.5 mg ME; more efficacious but expensive/less available. (Book p524)
Carbetocin (synthetic oxytocin octapeptide) – dose, half-life and restriction:
100 microgram slowly intravenously; half-life 40 minutes; not used for induction or for treating PPH
250 microgram intramuscularly; half-life 5 minutes; used to treat PPH
10 IU intramuscularly; half-life 20 minutes; used for induction of labour
1 mg intravenously; half-life 60 minutes; the standard treatment for PPH
Carbetocin is a long-acting oxytocin analogue given as 100 microgram for prevention at caesarean, not for induction or PPH treatment. (Book p524)
Misoprostol (PGE1) as a uterotonic in AMTSL is dosed:
600 microgram orally or sublingually, within a range of 400 to 600 microgram
25 microgram vaginally, repeated every six hours as required
800 microgram rectally, which is the WHO recommended single dose
200 microgram orally, which is the maximum dose the mother tolerates
In active management misoprostol is used where oxytocin is unavailable, in a dose of 400-600 microgram orally or sublingually. (Book p524)
Type of uterine contraction produced — oxytocin : methylergometrine.
Oxytocin: physiological, with relaxation between contractions — methylergometrine: tetanic, without relaxation
Oxytocin: tetanic, without relaxation between contractions — methylergometrine: physiological, with relaxation
Both drugs produce a tetanic contraction of the uterus that does not relax at all
Both drugs produce physiological contractions with complete relaxation between them
Oxytocin produces physiological contractions with relaxation, whereas ergometrine produces a sustained tetanic contraction and is unsafe before delivery. (Book p524)
Site of action and use – oxytocin : methylergometrine.
Oxytocin acts on both segments and is used for induction and AMTSL; ergometrine is only used after delivery
Oxytocin acts on the lower segment alone and is used for PPH; ergometrine induces labour
Oxytocin acts on the upper segment alone and is used for induction; ergometrine is first line for induction
Oxytocin ripens the cervix; ergometrine acts on the fundus and is used for augmentation
Oxytocin acts on the whole uterus and is used before and after delivery; ergometrine is used only after the baby is born. (Book p524)
Oxytocin bolus → hypotension; ME → hypertension. (Book p524)
Fill up: Oxytocin 10 IU is the first-line uterotonic, while carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha) is given as ______ microgram and must be avoided in ______.
Carboprost 250 microgram every 15 minutes up to eight doses is second line, but it can provoke severe bronchospasm in asthmatics. (Book p524)
Carboprost/dinoprostone (PGF2α) and tranexamic acid in the third stage are:
Not used in active management; tranexamic acid 1 g is added only when the risk of PPH is high
Both are first-line drugs of active management of the third stage in every delivery
Both are used only for induction of labour and never in the third stage or PPH
Both are contraindicated in the management of established postpartum haemorrhage
Prostaglandins are reserved for treating PPH rather than preventing it, and tranexamic acid is an adjunct where the risk is high. (Book p525)
Dinoprostone (PGE2) is used for ______ but is NOT recommended by WHO for ______.
Induction and augmentation of labour; not for AMTSL or PPH management
Postpartum hemorrhage; not recommended for induction of labour
Active management of the third stage; not for induction
Cervical ripening only; not recommended for augmentation
Dinoprostone (PGE2) is used for induction and augmentation of labour, but WHO does not recommend it for AMTSL or PPH management. (Book p525)
Delayed cord clamping (DCC) means clamping at ______ and is included in ______.
≥1 min (1–3 min); Anemia Mukt Bharat programme
DCC ≥1 min (1–3 min), part of Anemia Mukt Bharat. (Book p525)
About 80 mL more cord blood reaching the baby, giving extra iron and less neonatal anaemia
Prevention of postpartum haemorrhage in the mother after delivery
A lower risk of neonatal jaundice needing treatment with phototherapy
Prevention of retained placenta in the third stage of labour
Delayed clamping transfers about 80 mL more blood, roughly 50 mg of elemental iron, and reduces infant anaemia; it slightly increases jaundice. (Book p525)
Absolute indication for early cord clamping (ECC):
The need for neonatal resuscitation, as in birth asphyxia
An Rh-negative mother, to limit feto-maternal transfusion
Maternal HIV infection, to reduce the risk of viral transmission
Preterm delivery, to allow immediate paediatric assessment
Clamping is only brought forward when the baby needs resuscitation; otherwise delayed clamping is recommended, including in preterm births. (Book p525)
Relative indications for ECC include all EXCEPT:
Rh-negative mother with negative ICT (if ICT positive → DCC)
Relative ECC: Rh-negative mother ± ICT negative, fetal heart disease, excessive maternal bleeding. COVID-19 is an indication FOR DCC. (Book p525)
HIV-positive mothers – WHO/ACOG : national guidelines; and what reduces vertical transmission more?
WHO and ACOG advise delayed clamping; national guidance advises clamping once pulsation ceases; antiretrovirals matter more than timing
WHO advises early clamping and national guidance delayed clamping, with early clamping more protective
Both advise delayed clamping, and clamping timing matters more than antiretroviral therapy
Both advise early clamping, and early clamping reduces transmission more than antiretrovirals
Delayed clamping is advised for HIV-positive mothers because transmission is driven by viral load, which antiretroviral therapy controls. (Book p525)
Which of the following statements about delayed cord clamping is TRUE?
It is delayed for at least one to three minutes in babies who do not need resuscitation, and it does not raise the risk of postpartum haemorrhage
The cord must be clamped immediately in every birth to prevent postpartum haemorrhage
Delayed clamping is contraindicated in all preterm infants
Delayed clamping means waiting half an hour before clamping the cord
Delayed clamping improves neonatal iron stores and is especially valuable in preterm babies; it is combined with, not a substitute for, a uterotonic. (Book p525)
Step 3 of AMTSL uses the technique of ______ (a.k.a. ______) performed by ______.
Controlled cord traction; modified Brandt-Andrews technique; skilled birth attendant
Credé's method; fundal expression; any attendant
CCT = modified Brandt-Andrews technique, by a skilled birth attendant; Credé's method is outdated. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
Correct procedure of controlled cord traction:
Wait for separation signs, push the uterus up, then pull the cord forward during a contraction
Pull on the cord continuously from delivery, regardless of any signs of separation
Squeeze the fundus (Credé manoeuvre) while pulling the cord downwards firmly
Apply traction between contractions while an assistant presses on the fundus
Controlled cord traction: look for signs of separation, push the uterus upwards with one hand, then apply gentle downward-forward traction on the cord during a contraction. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
If the cord breaks during CCT, management is:
Manual removal under anaesthesia, sweeping the hand in the plane between the uterus and the placenta
Wait one hour for spontaneous expulsion before any intervention
An oxytocin bolus combined with firm fundal pressure
Emergency hysterectomy, since the cord can no longer be secured
Once the cord snaps, controlled traction is impossible, so the placenta is removed manually in the correct plane under anaesthesia. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
Pulling the cord before the placenta has separated risks ______; failure to find a plane between placenta and uterus suggests ______.
Uterine inversion; morbidly adherent placenta (placenta accreta spectrum)
Premature traction → uterine inversion; no cleavage plane → placenta accreta spectrum. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
Persistent bleeding after placental delivery with a retained part of placenta on USG suggests:
Retained lobe → placenta succenturiata or bilobata. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
Step 4 – intermittent assessment of uterine tone is done every ______ for ______; retained placenta/prolonged third stage is defined as placenta undelivered ______ after birth.
Tone every 15 min for 1–2 h; retained placenta = not delivered ≥30 min after baby. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
Thirty minutes after a normal delivery the placenta is still undelivered, there is no bleeding and the uterus is well contracted. What is the diagnosis and next step?
Retained placenta without haemorrhage — empty the bladder, wait up to 60 minutes and prepare for manual removal if it is still retained
Immediate manual removal of the placenta under general anaesthesia
Emergency hysterectomy, because this must be placenta accreta
Give ergometrine and apply strong traction to the cord to pull the placenta out
Without bleeding the third stage may safely be allowed up to an hour; traction beyond control risks cord avulsion and uterine inversion. (Book p526)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction & the fourth stage
Fourth stage of labour – duration, a normal maternal experience and monitoring intervals:
One to two hours after the placenta; physiological chills; observations every 15 minutes
Twenty-four hours after delivery; fever; vital signs taken hourly throughout
Thirty minutes after delivery; rigors; vital signs taken every five minutes
Six hours after delivery; sweating; vital signs taken every half hour
The fourth stage is the first one to two hours after delivery, when the woman may shiver and needs close observation. (Book p527)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
Advice given in the fourth stage and its possible complications:
Pass urine and take oral fluids within 2 hours; watch for PPH, tears, hematoma
Remain nil by mouth for a full 6 hours; watch for uterine rupture
Strict bed rest for 24 hours after delivery; watch for deep vein thrombosis
Keep the catheter in place for 12 hours; watch for postpartum infection
In the fourth stage the mother is advised to pass urine and take oral intake within 2 hours of delivery; the complications to watch for are PPH, perineal tears and vulval hematoma. (Book p527)
Steps 3 & 4: controlled cord traction, special cases & fourth stage
PPH is the most common cause of maternal mortality in India. Match the blood-loss definition – after vaginal delivery : after C-section : ACOG (any delivery).
PPH ≥500 mL after vaginal delivery, ≥1000 mL after C-section; ACOG ≥1000 mL after any delivery. (Book p528)
Which is NOT one of the three clinical definitions of PPH?
Excessive bleeding after delivery requiring blood transfusion
Blood loss with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia
Fall in hematocrit by ≥10% between admission and postpartum period
Clinical definitions: need for transfusion, hypovolemic signs, ≥10% hematocrit fall. Severe PPH (WHO) = ≥1000 mL. (Book p528)
Fill up: Primary PPH occurs within ______ of delivery, and secondary PPH runs from 24 hours to ______ afterwards.
Primary PPH is within 24 hours of birth and secondary PPH runs from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum. (Book p528)
Match the 4 Ts with the m/c examples – Tone : Trauma : Thrombin : Tissue.
Atonic uterus : perineal tear or rupture : bleeding disorders : retained placental tissue
Retained placental tissue : atonic uterus : perineal tear or rupture : bleeding disorders
Bleeding disorders : retained placental tissue : atonic uterus : perineal tear or rupture
Perineal tear or rupture : bleeding disorders : atonic uterus : retained placental tissue

The 4 Ts: Tone – atonic uterus (commonest overall and commonest primary PPH); Trauma – perineal or cervical tear, hematoma, rupture; Thrombin – bleeding disorders; Tissue – retained placental tissue (commonest secondary PPH). (Book p528)
The 'living ligature' of the uterus refers to:
The interlacing middle layer of myometrium, whose fibres compress the vessels as the uterus contracts
The round ligament, which anchors the uterus and kinks the ovarian vessels after delivery
The internal cervical os, which closes and compresses the cervical branch of the uterine artery
The decidua basalis, whose spiral arteries thrombose spontaneously after separation of the placenta
The middle myometrial fibres act as living ligatures; when they fail to contract and retract, the sinuses bleed and atonic PPH follows. (Book p528)
A woman undergoes postpartum dilatation and curettage for retained products of conception. What is she at the highest risk of, and what best prevents PPH in the first place?
Asherman syndrome; active management of the third stage of labour
Uterine inversion; an oxytocin bolus given with the anterior shoulder
Placenta accreta spectrum; routine misoprostol in the third stage
Endometritis; early clamping of the umbilical cord
Postpartum D&C carries the highest risk of Asherman syndrome; the best method of preventing PPH is active management of the third stage of labour. (Book p528)
Fill up: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss of ______ mL or more within 24 hours of birth, and the four Ts are tone, trauma, tissue and ______.
The four Ts are uterine tone, genital tract trauma, retained tissue and thrombin (coagulopathy); 500 mL defines PPH and 1000 mL severe PPH. (Book p528)
Maternal risk factors for PPH include all EXCEPT:
Previous history of PPH / advanced maternal age
H/O PIH in current pregnancy / anemia
Maternal: previous PPH, advanced age, obesity, multigravida, PIH in current pregnancy, anemia. (Book p529)
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
Placental risk factors for PPH are:
Placenta previa, abruptio placentae, placenta accreta spectrum and chorioamnionitis
A succenturiate lobe alone, which does not disturb the third stage
A velamentous cord insertion alone, which affects only the fetus
A circumvallate placenta alone, which is a harmless anatomical variant
Placental causes of PPH are previa, abruption, morbid adherence and infection; the others are variants that do not themselves provoke bleeding. (Book p529)
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
Uterine risk factors relate to overdistension, e.g.:
Twin pregnancy, gestational diabetes, polyhydramnios, macrosomia and a fibroid uterus
A bicornuate uterus, which overdistends and weakens the myometrium
Cervical incompetence with a short painless cervix in the second trimester
A uterine septum, which stretches the lower segment during pregnancy
Overdistension of the uterus exhausts the myometrium; congenital anomalies do not overdistend it, though they can predispose otherwise. (Book p529)
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
Which statement about intrapartum risk factors for PPH is TRUE?
Prolonged or precipitate labour, induction, instrumental delivery and general anaesthesia all raise the risk
Epidural analgesia and active management of the third stage raise the risk
Ambulation, continuous support and the left lateral position raise the risk
Oral fluids in labour and intermittent auscultation are intrapartum risk factors
Intrapartum risk factors exhaust or damage the uterus and birth canal; the measures in the other options are neutral or protective. (Book p529)
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
All of the following are specific risk factors for TRAUMATIC PPH EXCEPT:
Anaemia in the mother before delivery

Traumatic PPH follows tears and lacerations from operative delivery, malpresentation, obstructed or very fast labour and high parity; anaemia is a maternal rather than a traumatic risk factor. (Book p529)
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
All of the following predispose to uterine atony EXCEPT:
A short uncomplicated first stage in a multiparous woman
Overdistension of the uterus from twins or polyhydramnios
Prolonged or augmented labour with an exhausted myometrium
Grand multiparity with a fibroid uterus
Atony follows overdistension, exhaustion, parity, fibroids, infection and anaesthesia; a quick uncomplicated labour does not exhaust the uterus. (Book p529)
Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
First step in managing PPH (an obstetric emergency requiring a synchronised approach) is resuscitation, which includes all EXCEPT:
Large-bore IV cannula; blood samples for ABO/Rh, CBC, BT, CT; arrange blood
Resuscitation: IV cannula, blood samples, arrange blood, crystalloids 1000 mL/min, ABC, Foley catheter. (Book p529)
Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
After resuscitation, per-abdominal uterine massage finds a well-contracted uterus with normal tone. This:
Rules out atonic PPH and indicates traumatic PPH → P/V examination to find the cause
Normal tone → atonic PPH ruled out → traumatic PPH → P/V examination. (Book p529)
Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
If uterine tone is ↓ and maintained only by massage, this indicates ______; the next step is ______.
Atonic PPH: look for retained products preventing contraction, then continue management of atony
Traumatic PPH: suture the cervical and vaginal lacerations under anaesthesia
Uterine inversion: replace the fundus back through the cervix under anaesthesia
Amniotic fluid embolism: transfer to intensive care for ventilatory support
A uterus that contracts only while being massaged is atonic; the next step is to exclude retained tissue that is sustaining the atony. (Book p529)
Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
Immediately after delivery a woman loses 700 mL of blood. The uterus is boggy and reaches above the umbilicus, and the placenta has been expelled complete. What is the first step?
Call for help, rub up a contraction and give oxytocin while resuscitating with fluids and oxygen
Examine the genital tract under anaesthesia before doing anything else
Perform a manual exploration of the uterus straight away
A boggy uterus means atony, which is treated first by compression and uterotonics with simultaneous resuscitation; trauma is explored if bleeding persists. (Book p529)
Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
The three simultaneous steps in management of atonic PPH are:
Bimanual uterine massage + injection tranexamic acid + uterotonic drug
Bimanual massage (one hand on abdomen, one in vagina) + TXA + uterotonic. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid in PPH – timing and dose:
Within 3 hours; 1 g in 100 mL of normal saline given intravenously over 20 minutes
Within 24 hours; 500 mg given by intramuscular injection
Within 1 hour; 2 g given as a rapid intravenous bolus
At any time after the bleed; 1 g given orally as a single dose
Tranexamic acid 1 g in 100 mL saline over 20 minutes must be given within three hours; faster administration causes hypotension. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid dose is repeated if bleeding:
Persists ≥30 min or reappears within 24 h
Repeat if bleeding persists ≥30 min or reappears within 24 h. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Oxytocin in atonic PPH – WHO status, dose and cautions:
First-line drug recommended by WHO; 20-40 IU by infusion; avoid a bolus and avoid dextrose
Second-line drug; 10 IU by intravenous bolus, diluted in dextrose
Third-line drug; 5 IU intramuscularly, diluted in whatever fluid is to hand
Not used in postpartum haemorrhage because of the risk of water intoxication
Oxytocin is the WHO first-line uterotonic, given as 20-40 IU by infusion; boluses cause hypotension and dextrose causes hyponatraemia. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Natural – nonapeptide from paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus, stored in posterior pituitary, pulsatile release; synthetic – octapeptide stored at 2–8 °C
Natural – octapeptide from anterior pituitary; synthetic – nonapeptide at room temp
Natural – from supraoptic nucleus, stored in adrenal; synthetic – decapeptide
Natural: nonapeptide, paraventricular nucleus, posterior pituitary, pulsatile. Synthetic: octapeptide, 2–8 °C. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Mechanism, half-life and kinetics of IM oxytocin:
Raises intracellular calcium and decidual PGF2α; t½ 3-5 min; onset 3 min
Lowers intracellular calcium; t½ 40 min; onset 10 min
Raises cyclic AMP in the myometrium; t½ 1 h; onset 1 min
Blocks progesterone receptors; t½ 20 min; onset 5 min
IM oxytocin raises intracellular calcium and decidual PGF2α; half-life 3-5 minutes, onset 3 minutes, duration 1 hour, and it causes after-pains and milk ejection. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Fill up: Tranexamic acid is given as ______ g intravenously, and benefit is greatest when it is started within ______ hours of birth.
The WOMAN trial showed that 1 g of tranexamic acid given early, within three hours, reduces death from bleeding. (Book p530)
Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
Tetanic contractions, so it cannot be used before delivery; 0.2 mg intramuscularly, repeated in 2-4 hours
Physiological contractions; 0.5 mg intravenously, stored in clear glass vials
Tetanic contractions; 1 mg orally six-hourly, and requiring refrigeration
Uterine relaxation; 0.2 mg subcutaneously as a single dose
Methylergometrine 0.2 mg intramuscularly gives a sustained tetanic contraction; it is avoided before delivery and given slowly, if at all, intravenously. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
Contraindications to methylergometrine include all EXCEPT:
After delivery of first twin / heart disease / peripheral vascular disease
Rh-negative pregnancy / HIV on protease inhibitors (relative)
Asthma is a C/I to carboprost, not ME. ME C/I: after 1st twin, heart disease, PVD, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, Rh-negative, HIV on PIs. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
Syntometrine composition and note on carbetocin:
5 U oxytocin + 0.5 mg methylergometrine; expensive; carbetocin is used in AMTSL but not for PPH management
10 U oxytocin + 0.2 mg ME; cheap; carbetocin is PPH gold standard
Syntometrine = 5 U oxytocin + 0.5 mg ME (expensive, not readily available); carbetocin not for PPH treatment. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
Misoprostol in PPH – form, WHO strategy and dose:
Prostaglandin E1, the only uterotonic available as a tablet; WHO recommends 800 microgram sublingually
Prostaglandin E2, given as an intracervical gel in a dose of 0.5 mg for cervical ripening
Prostaglandin F2 alpha, given as 250 microgram intramuscularly every fifteen minutes
An oxytocin analogue, given as a 100 microgram slow intravenous bolus after delivery
Misoprostol is PGE1 in tablet form; 800 microgram sublingually is the WHO regimen for prevention where oxytocin is unavailable. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
Side effects and contraindication of misoprostol:
Hyperthermia and shivering with nausea and vomiting; contraindicated with a scarred uterus
Hypertension and headache; contraindicated in established maternal heart disease
Bronchospasm, since misoprostol provokes an attack in asthmatic women
Profuse watery diarrhoea; contraindicated in maternal pulmonary hypertension
Misoprostol causes fever, shivering and gastrointestinal upset; unlike carboprost it is safe in asthma but risky with a uterine scar. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
PGF2α; gold standard for PPH; 250 mcg IM every 15-40 min, max 8 doses; diarrhoea
PGE2; first-line alternative; 500 mcg by slow IV injection; pyrexia
PGE1; second-line agent; 1 mg IM repeated four-hourly; hypertension
PGI2; adjunct only; 100 mcg subcutaneously six-hourly; flushing
Carboprost (Hemabate) is PGF2α, the gold standard for PPH management, given as 250 mcg IM every 15-40 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses (2 mg); diarrhoea is the classic side effect. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
Contraindications to carboprost and the status of dinoprostone:
Asthma, pulmonary hypertension and suspected amniotic fluid embolism; dinoprostone is used off-label
Heart disease and Rh-negative status, with dinoprostone as the first-line drug
A scarred uterus only, with dinoprostone as the accepted gold standard
Diabetes mellitus, with dinoprostone given by intravenous infusion
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma and pulmonary hypertension; dinoprostone (PGE2) is used off-label per vaginam or rectum. (Book p531)
Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost

Match the second-line uterotonic with its dose and caveat — 1) Methylergometrine 2) Misoprostol 3) Carboprost … A) 800-1000 microgram rectally or sublingually, useful where injection or refrigeration is impractical B) 250 microgram intramuscularly every 15 minutes, contraindicated in asthma C) 0.2 mg intramuscularly, contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
Ergometrine raises blood pressure, misoprostol is the heat-stable standby, and carboprost is dangerous in asthma. (Book p531)
Sequence of uterotonics in the PPH management protocol:
Massage with tranexamic acid and oxytocin, then methylergometrine, then carboprost, with misoprostol as an add-on
Carboprost first, then oxytocin, then methylergometrine in that order
Misoprostol first, then oxytocin, then carboprost in that order
Methylergometrine first, then misoprostol, then oxytocin in that order
Oxytocin with tranexamic acid and massage is first line; ergometrine and then carboprost follow, with misoprostol as an adjunct. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
If unresponsive to drugs for >30 min, mechanical compression is used (continuing uterotonics) – principle and catheters:
Warm saline in an intrauterine catheter compresses the venous sinuses; the Bakri balloon holds up to 500 mL
Cold saline packing through a Foley catheter is the only mechanical option available
An air-filled balloon inflated to 2000 mL in a Bakri catheter tamponades the uterus
Gauze packing of the uterine cavity is the current standard first-line technique
Intrauterine balloons tamponade by compressing the venous sinuses; the Bakri is filled with warm saline up to about 500 mL. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
If tamponade is responsive, the catheter is removed after ______; if bleeding continues with unstable vitals the next step is ______.
Remove after 12–24 h if responsive; unstable vitals → uterine artery ligation. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
If bleeding continues but vitals are stable, the patient is shifted to OT with temporary measures such as:
External aortic compression at the umbilicus, and a military anti-shock garment
The Trendelenburg position with cold packs applied to the abdomen
Vaginal packing with intravenous fluids and nothing further
Fundal pressure combined with an intravenous oxytocin bolus
Aortic compression and a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment buy time while the woman is transferred to theatre. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
Compression sutures for PPH include (m/c first):
B-Lynch or Brace, then Hayman, Cho square, Pereira, Gunshella
McDonald, then Shirodkar, then the Wurm modification
O'Leary, then the Burch procedure, then Kelly plication
Halsted stitch, then the Lembert stitch, then the Connell stitch
Compression sutures for PPH are B-Lynch or Brace (commonest first), then Hayman, the Cho square sutures, Pereira and Gunshella. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
If bleeding continues after compression sutures – with radiointervention available : without radiointervention.
With radiology: uterine artery embolisation if she is stable — without: stepwise devascularisation through to hysterectomy
With radiology: immediate hysterectomy — without: embolisation performed by the obstetric team
With radiology: internal iliac artery ligation — without: embolisation by interventional radiology
With radiology: uterine packing — without: immediate hysterectomy for every woman
Embolisation suits the stable woman where interventional radiology exists; otherwise stepwise devascularisation ends in hysterectomy. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
Final steps if bleeding still continues – stable : unstable; and if hysterectomy fails to stop bleeding:
Stable: ligation of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery — unstable: subtotal hysterectomy; then pelvic pressure packing
Stable: total hysterectomy — unstable: internal iliac ligation; then a gauze pack
Stable: embolisation — unstable: a B-Lynch suture; then a Bakri balloon
Stable: aortic ligation — unstable: oophorectomy; then a vaginal pack
If she is stable, vessel ligation can preserve the uterus; if she is not, subtotal hysterectomy is faster and safer, with packing as a bridge. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery

Bleeding continues in an atonic postpartum haemorrhage despite oxytocin, ergometrine and carboprost. The uterus is now contracted, the placenta was complete and the genital tract is intact. What is the next step?
Insert a uterine balloon tamponade and prepare for surgical haemostasis if bleeding continues
Proceed directly to hysterectomy without any further measure
Give repeated doses of oxytocin and wait two hours
Repeat a manual removal of the placenta to be certain nothing remains
The escalation is balloon tamponade, then uterine compression sutures, vessel ligation and finally hysterectomy. (Book p532)
Management protocol: drugs, balloon, then surgery
Uterine artery ligation (O'Leary technique) is performed at:
Where the artery turns upwards in the broad ligament, taking a bite of myometrium and staying close to the uterus
At its origin from the internal iliac artery, before the vessel crosses the lateral pelvic wall
At the level of the cervicovaginal junction, below the point where the vessels enter the cervix
At the cornual end of the uterus, where it anastomoses with the ovarian artery near the fundus
The O'Leary stitch is placed where the uterine artery turns up beside the uterus, including myometrium so the suture cannot slip and avoiding the ureter. (Book p533)
Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
Success rate of bilateral uterine artery ligation:
About 85 per cent of cases, which is why it is attempted before hysterectomy
About 50 per cent of cases, so it is rarely worth attempting at all
About 99 per cent of cases, which makes hysterectomy almost unnecessary
About 30 per cent of cases, and only when performed before any drug
Bilateral uterine artery ligation controls bleeding in roughly 85 per cent of cases and preserves fertility, so it precedes hysterectomy. (Book p533)
Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
Shock index (SI) = heart rate ÷ systolic BP. Normal range and significance of SI ≥0.9:
Normal is 0.5-0.7; a value of 0.9 or more indicates transfusion need and higher mortality
Normal is 0.9-1.2; a value of 1.5 or more is the threshold for transfusion
Normal is 0.3-0.5; a value of 0.7 or more means she needs intensive care
Normal is 1.0-1.5; a value of 2.0 or more means hysterectomy is required
The shock index is normally 0.5-0.7; 0.9 or above signals significant loss, the need for transfusion and raised mortality. (Book p533)
Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
Packing of the uterus for PPH is:
Uterine packing is outdated; balloon tamponade is used instead. (Book p533)
Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
Fill up: The shock index is calculated as ______ divided by ______, and a value above 0.9 suggests significant occult blood loss.
Heart rate and systolic pressure are the earliest vital signs to change in haemorrhage, so their ratio flags occult loss before hypotension appears. (Book p533)
Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
Features of the human placenta and the plane of separation:
Deciduate, discoid, hemochorial; separates through zona spongiosa; most important factor = uterine contraction
Deciduate, discoid, hemochorial; uterine contraction is most important; plane = zona spongiosa. (Book p534)
Retained placenta (prolonged third stage) is defined as placenta not delivered:
More than 30 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 15 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 60 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 10 minutes after the delivery of the baby
A third stage longer than 30 minutes is a prolonged third stage, and active intervention is considered once that time has passed. (Book p534)
Placenta separated but not expelled (signs of separation present) = trapped placenta. Management:
Empty the bladder, give oxytocin and repeat controlled cord traction; if it fails, manual removal under short anaesthesia
Empty the bladder, give oxytocin and repeat controlled cord traction; if it fails, proceed straight to hysterectomy
Leave it with antibiotics for 24 hours and reassess the next morning before intervening
Give misoprostol into the vagina and wait for spontaneous expulsion over the next six hours
A trapped placenta needs a full bladder emptied, a uterotonic and controlled cord traction, escalating to manual removal if it is still retained. (Book p534)
Placenta attached to uterus but not invading myometrium – management:
Oxytocin with controlled cord traction, then manual removal under anaesthesia if the placenta is still retained
Oxytocin with controlled cord traction, then immediate hysterectomy if the placenta is still retained
Methotrexate to dissolve the adherent placenta, followed by surgical evacuation a week later
Conservative management with antibiotics and observation for 24 hours before any intervention
When the placenta is simply adherent and not bleeding, oxytocin and controlled cord traction come first, with manual removal as the next step. (Book p534)
Placenta invading the myometrium (morbidly adherent) is called ______ and managed by ______.
Morbidly adherent = placenta accreta spectrum → hysterectomy. (Book p534)
All of the following are recognised causes of retained placenta EXCEPT:
A cervical tear sustained during instrumental delivery
Morbid adherence of the placenta to the myometrium
Uterine atony with failure of placental separation
A constriction ring trapping an already separated placenta
Retained placenta follows adherence, atony or entrapment; a cervical tear causes traumatic bleeding, not retention. (Book p534)
Match PAS types by depth of chorionic villi – Accreta : Increta : Percreta.
Accreta attached to myometrium; increta into myometrium; percreta to or through serosa
Accreta invades the myometrium; increta reaches the serosa; percreta is superficial
Accreta reaches the serosa; increta is superficial; percreta invades myometrium
Accreta into endometrium; increta to serosa; percreta into the bladder
By depth of chorionic villi: accreta is superficially attached to the myometrium (commonest), increta invades into the myometrium, and percreta is attached to or through the serosa. (Book p535)
Risk factors and etiology of PAS:
Placenta previa, a previous caesarean, curettage or myomectomy; the cause is defective decidua with absent Nitabuch's layer
Multiparity alone, through an excessively thick and vascular decidua basalis
A twin pregnancy alone, through an unusually thick Nitabuch layer
Maternal anaemia alone, through a hyperplastic and overactive endometrium
Accreta spectrum follows endometrial damage: previa, scar, curettage or myomectomy, with loss of the Nitabuch layer and decidua basalis. (Book p535)
Investigation of choice for PAS and its findings:
Ultrasound with Doppler: placental lakes, loss of the retroplacental clear zone and an interrupted bladder line
Magnetic resonance imaging: a snowstorm appearance filling the whole uterine cavity
Computed tomography: ring enhancement of the myometrium around the placental bed
Hysteroscopy: direct visualisation of chorionic villi inside the uterine cavity
Ultrasound with Doppler is the investigation of choice; the snowstorm appearance belongs to a molar pregnancy, not to accreta. (Book p535)
Which of the following statements about placenta accreta is TRUE?
Deficient decidua basalis prevents normal separation, so attempting manual removal causes torrential haemorrhage
Placenta accreta is commonest in a first pregnancy with no uterine surgery
Manual removal of the placenta is always safe and should be the first treatment
A normal third stage in a previous pregnancy rules out accreta in this one
Accreta follows endometrial damage from surgery or curettage, and the correct management leaves the placenta in situ rather than forcing separation. (Book p535)
Uterine inversion is ______; on inspection the os is ______ in inversion and ______ in uterine prolapse.
Prolapse of the fundus into the uterine cavity; not visible; visible
Descent of cervix through introitus; visible; not visible
Rupture of the fundus; visible; visible
Retroversion of uterus; not visible; not visible
Inversion = fundus prolapses into cavity; os not visible in inversion but visible in prolapse. (Book p535)
Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
Classification by time after delivery – Acute : Sub-acute : Chronic.
Acute <24 h; sub-acute 24 h–4 wks; chronic ≥4 wks. (Book p536)
Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
Fundus into the cavity not beyond the os : fundus at the os : fundus outside the introitus : complete inversion
Dimple in the fundus : fundus at the os : fundus in the vagina : fundus outside
Fundus at the os : fundus in the vagina : fundus at the introitus : vagina everted
Fundus in the vagina : at the introitus : outside : with the bladder drawn in

By extent, inversion is graded: 1st the fundus dips into the cavity but not beyond the os; 2nd it reaches the os without protruding; 3rd it protrudes out of the introitus; 4th there is complete inversion of uterus and vagina. (Book p536)
Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
The m/c cause of uterine inversion and the nature of shock:
Iatrogenic from a mismanaged third stage; neurogenic shock first, then haemorrhagic shock
Spontaneous inversion with haemorrhagic shock alone and no neurogenic component at all
Associated with placenta previa, producing septic shock with rigors and hypotension
Caused by uterine fibroids, with cardiogenic shock from acute left ventricular failure
The commonest cause is mismanaged third stage; the initial neurogenic shock from stretching the pedicles is followed by haemorrhagic shock. (Book p536)
Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features

Match the degree of uterine inversion with its extent — 1) First degree 2) Second degree 3) Third degree … A) The fundus turns inwards but does not pass through the cervix B) The inverted fundus passes through the cervix and lies in the vagina C) The whole inverted uterus lies outside the vulva
Degrees are defined by how far the fundus has travelled: inside the cavity, through the cervix, or outside the vulva. (Book p536)
Examination findings in uterine inversion – P/A : P/V; and the clinical clue:
A cup-like depression below the umbilicus, with a globular mass in the vagina and immediate shock
A hard contracted fundus, with the cervix easily visible and only slow bleeding
The fundus high above the umbilicus, with an empty vagina and fever
A Bandl's ring across the abdomen, with bulging membranes and late shock
The fundus is absent abdominally or dimpled, a globular mass fills the vagina, and shock is immediate and out of proportion. (Book p537)
Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
First steps in managing acute uterine inversion:
Call for help and resuscitate, stop uterotonics, then manual replacement
Give an oxytocin bolus, remove the placenta, then replace the uterus
Proceed to immediate hysterectomy through an abdominal incision
Pack the vagina firmly and wait for the uterus to contract
The first steps in acute uterine inversion are to call for help and resuscitate, stop uterotonics such as oxytocin, then replace the uterus manually (Johnson's method). (Book p537)
Reposition last what prolapsed first; do not separate the placenta
Remove the placenta first, then replace the fundus into the pelvis
Push the cervix upwards first, then replace the uterine fundus
Apply steady traction to the cord until the uterus is fully delivered
Johnson's method: the part that prolapsed first is repositioned last, and the placenta is not separated, since separation increases haemorrhage. (Book p537)
If Johnson's method fails, the sequence is:
Repeat replacement under anaesthesia with a uterine relaxant, then Huntington's or Haultain's abdominal route
Immediate hysterectomy, since further attempts at replacement are futile
Hydrostatic reduction by O'Sullivan's method followed by Spinelli's vaginal repair
Vaginal packing with an oxytocin infusion to contract the uterus down
If Johnson's vaginal replacement fails, the next attempt needs anaesthesia and a relaxant, with abdominal routes as the fallback. (Book p537)
Huntington's: abdominal traction on the round ligaments — Haultain's: incising the constriction ring — outdated: O'Sullivan and Spinelli
Huntington's: vaginal repair — Haultain's: hydrostatic reduction — outdated: abdominal traction
Huntington's: incising the constriction ring — Haultain's: traction — outdated: embolisation
Huntington's: hydrostatic reduction — Haultain's: the Spinelli repair — outdated: abdominal traction
Huntington's pulls the fundus up with traction on the round ligaments; Haultain's incises the constriction ring from behind; the hydrostatic and Spinelli methods are historical. (Book p537)

Immediately after delivery of the placenta the uterus inverts through the cervix and the woman collapses with a pulse of 130/min and a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg. What is the correct sequence of management?
Resuscitate, replace the uterus at once by hydrostatic or manual reduction, then give a uterotonic once it is back
Give oxytocin first so that the uterus contracts, and only then attempt replacement
Remove the placenta if it is still attached before attempting any replacement
Proceed straight to hysterectomy without attempting replacement
Replacement must not wait for the placenta or for uterotonics; shock is neurogenic as well as haemorrhagic and needs simultaneous resuscitation. (Book p537)
Stop uterine relaxant → remove placenta → start oxytocin → start antibiotics
Start oxytocin → remove placenta → stop relaxant → antibiotics
1 stop relaxant, 2 remove placenta, 3 start oxytocin, 4 antibiotics. (Book p538)
Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) – alias and incidence:
Anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy, about 1 in 100,000 deliveries
Sheehan syndrome, occurring in about 1 in 1,000 deliveries
HELLP syndrome, occurring in about 1 in 10,000 deliveries
Mendelson syndrome, occurring in about 1 in 500 deliveries
Amniotic fluid embolism is also called anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy; it is rare at about 1 in 100,000 but catastrophic. (Book p538)
Pathophysiology of AFE begins with ______ and the amniotic fluid (fetal skin cells, debris, antigens) produces three effects:
A breach of the maternal-fetal interface lets fluid into the circulation, causing pulmonary vasospasm and then coagulopathy
A hypotonic uterus fails to compress the placental bed, causing haemorrhage, sepsis and renal failure
Placental abruption releases thromboplastin into the circulation, producing coagulopathy alone
Cord prolapse compresses the umbilical vessels, producing fetal hypoxia with no maternal effects
Erratic contractions breach the interface and open venous sinuses; the fluid then causes pulmonary vasospasm, cardiac failure and consumptive coagulopathy. (Book p538)
Clinical phases of amniotic fluid embolism — Phase I : Phase II.
Phase I: sudden hypoxia, hypotension and shock with little bleeding — Phase II: haemorrhage from disseminated intravascular coagulation
Phase I: heavy bleeding with an atonic uterus — Phase II: hypoxia from pulmonary vasospasm and right heart strain
Phase I: high fever with uterine tenderness — Phase II: septic shock with acute kidney injury
Phase I: severe hypertension and convulsions — Phase II: hepatic failure with profound hypoglycaemia
Phase I is respiratory and cardiovascular collapse with little bleeding, and phase II is the haemorrhagic phase from consumptive coagulopathy. (Book p538)
Clinical criteria for AFE diagnosis include all EXCEPT:
Unexplained shock with minimal bleeding / onset within 30 min of labour
Criteria: unexplained shock, onset within 30 min, breathlessness/shock, overt DIC, NO fever; also pulmonary vessel catheterisation. Management is ICU care; ↑ mortality. (Book p539)
Postpartum collapse – time of appearance: PPH : uterine inversion : AFE.
Within 24 h : within 24 h : within 30 min of delivery
Within 30 min : within 24 h : within 1 wk
Within 1 h : within 30 min : within 24 h
PPH and inversion within 24 h; AFE within 30 min. (Book p539)
Postpartum collapse examination – P/A and P/V findings: PPH : uterine inversion : AFE.
PPH: poor tone and heavy loss — inversion: a cup-like depression and a vaginal mass — AFE: both examination findings normal
PPH: entirely normal findings — inversion: poor uterine tone — AFE: a cup-like depression
PPH: a globular vaginal mass — inversion: heavy bleeding — AFE: poor uterine tone
All three conditions give entirely normal findings on both examinations
Postpartum collapse is triaged by examination: bleeding with an atonic uterus, an inverted uterus felt in the vagina, or a normal examination with sudden collapse from embolism. (Book p539)
Fill up: Amniotic fluid embolism typically begins with sudden ______ and ______, and is followed rapidly by bleeding from disseminated intravascular coagulation.
dyspnoea with cyanosis; hypotension and shock
The classic presentation is abrupt respiratory collapse and cardiovascular collapse during labour or soon after delivery, then coagulopathy. (Book p539)
Fill up: Vulval hematoma is a laceration of an underlying vessel; m/c cause and arteries involved ______.
Instrumental delivery; vulval from the internal pudendal artery, vaginal from the vaginal artery
Spontaneous labour; the bleeding comes from the uterine artery
Precipitate labour; the bleeding comes from the ovarian artery
Episiotomy; the bleeding comes from the inferior rectal artery
Vulval hematoma follows instrumental delivery (the commonest cause); vulval hematomas come from the internal pudendal artery and vaginal ones from the vaginal artery. (Book p540)
Which of the following statements about Vulval hematoma & broad ligament hematoma is TRUE?
Excruciating perineal pain with inability to pass urine, and a tense bluish tender swelling of the vulva
A painless soft swelling of the vulva with fever and offensive lochia after the delivery
Painless vaginal bleeding with an open cervical os in the first week after delivery
Pruritus with a watery discharge and superficial dyspareunia in the early puerperium
A vulval haematoma is intensely painful, causes retention of urine and appears as a tense bluish swelling that may extend into the thigh. (Book p540)
All of the following are Vulval hematoma & broad ligament hematoma EXCEPT:
Antibiotics and warm compress — Conservative: ice packs, analgesics, monitoring of vitals
Uterotonics and TXA — Conservative: ice packs, analgesics, monitoring of vitals
Vaginal packing — Conservative: ice packs, analgesics, monitoring of vitals
Conservative: ice packs, analgesics, monitoring of vitals. (Book p540)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with vulval hematoma & broad ligament hematoma presents with surgical drainage is for a large, expanding or very painful collection, or one that has caused shock. Indications for surgical management (incision & drainage with mattress-suture cavity closure):?
Larger than 5 cm, still enlarging, excruciating pain, or associated shock
Any haematoma at all that measures more than 1 cm across
Only once the haematoma has become clinically infected
Only when haematomas are present on both sides of the vulva
Surgical drainage is for a large, expanding or very painful collection, or one that has caused shock; small stable ones are managed conservatively. (Book p540)
Fill up: A supralevator collection is occult: ______ out of proportion to visible loss, from an upward extension of a cervical or vaginal tear.
Shock with little visible bleeding; from a cervical or vaginal tear extending upwards
Heavy vaginal bleeding from uterine atony after the delivery
Fever and pelvic pain from puerperal endometritis
A visible vulval swelling from a torn pudendal artery
A supralevator collection is occult: shock out of proportion to visible loss, from an upward extension of a cervical or vaginal tear. (Book p540)

Match the puerperal haematoma with its presentation — 1) Vulval haematoma 2) Infralevator vaginal or perineal haematoma 3) Supralevator or broad ligament haematoma … A) A tense, exquisitely tender swelling of the vulva that may extend into the thigh B) A swelling contained below the levator ani, seen as a bluish vaginal or perineal mass C) Occult blood above the levator ani that pushes the uterus up and to one side, sometimes with shock
Infralevator haematomas are visible; supralevator collections are occult and present late with shock out of proportion to visible loss. (Book p540)
Which of the following statements about Perineal tear: classification & repair is TRUE?
Vaginal mucosa : 1 + muscles : 2 + anal sphincter : 3 + rectal mucosa
1° vaginal mucosa; 2° + perineal muscles; 3° + anal sphincter; 4° + rectal mucosa. (Book p541)
All of the following are Perineal tear: classification & repair EXCEPT:
Under half the external sphincter : over half the external sphincter : both sphincters
Over half the external sphincter : under half the external sphincter : internal sphincter
Internal sphincter alone : external sphincter alone : rectal mucosa additionally
External sphincter partial : rectal mucosa involved : internal sphincter alone
Third-degree tears are subclassified as 3A (under 50% of external anal sphincter), 3B (over 50% of EAS) and 3C (internal and external anal sphincter). (Book p541)

A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks with perineal tear: classification & repair presents with first and second degree tears are repaired in the labour room under local anaesthesia like an episio. Repair setting – 1st & 2nd degree : 3rd & 4th degree; suture material:?
1st and 2nd degree in the labour room under local anaesthesia; 3rd and 4th in theatre
1st and 2nd degree in the labour room under local anaesthesia; all degrees in theatre
1st and 2nd degree at the bedside without anaesthesia; 3rd and 4th in theatre
All degrees are repaired in theatre under general or spinal anaesthesia

First and second degree tears are repaired in the labour room under local anaesthesia like an episiotomy; third and fourth degree tears are repaired in the OT under general or spinal anaesthesia, using Vicryl for both. (Book p541)
Fill up: Sequence of repair for 1st/2nd degree tear ______.
Vaginal mucosa continuous sutures → muscles interrupted sutures → vaginal skin mattress sutures
Muscles interrupted → mucosa mattress → skin continuous
Mucosa mattress → skin interrupted → muscles continuous
Mucosa continuous, muscles interrupted, skin mattress. (Book p541)
Which of the following statements about Perineal tear: classification & repair regarding Rectal mucosa, then internal sphincter, then is TRUE?
Rectal mucosa, then internal sphincter, then external sphincter end to end
External sphincter, then the rectal mucosa, then the internal sphincter
Vaginal mucosa, then the external sphincter, then the rectal mucosa
Perineal skin, then the internal sphincter, then the external sphincter
Repair of a 3rd or 4th degree tear proceeds from the rectal mucosa to the internal anal sphincter, then the external anal sphincter end to end, then the rest as for an episiotomy. (Book p541)
Timing of perineal tear repair – <24 h of delivery : >24 h of delivery.
Immediate repair : repair after minimum 3 weeks
<24 h immediate; >24 h wait minimum 3 weeks. (Book p541)
WHO recommendations to PREVENT perineal tear include all EXCEPT:
Controlled delivery of fetal head and guarding of perineum
Fundal massage and routine episiotomy are NOT recommended. (Book p541)
Fill up: A second-degree perineal tear involves the ______, whereas a third-degree tear involves the ______.
vaginal mucosa alone; the perineal body
Third- and fourth-degree tears extend into, or through, the anal sphincter and mucosa and must be repaired by an experienced operator in theatre. (Book p541)
Episiotomy is a surgically planned incision of the perineum to facilitate delivery of the fetal head; indications include:
Shoulder dystocia, instrumental delivery, the after-coming head of a breech and a rigid perineum
Every primigravida, to shorten the second stage and protect the pelvic floor
Every preterm delivery, to reduce intracranial haemorrhage in the preterm baby
Every twin pregnancy routinely, whatever the presentation or progress of labour
Episiotomy is a selective, not routine, procedure; the listed indications all need a rapid or atraumatic delivery. (Book p541)
At centre extending from introitus : at an angle of 60°
Median from introitus at centre; mediolateral at 60°. (Book p542)
After crowning; when the perineum climbs in breech; before traction with forceps
Before crowning; when the perineum climbs in breech; before traction with forceps
After crowning; at full dilatation regardless of descent; before forceps application
After crowning; when the perineum climbs in breech; after delivery of the head
Episiotomy is correctly timed after crowning, when the perineum climbs in breech delivery, and before or after forceps application but always before traction. (Book p542)
Median vs mediolateral episiotomy – muscle fibres cut, bleeding, repair, healing:
Median: less fibres, less bleeding, easy repair, quick healing; mediolateral: more, more, difficult, longer
Median: more, more, difficult, longer; mediolateral: less, less, easy, quick
Median: less fibres but more bleeding
Median cuts fewer fibres, bleeds less, repairs easily and heals quickly; mediolateral the opposite. (Book p542)
Median vs mediolateral – chance of gaping, dyspareunia and anal sphincter involvement:
Median: ↓ gaping, ↓ dyspareunia but anal sphincter involved; mediolateral: ↑ gaping, ↑ dyspareunia, sphincter not involved
Median: ↑ gaping, sphincter spared; mediolateral: ↓ gaping, sphincter involved
Median: less gaping/dyspareunia, but risk of anal sphincter extension; mediolateral: more gaping/dyspareunia, sphincter spared. (Book p542)
Vaginal mucosa, skin and subcutaneous tissue, the superficial perineal muscles and pudendal branches
The anal sphincter and the rectal mucosa, as in a fourth-degree tear
The levator ani muscle alone, with no skin or mucosal tissue
Bartholin's gland and the urethra, which lie within the incision line
An episiotomy cuts vaginal mucosa, skin and subcutaneous tissue, the perineal muscles and branches of the pudendal vessels and nerve. (Book p542)
Muscles CUT vs NOT cut in episiotomy:
Cut: pubococcygeus, transverse perinei, bulbospongiosus; not cut: anal sphincter
Cut: ischiocavernosus, external anal sphincter; not cut: bulbospongiosus
Cut: obturator internus and ischiocavernosus; not cut: pubococcygeus
Cut: external anal sphincter and ischiocavernosus; not cut: transverse perinei
An episiotomy cuts pubococcygeus and the deep and superficial transverse perinei and bulbospongiosus, but not the ischiocavernosus, ischiococcygeus, obturator or anal sphincter. (Book p542)
Rounded ends and an angulated blade
Sharp pointed ends and straight blade
Episiotomy scissors: rounded ends, angulated. (Book p542)
All of the following statements about a mediolateral episiotomy are true EXCEPT:
It is cut straight backwards in the midline to minimise bleeding
It is angled about 45 to 60 degrees away from the midline
It lowers the risk of extension into the anal sphincter compared with a midline cut
It bleeds more and is more painful afterwards than a midline episiotomy
A midline cut is the one made straight backwards; the mediolateral cut is angled away from the sphincter, which is why it is safer. (Book p542)
Malposition is defined by longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation, vertex presenting part and position:
Any position other than 1 to 5, that is ROP 6, DOP 7 or LOP 8
Any position other than the direct occipito-anterior position
Any of the positions numbered 1 to 5 in the textbook
The lateral positions LOT and ROT only, when persistent
Malposition is a longitudinal lie with cephalic presentation and vertex presenting part in any position other than 1-5, that is ROP 6, DOP 7 or LOP 8. (Book p543)
Most common OP positions in order and the causes:
ROP then DOP then LOP; android pelvis, then a deflexed head
LOP then DOP then ROP; anthropoid pelvis, then macrosomia
DOP then ROP then LOP; platypelloid pelvis, then a deflexed head
LOP then ROP then DOP; gynaecoid pelvis, then a deflexed head

The commonest OP positions in order are ROP, DOP and LOP; the causes are the android pelvis (commonest, the head occupying the posterior part because of the extra space) and then a deflexed head. (Book p543)
Incidence of OP position at term/onset of labour vs late labour, and parity associations:
About 10% at the onset of labour falling to about 2% as most rotate; malposition is commoner in nulliparous women
About 2% at the onset rising to about 10%, and commoner in multiparous women throughout
About 25% at the onset falling to about 5%, and commoner in nulliparous women throughout
About 10% throughout labour, with no association with parity at all
Most occipito-posterior heads rotate spontaneously, so the incidence falls from about 10% to about 2%; the malposition is commoner in nulliparas. (Book p543)
OP: flat lower abdomen, limbs near the midline, heart in the flank — OA: convex abdomen with the limbs behind
OP: convex abdomen with the limbs behind — OA: flat lower abdomen, limbs near the midline, heart in the flank
OP: heart loudest in the midline — OA: heart in the flank with a flat lower abdomen below the umbilicus
OP: limbs in the flank with the heart in the midline — OA: bulging flanks with limbs felt on both sides
In occipito-posterior the deflexed head leaves the lower abdomen flat, brings the limbs forwards and pushes the fetal heart out to the flank. (Book p544)
Engaging diameters – OP (deflexed head) : OA (well flexed head).
Occipitofrontal 11.5 cm / suboccipitofrontal 10 cm with delayed engagement : suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm
OP engages by occipitofrontal 11.5 cm/suboccipitofrontal 10 cm (delayed); OA by suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm. (Book p544)
Which of the following statements about occipito-posterior position is TRUE?
The anterior fontanelle is easily felt, the head is deflexed and labours are longer with severe backache
The sagittal suture lies in the transverse diameter and always rotates posteriorly
Vaginal delivery is impossible, so caesarean section is always required
The position is linked to the anthropoid pelvis but never to the android pelvis
Deflexion presents a larger diameter, so labour is longer and backache is prominent; most rotate anteriorly or deliver face-to-pubis. (Book p544)
Three possible outcomes in OP position and the m/c one:
Complete forward rotation, which is commonest; incomplete forward rotation; and persistent posterior rotation
Persistent posterior rotation, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and deep sacral arrest
Incomplete forward rotation, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and face-to-pubis delivery
Deep sacral arrest, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and persistent posterior rotation
Most occipito-posterior heads rotate forwards completely to occipito-anterior; the rest rotate incompletely or persist as occipito-posterior. (Book p544)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
Incomplete forward rotation – rotation achieved and causes:
One-eighth rotation (ROP to ROT); android pelvis, big baby, reduced liquor
Two-eighths rotation; an anthropoid pelvis with a large baby
Three-eighths rotation; a platypelloid pelvis with reduced liquor
No rotation at all; polyhydramnios with a large preterm baby
Incomplete forward rotation achieves only one-eighth rotation (ROP to ROT); the causes are the android pelvis (commonest), a big baby and reduced liquor. (Book p545)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
Deep transverse arrest is defined as:
The head stuck in the occipito-transverse position at the spines despite adequate contractions, usually with an android pelvis
The head arrested at the pelvic brim in the occipito-posterior position
The head arrested at the outlet in the occipito-anterior position
A face presentation arrested in the persistent mento-posterior position
Deep transverse arrest is failure of internal rotation from the transverse position at the level of the ischial spines. (Book p545)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
Management of deep transverse arrest — android pelvis : roomy pelvis.
Android pelvis: caesarean section — roomy pelvis: manual or Kielland rotation followed by instrumental delivery
Android pelvis: manual rotation then forceps — roomy pelvis: caesarean section without a trial of rotation
Both android and roomy pelvis: caesarean section in every case, since rotation is never successful
Both android and roomy pelvis: vacuum extraction as the first-line treatment in the second stage
Rotation then instrumental delivery is reasonable only when the pelvis is roomy; with an android pelvis caesarean is safer. (Book p545)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
Posterior rotation (ROP → DOP) is most commonly seen with:
Anthropoid pelvis, where the AP diameter exceeds the transverse
Android pelvis, where the transverse diameter exceeds the AP
Platypelloid pelvis, where the AP diameter is markedly reduced
Gynaecoid pelvis, where all diameters are round and roomy
Posterior rotation (ROP to DOP) is most commonly seen with the anthropoid pelvis, in which the AP diameter greatly exceeds the transverse. (Book p545)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
In the second stage the head is at station +2 in the occipito-transverse position after an hour of pushing, with good contractions, a normal pelvis and a normal CTG. What is the management?
Manual rotation to occipito-anterior, then instrumental delivery, or rotational forceps by an experienced operator; caesarean if these fail
Continue pushing for another two hours without intervention
Immediate caesarean section without attempting rotation
Symphysiotomy, because rotation is never appropriate in the second stage
Persistent occipito-transverse arrest can be resolved by manual or instrumental rotation when the pelvis is adequate and the operator is trained. (Book p545)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
Outcome of posterior rotation — anthropoid pelvis : other pelvis types.
Anthropoid: face-to-pubes delivery — other pelvis: deep sacral arrest with the head stuck
Anthropoid: deep sacral arrest — other pelvis: face-to-pubes delivery
Both pelves end in a face-to-pubes delivery after posterior rotation
Both pelves require caesarean section once rotation has gone posterior
The long antero-posterior diameter of the anthropoid pelvis permits face-to-pubes delivery; in other pelves the head arrests deeply. (Book p546)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
The m/c complication of face-to-pubes delivery and its implication:
Complete perineal tear, which is why episiotomy is indicated
Shoulder dystocia, managed by the McRoberts manoeuvre
Cord prolapse, needing an immediate caesarean section
The commonest complication of face-to-pubes delivery is a complete perineal tear, which is why it is an indication for episiotomy. (Book p546)
Outcomes of OP position & deep transverse arrest
Transverse lie – presentation : denominator : m/c position.
Shoulder presentation, denominator acromion, dorso-anterior m/c. (Book p546)
M/c outcome and causes of transverse lie:
Spontaneous rotation to cephalic or breech after 34 weeks; prematurity overall
Persistent transverse lie needing caesarean; uterine fibroid overall
Cord prolapse once membranes rupture; multiple pregnancy overall
Obstructed labour if untreated; cephalopelvic disproportion overall
In transverse lie the commonest outcome is spontaneous rotation to cephalic or breech after 34 weeks; the commonest cause overall is prematurity, and at term it is placenta previa. (Book p546)
Examination and complication of transverse lie:
Height less than period of gestation, fundus and pelvis empty; cord prolapse risk highest
Height more than period of gestation, head in the fundus; shoulder dystocia likely
Height equal to period of gestation, head in the pelvis; postpartum haemorrhage
Buttocks felt in the fundus, head ballotable above; face presentation likely

In transverse lie the uterine height is less than the period of gestation and both the fundal and deep pelvic grips are empty; it carries the highest risk of cord prolapse because the cervix is not closed by the head. (Book p546)
Fill up: A transverse lie at term with a live fetus is delivered by ______, and the gravest complication of a neglected case is ______.
caesarean section; rupture of the uterus
Neglected shoulder presentation stretches the lower segment until it ruptures; delivery is by caesarean section once the lie persists at term. (Book p547)
Indications for caesarean section in transverse lie (no mechanism of labour):
Two failed attempts at version, version contraindicated, or transverse lie in active labour
Only when the fetus is known to be alive at the time of diagnosis
Only in a primigravida with an unscarred uterus
Only once the membranes have ruptured spontaneously in labour
A transverse lie at term is delivered by caesarean when version fails or is contraindicated, or once labour is established. (Book p548)
Hand prolapse/neglected shoulder presentation – pathophysiology and management:
A vaginal delivery is attempted, the hand is pulled to rotate, obstructed labour with Bandl's ring follows, and caesarean is needed
The lie corrects spontaneously and internal podalic version delivers the fetus vaginally
Cord prolapse occurs first and forceps are applied to the after-coming head
The fetus converts to a breech, and breech extraction with decapitation is then performed
Neglected shoulder presentation is iatrogenic: traction on the prolapsed hand obstructs labour, and delivery must be by caesarean. (Book p548)
Indications for ECV and preliminary USG confirmations:
Breech and transverse lie, with ultrasound confirming lie, liquor, singleton pregnancy and no gross anomaly
Face and brow presentation, with ultrasound assessing the placenta alone
Twin pregnancy, with ultrasound determining chorionicity and amnionicity
Occipito-posterior position, with ultrasound measuring the biparietal diameter
Version is offered for breech and transverse lie after ultrasound confirms the lie, adequate liquor, a singleton and no major anomaly. (Book p546)
Outpatient, no anaesthesia, terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously, anti-D if Rh-negative, continuous monitoring

Stop at once, turn the baby back to its original position, and proceed to caesarean section
Continue the version quickly so that the procedure can be completed
Give oxytocin and deliver the baby vaginally as soon as possible

A gestation of 36 weeks, an anterior placenta and a maternal age above thirty-five years

ECV attempt outcomes – successful 1st attempt : fails 1st attempt → retry another day; successful 2nd : fails 2nd.

Success: induce immediately; failed first: await labour; failed second: caesarean at 37 weeks
Success: caesarean; failed first: await labour; failed second: induce with oxytocin
Success: await labour; failed first: await labour; failed second: a third attempt

A non-reassuring fetal heart rate pattern before the procedure

Face presentation – lie, presentation, presenting part, attitude, denominator:

Oligohydramnios with fetal growth restriction in a primigravida
Placenta previa with a gynaecoid pelvis and a well-flexed head

LMA is m/c; engaging diameter submento-bregmatic 9.5 cm (positions: mento-posterior, mento-anterior, mento-transverse). (Book p549)

Mento-anterior: caesarean section in every case — mento-posterior: vaginal delivery after manual rotation

Flexion in brow presentation; caesarean for a left mento-anterior face presentation

Match the malpresentation with its outcome — 1) Mento-anterior face presentation 2) Mento-posterior face presentation 3) Brow presentation … A) Presents the largest diameter of the fetal head, so spontaneous vaginal delivery is not possible B) Can deliver vaginally once the chin rotates to the front and the head flexes under the symphysis C) Cannot deliver vaginally, because the head cannot flex further in the cavity

Brow presentation occurs in ______ and the bony landmarks felt on P/V are ______.

Complete extension; the mentum and the nose of the fetus
Complete flexion; the posterior fontanelle and sagittal suture
Deflexion; both fontanelles felt with the orbital ridges

Engaging diameter and denominator in brow presentation:
Mento-vertical 14 cm; denominator frontal bone. (Book p549)
No mechanism of labour, so caesarean; early labour may convert to face or vertex
No mechanism of labour, so caesarean; early labour always converts to vertex
Manual conversion to a vertex presentation, then vaginal delivery in every case
A vacuum is applied to the brow for an immediate vaginal delivery in all cases

Fill up: The presenting diameter in brow presentation is the ______, which measures about ______ cm.
The partially extended head presents the mento-vertical diameter of 13.5 cm, the largest that the fetal head can offer, so it cannot negotiate a normal pelvis. (Book p549)
Breech is the m/c malpresentation with longitudinal lie and breech/podalic presentation. Match incidence – 28 wks : 34 wks : term.
About 25% at 28 weeks, 5% at 34 weeks and 3-4% at term, as most turn spontaneously
About 3-4% at 28 weeks, 5% at 34 weeks and 25% at term, as more turn with time
About 50% at 28 weeks, 25% at 34 weeks and 10% at term in most series
About 10% at 28 weeks, 3% at 34 weeks and 1% at term after routine version

Fill up: The commonest cause of breech overall is ______, and of recurrent breech is ______.

Match the posture – Flexed/complete breech : Frank breech : Knee presentation : Footling breech.
Hips and knees flexed : hips flexed, knees extended : hips extended, knees flexed : hips and knees extended
Hips flexed, knees extended : hips and knees flexed : hips and knees extended : hips extended, knees flexed
Hips and knees extended : hips and knees flexed : hips flexed, knees extended : hips extended, knees flexed
Hips extended, knees flexed : hips flexed, knees extended : hips and knees flexed : hips and knees extended
Complete: hips + knees flexed; frank: hips flexed/knees extended; knee: hips extended/knees flexed; footling: both extended. (Book p550)

Match the breech type with what is felt on vaginal examination — 1) Complete breech 2) Frank breech 3) Knee presentation 4) Footling breech … A) Anus and ischial tuberosities B) Heel, anus and ischial tuberosities C) Feet D) Knees

Fill up: Complete breech is the ______ common breech overall, but the commonest breech in a ______.
Complete breech is the least common breech overall and the commonest in a multigravida; frank breech is the commonest overall and in a primigravida. (Book p550)
Which statement about cord-prolapse risk in breech is TRUE?
Risk rises as the presenting part fits the cervix less well, so frank is lowest and footling highest
The risk of cord prolapse is identical for all four types of breech
Frank breech carries the highest risk and footling breech the lowest
Complete breech carries the highest risk and frank breech the lowest
Cord prolapse risk rises as the presenting part fits the cervix less well: frank breech is snug and lowest, complete is low, knee is higher and footling is highest. (Book p550)

Match the type of breech with its posture — 1) Frank breech 2) Complete breech 3) Footling breech … A) Hips and knees both flexed, so the feet lie beside the buttocks B) Hips flexed with both knees extended, so the feet lie up beside the head C) One or both legs extended below the buttocks, carrying the highest risk of cord prolapse

Fill up: Overall cord-prolapse risk ranks ______ above footling breech above knee presentation, and the commonest breech position is ______.
Cord prolapse risk ranks transverse lie above footling breech above knee presentation, and the commonest breech position is dorso-anterior. (Book p551)
A woman at 38 weeks is found to have a breech presentation and external cephalic version is being considered. What must ultrasound rule out before the version is attempted?

Placenta previa, oligohydramnios and a single loop of cord
Cord presentation, vasa previa and a velamentous insertion
Fetal hydrocephalus, duodenal atresia and bilateral renal agenesis

Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery

Shoulder dystocia with brachial plexus injury from traction on the extended arms
Uterine inversion from traction on the cord during delivery of the placenta
Cord avulsion with fetal exsanguination before the trunk has been delivered

Epidural analgesia, which abolishes the urge to push and prevents descent
Continuous cardiotocography, which alarms and forces unnecessary intervention

Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites
Emergency C-section facility, senior supervision, baby under 4 kg, IV fluids, CTG
Emergency C-section facility, senior supervision, baby up to 4.5 kg, oral fluids
Emergency C-section facility, registrar alone, baby under 4 kg, intermittent CTG
Emergency C-section facility, senior supervision, baby under 4 kg, no CTG needed

Full cervical dilatation with an empty bladder and rectum
A flexed head confirmed by ultrasound before the attempt
Continuous fetal heart monitoring and an experienced operator in theatre

The sacrum engages transversely and rotates through three-eighths of a circle

In breech, which part lies directly behind the pubic symphysis, and what is unique about the denominator?
