The sacrum itself, with the denominator behind the symphysis as it is in vertex
The posterior buttock, with the sacrum pointing anteriorly
The feet, which is why a breech has no denominator at all

Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
When spontaneous delivery of the buttocks does not occur — match the manoeuvre to the breech type: complete breech : frank breech.
Complete breech: groin traction — frank breech: Pinard's manoeuvre in the popliteal fossa
Complete breech: Pinard's manoeuvre — frank breech: groin traction
Complete breech: Lovset's manoeuvre — frank breech: Pinard's manoeuvre
Complete breech: Bracht's manoeuvre — frank breech: groin traction
A complete breech is delivered by traction in the groin; with extended legs the knees must be unlocked first by Pinard's manoeuvre. (Book p553)
Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
The Savage technique in breech delivery:
Wrapping the baby's lower body in a warm moist towel so the cord is not handled and vasospasm is avoided
Suprapubic pressure applied to the fetal head to keep it flexed during delivery of the after-coming head
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant to push the shoulders down through the pelvic brim
Rotating the fetal trunk through 180 degrees to bring the shoulders into the oblique diameter
The Savage technique keeps the baby warm and prevents handling of the cord, since touching it provokes vasospasm and fetal distress. (Book p553)
Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
Fill up: With the sacrum anterior, the breech engages in the oblique diameter of the inlet with the ______ diameter leading.
The bitrochanteric diameter (about 10 cm) is the engaging diameter of the breech, just as the bisacromial diameter serves the shoulders. (Book p553)
Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
Shoulder delivery in breech – the bisacromial diameter (12 cm) engages along the ______; the anterior shoulder touches levator ani and rotates ______.
Right oblique diameter; anteriorly by 1/8th of a circle
Bisacromial 12 cm along right oblique; anterior shoulder rotates anteriorly 1/8th; anterior shoulder then posterior shoulder/arm deliver. (Book p554)
Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
If the shoulders are not along the AP diameter, the first step is:
Hold the baby's back and rotate the shoulders into the antero-posterior diameter, then await spontaneous delivery
Perform Lovset's manoeuvre immediately without first rotating the shoulders
Apply fundal pressure to push the shoulders down through the pelvic brim
Apply Piper's forceps to deliver the head before the shoulders are released

Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
Fingers over the baby's back rotate the trunk so the posterior shoulder comes forward and delivers
Traction on the groin to bring the breech down onto the pelvic floor
Pressure in the popliteal fossa to flex the knee and deliver the leg
Suprapubic pressure while the baby hangs by its own weight to deliver the head
Lovset's manoeuvre rotates the trunk through 180 degrees so that first the posterior and then the anterior shoulder is released. (Book p554)
Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
Reach the cubital fossa with two fingers and deliver the arm
Apply Piper's forceps to the arm

Which of the following statements about delivering the shoulders in a breech birth is TRUE?

Lovset's manoeuvre is used to flex and deliver the after-coming head
The bisacromial diameter normally engages in the antero-posterior diameter of the outlet
The arms should be pulled down as soon as the axilla becomes visible, without rotating the trunk

Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
The after-coming head of breech is the ______ part delivered and is delivered by ______.
Head is the last part, delivered by flexion (opposite to vertex which delivers by extension). (Book p554)
The baby hangs by its own weight, then suprapubic pressure with the feet swung towards the mother's abdomen delivers the head
Two fingers are placed in the baby's mouth and traction is applied to the shoulders to flex the head
Piper's forceps are applied to the after-coming head while the body rests along the operator's arm
The baby's back is held upwards and the trunk is rotated to bring the head into the transverse diameter
Burns-Marshall relies on controlled hanging with suprapubic pressure and swinging the body upwards to deliver the head by flexion. (Book p554)
Bracht technique differs from Burns-Marshall in that:
Baby is not allowed to hang
Bracht = Burns-Marshall without suprapubic pressure. (Book p555)
Traction on the shoulders with malar flexion, the baby astride the operator's forearm
Traction in the groin with flexion of the neck from above
Fundal pressure from an assistant combined with jaw traction
Rotation of the trunk with suprapubic pressure applied to the head

Long forceps with pelvic, cephalic and perineal curves, used for the after-coming head
Short outlet forceps used for a head already on the pelvic floor
Rotational forceps with a sliding lock for a transverse head
Solid-blade forceps designed for a preterm after-coming head
Piper's forceps are long, with a perineal curve, and are applied to the after-coming head while an assistant holds the body up. (Book p555)
Prague manoeuvre is used for delivery of the head in ______ position, where the head is delivered by ______; the m/c position is ______ (head by flexion).

Match the manoeuvre with how the after-coming head is delivered — 1) Burns-Marshall technique 2) Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre 3) Piper's forceps … A) Two fingers on the maxilla flex the head while an assistant holds the body up and applies suprapubic pressure B) The baby is allowed to hang by its own weight so that the head flexes and delivers spontaneously C) Forceps are applied to the after-coming head while an assistant holds the baby's body out of the way

Entrapped after-coming head – preterm breech : term breech.
Preterm: Duhrssen incisions in the cervix at 2 and 10 o'clock — term: push the body back and deliver by caesarean
Preterm: push the body back and deliver by caesarean — term: Duhrssen incisions in the cervix at 2 and 10 o'clock
Preterm: immediate craniotomy to allow vaginal delivery — term: Zavanelli manoeuvre then caesarean section
Both preterm and term: Piper's forceps are the first and only option for the trapped head
Before viability the cervix is incised to release the head; at term the body is pushed back and the baby is delivered by caesarean. (Book p555)
Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
Complications of breech delivery and the m/c cause of death:
Intracranial haemorrhage is the commonest cause of death, with asphyxia and intra-abdominal injury
Shoulder dystocia is the commonest cause of death, with brachial plexus injury
Erb's palsy is the commonest cause of death, from traction on the extended arms
Fracture of the femur is the commonest cause of death in vaginal breech delivery
Rapid decompression and trapping of the after-coming head cause intracranial haemorrhage, the leading cause of death in breech. (Book p555)
Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
Twin pregnancy with the 1st twin cephalic and the 2nd in transverse lie
Singleton frank breech presenting at term in a primigravida
A footling breech in a primigravida at term, before labour
A preterm breech presenting before 34 completed weeks of gestation
Breech extraction is indicated in twin pregnancy with the first twin cephalic and the second twin in transverse lie. (Book p556)
Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
Deliver the first twin vaginally, then internal podalic version followed by breech extraction under anaesthesia in theatre
External cephalic version of the second twin, then an oxytocin infusion to deliver vaginally
Immediate caesarean section for the second twin as soon as the first twin has been born
Wait for spontaneous delivery of the second twin without any intervention for up to two hours
Breech extraction is performed in theatre under anaesthesia, because all the manoeuvres are done by the operator with no maternal effort. (Book p556)
Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
All of the following are recognised fetal complications of vaginal breech delivery EXCEPT:
Erb's palsy from traction on the extended arms
Intracranial haemorrhage from rapid decompression of the after-coming head
Fracture of the humerus, femur or clavicle during manipulation
Neonatal hypoglycaemia is a metabolic complication of diabetic pregnancy, not a mechanical complication of breech delivery. (Book p556)
Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
Prolonged second stage, fetal distress, and shortening the second stage for maternal disease
A prolonged first stage, and cephalopelvic disproportion in established labour
Breech presentation, and a transverse lie with the arm prolapsed
Placenta previa, and cord prolapse with the cervix only 4 cm dilated
Instrumental delivery is for the second stage: delay, fetal distress, or a maternal indication to avoid pushing. (Book p557)
Fully dilated os; Occiput/favourable position; Rotated head and Ruptured membranes; Consent and Contractions; Episiotomy, Engaged, Empty bladder; Pelvis adequate; CPD absent
Forceps blades ready; Obstetrician experienced; Room prepared; Consent obtained; Epidural sited; Pelvis assessed; Scissors available
Full term gestation; Occiput anterior; Rupture the membranes; Catheterise the bladder; Episiotomy cut; Push with pains; Stitch the perineum
Fetal heart checked; Oxygen running; Rotate the head fully; Cut an episiotomy; Extract the head; Pull steadily; Suture the tear afterwards

FORCEPS expands as: Fully dilated os; Occiput/favourable position; Rotated head + Ruptured membranes; Consent + Contracting uterus; Episiotomy + Engaged head + Empty bladder; Pelvis adequate; CPD absent. (Book p557)
Sagittal suture anteroposterior, rotation up to 45°, station at least +2
Sagittal suture anteroposterior, rotation up to 45°, station above +2
Any occipito-transverse position, rotation up to 45°, station at +2
Sagittal suture transverse, rotation up to 45°, station at least +2
A favourable position for instrumental delivery is the sagittal suture in the anteroposterior diameter with rotation of at most 45° (DOA, DOP, ROA, LOA) and station +2 or more. (Book p557)
Forceps vs vacuum – prerequisites differ how?

Forceps may be applied to an unengaged head, but the vacuum may never be

Best-suited case for vacuum and the choice in maternal heart disease:

A face presentation with the chin anterior; vacuum is preferred in heart disease
A breech presentation, where vacuum is preferred in maternal heart disease
A brow presentation, where forceps are preferred in maternal heart disease
Vacuum suits a rotated vertex at full dilatation; when maternal effort must be minimised, as in heart disease, forceps are preferred. (Book p557)
Fill up: Prerequisites for instrumental delivery include full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, an empty bladder and a head at or below the level of the ______.

A preterm fetus, intrauterine death with a macerated head, the after-coming head and face presentation
Maternal heart disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and a previous caesarean scar
An occipito-anterior position with the head already on the pelvic floor at full dilatation
A multiparous woman with a previously normal vaginal delivery at term

Absolute contraindications to any instrumental delivery:

Maternal cardiac disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and one previous caesarean section
Occipito-posterior position, a loose nuchal cord and lightly stained meconium liquor

Metal cups that are more traumatic, built up to 1.5 kg/cm2 over ten minutes

Disposable cups with the maximum pressure limited to 0.1 kg/cm2

All of the following are contraindications to vacuum extraction EXCEPT:
A cephalic presentation at full dilatation with the head engaged in the occipito-anterior position
Gestational age below 34 weeks, because of the risk of scalp and intracranial injury
A known fetal bleeding disorder or bone demineralisation
A face or brow presentation with an ill-defined flexion point
An engaged cephalic presentation at full dilatation is the indication for vacuum extraction; prematurity, coagulopathy and malpresentation are not. (Book p558)
A newer, smaller, portable disposable vacuum device used for occipito-anterior and posterior positions
A metal cup designed for delivery of the face presentation
A rotational forceps with a sliding lock for the transverse head
A fetal scalp electrode used to monitor the heart rate in labour
The Omnicup is a modern handheld vacuum device suitable for both occipito-anterior and occipito-posterior positions. (Book p559)
Handle, finger guard, lock, shank, heel and a fenestrated blade with pelvic and cephalic curves
Cup, chain, handle and hand pump for generating negative pressure
Blade, ratchet, teeth and serrations for gripping the fetal head firmly
Handle, spring and hook for applying traction to the fetal scalp
Each blade has a handle with finger guard, a lock, a shank, a heel and a fenestrated blade with pelvic and cephalic curves. (Book p559)
Advantages of fenestrations (windows) in the blade:
Lighter blades that grip well while compressing the fetal head less
Stronger traction through a wider surface of metal on the head
Rotation of the head by allowing the blades to slide independently
A better grip on the fetal scalp to prevent the blades slipping
Fenestration lightens the blade and reduces the compressive force transmitted to the fetal head without losing grip. (Book p559)
Types of lock — English lock (most common) : sliding lock.
English: two sockets, with the left blade introduced first — sliding: one socket that lets the blades slide
English: a single socket — sliding: two sockets with the right blade introduced first
English: a screw mechanism — sliding: a pivot joint between the two shanks
English: no lock at all — sliding: a ratchet that locks at fixed intervals
The English lock has a socket on each handle and closes only when the left blade goes in first; the sliding lock corrects asynclitism. (Book p559)
Named for the mother's left and right; held correctly the left socket faces up and the right socket faces down
Named for the operator's hands, with both sockets facing upwards when applied
Identified by blade length, since the left blade is noticeably longer
Identified by colour coding on the handle of each blade
Forceps blades are named for the side of the mother's pelvis; held correctly, the left blade's socket faces upwards. (Book p560)
Correctly applied forceps are identified by:
The lock closes easily and both blades lie equidistant from the sagittal suture along the occipito-mental diameter
The blades overlap slightly in the midline over the region of the anterior fontanelle
One blade lies over the face and the other over the occiput to grip the head firmly
The handles sit at 90 degrees to each other because the head is lying transversely
Correct application means the lock closes without force, the blades sit symmetrically along the occipito-mental diameter and the sagittal suture is midway. (Book p560)
Outlet forceps; short and light; total length 27.5 cm, shank 2.5 cm
Long rotational forceps; total length 35 cm, sliding lock
Forceps for the aftercoming head; total length 27.5 cm
Solid-bladed forceps; short and light, shank 2.5 cm
Wrigley forceps are outlet forceps, short and light, with a total length of 27.5 cm and a shank of 2.5 cm. (Book p560)
Long, the only forceps that can rotate the head, with a sliding lock; outdated
Short outlet forceps with a fixed English lock and no rotation; still used
Longest forceps designed for the aftercoming head in breech; still used
Solid-bladed forceps with a fixed English lock and no rotation; outdated
Kielland forceps are long, are the only forceps that can rotate the fetal head (rotation forceps), have a sliding lock, and are now largely outdated. (Book p560)
Piper's: the longest forceps, for the after-coming head — Tucker-McLane: the only forceps with a solid blade
Piper's: a solid blade for the head — Tucker-McLane: for the after-coming head
Piper's: a short outlet forceps — Tucker-McLane: the rotational forceps
Piper's: a sliding lock — Tucker-McLane: the shortest forceps available
Piper's are long forceps with a perineal curve for the after-coming head; Tucker-McLane are the only forceps with solid blades. (Book p560)

Match the forceps with its distinguishing feature — 1) Kielland's forceps 2) Piper's forceps 3) Simpson's forceps … A) A sliding lock with almost no pelvic curve, designed for rotation of the head B) Long forceps with a perineal curve for the after-coming head in a breech delivery C) Standard outlet forceps with both a pelvic and a cephalic curve for the flexed head
Kielland's slides to correct asynclitism and rotates, Piper's reaches the after-coming head, and Simpson's follows the curves of the pelvis and head. (Book p560)
Low forceps (m/c type) vs outlet (Wrigley) forceps criteria:
Low forceps: station +2 or more without reaching the perineum — outlet forceps: scalp visible at the introitus with the skull on the pelvic floor
Low forceps: at the level of the ischial spines — outlet forceps: station +1 with the head still above the pelvic floor
Low forceps: crowning with the head distending the perineum — outlet forceps: station +2 or lower inside the cavity
Low forceps: any station with the head not yet engaged — outlet forceps: the head still above the level of the ischial spines
Low forceps are the commonest type and are applied at station +2 or more; outlet forceps are only used when the scalp is visible. (Book p561)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Mid-cavity forceps (0/+1 station) and high forceps (−ve station) are:
Mid-cavity and high forceps are obsolete. (Book p561)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Direction of pull – ideal position and basis; low forceps pulls : outlet forceps pulls.
Low forceps: downward and backward, then downward, then downward and forward
Outlet forceps in lithotomy: downward, then downward and forward
Low forceps in the supine position: upward, then forward throughout
Outlet forceps in left lateral position: forward only throughout the pull

Pull is directed in lithotomy with the operator's hand on the maternal abdomen; low forceps pull downward and backward, then downward, then downward and forward, while outlet forceps pull downward then downward and forward. (Book p561)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Consent, adequate analgesia by epidural or pudendal block, and episiotomy
General anaesthesia, which is mandatory for all forceps deliveries
An oxytocin bolus given immediately before the blades are applied
A urinary catheter left in situ throughout the whole procedure
Prior to forceps delivery one must obtain consent, give adequate analgesia (epidural or pudendal block) and perform an episiotomy. (Book p561)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Fill up: Low forceps are applied when the leading point of the fetal skull is at station ______ or lower, while outlet forceps are applied when the scalp is visible at the introitus.
Low forceps means station +2 or more; outlet forceps are applied only when the scalp is visible without separating the labia. (Book p561)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Traction force for forceps – primigravida : multigravida.
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
M/c complication – forceps : vacuum; ease of use:
Maternal injury : fetal injury; forceps require more training, vacuum easier (m/c used)
Fetal injury : maternal injury; vacuum harder
Forceps → maternal injury; vacuum → fetal injury; vacuum easier and m/c used. (Book p562)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Forceps: facial nerve palsy and corneal injury — vacuum: cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage
Forceps: sixth nerve palsy and subgaleal bleed — vacuum: facial nerve palsy and corneal injury
Forceps: cephalhaematoma only — vacuum: corneal abrasion only
Forceps: subgaleal haemorrhage — vacuum: brachial plexus injury from the shoulders
Forceps injure the face and skull base; the vacuum produces scalp injuries, notably cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage. (Book p562)
Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
Failed forceps/vacuum is defined as ______ and managed by ______.
3 unsuccessful trials to deliver the head; C-section
3 unsuccessful attempts = failed instrumental delivery → C-section. (Book p562)

Fill up: Pfannenstiel incision is placed ______ and its feature is ______.
a finger-breadth above the symphysis pubis; cosmetic, rectus muscle not cut
a finger-breadth above the symphysis pubis; poor cosmetic result, rectus muscle cut
3 cm below the ASIS line; cosmetic, rectus muscle not cut
3 cm below the ASIS line; poor cosmetic result, rectus muscle cut
The Pfannenstiel incision sits a finger breadth above the pubic symphysis (low transverse); it is cosmetically good and the rectus muscle is not cut. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section
Which of the following statements about Joel-Cohen incision compared with Pfannenstiel is TRUE?
Joel-Cohen is straight rather than curved and sited about 3 cm below the line joining the ASIS
Joel-Cohen is curved rather than straight and sited lower close to the symphysis pubis
Joel-Cohen is a vertical midline incision carried down from the umbilicus to the symphysis
Joel-Cohen is a transverse incision placed at the level of the umbilicus with muscle cutting
Joel-Cohen is a straight, higher transverse incision with blunt dissection; Pfannenstiel is curved and lower with more dissection. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section
Which of the following statements about transverse skin incision for caesarean is TRUE?
Transverse incision gives less pain, stronger wound and better cosmesis but limits upper abdomen view
Transverse incision gives faster entry but causes more postoperative pain and weaker wound
Transverse incision gives better pelvic exposure though the scar is cosmetically less acceptable
Transverse incision causes less bleeding but results in a mechanically weaker wound postoperatively
Transverse incisions heal better and hurt less, but they limit access to the upper abdomen compared with a vertical incision. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section
Match the uterine incision with its description — 1) Sanger's 2) Kerr's 3) Kronig's … A) Classical upper segment vertical B) Lower segment transverse C) Low vertical
Sanger's is the classical vertical incision, Kerr's the standard lower segment transverse, and Kronig's a low vertical incision. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section
Fill up: Risk of scar rupture is ______ for classical caesarean and ______ for one previous LSCS.
Classical 4–9%; one LSCS 0.2–0.9%; multiple LSCS 0.9–1.8%; low vertical 1–7%. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section

Match VBAC eligibility with scar type — 1) Classical 2) One previous LSCS 3) Low vertical (Kronig) … A) Contraindicated B) May be allowed with counselling C) May be allowed, indicated for constriction ring
VBAC contraindicated after classical; ± after LSCS or low vertical (Krönig indicated for constriction ring). (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section

A 30-year-old woman with a previous classical caesarean at 28 weeks is counselled for the next pregnancy. She is now 36 weeks with no labour pains. What is the most appropriate plan regarding timing and mode?
Repeat caesarean at 36-37 weeks, since contractions become prominent after 37 weeks and raise rupture risk
Trial of labour aiming for vaginal birth at 40 completed weeks with continuous CTG monitoring
Repeat classical section at 39 completed weeks after confirming fetal lung maturity by amniocentesis
Induction of labour at 38 weeks using prostaglandins followed by oxytocin augmentation
A classical scar ruptures silently and catastrophically, so delivery is planned at 36-37 weeks before strong contractions begin. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section
Which of the following statements about VBAC guidelines after lower segment caesarean is TRUE?
ACOG says a trial may be offered whatever the number of scars; India says contraindicated with two or more
ACOG permits trial after one scar only; Indian guidelines permit trial after any number of scars
ACOG never offers a trial after any scar; India offers trial after two previous sections routinely
ACOG permits trial after three scars; India permits trial after one scar only with mandatory pelvimetry
ACOG allows a trial after any number of low transverse scars after counselling; Indian guidance treats two or more as a contraindication. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section

Match the caesarean incision with its description — 1) Pfannenstiel incision 2) Joel-Cohen incision 3) Classical uterine incision … A) A straight transverse skin incision higher on the abdomen with blunt dissection, less pain and less blood loss B) A curved transverse skin incision with a curved fascial cut and more dissection C) A vertical incision in the upper uterine segment, used for an anterior placenta or a very preterm lower segment
Joel-Cohen and Pfannenstiel are abdominal wall choices; the classical uterine incision is reserved because it rules out a future trial of labour. (Book p563)
Skin & uterine incisions for caesarean section

A 27-year-old woman with one previous LSCS at 34 weeks for fetal distress is now 38 weeks, cephalic, with adequate pelvis and no contraindication. She asks about options and success rates. What do you counsel?
Trial of labour succeeds in about 70% or elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks; avoid prostaglandins
Trial of labour succeeds in about 30% or elective repeat caesarean at 34 weeks with steroids
Elective repeat caesarean at 36 weeks only, since trial of labour is never offered after a scar
Induction with prostaglandins at 38 weeks followed by trial of labour in every woman with a scar
A trial of scar succeeds in roughly seven out of ten women; prostaglandins are avoided because they raise the rupture risk. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section
All of the following are increased risks associated with trial of labour after caesarean EXCEPT:
Bleeding, need for transfusion, uterine rupture, hysterectomy and fetal distress or death
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after caesarean
Severe perineal trauma and anal sphincter injury from vaginal delivery after previous scar
Post-term pregnancy and meconium aspiration syndrome unrelated to mode of delivery
A trial of labour trades anaesthetic and respiratory risk for rupture, haemorrhage and intrapartum fetal compromise. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section
All of the following are recognised risks of elective repeat caesarean EXCEPT:
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn, operative and anaesthetic risks and impact on future pregnancies
Uterine rupture in labour and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy from obstructed labour
Severe perineal trauma, pelvic floor dysfunction and anal sphincter injury after vaginal birth
Shoulder dystocia and Erb's palsy from vaginal delivery of a macrosomic fetus
Elective caesarean raises neonatal respiratory morbidity and complicates later pregnancies; it protects against perineal trauma and shoulder dystocia. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section
Which of the following statements about risk of scar rupture after caesarean is TRUE?
Rupture risk depends on type of previous incision, number of previous caesareans and inter-delivery interval
Rupture risk depends on maternal age alone, which determines tensile strength of the uterine scar
Rupture risk depends on fetal sex and birth weight, since a large baby stretches the scar in labour
Rupture risk depends on placental site alone, because a fundal placenta weakens the lower segment
Rupture risk tracks the scar itself — a classical scar, multiple scars and a short inter-delivery interval all raise it. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section
Fill up: Ideal inter-delivery interval after caesarean is ______ months; short interval is ______ months; minimum conception gap is ______ months.
Ideal ≥18 months; short = 12 months; minimum CS-to-conception gap 6 months. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section
Fill up: Anaesthesia level for painless labour is ______ and for caesarean section is ______.
Labour epidural T10; caesarean T4. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section

A 26-year-old woman is posted for elective caesarean at 39 weeks for breech presentation. Anaesthetist asks about ideal positioning to prevent supine hypotension. What is the ideal position and timing for non-medical elective CS?
Supine with 15° left lateral tilt; elective caesarean at 39 weeks for non-medical reasons
Supine with 15° left lateral tilt; elective caesarean at 37 weeks to avoid labour onset
Lithotomy position with pelvic wedge; elective caesarean at 39 weeks after lung maturity
Right lateral tilt with wedge under hip; elective caesarean at 40 weeks beyond expected date
The ideal position for caesarean is supine with 15° left lateral tilt or a wedge under the right hip, and elective caesarean for non-medical reasons is timed at 39 weeks. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section

A woman with one previous lower-segment caesarean section for fetal distress is at 39 weeks with a singleton cephalic fetus of estimated weight 3.4 kg and no other risk factors. How should she be counselled?
Offer a trial of labour after caesarean, since about seven in ten women succeed and the risk of uterine rupture is low
Insist on an elective repeat caesarean, because a trial of labour is never safe after a scar
Recommend induction with prostaglandins, which improves the chance of vaginal birth
Advise a home birth, since a previous lower segment scar needs no monitoring
With one previous low transverse scar the success rate is around 70-75 per cent and rupture risk under one per cent, but prostaglandins are avoided. (Book p564)
Previous caesarean: trial of labour vs repeat section
All of the following are absolute contraindications to VBAC EXCEPT:
Past history of CPD alone without current contracted pelvis or other scar complications
Previous classical caesarean, prior uterine rupture, myomectomy entering cavity or T-shaped incision
Contracted pelvis or cephalopelvic disproportion in the present pregnancy on clinical pelvimetry
Home delivery setting with no facility for emergency caesarean section or blood transfusion
Past h/o CPD is NOT a C/I; the others are. A T-shaped incision extends from LUS into upper segment. (Book p565)
Relative contraindications where repeat CS is preferred:
Macrosomia, post-term pregnancy, and malpresentation such as breech
Twin pregnancy, polyhydramnios, and a previous caesarean section
A previous vaginal delivery and a low transverse uterine scar
Maternal age above 30 and a short interdelivery interval
Relative contraindications where repeat caesarean is preferred are macrosomia, post-term pregnancy and malpresentation such as breech. (Book p565)
Fill up: The most important favourable marker for VBAC is ______ and a bad marker is ______.
previous vaginal delivery; previous puerperal sepsis in the scar
young maternal age; macrosomic fetus in present pregnancy
male fetus; twin pregnancy in present gestation
short maternal stature; post-term pregnancy beyond 40 weeks
Previous vaginal delivery, especially after a caesarean, predicts success; infection in the uterine scar predicts failure and rupture. (Book p565)
Maternal pulse rate, CTG monitoring, scar tenderness
Serial USG for scar thickness every hour
All of the following contraindicate a trial of labour after caesarean EXCEPT:
A single previous low transverse incision in the lower segment
A previous classical or T-shaped uterine incision
Previous uterine rupture or full-thickness myomectomy
Placenta previa or placenta accreta spectrum in the current pregnancy
One previous low transverse scar is the prerequisite for offering a trial of labour; upper segment scars and placental obstruction are contraindications. (Book p565)

A 29-year-old woman with one previous LSCS at 38 weeks presents at 39 weeks with Bishop score 4. She desires VBAC and needs induction. What is the recommended method for induction in previous caesarean?
Mechanical cervical ripening with Foley followed by oxytocin; prostaglandins are avoided
Misoprostol 25 mcg vaginally for ripening; oxytocin is avoided due to rupture risk
Dinoprostone gel for cervical ripening; mechanical methods are avoided in scarred uterus
Induction is never attempted after caesarean, so elective repeat caesarean is always performed
Induction of labour in a previous C-section is done by a mechanical method for cervical ripening followed by oxytocin; prostaglandins are avoided. (Book p566)

Match the procedure with its status in previous caesarean — 1) External cephalic version 2) Internal podalic version 3) Contracted pelvis … A) Relative contraindication B) Absolute contraindication C) Recurrent indication for caesarean
External version relative C/I; internal podalic version absolute C/I; contracted pelvis is a recurrent CS indication. (Book p566)
Transient tachypnea of newborn and postpartum endometritis
All of the following are indications for classical caesarean section (difficult lower segment access) EXCEPT:
Carcinoma cervix, dense bladder adhesions and placenta previa with large vessels over lower segment
Breech presentation, uncomplicated twin pregnancy and macrosomic fetus at term without obstruction
One previous lower segment scar alone with no other complicating factor in present pregnancy
Fetal distress at term and failed induction of labour where lower segment is accessible
Classical section is chosen when the lower segment cannot be reached or entered safely, not for the usual obstetric indications. (Book p565)
Classical caesarean indications & anaesthesia for caesarean
Perimortem caesarean section should be performed within:
Classical caesarean indications & anaesthesia for caesarean
M/c anaesthesia for caesarean and the preferred option in heart disease/PIH:
Spinal is m/c; heart disease and PIH → neuraxial/epidural. (Book p566)
Classical caesarean indications & anaesthesia for caesarean
Indications for general anaesthesia in caesarean/obstetric procedures:
Fetal distress, convulsions, and manoeuvres that need a hand inside the uterus, such as manual removal of the placenta
Elective caesarean at 39 weeks, an uncomplicated placenta previa and one previous lower segment scar
Maternal heart disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and an uncomplicated twin pregnancy
Prolonged labour, maternal request for sterilisation and a previous spinal anaesthetic
General anaesthesia is needed when speed matters or when the procedure needs uterine relaxation and a hand inside the uterus. (Book p566)
Classical caesarean indications & anaesthesia for caesarean
Fill up: In a perimortem caesarean section the baby should be delivered within ______ minutes of maternal cardiac arrest, through a ______ abdominal incision.
Delivery within four minutes improves both neonatal survival and maternal venous return, so a fast midline vertical incision is used. (Book p566)
Fill up: Puerperium = up to ______; fourth trimester = up to 12 weeks.
Puerperium = up to 6 weeks; fourth trimester = up to 12 weeks. (Book p567)
Which of the following statements about Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution is TRUE?
ACOG: an initial visit at 3 weeks and a final visit at 12 weeks — GOI: day 1, day 3, day 7 and 6 weeks
ACOG: day 1 and 6 weeks only — GOI: visits at 3 weeks and 12 weeks
ACOG: visits at 2, 4 and 6 weeks — GOI: day 1, day 7 and day 42
ACOG: a single visit on day 7 — GOI: a single visit at 6 weeks
ACOG restructures postnatal care as an ongoing process with a contact by 3 weeks and a comprehensive visit by 12 weeks; India schedules four early visits. (Book p567)
All of the following are Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution EXCEPT:
Just below the umbilicus; 20 weeks; cricket ball; 1000 g
At the xiphisternum; 36 weeks; football; 2000 g
At the symphysis; 12 weeks; tennis ball; 500 g
Midway to symphysis; 16 weeks; orange; 300 g
Just below umbilicus (≈20 wks), cricket-ball consistency, 1000 g; after 24 h fundal height falls 1.25 cm/day. (Book p567)

A 28-year-old woman at 2 weeks with definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution presents with the uterus halves to about 500 g in a week, is impalpable by two weeks at about 300 g, and completes. Uterine weight – after 1 week : 2 weeks : 4 weeks; and position at 1 and 2 weeks?
About 500 g at one week, 300 g at two weeks and 100 g by four weeks
About 300 g at one week, 100 g at two weeks and 50 g by four weeks
About 750 g at one week, 500 g at two weeks and 300 g by four weeks
About 1000 g at one week, 500 g at two weeks and 100 g by four weeks
The uterus halves to about 500 g in a week, is impalpable by two weeks at about 300 g, and completes involution at 100 g by four weeks. (Book p567)
Fill up: Involution = ______ size (not number), faster in nulliparous; USG normal by 8 weeks.
Involution = ↓ muscle size (not number), faster in nulliparous; USG normal by 8 weeks. (Book p567)
Fill up: The puerperium lasts about ______ weeks, and the uterus becomes a pelvic organ again at about ______ days after delivery.
The fundus descends roughly 1 cm a day and is no longer felt abdominally by about 10-14 days, with involution complete by six weeks. (Book p567)
Which of the following statements about Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function is TRUE?
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — The isthmus; 2–3 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — The fundus; 5 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — The vagina; 1 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — Obliterated; 4 cm
LUS → isthmus; cervix 10 cm → 2–3 cm for few days → closes. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
All of the following are Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function EXCEPT:
Pin-point : transverse slit-like — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Transverse slit : pin-point — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Round : stellate — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Slit : round — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function

A 28-year-old woman at 7 weeks with cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function presents with uterine artery doppler in the puerperium shows increased vascular resistance throughout the first 7 . Uterine artery Doppler in the puerperium shows:?
Raised vascular resistance throughout the first 7 weeks post-partum
Reduced vascular resistance for 6 months after delivery
Absent diastolic flow for the first 24 hours after delivery
No change at all from the antepartum Doppler findings
Uterine artery Doppler in the puerperium shows increased vascular resistance throughout the first 7 weeks post-partum. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
Fill up: Lochia (superficial decidual sloughing) components and sequence ______.
Decidua, blood, leucocytes and exudate; rubra, then serosa, then alba over 24-36 days
Blood alone; ten days of rubra followed by twenty days of alba
Mucus and pus; alba first, then serosa, then rubra
Amniotic fluid, lasting seven days in total after the delivery
Lochia is decidua, blood, leucocytes and serous exudate, passing through rubra, serosa and alba over roughly 24-36 days. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
Which of the following statements about Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function regarding 6 weeks; endometriosis; palm-size to 3–4 is TRUE?
6 weeks; endometriosis; palm-size to 3–4 cm after 2 weeks
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — 12 weeks; polyp; fist to 5 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — 1 week; fibroid; palm to 8 cm
Placental site: 6 weeks; m/c site for endometriosis; palm-size → 3–4 cm by 2 weeks. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
In partially/non-breastfeeding women – menstruation returns by ______; ovulation by ______ (earliest ______).
Menses 6–8 wks; ovulation ~7 wks (5–11), earliest 28 days. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function

Match the lochia with its timing and appearance — 1) Lochia rubra 2) Lochia serosa 3) Lochia alba … A) Red, containing blood, shreds of decidua and membranes, for the first three or four days B) Pinkish or brownish serous discharge from about day four to day ten C) Pale or yellowish white discharge continuing for several weeks after that
Rubra then serosa then alba is the normal sequence; offensive or persistently red lochia suggests endometritis or retained products. (Book p568)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
Contraception in the puerperium – non-breastfeeding : breastfeeding.
Non-breastfeeding: combined pills avoided for 21 days — breastfeeding: progestogen-only before an intrauterine device
Combined pills are preferred in both groups from the first postpartum day
An intrauterine device only for non-breastfeeding women, and nothing at all for breastfeeding women
Injectable progestogen only for non-breastfeeding women, and combined pills for breastfeeding women
Combined pills are avoided for 21 days because of thrombosis risk and they reduce milk supply; progestogen-only methods suit breastfeeding. (Book p569)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
Lactational amenorrhoea – mechanism and failure rate:
↑ prolactin inhibits GnRH → ↓ LH and FSH; pregnancy risk 4% per year
Prolactin → GnRH inhibition → ↓ LH/FSH; 4% failure per year. (Book p569)
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
Blood parameters after delivery include all EXCEPT:
Marked leucocytosis (≤25,000/µL) with ↑ granulocytes, relative lymphopenia, absolute eosinopenia
Marked thrombocytosis and high fibrinogen in 1st week
Leucocytosis up to 25,000, granulocytosis, relative lymphopenia, eosinopenia, thrombocytosis, high fibrinogen, ↓ Hb/Hct. (Book p569)
Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
Weight loss of 5-6 kg at birth, then 2-3 kg from diuresis, with a very high cardiac output for 24-48 hours
Polyuria with a weight gain of 2 kg and hypokalaemia from rapid sodium retention
An immediate weight loss of 10 kg with a persistently low cardiac output for two days
Oliguria with hypernatraemia and a falling fibrinogen from postpartum coagulopathy
Blood loss and diuresis account for early weight loss, and the cardiac output stays very high for one to two days, which matters in heart disease. (Book p569)
Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
Time for parameters to return to normal – blood volume : CO & HR : GFR : dilated ureter/renal pelvis.
Blood volume 1 wk; CO/HR 10 d; GFR 2 wks; ureter/pelvis 2–8 wks. (Book p569)
Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
Seen in multiparous women; oxytocin-driven contractions worse with suckling, settling by day 3
Seen in primiparous women; prostaglandin-driven, persisting for two weeks
Caused by retained placental fragments and needing uterine curettage
Caused by infected lochia and treated with a course of antibiotics
After-pains are intermittent oxytocin-driven contractions, commoner in multiparas, aggravated by breastfeeding and settling by the third day. (Book p569)
Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
Which of the following statements about normal puerperal changes is TRUE?
The leucocytosis of labour settles within about a week and after-pains are commoner in multiparous women
Haemoglobin falls steadily for six weeks because the red cell mass keeps shrinking
After-pains are commoner in primigravidas than in multiparous women
The raised blood urea of pregnancy persists for at least six weeks after delivery
After-pains are worse in multiparas and during breastfeeding; the leucocytosis settles and haemoglobin stabilises once haemodilution resolves. (Book p569)
Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
Causes of subinvolution of uterus (m/c first):
Retained placental fragments are commonest, then infection and incompletely remodelled vessels
Infection is commonest, with uterine fibroids the next most frequent cause
Anaemia is commonest, and breastfeeding delays involution further
Multiparity is commonest, with maternal obesity the next cause
Retained products are the commonest cause; breastfeeding releases oxytocin and actually helps the uterus to involute. (Book p570)
Excessive or prolonged bleeding with a uterus larger than expected for the postpartum day
Amenorrhoea with a small, well-involuted uterus on bimanual examination
High fever with a closed cervical os and no lochia being passed at all
A painless white discharge with itching and no abnormal bleeding
Subinvolution presents as prolonged or excessive lochia with a uterus that is bigger and softer than it should be for the day. (Book p570)
IOC is pelvic USG – findings for retained products : incompletely remodelled spiral artery.
Retained products: a thick vascular endometrium — remodelling: tubular hypoechoic areas in the myometrium
Retained products: a thin endometrium — remodelling: a uniformly small uterus
Retained products: free fluid in the pouch — remodelling: an adnexal mass
Retained products: an empty cavity — remodelling: a thick endometrium
Retained products show as a thickened vascular endometrium, while a remodelling defect shows tubular hypoechoic spaces in the myometrium. (Book p570)
Management of subinvolution and the caution:
A uterotonic first, then gentle curettage; vigorous curettage risks Asherman syndrome
Immediate hysterectomy, since a uterus that has failed to involute never recovers
Antibiotics alone, because subinvolution is always caused by occult endometritis
Methotrexate to dissolve the retained trophoblast, then a repeat scan in two weeks
A uterotonic is the drug of choice, with gentle curettage for suspected retained tissue; over-zealous curettage causes intrauterine adhesions. (Book p570)
All of the following predispose to subinvolution of the uterus EXCEPT:
Uterine fibroids or a retroverted uterus
Breastfeeding releases oxytocin and actually promotes involution; retained tissue, infection and fibroids delay it. (Book p570)
Prolactin peaks in the ______ and ______ after delivery; milk production is ______-dependent with the first stimulus being ______.
Third trimester; falls; prolactin; ↓ estrogen after placental delivery
Prolactin highest in 3rd trimester, falls after delivery; production prolactin-dependent, triggered by ↓ estrogen; ejection is oxytocin-dependent. (Book p570)
Colostrum contains more of everything than mature milk EXCEPT (mnemonic KFC):
Colostrum is poorer in K+, fat, carbohydrate and calcium. (Book p570)
Galactosemia or lactose intolerance in the baby
Maternal HIV infection in the Indian setting
Mastitis affecting one breast in the puerperium
COVID-19 infection in the mother after delivery
The absolute contraindication to breastfeeding listed is galactosemia or lactose intolerance in the baby. (Book p571)
Intravenous drug abuse, an active herpes lesion on the breast and untreated pulmonary tuberculosis
Maternal HIV infection, hepatitis B carriage and recent COVID-19 infection
Mastitis, a breast abscess and engorgement in the first postpartum week
Iron deficiency anaemia, gestational diabetes and treated hypothyroidism
Breastfeeding is encouraged in HIV on treatment, hepatitis B and mastitis; intravenous drug abuse, herpetic breast lesions and untreated TB are contraindications. (Book p571)
Which are NOT contraindications to breastfeeding?
HIV on treatment, COVID-19, mastitis, and hepatitis B positivity once the baby is immunised
Classic galactosaemia in the infant, which is an absolute contraindication
Untreated active pulmonary tuberculosis in the mother
An active herpes lesion on the breast itself
Breastfeeding continues in treated HIV, COVID-19 and mastitis, and in hepatitis B carriers once the infant has received immunoglobulin and vaccine. (Book p571)
Fill up: Milk ejection or the let-down reflex is mediated by ______ released in response to suckling, whereas milk synthesis depends mainly on ______.
Prolactin drives synthesis and oxytocin drives ejection; this is why breastfeeding causes after-pains and helps uterine involution. (Book p571)
Postpartum endometritis – m/c site and risk factors:
The placental site, after caesarean section, chorioamnionitis or prolonged rupture of membranes
The cervix, particularly after an operative vaginal delivery at term
The uterine fundus, after a short and uncomplicated labour
The cornua, which are the most exposed areas in a twin pregnancy
Infection begins at the raw placental site; caesarean, chorioamnionitis and prolonged rupture are the principal risk factors. (Book p571)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Presentation and management of postpartum endometritis:
Fever, subinvolution and uterine tenderness with offensive lochia; broad-spectrum antibiotics
Painless bleeding with a well-involuted uterus; evacuation of retained products
Profound shock with a flaccid uterus; emergency hysterectomy
Secondary amenorrhoea with hot flushes; hormonal replacement therapy
Endometritis presents with postpartum pyrexia, a tender poorly involuted uterus and offensive lochia, and is treated with antibiotics. (Book p571)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis – vessel, P/V finding, blood culture, imaging:
Ovarian vein, right more than left; cord-like structure; culture negative; MRI or CT
Uterine vein; a fluctuant mass on palpation; culture positive; ultrasound
Iliac artery; a pulsatile mass on palpation; culture positive; Doppler
Renal vein; nothing palpable on examination; culture negative; plain X-ray

Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis affects the ovarian vein (right more than left), shows a cord-like structure on P/V, has a negative blood culture because the infection is localized, and MRI or CT may show the thrombosed vein. (Book p571)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Key clinical features of septic pelvic thrombophlebitis:
Broad-spectrum antibiotics have no effect; clinical diagnosis
Persistent fever despite BSA; clinical diagnosis. (Book p571)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
On the fourth day after a caesarean section a woman develops a fever of 38.8 C with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
Postpartum endometritis — broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering aerobic and anaerobic organisms
Normal puerperal changes — reassurance and no treatment
A urinary tract infection — oral antibiotics alone
Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis — immediate anticoagulation alone
Fever with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia after caesarean is endometritis, treated with intravenous clindamycin and gentamicin or equivalent. (Book p571)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Management of septic pelvic thrombophlebitis – no thrombophlebitis evidence : evidence of thrombophlebitis.
No evidence: continue BSA and LMWH; evidence: heparin for 6 weeks
No evidence: stop all antibiotics; evidence: warfarin for 3 months
No evidence: heparin for 6 weeks; evidence: heparin for 48 hours
No evidence: surgery to ligate the vein; evidence: antibiotics only

Without evidence of thrombophlebitis, continue broad-spectrum antibiotics and LMWH, with heparin until 48 hours after the woman is afebrile; with evidence of thrombophlebitis, give heparin for 6 weeks. (Book p572)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Fever in a breastfeeding woman due to breast engorgement is characterised by:
Engorgement fever rarely ≥39 °C, lasts <24 h. (Book p572)
Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
Burning, numbness and tingling over the upper outer thigh/lateral hip after vaginal delivery indicates injury to:
The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, which is the nerve most often injured
The femoral nerve, compressed against the pelvic brim by the fetal head
The common peroneal nerve, compressed at the neck of the fibula
The obturator nerve, stretched by the descending head in the cavity
Meralgia paraesthetica is entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh under the inguinal ligament in labour. (Book p572)
Quadriceps weakness sparing adductors with sensory loss over anterior and medial thigh indicates:
Femoral nerve – 2nd m/c; adductors spared. (Book p572)
Foot drop after delivery is due to ______ injury from ______.
The common peroneal nerve, from prolonged squatting or pressure in the leg supports
The tibial nerve, injured by prolonged positioning in lithotomy
The sciatic nerve, injured by the epidural needle during analgesia
The femoral nerve, compressed by the forceps blades at delivery
Foot drop follows compression of the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck, classically from squatting or leg supports. (Book p572)
M/c nerves injured after caesarean section:
Post-CS: ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves. (Book p572)

Match the nerve injury with its clinical picture — 1) Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh 2) Femoral nerve 3) Common peroneal nerve … A) Foot drop and loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot after prolonged lithotomy or squatting B) Burning pain and numbness over the outer thigh from compression at the inguinal ligament C) Weakness of knee extension with a depressed knee jerk from compression against the pelvic brim
Meralgia paraesthetica, femoral neuropathy from the retractor or fetal head, and peroneal palsy from leg supports or squatting are the classic injuries. (Book p572)

q: A person has a 46,XX karyotype. How many Barr bodies would typically be seen on a buccal smear?
Barr bodies are not seen in females
Barr body count equals the number of X chromosomes minus one. 46,XX (2 X chromosomes) gives 1 Barr body; 46,XY (1 X chromosome) gives 0.
Which structure is the female homologue of the male bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland?
Bartholin's glands (greater vestibular glands) are homologous to the bulbourethral glands. Skene's/paraurethral glands are the homologue of the prostate.
The labia majora are embryologically homologous to which male structure?
The labia majora and scrotum both develop from the labioscrotal swellings — the same embryological origin.
In a newborn with ambiguous genitalia, what is considered the single best method to determine genetic sex?
Assessing external genitalia is the most common first step but is unreliable in ambiguous genitalia. Karyotyping is the definitive, best method.
The fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina all develop from which embryological duct?
The paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts give rise to the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina in a genetic female.
Which organ has a surface lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium, whose most common tumour type is an epithelial cell tumour?
The ovarian surface epithelium is a single layer of cuboidal cells; epithelial cell tumours are the most common ovarian tumour type arising from it.
The fallopian tube is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium. Its most common cancer is:
Tubal adenocarcinoma is the most common cancer of the fallopian tube, consistent with its columnar epithelial lining.

In the cervix, the exocervix (stratified squamous epithelium) most commonly gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma — the overall most common cervical cancer — while the endocervix (columnar epithelium) more typically gives rise to:
Endocervical columnar epithelium gives rise to adenocarcinoma, while the exocervix’s squamous epithelium gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma, the overall most common cervical cancer type.
In the Bartholin gland, the gland itself (cuboidal epithelium) most commonly develops which cancer?

The Bartholin gland proper is cuboidal and most commonly gives rise to adenocarcinoma; its duct (transitional epithelium) gives rise to transitional cell carcinoma, and its opening (squamous epithelium) to squamous cell carcinoma.
The fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina all share which embryological origin?
These structures all arise from the paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct, of mesodermal origin.
Unlike the rest of the vagina, the lower vagina and Bartholin’s gland both develop from the urogenital sinus, making their embryological origin:
Identical to the ovary’s genital-ridge origin
The lower vagina forms from the sinovaginal bulbs of the urogenital sinus (endodermal), unlike the upper vagina, uterus, cervix, and tubes, which are mesodermal (Mullerian).
Roughly what fraction of uterine blood supply comes via the ovarian artery anastomosis, versus the uterine artery itself?
About 80% of uterine blood supply is via the uterine artery, with roughly 20% via the anastomotic branch from the ovarian artery.
The right ovarian vein drains directly into which vessel, unlike the left?
The right ovarian vein drains directly into the IVC, while the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein first — an asymmetry relevant to imaging and vein thrombosis workups.
Which node group is NOT a primary drainage site for the cervix?

Cervical lymphatics drain chiefly to the hypogastric, obturator, parametrial, and external iliac nodes — not primarily to the superficial inguinal nodes, which matters for staging cervical cancer spread.
Lymphatics from the uterine cornu can travel alongside which structure to reach the superficial inguinal nodes — the same route implicated in round ligament pain?

Cornual lymphatics can accompany the round ligament through the inguinal canal to the superficial inguinal nodes, distinct from fundal drainage, which runs mainly to the paraaortic nodes via the ovarian vessels.
By the 'upper two-thirds vs lower one-third' rule, the lower third of the vagina mainly drains to which nodes?
The upper two-thirds of the vagina drains like the cervix (hypogastric/obturator/external iliac groups); the lower third drains like the vulva, to the superficial inguinal nodes.
The uterine artery is a direct branch of which vessel?
Anterior division of the internal iliac artery
Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
The uterine artery branches from the anterior division of the internal iliac (hypogastric) artery, typically alongside the superior vesical, vaginal, and middle rectal arteries.
The uterine artery crosses the ureter at roughly what distance from the cervix?
It crosses about 2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix, at the base of the broad ligament — the single most important surgical landmark in gynaecologic anatomy.
"Water under the bridge" describes the relationship between the uterine artery and which structure?
The ureter ("water") runs beneath the uterine artery ("bridge"). This crossing is the classic point of ureteric injury during hysterectomy.
A surgeon is clamping the uterine pedicle during an abdominal hysterectomy. Which structure is at greatest risk at exactly this step?
The ureter runs just beneath the uterine artery at the level of the internal os, so clamps placed too close to the cervix risk kinking or transecting it.
Which of these is NOT one of the classic "points of danger" for the ureter during pelvic surgery?
Pelvic brim, crossing the iliac vessels
Base of broad ligament, beneath the uterine artery
Near the lateral vaginal fornix, close to the cervix
At the umbilical port site in laparoscopy
The three classic danger points are the pelvic brim, the base of the broad ligament under the uterine artery, and near the lateral fornix/vaginal vault. The umbilicus is not one of them.
The ascending branch of the uterine artery anastomoses with which vessel near the uterine cornu?
This anastomosis gives the uterus a dual blood supply (internal iliac + aortic, via the ovarian artery) — one reason uterine artery embolisation for fibroids can leave residual perfusion.
The descending (cervicovaginal) branch of the uterine artery mainly supplies:
The descending branch supplies the cervix and upper vagina, while the ascending branch runs up along the body of the uterus toward the cornu.
Radial arteries in the myometrium give rise to basal arteries and which other paired vessels, shed with the functional endometrial layer each cycle?
Spiral arteries supply the functional layer and undergo vasospasm before menstruation, causing shedding. Failed trophoblastic remodelling of spiral arteries is also central to pre-eclampsia.
After bilateral uterine artery ligation for postpartum haemorrhage, bleeding can sometimes persist because of collateral flow from which vessel?
Because the ovarian artery anastomoses with the uterine artery near the cornu, its collateral flow can maintain some perfusion even after the uterine vessels are tied off.
The ovary's primary arterial supply comes from:
The ovarian artery, a direct branch of the aorta
The ovarian artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta (just below the renal arteries) and descends via the infundibulopelvic ligament — a separate origin from the uterine artery.
The angle of anteflexion, normally about 120°, is measured between:
Cervix and the body of the uterus
Anteflexion is the angle between the cervix and the body (corpus) of the uterus, normally around 120°.
The angle of anteversion, normally about 90°, is measured between:
Anteversion is the angle between the cervix and the vagina, normally around 90°.
On a per-vaginal exam of an anteverted uterus, which part is MOST easily palpated?
Posterior lip of the cervix only
In the more common anteverted position (about 80% of women), the fundus is easily felt and the cervix is comparatively difficult to palpate.
In a retroverted uterus, the fundus points toward the sacral promontory and is difficult to palpate on PV exam. Instead, which part is easily felt?
In a retroverted uterus, the cervix (with its posterior lip prominent) is easily felt, while the fundus is difficult to palpate — the reverse of the anteverted pattern.
The round ligament attaches the uterine cornu to which structure?
The anterior one-third of the labia majora
The round ligament runs from the uterine cornu, through the inguinal canal, to attach at the anterior one-third of the labia majora.
The round ligament's blood supply comes from Sampson's artery, which is itself a branch of:
Sampson's artery, supplying the round ligament, is a branch of the uterine artery.
The uterine artery arises from the ANTERIOR division of the internal iliac artery. What does the POSTERIOR division chiefly supply instead?
Muscles of the lower limb (gluteal region)

The posterior division of the internal iliac artery mainly supplies the gluteal/lower-limb musculature, unlike the anterior division, which supplies pelvic viscera including the uterus via the uterine artery.
In the surgical devascularisation ladder for intractable postpartum haemorrhage, after the uterine artery, which vessel is ligated next if bleeding continues?
The step-wise ladder for uncontrolled PPH escalates from uterine artery ligation, to ovarian artery ligation, to anterior division of the internal iliac artery if bleeding persists.
Why does uterine artery embolisation for fibroids typically leave vaginal blood supply intact?
The vagina has no significant blood supply
The uterine artery supplies the vagina only in childhood
Embolisation always spares the descending cervical branch
The vagina is supplied by the vaginal artery, not the uterine artery
The vagina’s blood supply comes chiefly from the vaginal artery rather than the uterine artery, so uterine artery embolisation generally spares it.
Which ligament is the chief mechanical support of the uterus and carries the uterine vessels at its base?
The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament runs from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic sidewall and is the main uterine support; it carries the uterine vessels at its base.
Which ligament is the embryological remnant of the gubernaculum and runs through the inguinal canal to the labium majus?
The round ligament corresponds developmentally to the gubernaculum testis — why it can stretch painfully in pregnancy ("round ligament pain"), and why canal-of-Nuck cysts occur along its course.
Which ligament gives the main posterior support to the cervix and upper vagina, and is plicated in McCall culdoplasty?
The uterosacral ligaments run from the cervix to the sacrum and are key posterior supports, surgically reinforced in vault-prolapse procedures like McCall culdoplasty.
The broad ligament is best described as:
A double fold of peritoneum draping the uterus, tubes and related structures
A dense fibromuscular band with no peritoneal covering
A ligament exclusive to the ovary
It's a peritoneal fold, not a true fibrous ligament — within its two layers run the uterine vessels, round ligament, ovarian ligament, and fallopian tube.
The male internal genitalia — seminal vesicle, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, and vas deferens — are remembered by which mnemonic?
SEED: Seminal vesicle, Epididymis, Ejaculatory duct, Vas Deferens — the male internal genitalia homologous to the female fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, and vagina.
Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination
The labia minora are the female homologue of which male structure?
The labia minora and penile urethra share the same embryological origin (urogenital folds).
Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination
The clitoris is the female homologue of which male structure?
The clitoris and penis are homologous structures, both developing from the genital tubercle.
Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination
The paraurethral (Skene) glands in females are homologous to which male structure?
Skene's (paraurethral) glands are the female homologue of the prostate gland.
Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination
Assessment of external genitalia, the most common method of sex determination, has which key drawback?
It cannot be performed before birth
It is not applicable/reliable in cases of ambiguous genitalia
It is more expensive than karyotyping
External genitalia assessment is the most common method but is unreliable when genitalia are ambiguous, making karyotyping the best method in such cases.
Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination
On karyotyping for sex determination, presence of a Y chromosome indicates a male, while its absence indicates:
An intersex state in all cases
Cannot be determined from karyotype alone
Presence of the Y chromosome determines a male karyotype; its absence indicates a female karyotype.
Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination
The ovarian artery, the main arterial supply of the ovary, is a branch of the abdominal aorta arising at which vertebral level?
The ovarian artery branches from the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level.
The ovary receives its nerve supply (T10, T11) via the ovarian plexus, which also supplies the broad ligament and:
The ovarian plexus (T10, T11) supplies the ovary, the lateral fallopian tube, and the broad ligament.
The ovary’s lymphatic drainage is to which lymph nodes, reflecting its embryological origin high in the abdomen?
The ovary drains to the paraaortic lymph nodes, consistent with its high abdominal embryological origin.
The fallopian tube’s arterial supply is split, with the lateral one-third supplied by the ovarian artery and the medial two-thirds supplied by:
The medial two-thirds of the fallopian tube is supplied by the uterine artery, and the lateral one-third by the ovarian artery.
The applied clinical relevance of the fallopian tube’s nerve supply (T11, T12, L1) is pain in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, occurring due to:
Pain in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy arises from stretching of the fallopian tube, transmitted via its T11, T12, L1 nerve supply.
The fallopian tube’s lymphatic drainage is mainly to the paraaortic lymph nodes, but its intramural part (along with the round ligament) can also drain to:
The intramural part of the fallopian tube, travelling with the round ligament, can drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
The uterus receives its nerve supply (T10–L1) via a named plexus called the:
The uterus is supplied by T10–L1 via the Frankenhauser ganglion, also known as the uterovaginal plexus.
In the lymphatic drainage of the uterus, the body of the uterus drains to the external and internal iliac lymph nodes, while the fundus drains to:
The fundus of the uterus drains to the paraaortic lymph nodes, while the body drains to the external and internal iliac nodes.
The cervix's arterial supply is from the descending cervical artery, which is itself a branch of the:
The descending cervical artery, supplying the cervix, is a branch of the uterine artery.
The cervix receives its nerve supply from which spinal segments?
The cervix is innervated by S2–S4.
The cervix's lymphatic drainage follows the mnemonic HOPE; this stands for hypogastric, obturator, paracervical, and:
HOPE: Hypogastric, Obturator, Paracervical, External iliac lymph nodes — the primary cervical drainage sites.
The vagina’s arterial supply, the vaginal artery, is a branch of which vessel?
The vaginal artery, supplying the vagina, is a branch of the internal pudendal artery.
The vagina’s nerve supply differs by region: the upper vagina is supplied by S2–S4, while the lower vagina is supplied by:
The lower vagina is supplied by the pudendal nerve, while the upper vagina is supplied by S2–S4.

Following the "upper two-thirds vs lower one-third" rule, the upper two-thirds of the vagina drains to the HOPE lymph node group, which lies in the pelvis, whereas the lower one-third drains to nodes reflecting its:
Direct drainage to deep inguinal nodes only

The lower one-third of the vagina, developing from the urogenital sinus, drains like external genitalia — to the superficial inguinal nodes — while the upper two-thirds drains internally to the HOPE nodes.
The vulva (pudendum) is primarily supplied by the internal pudendal artery, except for the mons pubis, which is supplied by the:
The mons pubis is supplied by the external pudendal artery, while the rest of the vulva is supplied by the internal pudendal artery.
The vulva’s nerve supply includes the pudendal nerve throughout, plus the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves supplying the:
The ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves supply the anterior-superior part of the vulva.
The posterior-inferior part of the vulva is additionally supplied by the pudendal nerve and:
The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
The posterior-inferior vulva is supplied by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, in addition to the pudendal nerve.

Besides the glans, the body and crura of the clitoris drain via the superficial inguinal nodes onward to the:
The body and crura of the clitoris drain to superficial inguinal nodes, which then continue to the deep inguinal nodes.
The vulva is also known by which alternative anatomical term?
The vulva, the external genitalia of females, is also known as the pudendum.
The uterine cavity is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium, but a key clinical note is that:
Cilia are present only after menopause
Cilia are lost at the onset of menstruation
Cilia regenerate every day regardless of cycle phase
The uterus is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium, but cilia are lost at the onset of menstruation.
The most common cancer of the uterus (endometrium) is:
Endometrial carcinoma (adenocarcinoma) is the most common uterine cancer, arising from the columnar glandular epithelium.
The endocervix is lined by columnar epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
The endocervix (columnar epithelium) most commonly gives rise to adenocarcinoma, while the exocervix (squamous epithelium) gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma.
The vagina is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
The vagina’s non-keratinized stratified squamous lining most commonly gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma.
The hymen is lined by which epithelium, and what is its most common cancer?
Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; squamous cell carcinoma
The hymen, like the vagina, is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and most commonly develops squamous cell carcinoma.
In the Bartholin gland, the duct is lined by transitional epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
The Bartholin gland duct (transitional epithelium) most commonly develops transitional cell carcinoma, distinct from the gland itself (adenocarcinoma).
The opening of the Bartholin gland is lined by squamous epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
The opening of the Bartholin gland (squamous epithelium) most commonly develops squamous cell carcinoma.
Embryologically, the ovary develops from the:
The ovary develops from the genital ridge, distinct from the Mullerian-duct origin of the tube/uterus/cervix/upper vagina.
The fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina (all of Mullerian/paramesonephric origin) are classified as having which germ layer origin?
Mullerian duct-derived structures (tube, uterus, cervix, upper vagina) are of mesodermal origin, while the lower vagina and Bartholin’s gland (from the urogenital sinus) are of endodermal origin.
On per speculum examination, the exocervix normally appears pink, while the endocervix (visible at the external os) appears:
On per speculum examination, the exocervix appears pink while the endocervix appears red, visible around the external os.
Approximately what proportion of women have an anteverted uterus (fundus pointing towards the pubic symphysis)?
About 80% of women have an anteverted uterus; the remaining 20% have a retroverted uterus (fundus towards the sacral promontory).

Which part of the fallopian tube is the narrowest, lying within the uterine wall itself?
The interstitial (intramural) part runs through the uterine wall and is the narrowest segment, acting as an anatomical sphincter.
The isthmus of the fallopian tube is the preferred site for which procedure?
The isthmus, the second-narrowest and most fibromuscular part, is the standard site for laparoscopic tubal ligation.
The ampulla is the most common site for which two clinically important events?
The ampulla is the widest, longest part with the most mucosal folds — the usual site of fertilization, and consequently the most common site of ectopic pregnancy.
Genital tuberculosis most commonly affects which part of the tube, and can cause which complication?
Genital TB most commonly involves the ampulla and can lead to bilateral cornual block, a recognised cause of infertility.
What is the investigation of choice to assess fallopian tube patency?
HSG (hysterosalpingography) is the standard investigation of choice for assessing tubal patency.
The ovary and fallopian tube together
The broad and round ligaments together

'Peg cells' are a normal histological finding in the lining of the:

Gonococcal infection of the fallopian tube classically leads to:

Hysteroscopic tubal sterilisation (e.g. the Essure method) targets which part of the fallopian tube, in contrast to the isthmus used for laparoscopic ligation?

Hysteroscopic sterilisation methods like Essure work at the interstitial (intramural) part of the tube, approached from inside the uterine cavity, unlike laparoscopic ligation which targets the isthmus.
An ovarian volume of 10 cc or more is classically associated with which condition?
Normal ovarian volume is about 6–7 cc; a volume of 10 cc or more is a classic supportive criterion for PCOS.
During intrauterine life the ovary descends into the pelvis with the help of which structure, which later splits into two ligaments?
Gubernaculum, into the ovarian and round ligaments
Mesonephric duct, into the round and broad ligaments

Urogenital ridge, into the broad and cardinal ligaments
The ovary is an abdominal organ in early development and descends via the gubernaculum, which the uterus later divides into the ovarian ligament (above) and round ligament (below).
The infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament of the ovary is deliberately preserved during which procedure?
It carries the ovarian vessels and nerves, so it is preserved whenever the ovary is left in place during hysterectomy.
A large ovarian mass causing pain along the medial thigh is most likely compressing which nerve?
The obturator nerve lies lateral to the ovary; a large ovarian mass pressing on it classically causes pain radiating along the medial thigh.
Posteriorly, the ovary is related to which two structures?
The ureter and internal iliac artery lie posterior to the ovary — a relationship relevant to injury risk during oophorectomy.
The ovary normally lies in which fossa on the lateral pelvic wall?
The ovary normally occupies the ovarian fossa of Waldeyer on the lateral pelvic wall.
Superiorly and anteriorly, the ovary is related to which vessel?
The external iliac artery lies superior/anterior to the ovary.
Medially, the ovary is related to the:
The ovarian ligament lies medial to the ovary, connecting it to the uterine cornu.
The mesovarium is the part of which structure that attaches to the ovary?
The mesovarium is the fold of broad ligament that attaches to and suspends the ovary.
The broad ligament can be divided into three parts by proximity to nearby structures. Which part lies closest to the fallopian tube?
The mesosalpinx is the part of the broad ligament closest to and enclosing the fallopian tube.
Which part of the broad ligament lies closest to the uterus itself?
The mesometrium is the largest part of the broad ligament, closest to and surrounding the uterus.
The surface of the ovary is covered by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium, beneath which lies a fibrous capsule called the:
Basement membrane only, with no capsule
The tunica albuginea is the fibrous capsule lying just beneath the surface (germinal) epithelium of the ovary.
Which follicle stage has a single layer of flattened follicular cells around the primary oocyte?
The primordial follicle is the earliest stage: a primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flattened cells.
A fluid-filled antral cavity first appears at which stage of follicular development?
The antral (tertiary) follicle is defined by the appearance of a fluid-filled cavity (the antrum), absent in earlier stages.

Granulosa cells, theca interna, theca externa
Theca interna, theca externa, granulosa cells
Theca externa, theca interna, granulosa cells

The outermost fibrous layer of the follicle
