The cumulus oophorus is the mound of granulosa cells that projects into the antrum, separating the oocyte from the antral fluid.
Hilar cells in the ovarian medulla are histologically homologous to which testicular cell type, relevant to a rare hormone-secreting tumour?
Hilar cells are homologous to testicular Leydig cells; a hilar cell tumour is a rare, androgen-secreting, masculinising ovarian tumour.
A primary follicle is distinguished from a primordial follicle by having:
Theca externa and interna layers already formed
A single layer of cuboidal (granulosa) cells around the oocyte, instead of flattened cells
The primary follicle has a single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells, replacing the flattened cells of the primordial follicle; multiple layers mark the secondary follicle stage.
Within the ovary, hilar cells and blood vessels are found chiefly in the:
The ovarian medulla contains the main blood vessels and hilar cells, while the cortex contains follicles at various stages.
Why does the uterus grow from roughly 60–80 g (non-pregnant) to about 1000 g at term?
The pregnant uterus grows mainly through hypertrophy (enlargement of existing smooth muscle fibres) rather than hyperplasia (new fibre formation).
The cervix-to-corpus ratio is about 2:1 (cervix larger than the corpus) at which life stage?
Before puberty the cervix is proportionally larger than the corpus (about 2:1); this reverses to roughly 1:3–1:4 by reproductive age.
At menopause, the cervix:corpus ratio returns toward roughly 1:1, mainly because of:
Postmenopausal atrophy affects the corpus more than the cervix, bringing the ratio back toward the prepubertal 1:1–2:1 range.
Moving anterior to posterior, which is the correct order of structures attached at the uterine cornu?
Round ligament, fallopian tube, ovarian ligament
Fallopian tube, round ligament, ovarian ligament
Ovarian ligament, fallopian tube, round ligament
Round ligament, ovarian ligament, fallopian tube
Anterior to posterior at the cornu: round ligament, then fallopian tube, then ovarian ligament.
The uterine isthmus lies between which two landmarks, and what does it become during pregnancy?
The internal os and external os; the cervical canal

The isthmus, between the anatomical and histological internal os, stretches during pregnancy to form the lower uterine segment (LUS).
Which two endometrial sublayers together form the 'functional layer' shed during menstruation?
The zona compacta and zona spongiosa together form the functional layer, which is shed each cycle; the zona basalis remains and regenerates it.
Endometrial thickness is typically greatest during which phase of the cycle?
Endometrial thickness peaks in the secretory phase (roughly 7–16 mm), exceeding even the late proliferative phase.
The myometrium's middle muscle layer is sometimes called the 'living ligature' because it:
Contracts around blood vessels to control bleeding after delivery
Physically stitches the uterine incision closed
Anchors the uterus to the sacrum
The interlacing middle layer of myometrium contracts after delivery to compress the blood vessels running through it, limiting postpartum bleeding.
The pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch) is the peritoneal reflection between the uterus and which structure?
The pouch of Douglas is the posterior peritoneal reflection between the uterus/upper vagina and the rectum — the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity.
Culdocentesis (needle aspiration via the posterior vaginal fornix into the pouch of Douglas) classically helps diagnose:

The total length of the fallopian tube is approximately:
The fallopian tube is approximately 10 cm long.

Red columnar epithelium visible outside the external os
Ectropion is eversion of the red endocervical (columnar) epithelium beyond the external os; it is physiological and does not require biopsy.
Physiological cervical ectropion is most commonly seen in:
High oestrogen states, especially pregnancy, are the most common physiological cause of ectropion, which can present with post-coital bleeding.
The cervical transformation zone is the area between the:
Original and the new squamocolumnar junction
At puberty, oestrogen and Doderlein bacilli drive squamous metaplasia, forming a new SCJ; the dynamic zone between the original and new SCJ is the transformation zone.
Most squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix arise at which site?
Endocervical canal, deep to the SCJ
The transformation zone (more than the SCJ itself) is the most common site for cervical squamous cell carcinoma; adenocarcinoma tends to arise from the endocervix.
The cervix is composed mainly of which tissue, with only about 10–15% smooth muscle fibres?
The cervix is predominantly collagen/connective tissue, with a comparatively small (10–15%) smooth muscle component.
Cervical effacement during labour occurs due to breakdown of collagen and:
Increased water content of the cervical tissue
Effacement results from collagen breakdown together with increased water content of the cervical connective tissue, softening and thinning the cervix.
On examination, a pinpoint external os is typical of a nulliparous cervix, while a transverse, slit-like os is typical of a:
Childbirth changes the external os from the nulliparous pinpoint shape to a transverse, slit-like multiparous shape.
The descending cervical artery, a branch of the uterine artery, runs prominently at which clock positions?
The descending cervical artery is prominent at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions of the cervix.
A paracervical block is deliberately avoided at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions because:
The descending cervical artery runs there, risking intravascular injection
Those are the safest injection sites
Injecting at 3 and 9 o’clock risks hitting the descending cervical artery; the block is instead given at 2, 4, 8, and 10 o’clock.
Which nodal involvement in cervical cancer is considered evidence of distant metastasis (Stage 4B) rather than routine pelvic spread?

The cervix normally drains to hypogastric, obturator, paracervical, and external iliac nodes. Superficial inguinal node involvement falls outside this pathway and signals distant metastasis (Stage 4B).
Sensory innervation of the cervix is chiefly via which ganglion/plexus?
The Frankenhauser (uterovaginal) plexus, fed by S2–S4, carries sensory fibres from the cervix.
Peritoneum covers which surface of the cervix?
Only the posterior surface of the cervix carries a peritoneal covering; the anterior surface does not.
The vaginal artery is homologous to which artery in males?
The vaginal artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery supplying the vagina and bladder base, is homologous to the inferior vesical artery in males.
Which vaginal wall is longer, and by roughly how much?
The posterior vaginal wall is longer than the anterior wall by about 2 cm.
Rugae — transverse folds of the vaginal wall — are considered:
The most specific gross feature of the vagina
Rugae are the most specific identifying feature of the vagina on inspection.
Of the four vaginal fornices, which is the deepest?
The posterior fornix is the deepest of the four fornices, and the usual entry point for culdocentesis.
Laterally, the vagina is related to all of the following EXCEPT:
The bladder is an ANTERIOR relation of the vagina. The cardinal ligament, ureter, and Bartholin gland are lateral relations.
The vaginal axis makes an angle of approximately 90° with the cervix. What is this angle called?
The vaginal axis meets the cervix at the angle of anteversion, normally about 90°.
The vaginal axis makes an angle with the horizontal of approximately:
The vaginal canal runs at roughly 45° to the horizontal in the standing position.
The vaginal epithelium is classically described as:
Non-keratinised stratified squamous, with no glands
The vagina is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium and, notably, has no glands of its own.
Since the vagina itself has no glands, vaginal discharge normally originates mainly from:
Cervical and endometrial gland secretions (plus Bartholin gland during intercourse)
Physiological vaginal discharge is mainly cervical and endometrial gland secretion, with a Bartholin gland contribution during intercourse.
Doderlein bacilli convert vaginal glycogen (built up under oestrogen’s influence) into:
Doderlein bacilli (lactobacilli) metabolise glycogen into lactic acid, keeping the vagina acidic.
Vaginal pH is typically most acidic during which state?
Pregnancy drives vaginal pH to its most acidic (about 3.5–4), reflecting increased Doderlein bacilli activity; menstruation and menopause instead shift pH alkaline.
On vaginal cytology, superficial cells with pyknotic nuclei predominate when which hormone is dominant?
Oestrogen-dominant states show pink, eosinophilic superficial cells with pyknotic nuclei; progesterone favours intermediate cells, and a low-hormone state favours parabasal cells.
Immediately after birth, vaginal pH is slightly acidic due to the influence of:
Residual maternal oestrogen keeps the newborn’s vaginal pH slightly acidic for the first couple of weeks of life.
Between about 2 weeks of age and puberty, vaginal pH becomes alkaline (6–8), mainly because:
The vaginal epithelium is absent at this age
Cervical secretions predominate, with Doderlein bacilli not yet established
Once maternal oestrogen wanes, Doderlein bacilli have not yet colonised the vagina, so cervical secretions predominate and pH is alkaline until puberty.
During menstruation, vaginal pH shifts alkaline (6–8) mainly because:
Menstrual blood is alkaline, temporarily shifting vaginal pH alkaline during menstruation.
At menopause, vaginal pH becomes alkaline again (6–8), reflecting:
Decreased Doderlein bacilli, from lower oestrogen and glycogen
Falling oestrogen after menopause reduces glycogen deposition, so Doderlein bacilli decline and pH becomes alkaline again.
For vaginal cytology (the hormonal maturation index), the sample is best taken from:
The upper one-third of the lateral vaginal wall
The upper one-third of the lateral vaginal wall is the most hormonally sensitive site and the standard sampling location for the maturation index.
The endocervix is also known as the:
The endocervix, close to the uterus, is also called the supravaginal part of the cervix.
The exocervix (the part of the cervix inside the vagina) is also known as the:
The exocervix is also called the portio vaginalis, as it lies within the vagina.
Cervical ectropion classically presents clinically with:
Cervical ectropion (with exposed red columnar epithelium) classically presents with post-coital bleeding.
In physiological cervical ectropion (as seen in pregnancy), biopsy is:

Physiological ectropion does not require biopsy, as it is a normal hormonally-driven finding.
The squamo-columnar junction (SCJ) is defined as the point where:
The cervix opens into the vagina
The cervix connects to the uterus
The uterine artery crosses the ureter

The SCJ is where columnar epithelium of the endocervix transitions into the squamous epithelium of the exocervix.
Originally (pre-puberty), the SCJ is located at the external os; at puberty, a new SCJ forms due to the effects of estrogen and:
At puberty, estrogen and Doderlein's bacteria drive formation of a new SCJ, distinct from its original pre-pubertal location at the external os.
The most common type of cervical cancer overall is:
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type of cervical cancer.
While SCC of the cervix most commonly arises at the transformation zone, adenocarcinoma of the cervix most commonly arises at the:
Adenocarcinoma, arising from columnar epithelium, most commonly arises at the endocervix.
The external os is defined as the point where:
The cervix opens into the vagina
The cervix connects to the uterus
The fallopian tube enters the uterus
The external os is the point where the cervix opens into the vagina.
The internal os is defined as the point where:
The cervix connects to the uterus
The cervix opens into the vagina
The internal os is the point where the cervix connects to the uterus.
In the HOPE mnemonic for cervical lymphatic drainage, the hypogastric lymph nodes are also known as:
Hypogastric lymph nodes are also known as internal iliac lymph nodes.
The nerve supply of the cervix arises from which spinal segments?
The cervix is innervated by S2–S4.
A paracervical block is safely given at the 2 and 4 o’clock, and 8 and 10 o’clock positions, specifically to avoid the descending cervical artery, found at:
The descending cervical artery lies at 3 and 9 o’clock, so paracervical block is given at 2, 4, 8, and 10 o’clock instead to avoid it.
The vaginal artery, supplying the vagina, is a branch of which vessel?
The vaginal artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery.
Besides the vagina itself, the vaginal artery also supplies the:
The vaginal artery supplies both the vagina and the base of the bladder.
Following the vagina's own lymphatic drainage pattern, the upper part drains to the HOPE lymph node group, while the lower part drains to:
The upper vagina drains to the HOPE nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
The vagina is best described anatomically as a:
Fibromuscular hollow tube connecting the cervix to the vulva (introitus)
Purely epithelial structure with no muscular wall
The vagina is a fibromuscular hollow tube, connected to the cervix at one end and opening at the vulva (introitus) at the other.
The peritoneum covers the vagina only over the upper one-third of which wall, forming the pouch of Douglas?
Peritoneal covering of the vagina is present only over the upper one-third of the posterior wall, forming the pouch of Douglas.
Anteriorly, the vagina is related to the bladder and:
Anteriorly, the vagina is related to the bladder and urethra.
Posteriorly, the vagina is related to the pouch of Douglas, the ampulla of the rectum, and the:
Posteriorly, the vagina is related to the pouch of Douglas, ampulla of rectum, and the perineal body.
Among the muscular lateral relations of the vagina are the levator ani, bulbospongiosus, and:
The lateral muscular relations of the vagina include levator ani, pubovaginalis, and bulbospongiosus.
At puberty, vaginal pH becomes acidic (around 4–5), primarily due to the appearance of:
Vaginal pH becomes acidic at puberty due to the appearance of Doderlein's bacilli, which convert glycogen to lactic acid.
Complete Coverage: Vaginal Histology, pH & Cytology
Doderlein's bacilli, responsible for the acidic vaginal pH of reproductive life, characteristically:
Are present from birth throughout life
Appear at puberty and disappear at menopause
Doderlein's bacilli appear at puberty (driven by estrogen and glycogen) and disappear at menopause.
Complete Coverage: Vaginal Histology, pH & Cytology
Since the vagina has no glands of its own, vaginal discharge is derived mainly from cervical discharge, with additional contributions from endometrial gland discharge and:
Vaginal discharge also includes contributions from endometrial gland discharge, and Bartholin gland discharge specifically during intercourse.
Complete Coverage: Vaginal Histology, pH & Cytology
On vaginal cytology, intermediate cells (blue/basophilic, with a small nucleus) predominate when which hormone is dominant?
Intermediate cells predominate when progesterone is the dominant hormone.
Complete Coverage: Vaginal Histology, pH & Cytology
Parabasal cells on vaginal cytology (blue/basophilic with a hazy outline and big nuclei) are seen when:
No hormone predominates (e.g., low estrogen and progesterone states)
Both estrogen and progesterone are markedly elevated
Parabasal cells appear when no hormone predominates, such as in hypoestrogenic states.
Complete Coverage: Vaginal Histology, pH & Cytology
Which artery lies POSTERIOR to the ureter, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions just after the ureter crosses it?
The common iliac artery lies posterior to the ureter and divides into internal and external iliac arteries just after the ureter crosses it at the pelvic brim.
The distance between the median sacral artery and the ureter — a landmark for the ureter's entry into the pelvis — is approximately:
This 3 cm landmark helps identify where the ureter enters the pelvis at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.
Among the three classic danger points for ureteric injury in hysterectomy, which is the SINGLE most common?
Pelvic brim, crossing the iliac vessels
'Water under the bridge' — the uterine artery crossing
At the internal os, near the cervix
The uterine artery crossing (‘water under the bridge’, about 2 cm lateral to the internal os) is the most common site of ureteric injury; the pelvic brim is the second most common.
The best intraoperative way to positively identify the ureter during pelvic surgery is to:
Look for a white, glistening tube
Watching for peristalsis is the most reliable way to positively identify the ureter intraoperatively.
Laterally, the external iliac artery is related to which two structures?
Obturator nerve and internal iliac vein
The iliopsoas muscle and genitofemoral nerve lie lateral to the external iliac artery.
Which two arteries lie ANTERIOR to the ureter as it courses through the pelvis?
Common iliac and internal iliac arteries
Internal iliac and superior vesical arteries

The ovarian artery (a direct aortic branch) and the uterine artery (from the anterior division of the internal iliac) both lie anterior to the ureter; the common and internal iliac arteries lie posterior to it.
Ranking the three classic areas of ureteric susceptibility in hysterectomy: 'water under the bridge' is most common and the pelvic brim is second most common. What is the third, remaining site?
At the internal os, near the cervix
At the pelvic sidewall near the sciatic notch
The third classic danger point is at the internal os, near the cervix — alongside the pelvic brim (2nd most common) and the uterine artery crossing / ‘water under the bridge’ (most common).
The peritoneum covering the uterine fundus
All the connective tissue and ligaments surrounding the uterus, between the uterus and the lateral pelvic wall

Parametrium is the collective term for the connective tissue and ligaments (including the cardinal ligament, carrying the uterine artery and ureter) between the uterus/cervix and the lateral pelvic wall — the tissue whose extent of removal defines the Piver-Rutledge hysterectomy types.
In a Type 1 (simple/total abdominal) hysterectomy, the uterine artery is clamped:
At its origin from the internal iliac artery
At the level of the internal os
At the site where the ureteric branch is given off
Type 1 hysterectomy clamps the uterine artery at the level of the internal os, without removing the parametrium.
Which type of hysterectomy removes the COMPLETE cardinal and uterosacral ligaments along with the upper two-thirds of the vagina?
Type 3 (radical) hysterectomy removes the complete cardinal and uterosacral ligaments and the upper two-thirds of the vagina, clamping the uterine artery at its origin.
Highest risk of ureteric injury among the three types
Type 2 (Wertheim's/modified radical) hysterectomy carries the highest per-procedure risk of ureteric injury of the three types.

Although Wertheim’s hysterectomy carries the highest per-procedure risk of ureteric injury, which type is the most common OVERALL cause of ureteric injury, simply because it is performed so much more often?
Type 1 (simple) hysterectomy is both the most commonly performed hysterectomy and, consequently, the most common overall cause of ureteric injury.
In Type 2 and Type 3 hysterectomy, which structures are additionally removed compared with Type 1, besides the uterus and cervix?
Types 2 and 3 both remove the fallopian tubes and ovaries along with the uterus and cervix, in addition to parametrial tissue, vaginal cuff, and lymph nodes.
Comparing all three Piver-Rutledge types, which is the ONLY one in which pelvic lymph nodes are NOT removed?
None — all three remove lymph nodes
Type 1 (simple) hysterectomy does not remove pelvic lymph nodes; both Type 2 and Type 3 do.
In Type 2 (Wertheim's) hysterectomy, how much of the vagina is removed, compared with Type 3?
Upper one-third (vs. upper two-thirds in Type 3)
None of the vagina is removed
Type 2 removes the upper one-third of the vagina, while Type 3 (radical) removes the upper two-thirds — alongside a correspondingly larger parametrial and ligament resection.
A supracervical (subtotal) hysterectomy involves removal of:
Only the uterus, with the cervix retained
Supracervical (subtotal) hysterectomy removes only the uterus; the cervix is retained.
Supracervical hysterectomy is particularly indicated in the setting of:
Supracervical hysterectomy, being quicker with less dissection, is a recognised option in the setting of postpartum haemorrhage.
Radical hysterectomy with lymph node dissection
Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH+BSO)
Panhysterectomy = TAH + BSO: total abdominal hysterectomy plus removal of both fallopian tubes and ovaries.
In a straightforward Type 1 (simple) hysterectomy, are the ovaries routinely removed?
No — they are only removed if there is a specific added indication, such as increased ovarian cancer risk
Yes, but only the left ovary
Simple hysterectomy does not routinely remove the ovaries; BSO is added only for a specific indication, converting it to a panhysterectomy (TAH+BSO).
Compared with abdominal hysterectomy, vaginal hysterectomy allows a shorter return to normal activity, but is generally limited to a uterine size up to about:
Vaginal hysterectomy is generally feasible for a uterus up to about 16–18 weeks in size; abdominal hysterectomy can accommodate any size.
A recognised disadvantage of laparoscopic hysterectomy, relative to open abdominal surgery, is:
Difficulty judging the extent of thermal injury, and lack of haptic feedback
Inability to remove any uterine size
Laparoscopic hysterectomy has a shorter recovery and smaller incisions, but carries the specific disadvantages of hard-to-judge thermal spread and no haptic feedback.
Which of these is an advantage specific to robotic hysterectomy?
3-D visualisation with scaled, more precise instrument movement
Lower overall cost than laparoscopic surgery
Robotic surgery offers 3-D views, motion scaling, and more precise movement with 7 degrees of freedom — traded off against high cost and no haptic feedback.
During an ABDOMINAL hysterectomy, which ligament/pedicle is clamped FIRST, working superior to inferior?
Round ligament, fallopian tube, and ovarian ligament pedicle
The abdominal approach clamps superior to inferior: round ligament/tube/ovarian pedicle first, then the uterine artery, then the cardinal ligament, then the uterosacral ligament.
During a VAGINAL hysterectomy the clamping order is essentially reversed. Which structure is clamped FIRST, working inferior to superior?
Vaginal hysterectomy clamps inferior to superior, starting with the uterosacral ligament, then the cardinal ligament, then the uterine artery, then the round ligament/tube/ovarian pedicle last.
Type 1 hysterectomy, also known as simple/total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH), is notable for being:
The most commonly performed hysterectomy overall, mainly for benign lesions
The type with the highest per-procedure ureteric injury risk
Type 1 (simple/TAH) is the most commonly performed hysterectomy overall, typically for benign lesions.
In Type 2 (Wertheim’s/modified radical) hysterectomy, the parametrium removed is specifically described as:
The complete cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
The medial half of the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
Only the uterosacral ligament, sparing the cardinal ligament
Type 2 hysterectomy removes the medial half of the cardinal ligament (CL) and uterosacral ligament (USL), compared to complete removal in Type 3.
In Type 2 (Wertheim’s) hysterectomy, the uterine artery is clamped at:
The site where the ureteric branch is given off
The level of the internal os
Its origin from the internal iliac artery
The level of the external os
Type 2 hysterectomy clamps the uterine artery at the site where the ureteric branch is given off, an intermediate level compared to Type 1 (internal os) and Type 3 (origin).

In the standard order of clamping during abdominal hysterectomy, the round ligament, fallopian tube, and ovarian ligament pedicle are clamped first; however, if oophorectomy is also indicated, this first step is modified to instead clamp at the:
If oophorectomy is indicated, the first clamp is placed at the infundibulopelvic ligament instead of the round ligament/tube/ovarian ligament pedicle, to also secure the ovarian vessels.
A disadvantage of robotic hysterectomy, beyond lack of haptic feedback and high cost, is that the bulky device:
Limits the movements of surgical assistants
Increases the risk of thermal bowel injury specifically
Requires a larger abdominal incision than open surgery
The bulky robotic device can limit the movements of surgical assistants around the patient.
Fossa navicularis is the depression located between which two structures?
Fossa navicularis is the shallow depression between the introitus and the fourchette.
The labia minora differ from the labia majora in that they contain:
Sebaceous glands only, with no hair, sweat, or apocrine glands
Unlike the labia majora (which has hair, sweat, sebaceous, and apocrine glands plus fat), the labia minora contain only sebaceous glands and no hair follicles.
The round ligament attaches to which part of the labia majora?
It does not attach to the labia majora
The round ligament terminates at the anterior one-third of the labia majora, after passing through the inguinal canal.
The clitoris is best described as:
A remnant of the mesonephric duct
Highly vascular erectile tissue, 1.5–2 cm long
The clitoris is highly vascular erectile tissue, normally about 1.5 to 2 cm in length.
Hart's line marks the junction between:
Keratinized (lateral) and non-keratinized (medial) epithelium of the labia minora
Hart's line divides the labia minora into a medial non-keratinized zone and a lateral keratinized zone.
The most common site for vulval cancer is:
The labia majora is the most common site for vulval cancer, more often than the area near Hart’s line.
The vestibule's boundaries are anterior = clitoris, posterior = fourchette, and lateral =
The labia minora form the lateral boundaries of the vestibule.
In the vestibule, the paraurethral (Skene's) gland ducts open on either side of which structure?
Of the vestibule's six openings, the paraurethral (Skene's) ducts open on either side of the urethral opening.
The Bartholin duct openings in the vestibule are located:
On either side of the urethra
On either side of, and posterior to, the introitus
The Bartholin duct openings sit posterolateral to the introitus, at roughly the 4 and 8 o’clock positions.
A hymen with multiple small sieve-like openings is called:
A cribriform hymen has multiple small, sieve-like openings, distinct from the single opening (annular), the split opening (septate), or the frilly edge (fimbriated) variants.
An imperforate hymen presents at puberty with which classic problem?
Cyclical pain without menstrual outflow, as blood cannot exit
With no outflow tract, an imperforate hymen causes cyclical pain from trapped menstrual blood (haematocolpos), without visible bleeding.
Pubarche (development of pubic hair) occurs due to androgen exposure and corresponds to which Tanner stage?
Pubarche corresponds to Tanner stage 3 of pubic hair development.
Hidradenoma of the vulva is a tumour of which structure, typically located on the labia majora?
Hidradenoma is a tumour arising from vulval sweat glands, characteristically on the labia majora.
Clitoromegaly is defined as clitoral length of:
Clitoromegaly is defined as a clitoral length of 4 cm or more.
Clitoromegaly noted AT BIRTH is most often due to:
Clitoromegaly present at birth reflects intrauterine androgen exposure, whereas clitoromegaly appearing at puberty reflects excessive androgens at that later stage.
A cyst located adjacent to the urethra is most likely a:
A paraurethral (Skene’s) gland cyst characteristically sits adjacent to the urethra.
A cyst found on the lateral wall of the vagina is characteristic of:
Gartner’s cysts arise on the lateral vaginal wall, from remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct.
Between the labia minora and majora, in the vestibule, outside the introitus
A Bartholin’s cyst forms between the labia minora and majora, within the vestibule, outside the introitus, at the site of the blocked gland/duct.
Gartner's cyst is a remnant of which embryological structure?
Gartner’s duct cysts are remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, which normally regresses in females.
The Bartholin gland is also known as the:
The Bartholin gland is also called the greater vestibular gland.
The Bartholin gland duct normally opens at which clock positions in the vestibule?
The Bartholin duct openings sit at the 4 and 8 o’clock positions in the vestibule, outside the introitus.
The Bartholin gland's normal function is to:
Produce acidic secretions for vaginal defence
The Bartholin gland produces alkaline secretions during intercourse, aiding lubrication.
An asymptomatic Bartholin's cyst under 3 cm is best managed by:
Incision and drainage with Word catheter
Small (<3 cm), asymptomatic Bartholin’s cysts are managed conservatively; larger asymptomatic cysts (>3 cm) warrant incision and drainage with Word catheter placement.
For a symptomatic Bartholin's cyst, incision and drainage is followed by insertion of a Word catheter mainly to:
Prevent recurrence by allowing epithelialisation of a new tract
The Word catheter is left in place for several weeks to allow a new epithelialised tract to form, reducing the chance of recurrence after drainage.
A recurrent Bartholin's cyst in a woman aged 40 or older (or postmenopausal) should be managed by:
Excision of the cyst with biopsy
In women 40 or older, recurrent Bartholin’s cysts are excised with biopsy to rule out Bartholin gland cancer; marsupialisation is preferred for recurrence under age 40.
Which of these is an indication for biopsy of an enlarged Bartholin gland?
A postmenopausal woman with an enlarged Bartholin gland
A cyst that resolves with conservative management
An enlarged Bartholin gland in a postmenopausal woman is a specific indication for biopsy, alongside a solid mass, a fixed cyst lining, or recurrence at age 40+.
The most common histological type of Bartholin gland cancer is:
Adenocarcinoma is the most common histological type of Bartholin gland cancer, typically occurring in postmenopausal women.
The fourchette is defined as the point where:
The fourchette is the point where the labia minora meet posteriorly.
The posterior commissure is defined as the point where:
The mons pubis meets the clitoris
The posterior commissure is the point where the labia majora meet posteriorly (distinct from the fourchette, which is where the labia minora meet).
The normal (non-enlarged) length of the clitoris is approximately:
The normal clitoris measures approximately 1.5–2 cm in length.
The clitoris is enclosed by the prepuce above and the ___ below.
The clitoris is enclosed by the prepuce above and the frenulum below.
The mons pubis is best described as:
The area between the labia minora
The junction of keratinized and non-keratinized epithelium
The hair-bearing area above the pubic symphysis
The mons pubis is the hair-bearing area located above the pubic symphysis.
After labia majora, the second most common site for vulval cancer is:
Labia majora is the most common site for vulval cancer, followed by the area along Hart's line.
A hymen with a dividing band of tissue splitting the vaginal opening into two is called:
A septate hymen has a septum dividing the vaginal opening into two openings.
A hymen with a frilly, fringed edge is termed:
A fimbriated hymen has a frilly/fringed edge and is a normal anatomical variant.
The Bartholin gland is located at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the labia, within the:
The Bartholin gland lies at the junction of the anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 of the labia, within the superficial perineal pouch.
Easily palpable as a firm nodule
A normal Bartholin gland is not palpable on examination.
The Bartholin gland ducts run in which direction before opening into the vestibule?
The Bartholin gland ducts course medially and forward before opening in the vestibule.
A Bartholin’s cyst classically presents as:
A rapidly growing painful mass with fever
An intermittent, painless, unilateral mass that enlarges during intercourse
Bartholin’s cyst classically presents as an intermittent painless unilateral mass, which enlarges during intercourse and may cause dyspareunia.
For a recurrent Bartholin’s cyst in a woman under age 40, the preferred management is:
Excision of the cyst with biopsy
In women under 40, recurrent Bartholin’s cysts are managed with marsupialisation; excision with biopsy is reserved for age ≥ 40 or postmenopausal women.
Unlike the painless Bartholin’s cyst, a Bartholin abscess presents with pain, induration, and:
A Bartholin abscess presents with pain, induration, and a warm, tender swelling — distinguishing it from the painless cyst.
The management of a Bartholin abscess is:
Conservative management alone, regardless of size
Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter
A Bartholin abscess is managed with incision and drainage, followed by insertion of a Word catheter to prevent recurrence.
Besides recurrence at age ≥ 40 and being postmenopausal, other indications for biopsy of an enlarged Bartholin gland include a solid mass and:
Cyst lining fixed to surrounding structures
A cyst under 1 cm in size
Fixation of the cyst lining to surrounding structures, along with a solid mass, are indications for biopsy.
Bartholin gland cancer typically occurs in which age group?
Bartholin gland cancer typically occurs in postmenopausal females.
The diagnostic criteria used for Bartholin gland cancer are known as the:
The Honan criteria are used for diagnosing Bartholin gland cancer.
The most common presenting symptom of Bartholin gland cancer is:
A vulval mass is the most common presenting symptom of Bartholin gland cancer.
The normal lymphatic drainage pathway of the vulva proceeds:
Deep inguinal → superficial inguinal → pelvic nodes
Pelvic → superficial inguinal → deep inguinal nodes
Superficial inguinal → deep inguinal → pelvic (external iliac) nodes
Directly from vulva to pelvic nodes in all cases
Vulval lymphatics normally drain superficial inguinal → deep inguinal → pelvic (external iliac) nodes in sequence.
The sentinel lymph node in vulval cancer is defined as:
The first lymph node to receive drainage from the tumour
A node found only on frozen section
The sentinel node is simply the first node in the drainage pathway to receive lymphatic flow (and potential metastasis) from the tumour.
Which dye/tracer combination is used for sentinel lymph node biopsy in vulval cancer?
Isosulphan blue dye and/or radiolabelled technetium-99 are used to identify the sentinel node in vulval cancer.
Clitoral lymphatics characteristically bypass the superficial inguinal nodes and drain directly to:
The lymph node of Cloquet (a femoral node)
Clitoral lymphatics can bypass the superficial inguinal nodes, draining directly to the lymph node of Cloquet.
A vulval tumour arising less than 2 cm from the midline (e.g. clitoris, fourchette, perineum) requires which lymph node dissection strategy, since its lymphatics cross to the opposite side?
Pelvic dissection only, sparing the groin
Midline structures (<2 cm from midline) have crossing lymphatics, so bilateral inguinofemoral dissection is required.
A tumour of the labia majora, more than 2 cm from the midline, has lymphatics that:
Always cross to the opposite side
Do not cross the midline, so unilateral dissection may be appropriate
Drain only to the pelvic nodes
Lateral structures (>2 cm from midline, e.g. labia majora) have lymphatics that do not cross the midline, so unilateral dissection may suffice.
Vulval cancer accounts for roughly what proportion of gynaecological cancers, with a mean age at diagnosis of about 65?
Vulval cancer makes up about 3–4% of gynaecological cancers, most common between ages 50–70 (mean 65).
The most common histological type of vulval cancer is:
Squamous cell carcinoma is by far the most common histological type of vulval cancer.
The second most common histological type of vulval cancer, after squamous cell carcinoma, is:
Melanoma is the second most common vulval cancer type, ahead of adenocarcinoma.
Which of these is NOT a recognised risk factor for vulval (squamous) cancer?
Herpes simplex virus is specifically noted as NOT a risk factor for vulval cancer, unlike HPV, lichen sclerosis, and VIN.
Condyloma acuminata (HPV-related genital warts) is a risk factor for vulval cancer, unlike:
Condyloma lata (a manifestation of secondary syphilis) is NOT a risk factor, in contrast to condyloma acuminata, which is HPV-related and IS a risk factor.
The most common presenting symptom of vulval cancer is:
Pruritus (itching) is the most common presenting symptom of vulval cancer, ahead of a mass/ulcer or pain.
The keratinising type of vulval SCC (about 60% of cases) is typically seen in older women (65–70) and is associated with:
Keratinising-type vulval SCC is linked to lichen sclerosis and differentiated VIN, is not HPV-driven, and is typically unifocal.
The warty type of vulval SCC (about 40% of cases) is typically seen in slightly younger women (55–60) and is associated with:
Warty-type vulval SCC is HPV-driven, arising from undifferentiated VIN, and is typically multifocal.
Which subtype of vulval SCC is characteristically multifocal, versus the other, which is typically unifocal?
The warty (HPV-driven) type is typically multifocal, while the keratinising type is typically unifocal.
In FIGO staging of vulval cancer, Stage I disease (tumour restricted to the vulva) is subdivided based on which two features?
Size (≤2 cm) and depth of invasion (≤1 mm)
Stage IA is ≤2 cm AND ≤1 mm depth of invasion; Stage IB is >2 cm OR >1 mm depth — a biopsy is required to assess this depth.
Stage III vulval cancer is defined by:
Tumour confined to the vulva alone
Stage III vulval cancer is defined by inguinofemoral lymph node involvement.
Which of these findings would classify vulval cancer as Stage IV?
Tumour size 3 cm with clear margins
Isolated inguinofemoral node involvement without fixation
Depth of invasion of 1.5 mm alone
Stage IV includes fixed/ulcerated groin nodes, pelvic node involvement, upper 2/3 vaginal/urethral/rectal involvement, or distant metastasis.
When a vulval growth is clearly visible, biopsy is best obtained using:
Excisional biopsy of the entire lesion only
A visible growth is sampled with Key's forceps or a wedge biopsy.
When no discrete growth is visible, but an area of vulva appears hypo/hyperpigmented or atrophied, the next step is:
A vulvoscopy-directed biopsy is used to evaluate abnormal-appearing vulval skin when no discrete growth is visible.
Stage IA vulval cancer (≤2 cm, depth ≤1 mm) is managed by:
Wide local excision with a 2 cm tumour-free margin
Stage IA disease is managed with wide local excision and a 2 cm tumour-free margin, without routine lymph node dissection.
Stage III and Stage IV vulval cancer are generally managed with:
Advanced (Stage III–IV) vulval cancer is generally managed with chemoradiation.
After radical vulval surgery, a large raw area combined with lymphoedema leads to prolonged immobility, raising the risk of:
Prolonged post-operative immobility from a large raw area and lymphoedema increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis.
When groin lymph nodes are PALPABLE and found positive for vulval cancer on frozen section, the recommended management is:
No dissection, proceed straight to chemoradiation
Palpable nodes positive on frozen section are managed with bilateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection.
If palpable groin nodes are negative for vulval cancer on frozen section, they should be managed:
With observation alone, no further workup
Palpable nodes that prove negative on frozen section are then managed following the same algorithm as non-palpable nodes.
For NON-palpable groin nodes, Stage IA disease WITHOUT lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) requires:
No lymph node dissection at all
Stage IA disease without LVSI carries minimal nodal risk, so no lymph node dissection is required.
For non-palpable nodes in any stage OTHER than IA, the recommended step is:
Bilateral dissection only if nodes are enlarged
Ipsilateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection or sentinel node biopsy
Beyond Stage IA, non-palpable nodes are evaluated with ipsilateral inguinofemoral dissection or sentinel node biopsy.
If ipsilateral node dissection/biopsy is positive on frozen section, the next step is:
Contralateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection (bilateral overall)
Switch directly to chemoradiation without further surgery
A positive ipsilateral result prompts contralateral inguinofemoral dissection too, making the procedure bilateral overall.
Unilateral-only groin dissection (when ipsilateral nodes are negative) is appropriate only if ALL of the following are met EXCEPT:
Tumour at least 2 cm from the midline
No local extension of the tumour
The three conditions for unilateral-only dissection are: tumour <2 cm, ≥2 cm from midline, and no local extension. LVSI is not one of the listed conditions.
The key histological difference between VIN and invasive vulval cancer is:
In VIN, the overlying (basement) membrane remains intact; in invasive cancer, it is broken with dysplastic cell spread
Invasive cancer never shows HPV changes
VIN keeps an intact basement membrane; invasive cancer is defined by its breach, allowing dysplastic cells to spread beyond it.
VIN 3 is characterised by dysplasia involving:
Only the lower third of the epithelium
The entire thickness of the epithelium, but without lymphatic or vascular invasion
VIN 3 involves the full thickness of the epithelium (compare VIN 1: lower third; VIN 2: two-thirds) but by definition has no lymphatic or vascular invasion.
VIN in YOUNGER women is typically:
Unrelated to HPV and usually progressive
More likely to progress to invasive cancer than VIN in older women
VIN in younger women is HPV-related, and about 90% regresses spontaneously.
VIN in OLDER women is typically:
Not HPV-related, associated with lichen sclerosis, and more likely to progress to invasive cancer
Identical in behaviour to VIN in younger women
VIN in older women is generally not HPV-related, is linked to lichen sclerosis, and carries a higher risk of progression to invasive cancer.
Within gynaecological cancers, sentinel lymph node biopsy is most established for vulval cancer, followed by:
Vulval cancer has the most established role for SLN biopsy in gynaecology, with cervical cancer next, and its use is now being explored across other gynaecological cancers too.
Outside gynaecology, sentinel lymph node biopsy is also well established in the management of all of the following EXCEPT:
SLN biopsy is well established in breast cancer, penile cancer, and malignant melanoma; testicular cancer is not part of this listed group.
In a small proportion of cases (about 0.5%), vulval lymphatics can bypass the inguinal nodes entirely and drain directly into the:
In about 0.5% of cases, vulval lymphatics drain directly into the pelvic nodes, bypassing the inguinal chain.
While clitoral lymphatics usually bypass the SILN and drain directly to the lymph node of Cloquet, they can rarely bypass both SILN and DILN to enter directly into the:
Rarely, clitoral lymphatics bypass both SILN and DILN, entering directly into the pelvic nodes.
When inguinofemoral lymph nodes are enlarged with clinical suspicion, dissection reveals metastasis in approximately what proportion of cases?
Enlarged, clinically suspicious nodes are positive for metastasis in about 75% of cases on dissection.
When inguinofemoral lymph nodes are NOT enlarged (no clinical suspicion), dissection still reveals micrometastasis in approximately what proportion of cases?
Non-enlarged nodes without clinical suspicion are positive for micrometastasis in about 25% of cases, justifying the staging algorithm for non-palpable nodes.
Comparing the two most common sites for vulval cancer, the ranking is:
Labia majora more common than labia minora
Labia minora more common than labia majora
Clitoris more common than labia majora
Perineum more common than labia majora
The labia majora is more commonly affected than the labia minora in vulval cancer.
Besides pruritus (the most common symptom), vulval cancer can also present with:
A lump, mass, or ulcer in the vulva
Vulval cancer can present with a lump, mass, or ulcer, in addition to pruritus.
Vulval cancer can also present with pain and urinary symptoms, occurring due to:
Pain and urinary symptoms in vulval cancer occur due to urethral involvement.
The predominant route of spread of vulval cancer is lymphatic, with a less common route being:
Vulval cancer spreads mainly via lymphatics, with vascular spread being less common.
Among HPV subtypes implicated in vulval cancer, which is more commonly associated than the other?
HPV 16 is more commonly implicated in vulval cancer than HPV 18 (both also cause cervical cancer).
Although not a general risk factor for vulval SCC, extramammary Paget’s disease of the vulva is specifically a risk factor for:
Squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva
Extramammary Paget’s disease of the vulva is a specific risk factor for adenocarcinoma of the vulva, distinct from the general SCC risk factors.
Stage II vulval cancer is defined by tumour spread to the lower one-third of the urethra, vagina, or:
Stage II vulval cancer involves spread to the lower 1/3rd of the urethra, vagina, or anus (as opposed to Stage IV, which involves the upper 2/3rds or rectum).
The most important prognostic marker in vulval cancer is:
Lymph node involvement is the single most important prognostic marker in vulval cancer.
VIN 1 is characterized by dysplasia involving:
The lower one-third of the epithelium
Only the basal layer, sparing the rest
VIN 1 involves dysplasia of the lower one-third of the epithelium.
VIN 2 is characterized by dysplasia involving:
The lower one-third of the epithelium
The entire epithelium, with no lymphovascular invasion
The entire epithelium, with lymphovascular invasion
VIN 2 involves dysplasia of about two-thirds of the epithelium, an intermediate grade between VIN 1 (lower 1/3rd) and VIN 3 (entire epithelium).
Trans-abdominal sonography (TAS), unlike trans-vaginal sonography (TVS), requires:
TAS requires a full bladder as an acoustic window; TVS does not.
TVS uses a higher frequency than TAS (roughly 5–10 Hz vs 3–5 Hz). What is the trade-off of this higher frequency?
Better resolution but reduced depth of penetration
Worse resolution but greater depth of penetration
Higher-frequency ultrasound gives better resolution but penetrates less deeply — fine for the closer transvaginal view, less suited to transabdominal imaging.
TVS is indicated when the uterus is not palpable per abdomen; TAS is preferred when:
The uterus IS palpable per abdomen
TAS is indicated when the uterus is palpable per abdomen; TVS is used when it is not.
According to newer diagnostic criteria, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound requires unruptured follicles numbering:
The follicle-count threshold for PCOS morphology was raised from ≥18 (older criteria) to ≥20 per ovary in newer criteria.
Ultrasound is the investigation of choice (IOC) for which two things?
Ultrasound is the IOC for diagnosing fibroids and for measuring endometrial thickness.
TVS is technically difficult in cases of vaginal narrowing, such as in:
A virgin patient or a postmenopausal patient
A pregnant patient in the second trimester
A patient with a retroverted uterus
Vaginal narrowing in virgin or postmenopausal patients can make TVS difficult to perform.
MRI is considered the best imaging modality for:
MRI is the best investigation for soft tissue evaluation, and is non-invasive and safe in pregnancy.
The junctional/transitional zone between the endometrium and myometrium, best seen on MRI, is normally:
The normal transitional zone is under 8 mm thick on MRI.
The ovaries are best visualised on which MRI sequence?
Ovaries are best visualised on T2-weighted MRI sequences.
In suspected adenomyosis, MRI supports the diagnosis when the transitional zone measures:
It cannot be assessed on MRI
A transitional zone ≥12 mm on MRI supports a diagnosis of adenomyosis, reflecting endometrial growth into the myometrium.
For Mullerian malformations, which imaging modality is considered the gold standard?
MRI is the gold standard for characterising Mullerian malformations, though 3D USG and combined laparoscopy/hysteroscopy also have roles.
PET scan is the investigation of choice (IOC) for assessing:
PET scan is the IOC for detecting nodal metastasis in ovarian cancer.
For Mullerian malformations, ultrasound serves as:
A co-incidental screening finding, with 3D USG as the investigation of choice among ultrasound modalities
An investigation that cannot detect these at all
Mullerian malformations are often picked up incidentally on routine ultrasound; among ultrasound techniques, 3D USG is the IOC, though MRI remains the overall gold standard.
MRI is used in endometrial carcinoma mainly to assess:
How much myometrium is invaded by tumour
In endometrial carcinoma, MRI is used to assess the depth of myometrial invasion, important for staging.
In cervical cancer, MRI is particularly useful for assessing:
MRI is valuable in cervical cancer for assessing parametrial invasion — involvement of the ligamentous tissue surrounding the uterus — which affects staging and management.
For assessing tubal patency, HSG serves as the investigation of choice, while which procedure is considered the gold standard?
HSG is the IOC for tubal patency, while laparoscopic chromopertubation (direct visualisation of dye spill from the fimbrial ends) is the gold standard.
Mullerian malformation may be picked up as an incidental finding during:
HSG performed for another indication, such as infertility workup
Mullerian malformations are sometimes discovered incidentally on HSG done to investigate infertility or other concerns.
When Mullerian malformation needs to be definitively characterised and other imaging is inconclusive, which combined procedure is used as a last resort?
Combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy, visualising both the exterior and interior of the uterus, is used as a last-resort definitive workup for Mullerian malformation.
In SIS, saline is infused into the uterine cavity via which device?
SIS distends the uterine cavity with saline delivered via a Foley's catheter, then is imaged by TVS.
On ultrasound during SIS, infused saline appears:
Saline appears black (anechoic) on ultrasound, making uterine pathology stand out clearly against it.
SIS is particularly indicated for evaluating:
SIS is indicated to evaluate suspected endometrial polyps and submucous fibroids.
Compared with plain TVS alone, SIS offers:
Better assessment of the ovaries specifically
Better visualisation inside the uterine cavity, since pathology stands out against the black saline background
A way to assess tubal patency, which TVS cannot do
SIS distends the cavity, giving superior visualisation of intracavitary pathology compared with TVS alone.
The dye used for HSG is:
A water-soluble iodinated radio-opaque dye (e.g. Urografin)
HSG uses a water-soluble iodinated radio-opaque dye such as Urografin, followed by serial X-rays.
The cannula classically used to instil dye through the cervix during HSG is the:
The Leech-Wilkinson cannula is the classic instrument used to instil dye during HSG.
HSG is ideally performed during which phase of the cycle, and why?
Late luteal phase, to assess the corpus luteum
Any time, timing does not matter
The pre-ovulatory phase (day 7–10), to avoid disrupting an early pregnancy
HSG is timed to the pre-ovulatory phase (D7–D10) since performing it later risks disrupting an early, unrecognised pregnancy.
Which of these is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to HSG?
Active pelvic infection (along with pregnancy and active genital TB) is a contraindication to HSG.
Why is active genital tuberculosis a contraindication to HSG?
The dye can be neutralised by TB bacilli
Dye forced through the fimbrial end can disseminate the infection
Pushing dye through the fimbrial end under pressure can disseminate active tuberculous infection, so HSG is avoided.
On HSG, a filling defect with a smooth outline is more suggestive of:
Polyps and fibroids classically produce smooth-outlined filling defects on HSG.
Multiple filling defects with irregular margins, described as a 'moth-eaten' appearance on HSG, are characteristic of:
Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) produces multiple irregular, 'moth-eaten' filling defects on HSG.
In a patient with genital tuberculosis presenting with infertility, HSG performed after a course of ATT is used mainly to:
After anti-tubercular treatment, HSG is used to check whether tubal patency has been restored.
A key limitation of HSG is that it:
Cannot be performed as an outpatient
Cannot visualise the exterior of the tubes and uterus
HSG only shows the internal contour/patency of the cavity and tubes — it cannot visualise their exterior surfaces.
A painful HSG procedure can cause cornual spasm, which on the film can be mistaken for:
Pain-induced cornual spasm is a recognised artifact that can mimic a true cornual block on HSG.
CO2 gas as a hysteroscopic distension medium is used only for:
CO2 gas is suitable only for diagnostic hysteroscopy — it cannot be used for therapeutic procedures.
Electrolyte-rich distension media (e.g. normal saline, Ringer's lactate) can be used only with which type of energy instrument?
Electrolyte-rich media conduct electricity, so they can only be used with bipolar instruments (unipolar current would disperse through the fluid).
Electrolyte-DEFICIENT media (e.g. glycine, sorbitol, mannitol) can be used with:
Only mechanical instruments, no energy source
Being non-conductive, electrolyte-deficient media can be used with both unipolar and bipolar instruments, but can lead to uterine perforation and fluid-related complications.
Fluid deficit during hysteroscopy is calculated as:
Total fluid used, regardless of outflow
Amount of fluid that comes out minus amount given
Amount of fluid given minus amount that comes out
A fixed value regardless of case
Fluid deficit = fluid instilled minus fluid recovered, and is closely monitored to avoid fluid overload.
The procedure should be stopped when fluid deficit reaches 1 litre with electrolyte-deficient media. What is the threshold with electrolyte-rich media?
There is no threshold with electrolyte-rich media
The safety threshold is 1 L for electrolyte-deficient media, but higher, at 2.5 L, for electrolyte-rich media.
Except for mannitol, electrolyte-deficient distension media are hypo-osmolar, which can lead to:
Hyponatremia, presenting with delirium and confusion
Absorption of hypo-osmolar electrolyte-deficient media (all except mannitol) can cause dilutional hyponatremia, presenting with delirium and confusion.
Normal intrauterine pressure during hysteroscopy is about 75–80 mmHg. What is the maximum safe pressure?
Intrauterine pressure during hysteroscopy should not exceed 150 mmHg.
Which of these is a contraindication to hysteroscopy, due to increased risk of fluid overload complications?
A history of one prior Caesarean section

Cardiopulmonary disease raises the risk of fluid-overload complications (pulmonary embolism, congestive cardiac failure, pulmonary oedema) during hysteroscopy, alongside pregnancy, pelvic infection, and cervical cancer.
Laparoscopy is considered the investigation of choice for which two conditions?
Laparoscopy is the IOC for endometriosis and for chronic pelvic pain.
Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing:
Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing PID, and laparoscopic chromopertubation is the gold standard for assessing tubal patency.
When HSG shows a bilateral cornual block, combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy is useful mainly to:
Treat the tubal block directly with a stent
Distinguish a true block from cornual spasm, by directly visualising both the exterior and interior
Replace the need for any further imaging

Since a painful HSG can mimic a block via cornual spasm, combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy directly visualises the exterior and interior to distinguish a true bilateral cornual block from this artifact.
The standard patient position for hysteroscopy is:
Hysteroscopy is performed with the patient in the lithotomy position.
For DIAGNOSTIC hysteroscopy, pain relief is typically achieved with:
Diagnostic hysteroscopy is usually done under a paracervical block with 1% xylocaine.
A paracervical block alone, same as diagnostic
Therapeutic hysteroscopy, being longer and more involved, generally requires general or regional anaesthesia rather than a paracervical block alone.
Besides cardiopulmonary disease, which of these is also a contraindication to hysteroscopy?
A single ovarian cyst under 3 cm
Pregnancy, pelvic infection, or cervical cancer
A history of one uncomplicated vaginal delivery
Pregnancy, active pelvic infection, and cervical cancer are all contraindications to hysteroscopy, alongside cardiopulmonary disease.
During laparoscopy, orientation on the screen follows the convention that:
Left and right are always reversed, mirror-image
The patient’s left and right correspond to your own left and right
Only the surgeon’s perspective matters, not a fixed convention
Orientation changes depending on the entry port used
By convention, the patient’s left and right on the laparoscopic view correspond to the viewer’s own left and right.
For Mullerian malformation, while MRI is the gold standard, ultrasound (specifically 3D USG) serves as the:
Investigation of choice for an initial/co-incidental assessment
Only modality that can diagnose it
While MRI is the gold standard for Mullerian malformations, 3D USG serves as the investigation of choice, often picking it up as a co-incidental finding.
Regardless of whether electrolyte-rich or electrolyte-deficient distension media is used, a shared risk during hysteroscopy is:
Both electrolyte-rich and electrolyte-deficient distension media carry a risk of uterine perforation during hysteroscopy.
The Wolffian duct is also known as the:
The Wolffian duct is the mesonephric duct; the Mullerian duct is the paramesonephric duct.
The Mullerian duct arises from invagination of coelomic epithelium; the Wolffian duct arises from:
The Wolffian (mesonephric) duct arises from intermediate mesoderm.
In intrauterine life, which duct develops FIRST and acts as a template for the other duct's formation?
The Wolffian duct develops first and acts as a template guiding Mullerian duct formation.
If the Wolffian duct fails to grow, what happens to the Mullerian duct?
It is also absent, since the Wolffian duct is its template
Because the Mullerian duct forms using the Wolffian duct as a template, failure of Wolffian duct growth leads to absence of the Mullerian duct too.
Mullerian duct anomalies are strongly associated with which other organ system’s anomalies, which should always be ruled out?
Renal anomalies are strongly linked to Mullerian duct anomalies (both derive from nearby structures during development) and should always be screened for.
The bilateral fold of coelomic epithelium carried by the Mullerian ducts goes on to form the:
The peritoneal fold carried alongside the fusing Mullerian ducts forms the broad ligament.
In females, the Mullerian duct forms the internal genital organs by which gestational week, while the Wolffian duct regresses shortly after?
In females, the Mullerian duct forms internal genital organs by 9 weeks, and the Wolffian duct regresses to remnants by 10 weeks (the reverse occurs in males).
All Wolffian duct remnants in the female are located in the:
Epoophoron, paroophoron, and Gartner’s duct — all Wolffian duct remnants — are found within the broad ligament.
The epoophoron is the ___ remnant of the mesonephric tubules, while the paroophoron is the ___ remnant.
The epoophoron is the cranial remnant and the paroophoron the caudal remnant of the mesonephric tubules.
Gartner's duct is a remnant of the:
Gartner's duct is a remnant of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct itself, distinct from the epoophoron/paroophoron (tubule remnants).
Gartner's cyst characteristically presents as a swelling on the:
Gartner's cyst arises along the antero-lateral wall of the vagina, following the course of the regressed Wolffian duct.
Compared with a cystocele, a Gartner's cyst is distinguished by being:
Reducible, with a positive cough impulse
Non-reducible, with an absent cough impulse
Unlike a cystocele (reducible, with cough impulse and preserved rugosities), a Gartner's cyst is non-reducible with no cough impulse.
The absence of vaginal rugosities over a Gartner's cyst is explained by:
Stretching of the vaginal epithelium over the cyst
The cyst being lined by rugae itself
It is a normal finding, unrelated to the cyst
The cyst stretches the overlying vaginal epithelium, effacing the normal rugal folds.
How does a Gartner's cyst differ from a Bartholin's cyst in location?
Both occur at the same site
Bartholin’s cyst is on the vaginal wall; Gartner’s is at the introitus
Gartner's cyst is on the vaginal wall; Bartholin's cyst is outside the vestibule, between the labia
Gartner’s cyst only occurs in the cervix
Gartner's cyst arises on the antero-lateral vaginal wall, while Bartholin's cyst arises outside the vestibule, between the labia minora and majora.
An asymptomatic Gartner's cyst is managed by:
Asymptomatic Gartner’s cysts require no intervention.
A symptomatic Gartner's cyst (e.g. causing difficult intercourse) is managed by:
Symptomatic Gartner’s cysts are managed by surgical removal.
Each of the two Mullerian ducts forms one lateral half of all of the following EXCEPT:
The fallopian tube of that side
The lower two-thirds of the vagina
The upper one-third of the vagina

Each Mullerian duct forms one fallopian tube plus half of the uterus, cervix, and upper one-third of the vagina; the lower two-thirds of the vagina comes from the urogenital sinus, not the Mullerian ducts.
Formation of the Female Genital Tract
The two Mullerian ducts initially lie lateral to the Wolffian ducts, then cross over them to:
Fuse with the urogenital sinus directly
The Mullerian ducts cross the Wolffian ducts and meet each other in the midline, led initially by the left duct.
Formation of the Female Genital Tract
Fusion of the two Mullerian ducts begins:
At the top (fundus) and proceeds downward
From the middle outward in both directions
Mullerian duct fusion starts inferiorly and proceeds upward.
Formation of the Female Genital Tract
After the Mullerian ducts fuse, a septum forms and then resolves. This septal resorption proceeds:
From below, upward, forming a single uterine cavity
Like the fusion itself, resorption of the intervening septum proceeds from below upward, ultimately forming a single uterine cavity with a dome-shaped fundus.
Formation of the Female Genital Tract
Complete fusion of the Mullerian ducts occurs by about ___ weeks, while the septum fully resolves by about ___ weeks of intrauterine life.
Complete fusion occurs by 10 weeks IUL; the septum resolves and endometrium differentiates by about 18–20 weeks (the 5th month).
Formation of the Female Genital Tract
Which of these structures develops independently of the Mullerian ducts and is therefore unaffected in Mullerian malformations?
The ovaries (from the genital ridge) and the lower one-third of the vagina (from the urogenital sinus)
The ovaries (genital ridge origin) and the lower vagina (urogenital sinus origin) are not Mullerian-derived, so they are spared in Mullerian malformations.
Formation of the Female Genital Tract
Class I Mullerian malformation (Mullerian agenesis) results in absence of the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, while:
Ovaries and ovulation remain normal, since the ovaries are not Mullerian-derived
Since the ovaries arise from the genital ridge (not the Mullerian ducts), ovarian function and ovulation are normal in Mullerian agenesis.
Class II malformation (only one Mullerian duct present) results in a unicornuate uterus with:
Two fallopian tubes and a full-width uterus
One fallopian tube, and the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina each reduced to half
A unicornuate uterus has a single fallopian tube, with the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina each present as only half their normal size.
In a unicornuate uterus with a non-communicating rudimentary horn, which complication is most likely if that horn contains functioning endometrium?
Unilateral dysmenorrhoea, from obstructed menstrual flow
A non-communicating rudimentary horn with functioning endometrium causes obstructed menstrual flow, presenting as unilateral dysmenorrhoea.
A communicating rudimentary horn in a unicornuate uterus specifically raises the risk of:
A communicating rudimentary horn allows sperm/embryo entry, raising the risk of pregnancy implanting within the rudimentary horn — a form of ectopic pregnancy.
On HSG, a unicornuate uterus classically shows:
Bilateral dye spill with a normal-shaped cavity
Single-sided dye spill with a banana-shaped uterine cavity
A unicornuate uterus shows single-sided spilling of dye (from the single fallopian tube) with a curved, banana-shaped cavity on HSG.
Unicornuate uterus is the Mullerian anomaly MOST strongly associated with:
Unicornuate uterus carries the strongest association with renal anomalies among the Mullerian malformations, and is also linked to ipsilateral renal agenesis.
Both Mullerian ducts present but failing to fuse, or fusing only at the vagina
Complete fusion with a persistent septum
Uterus didelphys occurs when both Mullerian ducts develop but fail to fuse (or fuse only in the region of the vagina).
Uterus didelphys typically presents with two complete uterine horns, two cervices, and:
Two vaginas, or occasionally a single vagina
A single fallopian tube shared between horns
Uterus didelphys usually has two vaginas, though the vagina may occasionally be single.
On HSG, uterus didelphys with two cervices requires:
A single cannula, as with a normal uterus
Two Leech-Wilkinson cannulae, one for each external os
Because there are two separate external ossa, two Leech-Wilkinson cannulae are needed to perform HSG in uterus didelphys.
A longitudinal vaginal septum can obstruct one hemivagina. If that side also has renal agenesis, the presentation classically includes:
Hematocolpos with dysmenorrhoea and a pelvic mass, plus ipsilateral renal agenesis
Obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis leads to hematocolpos on the obstructed side, presenting with dysmenorrhoea and a pelvic mass.
Which complication is specifically listed as NOT seen with either unicornuate uterus or uterus didelphys?
Transverse lie is specifically noted as a complication NOT seen with unicornuate uterus or uterus didelphys, unlike bicornuate and septate uterus.
In a bicornuate uterus (Class IV), both Mullerian ducts are present but fusion fails above the level of the:
Cervix (only the cervix and vagina are fused)
Vagina alone, with the cervix also separate
In bicornuate uterus, only the cervix and vagina are fused (single), while the uterine body remains as two separate horns.
The single BEST feature to distinguish a bicornuate uterus from a septate uterus is:
The angle between the uterine horns on HSG
The distance between the horns on HSG
The internal cavity shape on HSG
The external fundal contour — divided (bicornuate) versus smooth (septate)
The external fundal contour is the best differentiator: divided/notched in bicornuate uterus, smooth and normal in septate uterus — something HSG cannot show, since it only images the cavity.
On HSG, the internal cavity shape of bicornuate and septate uteri:
Cannot be reliably differentiated from each other

HSG cannot reliably differentiate bicornuate from septate uterus by cavity shape alone, since both show two separate horns internally; the external fundus (not seen on HSG) is the true distinguishing feature.
On HSG, an obtuse angle (>105°) and wider distance (≥4 cm) between the two uterine horns is more typical of:
Bicornuate uterus tends to show an obtuse inter-horn angle (>105°) and wider horn separation (≥4 cm), versus the acute angle (<75°) and narrower separation (<4 cm) of septate uterus.
In a septate uterus (Class V), the fundus:
Is divided externally, like a bicornuate uterus
Is NOT divided — the uterus appears externally normal, with an internal septum only
Cannot be assessed by any method
In septate uterus, fusion of the Mullerian ducts is complete and the fundus is not divided externally; only the septum (which failed to resolve) persists internally.
Arcuate uterus (Class VI), the mildest Mullerian anomaly, is characterised by a fundus that is:
Not dome-shaped (flat-topped or mildly dimpled), with the best reproductive outcome of all anomalies
Associated with the worst reproductive outcome
Arcuate uterus is the mildest anomaly, with a flat-topped or mildly dimpled fundus, and carries the best reproductive outcome of all the classes.
Diethylstilbestrol (DES) was historically given to pregnant women for which indication?
DES, a synthetic oestrogen, was historically given to women with a history of abortions, but proved teratogenic to the fetus.
The most common structural defect caused by in-utero DES exposure in a female fetus is:
Vaginal adenosis (areas of vagina lined by columnar epithelium)
Vaginal adenosis — columnar epithelium replacing normal squamous lining in patches of the vagina — is the most common DES-related defect.
The most common cancer associated with in-utero DES exposure is:
Clear cell carcinoma of the vagina/cervix
Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
Clear cell carcinoma of the vagina or cervix is the classic cancer risk associated with in-utero DES exposure.
The MOST SPECIFIC uterine finding in DES-exposed women (though a hypoplastic uterus is more common overall) is:
A T-shaped uterine cavity is the most specific (though not the most common) uterine finding associated with DES exposure; a hypoplastic uterus is the more common finding overall.
Unlike most other Mullerian anomalies, DES-related anomalies in FEMALE offspring are notably NOT associated with:

DES-exposed women have increased risks of breast cancer and premature menopause, and can develop cervical hoods/collars — but, unlike typical Mullerian fusion anomalies, are NOT particularly associated with renal anomalies.
In MALE fetuses exposed to DES in-utero, recognised complications include cryptorchidism, testicular hypoplasia, hypospadias, microphallus, and:

In male fetuses, DES exposure is linked to cryptorchidism, testicular hypoplasia, hypospadias, microphallus, and renal anomalies — note that renal anomalies ARE seen here, unlike in DES-exposed females.
The most common Mullerian anomaly overall is:
Septate uterus is the most common Mullerian anomaly, ahead of bicornuate uterus.
The most common overall presentation of Mullerian anomalies is:
Recurrent abortion is the most common presenting complaint across Mullerian anomalies.
Comparing reproductive outcomes, which pairing correctly ranks best to worst?
Arcuate best (better than uterus didelphys), septate worst
Arcuate uterus has the best reproductive outcome (better even than uterus didelphys), while septate uterus has the worst.
The Mullerian anomaly most strongly associated with renal anomalies is:
Unicornuate uterus carries the strongest association with renal anomalies (and with obstructed hemivagina) among Mullerian malformations.
Increased risk of renal anomalies is seen with essentially all Mullerian malformations EXCEPT:
Arcuate uterus, being the mildest anomaly, is the exception with no increased renal anomaly risk.
Recurrent abortion due to Mullerian anomaly most commonly occurs during which trimester?
Second-trimester loss is the most common timing for Mullerian-anomaly-related recurrent abortion.
Which specific Mullerian anomaly is most associated with FIRST-trimester abortion (as opposed to the second-trimester pattern typical of most anomalies)?
Septate uterus, with its poor vascularity septum, is specifically associated with first-trimester abortion, alongside being the anomaly most associated with recurrent abortion overall.
Ectopic pregnancy as a complication of Mullerian anomaly is most associated with:
Unicornuate uterus (in a communicating rudimentary horn)
Ectopic (rudimentary horn) pregnancy is most associated with unicornuate uterus.
Preterm labour due to altered uterine shape is most associated with:
Bicornuate uterus’s altered shape is particularly linked to preterm labour.
Breech presentation is most commonly associated with which anomaly, ahead of septate and bicornuate uterus?
Uterus didelphys is the most common anomaly associated with breech presentation, ahead of septate and bicornuate uterus; Mullerian malformations overall are the most common cause of recurrent breech.
Transverse lie in a Mullerian anomaly is associated with septate and bicornuate uterus, but is specifically NOT seen in:
Transverse lie is a recognised complication of septate and bicornuate uterus, but is specifically absent in unicornuate uterus and uterus didelphys.
In Mullerian anomalies with outflow tract obstruction, the typical sequence of complications proceeds:
Obstructed outflow leads first to hematometra (blood collection), which can then lead to endometriosis via retrograde menstruation.
Unilateral dysmenorrhoea in a Mullerian anomaly is classically associated with:
Uterus didelphys with two patent vaginas
Unilateral dysmenorrhoea points to an obstructed non-communicating horn, as seen in unicornuate uterus.
Although infertility from Mullerian anomalies is relatively rare, the anomaly most associated with it is:
Septate uterus is the anomaly most associated with infertility, though infertility overall is an uncommon presentation of Mullerian anomalies (often a co-incidental finding on HSG).
On routine clinical examination, Mullerian anomalies are generally not detectable, EXCEPT:
Septate uterus, felt as a midline ridge
Arcuate uterus, felt as a flattened fundus
Uterus didelphys, where two vaginas may be found
Bicornuate uterus, felt as two separate cervices
Clinical examination is generally unhelpful for Mullerian anomalies, except in uterus didelphys, where two vaginas may be found on exam.
As a first (screening) investigation, Mullerian anomalies are often picked up as a co-incidental finding on TVS done for recurrent abortions, or on HSG done for:
Mullerian anomalies are commonly co-incidental findings on TVS (done to work up recurrent abortion) or HSG (done to work up infertility).
Ranking the investigation pathway for Mullerian anomalies from initial screening to definitive last-resort workup:
3D USG (IOC) → MRI (gold standard) → combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy (last resort)

3D USG is the investigation of choice, MRI is the gold standard for full characterisation, and combined laparoscopy plus hysteroscopy is reserved as a last resort to directly visualise the exterior and interior.
Surgical correction of Mullerian anomalies (e.g. unification surgery for bicornuate uterus) is generally indicated for:
Recurrent abortion is the main indication for surgical correction of a Mullerian anomaly such as bicornuate uterus.
Unification surgery (metroplasty) for bicornuate uterus is known as Strassman metroplasty or:
Strassman metroplasty and Tompkin's metroplasty are both unification procedures for bicornuate uterus (the same surgery can also be used for uterus didelphys).
For a septate uterus, the modern surgical approach is:
Septate uterus is treated by hysteroscopic resection of the septum; the older abdominal approach was Jones metroplasty.
A recognised disadvantage of metroplasty is that it:
Improves fertility in all cases with no risks
Cannot be performed at all in modern practice
Requires delivery by Caesarean section and risks pelvic adhesions leading to infertility
Always requires removal of the ovaries
After metroplasty, subsequent delivery must be by Caesarean section, and the procedure risks pelvic adhesion formation, which can itself cause infertility.
Besides unilateral dysmenorrhoea, ectopic pregnancy, and unilateral renal anomalies, unicornuate uterus can also be associated with:
Unicornuate uterus can be associated with an ectopic ovary, in addition to unilateral dysmenorrhoea, ectopic pregnancy, and unilateral renal anomalies.
Complete Coverage: Mullerian Anomaly & DES Details
While a T-shaped uterus is the most SPECIFIC uterine finding in DES exposure, the most COMMON uterine finding is:
Hypoplastic uterus is the most common uterine finding in DES exposure, while T-shaped uterus is the most specific (though less common) finding.
Complete Coverage: Mullerian Anomaly & DES Details
In-utero DES exposure can lead to cervical abnormalities described as:
DES exposure can lead to cervical hoods/collars, in addition to vaginal adenosis and uterine anomalies.

Long-term (chronic) outcomes of in-utero DES exposure in females include increased risk of clear cell carcinoma and premature menopause, as well as increased risk of:

Mullerian anomalies carry an increased risk of Caesarean section delivery.

Pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) is another recognised obstetric complication of Mullerian anomalies.

Arcuate uterus, which is always palpably distinct

Bicornuate uterus, which is diagnosed by palpation alone

Clinical examination is generally not useful for Mullerian anomalies, except in uterus didelphys, which can show two vaginas/cervices on examination.
