The upper one-third of the vagina develops from the caudal fused part of the Mullerian duct, with which tissue origin?
The Mullerian-derived upper vagina is mesodermal in origin, forming the fibromuscular wall.
The lower two-thirds of the vagina develops from the sinovaginal bulb (from the urogenital sinus), with which tissue origin?
Mesenchymal only, with no epithelial contribution
The sinovaginal bulb is endodermal in origin, forming the epithelium of the lower vagina.
Where the upper and lower parts of the developing vagina meet, they initially form a:
A transverse vaginal septum forms transiently where the upper (Mullerian) and lower (sinovaginal bulb) parts meet.
The transverse septum formed during vaginal development normally dissolves by about:
The transverse septum normally dissolves by 20 weeks IUL, giving a single canalised vaginal canal.
Canalisation of the vagina is complete throughout its length EXCEPT at the:
Distal end, where the sinovaginal bulb meets the urogenital sinus proper (forming the hymen)
It is always complete with no exceptions
The distal-most point, where the sinovaginal bulb tissue meets the urogenital sinus proper, remains as a membrane — the hymen — which has an opening for menstrual outflow.
Both the hymen and the vagina share which epithelial lining?
Both the hymen and vagina are lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
Vaginal agenesis (complete absence of the vagina) is strongly associated with:
Vaginal agenesis is a rare condition strongly associated with Mullerian agenesis.
A key symptom pattern in vaginal agenesis is:
Painless amenorrhoea with no other symptoms
Cyclical abdominal pain WITHOUT visible menstruation (cryptomenorrhoea)
Vaginal agenesis presents with hidden menstruation and cyclical pain from outflow obstruction, without visible external bleeding, and an absent vaginal opening on exam.
A longitudinal vaginal septum (creating a hemivagina) is associated with:
A longitudinal vaginal septum, creating a hemivagina, is associated with uterus didelphys.
Complete absence of the sinovaginal bulb
Failure of resolution of the septum formed where upper and lower vagina meet
Transverse vaginal septum is caused by failure of the normal septum (formed at the junction of the Mullerian- and sinovaginal-bulb-derived vagina) to resolve.
Imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum share which common presenting complaint?
Both imperforate hymen and TVS present with outflow tract obstruction (cryptomenorrhoea).
The most common cause of cryptomenorrhoea (hidden menstruation) is:
Imperforate hymen is the most common cause of cryptomenorrhoea, ahead of transverse vaginal septum and vaginal agenesis.
A young woman presenting with primary amenorrhoea, cyclical pelvic pain, and urinary retention, but normal secondary sexual characteristics, should raise suspicion for:
An outflow tract obstruction such as imperforate hymen
Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea points to a purely anatomical outflow obstruction, not a hormonal or gonadal problem.
In cryptomenorrhoea, retrograde menstruation through the tubes increases the risk of developing:
Endometriosis, which itself causes dysmenorrhoea (the most common symptom)
Outflow obstruction promotes retrograde menstrual flow, raising the risk of endometriosis, whose most common symptom is dysmenorrhoea.
Blood collecting in the vagina (from outflow obstruction) is called:
Hematocolpos refers to blood collection within the vagina.
Blood collecting within the fallopian tube, from severe or prolonged outflow obstruction, is called:
Hematosalpinx refers to blood collection within the fallopian tube, the most proximal (and least common) site of collection in outflow obstruction.
In cryptomenorrhoea, the karyotype, gonads (ovaries), breast development, and axillary/pubic hair are all normal, because:
The problem is purely anatomical (outflow obstruction), not hormonal or gonadal
The ovaries are also affected but compensate
Cryptomenorrhoea from outflow obstruction is a purely structural problem; the 46,XX karyotype, ovaries, and secondary sexual characteristics are entirely normal.
Besides primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pelvic pain, cryptomenorrhoea from outflow obstruction can also present with:
Urinary retention, from pressure on the bladder/urethra
The distended, blood-filled vagina/uterus can press on the bladder and urethra, causing urinary retention alongside the classic cyclical pain and amenorrhoea.
Comparing site of obstruction: imperforate hymen occurs at the introitus, while transverse vaginal septum most commonly occurs:
In the upper part of the vagina
TVS most commonly occurs in the upper part of the vagina, well above the introitus.
On local examination, imperforate hymen classically shows a tense, bulging (sometimes bluish) hymen, whereas TVS typically shows:
A hymen that is completely absent
No bulging, because the thick fibrous septum lies higher up
With TVS, the hymen itself appears normal (no bulging) since the obstruction and thick fibrous septum lie further up the vaginal canal.
A positive cough impulse at the introitus is expected with:
Imperforate hymen shows a positive cough impulse at the introitus; TVS does not, since the obstruction is further up.
Hematometra (blood collection in the uterus) is:
Less common with TVS than with imperforate hymen
More common with transverse vaginal septum than with imperforate hymen
Hematometra is more common with TVS (less common with imperforate hymen), reflecting the septum’s more proximal location allowing collection to back up further.
Usually NOT associated with imperforate hymen, but must be ruled out with TVS
Urinary tract abnormalities are not typically linked to imperforate hymen, but TVS mandates renal imaging to rule them out.
MRI is considered essential in TVS to determine site, thickness, and rule out renal abnormalities, whereas in imperforate hymen, MRI is:
Imperforate hymen is usually a clinical diagnosis and does not require MRI, unlike TVS, where MRI is mandatory pre-operatively.
Management of imperforate hymen is a cruciate incision, while management of transverse vaginal septum is:
TVS requires surgical resection/excision of the septum, a more extensive procedure than the simple cruciate incision used for imperforate hymen.
In cryptomenorrhoea from outflow obstruction, hormonal profile (FSH, LH, oestrogen) is:
Not needed, since these levels are normal
Since the ovaries and hormonal axis are unaffected, hormonal profile testing is not needed in outflow-obstruction cryptomenorrhoea.
The first investigation for a suspected outflow tract obstruction is:
USG pelvis, to confirm the uterus is present and assess for hematometra/hematocolpos
USG pelvis is the first investigation, confirming uterine presence and assessing for hematometra/hematocolpos.
MRI is the investigation of choice mainly to:
Differentiate between imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum
Replace ultrasound as the first-line test
MRI’s main role here is to reliably differentiate imperforate hymen from TVS when the diagnosis is unclear.
In the work-up of a suprapubic bulge, catheterising the bladder and finding the bulge decreases in size indicates the swelling was:
If catheterisation reduces the bulge, the swelling was simply due to a full bladder.
If a suprapubic bulge persists despite catheterisation, the next step is:
USG pelvis to look for hematometra, with MRI if still in doubt
Reassurance, as this is a normal finding
A persistent bulge after catheterisation points to uterine swelling; USG pelvis is used to check for hematometra, with MRI reserved for cases still in doubt.
On examination of suspected outflow tract obstruction, per vaginal examination is:
Contraindicated in a virgin patient; per rectal exam is used instead, which may reveal an anterior swelling
PV exam is avoided in a virgin patient with suspected outflow obstruction; per rectal exam is used instead and may reveal an anterior swelling from the collected blood.
Using the local examination algorithm for outflow obstruction: an ABSENT introitus points toward vaginal agenesis, while a PRESENT introitus with no visible opening points toward:
A normal finding requiring no further workup
With the introitus present but no opening visible, imperforate hymen is the likely diagnosis; if a septum is felt through a present, open introitus, TVS is suspected instead.
The most common site for a transverse vaginal septum is the:
Lower part of the vagina, at the introitus
A transverse vaginal septum most commonly occurs in the upper part of the vagina, unlike imperforate hymen which obstructs right at the introitus.

The location of hematocolpos differs by condition: with imperforate hymen it collects in the lower vagina, while with transverse vaginal septum it collects in the:
Hematocolpos collects in the lower vagina with imperforate hymen, but in the upper vagina with transverse vaginal septum, reflecting the different obstruction sites.

At puberty, GnRH is released from the hypothalamus in which pattern?
A single large surge only at menarche
GnRH is released in a pulsatile manner from the hypothalamus, driving the HPO axis.
Which hormone is considered the initiator of the ovarian cycle?
FSH, released from the anterior pituitary in response to GnRH, is the initiator of the ovarian cycle.
The primary oocyte remains arrested in which stage until ovulation?
Primary oocytes are arrested in the diplotene (dictyate) stage of prophase I from fetal life until ovulation.
The earliest follicle stage, with a single layer of flat follicular cells, is the:
The primordial follicle has a single layer of flat follicular cells around the oocyte.
A follicle with a single layer of cuboidal cells around the oocyte is termed:
The primary follicle is defined by a single layer of cuboidal cells replacing the flattened cells of the primordial stage.
As the follicle differentiates into granulosa and theca cells, which receptors first appear?
FSH receptors appear on granulosa cells as the follicle differentiates, enabling FSH-driven growth.
Follicular growth up to the early pre-antral stage (about 70 days) is:
Early follicular growth, up to the early pre-antral stage, proceeds independently of FSH.
From the late pre-antral stage to the Graafian follicle (about 14 days), follicular growth becomes:
From the late pre-antral stage onward, follicular growth becomes FSH-dependent, culminating in the Graafian follicle after about 14 days.
The total time from primordial follicle to Graafian follicle is approximately:
The full journey from primordial follicle to Graafian follicle takes about 84–85 days (70 FSH-independent + 14 FSH-dependent).
Oestrogen, the main hormone product of granulosa cells, causes proliferation of the uterine endometrium. Giving unopposed oestrogen to a woman with an intact uterus raises the risk of:

Unopposed oestrogen (without progesterone) in a woman with an intact uterus drives endometrial proliferation, raising the risk of hyperplasia and cancer — hence oestrogen is never given alone in this setting.
Inhibin B, released by granulosa cells, provides negative feedback on FSH, causing atresia of all FSH-stimulated follicles EXCEPT:
Follicles in the contralateral ovary only
As FSH falls under inhibin B’s negative feedback, only the dominant follicle (most FSH-sensitive) survives; the rest undergo atresia.
A granulosa cell tumour is a feminising tumour (raised oestrogen) with which classic tumour marker?
Inhibin B is the classic tumour marker for granulosa cell tumours; AMH is a newer marker.
Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), the third hormone released by granulosa cells, is used clinically as a marker of:
AMH, produced by pre-antral and small antral follicles from puberty onward and proportional to follicle number, is used as a test of ovarian reserve.
The LH surge acts on LH receptors on the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle (receptors induced earlier by FSH) to cause:
Luteinisation of the granulosa cells, releasing progesterone
LH luteinises the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle, which then release progesterone — the main hormone of the luteinised follicle.
The LH surge also acts on theca cells, stimulating production of:
Androgens, later converted to oestrogen by granulosa-cell aromatase
LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens, which diffuse to granulosa cells for aromatisation into oestrogen.
Regarding oestrogen subtypes, adipose tissue specifically releases:
Adipose tissue specifically releases oestrone (E1), distinct from ovarian oestradiol (E2).
Ovulation is brought about by the:
Ovulation follows the combined FSH and LH surge but is specifically brought about by the LH surge.
At ovulation, resumption of meiosis I converts the primary oocyte into a:
Resumption of meiosis I at ovulation converts the primary oocyte into a secondary oocyte (plus the first polar body).
The LH surge initiates an oestrogen-dominant phase, which is then maintained by combined oestrogen and progesterone as the luteinised granulosa cells become the:
Luteinised granulosa cells form the corpus luteum, which maintains combined oestrogen and progesterone secretion.
The corpus luteum is typically formed on which day of a standard 28-day cycle?
The corpus luteum forms around day 14, right after ovulation.
Growth and continued activity of the corpus luteum is maintained by:
LH maintains the growth and secretory activity of the corpus luteum.
The corpus luteum reaches maximum activity approximately how many days after ovulation?
Corpus luteum activity peaks about 8 days after ovulation, around day 22 of a standard cycle.
The typical lifespan of the (non-pregnancy) corpus luteum is:
In the absence of pregnancy, the corpus luteum has a lifespan of about 12–16 days before degenerating.
Besides progesterone and oestrogen, the corpus luteum also secretes which hormone that provides negative feedback on FSH?
The corpus luteum secretes inhibin A, which negatively feeds back on FSH (distinct from inhibin B, secreted earlier by growing follicles).
In high concentrations, progesterone provides negative feedback on LH, which eventually causes:
High progesterone suppresses LH via negative feedback, and without adequate LH support, the corpus luteum degenerates.
The first half of the menstrual cycle, dominated by oestrogen, is known as the follicular phase, also called the:
The follicular phase is also known as the proliferative phase, named for its effect on the endometrium.
Which phase of the cycle has a FIXED duration of about 14 days, regardless of total cycle length?
The secretory (luteal) phase has a fixed 14-day duration; it is the follicular phase that varies in length between women.
Because the luteal phase is fixed at 14 days, the day of ovulation in any cycle can be estimated as:
14 days before the next expected menstruation
14 days after the last menstruation, always
Day 14 of every cycle regardless of length
It cannot be estimated without hormone testing
Since the luteal phase is a constant 14 days, ovulation can be calculated as 14 days before the next expected period, regardless of overall cycle length.
The oestrogen peak occurs how many hours before the LH peak?
The oestrogen peak precedes the LH peak by about 14–24 hours, triggering the LH surge.
The follicle size just before ovulation is typically:
The mature (Graafian) follicle typically measures 18–20 mm (at least 17 mm) just before ovulation.
Day 22 of a standard cycle corresponds to maximum corpus luteum size/activity and progesterone level, and is also notable for:
The point when all ovulation-confirming tests are done, with minimum FSH/LH
Day 22 marks peak progesterone and corpus luteum activity, minimum FSH/LH, and is when ovulation-confirming tests (like serum progesterone) are performed.
Mid-cycle (ovulatory) pain experienced by some women
Pain from an ovarian cyst rupture unrelated to ovulation
Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle, ovulatory pain experienced by some women.
The pathophysiology of Mittelschmerz pain involves:
Rupture of the antral cavity at ovulation, with fluid collecting in the pouch of Douglas
Rupture of the antral cavity at ovulation releases follicular fluid, which collects in the pouch of Douglas and irritates the peritoneum, causing pain.
Fluid in the pouch of Douglas seen on ultrasound around mid-cycle is:
Physiological fluid in the pouch of Douglas at mid-cycle is a normal finding associated with ovulation.
If pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum is maintained by hCG for approximately how long, protecting it from luteolysis?
hCG from the developing pregnancy maintains the corpus luteum, protecting it from luteolysis for up to about 10 weeks.
The corpus luteum of pregnancy contributes progesterone production (until the placenta takes over) and also secretes:
The corpus luteum of pregnancy secretes relaxin in addition to progesterone.
The superficial endometrial layer, shed during menstruation, is called the:
The zona functionalis is the superficial layer shed each cycle during menstruation.
The zona functionalis is supplied by which vessels, which are sensitive to hormonal changes?
Spiral arteries supply the zona functionalis and are hormonally sensitive, constricting to trigger shedding.
The zona basalis (deep layer) is NOT shed during menstruation and is supplied by:
Basal arteries, which are not hormonally sensitive
Spiral arteries, which are hormonally sensitive
No blood supply of its own
The zona basalis is supplied by basal arteries, which are insensitive to hormonal changes, allowing this layer to persist and regenerate the functional layer.
After menstruation, the zona basalis proliferates to:
The zona basalis proliferates after menstruation to regenerate the zona functionalis for the next cycle.
On ultrasound, the endometrium in the late proliferative/peri-ovulatory phase classically shows:
The late proliferative/peri-ovulatory endometrium shows a characteristic trilaminar (triple-line) appearance on ultrasound.
In the secretory phase, the endometrium on ultrasound appears:
Trilaminar, as in the late proliferative phase
Thick and echogenic, with posterior acoustic enhancement
The secretory-phase endometrium appears thick and echogenic with posterior acoustic enhancement on ultrasound.
In an anovulatory cycle, the absence of ovulation means there is no corpus luteum, and therefore no progesterone. This leads to:
Unopposed oestrogen driving endometrial proliferation, producing a weak endometrium that sheds irregularly
No change in bleeding pattern at all
Without progesterone to oppose it, oestrogen drives ongoing endometrial proliferation; the resulting weak, overgrown endometrium sheds unpredictably.
The classic bleeding pattern of anovulatory cycles — irregular, heavy, and painless — is known as:
This pattern is termed oestrogen breakthrough bleeding.
Dysmenorrhoea (from PGF2α-mediated uterine contractions) is characteristically seen only in:
Dysmenorrhoea requires the progesterone withdrawal and prostaglandin release that follow corpus luteum regression — a process unique to ovulatory cycles.
The combined oral contraceptive pill can help dysmenorrhoea partly because it:
By suppressing ovulation (making cycles anovulatory), the OCP removes the progesterone-withdrawal/prostaglandin trigger for dysmenorrhoea.
Primary dysmenorrhoea is defined as menstrual pain occurring:
Only with an underlying pelvic pathology
Primary dysmenorrhoea, by definition, occurs with no underlying pelvic pathology.
In the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory, which gonadotropin primarily acts on THECA cells?
LH acts on theca cells, stimulating androgen production.
In the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory, which gonadotropin primarily acts on GRANULOSA cells?
FSH acts on granulosa cells, driving aromatase activity and oestrogen production.
Granulosa cells possess aromatase but LACK which enzyme, meaning they cannot produce androgens on their own?
Granulosa cells lack 17α-hydroxylase, so they cannot make androgens independently and rely on theca-derived androgens for oestrogen synthesis.
Theca cells, stimulated by LH, produce androgens efficiently but LACK which enzyme needed to convert those androgens to oestrogen?
Theca cells lack aromatase, so they cannot convert their own androgens into oestrogen.
Because theca cells lack aromatase, the androgens they produce must:
Diffuse into neighbouring granulosa cells, which convert them to oestrogen
Remain in the theca cell permanently
Theca-derived androgens diffuse into adjacent granulosa cells, where FSH-induced aromatase converts them to oestrogen.
This division of labour — LH-driven theca cells making androgens, FSH-driven granulosa cells aromatising them to oestrogen — is known as:
This cooperative hormone-producing arrangement between theca and granulosa cells is the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory.
The LH surge is triggered when oestrogen reaches a sustained threshold of approximately:
A sustained oestrogen level of ≥200 picogram for 48 hours triggers positive feedback, causing the LH surge.
AMH concentration is directly proportional to:
AMH concentration is proportional to the number of follicles (formed by pre-antral and small antral follicles from puberty onward), making it a marker of ovarian reserve.
Besides inhibin B (the classic marker), a newer tumour marker for granulosa cell tumour is:
AMH is a newer tumour marker for granulosa cell tumour, in addition to the classic marker inhibin B.
Progesterone is present in small amounts even before ovulation, arising from:
Small amounts of progesterone from luteinised granulosa cells are present even before ovulation, providing positive feedback on LH and FSH.
The maximum progesterone level, reached around day 22 of a standard cycle, is approximately:
Maximum progesterone level (around day 22, one week before menstruation) is approximately 15 ng/mL.
On day 22 of the cycle, alongside maximum corpus luteum size and activity, FSH and LH levels are at their:
Day 22 corresponds to minimum FSH and LH levels, alongside maximum corpus luteal activity and progesterone.
From the beginning of the LH surge to its peak takes about 10–12 hours, while the LH surge overall (peak duration) lasts approximately:
The LH surge lasts approximately 32–36 hours in total, though it takes only 10–12 hours to reach peak from its start.
The first-line pharmacological management for primary dysmenorrhoea is:
NSAIDs are the first-line management for primary dysmenorrhoea (targeting PGF2\u03b1-mediated pain); OCPs are used if NSAIDs are insufficient, by making the cycle anovulatory.
In basic steroidogenesis, cholesterol is converted to pregnenolone via 17-alpha hydroxylase, and pregnenolone is then converted to androgen or progesterone via which enzyme?
3βHSD converts pregnenolone to androgen or progesterone in the basic steroidogenesis pathway.
GnRH is chemically classified as a:
GnRH is a decapeptide (10 amino acid) hormone.
GnRH is secreted from which hypothalamic nucleus?
GnRH is secreted from the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, in a pulsatile manner.
Downregulation of GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary
Sustained maximal LH and FSH release
Continuous, unlike pulsatile, GnRH exposure downregulates GnRH receptors on the anterior pituitary — the basis for continuous GnRH analogue therapy.
A LOW GnRH pulse frequency (about once every 90 minutes) preferentially favours release of:
Low-frequency GnRH pulses (about every 90 minutes) preferentially drive FSH release.
A HIGH GnRH pulse frequency (about once every 60 minutes) preferentially favours release of:
Higher-frequency GnRH pulses (about every 60 minutes) preferentially drive LH release.
GnRH neurons originate in the olfactory epithelium during intrauterine life and migrate to the hypothalamus along with the olfactory nerve. Failure of this migration causes:
Failed migration of GnRH neurons (alongside the olfactory nerve) from the olfactory epithelium to the hypothalamus causes Kallmann syndrome, explaining its associated anosmia.
Kallmann syndrome is inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder (involving the KAL-1 gene) and is:
More common in males than females
More common in females than males
Kallmann syndrome is more common in males than females, consistent with its X-linked recessive inheritance.
GnRH analogues (e.g. leuprolide, goserelin, buserelin) are:
Given only as a single lifetime dose
Orally inactive, given as subcutaneous injections
GnRH analogues are orally inactive and are given as subcutaneous injections, either continuously or in a pulsatile manner.
Pulsatile GnRH administration stimulates the HPO axis, raising LH, FSH, and oestrogen; this pattern is used therapeutically for:
Delayed puberty, Kallmann syndrome, and anovulation
Pulsatile GnRH is used to stimulate the HPO axis in delayed puberty, Kallmann syndrome, and for managing anovulation.
Continuous GnRH administration initially causes a flare (transient HPO axis stimulation), followed by:
Immediate downregulation with no initial flare
Downregulation of the HPO axis, lowering LH and FSH
Continuous GnRH causes an initial flare, then downregulates the HPO axis, ultimately lowering LH and FSH (and downstream oestrogen/androgen).
Continuous GnRH therapy (creating a hypo-oestrogenic/hypo-androgenic state) is used for all of these hyperestrogenic or hormone-sensitive conditions EXCEPT:

Continuous GnRH suppresses the axis and is used for hyperestrogenic/hormone-sensitive conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, ER+ breast cancer, hirsutism, precocious puberty, prostate cancer) — Kallmann syndrome, a hypogonadal state, instead needs pulsatile (stimulating) GnRH.
Adverse effects of continuous GnRH therapy, from hypo-oestrogenism, include hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and:
Continuous GnRH’s hypo-oestrogenic state produces menopause-like symptoms: hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and osteoporosis.
To counter these hypo-oestrogenic side effects during prolonged (≥6 months) GnRH analogue therapy, which strategy is used?
Low-dose oestrogen add-back therapy (e.g. using norethindrone, a progestogen with oestrogen-like action) mitigates hypo-oestrogenic side effects during prolonged GnRH analogue use.
Compared with GnRH analogues, GnRH antagonists (e.g. elagolix, cetrorelix) have the advantage of being orally active and:
GnRH antagonists are orally active and, unlike analogues, cause no initial flare — though they are more expensive.
LH and FSH are structurally classified as:
LH and FSH, released by the anterior pituitary, are glycoprotein hormones.
LH, FSH, TSH, and hCG all share a common:
Single unified structure with no subunits
LH, FSH, TSH, and hCG share an identical alpha subunit; each has its own distinct beta subunit conferring specificity.
In females, FSH receptors are located on:
FSH receptors in females are on granulosa cells (the male equivalent being Sertoli cells).
In females, LH receptors are located on:
LH receptors in females are on theca cells (the male equivalent being Leydig cells).
FSH itself induces the appearance of LH receptors on which cells of the dominant follicle, preparing the follicle to respond to the LH surge?
FSH induces LH receptors on the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle, priming it to respond when the LH surge occurs.
One key function of FSH is the selection of a cohort of follicles:
FSH drives the monthly selection of a cohort of growing follicles.
Selection of the single DOMINANT follicle from this cohort typically occurs around:
The dominant follicle is typically selected around day 8 of the cycle.
Final release of the ovum at ovulation occurs through:
Breakdown of collagen in the follicular wall
Collagen breakdown in the follicular wall (mediated by proteolytic enzymes under LH influence) allows final release of the ovum.
LH is responsible for triggering ovulation and for:
Selecting the initial cohort of follicles
Growth and maintenance of the corpus luteum
Beyond triggering ovulation, LH also drives growth and maintenance of the corpus luteum.
Alongside FSH, LH also contributes to the:
Formation of the primordial follicle pool at birth
Regression of the corpus luteum only
Selection of the dominant follicle exclusively
Final growth and maturation of the follicle
LH also contributes to the final growth and maturation stage of the follicle, alongside FSH.
Normal FSH and LH levels are each typically:
Normal FSH and LH levels are each below about 10 IU.
At menopause, falling oestrogen removes negative feedback, resulting in:
Loss of oestrogen’s negative feedback at menopause raises both LH and FSH.
In pregnancy, high oestrogen and progesterone levels result in:
High oestrogen and progesterone in pregnancy suppress LH and FSH via negative feedback.
In PCOS, the classic gonadotropin pattern is:
FSH normal, LH raised (an increased LH:FSH ratio)
PCOS classically shows normal FSH with raised LH, giving an increased LH:FSH ratio.
In androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY), the gonadotropin pattern is similar to PCOS:
Both FSH and LH markedly raised
Androgen insensitivity syndrome shares the normal-FSH, raised-LH pattern seen in PCOS.
While oestrogen normally exerts negative feedback on LH and FSH, sustained oestrogen levels above approximately 200 pg/mL switch this to:
Positive feedback, triggering the LH surge
Sustained oestrogen above roughly 200 pg/mL for about 48 hours switches feedback from negative to positive, triggering the LH surge.
Human Menopausal Gonadotropin (HMG) is composed of:
HMG is composed of equal parts, 75 IU LH and 75 IU FSH.
HMG is extracted from the urine of postmenopausal women, which is rich in gonadotropins due to loss of negative feedback.
HMG is used to treat anovulation due to pituitary ablation, and also in:
HMG is used both for anovulation from pituitary ablation and for controlled ovarian stimulation in IVF cycles.
A recognised disadvantage of HMG therapy is a 5–15% risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, and a roughly 30% risk of:
Because HMG stimulates multiple follicles, it carries a roughly 30% risk of multifetal pregnancy, alongside a 5–15% risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
The half-life (T½) of natural GnRH is approximately:
Natural GnRH has a very short half-life of approximately 2–4 minutes, necessitating pulsatile secretion.
A key clinical feature that helps distinguish Kallmann syndrome from Turner syndrome is that Kallmann syndrome patients typically have:
Unlike Turner syndrome, patients with Kallmann syndrome typically have normal height, alongside delayed puberty, infertility, and hyposmia/anosmia.
The management of Kallmann syndrome is:
Kallmann syndrome, being a hypogonadotropic state, is managed with pulsatile GnRH to stimulate the HPO axis.
Natural estrogen is a C18 steroid; natural progesterone is a:
Estrogen is a C18 steroid, while progesterone is a C21 steroid.
The four natural estrogens are estrone, estradiol, estriol, and:
The four natural estrogens are E1 (estrone), E2 (estradiol), E3 (estriol), and E4 (estetrol).
The predominant estrogen in reproductive-age women is:
Estradiol (E2) predominates in reproductive-age women and in pregnancy.
The predominant estrogen in menopausal and in obese women is:
Estrone (E1), produced peripherally in adipose tissue, predominates in menopausal and obese women.
The normal E2:E1 ratio is about 2:1; in obese women, this ratio:
In obese women, increased peripheral aromatisation reverses the normal E2:E1 ratio to about 1:2.
The most specific estrogen in pregnancy, derived from fetal DHEA-S, is:
Estriol (E3), derived from fetal adrenal DHEA-S, is the most pregnancy-specific estrogen.
The most commonly used synthetic estrogen in combined oral contraceptive pills is:
Ethinyl estradiol (EE) is the most commonly used synthetic estrogen in OCPs.
The synthetic estrogen most commonly used in hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is:
17-β estradiol is the synthetic estrogen most commonly used in HRT.
By potency, which of these synthetic estrogens is most potent?
Potency ranking is EE > CEE > E2 > E1 > E3 > E4, making ethinyl estradiol the most potent.
OCPs are classified by estrogen content; a 'low dose' pill contains:
Low-dose pills contain <50 mcg estrogen; high-dose ≥ 50 mcg; very low-dose <20 mcg.
First-generation progestins, such as norethindrone, have which distinguishing property?
Purely progestational, with zero androgenic effect
First-generation progestins like norethindrone have both androgenic and oestrogenic activity.
Which generation of progestins (e.g. desogestrel, norgestimate, gestodene) has the LEAST androgenic side effects among the numbered generations?
None; all generations are equally androgenic

Third-generation progestins (desogestrel, norgestimate, gestodene) have the least androgenic side effects among the numbered generations; 4th-generation progestins (drospirenone, dienogest) are actually anti-androgenic.
In the body, oestrogen synthesis proceeds from cholesterol through androgens via which enzyme?
Aromatase converts androgens to oestrogens in the final step of oestrogen synthesis.
Progesterone synthesis proceeds from cholesterol to pregnenolone, then to progesterone via which enzyme?
E2 (oestradiol) is mainly produced by granulosa cells (as in the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory); E1 (oestrone) is mainly produced by:
Adipose tissue, converting androstenedione via aromatase
Adipose tissue converts androstenedione to E1 (oestrone) via aromatase.
Since obese women have more adipose tissue, they characteristically have:
More adipose tissue means more peripheral aromatisation, raising E1 (oestrone) levels in obese women.
Aromatase inhibitors, such as letrozole, are used therapeutically to:
Reduce oestrogen production, useful in hyperestrogenic conditions
Stimulate ovulation directly without affecting hormone levels
By blocking aromatase, letrozole reduces oestrogen production, useful in hyperestrogenic conditions.
In a non-pregnant woman, progesterone is mainly sourced from the corpus luteum, more specifically from:
Theca cells of the dominant follicle
Luteinised granulosa cells (forming the corpus luteum) are the main progesterone source in a non-pregnant woman.
Progesterone (and androgen) receptors are initially intracytoplasmic, but must move where to actually function?
They function in the cytoplasm without moving
Progesterone and androgen receptors, though intracytoplasmic, must translocate into the nucleus to function.
In the circulation, oestrogen is mostly protein-bound, chiefly to:
Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), more than albumin
Oestrogen is mostly bound to SHBG (more than to albumin), with about 1% circulating free.
Progesterone, in contrast, is mainly bound to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), and notably:
Is bound mostly to SHBG, like oestrogen
Is NOT significantly bound to SHBG
Has no plasma protein binding at all
Unlike oestrogen, progesterone is not significantly bound to SHBG; about 2% circulates free.
The end metabolite of oestrogen is glucuronide; the end metabolite of progesterone is:
Oestrogen's main action on the endometrium is:
Progesterone supports the endometrium and induces secretory changes, but continuous administration can also cause an 'autoproliferative' action leading to:
Continuous progesterone can drive an autoproliferative action leading to endometrial hypertrophy.
Because of this autoproliferative action supporting endometrial regrowth in a controlled way, progesterone (in appropriate regimens) serves as:
A risk factor for endometrial hyperplasia only
The drug of choice (DOC) for endometrial hyperplasia
A contraindication in all endometrial disease
Progesterone (e.g. as continuous therapy) is the drug of choice for managing endometrial hyperplasia.
On the myometrium, oestrogen supports growth of the non-pregnant uterus, while progesterone supports growth of:
Both the non-pregnant and the pregnant uterus
Neither; progesterone has no myometrial effect
Only the cervix, not the uterine body
Progesterone supports myometrial growth in BOTH the non-pregnant and pregnant uterus, a broader role than oestrogen's.
Fibroids (myometrial tumours) are classically described as being:
Fibroids are dependent on both oestrogen and progesterone, not oestrogen alone.
In Turner syndrome, non-functional streak ovaries lead to low oestrogen and progesterone, resulting in:
Without adequate oestrogen/progesterone stimulation, the uterus in Turner syndrome remains infantile/hypoplastic.
On endometrial biopsy, the proliferative phase (first half of the cycle) shows simple tubular glands and:
Pseudostratification (nuclei at different levels) and telescoping of glands
The proliferative phase shows simple tubular glands, pseudostratification, and telescoping of glands.
The first histological sign of ovulation on endometrial biopsy is:
Subnuclear vacuoles are the first histological sign of ovulation on biopsy.
Subnuclear vacuoles are typically seen on which days of the cycle?
Subnuclear vacuoles classically appear on days 16–17 of the cycle.
Subnuclear vacuoles are more prominent in which phase, relative to the ovulatory phase itself?
Subnuclear vacuoles are more prominent in the early secretory phase than at ovulation itself.
As the early secretory phase progresses, the endometrial glands show:
Glands begin to coil as the early secretory phase progresses, preceding the more tortuous late-secretory appearance.
In the late secretory phase, the classic 'corkscrew' or 'sawtooth' gland appearance (tortuous glands) is seen around day:
Corkscrew/sawtooth tortuous glands appear around day 20 of the cycle.
Stromal oedema on endometrial biopsy is characteristically seen around day:
Stromal oedema is characteristically seen around day 22.
Lymphocytic infiltration of the endometrium, signalling the approach of menstruation, is seen around day:
Lymphocytic infiltration appears around day 26, just before menstruation begins.
Endometrial biopsy as a test for ovulation is:
Though histologically informative, endometrial biopsy is rarely used in current practice as an ovulation test.
Recognised indications for endometrial biopsy include abnormal uterine bleeding and:
Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) and suspected genital tuberculosis are recognised indications for endometrial biopsy.
Under oestrogen's influence, cervical mucus becomes thin, profuse, and:
Oestrogen makes cervical mucus thin, profuse, and watery, favourable for sperm penetration.
Under progesterone's influence, cervical mucus becomes:
Thin and watery, as with oestrogen
Progesterone makes cervical mucus thick, scanty, and viscous (non-stretchable/tacky).
The Spinnbarkeit test assesses cervical mucus:
The Spinnbarkeit test assesses the mucus's elasticity/stretchability, which is greatest under oestrogen dominance.
A positive ferning pattern on cervical mucus microscopy, appearing by day 7 of the cycle, is due to:
Increased sodium and chloride under oestrogen’s influence produce the ferning pattern by day 7.
At menopause, falling oestrogen reduces cervical mucus, contributing to:
Reduced cervical mucus at menopause contributes to senile vaginitis (vaginal dryness), managed with lubricants or local oestrogen.
Levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (e.g. Mirena) thicken cervical mucus, which is unfavourable for sperm penetration, and are associated with which additional benefit compared with copper IUDs?
A LOWER risk of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
By thickening cervical mucus, LNG-IUDs like Mirena carry a lower PID risk, in contrast to copper IUDs, which raise PID risk.
Oestrogen promotes ductal development and fat deposition in the breast; progesterone promotes:
Progesterone promotes glandular (lobular) development of the breast.
For contraception during lactation, combined OCPs are contraindicated, and the preferred option is:
No contraception is needed while breastfeeding
Progesterone-only contraceptives are the drug of choice during lactation, since oestrogen reduces milk secretion.
Oestrogen increases fallopian tube motility; progesterone decreases it. Failure of progesterone-only contraceptives, with reduced tubal motility, specifically raises the risk of:
Reduced tubal motility from progesterone-only contraceptive failure raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy.
A woman is found to have an ovarian tumour on ultrasound, with predominantly superficial cells on vaginal cytology (indicating high oestrogen). This picture suggests:
An oestrogen-secreting ovarian tumour with predominant superficial cells on cytology points to a granulosa cell tumour.
Vaginal cytology can be used as a test for ovulation when sampled around which day of the cycle?
Vaginal cytology sampled around day 22 can serve as a test for ovulation.
On breast tissue, unlike oestrogen and progesterone's effects on development, breast MILK SECRETION is:
Increased by oestrogen, unaffected by progesterone
Decreased by oestrogen; unaffected by progesterone
Oestrogen decreases breast milk secretion, while progesterone has no effect on it.
Regarding salt and water balance, oestrogen causes retention, while progesterone causes:
Progesterone promotes salt and water excretion, opposite to oestrogen’s retention effect.
Oestrogen increases bone mass and mineralisation and lowers serum calcium; in long bones, it also causes:
Oestrogen causes epiphyseal closure in long bones.
In precocious puberty, elevated oestrogen causes premature epiphyseal closure, resulting in:
Premature epiphyseal closure from early oestrogen exposure results in short final stature.
In menopause, falling oestrogen reduces bone mineral density, resulting in:
Loss of oestrogen’s bone-protective effect at menopause leads to osteoporosis.
Oestrogen increases clotting factors II, VII, VIII, and X, raising thrombosis risk with OCPs/HRT. This makes OCPs contraindicated in all of these EXCEPT:
OCPs are contraindicated in VTE history, coronary artery disease, stroke, and smokers over 35 — not in well-controlled hypothyroidism.
Because progesterone (unlike oestrogen) has no significant procoagulant effect, progesterone-only contraceptives:
Can be used in patients with a history of thrombosis
Progesterone-only contraceptives, lacking oestrogen’s procoagulant effect, can be used even in patients with a thrombosis history.
Progesterone raises basal body temperature (BBT) by approximately:
Progesterone raises BBT by about 0.5°C after ovulation.
Charting basal body temperature is used clinically as a:
Natural method of contraception and test for ovulation
BBT charting is used both as a natural contraceptive method and as a test to confirm ovulation.
Regarding LH, oestrogen levels below about 200 pg/mL exert negative feedback, while sustained levels at or above 200 pg/mL exert:
No effect on LH at all
Feedback only on FSH, not LH
Sustained oestrogen ≥200 pg/mL switches feedback on LH from negative to positive, triggering the LH surge.
Progesterone's feedback on FSH and LH is concentration-dependent: low concentrations give positive feedback, while high concentrations give:
A feedback effect only on prolactin
Low progesterone concentrations feed back positively on FSH/LH; high concentrations feed back negatively.
In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, LH, FSH, oestrogen, and androgens are all low, reflecting a defect at the level of the:
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism reflects a hypothalamic/pituitary defect, with everything (LH, FSH, sex steroids) low.
In hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, LH and FSH are HIGH while oestrogen/androgens are LOW, reflecting a defect at the level of the:
Gonads themselves, with loss of negative feedback on FSH/LH
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism reflects a gonadal defect; low sex steroids remove negative feedback, driving LH/FSH up.
The vaginal maturation index counts the ratio of parabasal, intermediate, and superficial cells. A ratio dominated by superficial cells (e.g. 0:30:70 or 0:40:60) suggests:
A superficial-cell-dominant ratio (e.g. 0:30:70) is characteristic of the proliferative phase.
A maturation index ratio of roughly 0:70:30 (intermediate cells dominant) suggests:
An intermediate-cell-dominant ratio (0:70:30) is characteristic of the secretory phase.
A maturation index of 100:0:0 (all parabasal cells) is characteristic of:
An all-parabasal-cell pattern (100:0:0) is characteristic of the low-oestrogen menopausal state.
Which of these hormones/receptors is membrane-bound, unlike oestrogen (intranuclear) or progesterone (intracytoplasmic)?
GnRH, LH, and FSH act via membrane-bound receptors, unlike the intracellular receptors of oestrogen and progesterone.
Regarding half-life, GnRH, FSH, and oxytocin all have a short half-life of about 3–4 minutes; LH's half-life is notably longer, at about:
LH's half-life (about 20 minutes) is notably longer than GnRH, FSH, and oxytocin (3–4 minutes each).
Which of these is NOT typically classified as a hyperestrogenic state?
Precocious puberty, endometriosis, fibroid, endometrial causes, and ovarian cancer are classified as hyperestrogenic states; androgen insensitivity syndrome is not.
Common risk factors for hyperestrogenic states include nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause, and:
Obesity (via increased peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen)
Obesity raises risk via increased peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen in adipose tissue.
Which of these is a PROTECTIVE factor against hyperestrogenic states?
Multiparity, along with pregnancy and physical activity, is protective against hyperestrogenic states.
Regular physical activity and pregnancy are both considered:
Pregnancy and physical activity are both protective against hyperestrogenic states.
Somewhat counterintuitively, smoking is protective against hyperestrogenic states and also against:
Smoking is also, counterintuitively, protective against pregnancy-induced hypertension — despite its many other well-established harms.
The first-line pharmacological option for hyperestrogenic states, which downregulates oestrogen receptors, is:
Progesterone, which downregulates oestrogen receptors, is the first-line pharmacological option.
Letrozole manages hyperestrogenic states by acting as a(n):
Aromatase inhibitor, blocking conversion of androgens to oestrogens
Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, blocking the conversion of androgens to oestrogens.
Danazol has anti-oestrogenic action but is limited by androgenic side effects such as:
Danazol's androgenic side effects include hirsutism, limiting its use despite its anti-oestrogenic action.
Considered the BEST pharmacological options for hyperestrogenic states are:
Continuous GnRH agonists and GnRH antagonists
Continuous GnRH agonists and GnRH antagonists are considered the best options among the pharmacological choices.
Selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) act as oestrogen agonists on some tissues and:
Agonists on all other tissues as well
Have no effect on any other tissue
SERMs act as oestrogen agonists on some tissues and antagonists on others — their defining mixed activity.
Clomiphene citrate's main clinical indication is:
Clomiphene citrate is used for ovulation induction.
Which finding on clomiphene citrate mandates immediate discontinuation of the drug?
Visual disturbance on clomiphene citrate is an indication for immediate drug discontinuation.
Raloxifene's clinical indications include osteoporosis and:
Raloxifene is indicated for osteoporosis and breast cancer, with no risk of endometrial cancer (unlike tamoxifen).
Unlike clomiphene and raloxifene, tamoxifen (used for breast cancer) carries a notable risk of:
Tamoxifen carries a notable endometrial cancer risk, unlike clomiphene and raloxifene, which do not.
Because tamoxifen is teratogenic, the recommended minimum gap between stopping tamoxifen and attempting pregnancy is:
A minimum 3-month gap is recommended between stopping tamoxifen and attempting pregnancy, given its teratogenicity.
Ospemifene, a SERM, is specifically used to treat:
Ospemifene is a SERM specifically used for vaginal dryness.
Bazedoxifene combined with oestrogen (approved for managing hot flashes) has the specific advantage of:
Increasing endometrial cancer risk, like tamoxifen
Preventing endometrial carcinoma while treating hot flashes and osteoporosis
This combination treats hot flashes and osteoporosis while preventing endometrial carcinoma — the opposite risk profile from tamoxifen.
Ormeloxifene is a component of which contraceptive?
Ormeloxifene is the active component of Centchroman (Chhaya), a non-hormonal-cycle weekly contraceptive.
Ulipristal, a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM), is used for fibroids and:
Ulipristal is an SPRM used for fibroid treatment and as an emergency contraceptive.
Mifepristone (RU486) acts as a progesterone antagonist and is used for medical abortion and:
Mifepristone, a progesterone antagonist, is used for medical abortion and for fibroids.
Unlike natural progesterone (a C21 steroid), synthetic progestins are classified as:
Synthetic progestins are C19 steroids (similar to androgens), which explains their androgenic side effects.
OCPs are classified by estrogen content into high dose (≥50 mcg), low dose (<50 mcg), and:
OCPs are classified as high dose (≥50 mcg), low dose (<50 mcg), and very low dose (<20 mcg) based on estrogen content.
The second-generation progestin, following first-generation norethindrone, is:
Levonorgestrel is the second-generation progestin, preceding the third generation (desogestrel, norgestimate, gestodene).
Fourth-generation progestins, including drospirenone (a spironolactone derivative) and dienogest, are notable for being:
The most androgenic of all generations
Estrogenic only, with no progestogenic action
Fourth-generation progestins (drospirenone, dienogest) are anti-androgenic, unlike earlier generations.
In pregnancy, progesterone is sourced from the corpus luteum in early pregnancy, with production later taken over by the:
Early pregnancy progesterone comes from the corpus luteum, with the placenta taking over later in pregnancy.
Regarding free (unbound, bioactive) hormone fraction, approximately what percentage of circulating progesterone is free, compared to estrogen?
Approximately 2% of circulating progesterone is free, compared to about 1% of estrogen.
The natural family planning method that relies on tracking cervical mucus changes to identify the fertile window is known as:
Billing's method is the natural method of conception/contraception based on cervical mucus characteristics.
The half-life of letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) is notably long, at approximately:
Letrozole's half-life is approximately 48 hours, much longer than hormones like GnRH, FSH, and oxytocin (3–4 minutes).
Among the adverse effects of clomiphene citrate (besides hot flashes and vaginal dryness), a recognised risk is:
Clomiphene citrate use carries an increased risk of twin pregnancy, due to multi-follicular development.
Unlike tamoxifen (which carries an endometrial cancer risk), clomiphene citrate and raloxifene share the advantage of:
Clomiphene citrate and raloxifene, unlike tamoxifen, carry no risk of endometrial cancer.
The menstrual cycle comprises the ovarian cycle and the uterine cycle. The ovarian cycle refers to:
Cyclical growth and shedding of the endometrium
Cyclical follicular growth leading to ovulation, followed by corpus luteum growth and degeneration
Changes in basal body temperature only
The ovarian cycle is follicular growth to ovulation, then corpus luteum growth and degeneration; the uterine cycle is the parallel endometrial growth and shedding.
Day 1 of the menstrual cycle is defined as:
The day the endometrium is thickest
Day 1 of the cycle is, by convention, the onset of menstrual bleeding.
By current (newer) criteria, a normal menstrual cycle length is considered to be:
Newer criteria define a normal cycle length as 24–38 days, updated from the previous 21–35-day range.
By current criteria, the normal number of days of bleeding is:
Newer criteria define normal bleeding duration as 4.5–8 days, updated from the previous 2–8-day range.
Normal cycle-to-cycle variation in length is considered to be:
A cycle-to-cycle variation of 2–20 days is considered within the normal range.
What proportion of women actually have a 'textbook' 28-day cycle?
Only about 15% of women actually have a 28-day cycle; considerable natural variation is normal.
Fewer than 9 cycles a year, with cycle length over 38 days (previously 35)
Oligomenorrhoea describes infrequent cycles (<9/year), with cycle length over 38 days (previously 35 days).
Frequent/short cycles, with length under 24 days (previously 21)
Polymenorrhoea describes frequent, short cycles, under 24 days (previously 21 days).
Menorrhagia (old terminology) is defined by increased blood loss (≥80 mL) together with a duration of bleeding of:
Menorrhagia combines increased blood loss (≥80 mL) with bleeding lasting more than 8 days.
Hypomenorrhoea (old terminology) describes scanty bleeding, defined as blood loss and duration of:
Hypomenorrhoea describes scanty bleeding: ≤20 mL, lasting under 2 days.
Which of these old terms describes cycles that are too INFREQUENT (long cycle length)?
Oligomenorrhoea describes infrequent (long-interval) cycles; polymenorrhoea is the opposite (frequent/short cycles).
The cutoff for oligomenorrhoea's cycle length has shifted with updated criteria from a previous threshold of 35 days to a current threshold of:
The oligomenorrhoea cycle-length threshold has been updated from 35 days to 38 days.
Metrorrhagia refers to irregular or intermenstrual bleeding.
Amenorrhoea (old terminology, as used here) refers to absence of menstruation for:
Amenorrhoea, in this context, refers to absence of menstruation for 3 months.
Metrorrhagia and oligomenorrhoea are distinguished by:
Metrorrhagia describing infrequent cycles, oligomenorrhoea describing irregular bleeding
Metrorrhagia describing irregular cycles, oligomenorrhoea describing infrequent (but still regular) cycles
Metrorrhagia is an irregular-cycle disorder (unpredictable timing), while oligomenorrhoea is a regular-cycle disorder (predictable, just infrequent).
Under newer terminology, a cycle length under 24 days is termed:
A cycle length under 24 days is now termed frequent menses (replacing ‘polymenorrhoea’).
Under newer terminology, a cycle length over 38 days is termed:
A cycle length over 38 days is now termed infrequent menses (replacing ‘oligomenorrhoea’).
Under newer terminology, blood loss over 80 mL is termed:
Blood loss over 80 mL is now termed heavy bleeding (replacing ‘menorrhagia’).
Under newer terminology, blood loss under 5 mL is termed:
Blood loss under 5 mL is now termed light bleeding (replacing ‘hypomenorrhoea’).
The newer terminology system replaces older terms like 'menorrhagia' and 'polymenorrhoea' with more descriptive terms based on:
Specific features (cycle length, volume, duration, regularity), each described independently
The newer system describes each feature (cycle length, volume, duration, regularity) independently, rather than bundling them into single eponymous terms.
Under newer terminology, a bleeding duration over 8 days is termed:
A bleeding duration over 8 days is now termed prolonged bleeding.
Under newer terminology, a bleeding duration under 4.5 days is termed:
A bleeding duration under 4.5 days is now termed shortened bleeding.
Under newer terminology, cycle-to-cycle variation greater than 20 days is termed:
Cycle-to-cycle variation over 20 days is now termed irregular cycles.
Heavy bleeding during a normal period
Acyclical episodes of bleeding occurring WITH an otherwise normal menstrual pattern
Bleeding that only occurs at menopause
Intermenstrual bleeding is acyclical bleeding occurring alongside an otherwise normal menstrual pattern.
The modern, functional definition of heavy menstrual bleeding is based on:
A blood loss volume of exactly 80 mL, measured precisely every cycle
Excessive bleeding that interferes with a woman's quality of life
Modern heavy menstrual bleeding is defined functionally — excessive bleeding that interferes with quality of life — rather than by a precise measured volume.
While the normal range of blood loss is 20–80 mL over 4.5–8 days, the AVERAGE values in a typical cycle are approximately:
The average blood loss per cycle is approximately 30–50 mL, over an average duration of about 4.5 days — distinct from the wider normal ranges (20–80 mL, 4.5–8 days).
AUB is classified into structural and non-structural causes using the PALM-COEIN system. Which of these is a STRUCTURAL cause?
Adenomyosis is one of the four structural (PALM) causes, alongside polyp, leiomyoma, and malignancy/hyperplasia.
In PALM-COEIN, which letter represents polyps?
'M' covers both malignancy (cervical/endometrial cancer) and hyperplasia (endometrial hyperplasia).
In PALM-COEIN, which letter represents ovulatory dysfunction (anovulation)?
'O' in COEIN stands for ovulatory dysfunction.
Iatrogenic causes of AUB (the 'I' in COEIN) include:
Iatrogenic causes include IUCDs and OCPs.
A specific PALM-COEIN diagnosis, such as AUB due to a polyp, is denoted as:
Each PALM-COEIN category is denoted with the AUB prefix plus its letter, e.g. AUB-P, AUB-A.
AUB of endometrial cause (endometritis) classically presents with cyclical heavy bleeding and:
Endometrial-cause AUB shows a normal-sized uterus on USG, distinguishing it from structural causes.
The pathogenesis of endometrial-cause AUB involves altered PGE:PGF2α ratio, increased fibrinolytic activity, and:
Progesterone levels remain normal in endometrial-cause AUB; the problem lies in local prostaglandin/fibrinolytic dysregulation.
In ovulatory dysfunction (anovulation), unopposed estrogen causes:
Estrogen breakthrough bleeding, giving irregular, heavy, painless cycles
Anovulation leads to unopposed estrogen and estrogen breakthrough bleeding: irregular, heavy, and painless.
Anovulatory AUB clinically presents with heavy bleeding and:
Anovulatory AUB presents with heavy bleeding alongside oligomenorrhoea (infrequent cycles).
Which of these features favours an ENDOMETRIAL cause over a structural cause of AUB?
An enlarged, irregular uterus on exam
A normal-sized uterus on USG with cyclical heavy bleeding
A normal-sized uterus with cyclical heavy bleeding points toward an endometrial (rather than structural) cause.
The most common cause of puberty menorrhagia is:
Anovulation is the most common cause of puberty menorrhagia, more common than coagulopathy.
In obese females, peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen in adipose tissue leads to continuous LH stimulation, resulting in:
Continuous (rather than cyclical) LH stimulation from persistent peripheral estrogen prevents a proper LH surge, causing anovulation.
Androgen excess causes anovulation through which mechanism?
A folliculotoxic effect preventing follicle maturation
Excess androgens have a folliculotoxic effect, preventing normal follicle maturation and thus ovulation.
Negative feedback on GnRH, lowering LH and FSH
Raised prolactin negatively feeds back on GnRH, lowering LH and FSH and causing anovulation.
Besides anovulation, hyperprolactinemia's suppression of LH/FSH also causes low progesterone, presenting as:
Low progesterone from hyperprolactinemia-driven anovulation presents as secondary amenorrhoea, alongside infertility.
Lactational amenorrhoea shares its mechanism with hyperprolactinemia-induced anovulation, since breastfeeding causes:
Breastfeeding raises prolactin, which suppresses the HPO axis, similarly to pathological hyperprolactinemia.
Key menstrual history parameters to assess in AUB include regularity, frequency, duration, and:
Regularity, frequency, duration, and volume are the four core menstrual parameters assessed in AUB history.
On general examination for AUB, besides vitals and pallor, it is important to check for thyroid enlargement and:
BMI, alongside vitals, pallor, and thyroid enlargement, is part of the general examination for AUB.
Classic examination signs of PCOS include hirsutism, acne, and:
Hirsutism, acne, and acanthosis nigricans are classic PCOS examination signs.
Bimanual pelvic examination assesses uterine size, contour, tenderness, fixity, and:
Bimanual exam assesses uterine size, contour, tenderness, fixity, and adnexal mass/tenderness.
Per vaginal and pelvic examination are generally:
Mandatory in every patient with AUB
NOT done in a virgin adolescent
Only done if bleeding is heavy
PV and pelvic examination are avoided in a virgin adolescent.
Relevant associated symptoms to ask about in AUB history include vaginal discharge, dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and:
Infertility, alongside vaginal discharge, dysmenorrhoea, and dyspareunia, is a key associated symptom to assess.
CBC and haemoglobin level in AUB workup are used mainly to assess:
CBC/Hb assesses the severity of blood loss.
BT, CT, and APTT (coagulation studies) are specifically indicated in AUB when there is puberty menorrhagia, low platelet count, or:
Coagulation studies are indicated for puberty menorrhagia, low platelets, or a coagulopathy history.
UPT and cervical cytology are specifically recommended in AUB workup for:
UPT and cervical cytology are recommended specifically for sexually active females.
USG in AUB evaluation is used mainly to detect:
USG is the main tool for detecting structural lesions in AUB workup.
Hysteroscopy is specifically indicated in AUB when there is an intracavitary lesion on USG, intermenstrual bleeding (suggesting polyp), or a history of curettage with AUB (suggesting):
A history of curettage with subsequent AUB raises suspicion for Asherman syndrome, an indication for hysteroscopy.
Endometrial sampling/biopsy is the investigation of choice for endometrial pathology; in India, the instrument commonly used is:
Worldwide, Pipelle or Vabra aspirator are commonly used; in India, Karman's cannula is the commonly used instrument.
In a reproductive-age woman with AUB, after a negative UPT, the preferred imaging is:
TVS is preferred over TAS in the reproductive-age AUB algorithm.
In a reproductive-age woman, endometrial biopsy is indicated if endometrial thickness exceeds:
Endometrial thickness over 12 mm is an indication for biopsy in reproductive-age women.
In a reproductive-age woman with AUB, endometrial biopsy is also indicated with a normal USG plus persistent bleeding, or in the presence of high-risk factors such as:
PCOS, granulosa cell tumour, or obesity
High-risk factors warranting biopsy include PCOS, granulosa cell tumour, and obesity.
According to FOGSI (India), perimenopause is considered to begin after age:
FOGSI (India) defines perimenopause as beginning after age 40; ACOG (worldwide) uses 45 years.
In a perimenopausal woman with AUB, the recommended workup is a UPT (irrespective of USG) plus:
Perimenopausal AUB workup includes UPT plus TVS and endometrial biopsy.
In a postmenopausal woman with AUB, if endometrial thickness on TVS is under 4 mm, initial management is a trial of tranexamic acid; if thickness is 4 mm or more, the next step is:
A thickness ≥4 mm in a postmenopausal woman warrants endometrial biopsy.
Tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic, reduces AUB blood loss by approximately:
Tranexamic acid reduces AUB blood loss by about 50%.
Tranexamic acid is well tolerated and effective particularly in cyclical bleeding with:
Tranexamic acid works well in cyclical bleeding with a normal-sized uterus.
Mefenamic acid, a prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor, is particularly indicated when AUB is accompanied by:
Mefenamic acid is specifically useful when AUB is accompanied by dysmenorrhoea.
As the sole first-line drug for AUB
In combination with tranexamic acid, not as first-line alone
Mefenamic acid is not used as a first-line drug alone; it is combined with tranexamic acid.
Ethamsylate reduces capillary fragility but, despite this mechanism, is:
Not effective in the management of AUB
The most effective AUB drug available
Despite reducing capillary fragility, ethamsylate is not clinically effective for managing AUB.
Combined OCPs manage AUB by stabilising the endometrium and by negative feedback on LH and FSH, which causes:
Anovulation, alongside contraception and ovarian suppression
OCPs stabilise the endometrium and, via LH/FSH suppression, cause anovulation, contraception, and ovarian suppression.
A standard OCP pack contains how many tablets?
A standard OCP pack contains 21 hormone tablets.
For contraceptive benefit, OCPs are started between which days of the cycle?
Any day, timing does not matter
OCPs are started between day 1 and day 5 of the cycle for contraceptive benefit.
In AUB management, a patient with haemoglobin under 10 g/dL is generally given OCPs:
Only as needed for bleeding episodes
Hb <10 g/dL warrants continuous OCP use for 3 months.
In AUB management, a patient with haemoglobin ≥10 g/dL is generally given OCPs as:
3 months continuously, same as low Hb
3 weeks of OCP followed by 1 week off, repeated for 3 cycles
Hb ≥10 g/dL is managed with 3 weeks OCP followed by 1 week off, for 3 cycles.
Estrogen upregulates progesterone receptors on the endometrium; progesterone, in turn:
Downregulates estrogen receptors, and only acts on estrogen-primed endometrium
Has no effect on estrogen receptors
Acts independently of any estrogen priming
Progesterone downregulates estrogen receptors and requires estrogen-primed endometrium to act.
In a patient with a THICK endometrium (estrogen having upregulated progesterone receptors), appropriate drug options include:
With a thick, progesterone-receptor-rich endometrium, OCPs or progesterone alone are appropriate.
In a patient with a THIN endometrium or prolonged/severe bleeding (few progesterone receptors present), the preferred approach is:
Estrogen followed by progesterone, or combined estrogen+progesterone (OCP)
With few progesterone receptors, estrogen is needed first (or combined as an OCP) to prime the endometrium before progesterone can act.
Progesterone's core action on the endometrium is to support it and:
Progesterone supports the endometrium and reduces shedding.
When given CONTINUOUSLY, progesterone downregulates estrogen receptors, leading to:
Endometrial atrophy, reduced blood loss, and amenorrhoea
Continuous progesterone causes endometrial atrophy, reducing blood loss and inducing amenorrhoea.
Continuous oral progesterone (without a break) for 3–6 months causes endometrial atrophy and is considered:
The preferred mode of oral progesterone use in AUB
Continuous oral progesterone is the preferred mode for AUB, producing endometrial atrophy.
Cyclical oral progesterone (day 14–25) supports the endometrium and is used in anovulatory DUB, but is less preferred mainly due to:
Compliance issues, and it offers no contraceptive benefit
Its high cost compared to other options
Cyclical progesterone is less preferred due to compliance challenges and lack of contraceptive benefit.
Mirena (a progesterone-releasing IUCD) causes endometrial atrophy and provides relief of AUB in approximately what proportion of cases?
Mirena provides relief of AUB in approximately 30–40% of cases.
Mirena is preferred for treating AUB in reproductive-age and perimenopausal women, and also for protecting against:
Mirena is preferred for treating AUB and for protecting against endometrial proliferation.
A key advantage of Mirena over continuous oral progesterone is:
Requiring daily dosing, improving adherence tracking
Good compliance and reduced need for hysterectomy
Mirena offers good compliance (no daily dosing needed) and reduces the need for hysterectomy.
The minimum duration of Mirena's presence per month required for its endometrial-protective effect is:
Mirena needs to be in place at least 12 days a month for its endometrial-protective effect.
GnRH analogues, used as second-line medical therapy for AUB, work by continuously lowering LH, FSH, and estrogen, which:
Reduces endometrial proliferation and blood loss
Continuous GnRH analogue use lowers LH/FSH/estrogen, reducing endometrial proliferation and blood loss.
A major disadvantage of GnRH analogue therapy for AUB is:
Expense and menopause-like symptoms from low estrogen
Increased fertility as a side effect
Weight gain as the only side effect
Its inability to reduce bleeding at all
GnRH analogues are expensive and cause menopause-like symptoms from hypo-estrogenism.
The maximum recommended duration of GnRH analogue use is:
GnRH analogue use for AUB is limited to a maximum of 6 months.
GnRH analogues are also used prior to which procedures, to reduce endometrial thickness beforehand?
GnRH analogues are used pre-operatively before surgery or endometrial ablation to thin the endometrium.
Ormeloxifene, now considered obsolete for AUB management, is a SERM that works by:
Antagonising estrogen's effect on the endometrium, causing atrophy
Ormeloxifene antagonises estrogen's endometrial effect, causing atrophy, though it is now considered obsolete for this indication.
For a STRUCTURAL cause of AUB, the general management approach is:
Treatment directed at the specific underlying cause
Structural causes are managed by treating the specific underlying cause (e.g. polypectomy for a polyp).
For a non-structural cause of AUB with bleeding controlled, management typically includes oral iron plus:
Once bleeding is controlled, oral iron plus maintenance drugs is the typical approach.
Indications for blood transfusion in AUB include puberty menorrhagia with haemoglobin under:
Blood transfusion is indicated in puberty menorrhagia when Hb is under 7 g/dL.
Before a planned surgery for AUB, blood transfusion is considered if haemoglobin is under:
Pre-operative blood transfusion is considered if Hb is under 10 g/dL.
Surgical management options for AUB include endometrial ablation, uterine artery embolisation (for fibroid), and hysterectomy, generally reserved for cases meeting BOTH of which conditions?
Young age and desire for more children
Failure of medical management AND a complete family
Surgical options are generally reserved for cases with BOTH failed medical management AND a completed family.
Hysterectomy for AUB is particularly considered in a perimenopausal woman with:
Hysterectomy is particularly considered in perimenopausal women with concomitant uterine pathology.
In a patient with severe bleeding for 15 days, normal USG, negative UPT, and a normal endometrial biopsy, one treatment option is IV oestrogen (ethinyl estradiol) 50 mg for 5 days, followed by:
IV oestrogen for 5 days is followed by progesterone in this acute management protocol.
Alternatively, in this scenario, tapering-dose OCPs can be used, with dosing frequency reduced over time. The FIRST 2 days are typically dosed:
The tapering OCP regimen starts with dosing every 4–8 hours for the first 2 days.
In the tapering OCP regimen for acute severe AUB, the middle 5 days are dosed 12-hourly, and the final 14 days are dosed:
The tapering schedule finishes with once-daily dosing for the final 14 days.
This tapering OCP approach for acute heavy bleeding relies on which underlying principle?
High-dose hormone exposure stabilising the endometrium, then gradually tapering
High initial hormone dosing stabilises the endometrium to control bleeding, then the dose is gradually tapered.
Endometrial ablation destroys the endometrial lining to a depth of approximately:
Endometrial ablation destroys the lining to a depth of about 4–6 mm.
First-generation endometrial ablation techniques (e.g. rollerball, laser, TCRE) are performed under hysteroscopic guidance, which carries:
An increased risk of fluid overload
A guaranteed need for hysterectomy afterward
Hysteroscopic guidance (needed for first-generation techniques) carries an increased risk of fluid overload from distension media.
Second-generation techniques (e.g. cryosurgery, hydrothermal ablation) are NOT performed under direct hysteroscopic view, meaning they carry:
A higher risk of fluid overload
The same risks as first-generation techniques
Only cryogenic risks with no other advantage
Since second-generation techniques avoid direct hysteroscopic distension, they carry no fluid overload risk.
Which of these is a contraindication to endometrial ablation?
A desire for future pregnancy/incomplete family
A desire for future fertility (incomplete family) is a contraindication, since ablation destroys the endometrium needed for implantation.
Endometrial ablation is also contraindicated in the presence of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer and:
Active pelvic infection, along with pregnancy, incomplete family, endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, and IUCD presence, is a contraindication to ablation.
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is defined as abnormal bleeding with a normal USG (no pelvic pathology), no coagulopathy, and:
DUB is a diagnosis of exclusion: normal pelvic anatomy on USG, no coagulopathy, and no medical/endocrine pathology.
Of all DUB cases, anovulatory DUB (AUB-D) accounts for about 80%, while ovulatory AUB (AUB-E/AUB-N) accounts for the remaining:
Anovulatory DUB makes up about 80% of cases (AUB-D), while ovulatory AUB accounts for the remaining 20% (AUB-E/AUB-N).
Besides coagulation and menstrual history, important history points in AUB evaluation include recent abortion and:
A history of IUCD insertion (along with recent abortion) is relevant, as both can be iatrogenic causes of AUB.
The gold standard investigation for endometrial pathology, combining fractional curettage with direct visualization, is:
Endometrial biopsy alone, done as an OPD procedure
Fractional curettage with hysteroscopy, done under general anaesthesia in the OT
Fractional curettage combined with hysteroscopy (done under GA in the OT) is the gold standard for endometrial pathology, though endometrial sampling/biopsy is the IOC as a simpler OPD procedure.
The dose of tranexamic acid used in AUB management is:
Tranexamic acid is dosed at 1 g thrice daily for 3–4 days in AUB management.
The dose of mefenamic acid used in AUB (with dysmenorrhoea) is:
Mefenamic acid is dosed at 500 mg thrice daily, used alongside tranexamic acid rather than as first-line alone.
For regularising menstrual cycles in AUB, the drug of choice (DOC) is:
OCPs are the drug of choice for regularising cycles in AUB, in addition to controlling blood loss and providing contraceptive benefit.
Regardless of the specific clinical scenario, blood transfusion is indicated in AUB when haemoglobin falls below:
5 g/dL, or if vitals are unstable

Blood transfusion is indicated for Hb < 5 g/dL or unstable vitals, regardless of the specific clinical context (distinct from the Hb <7 threshold in puberty menorrhagia or <10 before planned surgery).
The dose of ormeloxifene (a SERM, now largely obsolete for this indication) in AUB management is:
Ormeloxifene is dosed at 60 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, working by antagonising oestrogen’s effect on the endometrium (causing atrophy).
Surgical management of AUB (e.g., endometrial ablation, hysterectomy) is indicated only when BOTH of which conditions are fulfilled?
Patient preference alone, regardless of family status
Age over 40 alone, regardless of medical therapy tried
Failure of medical management AND a complete family
Surgical management requires both failure of medical management and a complete family — either alone is not sufficient.
The HPO axis is functional in intrauterine life, then becomes:
Progressively more active each year of childhood
Dormant after birth, reactivating at puberty
The HPO axis, functional in-utero, becomes dormant after birth and reactivates at puberty.
Dormancy of the HPO axis in childhood is maintained partly by central inhibition from which neurotransmitters?
GABA and neuropeptide Y are inhibitory neurotransmitters maintaining HPO axis dormancy.
Before puberty, the HPO axis shows high sensitivity to circulating oestrogen, such that even very low levels (E1 <10 pg) provide:
Negative feedback, keeping the axis suppressed
Feedback only on the adrenal gland
The prepubertal HPO axis is highly sensitive to oestrogen’s negative feedback, so even tiny amounts (from adrenal androgen aromatisation) keep it suppressed.
At puberty, the HPO axis becomes functional due to release of excitatory neurotransmitters, chiefly:
Kisspeptin (driving pulsatile GnRH release) and glutamate are the key excitatory drivers of pubertal HPO activation.
Leptin, released from adipose tissue, has which action on puberty onset?
A permissive action, supporting the onset of puberty
Leptin has a permissive role, supporting pubertal onset.
Because leptin correlates with body fat, obese girls tend to have:
Only delayed menarche but normal thelarche timing
Higher leptin from increased adipose tissue in obese girls is linked to relatively earlier puberty onset.
As the HPO axis becomes functional, GnRH is initially released:
Continuously throughout the day and night, from the very start
At high pulse frequency from the outset
Nocturnally, with low pulse frequency, before day-and-night release develops over 1–3 years
GnRH release starts nocturnally at low pulse frequency, evolving to day-and-night release over about 1–3 years.
In early puberty, the anterior pituitary initially releases predominantly:
FSH release predominates initially, with LH developing later.
Because LH release lags behind FSH in early puberty, the initial menstrual cycles are typically:
Completely absent for the first year
Without adequate LH surge capacity yet, early cycles are typically anovulatory.
The functional HPO axis pathway proceeds: hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (FSH/LH) → ovary, producing:
Estrogen and progesterone, acting on the uterus
The activated axis drives ovarian estrogen and progesterone production, acting on the uterus.
The growth spurt is the same for both sexes until about age 10.5, after which:
Girls' growth spurt is earlier and shorter; boys' is later and longer
Boys' growth spurt is earlier and shorter
There is no further sex difference
Girls' growth spurt starts earlier and is shorter; boys' starts later and lasts longer.
In females, puberty begins around age 10.5, with the very first sign being:
The growth spurt (skeletal growth) is the first sign of female puberty, even before it becomes visible.
The first VISIBLE sign of puberty in females, and the most specific marker, is:
Thelarche (breast budding) is the first visible sign and the most specific marker of puberty onset in females.
In females, menarche typically follows peak height velocity by about:
Menarche typically follows peak height velocity by about 6 months.
Average age of menarche is about:
Average age of menarche is about 12.5 years.
In males, puberty begins around age 11.5, with the first sign being:
Testicular enlargement is the first sign of male puberty, followed by penile enlargement, pubarche, and peak height velocity.
Tanner staging of breast and pubic hair development comprises how many total stages?
Tanner staging has 5 total stages, with stages 1–2 early and stages 4–5 late (mature) development.
Breast budding corresponds to Tanner stage:
Breast budding corresponds to Tanner stage 2.
Hair appearing on the mons pubis corresponds to Tanner stage:
Hair on the mons pubis corresponds to Tanner stage 3.
Hair appearing on the medial thigh corresponds to the LATE stage of development, Tanner stage:
Hair on the medial thigh corresponds to the late Tanner stage 5.
Adrenarche, the maturation of adrenal androgen secretion, is notable because it:
Occurs only after full HPO axis activation
Is independent of HPO axis activation and occurs under age 6
Adrenarche is independent of HPO axis (gonadarche) activation and occurs under age 6.
Adrenarche is biochemically indicated by DHEAS levels of:
Estrogen helps initiate the pubertal growth spurt partly by promoting anterior pituitary release of:
