Estrogen promotes anterior pituitary release of insulin-like growth factor (IGF), supporting the growth spurt.
Besides growth spurt initiation, estrogen's roles at puberty include breast development, menarche, and:
Bone mineralisation is one of estrogen's key roles at puberty, alongside growth spurt, breast development, and menarche.
Estrogen causes epiphyseal closure of long bones; in precocious puberty, this leads to:
Short final stature, from premature epiphyseal closure
Premature epiphyseal closure from early oestrogen exposure in precocious puberty results in short final stature.
Which of these is NOT typically listed as a role of estrogen at puberty?
Adrenarche is a separate, HPO-axis-independent process, not an action of oestrogen.
Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) occurring in a pubertal female
Bleeding limited to the first period only
Pubertal menorrhagia is AUB occurring specifically in a pubertal female.
The most common cause of pubertal menorrhagia is:
Anovulation is the most common cause of pubertal menorrhagia.
The second most common cause of pubertal menorrhagia is:
A coagulation defect is the second most common cause, after anovulation.
A coagulation defect should be specifically suspected in pubertal menorrhagia if there is a history of heavy bleeding at menarche, easy bruisability, profuse bleeding from wounds, or:
A single normal period before this episode
A family history of coagulation disorder
A family history of coagulation disorder, along with heavy bleeding at menarche, bruisability, and profuse wound bleeding, raises suspicion for an underlying coagulopathy.
In the workup of pubertal menorrhagia, USG is:
USG is not mandatory in the routine workup of pubertal menorrhagia.
Routine investigations in pubertal menorrhagia workup include haemoglobin, TSH, and a coagulation profile (bleeding time, clotting time, prothrombin time), plus UPT if the patient is:
UPT is added to the workup specifically if the patient is sexually active.
For MILD pubertal menorrhagia (Hb 10–12 g/dL), management is:
Oral iron, reassurance, and a menstrual diary/calendar
Mild cases are managed with oral iron, reassurance, and menstrual charting.
For MODERATE pubertal menorrhagia (Hb 8–10 g/dL), first-line management is:
OCPs, to reduce blood loss and regularise the cycle
OCPs are first-line for moderate cases, reducing blood loss and regularising the cycle.
If a patient with moderate pubertal menorrhagia refuses OCPs, tranexamic acid (500 mg three times daily for 5 days) can be used, though it:
Also regularises the cycle, just like OCPs
Is contraindicated in this age group
Reduces blood loss but does NOT regularise the cycle
Is the preferred first choice over OCPs
Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss but, unlike OCPs, does not regularise the cycle.
For SEVERE pubertal menorrhagia (Hb <8 g/dL, profuse bleeding for 15 days), initial treatment options include high-dose IV oestrogen (unavailable in India), ethinylestradiol 50 mg for 5 days, or:
Tapering-dose OCPs are an option for initial treatment of severe pubertal menorrhagia.
In the tapering OCP regimen for severe pubertal menorrhagia, dosing starts 8-hourly for the first 2 days, then 12-hourly, then once daily, over a total course of:
The full tapering course runs over 21 days: 2 days 8-hourly, 5 days 12-hourly, then 2 weeks once daily.
Maintenance therapy after severe pubertal menorrhagia is controlled includes OCP (once daily, day 5–25) for 6 cycles, or alternatively:
Tranexamic acid daily for a year
Progesterone for 10 days in each cycle, for 6 cycles
Progesterone for 10 days per cycle, for 6 cycles, is the alternative maintenance option.
Precocious puberty in females is defined as the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before age:
Precocious puberty in females is defined as secondary sexual characteristics appearing before age 8.
Precocious puberty in males is defined as the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before age:
Precocious puberty in males is defined as secondary sexual characteristics appearing before age 9.
Precocious puberty is more common in:
Precocious puberty is more common in females than males.
In isosexual precocious puberty, a female develops:
Female secondary sexual characteristics early, due to excess estrogen
No secondary sexual characteristics at all
Isosexual precocious puberty means early development of characteristics matching the person’s own sex, driven by excess estrogen in females.
In heterosexual precocious puberty, a female develops:
Accelerated but otherwise normal female puberty
Male secondary sexual characteristics, due to excess androgen
Heterosexual precocious puberty means development of characteristics of the opposite sex — in females, driven by excess androgen.
The most common overall cause of precocious puberty is:
Idiopathic precocious puberty is the most common cause overall, though brain tumours account for about 10% of cases.
Central (true) precocious puberty accounts for what proportion of cases, making it the more common type?
Central precocious puberty accounts for about 80% of cases.
Central precocious puberty results from premature activation of the HPO axis, causing:
Decreased GnRH, FSH, LH, and estrogen
Isolated estrogen elevation without gonadotropin change
Increased GnRH, FSH, LH, and estrogen, in that sequence
Premature HPO axis activation raises GnRH, then FSH/LH, then estrogen, in sequence.
Peripheral precocious puberty is NOT related to the HPO axis; instead, the source of excess hormone is the:
Peripheral precocious puberty arises from the ovary or adrenal gland directly, bypassing the HPO axis.
In peripheral precocious puberty, excess peripheral estrogen/androgen causes negative feedback, resulting in:
Excess peripheral hormone suppresses FSH/LH via negative feedback, since the axis is otherwise not driving the process.
Premature ovulation is a feature of:
Since central PP genuinely activates the HPO axis, it can result in premature ovulation, unlike peripheral PP.
Central precocious puberty is always isosexual, while peripheral precocious puberty can be:
Peripheral PP can be isosexual (excess estrogen) or heterosexual (excess androgen), unlike central PP, which is always isosexual.
Besides idiopathic causes, central precocious puberty can result from brain tumours (e.g. hamartoma, glioma, ependymoma) or:
CNS infection such as TB meningitis is another recognised cause of central precocious puberty.
A granulosa cell tumour of the ovary is a recognised cause of which type of precocious puberty?
None; it does not cause precocious puberty
A granulosa cell tumour secretes estrogen, causing isosexual peripheral precocious puberty.
Chronic hypothyroidism can cause isosexual peripheral precocious puberty because:
The alpha subunit of TSH is similar to that of LH/FSH, allowing cross-reactivity with gonadal receptors
Hypothyroidism always causes early puberty via unrelated mechanisms
It has no real mechanistic link and is coincidental
The shared alpha subunit between TSH and LH/FSH allows very high TSH to cross-react with gonadotropin receptors.
McCune-Albright syndrome is a recognised cause of:
McCune-Albright syndrome causes isosexual peripheral precocious puberty, via autonomous ovarian oestrogen production.
Androgen-producing ovarian tumours and congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) are causes of:
Excess androgen from these sources causes heterosexual precocious puberty.
The most common cause of heterosexual PRECOCIOUS puberty specifically is:
CAH is the most common cause of heterosexual precocious puberty specifically (PCOS is the most common cause of heterosexual development generally, at a later/normal age).
The classic triad of McCune-Albright syndrome includes café-au-lait spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and:
The McCune-Albright triad is café-au-lait spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty.
The underlying pathogenesis of McCune-Albright syndrome involves:
A chromosomal deletion on the X chromosome
A mutation in G-protein coupled (FSH) receptors, causing constitutive activation
A constitutively active G-protein coupled FSH receptor mutation drives the syndrome.
This constitutively active FSH receptor mutation in McCune-Albright syndrome directly:
Activates the ovaries, raising oestrogen independent of pituitary FSH
Only affects bone, with no hormonal consequence
The mutated receptor activates the ovary autonomously, raising oestrogen without needing pituitary FSH drive.
The single best investigation to differentiate central from peripheral precocious puberty is:
FSH and LH levels are the best investigation to distinguish gonadotropin-dependent (central) from gonadotropin-independent (peripheral) precocious puberty.
For HETEROSEXUAL precocious puberty specifically, additional investigations include testosterone, DHEA-S (to localise the source between ovary and adrenal), and:
17-OH progesterone, to rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia
17-OH progesterone is checked specifically to rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia in heterosexual PP.
Delayed puberty in females is defined as absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age 13, or absence of menarche by age:
Delayed puberty in females is defined by no secondary sexual characteristics by 13, or no menarche by 15.
Delayed puberty in males is defined as absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age:
Delayed puberty in males is defined as no secondary sexual characteristics by age 14.
Delayed puberty is overall more common in:
Delayed puberty is more common in males than females.
The most common cause of delayed puberty (in both sexes) is:
Constitutional delay is the most common cause of delayed puberty in both sexes.
Delayed puberty from low GnRH, associated with anosmia, points to:
Low GnRH with anosmia is characteristic of Kallmann syndrome.
A 46,XY karyotype with delayed puberty and female external phenotype suggests:
Androgen insensitivity syndrome presents with a 46,XY karyotype but female external phenotype, due to end-organ resistance to androgens.
Puberty is defined by all of the following EXCEPT:
The period involving transition from childhood to adulthood
Onset of development of secondary sexual characters

Permanent cessation of menstruation defines menopause, not puberty. Puberty is defined by the childhood-to-adulthood transition, onset of secondary sexual characters, and attainment of reproductive capacity.

The initial menstrual cycles at puberty are anovulatory, irregular, heavy, and characteristically:
Initial pubertal menstrual cycles are anovulatory, irregular, heavy in flow, and painless.

Menstruation occurring before the age of 10 years is specifically termed:
Precocious menstruation refers specifically to menstruation occurring before age 10 years, distinct from the broader term precocious puberty.

In the context of puberty, primary amenorrhoea is defined as failure of menarche within how many years of breast budding (thelarche)?
Failure of menarche within 3 years of breast budding defines primary amenorrhoea in this context.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
The most important secondary sexual character in females is:
Breast development is regarded as the most important secondary sexual character in females, driven by oestrogen and occurring in stages.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
Besides stimulating development of pubic and axillary hair, adrenarche in females is also associated with:
Adrenarche (adrenal androgen release) is associated with increased libido in females, in addition to pubic/axillary hair development.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
Besides anovulation (most common) and a coagulation defect (second most common), another recognised cause of pubertal menorrhagia is:
Thyroid dysfunction is listed as another recognised cause of pubertal menorrhagia, alongside anovulation and coagulation defects.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
In the evaluation of pubertal menorrhagia, per vaginal (PV) examination is:
Mandatory before any USG is done
Only omitted if the patient is anaemic
Per vaginal examination is contraindicated in virgin females during evaluation of pubertal menorrhagia.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
The three standard drug categories used in management of any abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), including pubertal menorrhagia, are tranexamic acid, combined OCPs, and:
Tranexamic acid, combined OCPs, and progesterone-only therapy are the three standard drug categories used across AUB management, including pubertal menorrhagia.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
The management of CENTRAL precocious puberty is with continuous GnRH (agonist) therapy or:
Central precocious puberty is managed with continuous GnRH agonist therapy or GnRH antagonists, both suppressing the prematurely activated HPO axis.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
The management of PERIPHERAL precocious puberty consists primarily of:
Since peripheral precocious puberty is not HPO-axis driven, management targets the underlying cause (e.g., ovarian/adrenal tumour, hypothyroidism) rather than suppressing GnRH.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
The drug of choice for management of delayed puberty (e.g., in Kallmann syndrome) is:
Pulsatile GnRH is the drug of choice for delayed puberty, in contrast to the continuous GnRH used to suppress central precocious puberty.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
PCOS, via chronic anovulation, is a recognised cause of:
PCOS (causing anovulation) is listed among the causes of delayed puberty, alongside constitutional delay, Kallmann syndrome, Turner syndrome, and androgen insensitivity syndrome.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
Recognised consequences of precocious puberty include risk related to the underlying cause, estrogen exposure at a young age, and:
Psychological and emotional stress is a recognised consequence of precocious puberty, alongside early oestrogen exposure and risks tied to the underlying cause.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
In the central vs peripheral precocious puberty comparison table, premature menarche (<10 years) is present (+) in central PP, while in peripheral PP it is:
Variable (\u00b1), occurring due to oestrogen breakthrough bleeding
Always present, identical to central PP
Peripheral PP shows variable (\u00b1) premature menarche, occurring due to oestrogen breakthrough bleeding rather than a mature ovulatory cycle.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
Since brain tumours account for about 10% of precocious puberty cases, MRI brain is indicated:
Only if neurological symptoms are present
Only in males with precocious puberty
In all females with precocious puberty
MRI brain is indicated in all females with precocious puberty, given that brain tumours account for about 10% of cases.
Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details
In the general investigation panel for precocious puberty, bone age estimation and FSH/LH are done alongside estrogen, TSH, MRI brain, and:
USG pelvis and abdomen rounds out the general precocious puberty workup, alongside bone age, FSH/LH, oestrogen, TSH, and MRI brain.

Menopause is defined as amenorrhoea of at least how many months, followed by permanent cessation of menstruation?
Menopause is defined as amenorrhoea ≥ 12 months followed by permanent cessation of menstruation.
The maximum number of ovarian follicles is present at which point in life?
Follicle number peaks at 6–7 million in the 5th month of intrauterine life, after which apoptosis reduces the number.
By birth, apoptosis has reduced the follicle count to approximately:
By birth, follicle number falls to about 1–2 million, down from a peak of 6–7 million in utero.
By puberty, the follicle count is approximately:
By puberty, roughly 4–5 million follicles remain, further reduced from the birth count.
A rebound increase in follicle number
Menopause corresponds to complete atresia of all ovarian follicles.
The average age of menopause is later worldwide than in India; the correct pairing is:
The average age of menopause is 51 years worldwide but 47 years in India.
Premature menopause is now more accurately termed:
Premature menopause is now termed primary ovarian insufficiency (POI).
POI is defined as menopause occurring before age:
POI (premature menopause) is defined as occurring before 40 years of age.
POI presents with secondary amenorrhoea and secondary infertility.
Late menopause is defined as non-occurrence of menopause in a female aged:
Late menopause is defined as non-occurrence of menopause by ≥ 55 years of age.
In late menopause, an endometrial biopsy is recommended because of increased risk of:
Late menopause carries an increased risk of endometrial cancer, so endometrial biopsy is advised.
The first sign of perimenopause (climacteric) is:
An increase in cycle length by ≥ 7 days
The first sign of perimenopause is an increase in cycle length of ≥ 7 days.
Menstrual cycles during perimenopause are typically:
Perimenopausal cycles are anovulatory and irregular.
STRAW staging divides the 3 phases of female adult life (reproductive age, perimenopause, menopause) into a total of:
STRAW staging divides the 3 phases of female adult life into 7 total stages.
Clinical criteria alone; no hormonal test is required
Menopause is a clinical diagnosis; no hormonal test is required (unlike POI, where lab testing is mandatory).
Unlike menopause, the diagnosis of POI requires:
POI diagnosis requires a mandatory laboratory test, in contrast to menopause which is a clinical diagnosis.
At menopause, which two ovarian hormones fall due to follicular apoptosis?
Follicular apoptosis at menopause leads to falling estrogen and androgen levels.
The predominant circulating estrogen after menopause is:
After menopause, estrone (E1) becomes the most common circulating estrogen.
AMH and inhibin levels after menopause are:
Both AMH and inhibin fall after menopause, reflecting depleted follicular reserve.
Loss of negative feedback from falling ovarian hormones at menopause leads to a rise in:
Loss of negative feedback causes a compensatory rise in FSH and LH.
Elevated FSH and LH excreted in the urine after menopause are together referred to as:
Urinary FSH/LH after menopause are referred to as HMG (Human Menopausal Gonadotropins).
A patient with secondary amenorrhoea and raised FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) should next have which test to confirm menopause/POI?
The next step in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism is measuring estrogen; low estrogen confirms menopause or POI.
Pregnancy can also cause secondary amenorrhoea, but is distinguished from menopause by which hormonal pattern?
Decreased estrogen and progesterone, decreased FSH and LH
Decreased estrogen, increased FSH and LH (same as menopause)
Increased estrogen and progesterone, increased FSH but decreased LH
In pregnancy, secondary amenorrhoea occurs with increased estrogen and progesterone, increased FSH, but decreased LH — unlike the menopausal pattern.
The most common symptom of menopause is:
Hot flushes (vasomotor symptoms) are the most common symptom of menopause.
Hot flushes occur because falling estrogen causes:
Resetting of the hypothalamic thermostat with a serotonin–norepinephrine imbalance
Falling estrogen resets the hypothalamic thermostat and causes a serotonin–norepinephrine imbalance, producing hot flushes.
The typical presentation of a hot flush is an intense heat sensation on the face, followed by:
A hot flush classically presents as a heat sensation on the face followed by sweating, sometimes with palpitations/tachycardia.
Hot flushes most commonly occur at night, when they are termed:
Night sweats, with associated disturbed sleep
Night-time hot flushes are termed night sweats and are associated with disturbed sleep.
A typical hot flush episode lasts less than 5 minutes and recurs approximately:
Each hot flush episode lasts under 5 minutes and recurs about 3–4 times.
Hot flushes, seen in perimenopausal and menopausal women, typically begin how long before menopause and subside how long after?
Begin 3–4 years before, subside 5 years after
Begin only after menopause, subside within a week
Begin at menarche, subside at menopause
Hot flushes begin 3–4 years before menopause and automatically subside about 5 years after menopause.
Severe hot flushes causing sleep disturbance or interference with daily activities represent:
The only indication for post-menopausal HRT
A sign of primary ovarian insufficiency exclusively
Severe hot flushes (with sleep disturbance or interference with daily activities) are the only indication for post-menopausal HRT.
Menopausal osteoporosis is best described as:
A quantitative bone defect with reduced bone mineral density
A pure vitamin D deficiency state
Osteoporosis is a quantitative bone defect — reduced bone mineral density (BMD).
Menopausal osteoporosis most commonly affects which type of bone?
Trabecular bone is most commonly affected in menopausal osteoporosis.
The three classic fracture sites at increased risk in menopausal osteoporosis are vertebral (T12–L3), neck of femur, and:
The three classic fracture sites are vertebral (T12–L3), neck of femur, and Colles fracture.
The investigation of choice for menopausal osteoporosis is:
DEXA scan is the investigation of choice for osteoporosis.
DEXA scanning is indicated at what age?
DEXA scan is indicated from age ≥ 65 years.
The preferred DEXA site is the 1st–4th lumbar vertebrae, which is favoured over:
Lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) are the preferred DEXA site, over the neck of femur.
On a DEXA report, comparing a patient's BMD to that of a young woman gives the:
The T-score compares a patient’s BMD to a young woman’s BMD; the Z-score compares it to a woman of the same age.
The drug of choice for menopausal osteoporosis is:
Bisphosphonates are the drug of choice for menopausal osteoporosis.
Drugs that act directly on osteoblasts (rather than osteoclasts) in osteoporosis management include teriparatide and:
Teriparatide and strontium act on osteoblasts, unlike bisphosphonates which act on osteoclasts.
Estrogen's cardioprotective effect includes raising HDL, lowering LDL, and increasing:
Nitric oxide in vascular endothelial cells
Estrogen increases nitric oxide in vascular endothelial cells, alongside raising HDL and lowering LDL.
At menopause, falling estrogen leads to:
Decreased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD)
Increased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD)
Only a change in bone density, with no vascular effect
Falling estrogen at menopause increases the risk of coronary artery disease.
The incidence of CAD in menopausal women particularly depends on:
CAD incidence depends on comorbidities and smoking habits.
Regarding HRT and cardiovascular disease, HRT is:
Only used to treat established CAD
HRT is never given to prevent CAD.
In women ≥ 60 years, HRT is associated with a slightly increased CAD risk, which is higher with:
Estrogen-only HRT compared to estrogen + progesterone HRT
Estrogen + progesterone HRT compared to estrogen-only HRT
In women ≥ 60 years, E+P HRT carries a slightly higher CAD risk than estrogen-only HRT; in women <60, HRT has no effect on CAD risk.
Senile/atrophic vaginitis is now termed genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
The genitourinary syndrome of menopause results from falling estrogen causing reduced cervical discharge and:
Falling estrogen reduces cervical discharge, resulting in vaginal dryness.
Urinary symptoms of genitourinary syndrome of menopause include increased urinary frequency, dysuria, frequent UTIs, and:
Urinary incontinence is among the urinary symptoms, along with increased frequency, dysuria, and frequent UTIs.
Genital symptoms of this syndrome include dyspareunia and:
Bleeding per vaginum due to the atrophic vagina
Bleeding per vaginum (due to the atrophic vagina) is a genital symptom, along with dyspareunia.
On local examination, the genitourinary syndrome of menopause classically shows shiny vaginal mucosa, thin atrophied mucosa, and:
Loss of vaginal rugosities is a classic local examination finding, along with shiny, thin, atrophied mucosa.
Which SERMs are known to worsen vaginal dryness?
Clomiphene, tamoxifen, and raloxifene are SERMs that can worsen vaginal dryness.
Which SERMs are actually useful in managing senile/atrophic vaginitis?
Ospemifene, and bazedoxifene combined with estrogen
Ospemifene, and bazedoxifene + estrogen, are the SERMs used to manage senile vaginitis (unlike clomiphene/tamoxifen/raloxifene, which worsen it).
For hot flushes, first-line management is HRT; if the uterus is intact, which regimen is used?
With an intact uterus, combined estrogen + progesterone HRT is used, since progesterone protects the endometrium.
For hot flushes, if the uterus is absent, HRT is given as:
With the uterus absent, estrogen-only HRT is appropriate since there is no endometrium to protect.
Second-line therapy for hot flushes (SSRIs) includes fluoxetine, paroxetine, and:
Venlafaxine, along with fluoxetine and paroxetine, is used as second-line SSRI therapy for hot flushes.
The SERM combination used for hot flushes is bazedoxifene with estrogen; which SERMs are contraindicated here as they can worsen hot flushes?
Raloxifene, tamoxifen, and clomiphene are contraindicated as they can worsen hot flushes.
Other (non-hormonal) drugs used for hot flushes include clonidine, gabapentin, isoflavenes, and:
Phytoestrogens (e.g. flax seed), along with isoflavenes, clonidine, and gabapentin, are non-hormonal options for hot flushes.
For osteoporosis, first-line therapy is alendronate; HRT is second-line, along with which SERM?
Raloxifene is the SERM option for osteoporosis management, alongside first-line alendronate and second-line HRT.
Other drugs for osteoporosis include tibolone (an estrogen + progesterone analogue), teriparatide, strontium, and:
Denosumab, a RANK ligand inhibitor, is another drug option for osteoporosis, along with tibolone, teriparatide, and strontium.
For senile vaginitis, first-line management is vaginal lubricants; second-line is local estrogen therapy, given as cream/gel, ring, or:
Local estrogen therapy for senile vaginitis can be given as cream/gel, pessary, or ring.
The daily calcium and vitamin D requirements are higher in menopausal women than in the reproductive age group; the menopausal requirements are:
1000 mg/day calcium and 600 IU vitamin D
800 mg/day calcium and 400 IU vitamin D
1200 mg/day calcium and 800 IU vitamin D
1500 mg/day calcium and 1000 IU vitamin D
Menopausal women require 1200 mg/day calcium and 800 IU vitamin D, higher than the reproductive age group’s 1000 mg/day and 600 IU.
Primary ovarian insufficiency is defined as exhaustion of ovarian follicles before age:
POI is defined as exhaustion of ovarian follicles before 40 years of age (premature menopause).
Among the causes of POI, the ovary is notable as the:
Organ most resistant to autoimmune damage
The ovary is the most radiosensitive pelvic organ, making chemo/radiotherapy an important cause of POI.
Besides chemo/radiotherapy, metabolic and infectious causes of POI include galactosemia and:
Galactosemia and mumps are recognised metabolic/infectious causes of POI.
Genetic syndromes associated with POI include Fragile X syndrome and:
Fragile X syndrome and Turner mosaic are the genetic syndromes associated with POI.
Clinical features of POI include hot flushes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, secondary infertility, and:
Secondary amenorrhoea with irregular cycles is a clinical feature of POI, along with hot flushes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and secondary infertility.
Confirming POI mandates FSH testing on two occasions, one month apart; an FSH ≥ 40 IU/L is:
Diagnostic of menopause but not POI
FSH ≥ 40 IU/L on two occasions one month apart is diagnostic of POI (FSH ≥ 25 IU is only suggestive, and <10 IU is normal).
Karyotyping is indicated in POI when there is short stature, or normal stature with age:
Karyotyping is indicated in POI for short stature, or for normal stature at age 30 years.
For a POI patient desiring fertility, the management of choice is:
IVF using the patient's own eggs only
IVF with donor eggs, with the embryo implanted in the patient's uterus
IVF with donor eggs, with the embryo implanted in the patient's own uterus, is the management of choice for infertility in POI.
For POI patients troubled by hot flushes, HRT should be continued until:
HRT for hot flushes in POI is continued until the age of normal menopause.
Menopausal symptoms are due to falling estrogen and are relieved by:
Menopausal symptoms result from falling estrogen and are relieved by post-menopausal HRT.
HRT is indicated in postmenopausal women with severe hot flushes and in:
HRT is indicated for post-menopausal severe hot flushes and for primary ovarian insufficiency (POI).
HRT is also indicated in ↓estrogen states from gonadal dysgenesis, such as Turner's syndrome and:
Turner's syndrome and Swyer's syndrome (both gonadal dysgenesis) are ↓estrogen states indicated for HRT.
HRT is indicated following surgical oophorectomy and in ↓estrogen states from:
Androgen insensitivity syndrome (a ↓estrogen state) and surgical oophorectomy are both indications for HRT.
If the uterus is absent, which type of HRT is used?
Estrogen-only HRT is used when the uterus is absent, since there is no endometrium to protect.
If the uterus is present, which type of HRT is used, and why?
Estrogen-only HRT, since progesterone increases cancer risk
E+P HRT, because progesterone protects the endometrium
With the uterus present, combined E+P HRT is used because progesterone protects the endometrium from cancer development.
In combined HRT, estrogen reduces hot flushes while progesterone's role is to:
Protect the endometrium from developing cancer
Progesterone's role in combined HRT is to protect the endometrium from developing cancer, while estrogen reduces hot flushes.
The minimum duration of progesterone required per cycle in HRT is:
A minimum of 12 days of progesterone per cycle is required in combined HRT.
The ideal duration of progesterone use in a woman on combined HRT is:
As long as estrogen is given
Not needed if BMI is normal
Ideally, progesterone should be given for as long as estrogen is given, to continuously protect the endometrium.
Giving unopposed estrogen (without adequate progesterone) in a woman with an intact uterus mainly risks:
Unopposed estrogen in a woman with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial cancer, which is why progesterone is co-administered.
Benefits of estrogen-only HRT include reduced hot flushes, reduced osteoporosis, and reduced chances of:
Estrogen-only HRT reduces hot flushes, osteoporosis, and chances of colorectal cancer.
A key disadvantage of estrogen-only HRT is increased risk of:
Estrogen-only HRT carries an increased risk of venous thromboembolism.
The increased VTE risk with estrogen-only HRT is lower with which route of administration?
The transdermal route carries a lower VTE risk compared to oral estrogen.
Estrogen-only HRT increases the risk of endometrial cancer specifically when:
The patient has had a prior hysterectomy
Estrogen-only HRT increases endometrial cancer risk only if the uterus is present (unopposed estrogen effect).
Estrogen-only HRT carries a variably increased (±) risk of:
Estrogen-only HRT is associated with a variably increased (±) risk of ovarian cancer.
Like estrogen-only HRT, combined E+P HRT reduces hot flushes, osteoporosis, and chances of colorectal cancer; unlike estrogen-only HRT, it also:
Has no effect on endometrial cancer risk
Unlike estrogen-only HRT, combined E+P HRT reduces the chances of endometrial cancer, because progesterone protects the endometrium.
A disadvantage shared between combined and estrogen-only HRT is increased risk of:
Both combined and estrogen-only HRT carry an increased risk of venous thromboembolism.
Combined E+P HRT carries a variably increased (±) risk of:
Like estrogen-only HRT, combined E+P HRT carries a variably increased (±) risk of ovarian cancer.
A disadvantage specific to combined E+P HRT (not listed for estrogen-only) is increased risk of:
Increased breast cancer risk is a disadvantage specific to combined E+P HRT.
Which statement correctly contrasts endometrial cancer risk between the two HRT types?
Both types increase endometrial cancer risk equally
Both types reduce endometrial cancer risk equally
E+P HRT reduces endometrial cancer risk, while estrogen-only HRT (with uterus present) increases it
Neither type affects endometrial cancer risk
E+P HRT reduces endometrial cancer risk (progesterone protects the endometrium), while unopposed estrogen-only HRT in a woman with a uterus increases it.
Fully protects against CAD in all age groups
Is specifically prescribed to prevent CAD
Does not protect against CAD in females ≥ 60 years; risk is actually increased
HRT does not protect against CAD in females ≥ 60 years — risk is actually increased in this group.
HRT does NOT increase the risk of:
HRT does not increase the risk of cervical cancer, unlike the other listed risks.
The maximum duration of HRT in a postmenopausal woman is:
The maximum duration of HRT in a postmenopausal woman is 5 years.
In women with POI, Turner's syndrome, or Swyer's syndrome, HRT duration extends:
Up to the age of normal menopause
In POI, Turner's syndrome, or Swyer's syndrome, HRT is continued up to the age of normal menopause (rather than the fixed 5-year postmenopausal limit).
General indications for continuing HRT include age less than 60 years and time since menopause onset less than:
HRT indication generally requires age <60 years and <10 years since the onset of menopause.
In a woman with hot flushes who has a contraindication to HRT, the drug of choice is:
Fluoxetine is the drug of choice for hot flushes when HRT is contraindicated.
The drug of choice for the estrogen component of HRT is:
17β-estradiol is the drug of choice for the estrogen component of HRT.
For estrogen administration in HRT, which route is preferred over oral?
The transdermal route is preferred over oral for estrogen administration in HRT.
The oral dose of 17β-estradiol is 1 mg/day, typically started at:
Oral 17β-estradiol is dosed at 1 mg/day, typically started at 0.5 mg/day.
The transdermal dose of 17β-estradiol is 0.05 mg/day, typically started at:
Transdermal 17β-estradiol is dosed at 0.05 mg/day, typically started at 0.025 mg/day.
Conjugated equine estrogen (CEE), once commonly used, is now considered:
Conjugated equine estrogen (CEE) is now considered obsolete.
The drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT is:
Micronized oral progesterone, at a dose of 100–200 mg/day
Micronized oral progesterone (100–200 mg/day) is the drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT.
Besides micronized oral progesterone, another drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT is:
Dydrogesterone is also listed as a drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT.
Absolute contraindications to HRT include a past history of DVT, stroke, and:
A past history of DVT, stroke, and coronary artery disease are contraindications to HRT.
HRT is contraindicated in women with a past history of:
A past history of breast cancer is a contraindication to HRT.
Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is a contraindication to HRT because it may indicate:
Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is a contraindication as it may indicate underlying endometrial cancer.
A history relevant to hepatic function that contraindicates HRT is:
A history of acute liver disease/biopsy is a contraindication to HRT.
Which lipid abnormality is an absolute contraindication to HRT?
Hypertriglyceridemia is an absolute contraindication to HRT.
HRT is contraindicated in women with:
Severe uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication to HRT.
Standard HRT does not provide any contraceptive benefit.
In perimenopausal women with hot flushes who also need contraception, which combination provides contraceptive benefit?
Estrogen combined with the Mirena (levonorgestrel IUS) provides contraceptive benefit in perimenopausal women with hot flushes.
Even in women with an absent uterus, E+P HRT (rather than estrogen-only) is indicated if there is a history of hysterectomy due to:
A history of hysterectomy due to endometrial cancer is an indication for E+P HRT even with an absent uterus.
E+P HRT is also indicated (despite an absent uterus) in women with a history of:
A history of endometriosis is an indication for E+P HRT even with an absent uterus, since endometriotic implants can still respond to unopposed estrogen.
Another indication for E+P HRT with an absent uterus is a history of:
A history of endometrioid tumor of the ovary is an indication for E+P HRT even with an absent uterus.
E+P HRT (despite the uterus being technically absent) is also used after:
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for benign disease
After supracervical/subtotal hysterectomy, residual endometrial tissue may remain, so E+P HRT is used.
In intrauterine life, adrenal androgens are converted to estrogen via which enzyme?
Adrenal androgens are converted to estrogen via aromatase in intrauterine life.
At puberty, androgens in females are produced by the ovary (theca interna cells) and:
At puberty, androgens are produced by the ovarian theca interna cells and the adrenal glands.
Androgens produced by the ovary include androstenedione, testosterone, and:
The ovary produces androstenedione, testosterone, and DHEA.
Which androgen is produced exclusively by the adrenal glands (not the ovary)?
DHEA-Sulphate is produced exclusively by the adrenal glands, unlike androstenedione, testosterone, and DHEA, which the ovary also produces.
Testosterone is converted to the more potent DHT by which enzyme?
Testosterone is converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5α-reductase.
A key feature distinguishing androgen metabolism in females is that:
Females cannot produce testosterone at all
5α-reductase is absent in females, so testosterone is not converted to DHT as it is in males.
The normal level of androgen (testosterone) in females is:
The normal androgen (testosterone) level in females is < 70 ng/dL.
Androgen receptors are located in the cytoplasm and act on:
Androgen receptors are intracytoplasmic and act on intranuclear receptors.
Circulating androgens bind predominantly to which protein, more than albumin?
Androgens bind predominantly to SHBG, more than to albumin.
Androgens have which effect on SHBG levels, in contrast to estrogen?
Both androgens and estrogen increase SHBG
Androgens decrease SHBG, while estrogen increases it
Both androgens and estrogen decrease SHBG
Androgens increase SHBG, while estrogen decreases it
Androgens decrease SHBG, while estrogen increases SHBG.
Functions of androgens in females include pubarche (growth of pubic and axillary hair) and:
Androgens contribute to pubarche and increased libido in females.
Androgen produced in the theca cell is converted to estrogen in the granulosa cell via:
Theca cell androgen is converted to estrogen in the granulosa cell via aromatase.
Estrogen produced in the granulosa cell promotes:
Granulosa cell estrogen promotes growth of follicles.
Excessive androgen within granulosa cells has which effect?
Excessive androgen in granulosa cells is folliculotoxic.
Excess androgen arrests follicular growth, inhibiting maturation into:
Excess androgen arrests growth and inhibits maturation into Graafian follicles, leading to anovulation.
Besides anovulation, excessive androgens in females can cause hirsutism and:
Excessive androgens can cause anovulation, hirsutism, and virilization.
Hirsutism is defined as growth of thick, coarse, terminal hair in a male pattern, commonly at the lips, chin, chest, and:
Common sites of hirsutism include lips, chin, periareolar area, and chest.
A female acquiring male secondary sexual characteristics
Virilization is defined as a female acquiring male secondary sexual characteristics.
Features of hirsutism (without virilization) include scarring acne and:
Hirsutism features include alopecia (male pattern baldness) and scarring acne.
Features specific to virilization (beyond hirsutism itself) include deepening of voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle mass, and:
Virilization features include hirsutism, deepening of voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle mass, and clitoromegaly.
Clitoromegaly, a feature of virilization, is defined as clitoral size:
Clitoromegaly is defined as clitoral size ≥ 1 cm.
A milder degree of the same testosterone elevation as hirsutism
Virilization reflects markedly increased testosterone, compared to only mildly increased levels in hirsutism.
Conditions associated with hirsutism (not virilization) include PCOS, idiopathic hirsutism, and:
Some cases of late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
Hirsutism is associated with PCOS, idiopathic hirsutism, and some cases of late-onset CAH.
In idiopathic hirsutism, androgen levels are:
In idiopathic hirsutism, androgen levels are normal.
Conditions associated with virilization include androgen-producing ovarian tumor and:
Virilization is associated with androgen-producing ovarian tumor and most cases of CAH.
The scoring system used for hirsutism is the modified Ferriman-Gallwey score, which assesses:
The modified Ferriman-Gallwey score assesses 9 sites, each scored 0–4.
A modified Ferriman-Gallwey score of what value or above is diagnostic of hirsutism?
A modified Ferriman-Gallwey score ≥ 8 is diagnostic of hirsutism.
The scoring system used specifically for virilization is the:
Virilization is scored using the Prader score, distinct from the Ferriman-Gallwey score used for hirsutism.
A serum testosterone level under 70 ng/dL indicates:
A serum testosterone < 70 ng/dL indicates normal androgen levels, as in idiopathic hirsutism.
A serum testosterone level of 70–200 ng/dL (mildly elevated) is seen in PCOS and:
A mildly elevated testosterone (70–200 ng/dL) is seen in PCOS and some cases of late-onset CAH.
A serum testosterone level above 200 ng/dL suggests an androgen-secreting ovarian tumor or CAH, associated with:
Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests an androgen-secreting ovarian tumor or CAH, with associated virilization.
The most common cause of hirsutism in a young female is:
PCOS is the most common cause of hirsutism in a young female.
The most common cause of rapid-onset hirsutism in a young female is:
An androgen-secreting ovarian tumor is the most common cause of rapid-onset hirsutism in a young female.
To differentiate PCOS from late-onset CAH, the screening test used is:
17-OH progesterone level is used to screen for CAH and differentiate it from PCOS.
A 17-OH progesterone level below 200 ng effectively:
A 17-OH progesterone level < 200 ng rules out CAH.
A 17-OH progesterone level between 200–800 ng, suspicious for CAH, is confirmed by:
A 17-OH progesterone level of 200–800 ng is suspicious for CAH and confirmed by ACTH stimulation test.
A 17-OH progesterone level > 800 ng confirms CAH.
The drug of choice for management of hirsutism is:
OCPs (low-dose pills with 3rd/4th generation progesterone) are the drug of choice for hirsutism.
The typical duration of OCP therapy for hirsutism before reassessment is:
OCP therapy for hirsutism is typically given for 6 months before reassessment.
One mechanism of OCPs in hirsutism is estrogen + progesterone suppressing LH and FSH, thereby reducing:
Estrogen + progesterone suppress LH and FSH, reducing androgen production.
A second mechanism of OCPs in hirsutism is estrogen increasing SHBG, which in turn:
Estrogen increases SHBG, which decreases free (bioavailable) testosterone.
If OCPs fail to control hirsutism, the next drug added is:
If OCPs fail, spironolactone is added.
Spironolactone, used as add-on therapy for hirsutism, works by which mechanism?
Spironolactone works via an anti-androgenic mechanism.
Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy because it can cause:
Ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus
Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy as it can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus.
Other drugs used in the management of hirsutism include cyproterone acetate, flutamide, finasteride, and:
Other drugs used for hirsutism include cyproterone acetate, flutamide, finasteride, and ketoconazole.
Among adjunct drugs for hirsutism, which is described as only slightly effective?
Metformin is noted as only slightly effective for hirsutism.
Eflornithine, used in hirsutism management, is administered as a:
Eflornithine is a topical drug used in hirsutism management.
The last resort in refractory hirsutism management is continuous GnRH therapy, which works by:
↓FSH only, with no effect on LH
Continuous GnRH therapy (last resort) works by decreasing LH, which decreases androgen production.
Which drug is specifically contraindicated in hirsutism because it can itself cause hirsutism as a side effect?
Danazol is contraindicated as it can itself cause hirsutism as a side effect.
Besides pharmacological therapy, an additional modality used for hirsutism management is:
Laser hair removal is an additional (non-pharmacological) modality for hirsutism management.
A single uniform disease with one defined cause
A group of symptoms with various presentations and different underlying pathophysiology
A purely genetic disorder with no environmental influence
A disease exclusive to obese women
PCOS is a group of symptoms with various presentations and different underlying pathophysiology.
The older/previous term for PCOS was:
PCOS was previously termed Stein-Leventhal syndrome.
Etiological factors in PCOS include environmental factors, lifestyle factors, and:
Genetic factors (a complex genetic trait), along with environmental and lifestyle factors, contribute to PCOS.
Genetic factors implicated in PCOS as a complex genetic trait involve chromosome 2 and:
Chromosomes 2 and 9 are implicated as complex genetic traits in PCOS.
The etiological factors of PCOS lead to excessive androgen production, defective folliculogenesis, insulin resistance, obesity, and:
Defect in gonadotropin secretion and action
These factors lead to excess androgen production, defective folliculogenesis, insulin resistance, defective gonadotropin secretion/action, and obesity.
In PCOS, the main source of excessive androgen production is:
The ovaries are the main source of excessive androgen production in PCOS.
In PCOS, the adrenal glands make only a minor contribution to androgen excess, reflected by an increase in:
The adrenal glands contribute a minor amount to androgen excess in PCOS, reflected by increased DHEA-S.
In PCOS, serum androgen (testosterone) levels are typically:
PCOS androgen levels are typically ≥ 70 ng/dL but < 200 ng/dL.
This degree of androgen elevation in PCOS (70–200 ng/dL) clinically leads to:
This mild-to-moderate androgen elevation in PCOS leads to hirsutism (not virilization, which needs markedly higher levels).
Folliculotoxicity of androgens in PCOS arrests follicular growth, preventing maturation into:
Folliculotoxic androgens arrest follicular growth, preventing maturation into Graafian follicles.
Complications of the androgen excess/dyslipidemia pathway in PCOS include increased risk of:
PCOS pathophysiology contributes to dyslipidemia and increased risk of coronary heart disease.
The dyslipidemia pattern associated with PCOS pathophysiology includes:
On ultrasound, PCOS shows small unruptured follicles (not true cysts) arranged along the ovarian periphery, giving a:
The peripherally arranged small follicles create a classic necklace appearance on USG.
Per the Rotterdam criteria, the number of follicles required per ovary to define polycystic morphology is:
The Rotterdam criteria require ≥ 12 follicles per ovary.
The Rotterdam criteria specify a follicle size of:
Follicles are 2–9 mm in size per the Rotterdam criteria.
Per the Rotterdam criteria, polycystic morphology can also be defined by ovarian volume of:
Ovarian volume ≥ 10 cc also satisfies the polycystic morphology criterion.
The American and European Societies use a stricter follicle count criterion of:
The American and European Societies use a stricter cutoff of ≥ 20 follicles, 2–9 mm size.
Anovulation is a direct cause of infertility in PCOS.
Anovulation means no corpus luteum forms, resulting in:
Without a corpus luteum, progesterone is decreased.
Due to low progesterone from anovulation, PCOS patients classically present with secondary amenorrhea or:
Secondary amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea (< 9 cycles/year) are classic presentations.
If pregnancy does occur in a woman with PCOS, low progesterone increases the risk of:
Low progesterone in PCOS increases the risk of abortion during pregnancy.
Oligomenorrhea in PCOS is defined as fewer than how many cycles per year?
Oligomenorrhea is defined as fewer than 9 cycles per year.
Anovulation in PCOS occurs due to folliculotoxicity of androgens and:
Anovulation results from both folliculotoxic androgens and absence of the LH surge.
Lab findings in PCOS include increased serum testosterone, increased DHEA-S, and a lipid pattern of:
PCOS lab findings show ↑LDL and ↓HDL, alongside increased testosterone and DHEA-S.
Progesterone levels in PCOS lab findings are typically:
Progesterone is decreased in PCOS due to anovulation.
AMH levels in PCOS are typically:
AMH is increased in PCOS, reflecting increased small antral follicles.
An AMH level of what value or above supports the diagnosis of PCOS (reflecting increased small follicles)?
An AMH ≥ 7.3 ng/mL supports the diagnosis, reflecting the increased number of small follicles.
The elevated AMH in PCOS reflects:
An increased number of small follicles
A decreased number of small follicles
Elevated AMH reflects the increased number of small antral follicles characteristic of PCOS.
Insulin resistance in PCOS contributes to dyslipidemia and leads to:
Insulin resistance contributes to dyslipidemia and leads to theca cell hyperplasia.
Theca cell hyperplasia from insulin resistance causes oversensitivity to LH stimulation, due to loss of the normal:
Loss of the normal cut-off (threshold) causes theca cell oversensitivity to LH stimulation.
The end result of theca cell oversensitivity to LH is:
Theca cell oversensitivity to LH results in increased androgen production.
Directly proportional to BMI in all cases
Insulin resistance in PCOS is independent of obesity — it occurs in both obese and non-obese patients.
Among PCOS patients, approximately what proportion are obese versus not obese?
Approximately 70% of PCOS patients are obese and 30% are not obese.
In all patients diagnosed with PCOS, OGTT (oral glucose tolerance test) should be performed every:
All PCOS patients should have OGTT performed every 2 years.
If insulin resistance is confirmed (positive) in a PCOS patient, OGTT should be repeated every:
If insulin resistance is present, OGTT is repeated yearly instead of every 2 years.
Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical manifestation of:
Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical manifestation of insulin resistance.
Acanthosis nigricans presents with skin that is:
Acanthosis nigricans presents as dark, velvety, and thick skin.
Common sites for acanthosis nigricans include the nape of the neck, axillary region, groin, and:
Common sites include the nape of the neck, axillary region, groin, and under the breast tissue.
The HAIRAN syndrome mnemonic in PCOS stands for hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and:
HAIRAN stands for Hyper-Androgenism, Insulin Resistance, and Acanthosis Nigricans.
HAIRAN syndrome is best understood as a triad reflecting:
The interconnection of hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and its skin manifestation
A distinct disease separate from PCOS
A diagnostic criterion of the Rotterdam criteria
HAIRAN reflects the interconnected pathophysiology of hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and its cutaneous manifestation (acanthosis nigricans).
Obesity is present in what proportion of PCOS patients?
Obesity is present in 40–80% of PCOS patients.
Not a defining feature of PCOS; PCOS can occur in thin individuals
A mandatory diagnostic criterion for PCOS
The primary cause of PCOS in all cases
Obesity is not a defining feature of PCOS — PCOS can occur in thin individuals too.
In adipose tissue, androgens are converted to estrogen via aromatase, leading to increased levels of:
Adipose tissue aromatization of androgens leads to increased estrone (E1).
This increase in estrone in obese PCOS patients causes estrogen breakthrough bleeding, presenting as:
Increased estrone causes estrogen breakthrough bleeding, presenting as menometrorrhagia.
The normal E2:E1 ratio is 2:1, but in an obese PCOS female this ratio shifts to approximately:
In an obese PCOS female, the E2:E1 ratio shifts to approximately 1:2 (favouring E1).
A thin PCOS patient, with normal estrogen levels, most commonly presents with:
A thin PCOS patient with normal estrogen levels most commonly presents with secondary amenorrhea.
An obese PCOS patient, with increased estrone, may present with secondary amenorrhea or:
An obese PCOS patient may present with secondary amenorrhea or menometrorrhagia (due to increased E1).
In PCOS, the underlying gonadotropin defect begins with an increased pulse frequency of:
The gonadotropin defect in PCOS begins with an increased pulse frequency of GnRH.
Increased GnRH pulse frequency in PCOS leads to increased secretion of which pituitary hormone?
Increased GnRH pulse frequency leads to increased LH secretion by the pituitary.
Persistently elevated LH throughout the cycle in PCOS results in:
Persistently elevated LH results in absence of the normal mid-cycle LH surge.
In PCOS, the typical FSH:LH ratio is:
The typical FSH:LH ratio in PCOS is 1:2 or 1:3 (versus normal 1:1).
In PCOS, FSH is typically normal while LH is:
FSH remains normal while LH is increased in PCOS.
The best time in the menstrual cycle to evaluate LH and FSH levels is:
Any day — timing does not matter
Day 2/day 3 of the cycle is the best time to evaluate LH and FSH.
In PCOS, which of the following hormones is typically increased?
Serum testosterone is increased in PCOS, while FSH, prolactin, and TSH remain unchanged.
Along with testosterone, PCOS shows increased levels of DHEA-S, LDL, AMH, LH, and (in obese females):
In obese PCOS females, estrone (E1) is also increased, along with testosterone, DHEA-S, LDL, AMH, and LH.
Which set of hormone levels remain unchanged in PCOS?
FSH, estradiol (E2), prolactin, and TSH remain unchanged in PCOS.
Which of the following is decreased in PCOS?
HDL, serum progesterone, and SHBG are all decreased in PCOS.
The decrease in SHBG seen in PCOS is due to the effect of:
Decreased SHBG in PCOS is due to the combined effect of androgens and insulin.
Given this hormonal profile, PCOS is best characterized by an elevated:
Both LH and FSH equally elevated
PCOS is characterized by elevated LH with normal FSH, giving the classic increased LH:FSH ratio.
The Rotterdam criteria for PCOS diagnosis include hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and:
Polycystic appearance of ovaries on USG
The three Rotterdam criteria are hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian appearance on USG.
Hyperandrogenism in the Rotterdam criteria can be defined biochemically (elevated serum testosterone) or:
Hyperandrogenism can be defined biochemically or clinically (hirsutism).
Ovulatory dysfunction in the Rotterdam criteria manifests as:
Ovulatory dysfunction manifests as secondary amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea.
How many of the three Rotterdam criteria must be present for a provisional diagnosis of PCOS?
Any 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria give a provisional diagnosis of PCOS.
After a provisional diagnosis of PCOS (2 Rotterdam criteria positive), the essential next step is to check:
17-OH progesterone levels, to rule out late-onset CAH
17-OH progesterone levels are checked next, to rule out late-onset CAH before confirming PCOS.
A 17-OH progesterone level below 200 ng in this workup:
A 17-OH progesterone level < 200 ng rules out CAH.
A 17-OH progesterone level above 800 ng in this workup:
A 17-OH progesterone level > 800 ng confirms late-onset CAH.
Which of the following is explicitly NOT a diagnostic criterion for PCOS?
Obesity is explicitly excluded from the diagnostic criteria for PCOS.
The LH:FSH ratio, though classically associated with PCOS, is:
The LH:FSH ratio, despite its classic association, is not a diagnostic criterion for PCOS.
Which of these is also NOT a diagnostic criterion for PCOS?
Insulin resistance, though central to PCOS pathophysiology, is not a diagnostic criterion.
Which of the following, though a common clinical feature of PCOS, is NOT part of the diagnostic criteria?
Menometrorrhagia, a common clinical feature, is not part of the diagnostic criteria.
The "necklace appearance" seen on USG in PCOS is:
Not itself a separate diagnostic criterion, but included within polycystic appearance
Diagnostic on its own without follicle counting
Only seen in POI, not PCOS
The necklace appearance is included within the polycystic appearance criterion, not a separate criterion.
In the workup of PCOS with secondary amenorrhea, the urine pregnancy test (UPT) is typically:
UPT is typically negative in this workup, ruling out pregnancy as the cause of amenorrhea.
In this workup, LH is typically:
LH is typically increased in this workup.
In this workup, FSH is typically:
FSH is typically normal in this workup.
TSH is checked and expected to be normal, because thyroid dysfunction causing amenorrhea would act via:
Thyroid dysfunction causes amenorrhea via negative feedback on GnRH, so TSH is checked to exclude this.
Serum prolactin is checked and expected to be normal, because hyperprolactinemia causing amenorrhea would act via:
Hyperprolactinemia causes amenorrhea via negative feedback on GnRH, so prolactin is checked to exclude this.
In additional workup, a progesterone challenge test is performed by giving progesterone for 5 days and stopping; a positive test shows:
A positive progesterone challenge test shows withdrawal bleeding after stopping the 5-day course.
A positive progesterone challenge test with increased LH, normal FSH, and secondary amenorrhea suggests:
This combination (positive test, ↑LH, normal FSH, secondary amenorrhea) suggests PCOS.
A positive progesterone challenge test with increased LH, normal FSH, but primary amenorrhea instead suggests:
The same hormonal pattern but with primary (not secondary) amenorrhea suggests androgen insensitivity syndrome.
Comparing PCOS to primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), both ovarian causes of secondary amenorrhea, the number of follicles is:
Increased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Decreased in PCOS, increased in POI
Follicle number is increased in PCOS but decreased in POI.
FSH levels differ between PCOS and POI as follows:
Increased in PCOS, normal in POI
Normal in PCOS, increased in POI
FSH is normal in PCOS but increased in POI.
LH levels in PCOS versus POI are:
LH is increased in both PCOS and POI, though the mechanisms differ.
Increased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Normal/decreased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Decreased in PCOS, increased in POI
Estrogen is normal or decreased in PCOS, but decreased in POI.
Increased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Decreased in PCOS, increased in POI
AMH is increased in PCOS (reflecting excess small follicles) but decreased in POI (reflecting depleted reserve).
The associated symptom typically seen with PCOS is hirsutism, whereas with POI it is:
PCOS is associated with hirsutism, while POI is associated with hot flashes/osteoporosis (menopausal-type symptoms).
Short-term complications of PCOS include menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, alopecia, infertility, and:
Insulin resistance is a short-term complication, along with menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, alopecia, and infertility.
Long-term consequences of PCOS include dyslipidemia, diabetes, and:
Coronary artery disease is a long-term consequence, along with dyslipidemia and diabetes.
Due to increased estrogen in obese PCOS females, long-term risks include endometrial cancer, NASH, and:
Increased estrogen in obese PCOS females raises risk of endometrial cancer, NASH, and variably ovarian cancer.
Due to obesity, long-term consequences of PCOS include sleep apnea syndrome and:
Obesity-related consequences include sleep apnea syndrome and anxiety/depression.
PCOS is also associated with a cluster of cardiometabolic abnormalities known as:
PCOS is associated with metabolic X (metabolic) syndrome.
Obstetric complications of PCOS include infertility (which is reversible) and abortion, the latter due to:
Decreased progesterone in PCOS contributes to increased abortion risk during pregnancy.
Due to underlying insulin resistance, pregnant PCOS patients are at increased risk of:
Insulin resistance in PCOS increases the risk of gestational diabetes during pregnancy.
Obstetric complications of PCOS also include pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) and:
PIH and stillbirth are recognised obstetric complications of PCOS.
In a patient presenting with hirsutism, acne, and irregular cycles, the appropriate next investigation is:
Serum testosterone levels are the appropriate next step in a patient with hirsutism, acne, and irregular cycles.
In a confirmed case of PCOS, baseline workup includes lipid profile, OGTT, and ultrasound to assess:
Baseline workup in confirmed PCOS includes lipid profile, OGTT, and USG to assess endometrial thickness.
In a reproductive-age PCOS patient, an endometrial thickness of what value or greater is an indication for endometrial biopsy?
An endometrial thickness ≥ 12 mm in a reproductive-age PCOS patient is an indication for endometrial biopsy.
Full-blown/classical PCOS (Phenotype A) is defined as a case where:
Only 1 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria is positive
Only 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria are positive
No Rotterdam criteria are met, but symptoms are present
Phenotype A (full-blown/classical PCOS) is defined by all 3 Rotterdam criteria being positive.
The 3 Rotterdam criteria that are all positive in classical PCOS (Phenotype A) are high testosterone levels, ovulatory dysfunction, and:
Polycystic appearance of ovary on USG
The third criterion is a polycystic appearance of the ovary on ultrasound, along with high testosterone and ovulatory dysfunction.
Management of PCOS is fundamentally based on:
The primary presenting feature of the patient
PCOS management is tailored to the patient\u2019s primary presenting feature (menstrual irregularity, infertility, hirsutism, or insulin resistance).
The four primary presenting features that guide PCOS management are menstrual irregularity (most common), infertility, hirsutism, and:
The four presenting features guiding management are menstrual irregularity (m/c), infertility, hirsutism, and insulin resistance.
The FIRST line management for PCOS, regardless of presenting complaint, is:
Lifestyle modification and weight loss is the universal first-line management step in PCOS.
Lifestyle modification and weight loss alone leads to spontaneous ovulation in what proportion of PCOS cases?
Lifestyle modification and weight loss alone leads to spontaneous ovulation in 5\u201310% of cases.
In all cases of PCOS, which condition must specifically be ruled out?
Hyperprolactinemia must be ruled out in all cases of PCOS.
If prolactin is elevated in a PCOS workup, the proposed mechanism is that prolactin acts on the adrenal glands, leading to:
Elevated prolactin acts on the adrenal glands to increase androgen production, a mechanism relevant to PCOS-like presentations.
In pubertal/young females, irregular menstrual cycles due to anovulation may normally persist for up to:
Irregular anovulatory cycles may persist for up to 3 years after menarche as a normal physiological phase.
A normal cycle length in this context is defined as:
A cycle length of 21\u201345 days is considered within the normal range.
Evaluation for menstrual irregularity is indicated if cycle length is \u226590 days, OR if irregularity persists beyond:
Evaluation is indicated for a cycle length \u226590 days, or if the irregularity continues beyond 3 years after menarche.
The first-line management (drug of choice) for menstrual irregularity in PCOS is:
Very low dose OCPs are the DOC for first-line management of menstrual irregularity in PCOS.
In the very low dose OCPs used for PCOS menstrual irregularity, the ethinyl estradiol component is dosed at:
Ethinyl estradiol is used at \u226420 mcg (very low dose) in this regimen.
The progesterone component of the very low dose OCP used for PCOS menstrual irregularity is a:
3rd/4th generation progesterone (e.g., MALA-D/MALA-N may be used)
3rd/4th generation progesterone is used (MALA-D/MALA-N may be used as options).
OCPs (estrogen + progesterone) act in PCOS by suppressing LH and FSH, leading to ovarian suppression, which in turn causes anovulation, decreased androgens, and:
Decreased natural estrogen, leading to endometrial thinning
Ovarian suppression from OCPs decreases natural estrogen, leading to endometrial thinning, alongside anovulation and decreased androgens.
The standard OCP regimen duration is:
The standard OCP regimen is 21 days (3 weeks on, 1 week off).
Advantages of OCPs in PCOS include regularising cycles, treatment of hirsutism, contraceptive benefit, and:
OCPs protect against endometrial cancer, in addition to regularising cycles, treating hirsutism, and providing contraception.
In PCOS-related hirsutism, OCPs act partly by decreasing LH/FSH (hence decreasing androgens), and partly through estrogen increasing:
OCP-derived estrogen increases SHBG, which binds testosterone and decreases the free (active) testosterone fraction.
Per this chapter\u2019s summary note, the overall drug of choice for PCOS is:
OCPs are noted as the overall DOC for PCOS.
As a 2nd line/alternative to OCPs for menstrual irregularity, progesterone is given cyclically every 12-14 days in the:
Only on day 1 of the cycle
Cyclical progesterone is given every 12\u201314 days in the 2nd half of the cycle.
The specific progesterone used in this regimen is medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), dosed at:
MPA is dosed at 10\u201320 mg for 5 days in this regimen, facilitating withdrawal bleeding.
Advantages of cyclical progesterone therapy include regularising cycles and a protective effect on the endometrium, specifically:
Decreased risk of hyperplasia and cancer, with a minimum duration of 12 days
Progesterone protects the endometrium (decreasing hyperplasia/cancer risk) when given for a minimum duration of 12 days.
Disadvantages of the progesterone-only regimen (compared to OCPs) include that it does not regularise cycles as reliably, and it provides no protective effect on the endometrium if given for:
If given for less than 12 days, progesterone provides no protective effect on the endometrium.
The very first step in managing infertility in PCOS is:
Advice weight loss, followed by a trial of natural conception with folic acid supplementation
The first step is advising weight loss, followed by a trial of natural conception with folic acid supplementation.
The 1st line management for PCOS infertility (after the initial step) is:
Pharmacological therapy with ovulation-inducing drugs is the 1st line management for PCOS infertility.
Among 1st line ovulation-inducing drugs, the overall drug of choice is letrozole, while the 2nd drug of choice is:
Letrozole is the DOC, with clomiphene citrate (CC) as the 2nd DOC among 1st line ovulation-inducing drugs.
2nd line drugs for PCOS infertility include CC+metformin, CC+dexamethasone, OCPs followed by CC, HMG, and:
Recombinant gonadotropins round out the list of 2nd line drugs, alongside CC+metformin, CC+dexamethasone, OCPs f/b CC, and HMG.
The 2nd line MANAGEMENT (procedure, not drug) for PCOS infertility is:
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is the 2nd line management approach (as a procedure) for PCOS infertility.
The 3rd line management for PCOS infertility is pulsatile GnRH or:
IVF is the 3rd line management option, alongside pulsatile GnRH.
Clomiphene citrate (CC) belongs to which drug class?
Clomiphene citrate is a SERM (Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator).
Clomiphene citrate is a non-steroidal drug that is:
Centrally acting, anti-estrogenic, causing ovulation induction
Peripherally acting only, with no central effect
CC is a non-steroidal, centrally acting anti-estrogenic drug that causes ovulation induction.
CC's central mechanism of action involves blocking estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary because:
CC's half-life is longer than estrogen's (T1/2 CC > T1/2 E)
CC\u2019s half-life is shorter than estrogen\u2019s
CC has no relation to estrogen half-life
Because CC\u2019s half-life exceeds that of estrogen, it occupies estrogen receptors longer, sustaining the false low-estrogen signal.
By blocking hypothalamic/pituitary estrogen receptors, CC causes the pituitary to falsely interpret this as low estrogen, leading to:
The false low-estrogen signal leads to increased LH and FSH release.
The rise in LH and FSH from CC\u2019s central action results in:
Maturation of multiple follicles and ovulation
Increased LH and FSH drive maturation of multiple follicles and ovulation.
CC's PERIPHERAL action involves binding to peripheral estrogen receptors in the endometrium and cervix, resulting in endometrial thinning and:
Peripheral anti-estrogenic action produces endometrial thinning and thick cervical mucus.
The endometrial thinning and thick cervical mucus from CC's peripheral action together make the environment:
Favourable only for implantation, not fertilization
CC's peripheral anti-estrogenic effects make the endometrium and cervix unfavourable for achieving pregnancy, despite inducing ovulation centrally.
With CC, the reported rate of ovulation is about 80%, while the pregnancy rate is only about:
Despite an 80% ovulation rate, the pregnancy rate with CC is only about 5\u201310%, reflecting its peripheral anti-estrogenic effects on endometrium/cervix.
The prerequisites for using clomiphene citrate are an intact HPO axis and:
An intact HPO axis and normal FSH levels are the two prerequisites for CC use.
The two components of clomiphene citrate are zuclomiphene and:
Enclomiphene, which potentiates the anti-estrogenic action
Enclomiphene (potentiating the anti-estrogenic action) and zuclomiphene are the two components of CC.
The half-life (T1/2) of clomiphene citrate is approximately:
CC has a half-life of about 2 weeks.
The starting and maximum doses of clomiphene citrate are:
2.5 mg OD starting, up to 7.5 mg OD maximum
500 mg OD starting, up to 1000 mg OD maximum
50 mg OD starting, up to 150 mg OD maximum
5 mg OD starting, up to 20 mg OD maximum
CC is started at 50 mg OD and can be increased up to a maximum of 150 mg OD.
Clomiphene citrate is administered for 5 days, specifically on cycle days:
CC is given for 5 days, on cycle days 5\u20139.
Follicular monitoring with CC begins from day 10 onwards, via TVS, performed:
Follicular monitoring is done daily or on alternate days via TVS starting day 10.
When follicles reach a size of 18-20 mm on CC, ovulation occurs naturally OR is triggered with:
At 18\u201320 mm follicle size, natural ovulation may occur, or hCG (acting like LH) is given as a trigger.
After the hCG trigger injection with CC, ovulation occurs after:
Ovulation occurs 32\u201336 hours after the hCG trigger injection.
After ovulation with CC (natural or triggered), the next step in management is typically:
Intrauterine insemination (IUI) commonly follows ovulation in the CC protocol.
The most common adverse effect of clomiphene citrate is:
Hot flushes, due to decreased estrogen
Hot flushes (due to decreased estrogen effect) are the most common adverse effect of CC.
The second most common adverse effect of clomiphene citrate is:
Ovarian cysts, due to increased LH and FSH
Ovarian cysts (due to increased LH and FSH) are the second most common adverse effect.
Besides hot flushes and ovarian cysts, other adverse effects of CC include headache, vaginal dryness, breast tenderness, and multiple pregnancies in what proportion of cases?
Multiple pregnancies occur in about 7\u201310% of CC cycles.
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) with clomiphene citrate is:
OHSS is the least common adverse effect associated with CC use.
Visual disturbances (diplopia, blurring of vision, scotoma) with clomiphene citrate are significant because they are:
An indication for immediate stoppage of the drug
Only seen with letrozole, not CC
Treated by increasing the CC dose
Visual disturbances with CC are an indication for immediate stoppage of the drug.
Advantages of clomiphene citrate over gonadotropin therapy include no risk of:
CC carries no risk of teratogenicity or ectopic pregnancy, unlike some other therapies.
In the CC vs letrozole comparison, clomiphene citrate is categorised as a SERM, while letrozole is categorised as:
Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, in contrast to CC, which is a SERM.
Letrozole's peripheral mechanism of action works by blocking aromatization of androgen to estrogen, which decreases estrogen and causes:
Increased negative feedback, decreasing LH and FSH
Loss of negative feedback, increasing LH and FSH
Reduced peripheral estrogen removes negative feedback, raising LH and FSH.
Letrozole's starting and maximum doses are:
50 mg OD starting, up to 150 mg OD maximum
2.5 mg OD starting, up to 7.5 mg OD maximum
500 mg OD starting, up to 1000 mg OD maximum
0.5 mg OD starting, up to 2 mg OD maximum
Letrozole is started at 2.5 mg OD, up to a maximum of 7.5 mg OD.
Letrozole's half-life, in contrast to CC's 2 weeks, is approximately:
Letrozole's half-life is about 48 hours, much shorter than CC's 2 weeks.
Regarding follicular development, CC typically produces multifollicular development, while letrozole produces:
Purely monofollicular development only, with no exceptions
Letrozole produces monofollicular plus multifollicular development, differing from CC\u2019s purely multifollicular pattern.
The risk of multiple pregnancies is lower with letrozole (3-7%) compared to CC, which carries a risk of:
CC carries a 7\u201310% risk of multiple pregnancies, higher than letrozole\u2019s 3\u20137%.
Regarding effect on endometrium and cervix, CC blocks estrogen receptors (thinning effect), while letrozole has:
No effect, hence increased chances of pregnancy
A thickening effect on the endometrium only
Letrozole has no adverse effect on endometrium/cervix, hence better pregnancy chances compared to CC.
Because letrozole doesn't have CC's adverse peripheral anti-estrogenic effects, its live birth rate is:
Markedly increased, making it the DOC
Letrozole's live birth rate is markedly increased compared to CC, making it the drug of choice.
Side effects of CC (hot flushes m/c, vaginal dryness) contrast with letrozole, which is:
Associated with more severe hot flushes
Never associated with any side effects
Well tolerated with no anti-estrogenic side effects, and rare headache
Letrozole is well tolerated, without anti-estrogenic side effects, with headache being rare.
Regarding teratogenicity, both CC and letrozole are reported as:
Both drugs are reported as not teratogenic in this comparison.
Regarding uses, CC is DOC for ovulation induction AND DOC for PCOS historically, while letrozole is specifically:
The DOC for PCOS (superseding CC for this indication)
Only used for infertility unrelated to PCOS
Letrozole has become the DOC for PCOS, given its superior live birth rate and tolerability.
The prerequisite shared by both CC and letrozole is:
Intact HPO axis and normal FSH level
Both drugs require an intact HPO axis and normal FSH level as prerequisites.
Contraindications shared by CC and letrozole include Sheehan syndrome, pituitary ablation, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and:
Kallmann syndrome is a shared contraindication, along with Sheehan syndrome, pituitary ablation, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (all reflecting a non-intact HPO axis).
CC combined with glucocorticoids (dexamethasone) is indicated in clomiphene-resistant PCOS with:
CC + glucocorticoids is used in clomiphene-resistant PCOS specifically with raised androgen (DHEAS) levels.
The principle behind CC + glucocorticoids is that glucocorticoids suppress the adrenal glands, leading to:
Glucocorticoids suppress the adrenal glands, decreasing androgen output.
CC combined with metformin is indicated in clomiphene-resistant PCOS with:
CC + metformin is used specifically in clomiphene-resistant PCOS with insulin resistance.
When OCPs are used with CC, the duration of OCP pretreatment is 2 months, followed by CC, working on the principle:
Increased LH leads to increased androgen
Decreased LH leads to decreased androgen
OCPs are given for 2 months (decreasing LH and androgen) before starting CC.
HMG (human menopausal gonadotropin) is sourced from:
HMG is sourced from the urine of postmenopausal women.
HMG contains 75 IU LH + 75 IU FSH, along with impurities.
HMG is indicated in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (as the DOC for ovulation induction in that setting), as a 2nd line drug for PCOS, and in:
HMG is used in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (DOC there), as a 2nd line PCOS drug, and in all cases of IVF.
Adverse effects of HMG include multiple pregnancies (15-30%), OHSS (5-15%), and:
Increased risk of spontaneous abortion is an adverse effect of HMG, along with multiple pregnancies and OHSS.
An advantage of HMG, despite its adverse effect profile, is:
HMG carries no teratogenicity risk, despite its risks of multiple pregnancy and OHSS.
Recombinant injectable FSH is described as a purified form of FSH, with the main disadvantage being:
Recombinant FSH is purified, but its main disadvantage is that it is expensive.
The principle of laparoscopic ovarian drilling is to burn the ovarian stroma, destroying theca cells, thereby:
Burning the ovarian stroma destroys theca cells, decreasing androgen production.
Advantages of laparoscopic ovarian drilling include no risk of multiple pregnancies and:
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling carries no risk of OHSS, in addition to no risk of multiple pregnancies.
The disadvantage of laparoscopic ovarian drilling is the risk of premature menopause/POI, occurring due to:
Follicular destruction from the drilling procedure risks causing premature menopause or POI.
The 'Rule of 4' for laparoscopic ovarian drilling specifies 4 sites, for 4 seconds, and:
The 'Rule of 4' specifies 4 sites, 4 seconds duration, and 40 watts power.
IVF is indicated in PCOS-related infertility when the patient is \u226535 years old AND has:
IVF is indicated when the patient is \u226535 years old and has additional factors contributing to infertility.
Spironolactone is contraindicated in PCOS patients seeking pregnancy because, being anti-androgenic, it can cause:
Ambiguous genitalia in a female baby
Ambiguous genitalia in a male baby
Spironolactone\u2019s anti-androgenic action can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus, so it is avoided when pregnancy is being pursued.
OCPs are generally contraindicated when trying to conceive in PCOS, except in which scenario?
Clomiphene-resistant cases (used as pretreatment before CC)
OCPs may still be used in clomiphene-resistant cases as pretreatment before CC, despite being generally avoided when actively trying to conceive.
SERMs capable of causing ovulation induction include clomiphene citrate, tamoxifen, and:
Raloxifene, along with clomiphene citrate and tamoxifen, is a SERM capable of ovulation induction.
