Ormeloxifene is a SERM that specifically:
Is the most potent ovulation inducer
Is identical in action to clomiphene citrate
Unlike clomiphene, tamoxifen, and raloxifene, ormeloxifene does not cause ovulation induction.
Ormeloxifene is a component of which contraceptive, marketed under the name \u2018Chaya\u2019?
Ormeloxifene is the active component of centchroman, marketed as \u2018Chaya\u2019.
The drug of choice for managing insulin resistance in PCOS is:
Metformin, an insulin sensitizer, is the DOC for managing insulin resistance in PCOS.
Indications for metformin in PCOS include insulin resistance, inability to lose weight, and:
Metformin is also indicated for ovulation induction when combined with CC, in addition to insulin resistance and difficulty losing weight.
Advantages of metformin in PCOS include helping with weight loss and:
Metformin has a mild anti-hirsutism action, in addition to aiding weight loss.
Metformin decreases the chance of gestational diabetes mellitus in PCOS patients and can be:
Used only in the first trimester
Continued during pregnancy, as it has no teratogenicity
Metformin can be safely continued during pregnancy, as it carries no teratogenicity, while reducing GDM risk.
In addition to the above, metformin also decreases the risk of which PCOS-related complication?
Metformin decreases the risk of OHSS in PCOS patients.
The most common cause of hirsutism is:
PCOS is the most common cause of hirsutism.
Besides PCOS and idiopathic hirsutism, recognised causes include androgen-producing ovarian tumour and:
An androgen-producing adrenal tumour is another recognised cause of hirsutism.
Cushing syndrome as a cause of hirsutism is characteristically also associated with:
Cushing syndrome presents with hirsutism plus diabetes and/or hypertension.
Pregnancy luteoma, a recognised cause of hirsutism, is best described as:
An adrenal tumour occurring only in pregnancy
A hyperplastic mass of luteinized ovarian cells (not a true tumour)
Pregnancy luteoma is a hyperplastic mass of luteinized ovarian cells, and is not a true tumour.
Theca lutein cysts, a cause of hirsutism, occur due to elevated hCG, which is structurally similar to which hormone\u2019s subunit?
hCG shares a similar alpha subunit with LH, explaining its role in causing theca lutein cysts.
Besides the structural/tumour causes, hirsutism can also result from an endocrine cause:
Hyperprolactinemia is listed among the causes of hirsutism.
Drugs specifically contraindicated in hirsutism (as they can worsen or cause it) include danazol and:
Gestrinone, along with danazol, is contraindicated in hirsutism.
Asherman syndrome is pathologically characterized by intrauterine adhesions and:
Asherman syndrome features intrauterine adhesions along with a thin and defective endometrium.
The highest risk factor for developing Asherman syndrome is:
Curettage performed post-partum carries the highest risk of causing Asherman syndrome.
The most common symptom GROUP seen in Asherman syndrome is:
Menstrual irregularities are the most common symptom group in Asherman syndrome.
Among the individual symptoms of Asherman syndrome, the single MOST common is:
Infertility is the most common individual symptom of Asherman syndrome (Infertility > 2\u00b0 amenorrhoea > hypomenorrhoea).
In the symptom frequency ranking of Asherman syndrome (Infertility > 2\u00b0 amenorrhoea > hypomenorrhoea), the SECOND most common symptom is:
Secondary amenorrhoea ranks second, after infertility, in symptom frequency.
In this same ranking, the LEAST common of the three main symptoms (infertility, 2\u00b0 amenorrhoea, hypomenorrhoea) is:
Hypomenorrhoea is the least common of the three ranked symptoms in Asherman syndrome.
Besides the ranked triad (infertility, 2\u00b0 amenorrhoea, hypomenorrhoea), other recognised symptoms of Asherman syndrome include secondary dysmenorrhoea and:
Recurrent abortions, along with secondary dysmenorrhoea, are other recognised symptoms of Asherman syndrome.
Which of the following is NOT a recognised cause of Asherman syndrome?
Chlamydial cervicitis is not listed as a cause; excessive curettage, genital TB, and schistosomiasis all are.
Asherman syndrome may follow surgical removal of retained products of conception, as well as:
D&C, along with removal of retained tissue, is a recognised cause of Asherman syndrome.
Among infectious causes, Asherman syndrome is recognised to occur secondary to genital tuberculosis and:
Schistosomiasis, along with genital TB, is a recognised infectious cause of Asherman syndrome.
The first investigation performed for suspected Asherman syndrome is:
TVS (transvaginal sonography) or a hormonal test
TVS or a hormonal test is the first investigation performed in suspected Asherman syndrome.
The screening test for Asherman syndrome is HSG (hysterosalpingography), which characteristically shows a:
HSG in Asherman syndrome characteristically shows a "moth eaten" appearance.
On HSG, a SINGLE filling defect with smooth outlines is more suggestive of:
A single filling defect with smooth outlines on HSG is more suggestive of a fibroid or polyp, not Asherman syndrome.
On HSG, MULTIPLE filling defects with irregular outlines are characteristic of:
Multiple filling defects with irregular outlines on HSG are characteristic of Asherman syndrome.
The diagnostic investigation of choice for Asherman syndrome, which is also therapeutic, is:
Hysteroscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic for Asherman syndrome, making it the investigation of choice.
In the secondary amenorrhoea workup for Asherman syndrome, the urine pregnancy test (UPT) result is:
UPT is negative in the Asherman syndrome workup for secondary amenorrhoea.
In Asherman syndrome, the serum LH, FSH, estrogen, prolactin, and TSH levels are typically:
LH, FSH, estrogen, prolactin, and TSH are all typically normal in Asherman syndrome, since the HPO axis itself is intact.
In Asherman syndrome, the progesterone challenge/withdrawal test result is:
The progesterone challenge/withdrawal test is negative in Asherman syndrome, since the damaged endometrium cannot respond and bleed.
The key distinguishing investigation that is uniquely negative ONLY in Asherman syndrome (among causes of secondary amenorrhoea with a negative progesterone challenge test) is the:
Combined progesterone AND estrogen withdrawal test
The combined progesterone and estrogen withdrawal test is uniquely negative only in Asherman syndrome, helping distinguish it from other causes of a negative progesterone challenge test.
The primary management of Asherman syndrome is:
Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is the primary management for Asherman syndrome.
After hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, intrauterine insertion of a Foley\u2019s catheter serves to:
A Foley\u2019s catheter is inserted into the uterine cavity after adhesiolysis to prevent re-adhesion of the walls.
Following adhesiolysis and Foley\u2019s catheter placement, estrogen and progesterone are given for how long to help build the endometrium?
Estrogen and progesterone are given for 3 months post-procedure to help rebuild the endometrium.
The complete 3-part management protocol for Asherman syndrome is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, plus intrauterine Foley\u2019s catheter insertion, plus:
The 3-part protocol is: hysteroscopic adhesiolysis + Foley\u2019s catheter (prevents re-adhesion) + estrogen/progesterone x 3 months (builds endometrium).
Secondary amenorrhoea is defined as absence of menstruation in a previously menstruating female for at least:
Secondary amenorrhoea is defined as absence of menstruation for \u226590 days in a previously menstruating female.
Evaluation for secondary amenorrhoea is also indicated if a female has fewer than how many menstrual cycles per year?
Fewer than 9 cycles per year is also an indication for evaluation of secondary amenorrhoea.
The most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea is:
Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea.
Lactation causes secondary amenorrhoea due to the effect of:
Lactational amenorrhoea occurs due to prolactin\u2019s suppressive effect on the HPO axis.
Recognised causes of secondary amenorrhoea include chronic anemia and:
Thyroid disorders, along with chronic anemia, are recognised causes of secondary amenorrhoea.
In a female of reproductive or perimenopausal age presenting with secondary amenorrhoea or AUB, the very first investigation performed is:
UPT is the first investigation performed, given pregnancy is the most common cause.
Besides UPT, the routine initial investigation panel for secondary amenorrhoea includes serum prolactin, serum TSH, LH & FSH, and:
Estrogen, along with prolactin, TSH, and LH/FSH, is part of the routine initial workup.
Prolactin is best classified as a:
The normal range of serum prolactin is approximately:
The normal serum prolactin range is <20\u201325 ng/mL.
The principal function of prolactin is:
Prolactin\u2019s principal function is milk synthesis.
Prolactin is secreted by which cells?
Prolactin is secreted by lactotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
Prolactin secretion follows a pulsatile pattern with diurnal variation, showing maximal secretion:
Prolactin secretion is pulsatile, with maximal secretion occurring in the early morning.
Hypothalamic TRH acts on the anterior pituitary to mainly stimulate TSH, and in small amounts also stimulates:
TRH stimulates TSH mainly, and prolactin in small amounts.
The principal inhibitor of prolactin secretion from the hypothalamus is:
Dopamine is the principal inhibitory regulator of prolactin secretion.
Elevated prolactin can be managed with dopaminergic drugs, specifically:
Cabergoline and bromocriptine are the dopaminergic drugs used to manage hyperprolactinemia.
The drug of choice for hyperprolactinemia in ALL females is:
Cabergoline is the DOC for hyperprolactinemia in all females.
Cabergoline's key pharmacological advantage is its:
Cabergoline has an increased half-life compared to bromocriptine.
The drug of choice specifically for a female with hyperprolactinemia presenting with infertility is:
Bromocriptine is the DOC in hyperprolactinemic females presenting with infertility.
Bromocriptine is preferred in the infertility setting due to its increased safety profile and because it is also:
Bromocriptine itself has an ovulation-inducing property, making it favourable in infertility.
In hypothyroidism (e.g., Hashimoto\u2019s thyroiditis), decreased T3/T4 abolishes negative feedback on TSH and:
Decreased T3/T4 abolishes negative feedback on both TSH and TRH.
The resulting increase in TRH (from hypothyroidism) stimulates increased TSH and also:
Increased TRH also stimulates increased prolactin, since TRH has a mild prolactin-releasing effect.
Given the hypothyroidism\u2013prolactin link, if serum prolactin is found to be elevated, the next appropriate step is to:
Because hypothyroidism can elevate prolactin, TSH should be checked whenever prolactin is found to be raised.
In the management algorithm for hyperprolactinemia, the first step after confirming elevated prolactin is to:
The first step is to repeat prolactin and TSH levels to guide further management.
If BOTH prolactin and TSH are elevated on repeat testing, the appropriate management sequence is:
Treat hypothyroidism with thyroxine, then treat the prolactin
Treat the prolactin first, then give thyroxine
MRI brain immediately, before any treatment
Hypothyroidism is treated first with thyroxine, after which the prolactin elevation is addressed.
If only prolactin is elevated (with normal TSH) on repeat testing, the next step is:
Repeat the test again in 1 year
With isolated hyperprolactinemia (normal TSH), MRI is done to rule out a prolactinoma.
A pituitary prolactinoma is classified as a MACROadenoma when tumour size is:
A macroadenoma is defined as tumour size \u22651 cm; a microadenoma is <1 cm.
The MOST common clinical feature of prolactinoma is:
Secondary amenorrhoea is the most common clinical feature of prolactinoma.
The SECOND most common clinical feature of prolactinoma is:
Infertility is the second most common clinical feature of prolactinoma.
Besides secondary amenorrhoea and infertility, other recognised features of prolactinoma include delayed puberty and:
Galactorrhoea, along with delayed puberty, is a recognised additional feature of prolactinoma.
Pressure symptoms of prolactinoma are more commonly seen with:
Pressure symptoms are more common with macroadenoma than microadenoma, given its larger size.
The specific visual field defect caused by pressure from a prolactinoma on the optic chiasm is:
Bitemporal hemianopsia is the classic visual field defect from chiasmal compression by a prolactinoma.
Besides visual disturbances, pressure symptoms of prolactinoma include headache and:
Cavernous sinus syndrome, along with headache and visual disturbances, is a recognised pressure symptom of prolactinoma.
The investigation of choice to detect a prolactinoma as a space-occupying lesion is:
MRI is the investigation of choice, showing prolactinoma as a space-occupying lesion.
Cases of prolactinoma managed with follow-up only (no treatment) include asymptomatic microadenoma, adenoma in pregnancy, and:
Adenoma in lactation, along with asymptomatic microadenoma and adenoma in pregnancy, is managed with follow-up only.
If visual disturbances develop during follow-up of a prolactinoma case being observed, the appropriate action is to:
The development of visual disturbances during follow-up is an indication to treat.
Medical management is indicated for symptomatic microadenoma and:
Medical management is used for symptomatic microadenoma and for macroadenoma/prolactinoma.
The drug of choice for medical management of macroadenoma/prolactinoma (without infertility as the chief complaint) is:
Cabergoline is the DOC for medical management of macroadenoma/prolactinoma.
In a prolactinoma patient presenting with infertility as the chief complaint, the drug of choice is:
Bromocriptine is the DOC when infertility is the chief complaint in prolactinoma.
Surgical management of prolactinoma is indicated if medical management for a certain duration shows no decrease (or an increase) in tumour size. This duration is:
Surgical management is considered if 4 months of medical management fails to decrease tumour size.
Surgical management of prolactinoma is also indicated when the prolactin level is:
A prolactin level \u226550 ng/mL is also an indication for surgical management.
In the HYPOTHALAMIC compartment of causes of secondary amenorrhoea (acting via decreased GnRH), recognised defects include stress, anorexia, bulimia, and:
Excessive exercise, along with stress, anorexia, and bulimia, is a recognised hypothalamic cause.
In hypothalamic-cause secondary amenorrhoea, LH, FSH, and estrogen are typically:
Hypothalamic causes show decreased LH, FSH, and estrogen due to reduced GnRH drive.
In hypothalamic-cause secondary amenorrhoea, MRI brain is typically:
MRI is normal in hypothalamic-cause secondary amenorrhoea, since the pituitary/hypothalamus are structurally intact.
Among PITUITARY causes of secondary amenorrhoea, the two recognised defects are prolactinoma and:
Sheehan syndrome, along with prolactinoma, is a recognised pituitary cause of secondary amenorrhoea.
Both prolactinoma and Sheehan syndrome (pituitary causes) show which hormonal pattern?
Decreased FSH, decreased LH, decreased estrogen
Both pituitary causes show decreased FSH, LH, and estrogen, reflecting pituitary failure.
On MRI, prolactinoma shows a space-occupying lesion, while Sheehan syndrome characteristically shows:
Sheehan syndrome characteristically shows an empty sella turcica on MRI, unlike the space-occupying lesion of prolactinoma.
Among OVARIAN causes of secondary amenorrhoea, POI (premature ovarian insufficiency/premature menopause) shows:
Increased FSH, increased LH, decreased estrogen, decreased AMH
POI shows increased FSH and LH, with decreased estrogen and decreased AMH, reflecting depleted ovarian reserve.
POI is notable as the ONLY condition (among these compartmentwise causes) where FSH is increased, a pattern termed:
POI is the only condition in this table showing hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (raised FSH with hypogonadism).
Besides menstrual disturbance, POI is specifically associated with other symptoms:
Hot flushes and vaginal dryness are specific additional symptoms associated with POI, reflecting the hypoestrogenic state.
PCOS, as an ovarian cause of secondary amenorrhoea, characteristically shows FSH normal/increased, LH increased, estrogen normal/increased, AMH increased, and a progesterone challenge test result of:
PCOS shows a positive progesterone challenge test, reflecting adequate estrogen priming of the endometrium.
Among UTERINE causes of secondary amenorrhoea, Asherman syndrome shows normal FSH, normal LH, normal estrogen, and a combined estrogen+progesterone challenge test result of:
Asherman syndrome shows a negative combined estrogen+progesterone challenge test, since the damaged endometrium cannot respond even with full hormonal priming.
Sheehan syndrome results from necrosis of the pituitary gland, most classically triggered by:
Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is the classic trigger for pituitary necrosis in Sheehan syndrome.
During pregnancy, the pituitary gland increases in size by approximately:
The pituitary gland enlarges by about 125% during pregnancy, increasing its blood demand.
This pregnancy-related pituitary enlargement increases blood demand, which\u2014if unmet due to PPH\u2014leads to:
Unmet blood demand during PPH leads to necrosis of the enlarged pituitary gland.
In Sheehan syndrome, failure of lactation occurs due to:
Failure of lactation in Sheehan syndrome results from decreased prolactin secretion.
The MOST common clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome is:
Failure of lactation is the most common clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome.
The SECOND most common clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome is:
Persistent amenorrhoea is the second most common clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome.
In Sheehan syndrome, among the pituitary hormones, the FIRST to decrease is:
Growth hormone is the first pituitary hormone to decrease in Sheehan syndrome.
In Sheehan syndrome, the LAST pituitary hormone to decrease is:
TSH is the last pituitary hormone to decrease in Sheehan syndrome.
The characteristic MRI finding in Sheehan syndrome is:
Empty sella turcica is the characteristic MRI finding in Sheehan syndrome, reflecting the necrosed and shrunken gland.
The workup of a case of secondary amenorrhoea begins by measuring:
The workup begins with measurement of FSH and estrogen.
If FSH is increased (>25 IU) and estrogen is decreased, this indicates:
Increased FSH with decreased estrogen indicates hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, pointing to POI.
If FSH is decreased or normal (\u226410 IU), the next step in the workup is:
With FSH decreased/normal (\u226410 IU), the next step is the Progesterone Challenge Test.
The Progesterone Challenge Test uses medroxyprogesterone acetate at a dose of:
The PCT protocol uses medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg BD for 5 days, then stopped.
If bleeding occurs after the PCT (PCT positive), the diagnosis is:
A positive PCT (bleeding occurs) points to PCOS.
If NO bleeding occurs after the PCT (PCT negative), the next step is:
A negative PCT leads to the combined estrogen + progesterone challenge test over 21 days.
If the E+P challenge test is NEGATIVE (no bleeding), the diagnosis is:
A negative E+P challenge test (no bleeding despite full hormonal priming) points to Asherman syndrome.
If the E+P challenge test is POSITIVE (bleeding occurs), the next investigation is:
A positive E+P challenge test is followed by MRI to localise a hypothalamic-pituitary cause.
On this follow-up MRI (after a positive E+P test), a NORMAL scan points to a:
A normal MRI (after a positive E+P test) points to a hypothalamic cause.
An MRI showing an EMPTY SELLA TURCICA (after a positive E+P test) points to:
An empty sella turcica on this follow-up MRI points to Sheehan syndrome.
An MRI showing a SPACE-OCCUPYING LESION (after a positive E+P test) points to:
A space-occupying lesion on this follow-up MRI points to a prolactinoma.
A pregnant female with an undiagnosed pituitary adenoma
Pituitary apoplexy classically occurs in a pregnant female with an undiagnosed pituitary adenoma.
The pathogenesis of pituitary apoplexy proceeds through postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) leading to:
PPH in a female with an undiagnosed adenoma leads to pituitary infarction and haemorrhage, i.e., pituitary apoplexy.
Symptoms of pituitary apoplexy include headache and visual disturbances, along with postpartum collapse due to:
Postpartum collapse in pituitary apoplexy occurs due to decreased ACTH (acute adrenal insufficiency).
Another recognised symptom of pituitary apoplexy is:
Hypoglycaemia is a recognised symptom of pituitary apoplexy, reflecting acute pituitary/adrenal failure.
The drug of choice for management of pituitary apoplexy is:
Corticosteroids are the DOC for managing pituitary apoplexy, addressing the acute adrenal insufficiency.
Absence of menstruation due to ovarian failure
Painful menstruation without any pelvic pathology
Hidden menstruation due to an obstruction in the outflow passage
Cryptomenorrhoea is hidden menstruation, occurring due to an obstruction in the outflow passage that prevents blood flow.
Cryptomenorrhoea characteristically presents with cyclical abdominal pain plus:
Cryptomenorrhoea presents with cyclical abdominal pain plus primary amenorrhoea, since menstrual blood cannot exit.
Recognised causes of cryptomenorrhoea include imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum, and:
Vaginal atresia, along with imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum, is a recognised cause of cryptomenorrhoea (outflow obstruction).
Mittelschmerz syndrome refers to pain occurring at the time of:
Mittelschmerz syndrome is pain occurring at the time of ovulation.
The characteristic presentation of Mittelschmerz syndrome is:
Pain that persists throughout the cycle
Mittelschmerz syndrome characteristically presents as midcycle pain, coinciding with ovulation.
Dysmenorrhoea is defined as pain occurring during menstruation.
In a patient presenting with cyclical abdominal pain, if primary amenorrhoea is ALSO present, the diagnosis to consider is:
Cyclical abdominal pain with primary amenorrhoea points to cryptomenorrhoea (hidden menstruation from outflow obstruction).
In a patient with cyclical abdominal pain and NO primary amenorrhoea, pain occurring at MID-CYCLE points to:
Mid-cycle pain (without primary amenorrhoea) points to Mittelschmerz syndrome, coinciding with ovulation.
In this same patient (no primary amenorrhoea), pain occurring DURING MENSTRUATION itself points to:
Pain occurring during menstruation itself (without primary amenorrhoea) points to dysmenorrhoea.
Primary dysmenorrhoea occurs due to the release of:
Primary dysmenorrhoea occurs due to release of PGF2\u03b1, causing uterine spasm.
By definition, primary dysmenorrhoea is NOT associated with:
Primary dysmenorrhoea occurs with no underlying pelvic pathology, unlike secondary dysmenorrhoea.
Secondary dysmenorrhoea occurs due to underlying pelvic pathology, the MOST COMMON of which is:
Endometriosis is the most common pelvic pathology causing secondary dysmenorrhoea.
Besides endometriosis, recognised pelvic pathologies causing secondary dysmenorrhoea include fibrosis, adenomyosis, and:
PID, along with endometriosis, fibrosis, and adenomyosis, is a recognised cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea.
The TYPE of pain in primary dysmenorrhoea is classically described as:
Primary dysmenorrhoea produces spasmodic-type pain, from uterine muscle spasm due to prostaglandins.
The type of pain in secondary dysmenorrhoea is classically described as:
Secondary dysmenorrhoea produces congestive-type pain, related to underlying pelvic pathology.
Only females who have never ovulated
Primary dysmenorrhoea typically affects young females, often soon after menarche.
Secondary dysmenorrhoea typically affects reproductive age females \u226530 years, given the time needed to develop underlying pathology.
Regarding pain ONSET, primary dysmenorrhoea begins with or just before menses and decreases within:
Primary dysmenorrhoea pain begins with/just before menses and decreases within 72 hours.
Regarding pain onset, secondary dysmenorrhoea begins:
Only during menses, resolving immediately after
Much before menses and remains after the onset of menses
Secondary dysmenorrhoea pain begins much before menses and persists after the onset of menses.
The SITE of pain in primary dysmenorrhoea is:
Primary dysmenorrhoea pain is centralised in the suprapubic area.
The site of pain in secondary dysmenorrhoea is:
Secondary dysmenorrhoea produces localised pain, reflecting the site of the underlying pathology.
Regarding pain PROGRESSION, primary dysmenorrhoea characteristically decreases on its own after physical activity, marriage, and:
Primary dysmenorrhoea characteristically improves after physical activity, marriage, and childbirth.
Regarding pain progression, secondary dysmenorrhoea characteristically:
Secondary dysmenorrhoea pain progressively increases over time, unlike primary dysmenorrhoea.
The management of primary dysmenorrhoea includes NSAIDs and:
OCPs, to make the cycles anovulatory
OCPs (to render cycles anovulatory) along with NSAIDs are used to manage primary dysmenorrhoea.
The management of secondary dysmenorrhoea is:
Secondary dysmenorrhoea is managed by treating the underlying pelvic pathology causing it.
The most common PHYSIOLOGICAL symptom of PMS is:
Mood swings are the most common physiological symptom of PMS.
The most common PHYSICAL symptom of PMS is:
Bloating is the most common physical symptom of PMS.
For a diagnosis of PMS, symptoms must interfere with routine activity and be seen in at least how many consecutive cycles?
Symptoms must be seen in at least 3 consecutive cycles for a diagnosis of PMS.
A key diagnostic criterion for PMS is that symptoms must resolve:
PMS symptoms must resolve after menstruation, as part of the diagnostic criteria.
For diagnosis of PMS, symptoms should characteristically be seen in the:
PMS symptoms should be seen specifically in the post-ovulatory (luteal) phase.
Consistent with the post-ovulatory requirement, PMS symptoms should NEVER be seen in the:
PMS symptoms should never be seen in the pre-ovulatory phase, per the diagnostic criteria.
A confirmed diagnosis of PMS requires:
Presence of any 2 of the 5 criteria
Presence of only the mood symptom
Presence of only the physical symptom
All 5 diagnostic criteria must be present together to confirm a diagnosis of PMS.
The drug of choice for PMS is:
Fluoxetine, an SSRI, is the DOC for PMS.
For insomnia associated with PMS, the drug used is:
Alprazolam is used specifically for insomnia in PMS management.
Evening primrose oil is specifically used in PMS management for:
Evening primrose oil is used specifically for breast tenderness in PMS.
Diuretics are used in PMS management specifically for:
Diuretics are used specifically for water retention in PMS.
Besides fluoxetine, alprazolam, evening primrose oil, and diuretics, another agent used in PMS management is:
Pyridoxine is another agent used in PMS management.
Lifestyle changes recommended for PMS \u2014 reducing sugar, salt, and caffeine intake \u2014 are specifically advised during:
The second half of the cycle
The first half of the cycle
These lifestyle changes are specifically recommended during the second half of the cycle (luteal phase).
Chronic pelvic pain is defined as pelvic pain persisting for at least:
Chronic pelvic pain is defined as pain persisting for \u22653 months.
The investigation of choice (IOC) for chronic pelvic pain is:
Laparoscopy is the IOC for chronic pelvic pain.
Besides chronic pelvic pain, laparoscopy is also the investigation of choice for:
Laparoscopy is also the IOC for endometriosis.
For PID specifically, laparoscopy is considered:
Laparoscopy is considered the gold standard investigation for PID (a step beyond being simply the IOC).
Endometriosis is defined by the occurrence of ectopic endometrium containing:
Endometriosis is defined by ectopic endometrial tissue containing both glands and stroma.
Endometriosis is a hormonally active condition that is:
Endometriosis is a hormonally active, estrogen-dependent condition.
In endometriosis, cyclical monthly shedding and bleeding of the ectopic endometrium leads to:
Cyclical shedding and bleeding of ectopic endometrium causes local inflammation and adhesion formation.
Endometriosis is best classified as a:
Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory condition.
Being estrogen dependent, endometriosis regresses during pregnancy due to increased:
Increased progesterone during pregnancy causes regression of endometriosis.
Endometriosis also regresses after menopause due to decreased:
Decreased estrogen after menopause causes regression of endometriosis, consistent with its estrogen-dependent nature.
Nulliparity is a risk factor for endometriosis because it is associated with:
Nulliparity increases cumulative lifetime estrogen exposure, raising endometriosis risk.
Besides nulliparity, recognised risk factors for endometriosis include early menarche and:
Late menopause, along with early menarche, increases estrogen exposure and endometriosis risk.
Unlike most other estrogen-dependent conditions (which correlate with obesity/high BMI), endometriosis is specifically associated with:
Endometriosis is distinctively associated with low BMI, unlike most other estrogen-dependent conditions which correlate with high BMI.
A recognised protective factor against endometriosis is:
Multiparity is protective against endometriosis, reducing lifetime estrogen/retrograde menstruation exposure.
Prolonged use of OCPs protects against endometriosis by increasing progesterone, leading to:
OCP-induced progesterone dominance causes endometrial thinning, protecting against endometriosis.
Smoking is protective against endometriosis via two mechanisms: decreasing local estrogen level and:
Smoking inhibits aromatase (reducing local estrogen conversion), in addition to decreasing local estrogen level directly.
The most common age group affected by endometriosis is:
Reproductive age (25\u201335 years) is the most common age group affected by endometriosis.
In teenage girls with endometriosis, one should suspect an underlying:
A M\u00fcllerian malformation should be suspected in teenage girls presenting with endometriosis.
In teenage girls, a M\u00fcllerian malformation increases the risk of endometriosis via:
Outflow obstruction from a M\u00fcllerian malformation increases retrograde menstrual flow, raising endometriosis risk.
A gene showing genetic predisposition to endometriosis is:
The K-RAS gene shows a positive genetic predisposition association with endometriosis.
The most common SITE of endometriosis is the:
The ovary is the most common site of endometriosis.
Endometriosis at the ovary is specifically termed a:
Ovarian endometriosis is termed a chocolate cyst or endometrioma.
In decreasing order of frequency, the site distribution of endometriosis is ovary > POD > broad ligament >:
Uterosacral ligaments follow broad ligament in the site-frequency order of endometriosis.
Rare sites of endometriosis include the spleen and:
The CNS, along with the spleen, is a rare site of endometriosis.
Endometriosis can also be seen at unusual sites such as the nose, lungs, and:
The umbilicus, along with the nose and lungs, is a recognised unusual site for endometriosis.
Endometriosis can also occur at surgical scars, such as after cesarean section and:
Episiotomy scars, along with cesarean section scars, are recognised sites for scar endometriosis.
Endometriosis at the ovary, POD, or uterosacral ligament is explained by the theory of retrograde menstruation, also known as:
Sampson\u2019s theory of implantation explains retrograde-menstruation-associated endometriosis at the ovary, POD, and uterosacral ligament.
Endometriosis at the umbilicus is explained by:
Halban\u2019s theory of lymphatic spread explains umbilical endometriosis.
Endometriosis at the lungs is explained by:
Ivanoff\u2019s theory of coelomic metaplasia explains pulmonary endometriosis.
Scar endometriosis (e.g., in a cesarean or episiotomy scar) is explained by:
Scar endometriosis is explained by direct implantation of endometrial cells during surgery.
Sampson's implantation theory explains the most common site (ovary) being more common than the:
Sampson's theory explains why the ovary is more commonly affected than the POD.
According to Sampson's theory, the most common EXTRAGENITAL site of endometriosis is the:
The sigmoid colon is the most common extragenital site of endometriosis per this theory.
Per Sampson's theory, endometriosis (via retrograde menstruation) is more common in females with short, frequent cycles, and:
Outflow tract obstruction (e.g., imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum)
Outflow tract obstruction, along with short/frequent cycles and M\u00fcllerian malformation, increases retrograde menstruation and endometriosis risk.
The most common symptom of endometriosis is:
Pain is the most common symptom of endometriosis.
Among the pain symptoms of endometriosis, ranked by frequency, the order is secondary dysmenorrhoea > chronic pelvic pain >:
Dyspareunia follows chronic pelvic pain in the frequency ranking of pain symptoms in endometriosis.
The SECOND most common overall symptom of endometriosis (after pain) is:
Infertility is the second most common overall symptom of endometriosis.
The THIRD most common overall symptom of endometriosis is:
Adnexal mass (chocolate cyst) is the third most common overall symptom of endometriosis.
A classically described presentation of endometriosis is a nulliparous female complaining of dysmenorrhoea and:
A nulliparous female with dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia is a classic endometriosis presentation.
The classical triad of endometriosis consists of secondary dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and:
The classical triad of endometriosis is secondary dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and infertility.
The mnemonic "VCC" for specific symptoms of endometriosis stands for vicarious menstruation, cyclical hematuria, and:
Catamenial hemothorax/pneumothorax is the third element of the "VCC" mnemonic for specific endometriosis symptoms.
Menstrual bleeding from sites other than the uterus
Vicarious menstruation is menstrual bleeding occurring from extra-uterine sites of endometriosis.
Hematuria occurring at the time of menstruation
Cyclical hematuria is hematuria occurring specifically at the time of menstruation, reflecting bladder endometriosis.
Catamenial hemothorax/pneumothorax refers to hemothorax or pneumothorax occurring:
Catamenial hemothorax/pneumothorax occurs during menstruation, reflecting thoracic endometriosis.
The menstrual abnormality classically seen in endometriosis is:
Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is the classic menstrual abnormality of endometriosis.
HMB in endometriosis occurs due to inflammation of the ovary and abnormal follicular growth, leading to:
Ovarian inflammation and abnormal follicular growth in endometriosis lead to anovulation, causing HMB.
Recognised causes of pain in endometriosis include adhesion formation, peritoneal inflammation, and:
Local prostaglandin production, along with adhesion formation and peritoneal inflammation, causes pain in endometriosis.
Deeper infiltration of endometriotic lesions leads to pain via:
Deeper lesion infiltration causes nerve irritation, contributing to pain.
The SEVERITY of pain in endometriosis correlates with the:
Pain severity in endometriosis correlates with the depth of the lesion.
Importantly, the severity of pain in endometriosis is:
Directly proportional to the extent of disease
Independent of the extent of disease
Pain severity is independent of the overall extent of disease, even though it correlates with lesion depth.
On per abdominal examination, findings in endometriosis are typically:
Per abdominal examination findings are typically not significant in endometriosis.
On per vaginal examination, the uterus in endometriosis is typically:
Normal size, retroverted and fixed due to adhesions, non-tender
The uterus is typically normal in size, retroverted and fixed (due to adhesions), and non-tender in endometriosis.
On per vaginal examination, adnexal findings in endometriosis may include:
Bilateral adnexal mass (chocolate cyst) with +/- tenderness
A bilateral adnexal mass (chocolate cyst) with variable tenderness is a recognised finding.
On per vaginal examination, the uterosacral ligament in endometriosis characteristically shows:
Uterosacral ligament nodularity is a characteristic examination finding in endometriosis.
The uterus is retroverted and fixed in endometriosis specifically due to:
Pelvic adhesions from endometriosis cause the uterus to become retroverted and fixed.
The FIRST investigation performed for suspected endometriosis is:
TVS is the first investigation performed for suspected endometriosis.
TVS in endometriosis is used to rule out other disorders and may show:
A definite diagnosis in all cases
TVS helps rule out other disorders and may show a chocolate cyst if present, though it cannot definitively diagnose or stage endometriosis.
The investigation of choice (IOC) for endometriosis is:
Laparoscopy is the IOC for endometriosis.
Laparoscopy in endometriosis serves a dual role, being both:
Purely investigational with no treatment role
Laparoscopy serves both diagnostic and therapeutic roles in endometriosis.
The GOLD STANDARD investigation for endometriosis is:
HPE is the gold standard investigation for confirming endometriosis.
The gold-standard HPE in endometriosis is performed on the:
HPE is performed on the endometrial implant tissue obtained during laparoscopy.
A chocolate cyst (endometrioma) forms due to:
Cyclical endometrial shedding within the ovary, causing bleeding and cyst formation
A chocolate cyst forms from cyclical endometrial shedding within the ovary, leading to bleeding and cyst formation.
The brown color of a chocolate cyst is due to:
Hemosiderin, from breakdown of old blood, gives the chocolate cyst its characteristic brown color.
The presence of a chocolate cyst indicates:
A chocolate cyst indicates severe endometriosis.
On USG, a chocolate cyst characteristically shows a ground glass appearance with:
Doppler flow within a solid component
A chocolate cyst shows a ground glass appearance with homogeneous internal echoes on USG.
Laparoscopic findings in endometriosis include chocolate cyst, adhesions inside the peritoneal cavity, and:
Peritoneal defects, along with chocolate cyst and adhesions, are a recognised laparoscopic finding.
Peritoneal defects seen on laparoscopy in endometriosis are termed:
Peritoneal defects in endometriosis are termed Allen-Masters syndrome.
Besides chocolate cyst, adhesions, and peritoneal defects, laparoscopy in endometriosis also shows:
Superficial peritoneal deposits are the fourth category of laparoscopic finding in endometriosis.
Red nodules seen on laparoscopy in endometriosis are also known as:
Red nodules are also known as red flame lesions.
Red flame lesions on laparoscopy indicate:
Red flame lesions indicate fresh endometriotic implants.
Black nodules seen on laparoscopy in endometriosis are also known as powder burn appearance or:
Black nodules are also known as powder burn appearance or gunshot appearance.
Black nodules (powder burn/gunshot appearance) on laparoscopy indicate:
Black nodules (powder burn/gunshot appearance) indicate old endometriotic lesions.
The uses of laparoscopy in endometriosis include visualization of the lesion, staging of disease, biopsy for HPE, and:
Therapeutic intervention, along with visualization, staging, and biopsy, is a key use of laparoscopy in endometriosis.
In the staging of endometriosis, MODERATE disease is characterized by:
SEVERE endometriosis is characterized by chocolate cyst and:
Severe endometriosis is characterized by chocolate cyst plus distortion of the pelvic cavity.
Surgical management of endometriosis (laparoscopy) is indicated primarily upon:
Surgical management is indicated primarily upon failure of medical management.
For mild/minimal endometriosis-related dysmenorrhoea, the approach is to treat it as:
Mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea is treated as primary dysmenorrhoea.
The 1st line treatment for mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea is:
OCPs are the 1st line treatment for mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea.
If the patient with mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea wants to conceive (and thus cannot use OCPs), the alternative 1st line option is:
NSAIDs are used instead of OCPs when the patient wants to conceive.
The 2nd line treatment for mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea is progesterone, given as either oral progesterone or:
MIRENA (levonorgestrel IUS), along with oral progesterone, is the 2nd line option.
The 3rd line treatment for mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea is:
Continuous GnRH analogs or GnRH antagonists form the 3rd line treatment.
If all 3 lines of medical management fail for mild/minimal endometriosis dysmenorrhoea, the next step is:
Laparoscopy follows failure of all 3 lines of medical management.
For MODERATE to SEVERE endometriosis-related dysmenorrhoea, the 1st line treatment is:
Continuous GnRH agonist or GnRH antagonist
Continuous GnRH agonist or GnRH antagonist is 1st line for moderate-severe disease, unlike the stepwise approach for mild disease.
If 1st line management fails in moderate-severe endometriosis dysmenorrhoea, the next step is:
Repeating the same drug at a higher dose
Laparoscopy follows failure of 1st line management in moderate-severe disease.
Danazol and gestrinone, used in endometriosis, share a common significant side effect of:
Both danazol and gestrinone share hirsutism as a significant side effect.
Letrozole, used in endometriosis management, works as a(n):
Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, reducing peripheral estrogen synthesis.
Mifepristone, used in endometriosis, works by leading to:
Mifepristone leads to endometrial atrophy, useful in endometriosis management.
The drug specifically NOT used in endometriosis (as it worsens pain) is:
Misoprostol (a PGE1 analog) increases pain and is specifically not used in endometriosis.
Laparoscopic management options for endometriosis include adhesiolysis, fulguration of implants, and:
Cystectomy (if indicated), along with adhesiolysis and fulguration, is a laparoscopic management option.
Besides adhesiolysis, fulguration, and cystectomy, laparoscopic management also includes pre-sacral neurectomy and:
LUNA, along with pre-sacral neurectomy, is a laparoscopic management option targeting pain pathways.
The LAST RESORT management for endometriosis is:
TAH is the last resort management for endometriosis.
TAH halts progression of endometriosis because it eliminates:
TAH eliminates retrograde menstruation, halting progression of the disease.
By eliminating retrograde menstruation, TAH ensures:
Complete regression of all existing implants
TAH prevents formation of new implants by eliminating retrograde menstruation, though it does not reverse existing implants/adhesions.
Causes of infertility in endometriosis include abnormal follicular growth, anovulation, and:
Distorted anatomy between tube and ovaries
Distorted anatomy between the tube and ovaries, along with abnormal follicular growth and anovulation, causes infertility in endometriosis.
In mild/minimal endometriosis-related infertility (with multiple contributing factors), the case is treated as:
Tubal factor infertility requiring IVF directly
Mild/minimal endometriosis infertility (multiple factors) is treated as unexplained infertility.
The management for mild/minimal endometriosis infertility (treated as unexplained infertility) is:
Clomiphene citrate plus IUI for 3 cycles is the management for mild/minimal endometriosis infertility.
If clomiphene citrate + IUI fails in mild/minimal endometriosis infertility, the next step is:
IVF follows failure of clomiphene citrate + IUI in mild/minimal endometriosis infertility.
In MODERATE to SEVERE endometriosis-related infertility, the predominant cause is:
Tubal factors predominate as the cause of infertility in moderate-severe endometriosis.
The management for moderate-severe endometriosis-related infertility (tubal factors) is:
IVF is the management for moderate-severe endometriosis infertility, bypassing the tubal factor.
An endometrioma (chocolate cyst) is a condition that:
Is best managed with OCPs alone
An endometrioma cannot be managed medically; it requires a structural/surgical approach when treatment is needed.
In a patient with an endometrioma who DESIRES pregnancy, the recommended approach is to:
Start IVF immediately without any surgery consideration
Not manage the cyst, to avoid risk of follicle destruction
The cyst is left unmanaged in a patient desiring pregnancy, to avoid the risk of follicle destruction from surgery.
If surgery IS eventually needed in a patient with an endometrioma desiring pregnancy, the procedure performed is:
Cystectomy (ovary-sparing) is the surgical procedure of choice, preserving fertility potential.
In a patient with an endometrioma who does NOT desire pregnancy, if the cyst is asymptomatic and <5 cm, management is:
An asymptomatic endometrioma <5 cm (in a patient not desiring pregnancy) is managed with USG follow-up.
In a patient with an endometrioma who does NOT desire pregnancy, if the cyst is symptomatic OR \u22655 cm, management is:
A symptomatic or \u22655 cm endometrioma is managed with laparoscopic cystectomy.
After laparoscopic cystectomy for a symptomatic or large endometrioma, the specimen should be sent for:
The excised specimen is sent for HPE to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy.
Medical management is specifically NOT useful for chocolate cyst, bladder endometriosis, and:
Bowel endometriosis, along with chocolate cyst and bladder endometriosis, does not respond to medical management alone.
CA-125 is characteristically elevated in endometriosis, typically to a level of:
CA-125 is characteristically elevated to \u2265100 IU in endometriosis.
MRI is specifically indicated in endometriosis for evaluating:
Only pelvic pain of unclear cause
MRI is specifically indicated for bladder and bowel endometriosis, rather than being used routinely in all cases.
Deep endometriosis of the rectosigmoid causes hypertrophy of the mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria, producing a characteristic MRI finding known as:
The mushroom cap sign is the characteristic MRI finding in deep rectosigmoid endometriosis.
Cyclical hematuria in endometriosis is caused by bladder endometriosis or:
A fistula between the uterus and rectum
A fistula between the uterus and bladder (utero-vesical fistula)
A utero-vesical fistula, along with bladder endometriosis itself, is a recognised cause of cyclical hematuria.
A fibroid (leiomyoma) is best described as:
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium
A benign smooth muscle tumour arising from the myometrium
A fibroid is a benign smooth muscle tumour arising from the myometrium.
An endometrial/endocervical polyp is best described as:
Ectopic endometrial glands within the myometrium
A polyp is a localised outgrowth of endometrium.
Adenomyosis is defined as endometrial tissue (glands and stroma) present within the myometrium, at a depth of at least:
2.5 mm from the basal layer of endometrium
Adenomyosis requires endometrial glands/stroma at least 2.5 mm deep from the basal layer of the endometrium.
Fibroid is most common in which age group?
Fibroid is most common in reproductive age females, 25\u201335 years.
Fibroid is most common in which parity group, reflecting hyperestrogenic conditions?
Fibroid is most common in nulliparous females, reflecting their hyperestrogenic state.
Polyp can be seen across all age groups, but its incidence:
Polyp incidence increases with increasing age.
The most common age group for polyp is:
The most common age group for polyp is 40\u201349 years.
Adenomyosis is most common in females of what age?
Adenomyosis is most common in females \u226540 years.
Adenomyosis is most common in which parity group (opposite to fibroid)?
Only in females who have never conceived
Adenomyosis is most common in multiparous females, in contrast to fibroid (most common in nulliparous females).
Fibroid is classically described as a(n):
Fibroid is an estrogen and progesterone dependent tumour.
Polyp incidence is increased in females using which drug?
Tamoxifen use is associated with increased incidence of polyps.
Adenomyosis is associated with endometriosis and fibroids.
The most common symptom of fibroid is:
HMB (heavy menstrual bleeding), with regular cycles
Fibroid's most common symptom is HMB, occurring with regular cycles.
Fibroid's most common symptom (HMB) was earlier termed:
HMB in fibroid was earlier termed menorrhagia.
In reproductive/perimenopausal age, a polyp's most common symptom is:
In reproductive/perimenopausal age, polyp presents with irregular/intermenstrual bleeding.
In postmenopausal women, a polyp's most common symptom is:
In postmenopausal women, polyp presents with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB).
Earlier, the most common cause of PMB was considered to be:
Endometrial atrophy was earlier considered the most common cause of PMB.
Currently, the most common cause of PMB is:
Currently, polyp (33%) has overtaken endometrial atrophy (30%) as the most common cause of PMB.
The most common symptom of adenomyosis is:
Adenomyosis's most common symptom is menorrhagia (HMB) plus secondary dysmenorrhoea.
Besides HMB, other symptoms of fibroid include secondary dysmenorrhoea, subfertility, pregnancy complications, and:
Pressure symptoms are another recognised symptom of fibroid.
Fibroid-related infertility is more accurately termed:
Fibroid causes subfertility (reduced, not absent, fertility), rather than absolute infertility.
Polyp, unlike fibroid and adenomyosis, characteristically has:
No other significant associated symptoms beyond the bleeding pattern
Polyp has no other significant associated symptoms beyond its characteristic bleeding pattern.
The other significant symptom associated with adenomyosis, besides its most common symptom, is:
Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is the other significant symptom of adenomyosis.
Rounded/oval and whorled, white, and firm
A fibroid grossly appears rounded/oval and whorled, white, and firm.
A fibroid arises from a broad base.
A fibroid is surrounded by a pseudocapsule, which is composed of:
Connective tissue containing blood vessels supplying the fibroid
The fibroid's pseudocapsule is connective tissue containing the vessels that supply it.
Grossly, a polyp appears as a:
Fleshy, red mass with a smooth surface
A polyp grossly appears as a fleshy, red mass with a smooth surface.
A polyp characteristically hangs from a:
Narrow base, within the uterine cavity
Fixed sessile base covering the whole cavity
A polyp hangs from a narrow base within the uterine cavity.
Grossly, adenomyosis results from the basal layer of endometrium infiltrating the myometrium, causing:
Basal endometrial infiltration causes myometrial hypertrophy and hyperplasia in adenomyosis.
This myometrial hypertrophy/hyperplasia in adenomyosis produces a uterus that is symmetrically enlarged, described as a:
The symmetrically enlarged uterus of adenomyosis is described as globular.
On cut section, adenomyosis characteristically shows:
Adenomyosis shows multiple haemorrhages within the myometrium on cut section.
On per abdominal examination, a fibroid presents as an abdomino-pelvic lump where the examiner is:
Able to easily converge fingers below the lump
Unable to converge fingers below the lump
Unable to palpate any lump at all
Only able to feel the lump on deep inspiration
The examiner is unable to converge fingers below a fibroid lump, since it arises from the pelvis.
The fibroid lump on P/A exam is characteristically:
A fibroid lump is characteristically midline, mobile, and firm.
The fibroid can enlarge, on P/A exam, up to the size of a pregnant uterus of:
A fibroid can enlarge up to the size of a 20-week pregnant uterus.
On per abdominal examination, polyp findings are typically:
Not significant/not applicable (polyps are not palpable abdominally)
Always palpable as a firm midline mass
Always palpable as a soft mobile mass
A polyp is not palpable on abdominal examination, being an intracavitary lesion.
On per abdominal examination, adenomyosis findings are typically:
Adenomyosis findings on abdominal examination are typically not significant.
On bimanual (P/V) palpation, a fibroid presents as an abdomino-pelvic mass that is:
A fibroid presents on P/V exam as a firm, mobile mass.
A key distinguishing feature of fibroid on P/V exam is that the mass:
Can be easily separated from the uterus
Is always separate from and mobile independent of the uterus
Is fixed to the pelvic side wall, not the uterus
Cannot be separated from the uterus
A fibroid mass cannot be separated from the uterus on bimanual exam, since it is a uterine tumour.
The uterus in fibroid is characteristically:
Fibroid produces an asymmetrically enlarged, non-tender uterus.
On P/V exam with a fibroid, movement of the abdominal mass is:
Not transmitted to the cervix at all
Only felt in the posterior fornix
Movement of the fibroid mass is transmitted to the cervix, confirming it is uterine in origin.
On P/V exam, a polyp typically presents with a uterus that is:
The uterus is typically normal on P/V exam in polyp.
On P/V exam, the uterus in adenomyosis is:
Adenomyosis produces a symmetrically enlarged, globular uterus on P/V exam.
The uterine size in adenomyosis on P/V exam corresponds to a pregnant uterus of:
Any size, with no characteristic limit
Adenomyosis enlarges the uterus to 10\u201313 weeks pregnant size, never exceeding 14 weeks.
Tenderness of the uterus in adenomyosis on P/V exam is referred to as the:
Uterine tenderness in adenomyosis is referred to as the Halban sign.
Adnexal tenderness in adenomyosis on P/V exam is:
Adnexal tenderness in adenomyosis is variable (+/-), not a fixed finding.
On USG, a fibroid appears as a well-defined hypoechoic mass arising from a:
A fibroid appears as a well-defined hypoechoic mass with a broad base on USG.
Is only seen in the cervix
A fibroid characteristically distorts the uterine cavity on USG.
A fibroid on USG may show a posterior finding of:
A fibroid may show posterior acoustic shadowing on USG.
The texture of a fibroid on USG is:
A fibroid's texture resembles the myometrium on USG, since it arises from smooth muscle.
When comparing SIS (saline infusion sonography) to TVS for detecting a submucous fibroid, which performs better?
SIS outperforms TVS in detecting submucous fibroids.
On Doppler, a fibroid characteristically shows:
A single feeding vessel to its centre
Doppler shows increased peripheral vascularity around a fibroid.
On USG, a polyp appears as a solid mass arising from a:
A polyp appears as a solid mass arising from a narrow base on USG.
The texture of a polyp on USG, unlike a fibroid, is:
Not the same as the myometrium
A polyp's texture is not the same as the myometrium, distinguishing it from a fibroid.
On Doppler, a polyp characteristically shows a single blood vessel extending up to its centre, known as the:
A single vessel extending to the centre of a polyp is termed the feeder vessel sign.
On USG, thickening of the uterine wall in adenomyosis is characteristically:
Adenomyosis characteristically shows greater posterior than anterior wall thickening.
The MOST SPECIFIC USG sign of adenomyosis is:
Collection of blood within the myometrium (myometrial cyst)
A myometrial cyst (blood collection within the myometrium) is the most specific USG sign of adenomyosis.
The alternating dark and light bands seen on USG in adenomyosis are termed the:
Alternating dark/light bands in adenomyosis are termed the Venetian blind appearance.
A further USG finding in adenomyosis is loss of demarcation between:
Loss of demarcation between endometrium and myometrium is a further USG finding in adenomyosis.
On HSG, a submucous fibroid characteristically shows:
A filling defect with smooth/regular outlines
A filling defect with irregular outlines (moth-eaten)
Free spill with no cavity distortion
A submucous fibroid shows a filling defect with smooth/regular outlines on HSG.
On HSG, a polyp shows a filling defect appearance that is:
Similar to that of a submucous fibroid (smooth/regular outlines)
A polyp's HSG appearance (smooth/regular filling defect) resembles that of a submucous fibroid.
On hysteroscopy, a submucous fibroid appears as a:
Fleshy, red mass with a smooth surface, arising from a narrow base
White, whorled mass with surface blood vessels, arising from a broad base
A submucous fibroid on hysteroscopy is a white, whorled mass with surface vessels, arising from a broad base.
On hysteroscopy, a polyp appears as a:
White, whorled mass, arising from a broad base
Fleshy, red mass with a smooth surface, arising from a narrow base
A polyp on hysteroscopy is a fleshy, red mass with a smooth surface, arising from a narrow base.
When AUB (abnormal uterine bleeding) is present, the 1st line investigations are UPT and:
TVS, along with UPT, is the 1st line investigation for AUB.
In a patient with AUB who is \u226540 years old, the 1st line investigation additionally includes:
Endometrial biopsy, to rule out hyperplasia/cancer
Endometrial biopsy is additionally performed in AUB patients \u226540 years, to exclude hyperplasia/cancer.
If the endometrial biopsy (in a patient \u226540 with AUB) is normal, and adenomyosis is suspected, the diagnosis is largely:
With a normal endometrial biopsy, adenomyosis is largely a clinical diagnosis.
The investigation of choice (IOC) for a submucous fibroid is:
Hysteroscopy is the IOC for a submucous fibroid.
Not routinely done, but may be done pre-operatively
MRI is not routine for fibroid but may be used pre-operatively for surgical planning.
The investigation of choice (IOC) for a polyp is:
Hysteroscopy, being both diagnostic and therapeutic, is the IOC for a polyp.
MRI is usually not required in adenomyosis, given it is largely a clinical diagnosis.
On MRI, the transition zone (TZ) thickness that suggests adenomyosis is:
A transition zone \u226512 mm on MRI suggests adenomyosis.
A transition zone (TZ) thickness that RULES OUT adenomyosis on MRI is:
A transition zone <8 mm on MRI rules out adenomyosis.
There is no established gold standard investigation for fibroid or polyp in this comparison; however, the gold standard investigation for adenomyosis is:
Histopathological examination after hysterectomy is the gold standard investigation for adenomyosis.
The HPE gold standard for adenomyosis demonstrates:
Endometrial glands confined only to the endometrial cavity
Endometrial glands present within the myometrium
HPE in adenomyosis demonstrates endometrial glands present within the myometrium.
Asymptomatic fibroid is managed with observation alone.
Medical management options for symptomatic fibroid include OCPs, continuous GnRH agonist, and:
GnRH antagonists, along with OCPs and continuous GnRH agonist, are medical management options for symptomatic fibroid.
Surgical management options for fibroid include myomectomy and:
Hysterectomy, along with myomectomy, is a surgical management option for fibroid.
Management of an endometrial polyp is:
An endometrial polyp is managed with hysteroscopic polypectomy.
Management of an endocervical polyp is:
An endocervical polyp is managed with a polypectomy hook.
The BEST management for adenomyosis is:
TAH (total abdominal hysterectomy), removing the uterus and cervix
TAH, removing the uterus and cervix, is the best management for adenomyosis.
If a patient with adenomyosis refuses TAH, the alternative management is:
LNG-IUCD (Mirena) is the alternative management if TAH is refused.
LNG-IUCD (Mirena) in adenomyosis works by causing:
LNG-IUCD works via endometrial atrophy in adenomyosis.
Benefits of LNG-IUCD (Mirena) in adenomyosis include endometrial atrophy, decreased blood loss, and:
Amenorrhoea, along with endometrial atrophy and decreased blood loss, is a benefit of LNG-IUCD in adenomyosis.
Fibroids are benign tumours arising from:
Smooth muscle cells of the uterus
Fibroids (leiomyomas) arise from smooth muscle cells of the uterus.
Fibroids contain varying amounts of fibrous tissue.
Most common pelvic tumours in females
Fibroids are the most common pelvic tumours in females.
Fibroids are estrogen and progesterone dependent tumours.
Fibroids possess receptors for estrogen, aromatase, and progesterone, with progesterone receptor activation leading to:
Progesterone receptor activation in fibroid leads to apoptosis (a negative regulatory effect).
Angiogenic factors implicated in fibroid growth include TGF-\u03b2 and:
EGF, along with TGF-\u03b2, is an angiogenic factor implicated in fibroid growth.
Fibroids are associated with chromosomal anomalies such as deletion, translocation, and duplication, occurring on chromosome number:
These chromosomal anomalies in fibroid occur on chromosome number 7.
Fibroids show a positive familial predisposition.
The effect of menopause on a fibroid is:
Fibroids regress after menopause, consistent with their estrogen/progesterone dependence.
The effect of OCPs on the SIZE of a fibroid is:
OCPs have no effect on fibroid size.
The effect of pregnancy on the SIZE of a fibroid is:
Pregnancy has no effect on fibroid size (though red degeneration can occur).
The most common TYPE of fibroid is:
Intramural fibroid (Type 4) is the most common type.
Regardless of final type, all fibroids begin as:
All fibroids begin as intramural fibroids, later evolving toward the endometrial or serosal surface.
The anatomical classification of UTERINE fibroids includes intramural (most common), submucosal, and:
Subserosal, along with intramural and submucosal, completes the uterine anatomical classification.
Among uterine fibroids, which is the MOST common subtype?
Intramural fibroid is the most common uterine subtype.
Just beneath the endometrium, projecting into the uterine cavity
A submucosal fibroid lies just beneath the endometrium, projecting into the cavity.
Just beneath the serosa, projecting outward
A subserosal fibroid lies just beneath the serosa, projecting outward from the uterus.
Extra-uterine fibroids are anatomically classified as cervical and:
Broad ligament fibroids, along with cervical fibroids, comprise the extra-uterine classification.
An ANTERIOR cervical fibroid characteristically causes urinary symptoms by:
Compressing the urethra, causing urinary retention
Rubbing against and irritating the bladder, causing increased urinary frequency
An anterior cervical fibroid irritates the bladder, causing increased urinary frequency.
A POSTERIOR cervical fibroid characteristically causes urinary symptoms by:
Increasing pressure on the urethra, causing urinary retention
Irritating the bladder, causing increased frequency
A posterior cervical fibroid increases pressure on the urethra, causing urinary retention.
A broad ligament fibroid is classified as "TRUE" when:
An intrauterine fibroid grows into the broad ligament
The fibroid arises directly from the broad ligament
A true broad ligament fibroid arises directly from the broad ligament itself.
A broad ligament fibroid is classified as "PSEUDO" when:
The fibroid arises directly from the broad ligament
An intrauterine fibroid grows into the broad ligament
A pseudo broad ligament fibroid is actually an intrauterine fibroid that has grown into the broad ligament.
In a TRUE broad ligament fibroid, the ureter is characteristically located:
In a true broad ligament fibroid, the ureter runs lateral to the fibroid.
In a PSEUDO broad ligament fibroid, the ureter is characteristically located:
In a pseudo broad ligament fibroid, the ureter runs medial to the fibroid \u2014 an important distinction surgically.
In the FIGO classification of submucosal fibroids, Type 0 refers to a fibroid that is:
Type 0 is a submucosal fibroid totally inside the uterine cavity.
Type 0 submucosal fibroids are generally pedunculated.
In the FIGO classification, Type 1 submucosal fibroid refers to a fibroid that is:
Type 1 is \u226550% inside the uterine cavity.
In the FIGO classification, Type 2 submucosal fibroid refers to a fibroid that is:
Type 2 is <50% inside the uterine cavity.
Per FIGO significance, Type 0 and Type 1 submucosal fibroids are best removed via:
Type 0 and Type 1 fibroids, being predominantly intracavitary, are removed hysteroscopically.
Per FIGO significance, Type 2 fibroids and beyond are best removed via:
No surgical removal is ever needed
Type 2 and beyond, being predominantly intramural, are removed via laparoscopy.
The most common presentation of fibroid overall is:
Fibroid is most commonly asymptomatic overall.
Among symptomatic presentations, the most common symptom of fibroid is:
HMB is the most common symptom among symptomatic fibroid cases.
Causes of HMB in fibroid include increased surface area of endometrium, increased uterine vascularity (due to increased estrogen), and interference with uterine contractility, along with:
Ulceration of a submucosal fibroid is another recognised cause of HMB.
The fibroid type most commonly causing HMB is:
Submucosal fibroid is the type most commonly causing HMB, given its direct endometrial contact.
Fibroid-related subfertility can occur due to impaired gamete transport, resulting from impaired tubal motility and:
Impaired uterine contractility, along with impaired tubal motility, causes impaired gamete transport in fibroid.
Fibroid can also cause subfertility by interfering with implantation, due to:
Distortion of the uterine cavity interferes with implantation in fibroid-related subfertility.
Another mechanism of fibroid-related subfertility is:
Displacement of the cervix away from the vaginal pool of semen
Blockage of the fallopian tube lumen in all cases
Cervical displacement away from the seminal pool is a mechanical cause of subfertility in fibroid.
The fibroid type most commonly causing subfertility is:
Submucosal fibroid is the type most commonly causing subfertility.
Associated with severe dysmenorrhoea in all cases
Associated with dyspareunia in all cases
If a fibroid does cause pain, it typically presents as:
Severe colicky pain radiating to the back
When painful, fibroid typically presents with pelvic pressure/pain.
Acute abdominal pain with fibroids is caused by torsion or:
Torsion or red degeneration of the fibroid causes acute abdominal pain.
Urinary pressure symptoms with fibroid are typically seen with:
Cervical fibroid typically produces urinary pressure symptoms.
Rectal pressure symptoms with fibroid are typically (and rarely) seen with:
A post-cervical fibroid rarely produces rectal pressure symptoms.
Endocrine symptoms recognised with fibroid include polycythaemia, hypercalcemia, and:
Increased prolactin levels, along with polycythaemia and hypercalcemia, are recognised endocrine effects of fibroid.
Pseudo Meig\u2019s syndrome, in the context of fibroid, consists of a pedunculated fibroid, right-sided pleural effusion, and:
Pseudo Meig\u2019s syndrome is the triad of pedunculated fibroid, right-sided pleural effusion, and ascites.
Pseudo Meig\u2019s syndrome, due to its presentation, mimics:
This triad mimics a malignant ovarian tumour, making the distinction clinically important.
Pseudo Meig\u2019s syndrome resolves spontaneously following:
Myomectomy leads to spontaneous resolution of pseudo Meig\u2019s syndrome.
A symptom specifically NOT seen with fibroid is:
Amenorrhoea is specifically noted as NOT being a feature of fibroid.
Recognised pregnancy complications with fibroid include preterm labor, IUGR, and:
Abruptio placentae, along with preterm labor and IUGR, is a recognised pregnancy complication with fibroid.
Additional pregnancy complications with fibroid include malpresentation, PPH, and:
Subinvolution, along with malpresentation and PPH, is a further pregnancy complication with fibroid.
In a fibroid, the MOST vascular part is the:
The periphery of a fibroid is its most vascular part.
In a fibroid, the LEAST vascular part is the:
The centre of a fibroid is its least vascular part.
Given this vascular pattern, degeneration of a fibroid begins from:
Degeneration begins from the centre, the least vascular part of the fibroid.
The MOST COMMON degeneration of fibroid is:
Hyaline degeneration is the most common degeneration of fibroid.
Homogeneous appearance of the fibroid, with loss of the whorled appearance
Hyaline degeneration produces a homogeneous appearance, with loss of the normal whorled pattern.
Calcareous degeneration is most commonly seen in:
Calcareous degeneration is most commonly seen in subserosal fibroid.
Calcareous degeneration begins from the periphery, unlike the typical centre-outward pattern.
On X-ray, calcareous degeneration shows a characteristic:
Calcareous degeneration shows a popcorn calcification/womb stone appearance on X-ray.
Sarcomatous degeneration is the least common degeneration of fibroid, at <0.5%.
Sarcomatous degeneration is most commonly seen in:
Sarcomatous degeneration is most commonly seen in intramural fibroid.
Clinically, sarcomatous degeneration is suspected in a peri/postmenopausal female with:

u: PK vs PD: The Two Definitions

Pharmacokinetics is the study of a drug's movement through the body after intake by any route; pharmacodynamics is the change the drug induces in the body. The figure flags absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion as the kinetic processes, and the drug, its binding to the target and the resulting effect as the dynamic events.

An oral drug is absorbed into the systemic circulation and may be distributed to adipose tissue — some drugs by redistribution. Adipose-seeking drugs are very short acting, highly lipid soluble and cross the BBB, like the anaesthetics propofol and thiopentone.

The circulating drug binds its target — most drugs bind reversibly — and the effect follows; breakdown of the bond frees the drug back into the circulation. The liver then breaks the remaining drug down to a water-soluble form, which is excreted mostly via the kidney and partly via the gut.
Four Ways Across the Biological Membrane

A drug in the intestinal lumen must cross the biological membrane to reach blood. The diagram draws four mechanisms — filtration, simple/passive diffusion (the most common), facilitated diffusion and active transport — with the first three bracketed as ATP-independent and only active transport needing ATP. The legend uses a Y for carrier and a triangle for drug.
Filtration & Simple Diffusion: The ATP-Free Routes

Filtration pushes the drug through membrane pores (example: subcutaneous insulin) with no ATP; simple/passive diffusion is the commonest mechanism of absorption and moves drug along its concentration gradient, straight through the lipid membrane rather than a pore. Neither uses a carrier and neither burns ATP.

Facilitated diffusion (GLUT receptors) uses a carrier but still runs along the gradient with no ATP, and GLUT absorption is gradient-based. Active transport (SGLT receptors) needs ATP and is independent of the gradient — SGLT1 sits on the small intestine and SGLT2 on the renal tubules. Together these two form 'carrier mediated transport'.

P-glycoprotein — the most common ABC pump, also called MDR1 — is an ATP-driven efflux pump. In the small intestine/liver most drugs cross the epithelial cell along the concentration gradient, but some are pumped back into the intestinal lumen, producing first-pass metabolism: the drug is excreted before it ever reaches the systemic circulation.

Efflux matters clinically: digoxin dosage is calculated on the amount lost to efflux. MDR1 pumps sit at the blood-brain barrier, so the opioid antidiarrhoeal loperamide acts on the GIT but cannot enter the brain; water solubility is another reason drugs stay out of the CNS. Placental MDR1 pumps protect the fetus, and hepatocyte MDR1 pumps drive bile acid excretion.
Pgp-Driven Resistance in Bacteria & Tumour Cells

The flowchart is short and ruthless: a bacterial or tumour cell develops a Pgp pump, the pump effluxes the drug, and the cell becomes resistant — the same pump that handles normal drugs becomes the engine of treatment failure.

Three columns summarise Pgp pharmacology: substrates (loperamide, cyclosporine, digoxin) are pumped out; inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital — like enzyme inducers) raise pump numbers and cause drug failure; inhibitors (verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, cyclosporine, itraconazole, neratinib, erythromycin/clarithromycin) lower pump numbers and cause drug toxicity. Cyclosporine is both substrate and inhibitor.
Effects of Pgp Blockade: The Interaction Table

The blockade table is pure exam gold: rifampicin → digoxin failure, clarithromycin → digoxin toxicity, cyclosporine → cholestatic jaundice, verapamil → reversal of drug resistance in cancer and bacteria, and quinidine → loperamide-induced central side effects. Each entry is a clinical interaction driven by the efflux pump.

Passive diffusion obeys one rule: lipid-soluble wins. A non-polar, unionised, neutral drug diffuses across the lipid membrane and is absorbed; a polar, ionised or charged drug is repelled by the charged membrane proteins, is lipid insoluble/water soluble, is not absorbed and is finally excreted.
The Criteria Table: LUNA for Absorption, WIPE for Excretion

One table decides everything: to be absorbed a drug must be lipid soluble, unionised, non-polar with the medium's pH equal to the drug's, and to be excreted it must be water soluble, ionised, polar with the pH of drug and medium unequal. The mnemonics are LUNA for absorption and WIPE for excretion.
Acidic in Acid, Basic in Base — and the Duodenum Rule

An acidic drug (aspirin) is unionised in the acidic stomach and a basic drug in the basic small intestine. Yet the unionised drug is maximally absorbed in the small intestine — duodenum — simply because of its enormous surface area, which beats the stomach's favourable pH.
Short Bowel Syndrome: Lose the Gut, Lose the Drug

Resection of the small intestine reduces drug absorption, so an oral drug may fail. Management is to increase the dose or change the route — a direct clinical application of surface-area-driven absorption.
Ion Trapping: Alkalinise for Acid, Acidify for Base

Excretion needs the drug ionised, hence the pH of drug and medium must differ. Acidic drug toxicity (aspirin, phenobarbital, methotrexate) is treated by alkalinising urine with bicarbonate; basic drug toxicity (amphetamine) by acidifying urine with ammonium chloride — vitamin C and cranberry juice are other urine acidifiers. Ionised drug is trapped and excreted.

For an acidic drug log [U]/[I] = pKa − pH; for a basic drug the ratio is inverted as log [I]/[U] = pKa − pH. pKa is the pH at which half the drug is ionised. An acidic drug of pKa 4 in gastric pH 2 gives a ratio of 100 — 99% unionised and 1% ionised, which is why absorption can occur.
IR, SR and CR: Three Shapes of a Release Curve

A tablet is either immediate release (IR) or extended release (ER), and ER splits into sustained release (SR) and controlled release (CR), the latter also called zero order CR. IR gives repeated sharp peaks with frequent dosing (indomethacin TID) and poor compliance; SR uses a polymer coating for a shorter peak and longer duration; CR coats the pores to give a flat plateau.
Bypassing the Stomach: Delayed Release & Enteric Coating

Two tricks avoid the stomach: delayed release, which delivers the drug to the small intestine (sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis), and enteric coating, which shields an acid-labile drug from gastric HCl (PPIs). One moves the release site, the other protects the drug.
Bioavailability: Definition, Factors and the AUC Formula

Bioavailability is the fraction of drug reaching the systemic circulation unchanged. From 100% intestinal absorption, a fraction is excreted and a fraction undergoes hepatic first pass metabolism, leaving only the rest in circulation. F = AUCoral/AUCiv × 100; AUC is the extent of absorption, and IV is the only route with 100% bioavailability.
IV bioavailability is 1, im/sc 0.75–1.0, and oral the widest range of 0.05–1.0 because first pass metabolism varies by drug. Remember the note: F tells you the extent, never the rate, of absorption.

On a plasma concentration-time curve, Cmax is the highest concentration achieved and Tmax is the time at which it occurs. Tmax is the marker of the rate of absorption, while AUC gives the extent — two different questions answered by two different parameters.
Bioequivalence: Branded, Generic, ANDA & the ±20% Rule

Bioequivalence means two pharmaceutically equivalent products with similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption. The branded drug is invented and patented for 20 years; the generic is a legal copy marketed after patent expiry, cheaper, approved through ANDA provided it is bioequivalent to the branded drug within ±20%.

AVD is the hypothetical volume of plasma in litres needed to account for all the drug in the body, intravascular and extravascular. A drug with a high AVD sits mainly in tissue; one with a low AVD stays in the systemic circulation. That is why it is only an 'apparent' volume.
AVD and the Loading Dose Formulas

AVD = D/C0 × f, where C0 is the initial plasma concentration and f is bioavailability (f = 1 for the IV route). Rearranged for practice, loading dose D = AVD × CT/f, so D ∝ AVD/f: a larger volume of distribution or lower bioavailability demands a bigger loading dose to hit the target concentration.
What Determines the Volume of Distribution?

Fat content drives vd: obesity raises it, athletes lower it, and women have more than men because of higher fat content. Lipid solubility raises vd, albumin binding lowers it (binding ∝ 1/vd) and tissue binding raises it. The drug's own chemistry and the patient's body composition both matter.
Digoxin: Distributed to Muscle, Dosed on Lean Mass

Digoxin leaves plasma for skeletal muscle, which outweighs the heart even though the heart is the target organ. Consequently digoxin's loading dose is calculated from lean body mass, not total body mass — dosing an obese patient on total weight overshoots.
High AVD = Dialysis Is a Waste of Time

With a very high vd the extravascular concentration is high and intravascular concentration is low, so dialysis can clear almost none of the drug — it is ineffective. Antidotes, not dialysis, are the treatment of poisoning by such drugs.
BADDOC: Drugs With High vd, and Their Antidotes

Remember BADDOC — Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, Opioids, Calcium channel blockers (with organophosphates alongside). These are not cleared by dialysis, so each has a specific antidote: flumazenil, glucagon (raises cAMP), ammonium chloride, digibind, naloxone, calcium gluconate and atropine.
Albumin vs α1 Acid Glycoprotein: Who Binds What

Albumin is the commonest plasma protein and binds acidic drugs — antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, warfarin and aspirin. α1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs — tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics such as beta blockers, amiodarone and lidocaine.
Displacement: Why Warfarin Plus Aspirin Bleeds

Warfarin and aspirin are both albumin bound. Given together they displace each other, each raising the other's plasma concentration of free drug — and the clinical result written in the margin is increased bleeding.
