Low Albumin Causes Toxicity, High AGP Causes Failure

A fall in albumin leaves more free drug and so more toxicity; a rise in α1 acid glycoprotein binds more drug and so lowers free drug and effect. The same principle explains why heavily albumin-bound drugs have a low volume of distribution — they stay in the plasma.
Clinical Applications: Nephrotic, Cirrhotic, Inflamed, Infarcted

Albumin falls in nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus — predict toxicity of albumin-bound drugs. α1 glycoprotein rises in inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease) and myocardial infarction — predict reduced free drug and reduced effect, as with lidocaine in MI.
Phase I and Phase II Metabolism: Two Steps to Excretion

Phase I breaks the drug down to yield a functional group, activating a prodrug or inactivating an active drug; Phase II then conjugates that group with a negatively charged moiety, making the drug ionized, water soluble and easily excreted. Placebo, by contrast, contains no drug at all.

Prodrugs are inactive as given and require metabolism for activation: proguanil, ramipril and other ACE inhibitors (except captopril and lisinopril), oxcarbazepine, omeprazole, dipivefrine, levodopa, racecadotril, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. Knowing the exceptions and the drug classes is what makes this list clinically usable.
Phase I Reactions (ORCHAD) and Phase II Conjugations

Phase I reactions follow ORCHAD — Oxidation (m/c), Reduction, Cyclization, Hydrolysis, Aliphatic and Aromatic hydroxylation, Deamination — all enabled by microsomal CYP450 enzymes. Phase II reactions are named after the conjugate added; glucuronidation is the most common and the only microsomal one, while glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation are non-microsomal.
CYP450 Nomenclature and the Enzyme Group

Cytochrome is a haem protein that binds oxygen and facilitates metabolism; the 450 refers to the 450 nm light absorbed by these enzymes first found in plant pigment. In CYP1A2 the number denotes the family, the letter the subfamily and the final number the geneisoform.
Substrate Map of the CYP Isoforms

CYP1A2 handles paracetamol, tacrine and theophylline; CYP2B6 handles 6-mercaptopurine and methyldopa; CYP2C9 handles phenytoin and warfarin. CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole but activates clopidogrel, and the two compete, so omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel; CYP2D6 metabolises psychiatric drugs, opioids and β-blockers and activates tamoxifen.
Ethanol, Paracetamol and the CYP3A4 Rule

Chronic ethanol consumption upregulates CYP2E1, which metabolises paracetamol far more than CYP1A2 does, so more NAPQI is generated and hepatotoxicity follows. CYP3A4 is the most common isoform, metabolising more than 50% of drugs — mifepristone being the quoted example.

Glucuronidation handles atazanavir, which can cause Steven Johnson syndrome, and irinotecan, which causes toxicity. Because the pathway itself is deficient in Crigler Najjar syndrome, both drugs are contraindicated in that condition.
Estrogen, Enterohepatic Circulation and OCP Failure

Estrogen is metabolised in the liver by Phase I (CYP3A4) and Phase II glucuronidation to a water-soluble conjugate that enters the small intestine. There gut bacterial glucuronidase releases lipid-soluble estrogen, which is reabsorbed — enterohepatic circulation extending its normal T½. Antibiotics kill these bacteria, shorten the T½ and cause OCP failure.

Acetylation substrates follow the mnemonic HIPS Dance — Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide and Dapsone — and all of them can cause drug induced SLE, often with arthralgia, rash and a positive ANA.
Enzyme Inducers vs Inhibitors: The Interaction Table

Inducers raise enzyme amount, increase metabolism and lower plasma concentration producing drug failure; inhibitors do the reverse and produce toxicity. Inducers: griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, St. John's wort. Inhibitors: acute alcohol, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice, diethylcarbamazine.
Clinical Significance: OCP Failure, Theophylline and Statin Toxicity

When rifampicin causes OCP failure the options are to change the contraceptive method (IUD or condoms), avoid enzyme inducers, or increase the dose of the interacting drug as with phenytoin and retigabine. Inhibitor toxicity is shown by erythromycin causing theophylline toxicity with arrhythmia and fibrillation, and clarithromycin causing statin toxicity.
Excretion: The Drug That Leaves the Body

Only the ionised, water-soluble, polar drug is excreted. The major organs are the kidneys — the most common organ of excretion — and the liver, which is the most common organ of metabolism, while saliva and sweat handle small amounts.

Tubular secretion (80%) dominates over filtration (20%). Only unbound drug is filtered; protein-bound drug, because of the negative charge of the basement membrane, is not filtered but is still secreted. Filtration depends on GFR and therefore gives a constant rate of excretion, so kidney disease directly reduces it.
Rate of Drug Elimination and Clearance

Rate of drug elimination is the amount of drug eliminated per hour (mg/hr) and equals plasma concentration (mg/ml) × clearance (ml/hr). Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per hour, not an amount of drug.
Two Ways to Dose: Infusion and Intermittent
Drugs are dosed either by continuous IV infusion or intermittently. The infusion (dosing) rate is also called the loading dose, while the repeated intermittent dose is the maintenance dose.
The Concentration-Time Curve of an Infusion

The curve has three phases: I the slowly rising state where absorption exceeds excretion, II the steady state plateau where infusion rate equals the rate of drug elimination, and III the declining state where excretion exceeds absorption. Infusion rate = plasma concentration × clearance, 4–5 half-lives are needed to reach steady state, and the dose depends on volume of distribution.
Maintenance Dose and the Bioavailability Factor

The intermittent dose, a.k.a. maintenance dose, is given at intervals to hold plasma concentration in steady state and depends on clearance. Maintenance dose = PC × CL × Time / f, where f is bioavailability (f = 1 for IV routes), so oral doses must be larger when bioavailability is incomplete.
Half-Life, Volume of Distribution and Clearance

Half-life is the time taken for the plasma level to fall by 50% and is proportional to volume of distribution ÷ clearance: T1/2 = 0.693 × vd/Cl = 0.693/kel, while kel = Cl/vd. Rising vd or falling clearance (as in renal failure) prolongs the half-life.
Zero Order vs First Order Kinetics (Table)

Zero order eliminates a constant amount of drug per hour (n = 0, RDE = constant); first order eliminates a constant proportion per hour (n = 1, RDE ∝ PC) as expressed in RDE = (PC)^n × Cl. Most drugs follow first order.
What Happens When the Dose Is Increased

With increasing dose, zero order shows rising T1/2, falling clearance and a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration with risk of toxicity; first order keeps T1/2 and clearance constant and the plasma concentration rises proportionately.
Saturation of Elimination and Pseudozero Order

Zero order kinetics reflects early saturation of elimination, first order reflects late saturation. The exceptions are the key exam points: zero order drugs follow first order at lower doses until saturation and are hence called pseudozero order, while first order drugs switch to zero order at higher doses after saturation.
The Example List: Alcohol, Phenytoin and the Rest

Zero order drugs are alcohol (true zero order), theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin; first order kinetics applies to most drugs. This is why a small phenytoin increment can cause toxicity and why alcohol levels fall linearly at a fixed amount per hour.

A drug's tendency to bind its target is affinity; the maximum effect it produces is efficacy, and efficacy is the clinically most important property because it fixes the ceiling of benefit. Potency is a different matter - the relative dose needed for a given effect, so the lesser the dose, the greater the potency. A graded (quantified) response, such as a change in BP, HR or blood glucose, is studied in an individual.
Quantal DRC: ED50, TD50 and LD50

The quantal DRC records a binary, all-or-none response (sedation, fertility) in a population, plotting the percentage of responders against log dose. ED50 is the dose at which half the population gets a therapeutic effect and marks potency, while TD50 (toxic) and LD50 (lethal, in animals) mark toxicity; on the graph the therapeutic curve sits leftmost and the lethal curve furthest right.

The therapeutic index measures safety: TD50/ED50 in humans and LD50/ED50 in animals. A low index, as with lithium, means safety only within a narrow dosage range and a high chance of toxicity, whereas a high index allows a wide range. The therapeutic window is the corridor between the minimum effective concentration (0.6 meq/L for lithium) and the minimum toxic concentration (1.5 meq/L) - below it there is no effect and above it toxicity.
Graded DRC: Height, Position and Parallel Lines

On the graded DRC (response versus log dose in an individual) efficacy is read from the height of the curve and potency from its position - more to the left means more potent. In the figure, efficacy runs B > A > C and potency PA > PB > PC, so drug A is the most potent yet B the most efficacious. Affinity is comparable only between drugs of the same MOA and only between parallel lines, which is why C is excluded and the order is A > B.
Full, Partial, Antagonist, Inverse: The Table

The interaction table grades four behaviours: a full agonist gives a maximum effect (+1 intrinsic efficacy), a partial agonist a submaximal effect (between 1 and 0), an antagonist no effect (0) and an inverse agonist an effect opposite to the receptor's nature (-1). Against endogenous full agonists these translate into mild, moderate and severe antagonism respectively. On the figure, A rises to maximal, B plateaus submaximally, C stays flat and D dips below the no-effect line.
Clinical Reading of Agonists and Antagonists

The single most useful clinical fact from this table is its footnote: antagonists are the most commonly used drugs, even though they exert no effect of their own. Adding a partial agonist to a patient already on a full agonist yields only mild antagonism, because a partial agonist can never match a full agonist's maximal response.

Antagonism is classified by mechanism, not by receptor: physical antagonism binds the substance (charcoal adsorbs alcohol from the intestine), chemical antagonism binds and neutralises it (heparin, an acid/-ve, is neutralised by protamine sulphate, a base/+ve; iron is chelated by dexrazoxane or deferiprone), and physiological antagonism uses opposite receptors - histamine via H1 constricts bronchi while adrenaline/salbutamol via β2 dilate them. Salbutamol is the best bronchodilator in asthma, but in COPD ipratropium or tiotropium is preferred instead because of cholinergic effects.
Competitive Reversible vs Irreversible and Non-competitive Antagonism

The table follows drug (A) through three rows: its normal effect, the addition of antagonist (B), and the effect of raising (A). In competitive reversible antagonism (A) and (B) compete for the same (enzymatic) site, so raising (A) restores the effect, Km rises, potency falls and Vmax/efficacy is unchanged. In competitive irreversible and non-competitive antagonism (B) occupies the allosteric part, raising (A) gives 'no reversal of antagonism', Vmax falls while Km and potency show no change.

The Michaelis-Menten equation is used to read the same table numerically: Vmax is the maximum velocity of the reaction between enzyme and drug (substrate) and stands for maximum effect, i.e. efficacy; Km is the concentration of drug at which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax and is proportional to 1/potency. So a competitive antagonist raises Km (potency falls) with Vmax untouched, while a non-competitive antagonist lowers Vmax with Km unchanged.
Receptors: Ligand Gated Ion Channel Receptors

Receptors begin with the fastest acting type, the ligand gated ion channel receptors (LGICR). Their examples are tabulated by substrate: GABA-A conducts chloride, glutamate has the NMDA, AMPA and kainate subtypes, while the nicotinic receptor and 5-HT3 are listed with a dash. The note to remember is that GABA-B is a GPCR, not an ion channel.

The nicotinic receptor is a pentamer of α, α, β, δ and ε subunits surrounding a lumen through which Na+ enters. Acetylcholine acts on the α subunit to open the channel, which is why the α subunit is marked most important in a receptor. Functionally, the same receptor gives contraction on muscle and depolarisation on a ganglion.

An enzymatic receptor carries an intracellular enzymatic domain; the ligand binds the receptor and the enzyme acts, the classic example being tyrosine kinase, where phosphorylation of tyrosine leads to cell proliferation. The four tabulated types are tyrosine kinase receptors (EGFR, VEGF-R, Her-2/neu R, insulin/IGF R), Janus kinase receptors (leptin/cytokine, prolactin, growth hormone), STKR (TGFR) and the guanylate cyclase receptor (ANP, BNP → ↑ cGMP → vasodilation).

Nuclear receptors are the slowest acting receptors because they work on gene transcription. Some already sit in the nucleus - estrogen, progesterone, vitamin A, T3/T4 and PPAR (α, δ, γ) receptors - while others (androgen, mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid and vitamin D receptors) wait in the cytoplasm and translocate to the nucleus only upon ligand binding.

GPCRs - also called serpentine, 7 transmembrane or heptahelical receptors - are the most common target for drugs. The α subunit is the most important and carries intrinsic GTPase activity; activation exchanges GDP for GTP and hydrolysis of GTP switches the signal off. GPCRs are classified by their α subtypes: s → Gs, q → Gq and i → Gi.

Gs signals through αs-GTP to activate adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which phosphodiesterase then metabolises. In cardiac and skeletal muscle cAMP causes contraction through calcium channel phosphorylation, while in smooth muscle it causes relaxation (myosin light chain phosphorylase activation and myosin light chain kinase inhibition) giving bronchodilation, vasodilation and uterine relaxation - the basis for ritodrine in labor, dobutamine in CHF and salbutamol in asthma (palpitations and tremors). Theophylline blocks phosphodiesterase 3, 4 in bronchi and milrinone blocks phosphodiesterase 3 in the heart, both used when β-blockers have already been given.

Gq works through αq-GTP to activate phospholipase C, which raises PIP2 and splits it into IP3 (a secondary messenger) and DAG. IP3 binds a receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, releasing Ca2+ and causing smooth muscle constriction - the pathway behind oxytocin, angiotensin and vasopressin 1 receptor effects, with α1, M1 and M2 as the feeding receptors. A separate note records that phospholipase A2 is responsible for the synthesis of prostaglandins.

Gi is present in the heart, where it lowers heart rate. Its receptors - M2, α2, H3 and 5HT1 - are autoreceptors. The αi-GTP limb lowers cyclic AMP while the Go limb (β, γ) lowers Ca2+; both converge on opening K+ channels and so produce relaxation.

G12/13 signals through Rho-GTP, which activates Rho-kinase and produces smooth muscle contraction, vasoconstriction and trabecular meshwork contraction. Three Rho-kinase inhibitors are shown: belumosudil, a new drug for graft versus host disease (RHO kinase is involved in leukocytosis), fasudil for vasodilation in angina, and netarsudil, which increases trabecular outflow and is used in open-angle glaucoma.

Indian drug schedules are read off the label: Schedule G carries the caution that the preparation is dangerous except under medical supervision and covers majority drugs such as antihypertensives and antidiabetics; Schedule H needs a registered practitioner's prescription, with Rx (in black) reusable on the same prescription and NRx (in red) for narcotics like codeine and benzodiazepines, issued once to avoid abuse potential; Schedule H1 (introduced in 2013) shows Rx in red and covers antibiotics against resistance; Schedule X shows XRx in red for narcotic/psychotropic drugs (amphetamine, methylphenidate, ketamine, pentobarbital) needing special licence and a register with prescription copy kept 2 years. Schedule P concerns expiry period, Schedule W generic-name marketing and Schedule Y clinical trials, import and manufacture of new drugs.

Pregnancy categories are ranked by safety A > B > C. Category A has risk absent to the fetus with maximum safety; B lacks human studies but is absent in animals and is safely prescribed; C has no human data with positive teratogenicity in animals; D and X are positive teratogenic in humans, D being used if benefit > risk (valproate in JME) and X being absolutely contraindicated (thalidomide).

Nine drug types are listed: prescription/legend (schedule H), OTC (anything other than schedule G, H, X), orphan drugs for rare diseases with low availability, street/illicit drugs of abuse (cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine), spurious drugs (imitating another drug's name or failing the intended purpose), misbranded drugs (false label information), adulterated drugs (unwanted substance), prototype drugs - the parental/most used drug of a group, e.g. morphine for opioids - and P (personal) drugs chosen on STEP criteria: safety, tolerability, efficacy and price. An orphan receptor is a receptor without a known ligand.

Development starts with non-mandatory preclinical trials in animals, which must be completed before the mandatory human phases I-IV. Preclinical steps are: draft a protocol describing the expectation of the drug and information on animals, submit it to the Animal Ethical Committee (AEC), get permission approved, then conduct the PCT under CPCSEA guidelines. The flow chart then enters clinical trials in humans, phase I being done in normal healthy individuals and later phases in patients.

A clinical trial opens with prerequisites: draft a protocol, submit it to the Human Ethical Committee, obtain approval, then conduct it under GCP (Good Clinical Practice) guidelines. Phase 0 is microdosing with 100 mcg or 1/100th of the normal dose as a radioligand-bound drug in normal healthy volunteers to determine pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics; if normal the trial moves to phase I, if abnormal (toxicity/efficacy) the trial is aborted.

The mandatory phases table compares the four phases: phase I (human pharmacology and toxicity study) determines toxicity, maximum tolerable dose, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in 30-100 normal healthy volunteers over 1-2 years in an open design; phase II (therapeutic exploratory trial) determines efficacy in 100-500 patients over 2-3 years by randomized control trial at a unicentric centre, and carries the maximum failure rate; phase III (therapeutic confirmatory trial) confirms efficacy in 500-3000 patients over 3-5 years by RCT/RUCT at multicentric centres; phase IV (postmarketing surveillance) looks for long term/rare ADRs in many thousands of patients in an open design. For toxic drugs such as anti-HIV and anticancer agents phases I and II are done simultaneously in patients, blinded designs are preferred over open in phases II-III, and all multicentric studies are phase III irrespective of population size.
Approval in Phase III and Phase V

The approval pathway runs from IND (Investigational New Drug) through confirming efficacy and safety for use, to a New Drug Application (NDA) submitted to CDSCO - Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation - in New Delhi, and ends with approval of the drug. Phase V is pharmacoepidemiology: its aim is to validate the toxicity claimed in phase IV using epidemiological studies, namely case control or cohort studies.

An ADR is an appreciably harmful reaction to a drug used for treatment or prophylaxis; management is treatment of the reaction plus prevention of future exposure, and an idiosyncratic ADR is genetic in origin. The types are remembered by ABCDEFG - Augmented (dose-dependent, e.g. captopril hypotension), Bizarre (dose-independent, e.g. hypersensitivity), Chronic (dose and duration dependent, e.g. steroid-induced hypothalamo-pituitary suppression), Delayed (seen after cessation, e.g. teratogenicity), End of use (withdrawal, e.g. opioid/clonidine) and Failure (e.g. rifampicin causing OCP failure).

Four hypersensitivity types are shown: type I anaphylaxis, type II hemolysis, type III drug-induced SLE (from drugs metabolised by acetylation such as isoniazid and procainamide) and type IV Steven-Johnson syndrome (carbamazepine, lamotrigine). The closing note maps lepra reactions: type 1 lepra reaction is type IV and type 2 is type III hypersensitivity.

Pharmacovigilance aims to maintain drug safety and runs under the Pharmacovigilance Program of India (PvPI), co-ordinated by the NCC at the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad (UP); it is similar to phase 4 clinical trials by pharmaceutical companies. VigiFlow is the software used at hospitals and medical colleges to report ADRs; the NCC processes them into a conclusive ADR report, sent to CDSCO, which may ban the drug and inform doctors and patients and also informs the international pharmacovigilance centre - the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC) in Uppsala, Sweden - whose Vigibase, the largest pharmacovigilance database, informs countries worldwide.

TDM rests on the principle that plasma concentration of a drug correlates well with its effect and side-effects. Indications are: non-quantifiable clinical effect (drugs with quantifiable effects like oral hypoglycemics and β blockers are excluded), low therapeutic index (aminoglycosides, anti-epileptics, tacrolimus, digoxin, anti-psychotics, lithium, theophylline), variable metabolism such as acetylation, checking compliance (anti-psychotics) and preventing damage to organ or fetus - e.g. an aminoglycoside for pseudomonas in renal failure, or valproate in pregnancy with folic acid 400 mcg/day without a history of NTD and 4000 mcg/day with it. TDM is determined only after steady state concentration is reached.

Pharmacogenetics/pharmacogenomics studies the effect of genetics or genome on drug action - genetics being based on DNA polymorphism and genomics on chromosomal changes. Genes code for enzymes and receptors, and the strength of these genes decides whether the response is toxic, strong, normal, weak or a failure. The acetylation example shows NAT1 individuals are fast acetylators and NAT2 individuals slow acetylators: high INH in slow acetylators causes hepatotoxicity while high INHA in fast acetylators causes neuropathy.

Malignant hyperthermia is due to RyR (ryanodine receptor) gene polymorphism and is triggered by succinylcholine, lidocaine and halothane, with dantrolene used for treatment. Increased expression of the gene raises RyR stimulation, releasing Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; ATP is then used for calcium reuptake and heat is released - the hyperthermia.

G-6-PD deficiency leads to hemolysis through the HMP shunt. The drugs to remember are glyburide, glibenclamide, sulfonamides, primaquine and tafenoquine (anti-malarials), dapsone, dabrafenib, menadione (vitamin K), methylene blue, anti-gout medication (pegloticase, rasburicase), nalidixic acid and nitrofurantoin.

CYP polymorphism explains several therapeutic failures: low action of CYP2C19 reduces activation of clopidogrel so MI develops despite medication; CYP2C9 with VKORC1 polymorphism gives a variable warfarin effect; and CYP2D6 polymorphism reduces drug effect - the reduced metabolism of psychiatric drugs causes toxicity, while reduced activation of tamoxifen lowers endoxifen levels and the drug fails.

Two further examples complete the page. Succinylcholine given with atypical pseudocholinesterase causes prolonged apnoea. A reduced effect of thiopurine methyl-transferase decreases metabolism of 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine, leading to increased toxicity.

The chapter opens with definitions. Pharmacology is the study of structure, effect (MOA), side effects and contraindications of drugs; pharmacotherapeutics is the study of a drug in service of disease (dose, route and response); pharmacognosy is the study of drugs derived from plants; chemotherapy is the use of drugs in cancer and infection; and pharmacy deals with compounding - mixing of drugs, now obsolete - and dispensing of drugs, with barcoding used to dispense the right drug and avoid errors. A drug is a chemical with a known structure that alters the pathophysiology for therapeutic gain.

Drugs come from four sources: natural (plants - quinine, digoxin, morphine from the poppy plant; animal peptides - insulin and heparin from porcine mucosa; microorganisms - antibiotics), semisynthetic or modified natural chemicals (apomorphine, a dopamine agonist used in parkinsonism), synthetic drugs made by rational drug designing - designed complementary to a receptor, binding and inhibiting, resulting in modification of the disease - and genetic engineering, the process of introducing a gene in a cell line to obtain a product, e.g. human insulin (gene) giving regular insulin (peptide).

Drugs carry a chemical name (long, based on structure), a generic/non proprietary name (abbreviated, e.g. propranolol, with tell-tale suffixes: -lol for β blockers, -pril for ACE inhibitors, -prazole for PPIs) and a branded/proprietary name given by the manufacturer. A compendium is a book of comprehensive organised drug information: the Indian Pharmacopoeia is made by pharmacists, covers structure, storage and purity, and is used by drug manufacturers and regulatory authorities, whereas the drug formulary is made by doctors, covers usage, mechanism of action, side effects and contraindications, and is used by doctors for prescribing. The note to remember is that a prescription must contain generic names.
Routes of Drug Administration: Local Drugs

Local drugs act at the site of application, increasing the effect of the drug while decreasing systemic side effects. Topically they are applied to skin (steroid antibiotics), mucous membrane (bladder cancer drugs) and eye (drugs used in glaucoma).

Intrathecal injection puts the drug into CSF by injection into the subarachnoid space by lumbar puncture; its uses are to bypass the blood-brain barrier (aminoglycosides in meningitis), and to give a local effect on brain/spinal cord with lidocaine and bupivacaine for lumbosacral anesthesia, methotrexate in CNS leukemia, and baclofen in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis - planted in the subarachnoid space, it releases muscle relaxant periodically. Intraarticular injection is exemplified by steroids in rheumatoid arthritis, while the intraarterial route goes directly into the artery supplying the organ, avoiding systemic circulation, and is used for head & neck cancer and hepatocellular cancer.
Enteral Routes: Oral, Rectal and Sublingual

Among enteral routes the oral route is the most common, being cost effective, convenient and safest, but it has maximum first pass metabolism (100% to the portal vein), the most variable absorption (difference in lipid solubility, food, intake, HCl) and poor absorption of large molecules like proteins; lipid soluble and small molecule drugs are used orally. The rectal route acts faster with 50% less first pass metabolism (50% portal vein, 50% IVC) but is inconvenient - diazepam is given rectally in children for febrile seizures, with midazolam preferred. Sublingual drugs are absorbed under the tongue into the SVC and then the heart, giving no first pass metabolism and fast cardiac effects (NTG is spat out after the desired result, since further absorption causes postural hypotension); disadvantages are cardiac side effects and teeth discolouration, and the drugs used are nitroglycerin, ergotamine, nifedipine (rapidly lowers BP compared with oral) and buprenorphine. Proteins are recognised by names ending in 'tide', 'mab' or 'ase'.

Parenteral routes: intravenous is the fastest, used in emergency, allows large volume and gives 100% bioavailability, but oily medium causes hemolysis and epinephrine is better intramuscular (IV causes ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest) - nicardipine is used in hypertensive emergency and furosemide in pulmonary edema. Intramuscular is self injectable with right expertise, risks infection through unsanitary or faulty techniques, and suits peptides, irritants and oily drugs (pain). Subcutaneous gives long duration of action from slow absorption from S.C. fat and is self injectable, but irritants cause skin necrosis; long acting insulin is given this way. Intranasal spray gives rapid effect and bypasses the BBB but only a limited dose of potent drugs can be given (GnRH agonist, sumatriptan, nicotine). The inhalational route has the fastest effect because the lung is highly vascularized; irritants cause cough. Afrezza is the fastest and shortest acting insulin, and inhalational gases have 100% bioavailability, while salbutamol, ipratropium and tobramycin (pseudomonas pneumonia) are given for a local effect.
Introduction to ANS: Components and Anatomy

The ANS has two components, parasympathetic and sympathetic, and is located in the neuraxis (brain + spinal cord). The parasympathetic is the cranio-sacral part - cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X from the brain stem plus the sacral outflow - while the sympathetic is the thoraco-lumbar part. Both use a two-neuron pathway: action potential travels along the 1st neuron to a ganglion (a collection of neuronal bodies) and then along the 2nd neuron to the organ, such as the pupil or the CVS (blood vessel, heart).
Physiology of Action Potential: Propagation Across a Neuronal Synapse

An action potential depolarises the presynaptic neuron, opening voltage gated Ca2+ channels; the resulting Ca2+ influx causes fusion of the vesicular and presynaptic membranes with exocytosis of neurotransmitter, which binds the post synaptic receptor. This opens Na+ channels, Na+ influx follows, and the post synaptic neuron depolarises to generate its own action potential. Neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles in the presynaptic terminal.

Parasympathetic outflow is cranio-sacral with ganglia near the site of action; sympathetic outflow is thoraco-lumbar with ganglia away from the site of action (pre/para vertebral). Both use nicotinic (Nn) ganglionic receptors that are sodium ion channels. Post-ganglionic parasympathetic receptors are muscarinic/nicotinic with acetylcholine as the transmitter throughout; sympathetic post-ganglionic receptors are α/β with norepinephrine, plus dopamine on renal blood vessels (D1 → vasodilatation → diuresis) and Ach at adrenals and sweat glands. Note: parasympatholytics (atropine, datura) block m3 on sweat glands causing absent sweating and hyperthermia, whereas sympatholytics have no action there. Drugs may act directly (binding the receptor) or indirectly (acting on the neurotransmitter).

ACh is synthesised from acetyl Co-A and choline by choline acetyl transferase, with choline reuptake as the rate limiting step and food as a minor source of choline. It enters the vesicle and is released; β-bungarotoxin blocks entry into the vesicle, botulinum toxin blocks vesicle release and aminoglycosides block Ca2+ influx. Released ACh acts on muscarinic and nicotinic receptors and is metabolised rapidly by acetylcholinesterase (AChE), which breaks ACh into acetate and choline. AChE has an esteratic site (breaks ester bonds) and a negatively charged anionic site, and the choline released is positively charged and reuptaken.
Clinical Significance: Nm Receptor Action and Uses of Botulinum

At the Nm receptor, aminoglycosides reduce muscular contraction by lowering ACh and cause neuromuscular toxicity treated with Ca2+ as DOC. Respiratory failure is the common end point of krait bite (β-bungarotoxin), myasthenia crisis, cobra toxin and food poisoning with botulism (which also causes floppy infant syndrome), and its management is ventilation. Botulinum toxin is used in tardive dyskinesia (torticollis/cervical dystonia, injected into the SCM), urge incontinence/overactive bladder, cosmetically for glabellar lines, for unrelaxed lower esophageal sphincter causing achalasia, and for migraine prophylaxis by reducing CGRP release.

Cholinergic receptors are of two types: muscarinic (m), which are GPCRs, and nicotinic (N), which are Na+ ion channels. Nicotinic muscular (Nm) receptors at the neuromuscular junction produce muscle contraction; nicotinic neuronal (Nn) receptors at adrenal glands raise medullary norepinephrine, then cortisol from the cortex and finally epinephrine released into plasma, at ganglia generate action potential, and in the CNS cause stimulation. In myasthenia gravis anti-ACh antibodies block Nm and decrease muscle contraction, giving fatigue, ptosis and respiratory failure (crisis).

Muscarinic receptors split by G protein: m1 and m3 work through Gq → ↑ Ca2+, while m2/m4 work through Gi/o → relaxation. m1 in the CNS raises cognition and in the GIT raises HCl secretion. m3 causes GIT contraction, detrusor contraction in the bladder, bronchoconstriction, ↑ salivation, miosis (pupil contraction) in the circular muscle of the iris, accommodation spasm in the ciliary muscle, and in blood vessels vasodilation > vasoconstriction by activating eNOS in the endothelium. m5/m4 (CNS) are shown with a dash, and m2 blockade in the heart slows the SA node (↓ heart rate) and AV node (↓ conduction).
In Alzheimer's disease there is ↓ ACh, so ↓ m1 stimulation and ↓ cognition. Treatment is with tacilifensin, an m1 agonist.

Cholinergic poisoning from organophosphates/carbamates gives miosis (pinpoint pupil) with lacrimation, ↑ salivation, bronchoconstriction with dyspnea, involuntary defecation, involuntary urination and ↑ sweating - the drug of choice being atropine. Anticholinergic poisoning from atropine and datura gives exactly the opposite picture: mydriasis, dry mouth, bronchodilation, constipation, urine retention and ↓ sweating - the drug of choice being physostigmine.

Cholinergic drugs are parasympathomimetics. Direct drugs stimulate muscarinic or nicotinic receptors themselves, while indirect drugs block acetylcholinesterase, raise acetylcholine and then stimulate m/n receptors. Direct agents are organised by structure into amides and choline esters; indirect agents are split into irreversible organophosphates and reversible tertiary or quaternary amines.
Direct Cholinergic Drugs: Amides, Pilocarpine and Cevimeline

Amides are lipid soluble, cross the BBB and therefore have central as well as peripheral effects, while choline esters are insoluble, do not cross the BBB and act peripherally on bladder, GIT and muscle. Pilocarpine and cevimeline are the amides, both useful for xerostomia; pilocarpine also contracts the pupil to increase trabecular outflow in glaucoma. The same contraction of accommodation muscles explains brow ache, accommodation spasm and tractional retinal detachment.
Choline Esters and Derivatives of ACh

Acetylcholine is destroyed in plasma by plasma, pseudo or butyryl cholinesterase, so it is systemically very short acting and is mainly remembered as a topical miotic in ocular surgery. Bethanechol, carbachol and methacholine differ by esterase resistance, receptor affinity, nicotinic side effects and uses. Bethanechol treats bladder and GIT atony, carbachol is topical because systemic use is limited by side effects, and methacholine provokes m3 bronchospasm in bronchial challenge testing.
Irreversible AChE Blockers and Organophosphate Poisoning

Organophosphates bind AChE and first produce a reversible phase with raised ACh, but ageing replaces phosphate bonds with stronger bonds and makes inhibition irreversible. Oximes can break the organophosphate-AChE link before ageing but become ineffective after ageing. Organophosphate poisoning is a cholinergic syndrome; atropine treats muscarinic features, while oximes reactivate AChE for nicotinic toxicity.
Reversible AChE Blockers: Mechanism and Tertiary Amines

Carbamates and non-carbamates are called pseudo-irreversible because they are long acting, yet they bind AChE with weak ionic bonds rather than aged organophosphate bonds. Edrophonium is the short-acting exception that only binds the anionic site, and oximes are not used for carbamate/non-carbamate poisoning. Tertiary amines cross the BBB, so physostigmine treats anticholinergic poisoning and synthetic agents are used for Alzheimer's disease.
Quaternary AChE Inhibitors and Myasthenia Gravis

Quaternary amines do not cross the BBB, so their action is peripheral. Edrophonium is a short-acting diagnostic drug for myasthenia gravis and separates myasthenic from cholinergic crisis by improvement versus worsening. Neostigmine is long acting for Nm and peripheral bladder/GIT uses, while pyridostigmine is the DOC for chronic myasthenia gravis; severe myasthenic crisis uses IVIG and newer chronic therapies lower antibodies.

Low-dose ACh lowers BP through m3-mediated vasodilation, and a larger dose gives a larger fall. If atropine blocks m3, ordinary ACh produces no BP effect. With high-dose ACh in the presence of atropine, ganglionic Nn stimulation releases norepinephrine, producing vasoconstriction and a pressor response.
Anticholinergic Drugs: Classification and Nicotinic Blockers

Anticholinergic drugs are parasympatholytics and are direct acting. They include muscarinic blockers and nicotinic blockers; nicotinic blockers are further separated into Nm muscular blockers and Nn neuronal or ganglionic blockers. Nm blockers relax skeletal muscle at the NMJ, whereas ganglionic blockers reduce sympathetic post-ganglionic norepinephrine release, producing vasodilation, antihypertensive action and postural hypotension.
Muscarinic Blockers: CNS, Eyes and Oropharynx

Muscarinic blockade in the CNS decreases cognition; scopolamine is remembered as a truth serum, an alternate narcoanalysis drug and the DOC for motion sickness as a transdermal patch. In the eye, muscarinic blockers cause passive mydriasis and cycloplegia; short-acting drops are used in adults, whereas potent atropine ointment is used in children and for uveitis-related indications. Glycopyrrolate decreases oropharyngeal secretions as a quaternary amine that does not cross the BBB, making it useful before anaesthesia to prevent aspiration.
Pulmonary Antimuscarinics, Inhalation Devices and Paradoxical Bronchoconstriction

Antimuscarinics in the lung cause bronchodilation and are classified by duration into SAMA, IAMA and LAMA. Ipratropium is the short-acting QID drug, tiotropium is DOC in COPD, and long-acting agents are add-on drugs in asthma or COPD. They are delivered by inhalation through pMDI or nebuliser, but paradoxical bronchoconstriction can occur from hypotonic solution, bromide or presynaptic m2 blockade that increases ACh and stimulates postsynaptic m3.

Atropine increases heart rate and AV conduction and is the DOC for conduction blocks such as digoxin toxicity and for bradycardia when the dose is at least 0.5 mg. Very low IV doses can paradoxically slow the heart through presynaptic muscarinic blockade. In the GIT, m1 blockers such as pirenzepine and telenzepine are obsolete anti-secretory drugs, while antispasmodics such as glycopyrrolate, dicyclomine and hyoscine reduce contraction and relieve abdominal pain or motion sickness.

Bladder antimuscarinics reduce detrusor contraction and treat urge incontinence. Selective m3 blockers such as darifenacin and solifenacin are contrasted with trospium, a quaternary amine useful when Alzheimer's disease is present because it does not cross the BBB. Non-selective drugs such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, flavoxate and fesoterodine can block brain m1 receptors and cause dementia on long-term use.
Physiology of Norepinephrine: Synthesis, Storage, Release and Metabolism

Norepinephrine synthesis begins with tyrosine and the rate-limiting enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, then proceeds through DOPA and dopamine before dopamine enters the vesicle through VMAT2 and is converted to norepinephrine by dopamine-β-hydroxylase. Released norepinephrine acts on α and β receptors, is metabolised by MAO and COMT, and is cleared by reuptake. Several drugs map exactly onto this diagram: metyrosine blocks tyrosine hydroxylase, reserpine/tetrabenazine derivatives block VMAT2, and cocaine, TCAs and SNRIs block reuptake.
Drugs Modifying NE/DA and Cocaine Dependence

Metyrosine lowers catecholamines by competitively inhibiting tyrosine hydroxylase and is used in malignant pheochromocytoma. VMAT2 blockers lower norepinephrine and dopamine: reserpine is now uncommon, tetrabenazine is DOC for Huntington chorea and Tourette-associated tics, and deutetrabenazine/valbenazine are long-acting derivatives used for tardive dyskinesia. Cocaine blocks NA and DA reuptake, raising DA and addiction potential; dependence is managed by keeping dopamine receptors engaged with bromocriptine and tapering.

Sympathetic receptors are GPCRs divided into α and β. α1 is mainly postsynaptic, centrally placed on the membrane and Gq-coupled; it contracts vascular, prostatic, bladder sphincter and radial iris smooth muscle but relaxes GIT through Ca2+-dependent K+ opening and hyperpolarisation. α2 is predominantly presynaptic and Gi-coupled; late stimulation reduces further NE release, causing central sympatholysis, but postsynaptic vascular α2 can vasoconstrict and pancreatic β-islet α2 reduces insulin to raise glucose.
Catecholamines, Blood Glucose and β Receptors

The notes compare m3 and α/β signalling and explain why catecholamines produce hyperglycemia: α1/α2/β2 stimulation is released during hypoglycemia, and the β2 liver/skeletal-muscle rise in glucose outweighs pancreatic insulin release. β receptors are Gs-coupled: β1 acts in heart and kidney to raise contraction, rate, conduction and renin, β2 relaxes smooth muscle but also causes tremor, palpitations, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia, and β3 relaxes bladder while stimulating adipocyte lipolysis.

Adrenergic drugs are sympathomimetics. They can act directly on α and β receptors or indirectly by increasing norepinephrine, which then stimulates α and β receptors. Direct agents are divided into catecholamines and non-catecholamines; catecholamines may be endogenous or exogenous, while non-catecholamines include α-agonists and β-agonists.

Epinephrine is the endogenous catecholamine that acts on α, β1 and β2 receptors and is a stronger cardiac stimulant than norepinephrine. It is DOC in cardiac arrest, anaphylactic shock and brittle asthma, with different dilutions/routes for cardiac arrest versus anaphylaxis. Other uses are prolonging local anaesthesia through vasoconstriction and glaucoma therapy with dipivefrine preferred; conjunctival pigmentation is linked to tyrosine, the common melanin precursor.

Norepinephrine acts on α1 and β1 and is a stronger vasoconstrictor than epinephrine because it lacks β2 vasodilation. It is given only IV for vasodilatory, cardiogenic and neurogenic shock, while IM use is contraindicated because of muscle necrosis. Dopamine is dose-dependent: low doses act on D1 for diuresis, intermediate doses on β1 for contractility, and high doses on α1 for vasoconstriction, but shock use raises mortality because of pro-arrhythmia.

Exogenous catecholamines are receptor-selective clinical tools. Dobutamine acts on myocardial β receptors, increases contraction without SA-node effect and is DOC in acute CHF; isoprenaline is a pure β1/β2 agonist with no α action. Fenoldopam and dopexamine combine D1 with α1 or β1 effects to lower BP, while droxidopa is a norepinephrine prodrug for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetic neuropathy.
α1 and Mixed α Non-catecholamine Agonists

α1 non-catecholamines produce vasoconstriction and are used for the mnemonic-like cluster PHEN: priapism, hypotension from spinal anaesthesia, mydriasis without cycloplegia and nasal decongestion. Midodrine is DOC for postural hypotension, while mephentermine, metaraminol and methoxamine treat hypotension. Apraclonidine has α1/α2 action, can cause mydriasis and lid retraction through raised calcium, and is used as an antiglaucoma drug in open-angle glaucoma.

α2 agonists reduce norepinephrine release to produce central sympatholysis and lower BP; if they cross the BBB they also cause sedation. Clonidine is the prototype and is used for Tourette-associated ADHD, withdrawal syndromes, postmenopausal hot flashes, hypertension and pre-anaesthetic medication, with rebound hypertension on withdrawal due to α2 down-regulation. Lofexidine treats opioid withdrawal, tizanidine is a muscle relaxant, α-methyldopa forms α-methyl-NE and is used in PIH, while guanfacine/guanabenz and brimonidine complete the list.

β3 agonists relax the urinary bladder and are the DOC drug class for overactive bladder or urge incontinence. The listed drugs are mirabegron and vibegron, with vibegron preferred. Mirabegron has more side effects than vibegron, including vascular headache, UTI from urine retention in a relaxed bladder, hypertension and nasopharyngitis; anticholinergic alternatives are darifenacin, solifenacin and trospium.
β2 Agonists: Duration, Asthma/COPD Use and Side Effects

β2 agonists are grouped by duration: SABA lasts about 4 hours, LABA about 12 hours, and VLABA about 24 hours. Terbutaline is the only adrenergic given subcutaneously, salbutamol can be nebulised for asthma/COPD, formoterol and salmeterol are pMDI twice-daily LABAs used as add-ons with ICS, and olodaterol/vilanterol are once-daily COPD-only VLABAs. Fast-acting β agonists are relievers in intermittent asthma, with formoterol plus ICS as DOC and salbutamol followed by ICS if unaffordable; tremor is the most common side effect, with hypokalemia, hyperglycemia and palpitations also listed.
Indirect Adrenergics, Cheese Reaction and Stimulants

Indirect adrenergics are norepinephrine displacers: a drug similar to NE enters the neuron, displaces NE from vesicles into the synapse, and produces α/β sympathomimetic stimulation. Intermittent dosing works, but continuous dosing depletes NE and turns into drug failure with sympatholysis. The cheese reaction is tyramine plus MAO-inhibitor physiology, and stimulant examples include methylphenidate, amphetamine and methamphetamine.

The chapter adds that guanfacine and guanabenz can lower BP through sympatholysis but are contraindicated in pheochromocytoma. For ADHD with a family history of drug abuse, the preferred DOC group is selective NE reuptake inhibitors such as atomoxetine and viloxazine. Narcolepsy drugs include solriamfetol, pitolisant, amphetamine, methylphenidate and modafinil; mixed-acting sympathomimetics stimulate α/β receptors directly and also raise NE levels, with ephedrine, pseudoephedrine and banned norephedrine as the examples.

The details section turns epinephrine dilutions into route-based facts: 1:1000 for SC/IM/endotracheal, 1:10,000 for IV/intracardiac/intraosseous, 1:100,000 for local vasoconstriction and 1:100,000 or 1:200,000 with local anaesthetic. Dale's phenomenon is the biphasic BP response to epinephrine: high adrenaline reaches the higher-threshold α response to raise BP, while low adrenaline acts on lower-threshold β2 receptors to lower BP. With α blockade the pressor limb is reversed to a pure fall, and with β blockade the response is re-reversed to an unopposed α1 steep rise.
Comparing Epinephrine, Norepinephrine and Isoprenaline on BP and HR

The final table compares α1/β1/β2 epinephrine, α1/β1 norepinephrine and β1/β2 isoprenaline. Norepinephrine gives the greatest mean BP rise but net bradycardia from reflex vagal tone, epinephrine raises mean BP with net tachycardia, and isoprenaline lowers diastolic/mean BP while driving the greatest HR rise with pro-arrhythmic action. Clinically, norepinephrine is preferred for most shock except anaphylaxis, where epinephrine is DOC because β2 bronchodilation matters; atropine blocks vagal reflex bradycardia and is paired with NE in neurogenic hypotension.
Direct Sympatholytics and Nonselective α Blockers

Anti-adrenergic drugs in this chapter are direct-acting sympatholytics, split first into α blockers and β blockers. α blockers are either nonselective α1+α2 blockers or selective α1/α2 blockers. Tolazoline is a small-vessel dilator for peripheral vascular disease/angiography, whereas IV phentolamine is the acute DOC for catecholamine excess situations such as cheese reaction, clonidine withdrawal and intraoperative pheochromocytoma hypertension.
Selective α2 Blockers and α1 Receptor Sites

The α2 blockers here are yohimbine and idazoxan, with yohimbine noted as a food supplement for erectile dysfunction, neuropathic pain and postural hypotension. α1 blockers dilate vessels but their adverse effects depend on α1 subtype: α1a in prostatic urethra and iris gives ejaculation/floppy-iris problems, while α1b/d vascular blockade gives venodilation-driven first-dose postural hypotension and lowers LDL.
α1 Blocker Uses and Scorpion Bite

Mixed α1a,b,d blockers such as prazosin, terazosin and doxazosin are used for BPH with hypertension and for scorpion bite. More selective α1a blockers, tamsulosin and silodosin, are BPH drugs, with tamsulosin also blocking α1d and silodosin having maximum side effects. Scorpion toxin has sympathetic and parasympathetic limbs: prazosin treats hypertension/pulmonary edema, atropine treats bradycardia, and severe priapism can need phentolamine.
β Blocker Classification by Selectivity, Generation and Vasodilation

β blockers are organized by β1/β2 selectivity and by special vasodilator mechanisms. First-generation agents are nonselective, second-generation agents are β1-selective, and third-generation drugs may add vasodilation through α blockade, β2 agonism, calcium-channel block, nitric oxide or potassium-channel opening. Remember the named drugs carefully because the chapter tests exceptions such as nebivolol, carvedilol, labetalol and tilisolol.
Partial Agonism, Membrane Stabilisation and Water Solubility

Some β blockers have intrinsic sympathomimetic/partial agonist activity; the mnemonic is 'Cause Partial Agonism' and pindolol has maximum action. This lowers bradycardia but makes these agents contraindicated after myocardial infarction and in migraine. Separate special groups include Na+ channel-blocking membrane stabilizers and water-soluble drugs that do not cross the BBB but are contraindicated in renal failure.
β Blocker Pharmacokinetic and Antioxidant Properties

The properties section gives high-yield extremes: nadolol has the longest half-life, esmolol the shortest because esterases metabolize it, carvedilol has maximum protein binding and celiprolol minimum protein binding. Esmolol is DOC intraoperatively and even for β blockade in asthmatics when necessary, while carvedilol and nebivolol are the antioxidant/cardioprotective examples.
β Blocker Adverse Effects: Brain, Bronchi, Glucose and Exercise

The side-effect mnemonic is 'BETA ONE in Heart, Kidney and metabolism.' Lipid-soluble β blockers cause central symptoms; bronchoconstriction makes asthma/COPD a contraindication; β blockade masks palpitations and tremors of hypoglycemia but not sweating; and β2 blockade causes exercise intolerance by reducing skeletal muscle contraction and blood glucose.
β Blocker Effects on Heart, Kidney and Metabolism

At the organ level β blockers reduce contraction, heart rate, conduction and renin release. Their metabolic effects differ by generation/selectivity: nonselective agents worsen the lipid profile, cardioselective agents improve it in the table, and first/second generations increase insulin resistance while third-generation agents decrease it.
Clinical Uses of β Blockers and Toxicity Antidote

β blockers are second-line antihypertensives overall, especially useful when renin is high or hypertension coexists with anxiety, migraine, tremor or hyperthyroidism. They are DOC in HOCM because lowering contraction reduces LV outflow obstruction, and they are used in aortic dissection, thyroid storm and glaucoma. Toxicity is treated with glucagon, which bypasses β blockade by stimulating adenylate cyclase and raising cAMP.
Cardiac Action Potentials and Vaughan Williams Classification

Part 1 starts from the action potential: myocardial cells contract and eject blood after an action potential, while the SA node spontaneously depolarizes to generate heart rate. Myocardial depolarization is Na+-driven, the plateau uses K+, Ca2+ and inward Na+ channels, and repolarization uses delayed-rectifier K+. The first antiarrhythmic map is Vaughan Williams: class I targets Na+ channels, class II β receptors, class III K+ channels, class IV Ca2+ channels and class V miscellaneous agents.
SVT/PSVT Pathology and AV Nodal Treatment Preference

SVT/PSVT is explained as a fast atrial rhythm driving AV nodal action, increasing ventricular rate and risking incomplete ventricular contraction, ventricular fibrillation and arrest. The treatment aim is to block the AV node. Adenosine is the IV DOC for acute management, β blockers such as esmolol/metoprolol are limited by bronchoconstriction, diltiazem/verapamil cover acute and long-term management, and oral digoxin is for long-term management.
Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter and Ventricular Arrhythmia Strategy

For atrial fibrillation/flutter, abnormal rate and disrupted rhythm come most commonly from ectopic functional atrial circuits. Management is split into ventricular rate control under 100 bpm by AV node block and rhythm control by blocking ectopic myocardial cells. Cardioversion is the treatment of choice acutely, β blockers are long-term DOC for rate control, and amiodarone is DOC among rhythm-control K+ blockers; ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation is treated by blocking myocardial cells, especially with amiodarone.
Class I Na+ Channel Blocker Classification and Electrophysiology

Class I drugs are divided into Ia, Ib and Ic. Ia drugs have intermediate Na+ blockade, open-state binding, significant K+ block, QT prolongation, maximum repolarization delay and prolonged PR; Ib drugs have very short closed-state blockade, K+ opening, QT shortening and normal AV/PR effects; Ic drugs have very long open-state blockade, maximum depolarization delay, normal QT and prolonged PR by blocking AP propagation.
Class Ia Drugs: Uses, Routes and Toxicities

Class Ia drugs are second-line rhythm-control drugs for atrial fibrillation/flutter and ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation. Quinidine is oral and classically causes torsades, diarrhea and α-block hypotension; procainamide is IV and causes ganglionic-block hypotension, leukopenia/infections, agranulocytosis and SLE; disopyramide is oral and anticholinergic, causing urinary retention, mydriasis, dry mouth, constipation and PR shortening by AV nodal stimulation.
Class Ib Drugs: Lidocaine, Mexiletine and Phenytoin

Lidocaine targets ischemic and digoxin-toxic ventricular tissue because persistently depolarized cells keep Na+ channels closed long enough for closed-state blockade. It is IV because of high first-pass metabolism, contraindicated/ineffective in atrial arrhythmias with small action potentials, and causes neurologic toxicity such as nystagmus, paresthesia and seizures. Mexiletine is the oral lidocaine derivative, and phenytoin is the antiepileptic Na+ blocker used for digoxin-induced ventricular tachycardia.
Class Ic Drugs and WPW Syndrome

Class Ic drugs are strongest Na+ blockers, and flecainide is the key named drug. In WPW syndrome, flecainide is DOC because blocking Na+ and K+ channels maximally increases refractory period in both normal cells and the accessory pathway. Pure AV nodal blockers such as digoxin, β blockers and CCBs are contraindicated in WPW because they increase conduction through the accessory pathway.
Class II, III, IV and V Antiarrhythmic Map

Part 2 re-lists the non-class-I antiarrhythmics. Class II contains β blockers; class III contains K+ blockers including bretylium, dofetilide, ibutilide, vernakalant, amiodarone and sotalol; class IV contains diltiazem/verapamil; and class V contains adenosine, MgSO4, atropine and digoxin. This opening map anchors the later details on AV nodal block, K+ blockade and miscellaneous drugs.
Class II β Blockers and Class IV Calcium Channel Blockers

Class II and class IV drugs both cause relative AV nodal block when used individually. β blockers are used for SVT/PSVT, idiopathic VT with reduced heart rate, ventricular premature beats and catecholamine-induced arrhythmias from pheochromocytoma or halothane. Diltiazem/verapamil are used for SVT/PSVT, but class II and IV must never be combined because total conduction block can result.
Class III K+ Channel Blockers and Amiodarone Spectrum

Class III drugs delay ventricular repolarization, producing QT prolongation and torsades risk. Ibutilide has the maximum torsades risk, whereas amiodarone has minimum torsades risk because it blocks K+, Na+, β and Ca2+ channels. Amiodarone is the broadest and longest-acting antiarrhythmic; ibutilide is the shortest-acting K+ blocker used IV for acute fibrillation/flutter attacks.

Amiodarone toxicity is dominated by iodine-related lung, liver, skin, thyroid and ocular problems. Pulmonary fibrosis needs baseline X-ray/PFT and is contraindicated in ILD; corneal deposits are whorl-like, usually asymptomatic and reversible; skin effects include ceruloderma and brown photosensitive pigmentation; and thyroid disease is more often hypothyroid in plain dwellers than hyperthyroid in hilly areas. Dronedarone lacks iodine, so it is less toxic but also less efficacious.
Adenosine: MOA, Route, Dosing and Uses

Adenosine acts on adenosine receptors to block the AV node through Gi, cause bronchoconstriction through Gq and vasodilate through Gs. Because it is rapidly taken up into cells and degraded orally by gastric acid, it must be given as an IV rapid push—6 mg, then 12 mg if there is no response. It is DOC for acute SVT/PSVT after vagal/carotid massage and can maintain controlled hypotension during surgery.
Adenosine Adverse Effects, Digoxin and Magnesium Sulfate

Adenosine commonly causes transient apnea and flushing; it may trigger atrial fibrillation by K+ channel opening and is contraindicated in asthma/COPD, atrial fibrillation and transplanted hearts because of denervation hypersensitivity. Digoxin blocks the AV node and is used as a chronic CHF inotrope plus SVT/PSVT drug. MgSO4 blocks Ca2+ channels to shorten QT and is DOC for acute torsades; congenital long QT is managed with β blockers and pacing, while acquired drug-induced long QT requires avoiding drugs.
Acute CHF Pathophysiology and IV Management

Acute CHF is most commonly caused by myocardial infarction. Acute myocardial injury decreases contraction, causes blood stasis in the heart, raises back pressure into the lungs, engorges pulmonary capillaries and extravasates plasma into parenchyma, producing pulmonary edema. Clinically the patient has chest pain and breathlessness; IV treatment of choice is dobutamine plus furosemide.
Acute CHF Inotropes and Pulmonary Edema Drugs

Acute CHF management combines drugs that increase contraction and drugs that quickly relieve pulmonary edema. Dobutamine stimulates β1-Gs to raise cAMP and contractility without affecting heart rate; PDE3 inhibitors raise cAMP as inodilators; levosimendan opens K+ channels and sensitizes myocardium to Ca2+. Furosemide venodilates via prostaglandins and diureses; if there is no response, nitroglycerin and then nesiritide can be considered.
Chronic CHF Compensation, Mortality and Oral Drug Classes

Chronic CHF follows gradual loss of output from cardiomyopathy/rheumatic disease, then compensatory catecholamines and RAAS. Compensation may maintain output but drives cardiac remodeling, oxygen demand and mortality; decompensation resembles acute CHF and lowers oxygen supply. Oral mortality-reducing drugs target β1 signaling, heart rate, vasodilation, RAAS and sodium/water retention, while furosemide and digoxin remain symptomatic drugs.
Newly Diagnosed CHF Approach and Neprilysin/Guanylate Cyclase Drugs

A newly diagnosed CHF patient first receives furosemide for symptoms, then a mortality-reducing foundation: sacubitril+valsartan if affordable is preferred to ACEI/ARB, otherwise ACEI/ARB are started low and titrated. β blockers are started while ACEI/ARB are being increased, beginning at suboptimal dose to prevent decompensation. Sacubitril raises BNP by inhibiting neprilysin, vericiguat raises cGMP through guanylate cyclase, and omapatrilat is obsolete because dual NEP+ACE inhibition caused fatal angioedema.

Digoxin comes from Digitalis lanata, has good oral absorption, a long 36-48 hour half-life and renal excretion. Digitalization takes 7-10 days, so therapeutic drug monitoring should begin after that to avoid false low values. The normal plasma range is 0.5-2.0 ng/mL, but the desired therapeutic range is 0.5-0.9 ng/mL; toxicity rises above 2.0 ng/mL and mortality in atrial fibrillation rises above 1.2 ng/mL.
Digoxin Cellular Mechanism and Ventricular Arrhythmias

At the cellular level, digoxin blocks the Na+-K+ ATPase pump. This raises intracellular Na+, blocks the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger, raises intracellular Ca2+ and increases myocardial contraction; extracellular K+ competes with digoxin binding, while diuretic-induced hypokalemia leaves more ATPase available and precipitates toxicity. In ventricles, delayed closure of Ca2+ channels causes DADs, extrasystoles, bigeminy, trigeminy, VT and finally VF, where defibrillation should be avoided.
Digoxin Toxicity Treatment and Organ-Level Heart Effects

Digoxin toxicity is treated according to rhythm: lidocaine or amiodarone for VT/VF, Digibind as the antidote, and no dialysis because distribution volume is high. At normal dose digoxin is parasympathomimetic with SA/AV nodal block but also raises atrial Ca2+, causing atrial tachycardia as the most specific arrhythmia; therapeutically it converts atrial flutter into atrial fibrillation, which is easier to control. At high dose it becomes sympathomimetic with increased heart rate and contraction.
Digoxin Adverse Effects, Contraindications and DIGOXIN Summary

The classic toxicity cluster is summarized by DIGOXIN: dialysis not done/Digibind, increased K+, gynecomastia, ocular effects/xanthopsia, increased arrhythmias, nausea-vomiting and Na+-K+ ATPase blockade. Nausea/vomiting is both earliest and most common. Toxicity risk rises with hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, MI and renal failure; digoxin is also contraindicated in HOCM and WPW.
Vasodilator Classification and Calcium Channel Blocker Comparison

Vasodilators are classified by hemodynamic target: arterial dilators lower afterload, venodilators lower preload and sodium nitroprusside is mixed. Calcium channel blockers split into non-DHP diltiazem/verapamil and DHP agents. Non-DHP agents are weaker vasodilators but late AV/SA nodal blockers used in arrhythmia, whereas DHPs are potent vasodilators with significant reflex tachycardia and no AV nodal block.
Calcium Channel Blocker Adverse Effects and Uses

Calcium channel blockers are first-line antihypertensives and DOC for Raynaud phenomenon; oral nimodipine prevents cerebral vasoconstriction after subarachnoid hemorrhage because it is lipid soluble and crosses the BBB. Their adverse effects reflect vasodilation and nodal block: headache is most common, amlodipine causes precapillary ankle edema prevented by low-dose amlodipine plus ACEI, verapamil causes constipation, and diltiazem/verapamil cannot be combined with β blockers.
Other Arterial Dilators: Hydralazine, Minoxidil, Diazoxide and Fenoldopam

Hydralazine blocks IP3-induced Ca2+ channels, opens K+ channels and increases NO; it is used for hypertensive emergency in pregnancy, though IV labetalol is the DOC, and can cause SLE/Sweet syndrome. Minoxidil is a potent K+ opener used orally as a second-line elderly antihypertensive and topically in androgenic alopecia; diazoxide is for insulinoma but can cause shock; fenoldopam is a D1 and α2 agonist.
Nitroglycerin Mechanism, Uses, Tolerance and Contraindications

Nitroglycerin is converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase to nitric oxide, which stimulates guanylate cyclase to raise cGMP and relax smooth muscle. cGMP is metabolized by PDE5, so sildenafil/tadalafil interact dangerously with nitrates. NTG is DOC sublingually for acute angina, patch/gel for prophylaxis, useful for MI pain and esophageal spasm, but causes tolerance prevented by an 8-hour nitrate-free nighttime interval and causes headache/Monday disease/postural hypotension.

Isosorbide dinitrate is an oral nitrate that undergoes first-pass denitration to active isosorbide mononitrate; IDN is used orally for angina prophylaxis and sublingually for acute angina. Isosorbide mononitrate has 0% first-pass metabolism and is used orally for long-term prophylaxis. Sodium nitroprusside is a mixed dilator metabolized to therapeutic NO and toxic cyanide/thiocyanate, so it is not preferred for hypertensive emergency/aortic dissection despite being effective.
RAAS Physiology, ACE Inhibition and Contraindications

The RAAS page maps liver angiotensinogen to angiotensin I through kidney renin, then lung ACE to angiotensin II, then aminopeptidases to angiotensin III and IV. ACE also behaves like kininase, so ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin, prostaglandins and substance P, causing dry cough and angioedema. Angiotensin II/III act through AT1 receptors on vessels, adrenals and glomeruli; RAAS blockers cause postural hypotension/hyperkalemia and are contraindicated in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis.
ACE Inhibitors, ARBs, Aliskiren and Captopril Test

The drug table gives ACE inhibitors, ARBs and direct renin inhibitors. ACE inhibitors include captopril, lisinopril, fosinopril, enalapril and IV enalaprilat; ARBs include losartan with PPARγ/uricosuric/TXA2 effects, telmisartan as the maximum PPARγ agonist, olmesartan and irbesartan with AV nodal AF rate control; aliskiren is the direct renin inhibitor. ACEI/ARBs are first-line for hyperreninemic HTN and DOC in HTN with DM, CKD, nephrotic syndrome and scleroderma; captopril testing differentiates renovascular from essential hypertension.
Mild to Moderate Hypertension: Classification and the Age-based Table

Antihypertensives are first classified by prescribing preference: first-line drugs are ACE inhibitors/ARBs, long-acting calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone), while second-line drugs are alpha blockers, beta blockers, the alpha-2 agonist clonidine, direct renin inhibitors (aliskiren) and spironolactone. The age-based table then explains the renin logic: young hypertensives are hyperreninemic and respond to ACE inhibitors/ARBs, whereas old hypertensives are hyporeninemic and respond to calcium channel blockers.
Clinical Approach: Newly Diagnosed Hypertension and Resistant Hypertension

In a newly diagnosed hypertensive without comorbidities, the choice follows age: below 55 years start ACE inhibitors/ARBs (they lower renin), above 55 years start calcium channel blockers (no effect on renin). If there is no response despite maximum dose after one month, combine A + C; if still no response after another month add the third first-line drug to make A + C + D. Resistance to three drugs of which one is a diuretic defines resistant hypertension, which is treated by adding spironolactone to counteract the raised aldosterone.

The comorbidity flowchart picks the drug by the associated disease: ACE inhibitors/ARBs for diabetes mellitus, CKD without edema, nephrotic syndrome and scleroderma; thiazides for CKD with edema, osteoporosis and renal insufficiency (metolazone being specific); alpha blockers (prazosin) for BPH; calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) for Raynaud disease and cyclosporine-induced HTN; and beta blockers for migraine, essential tremor, anxiety disorders, hyperthyroidism and stable angina.

Severe hypertension means uncontrolled blood pressure of 220/135 mmHg or more, and the next step is to assess for signs of end-organ damage. If end-organ damage is present it is a hypertensive emergency treated with IV drugs (hydralazine, enalaprilat, furosemide, labetalol as DOC in pregnancy, esmolol, nitroglycerine, nitroprusside and dihydropyridines); if end-organ damage is absent it is a hypertensive urgency treated with oral drugs (clonidine as DOC, captopril and nifedipine). End-organ damage signs are encephalopathy, retinopathy, CHF, pulmonary edema, renal failure and eclampsia.
Etiopathogenesis of Angina: Stable versus Variant (Prinzmetal)

Stable angina begins with a coronary atherosclerotic plaque that gradually reduces blood supply to the myocardium, so O2 supply falls; physical exertion then raises O2 demand and the imbalance produces the acute attack of ischemic pain. Variant (Prinzmetal) angina has no plaque-dependent supply problem in its core diagram: the coronary artery undergoes acute vasoconstriction (spasm) which acutely drops O2 supply to the myocardium and causes the ischemic pain.
Management of Angina: Acute Attack and Long-term Prophylaxis

The acute attack of angina is treated with sublingual nitroglycerine as the drug of choice. Its mechanism differs by type: in stable angina it lowers preload on the heart, thereby lowering myocardial O2 demand, whereas in variant angina it acts by coronary vasodilation. For long-term prophylaxis of variant angina, a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) is the drug of choice because it is long-acting and causes less reflex tachycardia; long-acting nitrates, which act as vasodilators, include oral/sustained-release/patch/gel nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate and isosorbide mononitrate.
Stable Angina: Aims of Therapy (Number of Attacks versus Mortality)

Stable angina therapy has two aims. The first is to reduce the number of attacks using calcium channel blockers, long-acting nitrates, beta blockers (best, as negative inotropes), ivabradine, ranolazine, nicorandil, fasudil, trimetazidine, allopurinol and the endothelin antagonist bosentan. The second aim is to reduce mortality due to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease with statins, aspirin (an anti-aggregant) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs.

Ivabradine is described as an AHA bradycardiac drug: it blocks the funny (Na+/K+) channels carrying the If current, blocking the SA node to lower heart rate while contraction remains normal. FDA approved for chronic CHF, it is used off-label for stable angina, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and postural tachycardia syndrome. Adverse effects are a higher risk of atrial fibrillation (from increased action of the functional circuit) and visual phenomena from If channel block in the retina - luminous phenomena (multiple coloured halos) and phosphenes (images of light perceived with closed eyes).

Ranolazine at normal dose blocks late inward sodium (LINA+) channels; at high dose it also blocks the delayed rectifier K+ channel, thereby blocking repolarization. Blocking late inward Na+ reduces intracellular Na+, which reduces Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity, lowers intracellular Ca2+ in the myocardium and so lowers O2 demand, while BP and heart rate stay normal in a normal person. FDA approved for stable angina, it is used off-label in HOCM and ventricular tachycardia, and its notable effects are a reduced risk of atrial fibrillation and a fall in HbA1c that reverses insulin resistance.
Other Antianginal Drugs: Nicorandil, Fasudil, Allopurinol, Bosentan and Trimetazidine

The remaining antianginals act on distinct targets: nicorandil opens K+ channels and causes vasodilation; fasudil is a Rho-kinase inhibitor that causes vasodilation; allopurinol produces vasodilatation and is also used in gout; bosentan is used in pulmonary hypertension; and trimetazidine blocks partial fatty acid oxidase (pFox), inhibiting metabolism of triglycerides (the main source of ATP in the heart) while promoting glycolysis in the heart, so O2 demand falls.
Sources of Lipids and the Physiology Diagram

Hypolipidemic drugs are used in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). The physiology page builds lipid handling from three sources: food entering the small intestine (cholesterol, triglycerides and bile acids, with ezetimibe blocking the NPC1L1 transporter and esterification by ACAT in the epithelial cell), storage in adipose tissue (where niacin blocks the adipocyte and hormone sensitive lipase releases free fatty acids in the fasting state), and synthesis in the liver. Enterohepatic circulation carries bile acids back through the duodenum; VLDL and chylomicrons reach the blood vessel, and the remnants of VLDL and chylomicrons are removed by the liver.
Cholesterol Synthesis, LDL Receptor Regulation and PCSK9 Drugs

When a cell requires cholesterol it makes it from citrate: ATP citrate lyase converts citrate to acetyl CoA (blocked by bempedoic acid), HMG CoA reductase converts HMG CoA to mevalonic acid (blocked by statins) and the pathway ends in cholesterol for bile acids and steroids. The same cholesterol need upregulates synthesis of the LDL receptor - the effect shared by statins, bempedoic acid, ezetimibe and bile acid binding resins. Plasma LDL reaching the cell is degraded to cholesterol, PCSK9 degrades LDL receptors, alirocumab and evolocumab are monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9, and inclisiran is a siRNA that blocks synthesis of PCSK9. Evinacumab blocks AngPTL-3 to block LPL and lower LDL cholesterol in FHC, while lomitapide is also used in familial hypercholesterolemia.

Niacin is highly toxic and therefore not preferred. It lowers free fatty acids, which lowers TG, VLDL and finally LDL; it is used to lower Lp(a) along with statin plus ezetimibe therapy and gives the maximum increase in HDL (more than statin) although this indication is obsolete. Its side effects are potent hepatotoxicity, insulin resistance progressing to diabetes mellitus and flushing caused by prostaglandin release with vasodilation, for which aspirin is the treatment of choice because it blocks cyclooxygenase and reduces prostaglandin synthesis.
Triglyceride-lowering Drugs: Omega-3 Fatty Acids, Icosapent and Fibrates

The TG-lowering group contains omega-3 fatty acids, icosapent and fibrates, with fibrates split into halogenated (clofibrate, bezafibrate, fenofibrate) and non-halogenated (gemfibrozil) agents. Icosapent is a derivative of omega-3 fatty acids that blocks release of VLDL by the liver and is used in familial hypertriglyceridemia. Fibrates stimulate PPAR-alpha, which increases LPL synthesis in capillary endothelium, lowering chylomicrons, VLDL, TG and LDL particles; they are DOC in hypertriglyceridemia, chylomicronemia syndrome and type III hyperlipoproteinemia, and fenofibrate also lowers uric acid like febuxostat. Their side effects are myopathy and gall stones, maximal with clofibrate.
LDL-lowering Drugs: Statins, Bempedoic Acid, Ezetimibe, PCSK9 Inhibitors, Inclisiran and Resins

The LDL-lowering indications are ASCVD such as angina, myocardial infarction and stroke, and any patient with raised LDL. The drugs are statins (the DOC, marked as the affordable oral drug class), bempedoic acid (affordable oral drug), ezetimibe (blocks NPC1L1 to reduce cholesterol absorption with upregulation of LDL receptors to lower plasma LDL), PCSK9 inhibitors given as intravenous monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab), inclisiran (small interfering RNA antagonists that block synthesis of PCSK9) and bile acid binding resins.

Bile acid binding resins are cholestyramine, colesevelam (preferred because of fewer side effects) and colestipol. They inhibit the enterohepatic circulation, so bile acid in the liver falls, cholesterol synthesis rises, demand for cholesterol and LDL rises, LDL receptors increase and plasma LDL finally falls. Their side effects are GI upset (diarrhea/bloating), hypertriglyceridemia, hyperchloremic alkalosis, reduced fat-soluble vitamins E/D/A/K and reduced absorption of other drugs. Uniquely among hypolipidemics they are safe and efficacious as DOC in pregnancy and children, because all other hypolipidemics are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Statins: Mechanism of Action and Pleiotropic Effects

Statins save lives by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme with maximum activity at night; the resulting effects are lowered LDL, VLDL and TG along with raised HDL and Lp-alpha. Beyond lipid lowering, statins have pleiotropic (non-hypolipidemic) effects: they are anti-aggregant, anti-coagulant, vasodilators through increased release of nitric oxide, antioxidants, anti-inflammatory and they stabilise the atherosclerotic plaque.

Statins are DOC in type II hyperlipoproteinemia and are used for ASCVD prophylaxis: primary prophylaxis in those with no prior attack but raised LDL/DM or a history of familial hypercholesterolemia, and secondary prophylaxis when there is a history of angina, MI or stroke. They are absorbed orally and taken up by the liver through OATP1B1; OATP1B1 is blocked by gemfibrozil and clarithromycin, producing statin toxicity, and clarithromycin also blocks glucuronidation and CYP3A4. All statins are CYP3A4 substrates except fluvastatin and rosuvastatin (CYP2C9) and pravastatin, which is excreted unchanged, is best in liver failure and is DOC for protease inhibitor induced dyslipidemia.
Statin Side Effects, Contraindications and Clinical Applications in ASCVD

Before starting a statin, baseline CPK and LFT are done although monitoring is not required. Side effects are myopathy (increased with fibrates), hepatotoxicity and hyperglycemia; contraindications are pregnancy and children below 11 years (pravastatin below 8 years), and if a fibrate must be combined, fluvastatin is relatively safer. In ASCVD with raised LDL, an LDL of 100-190 mg/dL plus a 10-year ASCVD risk of 5-20% gets a moderate dose statin while a risk above 20% gets a high dose; diabetes with risk below 20% gets moderate dose and 20% or more gets high dose; and clinical ASCVD gets high dose statins. If response is inadequate, ezetimibe or bile acid binding resins (affordable) or inclisiran can be added.
Management of Hypertriglyceridemia and Familial Hypercholesterolemia

Hypertriglyceridemia is managed according to the risk of ASCVD: when risk is present a statin is tried alone, icosapent is added on an inadequate response and fibrates are then added if the response is still inadequate; when ASCVD risk is absent, fibrates are the DOC for the raised TGs and icosapent is added. Familial hypercholesterolemia is treated with high dose statins as the DOC.
Diuretics: Definition and Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors

Diuretics are drugs that increase loss of water with or without solutes such as Na+ and Cl-, and they are used to manage hypertension, edema and drug toxicities (by increasing excretion). Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act at the proximal convoluted tubule and are given orally as dichlorphenamide, acetazolamide (most commonly used) and methazolamide, or as eye drops of brinzolamide and dorzolamide.
Relevant Physiology: PCT, Thick Ascending Limb and Collecting Duct
