The triangle is the symbol used throughout the diagram for the drug molecule, shown moving from intestinal lumen to blood vessel lumen. (Book p2)
Which set lists the four mechanisms of absorption across the biological membrane in the order i to iv shown in the diagram?
Filtration, simple/passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport
Simple diffusion, filtration, active transport, facilitated diffusion
Active transport, facilitated diffusion, filtration, simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion, active transport, filtration, simple diffusion
The diagram numbers the mechanisms i. Filtration, ii. Simple/passive diffusion (m/c), iii. Facilitated diffusion and iv. Active transport. (Book p2)
The brace labelled 'ATP not required' in the absorption diagram covers which mechanisms?
Filtration, simple/passive diffusion and facilitated diffusion
Filtration (i), simple/passive diffusion (ii) and facilitated diffusion (iii) are bracketed together as processes in which ATP is not required; only active transport needs ATP. (Book p2)
Of the four absorption mechanisms shown, which one alone requires ATP?
Active transport (iv) is the only mechanism annotated 'ATP required'; the other three lie inside the 'ATP not required' brace. (Book p2)
In the absorption diagram, the mechanism marked 'm/c' (most common) is:
Simple/passive diffusion carries the annotation 'm/c', i.e., it is the most common mechanism by which drugs cross biological membranes. (Book p2)
Which mechanism of absorption is carrier-mediated but does NOT require ATP?
Facilitated diffusion uses a carrier (e.g. GLUT receptors) but still follows the concentration gradient and needs no ATP, so it lies on the 'ATP not required' side of the diagram. (Book p2)
In the absorption diagram, filtration (i) carries the drug across the membrane through:
Filtration is drawn as a drug moving through a pore/channel in the biological membrane, with no carrier involvement. (Book p2)
The example of a drug absorbed by filtration given in the diagram is:
The diagram reads 'i. Filtration: Eg: Insulin (subcutaneous)' — insulin is the cited example of a drug absorbed through pores by filtration. (Book p2)
Filtration as depicted in the absorption diagram requires which of the following?
A concentration gradient but no ATP
Filtration sits under the 'ATP not required' brace: drug passes down its gradient through pores without ATP or a carrier. (Book p2)
The most common mechanism of drug absorption across biological membranes is:
The diagram marks simple/passive diffusion as 'm/c' — the most common route of drug absorption. (Book p2)
In the diagram, simple/passive diffusion (ii) is annotated as occurring:
Against the concentration gradient using ATP
Simple/passive diffusion is labelled 'along conc. gradient' — the drug moves from higher to lower concentration without ATP. (Book p2)
Filtration and simple/passive diffusion share which feature in the absorption diagram?
Both occur along the concentration gradient
Both are independent of the concentration gradient
Filtration and simple diffusion both sit under 'ATP not required' and both move drug down its concentration gradient; only filtration uses membrane pores. (Book p2)
Unlike simple/passive diffusion, filtration requires the drug to pass through:
Filtration is drawn as passage through a pore in the biological membrane, whereas simple diffusion is drawn crossing the membrane lipid directly. (Book p2)
Mechanism iii, facilitated diffusion, differs from simple diffusion in that it requires:
The diagram draws facilitated diffusion with a carrier (it lies under the 'Carrier mediated transport' bracket) while still moving drug along the concentration gradient. (Book p2)
The example of facilitated diffusion cited in the diagram is:
The diagram reads 'iii. Facilitated diffusion: Eg: GLUT receptors' — GLUT is the cited carrier for facilitated diffusion. (Book p2)
GLUT-mediated absorption, as annotated in the diagram, is based on:
The annotation reads 'GLUT absorption based on gradient' — GLUT carriers move substrate down its concentration gradient without ATP. (Book p2)
Yes, but only in the intestine
No, it lies under 'ATP not required'
Only when the gradient is reversed
Facilitated diffusion sits inside the brace marked 'ATP not required' in the diagram; it uses a carrier but no energy. (Book p2)
Mechanism iv, active transport, is characterised in the diagram as:
Along the concentration gradient, no ATP
Independent of concentration gradient and ATP
Independent of concentration gradient, ATP required
