The flowchart shows that after absorption a fraction is excreted and a fraction undergoes hepatic first pass metabolism, so only the remainder reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p7)
The formula for bioavailability given in the box is:
The box reads 'Bioavailability: AUCoral / AUCiv × 100'. (Book p7)
In the concentration-time curve, the area under the curve (AUC) represents the:
The text links the AUC to the 'Extent of Drug Absorption' — extent is measured by AUC, whereas rate is measured by Tmax. (Book p7)
The only route of administration with 100% bioavailability is:
'Only route with 100% B.V: I/V' — intravenous administration bypasses absorption and first pass metabolism. (Book p7)
On the concentration-time curve, which route gives the immediately maximal plasma concentration at time zero?
The curve is labelled 'IV max' at the highest point at zero time, while the oral curve rises later and shows a smaller AUC. (Book p7)
The oral curve in the concentration-time graph lies below the IV curve because of:
First pass metabolism and incomplete absorption
The smaller (oral) AUC compared with IV reflects the fractions lost to excretion and first pass metabolism before the drug reaches the systemic circulation, giving F < 1. (Book p7)
As per the table, the bioavailability of the IV route is:
The table lists IV → bioavailability '1', i.e., 100%. (Book p8)
As per the table, the bioavailability of the IM/SC route is:
The table lists im/sc → 0.75–1.0, slightly less than the intravenous route but still high. (Book p8)
As per the table, the bioavailability of the oral route is:
The table lists oral → 0.05–1.0, the widest range of all routes because first pass metabolism differs from drug to drug. (Book p8)
Which route shows the widest range of bioavailability in the table?
Oral spans 0.05–1.0, i.e., from 5% to complete bioavailability, whereas IV is fixed at 1 and im/sc at 0.75–1.0. (Book p8)
The note following the route table states that bioavailability does NOT indicate:
'Note: F does not indicate rate of drug absorption' — F measures the extent (AUC), not the speed, of absorption. (Book p8)
Maximum plasma concentration achieved by a drug
Time to reach the maximum concentration
'Cmax: maximum plasma conc achieved by a drug' — it is the peak of the plasma concentration-time curve. (Book p8)
Tmax is a marker of the:
'Tmax: marker of rate of drug absorption' — the sooner the peak occurs, the faster the absorption. (Book p8)
Two formulations of the same drug show Tmax of 1 hour and 4 hours respectively. This indicates a difference in:
Tmax is the marker of the rate of drug absorption; extent would instead be compared using AUC. (Book p8)
Which parameter reflects the extent, and which reflects the rate, of drug absorption?
The AUC measures the extent of absorption (and hence bioavailability), while Tmax is the marker of the rate of absorption. (Book p8)
On the rate-of-absorption graph, the peak of the plasma concentration (PC) curve corresponds to:
The graph marks Cmax at the top of the curve and Tmax on the time axis directly below it. (Book p8)
Bioequivalence is defined as two pharmaceutically equivalent compounds with similar:
'Bioequivalence: Two pharmaceutically equivalent compound with similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption.' (Book p8)
A branded drug is defined in the text as one which is:
A legal copy made after patent expiry
'Branded drug: One which is invented, patented for 20 years' — during this period no generic copy can be marketed. (Book p8)
A generic drug is defined as:
A legal copy of a new drug made after the patent expires
A drug invented and patented for 20 years
A drug with a different active moiety
'Generic drug: Legal copy of a new drug (Done after patent expires).' (Book p8)
The stated benefit of a generic drug is that it is:
'Benefit of a generic drug: Cheaper' — the generic contains the same drug but costs less. (Book p8)
For approval of a generic drug, the required application is:
'For generic drug approval: ANDA (Abbreviated New Drug Application)' — the abbreviated filing relies on bioequivalence rather than full clinical data. (Book p8)
The criteria for approving a generic drug is that it is bioequivalent to the branded drug within:
'Generic drug = Bioequivalent to Branded drug ±20%' — the generic must fall within ±20% of the branded product. (Book p8)
A generic formulation of a drug has an AUC 20% lower than the branded product, with a similar Tmax. It will be:
Rejected, since any difference is unacceptable
Approved only if Tmax is identical
Rejected, because AUC must be equal
The approval criterion is bioequivalence to the branded drug within ±20%; a 20% difference in AUC with similar rate falls within this limit. (Book p8)
Two generic products of the same drug are compared. Bioequivalence between them is judged by similarity of:
Bioequivalence means similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption; the approval limit against the branded drug is ±20%. (Book p8)
Which of the following is TRUE regarding F and Tmax?
F reflects the extent of absorption while Tmax reflects its rate
Both F and Tmax reflect the rate of absorption
Both F and Tmax reflect the extent of absorption
F reflects the rate of absorption while Tmax reflects its extent
F is derived from AUC and denotes the extent of absorption (and does not indicate rate), whereas Tmax is the marker of the rate of drug absorption. (Book p8)
Apparent volume of distribution (AVD) is defined as the:
Hypothetical volume of plasma in litres necessary to account for the total amount of drug in the patient's body
Actual volume of plasma in litres measured by dilution
Volume of drug solution administered intravenously
Volume of drug distributed to adipose tissue
'Hypothetical volume of plasma in litres necessary to account for the total amount of drug (intravascularly and extravascularly) in the patient's body.' (Book p9)
In the definition of AVD, the 'total amount of drug' refers to drug present:
The definition specifies the total amount of drug, both intravascularly and extravascularly, in the patient's body. (Book p9)
A drug with a high AVD is located mostly in the:
'Drug with ↑AVD → mostly in Extravascular compartment/Tissue.' (Book p9)
A drug with a low AVD is located mostly in the:
'Drug with ↓AVD → mostly in Intravascular compartment/Systemic.' (Book p9)
It is a hypothetical volume, not a real anatomical space
It is measured directly in plasma
It is calculated only for IV drugs
AVD is defined as a hypothetical volume of plasma in litres needed to account for the total drug in the body, not a real measured compartment. (Book p9)
The formula given for apparent volume of distribution is:
AVD = D(dose)/C0 × f, where C0 is the initial plasma concentration and f is bioavailability. (Book p9)
In the AVD formula, C0 represents the:
The arrow under the formula labels C0 as 'Initial plasma concentration' — the concentration extrapolated to zero time after IV dosing. (Book p9)
In the AVD formula, f stands for:
'f: Bioavailability' — and the text notes 'f = 1 in intravenous route'. (Book p9)
In which route is the value of f taken as 1?
'f = 1 in intravenous route' — the IV route has 100% bioavailability, so f = 1. (Book p9)
The formula given for loading dose is:
Loading dose: D = AVD × CT/f, where CT is the target plasma concentration. (Book p9)
In the loading dose formula, CT is the:
CT is labelled 'Target plasma concentration (constant)' — the concentration we wish to achieve and maintain. (Book p9)
As shown in the box, the loading dose is:
The text states 'D ∝ AVD/f': loading dose rises with a larger volume of distribution and falls with higher bioavailability. (Book p9)
If the AVD of a drug is increased, the loading dose must be:
'If AVD of a drug is ↑, Dose is increased to maintain CT' — a bigger apparent volume needs a bigger loading dose. (Book p9)
A drug has a large AVD and low bioavailability. Its loading dose will be:
Since D ∝ AVD/f, a big volume of distribution and a low f both increase the required loading dose to achieve the target concentration. (Book p9)
Which of the following is a factor determining apparent volume of distribution?
The factors listed are fat content, lipid solubility (pKa), albumin/plasma protein binding and tissue binding — gastric/urinary pH relate to ionisation, not distribution. (Book p9)
In obese individuals, the volume of distribution of a drug:
'Obesity: ↑ volume of distribution (vd)' — excess fat increases the compartment available to lipid-soluble drug. (Book p9)
In athletes, the volume of distribution of a drug:
Is equal to that in obesity
'Athletes: ↓ vd' — athletes have less fat and more lean tissue, lowering the apparent volume of distribution for fat-soluble drugs. (Book p9)
Regarding sex, the volume of distribution is greater in:
Females, because of higher fat content
Males, because of higher fat content
Females, because of higher muscle mass
Males, because of higher muscle mass
'Sex: F(↑ Fat content) > M' — women have more fat, hence a higher volume of distribution. (Book p9)
Which drug property is listed as a determinant of AVD?
'Lipid Soluble (pKa)' is listed among the factors determining AVD — a more lipid-soluble drug partitions into tissues and has a larger volume of distribution. (Book p9)
Plasma protein (albumin) binding is related to the volume of distribution as:
'Albumin binding (Plasma protein binding) ∝ 1/vd' — the more a drug is bound to plasma protein, the more it is retained intravascularly and the smaller its volume of distribution. (Book p9)
Which factor tends to hold drug outside the plasma and thereby raise the AVD?
Tissue binding is listed as a factor; drug bound in tissues is not in plasma, so the apparent volume of distribution is large. (Book p9)
A 20-year-old athlete and an obese diabetic man receive the same lipid-soluble drug. Compared with the obese man, the athlete will have:
A volume of distribution equal to plasma volume
Obesity increases vd while athletes have a lower vd; the higher fat content of an obese individual expands the drug's apparent distribution volume. (Book p9)
Which of the following factors would DECREASE the apparent volume of distribution of a drug?
Albumin binding is inversely related to vd (binding ∝ 1/vd), whereas tissue binding, obesity and lipid solubility all raise vd. (Book p9)
The example given for pattern of distribution is that digoxin distributes to:
'Distribution of Digoxin → Skeletal muscle > Heart' — the mass of skeletal muscle exceeds that of the heart. (Book p9)
Digoxin distributes to skeletal muscle more than to the heart because of the:
Greater affinity of skeletal muscle receptors
The diary attributes it to the greater mass ('d/t ↑ mass') of skeletal muscle compared with the heart, which is the target organ. (Book p9)
In the digoxin example, the heart is described as the:
The heart is labelled '(Target organ)' while skeletal muscle, being greater in mass, becomes the main distribution site. (Book p9)
The loading dose of digoxin is determined by:
Lean body mass and not total body mass
Total body mass and not lean body mass
'Hence loading dose is determined by lean body mass (not total body mass)' — fat contributes little to digoxin's distribution. (Book p9)
A morbidly obese patient requires a digoxin loading dose. Basing the dose on total body weight would:
Overdose the patient, because digoxin distributes to lean mass
Underdose the patient, because fat stores digoxin
Be correct, because fat binds digoxin
Have no effect on the dose
Because digoxin's loading dose is set by lean body mass and not total body mass, dosing a very obese patient on total weight would exceed the requirement. (Book p9)
A very high AVD leads to which pair of concentration changes?
'↑↑vd → ↑extravascular concentration; ↓intravascular concentration' — the drug is mostly outside the plasma. (Book p9)
Dialysis is ineffective in toxicity of drugs with a high AVD because:
The drug is largely outside the vascular compartment
The drug is too large to be dialysed
The drug is bound to dialyser membranes
The drug is metabolised during dialysis

With a high vd the extravascular concentration is high and the intravascular concentration low, so dialysis can remove only a negligible intravascular fraction — hence the note 'Dialysis is ineffective'. (Book p9)
In toxicity due to drugs that are not cleared by dialysis, treatment is with:
The text states 'Antidotes are given in toxicity' — for high-vd drugs the antidote, not dialysis, is the treatment. (Book p9)
A patient with organophosphate poisoning has a drug with a very high vd. The appropriate management per the text is:
Give the antidote atropine, as dialysis is ineffective
For high-vd drugs, dialysis is ineffective (low intravascular concentration) and antidotes are given — the table pairs organophosphates with atropine. (Book p9)
The mnemonic BADDOC lists drugs with:
The page is headed 'Drugs with ↑ vd: mnemonic: BADDOC.' — these are the drugs that are not cleared by dialysis. (Book p10)
In the mnemonic BADDOC, the letter 'O' stands for:
BADDOC = Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, opiOids, Calcium channel blockers; organophosphates are also listed in the table but O stands for opioids. (Book p10)
In the mnemonic BADDOC, the letter 'C' stands for:
BADDOC ends with Calcium channel blockers, which are treated with calcium gluconate. (Book p10)
In BADDOC, the two groups beginning with the letter 'B' are:
BADDOC = Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, Opioids, Calcium channel blockers. (Book p10)
The table of drugs with ↑vd is titled 'Drugs not cleared by dialysis', and the second column lists their:
The two columns are 'Drugs not cleared by dialysis' and 'Antidotes' — for each high-vd drug the specific antidote is given. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for benzodiazepine toxicity is:
Benzodiazepines → Flumazenil in the antidote table. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for beta blocker toxicity is:
Beta blockers (blocks GPCR) → Glucagon (↑cAMP): glucagon raises cAMP by a non-β-receptor route, bypassing the blocked receptor. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for amphetamine toxicity is:
Amphetamines → Ammonium chloride, the urine acidifier that traps the basic drug for excretion. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for digoxin toxicity is:
Digoxin immune Fab only by dialysis
Digoxin → Digibind in the antidote table; because digoxin has a high vd, dialysis would not clear it. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for opioid toxicity is:
Opioids → Naloxone, the opioid receptor antagonist. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for organophosphate toxicity is:
Organophosphates → Atropine, which reverses the muscarinic effects of the accumulated acetylcholine. (Book p10)
As per the table, the antidote for calcium channel blocker toxicity is:
Calcium channel blockers → Calcium gluconate, which supplies calcium to overcome the channel blockade. (Book p10)
Which drug-antidote pair is INCORRECTLY matched?
Calcium channel blockers are treated with calcium gluconate; naloxone is the antidote for opioids. (Book p10)
A patient with beta blocker overdose is unresponsive to atropine. Which agent from the antidote table should be given?
The table lists beta blockers → glucagon (↑cAMP); glucagon bypasses the blocked β receptor by increasing cAMP directly. (Book p10)
Why is haemodialysis NOT the treatment of choice in opioid overdose per this page?
Opioids have a high volume of distribution and are not cleared by dialysis
Opioids are too tightly protein bound
Opioids are cleared by the lungs
The table places opioids in the 'drugs not cleared by dialysis' group (BADDOC, high vd), so the antidote naloxone is used instead. (Book p10)
Which drug from BADDOC has a specific antibody fragment as its antidote?
The table pairs digoxin with Digibind; digoxin's large volume of distribution is why dialysis cannot clear it. (Book p10)
A patient with benzodiazepine overdose and a high AVD is given flumazenil rather than dialysis because:
Drugs in BADDOC are not cleared by dialysis
The table's very heading is 'Drugs not cleared by dialysis', listing benzodiazepines with flumazenil as the antidote — a direct consequence of their high volume of distribution. (Book p10)
Which of the following is NOT a member of the BADDOC group?
BADDOC = Benzodiazepines, Beta blockers, Amphetamines, Digoxin, Opioids, Calcium channel blockers; phenytoin is not part of this high-vd group. (Book p10)
The most important plasma protein binding acidic drugs, and the most common binding protein, is:
'Albumin → Binds to Acidic drugs (m/c)' — albumin is the commonest plasma protein that binds acidic drugs. (Book p10)
'α1 acid glycoprotein: Basic drugs' — basic drugs such as lidocaine and opioids bind α1 acid glycoprotein. (Book p10)
Which of the following is listed as a drug bound to albumin?
Antipsychotics are in the albumin column; lidocaine, tricyclic antidepressants and amiodarone bind α1 acid glycoprotein. (Book p10)
The antibiotics listed in the albumin column are:
The albumin list includes 'Antibiotics: sulfonamides'. (Book p10)
The anticoagulant listed as an albumin-bound drug is:
'Anticoagulant: warfarin' appears in the albumin column, together with aspirin. (Book p10)
Which set lists drugs bound to albumin as per the table?
Antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, warfarin and aspirin
The albumin column lists antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, antibiotics (sulfonamides), warfarin and aspirin. (Book p10)
Which set lists drugs bound to α1 acid glycoprotein?
Tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics (beta blocker, amiodarone, lidocaine)
The α1 acid glycoprotein column lists tricyclic antidepressants, opioids and antiarrhythmics — beta blockers, amiodarone and lidocaine. (Book p10)
Lidocaine, amiodarone and beta blockers are bound to:
These three antiarrhythmics are listed under α1 acid glycoprotein, the binding protein for basic drugs. (Book p10)
A basic drug such as an opioid will bind mainly to:
α1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs such as opioids, tricyclic antidepressants and antiarrhythmics; albumin binds acidic drugs. (Book p10)
Which pairing of drug and binding protein is correct?
Aspirin — albumin; lidocaine — α1 acid glycoprotein
Aspirin — α1 acid glycoprotein; lidocaine — albumin
Warfarin — α1 acid glycoprotein; opioids — albumin
Sulfonamides — α1 acid glycoprotein; amiodarone — albumin
Aspirin, warfarin, sulfonamides and antiepileptics are albumin bound (acidic drugs), while lidocaine, opioids, tricyclics and amiodarone bind α1 acid glycoprotein (basic drugs). (Book p10)
Warfarin and aspirin used together increase each other's plasma concentration, leading to:
The bracket linking warfarin and aspirin reads 'Increase each others plasma conc. if used together ↓ ↑Bleeding'. (Book p10)
Both warfarin and aspirin are bound to the same plasma protein. When given together, the result is:
Increased renal excretion of the free drug
Because both are albumin-bound, they compete for and displace each other, raising the free (unbound) concentration — hence the increased bleeding shown in the table. (Book p10)
As per the table, a fall in albumin produces:
↑ Free drug and ↑ risk of toxicity
↑ Free drug and ↓ risk of toxicity
The albumin column reads: ↓Albumin → ↑Free drug → ↑Risk of toxicity. (Book p10)
As per the table, an increase in α1 glycoprotein produces:
The α1 acid glycoprotein column reads: ↑α1 glycoprotein → ↓Free drug → ↓Effect. (Book p10)
The two plasma-protein changes have opposite clinical consequences, which are:
Less albumin leaves more free drug and risk of toxicity, whereas more α1 acid glycoprotein binds more drug, lowering free drug and effect. (Book p10)
A drug is 90% bound to albumin. In a patient with hypoalbuminaemia, the fraction of free drug:
Increases, raising the risk of toxicity
The table states that a fall in albumin raises the free drug concentration and therefore the risk of toxicity. (Book p10)
The inverse relationship between albumin binding and volume of distribution explains why drugs that are highly albumin bound:
Have a low AVD as they stay intravascular
Have a high AVD as they enter tissue
Albumin binding ∝ 1/vd, so a heavily albumin-bound drug remains largely in the intravascular compartment and has a low apparent volume of distribution. (Book p9)
Which statement about plasma protein binding and drug effect is correct?
Only the free (unbound) drug is active, so ↓albumin raises toxicity while ↑α1 gp lowers effect
Bound drug is the active form, so more binding means more effect
Protein binding has no relation to drug effect
↓Albumin and ↑α1 gp have the same clinical consequence
The table's 'effect on drugs' row shows ↓albumin → ↑free drug → ↑toxicity, and ↑α1 gp → ↓free drug → ↓effect: free drug, not bound drug, produces the effect. (Book p10)
Which condition is listed as a cause of decreased albumin?
Under ↓Albumin the text lists nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus; the inflammatory states and MI belong to the ↑α1 gp list. (Book p10)
Which set lists the causes of decreased albumin given in the table?
Nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis, IBD and myocardial infarction
Nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus are listed as conditions with ↓Albumin. (Book p10)
As per the table, α1 glycoprotein is increased in:
'↑α1 gp: Inflammatory — rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease; myocardial infarction'. (Book p10)
Which of the following is listed under inflammatory causes of increased α1 glycoprotein?
Rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease
Rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease are listed, along with myocardial infarction, as conditions that raise α1 glycoprotein. (Book p10)
A patient with nephrotic syndrome is prescribed an albumin-bound drug. Compared with a healthy adult, you should expect:
A higher free drug level and greater toxicity risk
A lower free drug level and reduced effect
No change in free drug level
Increased protein binding of the drug
Nephrotic syndrome causes ↓albumin; the table shows ↓Albumin → ↑Free drug → ↑Risk of toxicity. (Book p10)
A patient with myocardial infarction receives lidocaine. Because α1 glycoprotein is raised in MI:
Free lidocaine falls and its effect is reduced
Free lidocaine rises and toxicity occurs
α1 acid glycoprotein (which binds lidocaine, a basic drug) rises in MI, so free drug falls and the effect is reduced. (Book p10)
In a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, drugs bound to α1 acid glycoprotein will show:
Reduced free concentration and reduced effect
Rheumatoid arthritis raises α1 glycoprotein; the table shows ↑α1 gp → ↓free drug → ↓effect. (Book p10)
Which condition is NOT associated with a fall in albumin as per the table?
Myocardial infarction belongs to the ↑α1 glycoprotein group, not the ↓albumin group, which comprises nephrotic syndrome, CKD, liver cirrhosis and diabetes mellitus. (Book p10)
A patient with diabetes mellitus on a highly albumin-bound antiepileptic drug develops features of toxicity. The explanation is:
Low albumin raises the free drug fraction
High α1 glycoprotein raises the free drug fraction
Diabetes mellitus is listed among the causes of ↓albumin; with less binding protein there is more free drug and hence a risk of toxicity. (Book p10)
An elderly woman with liver cirrhosis is prescribed a warfarin-like albumin-bound drug. Which risk is increased?
Free drug toxicity due to low albumin
Reduced effect due to high albumin
Loss of the drug in urine
Liver cirrhosis lowers albumin; the table shows ↓Albumin → ↑Free drug → ↑Risk of toxicity. (Book p10)
Phase I metabolism of most drugs converts the active drug into:
The Phase I flowchart reads: most drugs (active) → drug broken down → inactivated, generating a functional group. (Book p11)
In Phase I metabolism, a prodrug (inactive) is:
Inactivated by conjugation with glucuronic acid
Broken down to a functional group and activated
Converted into a more lipid-soluble compound
The Phase I flowchart shows 'Pro drug (inactive) → drug broken down → Activated', with a functional group generated — this is how prodrugs are switched on. (Book p11)
The product of Phase I metabolism, common to both prodrug activation and drug inactivation, is:
Drug conjugated to a -ve charged moiety
Both arms of the Phase I flowchart converge on 'Drug + Functional group', which is then handed over to Phase II for conjugation. (Book p11)
Conjugation of the drug with a functional group
Oxidation of the drug by CYP450
Hydrolysis of the drug by esterases
Reduction of the drug by microsomal enzymes
The heading reads 'Phase II: Drug + Functional group', with an arrow labelled 'conjugate (-ve charged)' showing that Phase II attaches a conjugate to the Phase I product. (Book p11)
The conjugate added in Phase II metabolism carries which charge?
Variable charge depending on the drug
The Phase II diagram labels the conjugate '(-ve charged)'; this charged conjugate is what makes the metabolite water soluble. (Book p11)
Conjugation in Phase II renders the drug:
Ionised and water soluble, easily excreted
Volatile and excreted by the lungs
Phase II output: drug + functional group + conjugate → ionized and water soluble → easily excreted. (Book p11)
Which sequence correctly describes the two phases of drug metabolism?
Phase I conjugates; Phase II oxidises
Phase I generates a functional group; Phase II conjugates it
Both phases are performed only by gut bacteria

Phase I reactions create a functional group on the drug (oxidation being the most common), and Phase II then conjugates that group, making the drug ionised, water soluble and easily excreted. (Book p11)
The note about placebo states that placebo:
Contains a subtherapeutic dose of drug
Note: placebo does not contain any drug — it is used purely for the psychological (expectation) effect in trials. (Book p11)
Which antimalarial drug is listed as a prodrug?
The prodrug list begins with proguanil — an inactive compound activated by metabolism into its antimalarial form. (Book p11)
Regarding ACE inhibitors as prodrugs, the book states:
Ramipril and other ACE inhibitors are prodrugs, except captopril and lisinopril
Only captopril and lisinopril are prodrugs
No ACE inhibitor is a prodrug
'Ramipril & other ACE inhibitors (except Captopril, Lisinopril)' — captopril and lisinopril are already active, so they are the two exceptions to the prodrug rule. (Book p11)
Which pair of drugs from the prodrug list is used for Parkinson's disease or its related movement disorders?
The list includes 'Dipivefrine, Levodopa' — levodopa is the classic prodrug converted to dopamine in the brain. (Book p11)
Which antisecretory (antidiarrhoeal) drug is listed as a prodrug?
Racecadotril appears in the prodrug list; it is hydrolysed to its active enkephalinase-inhibiting metabolite. (Book p11)
Which two anticancer drugs are listed as prodrugs?
The list ends with 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine — both require intracellular metabolic activation to their cytotoxic nucleotides. (Book p11)
Which of the following pairs from the prodrug list are both used in acid-related disorders (ulcer disease)?
The third prodrug line lists 'Oxcarbazepine, Omeprazole'; omeprazole is activated in acid-secreting gastric parietal cells, and oxcarbazepine is reduced to its active metabolite. (Book p11)
Which of the following is NOT a prodrug as listed in the book?
Lisinopril (along with captopril) is specifically named as the exception — it is not a prodrug, unlike ramipril and the other ACE inhibitors. (Book p11)
A 60-year-old man on ramipril for hypertension has poor blood-pressure control. The reason ramipril needs metabolic activation is that it is a:
Prodrug requiring conversion to its active form
Drug with a very short half-life
Competitive inhibitor of its own metabolism
Ramipril is a prodrug (ramipril is converted to the active ramiprilat); prodrugs are inactive as given and must be metabolised before they act. (Book p11)
The mnemonic for Phase I reactions is:

ORCHAD stands for Oxidation, Reduction, Cyclization, Hydrolysis, Aliphatic hydroxylation, Aromatic hydroxylation and Deamination — the Phase I reactions. HIPS Dance, LUNJA and WIPE belong to other topics. (Book p11)
The most common (m/c) Phase I reaction is:
The list marks 'Oxidation (m/c)' — oxidation, catalysed chiefly by the CYP450 enzymes, is the commonest Phase I reaction. (Book p11)
Which of the following belongs to the Phase I reaction list?
Hydrolysis is one of the ORCHAD Phase I reactions; sulfation, glucuronidation and methylation are Phase II conjugation reactions. (Book p11)
Aliphatic hydroxylation and aromatic hydroxylation are classified as:
Both appear in the ORCHAD Phase I list (A = aliphatic hydroxylation, A = aromatic hydroxylation) and are carried out by microsomal CYP450 enzymes. (Book p11)
Phase I reactions are carried out by:
'Phase I reactions are enabled by microsomal CYP450 enzymes' — the cytochrome P450 system is the principal Phase I machinery. (Book p11)
Phase II reactions are named after:
The organ in which they occur
The Phase I reaction that preceded them
The heading states 'Phase II Reaction: Named after the conjugate' — e.g. glucuronidation is named after glucuronic acid added as the conjugate. (Book p11)
The most common (m/c) Phase II reaction, and the only microsomal one, is:
'Glucuronidation (m/c): microsomal' — glucuronidation is the commonest Phase II reaction and the exception that takes place in the microsomes. (Book p11)
Which group of Phase II reactions are non-microsomal?
Glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation
The brace labelled 'Non microsomal reactions' brackets glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation — glucuronidation is left outside because it is microsomal. (Book p11)
Which Phase II reaction is listed as microsomal?
Glucuronidation is annotated 'microsomal', while acetylation, glutathionation, glycination, methylation and sulfation are grouped as non-microsomal. (Book p11)
CY (cytochrome) is best described as a:
Heme protein that binds oxygen and facilitates metabolism
Conjugate added in Phase II metabolism
Pump that effluxes drugs from cells
Plasma protein that binds acidic drugs
'CY (cytochrome): Heme protein that binds oxygen → facilitates metabolism' — the haem iron is what allows CYP450 to oxidise drugs. (Book p12)
The '450' in cytochrome P450 refers to:
Enzymes discovered in plant pigment, absorbing light of 450 nm wavelength
The molecular weight of the enzyme in kilodaltons
The number of substrate families known
'P450: enzymes discovered in plant pigment, absorbs light of 450 nm wavelength' — the name comes from the spectral absorption peak of the reduced CO-bound pigment. (Book p12)
In the nomenclature CYP1A2, the numeral '1' denotes the:
'1 → denotes the family. A → subfamily. 2 → geneisoform number' — so CYP1A2 = family 1, subfamily A, isoform 2. (Book p12)
In the nomenclature CYP1A2, the letter 'A' denotes the:
The letter is the subfamily (A in CYP1A2); the first number is the family and the last number the geneisoform. (Book p12)
CYP1A2 is the example given in the book to illustrate which aspect of CYP nomenclature?
The microsomal location of CYP enzymes
The induction of CYP by rifampicin
Eg CYP1A2 is used to explain that the numeral denotes family, the letter the subfamily and the final numeral the geneisoform number. (Book p12)
Which drugs are metabolised by CYP1A2?
CYP1A2: paracetamol, tacrine and theophylline. (Book p12)
Which two drugs are metabolised by CYP2B6?
CYP2C9: phenytoin and warfarin — the basis of the classic warfarin-phenytoin interaction. (Book p12)
CYP2C19 performs which two opposite functions on its substrates?
It metabolises omeprazole and activates clopidogrel
It metabolises clopidogrel and activates omeprazole
It activates both omeprazole and clopidogrel
It metabolises both omeprazole and clopidogrel
CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole but activates clopidogrel — one enzyme, opposite clinical consequences for its two substrates. (Book p12)
In the CYP2C19 note, omeprazole and clopidogrel are described as:
Competitive inhibitors (substrates of the same enzyme)
Two drugs metabolised by different enzymes
They are bracketed as 'Competitive inhibitors (substrates of the same enzyme)' — both compete for CYP2C19. (Book p12)
A patient on clopidogrel after stenting is prescribed omeprazole for dyspepsia. The expected consequence is:
Omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel
Omeprazole increases the effect of clopidogrel
No interaction, as they act on different enzymes
Omeprazole increases clopidogrel levels causing bleeding
As stated: 'Omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel' — it competes with clopidogrel for CYP2C19, so less clopidogrel is activated to its active metabolite. (Book p12)
CYP2D6 metabolises which group of drugs?
Psychiatric drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics), opioids and β-blockers
CYP2D6 metabolizes psychiatric drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics), opioids and β-blockers. (Book p12)
Besides metabolising drugs, CYP2D6 is stated to activate:
Under CYP2D6: 'Activates: Tamoxifen' — CYP2D6 converts tamoxifen into its active metabolite endoxifen. (Book p12)
Chronic consumption of ethanol leads to:
The flowchart reads: ethanol — chronic consumption → CYP2E1 upregulation. (Book p12)
Following chronic ethanol consumption, paracetamol is metabolised to increased amounts of NAPQI, resulting in:
Chronic ethanol → CYP2E1 upregulation → paracetamol → ↑NAPQI → hepatotoxicity; CYP2E1-generated NAPQI is the toxic metabolite of paracetamol. (Book p12)
Paracetamol is metabolised predominantly by which enzyme, as noted in the flowchart?
'(Paracetamol metabolised by CYP2E1 >> CYP1A2)' — CYP2E1 accounts for the greater part, which is why alcohol-induced CYP2E1 upregulation predisposes to paracetamol hepatotoxicity. (Book p12)
An alcoholic with chronic liver disease takes an overdose of paracetamol. The risk of hepatotoxicity is high because:
CYP2E1 is upregulated, generating more NAPQI
CYP2E1 is inhibited, so paracetamol accumulates unchanged
Renal excretion of paracetamol is enhanced
Chronic alcohol upregulates CYP2E1, shifting more paracetamol to the toxic NAPQI pathway and causing hepatotoxicity. (Book p12)
The most common (m/c) CYP450 enzyme is:
'CYP3A4 (m/c): metabolises >50% of drugs' — it is the most common isoform, handling more than half of all drugs. (Book p12)
CYP3A4 metabolises >50% of drugs, and mifepristone is the example given. (Book p12)
The example of a drug metabolised by CYP3A4 given in the book is:
'metabolises >50% of drugs (eg: mifepristone)' — mifepristone is quoted as a CYP3A4 substrate. (Book p12)
Atazanavir causes which adverse effect through glucuronidation-related metabolism?
Under glucuronidation: 'Atazanavir (antiviral) — Cause → Steven Johnson syndrome'. (Book p13)
Under glucuronidation: irinotecan (anticancer) → toxicity (its glucuronidation by UGT determines the severity of diarrhoea and neutropenia). (Book p13)
Atazanavir and irinotecan are both contraindicated in:
The brace states 'Both drugs are c/i in Crigler Najjar syndrome' — glucuronidation is already defective there, so these glucuronidated drugs are contraindicated. (Book p13)
Estrogen is metabolised in the liver by:
Phase I with CYP3A4, then Phase II glucuronidation
Phase I with CYP2D6, then sulfation
In the flowchart, liver metabolism of estrogen = Phase I with CYP3A4 and Phase II glucuronidation, forming estrogen + glucuronic acid. (Book p13)
Estrogen + glucuronic acid, which is water soluble
Estrogen + sulfate, which is lipid soluble
Free estrogen, which is water soluble
Estrogen + glutathione, which is lipid soluble
Phase II glucuronidation yields 'estrogen + glucuronic acid (water soluble)', which is then excreted in bile into the small intestine. (Book p13)
In the small intestine, estrogen glucuronide undergoes:
Active transport into the portal vein
Small intestine: glucuronidase action by gut bacteria splits the conjugate, releasing 'estrogen broken down + lipid soluble'. (Book p13)
After gut bacterial glucuronidase acts on estrogen glucuronide, the estrogen becomes:
The deconjugated 'estrogen broken down + lipid soluble' is reabsorbed (returning to the liver along the arrow) — the basis of enterohepatic circulation. (Book p13)
Enterohepatic circulation of estrogen is described as producing:
The boxed label reads 'Enterohepatic Circulation: Extension of normal T½' — recycling through gut and liver keeps estrogen in the body longer. (Book p13)
Antibiotics interfere with estrogen recycling by:
Killing gut bacteria, reducing enterohepatic circulation of estrogen
The flowchart shows antibiotics (with a 'kill' symbol) → ↓enterohepatic circulation of estrogen — by removing the gut bacteria that deconjugate it. (Book p13)
The clinical consequence of antibiotics reducing enterohepatic circulation of estrogen is:
Antibiotics → ↓enterohepatic circulation → ↓T½ → OCP failure; the estrogen is cleared faster and contraceptive cover is lost. (Book p13)
A woman on oral contraceptive pills develops diarrhoea and is given antibiotics. Loss of contraceptive efficacy occurs because:
Gut bacteria are reduced, so estrogen is not deconjugated and recycled
The antibiotic induces CYP3A4 and destroys estrogen
The antibiotic binds estrogen in plasma
The antibiotic increases renal excretion of estrogen
Antibiotics lower gut bacteria and thus reduce enterohepatic circulation of estrogen, shortening its T½ and causing OCP failure. (Book p13)
The mnemonic for the drugs undergoing acetylation is:
HIPS Dance = Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide and Dapsone — the acetylation substrates. (Book p13)
Which of the following drugs undergo acetylation?
Hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide, sulfonamide and dapsone
The HIPS Dance list: Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide, Dapsone. (Book p13)
Which important adverse effect is bracketed against the acetylated drugs?
The brace against the HIPS list reads 'Can cause drug induced SLE' — hydralazine and procainamide are the classic culprits. (Book p13)
A patient on hydralazine for hypertension develops arthralgia, rash and a positive ANA. The likely diagnosis is:
Hydralazine belongs to the acetylated HIPS drugs (Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide, Dapsone) which can cause drug induced SLE. (Book p13)
Drug interactions in this chapter occur due to:
Changes in plasma protein binding only
Competition for renal tubular secretion only
'D/t microsomal enzymes induction or inhibition' — the drug interaction table is built entirely around CYP450 microsomal induction and inhibition. (Book p14)
↑ enzyme → ↑ metabolism → ↓ plasma concentration → drug failure
Inducers increase enzyme amount, so metabolism increases, plasma concentration falls and the drug fails to act. (Book p14)
↓ enzyme → ↓ metabolism → ↑ plasma concentration → drug toxicity
↑ enzyme → ↑ metabolism → ↓ plasma concentration → drug failure
Inhibitors reduce the enzyme, metabolism falls, plasma concentration rises and the drug becomes toxic. (Book p14)
Which group lists the enzyme inducers from the table?
Griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort
Quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin and valproate
Examples of inducers: griseofulvin, rifampicin, alcohol (chronic), benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort. (Book p14)
St. John's wort is described in the table as:
A plant used to treat depression, and an enzyme inducer
A herbal diuretic with no interactions
An enzyme inducer used for epilepsy
'St. John's wart (Plant used to treat depression)' is listed among the inducers — a herbal antidepressant that induces microsomal enzymes and can cause contraceptive failure. (Book p14)
Benzopyrene, an enzyme inducer in the table, is best known as:
Benzopyrene, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon of tobacco smoke, is listed among enzyme inducers (as it induces CYP1A1/1A2). (Book p14)
Which of the following are listed as enzyme inhibitors?
Acute alcohol consumption, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice and diethylcarbamazine
Griseofulvin, rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort

The inhibitor column lists acute alcohol consumption, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice and diethylcarbamazine. (Book p14)
Alcohol appears in the table as both inducer and inhibitor. The correct distinction is:
Acute consumption inhibits; chronic consumption induces
Acute consumption induces; chronic consumption inhibits
Both acute and chronic consumption inhibit
Alcohol is not an enzyme inducer
The table lists 'Alcohol (Chronic)' among inducers and 'Acute alcohol consumption' among inhibitors — the classic acute-inhibition, chronic-induction pattern. (Book p14)
Grapefruit juice is included in the table because it is:
Grapefruit juice appears in the inhibitor list — it inhibits CYP3A4 in the gut wall, raising levels of co-administered CYP3A4 substrates. (Book p14)
Diethylcarbamazine, listed as an enzyme inhibitor, is clinically used as:
Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the antifilarial agent listed among enzyme inhibitors. (Book p14)
Which of the following is an enzyme inducer?
Rifampicin is a classic microsomal enzyme inducer; cimetidine, ketoconazole and valproate are enzyme inhibitors. (Book p14)
Which one of the following is NOT an enzyme inhibitor?
Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer; cimetidine, ciprofloxacin and ketoconazole are all listed inhibitors. (Book p14)
In the interaction table, the effect of an inducer on metabolism and plasma concentration respectively is:
For inducers the cascade is ↑enzyme → ↑metabolism → ↓plasma concentration → drug failure. (Book p14)
Which statement about microsomal enzyme interactions is TRUE?
Inducers cause drug failure, while inhibitors cause drug toxicity
Inducers cause toxicity, while inhibitors cause failure
Both inducers and inhibitors cause failure

The summary of the table: inducers increase metabolism and lower plasma concentration, leading to drug failure; inhibitors reduce metabolism and raise plasma concentration, leading to toxicity. (Book p14)
In the case of OCP failure due to rifampicin, the clinical significance column advises:
Change the method of contraception (IUD or condoms), or avoid enzyme inducers, or ↑ the dose of drugs
Stop rifampicin immediately in all patients
Double the OCP dose and continue rifampicin
Add an enzyme inhibitor to the regimen
For OCP failure due to rifampicin the actions given are: change the method of contraception (IUD or condoms), or avoid enzyme inducers, or ↑ the dose of drugs (eg phenytoin & retigabine). (Book p14)
Which examples are given for increasing the dose of a drug when an enzyme inducer cannot be avoided?
The table cites '(Eg. Phenytoin & Retigabine)' as drugs whose dose is increased when an inducer has to be continued. (Book p14)
Erythromycin, an enzyme inhibitor, leads to theophylline toxicity causing:
Clinical significance of inhibitors: 1. Erythromycin → theophylline toxicity (↓ arrhythmia, ↓ fibrillation) — the arrows indicate the toxic manifestations. (Book p14)
Clarithromycin, an enzyme inhibitor, can precipitate:
'2. Clarithromycin → Statin toxicity' — by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism of statins, clarithromycin can cause myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. (Book p14)
A patient on theophylline develops arrhythmia after being started on erythromycin. The mechanism is:
Reduced renal tubular secretion of theophylline
Erythromycin inhibits the microsomal enzyme metabolising theophylline, so theophylline levels rise and arrhythmia/fibrillation result. (Book p14)
A patient on simvastatin develops muscle pain and raised CK after a course of clarithromycin. This is because clarithromycin:
Inhibits statin metabolism, causing statin toxicity
Induces statin metabolism, causing statin failure
Clarithromycin is a microsomal enzyme inhibitor → statin toxicity; less statin is metabolised, so levels rise and myopathy occurs. (Book p14)
Which type of drug is excreted from the body?
The chapter opens with 'Ionised / water soluble / polar drug' — only the water-soluble, polar form of a drug is available for excretion. (Book p15)
The two major organs of excretion are:
The major organs of excretion are kidneys and liver; minor routes (saliva, sweat) are mentioned separately. (Book p15)
The most common (m/c) organ for excretion is the kidney; the most common organ involved in metabolism is the:
The flowchart marks kidneys as the m/c organ for excretion, and the note states 'm/c organ involved in metabolism → Liver'. (Book p15)
Besides the major organs of excretion, some drugs are excreted through:
'Some drugs are excreted through saliva & sweat' — minor routes that can matter for drug detection and for side effects. (Book p15)
According to the table of excretory mechanisms, filtration accounts for what percentage of drug excretion?
The table columns are headed 'Filtration (20%)' and 'Tubular secretion (80%)'. (Book p15)
Which mechanism accounts for the majority (80%) of drug excretion?
Tubular secretion is labelled 80% while filtration is 20% — active tubular secretion is the dominant renal excretory mechanism. (Book p15)
Table row 'unbound drug': filtration (+) but tubular secretion (−); only the free, unbound fraction is filtered at the glomerulus. (Book p15)
Plasma protein (negative charge) bound drug is excreted by:
Table row 'Plasma protein (negative charge) bound drug': filtration (−) but tubular secretion (+); tubular secretion is the route by which protein-bound drug is still excreted. (Book p15)
Protein-bound drug is not filtered because of the:
Negative charge of the basement membrane
Positive charge of the basement membrane
Large size of the drug molecule alone
Absence of porins in the glomerulus
The table annotates filtration (−) for protein-bound drug as 'd/t −ve charge of basement membrane' — the negatively charged glomerular barrier repels the anionic protein-drug complex. (Book p15)
Variable charge, depending on the drug
The table specifies 'Plasma protein (negative charge) bound drug' — albumin and other plasma proteins are negatively charged. (Book p15)
A patient with hypoalbuminaemia has more unbound drug in plasma. For a drug cleared mainly by filtration, the effect is:
Increased filtration and greater excretion of the drug
No change, since filtration depends only on GFR
It is the unbound fraction that is filtered (+); when plasma protein is low, more drug is unbound, so more is filtered and excreted — the basis for altered dosing in nephrotic syndrome. (Book p15)
Filtration as a mechanism of drug excretion is dependent on:
GFR, giving a constant rate of excretion
Plasma protein binding, giving a variable rate
Tubular reabsorption, giving a zero-order rate
Hepatic blood flow, giving a first-order rate
Note: 'Filtration is dependent on GFR → Constant rate of excretion' — as long as GFR is stable, the filtered amount per unit time stays constant. (Book p15)
A patient with chronic kidney disease has a markedly reduced GFR. Which mechanism of drug excretion is most affected?
Filtration is dependent on GFR, so a fall in GFR directly lowers filtration-based excretion — the reason doses of renally excreted drugs must be reduced. (Book p15)
Rate of drug elimination (RDE) is defined as the:
Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body
Time taken for the drug to fall by half
Fraction of the dose reaching systemic circulation
Volume of plasma cleared of drug per hour
'Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body' — RDE is expressed in mg/hr. (Book p15)
RDE = plasma concentration × Clearance, with the units (mg/hr) = (mg/ml) × (ml/hr). (Book p15)
The units of plasma concentration, clearance and RDE respectively are:
The book writes (mg/hr) under RDE, (mg/ml) under plasma concentration and (ml/hr) under clearance — these units are how the three quantities fit together. (Book p15)
Plasma concentration is defined as the:
Concentration of drug present in each ml of plasma, in mg/ml
Total amount of drug in the body in mg
Volume of plasma containing 1 mg of drug
Amount of drug bound to plasma proteins
'Plasma conc: Conc of drug present in each ml of plasma → mg/ml.' (Book p15)
Drug clearance is defined as the:
Amount of plasma being cleared of the drug per hour
Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body
Volume of distribution of the drug
'Drug clearance: Amount of plasma being cleared of the drugs per hour' — clearance is a volume per unit time, not an amount of drug. (Book p15)
The two modes of drug dosing described are:
Continuous IV infusion and intermittent dosing
Under DRUG DOSING the two headings are (a) continuous IV infusion and (b) intermittent dosing. (Book p15)
Infusion rate / dosing rate is also known as the:
'Infusion rate / dosing rate: AKA loading dose' — a continuous infusion sets up the desired plasma level, whereas the repeated dose that sustains it is the maintenance dose. (Book p16)
In the concentration-time curve of an IV infusion, phase I represents:
Slowly rising state (infusion), where absorption > excretion
A loading dose given as a bolus
Phase I is the slowly rising state of infusion, during which absorption exceeds excretion so plasma concentration climbs. (Book p16)
Phase II of the concentration-time curve represents:
Peak concentration after a bolus dose
Phase II is the flat plateau — steady state plasma concentration, where infusion rate equals the rate of drug elimination. (Book p16)
At the plateau of the infusion curve, the relationship between infusion and elimination is:
Infusion rate = rate of drug elimination
Infusion rate > rate of drug elimination
Infusion rate < rate of drug elimination
The plateau is labelled 'Infusion rate = Rate of drug elimination' — the amount entering the body each hour equals the amount leaving, so the concentration stays steady. (Book p16)
Phase III of the curve is the declining state because:
The drug is redistributed to fat
Phase III is labelled 'Excretion > Absorption' — elimination now exceeds input, so plasma concentration falls. (Book p16)
The infusion rate required to maintain a desired plasma concentration is calculated as:
'Infusion rate = Plasma concentration × clearance' — the same relationship as RDE, since at steady state infusion must match elimination. (Book p16)
How many half-lives are required to attain steady state plasma concentration?
'4–5 T1/2 are required to attain steady state plasma concentration' — this is why a loading dose is given when an immediate effect is needed. (Book p16)
Continuous infusion dosing is stated to depend on:
Under the infusion curve, the bullet 'Depends on volume of distribution' applies to the infusion/loading dose, while the maintenance dose depends on clearance. (Book p16)
According to the page, attainment of steady state depends on:
For continuous IV infusion the page states that steady state depends on volume of distribution. (Book p16)
Intermittent dosing is also known as:
'Intermittent dosing: AKA maintenance dose' — the dose is repeated at intervals to hold the plasma concentration steady. (Book p16)
The purpose of the intermittent (maintenance) dose is to:
Maintain plasma concentration in steady state
'Dose given after a certain period of time to maintain plasma concentration in steady state' — maintenance dosing sustains, rather than establishes, the level. (Book p16)
'Depends on Clearance' — clearance governs how much drug must be replaced per unit time, whereas volume of distribution governs the loading dose. (Book p16)
The maintenance dose is calculated by the formula:
Boxed formula: maintenance dose = PC × CL × Time / f, where f is bioavailability. (Book p16)
In the maintenance dose formula, 'f' denotes:
[f: Bioavailability] — the fraction of the administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p16)
For intravenous routes, the value of f is:
'f = 1 in IV routes' — intravenous administration bypasses absorption barriers, so the entire dose reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p16)
A drug with a bioavailability of 0.5 is to be given orally instead of intravenously. To maintain the same plasma concentration, the oral dose must be:
Since dose = PC × CL × Time / f and f falls from 1 to 0.5, the required dose doubles — oral doses are higher than IV doses for this reason. (Book p16)
Half-life (T1/2) is defined as the time taken by a drug to:
Be completely eliminated from the body
'Time taken by a drug to decrease by 50% in plasma.' (Book p16)
Volume of distribution and inversely proportional to clearance
Clearance and inversely proportional to volume of distribution
Both volume of distribution and clearance
Neither volume of distribution nor clearance
T1/2 ∝ volume of distribution (vd) / Clearance (Cl) — a larger distribution volume prolongs half-life; a higher clearance shortens it. (Book p16)
The formula relating half-life to volume of distribution and clearance is:
T1/2 = 0.693 × vd/Cl — the constant 0.693 (ln 2) converts the first-order rate constant into half-life. (Book p16)
T1/2 = 0.693 / kel — half-life and the elimination rate constant are reciprocally related. (Book p16)
The elimination constant (kel) is equal to:
'Elimination constant (kel) = Cl / vd' — the fraction of the distribution volume cleared per unit time. (Book p16)
If the volume of distribution of a drug increases while clearance remains unchanged, the half-life will:
Since T1/2 = 0.693 × vd/Cl, a rise in vd with constant Cl lengthens the half-life — the drug is spread over a larger volume and cleared more slowly relative to its load. (Book p16)
In a patient with renal failure, clearance of a renally excreted drug falls. The expected effect on the drug is:
Shortened half-life with loss of effect
Because T1/2 ∝ vd/Cl, a fall in clearance prolongs T1/2; the drug stays in the body longer, so dose or interval must be adjusted. (Book p16)
Zero order kinetics means elimination of a:
Constant amount of drug per hour
Constant proportion of drug per hour
Increasing amount of drug per hour
Constant proportion of the dose per half-life
Table row 'elimination of': zero order = constant amount of drug per hour; first order = constant proportion of drug per hour. (Book p17)
First order kinetics means elimination of a:
Constant proportion of drug per hour
Constant amount of drug per hour
Saturating amount of drug per hour
First order: a constant proportion (fraction) of the drug present is eliminated per unit time, so the rate falls as concentration falls. (Book p17)
In the equation RDE = (PC)^n × Cl, the value of n for zero order kinetics is:
For zero order kinetics the table gives n = 0, so RDE becomes independent of plasma concentration (PC^0 = 1). (Book p17)
In the equation RDE = (PC)^n × Cl, the value of n for first order kinetics is:
For first order kinetics n = 1, so RDE ∝ PC — the rate of elimination is directly proportional to the plasma concentration. (Book p17)
When the dose is constant (Cl constant), zero order kinetics gives:
With constant dose and clearance: zero order → RDE = constant, because a fixed amount is eliminated per hour irrespective of concentration. (Book p17)
When the dose is constant (Cl constant), first order kinetics gives:
For first order kinetics RDE ∝ PC — elimination rate changes with concentration, unlike zero order where RDE stays constant. (Book p17)
Which statement comparing zero order and first order kinetics is correct?
Zero order eliminates a constant amount per hour; first order a constant proportion per hour
Zero order eliminates a constant proportion per hour; first order a constant amount per hour
Both eliminate a constant proportion per hour
Both eliminate a constant amount per hour
The first row of the table contrasts exactly this: zero order = constant amount per hour; first order = constant proportion per hour. (Book p17)
If the dose is increased, the half-life in zero order kinetics:
In the zero order column of the 'if dose increases' row, T1/2 shows an upward arrow — with a fixed amount eliminated per hour, a bigger dose takes longer to fall by half. (Book p17)
If the dose is increased, the half-life in first order kinetics:
In first order kinetics T1/2 is constant — half-life does not change with dose or concentration, which is why it is a characteristic value for the drug. (Book p17)
If the dose is increased, clearance in zero order kinetics:
The zero order column of the 'if dose increases' row shows CL with a downward arrow — because the eliminating system is saturated, clearance falls as the dose rises. (Book p17)
If the dose is increased, clearance in first order kinetics:
In first order kinetics CL is constant; clearance is a fixed volume of plasma cleared per hour regardless of dose. (Book p17)
With increasing dose, the rise in plasma concentration in zero order kinetics is:
Less than proportionate to the dose
Zero order: ↑ in PC is disproportionate (risk of toxicity) — because clearance falls with dose, a small dose increment can cause a large, dangerous rise in plasma level. (Book p17)
With increasing dose, the rise in plasma concentration in first order kinetics is:
First order: ↑ in PC is proportionate — doubling the dose doubles the plasma concentration, so toxicity risk is predictable. (Book p17)
In first order kinetics, if the dose is doubled the plasma concentration roughly:
Doubles, in proportion to the dose
First order gives a proportionate rise in PC with dose; the disproportionate, toxicity-prone rise belongs to zero order drugs. (Book p17)
Which variable is CONSTANT with increasing dose in first order but CHANGES (↑ T1/2, ↓ CL) in zero order kinetics?
Only the rate of drug elimination
In the 'if dose increases' row, first order keeps T1/2 and CL constant, whereas zero order shows T1/2 rising and clearance falling with dose. (Book p17)
Zero order kinetics is seen in drugs with:
Table row 'seen in drugs with': zero order — early saturation of elimination; the eliminating enzymes/transporters are overwhelmed even at ordinary doses. (Book p17)
First order kinetics is seen in drugs with:
First order kinetics is seen in drugs with late saturation of elimination — the eliminating systems have ample capacity at usual doses. (Book p17)
For a drug following zero order kinetics, the 'exception to the rule' occurs at:
Lower doses, where it follows first order kinetics until saturation — hence a.k.a. pseudozero order
Higher doses, where it follows first order kinetics after saturation
Lower doses, where it becomes truly zero order
All doses equally, as no exception exists
Zero order column, exception row: at lower doses these drugs follow first order kinetics until saturation, and are hence also called pseudozero order. (Book p17)
For a drug following first order kinetics, the 'exception to the rule' occurs at:
Higher doses, where it follows zero order after saturation
Lower doses, where it follows zero order before saturation
Higher doses, where it becomes pseudozero order before saturation
No dose, since first order never changes
First order column, exception row: at higher doses it follows zero order after saturation — once the enzymes saturate, elimination becomes a fixed amount per hour. (Book p17)
'Pseudozero order' is the term applied to drugs that:
Follow first order kinetics at lower doses until saturation
Follow zero order kinetics at all doses
Are excreted unchanged by the kidney
Zero order column: at lower doses they follow first order kinetics until saturation — hence aka pseudozero order; true zero order over the whole dose range is rare. (Book p17)
Elimination kinetics of a drug whose eliminating system is saturated even at therapeutic doses is best described as:
Zero order, because a constant amount is eliminated per hour
First order, because a constant proportion is eliminated per hour
Zero order only after a further rise in dose
Early saturation of elimination produces zero order kinetics — a constant amount per hour — with a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration as the dose increases. (Book p17)
Which drug is specified as following TRUE zero order kinetics?
The zero order example list writes 'Alcohol (true zero order)' — alcohol is eliminated at a fixed amount per hour at all relevant doses. (Book p17)
Which of the following sets are examples of zero order kinetics?
Alcohol, theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin
Most drugs used in clinical practice
Zero order examples: alcohol (true zero order), theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin. (Book p17)
The examples given for first order kinetics are:
First order column, examples row: 'most drugs' — the great majority of drugs are eliminated by first order kinetics. (Book p17)
A patient on phenytoin has the dose increased and develops nystagmus and ataxia. The likely explanation is:
Zero order kinetics giving a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration
First order kinetics with a proportionate rise in concentration
Phenytoin is listed among zero order drugs; here an increase in dose raises PC disproportionately (risk of toxicity) — the classic reason phenytoin needs careful, small dose increments. (Book p17)
In a patient with a very high blood alcohol level, the rate of fall of alcohol concentration is:
Constant per hour, regardless of concentration
Zero until the liver is saturated
Alcohol follows true zero order kinetics — a constant amount is eliminated per hour, so concentration falls linearly rather than exponentially. (Book p17)
The zero order examples theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin are grouped because their elimination shows:
The table lists these drugs under zero order kinetics, which is seen in drugs with early saturation of elimination. (Book p17)
Affinity of a drug refers to its:
Tendency to bind to the target
Maximum effect produced at the target
Relative dose required for a given effect
Duration of action at the receptor
In the flowchart, 'drug binds to target' corresponds to tendency to bind = affinity. (Book p18)
Efficacy of a drug is defined as the:
Tendency of the drug to bind its target
Relative dose needed to produce an effect
Safety of the drug in a population
The flowchart links 'produces effect' to the maximum effect produced, i.e. efficacy - which the book marks as clinically most important. (Book p18)
Of affinity, efficacy and potency, which is described as clinically most important?
The page marks efficacy with the note 'clinically most important', because it decides the maximum benefit a drug can give. (Book p18)
Potency of a drug refers to the:
Relative dose of a drug required to produce a particular effect
Maximum effect the drug can produce
Tendency to bind to its receptor
Potency = relative dose of a drug required to produce a particular effect. (Book p18)
A drug that produces the same effect at a LOWER dose is said to have:
The lesser the dose needed to bring about the effect, the greater the potency - potency and dose requirement are inversely related. (Book p18)
Which statement about potency and efficacy is correct?
Potency is a matter of dose, efficacy is a matter of the maximum response attainable
Potency is the maximum response and efficacy is the dose required
Both describe the same property of a drug
Both are independent of dose and response
Potency concerns the dose needed for a given effect, while efficacy is the maximum effect produced - two separate properties. (Book p18)
A quantal dose response curve records a response which is:
Quantal DRC: response is binary (present/absent), e.g. sedatives and fertility drugs, and is studied in a population. (Book p18)
Which drugs are given as examples for a quantal response?
Drugs modifying blood pressure and heart rate
The examples given under quantal DRC are sedatives and fertility drugs, where the effect either occurs or does not. (Book p18)
The quantal dose response curve is studied in:
The quantal DRC is studied in a population, in contrast to the graded DRC which is studied in an individual. (Book p18)
ED50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences:
ED50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences therapeutic effects. (Book p18)
TD50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences:
TD50 is the dose at which 50% of the population experiences toxic effects. (Book p18)
LD50 is the dose at which 50% experience:
LD50 is the dose at which 50% of animals experience lethal effects. (Book p18)
In the quantal DRC table, ED50 is used as a marker of:
The table marks ED50 as the marker of potency; TD50 and LD50 are markers of toxicity. (Book p18)
Which parameters are used as markers of toxicity in the quantal DRC?
LD50 only, since TD50 is not used
The marker column shows potency opposite ED50 and toxicity opposite both TD50 and LD50. (Book p18)
On the quantal dose response graph, response in % of population is plotted against:
The graph plots response in % population on the y-axis against log dose on the x-axis, with therapeutic, toxic and lethal curves and the ED50, TD50 and LD50 marked at the 50% line. (Book p18)
On the quantal graph, the curve lying to the LEFT is that of:
The therapeutic effects curve is leftmost since lower doses produce benefit, with toxicity and then lethal effects appearing further to the right. (Book p18)
The lethal effects curve on the quantal graph is:
Furthest to the right, because animals die only at the highest doses
Leftmost, because death occurs at low doses
Absent, because lethality is not studied
With log dose on the x-axis, lethal effects (in animals) appear furthest right, after the toxic effects curve. (Book p18)
Therapeutic index (TI) is a measurement of:
The page describes TI as measurement of the safety of a drug. (Book p18)
In HUMANS the therapeutic index is calculated as:
The book gives humans: TD50/ED50 and animals: LD50/ED50 for the therapeutic index. (Book p18)
In ANIMALS the therapeutic index is calculated as:
For animals the therapeutic index is LD50/ED50, whereas in humans it is TD50/ED50. (Book p18)
A drug with a LOW therapeutic index:
Is safe only in a narrow dosage range and has an increased chance of toxicity
Is safe over a wide dosage range
Has high efficacy but low potency
Cannot produce toxicity at any dose
Low TI means the drug is safe only in a narrow dosage range, with an increased chance of toxicity - lithium is the example given. (Book p18)
A drug with a HIGH therapeutic index is:
Safe in a wide dosage range
Safe only in a narrow dosage range
High TI means the drug is safe in a wide dosage range; low TI (lithium) means safety only in a narrow range. (Book p18)
Which drug is quoted as the example of a low therapeutic index?
Lithium is the example given for a low TI, which is why its plasma levels must be monitored. (Book p18)
In the lithium concentration-time curve, the therapeutic window lies between:
The figure marks lithium's therapeutic window from 0.6 meq/L (minimum effective concentration) up to 1.5 meq/L (minimum toxic concentration). (Book p18)
The lower boundary of the therapeutic window is the:
The lower dashed line is the minimum effective concentration - below it there is no effect. (Book p18)
The upper boundary of the therapeutic window is the:
The upper dashed line is the minimum toxic concentration; above it, toxicity occurs. (Book p18)
In the therapeutic window figure, the zone below the minimum effective concentration of lithium is labelled:
The grey zone below 0.6 meq/L is labelled 'no effect', the green zone is the therapeutic window and the red zone above 1.5 meq/L is toxicity. (Book p18)
What is the plasma concentration range of lithium that is toxic?
Plasma lithium above the minimum toxic concentration of 1.5 meq/L lies in the toxicity band of the figure. (Book p18)
The therapeutic window is best defined as the:
Range of plasma concentration between the minimum effective and minimum toxic concentrations
Dose at which 50% of a population responds
Range of doses with no effect
The figure shows the therapeutic window as the band of plasma concentration between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration. (Book p18)
A graded (quantified) response is seen with drugs modifying:
Blood pressure, heart rate and blood glucose levels
Graded response = quantified response, e.g. drugs modifying BP, HR and blood glucose levels, and it is studied in an individual. (Book p19)
The graded dose response curve is studied in:
The graded DRC is studied in an individual, whereas the quantal DRC is studied in a population. (Book p19)
On the graded DRC, the response is plotted on the y-axis and ______ on the x-axis.
The graded DRC graph plots response (0-100) against log dose, with the three sigmoid curves of drugs A, B and C. (Book p19)
In the graded DRC table, efficacy is described as:
Determined by response, the more the height the greater the efficacy
Determined by the dose, the further left the greater the efficacy
More to the right meaning greater potency
Efficacy is read off the height of the curve: more the height, greater the efficacy, giving the comparative order B > A > C. (Book p19)
According to the graded DRC table, the comparative order of efficacy is:
The table's comparative column for efficacy reads B > A > C, following the heights of the three curves. (Book p19)
In the graded DRC table, potency is determined by:
A lesser dose producing the same effect - the more to the left, the greater the potency
The maximum height of the curve
Potency: lesser dose for the same effect means greater potency, and graphically 'more to the left = higher potency'. (Book p19)
The comparative order of potency in the graded DRC table is:
The comparative column for potency reads PA > PB > PC, i.e. drug A is the most potent because its curve lies furthest left. (Book p19)
On the graded DRC, drug A is:
The most potent (leftmost) but not the most efficacious
The most efficacious (highest) but not the most potent
Both the most potent and the most efficacious
The least potent and the least efficacious
Drug A lies furthest left (highest potency, PA > PB > PC) while drug B gives the greatest height (highest efficacy, B > A > C). (Book p19)
On the graded DRC, drug B has:
Efficacy follows the height of the curve, and B has the greatest height, giving the order B > A > C for efficacy. (Book p19)
In the graded DRC table, affinity is described as:
Comparable between drugs of the same mechanism of action
Comparable between drugs of different mechanisms of action
Determined by the height of the curve
Independent of the position of the curve
Affinity is comparable between drugs of the same MOA, and only between parallel lines; more to the left means higher affinity. (Book p19)
As per the affinity column, affinity can be compared only between:
The table notes affinity is comparable between drugs of the same MOA - determined graphically 'only comparable between parallel lines'. (Book p19)
In the graded DRC table, the comparative order of affinity is:
A > B, because drug C is not parallel
With C not parallel to the others, affinity can only be compared between A and B - the table gives A > B. (Book p19)
Drug C in the graded DRC is excluded from the affinity comparison because:
C is not parallel to the other curves
The affinity column states the comparison holds only between parallel lines, and the table records 'A > B (C is not parallel)'. (Book p19)
Which statement correctly distinguishes efficacy from potency on a graded DRC?
Efficacy is judged by the height of the curve and potency by its position on the x-axis
Efficacy is judged by the position and potency by the height
Both are judged by the height of the curve
Both are judged by the slope of the curve
Height of the curve gives efficacy, while position along the log dose axis gives potency - the further left, the more potent. (Book p19)
The effect of a full agonist upon binding to its receptor is:
Opposite to the nature of the receptor
The drug receptor interaction table gives full agonists a maximum effect (curve A). (Book p19)
The effect of a partial agonist upon binding to its receptor is:
Partial agonists produce a submaximal effect (curve B), less than a full agonist whatever the dose. (Book p19)
An antagonist, upon binding to its receptor, produces:
An effect opposite to the receptor's nature
Antagonists have no effect of their own upon binding (curve C) - their action is seen only in the presence of an agonist. (Book p19)
An inverse agonist, upon binding to its receptor, produces:
An effect opposite to the nature of the receptor
The inverse agonist produces an effect opposite to the nature of the receptors (curve D), falling below the baseline of no effect. (Book p19)
In terms of net effect in the body when endogenous full agonists are present, a partial agonist produces:
With endogenous full agonists present, partial agonists give mild antagonism, antagonists moderate antagonism and inverse agonists severe antagonism. (Book p19)
Which agent produces moderate antagonism of endogenous full agonists?
The table's net effect row reads: partial agonist - mild antagonism, antagonist - moderate antagonism, inverse agonist - severe antagonism. (Book p19)
Which agent produces severe antagonism of endogenous full agonists?
Inverse agonists produce an effect opposite to the receptor's nature, which in the presence of endogenous full agonists amounts to severe antagonism. (Book p19)
Intrinsic efficacy, the mathematical representation of efficacy, for a FULL agonist is:
The table assigns intrinsic efficacy +1 to full agonists, between 1 and 0 to partial agonists, 0 to antagonists and -1 to inverse agonists. (Book p19)
The intrinsic efficacy of a partial agonist lies:
Partial agonists have an intrinsic efficacy between 1 and 0 - more than an antagonist but less than a full agonist. (Book p19)
The intrinsic efficacy of an antagonist is:
Antagonists have an intrinsic efficacy of 0, which corresponds to producing no effect upon binding. (Book p19)
The intrinsic efficacy of an inverse agonist is:
Inverse agonists are given an intrinsic efficacy of -1, matching their effect opposite to the nature of the receptor. (Book p19)
On the dose-response figure of drug receptor interactions, the curve that dips below the baseline of no effect represents:
Curve A is maximal (full agonist), B submaximal (partial agonist), C flat at no effect (antagonist) and D falls to the opposite effect (inverse agonist). (Book p19)
On the drug receptor interaction graph, the flat line at the level of no effect represents:
Curve C stays at 'no effect' across the dose range - the antagonist, which produces no action of its own. (Book p19)
According to the note on this page, the type of drug most commonly used among these is:
The note box states that antagonists are the m/c used, even though they produce no effect of their own. (Book p19)
Which pair of agents and intrinsic efficacy is correctly matched?
Correct values are +1 for full agonists, between 1 and 0 for partial agonists, 0 for antagonists and -1 for inverse agonists. (Book p19)
A patient on a full agonist for asthma is given a partial agonist at the same receptor. Which effect is expected?
Mild antagonism, because the partial agonist produces only a submaximal effect
Severe antagonism with complete loss of effect
No change, because both are agonists
An effect opposite to the receptor's nature
With an endogenous full agonist present, a partial agonist produces only a submaximal effect and therefore mild antagonism. (Book p19)
Comparing curves, which statement about a full versus a partial agonist is correct?
A full agonist reaches a maximal effect while a partial agonist plateaus at a submaximal effect
A partial agonist reaches a maximal effect while a full agonist is submaximal
Both reach the same maximal effect at different doses
Neither can be compared on a graded dose response curve
In the figure, A (full agonist) rises to maximal, B (partial agonist) plateaus at submaximal, C (antagonist) stays at no effect and D (inverse agonist) moves to the opposite effect. (Book p19)
Physical antagonism produces its effect by:

How does charcoal act in alcohol toxicity?
It adsorbs alcohol from the intestine
It neutralises alcohol chemically in the stomach
It blocks alcohol receptors in the brain
It increases alcohol metabolism in the liver

Binds the substance physically without reaction
Acts through a receptor of opposite type
Displaces the agonist from its receptor

Which cells are noted to contain heparin?

Which of the following is the example of a chelating agent for iron?

Irreversible binding to the same receptor

Histamine acting on H1 receptors causes:
In the physiological antagonism example, 'Histamine -(+)→ H1 causes → Bronchoconstriction'. (Book p20)
Which pair is used as the example of physiological antagonism of histamine?

Which drug does the page call the best bronchodilator in asthma?
An arrow from the salbutamol/adrenaline line carries the note 'Best bronchodilator in Asthma'. (Book p20)
Why is salbutamol NOT the best bronchodilator in COPD?
Because it is a β2 blocker
Because it has no bronchodilator action in COPD

Instead of salbutamol, which drug class is preferred for bronchodilation in COPD?

Which of the following is a physical antagonist?

To the left, with a higher maximum

Reversible competitive lowers efficacy; irreversible/non-competitive lowers potency

c: Patient Safety, OT Zones and Surgery Positions
Benign Conditions of Small and Large Bowel
Gall Bladder and Bile Ducts : Part 1
Gall Bladder and Bile Ducts : Part 2
u: A valid consent covers identification, diagnosis, the planned procedure, the surgeon, description, patient-specific and procedure-specific complications (any complication >1% incidence), benefits and the alternate procedure — signed by patient, surgeon and witness.

From narrow to wide: yellow 24G (13/10 ml/min), blue 22G (31/30), pink 20G (67/60), green 18G (96), gray 16G (236/240) and orange 14G (270) — the orange 14G is the shock cannula. The 24G/22G/20G trio is bracketed for paediatric patients.
The m/c IV complication is superficial thrombophlebitis — a tender, cord-like swelling at the cannulation site, managed with a topical heparinoid.

The checklist runs sign in (before induction of anaesthesia, ward to OT complex) → time out (before skin incision) → sign out (before the patient leaves the OT). Sign in confirms identity, marked site, procedure, written consent, known allergies and risk of >500 ml blood loss.
Safety Checklist: Time Out & Sign Out

Time out confirms patient site, procedure name and time, checks antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 30 min and the surgeon's anticipated blood loss. Sign out verifies instruments/sponge/needle count, specimen labelling with patient name and the anaesthetist's actual blood loss — and the book's note: there is no time in phase.

Actual blood loss = blood in suction − irrigation fluid, or wet mop weight − dry mop weight. A soaked mop holds 100 cc, a fist full of clots 500 cc, and mops carry a radio-opaque line so they are picked up on X-ray.

The OT complex flows through four zones: protective (change rooms, transfer bay, pre & post op rooms, ICU/PACU), clean (equipment store room, maintenance workshop — connecting protective to aseptic), aseptic (the OT itself) and disposal.
OT Positions: Supine, Trendelenberg & Reverse Trendelenberg

Supine/neutral is the m/c position for abdominal and breast surgeries.
