Empyema is pus in the pleural space, arising from pulmonary infection (unresolved pneumonia, bronchiectasis, TB, fungi, lung abscess), aspiration of an effusion of any cause, trauma (penetrating injury, surgery, oesophageal perforation), extrapulmonary subphrenic abscess, or osteomyelitis of ribs and vertebrae.

Three phases: exudative — fever and pus, a one-sided collection on CXR/CT, m/c Staph. aureus, treated by aspiration and antibiotics; fibrinopurulent — thickened pus and pleura needing a chest tube because aspiration fails; organized — thickened pleura entrapping the lung, needing pleural stripping/VATS with decortication.
Lung Cancer: Risk Factors and Small Cell Lung Cancer

Lung cancer follows smoking, pollution and asbestos; only 15-20% are resectable and immunotherapy has revolutionised treatment. Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma has the strongest smoking link, affects males more, carries a poor prognosis but is highly chemosensitive and produces the most paraneoplastic syndromes — Cushing's (ACTH), SIADH (ADH), acromegaly (GH-related peptide) and Lambert-Eaton (anti-VGCC). Pathology shows the Azzopardi effect with salt and pepper appearance; IHC is chromogranin and NCAM.
SVC Syndrome and Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lung

SVC syndrome is an oncological emergency with facial and cerebral edema ± seizures, diagnosed on CECT and treated with radiotherapy to shrink the tumour plus steroids. Squamous cell carcinoma sits centrally, is the m/c lung cancer in smokers, and can form a Pancoast tumor pressing the thoracic inlet (dyspnoea, stridor) or the sympathetic chain (Horner's: ptosis, miosis, enophthalmos, anhydrosis) — treated with radiotherapy plus immunotherapy.

Adenocarcinoma is the m/c lung cancer overall, commoner in females, peripheral and slow growing, developing in pre-existing cavities from TB or bronchiectasis, metastasising early, marked by NAPSIN A and ALK/RAS mutations.
Bronchoalveolar Carcinoma and Clinical Features of Lung Cancer

Bronchoalveolar carcinoma (adenocarcinoma in-situ) is multifocal, usually resectable with good prognosis, spreading along the broncho-alveolar lining in a lepidic pattern. Cough is the m/c symptom, with hemoptysis, pain and weight loss; brain is the m/c symptomatic metastasis while adrenal involvement is very common but asymptomatic.
Work-up: CXR first, HRCT as IOC for extent, biopsy for type (CT guided, mediastinoscopy — which also checks operability — or EBUS FNAC), and PET-CT as the staging IOC.

T1 is ≤3 cm surrounded by lung/visceral pleura without main bronchus involvement: T1a(mi) minimally invasive, T1a ≤1 cm, T1b >1-2 cm, T1c >2-3 cm. T2 is >3 to ≤5 cm, or main bronchus involvement sparing the carina, or visceral pleural invasion, or atelectasis/post obstructive pneumonitis reaching the hilum — T2a >3-4 cm, T2b >4-5 cm.

Surgery suits T1-T2 and T3 with N0/N1: lobectomy, pneumonectomy or sleeve resection through a posterolateral thoracotomy, risking bleeding, respiratory infection, persistent air leak and bronchopleural fistula. Squamous cell carcinoma is highly radiosensitive, and chemo/immunotherapy is the latest modality for all carcinomas, especially advanced disease.

Summary: SCC — M>F, central, smoking, hypercalcemia, P53, CIS precursor. Adenocarcinoma — F>M, peripheral, non smokers, migratory thrombophlebitis, K ras/EGFR/ALK, AIS and AAH precursors. Small cell — M>F, central, strongest smoking link, Cushing's and SIADH, L-myc, DIPNEH precursor. Large cell — M>F, peripheral, both smokers and non smokers, gynecomastia.
Histology, IHC and Benign Lung Tumors

Histology: SCC keratin pearls and desmosomes (CK, P63, P40); adenocarcinoma glands lined by pleomorphic cells (TTF-1, NAPSIN A); small cell salt & pepper chromatin, nuclear moulding, Azzopardi effect (NSE, chromogranin, synaptophysin); large cell large pleomorphic cells. Hamartoma is the m/c benign lung tumour — usually asymptomatic, sometimes cough or hemoptysis, a coin shaped lesion on CXR confirmed by CT and excised under VATS.

Mediastinal tumors by compartment: superior — lymphoma, thyroid, parathyroid; anterior — the 3 T's, thymoma (m/c mediastinal tumour), teratoma and terrible lymphoma; middle — cystic lesions, m/c pericardial cyst, plus lymphoma and mesenchymal tumors; posterior — neurogenic tumors, the m/c mediastinal tumour in children, and cystic lesions.

Thymoma is the m/c mediastinal tumour overall, sits anteriorly, is usually benign and associates with myasthenia gravis; small lesions go transcervically, large ones by VATS or thoracotomy. Masaoka staging: I encapsulated without microscopic capsular invasion; II macroscopic invasion into mediastinal fat or pleura with microscopic capsular invasion; III invasion into pericardium, great vessels or lungs; IVA pleural or pericardial dissemination; IVB lymphogenous or haematogenous metastasis.

The anterior mediastinum is the m/c extragonadal site for germ cell tumors, commoner in males; benign ones are teratomas while malignant ones raise αFP, LDH and β-hCG. Excise, and add chemotherapy if malignant.

A sebaceous cyst is a blocked hair follicle duct, so it can appear anywhere except palms and soles. The skin cannot be pinched over it, there is whitish discharge and the characteristic punctum; sometimes it hurts. It may become inflamed and infected, appear multiply on the scrotum and scalp, or harden into a sebaceous horn. Treat by excision of the cyst.

A dermoid cyst forms from epithelial tissue trapped along lines of embryonic fusion, classically at the outer canthus of the eye and post auricular region, fluctuant, and — unlike a sebaceous cyst — the skin CAN be pinched over it. Always X-ray/CT before surgery to rule out intracranial extension, then excise. An implantation dermoid follows injury, m/c after ear piercing, and is also excised.

Lipoma is an encapsulated collection of fat and the m/c swelling in the body. Skin pinches easily over it because it arises from subcutaneous tissue; it shows pseudofluctuation (expanding in one axis only) and a positive slip sign. Dercum's disease is multiple lipomatosis, benign and observed. Excise if painful or large, and watch closely lipomas of the retroperitoneum, thigh and between the shoulder blades for sarcomatous change.

Tuberculosis is the m/c pathological cause of cervical lymphadenopathy in India. Bacilli infect the nodes causing caseous necrosis, periadenitis mats them together, they coalesce and adhere to the deep fascia, and pus finally tracks through the fascia as a collar stud abscess — a cold abscess without signs of inflammation.
Diagnosis of Cold Abscess and Carbuncle

The cold abscess is a fluctuant cervical swelling confirmed by ANTIGRAVITY aspiration with Ziehl-Neelsen staining — aspirating from below risks a sinus tract — and treated with anti-tubercular therapy. A carbuncle is multiple small abscesses coalescing, m/c in diabetics, showing multiple pus points, m/c on the nape of the neck, drained through a cruciate incision.

A branchial cyst arises when the cervical sinus, formed by fusion of the 2nd and 6th arches, persists; it presents at the anterior border of SCM between the upper and middle thirds, fluctuant and transilluminant, treated by FNAC then excision. A branchial sinus/fistula comes from FAILURE of fusion of the 2nd and 6th arches, lies at the anterior border of SCM between the middle and lower thirds, and is excised.
Ulcers: Definition and Comparison of Types

An ulcer is a breach in epithelial or mucosal continuity. Compare the four: venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area with normal pulsations, dilated veins, normal sensation and sloping margins; arterial ulcers on the dorsum/lateral side with absent pulsations, painful, punched out; trophic ulcers on the sole or base of the great toe with normal pulsations, reduced sensation and punched out margins; diabetic ulcers in the same site with possibly absent pulsations, reduced sensation and punched out margins.

A varicose ulcer sits m/c at the medial malleolus, shallow, with pale granulation tissue, a hemosiderin-pigmented margin, and does not heal. Marjolin's ulcer is a squamous cell cancer developing in a long standing venous ulcer or burn scar, with raised everted margins, treated by wide local excision — radiotherapy is contraindicated because of scarring and recurrence.

Arterial ulcers come with loss of muscle mass and hair and shiny skin. Trophic ulcers afflict paralyzed patients and diabetics. Diabetic ulcers stem from microangiopathy and hyperglycaemia and are staged: 1 inflammation without breach, 2 superficial ulcer, 3 deep ulcer, 4 ulcer with osteomyelitis. Stage 1 needs antibiotics, diabetic control and off loading; stages 2-3 add debridement and VAC dressings at -125 mmHg; stage 4 requires amputation.

Read the edge: sloping means healing or venous; punched out means arterial, neuropathic, bed sores or syphilis; undermined means tuberculosis; rolled out and pearly white means basal cell carcinoma (rodent ulcer); raised, everted and cauliflower-like means squamous cell carcinoma.

Every instrument has 2 rings for gripping, multiple ratchets that prevent wear and tear, a joint — box or screw, the screw joint more often catching thread — and blades that are fenestrated or serrated.
Sponge Holder, Towel Clips and BP Handle

Rampley's sponge holder has a fenestrated serrated blade to grip sponges for part preparation. Towel clips hold towels after draping, pass and hold the suction catheter or cautery, and hold the tongue during tongue resection — Mayo's has hooks, Doyen's works by the pinch cork effect. The BP (Brad Parker) handle mounts blades and is held like a paint brush or in a palming grip.

Yankauer's suction cannula (plastic or metallic) suctions blood and fumes. Spring loaded forceps hold tissue: plain with transverse serrations and no teeth are relatively atraumatic; toothed grip tough structures but are traumatic; DeBakey's vascular forceps have minute serrations with raised edges for vessels; Russian forceps show transverse serration with a gap in between.

The needle holder grips the needle with criss cross serrations that stop it moving; hold the needle at the 1/3rd-2/3rd junction from the swaged and pointed ends, enter skin at 90°, and grip the needle with toothed forceps while suturing. Mayo scissors are heavy with a screw joint, for cutting sutures and sheaths.

Metzenbaum scissors are lighter tissue dissecting scissors and should not cut sutures; McIndoe scissors are finer still, for fine tissues in ophthalmic and ENT surgery. Skin suturing needs a needle holder, toothed forceps and scissors.

Non-self retaining retractors must be held. Skin hooks (single or double handled) hold raised flaps in mastectomy, thyroidectomy and parotidectomy. The cats paw and the fenestrated right angle Langenbeck retract superficial tissue — a broader Langenbeck serves cholecystectomy. The army navy/Czerney's retractor has one 90° end and one clawed end with a gap for suturing while retracted, and the Morris retractor is broader than Langenbeck's, preventing slipping with better grip and less weight.

Doyen's retractor retracts the bladder, its increased convexity easing retraction, while the malleable retractor retracts bowel in abdominal surgery. Self-retaining: mastoid retractors lock to retract superficial tissue in thyroid and parotid surgery; Balfour reaches deeper abdominal structures with a bar, blades and space to attach Doyen's; Bookwalter attaches a ring to the operating table with space for multiple retractors in complex abdominal malignancy surgery.
Spencer Wells are straight artery forceps of various sizes for holding bleeders; curved artery forceps give better visualization; the mosquito forceps is the smallest artery forceps.

Special forceps: Kelly's are big curved forceps with a gradual curve for abdominal surgery; right angle forceps tie pedicles; Allis, with serrations and teeth, traumatically holds tough sheath and fascia; Babcock, with a gap between two fenestrated ends, holds tubular structures — appendix, vas, fallopian tubes — without crushing; Kocher interlocks and crushes, holding tough structures and the cervix during hysterectomy.
Laparoscopic Instruments and the Veress Needle

Laparoscopic instruments are long because they work at depth, and insulated to stop cautery current leaking. The Veress needle makes pneumoperitoneum by the closed method; it is spring loaded with an outlet/inlet valve and a blunt tip in front that gives way to a bevelled tip on pressing, preventing tissue injury.

The 1st laparoscopic port goes in blindly. Trocars are sharp, blunt (Hassan's) or bladeless (Optiport, giving better visualization). Maryland's dissector — curved with artery-forceps-like serrations — is the workhorse of laparoscopic surgery.

Thoracotomy set: Farabeuf's periosteal elevator raises periosteum over the rib; Doyen's rib raspatory, one for each side, resects periosteum and muscles held with handle lateral, convexity upwards and tip downwards; the rib cutter has a blunt lower edge to spare the pleura (unlike the sharp bone cutter); the bone nibbler smooths sharp edges after cutting.

The Allison lung retractor's fenestrated blade lets the lung expand while retracted. Lung forceps resect small tissues such as hamartomas and nodules, their triangular end giving a bloodless field. Joll's thyroid retractor, now obsolete, uses 2 retractors on either side.

Vascular instruments: the bulldog clamp is self retaining with a pinch cork effect and serrations, clamping temporarily without crushing; the Satinsky clamp is curved with serrations for use over a pedicle with better visualization; the aneurysm needle is a J hook with an opening at the end for ligating an aneurysm.
Other Instruments: Ovum, Cheatle's and Stone Forceps

Ovum forceps have 2 convex fenestrated ends to remove retained placental or fetal tissue; Cheatle's forceps have 2 ends without a lock to pick up gauze. Cystolithotomy forceps have one complete ring for the thumb and an open part for the other four fingers, no lock so the stone is not crushed, and studs for grip. Pyelolithotomy forceps are obsolete, with varied angulations for calyceal access and transverse serrations without a lock.

Doyen's intestinal clamp is the non crushing bowel clamp, its longitudinal serrations preventing tissue crushing and stopping faecal spillage, while Payr's crushing clamp removes portions of bowel. Choledocholithotomy (Desjardin's) forceps, which have no serrations, bring down CBD stones.
q: As per the book, consent before a procedure must contain all of the following components EXCEPT:

Components of consent = identification, diagnosis, planned procedure, surgeon, description, patient-specific complications, procedure-specific complications, benefits, alternate procedure and sign of patient, surgeon and witness. (Book p1)
Which of the following is an explicit component of consent?
The planned procedure and the surgeon are explicit components of consent. (Book p1)
A procedure-specific complication must be explained to the patient when its incidence is:
Procedure specific complications = any complication > 1% incidence. (Book p1)
In addition to the planned procedure, consent must also discuss:
Consent includes benefits and the alternate procedure. (Book p1)
The consent form is signed by:
Consent requires the sign of patient, surgeon and witness. (Book p1)
In the color-coding of IV cannulas, the YELLOW cannula corresponds to gauge:
Yellow = 24G (max flow 13 (10) ml/min), the narrowest cannula in the chart. (Book p1)
The BLUE IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
Blue = 22G with a maximal flow of 31 (30) ml/min. (Book p1)
The PINK IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
Pink = 20G with a maximal flow of 67 (60) ml/min. (Book p1)
The GREEN IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
Green = 18G with a maximal flow of 96 ml/min. (Book p1)
The GRAY IV cannula corresponds to gauge:
Gray = 16G with a maximal flow of 236 (240 ml/min). (Book p1)
The ORANGE IV cannula, which is used in shock, corresponds to gauge:
Orange (used in shock) = 14G, the widest cannula, with a maximal flow of 270 ml/min. (Book p1)
The narrowest cannula in the color chart is:
The chart runs from narrow 24G (yellow) to wide 14G (orange). (Book p1)
The widest cannula in the color chart is:
14G orange is the widest cannula and is the one used in shock. (Book p1)
The maximal flow rate of the 16G gray cannula is:
The maximal flow rate of the 20G pink cannula is:
The maximal flow rate of the 14G orange cannula is:
Orange 14G (used in shock) has the highest maximal flow of 270 ml/min. (Book p1)
In the color chart, which group of cannulas is bracketed for paediatric patients?
Yellow (24G), blue (22G) and pink (20G) are grouped together for paediatric patients. (Book p1)
A cannula with a maximal flow of 96 ml/min is color-coded:
Green = 18G with maximal flow 96 ml/min. (Book p1)
The most common complication of an IV line is:
Superficial thrombophlebitis is the m/c complication of IV lines. (Book p1)
Superficial thrombophlebitis at a cannulation site presents with:
Features of superficial thrombophlebitis: tender, cord-like swelling. (Book p1)
The management of superficial thrombophlebitis at a cannula site is:
Management of superficial thrombophlebitis = topical heparinoid. (Book p1)
The three phases of the surgical safety checklist, in order, are:
Sign in → Time out → Sign out
Time out → Sign in → Sign out
Sign out → Sign in → Time out
Sign in → Sign out → Time out
The checklist flows Before induction of anaesthesia (sign in) → Before skin incision (time out) → Before patient leaves the operating room (sign out). (Book p2)
'Before induction of anaesthesia' (ward to OT complex) corresponds to which phase?
Sign in happens before induction of anaesthesia, in the ward to OT complex. (Book p2)
'Before skin incision' corresponds to which phase?
Time out is performed before skin incision. (Book p2)
'Before patient leaves the operating room' corresponds to which phase?
Sign out is completed before the patient leaves the operating room. (Book p2)
During sign in, the patient has confirmed all of the following EXCEPT:
At sign in the patient has confirmed identity, site (marked), procedure and written consent. (Book p2)
Which of the following is checked during sign in?
Sign in includes known allergies and the risk of >500 ml blood loss. (Book p2)
During sign in, the risk of blood loss greater than how much is assessed?
Sign in assesses the risk of >500 ml blood loss. (Book p2)
During time out, the team confirms:
Patient site, procedure name and time
Time out confirms patient site, procedure name and time. (Book p2)
At time out, antibiotic prophylaxis must have been given within the last:
Time out checks that antibiotic prophylaxis was given within the last 30 min. (Book p2)
During time out, the anticipated blood loss is estimated by the:
Anticipated blood loss at time out is given by the surgeon (actual loss at sign out is by the anaesthetist). (Book p2)
During sign out, which of the following is verified?
Sign out verifies instruments, sponge and needle count. (Book p2)
Specimen labelling during sign out must include:
Sign out includes specimen labelling (including patient name). (Book p2)
During sign out, the actual blood loss is documented by the:
Actual blood loss at sign out is recorded by the anaesthetist. (Book p2)
The note on the surgical safety checklist states that:
There is no time in phase
The book's note: 'There is no time in phase' — time out is a pause in workflow, not a timed interval. (Book p2)
The actual amount of blood loss is estimated as:
Dry mop weight − wet mop weight
Actual amount = blood in suction − irrigation fluid. (Book p2)
Alternatively, blood loss is estimated as:
Wet mop weight − dry mop weight
Wet mop weight + dry mop weight
Dry mop weight − wet mop weight
Blood loss can also be estimated as wet mop weight − dry mop weight. (Book p2)
A soaked mop represents a blood loss of:
Soaked mop = 100 cc of blood. (Book p2)
A fist full of clots represents a blood loss of:
Fist full of clots = 500 cc of blood. (Book p2)
Surgical mops carry a radio-opaque line so that they can be:
Mops have a radio-opaque line that is picked up on X-ray. (Book p2)
OT zoning = 1. Protective zone, 2. Clean zone, 3. Aseptic zone, 4. Disposal zone. (Book p2)
Which of the following belongs to the protective zone?
Change rooms, transfer bay, pre & post op rooms, ICU/PACU
Protective zone = change rooms, transfer bay, pre & post op rooms and ICU/PACU. (Book p2)
The clean zone connects the protective zone to the:
The clean zone connects the protective zone to the aseptic zone. (Book p2)
The equipment store room and maintenance workshop are in the:
Clean zone = equipment store room and maintenance workshop. (Book p2)
The aseptic zone of the OT complex is the:
The m/c position used for abdominal and breast surgeries is the:
Supine/neutral position is the m/c position used for abdominal and breast surgeries. (Book p3)
The Trendelenberg position (head end low, foot end up) is used in:
Trendelenberg position is used in pelvic surgeries. (Book p3)
The reverse Trendelenberg position is used in:
Reverse Trendelenberg is used in upper abdominal surgeries and in laparoscopic cholecystometry with right side up. (Book p3)
In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, reverse Trendelenberg is taken with the:
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy uses reverse Trendelenberg with right side up. (Book p3)
In laparoscopic cholecystectomy, CO2 collects below the right dome of the diaphragm, producing the m/c complication of:
CO2 collects below the right dome of diaphragm → right shoulder tip pain, the m/c complication. (Book p3)
Lithotomy position is used in all of the following EXCEPT:
Lithotomy is used for obstetric, gynecologic, urologic (TURP) and hemorrhoid surgeries — not posterior cranial fossa surgery. (Book p3)
The urologic procedure performed in lithotomy position mentioned in the book is:
Urologic procedures (TURP) are listed under the uses of lithotomy position. (Book p3)
In lithotomy position, if the legs are not supported properly, the nerve commonly injured is the:
Nerve injured if legs are not supported properly: common peroneal nerve. (Book p3)
The lateral (kidney) position is NOT used for:
Lateral/kidney position uses: thoracotomy, pyelolithotomy, nephrolithotomy, nephrectomy and breast reconstruction (latissimus dorsi flap). (Book p3)
A breast reconstruction operation performed in the lateral (kidney) position uses the:
Breast reconstruction in the lateral position uses the latissimus dorsi flap. (Book p3)
In the lateral (kidney) position, the increased risk of brachial plexus injury is due to:
Lateral position carries increased risk for brachial plexus injury d/t hyperextended arm. (Book p3)
The prone position is used for:
Spinal surgery and pilonidal sinus surgery
Prone position uses: spinal surgery and pilonidal sinus surgery. (Book p4)
The sitting / Fowler's position is used for:
Sitting/Fowler's position is used for posterior cranial fossa surgery. (Book p4)
An advantage of the sitting / Fowler's position is:
Bloodless field with reduced blood loss
Advantages of Fowler's: ↓ blood loss (blood less field) and ↑ exposure. (Book p4)
A disadvantage of the sitting / Fowler's position is:
Disadvantage of sitting/Fowler's position: ↑ risk of air embolism. (Book p4)
Obsolete, previously used for hemorrhoid/fissure surgeries
The m/c position for abdominal surgery
Used for posterior cranial fossa surgery
Jackknife position = obsolete position, previously used for hemorrhoid fissure surgeries. (Book p4)
A complication of the jackknife position is:
Complication of the jackknife position = positional asphyxia. (Book p4)
The Lloyd-Davis position is a combination of:
Lloyd-Davis position = Trendelenberg + lithotomy position. (Book p4)
The Lloyd-Davis position is used in:
Lloyd-Davis position is used in rectal cancer surgery. (Book p4)
As per the book, how much air sucked into a vein enters circulation and dysregulates cardiac functioning?
Air (50-100cc) sucked into vein → enters circulation → dysregulates cardiac functioning. (Book p4)
Air embolism is a risk in which of the following?
Risk factors for air embolism: thyroid/head & neck surgeries and sitting/Fowler's position. (Book p4)
The m/c presenting feature of an air embolism is:
Clinical features: sudden desaturation, dyspnea and hypotension. (Book p4)
Clinical features of air embolism include all of the following EXCEPT:
Features = sudden desaturation, dyspnea, hypotension — fever is not listed. (Book p4)
To prevent air embolism in the Fowler's position, the vein should be:
Prevention: 1. Ligate vein before cutting. (Book p5)
Air entry into the field is further prevented by:
Prevention of air embolism in Fowler's position: ligate vein before cutting and irrigate field. (Book p5)
Management of an air embolism begins with placing the patient in the:
Management starts with the Durant position, followed by aspiration of air. (Book p5)
Right side up (left lateral) + legs up
Durant position = right side up (left lateral) + legs up. (Book p5)
After the Durant position, air is removed by:
Aspiration using direct puncture / central line
Durant position is followed by aspirating air using direct puncture/central line. (Book p5)
The Durant position is used when:
Suspicion of air embolism is positive
The patient is bleeding into shock
The Durant position is used if suspicion of air embolism is (+). (Book p5)
An adverse event is defined as:
An incident that results in harm to the patient
An incident that could have harmed the patient
An incident that never reaches the patient
Adverse event = an incident that results in harm to the patient. (Book p5)
A near miss is an incident that:
Could have caused unwanted consequences but did not
Reaches the patient and causes injury
Near miss = an incident that could have resulted in unwanted consequences but did not. (Book p5)
A near miss is prevented from reaching the patient by:
A near miss does not reach the patient either by chance or through timely intervention. (Book p5)
Reaches the patient but results in no injury
Is by definition an adverse event
No-harm event = an incident that occurs and reaches the patient but results in no injury. (Book p5)
In a no-harm event, harm is avoided by:
In a no-harm event, harm is avoided by chance or due to mitigating circumstances. (Book p5)
The use of surgical blades, as stated in the book, is to:
The sharpest part of a surgical blade is its:
Belly of the blade: Sharpest. (Book p6)
The No. 11 blade is described as a:
Incision and drainage (I & D) of an abscess is a listed use of the:
No 11 Blade uses: Incision & drainage (I & D) of abscess. (Book p6)
Arteriotomy is a listed use of the:
No 11 Blade uses: I & D of abscess and Arteriotomy. (Book p6)
Suture removal is the listed use of the:
No 12 Blade uses: Suture removal. (Book p6)
The book's Types of Blades diagram includes all of the following EXCEPT:
The diagram shows No. 10, 11, 15, 22, 23 and the curved No. 12 - there is no No. 20. (Book p6)
While passing, a blade is passed:
Passed in kidney tray / pointed end facing towards self. (Book p6)
While passing a blade, its pointed end faces:
Passed in kidney tray / pointed end facing towards self. (Book p6)
Mounted on BP (Bard Parker) handle. (Book p6)
Langer's lines represent the orientation of:
Langer's lines: orientation of dermal collagen fibers. (Book p6)
An incision placed parallel to Langer's lines gives a:
Incision placed parallel: Good scar. (Book p6)
Muscle fibre action runs _____ to Langer's lines:
Muscle fibre action is perpendicular. (Book p6)
While planning an incision, one must avoid injury to:
Avoid injury to anatomical structures. (Book p6)
For a good cosmetic result, incisions are placed parallel to Langer's lines or:
Cosmetic factor: Parallel to Langer's lines / hidden in skin creases. (Book p6)
Which of the following is a factor while planning an incision?
Factors while planning an incision include adequate access. (Book p6)
In monopolar cautery, current flows from the machine to the:
The tip used in monopolar cautery is called the:
The correct order of the monopolar circuit is:
Machine -> Tip -> Cut/Coagulate -> Body -> Pad -> Machine
Machine -> Pad -> Body -> Tip -> Cut/Coagulate -> Machine
Tip -> Machine -> Pad -> Body -> Cut/Coagulate -> Tip
Machine -> Body -> Tip -> Pad -> Cut/Coagulate -> Machine
Circuit: machine -> Tip -> Cut/Coagulate -> to body -> Pad -> machine. (Book p7)
The cautery handpiece carries buttons for:
The handpiece is labelled Coagulation and Cutting. (Book p7)
The cautery pad is placed over a:
Cautery pad: Placed over well-vascularized area. (Book p7)
Have wide area of contact. (Book p7)
Small cautery pad: Burns at site. (Book p7)
With no cautery pad, the circuit is incomplete and:
No cautery pad: Circuit incomplete -> monopolar will not work. (Book p7)
Lateral spread of current in monopolar cautery causes:
Disadvantage: Lateral spread of current -> Thermal damage to nearby structures. (Book p7)
Current interferes with cardiac conduction. (Book p7)
Because it interferes with cardiac conduction, monopolar cautery is avoided in patients with:
Avoid in patients with cardiac pacemakers. (Book p7)
Current applied over a pedicle undergoes:
In a pedicle, the channelled current:
Monopolar cautery is avoided close to:
Avoid close to end arteries. (Book p7)
The uses of monopolar cautery are:
Monopolar cautery is avoided in all of the following EXCEPT:
Avoided in: CNS Sx, Parotid/Thyroid Sx, Ear lobule, Penile region, Patient with Pacemakers. (Book p7)
Which of the following regions is listed for avoidance of monopolar cautery?
Avoided in: CNS Sx, Parotid/Thyroid Sx, Ear lobule, Penile region, Patient with Pacemakers. (Book p7)
Parotid / Thyroid surgery appears in the book under:
Sites where monopolar cautery is avoided
Avoided in: CNS Sx, Parotid/Thyroid Sx, Ear lobule, Penile region, Patient with Pacemakers. (Book p7)
In bipolar cautery, the circuit is:
Bipolar cautery: Circuit completed locally. (Book p7)
Two prongs complete the circuit locally. (Book p7)
An advantage of bipolar cautery is:
Advantages: No cautery pad required. (Book p8)
Close to vital structures and end arteries
Safe close to vital structure and end arteries. (Book p8)
Cutting mode: Low voltage, continuous current. (Book p8)
Blend mode is a combination of:
Blend mode: Combination of cutting & coagulation mode. (Book p8)
Coagulation mode: High voltage, alternating current. (Book p8)
A type of coagulation with higher voltage peaks
A blend of two cutting modes
Fulguration mode: Type of coagulation with higher voltage peaks. (Book p8)
The fulguration waveform is labelled with:
Fulguration waveform labels Peak voltage and Average voltage. (Book p8)
Cutting current acts by heat causing:
Cutting current: Heat -> Cell water explosion. (Book p8)
Coagulation current: Dehydration + Protein Denaturation. (Book p8)
Dehydration + protein denaturation by coagulation current leads to:
Dehydration + Protein Denaturation -> Cell death. (Book p8)
Ligasure uses the body's _____ to seal & divide:
Uses body collagen & elastin to seal & divide. (Book p8)
Feedback mechanism: Regulate energy delivery. (Book p8)
Automatic discontinuation on seal closure. (Book p8)
Ligasure is used for vessels till _____ diameter:
A disadvantage of Ligasure is that it:
Cannot be used close to vital structures
Disadvantage: cannot be used close to vital structures. (Book p8)
The harmonic scalpel works on the:
Oscillatory blade: Oscillates between 2000-50000 Hz. (Book p8)
Protein denaturation + coagulation without heat production
Protein denaturation + coagulation without heat production. (Book p8)
An advantage of the harmonic scalpel is that it:
Can be used close to vital structures
Advantages: Can be used close to vital structures. (Book p9)
Which of the following is an advantage of the harmonic scalpel?
Advantages: Cut through scar tissue. (Book p9)
A disadvantage of the harmonic scalpel is that it is:
CUSA: Type of harmonic scalpel. (Book p9)
During CUSA, hepatocytes are susceptible to oscillatory fragmentation because of their:
Hepatocytes susceptible to oscillatory fragmentation d/t high water content and collagen. (Book p9)
Can aspirate gases as well. (Book p9)
Which of the following is a labelled part of the CUSA handpiece?
CUSA handpiece: CUSA tip, Irrigation port, Suction port, Power cable. (Book p9)
Features of both Ligasure + Harmonic Scalpel. (Book p9)
RFA: High frequency, alternating current. (Book p9)
Similar to electrocautery, RFA needs a:
Similar to electrocautery: Grounding pad needed. (Book p9)
RFA is used for liver tumour resection upto:
Use: Liver tumor resection upto 3 cm. (Book p9)
An advantage of microwave ablation is:
Advantages: No grounding pad required. (Book p9)
Compared to RFA, microwave ablation takes:
Advantages: Less time than RFA. (Book p9)
Open drains are described in the book as:
In the open-drain diagram, discharge from the abscess cavity ends up in a:
The open-drain diagram shows the drain leading from the abscess cavity to a soak dressing. (Book p10)
Closed: Empty into a container/bag. (Book p10)
The Romovac suction drain is a:
Romovac suction drain: Closed drain with -ve pressure. (Book p10)
A Romovac drain is used after all of the following EXCEPT:
Romovac used after mastectomy, thyroidectomy, neck dissection. (Book p10)
Which operation is a listed indication for a Romovac suction drain?
Romovac used after mastectomy, thyroidectomy, neck dissection. (Book p10)
A Romovac drain is avoided in the abdomen because it is a rounded drain with a risk of:
Avoided in abdomen d/t rounded drain risk of perforation. (Book p10)
The Romovac assembly diagram labels all of the following EXCEPT:
The Romovac diagram labels Connected to bag, Bag and Inserted to body. (Book p10)
The minivac drain is used after:
Minivac drain: used after sentinel LN biopsy. (Book p10)
The Jackson Pratt drain is a:
Jackson Pratt drain: -ve pressure drain. (Book p10)
The Jackson Pratt drain can be used in the abdomen because it has:
Jackson Pratt: Flat tubes -> Can be used in abdomen. (Book p10)
In the Jackson Pratt diagram, the squeezable reservoir is labelled as the:
The Jackson Pratt diagram labels the reservoir Bulb and the tube Flat. (Book p10)
In the Jackson Pratt diagram, the drainage tube is labelled as:
The Jackson Pratt diagram labels the reservoir Bulb and the tube Flat. (Book p10)
Abdominal drain: Closed drain, no -ve pressure. (Book p10)
A rounded suction drain that is avoided in the abdomen is the:
Romovac: avoided in abdomen d/t rounded drain risk of perforation. (Book p10)
A suction drain with flat tubes that can be used in the abdomen is the:
Jackson Pratt: Flat tubes -> Can be used in abdomen. (Book p10)
In the underwater seal bag, the tube is kept submerged underwater:
To prevent air being sucked in
Underwater seal bag: Tube submerged underwater (To prevent air being sucked in). (Book p11)
The underwater seal bag is connected to a:
Underwater seal bag: Connected to chest tube. (Book p11)
The most basic knot is the:
Square/Reef knot: most basic knot. (Book p11)
A square/reef knot is tied as:
One square throw followed by another square throw
Two throws followed by a single throw
Square knot: One square throw Followed by Another square throw. (Book p11)
When the crossings are the same (black over pink), the result is a:
Crossings are same (Black over pink): Reef or square knot. (Book p11)
When the crossings are opposite (black/pink), the result is a:
Crossings are opposite (Black/pink): Granny/slip knot. (Book p11)
The problem with a granny/slip knot is that its throws:
Granny/slip knot: Don't cross, Open up. (Book p11)
A slip knot is another name for a:
Crossings opposite: Granny/slip knot - Don't cross, Open up. (Book p11)
The surgeon's knot is tied as:
One throw followed by one throw
Surgeon's knot: 2 throws Followed by Single throw. (Book p11)
The reef knot is also called the:
Square/Reef knot: most basic knot - crossings same. (Book p11)
While suturing skin, the needle enters the skin at:
Skin suturing: Enter skin at 90 degrees. (Book p11)
As per the principles of suturing, the bite on each side is:
Principles of suturing: Bite on each side: x; Distance b/w 2 sutures: 2x. (Book p11)
As per the principles of suturing, the distance between 2 sutures is:
Principles of suturing: Bite on each side: x; Distance b/w 2 sutures: 2x. (Book p11)
Simple suture: Fail to cause eversion. (Book p12)
Mattress suture: Cause eversion; Hemostasis. (Book p12)
An advantage of mattress sutures is:
Mattress suture: Cause eversion; Hemostasis. (Book p12)
The vertical mattress suture passes at:
The same depth on both sides
Vertical mattress: passes Superficial and Deep. (Book p12)
The horizontal mattress suture passes at:
The same depth on both sides
The suture with the least cut through rate is the:
Horizontal mattress: Least cut through rate. (Book p12)
Subcuticular sutures are preferred because they are:
Subcuticular sutures: Cosmetically better (No marks). (Book p12)
The suture material for subcuticular closure is:
1-0 silk on a round body needle
5-0 vicryl on a round body needle
Subcuticular suture material: 3-0 monocryl on a cutting needle. (Book p12)
The knot used for closure of a continuous suture is:
Aberdeen's/Cobbler's knot for closure (of continuous suture). (Book p12)
The book's 'Other sutures' panel includes all of the following EXCEPT:
Other sutures: Continuous, Interrupted, Buried mattress, Lock and Purse string sutures. (Book p12)
Lock suture: Continuous suture with locking. (Book p12)
Lock suture: Distribution of tension. (Book p12)
The purse string suture is used to:
Purse string Suture uses: Bury appendicular stump; Cervical encerclage. (Book p12)
Cervical encerclage is a listed use of the:
Purse string Suture uses: Bury appendicular stump; Cervical encerclage. (Book p12)
The Far-Near-Near-Far suture is used for:
Far-Near-Near-Far suture uses: Obliteration of a large cavity. (Book p13)
Obliteration of a large cavity is the listed use of the:
Far-Near-Near-Far suture uses: Obliteration of a large cavity. (Book p13)
The shoe string technique is used for:
Shoe string technique uses: Fasciotomy wound closure. (Book p13)
Shoe string technique: Gradual tightening of suture. (Book p13)
Wound healing in the shoe string technique is by:
Shoe string technique: Healing by 3 degree intention / delayed 1 degree closure. (Book p13)
Round body: Splits tissue; Relatively atraumatic. (Book p13)
Round body: Splits tissue; Relatively atraumatic. (Book p13)
Round body needles are used for delicate structures (the B's) - all of the following EXCEPT:
Round body for delicate structures (B's): Bowel, Bladder, Blood vessels, CBD. (Book p13)
The common bile duct (CBD) is repaired with a:
Round body for delicate structures: Bowel, Bladder, Blood vessels, CBD. (Book p13)
Round body for delicate structures: Bowel, Bladder, Blood vessels, CBD. (Book p13)
Cutting/reverse cutting: Cuts tissue; more traumatic. (Book p13)
Cutting/reverse cutting: Cuts tissue; more traumatic. (Book p13)
Cutting needles are used for tough structures (the S's) - all of the following EXCEPT:
Cutting for tough structures (S's): Sheath, Skin, Fascia. (Book p13)
Cutting for tough structures (S's): Sheath, Skin, Fascia. (Book p13)
Sheath and fascia are sutured with a:
Cutting for tough structures (S's): Sheath, Skin, Fascia. (Book p13)
The swaged end of a needle is the:
End to which suture material is attached
Swaged end: End to which suture material is attached. (Book p13)
The swaged end forms what proportion of the needle?
The body (shaft) of the needle forms:
The needle is grasped with a:
Needle diagram: Point, Body (Shaft), Swaged end, Needle holder. (Book p13)
The tip of the needle is labelled as the:
Needle diagram labels: Point, Body (Shaft), Swaged end. (Book p13)
Color coding: Brown - Catgut; Violet - Vicryl; Blue - Prolene; Black - Silk. (Book p13)
Suture numbering: Suture diameter = 1/10th of a mm. (Book p13)
Suture numbering: No 1 -> Thickest ... 11.0 -> Finest. (Book p13)
Suture numbering: No 1 -> Thickest ... 11.0 -> Finest. (Book p13)
Suture numbering: No 1 -> Thickest; 1.0, 2.0 ... 11.0 -> Finest (Finesse increases). (Book p13)
The natural suture materials listed are:
Natural sutures are antigens (+) and hence:
Natural: Antigens (+) -> mount strong inflammatory reaction. (Book p14)
The synthetic sutures listed include all of the following EXCEPT:
Synthetic: Eg - Prolene, PDS, Vicryl. (Book p14)
Synthetic sutures are inert and cause:
Synthetic: Inert - Less tissue inflammation. (Book p14)
The most inert suture (least inflammation) is:
Most inert: Synthetic non absorbable (Least inflammation). (Book p14)
Monofilament sutures include all of the following EXCEPT:
Monofilament: Catgut, Prolene, PDS, Nylon, Monocryl. (Book p14)
Monofilament: Catgut, Prolene, PDS, Nylon, Monocryl. (Book p14)
Monofilament: Difficult to handle; Strong memory -> more knots. (Book p14)
Monofilament sutures have a strong memory, so they need:
Monofilament: Strong memory -> more knots. (Book p14)
Braided: Easier to handle; increased risk of infection. (Book p14)
A disadvantage of braided sutures is:
Braided: Easier to handle; increased risk of infection. (Book p14)
In the book's tree, absorbable and non-absorbable sutures are each divided into:
Classification tree: Absorbable (Natural/Synthetic) and Non-absorbable (Natural/Synthetic). (Book p14)
Catgut: Derived from submucosa of a sheep gut. (Book p15)
Catgut undergoes phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within:
Catgut: phagocytosis & enzymatic degradation within 7-10 days. (Book p15)
The tensile strength of chromic catgut lasts:
Chromic catgut: Tensile strength: 21-28 days. (Book p15)
Chromic catgut is completely absorbed in:
Chromic catgut: Complete absorption in 90 days. (Book p15)
Monocryl for subcuticular closure is used as:
Monocryl: Subcuticular: 3-0/4-0 cutting/reverse cutting needle. (Book p15)
Vicryl: Braided; Dissolves in 60-90 days. (Book p15)
Vicryl uses: CBD: 5-0; Bowel: 3-0; Bladder: 3-0 (Round body). (Book p15)
Vicryl for bowel and bladder repair is:
Vicryl uses: CBD: 5-0; Bowel: 3-0; Bladder: 3-0 (Round body). (Book p15)
Vicryl for CBD/bowel/bladder is mounted on a:
Vicryl uses: CBD/bowel/bladder - Round body. (Book p15)
Vicryl plus is coated with antibiotic triclosan, which:
Vicryl plus: Coated with antibiotic triclosan (decreased risk of infection). (Book p15)
Barbed vicryl: Thorns on suture. (Book p15)

u: Skin has three main layers, outside in: epidermis → dermis → hypodermis. The epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium, built in five sublayers. Outer to inner: corneum → lucidum → granulosum → spinosum → basale. Stratum corneum is dead, anucleate, keratin-packed — pure barrier tissue. Stratum lucidum only exists in thick skin — palms and soles. Stratum granulosum builds two granule types: keratohyaline granules and lamellar granules (a.k.a. Odland bodies / cementosomes).

Profilaggrin (inactive) is processed into filaggrin (active), which aggregates keratin filaments. A filaggrin mutation is linked to ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis. Desmosomes spot-weld keratinocytes together — most visible as "spines" in the stratum spinosum. Autoantibodies here cause the pemphigus group. Stratum basale = a single row of columnar cells with a central nucleus, a.k.a. stratum germinativum. Spinosum + basale together are called the Malpighian layer. Rete ridges are projections of epidermis down into the dermis; dermal papillae are the dermis pushing up into the epidermis — same interlocking border, opposite direction.

Normal epidermal transit time — basale to corneum — is about 4 weeks. It shortens sharply in psoriasis, driving faster, incomplete turnover. Keratinocytes make up ~90% of the epidermis, from ectoderm. Their structural hallmark is the keratin intermediate filament (KIF), which gives them structural integrity. The other 10% — three specialist cells, each with its own home and job.

The dermo-epidermal junction (DEJ) = basement membrane zone. Top to bottom: hemidesmosome–KIF complex → lamina lucida → lamina densa → sublamina densa. Papillary dermis (~10%): thin, loosely arranged collagen, holds the dermal papillae. Reticular dermis (~90%): dense, thick, mesh-like collagen. Collagen gives tensile strength — Type I is most abundant in skin, ahead of Type III (Type II belongs to cartilage, not skin). Elastic fibers give recoil. Key cells: fibroblasts (main ECM/collagen producers), mast cells (perivascular), macrophages, dermal dendrocytes. The gel-like ground substance filling the space around fibers and cells is made of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). Appendages living in the dermis: hair, nail, sweat gland, sebaceous gland.

The hypodermis = subcutaneous tissue. Main jobs: insulation and thermoregulation, via fat. Structurally: adipocytes grouped into lobules, separated by connective-tissue septa. "Panniculus" = fat, so panniculitis = inflammation of subcutaneous fat. Panniculitis is classified as septal or lobular, by where the inflammation centers.

Hyperkeratosis = thick stratum corneum. Parakeratosis = retained nuclei in the corneum. Wedge-shaped hypergranulosis → lichen planus. Absent/thin granular layer → psoriasis or ichthyosis vulgaris. Two edema patterns: intracellular ("ballooning degeneration," classic in HSV) vs intercellular ("spongiosis," classic in acute eczema). Acanthosis = thickened spinous layer. Acantholysis = lost desmosomal attachment → rounded "Tzanck" cells. Causes: autoimmune (pemphigus), infectious (bullous impetigo, SSSS, HSV), genetic (Hailey-Hailey, Darier). Dyskeratosis = abnormal, premature keratinization of single cells — seen in Darier disease, Bowen disease, SCC. Named microabscesses are diagnostic clues: Munro (corneum, neutrophils) & spongiform pustule of Kogoj (spinosum, neutrophils) → psoriasis · papillary-tip microabscess (neutrophils) → dermatitis herpetiformis · eosinophil-rich microabscess → pemphigus vegetans · Pautrier (atypical T cells) → mycosis fungoides.

Skin vitals: total skin weight is approximately 4–5 kg, covering a surface area of about 1.7 m². Naming convention: "vulgaris" in a disease name (e.g., ichthyosis vulgaris) signals it's the most common form of that condition. Layer-name origins: "lucidum" = clear; "granulosum" = granule (reflecting its prominent granules). On the non-keratinocyte cell table, two easy-to-miss overlaps: S100 positivity is shared by both melanocytes and Langerhans cells (not melanocyte-exclusive); and both melanocytes and Langerhans cells are classified as dendritic cells. Merkel cells are mechanoreceptors that are both slow-adapting and low-threshold. Collagen fibers make up about 70% of the dermis, providing tensile strength; elastic fibers provide elasticity and recoil. In acantholysis, loss of desmosomes converts polyhedral keratinocytes into rounded/circular keratinocytes with a prominent nucleus — these are the Tzanck/acantholytic cells.

Clinical diagnosis in dermatology rests on three pillars: morphology, configuration, and distribution. Flat, non-palpable lesions: under 1cm = macule; over 1cm = patch. Circumscribed, solid, raised lesions: under 1cm = papule; over 1cm = plaque; over 1cm with depth = nodule (think neurofibromatosis). Clear fluid-filled lesions: under 1cm = vesicle; over 1cm = bulla. Classic vesicular-rash causes: herpes labialis/zoster, varicella, hand-foot-mouth disease. Pus-filled lesions: pinpoint = pustule; larger = abscess. RBC extravasation into skin, by size: 1–2mm = petechiae; ≥3mm = purpura; over 1cm = ecchymoses. A wheal is a plaque that is pruritic, erythematous, edematous, and transient — the signature lesion of urticaria.

Secondary lesions are primary lesions modified by itching or treatment. Scale = visible exfoliation of the stratum corneum; scalp scaling suggests seborrhoeic dermatitis or psoriasis. Crust = dried serum/pus/blood; a golden-brown, "honey-colored" crust is classic for non-bullous impetigo. Erosion = loss of epidermis only (e.g. pemphigus vulgaris). An ulcer goes deeper — epidermis plus part or all of the dermis. Fissure = a linear, deep cleft (classic in eczema). Excoriation = scratch marks from scratching. Lichenification = thickened, hyperpigmented skin with exaggerated markings from chronic scratching. Atrophy = thinning of skin's structural components, seen as wrinkling (e.g. topical steroid abuse). Special lesions are specific to one disease: a burrow (wavy, grayish-white tunnel in the corneum) means scabies. Comedones (follicle plugged by sebum + keratin) mean acne vulgaris — black (open) from oxidized sebum, or white (closed). A three-zone target lesion means erythema multiforme.

Configuration describes how lesions are arranged. Grouped = clustered (herpes labialis). Dermatomal = along one nerve's territory (herpes zoster/shingles). Linear = line-shaped. Blaschkoid = wavy/whorled, following Blaschko's lines. Annular = ring-shaped, clear center, active periphery — seen in pityriasis rosea, mid-borderline (BB) leprosy, and tinea corporis. Discoid/nummular = coin-shaped, active both centrally and peripherally — seen in discoid lupus erythematosus and discoid eczema. Discrete = individual, separate lesions. Confluent = multiple lesions merging together. Distribution describes body location: acral (extremities), flexor or extensor aspect (extensor = elbows/knees), and photodistributed (sun-exposed areas).

Langer's lines = skin tension lines, running along dermal collagen fiber orientation. Surgeons cut along them; incisions across them risk hypertrophic scars. Blaschko's lines trace epidermal cell migration during embryonic development — V-shaped on the upper spine, S-shaped on the abdomen, roughly vertical on the limbs, spiralled on the scalp. Incontinentia pigmenti (X-linked dominant) follows these lines. Nikolsky sign: tangential pressure on skin causes the upper layer to separate from the lower. True Nikolsky (mechanism: acantholysis) is seen in pemphigus foliaceus, pemphigus vulgaris, and SSSS. Pseudo-Nikolsky (mechanism: keratinocyte necrosis) is seen in toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Diascopy (vitropression): press a glass slide over an erythematous lesion. Blanching = vasodilation (e.g. erythema). Non-blanching = RBC extravasation → purpura. Apple jelly nodules — yellowish-brown on diascopy — suggest granulomatous disease: lupus vulgaris, sarcoidosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Wood's lamp: an office procedure using UV light around 364 nm, filtered through nickel oxide and barium silicate glass. Infections: Microsporum species fluoresce blue/green; Trichophyton schoenleinii (causing favus) fluoresces dull blue. Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia) fluoresces yellow. Erythrasma (Corynebacterium minutissimum) fluoresces coral red, from coproporphyrin III. Pigmentary uses: an ash-leaf macule (tuberous sclerosis), vitiligo, and melasma all show enhanced, milky-white fluorescence. Metabolic uses: porphyria cutanea tarda causes pink urine under Wood's lamp; congenital erythropoietic porphyria causes red teeth (erythrodontia). KOH mount: scrape the active border of skin, nail, or hair → slide → microscope. Dermatophytosis shows refractile branching hyphae; pityriasis versicolor shows short hyphae + round spores ("spaghetti and meatballs"); chromoblastomycosis shows round, brown, thick-walled bodies (medlar/sclerotic/copper-penny bodies).

Tzanck smear: a cytodiagnostic test. De-roof a vesicle/bulla → scrape the floor/roof → slide → Giemsa stain → microscope. Round acantholytic cells with prominent nuclei point to the pemphigus group; multinucleated giant cells point to HSV-1, HSV-2, or VZV. Cryotherapy: liquid nitrogen at −196°C freezes tissue, changing osmolarity until cells rupture. Used for verruca vulgaris (warts) and keloids. Phototherapy uses UV radiation. NB-UVB = narrow-band UV-B (311±2 nm). PUVA = psoralen (a photosensitizer) plus UV-A (320–400 nm). Both are used for psoriasis, vitiligo, and atopic dermatitis.

Psoriasis: the name breaks down as "papulo" = papules/plaques, "squamous" = scales. It's a chronic, T-cell mediated, inflammatory disease of the skin (and other systems). Three groups of causes: signaling molecules (cytokines), genetic, and environmental. Proinflammatory cytokines rise: Th1 → IL-2, TNF-α, IFN-γ. Th17 → IL-17. Th22 → IL-22. Genetics: HLA-Cw6 → early-onset disease. HLA-B27 → psoriatic spondylitis. PSORS1 (susceptibility gene) → ~50% hereditary risk. Environmental triggers — drugs: lithium, antimalarials, beta-blockers, NSAIDs, sudden steroid withdrawal. Infections: Group A strep (triggers guttate psoriasis) and HIV. Also winter, alcohol, and smoking. Pathogenesis: epidermis shows hyperproliferation; dermis shows inflammation. Normal epidermal transit time (~28 days) drops to just 3–5 days in psoriasis.

Guttate psoriasis: seen in children, often after a sore throat/pharyngitis, triggered by Group A β-hemolytic strep. "Gutta" = raindrop-shaped lesions on the trunk. DOC: macrolide antibiotics. Pustular psoriasis: triggered by sudden withdrawal of systemic steroids. Sterile pustules coalesce into lakes/sheets of pus. Generalized forms: acute (Von Zumbusch type) and the pregnancy form (impetigo herpetiformis, a.k.a. pustular psoriasis of pregnancy). A localized form exists too. Erythrodermic psoriasis: erythema (with or without scaling) covering more than 90% of body surface area.

Psoriatic arthritis is seronegative (RF-negative) and erosive. Most commonly affected joint: distal interphalangeal (DIP). Most severe form: arthritis mutilans. "Sausage digits" (dactylitis) = fusiform digit swelling from inflammation. Classic X-ray finding: pencil-in-cup appearance. Chronic plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) is the classic type: red, scaly papules and plaques with silvery-white scale, distributed on the scalp and the extensor surfaces of elbows/knees.

Auspitz sign: the Grattage test — scraping a psoriatic plaque with a glass slide in stages. Scraping first accentuates the silvery-white scales, then reveals the Bulkeley membrane, then produces pinpoint bleeding spots — that final step is the Auspitz sign. Koebner's phenomenon (isomorphic response): new lesions of the original disease appear at sites of trauma on previously normal skin. True Koebner reflects an immunological response — psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo (rarer: Darier disease, lichen nitidus, Kaposi sarcoma). Pseudo-Koebner is autoinoculation of a viral infection along the trauma line — viral warts, molluscum contagiosum. Woronoff's ring: a hypopigmented ring surrounding a psoriatic lesion.

Nail pits (depressions in the nail plate) are the most common nail change in psoriasis — coarse, irregular, and deep, from a defect in the proximal nail matrix. Subungual hyperkeratosis: hyperkeratotic material builds up beneath the nail plate. Distal onycholysis: the nail plate separates from the nail bed distally. Oil drop sign / salmon patch: a pathognomonic finding from a nail-bed defect. Regional variations: scalp psoriasis (often mistaken for dandruff — identified by silvery-white scales) and flexural/inverse psoriasis (favors flexural surfaces instead of the usual extensor ones).

Stratum corneum: parakeratosis (abnormally retained nucleated cells) plus Munro's microabscess (a neutrophil collection). Stratum granulosum: thickness is decreased or absent. Stratum spinosum: thickness is increased (acanthosis), with its own neutrophil collection — the spongiform pustule of Kogoj. Dermal papillae: suprapapillary thinning, regular elongation of rete ridges, and dilated blood vessels.

Topical treatment by mechanism: to reduce scaling — emollients/moisturizers. Anti-inflammatory — topical steroids. To reduce DNA synthesis — coal tar, dithranol. To normalize keratinization — vitamin A analogue (topical retinoid, tazarotene) or vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol). Note: tazarotene is NOT used in acne. Phototherapy works by raising anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10. NB-UVB (narrow-band UV-B, 311±2 nm) vs PUVA (psoralen + UV-A, 320–400 nm) — psoralen is a photosensitizer that helps UV-A penetrate deeper. Combination regimens: Goeckerman = coal tar + NB-UVB. Ingram's = coal tar + NB-UVB + dithranol/anthralin.

Methotrexate: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; used for plaque, pustular, and erythrodermic psoriasis; watch for bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity (Category X). Cyclosporine: calcineurin inhibitor (↓IL-2), rapidly acting; used for severe erythrodermic psoriasis; watch for hypertension and nephrotoxicity. Acitretin (oral retinoid): modulates keratinocyte differentiation; used for pustular psoriasis; watch for hyperlipidemia, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity. Apremilast: PDE4 inhibitor, raising cAMP and anti-inflammatory cytokines; used for psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis; side effects: headache, diarrhea. Tofacitinib: JAK-STAT1/3 inhibitor; used for psoriatic arthritis; watch for infections, dyslipidemia, thromboembolism. Systemic steroids are generally contraindicated in psoriasis — the one exception: drug of choice for pustular psoriasis of pregnancy (impetigo herpetiformis), with cyclosporine as second-line there. Biologics give targeted cytokine inhibition — no organ-specific side effects, but expensive. IL-12/23 (shared p40 subunit) → ustekinumab. IL-23 → guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab. TNF-α → infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab. IL-17 → secukinumab, ixekizumab. IL-17 receptor → brodalumab. Psoriasis carries a systemic association with metabolic syndrome: obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia.

Lichen planus: a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory disease affecting skin, the oral cavity, and skin appendages (hair, nail). Triggers: dental amalgam (contains mercury), infections (Hepatitis B and C), and drugs (antimalarials). Skin symptom: pruritus. Classic lesion — the "6 P's": Purple (violaceous), Pruritic, Polygonal, Plain-topped, Plaques, Papules. Wickham's striae: a net-like, lacy white reticulate pattern on the lesion surface — best seen after applying oil, under a magnifying glass. Distribution: flexor surfaces. Lichen planus shows a true Koebner's phenomenon — also seen in psoriasis and vitiligo.
Lichen Planus — Oral, Nail & Hair Involvement

Oral cavity involvement occurs in 40–60% of patients — often asymptomatic, sometimes a burning sensation with spicy food. It shows the same lacy white reticulate pattern as the skin. Nails are affected in about 10% of patients. Most common change: thinning of the nail plate. Pathognomonic change: pterygium — a wing-shaped fold fusing the proximal nail fold to the nail bed as the nail matrix is destroyed. Severe cases can show anonychia (absent nails) or a "pup tent" sign (tenting of the nail). Hair involvement causes scarring alopecia, called lichen planopilaris — seen clinically as a perifollicular blue-grey hue.

Epidermis: hyperkeratosis (stratum corneum), wedge-shaped hypergranulosis (stratum granulosum), and acanthosis (stratum spinosum). Colloid/Civatte bodies = necrotic keratinocytes. Also seen: basal cell degeneration. A band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugs the dermo-epidermal junction, alongside a gap called the Max Joseph space. The rete ridges are saw-toothed. Band-like lymphocytes at the DEJ plus basal cell degeneration together define interface dermatitis. Treatment: topical or systemic steroids.

Word origin: "pityriasis" = scaling, "rosea" = red eruptions. It's an acute, self-limiting eruption. Trigger: viral infection — most commonly HHV-7, also HHV-6. Symptoms: usually asymptomatic, sometimes mild pruritus. Lesion sequence: a large herald patch appears first, followed by secondary scaly papules and oral/annular plaques, then mild pigmentary change, then slow fading. Total duration: 4–6 weeks. The herald patch is annular, with a collarette scale — attached at the outer edge, free at the inner edge. Hanging curtain sign: stretching the skin along the patch's long axis folds the scale in a pattern resembling a hanging curtain. Distribution follows the lines of Langer, long axis oriented down and out from the spine (parallel to the ribs) — giving a "Christmas tree" appearance. (Unrelated note: "Christmas tree cataract" is instead a feature of myotonic dystrophy.) Treatment: usually just counselling (self-limiting); topical steroids if pruritic; phototherapy if non-responsive.

A chronic, inflammatory papulosquamous disease. Hallmark: multiple follicular papules, described as "nutmeg grater" papules. Erythroderma: orange-red erythema (± scaling) covering >90% of body surface area, but with characteristic islands of sparing. Erythema progresses in a cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) direction. Palmoplantar keratoderma: thickened skin on the palms and soles. Treatment: oral retinoids, specifically acitretin (also used in pustular psoriasis).

Hair is an ectodermal appendage — a defining feature of mammals. Hair follicle layers, innermost to outermost: hair shaft → inner root sheath (IRS) → outer root sheath → glassy membrane → connective tissue sheath. The hair shaft itself, innermost to outermost: medulla → cortex → cuticle. The IRS, innermost to outermost: cuticle → Huxley's layer → Henley's layer. Longitudinally, the erector pili muscle attachment splits the follicle into upper and lower segments. The upper segment splits (at the sebaceous gland) into infundibulum (upper) and isthmus (lower) — the apocrine gland opens into the infundibulum. The lower segment splits (at Adamson's fringe) into stem (upper) and bulb (lower). Hair follicle stem cells are multipotent, located in the bulge (matching the erector pili attachment). Damage here causes scarring alopecia. Three hair types: lanugo (fine, soft fetal hair, shed in-utero), vellus (fine, unmedullated, soft; bulb in the reticular dermis), and terminal (coarse, medullated, thick; bulb in the subcutaneous tissue). Vellus→terminal conversion happens in hirsutism; terminal→vellus conversion happens in androgenetic alopecia.

The hair cycle has four stages: anagen (growth — 86% of hairs, up to 3 years, the longest phase), catagen (involution — 1% of hairs, just 3 weeks, the shortest phase), telogen (resting — 13% of hairs, ~3 months), and exogen (shedding). Normal hair growth rate: about 1 cm/month. Alopecia = hair loss, in two big categories. Non-cicatricial (non-scarring): follicles preserved, no visible inflammation, reversible. Cicatricial (scarring): follicles destroyed, inflammation present, irreversible. ("Cicatrix" = scar.) Non-cicatricial alopecia by pattern: patchy (alopecia areata, trichotillomania, non-inflammatory tinea capitis, secondary syphilis), diffuse (anagen effluvium, telogen effluvium), patterned (androgenetic alopecia), and systemic disease-linked (SLE, thyroid dysfunction).

Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disease targeting the pigmented anagen hair bulb. "Areata" means patchy/spotty. Scalp lesion: well-demarcated, circular, smooth surface, complete hair loss within the patch. At the margins: short, broken "exclamation mark" hairs — broad distally, tapering proximally. Nails show fine, regular, superficial pits (coarse/irregular/deep pits instead suggest psoriasis). Histopathology shows a peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate — a "swarm of bees" appearance. Bad prognostic factor: early age of onset. Patterns: ophiasis (band-like alopecia in the occipital area), alopecia totalis (complete scalp hair loss), alopecia universalis (complete body hair loss). Associations: atopy (a localized Type I hypersensitivity) and other autoimmune disease, especially thyroid dysfunction. Treatment: localized form — intralesional steroids (triamcinolone acetonide); extensive form — systemic steroids, azathioprine, or tofacitinib (a JAK1/3 inhibitor).

Trichotillomania is an obsessive-compulsive disorder involving pulling out one's own hair. Lesions: bizarre-shaped bald patches, broken hairs of varying length, perifollicular hemorrhage, and — unlike alopecia areata — incomplete hair loss within the patch. Complication chain: trichophagia (pathological hair-eating) → trichobezoar (a hair cast in the stomach) → intermittent gastric outlet obstruction. Tinea capitis (non-inflammatory) is fungal invasion of the hair shaft, in two types: black dot type (endothrix — infection inside the hair shaft; T. tonsurans/violaceum) and grey patch type (ectothrix — infection on the hair surface; Microsporum canis).

Secondary syphilis can cause a diffuse, non-cicatricial "moth-eaten" alopecia. Anagen effluvium: chemotherapy/radiotherapy acts on rapidly dividing cells, arresting hair growth in anagen (producing a dystrophic anagen hair) → hair loss after just 3–4 weeks. Telogen effluvium: severe systemic stress (post-pregnancy, infections like malaria/typhoid/COVID-19, or surgery) prematurely pushes follicles into telogen, where they sit for 3 months before shedding → hair loss after about 3 months. It resolves once the stressor is removed.

A patterned, non-cicatricial alopecia from genetic factors plus androgens: testosterone → (via 5α-reductase) → dihydrotestosterone (DHT) → hair thinning and alopecia. Pathology: shortening of the anagen phase, plus miniaturization of the hair follicle. In men: balding of the vertex plus frontotemporal recession, graded by Hamilton-Norwood grading. In women: central scalp thinning with the frontal hairline maintained, graded by Ludwig's grading. Treatment: minoxidil (increases anagen phase and follicle size; 2% for women, 5% for men), finasteride (inhibits 5α-reductase, blocking testosterone→DHT; 1mg dose, used in men and post-menopausal women), platelet-rich plasma therapy, and hair transplantation.

Cicatricial (scarring) alopecia arises from several disease categories. Papulosquamous disease: lichen planopilaris (lichen planus involving hair), showing a perifollicular blue-grey hue. Granulomatous disorder: sarcoidosis. Connective tissue disorders: discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE), discoid lesions of SLE, and linear morphea — a linear band of alopecia plus induration, dermal fibrosis restricted to the skin, resembling the strike of a sword ("en coup de sabre").

Inflammatory tinea capitis has two forms. Favus: caused by Trichophyton schoenleinii, endemic in Kashmir, producing yellow, cup-shaped crusts called scutula. Kerion: caused by zoophilic fungi (T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum), risk factors include contact with pet animals and childhood, presenting with a boggy, indurated scalp swelling, easily pluckable hair, and regional lymphadenopathy from the intense inflammation. Investigation for both: KOH mount. Other inflammatory causes of scarring alopecia: folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis of the scalp. An idiopathic cause: pseudopelade of Brocq, with a "footprints in snow" appearance and perifollicular concentric fibrosis on histopathology. Hidradenitis suppurativa: a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease of intertriginous sites (axilla, ano-genital region). Pathology: a hair follicle occlusion disease (previously thought to be an apocrine gland disease). Features: deep-seated red nodules, abscesses, sinuses, and scars. Treatment: antibiotics (clindamycin/doxycycline), oral retinoids (isotretinoin), and TNF-α inhibitors (adalimumab).

Sweat glands produce sweat, in two types. Eccrine glands: found all over the body (maximum in palms and soles), ducts open directly onto the skin surface, sympathetic cholinergic nerve supply (neurotransmitter: acetylcholine), and merocrine secretion (intact cell borders). Apocrine glands: found in the axilla and perineum, ducts open into the hair follicle (above the sebaceous gland), adrenergic nerve supply, and apocrine secretion (the apex of the cell pinches off). Modified apocrine glands: the mammary gland, Moll's gland (eyelid), and the ceruminous gland (external auditory canal).

Miliaria: obstruction of the eccrine sweat duct, favored by hot, humid climates. Classified by level of obstruction: miliaria crystallina (stratum corneum — tiny superficial vesicles that rupture immediately), miliaria rubra ("prickly heat" — stratum spinosum), and miliaria profunda (dermo-epidermal junction; "profunda" = deep). Bromhidrosis: offensive body odor. Chromhidrosis: production of colored sweat. Fox-Fordyce disease (a.k.a. apocrine miliaria — obstruction of the apocrine duct): pruritic, skin-colored papules in the axilla and areola. Treatment: topical steroids, topical retinoids.

Sebaceous glands produce sebum via holocrine secretion — the entire mature cell disintegrates to become the secretory product. Classified by association with the hair follicle. Present (the pilosebaceous unit: hair + sebaceous gland together) vs absent — ectopic sebaceous glands found without a hair follicle: upper lip/buccal mucosa (Fordyce spots), breast (Montgomery tubercles), eyelids (Zeis and meibomian glands), and the prepuce (Tyson's glands).

Acne vulgaris: a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit, with polymorphic lesions (comedones, papules, pustules, cysts). Pathogenesis chain: androgens stimulate the sebaceous gland → increased sebum production → outflow blocked by hyperkeratinization at the infundibulum → growth of Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium) → bacterial lipases convert triglycerides to free fatty acids → inflammation. Modifying factors: hot, humid climate; diet (high glycemic index foods and milk/dairy raise IGF-1, which blocks the sebaceous duct); emotional stress; oil-based facial cosmetics; genetic predisposition; hormonal factors (premenstrual flares in 70% of women; polycystic ovarian syndrome).

Grade 1 acne = comedones — folliculocentric lesions blocked by sebum and keratin. Open comedones (oxidized sebum) appear black; closed comedones (no oxidation) appear white. Grade 2 = papules/pustules; Grade 3 = more widespread inflammatory lesions; Grade 4 = nodulocystic acne (nodules plus cysts). Distribution: face (forehead, cheeks, chin), shoulders, chest, and upper back (chest + upper back = truncal acne). Acneiform eruption (drug-induced acne): sudden onset, caused by systemic steroids, isoniazid, or lithium. Distinguishing features: monomorphic lesions (all lesions look alike) and absence of comedones.

Differentiating acne from rosacea: acne shows comedones (present); rosacea does NOT have comedones, but does show papules/pustules/nodules and telangiectasia. Acne is associated with greasy skin; rosacea distributes on the central convexities of the face rather than acne's broader face/shoulder/chest/back pattern.
Acne general measures: cleansers, water-based (not oil-based) cosmetics, avoiding high-glycemic-index foods and dairy.
Topical therapy: retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene — first choice for comedonal acne), topical antibiotics (clindamycin, nadifloxacin), benzoyl peroxide (antibacterial + comedolytic), azelaic acid (antibacterial, reduces hyperpigmentation).
Systemic therapy: antibiotics (azithromycin, doxycycline, minocycline); oral isotretinoin for nodulocystic or therapy-resistant acne — side effects: cheilitis (most common), hyperlipidemia, rare hepatitis, teratogenicity (Category X — stop 1 month before conception). Oral contraceptives treat hormonal acne associated with PCOS.

Rosacea: a chronic, inflammatory, facial dermatosis distributed on the central convexities of the face, with periocular and perioral sparing. Pathogenesis: dysregulation of facial blood vessels causing vasodilation; the Demodex mite; and triggers that act as potent vasodilators — sunlight, spicy food, stress, alcohol, and hot beverages. Four clinical types: erythematotelangiectatic (photosensitivity, flushing, centrofacial erythema, telangiectasia), papulopustular, phymatous (a.k.a. "potato nose"/rhinophyma — irregular surface nodularities, prominent pores, from sebaceous gland hypertrophy and fibrosis), and oculo-rosacea (photophobia).

Rosacea can resemble SLE's malar rash — but SLE shows minimal papules/pustules, a true malar rash, and systemic symptoms (fever, arthralgia, myalgia) that rosacea lacks. General treatment: sunscreen, trigger avoidance, and avoiding topical steroids (which can worsen rosacea). Specific treatment: α-agonists like brimonidine (mechanism: vasoconstriction); antimicrobials — topical metronidazole, or systemic doxycycline/ivermectin. Rhinophyma treatment: early stages — oral isotretinoin; late stages — CO2 laser ablation.

The nail is an ectodermal appendage, on the dorsal aspect of the terminal phalanges, protecting the digit tip. Growth rate: fingernails ~3mm/month; toenails ~1mm/month (fingernails grow roughly 3x faster). Key structures: nail plate, nail bed, lunula (the semicircular pale area), cuticle (seals the nail apparatus, protects against trauma), proximal and lateral nail folds, nail matrix (produces the nail plate), and hyponychium. Paronychia = nail fold infection. Acute: caused by Staphylococcus aureus; erythema, edema, and pus in the nail fold; treated with antimicrobials (or surgical drainage plus antibiotics if an abscess is present). Chronic: caused by Candida albicans plus irritant contact dermatitis (from prolonged water contact); loss of cuticle, nail fold edema/erythema; treated with antifungals plus topical steroids.

Onychomycosis = fungal infection of the nail unit, caused by dermatophytes (tinea unguium), non-dermatophytes (Fusarium, Acremonium), or Candida. Clinical types: DLSO (distal lateral subungual onychomycosis) — yellow discoloration of the nail plate, the most common type. PSO (proximal subungual onychomycosis) — associated with HIV infection. WSO (white superficial onychomycosis) — superficial fungus on the dorsum of the nail plate. TDO (total dystrophic onychomycosis) — the end stage, with crumbling and dystrophy of the entire nail plate. Treatment: terbinafine (an allylamine) — 250mg once daily for 6 weeks (fingernails) or 12 weeks (toenails). Itraconazole (an azole) — pulse dosing of 200mg twice daily for 1 week each month; 2 pulses for fingernails, 3 pulses for toenails.

Pitting: depressions in the nail plate, from a defect in the proximal nail matrix. Causes: alopecia areata (fine, superficial, regular, geometric pits), psoriasis (coarse, irregular, deep pits), and eczema. Pterygium: a winged-shaped fold extending from the proximal nail fold to the nail bed, associated with lichen planus (dorsal pterygium). Beau's lines: a transverse/horizontal depression across the nail plate, from a temporary arrest of nail matrix activity. Associations: chemotherapy and severe medical illness.

Chromonychia means "colored nails." Blue/azure lunula: associated with Wilson's disease and argyria (silver intoxication). Yellow nail syndrome: a clinical triad of chronic respiratory illness (bronchiectasis/pleural effusion), primary lymphedema, and the yellow nail itself (cuticle loss, nail plate thickening, slow growth). Green nail syndrome: caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, via pyocyanin production. Leukonychia (white nails): true leukonychia (nail matrix defect) — Mees' lines (a single transverse white band, associated with chronic arsenic poisoning). Apparent leukonychia (nail bed defect): Muehrcke's bands (paired transverse white bands, associated with hypoalbuminemia), Lindsay's nail/half-and-half nails (proximal 50% white, distal 50% brown; chronic renal failure), and Terry's nail (proximal 90% white, distal 10% brown/pink; chronic liver disease).

Primary bullous lesions are fluid-filled: vesicles (under 1cm) and bullae (over 1cm). Bullae split further into flaccid (intraepidermal, wrinkled surface) and tense (subepidermal). Secondary lesions: erosions (focal/total loss of epidermis) and crusts (hard exudate). Bullous disorders fall into three broad categories: immunobullous disorders (autoimmune pathology), mechanobullous disorders, and inherited acantholytic disorders. Within immunobullous disorders, split level matters: an intraepidermal split gives the pemphigus group; a subepidermal split gives the pemphigoid group or dermatitis herpetiformis.

Desmosomes are proteins connecting keratinocytes to each other, present intraepidermally. Acantholysis = rupture/loss of desmosomes, turning polygonal keratinocytes into circular acantholytic (Tzanck) cells. Pemphigus target antigens: desmoglein, desmocollin, and the plakin group (desmoplakin, periplakin, endoplakin). Classification: pemphigus foliaceus (targets desmoglein 1; variant: pemphigus erythematosus) and pemphigus vulgaris (targets desmoglein 3 > 1; variant: pemphigus vegetans). Other types: IgA pemphigus (desmocollin), drug-induced pemphigus, and paraneoplastic pemphigus (plakins). Desmoglein 1 (→ pemphigus foliaceus): upper epidermis (between corneum and granulosum), subcorneal split, low oral mucosa concentration, no oral lesions. Desmoglein 3 (→ pemphigus vulgaris): deeper (between spinosum and basale), suprabasal split, high oral mucosa concentration, oral lesions in 90–95% of patients.

Pemphigus vulgaris is the most common pemphigus type, with a chronic course and IgG autoantibodies. Typical age: 40–60 years. Symptom: a burning sensation over lesions. Primary lesion: a flaccid bulla over normal skin that ruptures easily. Secondary lesion: erosions that extend with no healing tendency (from ongoing acantholysis). Sites: oral cavity, scalp, face, chest, back, limbs. On examination: Nikolsky sign — tangential pressure over normal-looking skin separates upper from lower epidermal layers. Bulla spread sign — tangential pressure over an existing bulla extends its margin into adjacent skin, with irregular, angulated margins. Oral cavity: lesions in 90–95% of patients, presenting as painful erosions.

Tzanck smear: shows acantholytic/Tzanck cells. Histopathology: the "row of tombstone" appearance — basal cells stay attached to the basement membrane (vertically, via intact hemidesmosomes) but detach from each other (laterally, from lost desmosomes). Split level: suprabasal. Direct immunofluorescence (the investigation of choice): immune deposits of IgG and C3, at an intraepidermal/intercellular site, in a characteristic "fish net" pattern. Treatment: immunosuppression — high-dose systemic steroids, or cyclophosphamide (side effect: hemorrhagic cystitis). For moderate/severe cases: monoclonal antibody therapy — rituximab, which inhibits CD20 on B cells.

Pemphigus foliaceus: targets desmoglein 1. Lesions: transient superficial bullae that rupture easily, leaving scales and crust; erythroderma affecting >90% of body surface area. Distribution: seborrhoeic areas (scalp, face, chest, upper back). Unlike pemphigus vulgaris, the oral mucosa is normal. Histopathology: subcorneal split with acantholytic cells. Pemphigus vegetans: a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris. "Vegetans" = vegetative/proliferative, cauliflower-like masses. Sites: flexures (axilla, groin). Drug-induced pemphigus: most commonly caused by D-penicillamine, also rifampicin and captopril. Paraneoplastic pemphigus: secondary to neoplasia, particularly non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and CLL.

Bullous disorders split into three types: immunobullous (subepidermal type — pemphigoid group and dermatitis herpetiformis), mechanobullous, and inherited acantholytic. The pemphigoid group arises from a defect in basement membrane zone (BMZ) proteins. BMZ layers, top to bottom: hemidesmosome-KIF complex → lamina lucida → lamina densa → sublamina densa. Each layer has its own antigen and disease link: HD-KIF complex (BPAG-1, keratin 5/14, BPAG-2) → bullous pemphigoid. Lamina lucida (BPAG-2, laminin) → bullous pemphigoid, cicatricial pemphigoid, pemphigoid gestationis, linear IgA bullous dermatosis. Lamina densa (laminin, collagen IV).
