Sublamina densa (collagen VII / anchoring fibrils) → epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. BPAG naming: "BP" = bullous pemphigoid, "AG" = antigen. BPAG-2 is a transmembrane protein. Laminin sits in both the lamina lucida and lamina densa. Collagen VII is the strongest portion of the BMZ. Molecular weights: BPAG-1 = 230 kDa, BPAG-2 = 180 kDa.

Bullous pemphigoid is a subepidermal blistering disorder. Autoantibody: IgG. Target protein: hemidesmosomes. Target antigens: BPAG-2, BPAG-1. Unlike the pemphigus group, acantholysis is absent in bullous pemphigoid — acantholysis is specifically a desmosomal-pathology feature. Typical age: 60–80 years. Primary lesion: tense, itchy bullae over a red base or normal skin, rupturing on scratching. Secondary lesion: erosions that tend to heal with no extension — a direct consequence of the absent acantholysis. Sites: flexures, lower abdomen, trunk. (Tense blisters are the expected finding in subepidermal pathology.) Oral mucosa lesions are seen in only 10–30% of patients — far less than pemphigus vulgaris's 90–95%.

Nikolsky sign is negative in bullous pemphigoid. Bulla spread sign: pressure over a bulla produces round, regular margins (unlike pemphigus's irregular, angulated spread). Asboe-Hansen sign: a variant of the bulla spread sign, using vertical pressure applied over the top of the bulla. Tzanck smear: eosinophilic cells present (the cause of erythema and itching); no acantholytic cells seen. Histopathology: subepidermal bulla with eosinophilic infiltrates. Direct immunofluorescence (investigation of choice): IgG and C3, deposited at the BMZ, in a linear pattern. Treatment: low-dose systemic steroids.

Linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD) splits by age: in adults it's called linear IgA disease (LAD), typically seen over 60 years. In children it's called chronic bullous disease of childhood (CBDC), seen under 5 years. Pemphigoid gestationis (a.k.a. herpes gestationis — a misnomer, unrelated to herpes) is bullous pemphigoid occurring in pregnancy. Target antigen: BPAG-2. Clinical features: urticarial raised plaques (from dermal edema) plus tense bullae, starting periumbilically and progressing to the lower extremities. Treatment: systemic steroids. Chronic bullous disease of childhood (CBDC): autoantibody IgA. Lesion: multiple vesicles in an annular pattern, described as a "cluster of jewels"/"string of pearls" appearance. Distribution: perioral and perineal region. Histopathology: neutrophilic infiltrates. Treatment: dapsone (drug of choice — inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis).

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease): a chronic, relapsing, pruritic immunobullous disease. Autoantibody: IgA. Target: epidermal transglutaminase 3. Split level: subepidermal. Genetics: HLA-DQ2, DQ8, B8. Associated systemic condition: gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac sprue). Typical age: 20–40 years. Lesions: primary — intensely pruritic papulovesicles ("dermatitis"); scratching produces secondary lesions — grouped excoriations (the "herpetiform" pattern plus scratch marks). Site: extensor aspect (scalp, back, elbow). Tzanck smear: neutrophils seen. Histopathology: subepidermal split/bulla with neutrophil accumulation at the dermal papillary tips — a papillary tip microabscess. DIF: IgA deposited at the BMZ and dermal papilla, in a granular pattern. Treatment of choice: a gluten-free diet (avoiding barley, rye, oats, wheat). Drug of choice: dapsone (inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis).

Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is classified as a mechanobullous disorder — induced by trivial mechanical trauma. Pathogenesis: genetic in origin (exception: EB acquisita, which is autoimmune/acquired, not genetic). BMZ proteins and their associated EB subtypes: keratin 5/14 defect → EB simplex. Laminin defect → junctional EB. Collagen VII defect → dystrophic EB. Clinical presentation: genetic predisposition (classic scenario: a child born via consanguineous marriage), with blisters appearing over areas of trivial trauma (classic scenario: a mother notices blisters just from handling her baby). Lesions: blisters/bullae at trauma-prone sites. Treatment: supportive management for lesions; gene therapy is the definitive treatment.
Inherited Acantholytic Disorders — Classification & Clinical Features

Two inherited acantholytic disorders: Hailey-Hailey disease and Darier disease. Both are autosomal dominant, with a defect in the Ca²⁺ ATPase pump of desmosomes. Hailey-Hailey: pathology predominantly acantholysis; chromosome 3; gene ATP2C1. Darier: pathology predominantly dyskeratosis (abnormal, premature keratinization); chromosome 12; gene ATP2A2. Hailey-Hailey disease (a.k.a. familial benign chronic pemphigus): primary lesion — flaccid vesicles (intraepidermal pathology), rupturing with friction at the axilla; secondary lesion — a macerated (soft, wet) plaque. Sites: flexures. Nail finding: longitudinal leukonychia. Darier disease (a.k.a. keratosis follicularis): hyperkeratotic (thick), dirty, warty, greasy papules. Sites: seborrhoeic areas (face, neck, chest, upper back). Nails: alternating white (leukonychia) and red (erythronychia) bands, plus V-nicking at the distal nail plate edge. Palms show pits. Oral cavity: papules coalesce into a "cobblestone" appearance.

Hailey-Hailey histopathology: suprabasal split, with a "dilapidated brick wall" appearance from partial acantholysis. Treatment: manage secondary bacterial/fungal infection; topical steroids to reduce inflammation. Darier disease histopathology: dyskeratotic cells in two forms — "corps ronds" (rounded cells, lower epidermis) and "corps grains" (grain-like cells, upper epidermis). Treatment: oral retinoids (acitretin).

Pyoderma = purulent bacterial infection of the skin ("pyo" = pus/purulent). Classified by hair follicle involvement. Follicular pyoderma (etiology: Staphylococcus aureus): folliculitis, furuncle/boil, carbuncle. Non-follicular pyoderma: localized (impetigo — superficial; ecthyma — deep) or spreading (erysipelas — superficial; cellulitis — deep). Folliculitis: infection of the hair follicle alone — a folliculocentric pustule. Treatment: topical antibacterials. Furuncle (boil): infection of the hair follicle plus perifollicular area — a red, indurated, tender nodule with a pus point. Treatment: topical antibacterials. Carbuncle: infection of multiple hair follicles plus contiguous areas — a red, indurated, tender nodule with multiple surface pustules. Site: nape of neck (most common). Strongly associated with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. Treatment: insulin for diabetes, parenteral systemic antibiotics, and surgical treatment (incision/drainage, debridement).

Impetigo = bacterial infection of the epidermis. Non-bullous impetigo (impetigo contagiosa): Group A Streptococcus and S. aureus; seen in children; golden-brown, honey-colored crusts; sites — perinasal and perioral areas. A rare, severe remote complication: post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Bullous impetigo: caused by S. aureus, which locally produces an epidermolytic toxin that lyses the epidermis, forming a bulla. Lesions: flaccid bullae with a varnish-like crust, on the trunk. Hypopyon sign: pus collects in the lower half of the bulla. Topical antibiotics used in dermatology: fusidic acid, mupirocin, and ozenoxacin — the latter two also have MRSA activity. Ecthyma: a deeper, ulcerative variant of impetigo, caused by Group A Streptococcus. Site: lower extremities (most common). Lesion: a chocolate-brown, thick, adherent crust overlying a purulent, irregular ulcer.

Erysipelas: upper half of the dermis plus lymphatics. Caused by Group A Streptococcus. Most common site: lower extremities (legs). Lesion: an erythematous, indurated, tender plaque with well-defined, raised margins. Cellulitis: lower half of the dermis plus subcutaneous tissue — deeper than erysipelas. Caused by Group A Streptococcus and S. aureus. Most common site: lower extremities. Lesion: an erythematous, indurated, tender plaque, but with ill-defined, diffuse margins (unlike erysipelas's sharp border). Treatment for these spreading infections: IV cefazolin or IV nafcillin.

SSSS = acute skin exfoliation caused by toxin-producing strains of S. aureus. Pathogenesis: a focus of infection (e.g. conjunctivitis, otitis media) → S. aureus produces an epidermolytic exotoxin → hematogenous spread → reaches the skin, targeting desmosomes (specifically the antigen desmoglein-1/DSG-1) → acantholysis. DSG-1 is mainly expressed in the upper epidermis, just below the stratum corneum. Clinical features: a history of a focus of infection; fever; periorificial erythema and crusting; skin tenderness; sheet-like epidermal peeling. True Nikolsky sign is positive. Oral lesions are absent (low DSG-1 concentration in oral mucosa). Differential diagnosis of sheet-like epidermal peeling: SSSS — normal mucosa; toxic epidermal necrolysis — hemorrhagic crust in the mucosa. Treatment: penicillinase-resistant penicillins (IV oxacillin, IV nafcillin); alternates — IV cefazolin, IV vancomycin.

Acute paronychia: nail fold infection caused by S. aureus. Predisposing factor: thumb sucking. Clinical features: nail fold erythema, edema, tenderness, plus pus collection. Treatment depends on abscess presence — absent: antimicrobials (cephalexin, dicloxacillin); present: surgical drainage plus antibiotics. Botryomycosis: a chronic, suppurative, granulomatous disease in response to a bacterial pathogen — despite the name, it's not a fungal infection (a misnomer). Most commonly caused by S. aureus; also Proteus, E. coli, Klebsiella. Lesions: nodules and ulcers. Erysipeloid: caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae. Risk factor: meat/fish handlers. Lesion: purplish erythema with painful edema. Treatment: penicillin.

Three named superficial bacterial skin surface conditions, grouped together. Erythrasma: caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum; asymptomatic, reddish-brown hyperpigmentation; sites — axilla, groin, toe-web spaces; Wood's lamp shows coral-red fluorescence (from coproporphyrin III). Treatment: topical fusidic acid, or systemic erythromycin/clarithromycin (macrolides). Trichomycosis axillaris: caused by Corynebacterium tenuis — despite the name, not a fungal infection (another misnomer). Clinical feature: yellow deposits/concretions over the axillary hair shaft. Site: axilla. Treatment: topical clindamycin, plus shaving the affected hair. Pitted keratolysis: caused by Micrococcus/Kytococcus sedantarius (not actually a Corynebacterium, but grouped here with the other two). Pathogenesis: increased sweating → increased bacterial growth → increased enzyme production that lyses keratin → pits. Clinical feature: pits/depressions. Sites: palms and soles. Treatment: Whitfield's ointment (3% salicylic acid + 6% benzoic acid).

Ecthyma gangrenosum: classic clinical scenario — Pseudomonas septicemia. Pathology: hemorrhagic necrosis of the skin. Lesions: necrotic, crusted ulcers. Hot tub folliculitis: classic history — bathing in an ill-maintained spa. Site: the "bathing trunk" area. Green nail syndrome: due to pyocyanin pigment production by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Cutaneous anthrax: caused by Bacillus anthracis. Classic history: contact with animals or animal products. Lesion — a "malignant pustule": starts as a painless papule, progressing to a black eschar surrounded by a rim of vesicles. Meningococcemia: caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Classic history: fever plus CNS symptoms (neck rigidity). Lesions: a petechial rash (non-blanching when pressed with a glass slide) and angular cutaneous infarcts. Scrub typhus: an acute, febrile, mite-borne infectious disease. Caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. Vector: the trombiculid mite; infective form: chiggers. Clinical features: fever plus malaise, CNS symptoms, and an eschar (a black scab surrounded by erythema). Differential diagnosis for an eschar: cutaneous anthrax (history of animal contact) and brown recluse spider bite. Treatment: doxycycline (drug of choice).

Mycobacterial skin infections split into cutaneous TB (extrapulmonary TB) and atypical mycobacterial infections (swimming pool granuloma, Buruli ulcer). Cutaneous TB itself splits into true cutaneous TB (direct invasion of the skin by M. tuberculosis) and tuberculids (a hypersensitivity response to M. tuberculosis, without direct invasion). True cutaneous TB depends on prior host sensitization. In an unsensitized host, the primary infection produces a TB chancre — an ulcer with an undermined edge. In a previously sensitized host, infection is termed secondary cutaneous TB. Secondary cutaneous TB is subclassified by bacterial load. Paucibacillary (low load, strong cell-mediated immunity): TB verrucosa cutis and lupus vulgaris. Multibacillary (high load, weak cell-mediated immunity) is further split by mode of acquisition: endogenous spread → scrofuloderma; autoinoculation → orificial TB; hematogenous spread → TB gumma and miliary TB.

TB verrucosa cutis (TBVC) — AKA warty TB / anatomist's warts. "Verrucosa" = rough, uneven, warty surface. Route: exogenous reinoculation in an already-sensitized host. Lesion: an indurated verrucous plaque. Site: extremities. Lupus vulgaris — "Lupus" refers to a wolf-bitten appearance. It is the most common cutaneous TB in adults. Routes: both exogenous and endogenous. Occurs with increased cell-mediated immunity (paucibacillary). Lupus vulgaris lesion: an annular, infiltrated (thickened) plaque. Centre: atrophy and scarring. Periphery: an active, advancing margin. Site: extremities, buttocks, face. Investigation — diascopy: pressing a glass slide on the lesion reveals a yellow-brown color, corresponding to granulomatous lesions called apple jelly nodules. Differentials for apple jelly nodules: lupus vulgaris, sarcoidosis, and cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Scrofuloderma — the most common cutaneous TB in children. Occurs with decreased cell-mediated immunity (multibacillary). Pathogenesis: an endogenous TB focus (lymph node/bone/fascia/joint — most commonly the cervical lymph node) directly invades the skin, forming painless subcutaneous nodules that rupture into the overlying skin, producing a draining sinus, undermined ulcers, and fibrotic scars. Site: neck, axilla. Orificial TB — a multibacillary form seen with decreased cell-mediated immunity, arising by autoinoculation from advanced internal TB (pulmonary, intestinal, or genito-urinary TB). Site (mucocutaneous junctions): lip, perianal, and genital areas. Treatment of cutaneous TB: standard antitubercular therapy for a total of 6 months — an intensive phase of HRZE for 2 months, followed by a continuation phase of HRE for 4 months.
Tuberculids: Lichen Scrofulosorum to Erythema Induratum

Tuberculids = a hypersensitivity response to M. tuberculosis, occurring with increased cell-mediated immunity and a positive Mantoux test. Classified by morphology: micropapular → lichen scrofulosorum; papular → papulonecrotic tuberculid; nodular → erythema induratum of Bazin. Lichen scrofulosorum: seen in children; asymptomatic, grouped lichenoid papules on the trunk; histopathology shows a perifollicular non-caseating granuloma. Differential — lichen nitidus ("nitidus" = shiny): also a child with asymptomatic papules, but identified by shiny lesions localized to the face, forearm, and shaft of the penis. Papulonecrotic tuberculid: seen in young adults; papules with central necrosis; site — lower extremities. Erythema induratum of Bazin: a lobular panniculitis with vasculitis (panniculitis = inflammation of subcutaneous fat); a red, tender nodule on the posterior aspect of the leg, healing with a scar. Differential — erythema nodosum: also red, tender nodules, but on the anterior aspect of the leg, healing without a scar.

Swimming pool granuloma (AKA fish tank granuloma) — caused by M. marinum. History: occupational exposure to contaminated fresh or salt water. Clinical feature: nodular lymphangitis — suppurative nodules distributed along the lymphatics of an extremity. Treatment: minocycline. Differentials for the nodular-lymphangitic pattern: sporotrichosis, nocardiosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, and tularemia. Buruli ulcer — caused by M. ulcerans. Pathogenesis: toxin-mediated — the toxin mycolactone causes tissue necrosis. Lesion: a painless ulcer with an undermined edge. Treatment of Buruli ulcer: rifampicin plus clarithromycin. If clarithromycin cannot be tolerated, substitute rifampicin plus injectable streptomycin for 8 weeks.
Viral Skin Infections Overview & Orolabial HSV

DNA viruses causing skin infection fall into five families: herpesvirus, poxvirus, HPV, enterovirus, and parvovirus B19. Herpesviruses are notable for establishing lifelong latency, causing persistent/recurrent infection. Orolabial herpes (HSV-1) — AKA fever blister / cold sore / herpes labialis. Presents as grouped vesicles at the lip margin. Treatment: oral acyclovir 400 mg TID for 5 days. Herpetic gingivostomatitis: a child presents with high-grade fever; oral vesicles rupture into erosions covered by a membrane. Herpetic whitlow: infection of the distal pulp of a finger; classically an occupational risk for dentists (direct digital contact with infected oral secretions).

Eczema herpeticum (Kaposi varicelliform eruption): disseminated, cutaneous HSV-1 infection — "herpes seen in patients with eczema." Associations: atopic eczema (defective skin barrier), cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (especially Sezary syndrome), and Darier's disease. Eczema herpeticum lesions: umbilicated vesiculopustules that rupture into multiple punched-out erosions covered by hemorrhagic crusts. Treatment: acyclovir — oral for mild disease, IV for severe disease. Erythema multiforme: HSV-1 is the most common trigger. Lesions are target lesions (3 zones) distributed over the extremities. Mollaret meningitis: a recurrent aseptic meningitis linked to HSV. HSV-2/genital herpes: grouped vesicles progress to discrete tender ulcers, which coalesce into polycyclic erosions.

Primary VZV infection = varicella/chickenpox; reactivation of latent virus = shingles. The classic varicella vesicle is described as a "dew drop on a rose petal." Lesions appear in crops, following the sequence: macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → scab. Because different crops appear at different times, varicella shows a pleomorphic rash — multiple lesion morphologies present simultaneously (a feature specific to chickenpox). The period of infectivity lasts until all lesions have crusted. Consequences of maternal varicella infection: congenital varicella (infection at <20 weeks gestation) → cutaneous dermatomal scar and limb atrophy. Neonatal varicella (maternal infection 5 days before to 2 days after delivery) → disseminated vesicular rash.

Herpes zoster: an acute, cutaneous, segmental eruption. Pathogenesis: varicella infection → latent virus in the dorsal root ganglion (sensory) → reactivation on exposure to risk factors (old age, HIV, lymphoreticular malignancies) → shingles. Clinical phases — pre-eruptive: fever, malaise, excruciating dermatomal burning pain. Eruptive: unilateral, dermatomal (most commonly thoracic), painful grouped vesicles on a red base. Complication: post-herpetic neuralgia — the most disabling complication; exhibits allodynia (a non-painful stimulus perceived as painful). Treatment of PHN: amitriptyline, pregabalin, gabapentin. Treatment of varicella/zoster: acyclovir 800 mg 5×/day for 7 days, or valacyclovir 1 g 3×/day for 7 days. Variants — Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: affects the frontal branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1); Hutchinson's sign (vesicle on the tip/side of the nose) predicts increased corneal involvement, due to shared supply by the nasociliary nerve. Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome): affects the geniculate ganglion; triad of facial nerve (VII) LMN palsy, otalgia, and vesicles in the external auditory canal. Investigation: Tzanck smear (positive in HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV) classically shows multinucleate giant cells.
Epstein-Barr Virus, CMV & Other Human Herpesviruses

EBV — Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever): classical triad of fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A characteristic drug reaction: giving ampicillin during EBV infection produces a maculopapular rash. EBV-associated malignancies: Burkitt's lymphoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Oral hairy leukoplakia: seen in HIV-infected patients; white, corrugated (ridged) plaques on the lateral border of the tongue; cannot be rubbed off. HHV-5 (CMV): produces an infectious-mononucleosis-like illness, with characteristic owl eye inclusion bodies. HHV-6 causes roseola infantum (exanthem subitum / 6th disease) in children — fever plus maculopapular rash, with red papules over the palate called uvulopalatoglossal (Nagayama) spots. HHV-7 is linked to pityriasis rosea. HHV-8 causes a group of lymphoproliferative diseases: Kaposi's sarcoma, multicentric Castleman's disease, and primary effusion lymphoma. Kaposi sarcoma is a multifocal, low-grade vascular tumour presenting as purplish/violaceous plaques or nodules, and is an AIDS-defining illness.

Molluscum contagiosum (MC): a benign, self-limiting viral infection of keratinocytes, caused by molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a poxvirus. MCV-1 affects children (face); MCV-2 affects adults (anogenital, sexually transmitted). Transmission: skin-to-skin; incubation 2 weeks to 6 months. Children: pearly white, centrally umbilicated papules (2–5 mm); pseudo-Koebner's phenomenon (new lesions along a scratch line from autoinoculation — also seen in viral warts). Immunosuppressed patients: giant (>1 cm), atypical, extensive, recalcitrant lesions. In HIV patients with molluscum-like lesions: skin only → disseminated molluscum; skin + lung → disseminated histoplasmosis; skin + CNS/meningitis → disseminated cryptococcosis. Complications: secondary infection (from scratching), conjunctivitis, and (in eyelid molluscum) superficial punctate keratitis. Histopathology: a cup-shaped invagination of epidermis into dermis containing Henderson-Patterson bodies (eosinophilic intracytoplasmic bodies). Treatment: often self-limiting; physical (curettage, cryotherapy) or topical imiquimod (a TLR7 agonist). Parapox virus: disease depends on the primary host. Sheep host → ORF virus → ecthyma contagiosum. Cow host → pseudocowpox virus → milker's nodule. (Note: ecthyma gangrenosum, a different entity, is caused by Pseudomonas, not a parapox virus.)

HPV: a DNA virus with tropism for squamous epithelium. Warts are benign HPV-induced proliferations of skin, classified as genital (condyloma acuminata — "acuminata" = pointed) or non-genital. Verruca vulgaris (HPV 2, 4, 27): skin-to-skin transmission; asymptomatic, well-circumscribed papules/plaques with a verrucous (rough) surface. Planar warts (HPV 3, 10): warts with a flat surface. Plantar warts — superficial: mosaic warts (HPV-2); deep: myrmecia (HPV-1). D/d myrmecia vs a corn: myrmecia is tender on lateral pressure; a corn (excess stratum corneum buildup from increased pressure) is tender on vertical pressure. Also: filiform warts, and periungual warts (difficult to treat). Treatment: topical (e.g., salicylic acid) or physical (electrocautery; cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen at −196°C). Epidermodysplasia verruciformis: autosomal recessive; HPV-5, 8; face — planar warts, trunk — pityriasis-versicolor-like hypopigmented macules; major complication — squamous cell carcinoma.

Hand-foot-mouth disease: caused by Coxsackie A16 and Enterovirus 71; papulovesicular lesions distributed on the palms, soles, buttocks, and the anterior oral cavity. Herpangina: caused by Coxsackie A1–A6, A8, A10, and Enterovirus 71; presents with high-grade fever and painful, papulovesicular, ulcerative lesions at the posterior oropharynx. Note: unlike hand-foot-mouth disease, herpangina has no skin lesion. Parvovirus B19 is a DNA virus. Erythema infectiosum (5th disease): affects healthy children; fever, malar erythema that spares the nasal bridge ("slapped cheek" appearance), and a reticulate, lacy (net-like) rash over the trunk. Papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome: erythema and edema of the hands and feet, with associated petechiae and purpura.

Superficial mycoses are fungal infections confined to the superficial skin layers/stratum corneum. Five classic diseases: pityriasis versicolor, tinea nigra, piedra, candida, and dermatophytoses. Pityriasis versicolor: etiological agent Malassezia globosa > furfur. Lesion: scaly ("pityriasis") perifollicular macules, with fine, branny, furfuraceous scales. "Versicolor" reflects a variety of colors: hypopigmented (most common) or hyperpigmented. Site: face, trunk (most common). The scratch test/Besnier's sign: scratching the fine scales with a fingernail produces prominent scales.
Pityriasis Versicolor: Pigment Mechanisms, Investigations & Treatment

Hypopigmentation mechanism: M. furfur produces azelaic acid, which inhibits tyrosinase, blocking melanin synthesis. Hyperpigmentation mechanism: the fungus induces formation of larger melanosomes. Investigation of choice: 10% KOH mount (dissolves keratin), showing round spores ("meatballs") and short hyphae ("spaghetti") — the classic "spaghetti and meatball" appearance. Wood's lamp: yellow fluorescence. Treatment: antifungals used are azoles and selenium sulphide (an antifungal with cytostatic properties). Note: griseofulvin and oral terbinafine are NOT used in pityriasis versicolor.

Tinea nigra: caused by Hortaea werneckii. Clinical features: asymptomatic hyperpigmented macules over the palms. Treatment: topical azoles. Piedra (trichomycosis nodularis): a superficial fungal infection targeting the hair shaft, with two types. Black piedra: Piedraria hortae, black nodules, hard consistency, tight attachment to the hair shaft. White piedra: Trichosporon beigelii, white nodules, soft consistency, loose attachment. Treatment of piedra: clipping of hair, topical azoles.

Mucocutaneous candidiasis is caused by Candida albicans. Oral candidiasis presenting as white plaques divides into pseudomembranous candidiasis/oral thrush (lesions can be rubbed off with a spatula) and chronic hyperplastic candidiasis. Oral candidiasis presenting as red/atrophic plaques divides by course. Acute form: AKA "antibiotic sore tongue," due to antibiotic use. Chronic form: AKA "denture mouth," due to denture use.

Candidial intertrigo ("inter" = between; "trigo" = folds): candidal infection of the skin folds. Predisposing factors: moisture and friction. Lesion: a macerated red plaque with peripheral satellite pustules. Site: groin/neck folds. Candidial balanoposthitis ("balano" = glans; "posthitis" = prepuce inflammation): lesion — radial fissures. Associated with diabetes mellitus. Candidial paronychia: predisposed by occupational exposure to wetness and detergents. Lesion: swelling of the nail fold, loss of cuticle. Investigations: KOH mount shows budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae; Sabouraud dextrose agar shows creamy white colonies. Treatment: fluconazole.

Dermatophytosis: superficial fungal infections involving keratinized tissue, caused by keratinophilic fungi. Three genera, distinguished by which tissues they can invade: Microsporum (skin, hair — NOT nail), Epidermophyton (skin, nail — NOT hair), Trichophyton (skin, hair, AND nail — all three). Pathogenesis: adhesion to superficial skin and tissues → invasion/growth into the stratum corneum → generation of an immune response.

Tinea capitis = dermatophyte involvement of the scalp. Non-inflammatory form (causes non-scarring alopecia): black dot/endothrix — infection inside the hair shaft causing hair breakage and visible black dots; etiology T. tonsurans, T. violaceum. Grey patch/ectothrix — itchy, scaly lesions with patchy alopecia; etiology M. canis. Inflammatory form (causes scarring alopecia): Favus — etiology T. schoenleinii, endemic to Kashmir, yellow cup-shaped crusts called scutula. Kerion — etiology zoophilic fungi (T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum); features: history of pet-animal contact, seen in children, boggy scalp swelling, easily pluckable hair, regional lymph node enlargement; investigation: KOH mount.
Tinea Corporis/Cruris, Onychomycosis & Other Regional Tineas

Tinea corporis/cruris: etiology T. mentagrophytes, T. rubrum. Lesion: an annular plaque with a clear center, itchy, with a raised, scaly periphery. Site: glabrous (non-hairy) skin, except palms, groin, soles. In the groin, it's called tinea cruris, AKA jock itch/dhobi itch. Onychomycosis: fungal infection of the nail unit. Features: yellow nail plate, subungual hyperkeratosis, absent pits. Most common clinical type: DLSO (distal lateral subungual onychomycosis). Tinea in other regions: face — tinea faciei; beard — tinea barbae; palms — tinea manuum; feet — tinea pedis, AKA athlete's foot (most common site: 4th toe web space). Tinea incognito ("incognito" = not recognizable): steroid-modified tinea. On steroid application: no resemblance to the classic presentation, reduced itch, lost active margin, diffuse scaling.
Antifungal Treatment: Topical, Systemic & Onychomycosis Regimens

Investigation for dermatophytosis: 10% KOH mount shows refractile branching hyphae. In tinea capitis: overall drug of choice is griseofulvin; if secondary to Trichophyton, terbinafine is preferred. Topical agents: azoles (MOA: inhibit 14-α demethylase, reducing conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol; e.g., luliconazole, ketoconazole, miconazole, clotrimazole) and allylamines (MOA: inhibit squalene epoxidase; e.g., terbinafine). Systemic drugs (course 4–6 weeks): itraconazole 100mg BD, terbinafine 250mg OD, fluconazole. Dermatophytic onychomycosis: terbinafine 250mg OD (6 weeks fingernails, 12 weeks toenails); itraconazole pulse dosing (200mg BD for 1 week/month — 2 pulses fingernails, 3 pulses toenails). Nail lacquer (topical nail paint): amorolfine 5%, ciclopiroxolamine 8%, terbinafine.

Subcutaneous (implantation) mycoses are characterized by traumatic inoculation of fungus into the skin. Sporotrichosis/Rose Gardener's disease: agent Sporothrix schenckii (a dimorphic fungus, spreading via lymphatics). History: thorn prick, usually in a gardener. Lesions: nodulo-ulcerative, extending proximally as linear lesions along the lymphatics (a "target" pattern of nodular lymphangitis). Differentials: nocardiosis, atypical mycobacterial infection (swimming pool granuloma), cutaneous leishmaniasis, tularemia. Histopathology: asteroid bodies (central basophilic yeast with radiating eosinophilic material). Treatment: cutaneous — itraconazole or saturated solution of potassium iodide; CNS — amphotericin B. Chromoblastomycosis/verrucous dermatitis ("chromo" = color/pigmented fungi; "verrucous" = rough/uneven surface): caused by pigmented (dematiaceous) fungi with melanin in their cell wall, found in soil — Fonsecaea compactum, Phialophora species. History: a farmer with vegetative trauma. Lesions: slow-growing verrucous plaques with black dots, and cauliflower-like lesions, on the extremities. Investigation: 10% KOH mount shows round, brown, thick-walled bodies — AKA medlar/sclerotic/copper penny bodies. Treatment: itraconazole.

Mycetoma: a chronic, suppurative, granulomatous disease. Etiologic classification: fungal (eumycetoma — Madurella grisea, Madurella mycetomatis) vs bacterial (actinomycetoma — Actinomadura madurae, Nocardia brasiliensis, Streptomyces species). Clinical features: more common in men; seen in agricultural workers after penetrating trauma; most common site — the foot. Classic triad: tumefaction (tumor-like swelling), multiple discharging sinuses, and granules from the sinuses (granules = colonies of the causative microbe). Granule color: black in eumycetoma, pale/cream/white in actinomycetoma. Eumycetoma: gram-negative septate hyphae (2–5 μm); histopathology shows granules surrounded by a suppurative granuloma with neutrophilic infiltrate; treatment is antifungals. Actinomycetoma: gram-positive filaments (0.5–1 μm); histopathology shows granules surrounded by homogeneous eosinophilic material; treatment is the Welsh regimen (cotrimoxazole plus amikacin).

Scabies is itchy and contagious, classified as a "water-washed disease" (linked to personal hygiene). Etiology: Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis (the itch mite) — a patient with normal immunity carries only 10–12 mites. Transmission: skin-to-skin contact, fomites. Incubation period: 4 weeks for a first infestation, but only 1–2 days on reinfestation. Clinical features: a history of nocturnal pruritus (the mite is active at night; itching reflects a hypersensitivity response to it), often with similar complaints among family members/contacts. Examination: excoriated papules and burrows (wavy, greyish-white tunnels specific to scabies, at the level of the stratum corneum, absent in animal scabies). Distribution follows the "Circle of Hebra": finger web spaces, medial wrist, medial forearm/arm, axilla, nipple, umbilicus, genitalia and groin. In adults, the face is spared — rich in sebaceous glands, its high sebum activity repels mites (hence permethrin is applied only below the neck).

Investigation: KOH mount of a skin scraping, looking for the scabies mite (identified by 2 anterior and 2 posterior pairs of legs), eggs, and fecal pellets (scybala). Complication: secondary bacterial infection. General treatment: antihistamines for pruritus; decontaminate clothes/bedding by washing in hot water; treat family members/close contacts too. Specific topical drugs: 5% permethrin (the best option; MOA — inhibits Na⁺ channels in the parasite, inducing paralysis; applied below the neck covering the entire body, left on 12 hours overnight then washed off, reapplied after 1 week for better efficacy); also benzyl benzoate emulsion, gamma benzene hexachloride, crotamiton (anti-pruritic properties), and precipitated sulfur (safe in pregnancy). Systemic therapy: ivermectin (oral dose 200 mcg/kg; MOA — binds glutamate-gated Cl⁻ channels, causing Cl⁻ influx, hyperpolarization, and mite paralysis).

Infantile scabies: unlike in adults, the face IS involved (facial treatment is required); vesicles appear on the palms and soles. Norwegian/crusted scabies: the most severe form. Predisposing factors: immunosuppression (HIV, lepromatous leprosy) or decreased skin sensation (neurologic disease). Pathogenesis: decreased immunity → no immune response to the mite → no/minimal pruritus → decreased scratching → mites are not dislodged → they proliferate massively in the stratum corneum (up to 2 million mites). Presents with hyperkeratotic crusted plaques and erythroderma (>90% BSA) ± scaling. Treatment: ivermectin, 5% permethrin, and salicylic acid (a keratolytic agent to remove the plaque). Nodular scabies: a hypersensitivity response to the scabies mite. Lesions: pruritic nodules at the axilla and scrotum. Treatment: anti-scabetic therapy plus intralesional steroid (to treat the hypersensitivity).

Pediculosis = louse infestation, classified by site: P. capitis (scalp hair), P. corporis (body hair), and pthiriasis pubis (pubic hair/eyelashes). Pediculosis capitis: etiology — head louse (Pediculus humanus capitis); transmission — close personal contact. Clinical features: more common in females; symptom — scalp pruritus. Examination: lice, and nits (eggs and lice) attached to one side of the hair; occipital lymphadenopathy can occur (from itching leading to secondary infection). Pediculosis corporis: AKA vagabond's disease (linked to decreased personal hygiene). Etiology — body/clothing louse (Pediculus humanis corporis). The louse lives in the seams of the patient's clothing and returns to the skin over the trunk to feed. Clinical features: pruritus, excoriations (also called morbus errorum).

Pthiriasis pubis: caused by the crab/pubic louse (Pthirus pubis); transmitted via sexual contact. Structural feature: the 2nd and 3rd pairs of legs end in pincer-like claws. Clinical features: pruritus, and maculae ceruleae — bluish macules over the lower abdomen, caused by an anticoagulant property in the louse's saliva. Treatment: pediculosis capitis and pubis both respond to permethrin 1%; pediculosis corporis is treated by disinfecting the clothing (since the louse lives there, not on the skin).
Cutaneous Larva Migrans, Larva Currens & Calabar Swellings

Cutaneous larva migrans: skin penetration by animal hookworm larvae (Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum). Pathogenesis: contact with soil containing animal excreta bearing the infective larval form → the larva enters the skin → serpiginous skin lesions, migrating at 1–2 cm/day. Classic history: barefoot walking on a beach. Lesion: a pruritic, elevated, migratory serpiginous tract. Treatment: ivermectin, albendazole. Larva currens (AKA "racing larva"): caused by Strongyloides stercoralis. Lesions: urticarial bands, migrating much faster — at 5–10 cm/hour. Treatment: ivermectin (DOC). Calabar swellings: caused by the African eyeworm, Loa loa. Lesions: painless, transient, non-pruritic swellings. Treatment: diethylcarbamazine (DOC).

Trypanosomiasis splits into African (sleeping sickness) and American (Chagas disease) forms. African/sleeping sickness: vector — tsetse fly; etiology — T. brucei. Subtypes: West African (early and late stages) and East African. West African trypanosomiasis shows posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, known as Winterbottom's sign. American/Chagas disease: vector — reduviid bug; etiology — T. cruzi. Acute stage: unilateral, painless palpebral edema, known as Romaña's sign, caused by sensitization to the bug's bite. A chronic stage also occurs.

Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the sandfly, and classifies into cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral forms. Cutaneous leishmaniasis further divides into Old World and New World forms. Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis: AKA Delhi boil/oriental sore; etiology — L. major, L. tropica. Skin lesion: a nodulo-ulcerative lesion with a central crust; on removing the crust, an ulcer with an elevated rim is revealed — the "volcano sign." New World cutaneous leishmaniasis: AKA Chiclero ulcer/gum tree harvester's ulcer; etiology — L. mexicana. Skin lesion: an ulcer affecting the cartilage of the ear. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis: etiology — L. braziliensis. Pathology: invasion and destruction of the nasopharynx. Skin lesion: mutilating lesions of the face and nose, known as espundia.

Visceral leishmaniasis: AKA Kala-azar; etiology — L. donovani, a parasite of the reticulo-endothelial system. Clinical features: fever, hepatosplenomegaly. Complication: Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) — caused by partial/inadequate treatment of kala-azar, leaving cutaneous sequelae. History: residence in Bihar or other high-caseload areas of India, with a past history of prolonged fever (kala-azar). Skin lesions: hypopigmented macules on the trunk, infiltrated nodules on the face. Investigations: Giemsa stain shows Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies (the amastigote form of the parasite); culture medium — NNN (Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle) media. Treatment: kala-azar — liposomal amphotericin B (DOC); PKDL — oral miltefosine. Differential diagnosis for hypopigmented macules and infiltrative nodules: lepromatous leprosy (nerve involvement, acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear).

Anogenital warts/condyloma acuminata: HPV-induced benign proliferations in the anogenital region. "Acuminata" means pointed. Etiology: low-risk HPV 6, 11 (90% of patients, most common) vs high-risk HPV 16, 18 (10% of patients). Clinical features — papules/plaques: asymptomatic, fleshy, pointed, pink. Hypertrophic masses: cauliflower-like lesions. Site: occurs at sites of maximum friction — males: coronal sulcus, frenulum; females: posterior fourchette. Histopathology: koilocytes seen (a squamous epithelial cell with a central hyperchromatic nucleus and a perinuclear halo). Complications: obstruction of labour (from large vulvar warts); laryngeal papillomatosis of the infant (from mother-to-child transmission via warts in the birth canal).

Non-pregnant treatment: podophyllin (a cytotoxic agent; MOA — binds the mitotic spindle, causing metaphase arrest and necrosis of the wart); imiquimod (an immune response modifier/modulator; MOA — a TLR7 agonist that releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, clearing the wart; 5% cream, applied topically thrice weekly, for up to 16 weeks). Pregnant treatment: cryotherapy (treatment of choice in pregnancy; agent — liquid N₂ at −196°C; MOA — freezing the warts); trichloroacetic acid 70–80% (a chemical cautery agent; MOA — coagulation of protein). Giant Condyloma/Buschke-Löwenstein tumour: treated with surgical excision.

Genital discharge disease is seen in urethritis and vaginal discharge syndrome. Urethritis: inflammation of the urethra, leading to urethral discharge. Etiopathogenesis: Gonococcal urethritis — Neisseria gonorrhoeae, incubation 2–5 days. Nongonococcal urethritis — Chlamydia trachomatis D-K serovar (most common), Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas vaginalis; incubation 7–14 days. Clinical features: Gonococcal — constitutional symptoms present, severe dysuria, profuse purulent discharge. Nongonococcal — constitutional symptoms absent, variable dysuria, scanty mucoid discharge. Note: Trichomonas vaginalis can also cause vaginal discharge.

Diagnostic criteria: 1 out of 3 criteria positive is needed to diagnose urethritis — visibly abnormal discharge (mucoid/purulent/mucopurulent); Gram stain of urethral swab (≥2 WBCs/oil immersion field); first void urine (≥10 WBCs/high power field). Gram staining findings: Gonococcal urethritis — gram-negative diplococci, seen intracellularly. Nongonococcal urethritis — no intracellular pathogens seen. Culture media: modified Thayer-Martin medium (a selective medium for gonococci). Contains vancomycin (inhibits gram-positive organisms), colistin (inhibits gram-negative organisms), nystatin (inhibits fungi), and trimethoprim (inhibits Proteus). NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test): sample — first void urine.

Gonococcal urethritis (CDC 2021): injection ceftriaxone IM, single stat dose (<150 kg: 500 mg IM; >150 kg: 1 g IM); add doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days only if chlamydial infection is not ruled out. Nongonococcal urethritis: tablet azithromycin 1 g stat, OR tablet doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days.

Vaginal discharge syndrome includes candidiasis, trichomoniasis, and bacterial vaginosis. Candidiasis: etiology — Candida albicans. Discharge: curdy white. Treatment: fluconazole. Note: Chrom agar is used to differentiate Candida species. Trichomoniasis: etiology — Trichomonas vaginalis, an anaerobic flagellate protozoan. Discharge: greenish-yellow, frothy. Cervix: "strawberry cervix"/colpitis macularis (multiple punctate hemorrhages). Treatment: metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days.

Bacterial vaginosis: a disease characterized by altered vaginal microflora — decreased Lactobacillus → decreased lactic acid → vaginal pH >4.5, alongside increased anaerobes (Prevotella, Mobiluncus, Gardnerella). Diagnosis — Amsel's criteria: any 3 of 4 findings positive confirms the disease: (1) vaginal discharge — homogenous, white, adherent; (2) vaginal pH >4.5; (3) whiff test/amine test — discharge + KOH produces a fishy odor (from released amines) = positive; (4) wet mount exam — >20% clue cells (a vaginal squamous epithelial cell covered by adherent bacteria, giving stippled borders). Treatment: metronidazole 500 mg PO BD for 7 days, OR metronidazole gel 0.75% (5g) intravaginally OD for 5 days, OR clindamycin cream 2% (5g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days.
Syndromic Management of STIs & NACO Kits 1–3

A syndrome is a collection of symptoms and signs pertaining to an STI. Syndromic management treats an STI based on clinical algorithms, without waiting for lab confirmation. Indications: resource-poor settings, unavailable lab services. Principle: treat the most common organisms responsible for the syndrome. NACO Kit 1/Grey — for urethral discharge, anorectal discharge, or cervicitis (vaginal discharge with cervical erosion/ulcer or mucopurulent discharge on speculum exam); targets gonococci (T. cefixime 400mg stat) and Chlamydia trachomatis (azithromycin 1g stat). NACO Kit 2/Green — for vaginal discharge syndrome; targets candidiasis (T. fluconazole 150mg stat) and trichomoniasis/bacterial vaginosis (T. secnidazole 1g BD). NACO Kit 3/White — for non-herpetic genital ulcer disease (no vesicles in history or on exam); targets primary syphilis (injection benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM stat, after a test dose) and chancroid (T. azithromycin 1g stat).

Kit 4/Blue — for non-herpetic genital ulcer disease in patients allergic to the penicillin test dose; targets syphilis (T. doxycycline 100mg BD for 15 days) and chancroid (T. azithromycin 1g stat). Kit 5/Red — for herpetic genital ulcer disease; targets herpes virus (T. acyclovir 400mg TID for 7 days). Kit 6/Yellow — for lower abdominal pain (pelvic inflammatory disease); targets gonococci (T. cefixime 400mg stat), Chlamydia (T. doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days), and anaerobes (T. metronidazole 400mg BD for 14 days). Kit 7/Black — for inguinal bubo; targets chancroid (azithromycin 1g stat) and LGV (T. doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days).

Congenital syphilis: transmitted mother to fetus in utero. Classified by timeline: early (within 2 years of life) vs late (>2 years). Early congenital syphilis triad: hepatosplenomegaly, snuffles (rhinitis), syphilitic pemphigus (vesiculobullous lesions). Also: Wimberger sign — bilateral erosion of the medial aspect of the upper tibia. Late congenital syphilis — Hutchinson's triad: Hutchinson's teeth (notched upper central incisors), interstitial keratitis (eyes), sensorineural hearing loss (ear). Also: saddle nose deformity; periosteitis — Olympian brow (frontal bossing), Higoumenakis sign (unilateral sternal end of clavicle), sabre tibia (anterior tibial bowing). Investigation of choice: infant VDRL titre is 4× (or more) greater than maternal VDRL titre. Diday-Kassowitz law: in an untreated syphilitic mother, successive pregnancies show a progressively lower likelihood of fetal infection — pregnancy outcomes improve over time.

Acquired syphilis: transmitted via sexual contact or blood transfusion. Classification by time from infection to diagnosis (WHO: 2 years; CDC: 1 year) into early acquired (primary, secondary, early latent) and late acquired (late latent, tertiary). Primary syphilis: period of infectivity 9–90 days. Genital lesion — a papule, AKA hard chancre/Hunterian chancre; characteristics: single, clean-based, indurated, non-tender, does not bleed on touch. Inguinal lymph nodes: bilateral, enlarged, non-tender, rubbery. Extragenital lesions: chancre over the lips (most common). Investigation of choice: dark ground microscopy of ulcer exudate, showing a slender organism with corkscrew motility.

Secondary syphilis results from hematogenous spread. Clinical features: constitutional symptoms (fever), generalized lymphadenopathy (the epitrochlear node is characteristic). Skin lesions: symmetric, non-pruritic, polymorphic (except vesicles and bullae); site — palms and soles. Buschke-Ollendorff sign: pressing the blunt end of a pin on the lesion elicits deep dermal tenderness. Mucosal lesions: condyloma lata ("lata" = flat; flat-topped moist lesions), mucosal patch (from breakdown of the mucosal area), and snail track ulcers (coalescing mucosal patches forming serpiginous lesions). Note: condyloma acuminata is a different entity, seen in anogenital warts. Non-scarring alopecia: described as "moth-eaten" alopecia.

Syphilis d'emblée ("d'emblée" = directly): occurs via blood transfusion or needle puncture wounds, with secondary syphilis bypassing the primary stage entirely — the chancre is absent. Investigation of choice: VDRL/rapid plasma reagin (RPR). Latent syphilis: no clinical features are present, but serology is positive. Classified into early latent (infectious) and late latent (non-infectious), using the same WHO (2 years)/CDC (1 year) cutoffs. Investigation of choice: enzyme immunoassay (EIA).

Tertiary syphilis has three stages: gummatous (a rubbery nodule that breaks open into an ulcer, with punched-out edges and a "wash-leather" slough), cardiovascular (aortic aneurysm — most commonly of the ascending aorta — and aortic regurgitation), and neurosyphilis. Neurosyphilis splits into general paresis of the insane (paralytic dementia, personality changes, psychiatric changes) and tabes dorsalis (degeneration of sensory neurons in the dorsal column, causing gait abnormalities from loss of proprioception, lancinating pain — severe in the face and extremities — and the Argyll Robertson pupil). Investigation of choice: CSF-VDRL. Relapsing syphilis ("redux" = to come back): early relapse — chancre redux (chancre recurs at the previous site); late relapse — pseudochancre redux (a gumma appears at the previous chancre site).

Drug of choice: injection benzathine penicillin, 2.4 million units, deep IM. Duration: early syphilis — 1 dose; late syphilis (except neurosyphilis) — 3 doses, once weekly. Neurosyphilis: injection aqueous crystalline penicillin (ACP), 18–24 million units IV, daily for 10–14 days (patient hospitalized). Note: benzathine penicillin does NOT cross the blood-brain barrier. Penicillin allergy: non-pregnant — doxycycline 100mg BD (early syphilis: 14 days; late syphilis: 28 days). Pregnant — desensitization with penicillin, then a therapeutic dose. Desensitization pathophysiology: repeated subthreshold penicillin doses cause antigenic determinants to bind IgE on basophils/mast cells without cross-linking, making cells unresponsive to higher doses. Complications of penicillin therapy: (a) hypersensitivity reaction — urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis; (b) Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — an acute febrile inflammatory reaction seen after starting treatment for spirochetal disease (also Lyme disease, relapsing fever), onset within hours. Pathogenesis: penicillin → lysis of spirochete → release of lipoproteins → release of cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8) → acute inflammatory reaction (fever, myalgia, hypotension, worsening of existing skin rashes). Treatment: self-resolving; symptomatic (NSAIDs for fever).

Chancroid: etiology — Haemophilus ducreyi; incubation period 3–7 days. Primary lesion: a pustule. Genital ulcer: AKA soft sore/soft chancre — multiple, necrotic-based, with a ragged and undermined edge; non-indurated, tender, bleeds on touch (contrast with the syphilitic hard chancre: single, clean-based, indurated, non-tender, does not bleed on touch). Inguinal lymph node: a bubo — a unilateral, enlarged, tender, suppurative lymph node, often with a concomitant genital ulcer. Investigation: Gram stain from ulcer exudate shows gram-negative coccobacilli in long parallel strands — the "school of fish"/railroad track appearance. Culture medium: Mueller-Hinton agar, 5% chocolatized horse blood agar. Treatment: tablet azithromycin 1g stat.

Herpes genitalis: etiology — HSV-2 (90%), HSV-1 (10%); incubation period 3–12 days. Lesion progression: vesicles (primary lesion) — fluid-filled lesions <1cm — rupture into a genital ulcer: multiple grouped ulcers with polycyclic margins. Inguinal lymph nodes: bilateral, enlarged, tender. Investigation: Tzanck smear (a cytodiagnostic technique) — deroof the vesicle, smear onto a glass slide, stain with Giemsa stain; findings — multinucleated giant cells (MNG). Treatment: tablet acyclovir 400mg TID for 7 days (the "Red Kit" in syndromic management).

LGV: etiology — Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1, L2, L3); tropism for genital lymphatics; incubation period 3–30 days. Primary stage: a genital ulcer — single, painless, herpetiform, and transient. Secondary stage: an enlarged inguinal lymph node (bubo) — unilateral in 2/3rds of cases, bilateral in 1/3rd. Groove sign of Greenblatt: enlarged lymph nodes above and below the inguinal ligament. A concomitant ulcer is typically absent (since the primary ulcer is transient). Tertiary stage/complications: genital elephantiasis, from LGV's affinity for genital lymphatics. In males: saxophone penis. In females: esthiomene (genital elephantiasis plus chronic ulcerations). Investigation of choice: NAAT. Treatment: doxycycline 100mg BD for 3 weeks.

Donovanosis: etiology — Klebsiella granulomatosis; synonym — granuloma inguinale; incubation period 8–80 days. Note: distinct from Leishmania donovani, which causes leishmaniasis (not donovanosis). Genital ulcer: single, painless; characteristic findings — beefy red, exuberant granulation tissue (due to high vascularity) that bleeds on touch. Inguinal lymph nodes are NOT involved directly; instead, a pseudobubo (a subcutaneous nodule in the inguinal region) may form. ("Granuloma" = subcutaneous nodule; "inguinale" = groin.) Investigation: crushed tissue smear — a small piece of ulcer tissue is crushed between two glass slides, smeared, and Giemsa-stained. Findings: a large mononuclear cell (Pund cell) containing intracellular Donovan bodies, showing a "closed safety pin" appearance (from bipolar condensation of chromatin). Treatment: tablet azithromycin 500mg daily or 1g/week, for 3 weeks and until the ulcer heals.

Genital ulcer disease can be approached by ulcer characteristics. Single, non-tender ulcers: primary syphilis, lymphogranuloma venereum, donovanosis. Multiple, tender ulcers: chancroid, genital herpes. Approach by inguinal lymph node involvement: NOT involved → donovanosis. Involved, non-tender → primary syphilis (rubbery nodes). Involved, tender, bilateral → check for a bubo: bubo absent → genital herpes; bubo present → check for a concomitant genital ulcer: ulcer present → chancroid; ulcer absent → LGV.
Clinical Spectrum & Classification of Hansen's Disease

The clinical spectrum of Hansen's disease (Ridley-Jopling classification) runs between two poles based on host cell-mediated immunity (CMI): the tuberculoid pole (good CMI, limited disease) and the lepromatous pole (poor CMI, disseminated disease), with a borderline spectrum in between. Ridley-Jopling types, in order of decreasing CMI: Tuberculoid (TT) → Borderline Tuberculoid (BT) → mid-borderline (BB) → Borderline Lepromatous (BL) → Lepromatous Leprosy (LL). Indeterminate leprosy: CMI not yet determined; occurs in children. Endemic regions: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu. Lesion: an ill-defined hypopigmented macule, without scaling or itching; site — face. Skin biopsy (investigation of choice): lymphocytosis around nerves (perineural) and appendages (periappendageal). Differential diagnosis: pityriasis alba ("pityriasis" = scaling present; a type of endogenous eczema).
Determinate Leprosy: TT vs LL Across 4 Criteria

Determinate leprosy is divided under the Ridley-Jopling classification based on 4 criteria, contrasted here between the two poles: Immunological: CMI — TT good, LL poor. Lepromin test — TT positive, LL negative. Microbiological: acid-fast bacilli (AFB) — TT few, LL numerous. Slit skin smear (SSS) for AFB — TT negative, LL positive. Clinical: skin lesions — TT 1–3, LL multiple. Symmetry — TT asymmetrical, LL symmetrical. Margins — TT well-defined, LL ill-defined. Number of nerves involved — TT one, LL multiple. Histopathologic: LL shows foamy macrophages with AFB (no granulomas form, due to poor immunity).

Tuberculoid leprosy (TT): number of skin lesions 1–3. Morphology: an annular plaque with central clearing. Side profile: the "saucer right way up" appearance (sloping inwards, with a raised outer margin). Tuberculoid granulomas destroy nerves (causing anesthesia), hair (causing alopecia), and sweat glands (causing anhydrosis) within the lesion.

Borderline Tuberculoid (BT): number of skin lesions 3–10. Feature: satellite lesions near the periphery. Margins: well-defined in some areas, less well-defined in others. Mid-borderline (BB): number of skin lesions 10–30. Morphology: polymorphic (varying sizes and shapes), giving a "geographic map-like" appearance. Margins: the outer sloping margin gives an "inverted saucer" appearance, while the inner punched-out margin gives a "Swiss cheese" appearance (together termed a dimorphous lesion).

Borderline Lepromatous (BL): almost symmetrical. Skin lesions: bilateral, multiple, almost symmetrical, with an inverted saucer appearance (also seen in BB). Nerve involvement: multiple, asymmetrically thickened. Lepromatous leprosy (LL): involves skin, nerves, AND internal organs (a systemic disease) — with symmetrical skin and nerve involvement. Skin lesions: macules, papules, nodules, diffuse infiltration. Nerves: thickened. Early features of LL: epistaxis (from nasal mucosa involvement), pedal edema (from autonomic damage). Late features: leonine facies (lion-like facies, from diffuse skin infiltration and madarosis), and glove-and-stocking peripheral neuropathy.

Lucio leprosy: AKA lepra bonita ("beautiful leprosy"); a diffuse, non-nodular form of LL, most common in Mexico. Face: myxedematous, shiny, with obliteration of wrinkles. The associated lepra reaction type is the Lucio phenomenon. Histoid leprosy: associated with relapse following dapsone monotherapy, and dapsone resistance. Skin lesions: painless, dome-shaped, firm nodules over otherwise normal-appearing skin. Pure Neuritic Hansen's Disease: no skin lesions; only peripheral nerve thickening.

A deformity is a visible alteration of the form, shape, or appearance of a body part. Deformity–cause pairs: lateral madarosis — hair follicle infiltration; saddle nose — nose infiltration; partial claw hand — ulnar nerve involvement; total claw hand — ulnar AND median nerve involvement; callosities (palms/soles) — trophic/nerve-related damage; foot drop — lateral popliteal nerve involvement; trophic ulcer (chronic ulceration on the plantar aspect of an anesthetic foot) — sensory impairment.
Cranial Nerve Involvement in Hansen's Disease

The facial nerve (CN VII, motor supply to the face) is most commonly involved — causing paralysis of orbicularis oculi, leading to lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eyelid). The trigeminal nerve (CN V, sensory supply to the face) involvement decreases corneal sensation. Both pathways converge to cause exposure keratitis → corneal ulcer → corneal opacity → increased predisposition to blindness. Notes: facial lesions carry a higher risk of triggering a lepra reaction; the great auricular nerve is a commonly examined peripheral nerve, easier to visualize than to palpate/feel.
Lucio Phenomenon & Cardinal Features for Diagnosis

Lucio phenomenon: seen in Lucio leprosy (a diffuse, non-nodular form of LL). Pathogenesis: blood vessels show vasculitis plus thrombosis. Clinical features: no fever; skin lesions are geometric, irregular ulcers with jagged edges and varying sizes. Cardinal features for diagnosis of Hansen's disease: diagnosis requires the presence of any 1 of 3 features — (1) a skin lesion: a hypopigmented or reddish patch with definite loss of sensation; (2) nerve involvement: thickening of a peripheral nerve plus loss of sensation (sensory deficit) and/or muscle weakness (motor deficit) in the area supplied by that nerve; (3) a slit skin smear positive for M. leprae.

Slit skin smear (SSS): demonstrates M. leprae in the skin. Procedure: pinch/squeeze the ear lobe → make a nick with a scalpel → obtain tissue fluid → process and stain for M. leprae. Sample sites: four standard sites — right ear lobe, right forehead, chin, and left buttock (males)/upper thigh (females). A sample from an active skin lesion may also be taken in some cases. SSS staining: bacilli stain red, using the modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain (with 5% sulphuric acid). Patterns: solid staining = live bacilli; fragmented or granular staining = dead bacilli.

Bacteriologic Index (BI): the density of bacterial load (live + dead bacilli) in the SSS, expressed in terms of oil immersion fields (OIF). Grading ranges from 6+ (>1000 bacilli/OIF) down to 1+ (1–10 bacilli/100 OIF). Morphologic Index (MI): the percentage of solid-staining (live) bacilli on SSS. Used to assess prognosis and response to therapy — a decreasing MI means decreasing live bacilli, indicating good prognosis and good response to therapy.
Skin Biopsy, Nerve Biopsy & Lepromin Test

Histopathology (HPE) of lepromatous leprosy: atrophy of the epidermis; a clear zone of Grenz (a subepidermal free zone with no cellular infiltrate); sheets of Virchow/lepra cells (foamy macrophages containing acid-fast bacilli). HPE of tuberculoid leprosy: a tuberculoid granuloma (dense infiltrates of lymphocytes and Langhans-type giant cells); the clear zone of Grenz is absent. Stain for demonstrating M. leprae on HPE: Fite-Faraco stain. Nerve biopsy: investigation of choice for Pure Neuritic HD. Best nerve for biopsy — upper limb: radial cutaneous nerve; lower limb: sural nerve. Note: avoid biopsying motor nerves, as this can cause deformities. Lepromin test: an intradermal test; a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction. Biphasic response: early reaction/Fernandez reaction (read at 48–72 hours) and late reaction/Mitsuda reaction (read at 3 weeks). Uses: prognosis (negative = bad prognosis); Ridley-Jopling classification; assessing immune resistance to M. leprae.
Classification for Treatment: Paucibacillary vs Multibacillary

For treatment purposes, Hansen's disease is classified as paucibacillary (PB) or multibacillary (MB). Skin lesions: PB — 1–5; MB — ≥6. Nerve thickening: PB — 0/1 nerve; MB — more than 1 nerve, irrespective of skin lesions. Slit skin smear for AFB: PB — negative; MB — positive at any site. Treatment duration: PB — 6 months; MB — 12 months.
MDT Drugs: Kits, Regimens & Side Effects

28-day kits (given by the Government of India): rifampicin 600mg once a month (day 1); dapsone 100mg per day (days 1–28); clofazimine (300mg once on day 1, then 50mg once daily days 2–28). This is the "Maroon Kit," part of multi-drug therapy under NLEP. National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023–2027: uniform multi-drug treatment with 3 drugs; duration 6 months PB, 12 months MB. Treatment in children (10–14 years): rifampicin 450mg/month; dapsone 50mg/day; clofazimine (150mg/month day 1, then 50mg on alternate days). Side effects: rifampicin — reddish-orange discoloration of secretions (e.g., urine), hepatitis. Dapsone — hematological effects (hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, methemoglobinemia), hepatitis. Clofazimine — hyperpigmentation, ichthyosis (fish-like scales), GI disturbances.
Newer Drugs & Treatment of Lepra Reactions

Newer drugs in leprosy: macrolides (clarithromycin); ansamycins (rifabutin, rifapentine); tetracyclines (minocycline); fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin). Treatment of lepra reactions: general management is to continue multidrug therapy for leprosy. Type-1 lepra reaction: DOC — systemic steroids; mild cases — NSAIDs. Type-2 lepra reaction: DOC — systemic steroids; also high-dose clofazimine, chloroquine, and thalidomide (MOA: inhibits TNF-α, a pro-inflammatory cytokine; side effect: teratogenicity). Treatment of a nerve abscess: incision plus surgical drainage plus steroids.

NLEP: launched in 1983. Elimination guideline: a prevalence of leprosy less than 1 per 10,000 population. Leprosy was eliminated as a public health problem in India on December 31, 2005. NLEP emblem symbolism: represents positive action and hope. The partially affected thumb symbolizes that leprosy can be cured, and that a leprosy patient can be a useful member of society. The lotus symbolizes beauty and purity. The rising sun symbolizes hope and optimism.
Prophylaxis: MW Vaccine & Single Dose Rifampicin

MW vaccine: uses the MIP strain (Mycobacterium indicus pranii). "Indicus" reflects that the strain was designed in India; "Pran" honors Dr. Pran, founder of NII (National Institute of Immunology). Uses: given alongside MDT as immunotherapy (enabling faster bacillary clearance); given to contacts of leprosy patients. SDR (Single Dose Rifampicin): indicated as chemoprophylaxis for contacts of leprosy. A "contact" is defined by close proximity and prolonged duration of close proximity (living/working/social activity) with a newly detected leprosy case — for 20 hours/week, for 3 months, within the past 1 year. Age criteria: adults and children ≥2 years. Contraindications to be excluded before dosing: leprosy, TB. Dosage: 600mg.

Melanocyte: located in the stratum basale; derived embryologically from the neural crest. Function: melanin production (precursor: tyrosine), providing protection from UV radiation. Markers: S100, Melan-A, HMB-45. Epidermal melanin unit (EMU): 1 melanocyte transfers melanosomes via dendrites to 36 keratinocytes; function — uniform skin color. Shades of color: the number of melanocytes is the same in fair and dark skin. Melanosomes are smaller in fair skin, larger in dark skin. Melanin type: fair skin — pheomelanin (yellowish-red); dark skin — eumelanin (brown-black).

Melasma: an acquired hyperpigmentary disease. Etiology: sunlight; endocrine causes (thyroid disorders); pregnancy (called chloasma — the "mask of pregnancy"); drugs (OCPs, phenytoin). Clinical features: hyperpigmented, symmetrically distributed brown macules; site — malar area, nose, mandibular area. Differential diagnosis: the malar rash of SLE (which is red in color, unlike melasma's brown). Treatment: general — sunscreen. Skin lightening agents (mechanism: tyrosinase inhibition) — hydroquinone, azelaic acid, kojic acid. Chemical peels (MOA: controlled exfoliation of skin) — glycolic acid, trichloroacetic acid. Note: Chikungunya fever can cause melasma-like pigmentation of the nose, called the "Chik sign."

Melanocytic nevus/moles: a benign proliferation of nevus cells (a type of melanocyte). Two types: congenital and acquired. Congenital melanocytic nevus: onset at birth; color — hyperpigmented; borders — well demarcated; surface — coarse, with hypertrichosis. If size exceeds 20cm, it's termed a giant congenital melanocytic nevus, carrying a 2–5% risk of melanoma. Acquired melanocytic nevus — three types by location: junctional nevus (at the dermoepidermal junction/DEJ; a flat, brown macule); compound nevus (DEJ plus dermis; a dome-shaped nodule, hyperpigmented); intradermal nevus (dermis only; a dome-shaped nodule, skin-colored).

Freckles: color — hyperpigmented, brownish lesions. Melanocyte number is normal, but activity is increased. Trigger: sunlight. Site: photo-exposed areas. Association: xeroderma pigmentosum (a nucleotide excision repair defect). Lentigenes: melanocyte number is increased, activity is normal. Association: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (autosomal dominant; lesions — mucosal lentigenes; associated with a GI polyp, specifically a hamartomatous polyp).

Café-au-lait macules (CALM): color — hyperpigmented. For diagnosing neurofibromatosis type 1, a patient needs ≥6 CALMs, each exceeding 5mm (prepubertal) or 15mm (post-pubertal) in size. McCune-Albright syndrome: skin — segmental CALM; bones — polyostotic fibrous dysplasia; endocrine — precocious puberty. Becker's nevus: onset — acquired during puberty; symmetry — unilateral; color — hyperpigmented; surface — hypertrichosis; site — chest, shoulder, upper back.
Dermal Melanocytosis: Mongolian Spot, Nevus of Ota & Ito

Dermal melanocytosis: AKA ceruloderma. Pathology: proliferation of melanocytes in the dermis. Color: blue to slate grey (due to the Tyndall effect). Mongolian spot: age — child; color — blue to slate grey; site — lumbosacral region; fate — spontaneously resolves. Nevus of Ota vs Nevus of Ito (both unilateral, both blue to slate grey): Ota — along V1, V2 of the trigeminal nerve; site — face, sclera (in two-thirds of patients). Ito — along the posterior supraclavicular nerve and lateral brachial cutaneous nerve; site — scapular, shoulder. Both treated with Q-switched Nd:YAG laser.

Disorders of hypo/depigmentation classify into congenital and acquired. Albinism: defect — tyrosinase. Types: ocular albinism (eyes only) and oculocutaneous albinism (eyes, skin, and hair). Chediak-Higashi syndrome: autosomal recessive; gene — LYST; defect in phagolysosome fusion. Clinical features: oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent infections, and giant granules in neutrophils on peripheral smear. Piebaldism: autosomal dominant; defect in the neural crest. Clinical features: a white forelock (a white bunch of hair on the forehead), and islands of normal skin within a white patch.

Nevus depigmentosus: onset — at birth. Defect: impaired transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes. Lesion: a hypopigmented macule with feathery margins. Nevus anemicus: defect — a vascular anomaly (not a pigmentary defect). Lesion: a congenital white patch caused by vasoconstriction. Pathogenesis: vasoconstriction → decreased blood supply → a hypopigmented/pale skin patch.

Vitiligo: an acquired, chronic depigmentary disorder. Pathogenesis: the autoimmune theory (most common) — autoimmunity destroys melanocytes, leaving them absent within the lesion. Clinical features: skin — a depigmented macule; hair — white hair/leukotrichia (a marker of bad prognosis). Classification: segmental, non-segmental, and unclassified/undetermined. Segmental vitiligo: onset — early childhood; lesion — unilateral, segmental, does not cross the midline; leukotrichia is common. Non-segmental types: acrofacial (face, head, plus distal involvement); mucosal (>1 site); vitiligo vulgaris (bilateral, symmetric — the most common type); universal vitiligo (>80–90% body involvement). Unclassified: focal vitiligo (small, isolated depigmented lesions). True Koebner's phenomenon/isomorphic response is seen in active vitiligo disease.

Vitiligo treatment is guided by body surface area (BSA) involvement. <20% BSA: topical steroids, topical tacrolimus (a calcineurin inhibitor). >20% BSA: phototherapy (narrow band UVB, 311±2nm), systemic steroids, azathioprine (an immunosuppressant). Chemical leukoderma: chemical-induced melanocyte destruction. Examples: bindi — para-tertiary butylphenol (PTBP); rubber footwear — monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH).

Eczema: a reaction pattern of the skin due to exogenous or endogenous causes. Classification: by morphology (acute, subacute, chronic) and by etiology (exogenous, endogenous). Acute eczema: signs of acute inflammation — erythema, edema, vesicles, oozing of fluid, crusting. Histopathology: spongiosis (intraepidermal intercellular edema, in the stratum spongiosum) is the hallmark of acute eczema. Subacute eczema: signs — erythema, scaling. Chronic eczema: due to prolonged scratching. Lichenification: hyperpigmented, thickening of skin, exaggerated skin markings.

Exogenous eczema divides into contact dermatitis (secondary to a substance), phytodermatitis (plant-induced), and photodermatitis (sunlight-induced). Contact dermatitis (CD): inflammation of skin secondary to contact with an inciting factor. Irritant CD: predisposition — all exposed individuals affected; mechanism — non-immune mediated, direct tissue damage; distribution — restricted to the site of contact; symptom — burning. Examples: acids, alkalis, detergents; diaper dermatitis (convex areas involved, folds spared). Allergic CD: predisposition — genetic; mechanism — immune mediated, type IV hypersensitivity; distribution — disseminates beyond the site of contact; symptom — itching. Most common allergens: nickel (metal), neomycin (topical antibiotic), potassium dichromate (cement), para-phenylenediamine/PPD (hair dye), para-tertiary butylphenol/PTBP (bindi). Patch test: diagnoses allergic contact dermatitis; based on type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity. Procedure: allergens applied to the back, read at 48 hours, best read at 96 hours.

Airborne contact dermatitis: substances released into the air settle over exposed skin, causing contact dermatitis. Parthenium hysterophorus (Congress grass): allergen — sesquiterpene lactones (SQL). Identification: white flower heads. Sites: exposed areas (face, upper eyelid, neck, V-area of chest). Diagnosis: photopatch test (patch test plus UV radiation). Treatment: acute — systemic steroids; long term — azathioprine (an immunosuppressant).

Seborrheic dermatitis (dandruff): pathogenesis — an inflammatory response to Malassezia yeast. Sites: scalp, face (nasolabial fold, retroauricular area). Scale: greasy, yellow. Severe forms occur in HIV and Parkinson's disease. Infantile seborrheic dermatitis is called cradle cap — greasy yellow scale in infants. Stasis eczema: other names — varicose/gravitational/venous eczema. Associated with chronic venous insufficiency. Importance: featured in the CEAP classification of varicose veins, at stage C4a (eczema/pigmentation).
Asteatotic Eczema, Pityriasis Alba, Nummular Eczema & Pompholyx

Asteatotic eczema/eczema craquelé: age — elderly. Pathogenesis: decreased skin lipid → dry skin. Lesions: itchy, scaly, with fissures. Pityriasis alba: "pityriasis" = scaly, "alba" = white. Age group: children. Lesion: hypopigmented, scaly macules. Association: dry skin/atopy. Differential diagnosis: indeterminate Hansen's disease (in which scaling is absent). Nummular/discoid eczema: lesion — coin-shaped (both centre and periphery active). Note: an annular lesion has an active periphery. Pompholyx/dyshidrotic eczema: lesion — pruritic, deep-seated vesicles, giving a "sago grain" appearance. Sites: sides of the digits.

Atopic Dermatitis (AD): a chronic, relapsing, inflammatory skin disease — an endogenous eczema triggered by exogenous factors. Also called "the itch that rashes" (itch → rash). Hallmark: pruritus. Atopy is defined as a localized type I hypersensitivity reaction. The "triad of atopy": atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma. Pathogenesis: a defective skin barrier causes dry skin; an increased IgE response to allergens occurs (driven by IL-4, IL-10, IL-13); a mutation of filaggrin (a filament-aggregating protein) contributes.
Atopic Dermatitis: Clinical Phases & Diagnostic Criteria

Clinical phases of AD: Infantile phase (up to 2 years) — lesions papulovesicular, exudative; sites — face, scalp, extensors. Childhood phase (2 years to puberty) — lesions red, scaly, excoriated papules and plaques; sites — flexors (cubital and popliteal fossa). Adult phase (>puberty) — lesions show lichenification; sites — flexors. Diagnosis: clinical examination (investigation of choice). Criteria: Hanifin and Rajka. (1) Pruritus — intermittent and intense; the hallmark of AD. (2) Typical morphology and distribution. (3) Chronic or chronically relapsing dermatosis. (4) Personal or family history of atopy.
Atopic Dermatitis: Skin & Eye Clinical Features

Skin clinical features of AD: xerosis (dry skin); ichthyosis (fish-like scales); white dermographism (from vasoconstriction); headlight sign (facial erythema that spares the perinasal and perioral area). Eye findings in AD: conical cornea → keratoconus. Cataract → anterior subcapsular cataract (shield cataract). Infraorbital skinfold → Dennie-Morgan fold. Lateral madarosis in AD → Hertoghe's sign.
Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome & Complications of Atopic Dermatitis

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: an X-linked recessive disorder; gene — WAS. Presentation in males: recurrent infections, atopic eczema, and microthrombocytopenia (small platelets). Complications of AD: infections — bacterial (Staphylococcus aureus), viral (eczema herpeticum — a disseminated cutaneous HSV-1 infection). Erythroderma: erythema ± scaling, affecting >90% of body surface area.

Topical treatment: for dry skin — emollients; for inflammation — topical steroids/tacrolimus. Systemic treatment: steroids; cyclosporine (a calcineurin inhibitor; side effects — nephrotoxicity, hypertension). Note on steroid dosage forms: for lichenification — ointment; for oozing — cream.

Crisaborole: route — topical. MOA — phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE-4) inhibitor. Indication — mild to moderate AD. Dupilumab: route — subcutaneous. MOA — binds the alpha-subunit of the IL-4 receptor, blocking signal transduction, targeting IL-4 and IL-13. Indication — moderate to severe AD.

Genodermatoses: genetic disorders with skin manifestations. Neurofibromatosis Type 1 = Von Recklinghausen's disease. Type 2 = bilateral vestibular schwannoma / MISME syndrome (Multiple Inherited Schwannomas, Meningiomas, and Ependymomas). Both are autosomal dominant. Genetics: NF-1 — gene NF1, chromosome 17, protein neurofibromin. NF-2 — gene NF2, chromosome 22, protein merlin/schwannomin. Skin manifestations of NF-1 — Cutaneous neurofibroma: benign tumor of the connective tissue of peripheral nerve sheath; onset adolescence; skin-colored papules to nodules; button hole sign — the lesion can be invaginated by finger pressure. Plexiform neurofibroma: arises from multiple nerve fascicles; congenital onset; a diffuse enlarging plaque; on palpation feels like a "bag of worms". Note: "bag of worms" is also used for a varicocele, due to a dilated pampiniform plexus of veins — a different structure with the same descriptive sign. Café au lait macule (CALM): hyperpigmented patch. Diagnostic criterion for NF-1 requires ≥6 macules, sized >5 mm prepubertally or >15 mm postpubertally. Skin fold freckles: hyperpigmented macules in the axilla and groin, called Crowe's sign — pathognomonic of NF-1. Eye manifestations of NF-1 — Lisch iris nodule: an iris hamartoma, best seen on slit-lamp exam, with normal visual acuity. Optic nerve/optic pathway glioma: presents with proptosis.
Tuberous Sclerosis: Genetics & Major Skin Signs

Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC), AKA Bourneville disease, is autosomal dominant. Genetics: TSC-1 — chromosome 9, protein hamartin. TSC-2 — chromosome 16, protein tuberin. Vogt's triad (mnemonic EPILOIA): Epilepsy, Low IQ/low intelligence, Adenoma sebaceum. Major skin manifestations — Ash leaf macules: the earliest skin lesion of TSC; hypopigmented; lanceolate shape (oval/rounded at one end, pointed at the other); diagnosed with a Wood's lamp. Adenoma sebaceum / facial angiofibroma: symmetric reddish-brown papules over the malar area, nasolabial folds, and nose — a characteristic feature of TSC. Shagreen patch: a leathery plaque in the lumbosacral region, composed of collagen (a collagenoma). Periungual fibromas (Koenen's tumours): onset at puberty.

TSC minor manifestations: Skin — confetti macules (hypopigmented); Dental enamel — pits; Gingiva — fibroma. TSC systemic features by organ: Kidney — renal angiomyolipoma. Lung — pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Heart — cardiac rhabdomyoma. Retina — retinal hamartoma. CNS — cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and SEGA (subependymal giant cell astrocytoma). Sturge-Weber Syndrome, AKA encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, has sporadic inheritance (unlike NF and TSC, which are autosomal dominant). Clinical manifestations: CNS — epilepsy; Eye — glaucoma; Skin — facial port-wine stain. Facial port-wine stain: pathology is a low-flow capillary vascular malformation. Present at birth, unilateral, and permanent. Color evolves from pink-red to purplish with age. Site: face. Treatment: pulsed dye laser (PDL).

Ichthyosis: a disorder of keratinization ("ichthy" = fish-like scales); characterized by scaling without inflammation. Classification — Congenital: ichthyosis vulgaris, X-linked recessive ichthyosis, lamellar ichthyosis. Acquired: from diseases (hypothyroidism, Hansen's disease, Hodgkin's lymphoma, HIV) or drugs (clofazimine, nicotinic acid, statins). Ichthyosis vulgaris: onset 3–12 months; autosomal dominant; defect in filaggrin; fine white scales; face and flexures are spared. X-linked ichthyosis: onset <3 months; X-linked recessive; defect in steroid sulfatase, causing accumulation of cholesterol sulfate (which cannot convert to cholesterol) → ichthyosis. Associations: keratosis pilaris (keratin accumulation within hair follicles) and hyperlinear palms.
