Lamellar ichthyosis: onset at birth; autosomal recessive; defect in epidermal transglutaminase-1; synonym ichthyosis nigra. Presentation: a translucent, parchment-like collodion membrane covers the neonate at birth, which over a few weeks gives way to dark, plate-like adherent (brown-black) scales that spare the palms and soles. Lamellar ichthyosis associations: ectropion (outward turning of the eyelid margin) and eclabium (outward turning of the lip); also corneal opacities and cryptorchidism (undescended testis). Note: epidermal transglutaminase-3 (a different enzyme) is the defect implicated in dermatitis herpetiformis, not lamellar ichthyosis. Treatment of ichthyoses: topical emollients; for lamellar ichthyosis, systemic oral retinoids (acitretin).

Incontinentia Pigmenti: a genetic ectodermal disease affecting skin, teeth, eyes, and lens. Inheritance: X-linked dominant. Distribution follows Blaschko lines (lines of embryologic cell migration). Patterns by site: spiralled — scalp; V-shaped — upper spine; S-shaped — abdomen; perpendicular — lower limbs. Skin manifestations progress through four stages: Stage I (Vesicular) — vesicular lesions along Blaschko lines. Stage II (Verrucous) — verrucous lesions replace the vesicles, with a rough, uneven surface. Stage III (Hyperpigmentation) — hyperpigmented lesions. Stage IV (Hypopigmentation) — hypopigmented lesions. Ocular manifestations: avascular peripheral retina, seen on fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA).

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP): an inherited DNA repair disorder causing cellular hypersensitivity to UV radiation. Inheritance: autosomal recessive. Defect: nucleotide excision repair (NER). Pathophysiology: UV radiation induces cellular DNA damage. Normally, NER excises the damaged DNA. In XP, defective NER leads to accumulation of damaged DNA → genomic instability → predisposition to carcinogenesis. Cutaneous manifestations: sunburn on minimal sun exposure; photophobia; freckles (melanocyte number is normal, but melanocyte activity is increased); skin carcinoma, particularly basal cell carcinoma; continuous sunlight exposure → photoaging → xeroderma (dry skin). Systemic manifestations: CNS — mental retardation, ataxia. Carcinoma — hematological malignancies (in addition to skin cancers). Treatment: photoprotection (sunscreen) and prevention of malignancy with retinoids, which modulate keratinocyte differentiation.

Histamine-mediated reactions follow a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Chief cell: mast cell. Immunoglobulin involved: IgE. Key mediator released: histamine. Clinical presentation is based on the vascular reaction pattern/response, spanning three entities of increasing severity: urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis. Urticaria: dermal edema; lesion is the wheal (itchy). Angioedema ("blood vessel swelling"): fluid accumulation in the affected area due to increased vascular permeability. Lesion: non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling. Level: subcutaneous tissue/submucosa. Site: lips and eyelids, due to their loose, scanty connective tissue. Anaphylaxis: acute, life-threatening, multisystem involvement. Skin — urticaria, angioedema. Respiratory system — bronchospasm. Cardiovascular system — hypotension. GIT — abdominal pain.

A wheal is a pruritic, elevated, edematous, transient plaque, characterized by central pallor with peripheral erythema. Dermographism is a sign elicited by stroking normal skin with a blunt object, producing an exaggerated wheal-and-flare response at the stroked site. Urticaria classification by duration: <6 weeks = acute; >6 weeks = chronic. Chronic urticaria is further divided by presence of an exogenous trigger: inducible (trigger present) vs spontaneous (no identifiable exogenous trigger — autoimmune or idiopathic). Types of inducible chronic urticaria: cold urticaria (triggered by cold temperature), aquagenic urticaria (triggered by water), solar urticaria (triggered by sunlight), cholinergic urticaria (triggered by exercise). Chronic spontaneous urticaria can be autoimmune or idiopathic in origin. Etiology of acute urticaria: Food — peanuts, seafood, food additives. Infection — parasitic (giardiasis, amoebiasis) or viral (hepatitis B, infectious mononucleosis). Drugs — NSAIDs. Aerosols — pollen, animal dander.

Cholinergic urticaria pathophysiology: trigger is physical exertion/exercise, which raises core body temperature. This stimulates eccrine sweat glands (supplied by sympathetic cholinergic fibres), causing release of acetylcholine, which produces characteristic pinpoint, itchy wheals. Treatment of chronic spontaneous urticaria — 2nd generation antihistamines: cetirizine, levocetirizine, loratadine, desloratadine, fexofenadine. Additional treatment options: monoclonal antibody omalizumab (targets IgE); calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine (side effects: hypertension, nephrotoxicity).

Hereditary Angioedema: autosomal dominant inheritance, caused by a C1 esterase inhibitor defect. Pathophysiology: normally, C1 esterase inhibitor inhibits the kallikrein system, the complement system, and Factor 12. When defective, it leads to activation of the complement system (causing ↓C4 levels, used as a screening test) and the kallikrein system — the latter converts HMW kininogen to bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability via B2 receptors, producing angioedema. Clinical presentation: recurrent episodes of angioedema, often precipitated by minor trauma. Involvement: skin, oropharynx, respiratory system, GIT. Lesions show no wheals, since histamine is not involved. Clinically significant: non-responsive to antihistamines and steroids (unlike histamine-mediated angioedema). Treatment goals: increase C1 esterase inhibitor — recombinant C1 esterase inhibitor, danazol, fresh frozen plasma. OR use target inhibitors: kallikrein inhibitors (ecallantide, lanadelumab) and B2 receptor inhibitors (icatibant).

Cutaneous Mastocytosis, AKA urticaria pigmentosa: a disease of mast cell proliferation in the skin lesions. Age group: children. Lesion: hyperpigmented skin lesions. Site: trunk. Clinical sign — Darier sign: stroking lesional skin with a blunt object causes degranulation of mast cells → release of histamine → erythema + urticarial halo at the site. Note — Pseudo-Darier sign: transient induration + piloerection (not erythema/urticaria) on stroking; due to hamartomatous proliferation of dermal smooth muscle; seen in congenital smooth muscle hamartoma, a different entity from mastocytosis. Diagnosis — Histopathology: metachromatic granules on toluidine blue stain. Metachromasia: when the color of the stained tissue differs from the color of the dye used. CD marker for mast cells: CD-117. Treatment: antihistamines; mast cell stabilizer — ketotifen.

Fixed Drug Eruption: an immunologic cutaneous adverse drug reaction. Mechanism: Type IV hypersensitivity. Pathogenesis: on first exposure to the drug, memory T cells are formed. On subsequent exposure, an immune response occurs at the same (fixed) site. Causes: NSAIDs, cotrimoxazole, tetracycline. Sites: mucocutaneous junctions (lips, glans penis) and limbs. Clinical features: a well-demarcated, circular, dusky red plaque with a dark centre and erythematous periphery. Onset of rash: first episode 7–10 days after drug intake; on re-intake, 30 minutes to 8 hours. Shows fixed-site recurrence on re-exposure, and heals with hyperpigmentation. Treatment: stop the offending drug; in severe cases, steroids (topical/systemic).

Erythema Multiforme (EM): an acute, immune-mediated, cytotoxic dermatitis that is self-limiting. Etiology: Infection — HSV-1 (most common), Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Drugs — antimalarials, NSAIDs, sulfonamides. Connective tissue disorder — SLE. Neoplasia — leukemia, internal malignancy. Types: EM minor (mild severity, mucosa not involved) vs EM major (severe, mucosa involved). Lesion: the target lesion, with 3 zones — centre: dusky purpura; intermediate: pale edema; periphery: erythema. Distribution: distal extremities, palms and soles; lesions are typically multiple. Treatment: treat the underlying cause (e.g., recurrent HSV-1 infection → acyclovir); systemic steroids (short course).

Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): an acute, life-threatening, severe mucocutaneous drug reaction. Etiology: drugs account for ≥90% of cases — NSAIDs (oxicam group), antiepileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), sulfonamides, antiretrovirals (nevirapine, abacavir), and allopurinol. HLA predisposition: HLA-B*1502 — carbamazepine toxicity. HLA-B*5801 — allopurinol toxicity. Pathogenesis of epidermal necrolysis: full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte necrosis → separation of the skin (lysis). Mediators: CD8 T cells and NK cells produce granulysin (a cytolytic protein), causing keratinocyte necrosis. IL-15 promotes and maintains CD8 T cells and NK cells. The Fas receptor (a death receptor): the causative drug binds the Fas receptor, triggering keratinocyte necrosis.

Classification of SJS/TEN by body surface area (BSA) involvement (calculated by rule of 9): <10% = SJS; 10–30% = SJS-TEN overlap; >30% = TEN. Clinical features: onset 1–4 weeks after drug intake; systemic symptom — fever. Skin: an atypical target lesion with 2 zones, distributed over the proximal extremities and trunk. Progression: diffuse erythema → bullae → sheet-like epidermal peeling (necrolysis). Pseudo-Nikolsky sign is positive: pathology is keratinocyte necrosis; procedure — tangential pressure applied over the skin causes separation of the upper from lower layers of skin. Mucosa: painful erosions with hemorrhagic crusts. Differential diagnosis for sheet-like epidermal peeling: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) vs TEN. In SSSS, mucosa is normal (pathology: ↓ Dsg-1 concentration). In TEN, mucosa shows hemorrhagic crusts. SCORTEN scoring: a severity-of-illness score in TEN that predicts mortality. Assessed first within 24 hours of presentation, and repeated after 3 days. Parameters (1 point each): age >40 yrs, malignancy present, heart rate >120/min, initial area of detachment >10%, serum bicarbonate <20 mmol/L, BUN >28 mg/dl, blood glucose >252 mg/dl. Mortality by score: 0–1 = 3%, 2 = 12%, 3 = 35%, 4 = 58%, 5 = 90%. Treatment: stop the offending drug; systemic steroids; cyclosporine (a T-cell inhibitor); IV immunoglobulin (acts as a Fas receptor antagonist).

Bleomycin-induced pigmentation: presents as flagellate (whip-like) dermatitis — diffuse, pruritic, distributed over the trunk and extremities; heals with hyperpigmentation. Mechanism of action: the enzyme hydrolase inactivates bleomycin. Hydrolase is deficient in the skin (leading to flagellate dermatitis) and in the lung (leading to pulmonary fibrosis) — explaining why these are the classic sites of bleomycin toxicity. Serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation: snake-like/linear hyperpigmentation seen in the skin overlying cutaneous veins. Causes: IV chemotherapy — 5-FU, cyclophosphamide, docetaxel, doxorubicin. Pathophysiology: IV chemotherapy drugs cause (1) endothelial injury and (2) subclinical thrombophlebitis, producing the linear hyperpigmented streak along the vein.

Lupus Erythematosus (LE): a multisystem autoimmune disorder with non-organ-specific antibodies, targeting cell nuclear antigens. Classification: Chronic Cutaneous LE (CCLE) — purely cutaneous. Subacute Cutaneous LE (SCLE) — mainly cutaneous, limited systemic involvement. Systemic LE (SLE) — widespread systemic disease. CCLE: most common form is Discoid LE (DLE). Site: face, scalp, ears. Lesion — the discoid plaque: central atrophy + scarring, peripheral hyperpigmentation, and adherent scales. DLE on the scalp causes scarring alopecia, with the Carpet Tack sign: adherent scales → follicular plugging → on removing the scale, its undersurface shows a "carpet tack" appearance. SCLE is the most photosensitive LE variant, producing a non-scarring rash. Associated antibodies: anti-La, anti-Ro. Two clinical forms: annular/polycyclic (annular and polycyclic plaques) and papulosquamous/psoriasiform.
Systemic LE: Skin, Oral & Hair Findings

In Systemic LE (SLE), skin rash can be malar or discoid. Acute cutaneous LE (malar rash): erythema of the malar area and nasal bridge, with characteristic nasolabial fold sparing. Oral ulcers in SLE: characteristically painless, occurring on the palate. Hair changes in SLE — Alopecia: non-scarring is the most common type; scarring alopecia occurs due to discoid lesions of SLE. Lupus hair: site — frontal hair; texture — fragile, unruly, short hair; association — a marker of a flare of disease activity.

Dermatomyositis (DM): an autoimmune connective tissue disease affecting skeletal muscles (causing proximal myopathy) and the skin. Gottron's papules (pathognomonic of DM): violaceous, flat-topped papules; site — metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and interphalangeal (IP) joints. Heliotrope rash: violaceous macular erythema; site — periorbital region (upper eyelid). Gottron's sign: violaceous macular erythema (distinct from Gottron's papules) at the MCP/IP joint (most common), olecranon process, elbows, medial malleoli, and patella. Mechanic's hand: hyperkeratotic fissuring at the tips and sides of the digits; associated with anti-Jo-1 antibodies. Named signs in DM, based on the site of violaceous macular erythema: V sign — anterior chest; Shawl sign — upper back/shoulder; Holster sign — lateral upper thigh. Nail features in DM: periungual erythema; ragged cuticle (Samitz sign); nail fold capillary telangiectasia.

Scleroderma: "sclero" = thickening; "derma" = skin. Two forms: localised cutaneous form/morphea (restricted to skin) and systemic sclerosis (involves multiple systems). Localised cutaneous form (morphea): early skin lesions are violaceous, indurated (hard, fibrosed) plaques; late skin lesions become ivory-white. Linear morphea: site — frontoparietal region; lesion — a linear indurated band of morphea; causes scarring alopecia, producing an "en coup de sabre" (blow of sword) appearance. Systemic sclerosis (SS) classification, based on the extent of skin thickening: Limited cutaneous SS — distal to the elbow/knee, and face. Diffuse cutaneous SS — distal + proximal to the elbow/knee, and trunk. CREST syndrome (seen in limited cutaneous SS): Calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.

Pathogenesis of Systemic Sclerosis (SS): (1) vascular dysfunction; (2) immune dysregulation; (3) increased Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) produced by fibroblasts → fibrosis. Skin features of SS: Hidebound/taut skin — skin cannot be pinched, due to thickening. Microstomia — perioral radiating furrows and difficulty opening the mouth, due to fibrosis. Decreased wrinkles with mask-like facies (expressionless face). Mat-like telangiectasia — dilated blood vessels. Extremity finding — Raynaud's phenomenon: episodic digital vasospasm, secondary to cold or emotional stimuli. 3 phases: (1) Pallor (due to decreased perfusion); (2) Cyanosis (due to deoxygenated blood); (3) Rubor (due to reperfusion). Other extremity findings: nail fold capillary telangiectasia; digital ulcer/gangrene and pitted scars. Pigmentation in SS: depigmented macules (white) combined with perifollicular pigment retention (brown) — together termed "salt and pepper" pigmentation.

Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), AKA IgA vasculitis, is a type of small vessel vasculitis. Features: skin lesion — palpable purpura, site — lower extremities. Platelet count: normal (distinguishing it from thrombocytopenic purpura). Behçet's Disease: a multisystemic disease, classified as a variable vessel vasculitis. Mucocutaneous lesions: recurrent oral ulcers — well-defined, yellow necrotic base, heal without scarring. Recurrent genital ulcers — sites: scrotum, vulva; heal with scarring. Skin lesions: Erythema nodosum — multiple red, tender nodules, on the anterior aspect of the leg. Also papulopustular lesions and acneiform nodules. Eye lesions: uveitis (anterior/posterior). Pathergy test: procedure — intradermal saline injection/prick with a needle, reading taken at 48 hours. Interpretation: positive if a papule/pustule forms.

Reactive Arthritis: inflammatory arthritis secondary to a distant focus of infection. Modes of acquisition: enterically acquired — Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter; sexually acquired (SARA) — Chlamydia trachomatis (with a history of urethritis). Reactive arthritis skin lesions: Circinate balanitis — well-demarcated, painless, circular erosions on the glans penis. Keratoderma blenorrhagicum — hyperkeratotic, crusted papules on the palms and soles. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) — Rheumatoid nodule: a painless subcutaneous nodule at pressure sites. Significance: indicates rapid progression of disease, increased severity of disease, and increased RA factor positivity. Acute Rheumatic Fever — Subcutaneous nodules: painless; smaller and shorter-lived compared to rheumatoid nodules; associated with carditis. Erythema marginatum (Acute Rheumatic Fever): non-pruritic pink macular erythema, with central clearing and outward peripheral expansion. Distribution: trunk, with sparing of the face.

Acanthosis Nigricans: morphology — hyperpigmented, velvety plaques; sites — axilla, neck. Causes: obesity (most common), diabetes, drugs, and internal malignancies (as a paraneoplastic manifestation). Pathogenesis in obesity: obesity causes ↑ circulating insulin → stimulates insulin-like growth factor (IGF) activation → stimulates keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation → Acanthosis Nigricans. Diabetic dermopathy: morphology — hyperpigmented, atrophic macules; site — anterior aspect of the leg. Significance: a marker of complications — diabetic nephropathy, neuropathy, and retinopathy. Necrobiotic disorders: "necrobiosis" = degeneration of collagen. Granuloma annulare: annular arrangement of papules; site — dorsum of extremities; association — diabetes mellitus. Differential diagnosis of an annular plaque with central clearing: Tinea corporis (scaling present, itching present) vs Granuloma annulare (scaling absent, itching absent/asymptomatic). Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum: a waxy-yellow, atrophic plaque with surface telangiectasia; site — anterior aspect of the leg; association — diabetes mellitus. "Lipoidica" refers to the fat content that causes the waxy-yellow appearance.

Sarcoidosis is a chronic granulomatous disease. Acute form / Löfgren's syndrome: Lung — bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; Skin — erythema nodosum (a panniculitis, i.e., inflammation of subcutaneous fat); other features — fever, arthralgia. Chronic form / Lupus pernio: the chronic, specific lesion of sarcoidosis. Lesion — a reddish violaceous plaque; site — central portion of the face. Lupus pernio associations: pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis of the upper respiratory tract, and bone cysts over the phalanges.

Primary systemic amyloidosis: association — plasma-cell dyscrasias; the deposited protein is the "AL" type of amyloid. Pathophysiology: amyloid deposition on the blood vessels of the skin (periorbital region) → ↑ fragility of blood vessels → trauma → rupture of blood vessels → pinch purpura (periorbital purpura elicited by pinching the skin). Pretibial myxedema, AKA thyroid dermopathy: lesion — non-pitting edema; site — anterior aspect of the leg; association — Graves disease (hyperthyroidism). Xanthelasma palpebrarum: "xanthos" = yellow; "palpebrarum" = eyelid margin. Lesion — symmetric yellow plaques; site — periorbital region. Associations: hyperlipidemia (Type 2, Type 4) and cholestasis. Note: can be present even with a normal lipid profile.

Lyme Disease: etiology — Borrelia burgdorferi; vector — Ixodes tick. Clinical features — skin rash: ECM (Erythema Chronicum Migrans), a target lesion. Breaking down the name: Erythema = red; Chronicum = progresses slowly; Migrans = migrates (expands). Differential diagnosis of target lesions — comparing Erythema Multiforme vs Lyme Disease: Number of target lesions: EM — multiple; Lyme — single. Site of target lesions: EM — distal extremities, palms and soles; Lyme — corresponds to the site of the tick bite.

Phrynoderma, AKA "toad skin": morphology — hyperkeratotic follicular papules; site — extensors (elbows/knees). Associations: essential fatty acid deficiency and vitamin A deficiency. Pellagra: "pella" = skin; "agra" = rough. Etiology — vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency. Diet association: maize and jowar. Aggravating factor: chronic alcoholism. Clinical features — the triad of pellagra: Diarrhoea, Dementia, and Photodermatitis (the photodermatitis is called Casal's necklace, a photosensitive rash around the neck). If untreated, this can progress to death. Acrodermatitis enteropathica: inheritance — autosomal recessive; gene involved — SLC-39A4; pathology — defective intestinal zinc absorption. Clinical features: age of presentation — 6 months. Clinical triad: Dermatitis (acral, periorificial), Diarrhoea, and Alopecia. Treatment: lifelong zinc supplementation.

Scurvy: cause — vitamin C deficiency. Clinical features: skin — perifollicular purpura/hemorrhage; hair — corkscrew hair. Note: "corkscrew motility" is a distinct, unrelated term seen in Treponema pallidum. Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency — Skin: nasolabial dyssebacea (abnormal sebaceous gland activity) and seborrheic dermatitis (dandruff-like feature). Oral cavity: angular stomatitis/cheilitis. Tongue: glossitis (magenta-coloured tongue). Eye: neovascularization of the cornea. Vitamin B12 deficiency: skin — hyperpigmentation of the dorsum of extremities; tongue — glossitis (beefy-red tongue); hair — canities (premature greying of hair). Note: a beefy-red genital ulcer is a separate entity — Donovanosis. Kwashiorkor (protein-energy malnutrition): skin lesions — flaky paint dermatoses and crazy pavement dermatoses. Hair lesion — the flag sign (an alternating pattern of hypopigmented and normal hair bands).

Necrolytic migratory erythema: "necrolytic" = necrosis of the epidermis; "migratory" = moves; "erythema" = red. Lesion — plaques with central clearing; site — periorificial areas, extremities. Association: glucagonoma (a tumor of the α-cells of the pancreas). Erythema gyratum repens: "erythema" = red; "gyratum" = coiled around a point; "repens" = crawl. Lesion — concentric bands of scaling (a "wood grain" pattern); sites — proximal extremities, trunk. Association: bronchogenic carcinoma of the lung. Trousseau syndrome: migratory thrombophlebitis; association — carcinoma of the pancreas. Sign of Leser-Trélat: association — GI adenocarcinoma. Presents as a rapid, multiple, sudden eruption of seborrheic keratosis. Note: seborrheic keratosis is a benign tumor of keratinocytes.

Panniculus = subcutaneous fat. Panniculitis = inflammation of subcutaneous fat. Types, based on which structure is inflamed: septae (connective tissue) inflammation → septal panniculitis; lobule (adipocytes) inflammation → lobular panniculitis. Erythema nodosum: "erythema" = red; "nodosum" = nodules. Definition: a delayed hypersensitivity response to various antigens. Triggers: idiopathic (most common cause); infections (Group A Streptococci, TB); drugs (OCPs, sulfonamides, iodides); inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease > ulcerative colitis); multisystemic disease (sarcoidosis); vasculitis (Behçet's disease — a variable vessel vasculitis). Clinical features: age group — children; often with a history of throat infection with Group A Streptococci. Lesion: red, tender nodules; site — anterior aspect of the legs; fate — heals without scarring. Histopathology: septal panniculitis. Treatment: symptomatic — NSAIDs for pain; definitive — treat the underlying cause/trigger.
Neutrophilic Dermatoses: Sweet Syndrome & Pyoderma Gangrenosum

Neutrophilic dermatoses share a common histopathology: dense, diffuse, dermal neutrophilic infiltrates. Two key diseases: Sweet syndrome and Pyoderma gangrenosum. Sweet syndrome (Acute Febrile Neutrophilic Dermatosis): important triggers — infections, pregnancy, hematological malignancies. Sweet syndrome clinical features: constitutional symptom — fever. Lesion: abrupt onset; morphology — red, tender papules and plaques; site — face, upper chest, upper back. Treatment: systemic steroids. Pyoderma gangrenosum: a misnomer — it is NOT a bacterial infection. Important triggers: rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's), and leukemia. Pyoderma gangrenosum clinical features: lesion — an ulcer; progression — rapid; painful; edge — undermined; hue — violaceous. Histopathology: dense, diffuse, dermal neutrophilic infiltrates (same as Sweet syndrome). Treatment: systemic steroids (it is treated as an immunological condition).

Lichen Nitidus: a chronic inflammatory disease of unknown etiology. "Nitidus" = shiny. Clinical features: age group — children. Lesion: asymptomatic, shiny papules; sites — forehead, shaft of penis, dorsum of extremities. Koebner's phenomenon: new lesions appear over sites of trauma. Histopathology: the "claw clutching ball" appearance — elongated rete ridges (the "claw") surrounding a chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate/lymphocytes (the "ball"). Treatment: usually self-resolving; if persistent, topical steroids. Cutis Marmorata: "cutis" = skin; "marmorata" = marbling. Cause: a physiological vascular response to cold. Age group: neonates. Lesion: symmetric, reticular (net-like pattern) marbling; sites — trunk and extremities. Management: resolves on warming the child.

Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH): a rare histiocytic disorder. Immunohistochemistry markers: CD207 (Langerin) — most specific; also S100 and CD1a. Disease spectrum by age of onset: at birth (congenital form) → Hashimoto-Pritzker disease (self-healing); <2 years → Letterer-Siwe disease; <5 years → Hand-Schüller-Christian disease; <8 years → Eosinophilic granuloma. Letterer-Siwe disease: course — acute disseminated form. Clinical features: bone lesions in 80% of patients; skin involvement in 50% (seborrheic dermatitis-like lesions, at the retroauricular and presternal areas); hepatosplenomegaly in 30% of patients. Hand-Schüller-Christian disease: clinical features — calvarial defects (skull), diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos. Eosinophilic granuloma: lesion — osteolytic; site — temporoparietal region.

Mycosis Fungoides / Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma (CTCL): a misnomer — it is NOT a fungal infection. Type of disease: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Tumour of: CD4 T cells. Course: indolent (slow, chronically progressive). Stages: (1) Patch, (2) Plaque, (3) Tumour, (4) Erythroderma (redness + scaling involving >90% of body surface area). Histopathology: cerebriform nuclei seen; Pautrier microabscess; epidermotropism (migration of malignant lymphocytes into the epidermis); malignant/atypical T-lymphocytes. Treatment: topical — nitrogen mustards; systemic — chlorambucil (chemotherapy); phototherapy — thin plaques: NB-UVB (311 ± 2nm); thick plaques: PUVA (Psoralen + UVA); TSEB — Total Skin Electron Beam therapy. Sézary syndrome: the erythrodermic phase of CTCL + leukemic variant of CTCL. Course: aggressive. Clinical triad: erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sézary cells (malignant T cells with cerebriform nuclei).

Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC): the most common primary skin malignancy. It is locally invasive, with rare metastasis. Pathway activated: Sonic Hedgehog pathway. Clinical features: lesion — most common site is the face (above the line joining the angle of the mouth to the lobule of the ear). Most common type: nodular type. Nodular BCC progression: translucent pearly nodule + surface telangiectasia → central necrosis → rodent ulcer, with a pearly, rolled-out edge. Treatment — Surgery: Mohs micrographic surgery — sequential removal of the tumour until the margin is negative for tumour cells; advantage — good cosmetic outcome. Targeted therapy: Sonic Hedgehog pathway inhibitors — Vismodegib and Sonidegib.
q: Going from the surface inward, what's the correct order of skin's three main layers?
The epidermis faces outward, sitting above the dermis, which sits above the fatty hypodermis.
Histologically, the epidermis is classified as:
Multiple stacked layers of flattened cells — the definition of stratified squamous.
Which layer is made of fully keratinized, dead cells with no nucleus?
'Corneum' = keratin. These dead, flattened corneocytes form the outermost shield.
The stratum corneum's barrier function works in two directions. What does it block?
Entry of microbes/irritants AND exit of water
It's a two-way barrier: keeps harmful things out, and limits transepidermal water loss.
Which epidermal layer exists only in the palms and soles?
Stratum lucidum ('clear layer') is unique to thick, glabrous skin.
In the palms, which layer sits directly beneath the stratum corneum?
Order in thick skin: corneum → lucidum → granulosum → spinosum → basale.
Which is the deepest epidermal layer, sitting directly on the dermis?
Stratum basale is the germinative layer — new keratinocytes are born here.
Alongside keratohyaline granules, the stratum granulosum also produces lamellar granules — also known as:
Lamellar granules are also called Odland bodies or cementosomes — they release lipid that helps seal the skin barrier.
Profilaggrin (inactive) → filaggrin (active) once processed in the granular layer.
What is filaggrin's main structural job?
It's the 'filament aggregating protein' — bundles keratin filaments to support the barrier.
A filaggrin mutation is classically linked to ichthyosis vulgaris and:
Both conditions share this barrier-protein defect.
The spiny look of the stratum spinosum comes from prominent:
Desmosomes are the intercellular 'spot welds' between keratinocytes here.
Autoantibodies against desmosomes cause which group of blistering disorders?
Losing desmosomal attachment is the defining mechanism of the pemphigus group.
Which layer is a single row of columnar cells with a central nucleus?
This is the dividing, germinative layer — stratum basale.
Another name for the stratum basale is the stratum:
'Germinativum' reflects its role generating new keratinocytes.
Which two layers together form the 'Malpighian layer'?
Stratum spinosum and stratum basale together = Malpighian layer.
Rete ridges are best described as:
Extensions of dermis into the epidermis
Projections of epidermis down into the dermis
Rete ridges = epidermis dipping down into dermis — the opposite direction from dermal papillae.
Extensions of dermis up into the epidermis
They interlock with rete ridges but point the opposite way — dermis reaching up into epidermis.
Normally, how long does it take a cell to migrate from the stratum basale to the stratum corneum?
About 4 weeks is the normal epidermal transit (turnover) time.
What happens to epidermal transit time in psoriasis?
Psoriasis is driven by markedly accelerated keratinocyte turnover, so transit time drops well below 4 weeks.
Roughly 90% of the epidermis is made of which cell, derived from ectoderm?
Keratinocytes are the epidermis's dominant cell population.
Keratin intermediate filaments (KIF) are the structural hallmark of which cell, giving it structural integrity?
KIF is the defining cytoskeletal feature of keratinocytes.
Which cell shows 'tennis-racket' shaped Birbeck granules on electron microscopy?
Birbeck granules with their racket shape are a Langerhans cell signature.
They're dendritic APCs, presenting antigen to T cells in lymph nodes.
Which markers are most specific for Langerhans cells (and Langerhans cell histiocytosis)?
CD207/langerin is the most specific Langerhans cell marker.
Which cell converts tyrosine into melanin?
Melanocytes synthesize melanin from tyrosine for UV protection.
Melanocytes are diagnostically important as the cell of origin for:
Which non-keratinocyte cell develops from the neural crest?
Melanocytes are neural-crest derived — unlike the other two.
Which cell is a fine-touch, slow-adapting mechanoreceptor?
Merkel cells couple with sensory nerves for fine touch.
A positive cytokeratin-20 stain points toward which cell/tumor?
CK20 is the classic marker for Merkel cells and Merkel cell carcinoma.
True or false: Langerhans cells and melanocytes sit in the same epidermal layer.
False — Langerhans in spinosum, melanocyte in basale
False — melanocyte in spinosum, Langerhans in basale
Langerhans cells live in the stratum spinosum; melanocytes live in the stratum basale.
The dermo-epidermal junction is also known as the ___ zone.
DEJ and basement membrane zone (BMZ) are synonyms.
Which dermal zone contains the dermal papillae and loosely arranged, thin collagen?
Papillary dermis is thin and loose — the reticular dermis is thick and dense.
Roughly what fraction of the dermis is reticular (vs papillary)?
Reticular dermis makes up about 90% of total dermal thickness.
Which collagen type predominates in normal skin?
Type I collagen dominates skin, giving it tensile strength.
Which collagen type is characteristic of cartilage rather than skin?
Type II collagen is the cartilage-defining collagen type.
Which dermal cell is the principal producer of collagen and ECM?
Fibroblasts are the dermis's main manufacturing cell.
Mast cells in the dermis are typically located:
Mast cells cluster around small dermal blood vessels.
Elastic fibers in the dermis mainly provide:
Which of these is NOT one of the four DEJ layers?
Stratum lucidum is an epidermal layer (palms/soles) — not part of the DEJ.
Between Type I and Type III, which collagen is more abundant in normal skin?
They're present in exactly equal amounts
Neither — skin has no Type III
Type I collagen dominates, with Type III present but secondary.
The gel-like 'ground substance' surrounding dermal fibers and cells is mainly made of:
GAGs form the hydrated gel that fills the space around collagen and dermal cells.
Which of these is NOT a skin appendage found in the dermis?
Stratum corneum belongs to the epidermis — hair, sweat and sebaceous glands are dermal appendages.
The hypodermis is also known as ___ tissue.
Hypodermis = subcutaneous tissue, sitting beneath the dermis.
What is the hypodermis's main physiological role?
Its fat content insulates and helps regulate body temperature.
In the hypodermis, adipocyte lobules are separated by:
Fibrous septa divide the fat into distinct lobules.
Panniculitis is classified histologically into which two patterns?
Named by whether inflammation centers on the septa or the fat lobules.
In the hypodermis, the connective-tissue septa function to:
Separate the fat into distinct lobules
Septa are the fibrous walls that divide the subcutaneous fat into lobules.
Septal panniculitis refers to inflammation centered on:
Septal panniculitis is named for inflammation localized to the septa between fat lobules.
Lobular panniculitis refers to inflammation centered on:
Lobular panniculitis is named for inflammation localized within the fat lobules themselves.
Retention of nuclei within the stratum corneum is called:
Para-keratosis: nuclei that should be gone are retained.
Thickening of the stratum corneum itself is called:
Hyper-keratosis = excess keratin build-up in the corneum.
Wedge-shaped hypergranulosis is a classic clue to:
That wedge-shaped thick granular layer is a lichen planus hallmark.
An absent or markedly thinned granular layer is seen in psoriasis and:
Both psoriasis and ichthyosis vulgaris show a thinned/absent granular layer.
'Ballooning degeneration' (intracellular edema) is characteristic of which infection?
Ballooning degeneration is classic in herpes simplex virus infection.
Intercellular edema in the epidermis, classic in acute eczema, is called:
Spongiosis = fluid pooling between keratinocytes, pulling them apart.
Loss of desmosomal attachment producing rounded 'Tzanck' cells is:
Acantholysis: keratinocytes lose their spiny attachments and round up.
Which is a genetic (not autoimmune/infectious) cause of acantholysis?
Darier disease and Hailey-Hailey disease are the genetic causes.
Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in the stratum corneum) point to:
Munro microabscesses are a psoriasis histology hallmark.
The 'spongiform pustule of Kogoj' — neutrophils collecting one layer deeper, in the stratum spinosum — points to:
Like Munro microabscesses, this is another psoriasis-specific neutrophilic pattern, just found in the spinosum instead of the corneum.
A neutrophilic microabscess at the dermal papillary tips is the histological signature of:
Papillary-tip microabscesses are classic for dermatitis herpetiformis, an immunobullous disease.
Which microabscess pattern is built from eosinophils rather than neutrophils or T cells?
Pemphigus vegetans is the eosinophil-predominant microabscess pattern.
Pautrier microabscesses, made of atypical T cells, suggest:
Pautrier microabscesses are characteristic of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides).
A saw-toothed rete ridge pattern on histology is classic for:
Regular elongation → psoriasis; saw-toothed → lichen planus.
Dyskeratosis is a feature shared by Darier disease and which malignancy?
Premature single-cell keratinization shows up in both Darier disease and SCC.
The skin weighs roughly 4–5 kg, making it the body's heaviest organ.
Total skin surface area is approximately:
Skin covers a surface area of about 1.7 square meters in an average adult.
In dermatological naming, the term "vulgaris" (as in ichthyosis vulgaris) indicates that a condition is:
"Vulgaris" is a naming convention flagging the most common variant of a condition.
The name "stratum lucidum" reflects this layer's:
"Lucidum" means clear, describing this thin translucent layer seen in thick skin.
The name "stratum granulosum" reflects this layer's:
"Granulosum" refers to its prominent keratohyaline and lamellar granules.
Besides melanocytes, S100 positivity is also characteristically seen in:
S100 stains both melanocytes and Langerhans cells — it isn't melanocyte-exclusive.
Besides Langerhans cells, which other non-keratinocyte cell is also structurally classified as a dendritic cell?
Melanocytes, like Langerhans cells, are classified as dendritic cells.
Merkel cell mechanoreceptors are best described as:
Merkel cells are slow-adapting, low-threshold fine-touch mechanoreceptors.
Collagen fibers make up approximately what fraction of the dermis?
Collagen fibers account for roughly 70% of the dermis, providing tensile strength.
In acantholysis, once desmosomes are lost, polyhedral keratinocytes round up and characteristically show a:
The resulting circular (Tzanck/acantholytic) cells characteristically show a prominent nucleus.
A regularly elongated rete ridge pattern on histology (as opposed to a saw-toothed pattern) is classic for:
Regular elongation of rete ridges is characteristic of psoriasis, while a saw-toothed pattern points to lichen planus.
A flat, non-palpable lesion under 1 cm is called a:
That same flat lesion, once it grows past 1 cm, is renamed a:
Patch = the larger (>1cm) version of a macule — still flat and non-palpable.
A circumscribed, solid, raised lesion under 1 cm is a:
That same raised lesion, once over 1 cm wide, is called a:
Plaque = the larger (>1cm) version of a papule.
A raised lesion over 1 cm that also has depth (not just width) is a:
Nodule adds a depth dimension on top of the plaque's size threshold.
Multiple nodules are a classic presenting sign of:
Neurofibromas classically present as multiple cutaneous nodules.
A clear fluid-filled lesion under 1 cm is a vesicle; once it grows past 1 cm, it becomes a:
Vesicle (<1cm) → bulla (>1cm), same clear-fluid content, different size.
Which of these is NOT a classic cause of a vesicular rash?
Psoriasis is a scaly plaque disease, not vesicular — the other three are classic vesicular-rash causes.
A pinpoint, pus-filled lesion is a pustule. A larger pus-filled collection is called a(n):
Abscess = a larger, deeper collection of pus.
By size, purpura refers to RBC extravasation of approximately:
Petechiae are smaller (1–2mm); purpura is ≥3mm; ecchymoses are the largest (>1cm).
A wheal is a plaque that is pruritic, erythematous, edematous, and:
Transience — coming and going within hours — is a defining wheal feature.
Wheals are the hallmark lesion of:
Urticaria (hives) is built entirely from wheals.
Secondary skin lesions arise when primary lesions are modified by:
Secondary lesions are primary lesions changed by scratching or treatment.
Visible exfoliation of the stratum corneum is called:
Scale is flaking/shedding of the outer keratin layer.
Scalp scaling is a clue to seborrhoeic dermatitis and:
Both seborrhoeic dermatitis and psoriasis classically scale on the scalp.
A golden-brown, 'honey-colored' crust is classic for:
Honey-colored crusting is the textbook description of non-bullous impetigo.
Focal or total loss of the epidermis alone (e.g. in pemphigus vulgaris) is called a(n):
Erosion is epidermis-only loss — shallower than an ulcer.
An ulcer differs from an erosion because it also involves loss of:
Ulcers extend past the epidermis into the dermis.
A linear, deep cleft in the skin — classic in eczema — is a(n):
Fissure = a deep linear crack in the skin.
Punctate or linear abrasions from scratching are called:
Thickened, hyperpigmented skin with exaggerated markings from chronic scratching is:
Lichenification is the skin's response to long-term rubbing/scratching.
Thinning of skin's structural components, seen clinically as wrinkling and classically from topical steroid abuse, is:
Atrophy = decreased or absent structural skin components.
A wavy, grayish-white tunnel in the stratum corneum is a burrow, pathognomonic for:
Burrows are made by the scabies mite tunneling through the corneum.
Comedones — plugged by sebum and keratin — are the hallmark lesion of:
Comedones are follicle plugs specific to acne vulgaris.
Which comedone type appears black, due to oxidized sebum?
Open comedones are exposed to air, so the sebum oxidizes and darkens.
A three-zone lesion — dusky red center, pale edematous middle, erythematous rim — is a target lesion, seen in:
The classic target/iris lesion defines erythema multiforme.
Clustered lesions, as seen in herpes labialis, are described as:
Lesions confined to the territory of a single nerve are called:
Dermatomal = following one nerve's sensory territory.
A dermatomal rash is the classic presentation of:
Shingles reactivates along a single dermatome.
A wavy, whorled configuration following developmental skin lines is:
Blaschkoid lesions trace Blaschko's lines of epidermal migration.
A ring-shaped lesion with a clear center and active edge is described as:
Which of these is NOT a classic cause of an annular pattern?
Psoriasis typically presents as plaques, not the classic annular ring pattern.
A coin-shaped lesion, active at both center and periphery, is called:
Discoid/nummular = coin-shaped, distinguishing it from annular's clear center.
Discoid lupus erythematosus and discoid eczema both show which configuration?
Both are named for their coin-shaped (discoid) lesions.
Individual, separately-present lesions are described as:
Discrete = standing apart from one another.
When multiple lesions merge together into one area, this is called:
Confluent = lesions running together, losing their individual borders.
A distribution limited to the extremities (hands/feet) is called:
A rash on the extensor aspect classically affects which joints?
Extensor surfaces = elbows and knees, the classic psoriasis distribution.
A rash confined to sun-exposed skin is described as:
Photodistributed = following the pattern of sun exposure.
Langer's lines run along the orientation of which dermal structure?
Langer's lines follow the direction dermal collagen fibers run.
Surgical incisions made ACROSS Langer's lines carry a higher risk of:
Cutting against the tension lines increases wound tension, favoring hypertrophic scarring.
Epidermal cell migration during embryologic development
Unlike Langer's lines (tension), Blaschko's lines trace developmental cell migration.
On the abdomen, Blaschko's lines characteristically form which shape?
Abdominal Blaschko lines are S-shaped; the upper spine is V-shaped, the scalp is spiralled.
Which genetic condition classically follows Blaschko's lines?
Incontinentia pigmenti (X-linked dominant) shows a distribution along Blaschko's lines.
The Nikolsky sign is elicited by:
Scraping a lesion with a blade
Pressing a glass slide over a lesion
Nikolsky sign = lateral/tangential pressure causing the epidermis to shear off.
A TRUE positive Nikolsky sign has which underlying mechanism?
True Nikolsky sign reflects loss of keratinocyte-keratinocyte adhesion — acantholysis.
Which of these shows a TRUE Nikolsky sign?
Pemphigus vulgaris (and foliaceus, and SSSS) shows a true, acantholysis-driven Nikolsky sign.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) shows a pseudo-Nikolsky sign, driven by:
In TEN, sheets of dying (necrotic) keratinocytes separate — a different mechanism from true acantholysis.
On diascopy, a blanching response indicates:
Blanching means the redness is from dilated vessels, which empty under pressure — e.g. erythema.
A non-blanching response on diascopy points to:
Non-blanching means the red color is fixed RBCs outside vessels, not blood you can push away.
Apple jelly nodules on diascopy suggest which category of disease?
The yellowish-brown 'apple jelly' color on diascopy is characteristic of granulomas.
Which of these is NOT a classic cause of apple jelly nodules?
Psoriasis isn't granulomatous — the other three are classic apple-jelly-nodule causes.
Wood's lamp uses UV light at approximately what wavelength?
Wood's lamp emits long-wave UV around 364 nm.
Which organism causing tinea capitis fluoresces blue/green under Wood's lamp?
Trichophyton schoenleinii, the cause of favus, fluoresces which color?
T. schoenleinii gives a dull blue fluorescence, distinct from Microsporum's blue/green.
Pityriasis versicolor fluoresces which color under Wood's lamp?
Malassezia (pityriasis versicolor) gives a yellow fluorescence.
Erythrasma, caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, fluoresces:
Erythrasma's coral-red glow is a classic Wood's lamp finding.
The coral-red fluorescence of erythrasma is due to which pigment?
Coproporphyrin III, produced by C. minutissimum, causes the coral-red glow.
An ash-leaf macule, identified under Wood's lamp, points to:
Ash-leaf macules are an early cutaneous clue to tuberous sclerosis.
Vitiligo and melasma both show which fluorescence pattern under Wood's lamp?
Both pigmentary conditions become more visible with a milky-white glow under UV.
Porphyria cutanea tarda is classically associated with which Wood's-lamp-related finding?
Urine in porphyria cutanea tarda fluoresces pink under Wood's lamp.
Red teeth (erythrodontia) under Wood's lamp suggest:
Erythrodontia is a hallmark of congenital erythropoietic porphyria.
For a KOH mount, the sample should be scraped from:
The center of the lesion only
The active border has the highest fungal yield.
Refractile, branching hyphae on KOH mount are characteristic of:
Branching hyphae are the classic dermatophyte (tinea) finding.
A 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH mount is classic for:
Short hyphae (spaghetti) plus round spores (meatballs) = pityriasis versicolor.
Round, brown, thick-walled 'copper-penny' bodies on KOH mount suggest:
Medlar/sclerotic/copper-penny bodies are the KOH signature of chromoblastomycosis.
A Tzanck smear samples fluid from a:
Tzanck smear requires de-roofing an intact vesicle or bulla.
Round cells with prominent nuclei on Tzanck smear — acantholytic cells — point to:
Acantholytic (Tzanck) cells are the pemphigus-group signature.
Multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear suggest infection with:
Multinucleated giant cells are classic for the herpesviruses (HSV-1/2, VZV).
Tzanck smear slides are stained with:
Giemsa stain is used to read the Tzanck smear.
Liquid nitrogen is the standard cryotherapy agent.
Liquid nitrogen freezes tissue at about −196°C.
Cryotherapy destroys tissue mainly by causing:
Osmolarity changes leading to cell rupture
Freezing shifts osmolarity until the cell membrane ruptures.
Which of these is a standard indication for cryotherapy?
Warts and keloids are classic cryotherapy targets; the others are treated with phototherapy instead.
NB-UVB phototherapy uses a wavelength of approximately:
Narrow-band UVB is centered around 311±2 nm.
PUVA therapy combines UV-A with which photosensitizing agent?
Which of these is NOT a standard indication for phototherapy?
Phototherapy treats psoriasis, vitiligo, and atopic dermatitis — melanoma is a UV-associated cancer, not a phototherapy target.
In the name 'psoriasis,' the 'squamous' part refers to:
Psoriasis is best classified as a chronic, inflammatory disease mediated mainly by:
Psoriasis is a T-cell mediated inflammatory disease.
Which T-helper subset produces IL-17 in psoriasis?
Th17 is defined by its signature cytokine, IL-17.
Which cytokines does Th1 characteristically produce in psoriasis?
Th1 produces IL-2, TNF-α, and IFN-γ.
Which HLA allele is linked to early-onset psoriasis?
HLA-Cw6 is associated with earlier disease onset.
Which HLA allele is linked to psoriatic spondylitis?
HLA-B27 links psoriasis to spondylitis, as in other seronegative arthropathies.
PSORS1, the main psoriasis susceptibility gene, confers roughly what hereditary risk?
PSORS1 carries roughly a 50% hereditary risk.
Which infection is the classic trigger specifically for guttate psoriasis?
Group A strep (often after pharyngitis) triggers guttate psoriasis.
Which of these is NOT a recognized drug trigger for psoriasis?
Lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials, NSAIDs, and steroid withdrawal are recognized triggers — penicillin is not on that list.
Psoriasis symptoms classically worsen in which season?
Normal epidermal transit time is about 28 days. In psoriasis, it drops to approximately:
Epidermal hyperproliferation shortens transit time to just 3–5 days.
In psoriasis pathogenesis, the epidermis shows hyperproliferation. What does the dermis show?
Dermal inflammation pairs with epidermal hyperproliferation in psoriasis.
Guttate psoriasis is most classically seen in which age group?
Guttate psoriasis is a childhood-predominant presentation.
Guttate psoriasis is typically preceded by:
A preceding streptococcal sore throat is the classic history.
The organism that triggers guttate psoriasis is:
Group A β-hemolytic strep is the trigger organism.
'Gutta' lesions in guttate psoriasis are described as:
Guttate psoriasis characteristically affects which body site?
The trunk is the classic site for guttate lesions.
The drug of choice for guttate psoriasis, targeting its streptococcal trigger, is a:
Macrolides treat the underlying strep trigger.
Generalized pustular psoriasis is classically triggered by:
Abrupt steroid withdrawal is the classic trigger for generalized pustular psoriasis.
In pustular psoriasis, sterile pustules coalesce into:
Coalescing sterile pustules form lakes or sheets of pus.
The acute, generalized form of pustular psoriasis is called the ___ type.
Von Zumbusch type is the acute generalized pustular psoriasis.
Pustular psoriasis occurring in pregnancy is also known as:
Impetigo herpetiformis = pustular psoriasis of pregnancy.
Erythrodermic psoriasis is defined by erythema affecting what proportion of body surface area?
Erythrodermic psoriasis involves over 90% of body surface area.
Psoriatic arthritis is RF-negative (seronegative) yet erosive.
The joint most commonly affected in psoriatic arthritis is the:
DIP joint involvement is the classic pattern in psoriatic arthritis.
The most severe, deforming form of psoriatic arthritis is called:
Arthritis mutilans is the most destructive psoriatic arthritis subtype.
Fusiform swelling of an entire digit due to inflammation is called:
The classic X-ray finding in psoriatic arthritis is the ___ appearance.
Pencil-in-cup describes the classic joint erosion pattern.
Chronic plaque psoriasis is also known as:
Psoriasis vulgaris = the common chronic plaque form.
In chronic plaque psoriasis, the scales are classically described as:
Silvery-white scale is the hallmark of plaque psoriasis.
Chronic plaque psoriasis classically distributes on the scalp and which surfaces of the elbows/knees?
Extensor surfaces (backs of elbows/knees) are the classic distribution.
The Auspitz sign is elicited using which bedside test?
The Grattage test — progressive scraping — is used to elicit the Auspitz sign.
In the Auspitz sign sequence, the first thing scraping reveals is:
Scraping first accentuates the scale, before deeper layers are reached.
Continued scraping in the Auspitz sequence reveals a thin membrane called the:
The Bulkeley membrane appears at the next stage of scraping.
The finding that finally defines a positive Auspitz sign is:
Pinpoint bleeding, from the exposed dermal papillary capillaries, is the Auspitz sign itself.
Koebner's phenomenon is also known as the ___ response.
'Isomorphic response' is the alternate name for Koebner's phenomenon.
Koebner's phenomenon is defined as new lesions of the original disease appearing at sites of:
Koebnerization occurs at trauma sites on previously unaffected skin.
TRUE Koebner's phenomenon reflects which underlying mechanism?
True Koebner is immunologically driven — unlike pseudo-Koebner's viral mechanism.
Which of these is a classic cause of TRUE Koebner's phenomenon?
Psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo are classic TRUE Koebner conditions; warts and molluscum are pseudo-Koebner.
Autoinoculation of a viral infection along the trauma line
Pseudo-Koebner spreads a viral infection (like warts) along a scratch line.
Which of these causes pseudo- (not true) Koebner's phenomenon?
Viral warts spread by autoinoculation — a pseudo-Koebner mechanism.
Woronoff's ring refers to a ___ ring seen around a psoriatic lesion.
Woronoff's ring is a zone of hypopigmentation surrounding the plaque.
The most common nail change in psoriasis is:
Nail pits are the single most common psoriatic nail finding.
Nail pits in psoriasis arise from a defect in the:
Pitting reflects a defect in the proximal nail matrix specifically.
Accumulation of hyperkeratotic material beneath the nail plate is called:
Subungual hyperkeratosis = keratotic buildup under the nail.
Distal separation of the nail plate from the nail bed is called:
Onycholysis is nail-plate separation from the bed, starting distally.
The oil drop sign (salmon patch) in nail psoriasis is pathognomonic and arises from a defect in the:
The oil drop sign reflects a nail-bed (not nail-matrix) defect.
Scalp psoriasis is often mistaken for dandruff, but is distinguished by:
Silvery-white scaling helps distinguish scalp psoriasis from simple dandruff.
Flexural (inverse) psoriasis, unlike classic plaque psoriasis, favors which surfaces?
Inverse psoriasis flips the usual pattern, favoring flexures instead of extensor surfaces.
Which nail finding is described as coarse, irregular, and deep?
These descriptors apply specifically to psoriatic nail pits.
Abnormal retention of nucleated cells in the stratum corneum, seen in psoriasis, is called:
Parakeratosis = retained nuclei in the corneum, a psoriasis hallmark.
A neutrophil collection within the stratum corneum in psoriasis is called:
Munro's microabscess sits in the stratum corneum specifically.
In psoriasis histology, the stratum granulosum is typically:
A thin or absent granular layer is part of the psoriasis histology triad.
Thickening of the stratum spinosum in psoriasis is called:
A neutrophil collection within the stratum spinosum in psoriasis is called the:
The spongiform pustule of Kogoj is Munro's microabscess's counterpart, one layer deeper.
Thinning of the epidermis directly above the dermal papillae in psoriasis is called:
Suprapapillary thinning is a classic psoriasis histology feature.
The rete ridge pattern in psoriasis is described as:
Regular elongation of rete ridges is seen in psoriasis (vs. saw-toothed in lichen planus).
The dermal papillae in psoriasis characteristically show:
Dilated papillary blood vessels feed the rapid epidermal turnover.
Which topical treatment category reduces scaling in psoriasis?
Emollients/moisturizers work specifically to reduce scaling.
Which topical treatment works as an anti-inflammatory in psoriasis?
Topical steroids are the anti-inflammatory mainstay.
Coal tar and dithranol work in psoriasis mainly by:
Both agents work by reducing epidermal DNA synthesis.
Tazarotene, a topical vitamin A analogue used in psoriasis, is notably NOT used to treat:
Despite being a retinoid, tazarotene is specifically not used for acne.
Calcipotriol is a topical vitamin ___ analogue used to normalize keratinization.
Calcipotriol is a vitamin D analogue.
Phototherapy works in psoriasis mainly by increasing which anti-inflammatory cytokine?
Phototherapy raises IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine.
NB-UVB phototherapy uses a wavelength of approximately:
Narrow-band UVB is centered around 311±2 nm.
In PUVA therapy, psoralen acts as a photosensitizer that mainly helps:
Psoralen sensitizes skin so UV-A can act more deeply and effectively.
PUVA's UV-A component uses a wavelength range of approximately:
UV-A in PUVA spans roughly 320–400 nm.
The Goeckerman regimen combines coal tar with:
Ingram's regimen combines coal tar and NB-UVB with:
Ingram's regimen adds dithranol (anthralin) to the Goeckerman combination.
Methotrexate works in psoriasis by inhibiting:
Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, halting DHFA→THFA conversion.
A major reproductive concern with methotrexate is that it is:
Methotrexate is Category X — strictly avoided in pregnancy.
Cyclosporine acts as a calcineurin inhibitor, reducing which cytokine?
Cyclosporine's calcineurin inhibition lowers IL-2 production.
Cyclosporine is the systemic treatment of choice for which severe psoriasis type?
Cyclosporine's rapid action suits severe erythrodermic psoriasis.
A major concern with cyclosporine therapy is:
Cyclosporine's key toxicities are hypertension and nephrotoxicity.
Acitretin, an oral retinoid, works in psoriasis by modulating:
Acitretin is the systemic drug of choice for which psoriasis type?
Acitretin is specifically indicated for pustular psoriasis.
Apremilast raises intracellular cAMP by inhibiting:
Apremilast is a PDE4 inhibitor, raising cAMP.
Apremilast is used for plaque psoriasis and:
Apremilast covers both plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.
Tofacitinib works in psoriatic arthritis by inhibiting:
Systemic steroids are generally contraindicated in psoriasis, EXCEPT as the drug of choice for:
Pustular psoriasis of pregnancy (impetigo herpetiformis) is the one accepted indication.
The main advantage of biologic therapy in psoriasis is:
Biologics avoid the organ-specific toxicity seen with older systemic drugs — though they're expensive.
Ustekinumab targets IL-12 and IL-23 by blocking their shared subunit:
Ustekinumab targets the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23.
Infliximab (with etanercept and adalimumab) targets TNF-α.
Which biologic targets the IL-17 receptor directly, rather than IL-17 itself?
Brodalumab uniquely targets the IL-17 receptor rather than the cytokine.
Psoriasis is systemically associated with metabolic syndrome, which includes obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and:
Type 2 diabetes rounds out the metabolic syndrome association with psoriasis.
Lichen planus is best classified as a chronic, ___-mediated inflammatory disease.
Lichen planus is chronic and immune-mediated.
Which of these is NOT a recognized trigger for lichen planus?
Amalgam (mercury), hepatitis B/C, and antimalarials are recognized triggers — sun exposure is not the classic trigger described.
Dental amalgam is thought to trigger lichen planus due to its content of:
Amalgam contains mercury, implicated as a contact trigger.
Which two hepatitis viruses are recognized triggers for lichen planus?
Hepatitis B and C are the linked viral triggers.
The main skin symptom of lichen planus is:
Itching (pruritus) is the predominant skin symptom.
In the '6 P's' of lichen planus, the first 'P' describes its color as:
Purple/violaceous color is one of the defining 6 P's.
The shape of a classic lichen planus papule is described as:
Polygonal shape is one of the 6 P's.
Unlike a dome-shaped papule, a lichen planus papule is:
Wickham's striae describe which pattern on a lichen planus lesion?
Wickham's striae are the lacy white reticulate surface pattern.
Wickham's striae are best appreciated by applying oil to the lesion and viewing it with a:
Oil plus magnification brings out the reticulate pattern.
Lichen planus classically distributes on which body surfaces?
Flexor surfaces are the classic lichen planus distribution.
Lichen planus shows a TRUE Koebner's phenomenon, a feature it shares with psoriasis and:
Psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo are the classic TRUE Koebner triad.
Oral involvement in lichen planus occurs in approximately what proportion of patients?
Oral lichen planus is quite common — 40–60% of patients.
Oral lichen planus can be asymptomatic, or cause a burning sensation with:
Spicy food is the classic oral-LP symptom trigger.
The pattern seen in oral lichen planus mirrors the skin's:

The apocrine gland opens at the infundibulum, the uppermost segment.

Adamson's fringe marks the stem/bulb boundary.

Follicles survive intact in non-cicatricial alopecia, allowing regrowth.

'Exclamation mark hairs' describes their tapered shape.

Trichobezoar is the resulting stomach mass.

The hair mass can intermittently obstruct gastric outflow.

Secondary syphilis classically causes which pattern of hair loss?

Chemo targets rapidly dividing anagen-phase cells.

Premature transition into telogen defines this condition.

Androgenetic alopecia is classified as which pattern of non-cicatricial alopecia?

Ludwig's grading applies specifically to female pattern hair loss.

Animal contact (zoophilic transmission) is the key risk factor.

The standard investigation for tinea capitis is:
KOH mount is the standard fungal investigation.

BP splits at the subepidermal level, unlike pemphigus.

Trichomycosis axillaris presents with yellow deposits/concretions over the:
The axillary hair shaft is coated with these characteristic yellow concretions.
Treatment of trichomycosis axillaris includes topical clindamycin and:
Shaving physically removes the colonized hair, aiding clearance.
The pathogenesis of pitted keratolysis begins with increased:
Excess sweating promotes bacterial overgrowth, starting the cascade.
In pitted keratolysis, bacterial enzymes create pits by lysing:
Keratin-lysing enzymes carve out the characteristic pits.
Pitted keratolysis classically affects the palms and:
Palms and soles are the classic pitted keratolysis sites.
Whitfield's ointment, used for pitted keratolysis, combines salicylic acid with:
Salicylic acid plus benzoic acid make up Whitfield's ointment.

6% benzoic acid pairs with the 3% salicylic acid.
Ecthyma gangrenosum classically occurs in the setting of:

The underlying pathology of ecthyma gangrenosum is:
Hemorrhagic necrosis defines the ecthyma gangrenosum lesion.
Ecthyma gangrenosum lesions present as necrotic, crusted:

Hot tub folliculitis is classically linked to a history of:
Poorly maintained hot tubs harbor the causative Pseudomonas.
Hot tub folliculitis characteristically affects which body region?
The area covered by a swimsuit — the 'bathing trunk' region — is classically affected.
Green nail syndrome results from bacterial production of:

Green nail syndrome is caused by:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the green nail syndrome pathogen.
Which of these three Pseudomonal skin conditions is linked to systemic septicemia rather than direct local infection?
Ecthyma gangrenosum is the systemic-septicemia-associated presentation, unlike the other two localized conditions.
The classic history in cutaneous anthrax involves contact with:
Occupational or incidental animal contact is the classic anthrax history.
The characteristic lesion of cutaneous anthrax is called a:
'Malignant pustule' is the classic name for the anthrax lesion.

A vesicular rim surrounds the characteristic black eschar.

Neck rigidity reflects the associated meningitis.
The petechial rash of meningococcemia is characteristically:
Non-blanching when pressed with a glass slide

Besides a petechial rash, meningococcemia can also cause:
Angular cutaneous infarcts are a further meningococcemia skin finding.
Scrub typhus is best classified as an acute, febrile, ___-borne infectious disease.
Scrub typhus is transmitted by mites, not ticks or mosquitoes.
Orientia tsutsugamushi is the scrub typhus organism.
The vector for scrub typhus is the:
The trombiculid mite transmits scrub typhus.
The infective form of the trombiculid mite in scrub typhus transmission is called:
Chiggers are the infective larval stage responsible for transmission.
The characteristic skin lesion of scrub typhus is a(n):
An eschar at the bite site is the scrub typhus hallmark.
The eschar of scrub typhus is described as a black scab surrounded by:
Surrounding erythema distinguishes the scrub typhus eschar's appearance.

Doxycycline is the scrub typhus treatment of choice.
Mycobacterial skin infections divide into cutaneous TB and:

Direct invasion of the skin by M. tuberculosis
True cutaneous TB is caused by direct bacterial invasion of the skin.

TB chancre classically shows an undermined ulcer edge.

TB verrucosa cutis is also known as:

TBVC results from exogenous reinoculation in a sensitized host.
The characteristic skin lesion in TB verrucosa cutis is:
TBVC presents as an indurated, verrucous (warty) plaque.
TB verrucosa cutis characteristically affects the:
The term "lupus" in lupus vulgaris refers to a:
"Lupus" here evokes a wolf-bitten look to the plaque.
Most common cutaneous TB in adults
Most common cutaneous TB in children
Only multibacillary form of cutaneous TB

Lupus vulgaris can result from both exogenous and endogenous spread.
Lupus vulgaris occurs in a host with:
Lupus vulgaris is a paucibacillary form reflecting strong CMI.

The centre of the plaque undergoes atrophy and scarring.
In the lupus vulgaris plaque, the periphery characteristically shows:
The periphery shows an active, advancing edge.

Granulomatous lesions, called apple jelly nodules

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is another classic cause of apple jelly nodules on diascopy.
Scrofuloderma is the most common cutaneous TB in:
Scrofuloderma is the leading cutaneous TB type in children.
Scrofuloderma occurs in a host with:
Scrofuloderma is a multibacillary form with weak CMI.
The most common focus of infection leading to scrofuloderma is the:
Cervical lymphadenitis is the classic source focus for scrofuloderma.

Direct invasion of the overlying skin

The nodules rupture into the skin, forming sinuses and ulcers.
The end result of scrofuloderma includes draining sinuses, undermined ulcers, and:

Neck and axilla are the classic scrofuloderma sites.

Hematogenous spread from a distant focus

Orificial TB is a multibacillary form seen with:

The intensive phase uses four drugs (HRZE) for 2 months.

The continuation phase drops pyrazinamide, using HRE for 4 months.

Tuberculids occur in a host with:
Strong CMI underlies the hypersensitivity reaction of tuberculids.

A positive Mantoux reflects the strong CMI in tuberculids.

The three morphologic categories are micropapular, papular, and nodular.

The histopathology of lichen scrofulosorum shows a:
A perifollicular non-caseating granuloma is characteristic.

Lower extremities are the classic site.

Erythema induratum of Bazin is best described as:
It is a lobular panniculitis combined with vasculitis.
Erythema induratum of Bazin characteristically involves the:
Posterior leg is the classic site, unlike erythema nodosum.
Unlike erythema nodosum, EI of Bazin heals with scarring.
Compared to erythema induratum of Bazin, erythema nodosum characteristically affects the:
Erythema nodosum classically involves the anterior leg (shins).
Unlike erythema induratum of Bazin, erythema nodosum heals:
Erythema nodosum heals without scarring, distinguishing it from EI of Bazin.
Swimming pool granuloma is also known as:
It is also called fish tank granuloma.
Swimming pool granuloma is caused by:
M. marinum is the causative organism.
The classic history in swimming pool granuloma involves occupational exposure to:
Contact with contaminated fresh or salt water is the classic exposure.
The characteristic clinical feature of swimming pool granuloma is:
Nodular lymphangitis is the hallmark presentation.
Nodular lymphangitis in swimming pool granuloma is described as suppurative nodules distributed along the:
The suppurative nodules track along the extremity's lymphatics.
The treatment of choice for swimming pool granuloma is:
Minocycline is the treatment of choice.

Lupus vulgaris is not part of the nodular-lymphangitis differential; sporotrichosis, nocardiosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, and tularemia are.
The pathogenesis of Buruli ulcer is best described as:
A bacterial toxin drives tissue necrosis in Buruli ulcer.
The toxin responsible for tissue necrosis in Buruli ulcer is called:

Painful ulcer with a punched-out edge
Painless ulcer with an undermined edge

Rifampicin combined with clarithromycin is first-line therapy.

Rifampicin plus injectable streptomycin for 8 weeks is the alternative regimen.
Skin viral infections are grouped into DNA-virus families including herpesvirus, poxvirus, HPV, enterovirus, and:

Herpesviruses establish latency, allowing lifelong persistent/recurrent infection.

Fever blister / cold sore / herpes labialis

Herpetic gingivostomatitis classically presents in a child with:

The erosions are covered by a membrane.
Herpetic whitlow involves infection of the:

Dentists are at particular risk from direct contact with infected oral secretions.

Rhinovirus is an RNA virus and is not part of this classification.

Latency in host tissue (e.g., ganglia) allows lifelong persistence and reactivation.
Eczema herpeticum is also known as:

Darier's disease is a listed association for eczema herpeticum.

Flaccid bullae with a varnish-like crust

Hemorrhagic crusting covers the punched-out erosions.

IV acyclovir is used for severe/disseminated disease.
The most common trigger for erythema multiforme is:

Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus produces:

Dew drop on a rose petal

Dermatomal burning pain precedes the visible rash.

PHN is highlighted as the most disabling complication.

Acyclovir 800 mg is given 5 times/day for 7 days.

Valacyclovir 1 g is given 3 times/day for 7 days.

Erythema infectiosum is also known as:

In "balanoposthitis," "posthitis" refers to inflammation of the:

Tinea involving the beard area is termed:

Tinea involving the palms is termed:

"Tinea incognito" refers to tinea that has become:

Itraconazole is the standard chromoblastomycosis treatment.

Mycetoma caused by bacteria is termed:

Actinomadura madurae, Nocardia brasiliensis, Streptomyces sp.

The most common site for mycetoma is the:

Pale/cream/white granules in mycetoma point to:

Scabies is classified as a "water-washed disease," linking it to:

Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis is the scabies mite.

Fomite transmission is a recognized route alongside direct contact.
The incubation period for a first scabies infestation is:
A first infestation takes about 4 weeks before symptoms appear.
The incubation period on reinfestation is much shorter, at:
Prior sensitization means reinfestation triggers symptoms almost immediately.
The pruritus of scabies is classically:
Nocturnal itching reflects the mite's nighttime activity.

The itch is an immune hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, not direct damage.
A useful history clue in diagnosing scabies is:
Scabies commonly clusters among close contacts and family members.
The lesion specific to scabies, described as wavy greyish-white tunnels, is the:
Burrows are the pathognomonic scabies lesion.
Burrows in scabies are found at which level of the skin?
The mite tunnels within the stratum corneum.

The distribution pattern of scabies lesions is called the:

2 anterior and 2 posterior pairs of legs

Topical imiquimod for anogenital warts is applied:
A thrice-weekly application schedule is standard.
Imiquimod treatment for anogenital warts may continue for up to:
Treatment courses can extend up to 16 weeks.
The treatment of choice for anogenital warts in pregnancy is:
Cryotherapy is preferred in pregnancy given the safety profile of the alternatives.
Cryotherapy for warts uses liquid nitrogen at a temperature of approximately:
Liquid nitrogen is applied at about -196°C.
Direct tissue freezing destroys the wart.
Besides cryotherapy, another option safe for use in pregnancy is trichloroacetic acid at what concentration?
70-80% concentration is standard for trichloroacetic acid wart treatment.
Trichloroacetic acid's mechanism of action is:
TCA works by chemically coagulating wart tissue protein.
Giant Condyloma, also known as the Buschke-Löwenstein tumour, is treated with:
Given its size and locally aggressive nature, surgical excision is required.
Genital discharge disease is seen in urethritis and:
These are the two syndromes grouped under genital discharge disease.
Urethritis is defined as inflammation of the urethra leading to:
Discharge is the defining clinical output of urethritis.
N. gonorrhoeae is the causative organism of gonococcal urethritis.
The incubation period for gonococcal urethritis is:
Gonococcal urethritis has a shorter incubation than nongonococcal urethritis.
The most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis is:
Chlamydia trachomatis D-K serovar is the leading NGU cause.
Besides Chlamydia, nongonococcal urethritis can also be caused by Ureaplasma urealyticum and:
Mycoplasma genitalium is another recognized NGU cause.
T. vaginalis is a recognized cause of NGU in addition to vaginal discharge.
The incubation period for nongonococcal urethritis is:
NGU has a longer incubation period than gonococcal urethritis.
Constitutional symptoms are typically present in:
Gonococcal urethritis more often produces systemic constitutional symptoms.
Dysuria tends to be severe in gonococcal urethritis and ___ in nongonococcal urethritis:
NGU dysuria is more variable in intensity compared to gonococcal urethritis.
Discharge in gonococcal urethritis is classically described as profuse and:
Profuse purulent discharge is characteristic of gonococcal urethritis.
Discharge in nongonococcal urethritis is classically described as scanty and:
Scanty mucoid discharge is characteristic of NGU.
Besides causing urethritis, Trichomonas vaginalis is also a recognized cause of:
T. vaginalis is a classic cause of vaginal discharge as well.
How many out of 3 criteria are needed to diagnose urethritis?
Just 1 of the 3 diagnostic criteria being positive is sufficient.
Visibly abnormal urethral discharge satisfying the diagnostic criteria may be mucoid, purulent, or:
Mucopurulent discharge is the third accepted discharge type.
On Gram stain of a urethral swab, urethritis is diagnosed with how many WBCs per oil immersion field?
2 or more WBCs per oil immersion field meets the criterion.
On first void urine analysis, urethritis is diagnosed with how many WBCs per high power field?
10 or more WBCs per high power field meets this criterion.
On Gram stain, gonococcal urethritis shows gram-negative diplococci located:
In clusters on the slide surface
Intracellular gram-negative diplococci are diagnostic of gonococcal urethritis.
On Gram stain, nongonococcal urethritis shows:
The absence of intracellular organisms helps distinguish NGU from gonococcal urethritis.
The selective culture medium for gonococci is:
Modified Thayer-Martin medium selectively grows gonococci.
In modified Thayer-Martin medium, vancomycin inhibits:
In modified Thayer-Martin medium, colistin inhibits:
Colistin suppresses competing gram-negative flora (other than gonococci).
In modified Thayer-Martin medium, nystatin inhibits:
Nystatin prevents fungal overgrowth in the culture.
In modified Thayer-Martin medium, trimethoprim inhibits:
Trimethoprim specifically suppresses swarming Proteus species.
The sample used for NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) in urethritis is:
First void urine is the preferred NAAT sample.
The CDC 2021 treatment for gonococcal urethritis centers on:
IM ceftriaxone as a single stat dose is the CDC 2021 mainstay.
For a patient under 150 kg, the ceftriaxone dose for gonococcal urethritis is:
500 mg IM is the standard dose for patients under 150 kg.
For a patient over 150 kg, the ceftriaxone dose for gonococcal urethritis is:
A higher 1 g IM dose is used for patients over 150 kg.
In treating gonococcal urethritis, doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days is added only if:
Chlamydial infection is not ruled out
Doxycycline covers possible co-infection with Chlamydia.
Nongonococcal urethritis can be treated with a single stat dose of:
A single 1g azithromycin dose is one first-line NGU option.
Alternatively, nongonococcal urethritis can be treated with doxycycline 100 mg BD for:
A 7-day doxycycline course is the alternative NGU regimen.
The route of administration for ceftriaxone in gonococcal urethritis treatment is:
Ceftriaxone for this indication is given IM.
The treatment guideline referenced for this urethritis regimen is from:
These specific regimens follow CDC 2021 guidance.
Vaginal discharge syndrome includes candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis, and:
Trichomoniasis is the third component of vaginal discharge syndrome.
Candida albicans is the classic vaginal candidiasis organism.
The vaginal discharge in candidiasis is classically described as:
Curdy white ("cottage cheese") discharge is characteristic of candidiasis.
The treatment for vaginal candidiasis is:
Fluconazole is the standard antifungal treatment.
Which agar is used to differentiate species of Candida?
Chrom agar's color reactions help distinguish Candida species.
Trichomonas vaginalis is the causative protozoan.
Trichomonas vaginalis is best classified as an:
T. vaginalis is an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan.
The vaginal discharge in trichomoniasis is classically described as greenish-yellow and:
Frothy, greenish-yellow discharge is characteristic of trichomoniasis.
The cervix in trichomoniasis shows a characteristic appearance called:
"Strawberry cervix" describes the punctate hemorrhagic cervical appearance.
Punctate hemorrhages give the cervix its "strawberry" speckled look.
The treatment for trichomoniasis is metronidazole, given at what dose and duration?
500 mg twice daily for 7 days is the standard trichomoniasis regimen described here.
Bacterial vaginosis is characterized by alterations in the:
A shift in the normal vaginal bacterial population defines BV.
Loss of protective Lactobacillus is central to BV pathogenesis.
Decreased Lactobacillus leads to decreased lactic acid and a vaginal pH:
Reduced lactic acid raises vaginal pH above 4.5.
Which anaerobic organisms characteristically increase in bacterial vaginosis?
These three anaerobes overgrow as Lactobacillus declines.
The diagnostic criteria for bacterial vaginosis are known as:
Amsel's criteria are the standard clinical diagnostic tool for BV.
How many of the 4 Amsel's criteria findings must be positive to diagnose bacterial vaginosis?
3 out of 4 positive findings confirms the diagnosis.
The vaginal discharge in bacterial vaginosis is described as homogenous, white, and:
An adherent quality distinguishes BV discharge.
The vaginal pH threshold used in Amsel's criteria is:
A pH above 4.5 is one of the four Amsel criteria.
The whiff/amine test becomes positive when vaginal discharge mixed with KOH produces a:
A fishy odor on KOH addition is a positive whiff test.
This fishy odor in the whiff test results from the release of:
