The clinical sign where a cutaneous neurofibroma can be pushed inward with finger pressure is called:
Button hole sign describes invagination of the neurofibroma on pressure.
A plexiform neurofibroma is typically present:
Plexiform neurofibromas, unlike cutaneous neurofibromas, have congenital onset.
On palpation, a plexiform neurofibroma classically feels like:
The multi-fascicular plexiform neurofibroma gives a 'bag of worms' feel, the same descriptor used for a varicocele.
A 'bag of worms' feel on scrotal examination, due to a dilated pampiniform venous plexus, describes a:
Varicocele shares the 'bag of worms' descriptor with plexiform neurofibroma, but the underlying structure differs.
For diagnosis of NF-1, café au lait macules must number at least:
≥6 café au lait macules is a core NF-1 diagnostic criterion.
The minimum size of a café au lait macule counted toward NF-1 diagnosis in a postpubertal patient is:
Postpubertal cutoff is >15 mm (versus >5 mm prepubertally).
Hyperpigmented freckling in the axilla and groin in NF-1 is termed:
Crowe's sign (skin fold freckling) is pathognomonic of NF-1.
Lisch nodules are hamartomas of the iris, seen in NF-1.
Lisch nodules are best visualized using:
Slit lamp exam is used to detect these small iris hamartomas.
An NF-1 patient with an optic nerve/optic pathway glioma classically presents with:
Optic pathway gliomas in NF-1 present with proptosis.
Tuberous Sclerosis Complex is also known as:
Bourneville disease is the eponym for TSC.
TSC is inherited in which pattern?
The TSC-1 gene is on chromosome 9 and encodes:
Hamartin is the TSC-1 gene product.
The TSC-2 gene, on chromosome 16, encodes:
Tuberin is the TSC-2 protein, distinct from TSC-1's hamartin.
The mnemonic 'EPILOIA' for Vogt's triad in TSC stands for epilepsy, low IQ, and:
EPILOIA = EPIlepsy, Low IQ, Adenoma sebaceum.
Vogt's triad in TSC consists of epilepsy, adenoma sebaceum, and:
Low intelligence is the third component alongside epilepsy and adenoma sebaceum.
Which is the earliest skin lesion to appear in Tuberous Sclerosis?
Ash leaf macules are the earliest cutaneous sign of TSC.
Ash leaf macules are best described as:
They are hypopigmented and lanceolate (oval at one end, pointed at the other).
Ash leaf macules are best diagnosed using:
A Wood's lamp accentuates hypopigmented macules for diagnosis.
Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibroma) classically presents as:
Symmetric reddish-brown papules on malar area, nasolabial fold, and nose
A leathery plaque over the lumbosacral spine
Adenoma sebaceum has this classic distribution and appearance, characteristic of TSC.
A shagreen patch is located in which region?
Shagreen patches classically occur over the lumbosacral spine.
A shagreen patch is histologically composed of:
Shagreen patches are collagenomas — collagen-rich leathery plaques.
Periungual fibromas in TSC, also called Koenen's tumours, typically have their onset at:
Koenen's tumours (periungual fibromas) typically appear at puberty.
Which TSC skin lesion is most useful for making an EARLY diagnosis in infancy, before adenoma sebaceum or periungual fibromas appear?
Since ash leaf macules are the earliest lesion, they aid early diagnosis before the other major skin signs emerge.
Confetti macules, a minor skin manifestation of TSC, are:
Confetti macules are small hypopigmented spots, a minor TSC skin criterion.
Which minor manifestation of TSC affects the dental enamel?
Dental enamel pits are a recognized minor TSC feature.
A gingival lesion seen as a minor manifestation of TSC is:
Gingival fibromas are a minor TSC diagnostic feature.
The renal lesion characteristic of Tuberous Sclerosis is:
Renal angiomyolipoma is the classic TSC kidney finding.
The pulmonary manifestation of TSC is called:
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is the characteristic TSC lung lesion.
The cardiac tumor associated with TSC is:
Cardiac rhabdomyoma is the classic TSC heart lesion, often detected prenatally.
The retinal finding in TSC is:
Retinal hamartomas are the characteristic TSC eye/retina finding.
SEGA, a CNS manifestation of TSC, stands for:
SEGA = Subependymal Giant cell Astrocytoma, arising from subependymal nodules in TSC.
Besides SEGA, the other CNS lesions seen in TSC include cortical tubers and:
Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules, along with SEGA, form the CNS triad of TSC.
Sturge-Weber Syndrome is also known as:
Encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis is the synonym for Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Unlike NF and TSC, Sturge-Weber Syndrome has which inheritance pattern?
Sturge-Weber occurs sporadically, unlike the autosomal dominant NF and TSC.
The classic triad of Sturge-Weber Syndrome affects CNS, eye, and:
CNS (epilepsy), eye (glaucoma), and skin (port-wine stain) form the Sturge-Weber triad.
The ocular manifestation of Sturge-Weber Syndrome is:
Glaucoma is the classic eye finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome.
The pathology underlying a facial port-wine stain is a:
Port-wine stains are low-flow capillary malformations.
A facial port-wine stain in Sturge-Weber syndrome is present:
At birth, and is unilateral and permanent
It is present at birth, typically unilateral, and persists permanently.
Over time, the color of a port-wine stain typically evolves from pink-red to:
With age, port-wine stains darken from pink-red toward purplish.
The treatment of choice for a facial port-wine stain is:
Pulsed dye laser targets the vascular malformation and is the standard treatment.
The term 'ichthyosis' refers to scaling that resembles:
'Ichthy' derives from the Greek for fish, describing the scale appearance.
A key feature distinguishing ichthyosis from eczema is that ichthyosis shows:
Ichthyosis is a disorder of keratinization without an inflammatory component.
Which of these is a CONGENITAL cause of ichthyosis rather than an acquired one?
X-linked recessive ichthyosis is congenital; the others are acquired causes.
Which drug is associated with ACQUIRED ichthyosis?
Nicotinic acid, along with clofazimine and statins, can cause acquired ichthyosis.
Ichthyosis vulgaris typically has its onset at:
Ichthyosis vulgaris classically appears between 3 and 12 months of age.
The inheritance pattern of ichthyosis vulgaris is:
The defective protein in ichthyosis vulgaris is:
A filaggrin defect underlies ichthyosis vulgaris.
In ichthyosis vulgaris, which sites are characteristically SPARED?
Ichthyosis vulgaris spares the face and flexural areas.
X-linked ichthyosis has its onset at:
X-linked ichthyosis appears earlier than ichthyosis vulgaris, before 3 months.
The enzyme defect in X-linked ichthyosis is:
Steroid sulfatase deficiency causes X-linked ichthyosis.
In X-linked ichthyosis, the enzyme defect leads to accumulation of:
Steroid sulfatase normally converts cholesterol sulfate to cholesterol; its deficiency causes cholesterol sulfate to accumulate.
Which of these is an association of X-linked ichthyosis?
Keratosis pilaris (keratin accumulation within hair follicles) and hyperlinear palms are X-linked ichthyosis associations.
Lamellar ichthyosis, unlike ichthyosis vulgaris, is present at birth.
The inheritance pattern of lamellar ichthyosis is:
The enzyme defect in lamellar ichthyosis is:
Epidermal transglutaminase-1 deficiency underlies lamellar ichthyosis.
Lamellar ichthyosis is also known by the synonym:
Ichthyosis nigra is the synonym reflecting the dark, brown-black scales.
At birth, a neonate with lamellar ichthyosis is typically covered by a:
A translucent, parchment-like collodion membrane covers the neonate at birth, evolving into scales over weeks.
In lamellar ichthyosis, the palms and soles are:
Unlike the trunk, palms and soles are spared in lamellar ichthyosis.
Ectropion in lamellar ichthyosis refers to:
Outward turning of the eyelid margin
Ectropion is eyelid margin eversion, seen in lamellar ichthyosis.
Eclabium in lamellar ichthyosis refers to:
Eclabium is outward eversion of the lip margin.
A defect in epidermal transglutaminase-3 (a different enzyme from transglutaminase-1) is classically associated with:
Transglutaminase-3 is the autoantigen in dermatitis herpetiformis, distinct from transglutaminase-1 in lamellar ichthyosis.
The systemic treatment used specifically for lamellar ichthyosis is:
Acitretin, an oral retinoid, is used for lamellar ichthyosis, in addition to topical emollients for general ichthyosis care.
Incontinentia Pigmenti is best described as a genetic disease affecting the skin, teeth, eyes, and:
Incontinentia Pigmenti is a genetic ectodermal disease involving skin, teeth, eyes, and lens.
The inheritance pattern of Incontinentia Pigmenti is:
Incontinentia Pigmenti is X-linked dominant, typically affecting females (often lethal in males).
The characteristic skin lesion distribution in Incontinentia Pigmenti follows:
Blaschko lines, reflecting embryologic cell migration, define the distribution pattern.
In Incontinentia Pigmenti, the scalp shows which Blaschko line pattern?
A spiralled pattern is seen on the scalp.
A V-shaped Blaschko pattern in Incontinentia Pigmenti is seen over the:
The V-shaped pattern occurs over the upper spine.
An S-shaped Blaschko pattern in Incontinentia Pigmenti is characteristically seen on the:
The abdomen shows an S-shaped pattern along Blaschko lines.
On the lower limbs, the Blaschko line pattern in Incontinentia Pigmenti is:
A perpendicular pattern is characteristic of the lower limbs.
The FIRST stage of skin involvement in Incontinentia Pigmenti is the:
Stage I is vesicular, with vesicles arranged along Blaschko lines.
In Stage II of Incontinentia Pigmenti, the vesicles are replaced by lesions that are:
Verrucous, with a rough uneven surface
Stage II is verrucous, characterized by a rough, uneven surface replacing the vesicles.
Stage III of Incontinentia Pigmenti is characterized by:
Stage III shows hyperpigmented lesions along the prior distribution.
The final (fourth) stage of Incontinentia Pigmenti skin involvement is:
Stage IV is hypopigmentation, the last of the four sequential stages.
The correct chronological order of skin stages in Incontinentia Pigmenti is:
The stages progress in this fixed sequence: vesicular, verrucous, hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation.
The ocular manifestation of Incontinentia Pigmenti is:
An avascular peripheral retina is the characteristic ocular finding.
The avascular peripheral retina in Incontinentia Pigmenti is best visualized using:
FFA demonstrates the avascular retinal periphery in Incontinentia Pigmenti.
Xeroderma Pigmentosum is best defined as:
An inherited DNA repair disorder causing UV hypersensitivity
XP is a DNA repair defect leading to cellular hypersensitivity to UV radiation.
The inheritance pattern of Xeroderma Pigmentosum is:
The specific DNA repair pathway defective in XP is:
NER is the pathway defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum.
In XP, defective NER leads to accumulation of damaged DNA, which causes:
Immediate cell death of all keratinocytes
Accumulated DNA damage causes genomic instability, driving carcinogenesis in XP.
A cutaneous feature of XP is sunburn that occurs with:
XP patients sunburn even on minimal sun exposure, reflecting their UV hypersensitivity.
In XP, freckling occurs due to:
Normal melanocyte number with increased activity
Decreased melanocyte number with increased activity
XP freckles show a normal number of melanocytes but increased melanocyte activity.
The most common skin malignancy associated with XP is:
Basal cell carcinoma is highlighted as the characteristic skin carcinoma in XP.
Continuous sunlight exposure in XP patients leads to photoaging and eventually:
Progressive photoaging in XP culminates in xeroderma, or dry skin.
Besides photophobia, a symptom of ocular involvement in XP, which CNS features may occur systemically in XP?
XP can have systemic CNS involvement with mental retardation and ataxia.
Besides skin cancers, XP patients are also predisposed to which systemic malignancies?
Hematological malignancies are a recognized systemic carcinoma risk in XP.
The primary preventive treatment strategy in XP is:
Since UV exposure drives the pathology, photoprotection with sunscreen is central to XP management.
Retinoids are used in XP to prevent malignancy because they:
Retinoids act by modulating keratinocyte differentiation, helping reduce malignancy risk.
Histamine-mediated emergencies are classically driven by which hypersensitivity reaction?
Type I (IgE-mediated, immediate) hypersensitivity underlies histamine-mediated emergencies.
The chief cell responsible for releasing histamine in these reactions is the:
Mast cells are the primary histamine-releasing effector cell.
Which immunoglobulin mediates the Type I hypersensitivity reaction seen in histamine-related disorders?
IgE cross-linking on mast cells triggers degranulation and histamine release.
The primary chemical mediator in this group of disorders is:
Histamine is the defining mediator that gives this disorder group its name.
The characteristic skin lesion of urticaria is the:
A wheal (itchy, edematous plaque) is the defining lesion of urticaria.
Angioedema differs from urticaria primarily because its swelling is:
Angioedema classically presents as non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling, unlike the itchy wheals of urticaria.
The fluid accumulation in angioedema occurs due to:
Increased vascular permeability drives fluid accumulation in the affected tissue.
Angioedema occurs at which tissue level?
Angioedema involves the deeper subcutaneous tissue or submucosa, unlike the superficial dermal edema of urticaria.
Angioedema characteristically affects the lips and eyelids because these sites have:
Loose, scanty connective tissue at these sites allows fluid to accumulate readily.
Anaphylaxis is acute, life-threatening, and involves multiple organ systems simultaneously.
In anaphylaxis, the respiratory system manifestation is:
Bronchospasm is the classic respiratory finding in anaphylaxis.
In anaphylaxis, the cardiovascular manifestation is:
Hypotension, due to vasodilation and increased permeability, is the classic CVS finding in anaphylaxis.
In anaphylaxis, the GIT manifestation is:
Abdominal pain is a recognized GIT feature of anaphylaxis.
Which skin findings can be seen in anaphylaxis?
Anaphylaxis's skin involvement includes both urticaria and angioedema.
A wheal is best described as a pruritic, elevated, edematous plaque that is:
Wheals are transient lesions, typically resolving within hours.
A wheal is characterized by central pallor surrounded by:
Central pallor with peripheral erythema is the classic wheal appearance.
Stroking normal skin with a blunt object
Dermographism is a bedside test performed by stroking normal skin with a blunt object.
An exaggerated wheal and flare response
The stroked area develops an exaggerated wheal-flare response in a positive test.
Urticaria is classified as ACUTE if its duration is:
Acute urticaria is defined as lasting less than 6 weeks.
Urticaria is classified as CHRONIC if it persists for:
Chronic urticaria is defined by duration beyond 6 weeks.
Chronic urticaria with an identifiable exogenous trigger is classified as:
Presence of an exogenous trigger defines the inducible subtype of chronic urticaria.
Chronic urticaria WITHOUT an identifiable exogenous trigger is classified as:
Absence of an exogenous trigger defines chronic spontaneous urticaria.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria can be further subdivided into idiopathic and:
Autoimmune and idiopathic are the two spontaneous urticaria subtypes.
Cold urticaria is an inducible subtype triggered specifically by cold temperature.
Aquagenic urticaria is triggered by contact with water, regardless of temperature.
Solar urticaria is triggered by sunlight exposure.
Which of the following is a recognized FOOD trigger for acute urticaria?
Peanuts, seafood, and food additives are classic acute urticaria food triggers.
Which parasitic infection is associated with acute urticaria?
Giardiasis and amoebiasis are parasitic infections linked to acute urticaria.
Which viral infections are associated with acute urticaria?
Hepatitis B and infectious mononucleosis are the viral causes noted for acute urticaria.
Which drug class is a recognized trigger for acute urticaria?
NSAIDs are a classic drug trigger for acute urticaria.
Cholinergic urticaria is specifically triggered by exercise/physical exertion.
In cholinergic urticaria, the exercise trigger acts by raising:
Increased core body temperature from exertion is the proximate trigger.
In cholinergic urticaria, which glands are stimulated as part of the pathway?
Eccrine sweat glands, supplied by sympathetic cholinergic fibres, are stimulated.
Eccrine sweat glands in cholinergic urticaria are innervated by:
Despite being part of the sympathetic system, eccrine glands use cholinergic (acetylcholine) neurotransmission.
The neurotransmitter released that directly produces wheals in cholinergic urticaria is:
Acetylcholine release from sympathetic cholinergic fibres triggers the wheal response.
The characteristic wheal morphology in cholinergic urticaria is described as:
Cholinergic urticaria classically produces small, pinpoint, itchy wheals.
The first-line pharmacologic treatment for chronic spontaneous urticaria is:
2nd generation antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, fexofenadine) are first-line for chronic spontaneous urticaria.
Which of these is a 2nd generation antihistamine used in chronic urticaria?
Fexofenadine is a 2nd generation antihistamine; the others are older, sedating 1st generation agents.
The monoclonal antibody used in refractory chronic urticaria targets:
Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used in refractory chronic urticaria.
The monoclonal antibody omalizumab used in chronic urticaria is named:
Omalizumab is the anti-IgE agent used for chronic urticaria not controlled by antihistamines.
Which calcineurin inhibitor may be used in chronic urticaria treatment?
Cyclosporine, a calcineurin inhibitor, is used in refractory chronic urticaria.
A key side effect of cyclosporine when used for chronic urticaria is:
Hypertension and nephrotoxicity are the classic cyclosporine side effects to monitor.
Hereditary Angioedema is inherited in which pattern?
Hereditary Angioedema follows autosomal dominant inheritance.
The underlying molecular defect in Hereditary Angioedema is in:
A defect in C1 esterase inhibitor is the core abnormality in Hereditary Angioedema.
Normally, C1 esterase inhibitor inhibits all of the following EXCEPT:
C1 esterase inhibitor regulates the kallikrein system, complement system, and Factor 12 — not mast cell degranulation directly.
In Hereditary Angioedema, a defective C1 esterase inhibitor leads to unchecked activation of the complement system, resulting in:
Decreased C4 levels result from unchecked complement activation and serve as a screening test.
The screening laboratory test for Hereditary Angioedema relies on measuring:
Low C4 levels are used as the screening test for Hereditary Angioedema.
In Hereditary Angioedema, unchecked activation of the kallikrein system converts HMW kininogen into:
Bradykinin, not histamine, is the key mediator generated via the kallikrein pathway in HAE.
Bradykinin produces angioedema by increasing vascular permeability via:
Bradykinin acts through B2 receptors to increase vascular permeability.
Recurrent episodes of angioedema in HAE are classically precipitated by:
Minor trauma is the classic precipitant of HAE attacks.
HAE can involve the skin, oropharynx, respiratory system, and:
GIT involvement (causing abdominal pain) is part of the HAE clinical spectrum.
Unlike histamine-mediated angioedema, HAE lesions characteristically show:
Since histamine is not the mediator in HAE, wheals are absent.
A clinically important feature of HAE is that it is:
Cured by a single antihistamine dose
Because bradykinin, not histamine, drives HAE, antihistamines and steroids are ineffective.
Which of these is used to directly increase C1 esterase inhibitor levels in HAE treatment?
Fresh frozen plasma (along with recombinant C1 Est Inh and danazol) raises C1 esterase inhibitor levels.
Danazol is used in HAE treatment because it helps:
Danazol is one of the agents used to raise C1 esterase inhibitor levels.
Ecallantide and lanadelumab used in HAE treatment work as:
Ecallantide and lanadelumab directly inhibit kallikrein, blocking bradykinin generation.
Icatibant used in HAE treatment acts as a:
Icatibant blocks the B2 receptor, preventing bradykinin's vascular permeability effect.
Cutaneous Mastocytosis is also known by the synonym:
Urticaria pigmentosa is the classic synonym for cutaneous mastocytosis.
Cutaneous Mastocytosis is characterized by proliferation of:
Mast cell proliferation within skin lesions defines cutaneous mastocytosis.
Cutaneous Mastocytosis most commonly affects which age group?
Cutaneous mastocytosis is predominantly a childhood disease.
The typical skin lesions of cutaneous mastocytosis are:
Hyperpigmented lesions are the classic presentation of cutaneous mastocytosis.
The most common site for cutaneous mastocytosis lesions is the:
The trunk is the typical site of involvement.
The Darier sign is elicited by:
Stroking lesional skin with a blunt object
Darier sign involves mechanically stroking the lesion to trigger mast cell degranulation.
Erythema plus an urticarial halo, from histamine release, defines a positive Darier sign.
The mechanism behind the Darier sign is:
Mechanical stroking triggers mast cell degranulation and histamine release, producing the sign.
The 'Pseudo-Darier sign' differs from the true Darier sign in that it produces:
Transient induration and piloerection, without erythema/urticaria
Pseudo-Darier sign lacks the erythema/urticaria of the true sign, showing induration and piloerection instead.
The Pseudo-Darier sign is caused by hamartomatous proliferation of:
Dermal smooth muscle hamartomatous proliferation underlies the Pseudo-Darier sign.
The Pseudo-Darier sign is seen in which condition?
Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma, a distinct entity, produces the Pseudo-Darier sign.
On histopathology, mast cells in cutaneous mastocytosis show metachromatic granules on which stain?
Toluidine blue stain highlights the metachromatic granules of mast cells.
The stained tissue color differing from the dye's own color
The tissue failing to take up any stain
Metachromasia describes a color shift between the dye and the stained tissue, as with toluidine blue and mast cell granules.
The CD marker used to identify mast cells is:
CD-117 (c-KIT) is the immunohistochemical marker for mast cells.
The mast cell stabilizer used in the treatment of cutaneous mastocytosis is:
Ketotifen, a mast cell stabilizer, along with antihistamines, is used in mastocytosis treatment.
Fixed Drug Eruption occurs via which hypersensitivity mechanism?
Fixed Drug Eruption is a Type IV (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction.
In Fixed Drug Eruption pathogenesis, the first drug exposure leads to formation of:
Memory T cells form on first exposure and mediate the reaction on re-exposure.
On subsequent drug exposure in Fixed Drug Eruption, the immune response occurs:
At the same (fixed) site as before
At a completely new site each time
The hallmark of fixed drug eruption is recurrence at the same fixed site.
Which of these drugs is a recognized cause of Fixed Drug Eruption?
Cotrimoxazole, along with NSAIDs and tetracycline, is a classic cause of fixed drug eruption.
A characteristic site for Fixed Drug Eruption is the:
Mucocutaneous junctions like the lips and glans penis are classic sites, along with the limbs.
The classic skin lesion in Fixed Drug Eruption is a:
A well-demarcated circular dusky red plaque, with a dark centre and erythematous periphery, is classic.
On the FIRST episode of Fixed Drug Eruption, the rash typically appears after:
First-episode onset is delayed, 7–10 days after drug intake.
On DRUG RE-INTAKE, a Fixed Drug Eruption rash appears within:
Because memory T cells are already present, re-intake produces a much faster reaction (30 min–8 hr).
Fixed Drug Eruption lesions characteristically heal with:
Complete resolution with no residual change
Residual hyperpigmentation at the healed site is characteristic.
The first step in managing Fixed Drug Eruption is:
Withdrawal of the causative drug is the essential first step.
In severe cases of Fixed Drug Eruption, treatment may include:
Steroids are used for severe fixed drug eruption cases, in addition to stopping the drug.
Erythema Multiforme is best characterized as:
EM is an acute, self-limiting, immune-mediated cytotoxic dermatitis.
EM is self-limiting, distinguishing it from more severe drug reactions like TEN.
The single most common infectious cause of Erythema Multiforme is:
HSV-1 is the most common (m/c) infectious trigger for EM.
Besides HSV-1, which other infection is a recognized cause of Erythema Multiforme?
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is another documented infectious trigger for EM.
Which connective tissue disorder is associated with Erythema Multiforme?
SLE is listed as a connective tissue disorder etiology for EM.
Which neoplastic conditions are associated with Erythema Multiforme?
Leukemia and internal malignancy are recognized neoplastic associations of EM.
EM minor differs from EM major in that EM minor:
EM minor is mild without mucosal involvement, while EM major is severe with mucosal involvement.
The classic skin lesion of Erythema Multiforme is the:
The target (iris) lesion is the hallmark of EM.
The target lesion of EM has how many zones?
The target lesion has 3 concentric zones.
In the target lesion of EM, the CENTRE zone shows:
The centre of the target lesion shows dusky purpura.
In the target lesion of EM, the INTERMEDIATE zone shows:
The intermediate zone shows pale edema, between the dusky centre and erythematous periphery.
In the target lesion of EM, the PERIPHERAL zone shows:
The outermost (peripheral) zone of the target lesion shows erythema.
The typical distribution of Erythema Multiforme lesions is:
EM classically distributes over the distal extremities, palms, and soles, usually as multiple lesions.
When Erythema Multiforme is due to recurrent HSV-1 infection, the appropriate treatment is:
Treating the underlying recurrent HSV-1 infection with acyclovir addresses the cause of EM.
For Erythema Multiforme, systemic steroids are typically given as:
A short course of systemic steroids is used given the self-limiting nature of EM.
An acute, life-threatening, severe mucocutaneous drug reaction
SJS/TEN is acute, severe, and life-threatening, driven primarily by drugs.
What proportion of SJS/TEN cases are attributable to drugs?
Drugs account for ≥90% of SJS/TEN cases.
Which NSAID subgroup is specifically implicated in SJS/TEN?
The oxicam group of NSAIDs is the specific subgroup implicated.
Which antiepileptic drugs are recognized causes of SJS/TEN?
Lamotrigine, phenytoin, and carbamazepine are the classic antiepileptic causes.
Which antiretroviral drugs are associated with SJS/TEN?
Nevirapine and abacavir are specifically listed as antiretroviral causes of SJS/TEN.
Besides antiepileptics and antiretrovirals, which other drug is a well-known cause of SJS/TEN?
Allopurinol is a classic cause of SJS/TEN, along with NSAIDs, antiepileptics, sulfonamides, and antiretrovirals.
HLA-B*1502 predisposes to toxicity from which drug?
HLA-B*1502 is specifically linked to carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN.
HLA-B*5801 predisposes to toxicity from which drug?
HLA-B*5801 is linked to allopurinol-induced SJS/TEN.
The fundamental pathological process in epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) is:
Full-thickness keratinocyte necrosis leading to skin separation
Full-thickness keratinocyte necrosis and subsequent skin lysis define epidermal necrolysis.
Which cells are the key mediators producing granulysin in SJS/TEN pathogenesis?
CD8 T cells and NK cells
CD4 T cells and B cells
CD8 T cells and NK cells produce granulysin, driving keratinocyte necrosis.
Granulysin, the key cytolytic protein in SJS/TEN, is produced by:
CD8 T cells and NK cells
Granulysin is a cytolytic protein released by CD8 T cells and NK cells.
IL-15 contributes to SJS/TEN pathogenesis by:
Promoting and maintaining CD8 T cells and NK cells
IL-15 sustains the CD8 T cell and NK cell populations that drive keratinocyte necrosis.
In the Fas receptor pathway of SJS/TEN, keratinocyte necrosis is triggered when:
The causative drug binds the Fas receptor
Complement deposits on the basement membrane
The offending drug binds the Fas (death) receptor, directly triggering keratinocyte necrosis.
The Fas receptor is best classified as a:
Fas is a death receptor that, when engaged, triggers apoptotic/necrotic cell death.
By body surface area involvement, SJS is defined as:
Less than 10% BSA involvement defines SJS.
By body surface area involvement, SJS-TEN overlap is defined as:
10-30% BSA involvement defines the SJS-TEN overlap category.
By body surface area involvement, TEN is defined as:
More than 30% BSA involvement defines TEN.
Body surface area involvement in SJS/TEN is calculated using the:
Wallace chart alone without rule of 9
The rule of 9 (as in burns assessment) is used to calculate BSA involvement.
SJS/TEN skin lesions typically appear after drug intake within:
Onset is 1-4 weeks after starting the causative drug.
A common systemic symptom accompanying SJS/TEN onset is:
Fever is a systemic symptom seen with SJS/TEN.
The skin lesion in SJS/TEN is described as an atypical target lesion with how many zones (vs 3 in EM)?
SJS/TEN's atypical target lesion has 2 zones, distinguishing it from EM's classic 3-zone target lesion.
The typical distribution of SJS/TEN lesions is:
SJS/TEN favors the proximal extremities and trunk, unlike EM's distal/acral distribution.
The progression of skin lesions in SJS/TEN follows which sequence?
Diffuse erythema → bullae → sheet-like epidermal peeling
This progression (erythema, then bullae, then sheet-like necrolytic peeling) is characteristic of SJS/TEN.
The Pseudo-Nikolsky sign in SJS/TEN is elicited by:
Tangential pressure over the skin causing separation of upper from lower layers
Stroking lesional skin to produce a wheal
Tangential pressure causing layer separation defines a positive Pseudo-Nikolsky sign, reflecting keratinocyte necrosis.
Mucosal involvement in SJS/TEN characteristically shows:
Painful erosions with hemorrhagic crusts are characteristic mucosal findings in SJS/TEN.
When differentiating sheet-like epidermal peeling, normal mucosa (with decreased Dsg-1 concentration as the underlying pathology) suggests:
SSSS spares the mucosa, unlike TEN, and its pathology involves decreased desmoglein-1.
Hemorrhagic crusts on mucosa, in the setting of sheet-like epidermal peeling, points toward:
TEN characteristically involves the mucosa with hemorrhagic crusts, unlike SSSS.
Predict mortality as a severity-of-illness score in TEN
Diagnose the causative drug in TEN
Grade the depth of keratinocyte necrosis
SCORTEN is a prognostic score predicting mortality in TEN.
SCORTEN is first assessed within how many hours of presentation?
SCORTEN is first calculated within 24 hours of presentation, then repeated after 3 days.
After the initial SCORTEN assessment, it is repeated after:
SCORTEN is repeated after 3 days to reassess severity.
Which of these is a SCORTEN parameter?
Heart rate >120/min is one of the seven SCORTEN parameters.
A SCORTEN score of 5 corresponds to a predicted mortality of approximately:
A SCORTEN of 5 predicts roughly 90% mortality, the highest risk category.
Cyclosporine, used in SJS/TEN treatment, works as a:
Cyclosporine acts as a T cell inhibitor in SJS/TEN management.
IV immunoglobulin, used in SJS/TEN treatment, is thought to act as a:
IV immunoglobulin is proposed to work by blocking the Fas receptor, interrupting keratinocyte necrosis.
Flagellate, whip-like streaks of dermatitis are the classic bleomycin-induced skin finding.
Flagellate dermatitis from bleomycin is typically:
The dermatitis is diffuse and pruritic in distribution.
The typical distribution of bleomycin-induced flagellate dermatitis is:
Trunk and extremities are the characteristic sites of involvement.
Bleomycin-induced flagellate dermatitis characteristically heals with:
Residual hyperpigmentation is typical after the dermatitis heals.
The enzyme responsible for inactivating bleomycin is:
Hydrolase normally inactivates bleomycin, limiting its toxicity.
Bleomycin toxicity preferentially affects the skin and lung because hydrolase is deficient in:
Low hydrolase activity in skin and lung explains why these organs are particularly susceptible to bleomycin toxicity.
Hydrolase deficiency in the lung, in the context of bleomycin toxicity, leads to:
Pulmonary fibrosis is the lung complication linked to bleomycin's reduced inactivation there.
Serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation is best described as:
A whip-like streak on the trunk
This distinctive linear, snake-like hyperpigmentation follows the course of cutaneous veins.
Which chemotherapy agent is a recognized cause of serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation?
5-FU, along with cyclophosphamide, docetaxel, and doxorubicin, is a recognized cause.
Besides 5-FU, which other agents cause serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation?
Cyclophosphamide, docetaxel, and doxorubicin round out the list of IV chemotherapy causes.
The pathophysiologic sequence behind serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation begins with IV chemotherapy drugs causing:
Endothelial injury is the initiating step in the pathway.
Following endothelial injury from IV chemotherapy, the subsequent step leading to serpentine hyperpigmentation is:
Subclinical thrombophlebitis follows endothelial injury, producing the linear hyperpigmented streak.
Lupus Erythematosus is best described as:
A Type I hypersensitivity reaction only
LE is a multisystem autoimmune disorder.
The antibodies in LE are characteristically:
LE antibodies are non-organ-specific, targeting cell nuclear antigens broadly.
The target antigens of LE autoantibodies are:
LE antibodies target cell nuclear antigens (ANA and related specificities).
Which LE subtype is purely cutaneous?
CCLE is restricted to the skin, unlike SCLE (limited systemic) and SLE (widespread systemic).
The most common form of Chronic Cutaneous LE is:
DLE is the most common CCLE form.
The classic sites for Discoid LE are:
DLE classically affects the face, scalp, and ears.
The discoid plaque of DLE shows central atrophy and scarring with:
Peripheral hyperpigmentation surrounds the centrally atrophic, scarred discoid plaque.
DLE causes scarring alopecia on the scalp, unlike the non-scarring alopecia typical of SLE.
The Carpet Tack sign in DLE is seen when:
Adherent scales are removed, revealing a carpet-tack undersurface
The skin is stroked, producing a wheal
A Wood's lamp is applied to the lesion
Removing the adherent scale of DLE reveals keratotic plugs on its undersurface, resembling carpet tacks.
The Carpet Tack sign results from a process of adherent scales leading to:
Follicular plugging underlies the carpet-tack appearance seen on the scale's undersurface.
Which LE subtype is the MOST photosensitive?
SCLE is the most photosensitive of the LE variants.
Unlike DLE, the rash of SCLE is characteristically:
SCLE produces a non-scarring rash, in contrast to the scarring seen in DLE.
Which antibodies are classically associated with SCLE?
Anti-La and anti-Ro antibodies are associated with SCLE.
Which of these is a recognized clinical form of SCLE?
Annular/polycyclic is one of the two SCLE forms, along with papulosquamous/psoriasiform.
The papulosquamous form of SCLE resembles which other skin disease clinically?
The papulosquamous/psoriasiform SCLE variant clinically resembles psoriasis.
In SLE, the acute cutaneous LE skin rash is also known as:
The acute cutaneous LE rash is the classic malar rash.
The malar rash of acute cutaneous LE involves erythema of the malar area and:
The malar rash extends across the malar area and nasal bridge.
A key feature distinguishing the malar rash from other facial rashes is:
Sparing of the nasolabial folds is a characteristic distinguishing feature of the malar rash.
Besides the malar rash, SLE skin rash can also present as which other type?
SLE skin rash can be malar (acute) or discoid in morphology.
Oral ulcers in SLE are typically located on the:
SLE oral ulcers are characteristically found on the palate.
A key feature of SLE-associated oral ulcers is that they are:
Unlike many other oral ulcer causes, SLE oral ulcers are characteristically painless.
The most common type of alopecia seen in SLE is:
Non-scarring alopecia is the most common alopecia pattern in SLE.
Scarring alopecia in SLE occurs due to:
Discoid (DLE-type) lesions on the scalp in SLE cause scarring alopecia.
Lupus hair specifically affects the frontal hairline.
The texture of 'lupus hair' is best described as:
Lupus hair is fragile, unruly, and short in texture.
The clinical significance of 'lupus hair' is that it is associated with:
Lupus hair serves as a marker of active disease flare.
Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune disease affecting the skin and:
DM affects skeletal muscles (causing proximal myopathy) along with the skin.
The muscle involvement pattern in DM is best described as:
DM classically causes proximal muscle weakness (proximal myopathy).
Which skin finding is considered PATHOGNOMONIC of dermatomyositis?
Gottron's papules are specifically noted as pathognomonic for DM.
Gottron's papules are best described as:
Gottron's papules are violaceous and flat-topped, distinguishing them from the macular Gottron's sign.
Gottron's papules are classically located over the:
MCP and IP joints are the classic sites for Gottron's papules.
The heliotrope rash of DM is located at the:
Heliotrope rash affects the periorbital region, especially the upper eyelid.
Heliotrope rash is a violaceous macular erythema, unlike the papular Gottron's papules.
Gottron's SIGN, distinct from Gottron's papules, is best described as:
Violaceous macular erythema over joints/bony prominences
Gottron's sign is a macular erythema, complementing the papular Gottron's papules.
Besides the MCP/IP joints, Gottron's sign can also be seen over the:
Olecranon process, elbows, medial malleoli, patella
Gottron's sign involves multiple bony prominences: MCP/IP joints, olecranon, elbows, medial malleoli, and patella.
Hyperkeratotic fissuring at the tips and sides of digits
Painless subcutaneous nodules on the hand
Mechanic's hand describes hyperkeratotic, fissured skin at the digit tips and sides, resembling a manual laborer's hands.
'Mechanic's hand' in DM is specifically associated with which antibody?
Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with the mechanic's hand finding, part of the antisynthetase syndrome.
The 'V sign' in DM refers to violaceous macular erythema over the:
The V sign describes erythema in a V-shaped distribution over the anterior chest.
The 'Shawl sign' in DM refers to violaceous macular erythema over the:
The Shawl sign describes erythema draped over the upper back and shoulders, like a shawl.
The 'Holster sign' in DM refers to violaceous macular erythema over the:
The Holster sign describes erythema over the lateral upper thigh, resembling a gun holster's position.
Samitz sign describes the characteristic ragged cuticle seen in DM.
Which of these is a recognized nail finding in DM?
Nail fold capillary telangiectasia, along with periungual erythema and ragged cuticle, is a DM nail feature.
Scleroderma is classified into which two main forms?
Localised cutaneous form (morphea) and systemic sclerosis
Morphea (skin-restricted) and systemic sclerosis (multi-system) are the two main forms.
Morphea, the localised cutaneous form of scleroderma, is restricted to:
Morphea is restricted to the skin, unlike systemic sclerosis.
Early skin lesions of morphea are characteristically:
Early morphea lesions are violaceous and indurated (hard, fibrosed).
Late-stage morphea skin lesions characteristically appear:
Late morphea lesions evolve to an ivory-white color as fibrosis matures.
Linear morphea classically affects which site?
The frontoparietal region is the classic site for linear morphea.
Linear morphea of the scalp can cause scarring alopecia producing which characteristic appearance?
'En coup de sabre' (blow of sword) describes the linear scarring alopecia band from linear morphea.
Systemic sclerosis is classified into limited and diffuse cutaneous forms based on:
The limited vs diffuse classification of SS is based on the extent of skin thickening/involvement.
In Limited cutaneous SS, skin involvement is:
Distal and proximal to elbow/knee, and trunk
Limited cutaneous SS involves skin distal to the elbow/knee, plus the face.
In Diffuse cutaneous SS, skin involvement extends to:
Distal and proximal to elbow/knee, and trunk
Diffuse cutaneous SS involves both distal and proximal areas relative to elbow/knee, plus the trunk.
CREST syndrome is seen in which form of systemic sclerosis?
CREST syndrome is characteristically associated with limited cutaneous SS.
In the CREST acronym, 'C' stands for:
Calcinosis cutis is the 'C' in CREST.
In the CREST acronym, 'E' stands for:
Esophageal dysmotility is the 'E' in CREST.
In the CREST acronym, 'S' stands for:
Which of these is one of the three key pathogenic mechanisms in systemic sclerosis?
Vascular dysfunction is one of the three core pathogenic mechanisms, along with immune dysregulation and fibrosis.
Which cytokine is increased in SS, produced by fibroblasts and driving fibrosis?
Increased TGF-beta produced by fibroblasts drives the fibrotic process in SS.
In SS, hidebound or taut skin is characterized by:
Skin that cannot be pinched, due to thickening
Skin that pinches easily due to atrophy
Thickened, taut (hidebound) skin cannot be pinched up, unlike normal skin.
Perioral fibrosis causes radiating furrows and difficulty opening the mouth (microstomia).
The facial appearance in SS, with decreased wrinkles, is described as:
Mask-like (expressionless) facies results from reduced wrinkling due to skin thickening.
Mat-like telangiectasia in SS refers to:
Mat-like telangiectasia describes visibly dilated cutaneous blood vessels seen in SS.
Raynaud's phenomenon is best defined as:
Raynaud's phenomenon is episodic vasospasm of the digital arteries.
Raynaud's phenomenon is classically triggered by:
Cold and emotional stimuli are the classic triggers for Raynaud's phenomenon.
In Raynaud's phenomenon, the FIRST phase (pallor) results from:
Pallor is the initial phase, due to decreased perfusion from vasospasm.
In Raynaud's phenomenon, the SECOND phase (cyanosis) results from:
Cyanosis follows as the static blood becomes deoxygenated.
In Raynaud's phenomenon, the THIRD phase (rubor) results from:
Rubor represents reperfusion, as blood flow returns after the vasospastic episode resolves.
Correct order of the 3 phases of Raynaud's phenomenon is:
The classic sequence is pallor, then cyanosis, then rubor.
Chronic digital ischemia in SS can result in:
Digital ulcers, gangrene, and pitted scars are complications of chronic digital ischemia in SS.
'Salt and pepper' pigmentation in SS consists of:
Depigmented macules with perifollicular pigment retention
White depigmented macules combined with brown perifollicular pigment retention creates the salt-and-pepper pattern.
In 'salt and pepper' pigmentation, the 'pepper' component refers to:
The brown perifollicular retained pigment corresponds to the 'pepper' component.
Henoch-Schönlein Purpura is also known as:
Immune complex vasculitis of large vessels
HSP is synonymous with IgA vasculitis.
HSP is classified as which category of vasculitis?
HSP is a small vessel vasculitis.
The characteristic skin lesion of HSP is:
Palpable purpura is the hallmark skin lesion of HSP.
HSP skin lesions are typically distributed over the:
HSP classically affects the lower extremities.
In HSP, the platelet count is typically:
A normal platelet count helps distinguish HSP (a vasculitic, non-thrombocytopenic purpura) from thrombocytopenic causes of purpura.
Behçet's Disease is classified as which type of vasculitis?
Behçet's Disease is classified as a variable vessel vasculitis, as it can affect vessels of any size.
Recurrent oral ulcers in Behçet's Disease are characterized by a yellow necrotic base and:
Oral ulcers in Behçet's heal without scarring, unlike the genital ulcers.
Recurrent genital ulcers in Behçet's Disease occur at the scrotum and vulva, and characteristically:
Only occur once in a lifetime
Unlike oral ulcers, genital ulcers in Behçet's heal with scarring.
Which skin lesion, consisting of multiple red tender nodules on the anterior leg, is seen in Behçet's Disease?
Erythema nodosum, with tender nodules on the anterior shin, is a Behçet's skin finding.
Besides erythema nodosum, which other skin lesions occur in Behçet's Disease?
Discoid plaques and carpet tack scale
Papulopustular lesions and acneiform nodules are additional Behçet's skin findings.
The eye involvement in Behçet's Disease is typically:
Uveitis, either anterior or posterior, is the classic ocular finding in Behçet's Disease.
Stroking the skin with a blunt object
The pathergy test uses an intradermal saline injection or needle prick to the skin.
The Pathergy test reading is taken at:
The pathergy test reading is assessed 48 hours after the procedure.
A positive Pathergy test is defined by the development of:
A papule/pustule at the injection site
Formation of a papule or pustule at the test site constitutes a positive pathergy test, supporting a Behçet's diagnosis.
Reactive arthritis is best defined as:
Inflammatory arthritis secondary to a distant focus of infection
A primary autoimmune joint destruction disease
Arthritis due to direct joint infection
Degenerative joint disease from wear and tear
Reactive arthritis occurs secondary to infection at a site distant from the joints, not direct joint infection.
Which organisms cause ENTERICALLY acquired reactive arthritis?
Enteric pathogens like Shigella, Salmonella, and Campylobacter cause the enterically acquired form.
Sexually Acquired Reactive Arthritis (SARA) is caused by:
Chlamydia trachomatis, with a history of urethritis, causes SARA.
Circinate balanitis, a skin lesion of reactive arthritis, presents as:
Circinate balanitis is well-demarcated, painless, and circular in appearance.
Circinate balanitis is located on the:
Circinate balanitis specifically affects the glans penis.
Keratoderma blenorrhagicum, a skin lesion of reactive arthritis, presents as:
Keratoderma blenorrhagicum shows hyperkeratotic crusted papules, distinct from circinate balanitis's erosions.
Palms and soles are the classic sites for keratoderma blenorrhagicum.
The rheumatoid nodule of Rheumatoid Arthritis is characteristically:
A painless subcutaneous nodule at pressure sites
An ulcer with yellow necrotic base
Rheumatoid nodules are painless subcutaneous nodules occurring at pressure sites.
The presence of rheumatoid nodules in RA is significant because it indicates:
Rapid progression and increased severity of disease
Rheumatoid nodules signal more aggressive, severe disease and higher RA factor positivity.
Subcutaneous nodules in Acute Rheumatic Fever, compared to rheumatoid nodules, are:
Acute rheumatic fever nodules are smaller and shorter-lived than rheumatoid nodules, though both are painless.
Subcutaneous nodules in Acute Rheumatic Fever are associated with:
Erythema marginatum alone without carditis link
Subcutaneous nodules in ARF are associated with carditis.
Erythema marginatum, seen in Acute Rheumatic Fever, is best described as:
Non-pruritic pink macular erythema with central clearing
Erythema marginatum shows non-pruritic pink erythema with central clearing and outward-expanding borders.
The distribution of erythema marginatum in ARF is:
Trunk, with sparing of the face
Face, with sparing of the trunk
Erythema marginatum affects the trunk while sparing the face.
The border behavior of erythema marginatum lesions is described as:
The periphery of erythema marginatum lesions shows outward expansion, giving the annular appearance.
Hyperpigmented velvety plaques, typically at the axilla and neck, define Acanthosis Nigricans.
The most common cause of Acanthosis Nigricans is:
Obesity is the most common (m/c) cause of Acanthosis Nigricans.
When Acanthosis Nigricans occurs due to internal malignancy, it is considered a:
Malignancy-associated Acanthosis Nigricans is a paraneoplastic phenomenon.
In obesity-related Acanthosis Nigricans, the pathogenesis begins with:
Obesity raises circulating insulin, which drives the downstream pathway to Acanthosis Nigricans.
In the pathogenesis of obesity-related Acanthosis Nigricans, increased insulin stimulates:
Elevated insulin activates IGF signaling, which then drives keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation.
Hyperpigmented atrophic macules on the anterior leg define diabetic dermopathy.
Diabetic dermopathy is typically located on the:
The anterior leg is the classic site for diabetic dermopathy.
The clinical significance of diabetic dermopathy is that it serves as a marker for:
Diabetic dermopathy signals an increased likelihood of microvascular complications: nephropathy, neuropathy, retinopathy.
Necrobiosis specifically describes collagen degeneration, the basis of the 'necrobiotic disorders' group.
Granuloma annulare presents as an annular arrangement of:
Granuloma annulare shows papules arranged in an annular (ring-like) pattern.
Granuloma annulare is classically located on the:
The dorsum of the extremities is the classic site for granuloma annulare.
Granuloma annulare is associated with which systemic condition?
Diabetes mellitus is the systemic association for granuloma annulare.
When differentiating an annular plaque with central clearing, the presence of BOTH scaling and itching favors:
Tinea corporis shows both scaling and itching, unlike the asymptomatic, non-scaling granuloma annulare.
Granuloma annulare, unlike tinea corporis, is typically:
Granuloma annulare lacks both scaling and itching, distinguishing it from tinea corporis.
Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum presents as a:
A waxy-yellow atrophic plaque with surface telangiectasia is characteristic of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum.
The surface of a necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum plaque characteristically shows:
Surface telangiectasia (dilated blood vessels) is a hallmark surface feature.
The term 'lipoidica' in necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum refers to:
The fat content causing a waxy-yellow appearance
Lipid deposition in the dermis alone
'Lipoidica' reflects the fatty, waxy-yellow character of the plaque.
Sarcoidosis is best classified as a:
Sarcoidosis is a chronic granulomatous disease.
The acute form of sarcoidosis is also known as:
Löfgren's syndrome is the acute presentation of sarcoidosis.
In Löfgren's syndrome, the characteristic lung finding is:
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is the classic lung finding in acute sarcoidosis (Löfgren's syndrome).
The characteristic skin finding in Löfgren's syndrome is:
Erythema nodosum is the skin manifestation seen in acute sarcoidosis.
Erythema nodosum is pathologically a form of:
Erythema nodosum represents panniculitis, inflammation localized to subcutaneous fat.
Besides bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and erythema nodosum, Löfgren's syndrome also features:
Fever and arthralgia round out the classic Löfgren's syndrome triad-like presentation.
The chronic form of sarcoidosis is also known as:
Lupus pernio is the chronic form of cutaneous sarcoidosis.
Lupus pernio is considered the chronic, ___ lesion of sarcoidosis.
Lupus pernio is specifically described as the chronic specific lesion of sarcoidosis.
The characteristic lesion of lupus pernio is a:
A reddish violaceous plaque is characteristic of lupus pernio.
Lupus pernio classically affects which site?
The central face is the classic site for lupus pernio.
Lupus pernio is associated with which pulmonary finding?
Unlike the acute form's hilar lymphadenopathy, lupus pernio (chronic form) is associated with pulmonary fibrosis.
Besides pulmonary fibrosis, lupus pernio is associated with sarcoidosis of the:
Upper respiratory tract sarcoidosis is a recognized lupus pernio association.
A skeletal finding associated with lupus pernio is:
Bone cysts over the phalanges are a recognized association of lupus pernio.
Primary systemic amyloidosis is associated with:
Plasma-cell dyscrasias (e.g., multiple myeloma) are the key association of primary systemic amyloidosis.
The type of amyloid deposited in primary systemic amyloidosis is:
AL (amyloid light chain) type amyloid is deposited in primary systemic amyloidosis, reflecting its plasma-cell origin.
In primary systemic amyloidosis, amyloid deposition on skin blood vessels occurs preferentially in the:
The periorbital region is the characteristic site of vascular amyloid deposition.
Amyloid deposition on blood vessels leads to which vascular change?
Amyloid deposition weakens vessel walls, increasing their fragility.
Following minor trauma, the fragile amyloid-laden vessels in primary systemic amyloidosis rupture, producing:
Pinch purpura is the characteristic periorbital purpuric sign resulting from vessel fragility and trauma.
Pretibial myxedema is also known as:
Thyroid dermopathy is the synonym for pretibial myxedema.
The lesion in pretibial myxedema is characterized by:
Non-pitting edema is characteristic of pretibial myxedema, distinguishing it from other causes of leg edema.
Pretibial myxedema is located on the:
The anterior leg is the classic site for pretibial myxedema, similarly to diabetic dermopathy but with a different lesion type.
Pretibial myxedema is associated with which endocrine condition?
Graves disease (hyperthyroidism) is the classic association for pretibial myxedema.
'Xanthos' is Greek for yellow, describing the lesion's color.
In 'Xanthelasma palpebrarum,' the term 'palpebrarum' refers to the:
'Palpebrarum' refers to the eyelid margin, the site of the lesion.
Xanthelasma palpebrarum lesions are best described as:
Symmetric yellow plaques over the eyelids define xanthelasma palpebrarum.
Xanthelasma palpebrarum is associated with hyperlipidemia of which types?
Type 2 and Type 4 hyperlipidemia are specifically associated with xanthelasma.
Besides hyperlipidemia, xanthelasma palpebrarum is also associated with:
Cholestasis is another recognized association of xanthelasma palpebrarum.
An important clinical note about xanthelasma palpebrarum is that it:
Can occur even with a normal lipid profile
Xanthelasma can be present even when the lipid profile is normal, so it doesn't always signal dyslipidemia.
Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative spirochete of Lyme Disease.
The vector responsible for transmitting Lyme Disease is the:
The Ixodes tick transmits Borrelia burgdorferi, causing Lyme Disease.
The characteristic skin rash of Lyme Disease is known by the abbreviation:
ECM stands for Erythema Chronicum Migrans, the classic Lyme Disease rash.
In 'Erythema Chronicum Migrans,' the term 'chronicum' indicates that the lesion:
'Chronicum' specifically denotes the slow, gradual progression of the lesion.
In 'Erythema Chronicum Migrans,' the term 'migrans' indicates that the lesion:
Is confined to a fixed size
'Migrans' describes the outward migration/expansion of the rash.
The 'erythema' component of ECM refers to the lesion being:
'Erythema' simply denotes the redness of the lesion.
When comparing target lesions, Erythema Multiforme typically shows how many lesions?
EM classically produces multiple target lesions, unlike Lyme Disease's typically solitary lesion.
In Lyme Disease, the number of target lesions (ECM) is typically:
Lyme Disease classically produces a single target lesion (ECM) at the tick bite site.
The site of target lesions in Erythema Multiforme is:
Corresponds to the site of tick bite
EM's target lesions favor distal extremities, palms, and soles.
The site of the target lesion (ECM) in Lyme Disease:
Corresponds to the site of the tick bite
Is confined to palms and soles
Unlike EM, Lyme Disease's target lesion appears specifically at the tick bite location.
A key distinguishing feature between EM and Lyme disease target lesions is:
The number and site of lesions
Number of lesions (multiple vs single) and site (distal extremities/palms/soles vs tick bite location) are the key differentiators.
Phrynoderma is also known by the descriptive name:
'Toad skin' describes the rough, papular texture of phrynoderma.
The characteristic morphology of phrynoderma is:
Extensor surfaces like the elbows and knees are the classic phrynoderma sites.
Phrynoderma is associated with deficiency of:
Essential fatty acids and vitamin A
Essential fatty acid deficiency and vitamin A deficiency are the associations for phrynoderma.
In the term 'pellagra,' 'pella' means skin and 'agra' means:
'Agra' translates to rough, describing the characteristic skin texture in pellagra.
Pellagra is classically associated with diets based on:
Maize and jowar-based diets, low in niacin/tryptophan, are classically linked to pellagra.
A recognized aggravating factor for pellagra is:
Chronic alcoholism aggravates pellagra, likely via poor nutrition and impaired niacin metabolism.
The classic triad of pellagra consists of diarrhoea, dementia, and:
Photodermatitis (Casal's necklace), along with diarrhoea and dementia, forms the pellagra triad.
The photosensitive rash around the neck in pellagra is called:
Casal's necklace describes the characteristic photodermatitis distribution around the neck in pellagra.
If pellagra is left untreated, the disease can progress to:
Untreated pellagra can be fatal, following the progression of its clinical triad.
Acrodermatitis enteropathica follows which inheritance pattern?
The gene involved in acrodermatitis enteropathica is:
SLC-39A4 encodes a zinc transporter, and its mutation causes acrodermatitis enteropathica.
The underlying pathology of acrodermatitis enteropathica is:
Defective intestinal zinc absorption is the core pathological defect.
Acrodermatitis enteropathica classically presents at what age?
Symptoms classically emerge around 6 months of age, often correlating with weaning from breast milk.
The clinical triad of acrodermatitis enteropathica consists of dermatitis, diarrhoea, and:
Alopecia, along with acral/periorificial dermatitis and diarrhoea, completes the classic triad.
The dermatitis of acrodermatitis enteropathica is characteristically distributed:
Acral (hands/feet) and periorificial (around mouth, eyes, etc.) areas are classically affected.
The treatment for acrodermatitis enteropathica is:
Lifelong zinc supplementation corrects the underlying deficiency and controls the disease.
Scurvy is caused by deficiency of:
The characteristic skin finding in scurvy is:
Perifollicular purpura/hemorrhage is the classic skin finding in scurvy, reflecting impaired collagen synthesis and vessel fragility.
The characteristic hair finding in scurvy is:
Corkscrew hair, from abnormal keratin formation, is characteristic of scurvy.
'Corkscrew motility,' distinct from corkscrew hair, is a term associated with:
Corkscrew motility describes the movement pattern of Treponema pallidum, unrelated to the hair finding in scurvy.
Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency causes which skin finding related to sebaceous activity?
Nasolabial dyssebacea, from abnormal sebaceous gland activity, is a riboflavin deficiency skin finding.
Besides nasolabial dyssebacea, riboflavin deficiency also causes which dandruff-like skin condition?
Seborrheic dermatitis is a recognized skin manifestation of riboflavin deficiency.
Riboflavin deficiency affecting the oral cavity presents as:
Angular stomatitis/cheilitis is the oral cavity manifestation of riboflavin deficiency.
Riboflavin deficiency causes which tongue finding?
A magenta-coloured tongue is characteristic of riboflavin deficiency glossitis, distinct from B12's beefy-red tongue.
Riboflavin deficiency can cause which eye finding?
Corneal neovascularization is an eye finding associated with riboflavin deficiency.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes skin hyperpigmentation typically located on the:
Dorsal extremity hyperpigmentation is characteristic of vitamin B12 deficiency.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes glossitis with a tongue described as:
A beefy-red tongue is characteristic of B12 deficiency glossitis, distinct from riboflavin's magenta tongue.
The hair finding in vitamin B12 deficiency is:
Canities, or premature greying of hair, is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency.
A beefy-red GENITAL ulcer (distinct from B12's beefy-red tongue) is characteristic of which infection?
Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) presents with a beefy-red genital ulcer, a distinct entity from B12 deficiency's tongue finding.
Kwashiorkor skin lesions are described using which two terms?
Flaky paint and crazy pavement dermatoses
Discoid plaques and carpet tack scale
Flaky paint dermatoses and crazy pavement dermatoses describe the characteristic Kwashiorkor skin changes.
The hair lesion characteristic of Kwashiorkor is the:
The flag sign, an alternating pattern of hypopigmented and normal hair, is characteristic of Kwashiorkor.
An alternating pattern of hypopigmented and normal hair bands
Progressive greying from root to tip
Alternating bands of hypopigmented and normally pigmented hair, reflecting periods of malnutrition and adequate nutrition, create the flag sign.
In 'necrolytic migratory erythema,' the term 'necrolytic' refers to:
'Necrolytic' describes epidermal necrosis, the defining histologic feature.
Necrolytic migratory erythema lesions are described as plaques with:
Central clearing within the plaques is a characteristic feature.
Necrolytic migratory erythema classically affects the:
Periorificial areas and extremities are the classic sites for necrolytic migratory erythema.
Necrolytic migratory erythema is associated with which tumor?
Glucagonoma, a tumor of pancreatic alpha-cells, is the classic association.
Glucagonoma arises from which pancreatic cell type?
Glucagonoma originates from the glucagon-secreting alpha-cells of the pancreas.
In 'erythema gyratum repens,' the term 'gyratum' means:
'Gyratum' describes the coiled, whorled configuration of the bands.
In 'erythema gyratum repens,' the term 'repens' means:
'Repens' conveys the crawling, ever-shifting quality of the bands.
The lesion pattern of erythema gyratum repens is described as:
Concentric bands of scaling (wood grain pattern)
A wood-grain pattern of concentric scaling bands is the distinctive appearance.
Erythema gyratum repens typically affects the:
Proximal extremities and trunk are the classic sites for erythema gyratum repens.
Erythema gyratum repens is most classically associated with:
Bronchogenic (lung) carcinoma is the classic malignancy associated with erythema gyratum repens.
Trousseau syndrome is classically associated with:
Pancreatic carcinoma is the classic malignancy linked to Trousseau syndrome.
The Sign of Leser-Trélat is associated with:
GI adenocarcinoma is the classic malignancy association for the Sign of Leser-Trélat.
The Sign of Leser-Trélat presents as:
Rapid, multiple, sudden eruption of seborrheic keratosis
A sudden, rapid, multiple eruption of seborrheic keratoses defines the Sign of Leser-Trélat.
Seborrheic keratosis, the lesion type seen in Leser-Trélat sign, is best classified as a:
Seborrheic keratosis is a benign keratinocyte tumor, notable here for its sudden proliferation as a paraneoplastic marker.
Panniculitis is inflammation localized to the subcutaneous fat layer.
Inflammation of the connective tissue septae within subcutaneous fat is termed:
Septal panniculitis specifically involves the connective tissue septae.
Inflammation of the fat lobules (adipocytes) within subcutaneous fat is termed:
Lobular panniculitis specifically involves the adipocyte-containing lobules.
Erythema nodosum is best defined as:
A delayed hypersensitivity response to various antigens
Erythema nodosum represents a delayed (Type IV-like) hypersensitivity response.
The MOST COMMON cause of erythema nodosum is:
Idiopathic cases are the most common overall, even though infections are a well-known trigger.
Which infectious organism is a classic trigger for erythema nodosum?
Group A Streptococci, along with TB, are classic infectious triggers for erythema nodosum.
Which drugs are recognized triggers for erythema nodosum?
OCPs, sulfonamides, and iodides are the drug triggers listed for erythema nodosum.
Between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which is more strongly associated with erythema nodosum?
Crohn's disease shows a stronger association with erythema nodosum than ulcerative colitis.
Which multisystemic granulomatous disease is a trigger for erythema nodosum?
Sarcoidosis (as in acute Löfgren's syndrome) is a classic multisystem trigger for erythema nodosum.
Which vasculitic condition can trigger erythema nodosum?
Behçet's disease, a variable vessel vasculitis, is a recognized trigger for erythema nodosum.
Erythema nodosum most commonly affects which age group?
Children are the typical age group affected by erythema nodosum.
The characteristic lesion of erythema nodosum is described as:
Red, tender nodules are the hallmark lesion of erythema nodosum, distinguishing it from painless nodules like rheumatoid nodules.
Erythema nodosum lesions are typically located on the:
The anterior legs (shins) are the classic site for erythema nodosum nodules.
Unlike genital ulcers in Behçet's disease, erythema nodosum heals without scarring.
Septal panniculitis is the characteristic histopathological finding in erythema nodosum.
The symptomatic treatment for erythema nodosum pain is:
NSAIDs are used for symptomatic pain relief in erythema nodosum.
The common histopathological feature shared by neutrophilic dermatoses is:
Dense diffuse dermal neutrophilic infiltrates define this group of dermatoses.
Which two diseases are classified under neutrophilic dermatoses?
Sweet syndrome and Pyoderma gangrenosum are the two neutrophilic dermatoses discussed.
Sweet syndrome is also known as:
Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis is the full descriptive name for Sweet syndrome.
Which of these is a recognized trigger for Sweet syndrome?
Hematological malignancies, along with infections and pregnancy, are recognized Sweet syndrome triggers.
A constitutional symptom characteristic of Sweet syndrome is:
Fever is the classic constitutional symptom accompanying Sweet syndrome.
The onset of skin lesions in Sweet syndrome is typically:
Sweet syndrome lesions have an abrupt onset.
The morphology of Sweet syndrome lesions is:
Red, tender papules and plaques characterize Sweet syndrome lesions.
Sweet syndrome lesions are typically distributed over the:
Face, upper chest, and upper back are the classic sites for Sweet syndrome.
The treatment for Sweet syndrome is:
Systemic steroids are the treatment of choice for Sweet syndrome.
Pyoderma gangrenosum is considered a misnomer because:
It is not a bacterial infection
Despite its name suggesting infection ('pyoderma'), it is not a bacterial infection.
Which rheumatological condition is a recognized trigger for pyoderma gangrenosum?
Rheumatoid arthritis is a recognized trigger for pyoderma gangrenosum.
Which gastrointestinal conditions trigger pyoderma gangrenosum?
Inflammatory bowel disease (both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's) is a recognized trigger.
Which hematologic malignancy is a recognized trigger for pyoderma gangrenosum?
Leukemia is listed as a trigger for pyoderma gangrenosum.
The characteristic lesion in pyoderma gangrenosum is a(n):
An ulcer, with rapid progression, is the characteristic pyoderma gangrenosum lesion.
The edge of a pyoderma gangrenosum ulcer is characteristically:
An undermined edge is a hallmark feature of pyoderma gangrenosum ulcers.
The hue of a pyoderma gangrenosum ulcer border is typically:
A violaceous hue at the border is characteristic of pyoderma gangrenosum.
The treatment for pyoderma gangrenosum, given its immunological basis, is:
Systemic steroids are used since pyoderma gangrenosum is treated as an immunological condition, not an infection.
Lichen Nitidus is best classified as:
A chronic inflammatory disease of unknown etiology
Lichen Nitidus is a chronic inflammatory condition with an unknown cause.
The term 'nitidus' in Lichen Nitidus means:
'Nitidus' translates to shiny, describing the lesion's surface quality.
Lichen Nitidus most commonly affects which age group?
Children are the typical age group affected by Lichen Nitidus.
Asymptomatic shiny papules define the Lichen Nitidus lesion.
Which of these is a classic site for Lichen Nitidus?
The shaft of the penis, along with the forehead and extensor extremities, is a classic Lichen Nitidus site.
The appearance of new Lichen Nitidus lesions at sites of trauma is called:
Koebner's phenomenon describes new lesions arising at trauma sites, seen in Lichen Nitidus.
The classic histopathological appearance in Lichen Nitidus is described as:
The 'claw clutching ball' appearance, from elongated rete ridges surrounding lymphocytic infiltrate, is characteristic.
In the 'claw clutching ball' histopathology of Lichen Nitidus, the 'claw' refers to:
Elongated rete ridges form the 'claw' that surrounds the inflammatory infiltrate 'ball'.
In the 'claw clutching ball' histopathology of Lichen Nitidus, the 'ball' refers to:
The lymphocytic/inflammatory infiltrate forms the 'ball' clutched by the rete ridge 'claw'.
The natural course of Lichen Nitidus is typically:
Lichen Nitidus is usually self-resolving over time.
If Lichen Nitidus persists, treatment options include:
Topical steroids are used for persistent Lichen Nitidus cases.
The cause of Cutis Marmorata is:
A physiological vascular response to cold
A genetic disorder of connective tissue
Cutis Marmorata is a normal physiological vascular response to cold exposure.
Cutis Marmorata is typically seen in which age group?
Neonates are the classic age group affected by Cutis Marmorata.
The lesion pattern in Cutis Marmorata is described as:
Symmetric reticular (net-like) marbling defines the Cutis Marmorata appearance.
The management for Cutis Marmorata is:
Since it's a cold-induced physiological response, simply warming the child resolves Cutis Marmorata.
Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis is best described as:
LCH is a rare disorder of histiocyte (Langerhans cell) proliferation.
The MOST SPECIFIC immunohistochemistry marker for Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis is:
CD207 (Langerin) is specifically noted as the most specific marker for LCH.
Besides CD207, which other markers are used in diagnosing LCH?
S100 and CD1a are additional immunohistochemistry markers used for LCH.
The congenital form of LCH, presenting at birth and self-healing, is called:
Hashimoto-Pritzker disease is the congenital, self-healing form of LCH.
A key feature of Hashimoto-Pritzker disease is that it is:
Associated with hepatosplenomegaly in most cases
Self-healing is the defining characteristic of the congenital Hashimoto-Pritzker form.
LCH presenting before age 2 years is classified as:
Letterer-Siwe disease is the LCH form presenting before 2 years of age.
The clinical course of Letterer-Siwe disease is:
Letterer-Siwe disease follows an acute, disseminated clinical course.
In Letterer-Siwe disease, bone lesions occur in what percentage of patients?
Bone lesions occur in 80% of Letterer-Siwe disease patients.
In Letterer-Siwe disease, skin involvement resembles which other dermatologic condition?
Skin lesions in Letterer-Siwe disease resemble seborrheic dermatitis, notably at retroauricular and presternal sites.
In Letterer-Siwe disease, hepatosplenomegaly occurs in approximately what percentage of patients?
Hepatosplenomegaly occurs in about 30% of Letterer-Siwe disease patients.
LCH presenting before age 5 years, with calvarial defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos, is classified as:
Hand-Schüller-Christian disease presents before age 5 with this classic triad.
The classic clinical triad of Hand-Schüller-Christian disease includes calvarial defects, exophthalmos, and:
Diabetes insipidus, along with calvarial defects and exophthalmos, forms this classic triad.
LCH presenting before age 8 years, limited to a single osteolytic bone lesion, is classified as:
Eosinophilic granuloma is the LCH form presenting before age 8 with an osteolytic lesion.
The lesion in eosinophilic granuloma is best described as:
Eosinophilic granuloma produces osteolytic bone lesions.
Eosinophilic granuloma classically affects which site?
The temporoparietal region of the skull is the classic site for eosinophilic granuloma.
Mycosis Fungoides is a misnomer because:
It is not a fungal infection
It does not affect the skin
It does not involve T cells
Despite its fungal-sounding name, Mycosis Fungoides is not caused by a fungus.
Mycosis Fungoides/CTCL is classified as a type of:
Mycosis Fungoides is a form of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, specifically a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
Mycosis Fungoides is a tumour of which cell type?
CD4 T cells are the malignant cell type in Mycosis Fungoides.
The clinical course of Mycosis Fungoides is typically:
Mycosis Fungoides follows an indolent, slowly progressive course.
The FIRST stage of Mycosis Fungoides is the:
The patch stage is the earliest stage of Mycosis Fungoides.
The correct order of Mycosis Fungoides stages is:
This is the classic progression: patch, plaque, tumour, then erythroderma.
The erythroderma stage of Mycosis Fungoides is defined by redness and scaling involving what percentage of body surface area?
Erythroderma requires involvement of more than 90% of body surface area.
On histopathology, the malignant lymphocytes in Mycosis Fungoides show characteristic:
Cerebriform (brain-like convoluted) nuclei are characteristic of the malignant T-lymphocytes in Mycosis Fungoides.
Clusters of malignant lymphocytes within the epidermis in Mycosis Fungoides are called:
Pautrier microabscess is the characteristic epidermal collection of malignant lymphocytes in Mycosis Fungoides.
The migration of malignant lymphocytes into the epidermis in Mycosis Fungoides is termed:
Epidermotropism describes this characteristic migration pattern.
Topical treatment for Mycosis Fungoides includes:
Topical nitrogen mustards are used in Mycosis Fungoides treatment.
The systemic chemotherapy agent used in Mycosis Fungoides is:
Chlorambucil is the systemic chemotherapy agent specifically noted for Mycosis Fungoides.
For THIN plaques of Mycosis Fungoides, the phototherapy of choice is:
NB-UVB is used for thin plaques, while PUVA is reserved for thicker plaques.
For THICK plaques of Mycosis Fungoides, the phototherapy of choice is:
PUVA, with deeper penetration, is used for thicker plaques.
TSEB, a treatment modality for Mycosis Fungoides, stands for:
TSEB stands for Total Skin Electron Beam therapy, used in Mycosis Fungoides management.
The erythrodermic phase of CTCL plus its leukemic variant
A separate disease unrelated to Mycosis Fungoides
The earliest patch stage of CTCL
Sézary syndrome is the erythrodermic, leukemic variant of CTCL/Mycosis Fungoides.
The clinical course of Sézary syndrome, compared to Mycosis Fungoides, is:
Sézary syndrome follows a more aggressive course than the indolent Mycosis Fungoides.
The clinical triad of Sézary syndrome consists of erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and:
Circulating Sézary cells (malignant T cells with cerebriform nuclei) complete the triad.
Sézary cells, seen circulating in the blood in Sézary syndrome, are characterized by:
Sézary cells show the same cerebriform nuclei seen in the tissue-based malignant lymphocytes of Mycosis Fungoides.
Most common skin malignancy in children only
BCC is the most common primary malignancy of the skin overall.
Basal Cell Carcinoma is best characterized by its growth pattern as:
BCC is locally invasive but rarely metastasizes, distinguishing it from more aggressive malignancies.
The molecular pathway activated in Basal Cell Carcinoma is the:
The Sonic Hedgehog pathway is the key driver pathway in BCC.
The most common site for Basal Cell Carcinoma is the:
The face, particularly above the line joining the mouth angle to the ear lobule, is the most common BCC site.
The most common histological type of Basal Cell Carcinoma is the:
Nodular BCC is the most common clinical/histological type.
A nodular BCC characteristically begins as a:
Translucent pearly nodule with surface telangiectasia
A translucent pearly nodule with surface telangiectasia is the initial nodular BCC presentation.
As a nodular BCC progresses, central necrosis leads to the formation of a:
Central necrosis in a nodular BCC produces the characteristic rodent ulcer.
The edge of a BCC rodent ulcer is classically described as:
A pearly, rolled-out edge is the hallmark border appearance of a BCC rodent ulcer.
The preferred surgical technique for Basal Cell Carcinoma, offering good cosmetic outcomes, is:
Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for its tissue-sparing, margin-controlled approach.
Sequential removal of tumour until the margin is negative for tumour cells
A single wide excision with a fixed margin
Freezing the tumour with liquid nitrogen
Using radiation to shrink the tumour before excision
Mohs surgery involves sequential tissue removal and margin examination until tumor-free margins are achieved.
A key advantage of Mohs micrographic surgery is:
By sparing healthy tissue through margin-controlled excision, Mohs surgery offers superior cosmetic results.
Targeted therapy for BCC works by inhibiting the:
Targeted BCC therapies specifically inhibit the Sonic Hedgehog pathway that drives tumor growth.
Which drug is a Sonic Hedgehog pathway inhibitor used in BCC treatment?
Vismodegib is a Sonic Hedgehog pathway inhibitor used for BCC.
Besides vismodegib, which other Sonic Hedgehog pathway inhibitor is used in BCC treatment?
Sonidegib is the other Sonic Hedgehog pathway inhibitor used for BCC.

c: Basic Anatomy and Physiology of Bone
Basic Terminology of Fracture and Healing
Upper Limb Trauma: Clavicle and Shoulder
Upper Limb Trauma: Arm and Elbow
Upper Limb Trauma: Forearm, Wrist and Hand
Lower Limb Trauma: Pelvis and Tests
Lower Limb Trauma: Hip Dislocation and Fractures
Lower Limb Trauma: Femur, Knee, Leg and Foot
Paediatric Orthopaedics: Trauma, Neck and Upper Limb
u: Bone as an osteon has three parts: organic osteoid, water, and inorganic mineral. Children carry more water, so their bones are softer. The mineral is calcium hydroxyapatite; the chief protein is Type I collagen, joined by osteocalcin and osteonectin.

Osteoblasts are mononuclear builders — they lay down osteoid matrix and are rich in ALP. Osteoclasts are multinucleated giants from monocyte aggregates — phagocytic resorbers rich in TRAP and carbonic anhydrase, with ruffled borders.

Osteocytes are mature, resting osteoblasts — the most numerous bone cells with the longest life. Bone strength rests on the blast–clast balance. Type 1 collagen: bone, meniscus, annulus fibrosis. Type 2: articular hyaline cartilage, nucleus pulposus.

Formation markers: ALP, Procollagen I, Osteocalcin, Osteonectin. Resorption markers: Hydroxyproline and Hydroxylysine (collagen breakdown bits), NRC telopeptide, TRAP. Notice ALP, TRAP, osteocalcin and osteonectin pull double duty.

Proximal to distal: epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis. Children have a physeal plate; adults keep only an epiphyseal line. The medullary cavity holds marrow in children, fat in adults, and is lined by endosteum.

Sharpey's perforating fibres pin the periosteum to bone. Periosteum covers all long bones except articular surfaces and sesamoids like the patella. Its outer fibrous layer provides nutrition; the inner cellular layer drives growth.
