The nutrient artery enters via the nutrient foramen with medullary vessels alongside. Metaphyseal vessels loop like hair-pins, slowing flow. Rich supply heals fast — but also spreads infection and tumours, helped by scarce macrophages.

Woven bone has jumbled collagen — weak, seen in children and fracture callus. Mature bone splits two ways: soft, cell-poor cancellous bone at the metaphysis; hard, cell-rich cortical bone at the diaphysis.

Cancellous bone is vascular: heals fast but risks infection and malunion. Cortical bone heals slowly and risks non-union. Remember the sting in the tail — intra-articular epiphyseal fractures end in osteoarthritis and a stiff joint.

The physis exists only in children and lengthens bone. Layers, epiphysis to metaphysis: germinal (most important) → proliferative → hypertrophic (weakest) → calcification → ossification. Complete germinal injury shortens the limb; partial injury bends it into varus/valgus. Thickness grows by apposition via endosteum and periosteum.
A fracture is a break in the bone cortex. Tenderness is the most consistent sign, but abnormal mobility with crepitus is pathognomonic. On X-ray, look for discontinuity of bone.
Five patterns with significant trauma: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental. Force decides pattern — pull snaps transverse, bend snaps butterfly, squash slants oblique, twist spirals.

Violent tendon pulls avulse the patella or olecranon. Without trauma, think pathological: local causes like cysts and radiation, or generalized disease led by osteoporosis — spine, then hip, then wrist.
Metastases love the proximal femur — hunt them with FDG-PET. Banana bones mean Paget's. Pain before the break means micro-fractures; Mirel's 8 or more means fix it before it snaps.
Sudden jumps in repetitive loading crack weight-bearing bones — tibia, fibula, metatarsal. The march fracture hits the 2nd metatarsal neck more than the shaft.
Stress pain comes before the break and rises with activity. X-ray lags 2–3 weeks; MRI is the investigation of choice, catching edema and occult lines. Stop the stressor, rest the limb.
Shin splints are medial tibial periostitis in runners — anteromedial pain, normal X-ray. At the 5th metatarsal base, Jones zones run 3-2-1: stress, true Jones, pseudo Jones.

Rigid fixation heals directly with no callus (primary). Micromovement heals indirectly through cartilage callus — stronger and more common (secondary). Timelines double by stage: days, weeks, months, years.
Stage by stage: blood collects, fibroblasts weave mesh, osteoblasts lay callus, callus hardens, osteoclasts sculpt native bone. A ruptured nutrient artery starts it all.
Callus is disorganised immature bone, visible at 2–3 weeks — squeeze it and it unites faster. Healing hates old age, smoking, open wounds, ischemia, and above all improper mobilisation.
No callus past 9 months is non-union — classically the lower tibial shaft. Hypertrophic ends are sclerosed with exuberant callus and just need stillness; atrophic ends are dead quiet and need graft.
Iliac crest is the graft goldmine. Ideal grafts make bone (genesis), scaffold bone (conduction), and recruit bone (induction). Calcium salts and PMMA conduct; BMP induces and speeds union.
Malunion heals crooked — clavicle most of all — and earns an osteotomy only if function suffers. Supracondylar humerus, Colles, intertrochanteric and femur follow the clavicle.
Non-union bones: tibial shaft, scaphoid, lateral humeral condyle, intracapsular femoral neck, talar neck. Malunion bones almost never non-unite — pick a side, as the note says.
Muscles displace the distal fragment; reduction restores anatomy against counter-force. Manual closed reduction uses hands alone, then plaster, then a check X-ray. Skin pulls 5–6 kg, skeleton 15–16.
Skin traction drags bandage to skin to soft tissue. Skeletal pins bite bone — upper tibia most often — using lignocaine, pins, an 11-blade, forceps, drill and Bohler's stirrup.

Threaded Denham pins grip osteoporotic calcaneum; smooth Steinmann pins suit normal tibia and femur. The upper tibial ritual: drape, deep local both sides, stab 2.5 cm below-behind the tubercle, dilate, drill through.
Finish the ritual: dress, lock the stirrup, hang rope weights, mount the splint. Watch for staph at the pin and ring sequestra at entry and exit. This traction serves IT and distal femur fractures.
Splints buy time. Thomas's fixed-traction splint — born for TB knees — rings the perineum for counter-traction, frees the patient to move, and loves femur fractures.
Bohler-Braun slides in the ward, gravity pulls back from a raised footend. Pulleys: A tibia, B femur, C saves the foot from dropping. Russell's variant serves the intertrochanteric femur.
Definitive rule one: is the joint surface involved? Intra-articular means open up and plate it. Extra-articular: close it and plaster — or plate the upper limb, nail the lower.
Open reduction sees the fracture and wins on accuracy — mandatory inside joints to dodge arthritis. POP is cheap and kind but clumsy, freezing joints above and below into atrophy and stiffness.
CRIF threads rods down the medulla under C-arm eyes, and locking screws stop spin. Quadriceps rips patellae, triceps rips olecranons — both get opened, fixed, and tension-band wired.
Open means the skin is breached — tibia and fingers suffer most, staph walks in, and the escaping hematoma spoils healing. Gustilo I is a sub-centimetre inside-out poke; II spans 1–10 cm.
Grade III is the danger zone: IIIa is filthy (sewage, farms, firearms, usually over 10 cm), IIIb is stripped of periosteum, IIIc has torn vessels.
Wound first, bone second. Wash with povidone and saline, cut away dead tissue. Close at once only if clean and edge-to-edge; delay if late, mangled, or neurovascularly hurt.

Grade I behaves like a closed fracture. Grades II–IIIa earn that privilege only if clean within 6–12 hours — otherwise they wear external frames, like all IIIb/IIIc. Never plate an open fracture: biofilm will feast.
External fixation holds bone from outside: Schanz pins bite above and below the wound, rods lock the pins, clamps and connecting bars complete the scaffold.
Stability grows with more pins, more rods, more planes — biplanar beats uniplanar. The Rail (limb reconstruction) system slides adjustable rods that squeeze and hold.

Ilizarov's rings are multiplanar and mightiest — squeeze or stretch at will, pins in any direction. Stretching bone across a gap (distraction osteogenesis) fills losses, straightens deformity, lengthens limbs.
Cut the cortex, then stretch 1 mm a day: callus stretches into new bone (callotasis). Around shattered joints, spanning frames bridge femur to tibia — think side-swipe and baby-car injuries.

Pins can cook bone into ring sequestra. Compartments can choke in high- or low-energy breaks, even open ones — distrust every drowsy patient. Amputation cuts through bone; disarticulation through joint.

Dead, dangerous or dumb limbs go: crush, PVD, frostbite, gas, tumour, missing limbs, polio. MESS 7+ amputates — velocity, ischemia time (king), shock, age — with limb-salvage and Ganga scores as backup.

Clean stumps close at once; infected or ischemic ones stay open (guillotine) for a second sitting. Bleed less with a tourniquet — unless ischemia caused it all. Cut bone 5 cm short, tie every vessel twice.
Sew muscle to bone (myodesis) for a sturdy stump — except in PVD, where muscle-to-muscle (myoplasty) survives better. Skew the flaps: posterior long, scar forward, prosthesis happy.
Arm levels run shoulder, midarm (transhumeral), elbow, midforearm (transradial), wrist, rays — forequarter takes the girdle. The blind gain pincers when radius and ulna split: Krukenberg.

Leg levels: hemipelvectomy, hip, above-knee (transfemoral), knee, below-knee (commonest), transmetatarsal, ray, toe. Gritti-Stokes caps femur with patella. In the foot: Syme's, Chopart (intertarsal), Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal).
Cut nerves loose and they ball into painful neuromas — excise them, or buzz with TENS. Phantoms haunt half to most amputees, melting distal-to-proximal. Stitch tight and flaps die.
Prostheses replace anatomy (a new leg); orthoses support it (a cock-up splint). Every limb has a socket for the stump, rods, a knee where rod meets device, and the terminal device itself.
Jaipur feet look real, bend, squat, walk barefoot on rough ground, and cost little — SACH feet are rigid, restricted, and dear. Wood, rubber core, vulcanized skin versus a solid block.
In children, hoard every millimetre of bone and disarticulate rather than cut — the growth plate stays safe. Stumps need redoing as they grow, but kids master prostheses fast.
Replant only clean, low-MESS parts. Rinse in saline, swaddle in wet gauze, seal in plastic, nest in ice (buys 12–24 hours), box it.
BB FAN of Virender Sehwag: Bone, Back (extensor) tendons, Front (flexor) tendons, Artery, Nerve, Vein, Skin. Bone first, skin last.
ATLS hunts life-then-limb threats in the golden hour: Airway (jaw thrust, spine still), Breathing, Circulation (stop the bleed), Disability (brain), Exposure (strip and warm).
Philadelphia collars freeze the neck. Pelvises can hide two litres of blood — squeeze with binders, hands or sheets, pour RL over NS, then frame the pelvis.
Damage control: do little, save life. Unstable, cold, acidotic, coagulopathic, fat-embolized patients get a quick frame, an ICU tune-up, and definitive surgery later.
Crush: squeeze long, starve muscle, then release a flood of toxins — kidneys clog with myoglobin, acids and potassium rise, calcium falls. Flood with fluids, alkalinize the urine.

Metabolic bone disease weakens bone into painful micro-fractures and pathological breaks. Calcium is ruled by PTH and vitamin D: low calcium fires PTH, kidneys activate vitamin D, gut drinks up calcium and phosphate.

PTH makes kidneys keep calcium and spill phosphate, and orders osteoblasts to flash RANKL — osteoclasts resorb, ALP climbs. Denosumab silences RANKL. Primary HPT is an adenoma that ignores all feedback.
Dead kidneys can't activate vitamin D: calcium crashes, PTH soars, bones sprout mixed lesions — renal osteodystrophy. Labs tell the tale: renal keeps phosphate high, vitamin-D lack drops it.

The grand map: mineral faults (HPT, rickets, osteomalacia) scramble calcium labs; collagen faults breed brittle bones and scurvy; cell faults swing Paget's and petrosis with lonely high ALP; osteoporosis hides with normal labs.
Rickets is vitamin-D starvation — usually just poor diet — plus gut, sun, liver, kidney, drug and mineral causes. Labs: calcium lowish, phosphate low, PTH and ALP high.

Skull softens first (craniotabes), forehead bosses, fontanelles linger, sutures gape. Ribs bead bluntly at the cartilage (rachitic rosary), sternum juts (pigeon), diaphragm dents soft ribs (Harrison).
Legs bend only after standing — never in infants. Bow legs lead, knock knees follow, windswept mixes both. Scorbutic beads differ: they bleed and hurt.
Varus hugs the midline, valgus flees it — at elbow (cubitus), hip (coxa), knee (genu). Bow legs versus knock knees: name every bend by joint and direction.
Children: rickets bows, idiopathy knocks, rickets windsweeps. Adults: arthritis rules both, RA windsweeps. Bow legs past age two mean rickets. Hips: vara under 130, valga over 135.
Rickets X-rays cup, splay, widen and fray at the growth plate. Healing is watched by film plus ALP: calcium steadies, PTH and ALP fall, phosphate climbs, Frenkel's white line seals the plate.
Young bones straighten with treatment; older ones need osteotomy once active. Adult twin osteomalacia loves young women: aching joints, sore bones, weak thighs — and milkman cracks.
Osteomalacia cracks into Looser's zones — femoral neck, clavicle, ribs, scapula, pubic rami — transverse pale bands. Hips protrude, femora bottle, pelvises turn triradiate and trefoil. Biopsy proves.
Blast vitamin D (Stoss lakhs at once), drip it daily, or pulse it weekly. Tumours can mimic it all; scanograms map leg deformity full-length.

No vitamin C, no mature collagen: cortices pencil-thin over ground glass, metaphyses line (Frenkel), zone (scorbutic) and spur (Pelkan), epiphyses ring (Wimberger). Gums bleed, knees ache bilaterally.
Vitamin C cures scurvy; Barton blends C and D lack. Primary HPT fires PTH regardless — usually an adenoma to excise. Secondary answers hypocalcemia, D lack, renal or liver failure.
HPT Bones: Skull to Brown Tumour
PTH dissolves bone: skull peppers, teeth lose lamina dura, fingers resorb radially, brown tumours (osteitis fibrosa cystica) fill with blood-born hemosiderin.
High calcium: painful bones, kidney stones, belly groans, mad mind (lazy, foggy, blue, mad). Renal bones stripe into Rugger Jersey spines.
Osteoporosis: good bone, too little of it. Menopause risks most, age causes most; steroids, heparin, Cushing's, stillness, space and RA join in. Bones peak at thirty, estrogen guards them.
Ageing tips formation below resorption: strength sinks, micro-cracks spread. Back aches first, fragility fractures (spine, hip, wrist) complicate most, spines bow into kyphosis.
Labs stay normal; films betray only after 30% vanishes — wedged, cod-fished, hip-snapped, wrist-cracked. Screen women past 65, men past 70, fractures past 50.
DEXA rules diagnosis — spine first, then hip and heel. T-scores grade against thirty-year-old peaks: −1 normal, −2.5 thin (osteopenia), beyond −2.5 porous, plus fracture severe.
Bisphosphonates (rise-, iban-, zoledronate) gag osteoclasts — first-line, but years of silence snap hips oddly, so holiday onto teriparatide. Denosumab, raloxifene and HRT back them up.

Teriparatide's PTH whispers wake only builders — severe disease's champion, brief and watched; abaloparatide echoes it, romosumab frees builders via sclerostin. Strontium does both but harms; cement (vertebro-) or balloon-lift-plus-cement (kypho-) props vertebrae.
Paget's: men's fifth-decade mystery — idiopathic mostly, SQSTM1 and paramyxovirus suspects, pelvis then tibia. Osteoclasts rage, builders overanswer, ALP soars through lytic, mixed, blastic acts.
Pagetic bones ache (commonest), run warm and thick, snap like bananas, squeeze cranial nerves 2-7-8 (deafness), harden ears, outgrow hats. Mosaic biopsy proves.

Lytic skulls flame (blade of grass), mixed frames pictures, ivories vertebrae, cottons wool; blastic skulls thicken (Tam O'Shanter). Zoledronate calms, calcitonin soothes; hearts fail high-output, bone can turn sarcoma.
Brittle bones (OI): COL1A1 collagen curse. Dominant Type I limps through recurrent breaks; recessive Type II stillborns, shattered in the womb on antenatal scans. Labs stay normal.
Same bone breaks again and again into deformity; thin sclerae blush blue with choroid; skin bruises easy. Braces guard, Seekh-Kabab rods realign.

The reckoning table: secondary/rickets/osteomalacia (Ca lowish, PTH up, PO4 down, ALP up), renal (Ca down-down, PO4 up-up), osteoporosis (all normal), primary (Ca up-up-up), Paget's (ALP up-up-up alone).

Clavicle breaks from a fall on an outstretched hand. The AP shoulder film labels clavicle, acromion, proximal humerus and the lateral scapular border — and the clavicle is the most commonly fractured bone at birth, in newborns and overall.
The tube meets the flat plate at the medial-2/3–lateral-1/3 junction, so it snaps there. SCM yanks the medial piece up while pectoralis and the arm's weight drag the lateral piece down.

Displacement heals crooked (malunion, the commonest trouble), the plexus and subclavian vessels sit in harm's way, and true non-union is very rare. Most clavicles heal in a figure-of-8, a sling, or both.

Velpeau binds clavicle fractures, acromion injuries and shoulder dislocations. Surgery is for open fractures, tenting skin, AC joint involvement, neurovascular injury and the floating shoulder — fixed by ORIF.
Plates-and-screws or an intramedullary implant fix the clavicle. Then meet the shoulder: a ball 4× its socket — hugely mobile, poorly stable, and the most commonly dislocated joint.
The cuff plus the long head of biceps hug the head dynamically. Static backup is the three glenohumeral ligaments — inferior most important — and the capsular folds.

The labrum deepens the socket, but inferior stays the weakest point — so dislocations run anterior > posterior > inferior. Anterior subtypes run pre-glenoid to the rare intrathoracic, subcoracoid commonest.
The dislocated arm lies abducted and externally rotated, contour flattened, adduction lost — usually after trauma or a FOOSH. It is an emergency: reduce immediately.
Hamilton's ruler bridges epicondyle to acromion, Dugas traps the hand from the far shoulder, Callaway's tape shows a fatter axilla, and Bryant's fold sags lower on the bad side.

The axillary nerve dies first — deltoid and teres minor go silent and the regimental badge patch tingles. Confirm on AP + lateral films, then reduce with Kocher's TEAM: Traction, External rotation, Adduction, medial rotation.
Try closed reduction under analgesia, then under anaesthesia's relaxed muscles, and only then open up. Stimson lets a prone patient's hanging, weighted arm pull itself back in.
After reduction, pouch or Velpeau to heal soft tissues and stop recurrence. The Hippocratic method is older school: foot for countertraction, arm for traction.

Recurrence tears the labrum antero-inferiorly (Bankart, commonest) or avulses the glenoid rim (bony Bankart), slackening the inferior ligament. Each new dislocation dents the head's posterolateral corner — Hill-Sachs.
Overall and late, recurrence rules; early, the axillary nerve suffers. Posterior dislocation is the violent-muscle one — seizures, high-voltage shocks, ECT — plus FOOSH and plain trauma.

Posterior attitude is adducted and internally rotated with contour preserved and pain present. The head glows like a light bulb on X-ray; reverse Bankart and reverse Hill-Sachs mirror the anterior lesions.

Hyperabduction erects the arm into luxatio erecta. Instability tests: fulcrum/crank/apprehension anteriorly, jerk posteriorly, sulcus inferiorly — and the unstable shoulder today gets arthroscopic Bankart/Hill-Sachs repair, not Bristow or Putti-Platt.

Osteoporotic postmenopausal women snap the surgical neck — the fracture line threading both tuberosities — and the axillary nerve is the casualty. Neeb's system then counts how many of the four parts have fled.
Neeb I–IV means 0, 2, 3 or 4 displaced parts among head, tuberosities and shaft — more parts, more AVN risk. Definitive care is open reduction with plates and screws.

The shaft runs from surgical neck to supracondylar ridges with the radial nerve spiralling in its groove. Closed care is a U-slab or hanging cast; open plating is best — and a hanging cast only works on an upright patient.

At the upper-2/3–lower-1/3 junction the nerve pierces the septum and gets snared — Holstein-Lewis wrist drop in a cock-up splint. Any radial palsy starts closed with a 3-month watch; failed recovery earns a conduction study, then exploration.

Around the elbow, supracondylar leads and lateral condyle follows. The elbow is a hinge — an ulnohumeral joint — whose 3-point bony triangle survives supracondylar fractures but breaks in every other elbow fracture.
Kids' thin, flat supracondylar bone makes this the childhood elbow fracture — a Salter-Harris II that is extraarticular. A FOOSH hyperextends it into posterior displacement.

Extension types push the fragment back; flexion types push it forwards. The extended-elbow fall plus triceps drag produces proximal migration, medial tilt-shift, internal rotation and the classic dorsal tilt.
Gartland I is undisplaced (POP at 90°), II cracks only the anterior cortex (POP if it reduces, wires if not), and III is fully displaced with a fish-tail — reduced and K-wired.
Blood lifts the fat pad into a sail; the swollen elbow fans into a fish-tail. Dunlop traction holds things temporarily while Baumann's angle judges the final reduction before ORIF.

Early disaster is neurovascular: brachial artery first, then compartment syndrome and Volkmann's, with nerves falling AIN > median > radial. AIN fibres ride the median nerve's exposed periphery — like CPN fibres in the sciatic nerve.
Late, malunion into gunstock varus leads, with myositis ossificans behind. Meanwhile the classic compartment cascade runs: arterial injury → FDP ischemia → hypoxia → swelling → self-strangulation.

The ischemic limb curls into Volkmann's posture — flexed elbow, pronated forearm, flexed wrist, clawed fingers. Pain on passive stretch screams first; pallor, paraesthesia, then late paralysis and very-late pulselessness follow.

The manometer rules: under 10 is normal, over 30 is compartment syndrome (use differential pressure in hypotension). Slit superficial and deep fascia everywhere, leave the wound open, then graft or vacuum-close.

Fixed Volkmann's deformity plus dead hand function earns a turnbuckle splint when mild, a Max Page slide when moderate, and bone shortening when severe. Overall the tibia causes compartment syndromes; in children, blame the supracondylar fracture.

Pink but pulseless: collaterals paint the hand while the compressed brachial kills the radial pulse — reduce the fracture. Malunion's medial tilt plus twist gunstocks the elbow but spares function; the French osteotomy straightens it.
Carrying angles run 0–15° in males, 10–15° in females. Massaging the fracture squeezes hematoma into muscle, where it turns to bone and freezes movement.

Myositis loves the brachialis and the elbow, and it alone freezes elbow motion after these fractures: NSAIDs and rest while angry, physio when quiet, excision if stuck. Elsewhere, long-bone trauma can fog the lungs with fat at 24–48 hours.

A varus-tinged FOOSH cracks the lateral condyle — intraarticular, Salter-Harris IV, triangle disturbed — the mirror of supracondylar. It joins intraarticular fractures, Monteggia/Galeazzi and femoral neck as must-fix fractures of necessity.

The extensor mass tugs the fragment into non-union while the dead lateral physis lets the medial side outgrow it — cubitus valgus stretching medial structures until the ulnar nerve tardily fails with tingling and a partial claw.

Lateral condyles get ORIF; the olecranon gets tension-band wiring that turns pull-apart into squeeze-together. Elbow dislocation — the childhood dislocation, usually posterior — reverses the 3-point triangle and flexes the arm.

Posterior dislocation plus coronoid plus radial head is Hotchkiss's terrible triad; its bowstring is a slack triceps. In toddlers the small radial head slips from its loose annular noose — nursemaid's elbow.
The nursemaid's arm hangs extended and pronated with a normal triangle and normal X-ray, and usually fixes itself — or one firm flex-and-supinate (or extend-and-pronate) click cures it.

The radius spins around a static ulna to pronate and supinate, with the TFCC guarding the DRUJ. Both-bone breaks are cast in supination up top, mid-prone in the middle, pronation down low — but plating both bones is best.

Monteggia pairs an upper-third ulna break (a must-fix necessity) with a dislocated radial head. Bado reads the head's escape: anterior (commonest), posterior, lateral, or anterior plus a radius fracture.
Plate the ulna, pin the PRUJ if needed, and watch the posterior interosseous nerve — fingers and thumb drop with feeling intact. Revision: shoulder loses axillary, supracondylar loses AIN first.
Galeazzi mirrors Monteggia: radius breaks, DRUJ/TFCC lets go — plate it. The lone ulna 'nightstick' from a defensive block takes either a cast or plates and screws.
A type-I Monteggia film and the ulnar nerve of posterior elbow dislocation close the notes. Then learn the wrist: volar-pointing lateral view, ulnar-pointing AP view, and all eight carpal labels.

The wrist table splits clean: extraarticular Colle's (dorsal) and Smith (volar) versus intraarticular Barton (rim plus sliding carpus) and Chauffeur (lone styloid). Colle's itself loves osteoporotic wrists snapping at the cortico-cancellous line in extension.

Dorsal plus lateral tilt forks the wrist like a dinner fork. Reduce with traction, palmar flexion, ulnar deviation into a hand-shaking, below-elbow cast — stiffness is the enemy — or plate it definitively.
Stiff fingers lead the trouble list, a forked malunion follows, then Sudeck's burning dystrophy, a snapped EPL, a squeezed median nerve in the carpal tunnel, and rarely non-union.
Smith is the flipped Colle's — volar slip, garden-spade dip, flexion fall. Barton drags the joint plus carpus and needs plates; Chauffeur chips just the radial styloid inside the joint.

She Looks Too Pretty Try To Catch Her: eight carpals with pea-small pisiform and big capitate. Capitate ossifies first at 2 months, pisiform last; fractures pick scaphoid, dislocations pick lunate and threaten the median nerve.
Young adults FOOSH onto the scaphoid waist until the snuffbox aches. Shoot an oblique view first — the line often hides — and call MRI for the invisible ones.

Scaphoid blood runs retrograde, so non-union rules and the proximal pole dies first. Waist breaks are commonest, proximal-pole breaks riskiest; undisplaced sips in a glass-holding cast, displaced earns a Herbert screw.

A torn scapho-lunate ligament gapes past 3–4 mm into a Terry Thomas grin (normal 2–3). Keinbock's rots the lunate; the lunate itself either spills like a coffee cup or sits tight while everything dislocates around it — Tavernier reduces it.
APL yanks thumb-base breaks: Bennett's partial piece slips out, Rolando's T/Y shatters in place. At the other end, the boxer's 5th metacarpal neck rests in a Jame's-position cast.

A ball jams the finger into hyperflexion and the extensor avulses — mallet. Jersey yanks the flexor in hyperextension instead. Both lose active DIP motion while passive survives, dropping dorsal or volar flecks.
Mallet's fleck rides dorsal, jersey's volar — FDP torn with FDS watching. Mallet splints with a stax or frog; the table leaves jersey's treatment blank.

The hip marries the femoral head to the acetabular cup. Learn every label — SI joint to obturator foramen on the pelvis, head to lesser trochanter on the femur — then trace Shenton's smooth arc, the first line to break in any hip disease.

The neck meets the shaft at 120–135°; smaller is vara, bigger is valga. The greater trochanter tip floats at the cup's centre — high means short leg, low means long — while the lesser trochanter winks in and out with rotation.

Dislocation and neck fracture both shatter Shenton's arc. Feel rotation: the leg swings out while the hip turns in, and vice versa. Pelvic breaks are high-energy — jumpers from heights snap U or H patterns.

Tiles asks one question: is the ring broken? Chips of ilium, ischium or the iliac spines stay stable — Duverney's wing included. A cracked ring is unstable, and Young-Burgess then reads the crashing force.
A head-on smash springs the pelvis open like a book — horizontally unstable. A side slam crushes it vertically into Malgaigne's same-side double break; the bucket handle mixes sides.

Bucket handle pairs one SI disruption with opposite rami breaks; complex force snaps all four rami into a straddle. All of them can bleed half to two litres from veins, spongy bone, soft tissue and the urethra — so run ATLS.

Squeeze outside bleeds, tamponade inside ones with binders or bed-sheets, pour in RL/NS, and fix the ring externally in compression. The acetabulum itself has two walls and two columns — Judet views catch the posterior wall most, and a spur flags both columns.
Gluteus medius and minimus, wired by the superior gluteal nerve, hold your pelvis level each step. If they fail, the sound side sinks after 30 seconds — SSS — and the ASIS of the good side drops.
Trendelenburg walkers lean their spine over the bad hip; polio-weak quads force a hand-to-knee push. Thomas then hunts hidden hip flexion — the well-leg raise test named for Hugh Owen Thomas.

Lie flat, watch the lordosis vanish as the good hip flexes, and the bad hip's secret flexion pops up — measure it with a goniometer. Then squeeze the calf: no plantar flick means the tendoachilles (Simmonds-Thompson) is torn.

The hip is a deep, faithful socket — concave cup plus the body's strongest ligament — so once reduced it rarely pops again. Pure means no accompanying break: dashboards drive the head backwards (commonest), deceleration or falls fling it forwards.

Posterior hips curl into F-AD-IR — internally rotated, knee kissing the other leg, medial foot on the bed. Anterior hips sprawl into F-ABD-ER — flexed, abducted, externally rotated, lateral foot down.

Posterior shortens, anterior lengthens. Both break Shenton's arc with the head sitting outside — but posterior hides the lesser trochanter in internal rotation while anterior flaunts abduction. Feel the head: buttock behind, groin in front, rectum if central — the head punched through into the pelvis, usually with a fracture.

A dislocated hip is an emergency racing AVN: reduce closed, repeat under anaesthesia if spasm wins, open if it still resists, then skeletal traction. Allis, Bigelow, Stimson and the East Baltimore lift are the moves — shoulders keep Kocher's.

Vessels die first (6–12 hours), the sciatic nerve drops the foot in posterior pops, and anterior pops threaten femoral vessels over nerve. Narath's warning: femoral pulse unfelt against a missing head while foot pulses survive — in dislocation, dysplasia or after head excision.

The capsule grips the intertrochanteric line between the trochanters — that line decides everything. Head blood climbs backwards, distal to proximal, led by the medial circumflex femoral artery with obturator and lateral circumflex help.

Above the line is intracapsular neck (50–60s women, trivial fall, mild Scarpa's ache); below it is extracapsular trochanteric (harder fall, angrier trochanteric pain). Age matches, everything else diverges.

The capsule leashes neck rotation under 45° with under an inch of shortening; trochanteric breaks flop past 45° with the foot's edge on the bed and over an inch lost. Neck starves into 45% AVN and 30% non-union; trochanteric bone, well-fed, merely heals crooked into vara.

Neck non-union has three excuses: synovial fluid rinses the clot, blood barely arrives, and no cambium brings baby osteoblasts. By address: sub-capital at the head's foot, transcervical through the neck, basicervical at the neck's foot.
Sub-capital tops the death list. Pauwels' then grades the neck's tilt: under 30°, 30–50°, over 50° — the steeper the slide, the bigger the slip and the bleaker the future, I beating II beating III.

Garden reads the trabecular handwriting: bending only (valgus-impacted), head-neck script broken, all three lines scrambled, then total divorce. Incomplete and undisplaced at stage I, completely displaced by IV — prognosis falls I to IV.

Under 65 and fresh (3 weeks): screw it closed with cannulated cancellous screws. Older breaks get an MRI verdict — dead heads earn muscle grafts (Meyers' quadratus femoris, Baksi's TFL, fibula), living ones earn an osteotomy, Pauwels's beating Mcmurray's.

Past 65, replace: half (Austin Moore, Thompson, best-of-breed bipolar) for virgin hips, total for arthritic ones. Hemi swaps head-and-neck alone; total adds the cup — and the CRIF film shows those cannulated screws at work.

Meyer's muscle pedicle feeds the dying head; Mcmurray's sliding cut medialises the shaft so weight vaults over the crack; Pauwels's wedge flattens the slide so standing hammers it shut. Fall plus hip pain with a clean X-ray still earns an MRI — occult necks hide.

Trochanteric breaks just need their angle bodyguarded: a proximal femoral nail with locking screws or a dynamic hip screw's lag-blade-plate quartet holds 120–135° against vara. The frail get Russel's traction and a derotation boot instead.

The thigh's tug-of-war: psoas and abductors flex and splay the top piece while adductors drag the bottom inward. RTA-grade violence (Winquist-Hansen) earns a Thomas splint first — ring roomy by 2 inches, length generous by 6 — then a locked nail.

A femur break stiffens the knee, may refuse to unite, can drain 1.5 litres into shock, and leaks marrow fat into the lungs. Fat embolism announces itself at 24–48 hours: speckled skin, gasping chest, clouded brain.

Not ARDS — GURDS: one major (axillary specks, PaO2 under 60, sinking consciousness, wet lungs) plus four minors (fever, fast pulse, thin blood, fat in spit and urine, jumping ESR, retinal flecks). Fix fractures early to prevent it; ex-fix, ICU, then finish.

Babies ride in a Pavlik, toddlers set in a spica, schoolkids flex on Enders/TENS wires, teens take adult nails. Under-2s can hang in gallows traction, and the clover-leaf Kuntscher grips the isthmus where straight nail meets curved bone.

A direct smash cracks the kneecap across and the quads yank the top half skyward — wire it like an olecranon (tension band, best) or tube it in plaster. Don't be fooled by the bipartite twin, usually bilateral and innocent.
A car bumper valgus-loads the standing knee into the lateral tibial plateau — plate it open. The tibial shaft below either hides in a patellar-tendon cast or gets the definitive locked nail.
Read the ankle three ways: AP (both malleoli, tibia, talus), lateral (talus on calcaneus) and mortise. One malleolus is lonely, two is Pott's, three is Cotton's.

Check nerves and vessels, reduce, recheck, then slab. Inversion-plus-toes-down snaps the body's most-sprained ligament (ATFL); rare eversion strains the deltoid. The pilon shatters the tibial ceiling, and a heel-drop fall flattens Bohler's angle while Gissane's gapes.

Jump for love and both heels plus the spine pay (lover's). Pilots crack the talar neck (aviator's) and gamble the body's blood — Hawkins I stays put, IV dislocates three joints, and a Hawkins stripe proves the bone still breathes.

Chopart splits the midfoot's intertarsal line; Lisfranc unkeys the tarso-metatarsal arch — the second metatarsal flees its cuneiform, the first gap widens, a fleck betrays the ligament. The 5th base zones out: pseudo-Jones avulses, true-Jones starves at the watershed, plain Jones sits beyond.

Fast crashes fracture; slow sport strains tendons (supraspinatus leads) and sprains ligaments (ankle's ATFL leads). Around the knee: collaterals guard outside the capsule, menisci float inside the synovium, cruciates hide inside the capsule but outside the synovium.

Walk the front of the knee bone by bone, then look down from above: the medial collateral clings to the medial meniscus (dooming it to tear together) while the lateral collateral floats free of its meniscus. Scopes diagnose best, MRIs investigate first.

Collaterals brace the coronal plane: bow-leg varus snaps the LCL, knock-knee valgus snaps the MCL — the knee's commonest ligament victim. Pain points to its side, and a 30°-bent stress test pries the guilty joint open.

Nine in ten collaterals heal in a brace; MRI's coronal blush confirms it. Then meet the twin shock-absorbing, rotation-taming crescents of type-I collagen — twisted most often into bucket handles, medial before lateral.

Meniscal misery arrives late: aching, puffy, and locking mid-stride when a flap jams the hinge. McMurray hyperflexes, twists and extends; Apley grinds the prone knee at 90° — inward grind accuses lateral, outward accuses medial.

Fingertips beat all: six joint-line points map each horn and body, front to back, medial then lateral. Sagittal MRI stages it — normal horns versus a heterogenous tear — but the scope has the last word. Only the red rim drinks blood; the white heart sips joint fluid.

Bloody red tears get stitched (meniscorrhaphy/meniscopexy); bloodless white tears get trimmed (menisectomy). Deeper inside, the cruciates police the sagittal plane — ACL leashing the tibia's forward slide and hyperextension, PCL its backward slide and hyperflexion.

Hyperextension hurls the ACL, dashboard hyperflexion snaps the PCL — one twist, one pop, a joint full of blood and a leg that gives way. Drawer at 90° (3 mm of slide), Lachmann at 15–20° (the best), pivot shift (the most specific).
The PCL sags backwards on the drawer and droops with gravity in Godfrey's hold. MRI investigates, arthroscopy confirms and then rebuilds — hamstring twins or patellar tendon as the new rope.

Scopes love knees most: instruments enter medially, the 4mm 30° eye laterally. The ACL itself is two ropes — posterolateral guarding extension, interrogated by Lachmann; anteromedial guarding flexion, caught by the drawer.
A Segond flake off the lateral tibia screams ACL. Twist the full recipe — femur in, knee bent, foot planted, tibia flung out — and the unhappy triad falls: MCL, ACL and medial meniscus together.

MRI frames the triad plane by plane. The Insall-Salvati ratio (tendon over patella, 0.8–1.2) names alta floaters that redislocate and baja sinkers. Finally: pivot shift for anterolateral spin-outs, dial test for posterolateral ones.
Painful regional conditions stand alone: repetitive microtrauma begets pain, and diagnosis is clinical — provoke the very movement that hurts. Shoulders arrive painful with no trauma history at all.
Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is periarthritis of the shoulder — self limiting, bilateral in 30%. Watch for it in uncontrolled diabetics and thyroid disorders.

Capsulitis causes pain, then thickening and fibrosis, then contracture — blocking active AND passive movement. Freezing = capsulitis (pain+, no stiffness); frozen = adhesions (pain down, stiffness up); thawing = resolution (both down).

Globally restricted ROM, rotation lost first (external > internal); X-ray normal, MRI shows capsulitis. General care — glycemic control (it may resolve spontaneously), physio, NSAIDs, steroids; specific care is adhesiolysis: manipulation under anesthesia or arthroscopic.

Impingement = painful arc syndrome in a ball-and-socket joint held by soft tissue more than bone: long head of biceps plus rotator cuff (supraspinatus above, subscapularis in front, infraspinatus and teres minor behind). The subacromial space between acromion and humeral head holds the bursa and supraspinatus tendon.

In a narrow space, abduction inflames the subacromial bursa, then the supraspinatus tendon; pain peaks at mid-abduction — the painful arc. Neer's raises the arm passively with a stable scapula; Hawkins-Kennedy elevates 90° in scapular plane and internally rotates. Conservative first; subacromial decompression if needed.

Supraspinatus tears most (then tendo Achilles); subscapularis is the forgotten tendon. Any tear drops stability and ends in arthropathy — degeneration in the old, trauma in the young. Pain rises against resistance; X-ray normal, MRI is IOC.

Abduction = supraspinatus (beer can, empty can, Jobe's); external rotation = infraspinatus and teres minor (horn blower's); internal rotation = subscapularis (lift off, belly press, bear hug). Empty can: 90° abduction, 30° flexion, full internal rotation; Jobe's: thumbs down in scapular plane.

Treat tears with rest from overhead work, physio, NSAIDs, steroids, arthroscopic repair. A chronic tear overloads the other stabilisers until the long head of biceps ruptures — its belly balls up distally as the Popeye sign.

TOS entraps the neurovascular bundle in the outlet bounded by both scalenes, clavicle and first rib — contents: brachial plexus and subclavian vessels. Culprits: odd neck posture, upper-lobe lung tumour, cervical rib at C7.

Shoulder pain radiating down the arm, pale hand; neurological signs mature into vascular claudication, and C8-T1 compression gives Klumpke's palsy. Plexus compresses before artery, artery before vein. Adson's (head to affected side), reverse Adson's (opposite), Wright's hyperabduction, Roo's 3-minute hand opening-closing; MRI is IOC; surgery excises first rib, cervical rib or the tumour.

Tennis = lateral epicondylitis of the common extensor origin (ECRB before longus), proved by Cozen's resisted wrist extension. Golfer's = medial epicondylitis of the common flexor origin (flexor carpi radialis), proved by reverse Cozen's resisted flexion.

Activity modification, NSAIDs, ortho-biologics and a counterforce brace that stops motion reaching the muscle origin. Blood boosts healing AND inflammation; PRP (WBCs removed) boosts healing only; stem cells come from fat, marrow and periosteum.

Stenosing tenosynovitis of APL and EPB in the first dorsal compartment, from overuse or rheumatoid arthritis. Women, radial styloid pain, Finkelstein's and Eichhoff's tests; rest, splint, steroid injections.

Cord-like fibrosis of palmar fascia contracts the finger — idiopathic mostly, also diabetes and alcohol; men, bilateral, ring finger at the MCP joint. Ectopic cousins: Peyronie's (penis) and Ledderhose (soles). Treat: conservative, collagenase, fasciectomy.
Trauma stenoses the A-1 pulley at the MCP, blocking the FDP tendon: the finger sticks shut, then snaps open on forceful extension. Women, ring finger, rheumatoid association.

Hyperabduction tears the thumb's ulnar collateral ligament (gamekeeper's/skier's thumb) — thumb spica, or surgery when a Stener lesion traps the adductor pollicis tendon in the gap. Bowler's thumb is a neuroma of the ulnar digital nerve from perineural fibrosis.

Ganglion — the commonest wrist swelling, dorsal over ventral, a unilocular synovial cyst full of mucinous fluid; aspirate, sclerose or excise. Compound palmar ganglion is a misnomer: TB or rheumatoid flexor-sheath inflammation bulging forearms and hand into an hourglass, pinched at the retinaculum.

A bone fragment parts at the bone-cartilage interface and locks the knee — knee over elbow, lateral part of the medial femoral condyle. Wilson's test: pain extending the internally rotated leg, eased by external rotation.

Loose bodies: osteoarthritic osteophytes overall and in the elderly, osteochondritis dissecans in the young. Many bodies at once means synovial chondromatosis — synovial metaplasia sprinkling cartilaginous bodies, a snowstorm on X-ray.

Chondromalacia patellae softens cartilage — idiopathic, female, the top cause of anterior knee pain, worse rising after long sitting (movie sign). Baker's cyst is a pulsion diverticulum of synovium behind the knee from OA or RA: prominent in extension, gone in flexion, USG diagnoses, excision treats.

Synovial sacs cut friction and let tendons glide; repetitive loading inflames them. Housemaid's knee = prepatellar, clergyman's knee = infrapatellar, student's elbow = olecranon, Haglund = retrocalcaneal (calcified bump), tailor's bunion = 5th metatarsal lateral, weaver's bottom = ischial.

Hallux valgus deviates the great toe laterally, swelling and hurting the first MTP — osteotomy fixes it. Gout mimics the pain but brings inflammation without deformity and needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals on aspiration.

AVN favours femoral head (Chandler's), proximal scaphoid pole (Preiser's) and talar body. Non-traumatic is idiopathic — sickle cell, Gaucher's, Caisson's, Perthes', alcohol; traumatic follows vascular disruption. Steroids raise femoral head pressure, choke its blood supply and infarct it.

Young men, bilateral in half (80% with steroid history). Antalgic limp, hip pain radiating to the knee, internal rotation and abduction restricted first — the sectoral sign. X-ray density changes lag weeks to months; the crescent sign marks early subchondral collapse.

MRI is IOC; bone scan shows the donut sign — a cold head ringed by normal uptake. Core decompression lowers pressure and revives flow, vascularised fibular grafts bring new vessels, and a destroyed head takes total hip replacement.
Three vascular watersheds: prolonged hip dislocation or femoral neck fracture kills the femoral head; scaphoid waist fracture kills the proximal pole; talar neck fracture kills the talar body.

Hawkin's sign — subchondral lucency on X-ray — reassures of viable, well-perfused bone; the snowcap sign caps a humeral head with AVN. Remember: intertrochanteric fractures malunite, and Hawkin's classification belongs to talus fractures.
Three tubes nest inside each other: epineurium wraps the nerve, perineurium wraps each fascicle, endoneurium wraps each axon. Blood vessels ride along the layers.

Cut completely and the distal segment undergoes Wallerian degeneration while the proximal stump balls into an end neuroma of naked sprouts — no further regeneration. Cut partially (sheath intact) and a neuroma in continuity bridges across, regenerating proximal-to-distal at 1 mm/day.

Percuss distal-to-proximal: a shock-like twang at the neuroma is Tinel positive. Non-progressive means end neuroma; progressive means neuroma in continuity regenerating. Higher injuries cripple more; recovering muscles march proximal to distal.

Neuropraxia = compression block, no neuroma, 100% recovery (tourniquet, Saturday night, crutch). Axonotmesis = axon down but a sheath intact, neuroma in continuity, <100% recovery, progressive Tinel and motor march (fractures, dislocations). Neurotmesis = complete transection, end neuroma, no recovery (lacerations, incised wounds).
Sunderland splits Seddon finely: Type I = neuropraxia; II = axon only; III = axon + endoneurium; IV = axon + endoneurium + perineurium; V = neurotmesis.

Tinel's tracks recovery; nerve conduction study is IOC for the injury type. Its best parameter, nerve conduction velocity, times the impulse down each segment — compression slows it — with electromyography alongside.
When to Observe, When to Explore

Neuropraxia: wait and watch with a splint against contracture. Closed fracture: splint, observe, NCS if months pass without recovery, then explore. Open fracture or an obvious sharp nerve injury: straight to surgical exploration.
Primary repair inside 6 hours, delayed primary at 7-18 days, end-to-end or end-to-side. When the ends won't meet, graft — sural nerve most commonly, saphenous as alternate.

After a year unrepaired the motor end plates die and tendon transfer borrows working muscle-tendon units. NERVE-GROW lists the good omens — neuropraxia, early repair, radial nerve, vascularity, end-to-end, growing children. Axonal confusion wires motor into sensory (gustatory tears) and spoils prognosis.

Mixed injury: sensory loss brings anesthesia and tingling; motor loss brings weakness plus antagonist overpull and deformity. Axillary nerve (C5, C6, mixed) drives deltoid and teres minor, feels the regimental badge area, and leaves the arm adducted, internally rotated.

Shoulder dislocation tops the causes, with surgical neck and glenoid fractures behind. Abduction runs supraspinatus 0-15°, deltoid 15-90°, serratus anterior and trapezius overhead. The map: arm anterior musculocutaneous / posterior radial; forearm anterior median / posterior interosseous; hand thenar median, hypothenar and intrinsics ulnar. Musculocutaneous loss leaves an extended, pronated forearm and numb lateral forearm.

Roots C5-T1 build trunks, divisions, cords; Erb's point conflates C5, C6 and the suprascapular nerve. Supraclavicular traction (birth dystocia, neck stretch) gives Erb's — best prognosis; infraclavicular (hyperabduction fall, presenting-arm traction) gives Klumpke's; combined is worst. Long thoracic (C5-7) wings the scapula; suprascapular loss adducts and internally rotates.

Erb's hits suprascapular, axillary and musculocutaneous — the adducted, internally rotated, extended and pronated policeman's/waiter's/porter's tip. Klumpke's (C8, T1) merges ulnar and median palsy into a fully clawed hand, and T1 sympathetic loss unmasks Horner's: ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, lost ciliospinal reflex. Splint it in the aeroplane splint.

The labourer's nerve is mixed: motor to forearm flexors and thenar muscles, sensory to lateral 3½ palm and only the tips dorsally. At the retinaculum it splits — deep branch (thenar motor + tip sensation) and superficial (palmar sensation). CTS squeezes the deep branch, sparing palmar feeling.
An autonomous zone is one nerve's private patch: index tip (median), little finger tip (ulnar), first web space dorsum (radial).

Arm: nothing. Forearm: every flexor except FCU and medial FDP (ulnar's share). Hand: the LOAF — lumbricals 1,2, opponens, abductor and flexor pollicis brevis — all thenar but adductor pollicis, which is ulnar.

Wrist lesions come from carpal tunnel, elbow lesions from supracondylar fractures — where AIN tops the injury order ahead of median, radial, ulnar. Wrist injury: numb lateral 3½, wasted thenar, ape thumb; add FPL/FDS/FDP loss at elbow. Opponens splint treats.

Pen test lifts the thumb (APB); pointing index/benediction exposes FDS+FDP failure with the unflexed index; AIN — purely motor to FPL and lateral FDP — shows a weak OK (Miloh-Nevin) sign with no sensory loss and an easy fist. Lunate dislocation can squeeze the median.

C8-T1 musician's nerve: forearm FCU and medial FDP; hand hypothenar, adductor pollicis, interossei (palmar adduct, dorsal abduct), lumbricals 3,4; senses medial 1½ all round. Cubital tunnel and Guyon's canal trap it; wrist lesions claw partially — complete clawing needs median too.

Knuckle bender splint supports the claw. Card test = palmar interossei (card slips), Egawa and fanning = dorsal interossei, book test = adductor pollicis with Froment's thumb-flexion cheat. Elbow lesions spare clawing because FDP's medial half dies too — the ulnar paradox: higher injury, lesser claw.

Most injured yet best prognosis — purely motor, extending elbow, wrist, fingers from the posterior cord. Long-head triceps branch fires first; ECRL is the first wrist extensor; PIN takes supinator, ECRB and finger extensors. Levels: radial head (PIN: finger+thumb drop), lateral condyle (+sensory), spiral groove (+wrist drop, m/c), axilla (+elbow extension lost). Below ECRL, no wrist drop.

Holstein-Lewis — humeral shaft fracture at the upper/lower third junction — entraps radial nerve, the m/c cause. Cock-up splint answers wrist drop: static extends wrist, dynamic also lets fingers flex. The summary tables pair every sign with its muscle, Froment to pincer grasp.

Sciatic injury behaves like CPN injury — peroneal fibres ride peripherally around the tibial core; hip surgeries top the causes. At the fibular neck the CPN splits: superficial everts and feels the dorsum, deep dorsiflexes and feels the first web. Fibular neck fracture drops the foot into equinovarus and a steppage gait; AFO splints it.

Trapped under the flexor retinaculum, the median — m/c entrapped nerve in the m/c entrapment neuropathy — burns at night along lateral 3½ fingers in middle-aged women, eased by shaking or hanging the hand. Idiopathic leads causes; myxedema, pregnancy, acromegaly, Colles' hematoma, gout, amyloid, diabetes follow. Durkan's 30-second compression is the best clinical test, NCS the IOC; rest-steroid-splint first, then release the ligament. Allen's test clears the hand's vessels before arterial lines.

Opponens pollicis, deep median branch, performs opposition — the single function CTS destroys completely. Meralgia paraesthetica burns the lateral thigh where the lateral cutaneous nerve ducks under the inguinal ligament, pinched by overweight and tight clothing.

Memorise the grid: cubital tunnel — ulnar behind medial condyle; Guyon's — ulnar under piso-hamate; pronator syndrome — median at pronator teres heads; Kiloh-Nevin — AIN in supracondylar fracture; cheiralgia — superficial radial at the styloid (watch, cuffs, bangles); meralgia — lateral femoral cutaneous under inguinal ligament; pyriformis — sciatic; tarsal tunnel — posterior tibial behind medial malleolus; Morton — interdigital nerve, 3rd-4th toe.

William Enneking, father of orthopaedic oncology, grades benign lesions by capsule — latent thick, active thin, aggressive breached (NOF, ABC, GCT) — and malignant ones by grade and compartment: low or high, intra (A) or extra (B), stage III metastasis.

Chondrocytes (cartilage formers: osteochondroma, enchondroma, chondroblastoma → chondrosarcoma) look lucent/hazy with calcification; osteoblasts (osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma → osteosarcoma) look dense/sclerosed; osteoclasts (giant cell tumor) destroy bone.

Haemangioma — benign vascular, spinal; simple bone cyst and fibrous dysplasia — mesenchymal, the latter swapping bone for fibrous tissue; Ewing's — malignant small round blue cell family rising from the medullary cavity.

Epiphysis: chondroblastoma while the growth plate shows (child), GCT once it closes (adult). Diaphysis: Ewing's, osteoid osteoma with aspirin-responsive night pains, adamantinoma. Metaphysis: osteosarcoma, osteochondroma, ABC, UBC, NOF, chondromyxoid fibroma. Osteoid osteoma lays the most matrix.

Truly benign: osteoid osteoma, simple bone cyst. Benign but with malignant potential: GCT, osteoblastoma, osteochondroma. Frankly malignant: chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, Ewing's, adamantinoma, chordoma.

Ewing's rules the first decade (peaks in the second); primary osteosarcoma is the commonest malignant bone tumour of children at 10-20; GCT/osteoclastoma at 30-40; secondary osteosarcoma (Paget's, radiation) and chondrosarcoma at 40-60; metastasis, myeloma, adamantinoma and chordoma after 60.

Insulted periosteum builds new bone to wall off pathology: thick and solid when indolent, thin and lamellated when aggressive. Onion peel = Ewing's, sunburst (calcified Sharpey's fibres) and Codman's triangle = osteosarcoma, solid = osteomyelitis.
Vascular tumours pulsate with a bruit — osteosarcoma most of all, then ABC, GCT and metastases from kidney and thyroid.

Polyostotic means multicentric — same bone or many, never metastatic: FD, GCT, enchondroma, osteochondroma. Non-ossifying fibroma is a cortical, eccentric, self-resolving metaphyseal defect of the first decade. Fibrous dysplasia replaces bone with fibrous tissue, loves the femur, and is usually monostotic.

Biopsy (best ix) reads Chinese letters; X-ray shows ground glass, RIND sign and shepherd crook deformity. McCune-Albright adds café au lait spots and precocious puberty; Mazabraud adds intramuscular myxomas.

Simple bone cyst: unilocular, symmetrical, centric, straw fluid, proximal humerus — aspirate with steroids/sclerosants or graft. Aneurysmal bone cyst: multiloculated, ballooning, eccentric, blood-filled, around the knee — extended curettage with liquid nitrogen, phenol or cement, the same extended curettage GCT gets.
A child's metaphysis with an open growth plate hosts the SBC; a cortical chip that breaks and falls free is the fallen leaf sign, one that hinges is the trap door sign.

ABC: child's metaphysis, multiloculated, MRI stacked with fluid-fluid levels — shared with GCT and telangiectatic osteosarcoma. Centric cystic lesions: SBC, enchondroma, Brodie's abscess; eccentric: GCT, ABC, NOF.
Cartilage-forming tumors are chondrocyte predominant and announce themselves with popcorn, ring-and-arc (O-ring) calcification - the club of chondroma, osteochondroma and chondrosarcoma.

Osteochondroma is the m/c benign bone tumor, m/c at the distal femur, a sessile or pedunculated mass that is aberrant growth-plate development. It grows epiphysis-to-metaphysis away from the joint, stops with skeletal maturity, and is not a true tumor.
Pain means bursitis first, then nerve compression or fracture. A cap over 2 cm on MRI, heavy cap calcification on X-ray, or growth persisting after skeletal maturity whispers chondrosarcoma.
Feel large, see small: the sub-2 cm cartilage cap hides from X-ray, while CT shows bone architecture matching normal. Cure is extraperiosteal excision after skeletal maturity.
Diaphyseal aclasis runs autosomal dominant through EXT 1,2 mutations, and 5% of the multiple lesions turn chondrosarcoma.
Enchondroma rules the small bones of hand and feet, sits metaphyseal, and gets extended curettage with bone graft.
Multiple enchondromas make Ollier's syndrome - very rare, 30% premalignant. When cavernous hemangiomas and lymphangiomas join in, it is Maffucci's.
The hand's commonest tumor is squamous cell carcinoma, not a bone tumor. Enchondroma's great mimic in fingers is spina ventosa - TB dactylitis.
Codman's tumor claims the child's epiphysis at 10-25 years: stippled calcification on film, chicken-wire calcification on biopsy, cured by excision curettage with autologous graft.

The m/c true benign tumor: diaphyseal, cortical, femoral. Prostaglandins from the central nidus kindle night pain that aspirin quenches; a lucent nidus ringed by dense sclerosis seals the diagnosis - NSAIDs, RFA or excision.
Osteoblastoma is osteoid osteoma grown past 2 cm in the spine, may ignore aspirin, carries a whisper of osteosarcoma risk - excise it.
Osteoclastoma: locally aggressive, epiphysio-metaphyseal, female-predominant, 20-40 years after skeletal maturity. Distal femur round the knee is the favourite seat, distal radius the classical one.

Eggshell crackling, a soap bubble of leftover trabeculae, giant cells around RANK-spewing mononuclear tumor cells. Extended curettage with liquid nitrogen, phenol or cement, then autograft - remember the six E's.
Giant-cell-rich company: NOF most common, ABC closest in resemblance. Under 5% turn malignant (3% of those fly to the lungs), but 30% come back locally.
The elderly spine's quiet vascular blotch: jail bars (corduroy) on X-ray, polka dots on axial CT, spine > skull > pelvis. Treat conservatively, by radiotherapy or vertebroplasty - bone cement.
Chondrosarcoma: 40-50 years, metaphyseal, in the pelvis and proximal femur as a calcified tumor with hyperglycemia as paraneoplasia. Endosteal scalloping and punctate calcification on film.

Children's commonest bone cancer: bimodal (1st decade 1°, older 2° via Paget/radiation), metaphyseal distal femur, radio-resistant, osteoid-forming. 15% already harbour lung micrometastases that can pop a pneumothorax.
Elevated periosteum draws Codman's triangle; calcified Sharpey's fibres burst into a sunburst. Classical intramedullary is the commonest of the four types.
Map: neoadjuvant chemo, surgery/limb ablation, adjuvant chemo. Drugs - the TID protocol: actinomycin, cyclophosphamide, bleomycin, high-dose methotrexate, doxorubicin, vincristine.

Ewing owns the 1st decade, peaks in the 2nd (5-20 yrs) as a high-grade diaphyseal femur mass in boys. Metastasis, male sex, fever, anemia, raised ESR, age over 14, leukocytosis, chemoresistance and relapse all darken the outlook.

It masquerades as infection with an onion-peel film; biopsy - the best test - shows small round blue cells in pseudo-rosettes, PAS-positive and diastase digestible, MIC-2 (CD99) positive, carrying t(11;22).

Radiosensitive yet radiotherapy is shunned for fear of recurrence; today it is chemotherapy with limb salvage and adjuvant radiation. Neuroblastoma, retinoblastoma and medulloblastoma share the small-blue-round-cell club.

Chordoma rises from notochord rests in the elderly sacrum; adamantinoma, a low-grade epithelial malignancy, soap-bubbles the tibial diaphysis; synovial sarcoma ignores synovium, born of capsule, bursae or tendon with t(x;18) SYT:SSX.

Metastasis is the commonest malignant bone tumor - breast, prostate, lung riding to the lumbar spine. Prostate blastic, kidney and follicular thyroid lytic, breast mixed; the winking owl is a eaten pedicle. Myeloma heads the malignant list, osteochondroma the benign, osteoid osteoma the true-benign.

Bone plus medullary cavity is osteomyelitis (metaphysis of long bone); joint is septic arthritis. Bacteria rule - pyogenes burn with severe periosteal reaction while TB smoulders with a limited one, except in the short bones of hand and foot where even TB flares.

Children and the elderly fall first - low immunity. The bloodstream seeds bone from a pre-existing focus most often; puncture wounds, surgery and open fractures inoculate directly, and a septic joint can chew its way into bone.
Staphylococcus aureus is king of musculoskeletal infection - the m/c cause of osteomyelitis overall, acute and chronic, in rich and poor countries alike, in HIV, open fractures and post-surgery.
Memorise the pairing grid: sickle cell - Salmonella diaphyseal (metaphysis means Staph); IV drugs - Pseudomonas; animal bite - Pasteurella; human bite - Eikenella; long parenteral lines - fungi.

Children break their femur distally then tibia; adults guard their vertebrae. The metaphysis beckons organisms: most vascular soil, hair-pin vessels with sluggish flow, and few patrolling macrophages.

The clock: organism lands in metaphysis <24 h with fever and pain; after 24 h an abscess pools; dead bone (sequestrum) drops inside it; periosteum builds the involucrum by about 10 days; a break in involucrum is cloaca, in skin a sinus - pus escapes.
A young child with high fever, painful swollen limb that he refuses to move - pseudoparalysis. Think septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, or scurvy's subperiosteal bleed.
Two-by-two: acute has fever-and-pain clinically and an abscess pathologically; chronic announces a sinus and hides a sequestrum.
Blood culture catches the bug half the time; WBC, ESR, CRP rise but accuse no one; serum procalcitonin alone is both sensitive and specific for acute osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
MRI sees marrow edema within 24 h; bone scan glows with Tc99, Ga67, In111-WBC; X-ray waits a day, shows soft tissue shadow by 48 h, and only at 7-10 days lifts the periosteal veil.

Biopsy from the site is gold standard. Within 24 h antibiotics may suffice, after 24 h add drainage; six weeks of antibiotics (2 IV, 4 oral) because bone drinks drugs poorly - track the fall of CRP, and splint, cool and elevate meanwhile.
Chronicity tops the list; pus may cross to the joint where the growth plate is missing - under 1 year or after fusion - and septicemia and growth disturbance complete the four.
Cut the timeline at 2 and 4 weeks: acute under two, subacute two-to-four, chronic beyond four - chronic is simply acute osteomyelitis that never died, wearing a sinus as its badge.
A dead, dense, devascularized island of bone floating in pus, wrapped in granulation tissue and involucrum, its haversian systems destroyed - the pathological signature of chronicity.
Shape names the disease: coral for Perthe's, ring for pins and stumps, tubular for pyogenic infection, feathery sandy for TB, fine sandy for viral, button-hole after radiation, ivory for syphilis.
X-ray unmasks sequestrum, involucrum and cloaca; dye through the sinus maps its track; biopsy remains gold standard - start broad-spectrum antibiotics and support the patient.

The operative ladder under antibiotic cover: sequestrectomy, curettage to the Paprika blush, saucerization, dead space filled with graft or cement, skin flapped or VAC'd at -75 to -125 mmHg - never on eschar or tumor.
Pathological fracture comes first, sinuses can turn squamous, and flare-ups and amyloidosis round out the toll of a chronic discharging wound.

Strong host, weak bug - infection walled off without sinus or sequestrum. Brodie's: subacute, proximal tibia, pus positive, dull ache with low fever, a lucent eye ringed by sclerotic rim - penumbra on MRI - treat with antibiotics ± debridement.
Garré's: the dry chronic twin - mandible more than tibia, no pus, no raised ESR, just bony hard swelling and bone gone rock-dense from excessive periosteal reaction; antibiotics suffice.

Pus in a joint is a surgical emergency - undrained it digests cartilage. Under-five children and the elderly, blood-borne Staph aureus (Pseudomonas in addicts, gonococcus in the sexually active), knee first, hip in infants - Tom Smith.
Swollen, red, exquisitely painful joint held still; the limb rests where the capsule is slackest - hip in FABER, knee at 5-30 degrees - and the knee offers a positive patellar tap.

Bloods and culture, an early film that shows little but a widened space, late destruction, MRI synovial thickening - and ultrasound-guided arthrocentesis that both names the culprit and relieves the joint.

Arthrotomy with irrigation and debridement is TOC; neglect lets collagenases strip cartilage until raw bones fuse - bony ankylosis. Disease fusion is ankylosis (bony from pyogenic/TB spine - stable, painless; fibrous from TB - mobile, painful, unstable), surgery's is arthrodesis.
Infant's septic hip under one year: pus and enzymes dissolve the cartilaginous capital epiphysis - chondrolysis - leaving a hypermobile, shortened limb with positive telescopy.

A post-viral, self-limiting 'observation hip' of 6-12 year olds: limp, mild fever, position of ease. Joint aspiration is the best divider, Kocher counts four points - weight bearing, >38.5°C, ESR >40, WBC >12,000 - the more, the more septic. Limp in a child: transient synovitis first.
The commonest hand infection runs around the nail - Staph aureus again; drain it, and if it sneaks under the nail bed, lift a piece of nail.
Pulp-space abscess of the distal phalanx, thumb first: a tense throbbing digit that can erode into bone or tendon; a vertical incision breaks the septae and lets the pus go.
Infected tendon sheath: finger held flexed, fusiform swelling, pain on passive extension and Kanavel's tap - antibiotics plus incision and drainage.

Koch's weak bacillus rides the blood from a primary focus - the lung - to settle in bone, where it rages far less than a pyogenes: less severe, paucibacillary, insidious. It picks the spine first (Pott's), then hip, then knee; within the spine dorso-lumbar beats dorsal beats lumbar, and children favour the cervical spine. The shoulder's dry 'caries sicca' and the fingers' air-filled 'spina ventosa' are the book's two named variants.

Pott's spine can strike four ways: paradiscally (the most common), centrally in the vertebral body, anteriorly - the wet exudative form of childhood - or posteriorly, the rarest of all. The paradiscal diagram lights up the para-vertebral bone and the disc between.

Paradiscal TB eats a three-bone sandwich: lower half of the upper vertebra, the disc, upper half of the lower vertebra - common somite, common sclerotome, common blood supply explain the triple hit. The lesion camps in front of the spinal cord, while the nerve slips out harmlessly through the intervertebral foramen.

The patient announces himself with low-grade fever, malaise, night pains and an evening temperature rise; the spine answers with back pain (earliest symptom) and paraspinal spasm (earliest sign). Spasm straightens the back into the military attitude with a cautious gait; collapse brings the cold abscess and a growing hump - one spinous process is a knuckle, two or three a gibbus, more than three an angular kyphosis.

The first X-ray whisper is narrowed disc space - disc destruction and dissection - later joined by a paravertebral abscess and vertebral lysis, but never by periosteal reaction, TB's tell-tale absence. MRI is the IOC, showing the disc and paradiscal disease in bone and cartilage; CT-guided biopsy remains the gold standard that names the organism. Left to itself, a neglected TB spine fuses into bony ankylosis - elsewhere in the body it fuses fibrously.

Pott's spine tightens its grip on the cord by three routes: granulation tissue pushing, inflammation swelling the cord, and a spinal artery thrombosis that can kill the cord within hours - rapid onset is the worst of the three. Early UMN signs (ankle clonus, exaggerated reflexes, extensor plantar) sound the alarm; bowel and bladder involvement late is the grave prognostic bell.

Prognosis runs on five dials: younger age, slow onset, early onset, short cord involvement (beyond 1 month is bad), and an active wet spine rather than a healed one. Compression by granulation tissue beats compression by bony deformity; the full recipe of older + rapid + late + longer + healed is the formula for despair.

The middle path: ATT for 18-24 months, rest and Taylor's brace. Improvement means continue; no improvement, neurological signs, or bowel-bladder sinking means to theatre - left anterolateral decompression, autologous bone grafting and spine stabilisation, with rib, transverse process, pedicle, vertebral body and affected disc all removed from the path of the cord.

Two lytic spine lesions, one disc as judge: on MRI a bad disc (involved) declares TB spine with good prognosis, a good disc (spared) declares metastasis with bad prognosis. On the plain film metastasis winks - the winking owl sign of a destroyed, absent pedicle.

TB hip opens quietly in the acetabulum and in Babcock's triangle, the immunologically weak patch of the femoral neck where monocytes and macrophages are deficient and the bacillus grows easily. The local story is a painful limb with antalgic gait, shortening and deformity.

Five stages from fluid to stone: I - synovitis, apparent lengthening, hip in flexion-abduction-external rotation as the distended capsule seeks ease; II - early arthritis, apparent shortening under 1 cm, hip swung to flexion-adduction-internal rotation; III - true shortening beyond 1 cm with cartilage loss; IV - small destroyed head against a large wandering acetabulum, the pestle and mortar; V - painful, unstable fibrous ankylosis.

Phemister's triad writes the X-ray: juxta-articular osteopenia first, peripheral osseous erosions, then narrowing of the joint space. Early treatment is ATT + rest + traction to save the head, with surgical decompression if it fails; late, deformity is corrected - total hip replacement is best (but wait 10-15 years for recurrence risk), Girdlestone excision when THA is contraindicated, or arthrodesis for the fixed hip.

The TB knee rests in 5-30 degrees of flexion - the position of ease for a joint that starts with synovitis and effusion. Late it locks into the PERF triple deformity: posterior subluxation of the knee, external rotation of the tibia, flexion of the knee. MRI (IOC) shows the synovitis, biopsy is gold standard; early ATT + rest + traction, late arthroplasty after 10-15 years or arthrodesis.

Margin notes that cross chapters: a non-healing sinus in chronic osteomyelitis means a sequestrum; no periosteal reaction in tubercular osteomyelitis; the spinous process is the vertebral part TB spares; paraplegia strikes the upper thoracic spine where the cord is thickest and easiest to compress. And Charcot's painless joint belongs to syphilis, DM and syringomyelia.

The child's bone is wetter, springier and wrapped in a thick periosteum: it bends rather than breaks, and the metaphysis can remodel deformities that would stay permanent in an adult. Water content, thick periosteum and remodeling potential are the paediatric skeleton's three gifts.

Bend the child's bone within physiological limits and it bows: the outer convex surface takes tension, the inner concave surface compression. Push past the limit and either the outer cortex breaks - a greenstick, like the stem of a growing tree, m/c in the radius, treated by osteoclasis of the intact cortex - or the inner surface buckles into a torus, a tubular cylinder at the base of a pillar, settled by a simple POP.
Three 'commonest' lines to hold: at birth the clavicle fractures, after a fall on an outstretched hand it is the supracondylar humerus, and overall the commonest fracture is still the clavicle.

A toddler's fracture is a spiral, undisplaced tibial fracture from a trivial accident; the thick periosteum supports it, the intact fibula lets the child still walk on it with a painful limp, and a POP cast is all it needs.

A shaken child leaves metaphyseal bruises - bucket handle fractures from violent to-and-fro shaking in children under 2, avulsing the capsule from the bone. Multiple fractures in different stages of healing, an inconsistent history with neglect, and long bone fractures in a non-ambulatory child send the X-ray scanogram out.

Growth marches from epiphysis to metaphysis through five layers: germinal (most important, the chondrocyte stem cells), proliferative, hypertrophic (weakest), calcification and ossification. Damage the germinal layer and you damage the future - at the knee, partial damage restricts the medial condyle and the leg bows into genu varus.

The Salter-Harris ladder starts gently: Type I splits the plate without touching the germinal layer (SCFE), and Type II - the m/c - adds a Thurston Holland metaphyseal fragment, as in supracondylar humerus fractures. Both spare the germinal layer, both grow normally on reduction, both carry a good prognosis.

From Type III upward the germinal layer burns: III runs toward the epiphysis (lower end of tibia), IV crosses every layer (lateral condyle of humerus) and both have a bad prognosis. Type V is the silent one - impaction crushes the plate, X-ray misses it, and it announces itself late as limb length discrepancy after a fall from height: the worst prognosis of all.

The wry neck starts as a birth injury to the SCM - breech, shoulder dystocia, forceps; ischemia turns the junction of its upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd, at the clavicular head, into a fibrotic cord. The head tilts, most often to the right; by 3 months the SCM tumor is palpable. Stretching corrects most cases themselves; miss the 1-year mark and it is surgical release - and an uncorrected year invites plagiocephaly. Acquired torticollis hides in vision problems and extra ocular muscle palsy.

In Sprengel's deformity the scapula never finished descending - an omovertebral bar held it - so it sits high and hypoplastic with a stiff shoulder, often alongside Klippel Feil's webbed neck. The Woodward operation frees it between 3 and 8 years; done after 8, neural traction injury becomes the new problem.

Klippel Feil is a segmentation defect of the cervical vertebrae: short webbed neck, low hair line, restricted movement, strong association with scoliosis. Madelung is the wrist's growth-plate failure: the distal radius stalls while the ulna keeps growing, the ulna crowds dorsally in the dinner fork deformity, and Darrach's procedure resects the terminal ulna.

Limb deficiency comes in three grades: amelia (both long and short bones absent - complete absence of limb), phocomelia (long bones absent, short bones present - thalidomide's signature), and hemi-melia, the longitudinal deficiency where the fibula is the m/c absentee (tibial hemimelia, or the absent radius of radial club hand). Holt-Oram, Fanconi, TAR and Vacter are its syndromic company.

Two rare pearls: cleidocranial dysostosis, with its skull and clavicle abnormality, congenitally absent clavicle and shoulders that can be brought close together; and Poland syndrome, the congenital absence of muscle, most often the pectoralis.

Two landmarks guard the child's hip: Shenton's line, arcing from the inferior margin of the superior pubic ramus to the medial head and neck - any pathology breaks it; and the neck-shaft angle, normal 130-135 degrees in adults, whose increase spells coxa valga and decrease coxa vara. The proximal femur carries a growth plate, its capital epiphysis being the head of the femoral epiphysis.

Injure the growth plate of the femoral head and the trochanter keeps growing while head and neck stop: the angle drops and coxa vara is born. It comes in infantile/primary and acquired/secondary forms (Perthes, SCFE), and the clinic tells the tale - Trendelenburg gait from failed abduction, obligate external rotation on flexion, limited abduction and internal rotation, and a shortened limb.
Congenital coxa vara traces back to damage of Fairbank's triangle, the vulnerable patch of the femoral neck. Do not confuse it: Babcock's triangle belongs to TB.

In SCFE the head stays home in the acetabulum while the neck slips - a Type I Salter-Harris fracture of the growth plate. It strikes boys at puberty (13-17 vs 11-14 for girls), overweight children, is idiopathic most often, and follows sex-hormone imbalance - hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, raised GH - which pushes bilaterality from 40% to 60%. Trethowan's line betrays it on the film: no longer cutting the head. Fix it: closed reduction, internal fixation, in situ pinning.

Osteochondrosis is a self-limiting, childhood, necrotic wobble of the epiphyseal ossification centres, sparked by a primary vascular event or repetitive trauma. Perthes (femoral epiphysis) is the m/c, then Kohler's (navicular), Freiberg's (lunate), Panner's (capitulum - elbow pain), Osgood-Schlatter (tibial tuberosity) and Sever's (calcaneal epiphysis).

Perthes - coxa plana, Legg-Calve-Perthes, Chandler's disease when it hits adults - is idiopathic spontaneous osteonecrosis. The femoral head drinks from two fountains: foveolar flow before 4, metaphyseal flow after 10; between 4 and 10 the supply shifts and the head stands exposed, so any insult lands as osteonecrosis.

Idiopathic and male, with protein S deficiency as its m/c association, 10-15% bilateral and a poor prognosis beyond age 6. It limps painlessly at first, pain later marching to the knee and groin, abduction and internal rotation stiff with obligate external rotors. MRI is the IOC (X-ray only shows late change); treatment sustains the head till vascularity resumes - no weight bearing, skin traction, Petrie/broomstick cast - and THA waits for skeletal maturity.

Once called congenital dislocation of the hip, DDH is idiopathic spontaneous subluxation of the femoral head from a flat, convex, shallow acetabulum - the head parked outside in utero. One in 1000 live births, girls over boys, left over right, 10% bilateral, favouring the first born breech female with a strong family history; Caucasians exceed Asians, perhaps because of how babies are carried.

Short limb, asymmetric thigh and gluteal folds, and Narath's absent femoral pulse against a present popliteal pulse under 3 months set the stage. Barlow (BAD) adducts and dislocates; Ortolani abducts and reduces the dislocated hip; Allis/Galeazzi finds the low knee in unilateral disease, and the Hilisic test speaks for bilateral DDH; the gait waddles and Trendelenburgs.

USG screens before 6 months; MRI confirms and plans. The child's acetabulum is triradiate cartilage of ilium, ischium and pubis, mapped by Hilgenreiner's line across its centres and Perkins' perpendicular off its lateral edge: the normal head sits in the inner, outer quadrant, the dysplastic head in the upper, outer.

The treatment clock: 0-6 months the Pavlik harness or von Rosen splint; 6-18 months open or closed reduction via Smith-Peterson approach; 18-36 months femoral osteotomy; beyond 3 years VDRO plus pelvic osteotomy (Salter, Pemberton); and past 10 years, total hip replacement after skeletal maturity.

Four shapes define the bowed child: genu varum bowing away from the midline, genu valgum knocking towards it, the windswept twist of one varus and one valgus leg, and genu recurvatum's excessive backward bend. In children rickets tops the list for varum and windswept while idiopathy wins for valgum; in adults osteoarthritis drives varum, rheumatoid arthritis drives valgum and windswept.

Blount's disease - infantile tibia vara - is bilateral idiopathic genu varum built on a proximal medial tibial physis defect, adding internal tibial rotation and genu recurvatum. Sifert Katz sign marks the clinic; metaphyseal beaking marks the film.

Acquired knee deformity follows malunion or growth plate injury, and the osteotomist corrects with wedges: open wedge lengthens the short side by filling extra bone, closed wedge shortens the long side by removing bone.

Three joints move the foot: the tibio-talar (ankle) plantar- and dorsiflexes, the subtalar inverts and everts, and the talonavicular with calcaneocuboid (mid tarsal) joints adduct and abduct the forefoot. The medial longitudinal arch gives the foot its concavity - lose it and it is flat, exaggerate it and it is cavus.

Ankle plantarflexion is equinus, dorsiflexion is calcaneus; subtalar inversion is varus, eversion is valgus.
