Talipes - the congenitally twisted foot - then names the combinations: cavus (high arch), equinus (plantarflexed), calcaneus (dorsiflexed), valgus (abducted, everted) and varus (adducted, inverted).

Club foot - CTEV, the m/c congenital abnormality of leg, ankle and foot, appearing like a golf club. One in 1000 live births, half bilateral, boys over girls, first born with breech presentation. The m/c form is congenital/primary and m/c idiopathic, but watch for spina bifida and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (muscle fibrosis to contracture to deformity); acquired club foot belongs to neuromuscular disorders like poliomyelitis.

A hypoplastic small talus displaces at the talonavicular joint, the foot destabilizes, and the Achilles and tibialis posterior pull it back and medially: talus in equinus and varus, calcaneus inverted, forefoot varus, ankle plantarflexed. The CAVE acronym maps it: Cavus (exaggerated medial arch), Adduction (talonavicular/mid tarsal), Varus (subtalar), Equinus (ankle) - with internal tibial rotation along for the ride.

Screen with the dorsiflexion test: the normal foot's dorsum touches the shin, the club foot will not dorsiflex even under strong pressure. Confirm with Kite's angle - the talocalcaneal angle, normally 30-40 degrees, collapsing to zero (parallel talus and calcaneum) in CTEV.

Start by 2 weeks and work Ponseti's order - Cavus, then Varus and Adduction, then Equinus - each manipulation held in an above-knee POP for a week, six to eight weeks overall, pivoting on the head of the talus. Kite's rival method starts at 1 month, corrects adduction-inversion then equinus on the calcaneocuboid fulcrum, below-knee casting for 6-9 months. Overcorrect and you make a rocker bottom foot, as does congenital vertical talus.

Recurrence is the enemy: the Dennis Brown splint works till the baby walks (and suffers low compliance), then CTEV shoes take over up to 3-5 years - worn at least 23 hours a day with the splint at sleep. The shoe is engineered against relapse: straight inner border against adduction, outer raise against varus, absent heel against equinus.

The late club foot stiffens with age and the surgery follows the clock: 1-3 years posteromedial soft tissue release with or without Ponseti manipulation (Turco releases the Achilles, tibialis posterior and FDL); 3-5 years, forefoot adduction turned bony, gets AMSTR plus Dilwyn Evans' calcaneocuboid fusion; 5-8 years, varus turned bony, adds Dwyer's wedge osteotomy; 6-10 years wedge tarsectomy; and beyond 10, triple arthrodesis fusing talonavicular, talocalcaneal and calcaneocuboid - which done before 10 fails to pseudoarthrosis. Josh's external stabilization system, on Ilizarov's principle, stands ready for deformity correction.

Achondroplasia, the m/c disproportionate dwarfism, is an FGFR3 mutation on chromosome 4 - autosomal dominant or sporadic - that blocks endochondral but not intramembranous ossification. Rhizomelic shortening with a normal trunk, normal IQ and sexual development; the face gives frontal bossing and saddle nose, the hands a starfish or trident span, the spine bullet-nose vertebrae, the pelvis a champagne glass. Shortening terminology: middle limb mesomelic, distal acromelic.

The spine is musculoskeletal (vertebral column) and neurological (cord plus roots). Four zones of vertebrae - cervical, thoracic/dorsal, lumbar, sacral - are joined by discs of annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus that segment the spine for mobility and absorb shock. Fracture the pars inter-articularis and it is spondylolysis; let it slip and spondylolisthesis follows, while the articular facets keep the spine aligned.

Denis splits the vertebra into three columns: anterior (anterior longitudinal ligament, anterior annulus, anterior 2/3rd of body), middle (posterior 1/3rd of body, posterior annulus, posterior longitudinal ligament) and posterior (pedicles, facets, lamina, spinous process with posterior ligaments). One column hurt means stable and conservative; two or more columns down means unstable and it goes to fixation surgery.

Fractures cluster at T12; dislocations haunt the cervical spine, where ligamentous stabilizers outweigh bony ones and the facets sit horizontally. In the lumbar region the vertical facets favour fracture over dislocation - and a cervical fracture carries the highest spinal cord injury risk. First aid: onto the back, support behind the neck, transport to the nearest hospital.

Jefferson's fracture - the m/c C1 (atlas) fracture - is axial loading bursting fragments outward away from the canal, so neurological deficits are spared. The open-mouth view and CT (best) display it; a stable ring is treated conservatively, while a torn transverse ligament demands atlanto-occipital fusion.

C2 fractures are odontoid (the m/c of C2) or Hangman's - a fracture of the C2 pars inter-articularis, spondylolysis of C2, that lets C2 dislocate over C3. Despite the violence, the cord usually spares the patient neurological deficit; RTA tops hanging as the m/c cause.

Whiplash is a soft tissue snap - hyperextension into flexion - leaving chronic neck pain with no deficits and normal X-ray/CT; a cervical collar settles it. Clay Shoveler's is the muscular twin: a shoveller's strong paraspinal and upper limb contraction avulses the C7 spinous process.

Dr. G.G. Chance's seat-belt (jack-knife) fracture is a complete transverse split - bony Chance through the vertebra, soft tissue Chance through ligament and disc. A lap belt without shoulder harness flexes the lumbar spine, transecting the cord through all three columns: an unstable fracture that paraplegises and demands stabilization and surgery.

Compression fractures are osteoporosis's flexion-compression wedge: the anterior column shortens, the posterior column holds. Burst fractures are significant trauma's axial loading: the anterior and posterior walls both bow convex. Different villains, different films.

SCIWORA - spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality - is the child's privilege of pliable bone: bone elasticity exceeds cord elasticity, the bone stretches, the cord does not, and paraplegia or quadriplegia arrives with no fracture on X-ray or CT. Only MRI confesses the injury.

Spinal shock is the temporary complete cessation of spinal cord function below the injury: anesthesia, flaccid paralysis, lost bowel and bladder control, silent reflexes. Recovery takes 24-48 hours to weeks, and the bulbocavernosus reflex - S2, S3, S4, elicited by tugging the Foley catheter till the anal sphincter contracts - is the first to return, marking the shock's end.

Neurogenic shock is the circulatory arm of spinal shock: loss of sympathetic outflow unleashes hyperactive parasympathetic tone, the heart bradycardias, vessels dilate, resistance falls, blood pools peripherally and pressure sinks. Contrast it with hemorrhagic shock, where blood loss buys a reflex tachycardia instead.

The cord climbs with the child: ending at the lower border of L3 at birth, it retreats to the upper border of L1 in the adult, throwing up brachial and lumbosacral bulges. Seven cervical vertebrae serve eight nerve pairs (thoracic and sacral twelve and five each); the cone-shaped conus medullaris caps the cord while the cauda equina tuft of roots drifts below, each root exiting under its own segment's pedicle.

L1 is the watershed: above it, cord (UMNL); below it, roots (LMNL). Above the lesion everything is normal either way; at the level, LMNL flaccidises with absent reflexes; below, UMNL spasms with exaggerated reflexes while LMNL keeps functioning normally - because the UMNL's inhibitory hand on the LMNL has been removed.

Every root owns a dermatome of skin, a myotome of muscle and a reflex. The myotome ladder runs C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension with wrist flexion, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction, then L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 toe extension, S1 ankle plantarflexion.
The reflex map: C5 biceps, C6 supinator (brachioradialis), C7 triceps, L3-L4 knee, S1 ankle. And the diaphragm breathes on C3, C4, C5 - an injury above C3 endangers the breath itself.
PIVD is a protrusion of the disc compressing the cord or nerves, most often at L4-L5, then L5-S1. Remember the jelly nucleus (type II collagen) wrapped in the tough fibrous annulus (type I collagen).

Abnormal loading and degeneration of the spine set the stage for a four-step cascade: degeneration → prolapse (bulging nucleus pulposus) → extrusion (AF breaks, NP comes out) → sequestration (extruded NP breaks away).

Canal stenosis comes from PIVD or from excessive abnormal bone growth of vertebral degeneration in OA, most often in the lumbar region. Contrast it with PIVD: stenosis is elderly and chronic, PIVD is young and acute.
Far lateral prolapse hits the exiting nerve root, while the common paracentral type impinges the traversing root. The most commonly injured nerve is L5, giving a lower motor neuron lesion picture.

Think heavy lifting history, low back ache and sciatica — back pain radiating to the lower limb that worsens with flexion, sneezing, coughing and prolonged sitting. PIVD is the most common cause of sciatica.

SLRT is positive when the hip cannot flex beyond 30-35° because raising the leg stretches the compressed nerve and produces pain. MRI is the IOC, and the neurological exam localizes the lesion by the nerve roots involved.

Climb the myotome ladder: C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension & wrist flexion, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction, then L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 toe extension, S1 ankle plantar flexion. Reflexes: C5 biceps, C6 supinator, C7 triceps, L3-4 knee, S1 ankle.
Conservative care is simple: rest in semi-fowler position (supine with 30-40° flexion of spine) plus physiotherapy.

Operate with total/hemi-laminectomy or laminotomy + discectomy when symptoms worsen despite conservative Rx, bowel & bladder are involved, a massive central prolapse compresses multiple roots, or cauda equina syndrome develops.

Conus (spinal cord, nucleus of Onuf S2; injury at L1) gives UMNL with LMNL features, symmetric areflexic flaccid paralysis and a normal knee reflex. Cauda (spinal nerves; large disc below L1) gives asymmetric LMNL with lost knee reflex. Both share saddle anaesthesia, bowel & bladder involvement and a lost ankle reflex.
LCS runs a straight line: spondylosis (OA of facet joints) → excessive bone formation → stenosis of the lumbar canal → neurogenic claudication.

LCS pain eases with flexion (sitting, leaning over, climbing upstairs) and worsens with extension (walking, standing upright). Neurogenic claudication starts in the back, is caused by standing and relieved by climbing stairs, with postural changes and normal pulses; vascular starts in the calf, is relieved by standing, caused by climbing, and has abnormal pulses.
LCS: elderly, slow & progressive onset, pain decreases on flexion. PIVD: young, acute onset, pain increases on flexion.
Spondylolisthesis is slipping of one vertebra over another, caused by trauma/fracture of the pars interarticularis.
On the scottie dog: spondylolisthesis loses its head (beheaded scottish terrier, m/c L5-S1), while spondylolysis wears a collar (scottish terrier with collar sign, m/c L5).
Meyerding grades by percentage of slip: I 0-25%, II 26-50%, III 51-75%, IV 76-100%, and V beyond 100% — that is spondyloptosis.

Back pain radiates to the lower limbs and palpation reveals the step sign — step off over the spinous process. Don't mix the -lo- words: spondylosis = degeneration (elderly), spondylitis = inflammation (AS), and spondyloptosis wears the inverted Napoleon hat sign.

AS is autoimmune: males > females, young, HLA-B27 (+), RF (-), with enthesopathy as the pathology. Sacroiliitis is the hallmark, morning stiffness improves with activity, and anterior uveitis is the classic association. On X-ray: bamboo spine (vertical syndesmophyte fusion) plus trolley track and dagger signs from ligament calcification.
DISH (Forestier disease) ossifies the anterior longitudinal ligament in the elderly. OPLL favours the cervical spine, also in the elderly — DISH is front, OPLL is back.

Scoliosis is lateral deviation of the spine by more than 10° from the central axis. The primary curvature is the largest curve; secondary curvatures are the smaller compensatory curves above and below it.

Spinal column deviation can be lateral, sagittal (forward bending) or rotational. Structural scoliosis is fixed and persists on bending forward; non-structural (postural/compensatory) has no rotational component and disappears on Adam's forward bending test — the screening test that separates the two.

Idiopathic (m/c, no visible anomaly) splits into infantile, juvenile and adolescent (m/c). Congenital scoliosis shows a visible anomaly → deformity with wedge, hemi, unsegmented bar or block vertebrae; neuromuscular is the third category.

Shoulder asymmetry, a laterally deviated spine and the rib hump of rotational abnormality; the deformity crowds the ribs and compresses thoracic and abdominal structures. Severity is measured by Cobb's angle between the abnormal vertebrae at both ends of the primary curvature.

The Risser sign gauges progression potential (proportional to growth potential — high in children, low in adults) and skeletal maturity by fusion of the iliac apophysysis with the iliac crest: grades 1-4 are 25/50/75/100% lateral ossification and grade 5 is complete fusion with the ilium.

Treatment hinges on severity & prognosis: low Cobb's + high Risser → braces (Milwaukee = cervical-thoraco-lumbo-sacral, Boston = thoraco-lumbo-sacral, Charleston); high Cobb's + low Risser → pedicle screw fixation with Harrington rods engaging all 3 spinal columns. Incidence is females > males, but prognosis is males > females.
Anatomy of a Joint & OA vs RA Joints

The knee joint has distal femur, synovium, articular cartilage on the articular surface of bone, joint capsule, synovial fluid and proximal tibia; damage to that cartilage makes every movement hurt. OA loves DIP, PIP and the 1st CMC (spares wrist & MCP), while RA loves MCP, wrist and PIP (spares DIP).
Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disease, born of age related degeneration or preexisting destruction of cartilage.

Primary idiopathic OA rules the single-joint knee (also spine, hand) and the generalized DIP. Secondary OA rides on preexisting pathology: intra articular trauma, developmental anomaly, AVN and overweight.

Cartilage degenerates, raw bone rubs on bone (pain + sclerosis), poor blood supply makes necrotic cysts, regenerating bone throws off osteophytes — and when those break loose, loose bodies roam freely in the joint.

OA hurts on active and passive movement, stiffens the joint, crepitates and deforms. Disuse withers the muscle — most often the vastus medialis. Bouchard's (PIP) and Heberden's (DIP) nodes mark the knuckles.

On X-ray: decreased joint space, bone-on-bone appearance, subchondral sclerosis, necrotic cysts & osteophytes and loose bodies. The medial side carries the load, so the space narrows medially first, bowing the leg into varus — OA is the m/c cause of bilateral genu varum.
Loose bodies in the knee: osteoarthritis is the m/c cause overall and in the elderly; osteochondritis dissecans wins in the young; and synovial chondromatosis makes multiple bodies.

Conservative care: lose weight to stop progression, physiotherapy with heat and strengthening exercises, walk with support and brace. Medications: NSAID acetaminophen, cartilage protectors (glucosamine, chondroitin sulphate) early on, and hyaluronic acid injections for lubrication.

Go definitive with arthroscopy (joint wash to remove loose bodies), high tibial/medial opening wedge osteotomy to correct varus deformity and pain, or arthroplasty to replace the damaged joint — unicondylar for the medial side, or TKR with femoral and tibial components (watch for patellar clunk syndrome).

THR replaces the head & neck of the femur plus the acetabular component. Then RA enters: the m/c inflammatory arthritis, a disease of synovium — systemic autoimmune, multisystem (lungs, heart, liver), erosive, females > males, symmetrical peripheral joints: MCP > wrist, PIP in the hand, knee and hip; axial rare (cervical spine); DIP spared. SLE is the only non-erosive inflammatory arthritis.
An antigen/antibody reaction ignites synovial inflammation and destruction, erosion marches from periphery to centre, pannus forms and devours the joint, and the sequence ends in subluxation.

RA shortens life expectancy and travels to the heart (carditis), pleura (pleuritis), lungs (Caplan) and blood (Felty). Diagnose with ↑ ESR/CRP, RF — the most sensitive marker, an IgM against the Fc portion of IgG — and Anti-CCP, the most specific.

RA X-ray: narrowed joint space, osteoporosis & hyperemia (juxta articular first, then generalized), marginal erosions, and no sclerosis, no osteophytes. Opposite of OA, which scleroses. De Quervain's synovitis targets the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

The RA hand deviates ulnarly at the fingers while the metacarpals deviate radially; boutonniere is PIP flexion with DIP extension, swan neck the reverse; mallet finger affects only the injured digit. The knee bows into bilateral genu valgum (children: rickets > RA; elderly: RA), wind swept and triple deformity. The foot shows hammer toes and hallux valgus; ulnar nerve palsy makes the claw hand.

Preserve function with physiotherapy; methotrexate is the DOC. DMARDs: leflunomide (immunosuppressant), infliximab/Adalimumab (TNF-α inhibitors), anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), rituximab (anti-CD20). Surgery: synovectomy for inflamed synovium, joint replacement and deformity corrections.

Four inflammatory spondyloarthropathies hit the spine and joints: ankylosing spondylitis (m/c), psoriatic, enteropathic (Crohn's/ulcerative colitis) and reactive (Shigella, chlamydia). All are seronegative (RA is RF positive), hit young males, run HLA B27 positive and accompany uveitis.

AS — Marie Strumpell/Bechterew's disease — is male-predominant, axial > peripheral, centred on the sacroiliac joint (also spine, hip). Gluteal/back pain with morning stiffness that improves with activity, ↓ lumbar movement, ↓ chest expansion (ribs fuse to spine) and anterior uveitis. Enthesitis at the ligament-tendon insertions erodes, regenerates abnormally and calcifies, restricting motion; first X-ray sign is sacroiliitis with sclerosis and ankylosis.

The bamboo spine fuses and squares the vertebrae with calcification between them: ligament inflammation builds syndesmophytes, curvature is lost, and bridging syndesmophytes lock the spine. The dagger sign calcifies the interspinous ligament; the trolley track sign calcifies paraspinal and interspinous ligaments.

Essential criterion: sacroiliitis — MRI is the IOC (earliest changes, iliac side > sacral side); supporting criteria add ↓ lumbar movement, ↓ chest expansion and inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness. Test with chest expansion measurement, Gaenslen's, FABER/figure-of-4 and pump handle for SI, and Schober for the lumbar spine (distance fails to increase on flexion). Treat with chest physiotherapy, swimming/cycling, NSAIDs and steroids.

When the spine fuses, think beyond AS: DISH (Forestier disease, elderly) flows candle-wax ossification down the anterior longitudinal ligament, while OPLL ossifies the posterior longitudinal ligament, m/c cervical, also in the elderly.

Psoriatic arthritis is erosive, females > males, asymmetrical oligoarticular, m/c at the DIP. CASPAR: psoriasis, RF -ve, X-ray changes, dactylitis (sausage digits), nail changes. Destructive ends: arthritis mutilans (total bone destruction) and the pencil-in-cup phalanx, with digits shortening and telescoping out.

Treat the psoriasis and give methotrexate. Hemophilia: A = factor 8 deficiency, B = factor 9 deficiency; recurrent bleeding destroys the synovium with inflammation. Pseudo tumors are muscle hematomas (iliopsoas > quadriceps) and painful joint swelling bleeds into the joint, m/c the knee.

The hemophilic knee rests flexed — its position of ease — and can end in arthritis mutilans. X-ray: widened intracondylar notch, lost joint space, juxta articular osteopenia, squared patella. Treat the bleed: factor replacement, compression bandage, ice pack; aspirate only for severe pain (infection risk).

Gout, the m/c crystal arthropathy, is a purine abnormality with raised uric acid (normal 3.5-6.5 mg/dl), striking the 1st MTP of middle-aged men; furosemide and aspirin precipitate attacks. A sudden uric acid swing drops crystals in cold peripheral joints, ignites local inflammation and damages the joint — tophi mark the acute attack.

X-ray: punched out lesion, joint destruction, overhanging bone (martel sign). The best investigation is synovial fluid analysis under light microscopy: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals.
Acute attack: only NSAIDs (indomethacin; aspirin is C/I) — colchicine brings GI disturbances. Never chase uric acid levels during an acute attack; it can precipitate more pain.

Chronic gout: xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat, rasburicase) and the uricosuric probenecid. Pseudogout deposits calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate — elderly, females > males, a/w hypothyroidism, m/c the knee; X-ray shows chondrocalcinosis (also in ochronosis/alkaptonuria, hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism) and the fluid holds polygonal, positively birefringent crystals.

The Charcot joint destroys itself silently — lost sensation and proprioception, m/c from diabetic peripheral neuropathy, favouring mid tarsal then tarso metatarsal joints (leprosy, syphilis-knee also). Look for a bag of bones, without pain. Fuse it with arthrodesis; arthroplasty is C/I.

u: Basic anatomy of the eyeball — shape, volume, site, axial length and the orbit

The chapter opens with four headline values of the eyeball: shape is aspherical (oblate spheroid), volume 6 ml, site the orbit (a bony cage), and axial length/antroposterior diameter 24 mm (2.4 cm). The 'Orbit containing eyeball' figure labels four structures of the orbit — the roof, the lateral wall, the medial wall and the floor — around the globe.
Outermost coat — cornea, limbus and sclera

The outermost layer has three components: the anterior 1/6th is the cornea (transparent, convex shaped, refractive power present), the limbus is the corneo-scleral junction, and the posterior 5/6th is the sclera (white, opaque, covered by the conjunctiva — a transparent mucous membrane). The anterior eye photograph labels the sclera, limbus and the iris with the pupil, both 'seen below cornea'.
Uveal tract and retina — middle and innermost coats

The middle layer is the uveal tract — explicitly labelled the vascular layer — with parts (anterior and posterior): a. iris, b. ciliary body, c. choroid. The innermost layer is the retina, a neurosensory layer that is present only posteriorly, not over the whole globe.
Structural anatomy — chambers, ciliary body and eye segments

The 'Structural anatomy of eyeball' cross-section labels the angle of AC, iris, pupil, zonules (ciliary zonules) and lens. The ciliary body has a pleated pars plicata, a flat pars plana (most avascular in uvea) and ciliary processes that secrete aqueous. The anterior chamber (AC) lies between cornea and iris, the anterior segment (AS) contains aqueous humour, and the posterior segment contains the vitreous — 1% hyaluronic acid with a gel-like consistency.
Aqueous humour — secretion, outflow and IOP

Aqueous humour is a fluid secreted from the ciliary processes at 2.3 µL/minute. Its function is to exert the intraocular pressure (IOP), measured by tonometry. Aqueous outflow is 0.25 µL/min/mm Hg, occurs via the angle of the AC (depth 3 mm, range 2.5–4.4 mm) and is measured by tonography — the tonometry-versus-tonography distinction is the key exam trap on this page.
Neurovascular supply of the cornea and the corneal blink reflex

The chapter opens with the cornea's avascularity (hence transparency), relative index 1.376 and converging refractive power +43D to +48D, then the sensory chain Trigeminal → Ophthalmic → Nasociliary → Cornea. The corneal blink reflex (stimulus: touch cornea with cotton wisp) runs afferent CN V → trigeminal nucleus → facial nucleus → efferent CN VII → orbicularis oculi → blinking; a broken efferent gives Bell's palsy with lagophthalmos, while no blinking marks corneal anaesthesia (causes: herpes keratitis m/c, diabetes, leprosy, topical medications ex. timolol, Acanthamoeba keratitis, contact lens wear, surgical trauma).
Corneal epithelial histology, layer thicknesses and the outermost/innermost table

The epithelial histology figure gives superficial squamous cells with microvilli (tear-film adhesion), middle wing-shaped cells and basal columnar cells that undergo mitosis and regenerate. The layers figure prints epithelium 50-80 µm, epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer 8-14 µm, stroma 490 µm, Dua's layer 0.5-13.9 µm, Descemet's membrane 10-12 µm and endothelium 5 µm, tagged can-regenerate (epithelium, Descemet's), thickest (stroma), strongest (Dua's). The epithelium is non-keratinized stratified squamous, and the outermost/innermost table is read with respect to the centre of the eyeball: cornea outermost anteriorly/innermost posteriorly, retina the reverse.
Bowman's membrane and the three grades of corneal opacity

Bowman's membrane is not a true basement membrane (so PAS — Periodic Acid Schiff — negative), is acellular, cannot regenerate and heals by scar formation causing corneal opacity and loss of vision. The opacity table grades nebular (faint: pupillary margin and iris details visible, maximum light, diffraction with distortion of image), macular (pupillary margin visible, iris details not visible) and leukomatous (most dense: both not visible, minimum light, rays don't cross the opacity, loss of vision).
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane, endothelium and specular microscopy

Stroma: thickest layer (90% of corneal thickness), type I collagen with keratan sulfate as the m/c GAG. Dua's layer / pre-Descemet's membrane is the strongest layer. Descemet's membrane is secreted continuously by endothelial cells and can regenerate; Schwalbe's line is its peripheral termination at the limbus near the anterior trabecular meshwork. Endothelium is the most metabolically active layer; zona occludens block aqueous entry, and breach causes oedema with haze/opacity. Specular microscopy: 3000 cells/mm² normal hexagonal mosaic, 2400 cells/mm² small breach compensated by polymegathism and polymorphism, 500 cells/mm² irregularities and large cavity = corneal decompensation from extended contact lens wear.
Sclera — extent, variable thickness, layers, scleritis versus episcleritis

The sclera covers the posterior 5/6th of the eyeball and is white d/t irregular collagen arrangement. Thickness varies: limbus 0.83 mm, thinnest posterior to the insertion of recti, thickest around the optic nerve. Layers: episclera (outermost, two vascular plexuses, merges with Tenon's capsule ~3 mm posterior to limbus), sclera propria (avascular collagen), lamina fusca (innermost). Scleritis (a misnomer) inflames the deep vascular plexus of the episclera with a bluish/violaceous hue and redness that remains after 2.5% phenylephrine; episcleritis inflames the superficial plexus, is idiopathic m/c, reddish, blanches on the test, and is managed supportively with NSAIDs and low-dose steroids.
Types of scleritis, scleromalacia perforans and the limbus

Scleritis splits into non-necrotizing and necrotizing; necrotizing further divides into with inflammation and without inflammation — the latter being scleromalacia perforans (m/c in women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, atrophy d/t inflammation, only deep bluish vessels, no pain, no congestion). The limbus is the corneo-scleral junction holding pleuripotent limbal stem cells (universal marker CD34, specific marker ABCG2) in the palisades of Vogt; their deficiency causes pterygium, treated by excision with a limbal stem cell autograft.
Components of the uvea and the anatomy of the iris

The uvea table splits iris plus ciliary-body pars plicata into anterior uvea (anterior uveitis), pars plana into intermediate uvea (intermediate uveitis) and choroid into posterior uvea (posterior uveitis). The iris is highly vascular, pigmented d/t melanocytes and of variable thickness; its thickest part is the collarette (boundary of pupillary and ciliary zones) and its thinnest part the root — the site of iridodialysis. Sphincter pupillae (miosis, parasympathetic inhibitory via CN III, final short ciliary nerve) opposes dilator pupillae (mydriasis, sympathetic excitatory: hypothalamus → C8-T1 ciliospinal centre → superior cervical ganglion → long ciliary nerve), with Pancoast tumour resection flagged as a risk to the SCG fibres.
Oculomotor branches, Horner's syndrome — neuron orders and HI MAPLE features

The oculomotor nerve's superior branch supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris; the inferior branch supplies inferior rectus and inferior oblique. Horner's syndrome is oculosympathetic palsy. First-order (central) causes: brainstem lesions, syringomyelia, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Wallenberg syndrome; second-order (preganglionic): Pancoast tumour, carotid and aortic aneurysm, neck lesions; third-order (postganglionic): cluster headache, ICA dissection, otitis media, cavernous sinus mass. Features run by the mnemonic HI MAPLE — heterochromia iridis (ipsilateral hypochromia, congenital cases only), inferior eyelid elevation (inferior tarsal muscle), miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis (Muller's muscle), loss of ciliospinal reflex and relative enophthalmos.
Diagnosing and localising Horner's syndrome — cocaine, apraclonidine and amphetamine tests

Muller's (superior tarsal) muscle and the CN III-supplied LPS elevate the eyelid. Detection: the cocaine test blocks NE reuptake — a normal pupil dilates, Horner's does not (no NE released); 1% apraclonidine keeps normal α2 > α1 selectivity but dilates Horner's through α1 denervation hypersensitivity (mushrooming). Localisation: 1% amphetamine (hydroxyamphetamine) releases NE into the cleft — dilatation places the lesion centrally or preganglionically, no dilatation post-ganglionically. The section photograph shows relative enophthalmos with right eye ptosis.
Pupil-size mnemonics, ciliary body functions and the mechanics of accommodation

Mydriasis causes run ITS COMB (internal ophthalmoplegia, tonic pupil/Holmes-Adie, sympathomimetics, closure-angle glaucoma, oculomotor palsy, mydriatics, belladonna poisoning); miosis causes run HI COPS (Horner's, pontine hemorrhage, iridocyclitis, clonidine, carbolic acid, organophosphates/opioids, parasympathomimetics, sleep/sedatives). The ciliary body secretes aqueous through its ciliary processes, offers the relatively avascular pars plana as the vitreous entry site, and accomplishes accommodation by contracting its muscles (↑ lens power) while relaxing the zonules. The near reflex = accommodation + convergence + miosis; far vision keeps muscles relaxed with tense zonules and a flat anterior surface, near vision contracts the muscles (↓ ring diameter), slackens zonules and raises anterior curvature, A-P diameter and lens power.
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia, spectacle types and spasm of accommodation

Presbyopia is physiological insufficiency of accommodation with onset around 40 years; correction is convex (+) spectacles, +1 D at 40 years and +0.5 D for every further 5 years, preferring progressives > D-bifocals >>> executive lenses. Monofocals suit patients needing only near vision (central hourglass power, restricted field), progressives give seamless near-intermediate-far coverage, D-bifocals lack intermediate vision and executive bifocals bisect the pupil and survive only in paediatric aphakia. Spasm of accommodation — continuous ciliary contraction — causes loss of far vision (pseudomyopia) and is treated with cycloplegic mydriatics: atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate.
Optic disc — the blind spot, its dimensions and the neuro-retinal rim

The retina is the innermost, neurosensory layer of the eye. The optic disc (OD) is the blind spot of Marriot (rods and cones absent), where all retinal layers terminate except the nerve fibres; it is the first, only visible and intra-ocular part of the optic nerve and the point where the nerve leaves the eyeball. Appearance: vertically oval, 1.5 mm (1500 µm) across, normal c/d ratio 0.3. The figure relation d(OD) = C (optic cup) + NRR (neuro-retinal rim) allows vessels to travel through, and NRR thickness runs Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal, becoming visibly thinner in glaucoma.
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and the ora serrata

The macula lutea is a yellowish spot temporal to the optic disc, 5.5 mm across. Within it the fovea (1.85 mm) carries the maximum concentration of cones and therefore the highest/best visual acuity (central vision); the foveola lacks a ganglionic layer; the umbo is the small central depression whose reflection of shone light is the foveolar reflex. The ora serrata is the anterior termination of the retina, marking the junction between ciliary body and choroid, and its significance is helping determine the site of intra-vitreal injection.
Routes of ocular drug administration — intravitreal, intracameral, topical, subconjunctival and sub-Tenon's

Intravitreal injection site depends on lens status: aphakia 3 mm, pseudophakia 3.5 mm, phakia 4 mm posterior to the limbus (the visible landmark), piercing sclera and pars plana; the procedure runs speculum → sterilise sclera infero-temporally → look upwards/inwards → caliper marking → 30G needle with slow twisting movements. Intracameral injection enters the anterior chamber (e.g. after a cataract incision). Topical is m/c used: drops before ointment, ointment ≥3 minutes after drops for longer contact. Subconjunctival and parabulbar/posterior sub-Tenon (PST, Nozik technique, below Tenon's capsule, used in intermediate uveitis) complete the list; episclera and Tenon's capsule fuse 3 mm posterior to the limbus.
Local ocular anaesthesia — lower-lid route, peribulbar versus retrobulbar, orbital anatomy

Local anaesthesia enters through the lower eyelid at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds: pull the lid down, pass a 24-25G needle along the floor of the eye, aspirate to rule out vessel injury, inject 5 ml and compress to avoid an IOP rise. Peribulbar (extraconal) is the better route; retrobulbar is intraconal. The orbital base is quadrangular and vessel-rich (hemorrhage risk) while the apex is conical; the annulus of Zinn is the tendinous ring origin of all EOMs except the inferior oblique; angles X (medial-lateral walls) and Y (both lateral walls) complete the figure.
Optic nerve — definition, total length and the four parts

The optic nerve collects the axons of retinal ganglion cells and measures 47-50 mm. Its parts: intraocular (disc) 1 mm — the shortest; intraorbital 25-30 mm — the longest, acquiring the myelin sheath and receiving the central retinal artery and vein 10 mm behind the eye inferomedially; intracanalicular 9 mm within the optic canal; intracranial 10-15 mm.
Blood supply of the eye — ophthalmic artery branches and the arterial circles

Internal carotid → ophthalmic artery → central retinal artery (inner 6 retinal layers, enters the ON); posterior ciliary arteries split into long posterior ciliary (pierces away from the ON, runs between sclera and choroid to the ciliary body and ciliary muscle, then anteriorly to the iris forming the major arterial circle for the ciliary process and the minor circle for the pupillary zone) and short posterior ciliary (pierce around the ON, supplying sclera, choroid and outer retina); seven muscular branches (2 SR, 2 MR, 2 IR, 1 LR) whose medial rectus branches form the anterior ciliary artery, piercing anteriorly behind the limbus to supply anterior sclera, ciliary process, iris and conjunctiva.
Development of the eye — timing, optic vesicle and lens placode, and the four derivative lists

Eye development begins on day 22 (end of week 3): downward growth gives elevations, deepening and the optic groove/sulcus (earliest indication), then evagination to optic vesicles. From day 27 lateral growth and lens formation begin: surface ectoderm thickens into the lens placode, the lens vesicle depresses and is engulfed by the optic vesicle, the placode pinches off, and the choroidal fissure closes by the 6th-7th week. Mesenchyme comes from mesoderm plus neural crest (superficial fibrous and deep vascular). Derivatives: surface ectoderm (lens, eyelid skin, corneal/conjunctival epithelium, tarsal glands), neural ectoderm (optic nerve, retina, vitreous, iris+CB epithelium, sphincter and dilator), neural crest (uvea, sclera, Descemet's, ciliary muscle), mesoderm (EOMs, vessel endothelium).
Coloboma — eyeball, eyelid and lens variants

Coloboma etymologically means a missing, mutilated part. Eyeball coloboma is a congenital malformation from non-closure of the choroidal fissure, affecting deep-mesenchyme derivatives (iris, ciliary body) and OV/OS derivatives (choroid, retina, optic nerve); typical coloboma lies infero-nasally (pear-shaped/key hole pupil) and atypical elsewhere; retino-choroidal (fundal) coloboma raises retinal-detachment risk and follows the Ida Mann classification. Eyelid coloboma is NOT fissure-related — an incomplete facial cleft/cryptophthalmos, m/c on the upper lid between middle and medial thirds, associated with Fraser, Goldenhar and Treacher Collins syndromes, and prevented from causing cosmetic blemish, exposure keratopathy and amblyopia by eyelid reconstruction. Lens coloboma is not a true coloboma: a large lens placode cannot pass the fissure and defective zonules notch the inferior lens.
The visual pathway — which fibres travel at each station

The retina generates visual impulses and the occipital cortex perceives the image; any lesion in between yields a visual field defect. Field-fibre mapping: nasal visual field → temporal fibres, temporal visual field → nasal fibres. The optic nerve carries I/L temporal + I/L nasal fibres; the optic chiasm is where nasal fibres cross, so it contains B/L nasal fibres; optic tract, LGB (the relay centre) and optic radiations (superior and inferior fibres) all carry I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres onward to the visual cortex.
Lesions 1-3 — optic nerve, optic chiasm and the junctional scotoma

All features are described for left-sided lesions. Optic nerve (I/L temporal + I/L nasal) → I/L anopia; macular/central fibres are most susceptible to ischemia and fail first, so the earliest defect is an ipsilateral central scotoma. Chiasmal: B/L nasal → bitemporal/heteronymous hemianopia (causes: 3rd ventricular glioma, pituitary adenoma from the sella inferiorly, craniopharyngioma from Rathke's pouch superiorly, ACA aneurysm with the chiasm under the ACA, carotid sinus thrombosis laterally); B/L inferonasal → bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia (earliest in pituitary adenoma); B/L superonasal → bitemporal superior quadrantanopia (earliest in craniopharyngioma). Junction of ON and OC (proximal ON, anterior knee of Wilbrand): I/L temporal + I/L nasal + C/L inferonasal → junctional scotoma, caused by meningioma.
Lesions 4-10 — lateral chiasm, tract/LGB/radiations, loops and the occipital cortex

Lateral chiasma (B/L temporal) → binasal hemianopia, very rare. Lesions 5 (OT), 6 (LGB), 7 (OR) → C/L homonymous hemianopsia. Superior OR (Meyer's loop) → C/L homonymous superior quadrantanopia, 'pie in the sky', mnemonic TIPS (Temporal Inferior Pie in the Sky), with temporal lobe features (uncinate fits, seizures, visual hallucinations). Inferior OR (Baum's loop) → C/L homonymous inferior quadrantanopia, 'pie on the floor', with parietal features (aphasia, acalculia, agraphia, apraxia if non-dominant). Occipital tip (macular representation) → C/L homonymous macular defect, 'cookie centre'; visual cortex except tip → C/L homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing; a complete occipital lesion gives C/L homonymous hemianopia and is rare.
Comparing tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects

OT/LGB/OR comparison: pupil abnormal (Wernicke's pupil) only in OT lesions; optic atrophy present bilaterally in OT (I/L superior and inferior, C/L bow-tie), present (+) in LGB, absent in OR (radiations are post-ganglionic); congruity incongruous for OT and LGB but congruous for OR; OT lesions associate with C/L hemiplegia and CN III palsy, caused by TB/syphilitic meningitis and PCA aneurysm; the LGB has 6 laminae — C/L fibres relay into 1, 4, 6 and I/L into 2, 3, 5. Miscellaneous: keyhole VFD from an incomplete LGB lesion; altitudinal VFD respects the horizontal midline (GOA — glaucoma, optic disc drusen, AION); central scotoma from any ON lesion (optic neuritis, MS m/c), toxic optic neuropathy/tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, hereditary optic neuropathy and cone dystrophy (Stargardt's).
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential

Cortical blindness follows bilateral cortical hemisphere lesions: B/L blindness, Anton's syndrome (denial of blindness), Riddoch phenomenon (statokinetic dissociation) and a pupil that remains normal. VEP is absent and separates functional from organic blindness; malingering and hysterical blindness instead show a normal VEP.
The pupillary reflexes and the light reflex overview

Four pupillary reflexes: near (accommodation, convergence, miosis), ciliospinal (pain in side of neck/trunk → I/L pupil dilation), psychosensory (stress/emotion → dilation) and the pupillary light reflex (PLR). PLR overview: dark room procedure; hand between the eyes separates the visual fields. Normal: bright light → constriction, low light → dilation. Illuminating one eye constricts the illuminated pupil (direct reflex) and the non-illuminated C/L pupil (consensual reflex).
The PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map

Afferent (I/L) limb: light on one eye → optic nerve; PLR fibres exit the optic tract before reaching the LGB to the pretectal nucleus (centre); PLR efferent neurons are primarily temporal. Efferent (B/L) limb: centre → internuncial neuron → B/L EWN (accessory nucleus for CN III) → B/L CN III → B/L ciliary ganglion → B/L short ciliary nerve → B/L sphincter pupillae constriction. ON, OC, OT are common to both the PLR and the visual pathway. Lesions of PLR: afferent — absolute/total (AAPO), relative (Marcus Gunn/RAPD), Wernicke's pupil; efferent — Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP), tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis.
Afferent pathway lesions — comparing AAPO and RAPD

AAPO (complete optic nerve lesion d/t trauma, end stage optic nerve disease): light reflex test shows I/L DLR and C/L DLR absent when the lesion side is illuminated; symptom I/L anopia. RAPD (incomplete ON lesion d/t optic neuritis, CRAO, retinal detachment — ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons): swinging flashlight test — on presentation B/L constricted, on stimulus B/L constrict on one eye, pupils dilate in the meantime on swinging, constrict again; repeat fatigues the lesioned ON → B/L dilation when the lesion eye is stimulated; no symptom. In both, pupils are always equal in size: isocoria.
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil

Wernicke's hemianopic pupil: I/L optic tract lesion → C/L homonymous hemianopia; light on the hemianopic/invisible VF gives no constriction, light on the normal VF constricts. ARP (efferent): causes — neurosiphilis (tertiary syphilis, may present with seizures/confusion), tabes dorsalis, aortic regurgitation; site — periaqueductal grey (affects I/L internuncial neurons) > posterior commissure (C/L internuncial neurons), usually B/L. Features: PLR B/L absent, accommodation/near reflex present (dorsal EWN carrying near reflex fibres is normal), no dilation with atropine, both pupils constricted on presentation (EWN receives neither excitatory/inhibitory signals). Mnemonic ARP PRA = Accommodation Reflex Present, Pupillary Reflex Absent.
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria workup

Tonic/Adie's pupil: ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve; causes — HZV ganglionitis, diabetes/alcoholism peripheral neuropathy, trauma; Holmes-Adie pupil = tonic pupil + ↓ deep tendon reflexes. I/L DLR ↓, CLR absent; near reflex present with slow vermiform dilating movements; denervation hypersensitivity constricts with 0.125% dilute pilocarpine (sphincter denervated → overexpression of receptors). Pharmacological mydriasis: drug action (e.g. atropine) supranuclear inhibition of EWN; does not dilate even with 1% pilocarpine. Anisocoria (difference ≥0.4 mm): greater in dark → abnormal pupil is constricted → 1% apraclonidine (positive = Horner's, negative = physiological); greater in light → abnormal pupil is dilated → 0.125% pilocarpine (constricts = tonic pupil; no constriction → 1% pilocarpine: constricts = 3rd CN palsy, neither = pharmacological mydriasis); abnormal shape = iris damage.
Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index

Conditions of the optic disc are representative of the optic nerve. Clinical features: (1) pallor of the OD d/t loss of vascularity — first classical sign; (2) loss of vascularity defined by the Rostenbaum index (ratio of small : large blood vessels) — normal >10, optic atrophy <7 (loss of small vessels on the OD); (3) visual field loss depends on the affected fibres — a patient may have 6/6 vision if central fibres are spared. Normal disc photograph: yellowish optic cup and pink/orange neuroretinal ring; atrophic disc: pale OD with reduced small vessels.
Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive

Primary (1°): atrophy without antecedent disc swelling — chalky white, well defined margins; shallow saucer-shaped cup; normal vessels; normal surrounding retina; causes: optic neuritis (m/c cause multiple sclerosis), tumors, trauma, hereditary, toxic. Secondary (2°): atrophy after disc swelling — dirty gray-white, ill-defined margins; cup filled up d/t swelling; peripapillary sheathing; hyaline bodies/drusen; causes: papilledema, papillitis, AION. Consecutive: atrophy d/t disease of the inner retina and its blood supply — waxy pallor, less sharply defined margins; normal cup; vessel attenuation; pathology seen; retinal diseases: retinitis seen CRAO/CRVO, healed vasculitis, panretinal photo-coagulation, retinitis pigmentosa.
Optic neuritis — types, the macular star and MS features

Optic neuritis = inflammation of the ON, an important cause of 1° atrophy. Parts of the ON: intraocular, intraorbital, intracanalicular, intracranial. Types: papillitis (intraocular) m/c in children — disc hyperemia, flame shaped haemorrhages in/around the disc; retrobulbar neuritis m/c in adults — no visible sign, loss of vision, associated with MS; neuroretinitis (papillitis + maculitis) — macular star appearance (exudates radiating from the macula), associated with viral infections. Macular star causes (NHAP): Neuroretinitis, Hypertensive retinopathy, Angioma (retinal), Papilledema. MS features (mnemonic a CuP mar): central scotoma, colour blindness (red ↓ green), unilateral (m/c) loss of vision, Uhthoff's phenomenon (↑ body temperature, e.g. during exercise → worsening of symptoms).
Optic neuritis — Pulfrich, pain, RAPD and the ONTT treatment

Pulfrich phenomenon: altered perception of kinetic objects (static → normal) d/t ON demyelination → ↓ speed of impulse conduction → inaccurate perception of fast moving objects. Pain in the eye is exaggerated with ocular movements (ON inflammation → extraocular muscle inflammation d/t common sheath → pain on movement). Marcus Gunn pupil/RAPD: earliest sign. Treatment (ONTT): steroids — IV methylprednisolone 1g/day × 3 days → oral prednisone 1mg/kg/day × 11 days; exclusive oral steroids C/I (↑ relapse). Criteria: vision at presentation <6/12; no previous episode of MS and/or optic neuritis; ≥1 demyelinating lesion on MRI. Outcome: hastens recovery, no change in visual outcome. Post-steroidal β-IFN (CHAMPS study): good outcome → ↓ MS occurrence. Glatiramer acetate 20 mg s/c. NMO/Devic's: demyelinating, m/c in young females, can be 2° to MS; pathology d/t aquaporin 4 (AQP-4 autoantigen); presentation B/L optic neuritis + transverse myelitis, ↑ relapse than MS alone.
Devic's workup, hereditary optic neuropathies and toxic/nutritional neuropathy

NMO investigations: NMO IgG (anti AQP-4) antibodies, lumbar puncture; management: disease control with steroids. Hereditary optic neuropathies: Kjer/dominant optic atrophy — autosomal dominant; Behr — autosomal recessive (ataxia, nystagmus, mental retardation); Wolfram/DIDMOAD (DI, DM, optic atrophy, deafness) — autosomal recessive (DI, DM, deafness); Leber's (LHON) — mitochondrial (maternal, m > F), point mutation at codon 11778, presents in 2nd/3rd decade, painless loss B/L > U/L, pupillary telangiectasia, pseudo-papillitis, 1° atrophy, central scotoma, papillomacular degeneration (pathognomonic), no treatment so far. Note: mitochondrial diseases do not generally have a gender predilection. Disc swelling causes: ↑ ICP → papilledema; pseudo-papilledema — LHON, methanol poisoning, near vision loss in hypermetropia, optic disc drusen, peripapillary myelinated nerve fibres. Toxic/nutritional (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia): drugs DICE (Digoxin, Isoniazid, Chloroquine, Ethambutol — most ophthotoxic), B1/B6/B12 deficiency, methanol poisoning; cecocentral scotoma; Rx hydroxocobalamin 1000 units weekly × 10 weeks. Papilledema: swelling of the OD d/t raised ICP — non-inflammatory (passive, hydrostatic), painless, B/L (except Foster Kennedy).
Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading and AION

Etiopathogenesis: raised ICP → pressure transmitted along subarachnoid space → pressure on the ON → blockage of anterograde flow/axoplasmic transport → stasis in the optic disc → extracellular edema (mechanical signs) and venous congestion (vascular signs). Acute: blurring of disc margins (earliest), elevated OD, Paton's lines (retinochoroidal folds around the OD d/t leakage of fluid); hyperemia/congestion of the OD, loss of venous pulsations, hemorrhages around the OD. Chronic: champagne-cork appearance. OD swollen → VFD: enlargement of the blind spot. ICP symptoms: papilledema (no LOV, normal light reflex, later 2° atrophy with gradual painless loss), horizontal diplopia (associated CN VI palsy), amaurosis fugax (brief cessation of axoplasmic transport; transient complete LOV, 30-60s episodes, total 6/6 recovery, diagnostic of stroke); headache (earliest sign, ↑ in morning, projectile vomiting, progressively worsens). Rx: depends on the underlying cause of ↑ ICP. Frisen's grading: 1 — 'C' shaped halo; 2 — circumferential halo, blurred margins; 3 — loss of major vessels around the disc; 4 — loss of vessels on the disc, ↑↑ swelling over disc; 5 — all vessels obscured, venous engorgement → congestion. AION: loss of blood supply to the anterior ON. Arteritic: giant cell arteritis (large vessel arteritis), temporal artery pathology, premonitory symptoms (pain, amaurosis fugax), B/L severe visual loss, corticosteroids. Non-arteritic (no vasculitis): occlusion of the short posterior ciliary artery; hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, collagen vascular diseases; painless, U/L moderate visual loss; experimental Rx levodopa + carbidopa × 3 weeks. Both: altitudinal field defects.
Congenital anomalies of the optic disc

Morning glory syndrome: U/L malformation of the OD; cause — peripapillary scleral defect d/t absence of lamina cribrosa; photograph shows a large OD with a radial (spoke wheel like) pattern of blood vessels. The lamina cribrosa is the fenestrated lamina of sclera that allows the ON fibres to pass; if absent → axial retrodisplacement of the ON; if the OD acquires myelination → white streaks around the OD. Myelinated nerve fibres: normal OD is non-myelinated; no visual loss.
Colour blindness — terminology, genetics and types

Terminology: primary colours — red (prota), green (deuta), blue (trita); pathology — anopia (non perception), anomaly (defect in perception). Congenital: X-linked recessive (m/c), m > F (carrier); red (L) and green (M) cone genes on chromosome X, blue (S) on chromosome 7; red ↓ green CB m/c. Acquired: ON diseases (eg d/t ethambutol) except glaucoma → red/green CB; macular disease except Stargardt's (cone dystrophy without CB) + sildenafil → blue/yellow CB; old age/digoxin → blue CB (xanthopsia, yellowish tinging). Types: dyschromatopsia — dichromatic (anopia for 1 colour, perceives 2 others: protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia — autosomal dominant) and trichromatic anomalous (perceives all 3 with anomalies in 1-2: protanomaly, deuteranomaly, tritanomaly); achromatopsia — red monochromat (black/white, autosomal recessive, total CB → hemeralopia/day blindness) and cone monochromat (perception of only 1 colour).

Ishihara chart: m/c used to detect CB, cannot detect tritan defects; 38 plates (numbers, lines) with ↓ false positives/false negatives. Hardy Rand Rittler: pediatric age group; 24 plates with shapes (O, Δ, ×). Both use the pseudoisochromatic principle. Others: Holmgren's wool test; Nagel's anomaloscope (most accurate for severity); Farnsworth Munsell 100 hue (most sensitive, detects all types, 85 hue caps); Farnsworth Munsell 15 hue (differentiates b/w congenital and acquired); lantern test (vocational CB testing).
Squint — definition, causes and the EOM action tables

Squint: deviation from binocular vision; overview — deviation of direction of vessels in one/both eyes and impairment in ocular movement. Causes: muscular disorders (myasthenia gravis, atrophy, dystrophy) and cranial nerve lesions (CN IV → superior oblique, CN VI → lateral rectus, CN III → other extraocular muscles; mnemonic SO4LR6O3). Anatomical actions: ability to be free from neural control, based on direction of tendons. Table: LPS — elevation of upper eyelid; MR — inward movement (adduction); LR — outward movement (abduction); cycloducts' 1°/2°/3° actions — SR elevation/intorsion/adduction, IR depression/extorsion/adduction, SO intorsion/depression/abduction, IO extorsion/elevation/abduction. Clinically visible: adduction, abduction, elevation, depression; invisible: intorsion (inward/nasal rotation), extorsion (outward/temporal rotation). Clinical actions: 1° actions predominate in the abducted eye, 2° in the adducted eye; use — to test actions of individual muscles.
Visual and orbital axes; BSV grades and formation

Visual and orbital axes: visual axis–orbital axis 23°; SR and IR muscle axes parallel to the orbital axis at 23° with the sagittal plane; LR muscle axis −45° with the sagittal plane; MR axis parallel to the sagittal plane. If the eye abducts by 23°, the visual axis and the muscle orbital axis coincide → vertical action predominates → SR → pure elevator. Clinical functions: pure elevation SR + IO; pure depression SO + IR; elevation in abduction SR; depression in abduction SO. BSV: formation of a composite image using both the eyes. Grades: 1 — simultaneous macular perception; 2 — fusion of similar images with minute retinal differences; 3 — stereopsis, binocular depth perception. Formation: synergistic muscles (same action, same eye — eg right SR + right IO, both elevation); yoke muscles/CN synergists (one from each eye, same direction — version); antagonistic muscles (opposite action, same eye — eg right LR and right MR).
Yoke pairs in action, Hering's and Sherrington's laws

Yoke pairs and net actions: left LR + right MR — levoversion; right LR + left MR — dextroversion; right SR + left IO — dextro-elevation; right IR + left SO — dextro-depression; right SO + left IR — levo-depression; right IO + left SR — levo-elevation; right SR + right IO and left SR + left IO — B/L elevation (sursumversion); right IR + right SO and left IR + left SO — B/L depression (deorsumversion). Hering's law of equal innervation: equal innervation to a pair of yoke muscles during any binocular movement (similar timing, amount of impulses, simultaneous contraction); applications — secondary deviation or inhibitional palsy. Sherrington's law of reciprocal inhibition: relaxation of yoke muscle antagonists. Formation of BSV: 4 muscles required (a yoke + antagonists); lesions → squint.
Classification of squint; comitant versus incomitant

Tree: squint → apparent deviation (pseudostabismus) and true deviation. True deviation → heterophoria (latent squint: deviation manifests under ocular stress, excessive near work) and heterotropia (manifest squint: visible always). Heterotropia → constant/concomitant (deviation remains constant in all directions of gaze) and incomitant (deviation varies in different directions of gaze). Table — comitant: 1° = 2° deviation, restriction absent, diplopia absent, head posturing absent, sensory anomalies present; incomitant: 1° < 2°, restriction present, diplopia present, head posturing present, sensory anomalies absent. 1° deviation: seen when the normal eye fixates; 2°: seen when the deviated eye fixates. Note: Hering's law — equal and simultaneous innervation flows through yoke muscles. Types of incomitant: paralytic (forced duction test negative — eye moves) and restrictive (forced duction test positive: diagnostic — eye does not move); forced duction test = try to move the eyeball being held at the limbus by forceps.
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint

Direction of deviation: ESO — inward (esotropia); EXO — outward (exotropia); HYPER — upward (hypertropia); HYPO — downward (hypotropia); INCYCLO — inward/nasal rotation (superior limbus rotates nasally); EXCYCLO — outward/temporal rotation (superior limbus rotates temporally). Consequences: diplopia (small angle squint) — images of the same object at non-corresponding retinal points (corresponding point of LE: nasal → temporal); motor adaptation — fusion (extra EOM work); sensory adaptation — ARC (new correspondence points, deviation up to 5°). Confusion (large angle squint) — images of different objects d/t both eyes looking at different objects; motor adaptation — change in head posture; sensory adaptation — suppression of the visual sensory impulse from the deviated eye → amblyopia (lazy eye): loss of vision without organic cause, no treatment.
Ocular movements, refraction, accommodative squint and fusional vergence

Examination of ocular movements: 9 directions of gaze — dextro-elevation (RSR + LIO), sursumversion (RSR + RIO, LSR + LIO), levo-elevation (RIO + LSR), dextroversion (RLR + LMR), primary position, levoversion (RMR + LLR), dextro-depression (RIR + LSO), deorsumversion (RIR + RSO, LIR + LSO), levo-depression (RSO + LIR). Refractory error: Snellen chart 6/6 normal; <6/6 → retinoscope. Accommodative squint: uncorrected hypermetropia → loss of near vision → overaccommodation + overconvergence → esotropia; treatment — spectacles. Fusional vergence: extra power of EOM to keep heterophoria from manifesting; tests — Livingston gauge, pencil, synoptophore, RAF rule (m/c used, a points measured); RAF ruler on nose: blurring point = near point of accommodation (normal 20y 8 cm, 50y >46 cm), diplopia point = near point of convergence (normal <10 cm); poor fusional vergence treated with orthoptic strengthening exercises.
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)

Objective tests: Hirschberg's, Bruckner's, cover-uncover, prism-bar cover. Subjective: ophthalmoplegic principle (Maddox rod, Maddox wing); haploscope principle (Lancaster RG, synoptophore). Hirschberg (corneal reflection): direction — DOOR (deviation opposite of reflection; CR nasal to centre → 15° exodeviation at pupillary margin); degree — 1 mm CR deviation = 7° squint/14 Δ (1 pd = 1/2°); CR at pupillary margin 15°/30 Δ, at limbus 45°/90 Δ (photographic chart 15/30/45°, clinical rule HCRT). Bruckner's: screening in infants; light through direct ophthalmoscope; examine fundal red reflex — equal b/w both eyes (normal), arc-like (refracting error), unequal (unequal squint).
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test

Cover test: confirm tropia (covered eye shows corrective movement); uncover test: diagnose phoria (deviation under cover, returns on removal). Mnemonic DOOM: deviation opposite of movement. PBCT: best and most accurate test for the measurement of degree of tropia; principle — neutralization, light through a prism deviates towards the apex; goal — prism power at which the eye appears normal on cover-uncover; mnemonic DOOB (deviation opposite of base of prism); orientation — ESO base-out, EXO base-in, hyper base-down, hypo base-up.

Maddox rod (diplopia principle): uses — measure/diagnose phoria at far fixation, macular function test, double Maddox rod test (measure cyclodeviation); results — dot on line: orthophoria; crossed diplopia: left exophoria/tropia; uncrossed: left esophoria/tropia. Maddox wing: diagnoses phoria at near fixation; obsolete. One test to differentiate tropia vs phoria: cover-uncover. Diplopia types: monocular (does not disappear on closing the normal eye — subluxation of lens, severe refractory errors/anisometropia, iridodonesis) and binocular (disappears if either eye is closed — squint d/t myogenic, neurogenic (3, 4, 6th nerve palsy), neuromuscular junction disorders (myasthenia gravis)). Tests: red-green glasses (easiest way), Lee's screen, Hess chart (most commonly used).
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV, depth perception)

Sensory anomaly tests differentiate: BSV (1 object 1 image), ARC (adaptation to diplopia), suppression (adaptation to confusion). Worth 4-dot: more common/more important > Bagolini; red on right eye, green on left eye; 4 dots — normal BSV/harmonious ARC; 5 dots — diplopia/non-harmonious ARC; 3 dots — RE suppression (d/t amblyopia); 2 dots — LE suppression. Bagolini striated glasses (RE 45°, LE 135°; light images perpendicular to striations): X — BSV or harmonious ARC; single line — RE suppression; diverging lines — diplopia, non-harmonious ARC. 4 prism test: differentiates BSV from central suppression scotoma in microtropia; after image test also listed. Stereopsis tests: two pencil (gross), Titmus fly (Polaroid vectographic), random dot stereogram — best (eliminates monocular clues): Lang, Frisby, Frisby-Davis distance stereotest.
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course

Paralytic squint: a type of incomitant squint. Features: diplopia; abnormal head posture; restriction of ocular movements (intended action of the paralysed muscle — vertigo); deviation opposite to the action of the paralysed muscle; 2° deviation > 1° deviation. Cause: 3rd, 4th, 6th nerve palsy. CN III (oculomotor) course: nuclear complex in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus — main motor nucleus (2 paired subnuclei: C/L SR and I/L MR, IR, IO; 1 unpaired subnucleus: both LPS) + Edinger-Westphal accessory nucleus (preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle — constriction). Fascicular: fibres pass through the red nucleus into the interpeduncular. Basilar: leaves the midbrain on the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle, between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries. Intracavernous: lateral wall above the trochlear nerve; superior and inferior branches; enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the annulus of Zinn. Intraorbital: superior division → LPS, SR; inferior division → IR, IO, MR.
CN III palsy — clinical features and special syndromes

Clinical features table: LPS (elevation of upper eyelid) → ptosis; SO/IR (elevation of eye) → hypotropia (downward deviation); medial rectus (adduction) → exotropia (outward deviation) → crossed diplopia; sphincter pupillae (miosis) → mydriasis with loss of pupillary light reflex; ciliary muscle (accommodation) → loss of near vision/near reflex. Photos: limited elevation of LE; primary gaze — LE ptosis + LE down and out; limitation of adduction; down and outward movement present. Special clinical features: vascular pathologies; uncal herniation; Benedikt's syndrome (red nucleus — CN III palsy + flapping tremors); Weber's syndrome (cerebral peduncle — CN III palsy + C/L hemiparesis); Nothnagel's syndrome (CN III palsy + cerebellar ataxia); nuclear CN III palsy — Daroff's rule: B/L ptosis, C/L SR weakness, B/L mydriasis and cycloplegia.
Vascular CN III palsy, treatment and aberrant regeneration

CN III diagram: pial vessels supply the superficial fibres (→ pupil); central deep fibres supplied by the vasa nervorum. Uncal herniation: only sphincter pupillae paralysed → mydriasis only. Vascular pathologies: caused by diabetes, hypertension; CN III palsy with pupillary sparing, near reflex absent, light reflex spared. Treatment: observation 6 months (regeneration d/t neurolemma — CNS oligodendrocytes, PNS Schwann cells) → surgery if no regeneration. Faulty regeneration → aberrant regeneration: pseudo-von Graffe sign (IR fibres supply LPS — on downgaze IR and LPS contract → depression of eye + elevation of upper lid → lid lag); pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupil (ciliary fibres supply sphincter pupillae — near vision → accommodation miosis, accommodation reflex present; or sphincter fibres completely damaged → pupillary light reflex absent).
CN IV (trochlear) palsy — course and Park's 3-step test

CN IV palsy: A/K/A superior oblique palsy; m/c congenital paralytic squint. Course: nucleus — midbrain at level of inferior colliculus; fascicular — curves around the aqueduct of sylvius and decussates; trunk — leaves the midbrain dorsally, between PCA and SCA; cavernous — lateral wall between oculomotor and ophthalmic nerves, through the superior orbital fissure OUTSIDE the annulus of Zinn; intraorbital — innervates the contralateral SO. Features (opposite to the paralysed action): intorsion → excycloptropia (head tilt to opposite side); depression → I/L hypertropia (chin down); depression in adduction → ↑ hypertropia on adduction, vertical diplopia on downgaze (face turns to opposite side). Note: C/L hypertropia only if the lesion is at the nucleus. Diagnosis — Park's 3-step test: step 1 identification of hypertropia (LE); step 2 hypertropia worse on opposite gaze; step 3 hypertropia better on opposite tilt (Bielschowsky head tilt).
Cyclovertical palsy note and CN VI (abducens) palsy

Note: cyclovertical muscle palsy (SR, IR, SO, IO) — diagnose with Park's 3-step test: 1. muscles causing hypertropia; 2. muscles causing lateral gaze; 3. muscles causing head tilt; the muscle implicated in all is the affected muscle. CN VI (abducens/lateral rectus) palsy: nucleus — pons, ventral to floor of 4th ventricle; fascicular — leaves brainstem at the pontomedullary junction; basilar — basilar cistern, crossed by AICA, Dorello canal, cavernous sinus; intracavernous — inferomedial in the lateral wall close to the ICA, orbit within the annulus of Zinn; intraorbital — ipsilateral lateral rectus. CN nuclei locations: III/IV — midbrain; V, VI, VII, VIII — pons; IX-XII — medulla. Pons syndromes: Foville (I/L 5/6/7/8 CN palsy + central Horner's), Millard-Gubler (I/L 6/7 CN palsy + C/L hemiplegia), Mobius (B/L 6/7 CN palsy). Features: limitation of abduction → inward deviation (LE esotropia); diplopia — uncrossed; I/L head posture; I/L horizontal gaze palsy.
Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests

Cerebral cortex: frontal cortex (FEF — frontal eye field, PEF — parietal eye field) initiates saccades (rapid, fixating movements) — horizontal controlled contralaterally, vertical bilaterally; occipital cortex initiates pursuits (slow following movements), controlled ipsilaterally. Both feed the brainstem cranial nerve nuclei. Vestibular apparatus (in the ear) maintains movement of head along with the eye → VOR (vestibulo ocular reflex) and optokinetic reflex. Tests: oculo-cephalic reflex (AKA Doll's reflex) — tests CN III, VI, VIII; eyes move opposite to the movement of head (in coma patients). Caloric test (injection of water into ear): cold water → opposite side nystagmus; warm water → same side nystagmus.

Horizontal gaze: centre — ipsilateral PPRF; saccadic movements to look towards the left/right side. Pathway of left gaze: initiation — C/L FEF (right) → I/L PPRF (left, centre) → I/L 6th nerve nucleus (drives the left LR) and via the C/L MLF → C/L 3rd nerve nucleus (drives the right MR yoke). PPRF: paraporentine/paramedian pontine reticular formation; MLF: medial longitudinal fasciculus.
Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome

Table: C/L FEF — I/L LR fails to contract, C/L MR fails to contract → left gaze palsy; I/L PPRF — same → left gaze palsy; C/L MLF — internuclear ophthalmoplegia (m/c cause multiple sclerosis): I/L LR can contract, C/L MR fails to contract → left gaze defect: I/L adduction absent, C/L abduction present. One and a half syndrome: I/L MLF → C/L gaze defect + I/L PPRF → I/L gaze palsy = 1½ defect; figure: primary gaze normal; right gaze (defect) d/t left MLF — partial loss of left gaze; left gaze (palsy) d/t left PPRF — completely loss of left gaze.
Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy

Vertical gaze (upgaze/downgaze) pathway: frontal and occipital centres → superior colliculus, rimLF, INC, posterior commissure → trochlear and oculomotor nerve nuclei. 1° centre — rimLF (rostral interstitial medial longitudinal fasciculus); 2° centre — INC (interstitial nucleus of Cajal). Etiology of vertical gaze palsy: 1. distal basilar artery ischaemia (m/c) — supplies rimLF; a. progressive supranuclear palsy — palsy: downgaze → upgaze → global → convergence, occurs in old age; 3. Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome — site: posterior commissure; m/c cause: pinealoma > hydrocephalus; features: upgaze palsy (supranuclear), Collier's sign (upper eyelid retraction), convergence — retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation (light reflex absent and near reflex present).
Restrictive squint — causes and Duane retraction syndrome

Restrictive squint causes: congenital — DRS (Duane retraction syndrome), Brown's syndrome, CFEOM (congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles); acquired — orbital trauma, orbital tumours. DRS table: Type I — limitation of abduction; retraction of globe + closure of palpebral fissure on adduction. Type 2 — limitation of adduction; retraction + closure on adduction. Type 3 — limitation of abduction and adduction; retraction + closure on abduction and adduction (d/t paradoxical innervation of both LR and MR). Type I pathology: LR gets supplied by the 3rd nerve instead of the 6th (paradoxical) — on abduction impulse via the 6th the LR does not act (no abduction); on adduction impulse via the 3rd both LR and MR contract → retraction of globe → closure of palpebral fissure.
DRS diagnosis, Brown's syndrome and comitant (accommodative) squint

DRS photograph series (Type I, left eye): right gaze — LE adduction present with closure of the left palpebral fissure; primary gaze — normal, no deviation; left gaze — LE abduction limitation. Diagnosis: forced duction test. Brown's syndrome: congenitally tight SO → ↓ movement of SO through the trochlea (bony hook) → contracture of SO → SO fails to relax → antagonist IO cannot relax → restriction of elevation in adduction. Comitant squint: m/c presentation — esotropia (convergent squint). Types: accommodative (refractive — esotropia associated with hypermetropia; non-refractive — d/t high AC/A ratio d/t ↑ convergence or ↓ accommodation, AC: accommodative convergence, A: accommodation; 1 D accommodation ~ 2° convergence) and non-accommodative. Non-refractive treatment: miotics (echothiophate), bifocal spectacles, surgery — bimedial recession (weakening of B/L medial recti), Faden surgery.
Essential infantile esotropia — prevention of amblyopia and surgery

Non-accommodative esotropia: AKA essential infantile esotropia; presentation 4-6 months of age; no refractory error; no neurological deficit. Associated with: latent horizontal nystagmus, inferior oblique overaction, dissociated vertical deviation, large angle deviation (≥15°/≥30 pd) → confusion → amblyopia of the deviated eye. Prevention of amblyopia: occlusion therapy — intermittent alternate patching of the normal eye (patch normal eye for x days ↔ patch deviated eye for x days, x = age in years); penalization — atropine drops in the normal eye. Prevention possible till 6 years of age (eyeball completes development by 6-7 years). Surgery (TOC): usually done at 1 year of age; for esotropia — recession of I/L MR (lengthening → weakening) + resection of I/L LR (shortening → strengthening).

Pseudo strabismus = apparent deviation. 2 types: pseudo eso, pseudo exo. Pseudo eso causes: 1. Telecanthus: ↑ ICD + normal IPD. 2. Epicanthus: extra congenital fold of skin connecting upper eyelid to lower eyelid in medial part. 3. Myopia. Pseudostrabismus photo labels TELECANTHUS.
Pseudo exo and myasthenia gravis features

Pseudo exo causes: 1. Hypertelorism: Increased ICD, Increased IPD (d/t wide set orbits). 2. ROP (Retinopathy of prematurity) D/t temporal displacement of macula. 3. Hypermetropia. Myasthenia gravis: m/c in young females. Pathology: Reduced Ach receptors. Fatigue worsens in evening (m/c feature). Ocular: Ptosis B/L, Diplopia, Cogan lid twitch sign (upshoot of eyelid when changing gaze from down to up), Orbicularis oculi weakness tested by forced opening of closed eyelids.
Myasthenia diagnosis — Tensilon and ice-pack tests

Diagnosis: Tensilon test: Inj 0.2 mg edrophonium (Anticholinesterase agent) → ↑ Ach. Before injection ptosis, after → improvement. Ice-pack test: Ptosis → ice pack application for 5 mins → ptosis improvement. Photo series shows B/L ptosis before, improved after.

q: The volume of the eyeball is:
The book lists the volume of the eyeball as 6 ml; 24 ml is a trap — 24 mm is the axial length, not the volume. (Book p1)
Fill up: The eyeball is aspherical — specifically an ______.
Shape of the eyeball: aspherical (oblate spheroid) — a sphere flattened at the poles, not elongated as in a prolate spheroid. (Book p1)
In the anatomy lab a student is asked for the site of the eyeball. Per the book, the eyeball is housed in the ______.
Site of the eyeball: the orbit, a bony cage; the figure 'Orbit containing eyeball' labels its roof, lateral wall, medial wall and floor. (Book p1)
The axial length (anteroposterior diameter) of the eyeball is:
Axial length/antroposterior diameter: 24 mm (2.4 cm) — one of the four headline values on the 'Basic Anatomy of Eyeball' block. (Book p1)
Match each attribute of the eyeball with its value — 1) Volume 2) Site 3) Axial length … A) 24 mm (2.4 cm) B) Orbit (bony cage) C) 6 ml
The book's four basic facts: shape aspherical (oblate spheroid), volume 6 ml, site orbit (bony cage), axial length/antroposterior diameter 24 mm (2.4 cm). (Book p1)
All of the following are labelled in the 'Orbit containing eyeball' figure EXCEPT:
The figure labels four structures of the orbit — roof, lateral wall, medial wall and floor; a posterior wall is not among the labelled structures. (Book p1)
Fill up: The cornea forms the anterior ______ of the outermost layer of the eyeball.
Layers → Outermost: anterior 1/6th is the cornea (transparent, convex shaped, refractive power present), the limbus is the corneo-scleral junction, and the posterior 5/6th is the sclera. (Book p1)
The posterior 5/6th of the outermost layer is formed by the:
Outermost layer: posterior 5/6th : Sclera — white (opaque) and covered by the conjunctiva (a transparent mucous membrane); the choroid belongs to the middle uveal tract. (Book p1)
All of the following are stated about the cornea EXCEPT:
The cornea is transparent, convex shaped and has refractive power; 'white (opaque)' is the description of the sclera, not the cornea. (Book p1)

Match each structure of the outermost layer with its description — 1) Cornea 2) Limbus 3) Sclera … A) Corneo-scleral junction B) White (opaque), covered by conjunctiva C) Transparent, convex, refractive power present
Cornea: transparent, convex, refractive power present; limbus: corneo-scleral junction; sclera: white (opaque), covered by conjunctiva (transparent mucous membrane). (Book p1)
Fill up: The sclera is covered by the ______, described as a transparent mucous membrane.
The sclera (posterior 5/6th of the outermost layer) is white (opaque) and covered by the conjunctiva — a transparent mucous membrane. (Book p1)
During dissection, a trainee points at the limbus and asks for its identity. The correct reply is:
The angle of the anterior chamber
The most avascular part of the uvea
The junction of iris and ciliary body
The limbus is defined in the layers flowchart as the corneo-scleral junction; the angle of the anterior chamber and the pars plana (most avascular in uvea) are separate structures. (Book p1)
Which of the following statements about the layers of the eyeball is TRUE?
The uveal tract is the innermost layer
The retina is present both anteriorly and posteriorly
The outermost layer consists of the cornea, limbus and sclera

Outermost = cornea (anterior 1/6th) + limbus (corneo-scleral junction) + sclera (posterior 5/6th). The uveal tract is the middle (vascular) layer, the retina (neurosensory layer) is present only posteriorly, and the sclera is white and opaque. (Book p1)
Which part of the eyeball is described as 'white (opaque)' and covered by a transparent mucous membrane?
Posterior 5/6th : Sclera — white (opaque), covered by conjunctiva (transparent mucous membrane); the iris belongs to the middle uveal tract. (Book p1)
The middle layer of the eyeball is the:
Layers → Middle: uveal tract (vascular layer) with parts (anterior and posterior): a. iris, b. ciliary body, c. choroid; the retina is the innermost, neurosensory layer. (Book p1)
All of the following are parts of the uveal tract EXCEPT:
Uveal tract parts (anterior and posterior): a. iris, b. ciliary body, c. choroid; the sclera is part of the outermost layer. (Book p1)
Fill up: The uveal tract is also referred to as the ______ layer.
The book explicitly labels the middle uveal tract as the 'Vascular Layer'; the neurosensory layer is the innermost retina. (Book p1)
The innermost layer of the eyeball is the retina, described in the book as the:
Innermost: Retina — a neurosensory layer, present only posteriorly; the vascular layer is the middle uveal tract. (Book p1)
Which statement about the retina is TRUE?
It forms the anterior 1/6th of the outer coat

The retina is the innermost neurosensory layer and is present only posteriorly; the middle layer is the vascular uveal tract, the anterior 1/6th is the cornea, and the limbus is the corneo-scleral junction. (Book p1)
A medical student must recite the three parts of the uveal tract in the book's order (a, b, c). The correct sequence is:
Uveal tract — Parts (anterior and posterior): a. iris, b. ciliary body, c. choroid, in that order. (Book p1)
The anterior chamber (AC) is the space:
Between the cornea and the iris
Between the iris and the lens
The structural anatomy diagram annotates 'Anterior chamber (AC): between cornea and iris'; the posterior chamber (PC) lies deeper, behind the iris. (Book p1)
Fill up: The posterior segment of the eyeball contains the ______.
Posterior segment: contains vitreous (1% hyaluronic acid, gel-like consistency); the aqueous humour is in the anterior segment. (Book p1)
Match each part of the ciliary body with its feature — 1) Pars plicata 2) Pars plana 3) Ciliary processes … A) Secrete aqueous B) Flat part; most avascular in uvea C) Pleated part
