Ciliary body: pars plicata (pleated), pars plana (flat) — most avascular in uvea; the ciliary processes secrete aqueous. (Book p1)
Which part of the ciliary body is pleated?
Ciliary body parts: pars plicata (pleated) and pars plana (flat, most avascular in uvea); the ciliary processes secrete aqueous. (Book p1)
Fill up: The pars plana is described as ______ in the uvea.
Pars plana (flat) — most avascular in uvea; the pleated part is the pars plicata. (Book p1)
During a slit-lamp teaching session a junior asks which structure secretes the aqueous humour. The book's answer is:
In the structural anatomy diagram the ciliary processes are annotated with 'secrete aqueous' — the source of aqueous humour. (Book p1)
The vitreous contains ______ hyaluronic acid, with a gel-like consistency.
Posterior segment: contains vitreous → 1% hyaluronic acid, gel-like consistency. (Book p1)
All of the following are labelled in the 'Structural anatomy of eyeball' diagram EXCEPT:

The diagram labels the angle of AC, iris, pupil, zonules/ciliary zonules, lens, ciliary body (pars plicata, pars plana), ciliary processes, AC, PC, anterior segment, sclera, choroid and retina; the corneal endothelium is not labelled. (Book p1)

Match each segment/chamber of the eyeball with its description — 1) Anterior chamber (AC) 2) Anterior segment (AS) 3) Posterior segment … A) Contains vitreous (1% hyaluronic acid, gel-like) B) Between cornea and iris C) Contains aqueous humour
AC: between cornea and iris; anterior segment (AS): contains aqueous humour; posterior segment: contains vitreous (1% hyaluronic acid, gel-like consistency). (Book p1)
In the structural anatomy diagram, the zonules (ciliary zonules) are shown attached to the:
The cross-section labels 'Zonules/ciliary zonules' spanning the ciliary body to the lens, suspending it behind the iris and pupil. (Book p1)
Which statement about the eye segments is TRUE?
The anterior segment contains the vitreous
The posterior chamber lies between the cornea and iris
The posterior segment contains the aqueous humour
The anterior segment contains the aqueous humour
Anterior segment (AS): contains aqueous humour; the anterior chamber (not the posterior chamber) lies between cornea and iris; the posterior segment contains the vitreous. (Book p1)
In the diagram, the vitreous contained in the posterior segment is annotated with which pair of features?
25% hyaluronic acid and a fluid consistency
1% hyaluronic acid and a gel-like consistency
No hyaluronic acid and a solid consistency
1% hyaluronic acid and a fluid consistency
Posterior segment: contains vitreous → 1% hyaluronic acid, gel-like consistency — the exact annotation in the structural anatomy diagram. (Book p1)
The rate of aqueous humour secretion is:
Aqueous humour — rate of secretion: 2.3 µL/minute; 0.25 µL/min/mm Hg is the outflow value and 6 ml is the eyeball volume. (Book p2)
Aqueous outflow: 0.25 µL/min/mm Hg — note the unit differs from secretion (2.3 µL/minute); outflow is pressure-dependent, hence per mm Hg. (Book p2)
The function of aqueous humour is to exert the intraocular pressure (IOP). IOP is measured by:
Aqueous humour function: exerts intraocular pressure (IOP) — measured by tonometry; tonography is reserved for aqueous outflow. (Book p2)
Aqueous outflow (0.25 µL/min/mm Hg) is measured by tonography, whereas the IOP it helps generate is measured by tonometry — the classic exam distinction. (Book p2)
Aqueous outflow occurs via the ______, whose depth is 3 mm (range 2.5–4.4 mm).
Aqueous outflow: 0.25 µL/min/mm Hg, via the angle of the AC — depth 3 mm (2.5 mm – 4.4 mm). (Book p2)
The depth of the anterior chamber, the route of aqueous outflow, is:
Via angle of AC → depth: 3 mm (2.5 mm – 4.4 mm), measured by tonography in the aqueous outflow block. (Book p2)
Fill up: Aqueous humour is a fluid secreted from the ______.
Aqueous humour: fluid secreted from the ciliary processes — the same structures annotated 'secrete aqueous' in the structural anatomy diagram. (Book p2)
Match each aqueous humour parameter with its value — 1) Rate of secretion 2) Outflow 3) AC depth (route of outflow) … A) 3 mm (2.5–4.4 mm) B) 0.25 µL/min/mm Hg C) 2.3 µL/minute
Rate of secretion 2.3 µL/minute; aqueous outflow 0.25 µL/min/mm Hg via the angle of AC, whose depth is 3 mm (2.5–4.4 mm). (Book p2)
The converging (refractive) power of the cornea printed in the book is:
The book lists the corneal refractive power as +43D to +48D and labels it the converging power; the cornea is avascular, which is why it is transparent. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex
Fill up: the relative refractive index of the cornea is ______.
Relative index of the cornea is 1.376 as printed beside the avascularity-transparency arrow on the neurovascular supply block. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex

Match the limb of the corneal blink reflex with its structure — 1) Afferent (sensory) 2) Nucleus relaying to the motor limb 3) Efferent (motor) 4) Effector … A) Facial nucleus B) Orbicularis oculi C) Trigeminal nerve (CN V) D) Facial nerve (CN VII)
The book's reflex chain runs: stimulus → afferent trigeminal (CN V) → trigeminal nucleus → facial nucleus → efferent facial nerve (CN VII) → effector orbicularis oculi → response blinking. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex

A 52-year-old man with Bell's palsy has his cornea touched with a cotton wisp: sensation is felt but no blink follows, and he cannot close the eye voluntarily. Which lesion site and sign does the book attach to this picture?
Trigeminal nucleus with loss of conjunctival sensation
Afferent limb (CN V) with corneal anaesthesia
Bell's palsy breaks the efferent (motor) facial nerve limb of the blink reflex; the book pairs a failed facial nerve with Bell's palsy and the inability to close the eye, lagophthalmos. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex
Which statement about the corneal blink reflex is FALSE per the book?
Its stimulus is touching the cornea with a cotton wisp
Its afferent limb travels in the trigeminal nerve (CN V)
It tests corneal motor power, not sensation
Its efferent limb travels in the facial nerve (CN VII)
The book defines the corneal blink reflex as the test of corneal sensation, not of motor power; the stimulus is touching the cornea with a cotton wisp and the response is blinking. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex
The book lists causes of corneal anaesthesia (the no-blinking pathway). All of the following appear in that list EXCEPT:

Listed causes of corneal anaesthesia are herpes keratitis (m/c), diabetes, leprosy, topical medications (ex. timolol), Acanthamoeba keratitis, contact lens wear and surgical trauma; vitamin A deficiency is not in the list. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex
The commonest (m/c) cause of corneal anaesthesia in the book's list is:
Herpes keratitis is flagged m/c among the causes of corneal anaesthesia; diabetes and leprosy follow in the same list. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex
Fill up the sensory chain to the cornea: Trigeminal → Ophthalmic → ______ → Cornea.
Sensory nerve supply of the cornea runs Trigeminal → Ophthalmic → Nasociliary → Cornea as printed in the neurovascular supply block. (Book p3)
Neurovascular supply of cornea and the corneal blink reflex

Match the corneal epithelial layer of the histology figure with its cells — 1) Superficial layer 2) Middle layer 3) Basal layer … A) Wing-shaped cells B) Columnar cells that undergo mitosis and regenerate C) Squamous cells bearing microvilli for tear-film adhesion

Corneal epithelial histology: superficial squamous cells carry microvilli for adhesion of the tear film, the middle layer is wing-shaped cells, and the basal layer of columnar cells can undergo mitosis and regenerate. (Book p3)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
Fill up: histologically the anterior (outermost) layer of the cornea, the epithelium, is a ______.
The book prints the epithelial histology as non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium under heading 1, Anterior (Outermost) Layer – Epithelium. (Book p4)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
Match each corneal layer with the thickness printed in the 'Layers of cornea' figure — 1) Epithelium 2) Bowman's layer 3) Stroma 4) Descemet's membrane … A) 8-14 µm B) 490 µm C) 50-80 µm D) 10-12 µm
Figure values: epithelium 50-80 µm, Bowman's layer 8-14 µm, stroma 490 µm, Descemet's membrane 10-12 µm (endothelium 5 µm, Dua's layer 0.5-13.9 µm). (Book p4)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
Per the book's outermost/innermost table, judged with respect to the centre of the eyeball, which pairing is CORRECT?
The table reads: cornea outermost lies anteriorly and innermost lies posteriorly; retina outermost lies posteriorly and innermost lies anteriorly. (Book p4)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
One corneal layer is described as acellular, unable to regenerate, healing by scar formation with corneal opacity and loss of vision. That layer is:

Bowman's membrane is acellular, cannot regenerate, heals by scar formation producing corneal opacity and LOV (loss of vision); epithelium and Descemet's membrane are the regenerating layers. (Book p4)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
All of the following are labelled in the 'Layers of cornea' figure EXCEPT:
The figure labels epithelium, epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer, stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium; lamina fusca belongs to the sclera, not this figure. (Book p4)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
The note beneath the epithelium heading states that 'outermost' and 'innermost' are judged with respect to:
The visual axis of the globe
The book's note reads: with respect to the centre of the eyeball — the reference point for the outermost/innermost table of cornea and retina. (Book p4)
Layers of the cornea — epithelial histology and layer thicknesses
Which statement about Bowman's membrane is FALSE?
It is acellular under light microscopy
It is not a true basement membrane of the epithelium
It is not stained by PAS reagent in sections
Bowman's membrane is not a true basement membrane, is not stained by PAS, is acellular and cannot regenerate — injury heals by scar formation, not by complete regeneration. (Book p4)
Fill up: Bowman's membrane is PAS-negative; the book expands PAS as ______.
PAS is expanded in the book as Periodic Acid Schiff reagent; Bowman's membrane is not stained by it because it is not a true basement membrane. (Book p4)

Match the corneal opacity with its bedside features — 1) Nebular (faint) 2) Macular 3) Leukomatous (most dense) … A) Pupillary margin visible, iris details not visible B) Pupillary margin and iris details both visible C) Pupillary margin and iris details both not visible

Corneal opacities table: nebular — pupillary margin visible (macroscopic) and iris details visible (microscopic); macular — pupillary margin visible, iris details not visible; leukomatous — both not visible. (Book p4)

A child is brought with a faint corneal scar: the pupillary margin and the iris details are both still seen behind it, and the book attributes distortion of the image to diffraction across such an opacity. The grade of opacity is:
Nebular (faint) opacity shows maximum distribution of visible light with a visible pupillary margin and visible iris details; diffraction through it causes distortion of the image. (Book p4)
In a leukomatous opacity the book says visible-light distribution is minimum because:
The pupillary margin reflects the light back
Light rays do not cross the dense opacity
Diffraction spreads the incoming light maximally
Iris details magnify the transmitted light
For leukomatous (most dense) opacity the figure shows light rays that don't cross the opacity, giving minimum light distribution and loss of vision. (Book p4)
The glycosaminoglycan flagged m/c in the corneal stroma is:
Stromal composition per the book: type I collagen fibres and glycosaminoglycans, with keratan sulfate marked m/c. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
The stroma occupies what share of corneal thickness per the book?
The stroma is the thickest corneal layer, 90% of corneal thickness (490 µm in the layers figure). (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
The book names the strongest corneal layer as:
Heading 4 states Dua's layer / pre-Descemet's membrane is the strongest corneal layer; the layers figure also tags it 'strongest'. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
Which statement about Descemet's membrane is FALSE?
Schwalbe's line is its peripheral termination at the limbus near the anterior position of the trabecular meshwork
It is secreted continuously by the underlying endothelial cells
It is secreted by the corneal epithelium and cannot regenerate

Descemet's membrane is secreted continuously by the underlying endothelial cells and can regenerate; Schwalbe's line is its peripheral termination at the limbus near the anterior trabecular meshwork. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
The corneal endothelium maintains transparency chiefly because:
It is the thickest corneal layer
It secretes the collagen fibrils of the stroma
It reflects ultraviolet light away from the retina
Endothelium with zona occludens prevents entry of aqueous into the cornea and maintains transparency; if injured or breached, corneal oedema and haze/opacity follow. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
On specular microscopy the book pairs corneal decompensation — irregularities with a large cavity — with which endothelial cell count?

The specular microscopy timeline: 3000 cells/mm² normal hexagonal endothelium, 2400 cells/mm² small breach with compensation, 500 cells/mm² irregularities and large cavity with corneal decompensation. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
Fill up: at 2400 cells/mm² the small endothelial breach is compensated by ______ (increase in cell size) together with polymorphism (change in shape).
The book's compensation row lists polymegathism (increase in size) and polymorphism (change in shape), which maintain tight-junction integrity and corneal transparency. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
A long-term soft contact-lens wearer presents with a hazy cornea; specular microscopy shows irregularities and a large cavity in the endothelial mosaic. The book's label for this state is:
The 500 cells/mm² column of the specular microscopy figure is annotated corneal decompensation d/t extended contact lens wear with a hazy cornea. (Book p5)
Stroma, Dua's layer, Descemet's membrane and endothelium
The sclera is the outermost covering of which fraction of the eyeball?
The sclera heading opens with: outermost covering of posterior 5/6th of eyeball. (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies
The scleral thickness at the limbus in the book's 'variable thickness of sclera' figure is:
The figure annotates the limbus with a scleral thickness of 0.83 mm; thinnest is posterior to the insertion of recti and thickest around the optic nerve. (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies
Match the scleral site with its thickness feature — 1) Limbus 2) Posterior to insertion of recti 3) Around the optic nerve … A) Thinnest B) 0.83 mm C) Thickest
Variable thickness of sclera: limbus 0.83 mm, posterior to insertion of recti thinnest, around the optic nerve thickest. (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies

Match the scleral layer with its description — 1) Episclera 2) Sclera propria 3) Lamina fusca … A) Avascular layer of collagen fibres B) Innermost layer C) Outermost layer with superficial and deep vascular plexuses that merges with Tenon's capsule about 3 mm posterior to the limbus

Scleral layers: episclera (outermost, highly vascular with two plexuses — superficial and deep near sclera proper — merging with Tenon's capsule ~3 mm posterior to limbus), sclera propria (avascular, collagen fibres), lamina fusca (innermost). (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies
Which statement about scleral inflammation is FALSE?
Scleritis is inflammation of the deep vascular plexus of the episclera
Episcleritis is inflammation of the superficial vascular plexus
Scleritis is a misnomer as sclera propria inflames
The commonest cause of episcleritis is idiopathic

Scleritis is labelled a misnomer precisely because it is inflammation of the deep vascular plexus of the episclera, not of the sclera proper; episcleritis involves the superficial plexus and is idiopathic m/c. (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies
A red eye is instilled with 2.5% phenylephrine during the vasoconstrictor test and the redness disappears with blanching. Per the book this result indicates:
Conjunctival foreign body, because the redness is localised
Acute angle closure, because the pupil is mid-dilated
Scleritis, because deep vessels do not constrict

In episcleritis the superficial vessels constrict, so after the test redness disappears and blanching occurs; in scleritis redness remains because inflamed deep vessels do not constrict. Reagent: 2.5% phenylephrine eye drops. (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies
The book's management of episcleritis is:
Topical antibiotics alone for six weeks then review
Immediate high-dose systemic steroids with a slow taper
Scleral buckling with cryotherapy to the episclera
Episcleritis management per the book: self resolving, resolves fast; supportive treatment with NSAIDs and low dose steroids. (Book p6)
Sclera — anatomy, layers and its pathologies
All of the following describe scleromalacia perforans in the book EXCEPT:
m/c in women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis

Scleromalacia perforans (necrotizing scleritis without inflammation) shows atrophy d/t inflammation, only deep bluish vessels, no pain and no congestion; it is m/c in women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. (Book p7)
Types of scleritis and the limbus
A 60-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has a quiet, uncongested eye; examination shows scleral atrophy with only deep bluish vessels and no pain. The book's diagnosis is:
Necrotizing scleritis with signs of inflammation (painful)
The types-of-scleritis tree puts scleromalacia perforans under necrotizing scleritis without inflammation, m/c in women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. (Book p7)
Types of scleritis and the limbus
Limbal stem cells sit in which structure per the book?
Site of limbal stem cells: limbal basal epithelial cells forming the palisades of Vogt (elevations and crypts); the limbus is the corneo-scleral junction that contains stem cells. (Book p7)
Types of scleritis and the limbus
Fill up: the universal marker of stem cells is CD34, while the specific marker of limbal stem cells printed in the book is ______.
The book lists universal marker of stem cell: CD34 and specific marker of limbal stem cell: ABCG2. (Book p7)
Types of scleritis and the limbus
Deficiency of limbal stem cells causes pterygium, which the book attributes to environmental factors. Its treatment per the book is:
A scleral patch graft without conjunctival tissue
Excision with a limbal stem cell autograft
Deficiency of LSC → pterygium, caused by environmental factors; Rx: excision and autograft with limbal stem cells. (Book p7)
Types of scleritis and the limbus

Match the uveal component with its uveal part and its inflammation — 1) Iris with pars plicata of the ciliary body 2) Pars plana of the ciliary body 3) Choroid … A) Intermediate uvea / intermediate uveitis B) Anterior uvea / anterior uveitis C) Posterior uvea / posterior uveitis

The components-of-uvea table pairs iris plus ciliary body pars plicata with anterior uvea (anterior uveitis), pars plana with intermediate uvea (intermediate uveitis) and choroid with posterior uvea (posterior uveitis). (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
The iris is pigmented because of which cell?
Anatomy of the iris: increased vascularity, pigmentation d/t melanocytes, and variable thickness. (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
The thickest part of the iris, which marks the boundary between its pupillary and ciliary zones, is the:
The iris figure labels the collarette as the thickest part and the boundary between the pupillary zone and the ciliary zone of the iris. (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
After blunt ocular trauma a patient shows a tear at the peripheral iris where it looks thinnest on gonioscopy. The book names this detachment of the iris:
The thinnest part of the iris is the root, labelled the site of iridodialysis (detachment of iris). (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris

Match the iris muscle with its action and autonomic control — 1) Sphincter pupillae 2) Dilator pupillae … A) Mydriasis under sympathetic (excitatory) control B) Miosis under parasympathetic (inhibitory) control
Sphincter pupillae produces miosis under parasympathetic (inhibitory) control; dilator pupillae produces mydriasis under sympathetic (excitatory) control. (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris

Match the sympathetic relay station of the dilator pathway with its order — 1) First order 2) Second order 3) Third order … A) Superior cervical ganglion to the eye along the internal carotid, ending in the long ciliary nerve B) Hypothalamus to the spinal cord's ciliospinal centre (C8-T1) C) Ciliospinal centre to the superior cervical ganglion, crossing the lung parenchyma

The sympathetic chain for the dilator: hypothalamus → 1° spinal cord ciliospinal centre (C8-T1) → 2° crossing lung parenchyma to the superior cervical ganglion → 3° along the internal carotid as the long ciliary nerve. (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
During resection of a Pancoast tumour the surgeon warns of damage to the sympathetic fibres heading to the superior cervical ganglion. Per the book's iris-supply table, the ocular consequence is:
Paralysis of the inferior oblique muscle
Loss of sympathetic supply to the eye
Loss of parasympathetic supply to the sphincter
The book flags resection of a Pancoast tumour as a risk of damage to SCG fibres at the second-order step, producing loss of sympathetic supply to the eye. (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
Which statement about the final nerve supply of the iris muscles is FALSE per the book?
The sphincter's final supply is the long ciliary nerve
The sphincter's post-ganglionic supply reaches it through the short ciliary nerve
The dilator's final supply is the long ciliary nerve
The parasympathetic route to the sphincter runs via the oculomotor nerve
Final nerve supply per the table: sphincter pupillae — infraorbital branch (to inferior oblique muscle) then short ciliary nerve (post ganglion); dilator pupillae — long ciliary nerve. (Book p8)
Components of uvea and anatomy of the iris
The book's oculomotor branch diagram lists the muscles of each division. All of the following are supplied by the INFERIOR branch of the oculomotor nerve EXCEPT:
None of these three is inferior-branch supplied
Superior branch supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris; inferior branch supplies inferior rectus and inferior oblique. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
Horner's syndrome is defined in the book as:
Oculoparasympathetic palsy of the ciliary ganglion (parasympathetic)
Sensory loss over the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (V1)
Horner's syndrome (HS) is oculosympathetic palsy, i.e. paralysis of the sympathetic supply to the eye. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome

Match the Horner's neuron order with a listed cause — 1) First order (central) 2) Second order (preganglionic) 3) Third order (postganglionic) … A) Pancoast tumour, carotid and aortic aneurysm, neck lesions B) Cluster headache, internal carotid artery dissection, otitis media, cavernous sinus mass C) Brainstem lesions, syringomyelia, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Wallenberg syndrome

First order (central, hypothalamus to ciliospinal centre C8-T1): brainstem lesions, syringomyelia, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, Wallenberg syndrome. Second order (preganglionic, to superior cervical ganglion): Pancoast tumour, carotid and aortic aneurysm, neck lesions. Third order (postganglionic, to dilator via long ciliary nerve): cluster headache, ICA dissection, otitis media, cavernous sinus mass. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
A 58-year-old diabetic presents with Horner's syndrome; MRI shows a lateral medullary infarct (Wallenberg syndrome). The book places this lesion at which neuron order?
The neuromuscular junction of the dilator
Wallenberg syndrome and syringomyelia, brainstem lesions and diabetic autonomic neuropathy are listed under the first-order (central) neuron, hypothalamus to ciliospinal centre (C8-T1). (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
The book's HI MAPLE mnemonic lists the clinical features of Horner's syndrome. All of the following belong to it EXCEPT:
Relative enophthalmos from the lid position
HI MAPLE: Heterochromia Iridis, Inferior eyelid elevation, Miosis, Anhydrosis, Ptosis, Loss of ciliospinal reflex, Relative Enophthalmos. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
Which statement about Horner's syndrome features is FALSE per the book?
Ptosis results from paralysis of Muller's muscle
Miosis results from paralysis of the dilator pupillae
The enophthalmos of Horner's syndrome is a true posterior displacement of the globe
Heterochromia iridis with ipsilateral hypochromia occurs only in congenital Horner's
The book calls the enophthalmos relative — ptosis plus inferior eyelid elevation give a sunken appearance; it is not true enophthalmos. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
Inferior eyelid elevation in Horner's syndrome is due to paralysis of which muscle?
Inferior eyelid elevation is paralysis of the inferior tarsal muscle, the analogue of Muller's muscle in the upper lid. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
Loss of which reflex is listed among the clinical features of Horner's syndrome?
HI MAPLE includes loss of the ciliospinal reflex among Horner's features. (Book p9)
Iris muscles, their autonomic supply and Horner's syndrome
Which two structures does the book credit with elevation of the eyelid?
Muller's muscle (superior tarsal) and LPS supplied by CN III
Orbicularis oculi (lid closure) and levator palpebrae inferioris
The note pairs Muller's muscle / superior tarsal muscle with LPS (supplied by CN III) as the elevators of the eyelid. (Book p10)
Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
Which statement about the cocaine test for Horner's syndrome is FALSE?
A normal pupil dilates because NE rises in the cleft
In Horner's there is no NE in the cleft, so no dilatation occurs
Failure to dilate after cocaine excludes Horner's syndrome
Cocaine test: blockade of NE reuptake dilates a normal pupil; in Horner's no NE is released, so there is no dilatation — failure to dilate confirms, not excludes, the syndrome. (Book p10)
Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
Fill up: with 1% apraclonidine, a normal eye keeps ______ selectivity (miosis), whereas Horner's shows denervation hypersensitivity of α1 receptors and dilates.
Apraclonidine (α agonist): normal selectivity α2 (miosis) > α1; in Horner's denervation hypersensitivity of α1 receptors (mushrooming) reverses selectivity to α1 > α2, dilating the pupil. (Book p10)
Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
To localise a confirmed Horner's syndrome the book uses 1% amphetamine (hydroxyamphetamine). No dilatation of the pupil after the test places the lesion:

Hydroxyamphetamine promotes release of NE into the post-synaptic cleft: dilatation means central or preganglionic disease, while no dilatation means the post-ganglionic (final) pathway is affected — post-ganglionic HS. (Book p10)
Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
A patient with right-eye ptosis and a smaller right pupil dilates after hydroxyamphetamine. Per the book's localisation tree, the lesion lies in:
The neuromuscular junction of Muller's muscle

Dilatation of the pupil after the amphetamine test indicates a central pathway (central HS) or preganglionic pathway (preganglionic HS) lesion; only absence of dilatation localises post-ganglionically. (Book p10)
Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
The photograph captioned in the Horner's section describes which combination?
Absolute enophthalmos with left eye ptosis
The clinical photograph is captioned 'Relative enophthalmos with right eye ptosis'. (Book p10)
Diagnosis of Horner's syndrome — pharmacological tests
The book's ITS COMB list gives causes of mydriasis. All of the following belong to it EXCEPT:

ITS COMB (mydriasis): Internal ophthalmoplegia, Tonic pupil, Sympathomimetics, Closure angle glaucoma, Oculomotor 3rd nerve palsy, Mydriatics, Belladonna poisoning; organophosphates belong to the miosis list. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
The HI COPS list gives causes of miosis. All of the following belong to it EXCEPT:

HI COPS (miosis): Horner's, Hemorrhage (pontine), Iridocyclitis, Clonidine, Carbolic acid, Organophosphates/Opioids, Parasympathomimetics, Sleep/Sedatives; tropicamide is a mydriatic in the ITS COMB list. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
Aqueous humour is secreted by which part of the uvea?
Pars plana of the ciliary body
Ciliary body functions: secretion of aqueous through the ciliary processes. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
The book prefers the pars plana as the site of entry into the vitreous cavity because:
It is the thickest uveal tissue of the eye
It secretes the vitreous gel directly
It contains the ciliary muscles of accommodation
Pars plana is the site of entry into the vitreous cavity because relative avascularity reduces the chances of bleeding. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
Which statement about accommodation per the book is FALSE?
Accommodation tightens the zonules to flatten the lens
Contraction of the ciliary muscles increases the power of the lens
Accommodation = contraction of ciliary muscles → increased lens power with relaxation of zonules, helping near vision; zonular tightening belongs to the relaxed (far-vision) state. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
The book lists three components of the near reflex. All of the following are components EXCEPT:
Components of the near reflex: accommodation, convergence (inward movement of both eyes) and miosis. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex

Match the visual state with its lens-zonule configuration — 1) Far vision (relaxed state) 2) Near vision with accommodation … A) Ciliary muscles contracted with reduced ring diameter, zonules slack, increased curvature of the anterior surface, increased A-P diameter and increased lens power B) Ciliary muscles relaxed, zonules tense, flat anterior surface
Zonules are tense in both states

The two figures: far vision shows relaxed ciliary muscles with tense zonules and a flat anterior surface; near vision shows contracted muscles (reduced ring diameter), slack zonules, increased anterior curvature, increased A-P diameter and increased lens power. (Book p11)
Pupil size mnemonics, ciliary body and the near reflex
Fill up: presbyopia is the ______ insufficiency of accommodation, producing difficulty with near vision.
Presbyopia is defined as physiological insufficiency of accommodation causing difficulty in near vision such as using phones or reading newspaper. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
Per the book's age rule for presbyopic correction, the add power required at 50 years of age is:
At 40 years +1 D is required and every additional 5 years adds +0.5 D: 45 years +1.5 D, 50 years +2 D. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
The book states presbyopia typically begins around which age?
Onset of presbyopia: around 40 years of age. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
The book's preference order for presbyopic spectacles is:
Rx: convex (+) spectacles with the preference progressives > D-bifocals >>> executive lenses; power depends on age. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation

Match the spectacle type with its book description — 1) Monofocal 2) Progressive lenses 3) D-bifocals 4) Executive bifocals … A) Cosmetically unappealing with no provision for intermediate vision B) Power restricted to a central hourglass configuration with no power in the peripheries, giving a restricted field of view C) Pupil bisected by the line between the lenses; obsolete except in paediatric aphakia D) Cosmetically appealing with seamless transition, covering near, intermediate and far vision

Monofocal (only near-vision patients): power restricted to centre hourglass, no power in peripheries, restricted field of view. Progressives: seamless, cosmetically appealing, cover near/intermediate/far. D-bifocals: cosmetically unappealing, no intermediate provision. Executive bifocals: pupil bisected by the line between lenses, obsolete except paediatric aphakia. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation

A 46-year-old tailor who has never worn glasses complains that threading a needle and reading his phone have become difficult, while distance vision is fine. The book's first-line correction for him is:
Patients only needing near-vision lenses (no existing distance glasses) are given monofocal spectacles; progressives/bifocals are for patients already using glasses for far vision. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
Spasm of accommodation produces which functional loss, and under what name?
Spasm of accommodation is a continuous state of contraction of the ciliary muscles causing loss of far vision, labelled pseudomyopia. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
The book treats spasm of accommodation with cycloplegia. Which drug group does it list?
Miotics — pilocarpine and carbachol eye drops
Beta blockers — timolol eye drops twice daily
Treatment is cycloplegia (relaxation of ciliary muscles) with drugs: mydriatics and cycloplegics — atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate. (Book p12)
Anomalies of accommodation — presbyopia and spasm of accommodation
The retina is described in the book as the innermost layer of the eye and as a:
The retina heading reads 'Retina - Innermost Layer of Eye' with the line 'Neurosensory layer'. (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim
Fill up: the optic disc is also called the blind spot of ______ because rods and cones are absent there.
Optic disc is AKA blind spot of Marriot, where rods and cones are absent. (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim
Which statement about the optic disc is FALSE per the book?
It is the point where the optic nerve leaves the eyeball
It contains the highest concentration of cones in the retina
All layers of the retina terminate at the optic disc except the nerve fibres
It is the first, only visible and intra-ocular part of the optic nerve
The maximum concentration of cones belongs to the fovea, not the optic disc; the disc is rod- and cone-free (blind spot of Marriot). (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim
The book's optic-disc appearance block gives the disc diameter as:
Appearance of the optic disc: vertically oval, diameter 1.5 mm / 1500 µm, normal c/d ratio 0.3. (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim
The normal cup-to-disc ratio printed beside the optic disc figure is:
Normal c/d ratio is given as 0.3 in the optic disc appearance list. (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim

Match the optic-disc relation printed in the figure — 1) d(OD) 2) NRR thickness order 3) Effect of glaucoma on the NRR … A) Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal B) Cup plus neuro-retinal rim C) The rim becomes visibly thinner

The figure states d(OD) = C (optic cup) + NRR (neuro-retinal rim), which allows vessels to travel through; NRR thickness runs Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal and becomes visibly thinner in glaucoma. (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim
A glaucoma suspect's disc photograph shows sectoral rim loss. Per the book's NRR thickness order, the rim sector that is normally the THICKEST — and therefore whose thinning is most telling — is the:
NRR thickness order is Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal, and the rim becomes visibly thinner in glaucoma. (Book p13)
Optic disc — blind spot, dimensions and neuro-retinal rim
The macula lutea is described as a yellowish spot situated:
At the centre of the optic disc
Macula lutea: yellowish spot, temporal to OD, diameter 5.5 mm. (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata
The diameters of the macula lutea and of the fovea per the book are:
Macula lutea diameter 5.5 mm; fovea diameter 1.85 mm with the highest/best visual acuity from the maximum concentration of cones (central vision). (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata
Fill up: within the macula, the ______ is the zone that does not have a ganglionic layer.
The macula figure labels the foveola as the area that does not have a ganglionic layer. (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata
The small bright spot seen when light is shone into the eye — the foveolar reflex — arises from which structure?
The scleral spur at the angle
The optic cup of the disc
Umbo is the small central depression; light shone upon the eye reflects and shines as a small bright spot — the foveolar reflex. (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata

Match the posterior-pole structure with its book feature — 1) Fovea 2) Foveola 3) Umbo 4) Ora serrata … A) Small central depression producing the foveolar reflex B) Maximum cone concentration giving central vision C) Anterior termination of the retina at the ciliary body-choroid junction D) Zone without a ganglionic layer

Fovea: 1.85 mm, maximum cones, central vision; foveola: no ganglionic layer; umbo: small central depression with the foveolar reflex; ora serrata: anterior termination of retina marking the ciliary body-choroid junction. (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata
The practical significance of the ora serrata given in the book is that it helps determine:
The centre of the visual field
The depth of the anterior chamber in mm
The angle of the anterior chamber
Ora serrata significance: helps determine the site of intra-vitreal injection; it is the anterior termination of the retina indicating the junction between ciliary body and choroid. (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata
All of the following are labelled in the book's macula figure EXCEPT:
The macula figure labels foveola, fovea and umbo; pars plicata belongs to the ciliary body, not this figure. (Book p13)
Macula lutea, fovea, foveola, umbo and ora serrata

Match the lens status with the book's intravitreal injection site — 1) Aphakia (absence of lens) 2) Pseudophakia 3) Phakia (normal crystalline lens) … A) 3.5 mm posterior to the limbus B) 3 mm posterior to the limbus C) 4 mm posterior to the limbus
Intravitreal injection site table: aphakia 3 mm, pseudophakia 3.5 mm, phakia 4 mm posterior to the limbus. (Book p14)
An intravitreal injection pierces which two structures on its way to the vitreous?
The book states the injection pierces sclera and pars plana. (Book p14)
Arrange the book's intravitreal injection procedure in order: which step immediately follows sterilising the sclera infero-temporally?
Marking the injection site with a caliper
Asking the patient to look up/in
Opening the eyes with a speculum first

Procedure order: speculum to open eyes → sterilise sclera infero-temporally → ask patient to look upwards/inwards → mark site with caliper → 30G needle inserted through sclera with slow twisting movements to reach the vitreous. (Book p14)
The needle gauge the book specifies for intravitreal injection is:
Injection with a 30G needle is inserted through the sclera with slow, twisting movements to reach the vitreous. (Book p14)
The visible landmark used to measure the intravitreal injection site behind the limbus is:
The figure labels the limbus as the visible landmark, with the intra-vitreal injection placed behind it. (Book p14)
A 66-year-old pseudophakic man is booked for an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. Measured from the limbus, the book's entry site for his lens status is:
3 mm posterior to the limbus only
Pseudophakia takes the 3.5 mm posterior-to-limbus site; aphakia 3 mm and phakia 4 mm. (Book p14)
An intracameral injection is defined by the book as an injection into:
The sub-Tenon's space below Tenon's capsule
The episcleral space above the sclera
The vitreous cavity behind the crystalline lens
Intracameral injection: injection into the anterior chamber (AC), e.g. after the incision during cataract surgery. (Book p15)
Which statement about topical ocular therapy is FALSE per the book?
Ointment is given before drops for absorption
Topical application is the most commonly used route
Eye drops are administered before ointment
Eye ointment is administered at least 3 minutes after drops
Topical is m/c used; eyedrops are administered before ointment, and ointment at least 3 minutes after drops because it provides a longer time of contact. (Book p15)
The posterior sub-Tenon (PST, parabulbar) injection is placed below which structure, and for which condition does the book use it?
Below Tenon's capsule, used in intermediate uveitis
Below the conjunctiva, used in conjunctivitis treatment
Below the sclera, used in scleritis
Below the choroid, used in posterior uveitis
Parabulbar or posterior sub-Tenon (PST) injection lies below Tenon's capsule (Nozik technique) and is used in intermediate uveitis. (Book p15)
Fill up: to keep a longer time of contact, eye ointment is administered at least ______ after the drops.
Eye ointment is administered ≥3 minutes after drops and provides a longer time of contact; drops always precede ointment. (Book p15)
In the injection-layers figure, the episclera and Tenon's capsule fuse at what distance behind the limbus?
The figure shows episclera and Tenon's capsule fusing 3 mm posterior to the limbus. (Book p15)
The book's site for local ocular anaesthesia is through the lower eyelid at:
The junction of the medial 1/3 and middle 1/3
The centre of the lower lid margin
Site: through the lower eyelid at the junction of middle 1/3 and lateral 1/3. (Book p15)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
The needle gauge and anaesthetic volume in the book's local anaesthesia procedure are:
Procedure: pull the lower lid down and insert a 24-25G needle through the lid along the floor of the eye, aspirate to rule out vessel injury, insert 5 ml of anaesthetic, then compress. (Book p15)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
Why does the book aspirate before injecting the local anaesthetic, and what follows the injection?
To test the pH; compression spreads the drug into the vitreous
To estimate the depth; compression prevents ptosis
To check for reflux; compression prevents corneal anaesthesia
Rule out vessel injury; compression limits IOP rise
Aspirate: rule out vessel injury; after inserting 5 ml of anaesthetic, post-injection compression over the eye avoids a rise of intra-ocular pressure. (Book p15)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
Fill up: peribulbar anaesthesia is injected into the ______ space, the route the book calls better.
Peribulbar (or) extraconal space is labelled the better route; retrobulbar occupies the intraconal space. (Book p16)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
Which statement comparing the two ocular anaesthesia spaces is FALSE per the book?
The retrobulbar (intraconal) route is labelled the better route
Peribulbar anaesthesia enters the extraconal (outside-cone) space
Retrobulbar anaesthesia enters the intraconal (within-cone) space
The peribulbar route is labelled the better (safer) route
The routes figure labels peribulbar (extraconal space) as the better route; retrobulbar is the intraconal space. (Book p16)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
The base of the orbit is quadrangular and, per the book, carries which surgical risk?
It holds blood vessels, raising hemorrhage risk
It contains the optic canal, risking blindness
It contains the lacrimal gland, risking dry eye
It contains the annulus of Zinn, risking ophthalmoplegia
Base of orbit: quadrangular shaped, contains blood vessels → increased chance of hemorrhage; apex of orbit is conical shaped. (Book p16)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
The annulus of Zinn is the common origin of all extraocular muscles EXCEPT:
Annulus of Zinn: tendinous ring, common origin for all EOMs except the inferior oblique. (Book p16)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
Match the orbital angle label of the anaesthesia figure with its definition — 1) X 2) Y … A) Angle between both lateral walls of the orbit B) Angle between the medial and lateral walls of the orbit
X is the angle of the optic canal
Figure keys: X = angle between medial and lateral walls of orbit; Y = angle between both lateral walls of orbit. (Book p16)
Local routes of ocular anaesthesia and the orbital spaces
The optic nerve is defined in the book as a collection of:
Axons of bipolar cells of retina
Optic nerve: a collection of axons of retinal ganglion cells, total length 47-50 mm. (Book p16)
The total length of the optic nerve per the book is:
Total length of the optic nerve: 47-50 mm. (Book p16)
Match the optic nerve part with its length — 1) Intraocular (disc) 2) Intraorbital 3) Intracanalicular 4) Intracranial … A) 25 to 30 mm B) 1 mm C) 10 to 15 mm D) 9 mm
Parts and lengths: intraocular (disc) 1 mm, intraorbital 25 to 30 mm, intracanalicular 9 mm, intracranial 10 to 15 mm. (Book p16)
Which statement about the optic nerve parts is FALSE per the book?
The second part acquires the myelin sheath
The third part (canal) is the longest
The first (intraocular) part is the shortest
The second (intraorbital) part is the longest
The third part lies within the optic canal, but the longest part is the second (intraorbital); the first is the shortest and the second acquires the myelin sheath. (Book p16)
The central retinal artery and vein enter the optic nerve at what distance behind the eye, and in which direction?
In the second part the central retinal artery and vein enter 10 mm behind the eye, inferomedially. (Book p16)

Match the branch of the ophthalmic artery with its book territory — 1) Central retinal artery 2) Short posterior ciliary artery 3) Anterior ciliary artery … A) Sclera, choroid and outer layer of retina B) Inner 6 layers of the retina, entering the optic nerve C) Anterior portion of sclera, ciliary process, iris and conjunctiva

Central retinal artery supplies the inner 6 layers of retina and enters the ON; short posterior ciliary arteries pierce around the ON supplying sclera, choroid and outer retina; anterior ciliary arteries supply anterior sclera, ciliary process, iris and conjunctiva. (Book p17)
The long posterior ciliary artery pierces the sclera:
Around the optic nerve, piercing with it
At the limbus, beneath the conjunctiva
Through the optic canal with the nerve
Away from the ON, sclera-choroid route

Long posterior ciliary artery pierces the sclera away from the ON, travels between sclera and choroid, reaches the ciliary body and supplies the ciliary muscle before passing anteriorly to the iris. (Book p17)
Match the arterial circle of the iris with its supply — 1) Major arterial circle 2) Minor arterial circle … A) Pupillary zone of the iris B) Ciliary process of the iris

Travelling anteriorly, the long posterior ciliary artery forms the major arterial circle supplying the ciliary process of the iris and the minor arterial circle supplying the pupillary zone of the iris. (Book p17)
The muscular branches to the recti number seven. The book's distribution is:
3 for MR, 2 for SR, 1 for IR, 1 for LR
2 for SR, 2 for MR, 2 for IR, 1 for LR
2 for SR, 2 for LR, 2 for IR, 1 for MR
Muscular branches to recti: 7 in number — 2 for SR, 2 for MR, 2 for IR, 1 for LR; the medial rectus branches form the anterior ciliary artery. (Book p17)
The anterior ciliary artery pierces the sclera:
At the equator of the globe
Anterior ciliary artery pierces the sclera anteriorly, posterior to the limbus. (Book p17)
All of the following are supplied by the anterior ciliary artery per the book EXCEPT:
The anterior portion of the sclera
Anterior ciliary artery supplies anterior portion of sclera, ciliary process, iris and conjunctiva; the choroid is supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries. (Book p17)
Development of the eye begins on which day of gestation per the book?
Day 27, the end of the 4th week
Day 33, the end of the 5th week
Day 22, the end of the 3rd week
Day 14, the end of the 2nd week
Development of the eye begins on Day 22 / end of the 3rd week of gestation. (Book p18)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives
The earliest indication of development of the eye in utero is the:
Downward growth produces elevations and deepening; the optic groove/sulcus is the earliest indication of development of the eye in utero, then evagination gives the optic vesicles. (Book p18)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives
Lateral growth with lens formation begins on day 27; the choroidal fissure closes by:
The choroidal fissure is a shallow groove that closes by the 6-7th week of gestation. (Book p18)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives
In the day-27 diagram, the thickened surface ectoderm opposite the optic vesicle is the:

The figure labels surface ectoderm and lens placode (LP) with OV (optic vesicle) and OS (optic stalk); the lens vesicle depression is then engulfed by the OV and the lens placode pinches off. (Book p18)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives

Match the mesenchymal source with its derivative — 1) Surface ectoderm 2) Neural ectoderm 3) Neural crest cells 4) Mesoderm … A) Optic nerve, retina, vitreous, epithelium of iris and ciliary body, sphincter and dilator pupillae B) Lens, skin of eyelids, epithelium of cornea and conjunctiva, tarsal/Meibomian glands C) Extraocular muscles and endothelial lining of blood vessels D) Uvea, sclera, Descemet's membrane and ciliary muscle

Derivatives: surface ectoderm — lens, eyelid skin, corneal and conjunctival epithelium, tarsal/Meibomian glands; neural ectoderm — optic nerve, retina, vitreous, iris+CB epithelium and iris muscles; neural crest — uvea, sclera, Descemet's membrane, ciliary muscle; mesoderm — extraocular muscles and vessel endothelium. (Book p19)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives
All of the following are neural-crest derivatives of the eye per the book EXCEPT:
Neural crest cells form the uvea (vascular layer), sclera, Descemet's membrane and ciliary muscle; the lens is a surface-ectoderm derivative. (Book p19)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives
The mesenchyme of the eye is formed by which two sources, and how does the neural-crest contribution divide?
Mesoderm + neural crest; crest gives fibrous and vascular mesenchyme
Ectoderm and endoderm; crest gives only sclera (fibrous)
Mesoderm and endoderm; crest gives only uvea (vascular)
Neural ectoderm and surface ectoderm; crest gives the lens (transparent)
Mesenchyme of the eye is formed by mesoderm and neural crest cells, the crest dividing into superficial (fibrous mesenchyme) and deep (vascular mesenchyme). (Book p19)
Development of the eye and its embryological derivatives
The word coloboma means, per its etymology in the book:
Etymology of coloboma: missing, mutilated part. (Book p19)
Eyeball coloboma is a congenital malformation due to:
Failure of the optic vesicle to evaginate
Eye ball coloboma: congenital malformation d/t non-closure of the choroidal fissure. (Book p19)
The pupil shape produced by an infero-nasal iris coloboma is described as:
The iris photograph shows an infero-nasal iris coloboma giving a pear-shaped pupil / key hole pupil. (Book p19)

Match the coloboma detail with the book's statement — 1) Structures affected from deep mesenchyme 2) Structures affected from OV and OS 3) Typical coloboma 4) Atypical coloboma … A) Any quadrant other than the infero-nasal B) Iris (and ciliary body) C) Choroid, retina and optic nerve D) Infero-nasal quadrant

Structures affected: deep mesenchyme derivatives — iris (ciliary body); from OV and OS — choroid, retina, optic nerve; typical coloboma — infero-nasal quadrant; atypical — any other quadrant. (Book p20)
A retino-choroidal (fundal) coloboma matters clinically because it increases the incidence of:

Retino-choroidal / fundal coloboma: increased incidence of retinal detachment; its types follow the Ida Mann classification, and the photo shows yellowish sclera seen through an oval defect. (Book p20)
Which statement about eyelid coloboma is FALSE per the book?
Its commonest site is the upper eyelid between the middle and medial thirds
It occurs via choroidal fissure non-closure
It does not occur due to choroidal/fetal fissure non-closure
It is an incomplete form of facial cleft / cryptophthalmos

Eyelid coloboma explicitly does NOT occur due to choroidal/fetal fissure non-closure; it is an incomplete form of facial cleft/cryptophthalmos, m/c on the upper eyelid between middle 1/3 and medial 1/3. (Book p20)
Eyelid coloboma is associated with all of the following syndromes in the book EXCEPT:
Associated syndromes: Fraser, Goldenhar and Treacher Collins; Down syndrome is not listed. (Book p20)
The complications of eyelid coloboma (cosmetic blemish, exposure keratopathy, amblyopia) are prevented by:
Complications — cosmetic blemish, exposure keratopathy, amblyopia (from keratopathy, refractive errors or dermoid in Goldenhar) — are prevented by Rx: eyelid reconstruction. (Book p20)

A newborn is noted to have an infero-nasal key-hole pupil; funduscopy shows an oval defect with yellowish sclera visible through it. The book attributes this eyeball defect to failure of closure of which embryonic structure?
Eyeball coloboma is d/t non-closure of the choroidal fissure; the fundal photo shows yellowish sclera through an oval defect and the iris coloboma gives the key-hole/pear-shaped pupil. (Book p20)
Which statement about lens coloboma is FALSE per the book?
Defective development of zonules produces a notch-shaped inferior defect
It results from choroidal fissure non-closure
It is not a true coloboma
The lens placode is too large to pass through the choroidal fissure
Lens coloboma is not a true coloboma: the lens placode is large and cannot go through the choroidal fissure; defective zonular development gives a notch-shaped inferior defect in the lens. (Book p20)
In the book's visual-pathway scheme, visual impulses are generated by the retina and the image is finally perceived in the:
Retina generates visual impulses and the occipital cortex perceives the image; a lesion along the visual pathway produces a visual field defect. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
Match the visual field half with the retinal fibres that carry it — 1) Nasal visual field 2) Temporal visual field … A) Nasal fibres B) Temporal fibres
Both are carried by nasal fibres
Both are carried by temporal fibres
The figure key: nasal visual field → temporal fibres; temporal visual field → nasal fibres. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
The optic nerve carries which fibre combination per the book?
Ipsilateral temporal plus ipsilateral nasal fibres
Contralateral temporal plus ipsilateral nasal fibres
Optic nerve (ON): I/L temporal + I/L nasal fibres. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
At the optic chiasm the event printed in the book is:
Decussation of half of the macular fibres only (macular)
Crossing of nasal fibres (chiasm holds B/L nasal)
Crossing over of temporal fibres (both eyes)
Relay of all fibres to the lateral geniculate body (LGB)
Optic chiasm (OC): crossing over of nasal fibres; it contains B/L nasal fibres. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station

Match the post-chiasmal station with its fibre content — 1) Optic tract 2) Lateral geniculate body 3) Optic radiations … A) Ipsilateral temporal plus contralateral nasal fibres B) Relay centre for the same fibre set C) Same fibres en route to the visual cortex
Optic tract, LGB (the relay centre) and optic radiations all carry I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres to the visual cortex. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
Fill up: at the optic chiasm the fibres that cross over are the ______ fibres, so the chiasm contains them from both eyes.
Optic chiasm: crossing over of nasal fibres; the chiasm therefore contains B/L nasal fibres while temporal fibres stay ipsilateral. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
Which statement about the book's pathway diagram is FALSE?
The optic chiasm contains bilateral temporal fibres
A lesion anywhere along the pathway gives a visual field defect
The lateral geniculate body is labelled the relay centre
The optic radiations are drawn as superior and inferior fibres
The chiasm contains bilateral NASAL fibres (crossing nasal fibres), not temporal fibres; LGB is the relay centre and the radiations split into superior and inferior fibres. (Book p21)
Visual pathway — fibre composition at each station
A left optic nerve lesion produces which field defect for the left-sided lesions described in the book?
Optic nerve lesion (I/L temporal + I/L nasal fibres) gives I/L anopia (blindness). (Book p22)
The earliest visual field defect in any optic nerve disease per the book is:
Macular/central fibres in the ON are most susceptible to ischemia and are affected first, so the earliest field defect is an ipsilateral central scotoma. (Book p22)

Match the chiasmal fibre group with its field defect — 1) Bilateral nasal fibres 2) Bilateral inferonasal fibres 3) Bilateral superonasal fibres … A) Bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia B) Bitemporal/heteronymous hemianopia C) Bitemporal superior quadrantanopia
Chiasmal lesions: B/L nasal → bitemporal/heteronymous hemianopia; B/L inferonasal → bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia; B/L superonasal → bitemporal superior quadrantanopia. (Book p22)

Match the cause with its direction of pressure on the chiasm in the book's list — 1) Pituitary adenoma 2) Craniopharyngioma 3) Anterior communicating artery aneurysm … A) From Rathke's pouch, superiorly B) From the sella turcica, inferiorly C) Laterally/compressing the chiasm lying under the ACA

Causes of chiasmal compression: 3rd ventricular glioma; pituitary adenoma from the sella turcica inferiorly; craniopharyngioma from Rathke's pouch superiorly; ACA aneurysm; carotid sinus thrombosis laterally — the chiasm lies under the ACA. (Book p22)
A 45-year-old with a pituitary adenoma compressing the chiasm from below undergoes perimetry early in the disease. The book's earliest expected defect is:
B/L inferonasal fibre involvement gives bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia, labelled the earliest VFD in pituitary adenoma (pressure from below). (Book p22)
A child with a suprasellar mass arising from Rathke's pouch shows an early field defect. Per the book it is:
Craniopharyngioma (from Rathke's pouch, superiorly) involves B/L superonasal fibres first, giving bitemporal superior quadrantanopia — the earliest VFD in craniopharyngioma. (Book p22)

Match the junctional (proximal optic nerve) lesion fibre set with its components — the anterior knee of Wilbrand lesion takes: 1) I/L temporal 2) I/L nasal 3) C/L inferonasal … producing the junctional scotoma. Which combination is printed?
Junction of ON and OC (proximal ON): anterior knee of Wilbrand lesion involves I/L temporal + I/L nasal + C/L inferonasal fibres, producing a junctional scotoma; cause: meningioma. (Book p22)
The book gives which cause for a junctional scotoma?
Junctional scotoma (junction of ON and OC, anterior knee of Wilbrand) — cause: meningioma. (Book p22)
Bilateral temporal fibre involvement at the lateral optic chiasm produces:
Lateral optic chiasma (B/L temporal fibres) gives binasal hemianopia, noted as very rare. (Book p23)

Match the post-chiasmal station with the field defect of its lesion — 1) Optic tract (5) 2) LGB (6) 3) Optic radiations (7) … A) Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia for all three B) Only the tract gives a hemianopsia C) Only the radiations give a hemianopsia D) The LGB gives a quadrantanopia
Lesions at 5 (OT), 6 (LGB) and 7 (OR) all involve I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres and give C/L homonymous hemianopsia. (Book p23)
Meyer's loop is which part of the optic radiations, and its lesion gives:
Inferior optic radiations — contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia (pie on the floor)
Inferior optic radiations — pie in the sky (temporal)
Superior optic radiations — contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia (pie in the sky)
Superior OR (Meyer's loop) carries superior I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres; its lesion gives C/L homonymous superior quadrantanopia, AKA pie in the sky. (Book p23)
The book's mnemonic TIPS stands for:
Tract inferior pie on the floor
Temporal inferior pie in the sky
Mnemonic TIPS = Temporal Inferior Pie in the Sky, for Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) lesions. (Book p23)
Temporal lobe disease features listed with Meyer's loop lesions include all of the following EXCEPT:
Temporal lobe disease features: uncinate fits, seizures, visual hallucinations; agraphia belongs to the parietal lobe list. (Book p23)
Baum's loop is which part of the radiations, and its lesion gives:
Inferior radiations — pie on the floor
Superior optic radiations — pie in the sky (temporal loop)
Inferior OR (Baum's loop) carries inferior I/L temporal + C/L nasal fibres; its lesion gives C/L homonymous inferior quadrantanopia, AKA pie on the floor. (Book p23)
Parietal lobe disease features listed with Baum's loop lesions include all of the following EXCEPT:
Apraxia if the non-dominant lobe is involved
Parietal lobe disease features: aphasia, acalculia, agraphia, apraxia (non-dominant lobe); uncinate fits belong to the temporal lobe list. (Book p23)
A lesion of the tip of the occipital cortex (macular representation) produces:
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing (sparing)
10a) Tip of cortex lesion (macular representation) gives C/L homonymous macular defect, AKA cookie centre defect. (Book p23)
Which statement about occipital lobe lesions is FALSE per the book?
A complete occipital lobe lesion gives macular sparing
A lesion of the visual cortex except its tip spares the macular representation
Cortical lesions except the tip give C/L homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing
A complete occipital lobe lesion gives C/L homonymous hemianopia and is rare
Complete occipital lobe lesion leads to C/L homonymous hemianopia (no sparing) and is rare; macular sparing belongs to cortex-except-tip lesions. (Book p23)
The abnormal pupil seen with an optic tract lesion is named:
In the OT/LGB/OR comparison table the pupil is abnormal in OT lesions — Wernicke's pupil — and normal in LGB and OR lesions. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects

Match the lesion site with the optic atrophy pattern — 1) Optic tract 2) LGB 3) Optic radiations … A) Present (+) B) Absent because the optic radiations are post-ganglionic C) Present bilaterally — I/L superior and inferior, C/L bow-tie pattern
Optic atrophy: OT — present bilaterally (I/L superior and inferior, C/L bow-tie pattern); LGB — present (+); OR — absent because optic radiations are post-ganglionic. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
Which statement about congruity of the visual loss is FALSE per the book's table?
Optic radiation lesions give congruous defects
Optic tract lesions give incongruous defects
Congruity of parameters of LOV: incongruous for OT and LGB, congruous for OR. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
The book lists associations and causes of optic tract lesions. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
TB/syphilitic meningitis and posterior cerebral artery aneurysm

OT lesions are associated with C/L hemiplegia and CN III palsy, caused by TB/syphilitic meningitis and posterior cerebral artery aneurysm; craniopharyngioma is listed under chiasmal causes. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
The lateral geniculate body is composed of how many laminae, and where do contralateral fibres relay?
Four laminae; C/L fibres relay into 1 and 2
Six laminae; C/L fibres relay into 2, 3 and 5
Three laminae; C/L fibres relay into all
LGB is composed of 6 laminae: C/L fibres relay into 1, 4, 6 laminae and I/L fibres into 2, 3, 5 laminae. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
Fill up: within the six laminae of the lateral geniculate body, ipsilateral fibres relay into laminae ______.
LGB laminae: C/L fibres relay into 1, 4, 6 laminae while I/L fibres relay into 2, 3, 5 laminae. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
A keyhole visual field defect is caused by:
Miscellaneous lesions: keyhole VFD — cause: incomplete LGB lesion. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
An altitudinal visual field defect is defined by respecting which boundary?
Altitudinal VFD respects the horizontal midline, appearing as B/L superior or B/L inferior loss. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
The book's GOA mnemonic lists causes of altitudinal defects. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
GOA: Glaucoma, Optic disc Drusen, AION (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy); optic neuritis is listed under central scotoma causes. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
The commonest cause behind optic-neuritis central scotoma in the book's list is:

Central scotoma causes include any ON lesion, e.g. optic neuritis with multiple sclerosis as the m/c cause; also toxic optic neuropathy/tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, hereditary optic neuropathy and cone dystrophy (Stargardt's disease). (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
All of the following are listed causes of central scotoma EXCEPT:

Central scotoma causes: any ON lesion (optic neuritis — MS m/c), toxic optic neuropathy/tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, hereditary optic neuropathy, cone dystrophy (Stargardt's disease); retinal detachment is not listed. (Book p24)
Optic tract, LGB and radiation lesions; miscellaneous field defects
Cortical blindness results from a lesion in:
Cortical blindness: lesion in bilateral cortical hemisphere. (Book p25)
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
Denial of blindness by a cortically blind patient is named:
Anton's syndrome: patient in denial of blindness. (Book p25)
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
Statokinetic dissociation in cortical blindness is called:
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
Which statement about cortical blindness is FALSE per the book?
The light reflex is lost with nerve damage
The pupils remain normal in cortical blindness
There is bilateral blindness of both eyes
In cortical blindness the pupil remains normal (the reflex arc is pre-cortical) while VEP is absent; bilateral blindness with Anton's and Riddoch phenomena completes the picture. (Book p25)
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
The investigation that differentiates functional from organic blindness in the book is:
VEP is absent in cortical blindness and differentiates functional from organic blindness. (Book p25)
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
A young woman claims total blindness after a stressful event; examination is unremarkable and the book's malingering/hysterical-blindness workup is planned. The expected VEP is:
Absent in the claimed eye only
Other uses of VEP: malingering and hysterical blindness show a normal VEP. (Book p25)
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
All of the following are clinical features of cortical blindness in the book EXCEPT:
Clinical features: B/L blindness, Anton's syndrome, Riddoch phenomenon, and a pupil that remains normal. (Book p25)
Cortical blindness and the visual evoked potential
Per the book, the near reflex has three components. Which set is printed?
The near reflex (first of the four pupillary reflexes) has 3 parts: accommodation, convergence and miosis. (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
Fill up: the ciliospinal reflex is triggered by pain in the side of the neck or trunk, producing ______.
Ciliospinal reflex: pain in side of neck/trunk → ipsilateral pupil dilation. (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
The book lists four pupillary reflexes. Which of the following is NOT among them?
The four pupillary reflexes: near (3 parts), ciliospinal, psychosensory and pupillary light reflex (PLR); VOR belongs to the vestibular apparatus, not this list. (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
Which statement about the light reflex procedure is FALSE per the book?
It is a dark room procedure
The hand is placed between the eyes to separate visual fields
Low light causes dilation of the pupil
Bright light causes dilation of the pupil
Procedure: dark room; hand between eyes → separate visual fields. Normal findings: bright light → constriction (not dilation); low light → dilation. (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
You test a patient's pupillary light reflex in a dark room and place your hand between his two eyes. Per the book the purpose is to:
Separate the visual fields of the two eyes
Block the consensual pathway to the opposite eye
The hand between the eyes separates the visual fields so each eye can be illuminated and read independently. (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview

Match the event with the pupil response in the book's figure — 1) Light shone on the left eye 2) Illuminated (left) pupil 3) Non-illuminated (right) pupil … A) Constricts by the direct reflex B) Constricts by the consensual reflex C) Source of the stimulus
Left stimulus: the illuminated pupil constricts (direct reflex) and the contralateral non-illuminated pupil constricts (consensual reflex). (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
Fill up: the consensual reflex is the constriction of the ______ pupil, that is, the pupil that is not illuminated.
Direct reflex = constriction of the illuminated pupil; consensual reflex = constriction of the C/L (non-illuminated) pupil. (Book p26)
Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
In the book's PLR pathway figure, where do the afferent fibres leave the visual pathway?
After relaying in the lateral geniculate body
In the retina before the optic nerve
Before reaching the LGB, exiting from the optic tract
Afferent (I/L) limb: light on one eye → optic nerve; PLR fibres exit from the optic tract before reaching the LGB and reach the pretectal centre. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map

Match the PLR pathway station with its labelled role — 1) Pretectal nucleus 2) Internuncial neuron 3) Edinger-Westphal nucleus … A) Accessory nucleus for CN III B) Centre of the reflex in the midbrain C) Relay from the centre to the EWN
Pretectal nucleus = centre; the internuncial (I/N) neuron relays to the B/L EWN; EWN = accessory nucleus for CN III. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
Fill up: the Edinger-Westphal nucleus supplies the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle and is the accessory nucleus of cranial nerve ______.
EWN (accessory nucleus for CN III) supplies the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
Which statement about the PLR pathway is FALSE per the book?
ON, OC and OT are common to the PLR and the visual pathway
The PLR efferent neurons are primarily temporal
The reflex stays strictly on the illuminated side only
The short ciliary nerve carries the final efferent limb

The efferent limb is B/L: from the centre via I/N neurons to both EWNs, giving direct and consensual responses; ON/OC/OT are common to both pathways; efferent neurons are primarily temporal. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
Which nerve–muscle pairing is the final efferent step of the PLR per the book?
Long ciliary nerve to the sphincter pupillae
Short ciliary nerve to the ciliary muscle
Long ciliary nerve to the ciliary muscle
Short ciliary nerve to the sphincter pupillae
B/L short ciliary nerves from the B/L ciliary ganglia supply the B/L sphincter pupillae, producing constriction. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
The book splits PLR lesions into afferent and efferent types. Which is NOT an efferent pathway lesion?
Efferent pathway lesions: Argyll Robertson pupil, tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis; Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) is an afferent pathway lesion. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map

Match the afferent pathway lesion with the book's label — 1) Total (absolute) afferent defect 2) Relative afferent defect 3) I/L optic tract lesion … A) Wernicke's pupil B) Absolute afferent pathway defect C) Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD)
Afferent pathway lesions: total/absolute → AAPO; relative → Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD); Wernicke's pupil is the optic-tract (hemianopic) pupil. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
Fill up: the book's efferent pathway lesion list is Argyll Robertson pupil, ______ pupil and pharmacological mydriasis.
Efferent pathway lesions: Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP), tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis. (Book p27)
PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
Which cause does the book give for an absolute afferent pathway defect (AAPO)?
Retinal detachment and end stage optic nerve disease
Complete optic nerve lesion d/t trauma or end stage optic nerve disease
AAPO: complete optic nerve lesion d/t trauma or end stage optic nerve disease. (Book p28)
All of the following are listed causes of an incomplete optic nerve lesion producing RAPD EXCEPT:
Retinal detachment, since the ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons
RAPD causes: optic neuritis, CRAO, retinal detachment (ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons); a complete optic nerve lesion (e.g. trauma) gives AAPO, not RAPD. (Book p28)
A 30-year-old with left optic neuritis undergoes the swinging flashlight test. On repeated swings to the affected (fatigued) left eye the book expects:
B/L constriction of both pupils on every swing
B/L dilation of pupils when the eye with the lesion is stimulated
Only the right pupil dilates on each swing
No change in either pupil with repeated swings

Swinging flashlight test in RAPD: on presentation B/L constricted; on stimulus B/L constrict on one eye; swinging to the other eye the pupils dilate in the meantime and constrict again; repeat (fatigue the lesioned ON) → B/L dilation when the lesion eye is stimulated. (Book p28)
Which statement about the light reflex in AAPO is FALSE per the book's table?
Light on the lesion side produces no constriction of either pupil
The I/L direct light reflex is absent
The C/L consensual reflex is absent
In AAPO light on the lesion side leaves both pupils un-constricted (I/L DLR and C/L DLR absent), yet the pupils remain always equal in size — isocoria. (Book p28)
Fill up: in both AAPO and RAPD the pupils are always equal in size, a condition the book names ______.
Pupils relative to each other: always equal in size — isocoria — in both afferent pathway lesions; anisocoria is the efferent hallmark. (Book p28)
Per the symptom row of the book's comparison table, what accompanies AAPO?
I/L anopia d/t the optic nerve lesion
Loss of accommodation on near effort
No symptom is listed in the table
Symptom row: AAPO — I/L anopia (d/t optic nerve lesion); RAPD — none (–). (Book p28)
A 68-year-old with acute left CRAO is examined. The book notes the ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons. The expected pupillary finding is:
A relative afferent defect in the right eye
A relative afferent defect in the left eye
Anisocoria with a dilated left pupil
An absolute afferent defect in the left eye
CRAO is an incomplete optic nerve lesion → RAPD in the affected eye; the pupils stay isocoric. (Book p28)

Match the finding with the lesion in the book's comparison — 1) I/L and C/L DLR absent when the lesion side is illuminated 2) Swinging flashlight test with dilation on the fatigued eye 3) Isocoric pupils in both lesions … A) Characteristic of RAPD B) Characteristic of AAPO C) Shared by AAPO and RAPD
The light reflex test (both DLRs absent on the lesion side) characterizes AAPO; the swinging flashlight test characterizes RAPD; isocoria is shared by both. (Book p28)
Which combination defines Wernicke's hemianopic pupil per the book?
Bitemporal hemianopia with a chiasmal lesion
Central scotoma with an optic nerve lesion
I/L homonymous hemianopia with an optic tract lesion
C/L homonymous hemianopia with an I/L optic tract lesion
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil: site of lesion — I/L optic tract; presentation — C/L homonymous hemianopia. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
Light is shone on the hemianopic (invisible) half of the field in a patient with Wernicke's pupil. Per the book the expected response is:
Light stimulus on the hemianopic/invisible VF → no constriction; light on the normal VF → pupil constriction. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
Which statement about the Argyll Robertson pupil is FALSE per the book?
It is a feature of tertiary syphilis (neurosiphilis)
The pupillary light reflex is B/L absent

ARP causes: neurosiphilis (tertiary syphilis, may present with seizures and confusion), tabes dorsalis, aortic regurgitation; PLR B/L absent; accommodation present; NO dilation with atropine. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
Fill up: the book's mnemonic for ARP, 'ARP PRA', stands for Accommodation Reflex Present and ______.
Mnemonic ARP PRA: Accommodation Reflex Present, Pupillary Reflex Absent. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
Match the ARP lesion site with the internuncial neurons it affects — 1) Periaqueductal grey 2) Posterior commissure … A) C/L internuncial neurons B) I/L internuncial neurons
