Periaqueductal grey affects I/L internuncial neurons; posterior commissure affects C/L internuncial neurons; lesions are usually B/L. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
Per the book, ARP lesions are usually:
Lesions in ARP are usually B/L. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
A 55-year-old with tertiary syphilis shows small constricted pupils that do not react to light but constrict on near effort. Per the book's postulate the presenting miosis persists because the EWN:
Is directly stimulated by the spirochaete
Receives neither excitatory nor inhibitory signals

On presentation both pupils are constricted; postulate: the supra-nuclear pathway is destroyed through the periaqueductal area/tectum (–), so the EWN receives neither excitatory/inhibitory signals → miosis. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
All of the following are listed causes of the Argyll Robertson pupil EXCEPT:
ARP causes: neurosiphilis (tertiary syphilis), tabes dorsalis, aortic regurgitation; papilledema is a cause of secondary optic atrophy, not of ARP. (Book p29)
Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil

Match the efferent lesion with its site of lesion in the book's table — 1) Tonic/Adie's pupil 2) Pharmacological mydriasis … A) Drug action: supranuclear inhibition of the EWN B) Ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve
Tonic/Adie's pupil: ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve; pharmacological mydriasis: drug action — supranuclear inhibition of the EWN (e.g. atropine). (Book p30)
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
All of the following are listed causes of the tonic pupil EXCEPT:
Tonic pupil causes: HZV ganglionitis, diabetes/alcoholism → peripheral neuropathy, trauma; Holmes-Adie pupil = tonic pupil + ↓ deep tendon reflexes. Horner syndrome is not in this list. (Book p30)
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
Per the book, Holmes-Adie pupil is:
Tonic pupil with ↓ deep tendon reflexes
Holmes-Adie pupil: tonic pupil + ↓ deep tendon reflexes. (Book p30)
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
Fill up: denervation hypersensitivity of the tonic pupil is demonstrated by constriction with ______ dilute pilocarpine.
Denervation hypersensitivity: the denervated sphincter pupillae overexpresses receptors (mushrooming), so it hyperreacts and constricts with 0.125% dilute pilocarpine. (Book p30)
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
Which statement about the tonic pupil is FALSE per the book?
The I/L pupil does not constrict to light while the C/L pupil constricts
The near reflex is present with slow, vermiform dilating movements
The two pupils are equal in size

The tonic pupil shows anisocoria (unequal pupil size), which differentiates it from afferent pathway lesions (isocoria); I/L DLR ↓ and CLR absent, near reflex present (slow vermiform), denervation hypersensitivity to 0.125% pilocarpine. (Book p30)
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
A 28-year-old's anisocoria is greater in the dark and the abnormal pupil is the smaller one. Per the book's algorithm the next test is:
Anisocoria greater in the dark → the lesion/abnormal pupil is the constricted one (the normal pupil can dilate in the dark, the abnormal one cannot) → 1% apraclonidine test. (Book p31)
Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm

Match the anisocoria pattern with the book's diagnosis — 1) Greater in dark, small pupil, apraclonidine positive (abnormal pupil dilates) 2) Greater in dark, small pupil, apraclonidine negative 3) Greater in light, dilated pupil, constricts to 0.125% pilocarpine … A) Physiological anisocoria B) Horner's syndrome C) Tonic pupil

Per the book's visual and orbital axes diagram, the visual axis makes an angle of ______ with the orbital axis, and the SR/IR muscle axes run parallel to the orbital axis at ______ with the sagittal plane.

Visual axis–orbital axis 23°; SR and IR–muscle axes parallel to the orbital axis at 23° with the sagittal plane; LR–muscle axis −45° with the sagittal plane; MR axis parallel to the sagittal plane. (Book p44)
Visual and orbital axes — why SR is a pure elevator
When the eye abducts by 23°, the visual axis and the SR's orbital axis coincide. Per the book the consequence is:
Vertical action predominates, making the SR a pure elevator
The SR acts as a pure depressor in that position
The SR loses all its action in that position
The LR becomes the pure elevator in that position
If the eye abducts by 23°, the visual axis and the muscle orbital axis coincide → vertical action predominates → SR → pure elevator. (Book p44)
Visual and orbital axes — why SR is a pure elevator
Match the clinical function in the book's diagram with its muscle — 1) Pure elevation 2) Pure depression 3) Elevation in abduction 4) Depression in abduction … A) SO B) SR + IO C) SO + IR D) SR
Pure elevation: SR + IO; pure depression: SO + IR; elevation in abduction: SR; depression in abduction: SO. (Book p44)
Visual and orbital axes — why SR is a pure elevator
Binocular single vision (BSV) per the book is the:
Loss of fusion of the two images
Formation of a composite image using both eyes
BSV: formation of a composite image using both the eyes. (Book p44)
Binocular single vision — grades and formation

Match the BSV grade with its definition in the book — 1) Grade 1 2) Grade 2 3) Grade 3 … A) Stereopsis, binocular depth perception B) Simultaneous macular perception C) Fusion of similar images with minute retinal differences
Grade 1: simultaneous macular perception; Grade 2: fusion of similar images with minute retinal differences; Grade 3: stereopsis, binocular depth perception. (Book p44)
Binocular single vision — grades and formation
Fill up: synergistic muscles in the book are 2 muscles with the same action in the same eye, e.g. right SR + right IO (both cause ______).
Synergistic muscles: 2 muscles with the same action in the same eye — eg right SR + right IO (both cause elevation). (Book p44)
Binocular single vision — grades and formation
Yoke muscles (CN synergists) in the book are a pair of muscles, one from each eye, enabling both eyeballs to move in the same direction — a ______ movement.
Yoke muscles/CN synergists: a pair of muscles, one from each eye, enabling both eyeballs to move in the same direction — version movement. (Book p44)
Binocular single vision — grades and formation
Which statement about antagonistic muscles is FALSE per the book?
They are 2 muscles with opposite action in the same eye
Example: right LR and right MR (abduction and adduction)
Example: right SR and left IO
A lesion of the yoke or antagonist muscles can produce squint
Antagonistic: 2 muscles with opposite action in the same eye (eg right LR and right MR). Right SR + left IO are yoke (version) muscles. (Book p44)
Binocular single vision — grades and formation

Match the yoke muscle pair with its net action in the book's table — 1) Left LR + right MR 2) Right LR + left MR 3) Right SR + left IO 4) Right IR + left SO … A) Levoversion B) Dextro-elevation C) Dextro-depression D) Dextroversion
Left LR + right MR — levoversion; right LR + left MR — dextroversion; right SR + left IO — dextro-elevation; right IR + left SO — dextro-depression. (Book p45)
Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
All of the following yoke pairs in the book's table produce depression or elevation movements EXCEPT:
Right SR + right IO and left SR + left IO (B/L elevation: sursumversion)

Right SO + left IR — levo-depression; right IO + left SR — levo-elevation; right SR + right IO and left SR + left IO — B/L elevation: sursumversion; right IR + right SO and left IR + left SO — B/L depression: deorsumversion. Levoversion (left LR + right MR) is a horizontal movement. (Book p45)
Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
Hering's law of equal innervation in the book states:
Equal innervation to a pair of yoke muscles
The antagonist always receives less innervation
Only one eye is innervated during version
Innervation decreases with the distance of gaze
Hering's law of equal innervation: equal innervation to a pair of yoke muscles during any binocular movement (similar timing, amount of nerve impulses, simultaneous contraction). (Book p45)
Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
The book lists applications of Hering's law. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
Equal and simultaneous innervation through yoke muscles

Applications: secondary deviation or inhibitional palsy; note: Hering's law — equal and simultaneous innervation flows through yoke muscles. The forced duction test is not an application of Hering's law. (Book p45)
Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
Fill up: Sherrington's law of reciprocal inhibition in the book is the relaxation of the yoke ______.
Sherrington's law of reciprocal inhibition: relaxation of yoke muscle antagonists (eg right MR contracted while right LR relaxed, and the yoke partner mirrors it). (Book p45)
Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
Per the book's BSV formation note, maintaining single vision requires ______ muscles — a yoke pair plus their antagonists; a lesion produces:
Formation of BSV: 4 muscles required — a yoke + antagonists; lesions → squint. (Book p45)

Fill up: in the book's classification tree, apparent deviation of squint is called ______.
Classification: squint divides into apparent deviation (pseudostabismus) and true deviation. (Book p46)

Match the true-deviation type with its definition in the book — 1) Heterophoria (latent squint) 2) Heterotropia (manifest squint) … A) Visible always B) Deviation manifests under ocular stress (excessive near work)
Heterophoria (latent squint): deviation manifests under ocular stress (excessive near work); heterotropia (manifest squint): visible always. (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
Heterotropia (manifest squint) in the book's tree splits into constant/concomitant and incomitant squint. All of the following statements about them are correct EXCEPT:
Concomitant: deviation remains constant in all directions of gaze
Incomitant: deviation varies in different directions of gaze
Incomitant: deviation is largest in primary gaze and zero in others
Constant/concomitant squint: deviation remains constant in all directions of gaze; incomitant: deviation varies in different directions of gaze. (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
Which row of the book's comitant vs incomitant table is FALSE?
Ocular movements: comitant — restriction absent; incomitant — restriction present
Sensory anomalies: comitant — present; incomitant — absent
Table: diplopia — comitant absent, incomitant present; head posturing — comitant absent, incomitant present; sensory anomalies — comitant present, incomitant absent. (Book p46)

A 7-year-old with a recent CN VI palsy complains of double vision and tilts his head. In the book's comparison table this pattern (diplopia present, restriction present, head posturing present, sensory anomalies absent) fits:
Incomitant squint: deviation varies with gaze, restriction present, diplopia present, head posturing present, sensory anomalies absent. (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
Fill up: in the book's diagrams, the 1° deviation is seen when the ______ eye fixates on an object, and the 2° deviation is seen when the deviated eye fixates.
1° deviation: deviation seen when the normal eye fixates on an object; 2° deviation: deviation seen when the deviated eye fixates on an object. (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
The note under the book's comparison table restates Hering's law as:
Only the fixating eye is innervated
Equal and simultaneous innervation flows through yoke muscles
Innervation is cut off in manifest squint
Note: Hering's law — equal and simultaneous innervation flows through yoke muscles. (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
Match the incomitant squint type with its forced duction test result in the book — 1) Paralytic squint 2) Restrictive squint … A) Positive — diagnostic (eye does not move) B) Negative (eye moves)
Types of incomitant squint: paralytic — forced duction test negative (eye moves); restrictive — forced duction test positive: diagnostic (eye does not move). (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
Under anesthesia, forceps hold the limbus of a patient's eye and the examiner attempts to move it. Per the book this is the forced duction test, and a positive (diagnostic) result means:
Forced duction test: try to move the eyeball being held at the limbus by forceps; positive = eye does not move (restrictive, diagnostic). (Book p46)
Classification of squint and the comitant/incomitant comparison
Match the deviation direction with its name in the book — 1) Inward 2) Outward 3) Upward 4) Downward … A) Exo (exotropia) B) ESO (esotropia) C) Hypo (hypotropia) D) Hyper (hypertropia)
Direction of deviation: ESO — inward (esotropia); EXO — outward (exotropia); HYPER — upward (hypertropia); HYPO — downward (hypotropia). (Book p47)

The book's rotational deviation pair includes incyclo (inward/nasal rotation) and excyclo (outward/temporal rotation). Which of the following is NOT a listed direction of deviation?
Listed directions: ESO (inward), EXO (outward), HYPER (upward), HYPO (downward), INCYCLO (inward/nasal rotation), EXCYCLO (outward/temporal rotation). (Book p47)

Fill up: in the book's figures, INCYCLO deviation is inward/nasal rotation, shown as the superior limbus rotating ______, while EXCYCLO deviation shows it rotating temporally.
INCyclo deviation — inward/nasal rotation (superior limbus rotates nasally); EXCyclo deviation — outward/temporal rotation (superior limbus rotates temporally). (Book p47)

Per the book's consequences table, diplopia as a consequence of squint is seen in:
Consequences of squint: diplopia — seen in small angle squint; confusion — seen in large angle squint. (Book p47)
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint

Match the consequence with its image formation in the book's table — 1) Diplopia 2) Confusion … A) Images of a different object d/t both eyes looking at different objects B) Images of the same object formed at non-corresponding points in both retinae
Both form images of the same object

Diplopia: images of the same object formed at non-corresponding points in both retinae (corresponding point of LE: nasal → temporal); confusion: images of a different object d/t both eyes looking at different objects. (Book p47)
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint
The motor adaptation of diplopia in small angle squint per the book is:
Amblyopia of the deviated eye, with no treatment
Suppression of the visual sensory impulse from the deviated eye
Fusion — extra work by the extraocular muscle to overcome the small angle
Anomalous retinal correspondence with deviation up to 5°
Motor adaptations: diplopia (small angle) — fusion, extra work performed by the extraocular muscle to overcome the small angle deviation; confusion (large angle) — change in head posture. (Book p47)
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint
Per the book, ARC (anomalous retinal correspondence) — formation of new correspondence points — occurs with deviation up to ______ degrees.
Sensory adaptation in small angle squint: ARC — anomalous retinal correspondence, formation of new correspondence points with deviation up to 5°. (Book p47)
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint

The sensory adaptations of large angle squint in the book's table include suppression of the visual sensory impulse from the deviated eye. This leads to amblyopia (lazy eye). All of the following describe it EXCEPT:
Loss of vision without organic cause
Amblyopia (lazy eye): loss of vision without organic cause — no treatment; it is a sensory adaptation (after suppression), not a motor adaptation. (Book p47)
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint
A 3-year-old with a large angle congenital squint does not complain of double vision. Per the book's table the explanation is:
Confusion with suppression of the deviated eye
Diplopia with fusion effort by the EOM
A change in head posture alone

Large angle squint gives confusion (images of different objects); the motor adaptation is a change in head posture and the sensory adaptation is suppression of the visual sensory impulse from the deviated eye → amblyopia. (Book p47)
Direction of deviation and the consequences of squint
Which statement about the consequences table is FALSE per the book?
Diplopia — image formation: images of the same object at non-corresponding retinal points
Diplopia — motor adaptation: change in head posture
Confusion — image formation: images of different objects
Confusion — sensory adaptation: suppression of the deviated eye
Change in head posture is the motor adaptation of CONFUSION (large angle), not of diplopia; diplopia's motor adaptation is fusion (extra EOM work). (Book p47)

Fill up: in the book's note on the diplopia column, the corresponding point of the left eye shifts from nasal to ______.
Diplopia image formation note: corresponding point of LE: nasal → temporal. (Book p47)

Examination of ocular movements: 9 directions of gaze, each with its acting muscle (1°, 2° and 3° gaze). (Book p48)

Match the gaze with its acting muscles in the book's 9-gaze figure — 1) Dextro-elevation 2) Sursumversion 3) Levo-depression … A) RSO + LIR B) RSR + RIO and LSR + LIO C) RSR + LIO
Dextro-elevation: RSR + LIO; sursumversion (B/L elevation): RSR + RIO and LSR + LIO; levo-depression: RSO + LIR. (Book p48)

Fill up: in the book's 9-gaze chart, dextroversion is achieved by ______.
Dextroversion: RLR + LMR; levoversion: RMR + LLR; deorsumversion: RIR + RSO and LIR + LSO. (Book p48)
Ocular movements, refraction, accommodative squint and fusional vergence
Per the book, visual acuity <6/6 on Snellen's chart indicates a refractory error, measured by the:
Measurement of refractory error: visual acuity — Snellen's chart (6/6 normal; <6/6: refractory error → measured by retinoscope). (Book p48)

A 5-year-old with uncorrected hypermetropia develops an inward deviation. Per the book the chain is loss of near vision → overaccommodation + overconvergence → esotropia. The treatment listed is:
Accommodative squint: uncorrected hypermetropia → loss of near vision → overaccommodation + overconvergence → inward deviation: esotropia; treatment — use of spectacles. (Book p48)
Ocular movements, refraction, accommodative squint and fusional vergence
Fill up: fusional vergence in the book is the extra power of the extraocular muscles to keep ______ from manifesting.
Fusional vergence: extra power of extraocular muscles to keep heterophoria from manifesting. (Book p48)
Ocular movements, refraction, accommodative squint and fusional vergence
Among the book's tests for fusional vergence, the RAF (Royal Air Force) rule is the:
Tests for fusional vergence: Livingston gauge test, pencil test, synoptophore, RAF (Royal Air Force) rule — m/c used, a points measured. (Book p48)

Per the book's RAF ruler diagram, moving the ruler until the patient reports diplopia marks the near point of convergence, normal is ______; moving it until blurring marks the near point of accommodation (normal 20y: 8 cm, 50y: >46 cm).
RAF ruler (placed on nose): move until blurring → near point of accommodation (normal 20y — 8cm, 50y >46cm); move until diplopia → near point of convergence (normal <10 cm). (Book p48)
Ocular movements, refraction, accommodative squint and fusional vergence

Match the deviation-measurement group with its tests in the book — 1) Objective test 2) Subjective — ophthalmoplegic principle 3) Subjective — haploscope principle … A) Lancaster RG test, synoptophore B) Maddox rod, Maddox wing C) Hirschberg, Bruckner, cover-uncover, prism-bar cover

Objective: Hirschberg's, Bruckner's, cover-uncover, prism-bar cover. Subjective: based on the ophthalmoplegic principle — Maddox rod, Maddox wing; based on the haploscope principle — Lancaster RG test, synoptophore. (Book p49)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)
The Hirschberg test in the book is also called the:
Hirschberg (corneal reflection) test: a. diagnosis of direction of deviation; b. measurement of degree of deviation. (Book p49)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)
Fill up: for Hirschberg direction of deviation the book's mnemonic DOOR stands for deviation ______ of reflection.
Mnemonic: DOOR — deviation opposite of reflection (e.g. CR nasal to centre → 15° exodeviation at the pupillary margin). (Book p49)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)
Per the book, 1 mm deviation of the corneal reflection from the centre of the pupil equals ______ of squint, i.e. 14 prism dioptres (1 pd = 1/2°).
Measurement of degree of deviation: 1 mm deviation of CR from centre of pupil = 7° squint / 14 prism dioptres; 1° = 2 pd (1 pd = 1/2°). (Book p49)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)
In the book's photographic degree-deviation chart, the CR at the pupillary margin equals 15°/30 Δ and the CR at the limbus equals:
CR at pupillary margin = 15°/30 Δ; CR at limbus = 45°/90 Δ; the photograph series shows 15°, 30° and 45° for ESO and EXO (clinical rule HCRT). (Book p49)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)
Per the book, Bruckner's test is a:
Screening procedure in infants — examine the fundal red reflex
A subjective test for phoria at far fixation in adults
A test of stereopsis and depth perception
A test of colour vision in the pediatric age group
Bruckner's test: screening procedure in infants; shine light on the eye through direct ophthalmoscope; examine fundal red reflex. (Book p49)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)

Match the Bruckner red reflex photograph finding with its interpretation in the book — 1) Equal reflex b/w both eyes 2) Arc-like reflex 3) Unequal reflex (R darker, L lighter) … A) Unequal squint B) Refracting error C) Normal red reflex
i. Red reflex: normal, equal b/w both eyes; ii. Arc-like reflex: refracting error; iii. Unequal squint (one darker, one lighter). (Book p50)
Measuring ocular deviation — objective tests (Hirschberg, Bruckner)
Match the cover test with its purpose in the book — 1) Cover test 2) Uncover test … A) Diagnose phoria B) Confirm tropia
Cover test: confirm tropia; uncover test: diagnose phoria. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test
Fill up: the book's mnemonic for the cover-uncover test, DOOM, stands for deviation ______ of movement.
Mnemonic: DOOM — deviation opposite of movement. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test

In the book's uncover test diagram, on presentation there is no deviation on stress; the affected exophoric eye is covered, deviation appears under cover, and on removal the eye moves back to normal. This test is used to:
Uncover test: diagnose phoria — deviation under cover, movement of the eye back to normal on removal. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test
The prism bar cover test (PBCT) in the book is the best and most accurate test for:
PBCT: best and most accurate test for the measurement of degree of tropia. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test
Fill up: the PBCT principle is neutralization — light passing through a prism deviates towards the ______.
PBCT principle: neutralization → light passing through a prism deviates towards the apex; goal — finding the power of prism at which the eye appears normal on cover-uncover test. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test
Match the deviation with the prism orientation during the test in the book — 1) ESO 2) EXO 3) Hyper 4) Hypo … A) Base-in prism B) Base-down prism C) Base-up prism D) Base-out prism
Orientation of prism: ESO — base out prism; EXO — base in prism; Hyper — base down prism; Hypo — base up prism. Mnemonic DOOB: deviation opposite of base of prism. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test
The book's PBCT mnemonic DOOB (deviation opposite of base of prism) guides prism orientation. All of the following pairings are correct EXCEPT:
Hyper uses a base-DOWN prism (not base-up); hypo uses base-up. (Book p50)
Cover–uncover test and the prism bar cover test
Per the book, a use of the Maddox rod test is to measure/diagnose:
Maddox rod test uses: 1. measure/diagnose phoria at far fixation; 2. macular function test; 3. double Maddox rod test — measure cyclodeviation. (Book p51)

Match the Maddox rod result (patient's view) with the book's diagnosis — 1) Dot on the line 2) Left exophoria/tropia 3) Left esophoria/tropia … A) Orthophoria (normal) B) Crossed diplopia C) Uncrossed diplopia
Results: dot on the line — orthophoria (normal); left exophoria/tropia — crossed diplopia; left esophoria/tropia — uncrossed diplopia. (Book p51)
All of the following are stated about the Maddox wing in the book EXCEPT:
It diagnoses phoria at near fixation
It is the most sensitive test for stereopsis
It is a subjective test based on the diplopia principle
Maddox wing: diagnoses phoria at near fixation; obsolete. It is not a stereopsis test. (Book p51)
Fill up: the book gives one test to differentiate between tropia and phoria: the ______.
Note: one test to differentiate between tropia and phoria — the cover-uncover test. (Book p51)
Monocular diplopia per the book is diplopia that does not disappear on closing the normal eye. Listed examples include all EXCEPT:
Monocular examples: subluxation of lens, severe refractory errors (anisometropia), iridodonesis; myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction disorder causing BINOCULAR diplopia. (Book p51)

Match the binocular diplopia cause group with its example in the book — 1) Myogenic cause 2) Neurogenic 3) Neuromuscular junction disorders … A) Myasthenia gravis B) 3rd, 4th, 6th nerve palsy C) Squint d/t myogenic cause
Binocular diplopia disappears if either eye is closed; squint d/t: myogenic cause; neurogenic (3, 4, 6th nerve palsy); neuromuscular junction disorders (myasthenia gravis). (Book p51)
All of the following are listed diplopia tests in the book EXCEPT:
Diplopia tests: red-green glasses (easiest way to check), Lee's screen, Hess chart (most commonly used). Amsler's grid is a retinal chart. (Book p51)
The easiest way to check for diplopia per the book is:
Red-green glasses: easiest way to check for diplopia; Hess chart: most commonly used for diplopia. (Book p51)
Match the sensory state with its meaning in the book — 1) BSV 2) ARC 3) Suppression … A) Adaptation to confusion B) 1 object 1 image C) Adaptation to diplopia
Tests for sensory anomalies differentiate: 1. BSV — 1 object 1 image; 2. ARC — adaptation to diplopia; 3. Suppression — adaptation to confusion. (Book p52)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)

Match the Worth 4-dot dots seen with the book's interpretation — 1) 4 dots 2) 5 dots 3) 3 dots (red not seen) 4) 2 dots (green not seen) … A) LE suppression B) Diplopia — non-harmonious ARC C) Normal BSV or harmonious ARC D) RE suppression (d/t amblyopia)
Worth 4-dot results: 4 dots — normal BSV/harmonious ARC; 5 dots — diplopia (non-harmonious ARC); 3 dots — RE suppression (d/t amblyopia); 2 dots — LE suppression. (Book p52)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)
Fill up: the book calls Worth's 4-dot test more common/more important than the ______ striated glasses test.
Worth's 4-dot test: more common/more important test > Bagolini striated glasses test. (Book p52)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)
Match the Worth 4-dot glass colour with the eye it is worn on in the book — 1) Red 2) Green … A) Worn on the right eye B) Worn on the left eye
Worth 4-dot method: red worn on the right eye; green worn on the left eye; 4 dots are shown. (Book p52)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)

Match the Bagolini striated glasses finding with the book's interpretation — 1) X (two crossing lines) 2) A single diagonal line 3) Two diverging lines … A) Diplopia — non-harmonious ARC B) Right eye suppression C) BSV or harmonious ARC
Bagolini results: X — binocular single vision or harmonious ARC; single line — right eye suppression; two diverging lines — diplopia, non-harmonious ARC. (Book p53)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)
The 4 prism test in the book is used to differentiate between BSV and ______ in microtropia (small angle squint).
4 prism test: used to differentiate between BSV and central suppression scotoma in microtropia (small angle squint); the after image test is the other listed test. (Book p53)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)
All of the following are listed tests for stereopsis (G3 BSV, depth perception) in the book EXCEPT:

Stereopsis tests: 1. two pencil test (gross stereopsis); 2. Titmus fly test (Polaroid vectographic images, matte-ean grey); 3. random dot stereogram test — best test, eliminates monocular clues (Lang, Frisby, Frisby-Davis distance stereotest). (Book p53)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)
Which statement about the stereopsis tests is FALSE per the book?
The Hess chart is the best test of stereopsis
The two pencil test assesses gross stereopsis
The Titmus fly test uses vectorographic images
The random dot stereogram test is the best test, used to eliminate monocular clues of depth perception
Best stereopsis test = random dot stereogram; the Hess chart is a diplopia chart (most commonly used for diplopia), not the best stereopsis test. (Book p53)
Sensory anomaly tests and stereopsis (G3 BSV)
Fill up: paralytic squint in the book is a type of ______ squint.
Paralytic squint is a type of incomitant squint. (Book p54)
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course
All of the following are listed features of paralytic squint in the book EXCEPT:

Features: diplopia; abnormal head posture; restriction of ocular movements (intended action of the paralysed muscle — vertigo); deviation opposite to the action of the paralysed muscle; 2° deviation > 1° deviation. (Book p54)
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course
The deviation in paralytic squint per the book is ______ to the action of the paralysed muscle.
Deviation: opposite to the action of paralysed muscle. (Book p54)
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course
In paralytic squint per the book, the 2° deviation is ______ the 1° deviation.
2° deviation > 1° deviation is a listed feature of paralytic squint. (Book p54)
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course
The cause of paralytic squint per the book is palsy of which nerves?
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course
The CN III nuclear complex is situated in the midbrain at the level of the:
Nuclear complex: situated in the mid-brain at level of superior colliculus. (Book p54)
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course
Match the CN III main motor nucleus subnucleus with its innervation in the book — 1) 2 paired subnuclei 2) 1 unpaired subnucleus … A) I/L MR, IR, IO and C/L SR B) Both LPS
Both innervate I/L MR, IR, IO

Paired subnuclei innervate C/L SR and I/L MR, IR, IO; the unpaired subnucleus innervates both LPS; Edinger-Westphal (accessory nucleus) sends preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle (constriction). (Book p54)
Paralytic squint — features and the CN III course

Match the CN III segment with its course in the book — 1) Fascicular 2) Basilar 3) Intracavernous 4) Intraorbital … A) Superior division supplies LPS and SR; inferior division supplies IR, IO and MR B) Runs in the lateral wall above the trochlear nerve; divides into superior and inferior branches; enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the annulus of Zinn C) Fibres pass through the red nucleus into the interpeduncular D) Leaves the mid-brain on the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle, between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

Course: fascicular — fibres pass through red nucleus into interpeduncular; basilar — leaves the mid-brain on the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle, between PCA and SCA; intracavernous — lateral wall above trochlear nerve, superior/inferior branches, enters orbit through superior orbital fissure within annulus of Zinn; intraorbital — superior division → LPS, SR; inferior division → IR, IO, MR. (Book p54)

Match the aberrant regeneration sign with its mechanism in the book — 1) Pseudo-von Graefe sign 2) Pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupil (ciliary muscle fibres supply the sphincter pupillae) … A) On downgaze both IR and LPS contract → depression of the eye + elevation of the upper lid → lid lag B) On near vision the ciliary muscle accommodates → sphincter miosis: accommodation reflex present

Months after a CN III palsy, a patient's upper lid elevates on downgaze, producing lid lag. Per the book this pseudo-von Graefe sign is because fibres of the ______ have started to supply the LPS.
Pseudo-von Graffe sign: fibres of the IR start to supply the LPS — on downgaze both IR and LPS contract. (Book p56)

Match the CN IV segment with its course in the book — 1) Nucleus 2) Fascicular 3) Trunk 4) Cavernous 5) Intraorbital … A) Leaves the midbrain on the dorsal surface, between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries B) Curves around the aqueduct of sylvius and decussates C) Midbrain at the level of inferior colliculus D) Lateral wall between oculomotor and ophthalmic nerves; passes through the superior orbital fissure outside the annulus of Zinn E) Innervates the contralateral superior oblique

CN IV course: nucleus — midbrain at level of inferior colliculus; fascicular — curves around aqueduct of sylvius and decussates; trunk — leaves midbrain dorsally, between PCA and SCA; cavernous — lateral wall between oculomotor and ophthalmic nerves, through superior orbital fissure OUTSIDE the annulus of Zinn; intraorbital — innervates contralateral superior oblique. Match the SO palsy manifestation with the patient's head posture in the book — 1) Excycloptropia 2) I/L hypertropia 3) Vertical diplopia on downgaze … A) Chin down B) Face turns to the opposite side C) Head tilt to the opposite side

Head posture: intorsion defect (excycloptropia) → head tilt to the opposite side; depression defect (I/L hypertropia) → chin down; depression-in-adduction defect (vertical diplopia on downgaze) → face turns to the opposite side. (Book p57)

Park's 3-step test: step 1 — identification of hypertropia (LE); step 2 — hypertropia worse on opposite gaze; step 3 — hypertropia better on opposite tilt. (Book p57)

Match the CN VI segment with its course in the book — 1) Nucleus 2) Fascicular 3) Basilar 4) Intracavernous 5) Intraorbital … A) Pons, ventral to the floor of the 4th ventricle B) Leaves brainstem at the pontomedullary junction C) Enters the basilar cistern, crossed by the AICA, through Dorello canal into the cavernous sinus D) Runs inferomedially in the lateral wall in close relation to the ICA; enters orbit within the annulus of Zinn E) Innervates the ipsilateral lateral rectus

Nuclei of CN: III, IV — midbrain; V, VI, VII, VIII — pons; IX, X, XI, XII — medulla. (Book p58)

Match the pons syndrome with its features in the book — 1) Foville syndrome 2) Millard-Gubler syndrome 3) Mobius syndrome … A) B/L 6/7 CN palsy B) I/L 5/6/7/8 CN palsy + central Horner's syndrome C) I/L 6/7 CN palsy + C/L hemiplegia
Syndromes affecting pons: Foville — I/L 5/6/7/8 CN palsy + central Horner's syndrome; Millard-Gubler — I/L 6/7 CN palsy + C/L hemiplegia; Mobius — B/L 6/7 CN palsy. (Book p58)

Match the vestibular test with its finding in the book — 1) Oculo-cephalic (Doll's) reflex 2) Caloric test — cold water 3) Caloric test — warm water … A) Opposite side nystagmus B) Tests CN III, VI, VIII — eyes move opposite to head movement (in coma patients) C) Same side nystagmus

Match the station in the book's pathway of left gaze with its role — 1) C/L FEF (right) 2) I/L PPRF (left) 3) I/L 6th nerve nucleus 4) C/L MLF → C/L 3rd nerve nucleus … A) Centre — drives the left LR B) Initiates the gaze C) Drives the left lateral rectus D) Drives the right MR (yoke muscle)

The C/L MLF carries the gaze signal to the C/L 3rd nerve nucleus, which drives the yoke (right MR). (Book p60)

Pursuit movements following a moving target

Convergence movements towards a near object
Horizontal gaze: saccadic movements to look towards left/right side. (Book p60)

Initiation comes from the contralateral FEF
The 6th nucleus drives the ipsilateral lateral rectus
The 6th nucleus drives the contralateral lateral rectus
The 6th nerve nucleus innervates the IPSILATERAL lateral rectus; the contralateral MR is driven via the C/L MLF to the 3rd nucleus. (Book p60)
In the book's horizontal gaze palsy table, the lesion that produces internuclear ophthalmoplegia is at the:
C/L MLF lesion: internuclear ophthalmoplegia — m/c cause multiple sclerosis. (Book p61)

Bitemporal hemianopia with a chiasmal lesion

C/L FEF or I/L PPRF lesion: I/L LR fails to contract and C/L MR fails to contract → left gaze palsy. (Book p61)

In the C/L MLF (INO) row the I/L LR CAN contract and the C/L MR fails to contract — the reverse of the false option. (Book p61)

Match the Parinaud syndrome feature with its description in the book — 1) Collier's sign 2) Convergence 3) Light-near dissociation … A) Upper eyelid retraction B) Light reflex absent and near reflex present C) Retraction nystagmus

Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome per the book: the site of lesion is the ______, and the m/c cause is ______.

Match the DRS type with the globe retraction/palpebral fissure closure in the book's table — 1) Type I 2) Type 2 3) Type 3 … A) On abduction and adduction (d/t paradoxical innervation of both LR and MR) B) On adduction C) On abduction

Comitant squint: m/c presentation — esotropia (convergent squint). (Book p64)

Rows → finger counting (FCCF+) → hand movements (HM+) → light perception (PL+) → patient blind. (Book p117)

Note: least acuity discernible via Snellen's chart: 1/60. (Book p118)
Principle per p118: each optotype subtends ___ at the nodal point when viewed from its respective distance; each segment subtends 1 minute.

Angle (in minutes) subtended at variable distance X per p118 equals:

Cardiff Acuity Test: used in both infants and toddlers; based on vanishing optotype. (Book p119)
Light stimulus → visual pathway → ↑ visual cortex activity → normal VEP
Principle: light stimulus → visual pathway → ↑ visual cortex activity → normal VEP. (Book p119)

Blink reflex present since birth; menace reflex develops around 5 months of age; VEP is objective. (Book p120)

Use: for diagnosis of presbyopia; distance of examination 30-35 cm (comfortable reading distance). (Book p120)

Power at posterior surfaces of cornea and lens are in the negative as light is moving from denser to rarer medium. (Book p121)

Radii of curvature: cornea anterior 7.7 mm, cornea posterior 6.8 mm, lens anterior 10 mm, lens posterior -6 mm. (Book p121)

Eye +58.6 D; cornea +43 D; lens +19 D

P 1.35 mm; N 7.0 mm; F2 24.13 mm from reference; F1 -15.7 mm. (Book p121)

Hypermetropia: ↓ refractory power → ↓ converging → image behind retina; corrective lenses (+). (Book p122)

Rays converge late behind the retina needing added plus power
Rays converge early; diverging lens refocuses on retina
The lens adds refractive power to the eye
The eye is too short axially
↑ Refractory power → early convergence → image anterior to retina → (-) diverging lenses correct. (Book p122)
In emmetropia per p122, parallel rays from infinity ___.
Parallel rays from infinity converge on retina. (Book p122)
Axial myopia per p123: 1 mm ↑ in axial length adds:

↓ Curvature of cornea/lens (↑ ROC) causes curvatural HYPERmetropia; myopia = ↑ curvature ↓ ROC. (Book p123)

Positional myopia: lens anterior; focal length ↓; power ↑; eg Weill Marchesani syndrome. (Book p123)
Floaters in high myopia per p123 are d/t:
Floaters present in high myopia d/t vitreous syneresis/liquefaction. (Book p123)
Half closure/half squinting of eyes in myopia per p123 improves vision because:

Cutting off of peripheral rays → central rays fall straight onto retina → improves vision. Hypermetropia: loss of near vision; over-accommodation → tired eyes/headache = asthenopia. (Book p123)

Match examination signs per p124 — 1) Myopic eyeball 2) Hypermetropic anterior chamber 3) Myopic squint 4) Hypermetropic squint … A) Small (↓AL); shallower than normal, prone to angle closure glaucoma B) Large (↑AL) → pseudoproptosis; deeper than normal C) Exophoria d/t convergence insufficiency D) Esotropia d/t overaccommodation → overconvergence
Myopia: large eyeball (↑AL) pseudoproptosis, deeper AC, exophoria; hypermetropia: small eyeball, shallow AC prone to ACG, esotropia. (Book p124)

Hypermetropia: angle kappa more than normal (>5°) → pseudoexotropia. (Book p124)

Hypermetropia: shot silk fundus, pseudo papillitis; myopia: tessellated/tigroid appearance; choroid red. (Book p124)
AL >26 mm or refractive power >6 D
Signs seen if pathological/degenerative myopia: AL >26 mm OR refractive power >6 D. (Book p124)

Increased RPE proliferation over the disc

Disparity in stretching → chorioretinal atrophy → underlying sclera visible (white). (Book p125)
Lacquer cracks per p125 are fine breaks in ___.
Fine breaks in Bruch's membrane (innermost layer of choroid) → underlying sclera visible (yellowish). (Book p125)
Areas of subretinal hemorrhage at macula
Foster Fuch spots: areas of subretinal hemorrhage at macula. (Book p125)
Ectatic scleral bulge d/t ↑AL stretching at normal IOP
Bulge lined by iris tissue at the limbus

Supertraction: vitreous pulls retina over optic disc → OD covered by retina → tilted OD (seen in very high myopia). (Book p125)

Myopia: concave/diverging glasses (negative power); hypermetropia: convex/converging lens (positive power). (Book p126)
Soft contact lenses are preferred in high myopia per p126 because:

Not done currently d/t unpredictable results. (Book p127)
Argon fluoride, 193 nm, photoablation → flattening → ↓ power

Contraindications to LASIK per p128 include all EXCEPT:
Refraction not stable for at least 12 months pre-op
Stable -3 D myopia for 2 years in a 25-year-old

Hydrogel; implanted in the sulcus anterior to lens

Concave: always virtual, erect, diminished image; convex: real and inverted (m/c), may produce virtual and erect image. (Book p129)

With the rule: vertical meridian more curved; against the rule: horizontal meridian more curved; oblique: perpendicular but not at 90°/180°. (Book p130)

Meridians not perpendicular; eg corneal scar, cataract
Corrected fully by a spherical lens

Match refractive types per p130 — 1) Simple myopic 2) Compound myopic 3) Simple hypermetropic 4) Mixed … A) Both axes myopic B) Axis 1 emmetropic, axis 2 myopic C) Axis 1 emmetropic, axis 2 hypermetropic D) One axis myopic, other hypermetropic

Cylindrical lenses have power 90° to their axis; only 1 axis has power. (Book p131)
Match per p131 — 1) Plano convex cylinder 2) Plano concave cylinder 3) Toric contact lens … A) For myopic astigmatism B) For hypermetropic astigmatism C) A lens with 2 surfaces with different powers
Plano convex for hypermetropic A; plano concave for myopic A; toric contact lens = lens with 2 surfaces with different powers. (Book p131)
Arrangement of light rays refracted through a toric surface

Circle of least diffusion placed on retina → clear image

Match per p133 table (C = convex, V = concave) — 1) With the rule, axis 180° 2) With the rule, axis 90° 3) Against the rule, axis 180° 4) Against the rule, axis 90° … A) - lens (C) B) + lens (V) C) + lens (V) D) - lens (C)

↑ Power at 90° → vertical power > horizontal power → with the rule astigmatism

c: CVS - Approach to Diagnosis & the Cardiac Cycle
u:
The general survey runs conscious/oriented/cooperative to build and nutrition to the vitals.
Vitals = pulse (rate, rhythm, volume, character, delay, vessel wall thickening, peripheral pulses), respiratory rate, blood pressure and temperature.
Temperature must be measured with a thermometer - never record 'afebrile' without one.
Then pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy and oedema complete the survey.

Fever (Harrison's 19e) = AM >98.9 F (>37.2 C) or PM >99.9 F (>37.7 C); normal range 36.5-37.5 C (97.7-99.5 F).
Evening rise is due to increased basal metabolic rate and skeletal muscle activity.
Sites beyond axilla/oral: rectum (higher than oral; lower oral readings from mouth breathing), lower oesophagus (core), tympanic membrane.

Fever raises the hypothalamic set point; hyperthermia is an uncontrolled rise that exceeds heat loss with an intact set point - so antipyretics fail.
Causes of hyperthermia: heat stroke; malignant hyperthermia (halothane); neuroleptic malignant syndrome (haloperidol, fluphenazine); serotonin syndrome (two or more serotonergic drugs).
Hyperpyrexia, Hypothalamic Fever & the Fever Cascade

Hyperpyrexia = fever >41.5 C (>106.7 F); causes CNS haemorrhage and severe infection.
Hypothalamic dysfunction usually gives subnormal, not supranormal, temperature.
Fever cascade: IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha -> hypothalamic endothelial cells -> PGE2 -> raised set point.

AUFI = fever <14 days without an organ-system-specific cause; say Dengue, Scrub typhus, Leptospirosis, Malaria, Enteric fever in that order and never volunteer Kala-azar.
PUO (Petersdorf and Beeson): >3 weeks, fever >101 on two occasions, uncertain despite 1 week inpatient evaluation; Harrison's adds no immunocompromise and an obligatory investigation set.
Variants: nosocomial, neutropenic, HIV-associated. PUO is atypical presentations of common illness, not typical presentations of rare illness.
Causes: infectious, neoplastic (including atrial myxoma), connective tissue disease and drug fever.

Auto-inflammatory diseases with characteristic fever: adult and juvenile Still's disease, familial Mediterranean fever (Robbins; colchicine), Behcet's syndrome, CAPS, PAPA and hyper-IgD syndrome.
Colchicine has exactly three listed uses: gout, pericarditis, FMF.
PAPA = Pyogenic arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum, Acne.

Pulse should rise about 10/min per 1 F of fever (about 18 per 1 C).
Relative bradycardia: enteric fever first week (heart block), viral fevers including dengue and yellow fever (Faget's sign), brucellosis, Weil's disease.
Relative tachycardia: acute rheumatic carditis, tuberculosis, polyarteritis nodosa, diphtheritic myocarditis.

Intermittent touches the baseline (quotidian, double quotidian, tertian, quartan); remittent swings >2 C (normal fluctuation 0.9 C) and never touches it; continued swings <=1 C and never touches it.
Named patterns: Pel-Ebstein (Hodgkin's lymphoma only), camel hump/double quotidian (kala-azar, gonococcal perihepatitis), step-ladder (enteric fever), undulant (brucellosis), relapsing (Borrelia), hectic (pent-up pus).
Charcot's intermittent fever = chills with RUQ pain and jaundice from a stone in the CBD.

Primary hypothermia is accidental exposure; secondary is failure of thermoregulation (CVA, overwhelming sepsis, low cardiac output after acute MI, endocrine failure, intoxication).
Signs and symptoms listed: altered sensorium from confusion to coma, tachypnoea, tachycardia, lethargy, shivering and pallor.

Anaemia and pallor are not interchangeable - anaemia is only one cause of pallor.
Examine in sunlight: lower palpebral conjunctiva, tip and dorsum of tongue, palatal mucosa, nail beds, palms and soles.
Pallor without anaemia (Kundu): shock, low cardiac output, hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism.
Anaemia classification: marrow production defect, ineffective erythropoiesis (nuclear and cytoplasmic), blood loss/haemolysis.

Look at the sclera through the upper palpebral conjunctiva - not the bulbar conjunctiva (mud and dust) - and ask the patient to look down.
Minimum bilirubin for clinical icterus is 2.5 mg/dL; the sclera is rich in elastic tissue where bilirubin deposits.
Tint: lemon yellow = mild haemolytic, orange yellow = moderate hepatocellular, greenish yellow = severe obstructive.

Bluish discolouration from reduced Hb or Hb derivatives (metHb/sulfHb) in small vessels; visible when reduced Hb exceeds 4 g/dL, i.e. SpO2 below about 85%.
It is the absolute, not relative, quantity of reduced Hb that matters - severe anaemia may show no cyanosis.
Central (saturation reduced or abnormal derivative) vs peripheral (slow flow, high extraction; oral mucosa and tongue underside spared).
Differential cyanosis: lower limb only = PDA with pulmonary hypertension and right-to-left shunt; upper limb only adds TGV; intermittent = Ebstein's anomaly.

Selective bulbous enlargement of the distal digit from subungual soft tissue deposition; Lovibond angle is the normal nail-to-nail-bed angle.
Minimum duration 2-3 weeks; the index finger is affected first.
Grades: 1 nail bed fluctuation, 2 increase in Lovibond angle, 3 drumstick/parrot beak, 4 hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

Suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema), thoracic malignancy (bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchial adenoma, mesothelioma), interstitial lung disease.
Clubbing is rare in COPD and TB. Cardiovascular: cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis, left atrial myxoma. GI: cirrhosis (especially PBC), inflammatory bowel disease.
Others: thyroid acropachy of Graves' disease and POEMS syndrome.

Pseudoclubbing preserves the Lovibond angle; per Kundu it is subperiosteal bone resorption without soft tissue proliferation.
Causes: leprosy, scleroderma, hyperparathyroidism, acromegaly, vinyl chloride workers with acro-osteolysis.
Most accepted theory: megakaryocytes bypass the lung, reach nail-bed arterioles and release PDGF. Other theories: neurogenic (vagal), humoral (GH/PTH/oestrogen), hypoxic (AV fistulae), ferritin.

Painful clubbing: bronchogenic carcinoma, lung abscess, infective endocarditis.
Unilateral clubbing: presubclavian coarctation of aorta (left-sided only), apical bronchogenic carcinoma, cervical rib, aneurysm of the subclavian or axillary artery.
Unidigital clubbing: hereditary, repeated local trauma, rarely median nerve injury. The index finger is affected first.

Significant nodes: any supraclavicular or epitrochlear node, inguinal >1.5 cm, others >1 cm.
Generalised = two or more non-contiguous areas (Harrison's says three, which the book calls impractical); persistent if more than 3 months.
Painful = infection or acute leukaemia; firm rubbery = lymphoma; fluctuant = suppurative; stony hard = metastasis; matted = tuberculous (benign) or lymphoma/metastatic (malignant).
Cervical levels: Ia submental, Ib submandibular, II-IV jugular, V posterior triangle, VI anterior triangle, VII superior mediastinal.

The Boloor insert on the neurological causes of clubbing adds syringomyelia, median nerve injury and hemiplegia.
It completes the respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and other groups given in the main text.

Boloor Fig. 2C.18 demonstrates grade 4 clubbing.
Grade 4 is defined by hypertrophic osteoarthropathy - periosteal reaction of the long bones with joint symptoms - not by the finger appearance alone.

Acute clubbing: subacute bacterial endocarditis, lung abscess, empyema. Reversible: lung abscess, empyema.
Unilateral: hemiplegia, aneurysm of the subclavian artery, Pancoast tumour. Unidigital: median nerve injury, trauma. Painful: bronchogenic carcinoma, SBE, lung abscess.
Clubbing with cyanosis: cyanotic congenital heart disease and ILD. Pseudoclubbing list adds leukaemic infiltration, thyroid acropachy, sclerodactyly, subungual tumours or cysts.
Differential clubbing (upper normal, lower clubbed) = PDA with reversal of shunt; reverse differential clubbing (upper clubbed, lower normal) = PDA + TGA + reversal of shunt.

Generalised lymphadenopathy groups: infections (HIV, infectious mononucleosis, TB), malignancies, autoimmune (SLE, Felty's, Still's), miscellaneous (sarcoidosis).
Non-pitting oedema: myxoedema, late filarial lymphoedema, scleroderma, angioneurotic oedema. Pitting: CCF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoproteinaemia, pericardial effusion, constrictive pericarditis, amlodipine.
Unilateral leg swelling: DVT, soft tissue infection, trauma, lymphoedema, immobility such as hemiplegia. Bilateral: heart failure, chronic venous insufficiency, hypoproteinaemia, lymphatic obstruction, drugs, Milroy's disease.

BP is the lateral force of the blood column per unit area of vascular wall. Cuff length about twice its width, average length 25 cm, bladder at least two-thirds of arm circumference.
Korotkoff 1 first low-frequency tapping; 2 softer and longer; 3 crisper and louder; 4 muffling (often absent); 5 disappearance. Normally phase 5 is the DBP; in severe AR phase 4 is taken.
Normal inter-arm difference 10-15 mmHg.

Auscultatory gap: sounds disappear after the systolic reading and return just above the diastolic value, seen in elderly hypertensives; it underestimates the systolic BP.
Avoid it by palpating the radial pulse, which persists through the gap.
Wide inter-arm difference: aortic dissection (haematoma occluding the subclavian artery) and subclavian steal syndrome.

Pulse pressure = SBP minus DBP; normal 30-60 mmHg.
Raised: exercise, AR, PDA, fever, anaemia, AV fistulas, beriberi, Paget's disease (bone fistulae), cirrhosis (intrahepatic and extrahepatic AV fistulae), pregnancy (placenta as a large AV fistula).
Narrow: aortic stenosis (outflow obstruction), constrictive pericarditis and cardiac tamponade (filling obstruction), with MS and DSS queried.

AHA/ASA Blood Pressure Categories on Book p15: Normal (<120 AND <80 mmHg) vs Elevated (120-129 AND <80 mmHg).
Hypertension Stage 1 = 130-139 OR 80-89 mmHg; Stage 2 = >=140 OR >=90 mmHg; Hypertensive Crisis = >180 and/or >120 mmHg.

Five cardinal CVS symptoms: breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations, syncope and pedal oedema (Dr. Hamide replaces pedal oedema with cough).
Dyspnoea is abnormal awareness of one's own respiration; orthopnoea is more severe than PND and reflects recumbent fluid shift from splanchnic/lower-limb beds.
NYHA Class I-IV is graded by both Dr. Hamide (unaccustomed, accustomed, day-to-day, rest) and Dr. Vivekanandan (if walking produces symptoms, consider Class III).

Normal daily physical activity benchmark is 1-2 flights of stairs.
Trepopnea (dyspnoea in right or left decubitus) is seen in dilated cardiomyopathy.
Platypnea (upright dyspnoea) and orthodeoxia (>=5% SpO2 drop upright) occur in LA thrombus, LA myxoma, hepatopulmonary syndrome (NO-mediated basal AV shunts), ASD and V/Q mismatch.
Chest Pain: Site, Onset, Nature, Radiation & Posture

Site: central = angina/ischaemia; retrosternal = oesophageal; epigastric radiating to chest = GI or angina.
Onset & nature: builds over minutes = MI/angina; immediate peak = aortic dissection, PE, spontaneous pneumothorax; burning pain can still be MI.
Radiation & posture: neck/jaw/arms = MI; interscapular back = dissection; trapezius ridge and relief on sitting upright leaning forward = pericarditis.

Boloor Table 3C.7 (p18-19) contrasts PND (sudden dyspnoea 2-2.5 h into sleep during REM from sympathetic surge and transient PCWP spike, with transient hypoxia) and orthopnoea (>400 mL recumbent venous shift with slow sustained PCWP rise and normal SpO2).
PND differentials: nightmares, panic attacks, nocturnal hypoglycaemia, OSA.
Orthopnoea differentials: COPD, gross obesity, acute asthma, gross ascites.

Post-meal pain (60-90 min) occurs in pancreatitis, cholecystitis, peptic ulcer and postprandial angina; NTG relieves both angina/MI and oesophageal spasm.
Non-ischaemic CVS chest pain includes AS/HOCM (LVH oxygen demand) and AR (diastolic coronary filling lost to regurgitation).
Variants: unstable, crescendo (never at rest), nocturnal/decubitus (severe CAD), walk-through (exercise vasodilation), silent MI (30%, elderly/DM), angina equivalents and second-wind angina.
CCS Angina Grading & Syncope vs Seizure

CCS stable angina: Grade 1 strenuous exercise only; Grade 2 slight limitation; Grade 3 walking 1-2 blocks or <1 flight of stairs; Grade 4 discomfort with any activity or at rest.
Exertional syncope points to fixed-output lesions (AS, HOCM).
Vasovagal syncope (<60 s, pale/grey, rare lateral tongue bite, rapid recovery) is separated from seizure (1-2 min tonic-clonic, red/blue, lateral tongue bite, >30 min post-ictal confusion).

Orthostatic syncope = fall in SBP >20 mmHg or DBP >10 mmHg within 3 min of standing (antihypertensives, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, anaemia).
Post-tussive syncope = violent coughing in lung disease raising intrathoracic pressure and reducing venous return.
CVS syncope splits into electrical (bradycardia, heart block, VT, SVT) and mechanical (AS, HOCM, PS, TOF, PE, and postural syncope in LA myxoma).

Palpitations (abnormal awareness of one's own heartbeat): exertional in regurgitant lesions, at rest in arrhythmia, followed by post-palpitation diuresis; in AR dyspnoea occurs much later than palpitations, whereas in MR they appear together.
Box 6.8 lists unilateral (DVT, infection, trauma, hemiplegia, lymphoedema) and bilateral leg oedema causes including drugs (NSAIDs, nifedipine, amlodipine, fludrocortisone), IVC obstruction, wet beriberi and Milroy's disease.
In cough with blood, always ask about melena and association with food.

Negative history screens RHF, RF, left-sided disease (voice change, dysphagia, oliguria), congenital spells/squatting, PHT (pulmonary apoplexy) and IE (stroke/TIA, haematuria).
Past history notes BMV in MS can cause MR; personal history checks IV drug abuse in suspected IE.
Drug schedule: digoxin 5 days on / 2 days off; diuretics and nitroglycerin at 8 am and 4 pm (avoiding nocturia and nocturnal hypotension).
History Summary & Pulse Rate, Rhythm, Volume & Delay

Warfarin is taken at 4 pm daily and benzathine penicillin every 21 days.
Normally femoral precedes radial pulse by a few ms (reversal = radiofemoral delay); in AF, variable diastolic filling causes weak contractions and an apex-pulse deficit.
VT (unchanged by vagal manoeuvres, cannon A waves and variable S1 from AV dissociation) is separated from PAT (abrupt termination with Valsalva/carotid massage, neck pounding).
Pulse Waveforms: Bisferiens, Bifid, Dicrotic, Anacrotic & Corrigan

Normal pulse has an anacrotic upstroke and dicrotic downstroke separated by the dicrotic notch at S2.
Pulsus bisferiens (two equal systolic peaks via Bernoulli effect) occurs in moderate AS + severe AR, HOCM and severe AR; bifid ('spike and dome') is classic for HOCM; dicrotic has its second peak in diastole (LV failure with low CO + high PVR); anacrotic has an upstroke notch (severe AS).
Corrigan/Waterhammer pulse is accentuated by raising the arm (gravity empties the radial artery and aligns it with the aorta).
Parvus et Tardus, Bigeminy, Paradoxus & Alternans

Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak low peak + slow wide upstroke) characterises AS; bigeminy pairs every sinus beat with a PVC (irregular rhythm), whereas regular alternating beats are pulsus alternans.
Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP drop, measured from expiration-only to inspiration+expiration Korotkoff sounds) occurs in tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, asthma/COPD and OSA/obesity; reversed pulsus paradoxus occurs in HOCM.
Pulsus alternans (LV dysfunction, sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ alternation) is detected by cuff when >10 mmHg.
CVS General Survey: PICCLE, Oedema Kinetics & Peripheral Signs

Check ruddy/suffused conjunctiva for polycythaemia of cyanotic heart disease, tongue/mucosa for central vs peripheral cyanosis, and clubbing (cyanotic HD, IE, LA myxoma).
Slow oedema pits >40 s (4 kg Na/water retention; treat with salt restriction); fast oedema pits <40 s (hypoproteinaemia); cardiac dependent oedema is presacral.
Check rheumatic nodules/joint swelling, IE stigmata (immunologic = Osler nodes, Roth spots, microscopic haematuria; vascular = Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages), and the Lighthouse sign of AR.
Peripheral Signs of AR & Hill's Sign

Peripheral AR signs 2-16: Becker's (retinal), Landolfi's (pupil), Muller's (uvula), De Musset's (head), Corrigan's (dancing carotids/waterhammer), locomotor brachii, Quincke's (nail bed), Rosenbach's (liver), Gerhardt's (spleen), Duroziez's (distal diastolic femoral murmur) and Traube's pistol-shot femorals.
Hill's sign (LL SBP >20 mmHg above UL SBP; popliteal/thigh cuff or posterior tibial/supramalleolar cuff): >20 mild, >40 moderate, >60 severe AR.
Hill's sign is a sphygmomanometer artefact from summation of reflected and forward waves (Jules Constant), and is falsely low in CHF and severe AS.

Inspect JVP, trachea and thyroid (if enlarged, look for thyrotoxic palpitations and eye signs), then chest shape: precordial bulge (left nipple displaced laterally/upward) vs pectus excavatum (backward bulge).
See-saw movement: RVH pulls the apex in while the precordium moves out in systole; LVH is the reverse. Back pulsations in coarctation = Suzman's sign.
Epigastric pulsations: RV origin coincides with the apex beat higher in the epigastrium; abdominal aortic origin occurs after the apex beat lower down.
JVP: Definition, RAP Formula, POLICE & IJV vs EJV

JVP = vertical height above the sternal angle (<=4 cm normal, since sternal angle is 5 cm above RA and normal RAP is <7 mmHg / 9 cm H2O; RAP mmHg = [JVP + 5] x 0.736; Harrison notes >4.5 cm at 30 deg).
POLICE separates JVP from carotid: non-Palpable, Occludable, Located between SCM heads lateral to carotid, drops on Inspiration, biphasic Contour, drops on Erection.
Right IJV is preferred over EJV (two 90-deg turns, fascial compression, sympathetic constriction) and over left IJV (left innominate vein compression in arteriosclerosis).
JVP Procedure, Non-pulsatile JVP & ACXVY Waves

Check JVP sitting first (if above clavicle), then at 45 deg; on inspiration mean JVP falls by suction while pulsations become more prominent from increased right-heart volume.
Non-pulsatile elevated JVP: bilateral = SVC obstruction; unilateral = innominate vein obstruction/thrombosis.
ACXVY: a = atrial contraction; c = tricuspid bulging in isovolumetric contraction (+ carotid component); v = venous return; x' (atrial relaxation) and x (systolic downward pull of tricuspid ring); y = atrial emptying.
Abnormalities of A, V, X & Y Waves (PAY TAX)

Prominent a wave = RVH (PAH, PE, PS); giant a wave = TS and marked LVH (Bernheim effect, before S1); cannon a wave (just after S1, RA vs closed TV) = intermittent in 3rd-degree block/VT, regular in junctional tachycardia, absent in SVT with aberrancy.
Equal a and v waves occur in RV failure and ASD ('left atrialization' of JVP because 4 pulmonary veins lower LA compliance).
PAY TAX: Constrictive Pericarditis gives a prominent Y descent; Cardiac Tamponade gives a prominent X descent (and blunted y descent); TR blunts the x descent and TS blunts the y descent.
Constrictive Pericarditis, Abdominojugular Reflux & Kussmaul's Sign

In constrictive pericarditis the adherent pericardium causes rapid early RV relaxation followed by sudden recoil — producing a rapid y descent and the catheterisation 'dip and square root' sign.
Abdominojugular reflux (periumbilical pressure >=15 s; positive if JVP rises >3 cm throughout) unmasks subclinical RV failure and confirms symptomatic LV failure.
Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical inspiratory JVP rise vs normal 3 mmHg fall): say RVMI first, then RV failure, TS, cor pulmonale, constrictive pericarditis and RCM — never tamponade (where septal bowing into the LV accommodates venous return and causes pulsus paradoxus instead).
Palpation: Apex Beat, DR POPE & Hyperdynamic vs Heaving

Apex beat = lowermost, outermost definite palpable cardiac impulse; report as '__ ICS, __ cm medial/lateral to MCL' and comment on character in the left lateral position.
Isovolumetric contraction rotates the heart counterclockwise (spiral muscle fibres) and LV ejection causes regression; LV vs RV apex gives a palpatory see-saw.
DR POPE = Dextrocardia (never say first; check right side if non-locatable), Rib, Pleural effusion, Obesity, Pericardial effusion, Emphysema; normal apex is L 5th ICS, 1/2 in medial to MCL, 1 ICS, ~2.5 cm2, <1/3 systole; contrast Hyperdynamic (volume overload) vs Heaving (pressure overload) vs Tapping (palpable S1).
Apex Shift, Abnormal Impulses, Thrills & Heave

LV enlargement shifts the apex downwards and laterally; RV enlargement shifts it only laterally.
Retracting apex (inward in systole, outward in diastole) = constrictive pericarditis and TR; hypokinetic = MI; double apex = HOCM ('second LV contraction'), severe AS with AR, and LBBB.
Thrill = palpable murmur (carotid AS shudder; A: AS/AR; P: PS, ASD/PDA; T: VSD; M: MR/MS); parasternal heave (2nd-5th ICS, midline to mid-MCL) is graded I-III (AIIMS) and caused by RVH or LA enlargement.
Pulsatile Liver, Epigastric Thumb Sign & Percussion

Thumb in epigastrium towards the shoulder: pulsation at the tip = RVH; pulsation at the pulp = aortic aneurysm.
Pulsatile liver: right hand on lower border, left fist on right lower ICS, breath held in deep inspiration; use JVP to time systole/diastole — expansile (TR) vs transmitted (aortic/RV), presystolic ('a' wave, TS) vs systolic (TR).
Cardiac percussion assesses liver span in suspected hepatomegaly and increased cardiac dullness in pericardial effusion.

Dr. Hamide's sequence: M (Apex) -> T (L 5th ICS) -> P (L 2nd ICS) -> AA1 (R 2nd ICS) and AA2 (Erb's point, L 3rd ICS, where the EDM of AR is heard best).
At AA1 the ESM of AS radiates to the carotids as a shudder and to the apex where it mimics MR (Gallavardin's phenomenon).
Levine and Freeman systolic murmur grading I/VI to VI/VI: thrill begins at Grade IV/VI; Grade VI/VI is audible with the stethoscope lifted off the chest.
Classical Murmurs & Heart Sound Intensity Table

Classical MS (****): loud S1, normal S2, high-pitched opening snap after S2 (diaphragm), followed by a low-pitched rough rumbling MDM +/- PSA (bell, left lateral position, mid-expiration).
Other apical MDMs: LA myxoma, Austin Flint (AR), Carey-Coombs (ARF), ball-valve LA thrombus, and high-flow states (MR, VSD, PDA, high-output, CHB); tricuspid MDMs: TS, high-flow (ASD, TR, TAPVR), RA myxoma.
AS and AR murmurs are best heard sitting leaning forward in expiration; Loud S1 (MS, hyperdynamic) vs Soft S1 (MR, calcific MS, TR, acute AR) and Loud/Soft A2 & P2.
Heart Sounds S1, S2, Split S2 in ASD, S3 & S4

Loud S1 in MS results from the dP/dt steep crossover slope (Curve A vs B) and wide leaflet closing excursion; other loud S1 causes include holosystolic MVP, LA myxoma, short PR interval and Ebstein's anomaly ('sail sound').
Split S1 (M1 20-30 ms before T1) widens in RBBB/Ebstein's; normal inspiratory S2 split is <0.03 s; ASD causes a wide fixed S2 split (increased low-resistance pulmonary hangout interval + reciprocal decrease in L-to-R shunt on inspiration, Perloff).
S3 reflects passive diastolic filling (physiological in children/athletes/pregnancy; pathological in MR/TR, high-output, CHD, HOCM, systolic HF with overly compliant dilated LV, HTN); S4 reflects atrial emptying into a stiff ventricle (HTN, CAD, severe AS, HOCM, RCM).
Added Sounds, OS vs S3 Table & Innocent Murmurs

Added sounds: opening snap (early diastole), ejection click (post-S1), midsystolic click, prosthetic mitral (closes at S1, opens at OS timing) and prosthetic aortic (opens at EC timing, closes at S2).
Standing widens the S2-OS gap in MS but narrows the A2-P2 gap; in the OS vs S3 table, treating HF makes OS louder whereas S3 is lost.
Pericardial knock = abrupt halt to early diastolic filling in constriction; pericardial rub is triphasic; innocent murmurs are <3/6, systolic/continuous (never pure diastolic), without thrill (Still's, venous hum, mammary souffle).
Dynamic Manoeuvres, Systolic Timing & 10 Named Murmurs

Carvallo's sign: inspiration increases all right-sided murmurs except pulmonic ejection; Valsalva/standing (low preload) increases HOCM and advances MVP click/murmur, whereas handgrip and rapid squatting decrease HOCM and delay MVP click/murmur.
Systolic murmurs by timing: Pansystolic (MR, TR, VSD), Early (acute MR, muscular VSD, acute TR), Mid (supravalvular AS, coarctation, AS, sclerosis, HOCM, flow, PS, ASD), Late (MVP, acute MI, TVP).
10 Named murmurs (****): Austin Flint, Carey-Coombs, Cole-Cecil, Cruveilhier-Baumgarten, Gibson, Graham Steell, Means-Lerman scratch, Roger's, Seagull and Still's.

Complete cardiovascular diagnosis order: 1. Etiology -> 2. Structural -> 3. Complications -> 4. Rhythm -> 5. Functional -> 6. Treatment Status -> 7. Precipitating Factor.
Worked model example (A-G): Rheumatic Heart disease (1) / Severe MS with Mild MR (2) / in Congestive Cardiac Failure (3) / with Atrial Fibrillation (4) / in NYHA Class III (5) / not on any treatment (6) / due to Infective Endocarditis (7).
The Cardiac Cycle: Atrial & Ventricular Timing (0.8 s)

Total cardiac cycle duration is 0.8 sec (8 sectors of 0.1 sec): inner ring = Atrial Systole (0.1 s) + Atrial Diastole (0.7 s); outer ring = Ventricular Systole (0.3 s) + Ventricular Diastole (0.5 s).
Ventricular systole (0.3 s): Isometric contraction -> Maximum ejection -> Reduced ejection; Ventricular diastole (0.5 s): Protodiastole -> Isometric relaxation -> Rapid inflow -> Diastasis -> Atrial systole (final 0.1 s).
Wiggers Diagram: Pressures, Volumes, Valves, ECG & Sounds

Seven phases (a-g): a = Atrial systole, b = Isovolumetric contraction, c = Rapid ejection, d = Reduced ejection, e = Isovolumetric relaxation, f = Rapid filling, g = Reduced filling (diastasis).
Valve crossovers: MV closes at a->b (S1); AV opens at b->c (~80 mmHg, peaking at 120 mmHg); AV closes at d->e (dicrotic notch, S2); MV opens at e->f (v-wave peak, followed by S3 in rapid filling).
LV volume is flat at EDV (~120-130 mL) during Phase b and flat at ESV (~50 mL) during Phase e; P wave precedes Phase a (4th sound), QRS precedes Phase b (1st sound), and T wave occurs in Phase d.
MS: Causes, Anatomy, Congenital Types & Variants

Harrison Table 263-1: RHD (~40% pure/predominant MS, fish-mouth valve), congenital, MAC, SLE, RA, methysergide, carcinoid, Lutembacher's, Hurler-Scheie/Fabry/Whipple, and LA outflow mimics (cor triatriatum, LA myxoma, pulmonary vein obstruction).
Mitral anatomy: 1 anterior leaflet, 3-lobed posterior leaflet, anteromedial & posterolateral commissures, chordae tendineae, lateral & medial papillary muscles; Congenital MS = supravalvular (fibrous ring), valvular, subvalvular (parachute = 1 papillary muscle; hammock = large/numerous papillary muscles).
Variants: Lutembacher (MS + ASD), Damped/Silent MS (RV forms apex in severe PAH so MDM disappears at apex), and Juvenile MS (<20 yr, rheumatic, severe MS & PAH, less AF, needs immediate surgery if symptomatic); gradual LA pressure rise -> protective PAH, sudden rise (AF) -> pulmonary oedema.
Etiopathogenesis, Clinical Features & Haemoptysis in MS

Up to severe MS, resting CO and EF are normal, but tachycardia abolishes the atrial kick and lowers CO (precipitants: fever, excitement, exertion, anaemia, paroxysmal AF, pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis).
PAH arises from passive backward transmission + reactive pulmonary arteriolar constriction ('second stenosis'); presystolic accentuation reflects atrial systole before S1.
Latent period ~2 decades; dyspnoea (J receptors, low compliance), palpitations (AF from pulmonary vein stretch), mitral facies, and 5 causes of haemoptysis: pulmonary apoplexy (bronchial vein rupture — #1), winter bronchitis, acute pulmonary oedema, pulmonary infarction, warfarin overdose.

Severity of MS: shorter S2-OS gap ('less'), longer duration of MDM ('more'), and features of pulmonary hypertension.
Complications: AF (thrombus most commonly in LA appendage/auricle), PAH/RVF/cor pulmonale, embolic stroke/limb/mesenteric ischaemia, haemoptysis, Ortner's syndrome (RLN -> hoarseness) & dysphagia; IE is very rare ('don't say it').
PAH (normal PAP 15-25/10 mmHg; PAH mean PAP >25 rest / >30 exercise, severe >60 exercise): low-volume pulse, prominent 'a' wave, 2nd ICS pulsation & dullness, diastolic shock (palpable P2), parasternal heave, and 6-event auscultation (S1, pulmonary EC, pulmonary ESM, loud P2 narrow split, Graham Steell, right S3).
OS, Absent PSA, Soft S1, DDs & ECG in MS

Opening snap (6 meanings): organic MS, pliable non-calcified valve, S2-OS gauges severity, amenable to surgery, significant MS, high LA pressure.
Absent PSA = AF, left heart failure, massive LA thrombus; Soft S1 in MS = co-existent MR, MV calcification, digitalis overdose (long PR), acute rheumatic carditis (long PR), AF, and damped MS (RV apex).
DDs: ASD (fixed S2 split, LSM ESM, functional TS), LA myxoma (positional murmur, fever, weight loss, anaemia, emboli, high IgG & IL-6), significant MR (no OS/loud P2, soft S1, loud PSM), severe AR (Austin Flint not presystolic, softens with vasodilators); ECG shows AF, P mitrale (bifid P), and RVH (tall R in V1-V2, deep S in V6).
CXR, Doppler Echo, Wilkins Score & Medical Management

CXR: straightening of left heart border (earliest, PA + LA appendage), double atrial shadow ('shadow within a shadow'), Kerley B lines (PVP 20-30 mmHg, costophrenic horizontal lines), and Kerley A lines (PVP >30 mmHg, towards hilum).
Doppler Echo: normal MVA 4-6 cm2, progressive >1.5 cm2, severe 1-1.5 cm2, very severe/tight/critical <1 cm2, enlarged LA >5.5 cm; Abascal/Wilkins score (mobility, thickness, subvalvular thickening, calcification x 4 pts = 16; <8/16 amenable to BMV).
Medical management: Penicillin V 250 mg BD (250 mg QID in ARF; lifelong in established HD), Digoxin 0.25 mg 5 days/wk OD for AF (+ oral Diltiazem/Atenolol if needed), Warfarin INR 2-3 indefinitely (AF or thromboembolism), and diuretics.
Emergency AF, Valvotomy, BMV & Prosthetic Valves

Emergency AF: rapid digitalisation 0.25 mg IV bolus, wait 2 h, repeat 0.25 mg up to max 1 mg, then beta-blockers if needed; Closed mitral valvotomy (pliable valve, no MR) uses the TUBBS transventricular dilator.
BMV: 5 criteria (significant symptoms, isolated MS, no MR, mobile non-calcified valve, no LA thrombus), 4 complications (emboli, perforation, MR, iatrogenic ASD), and 2 success criteria (50% fall in mean MV gradient + doubling of MVA).
Valve replacement (if MR or rigid/calcified valve): Mechanical prostheses (INR 2.5-3.5; caged-ball Starr-Edwards vs preferred tilting-disc/bileaflet St. Jude, Bjork-Shiley, Indian Chitra TTK — less space, less haemolysis, less strut fracture) vs Bioprostheses (porcine/pericardial/cadaveric; less thromboembolism, not useful <65 yr due to rapid deterioration).
Harrison's Table 264-1: Major Causes of Mitral Regurgitation (Book p56)

Inserted Harrison's table with two acute rows and a chronic hierarchy: Acute = IE, papillary muscle rupture (post-MI), chordal rupture/leaflet flail (MVP, IE), blunt trauma.
Chronic splits into Primary (affecting leaflets, chordae: myxomatous [MVP, Barlow's, forme fruste], rheumatic fever, healed IE, congenital [cleft, AV canal], radiation) and Secondary (leaflets/chordae 'innocent bystanders': ischemic CM, dilated CM, HOCM with SAM, AF with LA enlargement and annular dilation), plus Mitral annular calcification with its 'mixed' footnote.
The abbreviation key defines AF, AV, HOCM, IE, LA, LV, MI, MVP and SAM.
MR Causes: Acute vs Chronic (Book p57)

Acute MR: Endocarditis, Post-MI papillary muscle rupture (posteromedial), chordal rupture/leaflet flail due to MVP and IE, trauma.
Chronic MR: MVP, rheumatic fever, healed endocarditis, mitral annular calcification, congenital cleft, HOCM with SAM, dilated cardiomyopathy.
MR Haemodynamics: Chronic vs Acute (Book p57)

Chronic MR: gradual LA dilation with little pressure rise (very few symptoms), slow LV dilation, gradual LA and LV pressure rise from chronic volume overload; increased LV volume is often accompanied by reduced cardiac output (verify this).
Acute MR: rapid rise in LA pressure because of normal LA compliance, with marked symptomatic deterioration.

Dyspnoea (early, along with palpitations); Fatigue from decreased cardiac output; Palpitations from A fib and increased stroke volume.
Right heart failure appears in late stages.

Six entries in order: A fib; cardiomegaly with a displaced hyperdynamic apex; apical PSM ± thrill; soft S1, S3; signs of pulmonary venous congestion (crepts, oedema, effusions).
Signs of pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure complete the list.

ECG: left atrial hypertrophy, left ventricular hypertrophy / A fib. CXR: inverted moustache; enlarged LA, LV, pulmonary venous congestion, pulmonary oedema if acute.
Echo: dilated LA, LV; Doppler; cardiac catheterisation.
TR vs MR: Differentiating Features (Book p57)

TR has: murmur best heard in the tricuspid area, positive Carvallo's, hepatic pulsation, response to abdominojugular reflux (Vitam sign), giant V waves with deep Y descents (Lancisi sign), earlobe pulsation.
Acute MR produces an early systolic murmur because the undilated LA cannot buffer the regurgitant volume, so LV and LA pressures equalise in early systole itself.
MR Treatment — tail of the MR note (top of Book p58)

The MR '7. Mx' section closes at the top of Book p58: Medical = same as MS; vasodilators in severe cases may help in reducing R.
Surgical = MVR under open heart surgery, sometimes by mitral valvuloplasty or annuloplasty.
Anatomic Classification of Aortic Stenosis (Book p58)

Aortic stenosis is classified into 1. Supravalvular, 2. Valvular, 3. Subvalvular (a. Hypertrophic subaortic stenosis — HOCM; b. Fixed fibrotic subvalvular stenosis).
Only the Valvular level opens the 'Valvular aortic stenosis' subsection on p58; the other two are detailed on p61.

Three causes: rheumatic heart disease (almost always with mitral valve involvement + aortic regurgitation), congenital anomalies (bicuspid or unicuspid aortic valve), degenerative calcific stenosis.
Rheumatic AS is therefore never 'isolated' — the mitral valve is involved along with aortic regurgitation.
Valvular AS: Classification by Valve Area (Book p58)

Normal valve area = 3–4 cm². Severe AS <1 cm²; Moderate AS 1–1.5 cm²; Mild AS >1.5 cm².
Severity is graded strictly by valve area on p58, before any haemodynamic discussion.

LVOT obstruction -> concentric LVH (pressure overload); normal haemodynamic function for years without decline in CO, then eventual LV systolic dysfunction.
The hypertrophied LV has a high oxygen demand, so angina on exertion is common.

Presentation in the 6th–8th decade once severe (bicuspid disease presents sooner): exertional dyspnoea, angina pectoris (somewhat later), exertional syncope.
In isolated severe AS, left heart failure and pulmonary hypertension occur very late.
Valvular AS: Early Signs — Rhythm, BP, Carotid Pulse (Book p58)

Usually sinus rhythm; AF suggests associated mitral valve disease. BP usually normal early; late, stroke volume declines and pulse pressure falls.
Pulsus parvus et tardus 'rises slowly to a delayed peak'.
Harrison's Table 261-1: Major Causes of Aortic Stenosis (Book p59)

Inserted Harrison's table — valve lesion 'Aortic stenosis' with four etiologies: Congenital (bicuspid, unicuspid), Degenerative calcific disease, Rheumatic fever, Radiation.
Radiation appears only in the table, not in the p58 cause list.
Valvular AS: Auscultation & JVP Signs (Book p60)

Carotid shudder (thrill, especially left); soft S2 (cuspal calcification, prolonged LV ejection time); accentuated JVP a wave — Bernheim effect; laterally displaced apical impulse; systolic thrill.
