Ejection click (younger bicuspid patients; inaudible if calcified/rigid); low pitched rough rasping ejection (mid) systolic murmur, aortic area, sitting, breath held in expiration, radiating to carotids; Gallavardin effect (apical transmission confused with MR).

ECG — LVH; Doppler Echo; Chest X Ray; Cardiac catheterisation.
Only the ECG entry carries an elaborated finding (LVH); the other three are listed as-is.

Medical: severe AS — avoid strenuous physical activity; asymptomatic — ACE inhibitors and beta blockers; serial Echo.
Surgical indications: symptomatic severe AS, LV systolic dysfunction, bicuspid aortic valve disease, aneurysmal root/ascending aorta; procedures: Ross (declined use), percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty, TAVR.
Valvular AS: Determinants of Severity (Book p60)

Single second heart sound (LV systole prolongation), pulsus parvus et tardus, and a louder and later peaking murmur.
These bedside markers track worsening gradient severity as the obstruction progresses.

Localised discrete narrowing above the sinuses of Valsalva; murmur loudest at suprasternal notch/first right interspace, radiating more to the RIGHT carotid (arch diagram 'more towards R side').
a/w hypercalcaemia and elfin facies (wide set eyes, upturned nose, small chin, patulous lips, deep husky voice); stronger pulse/BP right arm and carotid; almost never with an ejection click.

Disproportionate asymmetric IV septal thickening; systolic bulge draws the anterior mitral leaflet medially -> LVOT obstruction (proximity-dependent).
Murmur increases with manoeuvres that decrease LV size (inspiration, tachycardia, amyl nitrite, standing after squatting); bifid pulse; double or triple apical impulse.
AS vs PS: Comparison Table (Book p61)

Murmur best heard at — AS right 2nd ICS, PS left sternal border; inspiration — AS decreases, PS increases; standing — makes the PS murmur louder on inspiration.
Ejection click — AS may be present, PS may be present but disappears in inspiration.
Harrison's Table 262-1: Major Causes of Aortic Regurgitation (Book p62)

Inserted Harrison's table — valve lesion 'Aortic regurgitation' with two etiology columns: Valvular (congenital bicuspid, endocarditis, rheumatic fever, myxomatous [prolapse], radiation, trauma, syphilis, ankylosing spondylitis).
Aortic root disease (aortic dissection, medial degeneration, Marfan syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, nonsyndromic familial aneurysm, aortitis, hypertension). The table says 'Medial degeneration'; 'Cystic' appears only in the p63 note.
AR Causes: Valvular, Root, Aortitis (Book p63)

Valvular: congenital bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis, myxomatous (prolapse), syphilis (Luetic Aortitis), ankylosing spondylitis, trauma; Root: dissection (displacement of the valves), cystic medial degeneration, Marfan's, bicuspid; plus c. Aortitis.
Bicuspid aortic valve is listed under BOTH valvular and root disease; Hypertension, radiation and nonsyndromic familial aneurysm are table-only entries.
AR Haemodynamics: Acute vs Chronic (Book p63)

Cascade: increased total stroke volume -> increased LVEDV (preload) -> dilation and eccentric hypertrophy -> eventual LV failure.
Acute severe AR (e.g. endocarditis): LV cannot compensate rapidly -> pulmonary oedema; chronic severe AR: asymptomatic for up to 10–15 years.

Palpitations can be an early complaint, seen for years before the exertional dyspnoea; angina can occur.
Then exertional dyspnoea, PND, orthopnoea.
AR Signs: Head to Toe (Book p63)

The '***Signs' list: peripheral signs (from head to toe); heaving apical impulse displaced down and out ('????'); pulsus bisferiens; diastolic thrill over the aortic area.
Systolic thrill over carotids/suprasternal notch need not mean accompanying AS; in severe AR, A2 is usually absent.

High pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur; best heard in the 3rd ICS along the left sternal border, sitting, breath held in expiration.
Characteristically early diastolic and loudest at Erb's point (neo aortic area) because of the aorta's orientation; if instead best heard in the aortic area, suspect an aortic aneurysm causing the AR.
AR Signs i–l — tail of the AR note (top of Book p64)

Right sternal border murmur -> aneurysmal dilation; a mid systolic ejection murmur can also be best in the aortic area, transmitted to the carotids.
Two eponymous murmurs are named without elaboration: Austin Flint and Cole Cecil.

ECG — LVH; Doppler Echo (color doppler: most sensitive for mild cases); cardiac cath.
CXR: cardiomegaly (cor bovinum / bovine heart), aortic root dilation (prominent aortic knuckle), aortic valve calcification (sus for concomitant AS).

As in MS (IE or syphilitic aortitis needs Rx); chronic + significant volume overload requires a vasodilator (hydralazine, nifedipine, or ACE inhibitor).
Surgery: AVR — ideal time after haemodynamic/echogenic evidence of LVdys but before significant symptoms.

Ostium secundum ASD = 90%; ostium primum ASD = 5%.
The primum type is commonly associated with Down syndrome or endocardial cushion defects.
Congenital HD — ASD: Syndromic Associations (Book p64)

Holt-Oram (triphalangeal fingerised thumb, sometimes abrachia or phocomelia); Patau — trisomy 13 (polydactyly, flexion deformity of fingers, simian crease, cleft lip and palate, microcephaly; ASD, VSD, PDA).
Edward — trisomy 18 (prominent occiput, low set malformed ears, rocker bottom feet, micrognathia, clenched fists; ASD, VSD, PDA); Ellis van Creveld (polydactyly, nail dysplasia, dwarfism); Lutembacher = MS + ASD.
Congenital HD — ASD: Atrial Fibrillation (Book p64)

The final point of the ASD section: atrial fibrillation is common in ASD.
This arrhythmic point closes the congenital heart disease page.
ASD: Symptoms, Signs & DDs — tail of the CHD section (top of Book p65)

Small ASDs are usually asymptomatic; large defects present with tachycardia, right/left heart failure, exertional dyspnoea.
Signs: associated PS, wide fixed split of S2 (narrowing with pulmonary hypertension), flow ESM across the pulmonary valve, flow MDM across the mitral valve; DDs: MS with pulmonary HTN, partial anomalous pulmonary venous connections, TAPVC with a large interatrial communication without pulmonary HTN. The page closes with the stubs 'TOF and VSD from peds' and 'Facies in congenital heart disease — Nice to know'.

ARF: children aged 5–14, rare >30 years; RHD peaks 25–40 years. Cause: Group A Streptococci.
Pathogenesis: molecular mimicry — immune response targeted at streptococcal antigens (M protein and NAG) also recognises human tissues.

Mitral stenosis is seen in 99% of RHD cases; 40% of cases have MS with MR; isolated MS in 25%.
38% have multi valve involvement; 35% aortic valve involvement; 6% tricuspid; the pulmonary valve is very rarely involved.

Latent period 1–5 weeks; the preceding infection is commonly subclinical but confirmable by antibody testing.
Most common complaints: polyarthritis (60–75%), carditis (50–60%).

Up to 60% of ARF patients progress to RHD; endocardium/myocardium/pericardium may be involved. Mitral valve almost always affected (sometimes with aortic); isolated aortic is rare.
Early damage -> regurgitation, then (recurrent episodes) thickening, scarring, calcification -> stenosis; characteristic carditis in previously unaffected patients is MR +/- AR; myocarditis may cause first degree AV block and softening of S1.

Hot, swollen, red, tender joints and polyarthritis; typically migrates over a period of hours; large joints, asymmetric.
Pain severe and disabling until anti-inflammatory therapy; characteristically sensitive to NSAIDs/Salicylates.

Sydenham's chorea: absence of other manifestations, prolonged latent period, more common in females; ALWAYS associated with carditis.
Head (darting tongue movements) and upper limbs; generalised or unilateral; emotional lability/obsessive-compulsive traits; resolves around 6 weeks, up to 6 months.

Erythema marginatum: pink macules clearing centrally with a serpiginous spreading edge; evanescent (appears/disappears before the examiner's eyes); trunk, sometimes limbs, almost never the face.
Subcutaneous nodules — the 3 P's: painless, pea sized, on bony prominences; days to weeks.

ESR, CRP; WBC count; ECG; chest X ray.
The two conditional entries: blood culture if febrile, and throat swab before giving antibiotics.

Antibiotics: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg PO bd / Amox 50 mg/kg daily x 10 days. Salicylates/NSAIDs for arthritis/arthralgia/fever once dx confirmed (no value in carditis/chorea); aspirin 50–60 mg/kg/day up to 80–100 mg/kg/day in 4–5 divided doses; naproxen 10–20 mg/kg/day in two divided doses.
Severe carditis: steroids (controversial) — prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day, max 3 weeks. Severe chorea: carbamazepine (1–2 weeks response, continue 1–2 weeks after remission); prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day with rapid weaning in very severe/refractory; IVIg not recommended except severe refractory chorea.

Primary: timely and complete treatment of group A streptococcal sore throat; penicillin within 9 days of onset prevents almost all ARF.
Secondary: Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 MU every 4 weeks — no carditis: 5 years or until 21; carditis without residual valve disease: 10 years or until 21; persistent valvular disease: 20 years or until 40 (each 'whichever is longer').
IE Diagnosis: Definite vs Possible (Book p69)

Definite: pathological criteria, 2 major + 1 minor, 1 major + 2 minor, or 5 minor.
Possible: 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor.
Duke Criteria: Major — Blood Cultures (Book p69)

Typical organisms from two cultures (Viridans streptococci, Streptococcus bovis, HACEK = Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), or community-acquired S. aureus/enterococci without a primary focus.
Other organisms from persistently positive cultures (two >12 h apart, or all of three/majority of four, first-last 1 h apart); single Coxiella burnetii culture or serology for Q fever, Bartonella, Chlamydia psittaci.
Duke Criteria: Major — Endocardial Involvement (Book p69)

Echocardiogram positive for IE: oscillating intracardiac mass without alternative explanation, abscess, or new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve.
Or NEW valvular regurgitation — worsening/changing a preexisting murmur is not sufficient.

Minors: predisposition (heart condition, injection drug use, previous IE, prosthetic material); fever >38°C; vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhages, subconjunctival petechiae, Janeway lesions); immunologic (glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth's spots, positive rheumatoid factor); microbiological evidence.
Pathological: positive microbiology or histology of pathologic tissue at surgery or autopsy (vegetations, valve tissue, embolic fragments, tissue/pus from intracardiac abscesses).
IE Prophylaxis — Old Regimens (Book p70, superseded)

Oral procedures: can take oral — amoxicillin; cannot take oral — ampicillin; ceftriaxone; allergy row — clindamycin; azithro (oral) / clindamycin; ceftriaxone (IV). RESP: same as oral; abscess/empyema drainage add strep viridans; staph — Vanco.
GU/GIT: not recommended (established infx/abx cover — enterococci: penicillin); SSTI: not for routine sx (infected tissue — penicillin; allergic or MRSA — Vance). The 2023 ESC + Duke-ISCVID pages supersede all of this, including prophylaxis.

Definite IE unchanged (2 major / 1 major + 3 minor / 5 minor); possible 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor. Blood-culture rules relaxed; second organism tier (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes, corynebacteria — typical only with intracardiac prosthetic material).
New microbiology (PCR, amplicon/metagenomic sequencing, in-situ hybridisation, Bartonella enzyme immunoassay); cardiac CT + 18F-FDG PET/CT major (no longer prosthetic-only); intraoperative inspection a new major; previous IE + transcatheter valves/CIEDs as new minors.

Native community-acquired: ampicillin + (flu)cloxacillin + gentamicin (allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin), 4–6 weeks; streptococcal fully sensitive: penicillin/ceftriaxone 4 weeks (2 weeks with gentamicin).
Prosthetic EARLY: vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin ≥6 weeks (assume MRSA; rifampicin 3–5 days later); LATE: as native + rifampicin if staph; right-sided/PWID: 2 weeks may suffice for uncomplicated tricuspid MSSA, look for septic pulmonary emboli; CIED: hardware extraction mandatory; culture-negative: HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma (prior antibiotics = commonest cause).
2023 Update: Team, Surgery, Stroke, POET (Book p71)

Endocarditis Team and Heart Valve Centre: every case discussed by cardiology, cardiac surgery, microbiology and imaging.
Surgery (three H's): heart failure (commonest/most urgent), uncontrolled infection (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, cultures >7 days, fungal/resistant), embolism prevention (>10 mm with embolus or severe valve disease, or isolated >15 mm). Stroke no longer an automatic bar (ischaemic without haemorrhage: no delay; ICH: defer ~1 month). POET: oral switch non-inferior in stabilised left-sided IE; OPAT not in the first 10 days, not with complications.
2023 Prophylaxis: The Principle (bottom of Book p71)

The principle since 2007 is unchanged: prophylaxis is confined to high-risk patients undergoing high-risk procedures.
Moderate-risk cardiac lesions no longer qualify.

Who (high risk only): prosthetic valve/material; previous IE; untreated cyanotic CHD or prosthetic-repair CHD (6 months, or lifelong with residual shunt/regurgitation); NEW 2023 — VAD or heart-transplant recipients with valvulopathy.
When: dental only (gingiva/periapical manipulation or oral-mucosa perforation) — NOT respiratory/GI/GU/dermatological/musculoskeletal without established infection. What: amoxicillin or ampicillin 2 g PO/IV single dose 30–60 min before (children 50 mg/kg); allergy — doxycycline 100 mg, clindamycin 600 mg, azithro/clarithro 500 mg; no cephalosporins with penicillin anaphylaxis. Oral hygiene and dental review outweigh prophylaxis; aseptic technique; discourage piercing/tattooing.

Proforma: cough with expectoration, haemoptysis, dyspnoea (rule out CVS causes), chest pain, fever/evening rise/weight loss/night sweats, cor pulmonale features, bronchiectasis complications, oedema, past TB?, occupational history**.
Unilateral chest pain usually points to RS causes; pleuritic pain increases on inspiration (coughing) — minimal effusion = pleural layers more in contact = more irritation; pleural disease gives dry cough and stabbing pain.

MRC grading preferred in RS — advantages: distance is checked, peer comparison, slope vs level ground.
Acute onset dyspnoea: pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism, acute COPD exacerbation, acute severe asthma, status asthmaticus, one more asthma.

Onset/duration (TB, chronic bronchitis); postural (post nasal drip, bronchiectasis, LHF 'orthopnoea equalii', tracheal mass); nocturnal (PND, asthma, cough-variant asthma, GERD, TPE); colour (mucopurulent-purulent = infection, serous/frothy pink = pulmonary oedema, blood-stained = bronchiectasis/TB/PE/carcinoma).
Bronchorrhoea >100 ml/day (tumbler 150–200 ml): bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema into a bronchus, necrotising pneumonia; foul smell = abscess/bronchiectasis; frank vs blood-stained.

Frank (blood only), spurious (URTI), pseudo (Serratia marcescens), endemic (Paragonimus westermani).
Severity: mild <100 ml/day, moderate 100–150 ml, severe up to 200 ml; massive >500 ml/day or >150 ml/hr or 100 ml/day for >3 days.

Airway: bronchitis (acute/chronic), bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchiectasis, body (foreign body) — repeated small haemoptysis/blood-streaked sputum highly suggests carcinoma; bronchial bleed more dangerous (systemic-circulation pressure).
Alveolar: pneumonia, fibrocavitary TB (Rasmussen aneurysm rupture), lung abscess, pulmonary oedema (pink frothy); interstitial: ILD (rare); vascular: PH, PE, PA fistula; CVS: MS, PE, PH, AV malformation; CVD: Wegener's, Goodpasture, vasculitis; infective: Weil's, fibrocavitary TB, invasive aspergillosis, paragonimiasis.

Causes: bronchiectasis, fibrocavitary TB, aspergillosis, paragonimiasis.
Management: intubate; volume resuscitation; blood transfusion; bronchoscopy with balloon tamponade / topical epinephrine or vasopressin.

Recurrent causes: bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, bronchogenic carcinoma; pseudohemoptysis = upper respiratory/oral bleeding.
Haemoptysis vs haematemesis: cough (not nausea/vomiting) with frothing; alkaline vs acidic pH; food particles and melaena with haematemesis. Cause of death: asphyxia from blood in the bronchial tree. Cor pulmonale history: RV failure or protein loss — also amyloidosis.
Causes of Dry Cough & Special Coughs (Book p77)

Dry cough: pleural pathologies, ILD, cough-variant asthma, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, atypical pneumonia, GERD, ACE inhibitors, RLN palsy.
Brassy cough (metallic, tracheal compression); bovine cough (non-explosive, RLN palsy); post-tussive syncope: high intrathoracic pressure -> decreased venous return -> decreased cardiac output.

Category; treatment taken? treatment completed? compliance?
Side effects experienced?

Modified MRC grades 0–4 verbatim; note: no 'breathlessness at rest'.
Advantages vs NYHA: slope vs level ground, peer comparison, distance checked; other classification — Sherwood Jones.
Breathlessness: JSCR Receptors & CVS vs RS (Book p78)

Dyspnoea receptors (JSCR): J (alveolar capillary junction), stretch (thoracic cage and lungs), chemoreceptors (carotid artery, aorta, medulla), respiratory muscle receptors.
CVS breathlessness: associated CVS cardinal symptoms; orthopnoea, PND. RS breathlessness: no associated CVS symptoms; orthopnoea may be present (asthma, COPD) but PND is specific to CVS.
Box 19.8: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Breathlessness (Book p79)

Seven conditions x History/Signs/CXR/ABG/ECG: pulmonary oedema, massive PE, acute severe asthma, acute COPD exacerbation, pneumonia, metabolic acidosis, psychogenic (* = valuable discriminatory feature).
Key rows: PE — normal CXR with oligemic fields, S1Q3T3/RBBB/T(V1–V4) inversion; asthma — hyperinflation only, up-PaCO2 in extremis, bradycardia in extremis; COPD — flapping tremor/bounding pulses, type II ABG; psychogenic — normal PaO2, down-down-PaCO2, carpopedal spasm.
Chest Pain: Origins & Character Table (Book p80)

Origins: parietal pleura, chest wall, mediastinal structures — NOT lung (autonomic innervation only).
Table: parietal pleura sharp/stabbing with inspiration (upper 6 ribs localised, lower ribs -> upper abdomen, diaphragmatic -> shoulder tip/neck); chest wall dull/aching, progressive, hinders sleep; mediastinal central/retrosternal.
Specific History Points in Suspected TB (Book p80)

Occupation of husband — high risk group for HIV; evening rise of temperature — due to TNFa;
contact history of tuberculosis.
Examination: Pulse, Pallor, Cyanosis, Clubbing (Book p81)

Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg is significant, reduces on treatment. Pallor — recurrent haemoptysis, bronchial ca, TB. Cyanosis — SpO2 <85%.
Clubbing in TB: post-TB bronchiectasis, scar carcinoma (adenocarcinoma), empyema, endobronchial TB.

Epitrochlear nodes are always pathologic — NHL, secondary syphilis, sarcoidosis, forearm/hand infections, tularaemia (rare), but not in TB (Dr. Hamide).
Scalene node: index finger between SCM and clavicle; head tilted to the same side; press firmly down towards the first rib.
Generalised & Mediastinal Lymphadenopathy; RS Oedema (Book p82)

Generalised — HIV, IM, sarcoidosis. Mediastinal — dull percussion on manubrium sterni, bronchial breathing below T4 spine (d'Espine sign) from subcarinal nodes.
RS oedema: cor pulmonale; protein loss in sputum (esp bronchiectasis); amyloidosis of long standing bronchiectasis.
Respiration: Rate, Distress Signs & Muscles (Book p82)

Normal rate 12-18/min; women thoraco-abdominal, men abdomino thoracic. Distress: alar nasii, pursed lip (PEEP), tracheal indrawing, accessory muscles, intercostal retraction.
Muscles (I always with E): inspiration — external intercostals/diaphragm + SCM, scalenes, pectoralis minor, trapezius; expiration quiet passive, active — internal intercostals, abdominal, quadratus lumborum.

Phlycten, choroid tubercles, scars/sinuses, scrofula; skin — lupus vulgaris (apple-jelly), erythema nodosum, verrucous cutis, scrofuloderma;
cold abscess/collar stud abscess; epididymo-orchitis.
Other Things in General Examination (Book p82)

Horner's syndrome in lung malignancies.
Signs of neurovascular compression: wasting of small muscles of hands.

Also Thinker's sign or Target sign: darkened/thickened skin on lower thighs and elbows.
Mechanism: air trapping flattens the diaphragm; sitting forwards improves it; hemosiderin from trapped RBCs -> brown discolouration.
Inspection of the Upper Respiratory Tract (Book p83)

Oral cavity — thrush, tonsils, halitosis -> lung abscess; nose — DNS, polyps;
pharynx — post nasal drip can cause respiratory symptoms and breathing difficulty.

Tracheal position affected mainly by the upper lobes; if no deviation — 'trachea appears central'.
Trail's sign: pretracheal fascia relaxes on the shifted side -> undue prominence of the clavicular head of SCM.
Chest Wall Inspection: Volume Loss, Symmetry & Shapes (Book p83-84)

Volume loss: shoulder droop, medial scapular border prominence (not winging), crowding of ribs. Ratios: normal 5:7, flat 1:2 (TB, fibrothorax), barrel 1:1.
Pectus carinatum (rickets) vs excavatum (funnel/cobbler's); Harrison's sulcus (chronic childhood respi disease, rickets); rachitic rosary.

Flail chest — paradoxical thoracic movement. Kyphosis (forward), scoliosis (lateral; convexity opposite the fibrosed lung).
Expansion: normal 5-8 cm; emphysema/ILD/ankylosing spondylitis <1 cm; apical (supraclavicular fossae), anterior (thumbs in front), posterior (TRAPS for upper lobes); metal end in front / on spines; full expiration first.

Turbinate hypertrophy/polyps; sinus tenderness = sinusitis. Kartagener's (situs inversus), Wegener's (necrotizing granuloma),
Samter's triad (aspirin-asthma-ethmoidal polyps), Young's (sinopulmonary + azoospermia), Churg-Strauss (asthma, eosinophilia, vasculitis, granuloma).
Surface Marking of Lungs & Lower Borders (Book p86-88)

Right 3 lobes, left 2. Oblique fissure: T2/T3 spinous process -> medial scapular border -> 5th rib MAL -> 6th rib MCL; RML by the horizontal fissure (4th rib sternal border, cuts at 5th rib).
Boloor p142/143 views; lower border LUNG 6/8/10 vs PLEURA 8/10/12; front (upper/middle lobes), back (lower lobe), axillary (all three).
Tracheal Position: Pushed/Pulled & CricoSternal Distance (Book p89)

Slight right deviation normal; pushed opposite — effusion, pneumothorax, apical tumour; pulled same — fibrosis, collapse; same-side in effusion — fibrosis/collapse, mesothelioma.
CricoSternal distance: number of fingers insinuated; reduced in COPD (mediastinum pulls the cricoid down).
Inspiratory Tracheal Descent & Tracheal Tug (Book p90)

Inspiratory tracheal descent — COPD — Campbell's sign.
Oliver's sign: chin raised, cricoid held up on deglutition; positive — downward tug (aortic arch aneurysm); false positive — tumour attached to the arch; false negative — non pulsatile thrombosed aneurysm.
Trachea: Normal Position & Trail's Sign (Book p91)

Normally central or slightly deviated to right. Trail's sign — ipsilateral fascia relaxes, SCM contracts -> prominent clavicular head.
Implication of tracheal shift: upper mediastinal shift; indicates upper lobe fibrosis or collapse.
Tracheal Palpation: Oliver's & Campbell's Sign (Book p92)

Oliver's sign: stand behind, hold cricoid, slight upward thrust; positive — downward pull with each heart beat (aortic aneurysm); false positive — tumour attached to abdominal aorta; false negative — thrombosed aneurysm.
Campbell sign: downward pull of the depressed diaphragm in long standing hyperinflation. Figs 3D.14/15 — tracing the trachea, feeling for resistance.
Chest Wall Tenderness, Subcutaneous Emphysema & Fremitus (Book p93)

Chest wall tenderness — empyema, pleuritis, infiltration of chest wall; then subcutaneous emphysema.
Fremitus: vocal (increased in consolidation, decreased in effusion), tactile (crackles, rhonchi), friction (pleural rub).

Transmission of sound: solid > liquid > air; ability to vibrate: air > liquid > solid.
VR/VF measure transmission (from vocal cords); percussion measures vibration. More lung-to-skin distance = more attenuation, vibration unchanged.

Consolidation (fluid, increased, DULL) vs hyperinflation (air, reduced, RESONANT) vs pleural effusion (STONY DULL) vs pneumothorax (reduced, Resonant) vs collapse (dull, solid like area).
Only consolidation INCREASES VR/VF; all others reduce it.

Anterior — hand by the side; posterior — head bent forward, hands on opposite shoulder; lateral — hands over head.
Nine areas (supraclavicular -> infra-axillary 4th-7th ICS; suprascapular -> infrascapular); liver dullness normal upper level 5th ICS, pushed down = emphysema.
Liver Dullness, Traube's Space & Grocco's Triangle (Book p95)

Left sided pathologies — also percuss Traube's space. Grocco's triangle — dullness against the spine at the base of the opposite lung,
posterior mediastinal pleura bulging into the contralateral hemithorax — pathognomonic of pleural effusion; figure labels incl. Garland's triangle.
Grocco's Triangle Red Box & Kronig's Isthmus (Book p96)

Red box: triangular dullness on the healthy back; base along 12th rib; apex at the upper fluid margin on the diseased side; internally vertebral line; externally apex-to-lateral-base.
Kronig's isthmus 5-7 cm (scalenus medius, acromion, clavicle, trapezius); stand behind, lateral to medial, clavicle not touched; up = emphysema, down = TB/apical tumour; tidal percussion.

6th rib superiorly, left midaxillary line laterally, left costal margin inferiorly; content — fundus of stomach; right side — left lobe of liver; left side — spleen.
Obliterated — effusion, splenomegaly, left lobe liver, full stomach, pericardial effusion; shifted up — diaphragmatic paralysis, left lower lobe collapse, left lung fibrosis; Castell's sign area.

Clavicle — stretch the skin, medial 1/3 with middle finger, dull note = secondary TB (apex).
Hydropneumothorax: shifting dullness (immediate), straight line dullness, succussion splash (hug and shake), silver coin sounds.
S Shaped Curve of Ellis & the 20-Second Rule (Book p97)

Ellis curve — moderate pleural effusion; highest in axilla, lowest near spine/sternum; capillary suction between the two pleura layers;
radiologically — scattering of X rays by the fluid. No 20-second wait like ascites (same compartment).

Low pitched, rustling; I:E = 3:1; no pause between phases.
Diminished in — bronchial asthma (silent chest), tumour, small effusion, pleural thickening.
Causes of Diminished Vesicular Breathing — Box (Book p97)

Reduced conduction: obesity/thick chest wall, pleural effusion or thickening, pneumothorax.
Reduced airflow: generalised (COPD), localised (collapsed lung due to occluding lung cancer).
q: The book opens general examination with 'conscious, oriented, cooperative', then build and nutrition status, then vitals. Which of the following is NOT part of the vitals as listed there?
Pulse - rate, rhythm, volume, character, delay, vessel wall thickening and peripheral pulses
Levels of cervical lymph nodes Ia to VII

Vitals in the book's opening section are pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure and temperature. Lymphadenopathy is a separate general-examination step, and the Ia-VII levels are described much later, under lymphadenopathy. (Book p3)
Temperature must always be measured with a ____; the book warns you must not write 'afebrile' without one.
Patient's own report of feeling hot
Axillary tactile comparison with the examiner's hand
The instruction is categorical: always measure the temperature with a thermometer and never record 'afebrile' on the basis of feel alone - tactile assessment is unreliable. (Book p3)
Which of the following is NOT one of the general-examination headings listed in the book's opening sequence?

The listed sequence runs: conscious/oriented/cooperative, build and nutrition, vitals, pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, oedema. Fundus examination is part of systemic examination, not this general survey. (Book p3)

Match each feature of lymphadenopathy to the description the book wants reported — 1) Site and number 2) Consistency 3) Tenderness 4) Shape and matting … A) Which node groups are enlarged and how many B) Soft, firm, hard or stony hard C) Painful or painless D) Whether nodes move together as a matted unit

For every lymph node enlargement the book asks you to report site, number of nodes, consistency, tenderness, shape, and whether the nodes are matted; the matted quality is deliberately separated from simple shape because it carries malignancy and tuberculosis meaning. (Book p3)
According to the Harrison's 19e definition quoted in the book, fever is defined by which pair of readings?
An AM temperature of >98.9°F (>37.2°C) or a PM temperature of >99.9°F (>37.7°C)
An AM temperature of >99.9°F (>37.7°C) or a PM temperature of >98.9°F (>37.2°C)
An AM temperature of >37.8°C or a PM temperature of >38.3°C
Any temperature above 37.0°C at any time of the day

Fever is an AM temperature above 98.9°F (37.2°C) or a PM temperature above 99.9°F (37.7°C). The afternoon threshold is set higher precisely because normal temperature is higher later in the day. (Book p3)
The normal body temperature range given in the book is:
Normal body temperature is 36.5-37.5°C, that is 97.7-99.5°F. Any definition of fever has to be read against this range and against the normal daily variation. (Book p3)
Why is the body temperature higher in the evening?
Because the hypothalamic set point is normally reset upward at night
Because of increased basal metabolic rate and skeletal muscle activity
Because evaporative heat loss falls when the ambient temperature falls at night
Because antipyretic tone from the circadian cortisol peak is lost in the evening

The book attributes the evening rise to increased basal metabolic rate and skeletal muscle activity; no set-point reset is involved, which is why the fever definition uses separate AM and PM thresholds. (Book p3)

Match each temperature-measurement site to the book's comment — 1) Rectum 2) Lower oesophagus 3) Tympanic membrane 4) Oral cavity … A) Reading lower than rectal, attributed to mouth breathing B) Generally higher than oral readings C) Temperature closely reflects core temperature D) The third alternative site listed, with no further qualification

Rectal temperatures are generally higher than oral readings; lower oesophageal temperatures closely reflect core temperature; the tympanic membrane is simply listed as another site; and the low oral reading is attributed to mouth breathing. (Book p3)

A patient with severe pneumonia is breathing rapidly through the mouth. His oral temperature reads 37.6°C while the rectal temperature is 38.6°C. According to the book the discrepancy is best explained by:
Mouth breathing lowering the oral reading, an important factor in patients with respiratory infections and rapid breathing
Rectal thermometry reading spuriously high in sepsis
A normal circadian difference between core and oral sites
Delayed equilibration of the rectal thermometer in tachypnoea

The lower oral readings are generally attributed to mouth breathing, which matters most in exactly this group - patients with respiratory infection and rapid breathing. This is why core sites (rectum, lower oesophagus) are preferred when accuracy matters. (Book p3)
What single feature separates fever from hyperthermia in the book's definition?
Fever is an elevation of body temperature that exceeds the normal daily variation and occurs with a rise in the hypothalamic set point
Fever is any temperature above 37.5°C while hyperthermia is any temperature above 41.5°C
Fever is caused only by infection while hyperthermia is caused only by drugs
Fever responds to cooling blankets while hyperthermia responds to antipyretics

Fever is a rise in temperature produced by a rise in the hypothalamic set point. Hyperthermia is an uncontrolled rise in body temperature that exceeds the body's ability to lose heat in the setting of an intact set point - hence antipyretics do not work. (Book p3)
A patient with heat stroke has a core temperature of 41.2°C. Antipyretics produce no fall in temperature. The best explanation is:
The hypothalamic set point is intact, so there is no new set point to lower - this is hyperthermia, not fever
The dose of antipyretic was inadequate for a temperature above 41°C
Antipyretics act only on peripheral heat loss and fail in humid environments
Heat stroke always causes hypothalamic damage and therefore a permanently reset set point
In hyperthermia the set point is intact; the problem is heat production exceeding heat loss, so antipyretics have no target. Cooling, not antipyresis, is the treatment. (Book p3)

Match each drug or setting to the hyperthermia syndrome the book attaches it to — 1) Halothane 2) Haloperidol and fluphenazine 3) Interactions of two or more serotonergic drugs 4) Environmental heat load … A) Neuroleptic malignant syndrome B) Malignant hyperthermia C) Serotonin syndrome D) Heat stroke

Anaesthetics such as halothane produce malignant hyperthermia by rapid uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in sensitive individuals; haloperidol and fluphenazine cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome; serotonin syndrome follows increased CNS serotonergic activity, typically with two or more serotonergic drugs; heat stroke is the environmental cause. (Book p3)
Which of the following is NOT listed under causes of hyperthermia?

The hyperthermia causes listed are heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome. Hypothyroidism belongs to the opposite end of the spectrum - it is one of the endocrine causes of hypothermia. (Book p3)
Which statement about fever and hyperthermia is correct?
True: Fever is an elevation of body temperature that exceeds the normal daily variation and occurs in conjunction with a rise in the hypothalamic set point
True: Antipyretics will not reduce the temperature in hyperthermia because the set point is intact
False: In hyperthermia the hypothalamic set point is raised, so antipyretics work well
False: Fever and hyperthermia are interchangeable terms for any temperature above 38°C

Fever = raised set point, so antipyretics work. Hyperthermia = intact set point, loss of heat exceeds the body's dissipating capacity, so antipyretics fail. The two are mechanistically different and are never interchangeable. (Book p3)
Fever above which temperature is called hyperpyrexia, and which two causes are named?
Above 41.5°C (>106.7°F); CNS haemorrhage and severe infection
Above 40.0°C (104°F); heat stroke and malignant hyperthermia
Above 41.5°C (>106.7°F); heat stroke and neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Above 39.5°C (103°F); severe infection and drug fever

Hyperpyrexia is fever above 41.5°C (>106.7°F) and the two causes the book names are CNS haemorrhage and severe infection. Note that heat stroke and NMS are causes of hyperthermia, a different category. (Book p4)
Which statement about hypothalamic fever is correct?
True: It is an elevated temperature caused by hypothalamic dysfunction
True: Hypothalamic dysfunction usually causes subnormal, not supranormal, temperature
False: Hypothalamic lesions characteristically produce sustained high fever above 41°C
False: Hypothalamic fever is simply another name for hyperpyrexia

Hypothalamic dysfunction as a cause of raised temperature is a real but uncommon event - the book stresses the paradox that hypothalamic disease usually causes subnormal rather than supranormal temperature. Hyperpyrexia is a different, higher-threshold concept. (Book p4)

Match each step in the mechanism of fever — 1) Pyrogenic cytokines 2) Cells they act on 3) Mediator produced 4) Final effect … A) IL-1, IL-6 and TNFα B) Hypothalamic endothelial cells C) PGE2 D) Rise in the hypothalamic set point

Infection or immune reactions release pyrogenic cytokines IL-1, IL-6 and TNFα; these induce hypothalamic endothelial cells to produce PGE2, which raises the hypothalamic set point and produces fever. This is the chain that antipyretics (COX inhibitors) interrupt. (Book p4)
The pyrogenic cytokines released by infection or immune reactions, which induce hypothalamic endothelial cells to make PGE2, are IL-1, IL-6 and ____.
The trio is IL-1, IL-6 and TNFα. IL-4, IL-10 and IFN-γ are not listed as pyrogenic cytokines in this cascade. (Book p4)
Which of the following is NOT part of the book's pyrogenic cytokine cascade that raises the set point?
The cascade is IL-1, IL-6 and TNFα acting on hypothalamic endothelial cells to produce PGE2. IL-4 is a Th2 cytokine with no role in this chain. (Book p4)
Acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) is defined in the book as:
Fever of <14 days without an organ-system-specific aetiology
Fever of >3 weeks that remains undiagnosed after one week of inpatient evaluation
Fever with a rash and no localising signs lasting more than 5 days
Fever of <7 days with a proven bacterial isolate from blood culture
AUFI is a clinical term for fever of less than 14 days without an organ-system-specific aetiology. The 3-week definition belongs to PUO, and the two must not be mixed up. (Book p4)
Match each cause of AUFI to the position in which the book asks you to say it — 1) First 2) Second 3) Third 4) Fourth 5) Fifth … A) Enteric fever B) Dengue C) Leptospirosis D) Scrub typhus E) Malaria
The order to say in our setting is Dengue, Scrub typhus, Leptospirosis, Malaria, Enteric fever. The order itself is examinable because it encodes local epidemiology. (Book p4)
In a viva on AUFI the examiner asks for the important causes 'in our setting'. Which statement reflects the book's instruction?
Never say Leishmaniasis/Kala-azar unless probed - it is an important cause of AUFI but not in our setting
Kala-azar should be named first because it is the commonest cause of AUFI
Kala-azar should never be mentioned at all in any answer on fever
Kala-azar is a cause of PUO only and never of AUFI

The book is explicit: say the local order (Dengue, Scrub typhus, Leptospirosis, Malaria, Enteric fever) and do not volunteer Kala-azar unless the examiner probes; it is an important cause of AUFI but not in our setting. (Book p4)
The Petersdorf and Beeson definition of PUO requires fever above 101 on at least two occasions, illness duration of more than ____, and uncertain diagnosis despite ____ of inpatient evaluation.
Petersdorf and Beeson: illness of more than 3 weeks duration, fever above 101 on at least two occasions, and diagnosis still uncertain despite 1 week of inpatient evaluation. (Book p4)
Which statement about the criteria for PUO is correct?
True: Fever above 101 on at least two occasions and illness duration of more than 3 weeks
True: No known immunocompromised state, and diagnosis uncertain after thorough history, examination and obligatory investigations
False: A known immunocompromised state is part of the classical definition of PUO
False: The obligatory investigation list for PUO includes bone marrow examination in every patient

Harrison's adds to the classical definition the absence of a known immunocompromised state and the requirement that diagnosis remains uncertain after thorough history, physical examination and a defined set of obligatory investigations - bone marrow is not among them. (Book p4)
Which investigation is NOT part of the obligatory investigation list for PUO given in the book?
USG abdomen and tuberculin skin test
Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy

The obligatory list is ESR, CRP, haemogram with PS, electrolytes, LFT, RFT, ANA, rheumatoid factor, urine analysis and culture, blood culture, CXR, USG abdomen and tuberculin skin test. Bone marrow is a second-line, cause-directed test. (Book p4)
Besides the classical form, the book lists nosocomial PUO, neutropenic PUO and ____-associated PUO.
The three variants named are nosocomial PUO, neutropenic PUO and HIV-associated PUO. Each has its own differential and its own obligatory work-up. (Book p4)
Which single statement best captures how PUO is usually caused?
PUO is usually caused by atypical presentations of common illnesses, not typical presentations of rare illnesses
PUO is usually caused by typical presentations of rare illnesses, not atypical presentations of common illnesses
PUO is usually caused by occult malignancy and should be investigated as such from the outset
PUO is usually a manifestation of an undiagnosed connective tissue disease

This inversion of the two possibilities is the single most useful line in the section: common diseases presenting atypically far outnumber rare diseases presenting typically, so the work-up stays anchored on common illness. (Book p4)

Match each group of PUO causes to an example from the book's list — 1) Infectious 2) Neoplastic 3) Connective tissue disorders 4) Drugs … A) Atrial myxoma B) Intra-abdominal abscess, including perinephric, perirenal, liver and subphrenic C) SLE, RA and vasculitides D) Drug fever

Infectious causes include HIV, TB, malaria, enteric fever, infective endocarditis, UTI, intra-abdominal abscess (perinephric, perirenal, liver, subphrenic) and pelvic inflammatory disease; neoplastic causes include leukaemia, lymphoma, GI malignancies, secondaries and atrial myxoma; connective tissue disorders include SLE, RA and vasculitides; drug fever is its own group. (Book p4)
A patient with prolonged fever, a raised ESR and an early diastolic 'tumour plop' has a left atrial mass on echocardiography. Within the book's PUO framework this is an example of:
A neoplastic cause of PUO - atrial myxoma is listed with leukaemia, lymphoma and secondaries
An infectious cause of PUO - the mass is a vegetation
A connective tissue cause of PUO - the mass is a sterile thrombus of vasculitis
A drug fever, since only drugs produce fever with a normal peripheral smear

Atrial myxoma is deliberately placed in the neoplastic list of PUO causes alongside leukaemia, lymphoma, GI malignancies and secondaries - a reminder that 'tumour' does not mean only solid organ malignancy or metastasis. (Book p4)
Which of the following abscess sites is NOT named in the book's list of intra-abdominal abscesses causing PUO?

The named sites are perinephric, perirenal, liver and subphrenic, together with pelvic inflammatory disease as a separate infectious cause. Psoas abscess, though a real cause of occult fever, is not on this list and is not what the examiner is quoting. (Book p4)
Which of the following is NOT one of the auto-inflammatory diseases in which fever is characteristic, as listed in the book?
Adult and juvenile onset Still's disease

The list is adult and juvenile onset Still's disease, familial Mediterranean fever, Behçet's syndrome, cryopyrin associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), PAPA syndrome and hyper-IgD syndrome. SLE appears in the PUO list as a connective tissue disorder, not as an auto-inflammatory periodic fever. (Book p4)
Familial Mediterranean fever has its pathogenesis referenced to ____ in the book, and its treatment is colchicine.
The pathogenesis of FMF is referenced to Robbins, and the treatment is colchicine - one of the only three diseases in which the book says colchicine is used. (Book p4)
The book gives three diseases in which colchicine can be used. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

The three uses are gout, pericarditis and familial Mediterranean fever. Behçet's syndrome is an auto-inflammatory disease with characteristic fever, but colchicine is not one of the three listed indications. (Book p4)
PAPA syndrome stands for Pyogenic arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum and ____.
PAPA = Pyogenic arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum, Acne. It is one of the auto-inflammatory diseases listed in which fever is characteristic. (Book p4)
CAPS, listed under auto-inflammatory diseases with fever, stands for:
CAPS = cryopyrin associated periodic syndromes, grouped with Still's disease, FMF, Behçet's, PAPA and hyper-IgD syndrome as auto-inflammatory causes of fever. (Book p4)
Which statement about hyper-IgD syndrome in the book is correct?
It is listed among auto-inflammatory diseases in which fever is characteristic
It is listed as a neoplastic cause of PUO
It is listed as a variant of PUO seen in HIV infection
It is listed as a drug fever caused by immunoglobulin therapy
Hyper-IgD syndrome appears in the auto-inflammatory fever list with Still's disease, FMF, Behçet's, CAPS and PAPA - all characterised by recurrent fever without infection or malignancy. (Book p4)
For every 1°F rise in body temperature, the pulse rate should rise by about ____.

The bedside rule is 10 beats per minute per 1°F (about 18 per 1°C) rise of temperature. A pulse that fails to rise this much is relative bradycardia; one that overshoots is relative tachycardia. (Book p5)

Match each cause of relative bradycardia to its identification — 1) Enteric fever, first week 2) Yellow fever 3) Weil's disease 4) Brucellosis … A) The pulse-temperature dissociation here is called Faget's sign B) Mechanism is heart block C) A variety of leptospirosis D) A zoonosis that classically gives relative bradycardia

Relative bradycardia in enteric fever (first week) is produced by heart block; in yellow fever the dissociation is called Faget's sign; Weil's disease is a variety of leptospirosis; and brucellosis is a classic cause. (Book p5)
A traveller returns with jaundice, bleeding, and a temperature of 39.5°C with a pulse of 78/min. The eponym for this pulse-temperature dissociation, when seen in this illness, is:

In yellow fever relative bradycardia is called Faget's sign. Kussmaul's sign is a paradoxical rise of JVP on inspiration; Osler's and de Musset's signs concern endocarditis and aortic regurgitation respectively. (Book p5)
The relative bradycardia of enteric fever in the first week is attributed to:
Increased vagal tone from mesenteric lymphadenopathy
The book gives the mechanism as heart block, and flags it as a point to read in more detail. This is distinct from the relative tachycardia seen with myocarditis (diphtheritic, rheumatic). (Book p5)
Which of the following causes relative bradycardia and NOT relative tachycardia?

Relative tachycardia belongs to acute rheumatic carditis, tuberculosis, polyarteritis nodosa and diphtheritic myocarditis; brucellosis is a cause of relative bradycardia, along with enteric fever, viral fevers and Weil's disease. (Book p5)
Which of the following is listed as a cause of relative tachycardia?
Enteric fever in the first week
Diphtheritic myocarditis joins acute rheumatic carditis, tuberculosis and polyarteritis nodosa in the relative tachycardia list. The other three options all cause relative bradycardia. (Book p5)
Intermittent fever is defined in the book as:
Fever present for several hours, which always touches the baseline sometime during the day
Fever that never touches the baseline but fluctuates by more than 2°C
Fever that does not fluctuate by more than 1°C during the day
Fever that recurs in cycles of one to two weeks

Intermittent fever is present for several hours and always touches the baseline at some point in the day; quotidian, tertian and quartan are its subdivisions. Never touching the baseline defines remittent and continued fevers instead. (Book p5)

Match each intermittent pattern to its timing — 1) Quotidian 2) Double quotidian 3) Tertian 4) Quartan … A) Paroxysm on alternate days B) Two-day interval between paroxysms C) Paroxysm of fever occurs daily D) Two spikes of fever in a single day
Quotidian = daily paroxysm; double quotidian = two spikes in a day; tertian = alternate-day paroxysm; quartan = a two-day interval between paroxysms. (Book p5)
Which group of conditions is listed as producing quotidian fever?

Quotidian (daily) paroxysms are seen in tuberculosis, UTI and septicaemia. Kala-azar and gonococcal perihepatitis give the camel-hump (double quotidian) pattern, and Borrelia gives relapsing fever. (Book p5)
Double quotidian fever - two spikes of fever in one day - is most commonly of which aetiology, and was commonly seen in which condition?
Double quotidian fever is commonly gonococcal in aetiology and used to be commonly seen in endocarditis - a historical association that still gets asked. (Book p5)

Match each fever to its organism or mechanism — 1) Benign tertian malaria 2) Malignant tertian malaria 3) Quartan fever 4) Charcot's intermittent fever … A) P. malariae B) P. vivax or P. ovale C) P. falciparum, also called aestivo-autumnal or Roman fever D) Chills with RUQ pain and jaundice from a stone obstructing the CBD

Benign tertian malaria is P. vivax/ovale; malignant tertian (falciparum, aestivo-autumnal, Roman) fever is P. falciparum; quartan fever with a two-day interval is P. malariae; and Charcot's intermittent fever is the cholangitic pattern of chills, RUQ pain and jaundice from a CBD stone. (Book p5)
A daily fluctuation of more than 2°C (3°F), and it never touches the baseline
A daily fluctuation of less than 1°C, and it never touches the baseline
Fever that touches the baseline once every day
Fever with two spikes in a single day
Remittent fever swings by more than 2°C (3°F) a day and never touches the baseline. For contrast, remember that the normal fluctuation of temperature is 0.9°C. (Book p5)
For contrast with the definition of remittent fever, the book notes that normal daily fluctuation of temperature is:
Normal fluctuation is 0.9°C, so a swing of more than 2°C is a large excursion indeed, and the definition of continued fever (no more than 1°C) sits far below it. (Book p5)

Match each fever pattern to its listed causes — 1) Remittent 2) Continued … A) Lobar pneumonia, second week of enteric fever, gram negative sepsis, acute rheumatic fever, meningococcaemia B) Amoebic liver abscess, acute bronchopneumonia, third week of enteric fever

Remittent fever is seen in amoebic liver abscess, acute bronchopneumonia and the third week of enteric fever; continued fever with minimal fluctuation is seen in lobar pneumonia (classically), the second week of enteric fever, gram negative sepsis, acute rheumatic fever and meningococcaemia. (Book p5)
Amoebic liver abscess, acute bronchopneumonia and the third week of enteric fever share which fever pattern?

All three are listed under remittent fever - a daily fluctuation of more than 2°C that never touches the baseline. Continued fever belongs to lobar pneumonia, gram negative sepsis, acute rheumatic fever and meningococcaemia. (Book p5)
The Pel-Ebstein (Ebstein-Cardarelli) pattern, in which fever cyclically increases and decreases in periods of one to two weeks, is called by that name:
Only when it is associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma - other cyclical fevers are simply called cyclical fevers
Whenever it is associated with any lymphoma, Hodgkin's or non-Hodgkin's
Only when it is associated with kala-azar
Whenever the fever period lasts longer than two weeks
The eponym is used only for the cyclical fever of Hodgkin's lymphoma; identical-looking cyclical fevers in other diseases are called cyclical fevers and nothing more. (Book p5)

Match each named pattern to its disease — 1) Camel hump pattern 2) Step-ladder pattern 3) Undulant fever 4) Relapsing fever … A) Brucellosis, with fever that rapidly rises and falls B) Kala-azar and gonococcal perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome) C) Enteric fever D) A cyclical fever caused by Borrelia infection
Camel hump = double quotidian pattern of kala-azar and gonococcal perihepatitis; step-ladder = enteric fever; undulant = brucellosis; relapsing = Borrelia. (Book p5)
The step-ladder pattern, in which fever stays at a baseline and then acutely rises to a new baseline, is characteristic of ____.
Step-ladder fever is the enteric fever pattern; the baseline holds, then climbs acutely to a new level. Brucellosis gives undulant fever, Borrelia relapsing fever, kala-azar the camel hump. (Book p5)
Which statement about fever patterns is correct?
True: Remittent fever never touches the baseline and fluctuates by more than 2°C
True: Continued fever does not fluctuate by more than 1°C and never touches the baseline
False: Intermittent fever never touches the baseline at any time during the day
False: The normal daily fluctuation of temperature is 2°C
Touching or not touching the baseline is the discriminator: intermittent fever always touches it, remittent and continued never do. Normal daily fluctuation is 0.9°C, not 2°C. (Book p5)
A patient from an endemic area has months of fever, massive splenomegaly and two temperature spikes each day. The camel hump (double quotidian) pattern here points to:

Camel hump pattern (double quotidian fever) is listed for kala-azar and gonococcal perihepatitis. Step-ladder fever belongs to enteric fever, undulant fever to brucellosis, and Pel-Ebstein fever to Hodgkin's lymphoma. (Book p5)
A patient has daily fever with wide swings (39.5°C to 35.8°C) and imaging shows a liver abscess. The pattern is hectic fever, and the book associates hectic fever with:
Any pent-up pus in the body, such as liver abscess, lung abscess, empyema and subphrenic abscess
The second week of enteric fever

Hectic fever is characterised by wide swings and is associated with any pent-up pus - liver abscess, lung abscess, empyema and subphrenic abscess. This is different from Pel-Ebstein fever of Hodgkin's lymphoma. (Book p6)
Which of the following is a primary cause of hypothermia as classified in the book?

Primary hypothermia is typically due to accidental exposure. Secondary hypothermia is failure of thermoregulation, and includes cerebrovascular accident, overwhelming sepsis, low cardiac output after acute MI, endocrine disease and intoxication. (Book p6)
Which of the following is NOT a secondary cause of hypothermia?

Immersion is a primary (accidental exposure) mechanism. The secondary list is failure of thermoregulation from CVA, overwhelming sepsis, low cardiac output following acute MI, endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, panhypopituitarism, adrenal insufficiency) and intoxication with drugs or alcohol. (Book p6)
An elderly woman is found drowsy with a temperature of 34.8°C, bradycardia and delayed reflexes; TSH is markedly raised. According to the book's classification her hypothermia is:
Secondary, from endocrine failure of thermoregulation
Not true hypothermia because her set point is intact
A drug-induced hypothermia until proven otherwise

Hypothyroidism is one of the endocrine causes of secondary hypothermia - thermoregulation fails rather than the environment overcoming it. The book's secondary list also includes panhypopituitarism, adrenal insufficiency, CVA, sepsis, low cardiac output and intoxication. (Book p6)
Which set of findings does the book list as the signs and symptoms of hypothermia?
Altered sensorium (confusion to coma), tachypnoea, tachycardia, lethargy, shivering and pallor
Altered sensorium, bradypnoea, bradycardia and absence of shivering

The book lists altered sensorium (confusion to coma), tachypnoea, tachycardia, lethargy, shivering and pallor. Note that clinically severe hypothermia can cause bradycardia, but that is not the list this book gives - answer what the source says. (Book p6)
Which statement about pallor and anaemia is correct according to the book?
Anaemia and pallor are not interchangeable terms - anaemia is only one of the causes of pallor
Pallor and anaemia are interchangeable terms because pallor always indicates anaemia
Anaemia is a clinical diagnosis and pallor is its laboratory confirmation
The book is emphatic: pallor is a physical sign with many causes, and anaemia is just one of them. This is why the examiner expects you to name causes of pallor without anaemia. (Book p6)

Match the instruction for examining pallor — 1) Where to examine 2) Which conjunctiva 3) Which part of the tongue 4) Which surfaces … A) Lower palpebral conjunctiva B) In sunlight C) Tip and dorsum D) Palms and soles
Examine in sunlight and look at the lower palpebral conjunctiva, the tip and dorsum of the tongue, the mucous membrane of the palate, the nail beds, and the palms and soles. (Book p6)
Which of the following is NOT one of the sites the book lists for examining pallor?
Tip and dorsum of the tongue

The bulbar conjunctiva is deliberately avoided - for icterus the book says we do not check through the bulbar conjunctiva because mud or dust can get easily deposited there. It is not a pallor site either. (Book p6)
Which of the following is listed as a cause of pallor without anaemia (Kundu)?
Shock and low cardiac output states

Kundu's list of pallor without anaemia is shock, low cardiac output states, hypothyroidism and hypopituitarism. The other options are anaemias - they produce pallor precisely because haemoglobin is reduced. (Book p6)

Match each arm of the aetiopathological classification of anaemia — 1) Marrow production defect 2) Ineffective erythropoiesis - defective nuclear maturation 3) Ineffective erythropoiesis - cytoplasmic maturation 4) Blood loss/haemolysis … A) B12/folate deficiency and myelodysplasia B) Bone marrow disorders and decreased stimulation from inflammation or renal disease C) Defects in haeme or globin synthesis D) Loss of red cells or their destruction

Marrow production defects include bone marrow disorders and decreased stimulation (inflammation, renal disease); ineffective erythropoiesis splits into defective nuclear maturation (B12/folate, myelodysplasia) and cytoplasmic maturation (haeme/globin synthesis); the last arm is blood loss and haemolysis. (Book p6)
Icterus is best looked for in:
The sclera through the upper palpebral conjunctiva
The sclera through the bulbar conjunctiva
The site is the sclera, viewed through the upper palpebral conjunctiva. The bulbar conjunctiva is avoided because mud or dust deposits there and can be mistaken for icterus. (Book p6)
The minimum serum bilirubin at which clinical icterus appears is:
Icterus needs a bilirubin of at least 2.5 mg/dL to become clinically visible. This is why jaundice is a relatively late sign of hyperbilirubinaemia. (Book p6)
Why is icterus checked in the sclera?
The sclera is rich in elastic tissue, where bilirubin preferentially gets deposited
The sclera has the highest blood flow per gram of tissue in the body
The sclera lacks lymphatics, so bilirubin cannot be cleared
The sclera has a thin epithelium that makes pigment visible earlier
Bilirubin preferentially deposits in elastic tissue, and the sclera is rich in it - which is also why the sclera is the classic first place that jaundice is noticed. (Book p6)

Match each tint of icterus to its severity and aetiology — 1) Lemon yellow 2) Orange yellow 3) Greenish yellow … A) Severe jaundice, obstructive aetiology B) Mild jaundice, haemolytic aetiology C) Moderate jaundice, hepatocellular aetiology
Lemon yellow = mild, haemolytic; orange yellow = moderate, hepatocellular; greenish yellow = severe, obstructive. The tint is a bedside clue to the underlying mechanism. (Book p6)
Why does the book ask the patient to look down while checking for icterus?
The perilimbal sclera is thinner than the posterior sclera, and looking down lets both perilimbal and posterior sclerae be compared
Looking down exposes the lower palpebral conjunctiva, the richest site of bilirubin deposition
Looking down relaxes the orbicularis oculi and prevents artefactual redness
Looking down increases conjunctival blood flow and makes mild icterus obvious

Since the perilimbal sclera is thinner than the posterior part, mild icterus is easier to appreciate posteriorly; asking the patient to look down lines up both the perilimbal and posterior sclerae so they can be compared. (Book p6)
A young man has mild jaundice, splenomegaly and anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count; his conjunctivae show a lemon-yellow tint. The book's tint for haemolytic jaundice is:
Lemon yellow is mild jaundice of haemolytic aetiology; orange yellow is moderate and hepatocellular; greenish yellow is severe and obstructive. (Book p6)
Cyanosis is defined (Harrison's 19e) as bluish discolouration of skin and mucous membranes due to accumulation in small blood vessels of:
Reduced haemoglobin or haemoglobin derivatives such as methaemoglobin and sulphhaemoglobin
Bilirubin and bile salts within the dermis
Reduced albumin-bound free fatty acids in the dermal plexus

The pigment responsible is reduced haemoglobin or a haemoglobin derivative (metHb/sulfHb) accumulating in the small vessels of the skin and mucous membranes - never oxygenated haemoglobin, which is bright red. (Book p7)
Cyanosis becomes apparent when the quantity of reduced haemoglobin exceeds:

Cyanosis appears when reduced haemoglobin exceeds 4 g/dL, which corresponds to an SpO2 of about 85% at least. Below that, the tissue appears normally coloured regardless of how the patient feels. (Book p7)
Cyanosis is indicative of an SpO2 of at least:
Cyanosis indicates an SpO2 below about 85%. A patient breathing room air with an SpO2 of 90% may look perfectly pink - a clinical trap. (Book p7)
A woman with a haemoglobin of 4 g/dL is profoundly breathless but has no cyanosis. The best explanation according to the book is:
It is the absolute, not the relative, quantity of reduced Hb that causes cyanosis, and her total Hb is too low to reach 4 g/dL of reduced Hb
Cyanosis is masked by anaemia-related pallor because conjunctival vessels are constricted
Cyanosis requires an abnormal haemoglobin derivative, which she lacks
Cyanosis cannot occur at any saturation above 70%, which she has not yet reached

Cyanosis needs an absolute quantity of more than 4 g/dL of reduced haemoglobin. In severe anaemia even a very low SpO2 may generate too little reduced Hb to produce the blue colour - so absence of cyanosis never excludes severe hypoxaemia. (Book p7)

Match each cyanosis concept to its description — 1) Central cyanosis 2) Peripheral cyanosis 3) Spared site in peripheral cyanosis 4) Intermittent cyanosis … A) Ebstein's anomaly B) Arterial oxygen saturation reduced or an abnormal Hb derivative present, with both mucous membranes and skin affected C) Slowing of blood flow with increased oxygen extraction from saturated arterial blood D) Mucous membranes of the oral cavity and underside of the tongue

Central cyanosis has a low arterial saturation or an abnormal derivative and involves both mucous membranes and skin; peripheral cyanosis reflects slow flow and increased extraction; in peripheral cyanosis the oral mucosa and underside of the tongue are often spared; intermittent cyanosis belongs to Ebstein's anomaly. (Book p7)
Which of the following is NOT a listed cause of central cyanosis?
Congenital heart disease with an anatomical shunt

Cold exposure produces peripheral cyanosis by vasoconstriction and diminished peripheral flow. Central cyanosis is listed as high altitude, anatomical shunts (congenital heart disease, pulmonary AV fistulas), haemoglobin anomalies and V/Q mismatch (extensive pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, COPD). (Book p7)
Which statement about hyperviscosity in cyanotic states is correct?
True: In iron-replete cyanosis, compensated erythrocytosis establishes equilibrium with the haematocrit, so hyperviscosity is rare
True: In iron-deplete cyanosis, erythrocytosis fails to establish equilibrium with the haematocrit, so hyperviscosity occurs
False: Hyperviscosity is commonest in iron-replete cyanosis because the haematocrit is highest
False: Iron deficiency protects cyanotic patients from hyperviscosity

Iron-replete patients develop proportionate erythrocytosis that reaches equilibrium with the haematocrit and rarely becomes hyperviscous. Iron-deplete patients fail to reach that equilibrium, so viscosity rises disproportionately - an argument for treating iron deficiency in cyanotic heart disease. (Book p7)

Match each distribution of cyanosis to its lesion — 1) Cyanosis of the lower limb only 2) Cyanosis of the upper limb only 3) Cyanosis that is intermittent … A) PDA with pulmonary hypertension and right-to-left shunt together with TGV B) Ebstein's anomaly C) PDA with pulmonary hypertension and right-to-left shunt

Differential cyanosis (lower limb cyanosed, upper limb spared) means a PDA with Eisenmenger physiology and right-to-left shunt; if the upper limb is cyanosed instead, TGV is added (reverse differential pattern); intermittent cyanosis is a feature of Ebstein's anomaly. (Book p7)
A child with a large untreated ventricular septal defect has cyanosis and clubbing confined to both legs, with pink upper limbs. The most likely lesion is:
PDA with pulmonary hypertension and right-to-left shunt
PDA with transposition of the great arteries
Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary stenosis

Lower-limb-only cyanosis is the differential cyanosis of a ductus arteriosus with pulmonary hypertension and reversal of shunt, so desaturated blood enters the descending aorta beyond the origin of the upper-limb vessels. Ebstein's anomaly gives intermittent cyanosis. (Book p7)
Clubbing is defined in the book as:
Selective bulbous enlargement of the distal portion of the digit due to deposition of subungual soft tissue
Diffuse enlargement of the proximal phalanx due to periosteal new bone formation
Bulbous enlargement of the digit with loss of the Lovibond angle caused by bony resorption
Thickening of the nail plate itself with preservation of the nail-bed angle

The key words are selective, distal and subungual soft tissue deposition. Bony resorption with a preserved Lovibond angle describes pseudoclubbing, and periosteal new bone formation describes hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. (Book p7)
The normal angle between the nail and the nail bed
The angle between the proximal and distal nail folds
The angle subtended by the distal phalanx and the middle phalanx
The angle between the nail plate and the terminal phalangeal joint line

The Lovibond angle is the normal angle between nail and nail-bed, measured at the profile of the finger. It increases in clubbing (grade 2) and is preserved in pseudoclubbing - which is exactly why the distinction matters. (Book p7)
The minimum duration required for clubbing to develop is:

Clubbing develops over a minimum of 2-3 weeks - a useful negative point: a finger that becomes bulbous over 24-48 hours is not clubbing, and the book's figure of 2-3 weeks also explains reversible clubbing after empyema or lung abscess resolves. (Book p7)
The first finger in which clubbing appears is:
Clubbing first appears in the index finger. This is stated twice - once in the general clubbing section and once at the end of the section on patterns of clubbing. (Book p7)

Match each grade of clubbing to its clinical description — 1) Grade 1 2) Grade 2 3) Grade 3 4) Grade 4 … A) Drumstick or parrot beak appearance B) Nail bed fluctuations C) Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy D) Increase in the Lovibond angle

Grade 1 is nail bed fluctuation (bogginess), grade 2 an increase in the Lovibond angle, grade 3 the drumstick/parrot-beak fingertip, and grade 4 hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. The grade is quoted in the viva with the sign, not the disease. (Book p8)
A patient with bronchogenic carcinoma has bulbous fingertips with a swollen, tender wrist and periosteal reaction on radiography of the forearm. The grade of clubbing is:
Grade 4, because hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is present
Grade 3, because the fingertip is drumstick shaped
Grade 2, because the Lovibond angle is lost

Grade 4 clubbing is defined by the presence of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, which is what the periosteal reaction and joint symptoms represent. Grades 1 to 3 describe only the finger changes. (Book p8)

Match each group of causes to the examples given — 1) Suppurative lung disease 2) Thoracic malignancy 3) Cardiovascular 4) Gastrointestinal … A) Cirrhosis (especially primary biliary cirrhosis) and inflammatory bowel disease B) Bronchiectasis, lung abscess and empyema C) Bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchial adenoma and mesothelioma D) Cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis and left atrial myxoma

Suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema), thoracic malignancy (bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchial adenoma, mesothelioma), cardiovascular causes (cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis, left atrial myxoma) and GI causes (cirrhosis - especially primary biliary cirrhosis - and inflammatory bowel disease) make up the list from Dr Vivekanandan. (Book p8)
Which statement about clubbing and chronic lung disease is correct?
True: Clubbing is rare in COPD and in tuberculosis
True: Left atrial myxoma is listed among the cardiovascular causes of clubbing
False: Bronchiectasis, lung abscess and empyema are diseases in which clubbing is rare

The book deliberately records that clubbing is rare in COPD and TB while it is common in suppurative lung disease, ILD and thoracic malignancy. Cardiac causes include cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis and left atrial myxoma. (Book p8)
Which of the following is LEAST likely to cause clubbing?

Clubbing is rare in COPD (and in TB); it is a feature of suppurative lung disease, malignancy and interstitial lung disease. This is one of the classic negative discriminations in a clubbing viva. (Book p8)
Thyroid acropachy, listed among other causes of clubbing, is:
A rare manifestation of Graves' disease with swelling of fingers and toes, clubbing and periosteal reaction of the extremity bones
A rare manifestation of hypothyroidism with thickening of the skin of the fingers
A paraneoplastic syndrome of thyroid carcinoma with clubbing and myxoedema
An autoimmune overlap syndrome with clubbing and pretibial myxoedema only

Thyroid acropachy occurs in Graves' disease - swelling of fingers and toes, clubbing and periosteal reaction of extremity bones. It is the reason thyroid disease appears in the causes of clubbing at all. (Book p8)
POEMS syndrome, listed under other causes of clubbing, stands for Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M protein and ____.

POEMS = Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M protein, Skin changes. It is worth remembering as a cause of clubbing that begins with a haematological plasma cell disorder, like the M protein itself. (Book p8)
A patient with treated Graves' disease develops clubbing, swelling of the fingers and toes and periosteal reaction of the long bones. The correct label is:

Thyroid acropachy is a rare manifestation of Graves' disease presenting with swelling of fingers and toes, clubbing and periosteal reaction of extremity bones. HOA would imply an intrathoracic neoplasm, not thyroid disease. (Book p8)
Bulbous enlargement of fingers or toes with preservation of the Lovibond angle
Bulbous enlargement of fingers or toes with loss of the Lovibond angle but no soft tissue proliferation
Clubbing associated with an underlying neoplasm
Clubbing that reverses completely after treatment of the primary disease

In pseudoclubbing the Lovibond angle is preserved. Per Kundu the mechanism is subperiosteal bone resorption in the phalanges without soft tissue proliferation - so the finger looks bulbous but the nail profile is unchanged. (Book p8)
Match each cause of pseudoclubbing — 1) Infective 2) Connective tissue 3) Endocrine 4) Occupational … A) Acromegaly B) Leprosy C) Vinyl chloride workers with acro-osteolysis D) Scleroderma
Pseudoclubbing is seen in leprosy, scleroderma, hyperparathyroidism, acromegaly and vinyl chloride workers with acro-osteolysis. All share bone resorption with a preserved Lovibond angle. (Book p8)
A worker in a vinyl chloride plant has bulbous finger tips; the nail-bed angle is normal and radiographs show acro-osteolysis. This is:

Preservation of the Lovibond angle with bone resorption is the signature of pseudoclubbing; vinyl chloride exposure with acro-osteolysis is one of its listed causes, along with leprosy, scleroderma, hyperparathyroidism and acromegaly. (Book p8)
The most accepted theory of clubbing in the book is:
Large megakaryocytes normally broken down in the pulmonary circulation reach the peripheral arterioles of the nail bed in lung disease and release PDGF, causing connective tissue proliferation
Vagal stimulation causes vasodilation and connective tissue growth in the nail bed
Growth hormone, PTH and oestrogen directly stimulate subungual fibroblasts
Persistent hypoxia opens deep arteriovenous fistulae which enlarge the fingertip

The megakaryocyte/PDGF theory is the most accepted: megakaryocytes are normally fragmented in the pulmonary circulation; in lung disease they reach the nail-bed arterioles intact and release platelet-derived growth factor, driving connective tissue proliferation. (Book p8)
In the most accepted theory of clubbing, the megakaryocytes reaching the nail-bed arterioles release ____, which causes proliferation of connective tissue.

The mediator is platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF). It explains why clubbing appears in conditions with right-to-left shunting and in suppurative lung disease, where megakaryocytes bypass the lung filter. (Book p8)

Match each theory of clubbing to its proposed mechanism — 1) Neurogenic 2) Humoral 3) Hypoxic 4) Ferritin … A) Vagal stimulation causes vasodilation B) GH, PTH and oestrogen cause vasodilation C) Persistent hypoxia opens deep AV fistulae D) Decreased systemic ferritin causes dilation of AV anastomoses

Neurogenic (vagal stimulation causing vasodilation), humoral (GH, PTH, oestrogen), hypoxic (persistent hypoxia opening deep AV fistulae) and ferritin (decreased systemic ferritin dilating AV anastomoses) theories are all listed in addition to the most-accepted megakaryocyte/PDGF mechanism. (Book p8)
Painful clubbing is listed in association with:
Bronchogenic carcinoma, lung abscess and infective endocarditis
Cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease
Cyanotic heart disease and interstitial lung disease

Painful clubbing belongs to bronchogenic carcinoma, lung abscess and infective endocarditis - three conditions in which the clubbing itself hurts, in contrast to the usual painless clubbing. (Book p9)
Which of the following is a listed cause of unilateral clubbing?
Presubclavian coarctation of aorta, with only left-sided clubbing
Presubclavian coarctation of aorta, with only right-sided clubbing
Atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger syndrome

Unilateral clubbing is described in presubclavian coarctation of aorta with only left-sided clubbing, apical bronchogenic carcinoma, cervical rib and aneurysm of the subclavian or axillary artery. (Book p9)
A young hypertensive patient has clubbing of the left hand only, with an absent left radial pulse. Among the listed causes of unilateral clubbing, the book's lesion here is:

Presubclavian coarctation of the aorta is the cause given that produces clubbing confined to the left side. An apical bronchogenic carcinoma, cervical rib and subclavian/axillary aneurysm are the other unilateral causes - each with its own localising signs. (Book p9)
Which of the following is NOT a listed cause of unidigital clubbing?
Unidigital clubbing is hereditary, follows repeated local trauma, and rarely follows median nerve injury. Bronchiectasis produces generalised clubbing, not single-digit clubbing. (Book p9)
Which finger is the first to be affected by clubbing?

The index finger is the first to be affected. Both the clubbing definition page and the closing line of the clubbing section state this, which is why it is a favourite one-line viva question. (Book p9)
According to the book, which node size is significant in the inguinal region?
Inguinal nodes are significant when larger than 1.5 cm; any other node is significant when larger than 1 cm; and any supraclavicular or epitrochlear node is significant however small it is. (Book p9)
Which nodes are significant whatever their size?
Anterior cervical and posterior triangle nodes

Any supraclavicular or epitrochlear node is significant at any size - these are the two sites where even a small node mandates explanation, and both are classic answers in a lymphadenopathy viva. (Book p9)
Generalised lymphadenopathy is best defined as involvement of:
Two or more non-contiguous lymph node areas - though Harrison's says three or more, which is not practical
All palpable node groups excluding the inguinal group
Three or more contiguous node areas only
Any two node areas including the two inguinal groups

The book prefers two or more non-contiguous areas and explicitly notes that Harrison's says three or more but that this is not practical. Persistent generalised lymphadenopathy means it lasts more than 3 months. (Book p9)
Persistent generalised lymphadenopathy is defined as lasting more than:

More than 3 months defines persistence. The distinction matters because transient generalised lymphadenopathy accompanies most viral illness, whereas persistence raises HIV, tuberculosis, lymphoma and connective tissue disease. (Book p9)

Match each lymph node character to its meaning — 1) Painful lymphadenopathy 2) Firm, rubbery nodes 3) Fluctuant nodes 4) Stony hard node … A) Suppurative nodes B) Metastasis C) Infectious aetiology or even acute leukaemia D) Lymphoma
Painful nodes suggest infection but can occur in acute leukaemia; firm, rubbery nodes suggest lymphoma; fluctuant nodes are suppurative; a stony hard node means metastasis. (Book p9)
Matted nodes - which feel connected and move together as a unit - are seen in:
Tuberculosis as the benign cause, and lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma as the malignant causes
Infectious mononucleosis as the benign cause, and acute leukaemia as the malignant cause
Sarcoidosis as the benign cause, and Hodgkin's lymphoma only
Suppurative lymphadenitis as the benign cause, and secondaries as the malignant cause
Matted nodes are benign in tuberculosis and malignant in lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma. The clue is in the matting together with the consistency and the site, not in enlargement alone. (Book p9)

Match each cervical node level to its region — 1) Ia 2) Ib 3) II, III and IV 4) V 5) VI 6) VII … A) Submental B) Submandibular C) Upper, middle and lower jugular D) Posterior triangle E) Anterior triangle F) Superior mediastinal

Ia submental, Ib submandibular, II-IV upper/middle/lower jugular, V posterior triangle, VI anterior triangle, VII superior mediastinal. The levels are used to describe neck nodes and to plan neck dissection. (Book p9)
A 22-year-old has a 3 cm firm, rubbery, painless lower cervical node with no other nodes palpable. Among the listed characters, firm rubbery nodes are said to be suggestive of:
Metastatic carcinoma from a head and neck primary
Firm and rubbery suggests lymphoma; fluctuant means suppurative; stony hard means metastatic deposit. Matted nodes would be more typical of tuberculosis. (Book p9)
The inserted Boloor reference page on Book p10 lists which group of causes of clubbing?
Neurological causes - syringomyelia, median nerve injury and hemiplegia
Cardiac causes - cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis and atrial myxoma
Endocrine causes - thyroid acropachy and acromegaly
Occupational causes - vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure

The Boloor insert supplies the neurological column of clubbing causes: syringomyelia, median nerve injury and hemiplegia. It complements the respiratory, cardiovascular and GI groups given in the main text. (Book p10)
Which of the following is NOT listed among the neurological causes of clubbing in the inserted reference page?
