When testing for pitting oedema on Book p30, what time cutoff separates slow oedema from fast oedema, what does each signify, and what is the treatment of slow oedema?
Slow oedema: pitting lasts >2 minutes (indicates lymphatic obstruction); Fast oedema: pitting lasts <10 seconds (indicates right heart failure); treated with albumin infusion
Slow oedema: pitting lasts >60 seconds (indicates hypoproteinaemia); Fast oedema: pitting lasts <60 seconds (indicates sodium retention); treated with fluid restriction

Slow oedema: pitting lasts >40 seconds (indicates 4 kg sodium and water retention in the extravascular compartment; treatment is salt restriction); Fast oedema: pitting lasts <40 seconds (due to hypoproteinaemia)

Match each peripheral sign on Book p30 to its description — 1) Subcutaneous nodules of rheumatic activity 2) Janeway lesions vs Osler nodes in IE 3) Roth spots and splinter haemorrhages in IE 4) Lighthouse sign of AR … A) Alternate flushing and blanching of the forehead B) Painless, pea-sized nodules over bony prominences / extensor aspects of long bones (alongside joint swelling) C) Janeway = non-tender erythematous macules on palms/soles; Osler = tender subcutaneous violaceous nodules on pads of fingers/toes D) Roth = exudative oedematous haemorrhagic retinal lesions with pale centres; Splinter = non-blanching reddish-brown lesions under the nail bed

Match each eponymous sign of aortic regurgitation on Book p31 to its clinical finding — 1) Becker's sign 2) Landolfi's sign 3) Muller's sign 4) De Musset's sign and Corrigan's sign … A) Changes in pupil size with cardiac systole B) Retinal artery pulsations C) Uvula pulsation D) Head bobbing [De Musset's] and dancing carotids [Corrigan's]

How does Book p31 define 'locomotor brachii', and what two cuff-and-artery combinations are given for measuring lower-limb systolic BP when testing Hill's sign?

Visible venous pulsations in the antecubital fossa; (1) popliteal artery with a calf cuff, or (2) anterior tibial artery with a thigh cuff
Systolic thrill over the axillary artery; (1) femoral artery at the mid-inguinal point, or (2) peroneal artery above the lateral malleolus

In Hill's sign on Book p31, what lower-limb minus upper-limb systolic BP thresholds correspond to mild, moderate and severe aortic regurgitation?

>20 mmHg = mild AR; >40 mmHg = moderate AR; >60 mmHg = severe AR
>15 mmHg = mild AR; >30 mmHg = moderate AR; >45 mmHg = severe AR
>30 mmHg = mild AR; >50 mmHg = moderate AR; >70 mmHg = severe AR

Direct intra-arterial catheterisation in a patient with severe AR and a +65 mmHg Hill's sign shows identical systolic pressures in the brachial and femoral arteries. How does Book p31 (citing Jules Constant) explain Hill's sign, and which two conditions produce a falsely low Hill's sign?
Hill's sign reflects true hydrostatic pressure amplification in the supine posture; it is falsely low in patent ductus arteriosus and hyperthyroidism

Hill's sign is caused by femoral arterial calcification; it is falsely low in coarctation of the aorta above the left subclavian artery

False: Severe aortic stenosis is a cause of a falsely low Hill's sign

In a patient with chronic severe aortic regurgitation and hepatosplenomegaly, you palpate systolic pulsations over both the liver and the enlarged spleen. Which pair of eponyms on Book p31 names these two findings?

Match each precordial inspection item on Book p32 to its description — 1) Clue to precordial bulge in males 2) Skeletal and pleuropulmonary causes of precordial bulge 3) Cardiac, pericardial and localised causes of precordial bulge 4) Backward bulge of the precordium … A) Ventricular hypertrophy, pericardial effusion, and localised bulging from a post-MI ventricular aneurysm B) Pectus excavatum C) Lateral displacement and elevation of the left nipple D) Scoliosis, kyphoscoliosis, rachitic deformity, bronchial carcinoma and pleural effusion

While inspecting the precordium tangentially from the left side (Book p32), you observe an inward movement of the apex accompanied by an outward movement of the precordium during systole (see-saw movement). What does this pattern signify, and what causes a visible parasternal heave?

Match each anatomical site of visible pulsation on Book p32 to its listed causes — 1) High thoracic region: 2nd right intercostal space 2) 2nd or 3rd left intercostal space 3) Suprasternal notch pulsation 4) Back pulsations … A) Coarctation of the aorta [Suzman's sign] B) Ascending aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation or dilation of the aorta C) Pulmonary artery dilation, hyperkinetic states or aneurysm of the aorta D) Can be physiological; pathological causes are aortic regurgitation and aortic arch aneurysm

A patient's JVP is measured at 5 cm vertically above the sternal angle. Using the two-step conversion formula on Book p33, how do you calculate the right atrial pressure (RAP) in mmHg?

Match each letter of the 'POLICE' mnemonic on Book p33 for JVP vs Carotid to its JVP characteristic — 1) P and O: Palpation and Occlusion 2) L: Location 3) I: Inspiration 4) C and E: Contour and Erection … A) Between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, lateral to the carotid B) Non-palpable and readily occludable C) Biphasic waveform that drops when sitting erect D) Drops with inspiration

Which of the following True/False statements accurately reflects the comparison between the internal jugular vein (IJV) and external jugular vein (EJV) on Book p33?

In an elderly, severely arteriosclerotic patient, the left jugular venous column appears elevated while the right IJV is normal. According to Book p33, why is the right IJV always preferred over the left IJV?

How is the abdominojugular reflux elicited according to Book p36, what defines a positive test, why does the JVP normally fall with abdominal compression, and what are its two clinical uses?

Apply the hand over the periumbilical area with fingers widely spread and press gradually, firmly and steadily inward for at least 15 seconds; positive if JVP rises by >3 cm throughout compression; normally abdominal compression obstructs femoral venous return so less blood reaches the RA; used to unmask subclinical RV failure and confirm symptomatic LV failure
Press sharply over the left iliac fossa for 3 seconds while the patient holds breath in expiration; positive if JVP rises by >1 cm transiently; used to diagnose superior vena cava obstruction
Compress the epigastrium for 60 seconds with the patient standing erect; positive if JVP falls by >5 cm; used to differentiate tricuspid stenosis from mitral stenosis
Percuss the right costal margin for 5 seconds; positive if a jugular venous thrill appears; used to confirm cardiac tamponade

Why does cardiac tamponade produce pulsus paradoxus but NOT Kussmaul's sign, whereas constrictive pericarditis produces Kussmaul's sign? (Book p36)

In tamponade, the RV can still accommodate the inspiratory increase in venous return by pushing the interventricular septum toward the LV (so there is no Kussmaul's sign, but decreased LV volume causes pulsus paradoxus); in constrictive pericarditis, RA pressure increases with inspiration but is not transmitted to the RV
In tamponade, the superior vena cava collapses completely during inspiration, preventing blood from entering the neck veins
In tamponade, the pericardial fluid is confined to the left ventricle and spares the right atrium and right ventricle
In constrictive pericarditis, the interventricular septum is absent, equalising systemic and pulmonary pressures

Item 23.d.v and 23.e on Book p36 explain: in constrictive pericarditis, right atrial pressure increases with inspiration because it is not transmitted to the constricted RV; in tamponade, by contrast, the RV can accommodate the increased inspiratory venous return by pushing the IV septum toward the LV — so there is no Kussmaul's sign, but there is pulsus paradoxus because of decreased LV volume. (Book p36)

Use the JVP to time systole and diastole (since both hands are on the abdomen); pulsations pushing both hands outwards are expansile (e.g. TR) whereas those felt only by the abdominal hand are transmitted (aortic or RV cause); pulsations coinciding with the JVP 'a' wave are presystolic (e.g. TS) whereas those after the 'a' wave are systolic (e.g. TR)

On Book p42, why is S1 loud in mitral stenosis (MS), and what do curves A ('Steep slope at crossover point') and B ('Shallow slope at crossover point') in the LA-LV pressure crossover diagram illustrate?

(i) dP/dt theory: elevated LA pressure forces the LV to reach a higher pressure to shut the mitral valve, so crossover occurs on a steeper part of the LV dP/dt curve (Curve A vs normal Curve B); and (ii) Wide closing excursion: the high AV pressure gradient at the onset of systole keeps the leaflets maximally separated so they close through a wider excursion

Citing Perloff's Physical Examination of the Heart and Circulation, Book p43 separately explains (i) why S2 is WIDELY split in ASD and (ii) why the split is FIXED across respiration. Which statement captures both mechanisms?

Rapid LV pressure overload with preserved LV volume and high LA pressures from the start
Immediate right atrial dilation with spared left-sided pressures

Which of the following True/False statements accurately reflects the MR haemodynamics on Book p57?

True: chronic MR causes gradual LA dilation with little increase in pressure, and therefore very few symptoms

A 60-year-old man, 4 days after an anterior MI, develops sudden dyspnoea, hypotension and bilateral pulmonary oedema with a new systolic murmur. Per Book p57, why does acute MR cause such marked symptomatic deterioration?
The LV becomes acutely pressure-overloaded, raising systolic LV pressure against a stenotic outflow
The non-compliant, undilated LA cannot buffer the regurgitant volume, so LA pressure rises rapidly
The right atrium fails to accept the regurgitant volume, isolating the pulmonary circuit
Atrial fibrillation shortens ventricular systole and prolongs the regurgitant orifice

Match the MR symptoms on Book p57 to their stated mechanism — 1) Dyspnoea 2) Fatigue 3) Palpitations 4) Right heart failure … A) Decreased cardiac output B) Early, along with palpitations C) Atrial fibrillation and increased stroke volume D) Occurs in the late stages

(Book p57)

Match the MR investigations on Book p57 to the findings the note lists for them — 1) ECG 2) CXR 3) Echo 4) Doppler; cardiac catheterisation … A) Inverted moustache, enlarged LA and LV, pulmonary venous congestion, pulmonary oedema if acute B) Dilated LA and LV C) Left atrial hypertrophy, left ventricular hypertrophy or A fib D) Listed as further investigations without elaborated findings

The characteristic CXR sign of mitral regurgitation on Book p57 is the inverted ____ silhouette, and in acute MR the film may additionally show ____.
snowman; cardiomegaly with a clear lung field

Match the six TR features of the TR-vs-MR list on Book p57 to their description — 1) Murmur site 2) Carvallo's sign 3) Hepatic pulsation 4) Response to abdominojugular reflux 5) Giant V waves with deep Y descents 6) Earlobe pulsation … A) Best heard in the tricuspid area B) Positive with inspiration C) Pulsation of the liver D) The 'Vitam sign' E) The 'Lancisi sign' F) Visible pulsation of the earlobe

A 55-year-old with acute MR from chordal rupture has a pansystolic murmur that begins very early in systole. According to Book p57, why is the murmur early systolic in acute MR?
The regurgitant orifice is small, so the jet is low-velocity and late in systole
Pulmonary artery pressure falls, delaying aortic valve closure

Atrial fibrillation shortens ventricular systole so the murmur ends early

A 66-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis exerts at work and develops chest pain. Which chain on Book p58 explains his haemodynamics?

RV failure from secondary pulmonary hypertension -> systemic venous congestion with angina

Book p58 haemodynamics: LVOT obstruction causes concentric LVH (pressure overload); this maintains normal haemodynamic function for years without decline in CO, but eventually the LV fails — systolic dysfunction; the hypertrophied LV has a high oxygen demand, thus angina on exertion is common. True: the hypertrophied LV has a high oxygen demand, so angina on exertion is common

Match the AS symptoms on Book p58 to their stated mechanism — 1) Exertional dyspnoea 2) Angina pectoris 3) Exertional syncope 4) Left heart failure + pulmonary hypertension in isolated severe AS … A) Increased pulmonary capillary pressure from increased LVEDP due to impaired relaxation of the poorly compliant hypertrophied LV B) Develops somewhat later, from increased oxygen demand C) Imbalance in vasoconstriction and vasodilation in exercising and non-exercising muscles D) Occurs very late

Usually sinus rhythm — AF suggests pulmonary hypertension; stroke volume rises late

falls rapidly to a low nadir

The 'carotid shudder' in AS (Book p60) is:

High pitched, blowing diastolic murmur at the apex

Harsh pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla

Transmission of the AS murmur to the apex, where it is confused with MR

widely spaced teeth; prominent chin; nasal twang

Book p63 root disease: i. Aortic dissection (Dissection causes AR due to displacement of the valves); ii. Cystic medial degeneration; iii. Marfan's; iv. Bicuspid aortic valve — the bicuspid valve is the one cause listed under BOTH the valvular and the root-disease headings. (Book p63)
All of the following are listed causes of aortic regurgitation on Book p63 EXCEPT:

Book p63 AR causes: valvular (congenital bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis, myxomatous, syphilis, ankylosing spondylitis, trauma), root disease (dissection, cystic medial degeneration, Marfan's, bicuspid), aortitis. Traumatic rupture of MITRAL chordae causes MR, not AR. (Book p63)
The root-disease cause the Book p63 note calls 'Cystic ____ degeneration' appears in the Book p62 table simply as '____ degeneration'.
Book p63 root disease ii reads 'Cystic medial degeneration', while Table 262-1 on Book p62 lists the root-disease entry simply as 'Medial degeneration'. (Book p63)
The AR haemodynamic cascade on Book p63: total stroke volume increases, so ____ (increased preload) occurs, and volume overload results in dilation and ____, until ultimately the LV fails.

Book p63 haemodynamics a: 'Total stroke volume increases -> Increase in LVEDV occurs (increased preload) -> Volume overload results in dilation and eccentric hypertrophy -> Ultimately, the LV fails'. (Book p63)
A 50-year-old with infective endocarditis develops acute severe aortic regurgitation and pulmonary oedema. Per Book p63, why does acute severe AR decompensate this fast?
His chronically dilated LV has already failed by the time he presents
The mitral valve is secondarily stenosed, raising left atrial pressure
In acute severe AR, as in endocarditis, the LV cannot compensate rapidly, so pulmonary oedema occurs
Right ventricular failure reduces LV preload, backing fluid into the lungs
Book p63 haemodynamics b: 'In acute severe AR, as in endocarditis, LV cannot compensate rapidly so pulmonary oedema occurs.' (Book p63)
Per Book p63, a patient with chronic severe aortic regurgitation can remain asymptomatic for up to ____ years.
Book p63 haemodynamics c: 'In chronic severe AR, the patients can be asymptomatic for up to 10–15 years.' (Book p63)
Per the AR symptom list on Book p63, palpitations can be an early complaint seen ____ before the exertional dyspnoea, and after angina the patient develops exertional dyspnoea, ____ and ____.
Book p63 symptoms: a. Palpitations can be an early complaint — can be seen for years before the exertional dyspnoea; b. Angina can occur; c. Then exertional dyspnoea, PND, orthopnoea. (Book p63)
The FIRST sign entry of the AR sign list on Book p63 is:
A giant v wave in the JVP
Book p63 sign a (the list is even marked '***Signs' in the note): 'Peripheral signs (from head to toe)' — the first entry, before any specific impulse or murmur. (Book p63)
Which apical-impulse finding is listed as a sign of AR on Book p63?
Pulsus alternans recorded at the apex
Heaving apical impulse, displaced down and out — annotated '????' in the note
An apical impulse that vanishes on inspiration
Book p63 sign b: 'Heaving apical impulse???? Displaced down and out' — the note itself flags this line with question marks. (Book p63)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the AR signs on Book p63?
False: in severe AR, A2 is usually absent
True: a systolic thrill may be felt over the carotids and suprasternal notch and need not mean there is an accompanying AS
True: pulsus bisferiens is not a listed sign of AR
False: a diastolic thrill over the aortic area is a listed sign of AR

Book p63 signs c–f: c. Pulsus bisferiens; d. Diastolic thrill over aortic area; e. Systolic thrill may be felt over the carotids and suprasternal notch and need not mean there is an accompanying AS; f. In severe AR, A2 is usually absent. (Book p63)

Match the AR murmur details on Book p63 to their statement — 1) Quality 2) Characteristic timing and site 3) Position for auscultation 4) Why it is best heard at Erb's point … A) High pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic B) An early diastolic murmur best heard over Erb's point (neo Aortic area) C) Sitting position with the breath held in expiration D) Because of the orientation of the aorta

Book p63 signs g–h: g. High pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur, best heard in the 3rd ICS along the left sternal border in the sitting position with breath held in expiration; h. Characteristically an early diastolic murmur best heard over Erb's point (neo Aortic area) because of the orientation of the aorta. (Book p63)
A patient's aortic regurgitation murmur is better heard in the aortic area than at Erb's point. According to Book p63, what does that site discrimination suggest?
An aortic aneurysm causing the AR

Book p63 sign h: the AR murmur is characteristically best heard over Erb's point (neo Aortic area) because of the orientation of the aorta — 'However, if the AR murmur is better heard in the Aortic area, it suggests an aortic aneurysm causing AR'. (Book p63)
All of the following are listed signs of AR on Book p63 EXCEPT:
Diastolic thrill over the aortic area
Peripheral signs from head to toe

Pulsus parvus et tardus is the CAROTID pulse of aortic STENOSIS (Book p58); the p63 AR list instead includes pulsus bisferiens, diastolic thrill over the aortic area and peripheral signs from head to toe. (Book p63)
A patient's aortic regurgitation murmur is best heard over the right sternal border rather than at Erb's point. According to Book p64, what does that suggest?
That the regurgitation is due to aneurysmal dilation
Book p64 sign i: 'When the murmur is best heard over the right sternal border, it suggests that the regurgitation is due to aneurysmal dilation.' (Book p64)
AR Signs i-l (top of Book p64)
Per Book p64, which additional systolic finding can be present with aortic regurgitation?
A mid systolic ejection murmur best heard in the aortic area and transmitted to the carotids
A pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
A mid diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap
A continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle
Book p64 sign j: 'A mid systolic ejection murmur can also be heard best in the aortic area and transmitted to the carotids'. (Book p64)
AR Signs i-l (top of Book p64)
Book p64 names two eponymous murmurs as signs k and l of aortic regurgitation, without elaborating them: the ____ murmur and the ____ murmur.
Book p64 signs k–l: 'k. Austin Flint murmur-  l. Cole Cecil murmur-' — the note lists the eponyms only, with nothing after the dashes. (Book p64)
AR Signs i-l (top of Book p64)
In the AR investigation list on Book p64, the only sub-item elaborated is under Doppler Echo: color doppler is the ____ for ____.
Book p64 investigations: b. Doppler Echo — i. 'color doppler : most sensitive for mild cases'. (Book p64)

Match the three CXR findings of AR on Book p64 to their sign — 1) Cardiomegaly 2) Aortic root dilation 3) Aortic valve calcification … A) Cor bovinum / bovine heart B) Prominent aortic knuckle C) Sus for concomitant AS
Book p64 CXR findings: i. cardiomegaly -> cor bovinum / bovine heart; ii. aortic root dilation -> prominent aortic knuckle; iii. Aortic valve calcification -> sus for concomitant AS. (Book p64)
All of the following are listed investigations for AR on Book p64 EXCEPT:

Book p64 AR investigations: a. ECG — LVH; b. Doppler Echo (color doppler most sensitive for mild cases); c. CXR (three findings); d. Cardiac cath. Holter/ambulatory BP monitoring is not listed. (Book p64)

Match the AR management entries on Book p64 to their detail — 1) Baseline medical 2) Chronic + significant volume overload 3) Surgical treatment 4) Ideal time for surgery … A) As in MS (IE or syphilitic aortitis needs Rx) B) Requires a vasodilator (hydralazine, nifedipine, or ACE inhibitor) C) AVR D) After haemodynamic / echogenic evidence of LVdys but before significant symptoms

Book p64 AR management: a. as in MS (IE or syphilitic aortitis needs Rx); b. chronic + significant vol overload: requires vasodilator (hydralazine, nifedipine, or ACE inh); c. Sx: AVR; ideal time: after haemodynamic / echogenic evidence of LVdys but before significant symptoms. (Book p64)
A patient with chronic aortic regurgitation is found to have active infective endocarditis. What does the Book p64 AR management line ('as in MS …') say must happen here?
The MS-style medical regimen proceeds, but IE or syphilitic aortitis needs Rx
Vasodilators are withheld until the endocarditis is cured
Immediate AVR regardless of haemodynamic status
No medical therapy — surgical AVR alone
Book p64 management a: 'as in MS ( IE or syphilitic aortitis needs Rx )' — the parenthetical singles out IE and syphilitic aortitis as conditions that require treatment. (Book p64)
For chronic AR with significant volume overload, Book p64 requires a vasodilator — listing ____, ____, or ____.
Book p64 management b: 'chronic + significant vol overload : requires vasodilator ( hydralazine , nifedipine , or ACE inh )'. (Book p64)
In the ASD types on Book p64, ostium secundum ASD accounts for ____% and ostium primum ASD for ____%.
Book p64 ASD types: a. Ostium secundum ASD — 90%; b. Ostium primum ASD 5%. (Book p64)
Ostium primum ASD on Book p64 is commonly associated with:
Marfan syndrome or a bicuspid aortic valve
Down syndrome or endocardial cushion defects
Turner syndrome or coarctation of the aorta
Klinefelter syndrome or mitral valve prolapse
Book p64: 'Ostium primum ASD 5% — commonly associated with Down syndrome or endocardial cushion defects'. (Book p64)

Match the five syndromic ASD associations on Book p64 to their listed detail — 1) Holt-Oram syndrome 2) Patau syndrome 3) Edward syndrome 4) Ellis van Creveld syndrome 5) Lutembacher syndrome … A) Triphalangeal (fingerised) thumb, sometimes abrachia or phocomelia B) Trisomy 13 C) Trisomy 18 D) Polydactyly, nail dysplasia, dwarfism E) MS + ASD

Book p64 syndromic associations: a. Holt-Oram (triphalangeal fingerised thumb, sometimes abrachia or phocomelia); b. Patau (trisomy 13); c. Edward (trisomy 18); d. Ellis van Creveld (polydactyly, nail dysplasia, dwarfism); e. Lutembacher — MS + ASD. (Book p64)

Match the three Patau syndrome entries on Book p64 to their detail — 1) Chromosomal basis 2) Phenotype 3) Cardiac lesions … A) Trisomy 13 B) Polydactyly, flexion deformity of fingers, simian crease, cleft lip and palate, microcephaly C) ASD, VSD, PDA
Book p64 Patau syndrome: i. Trisomy 13; ii. Polydactyly, flexion deformity of fingers, simian crease, cleft lip and palate, microcephaly; iii. ASD, VSD, PDA. (Book p64)

Match the three Edward syndrome entries on Book p64 to their detail — 1) Chromosomal basis 2) Phenotype 3) Cardiac lesions … A) Trisomy 18 B) Prominent occiput, low set malformed ears, rocker bottom feet, micrognathia, clenched fists C) ASD, VSD, PDA
Book p64 Edward syndrome: i. Trisomy 18; ii. Prominent occiput, low set malformed ears, rocker bottom feet, micrognathia, clenched fists; iii. ASD, VSD, PDA. (Book p64)
All of the following are listed features of Edward syndrome on Book p64 EXCEPT:

Edward syndrome (Book p64): prominent occiput, low set malformed ears, rocker bottom feet, micrognathia, clenched fists. Polydactyly belongs to Patau syndrome (and Ellis van Creveld), not Edward. (Book p64)
All of the following are listed under the syndromic associations of ASD on Book p64 EXCEPT:

The five listed syndromic associations (Book p64) are Holt-Oram, Patau, Edward, Ellis van Creveld and Lutembacher (MS + ASD). Williams syndrome is not listed here — the elfin-facies/hypercalcaemia phenotype appears on p61 beside supravalvular AS. (Book p64)
The skeletal entry of Holt-Oram syndrome on Book p64: a triphalangeal (fingerised) thumb, sometimes ____ or ____.
Book p64 Holt-Oram syndrome: 'Triphalangeal (fingerised) thumb, sometimes abrachia or phocomelia'. (Book p64)
The third and final point under ASD on Book p64 states:
Atrial fibrillation is common in ASD
Complete heart block is common in ASD
Supraventricular tachycardia is common in ASD
Ventricular ectopy is common in ASD
Book p64, ASD point 3: 'Atrial fibrillation is common in ASD'. (Book p64)
Per Book p65, small ASDs are usually ____, whereas large defects present with features like tachycardia, right heart failure, left heart failure and exertional dyspnoea.
accompanied by a loud single S2

Book p65, ASD '4. Symptoms and signs': a. Small defects are usually asymptomatic; b. Large defects present with features like tachycardia, right heart failure, left heart failure, exertional dyspnoea. (Book p65)
ASD: Symptoms, Signs & DDs (top of Book p65)

Match the five ASD sign entries on Book p65 to their detail — 1) Associated PS 2) S2 3) S2 with pulmonary hypertension 4) Flow ESM 5) Flow MDM … A) Can be present B) Wide fixed split of S2 C) Split is narrowed with the development of pulmonary hypertension D) Across the pulmonary valve E) Across the mitral valve

Book p65, ASD '5. Signs': a. Associated PS can be present; b. Wide fixed split of S2; c. S2 split is narrowed with the development of pulmonary hypertension; d. Flow ESM across pulmonary valve; e. Flow MDM across mitral valve. (Book p65)
ASD: Symptoms, Signs & DDs (top of Book p65)

Match the three ASD differential diagnoses on Book p65 to their detail — 1) MS with pulmonary HTN 2) Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connections 3) Total anomalous pulmonary venous connections … A) Listed first as DD a B) Listed second as DD b C) With a large interatrial communication without pulmonary HTN

Book p65, ASD '6. DDs': a. MS with pulmonary HTN; b. Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connections; c. Total anomalous pulmonary venous connections with a large interatrial communication without pulmonary HTN. (Book p65)
ASD: Symptoms, Signs & DDs (top of Book p65)
The two pointer stubs that close the congenital heart disease section on Book p65 are:
'TOF and VSD from peds' and 'JVP waves in CHD'
'PDA and PPHN from peds' and 'Facies in CHD — must know'
'TOF and AVSD from peds' and 'Facies in CHD — Nice to know'
'TOF and VSD from peds' and 'Facies in congenital heart disease — Nice to know'
Book p65 closes the CHD section with two stubs: 'TOF and VSD from peds' (both terms underlined) and 'Facies in congenital heart disease- Nice to know'. (Book p65)
ASD: Symptoms, Signs & DDs (top of Book p65)
Per Book p65, acute rheumatic fever is most commonly a disease of children aged ____, is rare in people over ____, while RHD peaks between ____.
Book p65 RF point 1: 'Acute Rheumatic Fever is most commonly a disease of children aged 5–14. They are rare in people >30 years. RHD however peaks between 25–40 years.' (Book p65)
The pathogenesis of ARF on Book p65 is molecular mimicry: the immune response targeted at the streptococcal antigens ____ and ____ also recognises human tissues.
Book p65 RF point 3: 'Pathogenesis — molecular mimicry: immune response targeted at streptococcal antigens (M protein and NAG) also recognises human tissues.' (Book p65)
The cause of rheumatic fever on Book p65 is:
Book p65 RF point 2: 'Cause — Group A Streptococci'. (Book p65)
In the RHD statistics on Book p65, mitral stenosis is seen in ____% of cases, isolated MS in ____% of cases, and multi-valve involvement in ____% of cases.
Book p65 RF statistics: a. Mitral stenosis is seen in 99% of RHD cases; b. 40% of cases have MS with MR, isolated MS in 25%; c. 38% have multi valve involvement. (Book p65)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the RHD statistics on Book p65?
False: 6% of RHD cases have tricuspid valve involvement
True: 35% of RHD cases have aortic valve involvement
True: the pulmonary valve is commonly involved in RHD
False: isolated MS is seen in 25% of RHD cases
Book p65 statistics c: 38% multi valve involvement, 35% aortic valve involvement, 6% tricuspid valve involvement, 'Pulmonary valve is very rarely involved.' (Book p65)
All of the following figures appear in the RHD statistics on Book p65 EXCEPT:
The statistics on Book p65: MS 99%, MS with MR 40%, isolated MS 25%, multi valve 38%, aortic 35%, tricuspid 6%, pulmonary very rare. There is no isolated-tricuspid-stenosis figure. (Book p65)
The ARF latent period on Book p66 is ____, and the preceding infection is commonly ____ but can be confirmed by antibody testing.
Book p66 RF point 5a: 'Latent period of 1–5 weeks. The preceding infection is commonly subclinical but can be confirmed by antibody testing.' (Book p66)
The most common presenting complaints of ARF on Book p66 are polyarthritis in ____% of cases and carditis in ____%.
Book p66 RF point 5b: 'm/c c/f — polyarthritis (60–75%), carditis (50–60%)'. (Book p66)
Which of the following is NOT stated about the most common presenting complaints of ARF on Book p66?
Carditis is the second listed complaint (50–60%)
Both polyarthritis and carditis are listed as the m/c c/f
Book p66 lists exactly: 'm/c c/f — polyarthritis (60–75%), carditis (50–60%)'. No rash figure is given. (Book p66)
Per Book p66, up to ____% of patients with acute rheumatic fever progress to RHD.
Book p66 RF point 6a: 'Up to 60% of patients of ARF progress to RHD. Endocardium/myocardium/pericardium may be involved.' (Book p66)
Which statement about valve involvement in ARF is on Book p66?
The mitral valve is almost always affected, sometimes together with the aortic valve; isolated aortic valve involvement is rare
The aortic valve is almost always affected, and isolated mitral involvement is rare
The tricuspid valve is almost always affected
The pulmonary valve is the most commonly affected valve
Book p66 RF point 6b: 'Mitral valve is almost always affected, sometimes together with the aortic valve. Isolated aortic valve involvement is rare.' (Book p66)
Early valvular damage in ARF (Book p66) leads to ____, and over ensuing years — usually after recurrent episodes — leaflet thickening, scarring, calcification and eventually ____ may develop.

Book p66 RF point 6c: 'Early valvular damage leads to regurgitation. Over ensuing years, usually as a result of recurrent episodes, leaflet thickening, scarring, calcification and eventually valvular stenosis may develop.' (Book p66)
The characteristic manifestation of carditis in previously unaffected individuals (Book p66) is:
Book p66 RF point 6d: 'The characteristic manifestation of carditis in previously unaffected individuals is MR, sometimes accompanied by AR.' (Book p66)
Myocarditis in ARF may lead to ____ and ____, per Book p66.
first degree AV block; softening of S1
third degree AV block; loss of S2
first degree AV block; accentuation of S1
second degree AV block; an S3 gallop
Book p66 RF point 6e: 'Myocarditis — may lead to first degree AV block and softening of S1.' (Book p66)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the ARF heart-involvement section on Book p66?
False: endocardium, myocardium or pericardium may be involved in ARF carditis
True: up to 60% of ARF patients progress to RHD
True: isolated aortic valve involvement is common in ARF
False: early valvular damage leads to regurgitation

Book p66: 6a — up to 60% of ARF patients progress to RHD and endocardium/myocardium/pericardium may be involved; 6b — isolated aortic involvement is rare; 6c — early damage leads to regurgitation. (Book p66)

Match the five joint-involvement entries of ARF on Book p67 to their detail — 1) Appearance 2) Course 3) Distribution 4) Pain 5) Drug response … A) Hot, swollen, red, tender joints and polyarthritis B) Typically migrates over a period of hours C) Large joints, asymmetric D) Severe and disabling until anti-inflammatory therapy is commenced E) Characteristically sensitive to NSAIDs/Salicylates

Book p67 RF point 7: a. Hot, swollen, red, tender joints and polyarthritis; b. Typically migrates over a period of hours; c. Commonly affects the large joints and is asymmetric — pain severe and disabling until anti-inflammatory therapy is commenced, characteristically sensitive to NSAIDs/Salicylates. (Book p67)
A child with ARF has arthritis that shifts from the knee to the ankle over a few hours, with hot, swollen, red, tender joints. Which description on Book p67 fits this course?
ARF arthritis is classically fixed in a single small joint
It typically migrates over a period of hours, commonly affects the large joints asymmetrically, and is characteristically sensitive to NSAIDs/Salicylates
ARF arthritis is symmetric and involves the DIP joints
ARF arthritis is unresponsive to anti-inflammatory therapy

Book p67 RF point 7: hot, swollen, red, tender joints and polyarthritis; typically migrates over a period of hours; commonly large joints and asymmetric; severe and disabling until anti-inflammatory therapy; characteristically sensitive to NSAIDs/Salicylates. (Book p67)

Match the six chorea entries of ARF on Book p67 to their detail — 1) Presentation pattern 2) Carditis association 3) Head predilection 4) Distribution 5) Neuropsychiatric association 6) Duration … A) Commonly occurs in the absence of other manifestations, prolonged latent period, more common in females B) Always associated with carditis C) Characteristic darting movements of the tongue, and upper limbs D) May be generalised or restricted to one side of the body E) Emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits F) Usually resolves around 6 weeks, but may take up to 6 months

Book p67 RF point 8: a. Sydenham's chorea — absence of other manifestations, prolonged latent period, more common in females; b. Always associated with carditis; c. Head — darting tongue movements, upper limbs; d. Generalised or one side; e. Emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits; f. Resolves around 6 weeks, up to 6 months. (Book p67)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the chorea section on Book p67?
True: Sydenham's chorea is more common in females
False: chorea is always associated with carditis
True: chorea most often first affects the distal lower limbs
False: chorea itself usually resolves around 6 weeks, but may take up to 6 months

Book p67 RF point 8a–f: Sydenham's chorea more common in females with a prolonged latent period; always associated with carditis; head (darting tongue) and upper limbs; generalised or unilateral; emotional lability/OC traits; resolves around 6 weeks, up to 6 months. (Book p67)
All of the following are listed features of ARF chorea on Book p67 EXCEPT:

Book p67 chorea entries: darting tongue/upper-limb movements, generalised or one-sided, emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits, always with carditis. 'Masked facies with hypokinetic jerking' is not on the list. (Book p67)
Erythema marginatum on Book p67 begins as pink macules that clear ____, leaving a ____ spreading edge; the rash is evanescent, appearing and disappearing before the examiner's eyes.

Book p67 RF point 9a–b: erythema marginatum begins as pink macules that clear centrally, leaving a serpiginous spreading edge; the rash is evanescent, appearing and disappearing before the examiner's eyes. (Book p67)
Where does erythema marginatum usually occur, per Book p67?
Face and neck, sometimes the trunk
Trunk, sometimes the limbs, but almost never the face
Book p67 RF point 9c: 'Usually occurs on the trunk, sometimes on the limbs, but almost never on the face'. (Book p67)
The subcutaneous nodules of ARF on Book p67 are remembered by the 3 P's: ____, ____, and on bony prominences, lasting a few days to a few weeks.
Book p67 RF point 9d: 'Subcutaneous nodules — 3 P's — painless, pea sized, on bony prominences. Last for a few days to a few weeks.' (Book p67)

Match the ARF investigation entries on Book p67 to their condition — 1) Blood culture 2) Throat swab 3) ESR and CRP 4) WBC count … A) If febrile B) Before giving antibiotics C) Listed as entry a without a condition D) Listed as entry b without a condition
Book p67 RF point 10: a. ESR, CRP; b. WBC count; c. Blood culture if febrile; d. Throat swab before giving antibiotics; e. ECG; f. Chest X ray. (Book p67)
A febrile child is being evaluated for ARF and antibiotics are about to start. Per the Book p67 investigation list, which sequencing rule must be respected?
Chest X ray before the ESR
WBC count only after penicillin has been started
Book p67 RF point 10d: 'Throat swab before giving antibiotics' — and 10c adds blood culture if febrile. (Book p67)
The ARF antibiotic regimen on Book p67: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg PO bd / Amox 50 mg/kg daily for ____ days.
Book p67 RF point 11a: 'Antibiotics — Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500mg PO bd/Amox 50 mg/kg daily for 10 days.' (Book p67)

Match the seven treatment entries of ARF on Book p67 to their detail — 1) Antibiotics 2) Salicylates/NSAIDs — indications 3) Salicylates/NSAIDs — no value in 4) Aspirin dosing 5) Naproxen 6) Severe carditis 7) Severe chorea … A) Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500mg PO bd / Amox 50 mg/kg daily for 10 days B) Arthritis/arthralgia/fever once the dx is confirmed C) Treatment of carditis and chorea D) 50–60 mg/kg/day up to 80–100 mg/kg/day in 4–5 divided doses E) 10–20 mg/kg/day in two divided doses, an alternative F) Steroids — controversial; prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day for a few days, maximum 3 weeks G) Carbamazepine; continued 1–2 weeks after symptoms subside

Book p67 RF point 11: a. Antibiotics (Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500mg PO bd/Amox 50 mg/kg daily x 10 days); b. Salicylates/NSAIDs for arthritis/arthralgia/fever once dx confirmed — no value in carditis and chorea — aspirin 50–60 mg/kg/day up to 80–100 mg/kg/day in 4–5 divided doses, monitor for salicylate toxicity, naproxen 10–20 mg/kg/day in two divided doses as alternative; c. Severe carditis — steroids controversial, prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day, max 3 weeks; d. Severe chorea — carbamazepine, response 1–2 weeks, continue 1–2 weeks after remission. (Book p67)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the salicylate/NSAID and steroid/chorea therapy on Book p67?
True: salicylates and NSAIDs are of no value in the treatment of carditis and chorea
False: aspirin is dosed at 50–60 mg/kg/day, up to 80–100 mg/kg/day in 4–5 divided doses
True: IVIg is recommended for every case of chorea
False: prednisolone for severe carditis is 1–2 mg/kg/day for a few days, maximum 3 weeks

Book p67 RF point 11b–d: salicylates/NSAIDs treat arthritis/arthralgia/fever once dx is confirmed and are of no value in carditis and chorea; aspirin 50–60 mg/kg/day up to 80–100 mg/kg/day in 4–5 divided doses with salicylate-toxicity monitoring; IVIg is NOT recommended except severe chorea refractory to other treatments; prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day max 3 weeks for severe carditis. (Book p67)

Severe ARF chorea on Book p67 can be controlled with ____, with response possibly not seen for 1–2 weeks and the drug continued 1–2 weeks after symptoms subside; IVIg is not recommended except in ____.
haloperidol; severe chorea refractory to other treatments
carbamazepine; severe chorea refractory to other treatments

Book p67 RF point 11d: 'Severe chorea can be controlled with Carbamazepine. Response may not be seen for 1–2 weeks and the medication should be continued for 1–2 weeks after the symptoms subside… IVIg is not recommended except in severe chorea refractory to other treatments.' (Book p67)
All of the following are stated about salicylate/NSAID therapy in ARF on Book p67 EXCEPT:
Used to treat arthritis/arthralgia/fever once the dx is confirmed
Of no value in the treatment of carditis and chorea
First-line for severe carditis instead of steroids

Book p67: salicylates/NSAIDs treat arthritis/arthralgia/fever once the dx is confirmed, are of no value in carditis and chorea, and salicylate toxicity must be monitored. For severe CARDITIS the note lists (controversial) steroids — salicylates are not first-line for it. (Book p67)
Per Book p68, if commenced within ____ days of sore throat onset, a complete course of penicillin prevents almost all cases of ARF from developing.
Book p68 RF point 12a.ii: 'If commenced within 9 days of sore throat onset, a complete course of penicillin will prevent almost all cases of ARF from developing.' (Book p68)

Match the three secondary-prophylaxis durations on Book p68 to their rule — 1) RF without carditis 2) RF with carditis but no residual valvular disease 3) RF with persistent valvular disease (clinical or subclinical) … A) 5 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer B) 10 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer C) 20 years after the last attack or until 40 years of age, whichever is longer

Book p68 RF point 12b: ii. RF without carditis — 5 years or until 21 (whichever longer); iii. RF with carditis but no residual valvular disease — 10 years or until 21 (whichever longer); iv. RF with persistent valvular disease, clinically or subclinically evident — 20 years or until 40 (whichever longer). (Book p68)
The secondary prevention regimen on Book p68 is Benzathine penicillin G ____ every 4 weeks.
Book p68 RF point 12b.i: 'Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units every 4 weeks.' (Book p68)
A 26-year-old with RF with carditis but no residual valvular disease had her last attack 4 years ago. Per Book p68, how long does secondary prophylaxis continue?
Until 10 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer — i.e., 6 more years from the last attack
Until 5 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer
Until 20 years after the last attack or until 40 years of age, whichever is longer
It stops now — prophylaxis is never required beyond age 21

Book p68 point 12b.iii applies: 'RF with carditis but no residual valvular disease — for 10 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer.' Last attack at age 22 -> 10 years runs to age 32, so 6 more years. (Book p68)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the prevention section on Book p68?
True: secondary prophylaxis for RF without carditis lasts 10 years or until 21 years of age
False: penicillin started within 9 days of sore throat onset prevents almost all cases of ARF
True: timely and complete treatment of group A streptococcal sore throat with antibiotics is primary prevention
False: RF with persistent valvular disease requires 20 years or until 40 years of age, whichever is longer

Book p68: primary prevention = timely and complete treatment of group A streptococcal sore throat with antibiotics (within 9 days prevents almost all ARF); RF WITHOUT carditis gets 5 years/21, and persistent valvular disease gets 20 years/40. (Book p68)
Definite IE on Book p69 is diagnosed by the pathological criteria, or 2 major + ____, or 1 major + ____, or ____ minor.
Book p69 IE diagnosis, definitive: i. pathological criteria; ii. 2 major + 1 minor; iii. 1 major + 2 minor; iv. 5 minor. (Book p69)
Possible IE on Book p69 is:
Book p69 IE diagnosis b: 'possible : 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor'. (Book p69)
All of the following are combinations for DEFINITE IE on Book p69 EXCEPT:
Definite IE (Book p69): pathological criteria, 2 major + 1 minor, 1 major + 2 minor, or 5 minor. '1 major + 1 minor' is only the first possible-IE combination (alongside 3 minor). (Book p69)

Match the four blood-culture major-criteria entries on Book p69 to their detail — 1) Typical organisms from two blood cultures 2) The 'or' entry within typical organisms 3) Other organisms from persistently positive cultures 4) Single positive culture / serology … A) Viridans streptococci, Streptococcus bovis, HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) B) Community-acquired Staphylococcus aureus or enterococci in the absence of a primary focus C) Two positive cultures of samples drawn >12 hours apart, or all of three or a majority of four separate cultures (first and last sample drawn 1 hour apart) D) Single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii, or positive serology for Q fever, Bartonella species and Chlamydia psittaci

Book p69 major criteria, blood cultures positive: typical microorganisms from two blood cultures (Viridans streptococci, Streptococcus bovis, HACEK group — Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), OR community-acquired S. aureus or enterococci without a primary focus; OR other organisms from persistently positive cultures (two positive cultures >12 h apart, or all of three / majority of four, first and last 1 h apart); OR single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii or positive serology for Q fever, Bartonella species and Chlamydia psittaci. (Book p69)
The HACEK group in the Book p69 major criteria comprises ____, ____, ____, ____ and ____.
Book p69: HACEK group = (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella). (Book p69)

A patient grows an organism that is not on the typical list, in cultures from draws 14 hours apart. Per the Book p69 major criteria, what defines 'persistently positive' blood cultures for other microorganisms?
A single positive culture from any draw
Two positive cultures drawn within 6 hours of each other
Two positive cultures of blood samples drawn >12 hours apart, or all of three or a majority of four separate cultures with the first and last sample drawn 1 hour apart
One positive culture from two separate venipunctures on the same day

Book p69: other microorganisms consistent with IE from persistently positive blood cultures defined as — two positive cultures of blood samples drawn >12 hours apart, or all of three or a majority of four separate cultures of blood (with first and last sample drawn 1 hour apart). (Book p69)

Match the four echocardiographic entries that make the echo 'positive for IE' on Book p69 to their detail — 1) Oscillating mass 2) Abscess 3) Prosthetic valve 4) Valvular regurgitation … A) Oscillating intracardiac mass without alternative explanation B) The second listed echocardiographic entry C) New partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve D) New valvular regurgitation (worsening or changing of preexisting murmur not sufficient)

Book p69 major criteria: evidence of endocardial involvement — echocardiogram positive for IE: oscillating intracardiac mass without alternative explanation, or abscess, or new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or new valvular regurgitation (worsening or changing of preexisting murmur not sufficient). (Book p69)
Per the Book p69 major criteria, why is a 'worsening or changing of preexisting murmur' explicitly not sufficient?
Murmur changes cannot be recorded on echocardiography
Only a NEW valvular regurgitation satisfies the echocardiographic major criterion
It implies the murmur is rheumatic in origin
A preexisting murmur excludes infective endocarditis
Book p69: the echocardiographic entry requires NEW valvular regurgitation — 'worsening or changing of preexisting murmur not sufficient'. (Book p69)
A positive echocardiogram for IE on Book p69 shows an oscillating intracardiac mass without alternative explanation, or ____, or a new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or ____.
new valvular stenosis; new atrial septal defect
Book p69 echo entries: oscillating intracardiac mass without alternative explanation, or abscess, or new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or new valvular regurgitation. (Book p69)

Match the four minor-criteria bullets on Book p69 to their content — 1) Predisposition 2) Fever 3) Vascular phenomena 4) Immunologic phenomena … A) Predisposing heart condition, injection drug use, previous infective endocarditis, or prosthetic valve or material B) Temperature >38°C C) Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhages, subconjunctival petechiae, Janeway lesions D) Glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth's spots, positive rheumatoid factor

Book p69 minor criteria: predisposition (heart condition, injection drug use, previous IE, prosthetic valve or material); fever >38°C; vascular phenomena (major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhages, subconjunctival petechiae, Janeway lesions); immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth's spots, positive rheumatoid factor). (Book p69)

Match the five physical findings on Book p69 to the minor-criteria list they belong to — 1) Janeway lesions 2) Osler's nodes 3) Roth's spots 4) Subconjunctival petechiae 5) Glomerulonephritis … A) Vascular phenomena list B) Immunologic phenomena list C) Immunologic phenomena list D) Vascular phenomena list E) Immunologic phenomena list

Book p69: vascular phenomena include major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhages, subconjunctival petechiae and Janeway lesions; immunologic phenomena include glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth's spots and positive rheumatoid factor. (Book p69)

The 'microbiological evidence' minor criterion on Book p69: a positive blood culture that does not meet a major criterion, or ____ evidence of active infection with organisms consistent with infective endocarditis.

Book p69 minor criteria: 'Microbiological evidence: Positive blood culture but does not meet a major criterion or serological evidence of active infection with organisms consistent with infective endocarditis'. (Book p69)
The pathological criterion on Book p69 is:
Two positive blood cultures from separate venipunctures
Positive microbiology or histology of pathologic tissue material attained at surgery or autopsy (vegetations, valve tissue, embolic fragments or tissue/pus from intracardiac abscesses)
A vegetation seen only on cardiac CT

Book p69: 'Pathological criteria — Positive microbiology or histology of pathologic tissue material attained at surgery or autopsy (vegetations, valve tissue, embolic fragments or tissue/pus from intracardiac abscesses)'. (Book p69)

Match the four cells of the 'for oral procedures' prophylaxis table on Book p70 to its regimen — 1) Can take oral (no allergy) 2) Cannot take oral (no allergy) 3) Can take oral + penicillin allergy 4) Cannot take oral + penicillin allergy … A) Amoxicillin B) Ampicillin ; ceftriaxone C) Clindamycin ; azithro D) Clindamycin ; ceftriaxone

Book p70 oral-procedures table: penicillin row — can take oral: amoxicillin; cannot take oral: ampicillin; ceftriaxone. Penicillin-allergy row — can take oral: clindamycin; azithro; cannot take oral: clindamycin; ceftriaxone. (Book p70)
For RESP procedure prophylaxis on Book p70, abscess/empyema drainage requires adding coverage for ____, and staph is covered with ____.
Book p70 prophylaxis — RESP: i. same as oral; ii. abscess/empyema drainage include below; iii. strep viridans; iv. staph : Vanco. (Book p70)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the old prophylaxis page (Book p70)?
True: GU or GIT prophylaxis is not recommended, but in patients with established infection or under antibiotic cover, enterococci are covered with penicillin
False: SSTI prophylaxis is not recommended for routine surgery
True: clindamycin; azithro is the first-line non-allergic oral regimen
False: if SSTI surgery involves infected skin or musculoskeletal tissue and the patient is allergic or MRSA, Vance is used

Book p70: GU or GIT — not recommended; pts with established infx or under abx cover to prevent sepsis during procedure: enterococci — penicillin. SSTI — not recommended for routine sx; if sx involves infected skin or musculoskeletal: anti strep or staph — penicillin; if allergic or MRSA — Vance. (Book p70)
The highlighted note at the foot of Book p70 states:
The 2023 ESC guideline and 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria have superseded the above — see the UPDATE pages that follow, including prophylaxis
The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria replace only the diagnosis table, not prophylaxis
The p70 prophylaxis regimens remain current for RESP procedures
The 2015 ESC guidelines supersede this page
Book p70, foot note: '* IE — 2023 ESC guideline and 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria have superseded the above. See the UPDATE pages that follow, including prophylaxis.' (Book p70)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects what Duke-ISCVID changed (Book p71)?
False: the separate-venipuncture / defined-time-interval blood-culture requirement has been removed
True: definite IE is unchanged in structure — 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor
True: cardiac CT and 18F-FDG PET/CT became major imaging criteria only for prosthetic valves
False: previous IE is now a predisposing condition

Book p71: definite IE unchanged in structure — 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; possible IE 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor. Cardiac CT and 18F-FDG PET/CT are now major imaging criteria — no longer restricted to prosthetic valves; intraoperative inspection by the surgeon is a NEW major clinical criterion. (Book p71)

Match the six Duke-ISCVID changes on Book p71 to their detail — 1) Blood-culture rules 2) Typical organism list 3) New microbiological methods 4) Imaging major criteria 5) Intraoperative inspection 6) New minor criteria … A) Relaxed — the separate-venipuncture / defined-time-interval requirement has been removed B) Expanded, with a second tier that counts as typical only if intracardiac prosthetic material is present (e.g. coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes, corynebacteria) C) PCR, amplicon and metagenomic sequencing, in-situ hybridisation, and enzyme immunoassay for Bartonella D) Cardiac CT and 18F-FDG PET/CT are now major imaging criteria — no longer restricted to prosthetic valves E) A new major clinical criterion by the surgeon F) Previous IE is now a predisposing condition; predisposing lesions broadened (transcatheter valves, CIEDs)

Book p71 'DIAGNOSIS — WHAT DUKE-ISCVID CHANGED': blood-culture rules relaxed (separate venipunctures at defined time intervals removed); typical organism list expanded with a prosthetic-material second tier; new microbiological methods (PCR, amplicon/metagenomic sequencing, in-situ hybridisation, enzyme immunoassay for Bartonella); imaging majors widened (cardiac CT, 18F-FDG PET/CT, no longer prosthetic-valve-only); intraoperative inspection a new major clinical criterion; new minors (previous IE a predisposing condition; transcatheter valves, CIEDs added). (Book p71)
Which organisms count as typical ONLY if intracardiac prosthetic material is present (the Duke-ISCVID second tier, Book p71)?

Book p71: a second tier was added of organisms that count as typical only if intracardiac prosthetic material is present (e.g. coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes, corynebacteria). (Book p71)
The new microbiological methods accepted by Duke-ISCVID (Book p71): ____, ____ and metagenomic sequencing, in-situ hybridisation, and enzyme immunoassay for ____.
Book p71: 'New microbiological methods accepted: PCR, amplicon and metagenomic sequencing, in-situ hybridisation, and enzyme immunoassay for Bartonella.' (Book p71)

Match the six rows of the management-by-type table in the 'FIVE BUCKETS' section (Book p71) to their regimen — 1) Native valve, community-acquired 2) Prosthetic valve, EARLY (<12 months) 3) Prosthetic valve, LATE (>12 months) 4) Right-sided / PWID 5) CIED-related 6) Culture-negative … A) Ampicillin + (flu)cloxacillin + gentamicin; penicillin allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin — 4–6 weeks B) Vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin; ≥6 weeks; usually nosocomial staphylococci — assume MRSA; rifampicin added 3–5 days after starting the other two, once bacteraemia is clearing C) As for native valve, plus rifampicin if staphylococcal — ≥6 weeks D) Cover S. aureus — (flu)cloxacillin, or vancomycin/daptomycin if MRSA risk — 2 weeks may suffice for uncomplicated tricuspid MSSA IE E) As for staphylococcal IE — complete hardware extraction is mandatory; new device at a different site once cultures are clear F) Cover HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma — serology + PCR

Book p71 table: Native valve community-acquired — ampicillin + (flu)cloxacillin + gentamicin (allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin), 4–6 weeks; Prosthetic EARLY — vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin, ≥6 weeks, assume MRSA, rifampicin 3–5 days later; Prosthetic LATE — as native + rifampicin if staphylococcal, ≥6 weeks; Right-sided/PWID — (flu)cloxacillin or vancomycin/daptomycin, 2 weeks may suffice for uncomplicated tricuspid MSSA; CIED — as staphylococcal IE, hardware extraction mandatory; Culture-negative — cover HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma, serology + PCR. (Book p71)
For streptococcal, fully sensitive native-valve IE (Book p71), penicillin or ceftriaxone runs for ____ weeks — or ____ weeks if combined with gentamicin.
Book p71: 'Streptococcal, fully sensitive: penicillin or ceftriaxone 4 weeks (2 weeks if combined with gentamicin)'. (Book p71)
A patient 3 months after prosthetic aortic valve implantation presents with IE. Per the 2023 table (Book p71), the empirical regimen is:
Vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin for ≥6 weeks — assume MRSA — with rifampicin added 3–5 days after starting the other two, once bacteraemia is clearing

Book p71 Prosthetic valve, EARLY (<12 months): Vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin; ≥6 weeks; usually nosocomial staphylococci — assume MRSA; rifampicin added 3–5 days after starting the other two, once bacteraemia is clearing. (Book p71)
The right-sided / PWID row of the 2023 table (Book p71) states:
A minimum of 6 weeks is mandatory for all right-sided IE
2 weeks may suffice for uncomplicated tricuspid MSSA IE, and septic pulmonary emboli must be looked for
Rifampicin is mandatory for all PWID IE
Hardware extraction is mandatory in PWID IE

Book p71: Right-sided / PWID — cover S. aureus ((flu)cloxacillin, or vancomycin/daptomycin if MRSA risk); '2 weeks may suffice for uncomplicated tricuspid MSSA IE. Look for septic pulmonary emboli'. (Book p71)
In the culture-negative row of the 2023 table (Book p71), examiners should ask about prior ____, because that is the commonest cause of culture negativity.
Book p71 Culture-negative row: 'Serology + PCR. Ask about prior antibiotics — the commonest cause of culture negativity'. (Book p71)
All of the following are on the culture-negative coverage list in the 2023 table (Book p71) EXCEPT:
Book p71 Culture-negative: 'Cover HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma'. Nocardia is not on the list. (Book p71)

Match the three H's of surgery indications on Book p71 to their detail — 1) Heart failure 2) Uncontrolled Infection 3) Prevention of Embolism … A) From valve destruction — the commonest and most urgent B) Abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, persistent positive cultures >7 days, fungal or resistant organism C) Vegetation >10 mm with an embolic event, or >10 mm with severe valve stenosis/regurgitation, or isolated vegetation >15 mm

Book p71 'Surgery indications (the three H's)': Heart failure from valve destruction — the commonest and most urgent; uncontrolled Infection (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, persistent positive cultures >7 days, fungal or resistant organism); prevention of Embolism (vegetation >10 mm with an embolic event, or >10 mm with severe valve stenosis/regurgitation, or isolated vegetation >15 mm). (Book p71)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the 2023 stroke-and-surgery guidance (Book p71)?
True: after an ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage, surgery need not be delayed if otherwise indicated
False: after intracranial haemorrhage, surgery should be deferred about a month
True: stroke remains an automatic bar to surgery
False: heart failure from valve destruction is the commonest and most urgent surgery indication

Book p71: 'Stroke is no longer an automatic bar to surgery. After an ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage, surgery need not be delayed if otherwise indicated. After intracranial haemorrhage, defer about a month.' (Book p71)

The POET trial on Book p71: in stabilised left-sided IE, switching to oral antibiotics to complete the course is ____; OPAT is endorsed for selected stable patients — not in the first ____ days, not in the presence of ____.

Book p71: 'Partial oral therapy (POET trial): in stabilised left-sided IE, switching to oral antibiotics to complete the course is non-inferior. OPAT is endorsed for selected stable patients — not in the first 10 days, not in the presence of complications.' (Book p71)
The 2023 ESC recommendation on the Endocarditis Team and Heart Valve Centre (Book p71) states:
Every case is discussed by cardiology, cardiac surgery, microbiology and imaging
Only prosthetic-valve cases require team discussion
Discussion is limited to cardiology and microbiology
Surgery is consulted only after a negative echocardiogram
Book p71: 'Endocarditis Team and Heart Valve Centre — a formal 2023 ESC recommendation. Every case discussed by cardiology, cardiac surgery, microbiology and imaging.' (Book p71)
The prophylaxis principle stated in section 3 at the foot of Book p71 is:
Since 2007: prophylaxis for every cardiac lesion undergoing a dental procedure
Since 2007: prophylaxis is confined to high-risk patients undergoing high-risk procedures — moderate-risk cardiac lesions no longer qualify
New in 2023: moderate-risk lesions now qualify
Prophylaxis for all oral-mucosa procedures in every patient

Book p71, section 3 'PROPHYLAXIS — WHO, WHEN, WHAT': 'The principle since 2007 is unchanged: prophylaxis is confined to high-risk patients undergoing high-risk procedures. Moderate-risk cardiac lesions no longer qualify.' (Book p71)
2023 Prophylaxis: The Principle (bottom of Book p71)

Match the four high-risk patient categories on Book p72 to their description — 1) Category 1 2) Category 2 3) Category 3 4) Category 4 … A) Prosthetic valve — surgical or transcatheter — or any prosthetic material used for valve repair B) Previous infective endocarditis C) Untreated cyanotic congenital heart disease, or CHD repaired with prosthetic material — for 6 months after the procedure, or lifelong if a residual shunt or regurgitation persists D) NEW in 2023 — recipients of a ventricular assist device or a heart transplant with valvulopathy

Book p72 WHICH PATIENTS (high risk only): 1. Prosthetic valve (surgical or transcatheter) or any prosthetic material used for valve repair; 2. Previous infective endocarditis; 3. Untreated cyanotic CHD, or CHD repaired with prosthetic material — 6 months after the procedure, or lifelong if a residual shunt or regurgitation persists; 4. NEW in 2023: recipients of a ventricular assist device or a heart transplant with valvulopathy. (Book p72)

Match the 2023 prophylaxis procedure and regimen details on Book p72 — 1) WHICH PROCEDURES 2) NOT recommended 3) REGIMEN (single dose, 30–60 min before) 4) Penicillin-allergy regimen … A) Dental only — manipulation of the gingiva or the periapical region of the teeth, or perforation of the oral mucosa B) Respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, dermatological or musculoskeletal procedures in the absence of established infection — the point examiners test C) Amoxicillin or ampicillin 2 g PO/IV (children 50 mg/kg) D) Doxycycline 100 mg, or clindamycin 600 mg where still used; azithromycin/clarithromycin 500 mg are alternatives

Book p72: WHICH PROCEDURES — dental only (gingiva/periapical region or perforation of oral mucosa); NOT recommended for respiratory, GI, GU, dermatological or musculoskeletal procedures without established infection ('this is the point examiners test'); REGIMEN — amoxicillin or ampicillin 2 g PO/IV (children 50 mg/kg); penicillin allergy — doxycycline 100 mg, or clindamycin 600 mg where still used; azithromycin/clarithromycin 500 mg alternatives. (Book p72)
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the 2023 prophylaxis regimen (Book p72)?
True: cephalosporins can be used safely in patients with anaphylaxis to penicillin
True: cephalosporins must not be used in patients with anaphylaxis to penicillin
False: doxycycline 100 mg is an alternative in penicillin allergy
False: amoxicillin or ampicillin 2 g PO/IV (children 50 mg/kg) is the single-dose regimen

Book p72: 'Cephalosporins must not be used in patients with anaphylaxis to penicillin'; the single dose is amoxicillin or ampicillin 2 g PO/IV (children 50 mg/kg), with doxycycline 100 mg or clindamycin 600 mg (where still used) and azithromycin/clarithromycin 500 mg as allergy alternatives. (Book p72)
The 'ALWAYS, FOR EVERYONE' column on Book p72 states:
Antibiotic prophylaxis matters more than oral hygiene

Good oral hygiene and regular dental review matter more than antibiotic prophylaxis — the cumulative bacteraemia of daily chewing and brushing far exceeds that of a single dental visit; aseptic technique for all vascular access and invasive procedures; discourage piercing and tattooing
Tattooing is safe for high-risk cardiac patients
Vascular access requires no special technique in IE patients

Book p72 ALWAYS, FOR EVERYONE: 'Good oral hygiene and regular dental review matter more than antibiotic prophylaxis — the cumulative bacteraemia of daily chewing and brushing far exceeds that of a single dental visit. Aseptic technique for all vascular access and invasive procedures. Discourage piercing and tattooing.' (Book p72)
The single 2023 prophylaxis dose is given ____–60 minutes before the procedure, per Book p72.
Book p72 REGIMEN header: '(single dose, 30–60 min before)'. (Book p72)
All of the following are 2023 HIGH-RISK patient categories for IE prophylaxis on Book p72 EXCEPT:
A moderate-risk cardiac lesion without previous IE

Book p72 high-risk categories: prosthetic valve/material, previous IE, untreated cyanotic CHD (or prosthetic-repair CHD for 6 months/lifelong), and the 2023 addition of VAD/heart-transplant recipients with valvulopathy. Moderate-risk cardiac lesions no longer qualify (Book p71). (Book p72)
For CHD repaired with prosthetic material (Book p72), prophylaxis lasts for ____ months after the procedure, or lifelong if a residual shunt or regurgitation persists.

Book p72 category 3: 'Untreated cyanotic congenital heart disease, or CHD repaired with prosthetic material — for 6 months after the procedure, or lifelong if a residual shunt or regurgitation persists'. (Book p72)

Match the nine entries of the respiratory history proforma on Book p75 to their detail — 1) Cough with expectoration 2) Haemoptysis 3) Dyspnoea 4) Chest pain 5) Constitutional features 6) Cor pulmonale 7) Bronchiectasis 8) Past history 9) Occupational history … A) First bullet of the proforma B) Second bullet C) MRC grading is preferred in RS D) Unilateral pain usually points towards RS causes E) Fever, evening rise of temperature, weight loss, night sweats F) Features suggestive of right heart failure (cor pulmonale) G) If suspecting bronchiectasis, its complications H) Past history of TB? I) The double-asterisked entry

Book p75 proforma: cough with expectoration; haemoptysis; dyspnoea (rule out CVS causes of breathlessness); chest pain; fever/evening rise/weight loss/night sweats; features suggestive of right heart failure (cor pulmonale); if suspecting bronchiectasis, its complications; oedema; past history of TB?; occupational history**. (Book p75)
Pleuritic chest pain on Book p75 characteristically increases on ____ (coughing).
deep inspiration only, never with coughing
Book p75: 'Pleuritic chest pain characteristically increases on inspiration (coughing). Pleural disease can be associated with dry cough and stabbing type of chest pain.' (Book p75)
A patient with a MINIMAL pleural effusion has intense pleuritic chest pain. Per Book p75, why is the pain greater when the effusion is minimal?
A minimal effusion compresses the bronchus
A minimal effusion is usually infected
With minimal effusion the layers of the pleura are more in contact, causing more irritation
Pain is independent of effusion volume
Book p75: 'If the pleural effusion is minimal, the layers of the pleura are more in contact which causes more irritation leading to more pain.' (Book p75)
For dyspnoea, Book p75 prefers the ____ grading in RS, whose advantages are that distance is checked, peer comparison, and ____ vs level ground.
Book p75: 'Dyspnoea — MRC grading is preferred in RS. The advantages are: distance is checked, peer comparison and slope vs. level ground'. (Book p75)
The acute-onset dyspnoea list on Book p75: pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism, acute exacerbation of COPD, acute severe asthma, ____, one more asthma.
Book p75: 'Acute onset dyspnoea — pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism, acute exacerbation of COPD, acute severe asthma, status asthmaticus, one more asthma'. (Book p75)

Match the seven cough-and-expectoration history points on Book p75 to their cause lists — 1) Onset, duration 2) Postural variation 3) Diurnal variation — nocturnal cough 4) Mucopurulent to purulent colour 5) Bronchorrhoea >100 ml/day 6) Foul smell 7) Blood … A) TB, chronic bronchitis B) Post nasal drip, bronchiectasis, left heart failure (orthopnoea equalii), mass on trachea C) Post nasal drip, PND, bronchial asthma, cough variant asthma (no wheeze), GERD, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia D) Bronchial/pneumonia infection E) Bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema rupturing into a bronchus, necrotising pneumonia F) Lung abscess, bronchiectasis G) Frank haemoptysis vs blood stained sputum

Book p75: onset/duration — TB, chronic bronchitis; postural variation — post nasal drip, bronchiectasis, left heart failure (orthopnoea equalii), mass on trachea; nocturnal cough — post nasal drip, PND, bronchial asthma, cough variant asthma (no wheeze), GERD, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia; mucopurulent-purulent — bronchial/pneumonia infection; quantity — bronchorrhoea >100 ml/day (bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema rupturing into a bronchus, necrotising pneumonia); smell — foul in lung abscess, bronchiectasis; blood — frank haemoptysis vs blood stained sputum. (Book p75)
Bronchorrhoea on Book p75 is defined as expectoration of more than ____ ml/day, with one tumbler approximating ____–200 ml.
Book p75: 'Quantity — bronchorrhea >100 ml/day (1 tumbler approx. 150–200 ml)'. (Book p75)
All of the following are listed causes of bronchorrhoea (>100 ml/day) on Book p75 EXCEPT:
Book p75 bronchorrhoea causes: bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema rupturing into a bronchus, necrotising pneumonia. Simple chronic bronchitis is not on that list. (Book p75)

Match the four special haemoptysis types on Book p76 to their definition — 1) Frank haemoptysis 2) Spurious haemoptysis 3) Pseudohemoptysis 4) Endemic haemoptysis … A) Expectoration of blood only B) Secondary to URTI C) Serratia marcescens D) Paragonimus westermani
Book p76: Frank haemoptysis — expectoration of blood only; Spurious — secondary to URTI; Pseudohemoptysis — Serratia marcescens; Endemic — Paragonimus westermani. (Book p76)
Haemoptysis severity on Book p76: mild is below ____ ml of blood loss per day, moderate is 100–150 ml, and severe is up to ____ ml.
Book p76 severity: Mild <100 ml/day; Moderate 100–150 ml; Severe up to 200 ml. (Book p76)
Massive haemoptysis on Book p76: more than ____ ml/day, or a rate above 150 ml/hr, or 100 ml loss per day for more than ____ days.
Book p76: Massive — '>500 ml/day or Rate >150 ml/hr or 100 ml loss per day for more than 3 days.' (Book p76)
The airway causes of haemoptysis on Book p76: Bronchitis (acute and chronic), ____, bronchiectasis and ____.
Book p76 (Dr. Vivekanandan's list), Airway: Bronchitis (Ac & Chr), Bronchogenic Ca, Bronchiectasis and Body (Foreign body). (Book p76)
Per the note on Book p76, why is a bronchial bleed more dangerous than a pulmonary artery bleed?
The pulmonary artery carries more blood volume
Bronchial arteries are smaller and spasm more
The bronchial arteries are part of the systemic circulation at a much higher pressure than the pulmonary circulation

Book p76 note: 'Bronchial bleed is more dangerous than a pulmonary artery bleed because the bronchial arteries are a part of the systemic circulation which are at a much higher pressure than the pulmonary circulation.' (Book p76)
A history of repeated small haemoptysis / blood-streaked sputum is highly suggestive of (Book p76):
Book p76 note: 'h/o repeated small haemoptysis/ blood streaked sputum is highly s/o carcinoma.' (Book p76)

Among the alveolar causes on Book p76, TB is specified as fibrocavitary TB due to rupture of ____ aneurysms (dilated pulmonary arteries surrounding the cavity), and acute pulmonary oedema presents with ____ sputum.

Book p76 Alveolar: pneumonia; TB — 'Fibrocavitary TB (don't just say TB) due to rupture of Rasmussen Aneurysms (dilated pulmonary arteries surrounding the cavity)'; lung abscess; acute pulmonary oedema (pink frothy sputum). (Book p76)

Match the four remaining cause groups on Book p76 to their members — 1) Interstitial 2) Vascular 3) CVS 4) Collagen vascular disorders … A) ILD (rare) B) Pulmonary HTN, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary AV fistula C) Mitral stenosis, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, AV malformation D) Wegener's, Goodpasture syndrome, other vasculitis

Book p76: Interstitial — ILD (rare); Vascular — Pulmonary HTN, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary AV fistula; CVS — Mitral stenosis, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, AV malformation; Collagen vascular disorders — Wegener's, Goodpasture syndrome, other vasculitis. (Book p76)
All of the following are listed infective causes of haemoptysis on Book p76 EXCEPT:

Book p76 infective causes: Weil's disease (severe Leptospirosis), Fibrocavitary TB, Invasive Aspergillosis, Paragonimiasis. Goodpasture syndrome is under collagen vascular disorders, not infective causes. (Book p76)
The four causes of massive haemoptysis on Book p76 are:
Mitral stenosis, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, AV malformation
Book p76 Massive haemoptysis causes: Bronchiectasis, Fibrocavitary TB, Aspergillosis, Paragonimiasis. (Book p76)

Match the three discriminators between haemoptysis and haematemesis on Book p77 to their detail — 1) Associated features 2) pH 3) Food particles / melaena … A) Associated with cough, not with nausea and vomiting; frothing present B) Alkaline — haematemesis is acidic C) Food particles may be present in haematemesis, which may be associated with melaena

Puffiness and swelling in a patient with cor pulmonale on Book p77 results from pulmonary artery hypertension causing ____ failure, or from protein loss in the expectoration — and can also be due to ____.

Book p77: 'h/s/o cor pulmonale — puffiness and swelling d/t pulmonary artery hypertension causing RV failure or even due to protein loss from the expectoration. Can also be due to amyloidosis.' (Book p77)

Match the eight causes of dry cough on Book p77 to their position — 1) First three 2) Next three 3) Last two … A) Pleural pathologies, interstitial lung disease (ILD), cough-variant asthma B) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, atypical pneumonia, GERD C) ACE inhibitors, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy

Match the five Modified MRC grades on Book p78 to their description — 1) Grade 0 2) Grade 1 3) Grade 2 4) Grade 3 5) Grade 4 … A) No breathlessness, except with strenuous exercise B) Breathlessness when hurrying on level ground / walking up a slight hill C) Walks slower than peers on level ground / has to stop for breath while walking at own pace D) Stops for breath after walking about 100 m or after a few minutes on level ground E) Too breathless to leave the house / breathless when dressing and undressing

According to the note under the MRC scale on Book p78, which of these is NOT on the scale?

Too breathless to leave the house
Walks slower than peers on level ground

Per Book p78, the MRC advantages over NYHA are that ____ vs level ground is checked, peer comparison, and distance is checked; the other named classification is the ____ classification.
Book p78: 'The advantages vs NYHA are: slope vs. level ground, peer comparison and Distance is checked. Other classification — Sherwood Jones classification'. (Book p78)

Match the receptors involved in dyspnoea (JSCR) on Book p78 to their location — 1) J receptors 2) Stretch receptors 3) Chemoreceptors 4) Respiratory muscle receptors … A) Alveolar capillary junction B) Thoracic cage and lungs C) Carotid artery, aorta, medulla D) The fourth of the four listed receptor groups

Match the two columns of the breathlessness table on Book p78 to their content — 1) CVS breathlessness 2) RS breathlessness … A) Associated CVS cardinal symptom(s); orthopnoea, PND B) No associated CVS symptoms; orthopnoea may be present (asthma, COPD), but PND is specific to CVS

Book p78 table: CVS breathlessness — associated CVS cardinal symptom(s); orthopnoea, PND. RS breathlessness — no associated CVS symptoms; orthopnoea may be present (asthma, COPD), but PND is specific to CVS. (Book p78)

Match the seven conditions of Box 19.8 on Book p79 to their History column — 1) Pulmonary oedema 2) Massive pulmonary embolus 3) Acute severe asthma 4) Acute exacerbation of COPD 5) Pneumonia 6) Metabolic acidosis 7) Psychogenic … A) Chest pain, palpitations, orthopnoea, cardiac history B) Risk factors, chest pain, pleurisy, syncope, dizziness C) History of asthma, asthma medications, wheeze D) Previous episodes, smoker — in type II respiratory failure may be drowsy E) Prodromal illness, fever, rigors, pleurisy F) Evidence of diabetes mellitus or renal disease, aspirin or ethylene glycol overdose G) Previous episodes, digital or perioral dyssaesthesia
