Match the ABG patterns in Box 19.8 on Book p79 to their condition — 1) Acute severe asthma 2) Acute exacerbation of COPD 3) Metabolic acidosis 4) Psychogenic 5) Pulmonary oedema … A) Down-PaO2, down-PaCO2 — with up-PaCO2 in extremis B) Down or down-down-PaO2, up-PaCO2 (type II failure ± up-H+; up-HCO3 in chronic type II failure) C) PaO2 normal, down-PaCO2, up-H+ D) PaO2 normal, down-down-PaCO2, up-H+ E) Down-PaO2, down-PaCO2

Box 19.8 ABG (Book p79): Acute severe asthma — down-PaO2, down-PaCO2 (up-PaCO2 in extremis); Acute COPD exacerbation — down or down-down-PaO2, up-PaCO2 (type II failure ± up-H+; up-HCO3 in chronic type II failure); Metabolic acidosis — PaO2 normal, down-PaCO2, up-H+; Psychogenic — PaO2 normal, down-down-PaCO2, up-H+; Pulmonary oedema — down-PaO2, down-PaCO2. (Book p79)
Box 19.8: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Breathlessness

Match the ECG rows of Box 19.8 on Book p79 to their condition — 1) Pulmonary oedema 2) Massive pulmonary embolus 3) Acute severe asthma 4) Acute exacerbation of COPD 5) Pneumonia 6) Metabolic acidosis 7) Psychogenic … A) Sinus tachycardia, ischaemia, arrhythmia B) Sinus tachycardia, RBBB, S1Q3T3 pattern, T-wave inversion (V1–V4) C) Sinus tachycardia (bradycardia in extremis) D) Normal, or signs of right ventricular strain E) Tachycardia F) Left blank in the table G) Left blank in the table

Box 19.8 ECG (Book p79): Pulmonary oedema — sinus tachycardia, ischaemia, arrhythmia; Massive PE — sinus tachycardia, RBBB, S1Q3T3 pattern, T(V1–V4) inversion; Acute severe asthma — sinus tachycardia (bradycardia in extremis); Acute COPD exacerbation — normal or signs of right ventricular strain; Pneumonia — tachycardia; Metabolic acidosis and Psychogenic — blank. A patient presents with acute breathlessness, central cyanosis and raised JVP, but NO signs in the lungs, with shock (tachycardia, hypotension). Per Box 19.8 (Book p79), the ECG pattern expected in this condition is:
Sinus tachycardia with bradycardia in extremis

Box 19.8: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Breathlessness
The pneumonia row of Box 19.8 (Book p79) includes:
Flapping tremor, bounding pulses; hyperinflation with bullae

Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects Box 19.8 (Book p79)?

True: metabolic acidosis presents with hyperventilation accompanied by heart or lung signs

Chest pain can originate from the parietal pleura, chest wall and mediastinal structures — but NOT the lung. Per Book p80, why not the lung?
The lung has only autonomic innervation, so it does not cause chest pain
The lung is supplied only by the sympathetic trunk
Chest pain always originates from the heart

Book p80: 'Chest pain — can originate from the parietal pleura, chest wall and mediastinal structures. NOT LUNG because the lung has only autonomic innervation, it does not cause chest pain.' (Book p80)

Match the three origins of chest pain in the Book p80 table to their character and causes — 1) Parietal pleura 2) Chest wall 3) Mediastinal structures … A) Sharp, stabbing, intensified by inspiration or coughing — pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, fractured ribs B) Dull, aching, unrelated to respiration, progressively worsens and hinders sleep — invasion, trauma, compression C) Central, retrosternal, no relation to respiration — lung cancer, lymphoma, thymoma, mets

Book p80 table: Parietal pleura — sharp, stabbing, intensified by inspiration or coughing (causes: PE, pneumonia, pneumothorax, fractured ribs); Chest wall — dull, aching, unrelated to respiration, progressively worsens and hinders sleep (invasion, trauma, compression); Mediastinal structures — central, retrosternal, no relation to respiration (lung cancer, lymphoma, thymoma, mets). (Book p80)

In the parietal pleura column of Book p80: upper 6 ribs irritation causes ____ pain, lower rib pleural irritation can radiate to the ____, and diaphragmatic pleural irritation is referred to the ____.

Book p80 parietal pleura cell: 'Upper 6 ribs irritation -> localised pain. Lower rib pleural irritation can radiate to the upper abdomen. Diaphragmatic pleural irritation is referred to the shoulder tip/neck.' (Book p80)

Match the three specific history points in a suspected case of tuberculosis on Book p80 to their detail — 1) Occupation of husband 2) Evening rise of temperature 3) Contact history … A) High risk group for HIV B) Due to TNFa C) The third listed TB history point

Book p80 'Specific history points in a suspected case of Tuberculosis': occupation of husband — high risk group for HIV; evening rise of temperature — due to TNFa; contact history of tuberculosis. (Book p80)
On Book p81, pulsus paradoxus above ____ mmHg is significant, and it reduces on treatment.

Match the three causes of pallor in RS on Book p81 to their position — 1) First listed 2) Second listed 3) Third listed … A) Recurrent haemoptysis B) Bronchial ca C) TB

The four clubbing-in-TB causes on Book p81: post-TB bronchiectasis, ____ (it's an adenocarcinoma), empyema and ____.
Book p81: 'Clubbing in TB — post TB bronchiectasis, scar carcinoma (it's an Adenocarcinoma), empyema, endobronchial TB'. (Book p81)
A palpable epitrochlear node is always pathologic (Book p81) — causes: NHL, secondary syphilis, sarcoidosis, infections of forearm/hand, tularaemia (rare) — but NOT in ____, per Dr. Hamide.

To palpate the scalene node on Book p81: place the index finger between the ____ and the ____, ask the patient to tilt the head to the same side and press firmly down towards the first rib.

The three causes of generalised lymphadenopathy on Book p82: ____, ____, and sarcoidosis.

Match the three causes of oedema in RS on Book p82 to their position — 1) First listed 2) Second listed 3) Third listed … A) Cor pulmonale B) Protein loss in the sputum, esp in bronchiectasis C) Amyloidosis due to long standing bronchiectasis

The normal respiratory rate on Book p82 is ____–18/min; women breathe ____, men breathe ____.

Match the five signs of respiratory distress on Book p82 to their detail — 1) Alar nasii 2) Pursed lip breathing 3) Indrawing 4) Accessory muscles 5) Intercostal retraction … A) Enlargement B) Helps like PEEP C) Of the trachea D) Like sternocleidomastoid and recti E) Listed last in the distress list

Book p82 distress signs: alar nasii enlargement; pursed lip breathing — help like PEEP; indrawing of trachea; use of accessory muscles like sternocleidomastoid and recti; intercostal retraction. (Book p82)

Match the four muscle-of-respiration entries on Book p82 to their detail — 1) Inspiration — principal 2) Inspiration — accessory 3) Expiration — quiet breathing 4) Expiration — active … A) External intercostal muscles, diaphragm B) Sternocleidomastoid (elevates sternum), scalenes (elevate upper ribs), pectoralis minor, trapezius C) Passive D) Internal intercostals (pulls ribs down), abdominal muscles (pull ribs down, compress abdominal contents pushing diaphragm up), quadratus lumborum (pull ribs down)

Book p82: Inspiration — principal: external intercostals, diaphragm; accessory: SCM (elevates sternum), scalenes (elevate upper ribs), pectoralis minor, trapezius. Expiration — quiet: passive; active: internal intercostals, abdominal muscles, quadratus lumborum. (Book p82)
The 'I always with E' mnemonic on Book p82 means:
Inspiration -> external (intercostals); vice versa for expiration
Book p82: '**Muscles of respiration — I always with E (insp -> external; vice versa)'. (Book p82)

Match the first four external markers of tuberculosis on Book p82 to their detail — 1) Phlycten 2) Choroid tubercles 3) Scars/sinuses 4) Scrofula … A) Small pinkish yellow nodule near the limbus B) Not visible to naked eye C) The third listed marker D) Tuberculous lymphadenitis (painless) in cervical region usually, can be non-TB

Book p82 TB markers: 1. phlycten — small pinkish yellow nodule near the limbus; 2. choroid tubercles — not visible to naked eye; 3. scars/sinuses; 4. scrofula — tuberculous lymphadenitis (painless) in cervical region usually, can be non-TB. (Book p82)

Match the four cutaneous TB forms on Book p82 to their detail — 1) Lupus vulgaris 2) Erythema nodosum 3) Tuberculous verrucous cutis 4) Scrofuloderma … A) Painful cutaneous granuloma with apple-jelly nodules — nose, eyelids, cheek, ear, neck B) The second listed skin form C) Direct inoculation of TB over skin -> solitary plaque with central involution and atrophic scar D) Direct skin extension from TB of LN, bones and joints

The 'other things in G/E' on Book p82: Horner's syndrome in lung malignancies, and signs of neurovascular compression — wasting of the ____.
Book p82: 'Other things in G/E: 1. Horner's syndrome in lung malignancies; 2. Signs of neurovascular compression: wasting of small muscles of hands'. (Book p82)
Dahl's sign on Book p83 is also known as the ____ sign or the ____ sign.

Hemosiderin released from red blood cells trapped in the skin at the contact points

Match the three URT inspection entries on Book p83 to their detail — 1) Oral cavity 2) Nose 3) Pharynx … A) Thrush (immunocompromised state), tonsils; poor oral hygiene, halitosis -> lung abscess B) DNS, polyps C) Post nasal drip — even these can cause respiratory symptoms and breathing difficulty

Book p83: oral cavity — thrush (immunocompromised state), tonsils; poor oral hygiene, halitosis -> lung abscess; nose — DNS, polyps; pharynx — post nasal drip, 'cause even these can cause respiratory symptoms and breathing difficulty'. (Book p83)
The tracheal position is affected mainly by the ____ lobes, per Book p83.

Trail's sign (Book p83): the pretracheal fascia encloses the clavicular head of SCM on both sides; when the trachea shifts to one side, the fascia on that side ____, making the clavicular head more prominent.

When the trachea is shifted to one side, the fascia on that side relaxes, making the clavicular head more prominent.' (Book p83)
The signs of lung volume loss on Book p83: shoulder droop, prominence of the medial border of the scapula (don't call it ____) and crowding of ribs.

Match the four chest shape abnormalities on Book p83 to their detail — 1) Flat chest 2) Barrel chest 3) Pectus carinatum 4) Pectus excavatum … A) AP:transverse 1:2 — seen in pulmonary TB, fibrothorax B) 1:1 — infancy, old age, emphysema, acromegaly C) Pigeon chest — associated with rickets; forward protrusion of sternum with depression on either side D) Funnel chest, cobbler's chest — sunken appearance of sternum, most commonly a cup-shaped concavity

Match the chest-movement examination items on Book p85 to their technique — 1) Apical chest expansion 2) Anterior thoracic movement 3) Posterior thoracic movement — lower lobes 4) Posterior thoracic movement — upper lobes … A) Put hands over the supraclavicular fossae B) Hand placed on side of chest with thumbs in front; separation of thumbs with respiration observed C) Same as anterior D) Place hand over the TRAPS and compare movements

Match the five syndromes of significant URT findings on Book p86 to their feature lists — 1) Kartagener's syndrome 2) Wegener's granulomatosis 3) Samter's triad 4) Young's syndrome 5) Churg-Strauss syndrome … A) Recurrent sinusitis with ciliary dyskinesia, bronchiectasis, situs inversus, male infertility B) Necrotizing granuloma C) Aspirin sensitivity, bronchial asthma, ethmoidal polyps D) Sinopulmonary disease, azoospermia E) Asthma/allergic rhinitis, eosinophilia, vasculitis, granuloma

The first two significant upper respiratory tract findings on Book p86 are:

In the surface marking of the lung on Book p86, the right side has ____ lobes and the left side ____ lobes.

Match the course of the major interlobar (oblique) fissure on Book p86 to its points — 1) Starting point 2) Along 3) Crossing 4) Reaching … A) The T2/T3 spinous process B) The medial border of scapula C) The 5th rib in the mid axillary line D) The 6th rib in mid clavicular line

Book p86: 'Draw a straight line (minor interlobar fissure/horizontal fissure) from the 4th rib at right sternal border towards the midaxillary line cutting the major interlobar fissure at 5th rib. The triangular area represents RML.' (Book p86)
Surface Marking of Lungs & Lower Borders
The inserted Boloor p.142 reference on Book p87 shows the surface marking of lung fissures and lobes in which views?
Book p87 (Boloor p.142): Fig 3D.2 anterior view, Fig 3D.3 posterior view, Fig 3D.4 right lateral view of the chest showing the interlobar fissures and lobes. (Book p87)
Surface Marking of Lungs & Lower Borders
Fig 3D.5 on Book p88 shows the ____ lateral view of the chest, displaying the left major interlobar fissure.
Book p88: 'Fig. 3D.5: Left lateral view of chest showing left major interlobar fissure.' (Book p88)
Surface Marking of Lungs & Lower Borders
The lower border of the LUNG on Book p88 is the 6th/8th/10th rib in the midclavicular/midaxillary/scapular lines, while the PLEURA reaches the ____, ____ and ____ ribs in the same lines.
Book p88 (Boloor p.143, the 6/8/10 vs 8/10/12 rule): Lung — 6th (midclavicular), 8th (midaxillary), 10th (scapular); Pleura — 8th, 10th, 12th. (Book p88)
Surface Marking of Lungs & Lower Borders

Match the three examination positions on Book p88 to what is predominantly assessed — 1) Front examination 2) Back examination 3) Axillary examination … A) Upper and middle lobes B) Lower lobe pathology C) All three lobes
Book p88 table: front examination — predominantly upper and middle lobe; back examination — predominantly lower lobe pathology; axillary examination — all three lobes can be assessed. (Book p88)
Surface Marking of Lungs & Lower Borders
Which of the following True/False statements correctly reflects the tracheal position rules on Book p89?
False: slight tracheal deviation to the right is normal
True: slight tracheal deviation to the right is normal
True: an apical tumour pulls the trachea to the same side
False: in effusion, a shift to the same side suggests co-existent fibrosis/collapse or mesothelioma

Book p89: slight tracheal deviation to the right is normal; pushed to the opposite side — pleural effusion, pneumothorax, apical tumour; pulled to the same side — fibrosis, collapse; shifted to the same side in effusion — co-existent fibrosis/collapse, mesothelioma. (Book p89)

Match the three tracheal deviation categories on Book p89 to their causes — 1) Pushed to the opposite side 2) Pulled to the same side 3) Shifted to the same side in effusion … A) Pleural effusion, pneumothorax, apical tumour B) Fibrosis, collapse C) Co-existent fibrosis/collapse, mesothelioma

Book p89: pushed to the opposite side — pleural effusion, pneumothorax, apical tumour; pulled to the same side — fibrosis, collapse; shifted to the same side in effusion — co-existent fibrosis/collapse, mesothelioma. (Book p89)
The crico-sternal distance on Book p89 is measured as the number of ____ that can be insinuated; it is reduced in COPD because the mediastinum is pulled down, pulling the ____ downward.
Book p89: 'CricoSternal distance: Measured as number of fingers that can be insinuated. Reduced in COPD bc the mediastinum is pulled down pulling the cricoid also downward.' (Book p89)
Inspiratory tracheal descent in COPD on Book p90 is called ____'s sign.
Book p90: 'Inspiratory tracheal descent — COPD — Campbell's sign'. (Book p90)

Match the five entries of Oliver's sign on Book p90 to their detail — 1) Technique a 2) Technique b 3) Positive 4) False positive 5) False negative … A) Patient's chin is raised B) Cricoid cartilage held up on deglutition on either side with fingers of both hands C) Downward tug felt — aortic arch aneurysm D) Mediastinal tumour attached to the arch E) Non pulsatile thrombosed aortic aneurysm

Book p90 Oliver's sign: patient's chin is raised; cricoid cartilage held up on deglutition on either side with fingers of both hands; positive — downward tug felt — aortic arch aneurysm; false positive — mediastinal tumour attached to the arch; false negative — non pulsatile thrombosed aortic aneurysm. (Book p90)
Per Book p91, the trachea is normally:
central or slightly deviated to the left
slightly deviated to the right on expiration
central or slightly deviated to right
Book p91: 'Trachea: Normally central or slightly deviated to right.' (Book p91)

In the Trail's sign mechanism on Book p91, the investing layer of cervical fascia splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and continues as the pretracheal fascia; on tracheal shift, the fascia over the ipsilateral SCM ____, the SCM goes into a state of ____, and the clavicular head becomes prominent.

Book p91: 'When there is tracheal shift to one side, the fascia covering the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid relaxes. The sternocleidomastoid goes into a state of contraction making the clavicular head prominent.' (Book p91)
The clinical implication of tracheal shift on Book p91: it suggests a ____ shift and indicates ____.
upper mediastinal; upper lobe fibrosis or collapse
lower mediastinal; lower lobe fibrosis or collapse
Book p91: 'Clinical implication of tracheal shift: It suggests upper mediastinal shift. Indicates upper lobe fibrosis or collapse.' (Book p91)
The Oliver's sign technique on Book p92: stand ____ the patient, hold the cricoid cartilage and give a slight ____ thrust.
Book p92: 'Stand behind patient and hold cricoid cartilage give a slight upward thrust.' (Book p92)

Match the four entries of Oliver's sign on Book p92 to their detail — 1) Positive test 2) Negative test 3) False positive 4) False negative … A) Downward pull with each heart beat suggestive of aortic aneurysm B) Normal C) Mediastinal tumor attached to abdominal aorta D) Thrombosed aortic aneurysm

Book p92 Oliver's sign: positive — downward pull with each heart beat suggestive of aortic aneurysm; negative — normal; false positive — mediastinal tumor attached to abdominal aorta; false negative — thrombosed aortic aneurysm. (Book p92)
Comparing the two Oliver's sign pages: the false positive on Book p90 is a mediastinal tumour attached to the ____, while on Book p92 it is attached to the ____.
Book p90: 'False positive — mediastinal tumour attached to the arch'; Book p92: 'False positive — mediastinal tumor attached to abdominal aorta'. (Book p92)
Tracheal descent on inspiration (Campbell sign) on Book p92 is due to the downward pull of the depressed diaphragm in long standing ____ of lung.
Book p92: 'Tracheal descent on inspiration (Campbell sign): Due to downward pull of the depressed diaphragm in long standing hyperinflation of lung.' (Book p92)
Figs 3D.14 and 3D.15 on Book p92 show:
Oliver's sign from behind; tracheal tug from the front
Chest expansion measurement; apical impulse palpation
Clavicular head prominence; tracheal shift to the left
Tracing the trachea down with the middle finger; insinuating the middle finger between the trachea and sternal head of sternocleidomastoid and feeling for resistance

Book p92: Fig 3D.14 — tracing the trachea down with the middle finger; Fig 3D.15 — insinuate the middle finger between the trachea and sternal head of sternocleidomastoid, and feel for resistance. (Book p92)
Chest wall tenderness in the respiratory system (Book p93) is seen in:
Empyema, pleuritis, infiltration of chest wall
Book p93: 'Chest wall tenderness — Empyema, pleuritis, infiltration of chest wall'. (Book p93)
Chest Wall Tenderness, Subcutaneous Emphysema & Fremitus
The finding listed on Book p93 immediately after chest wall tenderness is:
Book p93: the line 'Subcutaneous emphysema' follows 'Chest wall tenderness — Empyema, pleuritis, infiltration of chest wall'. (Book p93)
Chest Wall Tenderness, Subcutaneous Emphysema & Fremitus

Match the three fremitus types on Book p93 to their detail — 1) Vocal 2) Tactile 3) Friction … A) Increased in consolidation, decreased in effusion B) Palpable added sounds — crackles, rhonchi C) Palpable pleural rub
Book p93 fremitus: vocal — increased in consolidation, decreased in effusion; tactile — palpable added sounds: crackles, rhonchi; friction — palpable pleural rub. (Book p93)
Chest Wall Tenderness, Subcutaneous Emphysema & Fremitus

Match the four physics entries on Book p93 to their detail — 1) Transmission (speed) of sound 2) Ability to vibrate 3) VR/VF measures 4) Percussion measures … A) Solid > liquid > air B) Air > liquid > solid C) The medium's ability to transmit sound (from vocal cords) D) The medium's ability to vibrate

Book p93: transmission (speed) of sound — solid > liquid > air; ability to vibrate — air > liquid > solid; VR/VF measure the medium's ability to transmit sound (from vocal cords); percussion measures the medium's ability to vibrate. (Book p93)
For lesions where the lung-to-skin distance is altered (Book p93): as distance increases, ____ of the sound produced (VF/VR/breath sound) increases, while the nature of vibration of the medium ____.
Book p93: 'Lesions where LUNG to SKIN distance is altered — as distance increase — more attenuation of sound produced (VF/VR/BREATH SOUND) while nature of vibration of medium remain same'. (Book p93)

Match the five pathologies in the Book p94 table to their VR/VF and percussion — 1) Consolidation 2) Hyperinflation 3) Pleural effusion 4) Pneumothorax 5) Collapse … A) Increased (fluid sound faster) — DULL (fluid vibrate less) B) Reduced (air sound slower) — RESONANT (air vibrate more) C) Reduced (lung-chest distance more) — STONY DULL D) Reduced — Resonant (air vibrate more) E) Reduced — Dull (collapse forms solid like area)

Book p94 table: Consolidation — fluid in parenchyma — increased — DULL; Hyperinflation — more air in parenchyma — reduced — RESONANT; Pleural effusion — fluid around lung, lung far from chest wall — reduced — STONY DULL; Pneumothorax — air around lung, lung far from chest — reduced — Resonant; Collapse — lung far from chest — reduced — Dull (collapse forms solid like area). (Book p94)
In the Book p94 table, consolidation is described as ____ in the parenchyma, while hyperinflation is described as ____ in the parenchyma.
Book p94: consolidation — 'fluid in parenchyma'; hyperinflation — 'more air replaced in parenchyma'. (Book p94)
A patient shows STONY DULL percussion with reduced vocal/tactile fremitus because the lung is far from the chest wall. Per the Book p94 table, the pathology is:
Book p94: pleural effusion — fluid around lung + lung far from chest wall — VR/VF reduced — percussion STONY DULL. (Book p94)
Which of the following True/False statements is consistent with the Book p94 table?
False: pneumothorax percussion is resonant because air vibrates more
True: pneumothorax percussion is resonant because air vibrates more
True: hyperinflation increases VR/VF because air conducts sound slower
False: collapse gives a dull note because collapse forms a solid like area
Book p94: pneumothorax — reduced VR/VF, percussion resonant (air vibrate more); hyperinflation — reduced VR/VF (air sound slower); collapse — dull (collapse forms solid like area). (Book p94)
In the Book p94 table, all of the following pathologies REDUCE VR/VF EXCEPT:
Book p94: consolidation — INCREASED VR/VF (fluid conducts sound faster); hyperinflation, pleural effusion, pneumothorax and collapse — all reduced. (Book p94)

Match the three percussion techniques on Book p95 to their hand position — 1) Anterior percussion 2) Posterior percussion 3) Lateral percussion … A) Hand by the side B) Head bent forward, hands on opposite shoulder C) Hands held over head
Book p95: anterior percussion — hand by the side; posterior percussion — head bent forward, hands on opposite shoulder; lateral percussion — hands held over head. (Book p95)

Match the nine percussion areas in the Book p95 table to their row/limit — 1) Supraclavicular 2) Clavicular 3) Infraclavicular 4) Mammary 5) Axillary 6) Infra-axillary 7) Suprascapular 8) Interscapular 9) Infrascapular … A) 2nd row of the anterior column B) 3rd row — up to 2nd ICS C) 4th row — 2nd to 6th ICS D) 5th row — up to 4th ICS E) 6th row — 4th to 7th ICS F) 1st row of the posterior column G) 2nd row of the posterior column H) 3rd row of the posterior column I) 1st row of the anterior column

Book p95 areas table — Anteriorly: supraclavicular, clavicular, infraclavicular (up to 2nd ICS), mammary (2nd to 6th ICS), axillary (up to 4th ICS), infra-axillary (4th to 7th ICS); Posteriorly: suprascapular, interscapular, infrascapular. (Book p95)
The normal upper level of liver dullness on Book p95 is the ____ ICS; if pushed down, it suggests emphysema (primary or ____).
Book p95: 'Normal upper level of liver dullness is the 5th ICS. If pushed down, it suggests emphysema (Primary or compensatory)'. (Book p95)
In left sided pathologies, per Book p95 you should also percuss over:
Book p95: 'In left sided pathologies, percuss over Traube's space also'. (Book p95)
A triangular area of dullness on percussion against the spine at the base of the OPPOSITE lung (Book p95) — its reason and significance are:
The scapula overlying the base; pathognomonic of TB
The posterior mediastinal pleura may bulge into the contralateral hemithorax in the presence of a pleural effusion — pathognomonic of pleural effusion
Lateral displacement of the heart; suggestive of pneumothorax
Depression of the diaphragm; suggests hyperinflation

Book p95: Grocco's triangle — area of dullness on percussion against the spine on the base of the opposite lung (possibly due to posterior mediastinal shift); in pleural effusion the posterior mediastinal pleura may bulge into the contralateral hemithorax; pathognomonic of pleural effusion. (Book p95)
The figure labels on Book p95: the ____ triangle of hyperresonance; area of compression atelectasis above ____ effusion; and massive effusion with ____ dullness.

Book p95 figure labels: 'Garland's triangle of hyperresonance', 'Area of compression atelectasis above massive effusion', 'Massive effusion with stony dullness' (also scapula, Grocco's triangle of dullness). (Book p95)

Match the five entries of the Book p96 red box (Grocco's triangle detail) to their detail — 1) Position 2) Base 3) Apex 4) Internally 5) Externally … A) Triangular area of dullness at the back of chest on the healthy side B) Horizontally along the 12th rib C) At the level of upper margin of fluid on diseased side D) Vertebral line E) Line joining the apex and lateral base

Book p96 red box: triangular area of dullness at the back of chest on the healthy side; base — horizontally along the 12th rib; apex — at the level of upper margin of fluid on diseased side; internally — vertebral line; externally — line joining the apex and lateral base. (Book p96)
Grocco's Triangle: The Red Box & Kronig's Isthmus
Kronig's isthmus on Book p96 is a band of resonance of ____ cm over the supraclavicular fossa.
Book p96: 'Kronig's isthmus — Band of resonance 5-7 cm over the supraclavicular fossa.' (Book p96)
Grocco's Triangle: The Red Box & Kronig's Isthmus

Match the four borders of Kronig's isthmus on Book p96 to their detail — 1) The first listed border 2) Laterally 3) Anteriorly 4) Posteriorly … A) Scalenus medius B) Acromion process C) Clavicle D) Trapezius
Book p96 Kronig's isthmus borders: scalenus medius; acromion process laterally; anteriorly clavicle; posteriorly trapezius. (Book p96)
Grocco's Triangle: The Red Box & Kronig's Isthmus

Kronig's isthmus percussion on Book p96 is done by standing ____ the patient, from ____ to medial, without touching the ____. An increase in size suggests emphysema; a decreased size suggests TB/apical lung tumour.

Book p96: 'This percussion is done by standing behind the patient, from lateral to medial; clavicle not touched. It indicates the condition of the lung apex. Increase — emphysema; decreased size — TB/apical lung tumour.' (Book p96)
Grocco's Triangle: The Red Box & Kronig's Isthmus
Tidal percussion on Book p96 is used to differentiate ____ pathologies.
Book p96: 'Tidal percussion — infradiaphragmatic vs. supradiaphragmatic pathologies.' (Book p96)
Grocco's Triangle: The Red Box & Kronig's Isthmus

Match the four borders/content of Traube's space on Book p96 to their detail — 1) Superiorly 2) Laterally 3) Inferiorly 4) Content … A) 6th rib B) Left midaxillary line C) Left costal margin D) Fundus of the stomach
Book p96: Traube's space — 6th rib superiorly, left midaxillary line laterally, left costal margin inferiorly; content — fundus of the stomach. (Book p96)

Match the five relation entries of Traube's space on Book p96 to their detail — 1) Right side 2) Left side 3) Superiorly 4) Inferiorly 5) One obliteration cause … A) Left lobe of the liver B) Spleen C) Left lung resonance D) Left costal margin E) Left pleural effusion
Book p96: right side — left lobe of the liver; left side — spleen; superiorly — left lung resonance; inferiorly — left costal margin; obliterated in — left pleural effusion (among others). (Book p96)
Traube's space is obliterated in left pleural effusion, massive splenomegaly, enlarged left lobe of liver, full stomach, and ____, per Book p96.
Book p96: obliterated in — left pleural effusion, massive splenomegaly, enlarged left lobe of liver, full stomach, massive pericardial effusion. (Book p96)
Traube's space is shifted upwards in left diaphragmatic paralysis, left lower lobe collapse, and ____, per Book p96.
Book p96: shifted upwards in — left diaphragmatic paralysis, left lower lobe collapse, fibrosis of left lung. (Book p96)
The label on the Book p96 Traube's space figure points to the 'area to percuss for ____ sign'.
Book p96 figure (Marisa Bonofiglio): labels include sternum, (L) ANT axillary line, 6th rib, costal margin, Traube's space, and 'Area to percuss for Castell's sign'. (Book p96)
In clavicular percussion on Book p97, you ____ the skin below, percuss the ____ 1/3 with the middle finger (fewer muscle attachments there), and a dull note over it represents ____ TB.

Book p97: 'Percuss the clavicle — stretch the skin below. Percuss the medial 1/3 with your middle finger because there are less muscle attachments on the medial 1/3. Purpose — near the apex of the lung. So a dull note over here would represent a secondary TB.' (Book p97)
You find the upper border of posterior dullness and ask the patient to lean forward (Book p97). If the dullness is seen IMMEDIATELY, it is suggestive of:
hydropneumothorax — even effusion has shifting dullness, but it will take time
simple pleural effusion — it shifts immediately

Book p97: 'Shifting dullness — find the upper border of posterior dullness, then ask the patient to lean forward. If the dullness is immediately seen then it is suggestive of hydropneumothorax. Even effusion will have shifting dullness, but it will take time.' (Book p97)

Match the four hydropneumothorax findings on Book p97 to their detail — 1) Straight line dullness 2) Succussion splash 3) Silver coin sounds 4) Shifting dullness … A) Listed as a hydropneumothorax sign B) Percuss the upper limit of dullness, hug the patient and shake him — a splash like over a stomach containing air and fluid C) Hit one coin with the other, stethoscope on the back — clinking sounds audible D) Find the upper border of posterior dullness, lean forward — immediate dullness

Book p97: straight line dullness — hydropneumothorax; succussion splash — percuss the upper limit of dullness, stethoscope just above it, hug and shake the patient, splash like stomach with air and fluid; silver coin sounds — hit one coin with the other, steth on the back, clinking audible in hydropneumothorax; shifting dullness — immediate on leaning forward. (Book p97)
The S shaped curve of Ellis on Book p97 (moderate pleural effusion, uppermost dullness highest in the axilla, lowest near the spine posteriorly and sternum anteriorly) is attributed to:
capillary suction between two layers of pleura
surface tension of the pleural fluid

Book p97: 'S shaped curve of Ellis — seen in moderate pleural effusion. Uppermost dullness is highest in the axilla. Lowest in spine posteriorly and near sternum anteriorly. Reason — capillary suction between two layers of pleura.' (Book p97)
S shaped Curve of Ellis & the 20-Second Rule
The S shaped curve of Ellis is also seen radiologically, per Book p97 believed to be due to:
scattering of X rays by the fluid
Book p97: 'Also seen radiologically, believed to be due to scattering of X rays by the fluid'. (Book p97)
S shaped Curve of Ellis & the 20-Second Rule

In shifting dullness due to hydropneumothorax, per Book p97 you don't wait ____ seconds like in ascites — in the abdomen air and fluid are in different compartments so time is needed for bowel loops to move, whereas in the lung air and fluid are in the same compartment.

Book p97: 'we don't wait for 20 seconds like ascites because in the abdomen the air and fluid are in different compartments... Whereas in the lung, the air and fluid are in the same compartment so there is no need to give time for movement.' (Book p97)
S shaped Curve of Ellis & the 20-Second Rule

Match the four vesicular breath sound entries on Book p97 to their detail — 1) Pitch/nature 2) Inspiration : Expiration 3) Pause 4) Diminished VBS in … A) Low pitched, rustling in nature B) 3:1 C) No pause between end of inspiration and beginning of expiration D) Bronchial asthma (silent chest), tumour, small effusion, pleural thickening

Book p97 vesicular breath sounds: low pitched, rustling in nature; inspiration: expiration is 3:1; no pause between end of inspiration and beginning of expiration; diminished VBS — bronchial asthma (silent chest), tumour, small effusion, pleural thickening. (Book p97)

Match the five causes of diminished vesicular breathing in the Book p97 box to their category row — 1) Obesity/thick chest wall 2) Pleural effusion or thickening 3) Pneumothorax 4) Generalised, e.g. COPD 5) Localised, e.g. collapsed lung due to occluding lung cancer … A) Reduced conduction — 1st listed B) Reduced conduction — 2nd listed C) Reduced conduction — 3rd listed D) Reduced airflow — generalised E) Reduced airflow — localised

Book p97 box 'Causes of diminished vesicular breathing': Reduced conduction — obesity/thick chest wall, pleural effusion or thickening, pneumothorax; Reduced airflow — generalised, e.g. COPD; localised, e.g. collapsed lung due to occluding lung cancer. (Book p97)
